en: Mokṣopāya, Chapter 1: Detachment, First canto.
Salutation to that Soul of the Universe, the all-pervading one whose nature is luminosity, who shines as light within me— in heaven, on earth, in space, and both outside and inside.

He who possesses the conviction, "May I, who am bound, become liberated," is neither one who knows that [reality] ultimately, nor one who does not know it; he alone has the qualification for this scripture.
Vālmīki:
Having first reflected upon the means to the story, one who then reflects upon these means to liberation is wise; he is not born again.
O crusher of enemies, having first composed these means of narration in this work called the Rāmāyaṇa, which yield great fruit, in ancient times—
To this disciplined and wise disciple, Bharadvāja, he,
with one-pointed mind, gave the beautiful jewels, just as the ocean gives them to a suppliant.
Then these methods of discourse were proclaimed by the wise Bharadvāja in the presence of Brahmā, in a certain thicket on Mount Meru.
Then the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds and the magnanimous one, being pleased with him, said: "O son, choose a boon."
Bharadvāja said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, this boon is pleasing to me today:
please declare that by which these people may be liberated from suffering."
Brahmā said:
"Quickly and with great effort, request the preceptor Vālmīki;
by him this faultless Rāmāyaṇa was begun."
When that is known, a person shall cross over from all delusion by means of it,
just as one crosses to the far shore of the ocean by means of a bridge endowed with boundless virtues.
Having spoken thus to Bharadvāja, the Supreme Lord, the Creator of all beings, went together with Bharadvāja to my hermitage.
Quickly honored by me with water for the feet, the guest-offering, and other rites, that god—who is devoted to the welfare of all beings—spoke to me, O Great Being: MU_1.1.12.
O blameless and excellent sage, because of this account of Rāma’s true nature, you must not abandon your endeavor until its completion.
By means of this knowledge, this world will swiftly cross over the peril of saṃsāra, just as one crosses the ocean quickly by means of a ship.
"I have come here specifically to tell you this very purpose:
for the sake of the welfare of the world, compose a scripture"—thus spoke the Unborn One.
From that meritorious hermitage of mine, he vanished in an instant;
in a mere moment, he rose up loftily like a wave of water.
When that Blessed One had departed, I was filled with wonder;
once again, with a clear mind, I questioned Bharadvāja there.
"What was this that was proclaimed by Brahmā? O Bharadvāja, tell me quickly!
When thus addressed, O sinless one, Bharadvāja spoke again to me: MU 1.1.18.
Bharadvāja said:
"This has been stated by the Blessed One: 'Compose the Rāmāyaṇa quickly for the welfare of all the world—a boat for the ocean of saṃsāra.'"
And tell me, O Blessed One, how Rāma and the high-minded Bharata conducted themselves in this narrow strait of saṃsāra.
Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, as well as the illustrious Sītā,
and those highly intelligent sons of ministers who were the followers of Rāma.
Tell me clearly how you have attained this state free from suffering;
in that same way, I shall cross over [the ocean of existence] together with the people.
O Indra among kings, when I was thus respectfully addressed by Bharadvāja,
I then proceeded to speak in order to carry out the command of the Lord.
Listen, dear Bharadvāja; I shall speak to you according to what was asked, by hearing which you will be able to cast far away all delusion.
O wise one, conduct yourself in such a way that, when so conducted, you may be happy—
just as the lotus-eyed Rāma did with an intellect entirely unattached.
Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and the high-minded Śatrughna;
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, Sītā, and likewise Daśaratha.
Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, who were established in their purpose and free from conflict, had reached the further shore of awakening, as did the other eight ministers.
Ghṛṣṭi, Vikuṇṭha, Bhāma, and Satyavardhana;
Vibhīṣaṇa, Suṣeṇa, Hanumān, and likewise Indrajit.
These twenty-eight are declared to be great-souled ones who are liberated while living, whose minds are free from passion, and who follow whatever has come to them.
O son, if you conduct yourself exactly as they took, gave, grasped, stayed, and remembered, then you are indeed liberated from all distress.
Having attained supreme yoga, the noble being who has fallen into the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra experiences neither sorrow nor dejection; free from fever, he remains eternally satisfied.
The Second Chapter, named "Sūtramātra," [ends]. Bharadvāja:
O Brahmin, having first described the state of one liberated while living, tell me in due order how Rāghava became eternally happy; so that I too may become happy.
Vālmīki:
O holy one, for this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky, I consider its non-recollection to be better than its remembrance; indeed, forgetting it is preferable.
Without the cognition of the absolute non-existence of the visible object, that [emptiness] is never experienced by anyone at any time; therefore, let that cognition be sought after.
And that [liberation] is indeed possible here; for that purpose, this scripture has been composed. If you listen to it, you will attain reality, and not otherwise.

O sinless one, through this inquiry, it is experienced that this delusion of the world, though visible, does not exist at all— just as color does not exist in space— due to the absence of mental fatigue.
When the cleansing of the mind's objects of perception is accomplished through the realization that "the visible does not exist," then the supreme bliss of Nirvana has arisen.
Otherwise, for you who wallow in the pits of the scriptures,
there will be no peace even after many eons, as your knowledge here remains unrefined.
The renunciation of latent impressions is said to be the supreme liberation;
O Brahman, this is that stainless path which illuminates knowledge.
But when latent impressions have been exhausted, the mind dissolves quickly,
O Brahmin, just as a particle of frost vanishes when the continuity of cold has ceased.
This body, a cage of elements, is sustained by latent impressions (vāsanā),
just as a multitude of pearls is strung together by a fine thread placed within.
Impression (vāsanā) is said to be of two kinds: pure and likewise impure. The impure is the cause of birth; the pure is the destroyer of birth.
The wise declare that impure latent impression (*vāsanā*) is dense with the form of ignorance, characterized by thick egoism, and the cause of rebirth.
Having abandoned the sprout of rebirth, she remains like a parched seed; known as "Pure," she persists until the end of the body, having realized that which is to be known.
In embodied beings who are liberated while living, there exists a pure latent impression (vāsanā) that prevents rebirth; it remains within the body like the after-effect of a spinning wheel.

Those of great intellect whose latent impressions are purified so that they no longer become vessels for the miseries of rebirth, and who have known that which is to be known, are called liberated while living.
I shall fully explain to you how the high-minded Rāma attained the state of liberation while living, for the sake of pacifying old age and death.
O Bharadvāja of great intelligence, listen to this auspicious method of Rāma; I shall speak it, and by that very means you will understand everything in every respect.
Having departed from the house of learning, the lotus-eyed Rāma spent his days at home, free from all fear, engaged in various pastimes.
Then, as time passed while that king protected the earth,
his subjects remained free from sorrow and devoid of all affliction.
Once, the mind of the virtuous Rāma became intensely eager to behold the series of hermitages belonging to the sages at the sacred fords.
Having reflected thus, Rāghava approached his father’s feet and grasped them by the claws and downy hair, like a swan seizing two fresh lotuses.
Rāma:
Father, my mind is indeed intensely longing to see sacred fords, temples of the gods, forests, and shrines.
Therefore, you ought to make this former request of mine fruitful;
for there is no petitioner in the world, O dear one, who has ever been treated with contempt by you.
Thus entreated by Vasiṣṭha, the king then deliberated and released Rāma first, even though he was the one who had come as a petitioner.

On an auspicious day under a favorable constellation, Rāghava, his body adorned with auspicious ornaments and having had benedictions pronounced by the twice-born, set out together with his two brothers.
Accompanied by a few affectionate and excellent princes, as well as by Brahmins sent by Vasiṣṭha who were well-versed in the scriptures.
Having been adorned by his mothers, who offered him blessings as they embraced him again and again,
he departed from that house, intent upon his pilgrimage.
He departed from his own city, honored by the citizens with the sound of musical instruments,
and gazed upon by the city women with eyes curved like swarms of bees.
He was showered by the villagers with handfuls of parched grain offered from their lotus-like hands, appearing like the Himalaya mountain covered in snow.
Winning over the hosts of Brahmins, hearing the blessings for the people,
and surveying the horizons of all directions, he wandered through the forest.
Then, starting from his own realm of Kosala and proceeding in due order,
he beheld [the lands] preceded by bathing, giving, austerity, and meditation.
Rivers, sacred fords, holy groves, and sanctuaries;
jungles at the edges of forests, and the shores of oceans and mountains.
The Mandākinī, which resembles the moon; the Kālindī, with its stainless blue lotuses;
the Sarasvatī, the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī.
The Veṇā and the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Nirvindhyā and the Sarayū, as well as the Carmaṇvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāśā, and the Bāhudā.
Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, and likewise Gayā;
Vārāṇasī, Śrīgiri, Kedāra, and likewise Puṣkara.
And Mānasa, Kramasaras, as well as Uttaramānasa,
Vaḍavā, Maḍavā, and the multitude of tirthas together with their siblings.
The great sacred ford of Agnitīrtha, as well as Indradyumna-saras,
the lakes and ponds, and likewise the series of oblong ponds and wells.
[He saw] his master Kārttikeya, as well as the Sālagrāma Hari,
and the sixty-four sacred sites of Hara, the lord of Girijā.
The shores of the four oceans, variegated with many wonders;
the caves and groves of the Vindhya mountains; and the regions of the principal mountain ranges.
And likewise, he saw the auspicious and purifying hermitages of the great royal sages, as well as those of the brahminical sages, of the gods, and of the brahmins.
Again and again, that bestower of honor wandered with his two brothers through all the regions of the earth, even to the four ends of the quarters.

Honored by gods, kinnaras, and men, the joy of the Raghus, having surveyed this entire earth, returned to his own home like the Lord who has wandered through the quarters and reached the world of Śiva.
The third canto, titled "The Undertaking of the Pilgrimage," by Vālmīki.
Scattered with handfuls of parched grain and flowers by the city-dwellers,
the glorious Jayanta entered his home like [Indra] entering heaven.
Then Rāghava, having arrived first, bowed down to his father, Vasiṣṭha, his maternal kinsmen, the Brāhmaṇas, and the elders who were his teachers.
Then Rāghava could not contain himself amidst the repeated embraces and greetings of his friends, mothers, father, and the assembly of brahmins.
While that son of Daśaratha remained firm, the quarters of the sky seemed to reel from his mutual, sweet, and pleasing conversations,
as if from the soft sounds of bamboo flutes.
Many days have passed here with the festival of Rāma’s arrival,
which releases the people into great joy and is filled with the clamor of playful revelry.
From that time forth, Rāghava lived happily in his home,
describing the various customs and regional practices found here and there.
Having risen in the morning and performed the twilight devotions according to the prescribed rule, Rāma then beheld his father, who was seated in the assembly hall like Indra himself.
Having spent a fourth part of the day with Vasiṣṭha and the others, he remained engaged with them in highly varied conversations that were filled with wisdom and attended with great respect.
Permitted by his father and surrounded by a vast army,
he went to the forest teeming with boars and buffaloes, out of a desire for the hunt.
Then, having returned home and performed his ablutions and other rites in due order,
he ate together with his friends and kinsmen and passed the night with his companions.
Rāghava, whose daily conduct was of this nature, returned with his two brothers from his pilgrimage and dwelt in his father’s house.

The sinless prince passed his days with such activities as were pleasing to the king’s conduct— activities that were like moonlight in the hearts of the virtuous and as delicate as the essence of the nectar of sacred learning.
The Fourth Sarga, titled "The Description of Daily Life," by Vālmīki.
Then, while the sixteenth year was current, the descendant of Raghu [Rāma] remained there,
as did Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa, who followed Rāma.
While Bharata remained constantly in his maternal grandfather’s house in happiness,
the queen protected this entire earth according to the law.
And for the sake of his sons' welfare, King Daśaratha— possessed of great wisdom, skilled in counsel, and knowledgeable in statecraft— conferred daily with his ministers.
When his pilgrimage was completed, Rāma, remaining in his own home,
grew thinner day by day like a clear lake in autumn.
Gradually, his large-eyed face took on a pallor,
like a white lotus with petals blossoming from ripeness, adorned with a row of rice stalks.
With his hands resting upon the surface of his cheeks, seated in the lotus posture,
he became silent and inactive, overcome by deep reflection.
Emaciated in body, filled with anxiety, exhausted, and deeply dejected,
he said nothing to anyone, appearing as if fixed in a painting.
Being entreated again and again by his attendants out of weariness,
he performed his daily ritual observances with his lotus-like face withered.
Thus, beholding Rāma, who was distinguished among sages and a mine of multitudes of virtues, his two brothers fell into that very same state.
Thus, while those sons were distressed and emaciated,
the protector of the earth, together with his wife, fell into a state of helplessness due to anxiety.
"O son, what is this heavy anxiety of yours? Thus he questioned Rāma again and again with affectionate words, but Rāma did not tell him.
Having said, "Father, I have no sorrow at all," the lotus-petal-eyed Rāma remained silent, sitting upon his father's lap.
Then King Daśaratha asked Vasiṣṭha, the best of speakers and knower of all affairs, "Is Rāma distressed?"
"There is a reason for this, O illustrious one; let there be no sorrow for you, O King. Thus addressed by the sage Vasiṣṭha, the king was filled with anxiety.

The virtuous do not harbor anger, dejection, or widespread joy on account of a trivial cause; O King, in this world, great beings do not undergo transformation except through the impulse of creation or destruction.
The fifth canto, titled "Lamentation over Emaciation," by Vālmīki.
When the Lord of Sages had spoken thus, the king remained silent for some time, filled with doubt, weary, and waiting.
While all the queens in the royal palaces were utterly exhausted and remained vigilantly attentive to Rāma’s movements on every side, [Kaikeyī acted].
At that very time, however, a great seer known as Viśvāmitra arrived at Ayodhyā to see that lord of men.
Then, it is said, the sacrifice of that wise man who desired dharma was indeed devastated by Rākṣasas, who were intoxicated by their power of illusion, heroism, and strength.
For the sake of protecting that sacrifice, he desired to see the king;
for that sage was not able to attain that ritual without obstacles.
Then, intent on their destruction, Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of ascetic power and possessed of great luster, set out for the city of Ayodhyā.
Desiring an audience with the king, he spoke to the gatekeepers:
"Quickly announce that I, Kauśika, the son of Gādhi, have arrived."
Having heard those words of his, all the gatekeepers went to Rājagṛha,
their minds agitated, impelled by that speech.
Having gone to the royal palace, they then informed the lord of the gatekeepers that the seer Viśvāmitra had arrived.
Then, approaching the king who was seated out of place and surrounded by a circle of royal attendants, that staff-bearer, acting with haste, addressed him.
O King, at the gate stood a glorious man of great splendor, radiant like the rising sun, with a mass of matted hair as red as flames.
He made that region rich with yak-tail fans and banners, and filled with horses, elephants, men, and weapons, so that it was strewn with gold by their splendors.
The female staff-bearer quickly spoke to us in a humble voice, saying, "Inform the King that the sage Viśvāmitra has arrived."
Having heard these words of Yashthika, that best of kings,
together with his ministers and his vassals, rose up from his golden seat.
On foot alone, he was protected by a great multitude of kings,
praised by his vassals, and accompanied by Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva.
He went to the place where that great sage Viśvāmitra was;
he saw the tiger among sages stationed at the entrance.
For some reason, he had come to the surface of the earth like the sun,
pervading it with his brahminical splendor and his great kṣatriya power.
His shoulders were covered by a creeper of matted hair, perpetually withered by old age and made coarse by the expansion of his ascetic penance, like a mountain shrouded by clouds at twilight.
He bore a radiant body that was both tranquil and lovely, luminous yet unimpeded, modest yet possessed of a majestic form.
With a splendor that was both charming and most formidable, serene yet restless, profound and overflowing, he delighted the people.
He held in his hand a single, flawless, smooth lute— a companion to the state of infinite life— while his own mind remained unfading.
Because his mind was overcome with compassion, he seemed to drench these subjects with nectar through his glances, which were serene and sweet.
With white and dark outer corners of the eyes and high, fair eyebrows,
he bestows both bliss and fear within the beholder.
Beholding the sage from afar, the king, with his body bowed low, prostrated himself so that the ground was adorned by the garlands of jewels falling from his crest.
There, the sage also greeted the lord of the earth with a sweet and noble voice, just as the sun greets Indra.
Then all the twice-born ones, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
honored him with due respect, following the sequence beginning with a welcome.
Daśaratha:
O virtuous one, we have been graced by you with this radiant appearance, which has come upon us unexpectedly— just as beds of lotuses are graced by the sun.
O Sage, through the sight of you today, we have attained that blissful joy which is beginningless, unshakable, and free from all states of woe.
Today we truly stand at the forefront of those who act in accordance with dharma,
since we have become the object of your arrival.
Thus conversing there, the kings and the great seers took their seats in the assembly hall and sat down together.
Seeing that the sage had arrived, blazing with splendor, the king was struck with awe;
yet, with a joyful countenance, he himself offered the guest-offering (arghya).
Having accepted the guest-offering from the king according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
he honored the king by performing a circumambulation.
Honored by the king, he then, with a joyful countenance,
inquired after the welfare and the well-being of that lord of men.
Having met with Vasiṣṭha, that bull among sages smiled and,
having honored him as was fitting, then inquired after his well-being.
Having met together and honored one another for a moment as was appropriate,
they all, with joyful minds, entered the residence of the great king.
Seated upon their respective appropriate seats, their mutual splendor increasing, they all respectfully inquired after one another’s well-being.
To that wise Viśvāmitra who was seated,
he repeatedly offered water for his feet, the guest-offering, and cows.
Having honored Viśvāmitra according to the prescribed rites,
the king, with palms joined in reverence, disciplined in mind, and joyful at heart, spoke these words.
Just as the attainment of nectar, just as rain in a time of drought,
and just as the recovery of sight for the blind— such is your arrival.
Just as the acquisition of desired wealth for one without offspring, the birth of a son,
and the attainment of an object seen in a dream, so too is this arrival of yours.
Just as there is union with what is desired, just as there is the arrival of what is wished for,
and just as there is the recovery of what was lost— such is your arrival.
Just as there is joy for one who has died upon returning through travel in the sky, so too, O Brahmin, is there joy from your arrival; welcome to you, O great sage!
For whose heart would residence in the world of Brahmā not bring joy?
O Sage, your tradition is likewise; I tell you this as the very truth.
And what is your supreme desire? What may I do for you?
You have arrived as a worthy recipient for me, O Brahmin, endowed with the highest righteousness.
Worthy of being addressed by the title "royal seer" (rājarṣi), you have illuminated the people through your asceticism;
having subsequently attained the status of a "brahmin seer" (brahmarṣi), you are worthy of my worship, O Blessed One.
Just as joy would arise in me from being sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
so does the joy from seeing you cool my innermost being, as it were.
Free from desire, fear, and anger, devoid of passion and free from affliction— O Brahman, it is most wonderful that you have come to me.
And I, O best among those who know what is to be known, perceive myself as free from stain, situated in an auspicious field, like the lunar orb emerged from the water.
I consider your arrival to be like that of Brahmā himself in person;
O Sage, I am purified and graced by your visit.
O holy one, by the merit of your arrival,
that which has delighted me today makes my birth fruitful and my life well-lived.
Having seen you arrived here, having honored and bowed to you,
I bow within my very self, just as the ocean bows when it beholds the moon.
O bull among sages, whatever task you have come for and whatever purpose you serve—know that it is already accomplished; for you are indeed highly venerable to me.
O Kauśika, you ought to perform your own duty through reflection;
for, O Blessed One, there is nothing that is not to be given to you, whatever may be offered.
And you ought to deliberate upon the task according to dharma;
I shall be the doer of it all for you, while you are the supreme deity.
Having heard these exceedingly sweet words, spoken with humility by one who knows the truth and pleasing to the ear,
the bull among sages attained supreme joy, for they were distinguished by virtues due to the power of his own renowned qualities.
The sixth canto, titled "The Arrival of Viśvāmitra," by Vālmīki.
Having heard those words of the lion among kings, which were so wonderfully extensive,
the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, his hair standing on end with joy, spoke.
O tiger among kings, this is indeed worthy of you alone upon this earth—
you who are born of a great lineage and who abide by the will of Vasiṣṭha.
O tiger among kings, carry out the decision regarding that matter which is in my heart; uphold righteousness.
"O bull among men, I was observing a vow for the sake of attaining perfection;
however, terrible Rākṣasas stood in my way to create obstacles."
But whenever I worshipped the assembly of gods with a sacrifice,
on each such occasion the night-stalkers would destroy that very sacrifice of mine.
When that sacrifice had been performed many times, those leaders of the rākṣasas strewed the earth with flesh and blood.
When that assembly of sacrifices had thus become desolate, I,
having exerted myself in vain, lost my enthusiasm and departed from that place.
O King, my mind does not incline toward releasing anger;
for such was that deed, and no curse can take effect against it.
And such is my forbearance, O King, regarding that great sacrifice;
through your favor, may I attain its great fruit without obstacle.
You ought to protect me, who am distressed and have come seeking refuge;
for the hopelessness of those who seek is indeed a defeat for the virtuous.
You have a glorious son, a hero who tears asunder the Rākṣasas; he possesses the prowess of a proud tiger and is like Mahendra himself—Rāma.
O tiger among kings, you ought to give me that son Rāma, whose valor is truth, the heroic eldest one who still wears the sidelocks of youth.
For, protected by me through my own divine splendor,
he is indeed capable of crushing the heads of those Rākṣasas who do him harm.
And I shall bring about for him manifold and infinite welfare,
by which he will become worthy of worship even by the three worlds.
And having encountered him, the night-stalkers were unable to stand their ground,
like deer in a forest upon seeing an enraged lion in battle.
No man other than the descendant of Kakutstha dares to fight them,
just as no one dares to fight enraged, intoxicated elephants except for lions.
For those wicked ones, intoxicated by their own prowess in battle, are like the Kālakūṭa poison;
they are the servants of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, resembling the wrathful God of Death himself.
O tiger among kings, they shall not withstand the arrows of Rāma,
which will fall incessantly like showers of dust from a cloud.
And you ought not, O King, to harbor affection for your son;
there is nothing in this world that must not be given away by one who is great-souled.
Ah, now I truly understand; know that those Rākṣasas have been slain, for wise people such as we do not engage in action when there is doubt.
I know the high-souled Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses;
so too does the greatly effulgent Vasiṣṭha, as well as those others who possess far-sighted vision.
If righteousness and great fame are established in your mind,
then you ought to grant me your own desired son.
And my sacrifice shall last for ten nights, in which the Rākṣasas— my enemies who create obstacles to my sacrifice— must be slain by Rāma.
O descendant of Kakutstha, let all your ministers, headed by Vasiṣṭha, grant their permission in this matter; therefore, O Rāma, bid him farewell.
O knower of time, O Rāghava, act in such a way that this time does not pass me by; may prosperity be yours, and do not set your mind on grief.
Even a minor task, when performed at the proper time, becomes a source of benefit;
whereas even a great task, through its mistimed performance, results in emptiness of utility.
Having spoken these words, which were consistent with dharma and purpose, the righteous and highly effulgent Viśvāmitra, lord of sages, became silent.

Having heard the words of the eminent sage, the one of great power remained silent, for he knew that this was what ought to be said; yet a wise man finds no satisfaction through speech lacking in logical consistency, nor does the world find contentment when its heart's desire remains unfulfilled.
The seventh canto, titled "Viśvāmitra’s Speech," by Vālmīki.

Having heard those words spoken by Viśvāmitra, that tiger among kings remained motionless for a moment and then spoke this piteously: "O Brahmin, I am indeed bound by the bond of dharma; yet, O best of sages, I am unable to abandon my daughter."
"This lotus-eyed Rāma is less than sixteen years of age;
I do not see in him the fitness for battle with the rākṣasas."
O Lord, this is a full Akṣauhiṇī army of which I am the master;
surrounded by it, I shall give battle to the flesh-eaters.
For these servants are brave, valiant, and skilled in weapons; and I myself, bow in hand, am their protector at the forefront of the battle.
With these, I shall give battle to your enemies— even those as great as Mahendra— as a lion does with rutting elephants.
But Rāma is a child among armies; he does not know the difference between strength and weakness, for no ground of battle other than the inner apartments has ever been seen by him.
He was neither equipped with supreme weapons nor skilled in combat;
nor was he an expert in the frowns of warriors at the forefront of battle.
He always frequented only the flower groves, the city parks, and the bowers within the gardens and forests.
He knows how to sport together with the princes upon his own courtyards, which are strewn with offerings of flowers.
But today, O Brahmin, due to the reversal of my fortune, I have become exceedingly pale and emaciated, like a full-grown green lotus struck by frost.
He is unable to eat his food nor to stroll in the garden of his home;
with his soul overwhelmed by inner anguish, he remains merely silent.
O leader of sages, for his sake, I, together with my wife and servants,
have surely reached a state of exhaustion, like a rain-cloud in autumn.
"Such is this young son of mine, rendered helpless by mental anguish;
how can I give him to you to fight with the night-stalkers?"
O holy one, O great-minded one, this affection for a son leads to happiness even more than association with young women, even more than the essence of nectar, and even more than sovereignty.

Those things which have miserable endings, involve great undertakings, and bring weariness to the three worlds—even the virtuous do not resort to them out of affection for their sons; of this there is no doubt.
O tiger among sages, men easily renounce their vital fluids, wealth, and wives; but they do not renounce their sons, for such is the nature of living beings.
"The Rākṣasas are performers of cruel deeds and experts in treacherous warfare;
let Rāma fight them"—even such a statement is exceedingly difficult to endure.
Separated indeed from Rāma, I cannot bear to live for even a moment;
though I long for life, you ought not to take Rāma away.
"O Kauśika, nine thousand years have passed for me;
these four sons were produced by me with great hardship."
Among them, the lotus-eyed Rāma is the preeminent one;
without him, those other three cannot sustain their lives.
If that very Rāma is being led by you toward the Rākṣasas,
then know me to be as good as dead this instant, bereft of my son.
For my love for these four sons is indeed supreme;
since Rāma is the eldest and consists of righteousness, you ought not to take him away.
O Sage, if it is your desire to destroy the army of the night-stalkers,
then take with you this force, complete with its four divisions, along with me.
What is the prowess of those Rākṣasas? Whose sons are they, and how did they come to be?
What is their size, and who are they? Describe these things clearly to me.
O Brahmin, how should Rāma strike those Rākṣasas who fight with deceit— either by means of my forces or by me himself?
"Tell me everything, Blessed One, how I must stand in battle against those wicked beings, for the Rākṣasas are indeed arrogant in their prowess."
For it is heard that there was a great hero, a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa,
who was the brother of Vaiśravaṇa himself and the son of the sage Viśravas.
If that evil-minded one indeed creates an obstacle to your sacrifice,
then we shall not be capable of facing him in battle, O evil-souled one.
O Brahmin, from time to time, beings of diverse and vast power and prosperity attain their exaltation among all creatures, and by the force of time, they dissolve away.
Today, at this time, we are not capable of standing before your enemies, Rāvaṇa and the others; such is the certainty of destiny.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, show favor toward my little son;
for you are indeed the incomparable deity for me, who am so ill-fated.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, monkeys, and serpents were not able to fight Rāvaṇa; how much less so human beings in battle?
He assumes the vigor of those great heroes who consume nectar;
therefore, we are not capable of contending with him in battle, nor can we withstand his boons.
This was one such time when even the virtuous were rendered frail;
for there Rāghava too fell into a state of wretchedness, worn down by old age.
Or else, O Brahmin, tell me, you who resemble a god, where indeed shall I release this son of mine—this salt, the destroyer of the sacrifice, born of honey? MU 1.7.35
If you do not wish this, O Brahmin, then I myself am at your command;
otherwise, however, I see no eternal victory for myself.
Having spoken these gentle words, he became overwhelmed with fear and sank into the turbulent uncertainty regarding the sage’s doctrine;
like one being swept away in an ocean with surging waves, that great-souled man could not discern even a single drop of certainty.
The eighth canto, titled "The Words of Daśaratha," by Vālmīki.
Having heard those words of his, whose syllables were choked with affection,
Kauśika, filled with indignation, replied to the lord of the earth.
Viśvāmitra:
Having promised "I shall do it," do you wish to abandon your vow?
Having been a powerful lion, you now desire the state of a deer.
This reversal of fortune is unbecoming for this lineage of the Raghavas;
never indeed do dark rays arise from the cool-rayed moon.
If you are unable, O King, I shall depart as I came;
having failed in my vow, O descendant of Kakutstha, may you remain happy along with your kinsmen.
Vālmīki: Then, when that great-souled Viśvāmitra was overcome with anger,
the entire earth trembled and the gods were seized by fear.
Perceiving that the Great Sage, the friend of the world, was overcome by anger, the wise Vasiṣṭha— steadfast, firm in his vows, and intelligent— spoke these words.
Vasiṣṭha:
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, you, the illustrious Daśaratha, are like another Dharma incarnate; you are adorned with virtues throughout the three worlds.
Being possessed of wisdom and firm in your vows, you ought not to abandon the Dharma;
you ought to carry out the word of the Sage, the Lord of the Three Worlds.
Renowned throughout the three worlds and endowed with righteousness and glory, practice your own duty; you ought not to abandon dharma.
O King, since they have promised "I shall do it" but have not performed it for you, your merit from sacrifices and charitable works will perish; therefore, release Rāma.
Guarded by that lion among men as nectar is by fire,
the Rākṣasas shall not behold him, whether he has mastered the divine weapons or not.
Even though you are born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and are yourself Daśaratha,
if you do not uphold my word, who else will?
Living beings do not abandon the boundaries established by the conventional usage formulated by you and others; therefore, you ought not to discard them here.
He is Dharma incarnate; he is the foremost among the courageous;
he is preeminent in wisdom in this world and the ultimate refuge of asceticism.
He knows the various weapons throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
no other man knows them, nor will anyone ever know them.
O King, neither any of the celestial sages, nor the immortals, nor the rākṣasas, nor the nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas are equal to him.
In former times, when he ruled his kingdom, Bhṛśāśva gave this weapon— which was exceedingly difficult for enemies to conquer— to Kauśika.
For those sons of Bhṛśāśva, resembling the sons of Prajāpati—
heroes, radiant and of great prowess— followed after him.
Jayā and Suprabhā were the two slender-waisted daughters of Dakṣa;
their offspring were one hundred in number, exceedingly difficult to conquer.
In former times, Jayā, having obtained a boon, gave birth to five hundred sons for the destruction of the asura armies; they were indestructible and able to assume any form at will.
Suprabhā gave birth to another fifty sons,
known as the Saṅgharṣas, who were invincible, difficult to revile, and exceedingly powerful.
Such is the heroism and great splendor of the great sage Viśvāmitra;
you ought not to entertain a wavering thought regarding Rāma’s departure.

While this Lord of Sages, who consists of the Great Being, stands nearby, even a man who is virtuous attains immortality when death arrives; do not fall into despondency like one who is utterly deluded.
The Ninth Sarga, titled "Vasiṣṭha’s Speech," by Vālmīki.
While Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus, King Daśaratha, intending to send forth his son, summoned Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Daśaratha:
O doorkeeper, bring quickly and without hindrance the mighty-armed Rāma, whose prowess is truth, together with Lakṣmaṇa, for the sake of the sage.

Thus dismissed by the king, he went to the inner apartments of the palace and, returning in just a moment, spoke to the lord of the earth: *iti rājñā visṛṣṭo 'sau gatvāntaḥpuramandiram / muhūrtamātreṇāgatya samuvāca mahīpatim //*MU_1,9.3//* Thus dismissed by the king, he went to the inner apartments of the palace and, returning in just a moment, spoke to the lord of the earth.
O King, Rāma, who had crushed all his enemies with his arms, sat dejected in his palace at night, like a bee within a lotus.
"I shall come in a moment," he says, yet he meditates all alone;
with a weary mind, he does not wish to remain in the presence of anyone.
When he had spoken thus, the protector of the earth consoled all those followers of Rāma and questioned them in due order.

When asked by the king, "In what manner and in what state is Rāma? the dejected servants of Rāma spoke these words to the lord of the earth: "O King, having heard that you have been defeated in battle by the sons of Daśaratha, Rāma has gone to the hermitage of the sage Atri, accompanied by his wife and younger brother. The king then said: "I shall go there myself; let my army remain here. Having spoken thus, the king set out with a small force, accompanied by his ministers. Having reached the hermitage, he saw the sage Atri, who was seated upon a seat of kuśa grass. He prostrated himself at the feet of the sage and sat down before him. Then the sage addressed the king: "O King, why have you come here? Tell me the reason for your arrival. The king replied: "O holy one, I have come here because I am unable to endure the sight of my enemy, Rāma, who has surpassed me in battle. The sage said: "O King, do not speak thus. You are a great warrior and a protector of the earth. It is not fitting for you to be distressed by this. O King, go back to your own city and rule the earth with justice. The king said: "O holy one, I cannot return without having seen Rāma. I must see him and then return to my kingdom. The sage said: "If it is so, then stay here for a short while until Rāma returns from his pilgrimage. The king agreed and remained there. After some time, Rāma returned from his pilgrimage and approached the sage Atri. He prostrated himself at the sage's feet and sat down before him. The sage then addressed Rāma: "My son, why have you come here? Tell me the reason for your arrival. Rāma replied: "O holy one, I have come here because I wish to see the king, who has been defeated by me in battle. The sage said: "My son, go and see the king. Do not cause him any distress. Rāma then went to the king and prostrated himself at his feet. The king embraced him and said: "My son, you have performed a great feat in defeating me in battle. Rāma replied: "O King, it was not through my own power that I defeated you, but through the grace of the gods. The king said: "My son, I am pleased with you. Ask for whatever boon you desire. Rāma replied: "O King, if you are pleased with me, then grant me this boon: that I may never again face defeat in battle. The king granted him this boon and dismissed him. Rāma then returned to his own city and ruled the earth with justice. Thus ends the story of Rāma’s victory over the king. May it be auspicious.
O Lord, we who support this frail body of ours are exhausted,
O All-pervading One, now that your son Rāma has withered away from fatigue.
Ever since Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals,
arrived from his pilgrimage accompanied by the brahmins, he has been dejected in spirit.
Through our diligent prayers, he— his countenance unfaded at evening— performs or does not perform his daily duties according to his own inclination.
At the conclusion of his bathing, worship of the gods, and customary rites,
the Lord, though entreated, does not eat food because he is weary and lacks satisfaction.
In the courtyard, he does not sport with playful dalliances alongside the women of the inner apartments who have set up swings,
like a cātaka bird that does not play with the waters of the earth.
O King, the array of armlets and bracelets set with rubies and pearls does not delight him, just as the sky [does not delight] one who is helpless from being struck by lightning.
In these vine-circled dwellings, where playful women move restlessly and the breezes carry the scent of flowers, he becomes filled with extreme despondency.
Whatever is delightful, appropriate, sweet, charming, or heart-captivating,
one suffers because of that very thing as if with eyes filled with tears.
"Why do these women, who bring only suffering, appear before me and move so restlessly?"— thus he censures the amorous women amidst their graceful dances.
Food, sleep, bathing, pleasure, drink, and sitting—
he does not delight in these when they are censured, as if they were the behavior of a madman.
"What is prosperity? What is adversity? What is home? What is striving?
Everything is indeed unreal"—having said this, he remains alone in silence.
He does not give rise to jests, he does not sink into enjoyments, nor does he remain occupied with worldly affairs; he maintains only silence.
Women with creeper-like tresses swaying and eyes rolling in playfulness do not bring him joy, just as does a doe to a tree in the forest.
In solitary places, at the ends of the earth, on riverbanks, and in forests— indeed,
in wildernesses devoid of living beings— he finds delight as if he were a slave for sale.
O King, by his turning away from the giving of clothing, drink, and food, he follows the path of those ascetics who possess the character of wandering mendicants.
Dwelling alone in a region devoid of people, O Lord of Men,
he neither laughs with a singular intellect, nor sings, nor weeps.
Having assumed the lotus posture with a mind empty of thought, he remains seated alone, resting his cheek upon the palm of his left hand.
He does not take up pride, nor does he desire sovereignty;
he neither rises nor sets amidst the fluctuations of pleasure and pain.
We do not know what he has become, what he does, what he strives for, what he meditates upon, what he approaches, or how he pursues it.
Day by day he grows emaciated; day by day he turns pale;
day by day he loses his passion, like a tree at the end of autumn.
O King, Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa followed him;
they were exactly like him, as if two reflections of him had arisen.
Although questioned again and again by his servants, kings, and mothers,
he said nothing at all and remained silent and motionless.
"Do not set your mind upon enjoyments that are pleasing only at first sight"—
thus does a virtuous friend advise a worthy person standing by his side.
Amidst women delightful with various luxuries and amidst social conversations, one who lacks affection perceives only their destruction, as if it were standing right before him.
He sings again and again with a falsetto (*kākali*), through gestures alone that are devoid of rhythmic flow, sweetness, effort, and fixed placement of words.
When an attendant standing at his side says, "Become an emperor," the sage,
with a distracted mind, laughs at him as if he were a madman prattling on.
He does not listen when something is spoken, nor does he look at what is before him;
he shows contempt everywhere, even toward matters of great importance.
Even regarding a lotus in the sky or a great forest in the sky,
the thought "how can this be so?"— such wonder does not arise in him.
Even when situated in the midst of beloved women, the arrows of Love do not pierce his mind, which is as difficult to breach as a great rock by torrents of water.
"Why do you desire wealth, which is but the sole refuge in times of calamity? Having thus instructed him, he bestows his entire possession upon the seeker.
"This is adversity, this is prosperity"—this delusion, consisting of mental construction, has arisen in the mind; thus he sings out from grief.
"Alas, I am ruined! I am helpless!"—even while crying out thus, people do not attain dispassion; rather, they simply say, "How strange! MU 1.9.39.
While Rāma, the destroyer of enemies and a great tree in the forest of the Raghus,
remains in this state, we have come to extreme distress.
O mighty-armed one, O lotus-petal-eyed one, we do not know what we should do for him whose mind is such; for you alone are our refuge in this matter.
O Lord, he disregards a king, or a learned brahmin, or even his foremost preceptor, laughing at them as if they were a mere animal, remaining unperturbed.
Having reached the firm conclusion that this vast proliferation known here as the "world" which has arisen is neither a real entity nor indeed the Self, he remains established [in that realization].
Neither in woman nor in himself, nor in a friend, nor in a kingdom, nor in a mother;
neither in prosperity nor in adversity—there is no limit to his attachment, whether within or without the Lord.
He is free from attachment, free from hope, free from desire, and without a basis;
he is liberated from delusion, and because of that, we are tormented.

"What is the use of wealth? What is the use of mothers? What is the use of a kingdom? What is the use of worldly effort?"—thinking thus with firm resolve within himself, he stood ready to give up his life.
He experienced the utmost distress regarding enjoyments, life-span, kingdom, friends, father, and mother,
like a cātaka bird during a drought.
O Lord, for one whose nature is such, the expansive web of saṃsāra, though endowed with all its splendors, acts as a counter-poison.
Who indeed on this earth could be such a Great Being,
capable of establishing him in this worldly conduct?
Thus, may he who is devoted to compassion arise sufficiently to rescue this calamity that has come upon us, spreading like the extension of branches.

Having cast away delusion from the mind, the high-minded one indeed leads all those who are afflicted to goodness; just as the sun, dispelling darkness on earth, brings about its own fruitfulness by attaining the state of a light-giver.
The tenth canto, titled "Rāghava’s Despair," by Viśvāmitra.
If this is so, then let your honors quickly bring that highly wise delight of the Raghus here, as lions might bring a deer.
This delusion of the Lord of the Raghus arose neither from calamities nor from passion;
this awakening, produced by discernment and dispassion, is of great consequence.
"May Rāma come here in an instant; we shall dispel his delusion right here in an instant, just as the Maruts disperse a thick cloud from a mountain."
O descendant of Raghu, when this delusion has been skillfully cleansed away,
you will find rest in that supreme state, just as we have.
Having attained truth, joy, wisdom, and tranquility,
he will reach fullness and a sublime complexion, as if having drunk the nectar of immortality.
And the honorable one, with a fully satisfied mind, will maintain his own traditional course of legal practice in its entirety and without interruption.
There will be a Great Being who knows the higher and lower states of the world,
who is indifferent to conditions of pleasure and pain, and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal.
When the Lord of Sages had spoken thus, the king, his heart fulfilled,
dispatched a succession of messengers once again to bring Rāma back.
And after this much time, Rāma rose from his seat in his own home to go into the presence of his father, like the sun rising from a mountain.
Accompanied by a few servants and his two brothers,
he arrived at that holy assembly hall of his father, which was like the heaven of the Lord of the Gods.
Then Rāma saw Daśaratha from afar,
surrounded by a multitude of kings like Vāsava by a host of gods.
It was attended on both sides by Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra,
and protected by a multitude of ministers who were experts in the meaning of all the scriptures.
He was attended by lovely women holding beautiful chowries,
standing in their appropriate places like the cardinal directions personified.
Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others, as well as Daśaratha and his kin,
beheld from afar Rāghava approaching like Guha.
He was resorted to by all who sought his service, both because of his pride in supporting sentient beings— as the Himalayas are resorted to for their coolness— and because of his profound voice.
Gentle, with an even and auspicious appearance, noble in discipline and vigorous,
his body was lovely and serene— a vessel for the highest good.
With the onset of youth fully dawning, adorned by both exertion and tranquility,
free from agitation and effortless, his desires were almost entirely fulfilled.
Having contemplated the course of the world, which is the domain of pure qualities,
it was as if approached by those very qualities out of a singular longing for his great being.
He reveals the unsurpassed reality within the hollow of his inner organ, which is filled with noble essence, by means of an undisturbed state of consciousness.
Thus, the scion of Raghu, adorned with a multitude of virtues, was visible from afar,
his body like a sprout clothed in a white, pure, and translucent silken garment.
He prostrated with his head, whose beautiful crest-jewel was shimmering, possessing the splendor of a mountain swaying upon the trembling earth.
First he honors his father, then the sages with single-minded devotion; thereafter the Brahmins, then his kinsmen, and then his teachers who possess superior virtues.
And having observed it himself, he accepted with a slightly sweet voice that succession of prostrations performed by the royal assembly.
Having received the blessings from the two sages, Rāma, his mind at peace and as beautiful as a celestial being, approached the holy presence of his father.
Then that lord of the earth, delighted by his prostration at his feet,
quickly embraced him upon his head and kissed him again and again.
Likewise, that slayer of enemy heroes embraced Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa with deep affection, just as a royal swan embraces a lotus.
Then, as the king said, "Child, stay on my lap," he settled instead upon a garment spread on the ground by his attendants.
Daśaratha:
My son, you have attained discernment and are a vessel for all that is auspicious;
like an ordinary person, you should not subject yourself to weariness with an aged intellect.
By one such as you who practices what has been taught by aged brahmins and gurus, the meritorious state is attained; it is not attained by one who pursues delusion.
O son, calamities remain far away and fragile for as long as no opening is given to delusion.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O mighty-armed prince, you are a hero; for by you these enemies that are the objects of the senses—so difficult to cut away and so difficult to restrain—have been conquered."
Why do you sink, like one ignorant of the truth, into this ocean of delusion— fathomless with its waves, profound, and characterized by dullness?
Viśvāmitra:
O mind, whose eyes are like a cluster of swaying blue lotuses, tell me: having abandoned your fickleness, for what reason do you now become deluded?
Upon what do they rest? To what extent, by what means, and for how long do those anxieties plunder the mind, like rats a house?
I believe you are not the ultimate object of mental agonies that are ill-suited to you;
for he who remains steadfast when faced with calamities has already conquered those very agonies.
Speak quickly whatever you desire, and you shall obtain it without fault;
furthermore, by this means, all mental afflictions shall no longer overcome you.

Having heard these words of the supreme sage, which were filled with the elegance of appropriate meaning, that banner of Raghu’s lineage abandoned his grief— just as a peacock ceases its lamentation when a rain-cloud thunders, having inferred the fulfillment of its desired aim.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Consolation of Rāghava," by Vālmīki.
Thus questioned by the lord of sages, Rāghava, having been comforted,
spoke words that were beautiful, steady, full of meaning, and measured.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, now that I have been questioned by you, I shall relate it exactly as it is, even though I am ignorant; for who can transgress the words of the virtuous?
I, for my part, was born here in this paternal home;
in due course I attained growth, acquired knowledge, and have remained established therein.
Then, O leader of sages, becoming devoted to righteous conduct, I wandered over the earth girdled by the oceans for the purpose of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Then, after such a length of time, my own discernment stripped away this attachment to cyclic existence from within me, just as a river current sweeps away a creeper from its bank.
My mind being encompassed by discernment, I myself thereafter reflected upon this with an intellect devoid of interest in enjoyments.
What indeed is this so-called happiness, alas, that consists in this wandering through saṃsāra,
where the world is born for the sake of death and dies for the sake of birth?
All these beings, including those that move and those that are stationary, remain established in their own states;
yet they are the masters of calamities, evil by nature, and the very grounds of worldly existence.
Like iron filings, phenomena are mutually unattached;
they cling together solely through their own mental construction.
This expansive world is seen as dependent upon the mind;
yet the mind itself appears here as non-existent—by what have we been utterly deluded?
Alas, we of deluded intellect have been sold for nothing,
like bewildered deer in the forest lured by the water of a mirage from afar.
Not sold by anyone, yet remaining as if sold; alas, we are all fools, even though we know Śambara.
What indeed are these so-called enjoyments within these manifold phenomena, which are utterly wretched?
For we have remained here in vain through delusion, fixed in our attachments.
Remaining for a long time in ignorance within this dense forest, we fools have fallen into delusion in vain, like bewildered deer in a pit.
What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments? Who am I, and what is this that has come?
Let that which is false remain false; for whom indeed has anything truly come into being?
O Brahmin, as I reflected in this way, a distaste for all worldly existences then arose within me, just as it does for a traveler in the desert wastes.
Therefore, O Blessed One, tell me this: what is it that perishes? What is it that is born again? And what is it that increases?
Old age, death, calamity, birth,
and prosperity revolve again and again through their manifestation and disappearance.
Behold! By those very same trivial emotions, we have indeed been reduced to a state of decay, like mountain trees battered by the winds.
Like insentient beings, people stand about making sounds through the winds called "vital breaths," just as hollow bamboo flutes produce sound in vain.
"How can this suffering be stilled?"— thus am I tormented by anxiety,
like an old tree by a fierce fire dwelling within its hollow.
Although my heart is as solid as a stone due to the suffering of saṃsāra,
I do not weep with falling tears merely out of fear for my own world.
But my mental states, empty and devoid of the moisture of dry lamentation, perceive through solitude alone, with discernment established within the heart.
I am utterly bewildered as I reflect upon this state composed of existence and non-existence;
like a fortunate man [unaware] of his poverty, I remain far removed from the anxieties of saṃsāra.
Fortunes, intent on deception, utterly delude the activity of the mind, utterly shatter one's virtues,
and bestow a web of suffering.
Wealth, which turns toward a mass of anxieties, does not lead to my joy;
nor do houses filled with wives, like those of men beset by calamities.
O Sage, my mind finds no peace through constant reflections on the various states of defilement, which are fashioned from ever-perishing causes; it is like that of a wild elephant bound in chains.

At every turn, in this world where the light of sharp delusion has fallen like a mist during the night, the wicked—those clever thieves who seize objects of sense by force—have set out and exerted themselves in every direction to plunder the very faculty of discernment.
O wise ones, tell me: who are the true warriors capable in battle against them today?
The twelfth canto, titled "The First Lamentation," [of] Rāma.
O Sage, this prosperity has been devised for diversion in this cycle of existence; yet even that, alas, surely brings about ruin through total delusion.
Like a river in the rainy season, it pours forth vast, dull surges within, abundant with excitement and agitated by a lack of order.
Many daughters of anxiety, uttered with much restlessness, arise from her,
just as the flickering waves arise from a river.
For this unfortunate woman does not fix her step upon one place; like a bewildered girl, she runs hither and thither with no settled course.
Producing an intense burning sensation when her limbs are touched,
she brings about only her own destruction within, like a streak of lamp-soot.
Indeed, like the common folk of a king, fools— without any investigation into merits and demerits— cling to one who has mounted a difficult position, even though he stands by their side.
Through various actions, this [mind] undergoes expansion;
it spreads like a flow of milk from the force of the venomous serpent of the afflictions.

People remain cold and gentle in touch toward both strangers and their own kin only so long as they have not been made harsh by prosperity, just as frost remains soft until it is driven away by a whirlwind.

Those who are wise, heroic, grateful, refined, and gentle— by their splendor, they have rendered even the handful of dust as if it were precious gems, yet they themselves are soiled by that very prosperity.
"O Blessed One, wealth does not lead to happiness; indeed, it leads only to suffering.
Without being guarded, it brings about destruction, just as a poisonous creeper brings about death."
The illustrious man, the one who is beyond reproach, and the hero who does not boast—
these three types of men, who possess equanimity and sovereignty, are difficult to find.
For this is a treacherous and dense cave for those who experience suffering,
a great forest on the Vindhya mountains for the lordly elephants of thick delusion.

It is a moonlight for the night-lotus of the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause, a moonlight for the water-lily of suffering; it is a whirlwind for the lamp of right vision, and a river surging with a flood of waves.
It is the path to the mountain of the clouds of agitation, the increaser of the poison of despondency,
the field for the weeds of conceptual constructions, and the pit for the snakes of evil enjoyments.
She is the frost to the creepers of dispassion, the night of transformation for the owls of passion, the fangs of Rahu to the moon of discernment, and the moonlight for the lotuses of goodness.
Like Indra’s bow, it is captivating with its various flickering colors;
like a shimmering flash of lightning, it arises and perishes, resting upon the dull-witted.
Fickle and devoid of delight, she is like a female mongoose born of a mongoose;
she is a mirage, the cause of intense delusion and the intent to deceive.
Like a wave in its singular form, not taking a step for even a moment; like the flickering flame of a lamp, she is extremely difficult to comprehend in her range of movement.
Like a lioness, she strikes down the prideful herds of elephants;
like the edge of a sword, she is cool yet sharp, resting upon a sharp intention.
I do not perceive, through this ill-fated fortune that is afflicted by its objects and overwhelmed by misfortune, even the slightest happiness apart from suffering.
Fortune, once driven out through the door by the enemy of darkness (the sun), returns again;
alas, she has lost her place in the heart, shameless and finding refuge with the wicked!

The goddess of fortune (Lakṣmī) captivates the movement of the mind, yet she is difficult for the miserly to achieve and is momentarily fleeting; her body emerges from the midst of a swarm of serpents, like a flowering creeper rising from a chasm.
The thirteenth canto, titled "The Banishment of Lakṣmī," Canto 13:
Rāma.
The body departs unexpectedly, like a madman, abandoning its life which is as fragile as a drop of water hanging from the tip of a sprout’s corner.
For those whose minds are worn out by attachment to the poison of sense objects,
and who lack mature self-discrimination, life is merely a cause of exhaustion.

But for those who have understood that which is to be known and have come to rest in the expansive state, being fully at ease regarding both existence and non-existence— for them, life becomes a source of happiness.
O Sage, we have reached a firm certainty established through limited forms; yet, amidst this mass of lightning in the clouds of saṃsāra, we find no peace in our lifespan.
It is as reasonable to wrap the wind, to break open space,
or to tie together waves, as it is to place one's reliance on life.
Like a thin autumn cloud, like an oilless lamp,
or like a flickering wave, it is perceived only as having already passed away.

I may still harbor the hope of grasping the moon’s reflection in a wave, a flash of lightning in a mass of clouds in the sky, or the transient stability of life; but I no longer place my trust in a lifespan whose duration has already passed.
With an unresting mind, the deluded person strives for a long, empty life solely for the sake of suffering, like a female mule conceiving within her womb.
O King, in this ocean of creation, water is but foam amidst the wandering of saṃsāra; life is but sap within the creeper of the body—it does not please me.
That by which what is to be attained is fully attained, by which one no longer grieves,
and which is the locus of supreme bliss— that is called true life.
For even trees live, and deer and birds live;
but he alone truly lives whose mind does not live by means of mentalizing.
Only those beings born in this world have lived a truly virtuous life who are not born here again; know this, O you who are like donkeys!
The scripture is a burden to one lacking discrimination; knowledge is a burden to one possessed by passion;
an unpeaceful mind is a burden; and for one who does not know the Self, the body is a burden.
Form, life-span, mind, intellect, ego, and likewise one's endeavors—
all these lead to suffering for the person of deluded intellect, just as a burden does for the bearer of that burden.
Life is a state where the mind never finds rest, the supreme abode of calamities,
a nest for the birds of disease, and a firm source of exhaustion.
Casting aside daily weariness, one should strive steadily and without ceasing; for in time, the pit of birth is quickly filled up.
The body is consumed by fierce diseases that rest within its cavities and inflict the burning pain of poison, just as the forest breeze is swallowed by savage serpents.
Like an old tree being dragged down by cruel woodworms, one is pulled toward suffering by base and intrusive afflictions that constantly produce fragmentation.
Surely, like a rat by a cat, one is constantly observed by death for the purpose of swiftly swallowing away one's dense pride.
By old age, which is pregnant with qualities such as pride yet itself empty, powerless, and subject to control, one’s food is digested just as it would be by a voracious eater.
In just a few days, having recognized its worthlessness,
youth is cast off with disdain, just as a wicked person is abandoned by a virtuous one.
Form is constantly coveted by Death, the enemy of destruction, who is the kinsman of old age and death, just as a beautiful woman is desired by a supreme libertine.
In this world, there exists nothing so utterly devoid of quality— whether stable or fleeting, whether excellent or worthless— as this life acquired through death.
The fourteenth canto, titled "Censure of Life," from the Rāmāyaṇa.
Risen up in vain through delusion, it grows in vain;
I am terrified by this enemy of false egoism, which consists of falsehood.
It is solely through the power of egoism that this world, appearing in manifold forms, inflicts the torment of a treasury of defects upon those who are most wretched.
Through the power of egoism comes calamity; from egoism come distressing anxieties;
through the power of egoism comes worldly striving; egoism itself is a great delusion.
Relying upon that supreme and long-standing enemy, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), I neither eat nor do I drink water; how much less, O Sage, could I enjoy worldly pleasures?
The long rope of saṃsāra, which deludes my mind,
has been stretched out by the fault of egoism, just as a snare is set by a hunter.
Those sufferings which are long-lasting, harsh, and great,
born from the sense of "I," have gone away like *khadira* thorns.
I renounce the ego, which has the moon of tranquility as its mouth, the great thunderbolt of the lotus of qualities, and the autumnal clouds of knowledge.
I am not Rāma, nor do I have desire for worldly objects, nor does my mind dwell upon them;
I wish to remain tranquil within my own self alone, just like a Jina.
Whatever has been enjoyed, done, or taken by me under the influence of egoism—all that is indeed non-substantial; the substance is only the emptiness of egoism.
O Brahmin, if there is such a thing as "I," then I am pained in adversity and happy in prosperity; therefore, the wealth is the state of being without egoism (anahaṅkāritā).
O sage, having abandoned the ego and with a tranquil mind, I remain free from agitation, finding an unshakable refuge within the flood of sensory enjoyments.
O Brahmin, as long as the cloud of egoism expands,
so long does the cluster of blossoms of the *kuṭaja* tree of craving continue to bloom.
When the dense cloud of egoism has been stilled, the lightning-vine of craving will swiftly vanish somewhere, like the flickering of a lamp’s flame that has gone out.
In the great Vindhya mountain of egoism, the intoxicated elephant of the mind roams about with the crashing thuds of its limbs, like a rain-cloud with its peals of thunder.
In this great cavern of the body, this lion of dense egoism which shines forth expansively— it is by means of this that the entire world is stretched out.
The succession of many births, strung upon the fine threads of craving,
has been fashioned by the fierce hunter of egoism into a necklace around his neck.
Sons, wives, and kin— this entire web, devoid of the power of mantra,
has been spread out here by this enemy of false ego.
When this notion of "I" has been wiped away by one who is himself free from distress,
all mental anxieties are indeed wiped away.
When the cloud of "I" has subsided and gradually becomes perfectly tranquil, the mist of the mind's conceptualization and delusion vanishes somewhere beyond reach.
O Brahmin, for me, whose mental state is free from egoism yet who is sinking in grief due to my own folly, you ought to tell me whatever is appropriate in this matter.
I shall not take refuge in that which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, situated within, and abandoned by the highest virtue;
that locus of egoism which is exceedingly painful on all sides—O Great-Souled One, instruct me with what remains.
The fifteenth chapter, titled "Aversion to Egoism," [ends]. Rāma:
Worn out by the defects [of the senses], the flickering mind wavers from the noble practice cultivated by the wise, like a tuft of *tapiñjala* grass swayed by the wind.
It runs aimlessly and distractedly here and there,
wretchedly further and further away from its goal, just like a stray dog in a village.
One attains nothing anywhere, even through the acquisition of great wealth;
it reaches no end or fullness, like a small water-vessel with water.
The mind is eternally empty, yet it is ensnared by the net of various desires;
it does not attain even the slightest peace, like a deer strayed from its herd.
Maintaining a state as flickering as a wave and subject to being cut and shattered,
the mind does not attain tranquility even for a moment.
The mind, agitated by its own conceptualizations, rushes in all ten directions,
like the waters of the milk-ocean stirred up by the gentle striking of Mount Mandara.
I am not able to stem this great ocean of mental delusion, which has waves, ripples, and whirlpools, and is garlanded with the crocodiles of illusion.
O Brahmin, like a deer captivated by the mind, one who longs for the sprouts of grass that are enjoyments runs far away, without considering the fall into the abyss.
My mind never abandons that state of being mangled and shattered by its agitated activity, just as the ocean never ceases its turbulence.
With its flickering mode of activity, the mind— agitated by a multitude of anxieties—
does not fix its steadiness upon any one thing, like a lion in a cage.
The mind, mounted upon the chariot of delusion, seizes the happiness of tranquility from the body—
having exerted its effort— as a swan extracts milk from water.
O Lord of Sages, the fluctuations of the mind lie dormant upon the bed of manifold conceptual constructions and do not awaken; therefore, I am tormented and distressed.
O Brahmin, I am bound by my mind, which is woven together with the threads of craving through firm knots, like a bird caught in a net.
O Sage, I am consumed by my mind as dry grass is by fire— with the constant smoke of indignation and the dense flames of anxiety.
O Brahmin, my mind has become dull through cruelty and follows after its wife, craving; it has been devoured by me like a corpse by a fierce dog.

O Brahmin, I have been carried away by the mind— which is insentient in nature and characterized by a movement that tosses like trembling waves— just as a tree on a riverbank is swept away by a torrent.
To fall into intermediate states and to be assailed by emptiness,
I have been driven far away by my mind, like a blade of grass by a fierce wind.
Constantly intent on crossing this ocean of saṃsāra, I have been dammed by my own evil mind, just as a flood of water is held back by a bridge.
As I was departing from the underworld and returning from the underworld,
I have indeed been bound by my mind, like a well-wood is encircled by a rope.
I have been seized by my own mind— which is false yet expansive in form and fragile under scrutiny— just as a child is seized by a Vetāla spirit.
O Brahmin, his mind is more fiery than fire, his course more difficult than even a mountain, and his grasp of the mind more unassailable than even a diamond.
The mind falls upon its objects like a bird upon pieces of meat;
in an instant it reaches detachment, like a child from his playthings.
O Father, this ocean of the mind— insentient by nature, restless, possessing the movement of vast whirlpools, and filled with the serpents of one's desires— draws me away from afar.
O virtuous one, the restraint of the mind is more difficult than even drinking up the great ocean, or leaping over Mount Sumeru, or even consuming fire.
The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist, and when it is extinguished, the world is extinguished. Therefore, that mind must be treated with diligent effort.

Surely these hundreds of joys and sorrows have come from the mind, just as forests emerge from the best of mountains; I believe, O Sage, that they truly dissolve away when that mind has been thinned through the power of solitude.
I have risen up with my mind intent on conquering that enemy against whom the great ones have fixed their hope for victory over all virtues;
yet, due to the absence of inner delight, I do not welcome worldly prosperity—which is dull, impure, and vast—any more than the moon welcomes a mass of clouds.
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Mind's Lack of Self-Nature," [ends with] Rāma:
In this world, by means of insatiable craving— the night of the darkness within the heart—
swarms of owls that are the mental afflictions roam through the sky of consciousness.
My essence and tenderness have been consumed by this anxiety, which brings internal burning; I am being withered away by it, just as mud is dried up by the radiance of the sun.
In the great forest of my mind, which is crowded with the darkness of delusion and empty, the demoness of hope dances wildly and is utterly intoxicated.
With frost formed from dust and radiant with heaps of gold,
this cluster of Ashoka blossoms surely puts forth its bloom within my mind.
Enough with this craving that devours the inner disposition;
it leads to turbulent agitation, like a wave in the ocean.
Upon the mountain of my body, the river of craving flows with surging waves; it possesses a form most turbulent, and its roar is that of unrestrained billows.
Like an old blade of grass driven by a whirlwind, this *citta*-cātaka has been led away somewhere by a turbid intellect that has arisen to obstruct its momentum.
Whichever excellence of virtue I have studied and take as my refuge,
craving cuts it away from me, just as a field mouse gnaws through a stringed instrument.
Like a withered leaf in milk, like a decayed blade of grass in the wind,
or like an autumn cloud in the sky, I wander in the whirlpool of anxiety.
We, whose intellects lack the capacity to reach our own true abode,
are bewildered in the snare of thought, like birds caught in a net.
O dear one, I have been so scorched by the flame called craving that I do not expect its burning to be extinguished even by nectars.
Having gone far, far away from here, and having met again and again,
the mare of craving, intoxicated and rushing, wanders swiftly toward the ends of the quarters.
Thirst, clinging to the insentient, causes one to go up and down;
it is perpetually agitated, knotted, and as fierce as the rope of a waterwheel.
Like a powerful ox driven by a rope knotted within its body and pulled with frantic urgency, so is a person driven by craving.
Driven by the constant craving for sons, wives, and kin— a craving as dark as night— the Kirātī weaves a net here among the worlds, just as she does among the birds.
Like the night of the dark fortnight, craving terrifies even the wise, blinds even the eye of wisdom, and exhausts even the joyful.
Crooked, soft to the touch, and signaling the imbalance of poison,
craving burns like a black female serpent even when only slightly touched.
Bestowing an illusory nature, miserable and bestowing misfortune, craving shatters the hearts of men like the demoness Kṛṣṇā.
O Brahmin, the lute of craving—its strings worn out by weariness and wrapped within its hollow belly—does not shine even in the presence of bliss. MU_1,16.19.
The creeper of the abyss of craving is eternally exceedingly filthy, characterized by bitter madness; it is long, slender, and thick with affection.
Bringing no joy, empty, utterly fruitless, and excessively haughty;
inauspicious and cruel, craving is like a withered flower-cluster.
Even when the mind is not won over, craving pursues everything; yet it obtains no fruit at all, like an aged woman longing for a lover.
In the great dance of saṃsāra, crowded with various sentiments,
upon the stages of the vast expanse of worlds, craving is the aged dancer.
In the long wilderness of saṃsāra, the poisonous creeper of craving has spread wide; it is mounted upon the blossoms of old age and bears a succession of fruits that are both falls and rises.
When it can no longer do so, even then it adopts a dancing gait;
craving dances without joy like an aged dancer.
When the mist thickens, the light fades; when it arrives, the peahen of craving, restless with thirst, sets her foot upon the floods of suffering.
Abounding with dull waves and for long remaining utterly empty within,
the river of craving momentarily attains a surge of splendor during its monsoon season.
Leaving behind that which has perished, craving moves from one man to another like a restless bird flying from tree to tree.

Though she has already reached her goal, she sets foot even on what is unassailable; though she is satisfied, she still seeks further fruit; she does not remain long in one place—such is the restless female monkey of craving.
"Having done this, one arrives at that"—all of this is utterly inconsistent;
yet craving strives incessantly, like some divine impulse."
In one moment it descends to the underworld, in another it ascends to the vault of heaven;
in a moment it wanders through the groves of the quarters—such is the bee of craving upon the lotus-heart.
Craving alone is the long-lasting giver of suffering among all the defects of saṃsāra;
it casts even one dwelling in the inner apartments into extreme distress.
The row of clouds that is craving— dense with the mist of delusion and obstructing the supreme light— bestows the highest dullness.
For all the multitudes of living beings wandering in the cycle of existence,
craving is the binding rope that weaves together the garlands of their minds.
Thirst is of variegated colors, devoid of qualities, long-lasting, and of a soiled nature; it is empty, the abode of emptiness, and possesses the character of Indra’s bow.
A thunderbolt to the crops of virtue, a fruitful autumn turned into a calamity,
frost to the lotus of prosperity, and a long night to those shrouded in darkness.
She is the actress in the drama of saṃsāra, the female bird dwelling in the body-abode,
the doe in the forest of the mind, and the lute for the song of passion.
It is a wave in the ocean of worldly affairs, a chain for the elephant of delusion,
as beautiful as a banyan tree at the crossroads, and a moonlight for the night-lotus of suffering.
She is a single jewel-casket for the sufferings of old age and death;
she is a woman eternally intoxicated by the charms of mental anguish and physical disease.
For a moment craving is pure light, for a moment it is a fragment of darkness;
for a moment it is like the path of the sky, and for a moment it is dense with mist.
Let craving go to its pacification for the sake of calming the exertion of activity,
just as the thick, dark night vanishes for the sake of warding off demons.
This world remains deluded, mute, and with its inner disposition agitated,
for as long as it continues to pursue the cholera-like poison of craving.
This world, when freed from anxiety, abandons all suffering;
indeed, the abandonment of anxiety is said to be the mantra for the cholera of anxiety.
Handling grass, stones, wood, and all else with the suspicion that it might be meat,
one’s inner craving throbs like a female fish in a lake.
The pain of disease residing in the limbs and the thirst [for existence] quickly bring even a man of profound depth to the surface,
