just as the rays of the sun bring a lotus to the surface.
Hollow within, knotted, and possessing long, sprout-like thorns,
craving is like a bamboo creeper that constantly bears the luster of a pearl gem.
Oh, how truly wonderful! Even those of great intelligence cut through craving—which is so difficult to sever—with the stainless sword of discernment.
Neither the edge of a sword, nor a vajra-fire, nor the glowing sparks of heated iron are so sharp,
O Brahmin, as this craving that resides within the heart.
Black as collyrium with sharp tips, possessing long wicks of craving, they are luminous yet touchable only by burning; cravings are like the flames of a lamp.
Even the wisest man, even the hero, even the steadfast— desire alone makes such a supreme among men as light as a blade of grass in the blink of an eye.
The great Vindhya forest of craving is vast and dense, terrifying, composed of thickets, nets, and dust; it is filled with blinding darkness and fierce frost.

Desire alone, having found its mark within all worlds, remains in the universe like a power inherent in the sweet waters of the milk-ocean, though it has become difficult to perceive as if it were standing right before one's eyes amidst the rows of flickering waves.
The seventeenth canto, named "The Censure of Thirst," ends here.
Rama.
The body, dense with the strings of moist intestines, subject to change, and filled with feverish heat, throbs within this cycle of existence; even that serves only for suffering.
Though ignorant, he resembles one who knows that [reality], for his self-experience is turned inward;
though capable by means of reasoning, he is to me incapable, being neither inert nor conscious.
Situated between the dull-witted and the enlightened, with a mind swinging in indecision, such a person is neither a man of discernment nor a fool; he merely fosters delusion.
With a little he attains joy, and with a little he falls into distress;
there is no object of grief equal to the body, which is base and devoid of virtue.
He is perpetually adorned by a mouth that is like a blossoming flower, beautiful with its filaments of teeth, and ever-changing as it opens and closes.
With the multitude of his arms as its branches, well-supported by the pillars of his teeth, with his eyes as bees covering its bark, and the great fruit upon the pedestal of his head; //MU_1,17.6//
With streams of flowing tears for its currents, hands and feet for its beautiful sprouts,
ankles for its joints, it is the dwelling place for the birds of the multitude of tasks.

This tree of the body, possessing its own shade, is the resting place for the multitude of travelers that are living beings; who owns it as their own, and who is a stranger to it? For what reliance or non-reliance can there be here?
When the boat and the body— both of which are grasped again and again for the purpose of crossing over the burden— belong to no one, for whom could there be the notion of a "self"?
In this empty forest called the body, crowded with many pits and filled with countless trees that are its hairs, who can find any sense of security?
In this firm body-drum, bound together with skin, sinews, and bones,
I do not remain within it— like a cat in a drum that never ceases its sound.
Grown within the forest of saṃsāra, the monkey of the flickering mind takes the form of a wish-fulfilling flower-cluster, yet it is gnawed by the woodworms of long-standing suffering.
This glorious tree has craving for its female serpent-dwelling, anger for its crow-nest,
smiles for its flowers, and the great fruits of good and evil.
With his trunk as a sturdy stem, a network of arms as a cluster of creepers, and hands as beautiful blossoms,
all the sprouts of his limbs were set in motion by the wind.
He was the support for all the birds of the senses, possessed of well-formed knees and beautiful skin; endowed with a luster full of vitality, he was frequented by travelers in the form of desire.
Upon its head grew a long row of hair like blades of grass;
its hollow interior was a nest for the aged vultures of egoism.
This tree of my body, its roots being the web of latent impressions that have burst forth, is weak in form; this cessation of exertion does not lead to my happiness.
O Sage, the body is the great house for one who dwells within the ego; let it roll about or attain stability—what does that matter to me?
This house of the body is not desired by me, for its senses are like tethered cattle, its courtyard is the leaping field of craving, and all its limbs are stained with the dust of passion.
This house of the body is undesirable to me; it is a hollow space constricted by the friction of wood-like bones and bound together by strings of entrails.
This house of the body is not pleasing to me: its strings of sinews are stretched out, it is made muddy by the water of blood, and it is whitened by the moss of old age.
I do not desire this house of the body, which maintains its stability through the infinite activities performed by the painter of consciousness, and which has false delusion as its great pillar.
This house of my body is undesirable: it resounds with the cries of children in distress, it is charming only by virtue of a comfortable bed, and its maidservants are consumed by wicked desires.
This house of the body is not desired by me; it is crowded with the vessels and utensils of the array of sense-objects rich in impurity, and it is encircled by the brine of ignorance.
This house of my body is undesirable, for it has ankles of *gulgulu* resin, knees resting upon high pillars, and is made very firm with the timber of long arms.
O Brahmin, this house of the body is not pleasing to me, for it has the eyes as its open windows, the interior courtyard where wisdom plays, and anxiety as its daughter.
This house of the body is not desired by me, for its moon-chamber— the beauty of the ears— is covered by the roof-tiles of the hair on the head, and its balconies are the exceedingly long fingers.
With the sprouts of thick hair growing from every part of its walls,
and its seats and vessels completely empty, this house of my body is not desired by me.
This house of my body is undesirable, for its interior is made resonant by the nails, the navel, and the breaths, while the wind within produces a whistling sound.
This body-house of mine is undesirable, for it is filled with the incessant force of winds agitated by inhalation and exhalation, and it is riddled with wide-open windows in the form of the eyes.
This house of the body is not desired by me; its door to the mouth is terrifying, overrun by the monkey of the tongue, and fragments of teeth and bones are visible within.

This house of my body, though once smooth with the plaster of youth and made unstable by the movement of its mechanical parts, is no longer desired as it has been excavated by the relentless rat of the mind.
For a moment my body-house shines with the light of a smile-lamp, beautiful with bliss; for a moment it is pervaded by floods of radiance, yet it is not desired [by me].
This body of mine is not desired by me; it is the abode of all diseases, a city of wrinkles and grey hair, and a forest of the deer of all mental afflictions.

This forest of the body is not desired by me; it is treacherous with the agitation of the senses and the constellations, empty, hollow and pithless, and its heart-thicket is a dense thicket of darkness.
O lords of sages, I am unable to sustain this abode of a body,
just as one of little strength cannot lift an elephant sunk in the mud.
What is the use of prosperity, what of the body, what of desire, and what of worldly effort?
In just a few days, Time cuts away everything.
O Sage, tell me: what beauty can there be in this body, composed of blood and flesh, which is both internal and external, and whose sole nature is destruction?
O dear one, what reliance can a wise person have on those ungrateful bodies which do not follow the life-principle at the time of death? Alas! MU_1,17.39.
As long as this body— trembling like the tip of an elephant’s ear in rut and fragile as a dangling drop of water—
does not abandon me, so long shall I abandon it.
This body-sprout is flickering with the movement of the wind, fragile, worn out, thin, and round; it is undesirable, being both harsh and sapless.
Having eaten and drunk for a long time that which is as delicate as young shoots,
it reaches a state of attenuation and pursues its destruction without effort.
Indeed, that ordinary body feels no shame while repeatedly experiencing those very same pleasures and pains, which consist of both existence and non-existence.
Having exercised sovereignty for a very long time and having enjoyed the glory of wealth and power, why is this body maintained, which attains neither height nor stability?
At the time of old age it undergoes decay, and likewise at the time of death it meets its end;
for one who does not perceive the distinction, the body is exactly the same for both the wealthy man and the beggar.
Within the belly of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the midst of the cavern of craving,
this mute tortoise of a body remains asleep, though it is called "liberated."
In this ocean of saṃsāra, numerous pieces of wood that are human bodies are carried along, all equally fit for the single purpose of being burned; among them, who can be known as a "man"?
For the discerning person, there is no purpose whatsoever in this physical body, which is long subject to corruption, unstable, and destined for the fruit of downfall.
Having suddenly reached old age within the mire-filled pools of the bathhouse,
it is not known where or how this frog-like body will soon depart.
Bodies, which are like restless winds and whose undertakings are devoid of essence,
are seen here by no one as they travel along the path of dust.
O Blessed One, the movement of the wind, of a lamp, and of the mind as they go is known,
but not so the coming and going of our body and arrow.
Fie, fie again and again upon those who have their hopes bound to bodies and whose hopes are bound to the maintenance of the world— those who are intoxicated by the wine of delusion!
"I am not the body, nor is the body mine; this [body] is not I.
O Sage, those whose minds rest thus are the supreme persons.
Abounding in honor and dishonor, and delightful through great gain,
those things perceived as defects destroy a man whose attachment is bound solely to the body.
We have been deceived by the guile of the subtle-bodied demoness who dwells within the attachment to the body— the wondrous manifestation of egoism.
Alas, all this wretched wisdom has been deceived by this vile eye of false knowledge, which is bound to the body; it remains alone in its misery.
That self-slayer who possesses not even the slightest truth deceives the people with his wondrous, burnt body.
In just a few days, this withered sprout of a body falls away effortlessly, like a drop from the water of a mountain stream.
This body is soon to perish, like a bubble upon the ocean;
it flickers in vain amidst the revolution of activities, yielding no fruit.
O twice-born one, I have no reliance for even a moment upon this body— a city produced by dreams and delusion, a transformation of false knowledge, whose dissolution is most evident.
He who has determined stability in lightning, in autumnal clouds, and in the cities of the Gandharvas— he places his trust in physical conflict.

Having cast aside like a blade of grass this wretched body— which is ever-vulnerable to a succession of calamities, which achieves victory only over those of deceitful conduct, and which is the seat of every defect— I now abide in happiness.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "Loathing the Body," from the Rāmāyaṇa.
Even having obtained birth in this ocean of worldly existence— which is characterized by instability and surging with the waves of karmic duties— childhood leads only to suffering.
Incapacity, misfortune, craving, muteness, dull-wittedness,
greed, restlessness, and wretchedness— all these prevail in childhood.
In states of rage, weeping, and ferocity, as well as those shattered by wretchedness,
childhood is a bondage, like a tethering post for female elephants.
Neither in death, nor in old age and disease, nor in adversity, nor even in youth,
do those anxieties cut through the heart as they do in childhood.
The undertaking of animal births is utterly despised by all;
the fickle conduct of the foolish brings suffering even beyond death.
To whom can childhood— merely a fragile reflection of dense ignorance consisting of various fancies, with the mind already cut and shattered— bring happiness?
In childhood, when one is constantly gripped by fear at every step due to a mind darkened by dullness, what calamity could there be that would not cause even greater fear?
O you of evil intent, through playful diversions, wicked amusements, and harmful desires, the fool incurs supreme delusion and powerful calamity.
Childhood, with its onset muddled by conceptual constructions, its difficult playfulness, and its precarious foundation, serves only to discipline a person, not to bring peace.
Whatever faults, whatever misconducts, whatever evil courses, and whatever wicked anxieties there may be—
all these are established in childhood, like owls in a ruined dwelling.
O Brahmin, may those foolish men of ruined intellect— who, with their minds clouded by vain thoughts, declare that childhood is delightful— be cursed!
Where the restless mind flickers amidst its fluctuations,
how can even the sovereignty over the three worlds bring satisfaction?
O Sage, for all sentient beings indeed, in all their states, the mind becomes ten times more restless in childhood.
The mind is restless by its very nature, and childhood is the height of restlessness; O dear one, when these two are joined together, how can there be an end to this wicked fickleness?
O Brahmin, the fickleness of the mind was learned from the eyes of women, from masses of lightning, from garlands of flames, and from the waves— perhaps since childhood.
Indeed, childhood and the mind are observed to be like two brothers, constantly unstable in all their activities.
All wicked spirits, all faults, and all evil intentions subsist upon childhood alone, just as men depend upon one who possesses wealth.
If a child does not obtain something new and delightful every single day,
he falls into a swoon from the force of his craving.
With a little he comes under control, and with a little he undergoes change;
the fool delights in impurity, just like a dog.
With a face constantly streaming with tears, his mind benumbed within the mud,
the infant is like a patch of ground heated by the sun and drenched by rain.
Devoted to fear and food, wretched, and desiring only what is seen,
the child possesses a restless intellect and a body that leads solely to suffering.
Failing to obtain the things desired by his own imagination, the weak-minded fool suffers with an afflicted intellect, as if his heart were being cut out.
O Sage, those sufferings of a fool— which have their targets attained through evil efforts and which are intensified by many factions— do not belong to anyone else.
Like a weakling tormented by a powerful horse, the fool is constantly afflicted by a mind that frolics according to its desires, just as a forest glade is scorched by the summer heat.
A youth who has entered the house of learning undergoes supreme torment,
as terrifying as the unevenness of poison, like a lordly elephant at its tethering post.
Consisting of various desires, this false conceptualization born of imagination—
the fragile disposition of childhood— leads to suffering that is exceedingly long-lasting.
How could that folly, by which one desires to eat frozen snow and to seize the moon from the sky, ever lead to happiness?
O one of great intelligence, what distinction is there between an insentient stone, which is incapable of warding off cold and heat, and a foolish tree?
Intent on eating, they desire to fly up with their two wings;
children, possessing the nature of birds, are constantly devoted to fear and food.
In childhood there is fear of the teacher, and likewise of the mother and the father;
there is fear of people and of elder children—childhood is a temple of fear.

O Great Sage, in this world, even for one who has taken refuge in You— though Your intent is unassailable by any state of fault and You are free from the play of non-discrimination— the childhood of worldly existence does not provide sufficient satisfaction to anyone at all.
The nineteenth canto, titled "Disgust for Childhood," ends with Rāma.
Then, having abandoned the miseries of childhood, a man whose mind is afflicted ascends the dizzying precipice of youth for the sake of his own downfall.
In that state, the dull-witted person, following the fluctuations of his own restless mind which possesses infinite diversions, goes from sorrow to even greater sorrow.
Helplessly oppressed by the demoness of desire, who dwells within the cavity of one's own mind and causes manifold agitation, one is overcome by force.
Just as one who is powerless hands over his own son to the flames, so too does he surrender his mind to thoughts of fickle nature on all sides, like wayward women.
Those various faults arising from wicked undertakings ravage that youth of such disposition; yet, O Sage, those very faults are not even seen there.
Those people who have not been destroyed by youth— which, like the seed of the great hell, causes one to wander incessantly— have indeed been destroyed by nothing else.
He who has crossed over the terrifying land of youth— which consists of manifold pleasures, is variegated, and is filled with a multitude of diverse events— is called wise.
Youth does not please me, for its form is radiant only for a moment, it possesses the restless thundering of dense clouds, and it is constantly illuminated by flashes of lightning.
Abounding in various whirlpools, mired in mud, and possessing a dull depth;
fragile as breaking waves and terrifying—I do not take pleasure in this youth of mine.
Youth, which stands at the forefront of all men, enchanting for but a moment,
and resembling a city of the Gandharvas— this youth of mine does not please me.
Indeed, youth— which lasts no longer than the flight of an arrow, which is pleasant yet radiant with suffering, and which constantly brings the affliction of burning— does not please me.
Sweet, delicious, and bitter, yet corrupting and a mere ornament of the faults—
this youth of mine, resembling the surging waves of wine, does not please me.
Unreality appearing like reality, soon bringing about deception—
youth, which is like union with a woman in a dream, does not please me.
Youth, flickering like a flash of lightning, falsely constructed as a cycle, and resembling a whirling firebrand— this youth of mine does not please me.
Tender, expansive, and noble within, yet empty at its core and perishing in an instant— this youth of mine, resembling an autumn cloud, does not please me.
"Youth does not please me; it is delightful only at first sight, its inner nature is devoid of true reality, and it is like union with a courtesan."
Whatever misdeeds there may be, they all bring about every kind of suffering; they manifest in youth just as great portents appear at the end of an eon.
Even the Blessed One fears the night of ignorance that is youth, which creates darkness within the heart and assumes a terrifying form.
This delusion of youth causes extreme confusion, which utterly forgets virtuous conduct and brings about a failure of the intellect.
In youth, a living being is consumed by the unassailable fire born of separation from a beloved within the heart, just as a tree is consumed by a forest fire.
For even a mind that is expansive, serene, and pure may become turbid in youth, just as a river becomes so during the rainy season.
A river, though terrifying with its dense waves, can be dammed;
but not so thirst, which is flickering with youth and agitated within.
"She was my beloved; those were her full breasts; those were her charms; that was her face"—through such thoughts regarding youth, a person falls into a state of decay.
In this world, the virtuous honor a young man afflicted by ever-increasing thirst, and not one who is base and devoid of desire, like a withered scrap of straw.
Indeed, youth is the eternal tethering post for the great elephant of pride— the one blinded by intoxication and bearing the pearls of its own faults— for the very purpose of its destruction.
Youth is a new forest for trees whose roots are the vastness of the mind, which harbor the venomous serpents of faults, and whose trunks are anger and weeping.
Know that youth is a lotus flower: crowded with the filaments of passion, filled with the petals of false conceptualizations, and serving as a pond for the bees of evil thoughts.
Fresh youth is the abode of the birds of mental and physical afflictions, which frequent the shores of the lake of the heart and prey upon both the virtuous and the wicked.
The ocean, whose playful waves are insentient and beyond counting,
has reached its full maturity, disregarding all boundaries.
Then, the uneven wind of youth stood ready to remove the dust from all the leaves of virtue, in order to sweep it away.
The fierce dust-storms of youth, agitated by the wind of the senses, turn the face pale and reach the highest peak of harshness.
The exuberance of youth awakens a multitude of faults, cuts down the series of virtues, and is the very playfulness of men's misfortune.
Having bound the restless bee of the mind to the pollen of the lotus-body,
this moon of youth deludes man.
The lovely creeper of youth, sprouted from the thicket of the body,
intoxicates the bee of the mind as soon as it has attached itself and reached its full maturity.
The deer of the mind, rushing toward the mirage of youth that arises from the heat of the body's vital winds, fall into a treacherous pit.
The moonlight of youth for my body, the mane of the lion of my mind,
and the wave of the ocean of my life— this youth does not please me.
This autumn of youth has borne fruit for only a few days within the wilderness of the body; indeed, you ought not to place your trust in it.
In an instant, this bird of youth flies away from the body,
just as the wish-fulfilling gem slips from the hand of one with little fortune in a mere moment.
Whenever youth ascends to its highest peak, the passionate desires leap up; at that time, they lead only to destruction.
Right then do the demons of passion and hatred prowl about;
they do not set until the night of youth has come to an end.
Exercise compassion toward youth, which is full of various duties, miserable, and fleeting like a moment— toward it as if toward a dying son.
That man who, out of delusion, feels joy because of youth which is subject to momentary destruction, is indeed considered a great fool— a human deer.
That person of wicked intellect who desires youth, which is intoxicated by pride, delusion, and arrogance,
will soon be joined with remorse.
They alone are righteous, they alone are great-souled, and they alone are true men on this earth,
O virtuous one, who have happily crossed over the perilous strait of youth.
The ocean, though filled with formidable sea-monsters, can be crossed with ease;
but not so the ocean of youth, which is fraught with faults and surging with waves of passion.
Adorned with discipline, the abode of noble beings, radiant with compassion, and encircled by virtues— indeed, O dear one, such a youth is rare in this world, like a forest situated in the sky.
The twentieth canto, titled "The Censure of Youth," ends with the word "Rāma."
And in this woman, who is a doll of flesh with a cage of limbs moving by machinery, and who abounds with sinews,
bones, and joints— what indeed is beautiful?
Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, and tears from the eye, look closely at it; if it is not beautiful, why do you delude yourself in vain?
"Here are the hairs, here is the blood"—this is the body of a woman.
What can a person of vast resolve do with this censured thing?
Those very limbs which were repeatedly cherished with garments and ointments,
flesh-eaters now tear apart for all embodied beings.
In which [woman] pearls were seen upon her breast, radiant with luster, resembling the surging currents of the Gaṅgā water sparkling on the slopes of Mount Meru’s peaks.
In cremation grounds at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is at another time devoured by dogs like a small morsel of food.
Just as the limbs of a camel in the forest are smeared with blood, flesh, and so forth, so too are the limbs of a passionate woman; for what attachment can there be even to that?
The mere quality of being delightful at first sight is attributed to a woman;
I believe, O Sage, that even this does not exist here, for she is the sole cause of delusion.
What distinction is there here between intoxicating wine, which bestows expansive joy while first agitating one's passion, and a woman who causes transformation?
O Sage, the elephants of human beings, tethered to the hitching post of the tongue,
do not attain awakening even by means of the long goads of tranquility.
Bearing hair like soot, naturally sharp and always like the flames of the fire of evil deeds, women burn a man like straw.
They are to be revered, they are great-souled ones, and they alone are true men on this earth,
who have easily crossed over the perilous strait of youth, O virtuous one.
For women are both beautiful and terrible— the firewood for the fires of hell— blazing even from afar, and though full of moisture, they are dry.
Her dark tresses were scattered like thick darkness, her eyes were like shimmering stars,
her face was like the orb of the full moon, and she smiled like a cluster of night-lotuses.
Fickle in her play yet harsh, she brings about the destruction of one's purpose;
she is a woman who utterly deludes the intellect, a long night for the seeker.
Delightful and sweet with flowers, her hands shining like tender sprouts,
rich in the playful movements of her bee-like eyebrows, she bears clusters of blossoms as her breasts.
With limbs as pale as the filaments of flowers, intent on slaying men,
this beloved and most formidable creeper of poison bestows supreme helplessness.
By the mere sound of her sighing,
the beloved, eager to crush the serpent, draws the creature from its hole like a female elephant drawing a snake.
Women are the snares for binding the limbs of those bird-like men whose minds are deluded, set by the hunter named Desire.
O Brahmin, the intoxicated elephant of the mind remains bound like a mute by the chain of passion within the vast tethering-post of the *lalanā*.
For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, moving within the hollow of their karma,
a woman is the baited hook on the line of evil latent impressions.
Like a manger for horses, like a tethering post for elephants,
or like a lotus pond for bees, beautiful-eyed women are the bond that binds men.
O Sage, this manifold and variegated realm of enjoyment consists of diverse flavors;
for it is by depending upon women that it attains its supreme stability here.
May this woman of mine, who is a casket for all the jewels of faults and a constant chain of suffering, be enough for me!
What use have I for the breast, or for the eyes, or for the hips, or for the eyebrows— these things which consist of nothing but flesh, mere insubstantiality?
O Brahmin, in just a few days, a woman goes to ruin: here the flesh, there the blood, and there the bones.
O Sage, those women who were cherished by their husbands with soft cotton pillows now sleep upon the ground of the ancestors, their limbs separated from one another.
O Brahmin, that upon which thick, fresh moisture has settled, and where the beauty of leaf-sprouts has been arranged by her lover— that very thing withers away in the forest.
The hair becomes like the bristles of a yak-tail fan upon the trees of the cremation ground;
and the bones shine like stars upon the circle of the earth within a few days.
The dust particles drink the blood, and many carnivorous creatures devour it; the flames of the fire consume the skin, and the vital breaths depart into space.
Thus, I have described to you this imminent state of the limbs of women; why do you pursue such delusion?
How indeed could one endowed with intelligence [not understand] that this [channel] called *lalanā* is the configuration resulting from the conjunction of the five elements, because it conveys taste?
The anxiety that pursues one's beloved becomes a dense thicket with spreading branches, abounding in bitter and sour fruits, and reaches the height of its full expansion.
In some cases, the mind— confused and blinded by greed for wealth—
attains supreme delusion through its very reality, like a deer strayed from the herd.
A youth devoted to young women reaches the highest state of pitiability,
like an elephant bound in a pit in the Vindhya mountains out of greed for a female elephant.
He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one without a wife, there is no ground for enjoyment. By abandoning a woman, the world is abandoned; by abandoning the world, one becomes happy.

O Brahmin, I do not delight in enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight but fraught with long-lasting misery, and as fragile as the wing of a bee; out of fear of death, disease, old age, and the like, I seek peace and shall go with effort to the supreme forest.
The twenty-first canto, titled "Contempt for Women," [from] Rāma.
For childhood is insatiable, as it drinks up youth;
and later, old age consumes youth—behold their mutual harshness!
Just as a thunderbolt destroys a lotus, as a whirlwind disperses an autumnal cloud,
and as a river erodes a tree on its bank, so does old age wither the body.
Lustful women look with equal indifference upon a man whose limbs are all slack and long, and whose body is decayed by old age, as they do upon a young camel.
When people are seized by old age, which torments them with labored breathing and exhaustion, wisdom flees in flight like a woman whose husband has been slain and who is being taken by a rival wife.
Servants, sons, wives, kinsmen, and friends likewise laugh at a man trembling with old age, as if he were a madman.
Greed indeed approaches one who is old, lacking wisdom, wretched, and deficient in virtues and prowess, just as a vulture alights upon a tree that is not very tall.
In old age, a long-standing longing— consisting of the fault of wretchedness, burning within the heart,
and the sole companion of all calamities— increases.
"What painful and most terrible thing must I do for the sake of the next world? Indeed, in old age, this fear increases—a fear that is impossible to remedy."
"What am I, a wretched man? What indeed shall I do, or how shall I remain? I shall simply maintain silence"—such dejection arises in old age.
In old age, greed arises with a longing to enjoy, yet it cannot be indulged; indeed, the heart is scorched by the frailty of one's power.

As long as the old female crane, worn out by age and emitting the cawing sounds of coughing, cries out while perched upon the top of the tree of the body, which is infested with the serpents of disease.
Just then, O Sage, a death-owl, desiring the thick darkness of night, was seen arriving swiftly from somewhere or other.
The evening twilight, as soon as it has arisen, pursues the darkness;
old age, as soon as it is seen upon the body, pursues death.
O Brahmin, as soon as she sees from afar the tree of the body in full bloom with old age, the female bee of death quickly approaches the man with great eagerness.
An empty city appears; a tree with its branches lopped off appears;
a region suffering from drought appears; but a body worn out by old age does not appear [as such].
Like a vulture seizing its prey, old age swiftly devours a man, causing him to cough as if to swallow him in a single moment.
As soon as she sees it, old age seizes the body instantly and, like a young maiden, swiftly plucks away the white water-lily of youth from its head.
Making a whistling sound, this wind, harsh with dust, withers this body— already worn out— as a gale withers the sprout of a tree.
Stricken by old age, the body, having reached a state of decay,
bears the beauty of a withered lotus strewn over with a mass of frost.
Like the rising moonlight of old age upon the mountain-peak of his head,
this [old age] causes the water-lily of coughing— already agitated by wind— to blossom.
Beholding the head of a man— like a ripened pumpkin— rendered grey by the alkali of old age, Time, it is said, is the Lord who devours it.
The son of Jahnu (Yayāti), exerting himself against old age, swiftly cuts away the roots of this body, which is like a tree on a riverbank, while its life-span is still wavering.
The old cat, nourished by the mice of youth that have been devoured,
attains the highest exhilaration, greedy for the flesh of the body.
There is nothing in this world so inauspicious as the female jackal born of the body that cries out with the sound of old age.

This flame of old age blazes forth, consisting of the smoke and darkness of suffering, accompanied by coughing, labored breathing, and whistling sounds; indeed, by it, this person is utterly consumed.
O dear one, through old age the slender body of men becomes crooked, its sprouts of white hair falling away, like a flowering creeper bent down by its blossoms.
O Sage, the elephant of death surely uproots in an instant the camphor-tree of the body, which is as white as aged camphor.
O Sage, as King Death approaches, with old age as his white fly-whisk, the army of his own mental afflictions and diseases marches ahead.
O Sage, behold those who were never defeated in battle by enemies who crushed the peaks of mountains, yet have now been swiftly conquered by this old, decrepit ogress!
Within the interior of the body-dwelling, white with the frost of old age,
the infant senses are not able to move even slightly.
Upon this body-staff, which has reached the pinnacle of this fragrant chamber of the wandering through saṃsāra,
the beauty of the fly-whisk named "Old Age" shines resplendently.
O Sage, while the city of the body remains white with the rising moon of old age,
the night-lotus of death blooms in an instant.
Within the inner apartments of the body, which are white with the plaster of old age,
women dwell happily amidst incapacity, suffering, and calamity.
O Sage, where old age— foremost among all forms of non-existence— overcomes living beings, what consolation can there be here for one of dull intellect like me?
What is the use of that miserable life lived under such a wretched grasp, since even one who has reached old age continues to live?
For in this world, O dear one, old age—which remains unconquered by men—overcomes all their desires.
The twenty-second canto, titled "Aversion to Old Age," ends here. Rāma.
By those of small intellect, who have imagined numerous conceptual constructions through their own fabrications,
the delusive confusion of saṃsāra has been brought to a state of heightening.
How could the wise have any reliance here upon this cage of a web?
Only fools desire to grasp a fruit reflected in a mirror.
Even here, this fragile cultivation of happiness exists;
yet time cuts it away entirely, just as a rat gnaws through a thread.
There is nothing here that this all-devouring time does not swallow up;
it consumes every created world, just as the submarine fire devours the great ocean.
As the Great Lord, Time is terrible by virtue of its universal commonality;
it is intent upon devouring this entire existence of the perceptible world.
Even for the great, O Lord, Time waits not even for a moment;
having become the soul of the universe, it swallows the infinite world.
Manifesting slightly through forms known as ages, years, and kalpas,
he whose nature is invisible abides pervading all things.
Those things which are delightful, those which are auspicious undertakings, and even those as massive as Mount Sumeru—
all are swallowed up by Time, like serpents by a young camel.
Merciless, hard, cruel, harsh, wretched, and base—
there is nothing that this Time has not yet swallowed even today.
Time, whose mind is solely intent on devouring, consumes even mountains; this great consumer is never satiated, despite its infinite floods of enjoyments.
Time takes away, destroys, creates, consumes, and slays; indeed, in the dance of saṃsāra, it acts through various forms like an actor.
Established in its own divisions, it incessantly shatters the seeds of the elements within the world,
like a parrot pecking at pomegranate seeds with its beak because they have no substance.

The elephant that sustains the rows of living beings among the flourishing populace roams about, its tusks— the tips of which are auspicious and inauspicious— tearing away the sprouts of worldly existence.
The vast forest of Brahmā stands encompassing the expansive tree whose fruit is the cosmic egg—the very marrow of Viriñca. MU 1.22.14.
Creating clusters of days filled with the female bees of nights,
and creeper-like branches of years and kalpas, he is never at all weary.
O Sage, this crest-jewel of rogues is not shattered even when split, nor is it consumed even when burnt; it is not seen even when it is clearly visible.
In a single moment,
it sufficiently raises up something and utterly destroys something else, spreading out like a vast kingdom of the mind.
With his conduct, which was like that of a wanton woman of depraved dalliance and nurtured by hardship,
he remained there, stirring the people about like a cook stirring a soup with a ladle.
Through the expansion of his own self, he is intent on assimilating everything— straw, dust, Mahendra, Sumeru, a leaf, and the ocean— into himself.
Cruelty is fully contained right here; greed is established right here;
all misfortune is right here, and all fickleness is right here.
Playfully impelling the sun and moon, he sports here in the expanse of the sky like a child with his own two cheeks upon which betel-nut has been spat.
With a form encircled by garlands of the bones of all living beings,
he sports like Time at the end of an aeon, fashioning his own fictions.
At the end of the eon, Mount Meru trembles in the sky from the winds issuing from the limbs of this wild dance, like the bark of a birch tree tossed by the gales.
Having become Rudra, he becomes Mahendra, then the Grandfather (Brahmā), Śukra, and Vaiśravaṇa; and again, he becomes nothing at all.

He sustains within himself successions of creations that arise effortlessly and are yet destroyed— immeasurably radiant, some different and others not different from one another, just as the ocean contains its own waves.
Standing there, he was stripping from the trees called Mahākalpa the ripe clusters of fruit that were the hosts of gods and asuras.
He has attained the state of a vast tree for the multitudes of cosmic egg-figs that fall down, humming with swarms of restless gnats.
Accompanied by his beloved Action, he alone delights his body with the night-lotus of pure existence, which is in full bloom under the moonlight of consciousness.
He remained standing, leaning upon his own body as a firm seat, which was as lofty as a great mountain and extended to the very limits of the infinite realms of misery.

In some places he contemplates his own nature as dark as the deepest shadow, in some places as pervaded by radiant splendor, and in both cases, he remains meditating on it as being sequentially devoid of both.
Through his own essential being, which has been concentrated by the essence of countless transmigrations,
he has come to a state of fixed footing, as if weighed down by a heavy burden.
It does not weary, it does not die, it does not come, nor does it go;
it neither sets nor rises, even throughout hundreds of great eons.
He passes his time by himself through the mere play of initiating the world with effortless ease, having attained a state free from egoism.
He remained, superimposing upon the lakes of his own self a series of day-lotuses turbid with the mud of night and a whirlpool of ritual actions.
Taking up the night as a terrifying broom of black bristles,
he sweeps the golden dust of light all around the earth.
Moving the sun-lamp with his finger around the corners of the house of the world, he gazes out of compassion to see what exists and where.
Beholding with the eye of the sun the days that have reached their full maturity in an instant,
he devours this world like an old forest, [consuming] the fruits that are the guardians of the worlds.
Death, like a casket, gradually deposits the jewels of the world— those distinguished by their virtues— into its formidable hollow, which is strewn with the dilapidated huts of the universe.
That very series of world-jewels which is abundantly filled with virtues,
he cuts away further, as if having placed it upon his body for the sake of ornament.
The fickle moon constantly and excessively encircles the night-lotus garland that follows him day by day, with the stars as its filaments.
The mountain, the spider, the cloud, the mountain peak, the world, the spider, and the butcher— every day, having sprinkled them, he drinks even the red drops of the stars.
He is the moon to the lotus of youth and the lion to the elephant of life;
there is nothing, whether trivial or significant, that he does not steal away.
Through the playful sport of cosmic cycles, by which living beings are ground down and cast away,
and through the laughter of the submergence and emergence [of phenomena], he rejoices in his own self by means of his own self.
He is the doer, the enjoyer, and the destroyer; he is the rememberer who has attained the state of all things.
He performs this entire universe, yet he does nothing at all.

Indeed, manifesting and suddenly concealing his entire body— which encompasses both the auspicious and the inauspicious and is devoid of any internal distinction— the power of Time sports here among men.
The twenty-third canto, titled "The Censure of Time," ends here. Rama: [End].
Of this prince, whose play was so formidable that all calamities were cast far away, and who possessed the unmeasured power of Time within this cycle of existence.
In this world, which is like a tattered jungle-net, the hunt is pursued by the wretched and deluded multitudes of living beings and wild animals.
The great ocean at the end of the aeon is a delightful pleasure-pool, wherein the beautiful submarine fire blazes like a lotus in one quarter.
The turning of the aeon occurs through those very worlds, which have become rich with pungent, bitter, and sour elements, along with oceans of curd and milk, once they have all become exhausted.
Caṇḍī, who moves with fourfold gait and is accompanied by the entire host of Mothers,
is a she-wolf that drags away the human deer situated in the forest of saṃsāra.
The earth is the palm of her hand, and the earth is her wine-cup filled with nectar,
garlanded by swarms of hovering bees amidst lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lilies.
Roaring, with a formidable lashing of his tail, Nṛsiṃha is within the cage of his arms;
with a mane and broad, thick shoulders, he is a lovely pet bird at play.
Sweet-voiced with a lute made of bottle-gourd, possessing the stainless luster of the autumnal sky,
the Lord Mahākāla is indeed like a playful young cuckoo.
With a form of incessant radiance, casting forth the thunderbolt of the arrows of suffering,
the bow named Non-Contemplation vibrates everywhere.

Increasing his supreme, shimmering playfulness, wandering about, snatching away, sporting, and tearing asunder, Time— here like a monkey agitated by the decay of the aged world— strives with his body quivering.
The twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Play of Time," ends with Rāma.
In this very world, another who is like a crest-jewel among all misfortunes acts; thus, people speak of him as "Fate" and "Time."
Apart from mere activity,
no other form of that which consists of its own internal vibration is perceived, nor is any intended action [of karma] observed.
Therefore, this entire succession of beings, eternally delicate,
has been brought to a state of extreme distress by suffering, like a garland of snow by heat.
Whatever expanse of the world is seen here, that is his theater of dance; herein he performs his dance.
And thirdly, bearing the extremely terrible name Kṛtānta,
Fate dances in this world in the intoxicated form of a Kāpālika.
O Sage, for Kṛtānta dances incessantly and without ceasing, while Niyati, his beloved, is ever his supreme object of passion.

The remainder is Śeṣa, white as the digit of the moon; and the stream of the Gaṅgā—these two, appearing like sacred threads (upavīta) and the absence thereof (avīta), rest upon the chest of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).
The orbs of the moon and sun are the golden bracelets on his wrists;
the playful lotus in his hand has the cosmic egg as its pericarp.
The single sky is like the garment of the one ocean, washed by its waters, strewn with the stars as its beads, and possessing the moving Puṣkara and Āvarta clouds as its fringes.
In the presence of one of such a nature, Nityakāminī,
whose passion never subsides, dances with her various undertakings.
Within the hollow of the pavilion of the world, she is intent on dancing; her nature is unimpeded movement, and she is ever-active in coming and going.
With beautiful ornaments upon her limbs, she was a series of celestial realms;
her vast, hanging mass of hair reached down to the netherworld (Pātāla) from the sky.
And Narakālī, a garland of anklets filled with a tumultuous clamor,
is strung upon the thread of evil deeds and dangling from her feet that tread upon the underworld.
On the canvas of her face during the night, Citragupta painted a musk tilaka, prepared by her friend Kriyā.
Assuming the form of Kālī at the end of the aeons, this goddess dances again amidst the multitude of ritual activities, with the solid mountains resounding with her clear roar.
Behind him were the dangling, wandering children with peacock-feather chariots,
terrifying with the great, resonant *bhāṅkāra* sounds from the wide cavities of their three eyes.
With the hair on the head of Hara, bestowed by the long, dangling autumn moon, serving as chowries for Gaurī’s high, beautiful, and pale tresses of mandāra flowers; //MU_1,24.17//
With skull-bowls as terrifying as mountains in a state of wild dance,
and with begging-bowls in the form of Indra’s body possessing a thousand resonating apertures;
With its dry skeletons and the breaking of skull-staffs filling the sky,
it terrifies even itself, though it is as dark as a black cloud.
With her beautiful lotus-garland of the wheel that is the head of Viśvarūpa,
she shines as she dances through the great kalpas.
It is said that at the end of the eon, even Tumburu and the other celestial musicians flee from her due to the terrifying sounds of the drums of the intoxicated Puṣkarāvarta clouds.
At the end of the dance of Death, who laughs with the orb of the moon and wears as a crest the sky—beautiful with the moonlight of its stars—as a peacock feather; //MU_1,24.22//
In one ear there is a long Himalaya, a ring;
in the other, too, is the great Meru, lovely as a golden pericarp.
Right here, the two dangling earrings are the sun and moon;
the regions of her cheeks are the Lokāloka mountain range, which forms her girdle all around.
Moving here and there, the lightning,
colored like a golden bracelet, shines like a strip of cloud-silk fluttered by the wind.
With maces, spears, pikes, darts, lances, and clubs—
sharpened weapons gathered together like the Destroyer himself, intent on annihilating the multitude of living beings.
Upon the long noose of the bonds of saṃsāra, cast by the hand of Time,
this garland shines, strung with the great threads of his remaining enjoyments.
The row of bracelets formed by the seven oceans, radiant with the brilliance of the jewels in the sea-monsters that gleam with life, serves as an ornament for his two arms.
The great whirlpool of worldly activity, the succession of pleasure and pain,
filled with passion (rajas) and dark with ignorance (tamas)— his line of body hair shines like this.

At the end of the aeon, Maheśvara, having thus withdrawn that dance-performance so fierce with its frantic *tāṇḍava*— which was of such a nature— along with the creation itself, [the Lord of Death] Kṛtānta likewise withdrew.
Furthermore, she displays this playful dance of laughter, which embodies all forms and is adorned with the dramatic gestures of old age, suffering, and sorrow.
Again and again he creates worlds, forests, other realms, and the arrangement of the multitude of living beings,
as well as the beautiful fashioning of conduct and all that is moving and unmoving— just as a child tirelessly constructs figures out of mud.
The twenty-fifth canto, named "The Play of Destiny," Canto 25;
Rāma:
And since this very cycle called saṃsāra has thus come to pass for these [beings], O great sage, what reliance could those like me have here upon time and the other factors?
We stand as if sold by these cheats, such as fate and the like,
who are clever in their deceptions— like bewildered forest deer.
This ignoble conduct is like Time with its mouth agape;
it incessantly casts the world into the ocean of calamity.
In the end, fate, through its cruel workings, consumes the world with its evil desires,
just as fire burns with flames that resemble flowers.
When the beloved form of a single desire unsettles one's fortitude,
it is destiny— fickle by its very nature due to being feminine— that turns toward restriction.
Like a serpent swallowing air, the End-maker (Kṛtānta), whose conduct is cruel, having brought the world-body to old age, incessantly devours the multitude of beings.
The king of Yama, who is merciless, does not show compassion even for one who is suffering;
a person whose conduct is characterized by mercy toward all beings has become rare to find.
O Sage, all classes of beings whose nature is fragile and insignificant are for nothing but suffering and endless ruin; they are dreadful realms of greed.
Life is exceedingly flickering, while death alone is cruel;
youth is extremely unstable, and childhood is carried away by dullness.
The world is stained by the impurity of time; kinsmen are the bonds of existence;
enjoyments are the great diseases of worldly life; and craving is but a mirage.
It is true that the senses themselves have become enemies;
the self strikes itself with its own hand, for the mind is indeed the enemy of the mind.
Egoism leads to blemish; intellects are fragile;
actions yield evil fruits; and pastimes have become centered on women.
Women have been rendered devoid of charm, though they possess the objects of desire; the poetic sentiments have become flagrant with defects, having fallen into a state of flavorlessness.
An entity is grasped as a non-entity, and the mind is given over to the ego-sense;
since entities are obstructed by non-existence, the end of existence is not attained.
O virtuous one, the mind, its interior agitated, suffers in vain;
the serpent of passion frolics about and does not approach dispassion.
When the vision is struck by the quality of passion (rajas), darkness (tamas) increases;
and the essence of being (sattva), the ultimate reality, is not attained, being exceedingly remote.
Stability has become instability; death is on the verge of arrival;
fortitude falls into despondency; and delight is fixed upon that which is unreal.
The intellect is clouded by dullness, the body is intent solely on falling,
old age seems to blaze within the frame, and past misdeeds erupt with a thunderous roar.
With effort, youth passes away; association with the virtuous remains far off;
no certain refuge exists anywhere, and truthfulness does not arise in any place.
The mind becomes utterly bewildered within; joy has departed far away;
compassion does not blaze forth, and baseness approaches from afar.
A person intent on rising and falling moves from steadiness to unsteadiness;
association with the wicked is easily found, but meeting with the virtuous is difficult to obtain.
All things are subject to coming and going; this cultivation is the bond of existence.
It is merely the succession of beings that is led perpetually somewhere or other.
For even the directions are no longer seen, and even place has ceased to be designated;
even mountains crumble away—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even the oceans run dry and even the stars perish;
even the perfected ones do not achieve perfection—what hope, then, for a person such as I?
Even the sky is devoured by non-existence, and even the world is shattered; even the earth falls into distress—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even the Dānavas are torn asunder; even Dhruva’s life is not secure;
even the immortals are slain—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even Śakra is assailed by other Śakras, and even Yama is subject to restraint;
even for Vāyu there is a state of non-Vāyu—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Even the moon reaches the state of the sky; even the sun suffers fragmentation;
even fire falls into ruin—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?

Even Parameṣṭhin, though he has reached the ultimate state, undergoes decline; even the Unborn takes on the form of Hari; and even Bhava enters into non-existence—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
Time falls into fragments, and even destiny is led away;
even space dissolves into the infinite—what reliance, then, can there be on a person such as I?
By some inscrutable form, through a tantra that is inaudible, unutterable, and difficult to perceive,
worlds are mimicked by one who causes delusion.
Having attained even a fraction of egoism, there is no one in the three worlds who is not afflicted by that which dwells within them all.
Like a stone upon a mountain crag, the sun, together with its horses and charioteer,
is perpetually whirled around, powerless like a forest boulder.
The terrestrial globe, the abode of the hosts of gods and demons dwelling within it,
is encircled by the wheel of celestial spheres, like a ripe walnut by its husk.
In heaven the gods, on earth the men, and in the netherworld the asuras and serpents—
all are reduced to a state of decay in a mere moment by the power of time.
And desire, having acquired its prowess through the fire of conflict with the lords of the world,
leaps about after having assailed the world by means of sheer transgression.
Spring, like an intoxicated elephant, with its rutting ichor in the form of falling blossoms, fills the circle of the quarters with fragrance and leads the heart toward crookedness.
Even great discernment is unable to clarify the mind when its form has been gazed upon by the eyes of women full of passion.
I consider only the Buddha to be truly happy, for his mind is cooled by its own welfare, whereas others are scorched by a distress born of their desire to help others.
Who is able to count the waves of the ocean of life, which arise and perish, falling into the submarine fire of Time?
All men indeed, through delusion, fall into the snare of evil desires;
like deer caught in a thicket of faults, they are swallowed up in the wilderness of birth.
In this world, through those evil deeds, the lifespan of people in the succession of births is exhausted;
for we do not know the fruit of those deeds, which is like a noose made from the branches of a tree in the sky, even though we are seekers of discernment.

"Today is a festival, this is the season, likewise here is a procession; these are your kinsmen, this is happiness, that is a special enjoyment"—thus, constructing a web of his own vain conceptualizations, the world falls away with its fickle and fragile intellect.
The twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of Wicked Amusements," Canto 26:
Rāma.
Moreover, dear father, in this nature of the world, whether it be exceedingly desolate or delightful,
there is not even the slightest collection of objects by which the mind attains supreme rest.

When childhood has passed and the deer of life, restless with imagined play, has wandered into the caves of old age, and the little body has reached a state of decay, the world suffers only in its utter desolation.
Having cast far away the lotus-plant of the body, struck by the frost of old age,
and once the bee of life has departed in an instant, the lake of worldly existence for all people has dried up.
Whenever it surely reaches ripeness, then and there this vine of the human body bows down; shattered by the weight of old age and its few remaining fresh blossoms.

In this world, the river of craving flows on, its powerful current sweeping away the entire multitude of infinite objects; it is adept at eroding the roots of the sturdy tree of contentment that stands upon its bank.
The ship of the body, bound with the fastenings of skin, tossed about and wandering in the ocean of existence,
flows downward and is overwhelmed by the five crocodiles known as the sense-faculties, over which it has no control.

These deer of the mind, roaming in the forest of the creeper of craving, wander through the hundreds of branches of the trees of sensual desire; though they exhaust themselves, they do not obtain the fruit.

In times of hardship, their dejection and delusion are cast far away; amidst sovereign powers, they are pleasing with minds free from arrogance; such great men, whose inner hearts remain unshaken by beautiful women, are exceedingly difficult to find nowadays.
Those who cross the ocean of battle, with its waves consisting of throngs of elephants, are not heroes in my view;
rather, those alone are heroes here who cross this ocean of the senses, which has the mind for its waves.

No action whatsoever is seen belonging to anyone that results in a delightful, untainted ultimate fruit— such that, having attained it, the world finds rest, its mental fluctuations struck down by false hopes.
Those who fill the world with their fame, the hollows of the quarters with their majesty, their homes with their splendor, and prosperity with the strength of their virtue—
those men, whose bonds to the Dharma remain unbroken, are not easily found in this world.
Whether situated within the walls of a mountain crag or dwelling inside a fortress of diamond,
all fortunes and all calamities, with their full force kindled, constantly come upon everyone.
Sons, wives, and wealth are fashioned by the intellect as if they were an elixir, my dear;
yet none of these provide any benefit in the end, for they result in a most painful swoon of suffering.
Filled with despair and having reached a precarious state at the end of his physical life and youth,
the person who has grown old burns within, remembering his own past states that are now empty of the Abhidharma.
Having spent the initial days with activities emaciated by the pursuit of desire, wealth, and dharma,
by what means can a man’s mind— fickle and as restless as the tail-feathers of a peacock— attain rest?

Even when results of actions that were previously set in motion—resembling the lofty waves of a river—arrive by the power of fate with forms not at all anticipated, people mock them; for the world has diverse tastes.
These and those tasks, which have been visualized as being endlessly delightful,
wear out the minds of people through the pursuit of pleasing one's wife until their very hair turns grey with old age.
Just as the withered leaves of trees, having come together at birth, quickly go to their dissolution,
even so do worlds devoid of self-discernment, having come together, depart from somewhere by means of the days.

Having wandered here and there to a great distance and entered his home at the close of day, when the sun has set— leaving behind the company of discerning people and the performance of virtuous deeds— who can find sleep?
While all enemy forces have been routed and prosperity has arrived from every side,
one enjoys these pleasures— only so long as death does not arrive from somewhere.

Deceived by these entities whose forms are increased from somewhere yet are trivial, which are seen for a moment and then perish, the people in this world do not perceive what has come nor what has gone—alas! MU_1,26.21.

Those who, having forcibly attained corpulence, remain bound to the body, are indeed made into "black-faced" (kālamukha) sacrificial animals by people desiring to depart; for them, the bonds of karma are destroyed. MU 1.26.22.
This restless multitude on earth comes incessantly with haste and goes away without ceasing with haste; it is like a garland of waves, momentary in its destruction.

Intent solely on taking away the lives of men, women steal the mind through their captivating charm; with red lips and eyes as flickering as bees, they are like poisonous trees with trembling creepers.
Coming from here and from there, bound by a mere convention of commonality,
the illusory practice of men regarding wife and friend is equal to a fleeting attachment during a journey.
Just as in the lights of lamps whose many wicks have been consumed and which are bound by excessive oil—
illusory manifestations of saṃsāra that are flickering and unreal— the true reality is not known.
This wheel of the breast, which is the very engine of worldly existence, though as fragile as a bubble in the monsoon rain,
produces in the mind of the heedless person the conviction that it is long-lasting and stable.
Splendor has been extinguished by the power of wretchedness; virtues now remain in a state of decay.
Comfort has retreated far away from people, like the winter from lotus ponds.
When a tree, having repeatedly approached by the power of fate and caused injury with the weight of its own body,
is cut down there by axes— what occasion indeed is there for consolation in that?

Even from the company of a person who is charming but whose conduct is exceedingly corrupt, and who has arisen for the sake of inner destruction— just as from a poisonous tree— one now encounters only a state of fainting.
Which are those directions in which there are no defects? Which are those quarters in which there is no burning pain of suffering?
Which are those beings in whom there is no fragility? Which are those actions in which there is indeed no illusion?
Even the Viriñcas, who live for a single kalpa, perish when the calculation of the multitude of kalpas is completed;
therefore, within the web of time which possesses all its parts, even the notions of shortness and length are unreal.

Everywhere the mountains consist of stone, the earth of clay, and the trees of wood; likewise, people consist of flesh, their existence bound by human nature. There is nothing here that is unprecedented or devoid of transformation.

Pervaded by consciousness and bound together like a mass of water, this collection of atoms situated in space is perceived through the distinct divisions of the characteristics of objects; other than this, nothing else exists.

In this world of the wise, O virtuous one, there is a wonder that causes amazement in the minds of men; yet such a thing, possessing a form as variegated as a painting, never at any time becomes an object for anyone, even in a dream.

Even now, though the vastness of conceptualization has departed like the fruit of a creeper in the sky, for those untouched by even a fragment of greed, there arises not even a story composed of noble deeds.
Desiring to attain the station of the supreme ones, the world today is ruined by its own mind;
it falls fearlessly from the mountain peak like a beast, out of longing for the leaves of a dark blue creeper.
With their branches of foliage, flowers, and fruits merely the deceptive shadows of shoulders cast across the space between them,
and their wealth utterly destroyed, the trees of the ravines and the men of today are both alike.
In some places people wander through regions beautiful with gentleness, and in others through terrifying ones,
moving through these uninterrupted transitions like black antelopes through forest thickets.

Whose minds are not astonished by the deeds of this world— which, day by day, produce both terrifying and delightful events that agitate all men, yet result in bitter fruits that destroy one's rising hopes— perpetrated by the deceitful?
People are attached to desire and intent on practicing various base arts; even in this world, a virtuous person is not easily found today, even in a dream.
All actions, due to their connection with suffering, are surely distressed and wretched; I know not how this life-like state is to be conducted.
The twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition of Impermanence," [ends].
Rāma:
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether moving or stationary,
all that is unstable, O Brahmin, resembling a union in a dream.
O Sage, that which is seen today as a dug-out pit resembling a dried-up ocean shall, by morning, become a mountain enveloped in clouds.
That mountain, vast as a forest array and having licked the very sky, in just a few days reaches the level of the earth or turns into a well.
That very limb which today is clothed in silk garments, garlands, and ointments,
tomorrow shall be naked and cast far away into a pit.
In that very place where today a city was seen, bustling with diverse activities, in just a few days there arises the state of a desolate wilderness and a desert.
O King, that man who today stands as a radiant sovereign over the realms will, in mere days, be reduced to a heap of ashes.
The great and terrifying forest, which resembles the vault of the sky and whose space is covered by banners— that very same thing becomes a city.
O Sage, that formidable forest grove which once shone, entwined with creepers, now in just a few days attains the state of a desert land.
Water becomes dry land, and dry land becomes a watery place;
indeed, the entire world, including its wood, water, and grass, undergoes total inversion.
Youth, childhood, the body, and accumulations of wealth are impermanent;
they pass incessantly from one state to another, like waves.
In this world, life is as flickering as the flame of a lamp in the wind; the splendor of all things in the three realms is like the flash of lightning.
This vast succession of beings falls into error,
like a heap of seeds that sprouts again and again without end.
With the heavy cloth of the dust of many beings tossed about by the wind of the mind,
she is adorned with the graceful gestures of falling, rising, and turning.
This worldly existence is perceived as a state produced by delusion,
like an actress on the stage of saṃsāra who has begun her performance with a whirlwind dance.
It produces the delusions of a city of Gandharvas and is enchanting through its noble conduct, which is as graceful as the play of a sidelong glance.
O Brahmin, repeatedly casting forth a light as flickering as lightning, the passion for worldly existence shines like a woman intoxicated by dancing.
Those days were great; those were our riches and those our deeds.
Everything has become a mere memory, and we too shall depart in an instant.
It perishes day by day and is born again day by day;
even today there is no end to this burnt-out cycle of existence, whose form has been destroyed.
Men go to the state of animals, and animals even to the state of men; gods likewise become non-gods. O Lord, what indeed is stable here in this world?
Creating a web of rays again and again, the sun passes through days and nights;
having traversed the duration of time, it gazes upon the limit of destruction.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all classes of beings alike hasten toward destruction, just as bodies of water do before the submarine fire.
The sky, the earth, the wind, space, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—
all these are the fuel that has been completely dried up by the submarine fire of destruction.
Wealth, kinsmen, servants, friends, and all possessions—
all these have become tasteless for one who is terrified by the fear of destruction.
These entities in the world remain savory to the wise man only so long as the evil demon of destruction has not entered the path of his memory.
In one moment sovereignty arrives, and in another moment poverty comes;
in one moment there is freedom from disease, and in another moment the onset of illness.
Who indeed, even among the wise, has not been deluded by this great worldly delusion, which produces error at every moment?
For a moment the circle of the sky was smeared with the mire of darkness;
for a moment it was beautiful with a soft radiance flowing like molten gold.
At one moment its hollows were encircled by garlands of clouds dark as blue lotuses;
at another moment it resounded with a tumultuous roar, and at another it remained silent.
At one moment it is the play of the stars; at another, it is adorned by the sun;
at one moment it brings delight through the moon; and at another, it is entirely forsaken by them all.
Who, even if wise, would not fear this worldly existence, which is characterized by coming and going, by persistence and destruction? MU_1,27.30
Calamities come for a moment, and prosperity comes for a moment;
birth and death likewise come for a moment, O Sage—what indeed is not momentary?
In the past one was born here as one thing, and by other days he has become quite another.
O Blessed One, is there anything whatsoever that remains stable, even for a single moment?
The nature of a cloth is seen in a jar, and the state of a jar is seen in a cloth;
there is nothing that has not been seen, for cyclic existence is a perversion.
A hero slain by a coward—even a single man slaying a hundred—is a case where commoners have attained lordship; thus the entire world turns upside down.
This multitude of people constantly pursues error,
like a succession of waves arising from the perception of the dull movement [of water].
Childhood lasts but a few days today, then comes the beauty of youth, and after that, old age;
since even the body possesses no single fixed form, what stability can there be in external objects?
In one moment the mind attains joy, in another it falls into despondency;
in a moment it reaches a state of serenity—in every respect, the mind is like an actor.
In one direction this rule creates one thing, in another a different thing, and in yet another a further thing; thus fashioning reality, it never comes to weariness, like a child at play.
The Creator gathers this world that has arisen here, intoxicates it, devours it, slays it, strikes it down, and makes it his own through hundreds of calamities and upheavals.
In one moment [he creates] one thing, in another day something else, and in the morning yet another; though he fashions these here and there with skill in deception, Fate is not seen by anyone.
What exists today does not exist tomorrow morning; what exists tomorrow morning does not exist today; and what exists at another time does not exist today—everything turns around again and again.
In this world, sufferings are continuous and pleasures are rare;
they revolve around a person constantly, like nights and days.
For people subject to worldly existence, who are partakers of appearance and disappearance, neither misfortunes nor prosperities attain stability.
This wicked one, who causes everyone to fall from step to step in times of calamity,
stands as a mere fragment of the Time of Destruction (Kāla), having effortlessly overturned everything.
The floods of fruits from the succession of beings in the three worlds— divided by the ripening of favorable and unfavorable conditions—
fall day after day from the vast trees of saṃsāra, blown down by the wind of time.
The twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Overcoming of Delusion," Canto 28:
Rāma.
Thus, when the great mind has been consumed by the forest fire of delusion,
desires for enjoyments no longer flicker, like mirages in lakes.
Day by day, the wandering through cyclic existence becomes exceedingly bitter,
like a neem branch whose flavor intensifies as it ripens with time.
O King, wickedness increases and goodness diminishes day by day within the hearts of people, which have become as harsh as the karañja thorn.
The boundaries on earth are instantly shattered in every direction,
like parched *māṣa* beans, with a sharp and harsh clanging sound.
For lords of the earth who dwell on kingships and heaps of enjoyments,
a life of solitary conduct— free from the sprout of anxious thought— is better than being burdened by such concerns.
My garden is not for my delight, nor are my riches for my pleasure;
the hope for wealth brings me no joy; I am at peace along with my mind.
The world is impermanent and unhappy, and craving, my dear, is difficult to bear;
my mind is struck by restlessness—how shall I attain peace?
I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;
I remain just as I am, free from all feverish distress.
What use have I for sovereignty, what use for enjoyments, what use for wealth, or what use for undertakings?
By the power of egoism, all of that has dissolved away from me.
Those who strive for the sake of liberation from those firm knots of the senses that are fastened upon the rope of the series of births are the best.
The minds of proud women were crushed by the god whose banner is the sea-monster,
just as a delicate lotus is crushed by the trampling of an elephant's hooves.
O Lord of Sages, if today one’s mind is not treated with a healthy intellect, then what opportunity indeed remains, and from where could it come, for the further treatment of the mind?
Poison is the inequality of sense objects; poison is not said to be [ordinary] poison.
Sense objects destroy future lives, whereas ordinary poison destroys only a single body.
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither friends nor kinsmen,
neither life nor death bind the mind of the wise man.
Therefore, O Brahmin, best among those who know the past and the future,
please instruct me quickly so that I may become one who knows, free from sorrow, fear, and exertion.
Enmeshed in a web of latent tendencies, crowded with the thorns of suffering,
and abounding in falls and upheavals, the forest of ignorance is of terrifying form.
O Sage, I am able to endure the fierce crushing of the saw—
the calamity as deadly as poison arising from the activities of saṃsāra.
"This does not exist, this exists"—such is the delusion of worldly people;
this [wisdom] shakes the flickering mind as the wind disperses a mass of dust.
The collection of living beings, strung upon the threads of craving like a string of pearls,
has the mind as its leader, which is eternally manifest through its connection with the pure aspect of consciousness.
I shall tear asunder this necklace of saṃsāra, adorned with the serpent of Time and strung with aversion, just as a lion rends a cruel snare.
O best among the knowers of reality, quickly dispel with some lamp of knowledge the mist of mental darkness within the forest of my heart.

O Great-souled One, those mental afflictions do not even exist here for you; they do not reach destruction, just as thick darkness is destroyed by the moon through its union with the minds of the most excellent beings.

Life is as fragile as water dripping from the petals of a lotus-cluster shaken by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds; and the rushing current of the waters of youthful indulgence is ever-tossing.
Having realized this, I have quickly and firmly sealed my mind with the mountain-like seal of steadfastness for the sake of lasting peace.
The twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Exposition of Non-Attachment to All Things," [ends with] Rāma:
Thus beholding the world submerged in the mire of mental constructions— a hollow pit of perilous and surging multitudes of calamities— the mind [was stirred].
My mind seems to reel as if in a whirl, and a great confusion arises;
my limbs tremble like the leaves of an ancient tree.

A mind that has not attained the practice of supreme contentment and is agitated by its own restlessness fears this world, having no secure refuge, like a young girl under the power of one with little strength.
These fluctuations of the internal organ roll about amidst conceptual constructions,
like female deer lured by false appearances from their mountain caves.
Fallen from the abode of discernment and rooted in misery rather than the state of the virtuous,
these wretched senses— sight and the rest— are like those who have entered a blind well.
Thought, dependent on the Lord of Life, neither remains stationary nor proceeds according to its desire, like a wife in the house of one who is unkind.
Having worn out all things, my fortitude has fallen into a state of distress— neither relinquishing nor yet sustaining them— like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having cast aside all objects, non-abiding is established;
and by grasping and then relinquishing the self, abiding is established.
My mind is mocked by an internal support that wavers and yet remains unmoving,
like the root of a tree that has been cut down by a poor man.
This mind, flickering, expansive, and wandering through the various worlds,
does not abandon its agitation, just as an immortal [does not leave] his own celestial chariot.
Therefore, what is that excellent state of stability— non-empty, effortless, free from limiting conditions, and beyond delusion— in which no doubt exists?
All undertakings and enterprises, as well as good people such as Janaka and others, were solely devoted to worldly activity; how then did they attain the state of excellence?
O bestower of great honor, how is it that a person here is not smeared by the mire of saṃsāra, even though it clings to their limbs in abundance?
Relying upon what view do you great-souled ones, free from defilement, live as liberated beings while yet alive and wander here in this world?
How can sense objects— which entice only toward fear, which are the food of the serpent of enjoyment, and whose power is of a fragile nature— ever attain the state of being auspicious?
How can the lake of the intellect, trampled by the elephant of delusion and its inner waters defiled by stains, attain supreme clarity?
How is it that a person, though dwelling within saṃsāra itself and engaging in worldly affairs,
does not incur bondage, just as water on a lotus leaf?
Creating this entire world as if it were himself or as if it were a blade of grass,
how can he attain supremacy without touching the mind's passion?
Having followed the conduct of which Great Being who has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence, does this person proceed without committing evil deeds?
What is that which is appropriate and beneficial? What would be that appropriate fruit?
And how indeed should one conduct oneself in this discordant cycle of existence?
Therefore, O Lord of this world, tell me something by which I may understand the beginningless and endless, unstable course of the Creator’s activity.
O Brahmin, act so that the cleansing of the impurities of my mind— the moon within the space of the heart— may come to pass without obstacle.
What here should be accepted, what should be rejected, or what is otherwise?
How may this flickering mind come to rest, like a mountain?
By what purifying mantra is this cholera of miserable transmigratory existence—
