causing hundreds of hardships— pacified without effort?
How may I attain within myself that coolness, which is like the unceasing full moon of the Rākā night— the blossoming cluster of the tree of bliss?
Just as I no longer grieve within after attaining internal fullness,
so may you, who are virtuous and knowers of reality, instruct me further.

O Great-Souled One, why do conceptual constructions so excessively torment the mind here— which is empty of any resting-place other than the supreme state of bliss— just as dogs in a forest devour the body of a small creature?
The thirtieth canto, named "The Purpose," from the Rāmāyaṇa.
While life is as fragile as a drop of water hanging from a leaf trembling on a tree in the wind, and the body is as delicate as a digit of the cool-rayed moon of Lord Īśāna;
In this circle of snares consisting of the gathering of friends and kinsmen— which is as fragile as the throat-skin of a frog croaking in a field of ripening grain— [beings are ensnared].
In the dense cloud of the mist of delusion, which is made manifest by the lightning-flashes of base desires stirred up by the wind of latent impressions, there resounds a heavy thunder.
When greed— the peacock of desire— is fierce, restless, and intensely active, it dances a wild *uttāṇḍava* dance within the blossoming *kuṭaja* tree of misfortune, bursting it open with a loud crash.
In this cruel cat of Death, who carries off all living beings as mice, whose movement is silent and imperceptible, and who pounces from somewhere above— where can there be safety?
What is the means? What is the way? What is the reflection? What is the refuge? By what means might this forest of life, which yields such inauspicious results, not come to be?
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all,
that does not become pleasing to a man of wise intellect, even if it were something trivial.
For how can this world, which is burnt by saṃsāra and agitated by incessant mental constructions, become sweet-tasting— being devoid of essence— unless through the state of a fool?
By what means can the poison of hope be made delightful through a bath of milk?
It becomes so only through the white blossoms of [virtuous] deeds, just as a beautiful creeper is refreshed by honey.
By what means can the stain of desire be wiped away from that moon of the mind, which, though possessing the luster of nectar, has not yet arisen free from impurity through the process of cleansing?
By whom should one navigate the pathways through the forest of saṃsāra, having seen the course of worldly existence and having destroyed both the seen and the unseen?
How is it that the great diseases of passion and hatred, preceded by the pursuit of enjoyments and characterized by extreme impurity, do not afflict a living being wandering in the forest of saṃsāra?
And how is it that one, even when falling into the fire of heroic passion, is not consumed,
just as mercury is not burnt by fire because of its mercurial essence?
For it is said that in this world, without the performance of worldly activities,
existence is not possible, just as for one who has fallen into the ocean, there can be no water.
Free from passion and hatred, and devoid of pleasure and pain,
there is no performance of ritual action here, just as a flame of fire is devoid of burning.

O most excellent ones, tell me that method by which the destruction of the pride of mind-cherishing—which is the source of suffering in the three worlds—can occur without [relying on] mere reasoning. MU_1,30.16.
Tell me that supreme state which, through the practice of worldly activity, brings suffering no more to me; or else, tell me that highest path for one who has ceased all worldly activity.
How, by whom, or what was performed previously by that person of supreme mind, whereby his most purifying mind now attains this ultimate rest?
O Blessed One, as you know, please tell me for the sake of dispelling delusion that by which you, the virtuous ones, have attained freedom from suffering.
Or else, O Brahmin, if no such reasoning exists,
or if someone does not clearly state it to me even though it exists.
Yet, I myself do not attain that unsurpassed rest;
therefore, having abandoned all worldly effort, I have entered into a state of egolessness.
I shall not eat, nor shall I drink water; I do not put on a garment;
I perform no activity such as bathing, giving gifts, or eating.
I do not remain attached to my duties, whether in times of prosperity or in times of adversity;
O Sage, I desire nothing except the relinquishing of this body.
Free from doubt, devoid of the sense of "mine," and rid of envy,
I remain here in silence alone, as if fixed in a painted image.
Then, gradually abandoning even the consciousness of inhalation and exhalation,
I shall cast off this useless structure known as the body.
Neither am I his, nor is my body mine; I am extinguished like a lamp without oil.
Having renounced everything, I shall cast off this physical frame.
Having spoken thus, Rāma— delightful as the stainless moon and whose mind was blossomed by profound discernment—
became silent before the great ones, like a peacock ceasing its cry out of exhaustion from the sound of thunderclouds.
The thirty-first canto, titled "The Question of Rāghava," by Vālmīki:
While that prince Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, was speaking these words that bring about the cessation of mental delusion, [the sage spoke].
All those present there became filled with wonder, their eyes wide open,
as if the hairs on their bodies had risen upward to hear the words, holding them like garments.
Those whose entire worldly tendencies have been cast off by the tendency toward cessation remain for a moment as if tossed by the waves of the ocean of nectar.
Those songs of the noble Rāma were heard by listeners whose hearts were overflowing with joy, as if they were fixed within them like figures in a painting.
[He was surrounded] by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra seated in the assembly,
and by ministers headed by Jayanta and Ghṛṣṭi, who were experts in counsel.
By kings such as Daśaratha, by citizens including those of mixed parentage (pāraśava),
by vassal lords and princes, and by Brahmins who discourse upon the Veda.
Likewise, with servants and ministers, with birds confined in cages, with pet animals devoid of movement, and with horses that had ceased chewing; MU_1,31.7.
And by the throngs of women led by Kausalyā, who stood at their own windows with the sound of their ornaments stilled and themselves motionless; MU_1,31.8.
The birds dwelling in the garden creepers and even those nesting in the eaves remained with their flocks undisturbed and ceased their chirping.
By the Siddhas and the sky-dwellers, as well as by the Gandharvas and Kinnaras,
and by the foremost of sages headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha;
And by others— lords of the gods, vidyādharas, and great serpents— those words of Rāma, which possessed manifold meanings and were most noble, were heard.
Then, while the lotus-eyed Rāma— so beautiful as to be like the moon in the sky of the Raghu dynasty— remained silent;
Accompanied by voices of acclaim uttered by the assembly of perfected beings (siddhas),
a rain of flowers fell from the sky like a canopy.
Resounding with the humming of pairs of bees resting within the buds of *mandārava* flowers,
it delighted men who were intoxicated by the beauty and fragrance of wine.
Like a succession of stars scattered by the wind in the sky,
it was like the flash of a celestial woman’s laughter fallen upon the surface of the earth.
It fell like a single row of drops from an autumn cloud during the rains,
or like a succession of balls of fresh butter being cast down.
Noble as a rain from the Himavat, resembling a mass of pearl necklaces, like a garland of rays from the moon, and like a succession of waves of milk; MU_1,31.17.
Enveloped by the fragrance of filaments, with swarms of bees hovering about,
it was stirred by a breeze sweet with the song of sighing blossoms.
With its clusters of ketaka flowers fluttering about, its throngs of kairava lilies spreading forth,
its circles of kunda blossoms falling down, and its abodes of blue water-lilies turning and swaying.
Filling the courtyards, houses, gardens, and rooftops of the city,
she was gazed upon by the excellent women residing in the city who craned their necks.
A rain from the cloudless sky, resembling blue lotuses, fell without disturbance;
it was something never seen before by anyone, and it inspired wonder in all people.
Never seen before, impelled by the hands of the multitude of perfected ones (siddhas),
that rain of flowers fell during a quarter of a muhūrta.

When the assembly hall was filled with light and the rain of flowers had subsided, those members of the assembly heard these words spoken by the hosts of Siddhas: imān siddhagaṇālāpāñ śuśruvus te sabhāsadaḥ // MU_1,31.23 //
Wandering all around the heavens for an entire kalpa among the hosts of perfected beings,
we have today heard this unprecedented elixir for the ears.
Indeed, that noble speech which was uttered by this moon of the Raghu dynasty,
out of his state of freedom from passion, lies beyond the reach even of the Lord of Speech himself.
"Oh, what great merit has been gained by us today, having heard these words issuing from the mouth of Rāma, which bring the refreshment of nectar to the intellect!"

Because the Joy of the Raghus has spoken what is fitting— beautiful with the nectar of tranquility and having attained the state of supreme excellence out of reverence— we have been instantly awakened by him.
The thirty-second canto, titled "The Acclamation of the Sky-dwellers," ends with the perfected ones (siddhas).
It is appropriate to hear the decision regarding this purifying speech uttered by the Banner of the Raghus,
as it is about to be declared by the great seers.
"O foremost of sages, headed by Nārada, Vyāsa, and Pulaha,
may all you great ṛṣis come here without hindrance!"
Let us fly all around this holy assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha,
just as bees hover about a lotus pond filled with dense golden lotuses.
Vālmīki:
Having spoken thus,
that entire divine succession of sages, dwelling in their celestial abodes, descended together into the assembly there.
The Lord of Sages sat upon the back of the wind stationed at the summit, his lute sounding, while Vyāsa— dark as a cloud swollen with water— stood nearby, gazing intently at him.
It was adorned by the leaders of sages such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Pulastya,
and protected by Cyavana, Uddālaka, Uśīra, Śaraloman, and others.
From their mutual contact, there arose one with a misshapen deer-skin,
possessing trembling eyes, a rosary, and bracelets, and holding a beautiful water-pot.
Like a row of stars enhancing each other's beauty,
it was like another shower of flowers, or like a second solar orb.
Vyāsa shone there like a cloud amidst a host of stars;
Nārada shone there like the moon amidst a multitude of stars.
Pulastya shone there like the lord of the gods among the deities,
and Aṅgiras shone like the sun among the gods.
Then, as this army of Siddhas descended from the sky with joy,
the assembly hall of Daśaratha’s son rose up, filled with sages.
Intermingled, those sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers shone forth,
their bodily splendors enveloping one another as they illuminated the ten directions.
With hands holding flutes and bells, bearing playful lotuses, their hair-tips entwined with sprouts of dūrvā grass, and their locks adorned with crest-jewels; MU_1,32.13.
Their matted hair was tawny like a forest fire, their heads were adorned with crowns and garlands,
and they wore rosaries upon their forearms as well as rings set with rubies.
Some were clothed in rags and bark, while others were draped in garlands and silk;
some had their waist-bands dangling, and others wore shimmering clusters of pearls.
In an instant, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra honored those great hosts of sky-dwellers with offerings of water for the feet, water for the guest-reception, and with their words.
The king honored the multitude of Siddhas with every form of conduct,
and the multitude of Siddhas likewise greeted the king with inquiries concerning his welfare.
Having received mutual hospitality through various expressions of affectionate zeal,
those who move through the sky and those who dwell upon the earth sat down upon their seats.
With words, a rain of flowers, and cries of "Well done!",
they honored Rāma from all sides as he stood bowed before them.
And there, resplendent with royal fortune,
he took his seat along with Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and Vāmadeva as his ministers.
Nārada the son of a god, Vyāsa the bull among sages, Marīci, Durvāsas, and likewise the sage Āṅgirasa; MU 1.32.21.
Kratu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Śaraloman, the lord of sages Vātsyāyana, Bharadvāja, and Vālmīki, the bull among sages; MU_1,32.22//
Uddālaka, Ṛcīka, Śaryāti, and Cyavana; likewise Ūṣmapa, Ghṛtārcis, Śāluḍi, and Vāluḍi.
These and many others, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
who were high-souled and had realized that which is to be known, stood there as leaders.
Together with Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, those learned sages, Nārada and the others, spoke these words to Rāma, whose face was cast down in humility.
Oh, how wonderful! The prince has uttered words endowed with auspicious qualities, filled with the essence of most noble dispassion.
The meaning of the sentences is fully established, easy to understand, appropriate, clear, noble,
worthy of being practiced with affection, undisturbed, and unerring.
Whom would these words spoken by Rāghava— not obscure, clear, pleasing, nourishing, and satisfying— not fill with wonder?
From among a hundred [poets], the speech of that single one who possesses all-encompassing noble wonderfulness becomes uniquely capable of bestowing the desired object.
O Prince, without you, whose [new] creeper of wisdom— endowed with the fruit of discernment— could thus attain such blossoming?
That man is considered truly enlightened in whom the flame of the lamp of wisdom dwells within the heart, blazing brightly like that of Rāma and providing illumination.
Many machines made of blood, flesh, and bone, stretched out extensively, draw away objects; among them, there is nothing conscious.
Beasts, utterly deluded, do not reflect upon saṃsāra; they undergo again and again the suffering of birth, death, and old age.
Only rarely and in some place is a single person seen whose disposition is pure and who is worthy of reflection upon his past and future, such as this slayer of enemies.
For those who possess auspicious forms and yield the fruit of unsurpassed wonder are rare in this world, like mango trees.
Right view, which is the wonder of one's own discernment regarding the birth of the world,
appears as something entirely different within this noble-minded person.
Worlds that are easy to attain and full of fortune abound with trees laden with fruit and foliage; however, sandalwood trees do not grow in every land.
It is true that there are trees in every forest possessing fine fruits and foliage;
however, the clove tree, with its unprecedented wonder, is not always easily found.
Like moonlight from the cool-rayed moon, like a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree, or like a trail of fragrance from a flower— so was wonder beheld from Rāma.
O best of the twice-born, from this burnt-out cycle of existence fashioned by the creation of fate and unrestrained wickedness, the essence is indeed extremely difficult to find.
Those who, as repositories of glory, strive with their intellect to attain the essence, are the fortunate ones;
they alone are counted among the foremost of the virtuous and are the best of men.
"In these three worlds, there is no one equal to Rāma;
he is discerning, noble-souled, and great-souled—this is our conviction."
Even though it produces wonder in all the world, if that which is desired by the heart of Rāghava does not bear fruit, then we sages ourselves are clearly the ones whose intellects have failed.

The chapter titled "The Fall of the Assembly of Siddhas, Munis, and Īśvaras," namely the second chapter, the Section on Dispassion (*vairāgyaprakaraṇa*), is completed. Section: The Conduct of One Desiring Liberation (*mumukṣuvyavahāra*).
The First Canto: Vālmīki.
When these words had been spoken by the great Nārada while he was present in the assembly, [Vālmīki...]
Viśvāmitra also spoke with affection to Rāma, who had gone before him.
Viśvāmitra said:
O Rāghava, best among the wise, there is nothing further for you to know;
by your own subtle intellect, you have understood everything.
Only a slight amount of cleansing is required for you,
whose mirror of excellent intellect is eternally pure by its very nature.
Like the intellect of Śuka, the son of the Blessed Vyāsa, your mind,
though it has already known all that is to be known, requires only internal rest.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, how was it that the intellect of Śuka, the son of the venerable Vyāsa,
did not find rest even at the beginning, yet later found rest through his intellect?
Viśvāmitra said:
O Rāma, listen to this account of the son of Vyāsa, which I am describing in accordance with my own life story, and which serves as the cause for the end of all births.
This venerable Vyāsa, possessing the splendor of the sun and resembling the color of collyrium, is seated upon a golden throne at the side of your father.
To him was born a son named Śuka, whose face was like the moon, who was skilled in statesmanship,
possessed of great wisdom, and who stood as if the sacrifice itself had taken embodied form.
As he thoroughly investigated this worldly course within his heart,
a profound sense of discernment indeed arose in him just as it had in you.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, by means of his own discernment and having investigated for a very long time, he himself attained that which is beautiful and true.
Because his mind did not find rest even when the supreme reality was attained by itself,
he could not gain the conviction within himself that "this is not the reality."
His mind alone ceased its agitation regarding enjoyments, which were fraught with manifold calamities, just as a *cātaka* bird ceases its longing for waters from the earth.
Once, that one of stainless wisdom, with devotion, questioned his father, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who was staying in a secluded place on Mount Meru.
O Sage, how has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen?
How does it come to rest? To what extent, by whom, and when does it occur?
Thus questioned by his son, the sage Vyāsa, who knows the self, explained everything that was to be said to him exactly and without flaw.
"I already knew this before," thought Śuka to himself; thus, with his pure intellect, he did not hold his father's words in high regard.
The venerable Vyāsa, having understood his son’s intention to be such, replied again to his son: "I do not know [this] in its true essence."
There exists on the surface of the earth a king named Janaka;
he knows that which is to be known exactly as it is, and from him you shall obtain everything.
Thus addressed by his father, Śuka departed from Sumeru for the surface of the earth and reached the city of Videha,
which was protected by Janaka.
O King, that son of Vyāsa, Śuka, having been announced by the gatekeepers to the great-souled Janaka, stood there at the door.
Thinking with disdain, "Let this [instruction] remain as it is for the sake of Śuka’s inquiry," Janaka spoke thus and remained silent for seven days as well.
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the inner apartments;
there he remained for seven days, dwelling in that very place with a distracted mind.
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the inner apartments for seven days, thinking, "The king is not to be seen for that long."
There, Janaka cherished Śuka, whose face was like the moon, with intoxicatingly beautiful women, sumptuous foods, and an abundance of enjoyments.
Those enjoyments and those sorrows did not shake the mind of Vyāsa’s son,
just as a gentle breeze cannot move a mountain that is firmly rooted.
There Śuka remained, alone, tranquil, pure, silent, and joyful in mind, like the full moon.
King Janaka, having brought back Śuka whose true nature was now fully realized,
looked upon him with a joyful heart and bowed down to him.
"Having completed all duties for the world and attained every desire,
what is it that you wish for?"— thus he spoke to him, having quickly offered a welcome.
Śuka said:
O Guru, how has this grand display of saṃsāra arisen?
How does it come to rest? Tell me this properly and quickly.
Viśvāmitra: When questioned by Janaka, Śuka spoke in that same manner as had previously been declared by his high-souled father.
Śuka said: "I myself already knew this previously through discernment;
this much alone was stated by my father when he was questioned."
O best among those skilled in speech, you too have stated this very same point;
and this indeed is the meaning of the statements observed throughout the scriptures.

Just as this [world], which arises from one's own conceptual construction, is exhausted through the exhaustion of that very conceptual construction, so too is saṃsāra—once it has been "burnt away"—exhausted; such is the certainty that it is devoid of essence.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, tell me this truly and purely:
may my mind find rest in you, so that the world no longer wanders in delusion.
Janaka: O Sage, there is no other certainty beyond this;
you have known this yourself and have heard it again from a teacher.
In this world, there exists only the one, unbroken conscious Self, and nothing else;
bound by the power of volition, it is liberated when free from volition.
But for that great-souled one by whom this knowable has been clearly known,
detachment from enjoyments or from all that is visible has arisen here in this world.
O Great Hero, your mind has already reached detachment from enjoyments that are like long-lasting diseases; what else do you wish to ask?
The fullness of the great treasury of omniscience did not arise for your father while he remained in extensive asceticism in the same measure as it has arisen for you.
I am indeed superior to Vyāsa, for I am his disciple and his son;
yet you are even more distinguished than I, owing to the attenuation of your desire for enjoyment.
Everything that was to be attained has been attained by you, whose mind is now full;
O Brahmin, you do not fall back into the realm of the visible—you are liberated, so cast away delusion.
Having been thus instructed by the high-souled Janaka,
Śuka became silent and rested in the pure, supreme reality.
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, effortless and with all doubts severed,
he went to the faultless peak of Mount Meru for the sake of meditative absorption.
Having remained there for ten thousand years in a state of non-conceptual meditative absorption, he was extinguished within himself like a lamp devoid of oil.
Then, in that pure and sanctifying state which is itself stainless and free from the blemish of temporal distinctions,
this Great Soul attained oneness, with all duality dissolved, like a drop of water in the ocean.
The second canto, named "The Quenching of Śuka," by Viśvāmitra.
O Rāma, only that much of the removal of the mental impurities of that son of Vyāsa is appropriate for you as has been utilized by you.
O Lord of the Earth, by this [knowledge] everything that is to be known has been understood without remainder;
for him, worldly enjoyments do not provide pleasure, just as diseases do not to one of sound intellect.
This is indeed the characteristic of a mind that has known what is to be known:
that all varieties of enjoyments no longer taste sweet to it.
Through the contemplation of enjoyments, the bondage arising from unreal things attains firmness;
through that very same [contemplation] when it is stilled, the bondage in the world reaches attenuation.
O Rāma, the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is called liberation by the wise;
the firmness of the latent impressions regarding objective entities is designated as bondage.
For most men, there occurs an approach to the reality of the Self;
subsequently, a distaste for sense objects arises from [the realization of] their worthlessness.
The wise man who knows that, having known what is to be known, sees correctly;
to that great soul, enjoyments do not taste sweet by force.
He for whom worldly enjoyments no longer hold any appeal on this earth, even without such motives as fame and the like, is called one liberated while living.
O dear one, as long as that which is to be known has not been realized,
a person finds no dispassion toward sense objects, just as a creeper does not grow in a desert land.
Therefore, O scion of Raghu, know that you have already known what is to be known,
since these delightful lands of enjoyment do not please him.
Upon hearing directly from the presence [of the sage] that "this which Rāma knows is indeed the Reality," a tranquility of mind arises within the descendant of Raghu.
The intellect of Rāma requires only rest in the state of absolute oneness, just as the beauty of autumn requires rest upon the waters.
In this matter, may the illustrious and venerable Vasiṣṭha provide the means for the high-souled Rāghava to find rest for his mind.
He is the lord and eternal family preceptor of all the descendants of Raghu;
he is omniscient, all-seeing, and possesses stainless vision of the three periods of time.
O venerable Vasiṣṭha, do you perhaps remember what you yourself [said] previously,
for the sake of pacifying our enmity and for the welfare of great-souled beings?
On a peak of the Niṣadha mountain, crowded with *sarala* trees,
much knowledge was taught by the Lord Brahmā to the sages.
O Brahmin, by that reasoned knowledge indeed this latent impression (vāsanā) of the transmigrating being surely comes to rest, just as darkness does before the sun.
O Brahmin, quickly teach that very same reasoned knowledge to Rāma, who dwells at the end of his journey, by which he shall attain rest.
This is by no means a hardship, for Rāma is free from all taint;
just as a face reflects effortlessly in a stainless mirror.
O virtuous one, that knowledge, that meaning of the scriptures, and that unimpaired proficiency which is imparted to a detached and worthy disciple— [that alone is true learning].
Whatever is taught to one who is not a disciple and who lacks dispassion becomes impure, like cow’s milk poured into a dog’s skin.
Those who are free from passion, fear, and anger, who are devoid of the sense of "mine," and whose sins have fallen away—
whatever such persons as you say, upon that the intellect here finds its rest.
When this had been said by the son of Gādhi, those sages, headed by Vyāsa and Nārada, honored him for that very matter, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then the illustrious sage Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great splendor, standing by the side of the king like Brahmā’s son Brahmā himself, spoke.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sage, I shall carry out what you command for me without obstacle;
for who, even if capable, is able to transgress the word of the virtuous?
For today, with the light of knowledge, I shall dispel the darkness of mind in the princes, Rāma and the others, just as one dispels the darkness of night with a lamp.
I remember all of it without omission for the sake of calming the delusion of saṃsāra—
that knowledge which was formerly proclaimed on Mount Niṣadha by the Lotus-born One.
Vālmīki:

Having spoken thus, that great-souled Vasiṣṭha— whose venerable luster was enhanced by his girded robes— declared this for the sake of pacifying ignorance, which brings about the singular awakening to the supreme state.
The third canto, titled "The Words of Viśvāmitra," [ends with] Vasiṣṭha:
I shall now relate that very knowledge which was previously spoken by the Lotus-born Lord at the beginning of creation for the sake of the peace of the world.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, you shall indeed relate the extensive compendium on liberation;
however, for now, dispel this doubt that has arisen within me."
Śuka’s father was the omniscient teacher Vyāsa, the great sage who was liberated while in the body; how could his son not be liberated? How indeed could he not be liberated?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Even the motes of dust in the three worlds, which vanish as they repeatedly rise and fall within the light of the supreme sun, do not admit of being numbered.
And as for those millions of beings in the three worlds who exist at present,
they cannot possibly be numbered by anyone at all.
In the supreme ocean, there will arise waves that are the creations of the world;
there is not even a mention of anyone who could count them all.
Rāma said:
It is appropriate to investigate those successions of world-creations that have been and those that will be; what need is there to speak of those that are currently present?
Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, whatever being— whether animal, human, god, or otherwise— perishes,
it perceives this [world] in that very place and at that very time.
Within his own heart, the unborn one— whose nature is space— experiences the three worlds as space itself through his mental body, which is known as the *ātivāhika*.
In this way, millions of beings have died, are dying, and will die;
for these worlds of living creatures have arisen one after another.
Like a whirlwind or an earthquake, like a child terrified by a demon,
like a string of pearls in the stainless sky, or like a tree and a vehicle that do not move.
Like a city within the consciousness of a dream, or like trees appearing in the sky born of memory,
one who has died experiences the wandering of the world within oneself.
There, through excessive transformation, that very [space] attains density;
thus, this world manifests here within the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa).
Furthermore, in that very same place, one who experiences birth, death, and so forth imagines a world beyond; and having died there, one likewise [imagines] it again.
Within that are other persons, and within them yet others;
these worlds appear like the layers of a plantain tree.
Neither the collection of great elements such as earth, nor the sequences of the world, exist for those who have died; yet even so, they still experience the delusions of the world.
Thus, this ignorance is infinite, abounding in manifold productions;
it is a long river for the dull-witted, a stream surging with the waves of world-creation.
O Rāma, in the vast ocean of ultimate reality, the waves of creation repeatedly roll forth— both those very same ones and many others in great abundance.
Some are similar in every respect through their lineage, conduct, mind, and qualities;
some are similar by half; and some are extremely different.
There, I remember this sage Vyāsa as the thirty-second,
through the vision of knowledge that arises according to its possibility and is like a mirror.
Among those, twelve other mental states are equal to those belonging to the family-form;
ten have forms entirely common [to all], while the remaining ones are distinct from the family-form.
Even now there will be others such as Vyāsa and Vālmīki,
as well as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, and likewise yet others.
Multitudes of various asuras, ṛṣis, and gods arise in great numbers together, and at times they dissolve again, each separately.
I know that there were seventy-two Tretās of Brahmā, there are, and there will be; I know that he is indeed another, as is the world, and both you and I.
Thus, in due course, this tenth incarnation of the far-sighted sage Vyāsa, whose deeds are marvelous, is clearly perceived.
We have been joined with Vyāsa and Vālmīki many times;
we ourselves have appeared in these various forms, though our underlying intention remains the same.
Indeed, he must once again compose this very history called the Bhārata here on earth for eight more ages.
Having divided the Vedas and brought his lineage to preeminence through this [work],
and having thereafter attained the status of a Brahman, he shall bring about the liberation of the people of Videha.
Free from sorrow and fear, peaceful, liberated, with all conceptual constructions gone— this Vyāsa is described as one who is liberated while living, having conquered his own mind.
In each and every creation, living beings are born again and again with equal wealth, kin, age, actions, learning, wisdom, and conduct.
In some cases, these [worlds] come into being or cease to be through hundreds of creations;
yet at other times, this illusion is thus devoid of any end.
This vast succession of beings proceeds toward perversion,
like a heap of seeds being sown incessantly again and again.
In that very same configuration, and again in another,
the forms of creation proceed repeatedly like waves from the ocean of time.
With an inwardly comforted mind, his conceptual constructions diminished, consisting of the essence of his own true nature,
and satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace, the wise one remains free from all veils.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Repeated Experience of Creation," by Vasiṣṭha.

Just as the water-ness of water remains the same whether it is in the state of gentle waves or [still] water within the ocean, so too is the state of being liberated from both "having a body" and "not having a body."
[The Blessed One said: "Whether liberation for you consists of having a body or being bodiless, it is dependent upon an object.
For one who has not tasted food, how can there be an experience of that food?"
O best of sages, we see him before us as one liberated while living, like an ordinary object; yet we do not know his inner disposition.
Vasiṣṭha said:
What difference can there be between those who are liberated while in the body and those who are liberated beyond the body, since they are all of the nature of non-duality?
It is the very same water that exists both in the state of a wave and in its state of calmness.
There is not even the slightest difference between liberation while embodied and disembodied liberation;
whether it be with movement or without movement, it is indeed the wind that is called "air."
Whether with a body or without a body, liberation is not an object of valid cognition for us;
for when its own oneness exists as indivisible, [it is self-evident].
Therefore, listen now to this very subject at hand, which is an ornament for the ears—
the knowledge being taught by me, which destroys the blindness of ignorance.
For indeed, O descendant of Raghu, everything here in this world is always obtained by everyone through human effort properly applied.
For here, like the moon, a cool refreshment arises in the heart;
in the attainment of the fruit of one's exertion, it comes from human effort alone and from nothing else.
That which is not seen through direct perception as having a fruit resulting from human effort—
such as "fate" (daiva) imagined by deluded and dull-witted people— does not exist at all.

That movement of the body which is directed by the mind according to the teachings of the scriptures of the virtuous is human effort; that alone is fruitful, while all else is the behavior of a madman.
Whatever object a person desires and strives for in due order,
he will certainly attain it, provided he does not turn back halfway.
Indeed, by means of human effort, a certain distinguished being attained the state of Śakra, which is as beautiful as the sovereignty over the three worlds.
Only a rare flash of consciousness, through human effort and sudden realization, attains the state of Brahman within its lotus-abode.
Through his own essential human effort alone, this certain man has attained the state of Puruṣottama, the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Through human effort alone, a certain embodied being here has attained the state of having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, by means of the practice of turning the body.
Know that human effort is of two kinds: past and present. Past effort is quickly overcome by present human exertion.
By those who are diligent, firm in their practice, and endowed with wisdom and enthusiasm, even Merus are swallowed; what need is there to mention former human efforts?
That state of manhood which consists of the supreme human effort governed by the scriptures leads to the attainment of the full weight of desired fruits; indeed, any other kind leads to misfortune.
In one state of existence, due to the power of his own wretched condition, a man might slowly obtain from a single cup pressed by the tip of a finger many drops of rinsing water;
in another state, the earth—adorned with oceans, mountains, cities, and islands—would not even be sufficient for him when it comes to making the appropriate distribution of what must be done.
The fifth canto, titled "The Commencement of Manly Effort," by Vasiṣṭha:
Thus, for those who dwell according to the scriptures, activity itself is the first [step],
serving as the means for accomplishing all actions, just as light is for the various colors.

That which is merely desired by the mind, but not accomplished through action in accordance with the scriptures, is like the play of a madwoman; it is enchanting, yet it does not achieve any real purpose.
Just as it is intended by whomsoever, so it is experienced by that person;
let it be one's own karma alone, for there is no other separate thing called "fate."
Human effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures.
Among these, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the ultimate goal.
Two human endeavors, equal in strength, fight like two rams;
between that which belongs to oneself and that which belongs to another, the one with greater force prevails.
Where misfortune is encountered even through effort prescribed by the scriptures,
one should understand that there one's own past human effort is more powerful than the effort of the one causing the misfortune.
Relying on supreme human effort and grinding his teeth against his teeth,
one who is intent on the auspicious should overcome past inauspicious human effort.
The thought that "this past human effort compels me" must be forcibly cast underfoot; for it is not superior to direct perception.
To that same extent, one should strive with effort according to one's own human capacity,
until past karma naturally subsides.
A past fault is undoubtedly pacified by present virtues;
for here we have the illustration of the destruction of yesterday's fault by today's virtues.
Having cast aside false destiny, one should strive with a mind constantly applied to effort to bring about the crossing over of saṃsāra for the sake of prosperity by establishing it within oneself.

One should not associate with those who lack exertion, for they are like human donkeys; rather, one should apply oneself according to the scriptures for the sake of accomplishing success in both worlds.
One must emerge from this cavern of saṃsāra by one's own strength,
relying on human effort, just as Hari [emerged] from the cage of his enemies.
Day after day, a person should examine his own conduct;
he should abandon that which is equal to the behavior of beasts and take refuge in that which is appropriate for the virtuous.
Having tasted something soft at home, such as the abundance of beloved food and drink,
one should not let one's life be reduced to ashes like an insect in a wound.
Through auspicious human effort, an auspicious result is swiftly attained;
through inauspicious effort, an inauspicious one is always obtained. That which is called "destiny" is nothing at all.
He who, disregarding what is directly perceived, relies on inference alone, should flee upon seeing these two [objects] with his own eyes and thinking, "These are two snakes."
Seeing the faces of those of deluded intellect who say, "Fate impels me," and whose vision regards the unseen as supreme, Lakṣmī turns away.
Therefore, by human effort, one should resort to complete discernment;
one should thoroughly investigate the scriptures whose purpose consists of the knowledge of the Self.
Fie upon the wicked desires of those fools who, while contemplating their own goals in their minds according to the scriptures, fail to accomplish them through their own efforts! MU 2.5.20.
Human effort is not infinite, nor is it that which is desired by its very name;
for even with great exertion, oil is not obtained from a stone.
Just as a jar is limited, and just as a cloth is limited,
so too is the purpose of man for you fixed and established within a definite measure.
And that [scripture] bestows its own fruit through the study of its meaning, the company of the virtuous, and right conduct;
this is its inherent nature, for otherwise it would lead to misfortune.
This is the true nature of the individual soul; no man who conducts himself in this manner ever finds his efforts to be fruitless.
Even other supreme men, though afflicted by the suffering of wretchedness and poverty,
have attained equality with the Lord of the Gods through human effort alone.

Indeed, by means of those qualities— such as study of the scriptures and association with the virtuous— which have been practiced thus from childhood, one's own true goal is attained through human effort.
Those of evil intellect who think that what is seen, experienced, heard, or done by them has arisen from fate are destroyed.
If laziness did not exist in this world, who would not be wealthy or highly learned?
It is because of laziness that this earth, bounded by the oceans, is filled with human cattle who are destitute.

When childhood has passed— restless with incessant play— a man should, from the age of adolescence and its ornaments onward, diligently apply himself to the investigation of his own virtues and faults through association with the virtuous, thereby awakening his intellect to the true meaning of words and their referents.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The sixth canto, named "The Establishment of Manhood," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, having cast far away that which is other than human effort and destiny,
one should by force rescue the living soul through the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures.
"In whatever measure there may be effort, in that same measure shall the fruit arise;
thus, human exertion alone exists—let that very thing be your destiny."
Just as at a time of suffering one exclaims "Alas, what misery! when afflicted by pain, so too is the expression "Alas, fate! a synonym for the word "misery."
There exists no such thing as "destiny" (daiva) that takes a form other than one's own prior karma;
it can be overcome here in this world by a fool through his own powerful effort, just as one might defeat a strong man.
Just as yesterday’s evil conduct is quickly brought to a state of purity today by beautiful conduct, so too is one's former misdeed.
Those who strive for its conquest, yet are not greedy for even a fraction of gain—
they are fools, commoners, and wretched, remaining dependent on fate.
When an action performed through human effort is destroyed by fate,
it should be understood that in such a case, the power of human effort is stronger.
Just as one of two fruits on the same stalk is hollow and empty,
so too does effort manifest there for the sake of experiencing its flavor.
Since even those things that have attained perfection among the states of the world go to destruction,
one should recognize therein the great power of the effort that causes decay.
Whatever a mendicant king forcibly takes from the elephant of good fortune belongs to the great fruit of the efforts of the ministers, the elephants [of state], and the citizens.
Just as food, having been seized by the power of the teeth, is ground down,
so too is a small amount of manly effort crushed when seized by a hero.
For it is observed that even those great beings who exert themselves are treated with contempt;
they are employed by others in various tasks at will, like clods of earth.
Whatever human effort there may be of one who is capable, whether visible or invisible,
that is perceived as "fate" by the incapable person who lacks wisdom within himself.
It is established that for all beings, the powerful effort of a being is what is called destiny;
this is clearly evident even among stationary things that possess presiding deities.
The innate wisdom of the teachers, ministers, elephants, and citizens— which is beyond conceptualization—
is that which creates and sustains the kingdom of the mendicant, thereby maintaining the stability of all beings.
The present destroys the past, and the past forcibly destroys the present;
in this constant oscillation of human action, he who remains unperturbed is the victor.

Between these two, that of the present day alone would possess greater strength through direct perception; therefore, destiny can be overcome with effort by a fool, just as a youth overcomes an elder.
Whether the harvest acquired over a year is carried away by a cloud,
it is the human effort of that cloud which triumphs, for it possesses superior exertion.
Even when wealth acquired through gradual effort is lost, one should not feel distressed;
where my strength was powerless, what cause for lamentation is there?
If I undergo suffering for the sake of that which I cannot achieve,
then it is more fitting for me to weep every day at my own unattained death.
All these states of the world manifest according to the influence of place, time, action, and substance; may he who possesses superior effort be victorious!
Therefore, relying on human effort, and having brought your wisdom to purity through excellent scriptures and the company of the virtuous, cross over the ocean of saṃsāra.
These two fruits of human endeavor—the one from the past and the one pertaining to this life—are like fruit-bearing trees;
yet, of these two, the human endeavor pertaining to this life is more victorious.
The ignorant creature who does not destroy his meager past karma through auspicious endeavors is not the master of his own speech, mind, happiness, or suffering.
But he who possesses noble wonder and dwells in virtuous conduct emerges from the delusion of the world, like a lion from its cage.
"He is impelling me to act thus"— in such a useless and false imagination,
whoever persists while abandoning what is evident should be shunned from afar as a base person.
Regarding the thousands of legal disputes that arise and pass away,
one should conduct oneself among them according to the scriptures, having abandoned both pleasure and pain.
For one who does not abandon their own established boundaries as prescribed by the scriptures,
all jewels come to attend upon them, just like those from the ocean.

The wise have designated by the word "human effort" (pauruṣa) the state of being solely intent on the exertion required for the task that achieves one's own goal; when constrained by scripture, that effort leads to success.

The capacity of action, which is by nature characterized by vibration, to accomplish its own purpose is itself inferred by an intellect sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures.
The wise know the ultimate truth to be infinite and the bliss of equanimity; those from whom this is attained forever—those scriptures and virtuous ones—are to be served.
If that which is prior human effort is designated by the word "fate" (daiva), then this is appropriate;
we do not object to this name.
Those fools who have imagined a destiny other than this have gone to their ruin;
by one's own human effort alone, the welfare of both worlds is eternally secured.

Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains splendor through good conduct today, so too does today’s [conduct] depend on what preceded it; therefore, strive with effort to be one who performs virtuous deeds.
When a result is seen to arise from human effort alone, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand,
the fool rejects this direct perception and sinks into the delusion of fate.

O one of auspicious intent, disregard that destiny which is devoid of all causes and effects, imagined merely through the power of one's own conceptual constructions; instead, take refuge in your own human effort, which is composed of reality.

When that fruit which has been conceived by the scriptures and by the local customs flourishing through the conduct of the virtuous—having become deeply rooted over a very long time—vibrates within the heart, the mind does not turn toward anything else; they call this sequence of limbs "human effort" (pauruṣa). (MU 2.6.37)
Having realized that this state of being a man is the fruit of human effort, one must always be devoted solely to personal exertion;
then, through service to true scriptures, virtuous people, and the learned, that state may be led to its highest fulfillment.

One should exert effort in serving noble people, being constantly convinced that one’s own human effort— when practiced with a mind made beautiful by the discernment of both destiny and personal exertion— is what always triumphs.
Having understood that this disease consisting of the continuous chain of births is cured only by innate human effort in this life,
may this living being bring about peace through the unfailing supreme medicine of serving the most excellent sages with a mind full of contentment.
The seventh canto, titled "The Refutation of Fate," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having obtained a body free from disease and afflicted by few misfortunes,
one should thus compose the self so that it is not born again.
He who seeks to overcome destiny through human effort shall conquer his every desire, both in this world and in the next.
Those who, having abandoned exertion, remain devoted solely to fate—
haters of themselves— destroy their own virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
The vibration of consciousness, the vibration of the mind, and the vibration of the senses—these are the forms of the human goal; from these, the arising of the fruit occurs.
Just as the mind experiences [an object], so it undergoes internal vibration;
in that very way the body moves, and in that very way there is the state of being the enjoyer of the fruit.
This has been established since childhood: that wherever and however it may be, destiny is never seen to prevail; therefore, human effort triumphs.
O Lord of Gods, by virtue of his human effort this preceptor Bṛhaspati attained his status,
and Śukra likewise assumed the position of the preceptor of the Daityas through human effort.
O virtuous one, even those best of men who were afflicted by the suffering of wretchedness and poverty have attained a status equal to that of the Lord of the Gods through human effort alone.
Those who were great and rich in power, the abodes of various wonders,
have become guests of hell solely through the fault of their own human pride.
Through the power of one's own human effort alone, the various classes of beings have evolved through thousands of existences and diverse conditions.
The threefold establishment [of the means] occurs through scripture, through the teacher, and indeed through oneself;
this applies to every human goal, and never to fate.
One should diligently cause the mind that has entered into unwholesome states to descend into wholesome ones; this is the swift summary of the meaning of all the scriptures.
"O son, practice with diligence that which is beneficial, that which is not trivial, and that which is free from downfall"— thus stand the teachers.
"In whatever measure my effort is directed toward a result, in that same measure the fruit quickly follows;
thus, I am the enjoyer of the fruit through human exertion alone, and not through destiny."
Success is seen to arise from human effort; the course of the wise is one of exertion.
Destiny is merely a consolation for those of feeble intellect when faced with suffering.
In the world, the human sequence— such as traveling to another country— is always observed to result from valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) headed by direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The enjoyer is satisfied, not the non-enjoyer; the goer goes, not the non-goer;
the speaker speaks, not the non-speaker; thus human effort bears fruit for men.
Through human effort, those of sound intellect cross over insurmountable crises without exertion, but not by means of this state of muteness.
Whoever exerts effort in whatever manner, that very person alone reaps the corresponding fruit;
for no one here attains a result by remaining silent.
Through auspicious human effort, an auspicious fruit is obtained; through inauspicious effort, an inauspicious one, O Rāma. Do as you wish.
The attainment of the fruits of human effort here, occurring according to the influence of place and time—
whether it be attained slowly or quickly— is traditionally known as destiny (*daiva*).
Fate is not seen by the eye, nor does it exist in another world;
what is called "fate" in the world is simply the fruit of one's own past actions.
A person is born in this world, grows, and then decays again;
yet fate is not seen therein as the one possessing childhood, youth, and old age.
The movement from one place to another, the holding of objects in the hand,
and likewise the activity of the limbs, are brought about by human effort and not by fate.
The wise have designated as the term "human effort" (pauruṣa) the state of being solely intent on the exertion required to achieve a goal; by means of this, everything is attained.
But that state of being solely intent on effort toward an action that results in the attainment of what is useless is called "the behavior of a madman," for nothing at all is attained by it.

The capacity of action, which is by nature characterized by movement, to accomplish its own purpose is itself raised up by an intellect sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures.
The wise know one's own ultimate reality to be infinite and the bliss of equanimity;
therefore, those scriptures and virtuous teachers from whom this is attained with effort are to be served.

The quality of good scriptures and the like increases through the intellect, and the intellect increases the qualities of good scriptures and the like; these two grow mutually through practice, like a lake and a cloud over time.
Through qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, practiced sufficiently from childhood, one’s own beneficial goal is attained by human effort.
The Daityas were conquered by human effort, the activities of the world were established, and the worlds here were fashioned by Viṣṇu through exertion, and not by fate.
O Raghunātha, in this world where human effort is the cause, exert yourself long and diligently so that,
O fortunate one, you may not fearlessly fall into the state known as that of trees and reptiles.
The eighth canto, titled "The Demonstration of Manly Effort," by Vasiṣṭha.
It has no form, nor actions, nor a locus, nor prowess;
what is this so-called "fate" that is said to be as potent as false knowledge?
Those utterances which, regarding the attainment of the fruits of one's own actions, declare "this is thus," have come to be established under the name of "fate" (daiva).
In the same way, those of deluded intellect have firmly concluded that destiny exists; they grasp at it through their lack of understanding, just as one might seize a snake thinking it to be a rope.
Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains beauty through good conduct today, so too does today’s [conduct] depend on what preceded it; therefore, strive with effort to be a performer of virtuous deeds.
That fool of wicked mind for whom destiny is established by fallacious inference should say to the fire: "Let there be burning from destiny, or let there not."
If destiny alone is the agent of action for a person in this world, what is the use of exertion?
Destiny itself will perform the acts of bathing, giving, eating, and conduct.
Or what is the use of the instruction of the scriptures? This person is indeed mute;
he is merely moved by destiny—what can be taught here to whom?
And in this world, no lack of movement is observed except in the case of a corpse;
since movement results in the attainment of fruits, destiny is therefore useless.
Nor can there be joint agency between the formless divine and that which possesses form;
for even when the hands and other limbs exert effort, nothing is ever accomplished by the divine alone.
Moreover, this destiny is not experienced here in the same way as the cognition of the mind; indeed, [this is known] even to cowherds. Therefore, the wise always maintain that destiny does not exist.

If the object is distinct from cognition, then what is the difference between them? If it is merely a conceptual construction, why is it not assumed to be the work of a person? If it is a means of valid cognition, why is it not considered human?
Since that which is formless has no contact with that which possesses form— just as there is none between the sky and a corporeal body—
and since only that which is corporeal is seen to be joined [with another], therefore destiny does not exist.
Furthermore, there exists another who is the director of all beings within those three worlds; let the multitudes of beings lie down, for destiny shall accomplish everything.
"I have been thus appointed by destiny; what can I do while remaining in such a state?"—this is merely a word of consolation, for in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as destiny.
Fate was imagined by the deluded; those devoted to it have gone to ruin, while the wise, through human effort, have attained the highest state.
Tell me, by whom among those who are brave, those who are courageous, those who are wise, and those who are learned— by whom, indeed, in this world— is fate proclaimed?
If one whose long life has been determined by those who know the times should live even with his head severed, then that is simply the supreme destiny.
O Raghava, if one who is not even taught by those who know the proper time is nonetheless determined to possess wisdom, then that is the supreme destiny.
O Rāma, by the sage Viśvāmitra, having cast fate far aside,
brahminhood was attained through human effort alone and not otherwise.
O Rāma, by these other men who have attained the state of sages,
the power of traveling through the sky for a long time was achieved through human effort alone.
Having destroyed the hosts of gods through human effort alone, the lords of the Dānavas established their empire within the three worlds.
By their sheer power and through human-like effort alone, the lords of the gods forcibly seized from the Dānavas the expansive world, which had been torn asunder and shattered.
By Rama’s human effort alone was the water held back by a clever device for a long time in the basket; fate was not the cause there.
O Rāma, in matters of seizing, taking, and the agitation of confusion and delusion, it is seen that power resides in human effort, not in destiny, just as it does in the case of medicine.

O you of auspicious intent, disregarding fate— which is devoid of all causes and effects, imagined through the power of one's own conceptual constructions, and composed of unreality— take refuge in supreme human effort.
The ninth canto, titled "The Refutation of Fate," Canto Nine;
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, enough with this foundation!
O Brahmin, tell me that which is called "fate" (daiva) in the world; what indeed is it?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, human effort alone is the agent of all actions and not anything else;
it is the enjoyer of the fruit everywhere, and destiny is not the cause therein.
Destiny does nothing at all; it neither acts nor enjoys, it does not exist, it is not seen, and it is not respected—it is merely such a mental construction.
For those who possess fruits, the attainment of either auspicious or inauspicious results from an action accomplished here through human effort is designated by the term "fate" (daiva).
The constant attainment of desired or undesired objects brought about by human effort—
whether that attainment is desirable or undesirable— is designated by the term "fate" (daiva).
But that goal which is inevitably destined to be realized, and which is the sole means for achieving the purpose of man—
that is what is designated by the term "fate" (daiva) in this collection of worlds.
But for no one in the world, O Rāghava, does destiny—indeed, which is like the sky—do anything at all; it neither acts nor refrains from acting.
When the human effort has been accomplished, that statement regarding the arising of good or bad results which asserts, "This is situated thus," is called destiny (daiva).
"In this way my intellect arose; indeed, in this way my conviction was formed"—when such an attainment of the fruit of action occurs, that is called destiny (daiva).
That which expresses the sense that "it is thus" regarding the attainment of desired or undesired results,
being a mere word for consolation, is called destiny (daiva).
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, how is it that you have brushed aside this which was previously called "destiny" (daiva)— namely, that which has been accumulated through past actions?
Vasiṣṭha:
Well said, O Rāghava; you understand. Listen, and I shall tell you everything by which your mind will become firm in the conviction that there is no destiny.
That very latent impression (vāsanā) which previously existed in abundance as something submerged,
has indeed undergone transformation into the state of action (karma) for human beings.
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) a living being possesses, that very karma it becomes in an instant;
for it is not at all tenable that one karma should result in a different state of existence.
One who desires a village reaches a village, and one who seeks a city reaches a city; whatever one’s latent impression (vāsanā) may be, so does that person strive for it.
Whatever action was performed here in the past with intense urgency,
that very thing is indeed expressed by the synonymous term "fate" (daiva).
Thus, destiny is one's own actions, and action is one's matured latent impressions;
latent impressions are nothing other than the mind, for the mind is indeed remembered as the person (puruṣa).
What is called "fate" consists of those very actions; O virtuous one, action is indeed the mind.
For the mind is the person; therefore, it is certain that there is no such thing as fate.
For whatever direction a being's single mind exerts itself,
it surely attains that very thing by its own power, and not through destiny.
O Rāma, the wise have declared that *manas*, *citta*, *vāsanā*, *karman*, *daiva*, and one's own resolve (*svaniścaya*) are the designations for the human will.
O Rāma, just as a man of such a name exerts himself constantly with firm resolve, he likewise attains the fruit in full measure.
Thus, O scion of Raghu, everything is obtained here through human effort and by no other means; therefore, may that [effort] grant you prosperity.
Rāma:
O Sage, I remain exactly as my past web of latent impressions impels me; being wretched, what can I do?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"For this very reason, O Rāma, you shall attain eternal welfare through human effort alone, brought about by your own exertion, and not otherwise."
O Rāma, there exists for you a prior accumulation of two kinds of latent impressions— both auspicious and inauspicious— or else one or the other of the two.
If you are led there today by a pure flood of latent impressions, then,
through that very auspicious process, you shall attain the eternal state.
If, however, an unwholesome state of being should involve you in a crisis,
that former habit must be overcome by you with effort and force.
O wise one, you are pure consciousness alone; you are not the body, which is inert by nature.
If that very consciousness is perceived by another, then where indeed could you yourself be found?
But if another causes you to perceive, then since you do not exist [at that time], who else could there be? And who would cause that other to perceive? Therefore, an infinite regress is not real.
The river of latent impressions, flowing along both auspicious and inauspicious paths,
must be directed onto the auspicious path through human effort.
O best among the strong, one should, by means of human effort and power, draw one's own mind away from unwholesome things and establish it only in wholesome ones.
The mind of a living being wavers from the unwholesome to the wholesome, and from that again to the other; like a beast, it must therefore be guarded at all times.
One should quickly protect the child-like mind through the consolation of equanimity— not abruptly, but gradually— by means of human effort and exertion.
O Rāma, the flood of latent impressions (vāsanā), whether auspicious or inauspicious, was previously made dense by you through practice; today, make the auspicious one dense.
O crusher of enemies, know that when, by the force of prior practice, your latent impressions (vāsanā) arise, then you should recognize the fruitfulness of that practice.
O sinless one, even now your latent impression (vāsanā) attains density through the power of habituation; therefore, apply yourself to the practice of the auspicious.
If your latent impression (vāsanā) has previously become dense through lack of practice, it will not increase now either; therefore, my dear, be happy.
Even when there is doubt, gather only what is exceedingly wholesome;
for in this increase of latent impressions, no fault whatsoever arises from the wholesome.
"Whatever one practices in this world, one becomes that very thing"—
this is seen among the wise, from childhood onwards, as a truth free from doubt.
Therefore, endowed with auspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*), strive here for your own welfare by relying on supreme human effort and conquering the five senses.
As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not yet known that supreme state, practice what has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures.
Therefore, once the true nature of things has been understood through the ripening of the austerities,
you, being free from affliction, must surely abandon even this auspicious flood of meditative cultivation.

Following that which is most auspicious and practiced by the noble ones with a mind perceiving its delightful nature, attain the state that is forever free from sorrow; and having subsequently relinquished even that, abide well in perfection.
The tenth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into Karma," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, relying on human effort for the sake of your ultimate welfare— which is your eternal kinsman—
make your mind one-pointed and listen to these words of mine.
Quickly restraining with human effort those senses that have mounted the chariot of desire and are falling upon intermediate objects, lead them to equanimity.

For the sake of attaining success both in this world and the next, I shall expound this compendium, which is equal to the essence [of all knowledge], bestows the fruits of human goals, and consists of the means to liberation.
Having abandoned the latent tendencies of saṃsāra so as not to grasp at them again,
they have taken up perfect tranquility and contentment with a noble mind.

Having made the mind equanimous within the Self through continuous reflection, one should hold it steady upon the subject matter of the investigation into the meaning of the preceding and following statements.
O Rāma, listen to this means of liberation that is about to be described; it brings about the destruction of pleasure and pain and is the sole means for attaining supreme bliss.
Having heard this discourse on liberation together with all those who possess discernment,
you shall attain the state free from suffering, wherein no destruction exists.
This was spoken in a former age by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin;
it brings about the destruction of all suffering and is the supreme consolation for the intellect.
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, by whom was this told previously by the Self-born One (Svayambhū), and how was it obtained by you? Tell me, O Lord.
Vasiṣṭha said:
There exists the sky of consciousness, whose nature is infinite manifestation, all-pervading, the refuge of all, and whose essence is indestructible; it is the lamp within all things.
From that [state], which possesses the form of both vibration and non-vibration, Viṣṇu was born,
like a wave from the ocean filled with the essence of vibration.
From that lotus of the heart, which has Mount Sumeru as its pericarp, the cardinal directions as its petals,
and the stars as its filaments, the Supreme Lord was born.
He, who was garlanded by a circle of sages and lords of gods who were masters of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas,
created the entire creation as the mind creates a flood of mental constructs.
In this corner of Jambudvīpa, in the region named Bhārata,
he created people who were overwhelmed by mental anguish and physical disease.
It is intended for those despondent over existence and non-existence, and is devoted to the destruction of portents;
in this creation, it is the supreme means for the nourishment of all classes of beings.
Seeing the suffering of those people, the Lord, the creator of all worlds,
was moved by compassion, just as a father is by the suffering of his son.
"Who will bring an end to the suffering of these whose hopes are destroyed and whose lives are spent? Thus the Lord of Beings reflected with one-pointed concentration for a moment.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, created once again austerity, righteousness, charity, truth, and the sacred fords.
Having created this, the divine Creator of beings reflected once more:
"By means of this [Veda], there shall be no end to the suffering of men," he thought himself.
That which is called Nirvana is the supreme bliss, by means of which a person is neither born nor dies; it is obtained through knowledge alone.
For a living being, knowledge alone is the means for crossing over saṃsāra;
austerity, charity, and pilgrimage are proclaimed to be inferior means.
Therefore, for the sake of liberating these great-souled people from suffering,
I shall now swiftly reveal a fresh means of crossing over.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Brahmā, seated upon a lotus,
formed a mental resolve and brought me, this [universe], into existence.
O sinless one, having arisen from somewhere or other, I quickly appeared before that father of mine, as swiftly as one wave rises after another.
The Protector, bearing his water-pot, was saluted and greeted by me, who likewise bore a water-pot; he, bearing his rosary, was saluted by me, who likewise bore a rosary.
Having said to me, "Come, my son," he joined me with his hand upon the northern petal of his own lotus, like the cool-rayed moon to a white cloud.
Clad in a deer skin, with his own garment being a deer skin,
my father Brahmā spoke to me as a swan speaks to a crane.
O son, for a mere moment your mind, as fickle as a monkey,
has been overcome by ignorance, just as the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu.
Thus, having been cursed by him immediately after my reflection,
I, the twice-born, forgot my entire stainless true nature.
Then, overcome by dejection and tormented by suffering and grief, I remained with a mind awakened to the truth, like a base person who has been born [into such a state].
"How has this fault called 'saṃsāra' come to be? Alas!"—having thought thus within himself, he remained silent.
Then my father said to me: "Son, why are you sorrowful?
Ask me about the destruction of suffering, and you shall be forever happy."
Then, seated upon the petal of a golden lotus, I questioned that Blessed One, the creator of all worlds, regarding the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.
"How indeed has this great suffering come upon this saṃsāra,
and how is it exhausted for a living being?"— thus was I questioned by him.
That knowledge has been declared at great length, by knowing which it is the supreme purifier;
indeed, I am as if even superior to my father.
Then the Creator of the world, the speaker and the cause of all things, spoke to me, who had realized what is to be known and was established in my own true nature: *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.10.36*

Having reduced you to a state of ignorance through a curse, I have made you my questioner for the sake of the spiritual perfection of all people, so that the essence of this knowledge may be revealed.
Now, with your curse stilled, you have attained supreme awakening;
you stand as one with the Self, like gold [distinguished] from gold.
O virtuous one, go now upon the surface of the earth to Bhārata-varṣa, situated within Jambūdvīpa, for the sake of favoring the world.
In that regard, O son, those of great intelligence who are devoted to the section on ritual action should be instructed by you, step by step, according to the sequence of the ritual section.
O virtuous one, those whose minds are dispassionate, who possess great wisdom, and who are free from attachment, should be instructed by you with knowledge that bestows bliss.
Thus commissioned by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā,
I remain here, O Rāghava, as long as the succession of beings endures.
"There is indeed nothing at all that remains to be done by me here; thus, with this conviction, I remain established on the earth.
With a disposition that is utterly tranquil, as if my intellect were perpetually asleep, I perform my duties, yet I do nothing at all."
The eleventh canto, titled "The Descent of Knowledge," by Vasiṣṭha.
All this has been told to you regarding the descent of knowledge upon earth,
as well as my own endeavor, which was ordained by the Lotus-born One.
O sinless one, because of the ripening of great merit, my heart is today intensely yearning to hear this supreme knowledge from you.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how was the intention of the Supreme Lord Parameṣṭhin directed toward the descent of knowledge into the world immediately after the creation?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Within the supreme Brahman, Brahmā himself is born eternally through the power of his own nature, consisting of vibration like a wave in the ocean.
Having thus created this extensive creation,
the Supreme Lord beheld all the destinies of that creation, existing in the past, present, and future.
When the time for the performance of ritual acts belonging to the Kṛta age and the others had come to an end,
the Lord, observing the delusion of the worlds, was moved by compassion.
Then the Lord, having created me and repeatedly endowed me with knowledge,
dispatched me to the surface of the earth for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of the world.
Just as I was dispatched by him, so too were many other great seers,
headed by Sanatkumāra, Nārada, and others.
Through the sequence of ritual action and merit, as well as through the sequence of knowledge,
they were proclaimed in order to uplift the world, which is bound by the great delusion of the mind.
Then, in ancient times, when the Kṛta Yuga had come to an end, those great ṛṣis [observed] that the pure sequence of ritual action had gradually diminished upon the earth.
For the purpose of establishing the sequence of ritual actions and for the regulation of boundaries,
kings were appointed according to the division of separate territories.
Furthermore, many treatises on Smṛti and treatises on sacrifice were composed and proclaimed on this earth for the sake of accomplishing dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
While this wheel of time continues to turn, and that sequence has thus dissolved,
people remain daily intent on eating and devoted to the acquisition of rice.
Conflicts have arisen among kings for the sake of sense-objects,
and living beings on earth have frequently fallen into a state deserving of punishment.
Then, gradually becoming incapable of protecting the earth without war, the kings,
along with their subjects, fell into a state of wretchedness.
For the sake of dispelling their dejection and for the purpose of correctly establishing the process of creation,
great visions of knowledge were then proclaimed by us and others.
This is the science of the inner self; therefore, it was first described among kings.
Subsequently, as it spread throughout the world, it is called the "royal science" (rājavidyā).
O Raghava, having understood this supreme scripture on the inner self— the royal science and royal secret— kings have attained the state beyond all suffering.
Now, O Rāma, after many kings of stainless fame have passed away,
you have been born here today on this earth from this Daśaratha.
O crusher of enemies, this beautiful dispassion, which is free from external causes, has arisen in your mind as it became exceedingly serene; it is truly purifying.
For indeed, O Rāma, even for every capable and discerning virtuous person, dispassion arises preceded by a specific cause; such is the passionate (rājasa) type.
But this unprecedented state that has arisen in you— a dispassion toward worldly objects that causes wonder among the wise— is sattvic, born of your own discernment, and without external cause.
Who indeed would not become dispassionate upon seeing the loathsome and the foul?
But for the virtuous, supreme detachment arises from discernment alone.
Indeed, those great ones of vast wisdom, in whom dispassion arises even without a sign, they alone possess stainless minds.
For a living being shines with an intellect that is detached through the reflective awareness of the wonder of its own discernment, just as a youth shines with a forest garland.
Those who, having discerned this structure of saṃsāra through discrimination,
attain dispassion— they alone are the supreme among men.
Having investigated this again and again by the power of one's own discernment,
one must forcibly abandon this magical illusion, both externally and internally.
Who would not become dispassionate upon seeing the cemetery, calamity, and wretchedness?
That supreme excellence is dispassion which arises spontaneously from within.
Possessing uncontrived dispassion and having attained full greatness,
you are worthy of the essence of knowledge, just as soft soil is for a seed.
Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the Protector, the Supreme Self,
a virtuous intellect such as yours pursues discernment.

Through the sequence of ritual actions, through great austerity, through observance of rules, through charity, through pilgrimages to sacred fords, and through discernment cultivated over a long period of time; //MU_2,11.31//
When evil deeds have come to an end and there is an investigation into the ultimate truth,
the intellect of a living being is set in motion by a chance occurrence.
People devoted to ritual action, though diligent, continue to revolve here in this world like the turning of a wheel, as long as they do not behold the supreme state.
Having seen this cycle of existence as it truly is, and having abandoned the mind absorbed in it, they go to the supreme state like elephants freed from their tethering posts.
O Rāma, this wandering in saṃsāra is a treacherous and endless pursuit;
like a great thread, it is not destroyed without knowledge, even when the body has been cast off.
