O scion of Raghu, it is by the very raft of the application of knowledge that those of great intelligence have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross, and not by any other means.
Listen with an attentive mind to this method of knowledge, which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra, by means of this constant attentiveness.
O blameless one, because the ways of suffering in the world involve endless turmoil,
these burn within for a long time unless there is a remedy.
O Raghava, by what means can the dualities of suffering— such as cold, wind, and heat—
be endured even among the virtuous, except through the application of knowledge?
Afflictions of sorrow fall upon a foolish man at every step and at their appointed time, and they consume him just as a flame of fire consumes straw.
Mental anxieties do not burn the wise man who has realized true knowledge and possesses right vision,
just as the flames of fire do not consume a forest during the rainy season.
Even when the desert wind of saṃsāra, which revolves with mental and physical afflictions,
is agitated, the knower of reality is not broken, like the wish-fulfilling tree.
Therefore, in order to know reality, only a wise person should diligently and with affection question another wise person who is authoritative and awakened in soul.
The speech of an authoritative person who has been questioned should be carefully received by one of superior mind, just as saffron is gathered with a cloth.
O best among those skilled in speech, there is no one more foolish than that man who questions a person who does not know reality and whose words are not to be accepted.
There is no one more base than that person who, when questioned with effort by an authoritative speaker who knows the truth,
does not carry out his word.
Having first ascertained through the effects whether the speaker possesses knowledge of that matter or lacks it,
the man who then poses a question is a wise inquirer.
The fool who poses a question without first determining the speaker shall be a base interrogator; he is not a fit vessel for matters of great significance.
When the intellect is blameless and capable of reconciling what precedes and follows,
one should speak when questioned by a wise person, but not to one who is base and possesses the nature of a beast.
The wise in this world call that man the most foolish who speaks without first considering whether the meaning he offers is valid or suitable for the questioner.
O descendant of Raghu, you are an exceedingly great repository of virtues and an inquirer;
I am one who knows how to speak, and this is the union of us two.
O you who are skilled in words and their meanings, whatever I say should be determined by you with effort as being this very reality, and held unshakably in your heart.
You are great, you are dispassionate, and you are a knower of the true state of living beings;
in you, the reality takes root within, just as saffron water clings to a cloth.
Your wisdom, which is supremely attentive and discerns the ultimate truth, enters into the object like the sun’s radiance into the midst of water.
Whatever I say to you should be taken to heart and applied with effort;
otherwise, I am not to be questioned by you here in vain.
For the mind, O Rāma, is fickle—a monkey in the forest of saṃsāra;
having restrained it with effort within the heart, one should listen to the wisdom of the ultimate truth.
Having kept for a long time at a great distance those who lack discernment, the ignorant, and people who delight in the company of the wicked, one should indeed honor the virtuous.
Through constant association with the virtuous, discernment arises;
enjoyment and liberation are said to be the two fruits of the tree of discernment.
At the gateway to liberation, four gatekeepers are proclaimed:
tranquility, discernment, contentment, and fourthly, association with the virtuous.
These four, or else two or three, should be served with diligence;
they forcibly open the door to the royal palace of liberation.
Or, having abandoned all other efforts, one should resort with every exertion to even a single [virtuous quality],
for when that one is brought under control, all four likewise come under control.
For one who possesses discernment is the vessel for sacred learning, knowledge, austerity, and splendor;
he is like the sun, the form of all ornaments, among all radiant lights.
For the dullness of wisdom in those who lack consciousness becomes solidified,
like water turning into the state of a stone due to its sluggishness.
But you, O Raghava, with your heart blossomed by kindness, virtuous qualities, and insight into the meaning of the scriptures, abide like a lotus at sunrise.
O noble-minded one, only a living being whose ears have been cleared is fit to hear and understand this vision of knowledge, just as one whose ears are open can perceive the sound of a lute.
O Rāma, that state where no destruction exists is attained through the yoga of dispassion and practice, and by the perfection of equanimity and goodness.
Through the scriptures, preceded by association with virtuous people, and through excellent austerity and self-restraint,
one should first increase wisdom alone for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra.
One should strive to destroy folly, which is the fierce watering of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra, the abode of calamities, and the collyrium for the night of delusion.
Know that this very thing is the supreme destroyer of ignorance:
namely, that this scripture is being contemplated with an intellect somewhat refined.
When the serpent-hole of wicked desires leaps within the heart through folly,
the mind undergoes contraction, like a piece of leather placed over a fire.
In one who possesses wisdom, this vision of reality becomes serene,
just as the sight [of the moon] is clear when the orb of the moon is complete and stainless, free from clouds.
He whose mind is expansive and endowed with the beautiful skill of investigating what precedes and what follows is called a true man.
With your blossoming, white, mind-stealing heart— cool-rayed through its excellent discernment and endowed with virtues— you shine like the stainless moon in the sky.
The twelfth canto, titled "The Characteristics of the Speaker and the Questioner," by Vasiṣṭha.
O Rāghava, you are worthy of honor with a fulfilled mind; you know how to inquire and you understand what is said, and for that reason I have proceeded to speak out of respect.
Having established the mind within the self— free from passion and ignorance and following pure goodness— be steady to hear this knowledge.
The entire array of qualities of an inquirer exists in you,
and the series of qualities of a speaker resides in me, just as the wealth of jewels is found in the ocean.
O Sage, you have attained dispassion born of discernment and non-attachment,
just as a moonstone becomes moist when struck by the rays of the moon.
Since childhood, you have long been practiced in pure virtues; being yourself pure, these virtues are as continuous and extensive as the fibers of a lotus stalk.
Therefore, listen; I shall tell you a tale, for you alone are its worthy recipient.
Indeed, without the moon, the white water-lily does not bloom in its pure splendor.
Whatever undertakings there may be and whatever views there may be,
they all indeed come to complete rest when that state is seen.
If there were no resting of consciousness for one of noble mind,
then who in this cycle of existence could endure to bear such anxiety?
Through the attainment of the Supreme, all mental fluctuations dissolve,
like the rocks of the principal mountains from contact with the multitude of suns at the end of a kalpa.
O Rāma, the unbearable cholera-like affliction caused by the onset of the poison of saṃsāra is pacified by the purifying Gāruḍa mantra of yoga.
And that yoga, consisting of the knowledge of ultimate reality, is indeed obtained through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures in the company of a virtuous person.
For it must be understood that when this investigation is performed here, there is necessarily the complete cessation of all suffering.
Therefore, those who possess the vision of inquiry should not be viewed with contempt.

By the power of inquiry, a person endowed with right vision—having cast off this entire cage of worldly existence like a snake sheds its ripe skin—is freed from the fever of passion; with a cooled inner heart, he beholds the whole world as if it were a mere plaything. (MU 2.12–13)
For one who possesses wrong view, this supreme suffering exists;
for this disease of saṃsāra is exceedingly treacherous,
biting like a serpent and cutting like a sword.
It pierces like an arrow;
it entangles like a rope;
it burns like fire.
It blinds like the night;
it renders one helpless like a harsh stone falling unexpectedly;
and it carries away wisdom.
It destroys stability,
casts one into the blind well of delusion,
and wears one down with craving.

There is no suffering whatsoever that a transmigrating being does not encounter. This chronic cholera of the poison of sense-objects is indeed said to be incurable; if it is not treated, it leads to the production of various results that result in a multitude of hells.
Where the falling of a hundred sharp swords is like the striking of a blue lotus; where the burning of fire is like a sprinkling of snow;
and where the cutting off of limbs is like the application of sandalwood paste.

The crushing of limbs by the whirling wind within; the incessant falling of a multitude of chowries and iron arrows shaken by the flames of unceasing fire; the raining of spray from cooling shower-houses that would dispel the summer heat;
and the severing of the head—these are pleasant sleep.
The sealing of the tongue, proficiency,
and great accumulation— O Rāghava, one must not treat with indifference this wheel of saṃsāra, which is so harsh with thousands of such painful exertions.
Indeed, this must necessarily be investigated.

And it should be understood in this way: that indeed there is the attainment of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) through inquiry (*vicāra*). Furthermore, O moon of the Raghu dynasty, if these great sages, great seers (*maharṣi*), brahmins, and kings did not have their bodies enveloped by the armor of knowledge (*jñānakavaca*), [they would not have attained such excellence].

How is it, then, that even those who cannot endure suffering remain with minds constantly joyful while experiencing the torments of saṃsāra, which consist of suffering and are preceded by the activity of darkness? For here:
Free from curiosity and devoid of the disturbances of conceptual construction, just as Hari, Hara, Padmaja, and the others abide,
so do those supreme among men— having attained the lamp of the self and possessed of awakened intellects— abide in this world.
And so it is:
when delusion has been utterly exhausted, when the dense cloud of ignorance has dissolved, when reality has been fully known and the beloved Self has been attained;

when, having deliberated with the Noble Ones, the truth has been seen by the intellect as both existence and non-existence have lost their substance—this wandering of the world is but a source of delight.

Moreover, O Rāghava: when the essence of consciousness has become serene within the heart, when the Supreme Being dances with full majesty, when all perceptions of worldly activity have expanded into a state of total absorption,
and when the constructions of the internal organ subside into peace— then, once the Reality is perceived by the intellect, this worldly wandering becomes a source of delight.
Moreover:
The chariot is the expansive body, the arrangement of horses is the movement of the senses, and the motion is from the wind; I am the unperceived, infinite, and peerless one.
Whether beyond or within, I, the embodied soul, wander through the world—this wandering in the world is a delight when the reality is seen with a faultless intellect.
The thirteenth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Greatness of Reality," by Vasiṣṭha.
Holding fast to this view, those of great intellect and nourished souls move about without arrogance, like great beings who have attained their goal.
They do not grieve, they do not beg, and they do not desire good or evil;
they perform everything, yet they perform nothing at all.
They remain established in their own natural state, they bring others to that same state,
and they proceed [in life] free from the dualistic notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, abiding in their own self.
They come and yet do not come; they go to the forest and yet do not go. They do not act and yet they act; they speak and yet they do not speak.
Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever views there may be, and whatever perceptions of what is to be rejected or accepted— these all perish once the state has been realized.
The mind that has abandoned all worldly attachment and possesses a sweet disposition attains happiness from every side, remaining like the orb of the moon.
Even the undertaking of emanations, even that which has cast aside all curiosity,
does not find room within oneself, just as an elixir does not fit within the moon.
He performs no magical illusions, nor does he pursue latent impressions;
having cast off the fickleness of a child, he shines forth as the fullness itself.
For such states of being are obtained from the perception of the reality of the Self, and not from anything else.
Therefore, throughout one's life, a person must seek the Self through inquiry, worship it, and know it; nothing other than this. (MU 2.13.9)
Where there is a single harmony between one's own experience, the excellent scripture, and the teacher,
by means of that continuous practice, the Self is beheld.
One who disregards the meaning of the scriptures and treats great men with contempt should not, even when fallen into painful calamity, fall into equality with the foolish.
Neither disease, nor poison, nor calamity exists upon the surface of the earth that causes such distress to men as the folly residing within their own bodies.
Just as this treatise is fit to be heard by those with some degree of refined intellect,
there is no other treatise whatsoever that so effectively dispels ignorance.
This is worth hearing, bringing happiness, beautiful with its narratives and parables,
and entirely consistent with the meaning of the words of the scriptures.
Those calamities which are difficult to overcome and those empty, wretched births— all these are produced from folly, just as thorns grow from the khadira tree.
O Rāma, it is better to wander for alms with a bowl in hand through the streets of the Caṇḍāla dwellings than to lead a life destroyed by folly.
Having attained this light consisting of the means to liberation,
no person shall ever again fall into blindness, even within the darkness of delusion.
The night-blooming lotus of humanity, darkened by craving,
contracts until the stainless radiance of the sun of discernment has arisen.
For the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, one should realize the true nature of the self through the authority of the Guru and the scriptures, together with kinsmen such as myself.
O Rāghava, conduct yourself here just as Hari, Hara, and others, as well as other Brahman-sages, move about as those liberated while living.
In this world, sufferings are infinite while happiness is like a mere moment or fraction of a second;
therefore, one should not fixate one's view upon pleasures that are followed by suffering.
That state which is infinite and effortless should be striven for with diligence by a person of discernment for the sake of attaining the essential goal.
These very persons are the supreme among men, the vessels for the goal of human life,
whose minds— free from the fever of worldly passion— rest upon the unsurpassed state.
Know those of wicked mind who are satisfied with mere enjoyments, food, sovereignty, and other such pleasures, to be like blind *duṇḍubha* snakes.
Those who are devoted to the deceitful, the wicked, those intent on evil deeds, to enemies disguised as friends, and to those who indulge in sensual pleasures; MU_2,13.25.
Those fools, whose intellects are dulled by delusion, go from difficulty to difficulty, from suffering to suffering, from fear to fear, and from one hell to another.
O Rāma, the two states of pleasure and pain— each eager to destroy the other— are never conducive to the highest good, for they are as transient as the flickering of lightning.
Know those high-souled men like you, who are dispassionate and perfectly secluded, to be worthy of veneration, for they alone partake both in worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Relying upon supreme discernment through the yoga of dispassion and practice,
one shall cross over this terrible river of saṃsāra and its calamities.
A discerning person who understands this world should not sleep within the illusions of saṃsāra, for they bestow the stupor and delusion of a toxic faint.
He who, having encountered this saṃsāra, remains indifferent to it,
lies within a high, blazing house made of straw.
That state, reaching which they do not return and attaining which one no longer grieves, is indeed attainable here through intelligence; of this there is no doubt.
If that [self] does not exist, what fault would there be for you through such investigation?
If it does exist, then you shall have crossed over the ocean of existence.
When a person's inclination here is directed toward investigating the means to liberation,
then he is said to be one who partakes in liberation.
A state of well-being that is unfailing, free from apprehension, and devoid of delusion does not exist within the three worlds without the state of absolute liberation (*kevalībhāva*).
In attaining that— attaining the supreme— neither afflictions are of use,
nor do friends assist, nor wealth, nor kinsmen.
There is no movement of hands or feet, nor travel to another land; it is not accomplished through an excess of afflictions, nor does it depend upon sacred fords or shrines.
That state is attained solely through the conquest of the mind alone— by means of an action whose sole purpose is human effort and whose function is the unification of latent impressions.
By abandoning the webs of suffering, that state— which is to be accomplished through solitude alone and is certain through one-pointed inquiry— is attained by a man.
By one seated upon a comfortable seat, reflecting upon that for oneself,
there is no sorrow once that state is attained, nor is one born again.
The virtuous know that to be the ultimate limit of the essence of all happiness; they call that supreme elixir the unsurpassed outflow [of liberation].
Because all states of existence are subject to decay, there is no happiness at all in either heaven or the human realm; it is like water in mirages.
Therefore, the conquest of the mind is to be contemplated; it is tranquility, the means for achieving contentment.
From that, the enjoyment of infinite tranquility is attained; hence, bliss is obtained.
Whether by a living being, one who is moving, one who is wandering, or likewise one who is falling;
whether by a *rakṣasa*, a *dānava*, a god, or even a human.
Having attained that supreme bliss born from the pacification of the mind, one reaches the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment, which has the blossoms of tranquility in full bloom.
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, one who does not accumulate a multitude of undertakings neither abandons nor craves them, remaining like the sun stationed in the sky.
The mind that is profoundly tranquil, utterly transparent, rested, and free from delusion;
that which is effortless and devoid of longing—neither desires nor rejects anything.
Listen now to these gatekeepers at the door of liberation in their proper order;
by devotion to even one of them, one enters the door of liberation.
The long desert expanse of saṃsāra, with its states of suffering and defects,
attains coolness for a living being through the cooling water of tranquility.
Through tranquility, the highest good is attained, for tranquility is the supreme state;
tranquility is auspiciousness, tranquility is peace, and tranquility is the warding off of delusion.
For a man who is satisfied by tranquility, whose self is cool and clear,
and whose mind is contented through peace, even an enemy becomes a friend.
For those whose inner disposition is adorned by the moon of tranquility,
their supreme purity arises like that of the oceans of milk.
Those virtuous ones in whose hearts the lotus of tranquility has blossomed within the sheath of the heart-lotus are indeed like Hari, possessing two lotus-hearts.
Those whose stainless moon-like faces shine with the beauty of tranquility—
they are these lords of their clans, worthy of homage, who have surpassed the moon itself in loveliness.
The splendors existing within the belly of the three worlds do not bring such joy as the manifestations of peace, which are equal to the wealth of universal sovereignty.

Whatever sufferings, whatever cravings so difficult to endure, and whatever mental anxieties there may be— all of these perish within those whose minds are peaceful, just as darkness vanishes before the suns.
For the mind of all beings follows after serenity; it does not do so toward the moon as it does toward a person who is tranquil and has inspired wonder.
In a virtuous person who possesses tranquility and friendliness toward all living beings, the supreme reality reveals itself spontaneously.
Just as toward a mother, all beings here place their trust in one who is tranquil, whether they encounter hardships or gentleness.
A person does not obtain such happiness through the drinking of elixirs nor through the embrace of Fortune as they do through inner tranquility.
O Rāghava, comfort the mind, which is enveloped by all manner of mental and physical afflictions and overcome by the threefold bond of craving, with the sprinklings of the nectar of tranquility.
Whatever you do and whatever you eat with a mind cooled by tranquility, that will taste exceedingly sweet and delicious to you, my dear; nothing else does so in the mind.
O Rāghava, I believe that even those limbs which have been severed grow back again by means of that peace and bliss which the mind attains when bathed in the nectar-essence of tranquility.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Daityas, nor enemies,
nor tigers, serpents, and the like, harbor hostility toward one who abides in tranquility.
Those who have all their limbs well-armored with the nectar-like armor of tranquility are not pierced by sufferings, just as arrows cannot penetrate a diamond rock.
A king, even when surrounded by ministers and the ladies of the inner court, does not shine in such a manner as he does when adorned with tranquility through a balanced and healthy mode of conduct.
A person does not attain such satisfaction by seeing something dearer than their own life as they do upon beholding a person who is peaceful and of tranquil disposition.
He who conducts himself well with a conduct that is disciplined, tranquil,
and approved by the world lives truly in this life, and no other.
Whatever good deed one who is undisturbed in mind and tranquil performs,
all these beings rejoice in it.
Having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled what is pleasant or unpleasant,
he who neither rejoices nor desponds is said to be at peace.
He who is equal toward all things, neither desiring nor rejecting,
having conquered his senses through effort— he is called "peaceful."
He whose mind is as clear as the orb of the moon and remains undisturbed even in death, festivals, or battles— he is called "peaceful."
Even while remaining, he does not remain as if he were; he neither rejoices nor becomes angry.
He whose mind is like one in deep sleep and who is established in his own self is said to be "peaceful."
He whose joyful gaze, beautiful with the flow of nectar, extends toward all people, is called "peaceful."
He whose actions are perceived with a clear and pure intellect, such that they are exactly the same internally as they are externally, is said to be "peaceful."
Even in the midst of endless calamities, even when the world is being consumed at the end of an aeon,
he whose mind is not agitated by trivial things is said to be "peaceful."
He who has attained inner coolness and does not sink into worldly objects, who engages in practical affairs without being deluded— he is called "peaceful."
He whose mind, ever engaged in its own activity, remains like space and incurs no stain— that one is called "peaceful."
Among ascetics, the learned, sacrificial priests, and kings—
among those who are powerful and rich in virtues— it is only the man of tranquility who truly shines.
For the great ones who possess virtuous qualities and whose minds are absorbed in tranquility, bliss arises from the heart, just as moonlight emerges from the cool-rayed moon.
The glorious tranquility (*śama*) shines forth as the boundary of all multitudes of virtues, the singular ornament of manliness, and the place of fearlessness in times of distress.
Having taken refuge in that supreme state—tranquil, immortal, unassailable, and cherished by the noble—you have set forth for the highest goal;
O son of Raghu, like those of great majesty, follow that very same path for the sake of perfection.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of Tranquility," by Vasiṣṭha.
One who knows the cause should, with a mind purified by the stainless understanding of the scriptures and with a self restrained, engage in inquiry.
Having attained sharpness through reflection, the intellect perceives the supreme state;
for reflection is indeed the great medicine for the long-lasting disease of saṃsāra.
The forest of calamities, whose form is made to sprout by endless desires,
does not grow again once it has been cut down by the saw of discernment.
O one of great wisdom, in delusions, the loss of kinsmen, calamities, and errors— in all these indeed, discernment is the refuge of the virtuous.
Without discernment, there is no means whatsoever for the pacification of suffering;
through discernment, the minds of the wise abandon the unwholesome and attain the wholesome.
Strength, intelligence, vigor, discernment, and the fruit of action—
all these bear fruit for the wise man through inquiry alone.
Relying on expansive discernment, which is a great lamp for what is appropriate and inappropriate and the means for accomplishing one's desires, one shall cross over the ocean of saṃsāra.
The noble lion of inquiry, being a pure self, tears asunder the great elephant of delusion whose lotus-heart has been mangled.
That even the deluded, by the power of time, have reached the supreme state in this world is the unsurpassed manifestation of the lamp of inquiry.
Kingdoms, abundant wealth, vast enjoyments, and eternal liberation—
O Rāghava, these are the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry.
Those minds of the great here that delight in solitude do not sink in adversity, just as gourds do not sink in water.
Those who conduct themselves with an intellect that captivates through the arising of discernment indeed become the recipients of most exalted fruits.
The successions of sorrows are the blossoms of the *karañja* trees of non-investigation, which reside in the forest of the fool’s heart and obstruct the expansion of hope.
O Rāghava, may that sleep— which is as dark as powdered collyrium, which possesses the fragrance of wine, and which consists of a lack of discernment— come to an end for you.
Even during great calamities or long-lasting hardships, a man devoted to right reflection does not sink into delusions, just as a mass of light does not sink into darkness.
He in whose clear mental lake the multitude of lotuses that are inquiry has surely blossomed shines like the Himalayas.
For one whose intellect is devoid of discernment and has fallen into dullness,
a thunderbolt arises from the moon, like that which befell the child Yakṣa in vain.
O Rāma, that lowest of men who lacks discernment must be abandoned from afar; he is a pit of misery, a termite mound, and a springtime for the creepers of calamity.
Whatever undertakings are ill-conceived, whatever conducts are wicked, and whatever anxieties are base— all these appear without scrutiny like ghouls in the darkness.
O scion of Raghu, keep far away from him who lacks discernment, who is like a solitary, withered tree, and who is incapable of performing virtuous deeds.
For when the mind of a living being is secluded and freed from the helplessness of desire,
it attains supreme bliss within itself, like the full moon.
Discrimination, once arisen, thoroughly cools the entire body and adorns it exceedingly,
like a fresh moonlight adorning the world.
For a living being, the investigation of the intellect— which is the white fly-whisk for the banner of ultimate truth— shines forth like the moon in the night.
States that are delightful when investigated shine forth, illuminating the ten directions;
they gleam like the sun, having shattered the disease of the fear of repeated existence.
For a fool, a life-taking Vetāla conjured by the delusion of his own mind dissolves through inquiry, even as it appears in the darkness of night.
All worldly phenomena are charming only so long as they are not investigated;
their true existence is non-existent, for they fall apart under scrutiny.
The long-standing vampire of saṃsāra, imagined by a person's own deluded mind and bestowing manifold suffering, dissolves through inquiry.
Know this state of absolute oneness to be equally pure, free from affliction, infinite, and independent— the fruit of the tree of intense discernment.
By him, through his unwavering state and the vast, manifest splendor of his majesty,
there arises a desirelessness like the coolness produced by the risen moon.
By means of that great medicine for the fever of anxiety, which is established in the mind of the virtuous and bestows the state of excellence, he neither desires nor abandons anything.
That mind, having attained a vast manifestation with that as its constant object,
neither sets nor rises, like the sky which is exceedingly expansive within.
It neither abandons nor takes up, it neither suffers nor finds peace;
merely observing like a witness, it remains within itself as the world.
It neither subsides, nor does it abide within or without;
it neither adopts inaction, nor does it sink into action.
He remains equanimous toward what has passed and follows what has arrived;
neither agitated nor excessively unagitated, he shines like the full ocean.
With such a mind, the great-souled ones of noble intent—
yogins who are liberated while living— indeed wander about in this world.
Having dwelt for a very long time, as long as they desire,
those steadfast ones finally cast off the body and attain the pervasive state of absolute oneness.
Even in times of adversity, a wise person should strive with effort and by means of their own countermeasures to reflect: "Who am I, and whose is this cycle of existence? MU 2.14.37.
O Raghava, a king understands the difficulty,
doubt, fruitlessness, or success of a task only through careful deliberation, and not otherwise.
The established tenets of the Vedas and Vedānta, which are the cause of stability,
are determined through inquiry, just as the features of the earth are discerned at night by means of a lamp.
The beautiful-eyed one sees what is not lost even in darkness, what is not obscured even amidst great brilliance, and even what is concealed, by means of discernment.
For one who is blind to discernment is like one born blind; such a person of evil intellect is an object of pity for all.
But he whose soul is discernment possesses divine vision and triumphs over all things.
Consisting of the Supreme Self, to be protected, and the sole means to great bliss—
this wondrous power of discernment must not be abandoned for even a single moment.
A man who is charming in his discernment is pleasing even to the great, just as a fully ripened mango fruit is delightful.
Men whose minds delight in reflection, who know the upward path, do not fall again and again into the various pits of suffering.
Neither does a sick man nor one shattered by hundreds of misfortunes wail as much as the ignorant man whose soul is ruined by a lack of discernment.
Better is the state of being a worm in the mud, better is being a thorn in a pit, better is dwelling in a blind cave than the lack of discernment in a human being.
One should abandon that which is the natural abode of all misfortune, despised by all the virtuous, the ultimate limit of all instability, and devoid of reflection.
A great-souled person must always be engaged in inquiry;
for indeed, inquiry is the support for those falling into the dark well of worldly existence.
By supporting oneself with one's own self and investigating through inquiry,
one may cause the deer of one's own mind to cross over the ocean of delusion that is saṃsāra.
"Who am I? How has this fault called saṃsāra come upon me?"—such an investigation according to reason is called "vicāra" (discernment).
The heart of the dull-witted and unreflective person has long been made like a stone— blind, deaf, and noisy with delusion, leading only to suffering.
For here, O Rāghava, regarding views that grasp at existence or non-existence and those that involve acceptance or rejection,
no reality whatsoever is properly known except through inquiry.
Through inquiry, reality is known; from reality, there is rest in the Self.
Then, when the mind is stilled, all suffering comes to an end.
Success indeed bears fruit on earth for actions that attain manifestation from the highest source;
may this [truth], when examined with the eye of clear discernment, shine forth even for you who are possessed of tranquility.
The fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of Discernment," by Vasiṣṭha.
Contentment is indeed the highest good; contentment is said to be happiness.
O slayer of enemies, one who is contented attains supreme rest.
For the virtuous who are happy in the sovereignty of contentment and whose minds have long found rest, even a universal empire is like a blade of withered grass.
O Rāma, an intellect endowed with contentment regarding the conditions of worldly existence is never distressed,
remaining unperturbed even amidst adversities.
For those who have attained supreme satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment, this incomparable splendor of enjoyments acts like a potent poison.
These waves of nectar-like flavor do not satisfy one in the same way as contentment,
which possesses a sweet taste and destroys all defects.

Having abandoned the desire for what has not been attained and having reached equanimity toward what has been attained, he who is inwardly free from distress at the sight of suffering is called "contented" in this world.
As long as the mind does not attain contentment within itself by means of the Self,
calamities continue to arise from the forest of the mind like creeping vines.
The mind, cooled by contentment and possessing the vision of pure gnosis,
attains full blossoming, just as a lotus does under the rays of the sun.
When the mind is rendered helpless by the powerlessness of desire and is devoid of contentment,
knowledge does not reflect within it, just as an image does not appear on a tarnished mirror.
The lotus of man does not undergo contraction through the night of dense ignorance for him,
in whom the sun of contentment has eternally risen.
Even though he possesses nothing, that person enjoys the happiness of sovereignty,
provided his mind is contented and liberated from mental anguish and physical disease.
He who does not long for what has not been attained, and who enjoys what has been attained in due order— he, O gentle one, is of good conduct and is called "contented."
In the mouth of the great one who is fully satisfied with contentment and whose mind is complete— pure like the ocean of milk— the Goddess of Fortune shines resplendently.
Relying fully upon perfection within one's very own self by means of the self itself,
one should abandon craving everywhere through manly effort.
For one who is filled with the nectar of contentment, a natural coolness arises within the heart;
for one who is not empty [of it], stability becomes eternal, like that of the moon.
With minds nourished by contentment, those of great prosperity attend upon him like servants, having entered into a state of servitude.
When the person remains established in the self by the self alone, pure and contented,
all mental anxieties are pacified instantly, like dust in the rainy season.
A person shines like the full moon through a constant, pure mode of conduct that is free from blemish and named "coolness."
The world finds such satisfaction in beholding the face of a man beautiful in its symmetry as it does not find through the acquisition of wealth.
O descendant of Raghu, even the great sages who traverse the heavens bow down to that stainless king of men, who is adorned here by his equanimity, his wisdom, and his possession of virtues.
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of Contentment," by Vasiṣṭha:
O one of great intelligence, the company of the virtuous especially benefits all people here in this world for the purpose of crossing over saṃsāra.
Those great-souled ones who protect the auspicious flower of discernment, born from the tree of association with the virtuous, are the vessels for the glory of its fruit.
The empty becomes crowded, even death turns into a festival,
and misfortune appears like prosperity when one meets with a gathering of wise men.
Victorious in this world is the association with the virtuous—the frost to the lotus-pond of worldly existence, and the wind that dispels the mist of delusion. It alone is truly good.
Know that association with the virtuous is the supreme nourishment for the intellect, the felling of the tree of ignorance, and the complete departure from mental anxieties.
From association with the virtuous, the supreme lamp of discernment arises—
truly as enchanting and radiant as a cluster of blossoms from an aśoka tree.
The splendors of association with the virtuous bestow an unsurpassed, eternal, and abundant bliss that is free from misfortune and free from affliction.
Even by men who have fallen into a most miserable state and have become helpless, association with the virtuous must not be abandoned even in the slightest degree.
In this world, associations with the virtuous are illuminators of the auspicious path of the righteous;
they are the rays of the sun of knowledge that dispel the darkness within the heart.
For one who has bathed in the Ganges of association with the virtuous— cool and pure with its waters of tranquility—
what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices?
O sinless one, if there exist holy men who are free from passion, whose doubts are severed, and whose knots have been untied, what is the use of austerities or the visiting of sacred fords?
Those whose minds are at rest are indeed worthy of worship with the utmost effort;
for the virtuous are to be gazed upon just as jewels are by a poor man.
The intellect of the wise, graced by the beauty of association with the virtuous, always shines forth like a lotus in the midst of a host of celestial nymphs.
By that fortunate one, through whom association with the virtuous was never abandoned, the state of being a "forelock" at the tip of the foot of stainless grace was made manifest.
Those who have severed the knots, who know that reality, who are virtuous, and who are esteemed by all—
these should be served by every means, for they are indeed the means [for crossing] the ocean of existence.
These very people have become like dried fuel for the fires of hell—
those virtuous ones who, with ease, beheld the fires of hell as if they were mere water.
The uneven delusion that poverty, death,
and suffering are [the ultimate] is completely pacified by the medicine of association with the virtuous.
Contentment, association with the virtuous, reflection, and likewise tranquility—
these alone are the means for men to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Contentment is the supreme gain; the company of the virtuous is the supreme goal;
reflection is the supreme knowledge; and tranquility is indeed the supreme happiness.
These four are the stainless means for shattering cyclic existence;
those who have practiced them have crossed over the ocean of existence, which has delusion as its waters.
O best among the wise, when even one of these has been practiced until its stainless arising, all four are indeed considered practiced.
Even a single one among all these is like the source of birth for all;
therefore, for the sake of complete accomplishment, one should diligently rely upon one [of them].
But the company of the virtuous, contentment, and discernment proceed without deliberation toward pure tranquility, like currents in the ocean.

In a living being who frequents the company of the virtuous, discernment, contentment, and tranquility flourish, just as the splendors of the wish-fulfilling tree do for one who has taken refuge beneath it.
In a person endowed with contentment, reflection, tranquility, and the company of the virtuous proceed,
just as beauty and other qualities manifest in the full moon.

In one who possesses right understanding and engages in reflection, contentment, peace, and association with the virtuous proceed, just as the glories of victory attend a preeminent minister in matters of statecraft.
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, having conquered the mind— one of these which is eternal— by human effort, one should diligently apply oneself to virtue.
Relying on supreme human effort and having conquered the elephant of the mind,
as long as even a single virtue is not attained, there is no higher state.
O Rāma, grind your teeth against each other with manly effort until your mind is firmly resolved upon the acquisition of virtue.
Whether you are a god, a yakṣa, a human, or even a tree,
O mighty-armed one, there is no means whatsoever for you here [to escape] until then.
When even a single quality has borne fruit and attained strength,
all the defects of the undiscerning mind quickly perish.
When virtue increases, virtues that bring about the destruction of faults increase;
when fault increases, faults that destroy virtues increase.
For in this great forest of the mind, the swift river of latent impressions (vāsanā),
with its vast banks of the auspicious and inauspicious, flows constantly among living beings.
For she is carried along by her own effort toward whichever bank she is cast; she flows by that very path—do as you wish.

O one of excellent mind, gradually lead the great river of your own nature along the auspicious banks within the forest of the mind by means of the speed of human effort; for by that, you will not be carried away even slightly in this world.
The seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, O Raghava, you who possess such solitude of mind are worthy to hear the words of knowledge, just as a king is worthy to hear the discourse on statesmanship.
Pure, possessing a great disposition for pure consciousness,
and free from attachment to the dull, he is fit [for liberation], like the autumnal sky for the moon.
Supported by this unimpaired splendor of virtue,
listen to these words about to be spoken, which remove the delusion of the mind.
For that person for whom the wish-fulfilling tree of merit stands bowed under the weight of its fruit,
this effort to hear [this teaching] arises for the sake of liberation.
One who is worthy becomes a vessel for those purifying and sublime words that grant the singular realization of the Supreme; the base person does not.
This compendium, equal in essence to the *Sāra*, is named the *Mokṣopāya*; consisting of thirty-two thousand verses, it bestows liberation when understood.
Just as light proceeds from a lamp that has been lit while one is awake,
even against one's will, so too shall nirvana come about through this [practice].
Whether known by oneself or heard from another, it bestows happiness solely through the pacification of delusion;
when described as the words of a reliable authority, it immediately acts like a wave of nectar.
Just as the delusion of a snake in a rope perishes through inspection,
so too does the suffering of saṃsāra come to rest through this contemplation.
In this work, there are six chapters consisting of sentences with logically consistent meanings, each composed separately, and containing well-spoken essences of illustrative examples.
The first chapter, titled "Dispassion," has been proclaimed;
by means of it, dispassion increases like a tree in a desert through irrigation.
When this text of one thousand five hundred verses is reflected upon within the heart,
pure luminosity arises, like the clarity in a gem that has been polished.
Thereafter, a chapter titled "The Conduct of One Seeking Liberation" was composed; it consists of approximately one thousand verses and is beautiful with its string of well-spoken words.
For when the inherent nature of men who seek liberation is described,
it is understood that one of such a nature is fit for liberation.
Then follows the section on origination, consisting of parables and narratives,
comprising five thousand verses, which establishes the nature of consciousness.
The splendor of the world, consisting of the seer and the seen, takes the form of "I" and "you"; that wherein this is described as being neither arisen nor as if arisen is the Jāgatī.
Upon hearing which, this entire world— including ourselves, you, all its expansions, as well as the space of the worlds and the mountains— is understood within the interior of the ear.
Free from the grasping of a solid mass, without foundations and without mountains, devoid of the primary elements such as earth and the rest, it is like a city created by mere imagination.
It has the appearance of entities perceived in a dream, it is as expansive as a kingdom of the mind, and it is like a city of the Gandharvas— an apprehension devoid of objective reality.
It appears like the delusion of two moons, spread out like the water of a mirage,
resembling mountains seen from a moving boat, and is utterly devoid of any attainment of reality.
Resembling a phantom that deludes the mind, yet seedless and luminous;
appearing like inspired eloquence regarding the meaning of the teaching, it is comparable to a string of pearls in the sky.
Just as the state of being a bracelet [is unreal] in gold, just as the state of being a wave [is unreal] in water,
and just as blueness [is unreal] in the sky, so too has this [universe] arisen as something non-existent.
Without walls and devoid of colors, yet captivating to the mind;
like a painting in a dream or in the sky, it shines forth without action for a long time.
Just as a variegated fire possesses the nature of fire even though it is not [ordinary] fire,
so too does [the Lord], though being unreal in essence, assume the form and meaning of the word "world."
It rose up like a stone leaf rich with a garland of wave-lotuses,
appearing like a mass of impurity from the powder produced by the whirring of the discus.
Like a forest in summer with withered leaves, fallen and lost, and devoid of sap; resembling the frantic dance of those intent on death, it provokes the laughter of stone women.
The solitary dancing within a house of darkness is the behavior of a madman;
[but when that darkness] has its mist of ignorance stilled, it is the autumnal sky of pure consciousness.
It is as if carved upon a pillar, or depicted on a painted wall;
it is fashioned from clay, yet it possesses consciousness—or rather, it is devoid of consciousness.
Then the fourth section, concerning stability, was composed;
it consists of three thousand verses and is filled with well-spoken narratives and legends.
Thus, the world has come to abide in the form of the sense of "I," fully developed through the sequence of the seer and the seen; this has been described here.
"This delusion of the world, resplendent throughout the expanse of the ten directions,
has thus come to increase"— this is what is said there concerning its long duration.
Then follows the *Upaśāntiprakaraṇa*, consisting of five thousand [verses];
this fifth section is declared to be purifying and beautiful through the lineage of the sages.
"The delusion that 'this world,' 'I,' and 'you' exist has arisen"—
it is in this summary of verses that it is explained how this [delusion] is pacified.
When the chapter on tranquility is heard, cyclic existence is stilled;
that which was previously perceived through delusion is now seen clearly as merely a slight attainment.
Reduced to a hundredth part, it remains in the form of extinguished delusion,
residing within the mind of another's conceptualization, like the unreal splendor of a city in a dream.
It is as unobtainable as the roar of a battle in a dream occurring at one's own side,
and like the terrifying sound of a thunderbolt from a cloud whose fury has subsided.
She is like a city created by the imagination of a forgotten dream;
she possesses a dark-complexioned body, like one who will soon attend the festivals in the gardens of a future city.
It is like the experience of the meaning of a fierce story being told by a tongue that has vanished;
it is like a wall-surface pervaded by a painting whose colors have not yet been applied to the mind.
When forgotten, it is like a city of imagination;
though possessing the splendor of all seasons, it has never arisen, yet its excellent form appears as if manifest.
It is colored by the essence of spring with the form of future excellent flowers,
and is like a river of calm water whose surging waves are hidden within.
The sixth chapter, titled "Nirvāṇa," has thus been proclaimed;
the extent of the remaining text should be known as that which bestows great benefit.
Upon that Buddha, the listener becomes one who has attained nirvāṇa, with all conceptual constructions stilled;
he is the self-luminous essence beyond the object of thought, the nature of pure consciousness, free from all affliction.
Transparent as the treasury of the supreme ether, with all wandering through existence stilled,
he has brought the journey of the world to its conclusion and remains well-established, having accomplished what was to be done.
He is a vajra-pillar for all extended undertakings, resembling the sky;
he is supremely satisfied, having swallowed the entire web of the world exactly as it exists.
Having become like space, his mental engagement with the perception of all forms has ceased entirely;
he is abandoned by the states of cause, effect, agency, that which is to be rejected, and that which is to be accepted.
Though possessing a body, he is bodiless; though within saṃsāra, he is beyond transmigration; consisting of pure consciousness, he is like the interior of a solid stone.

Even while the sun of consciousness shines in the world, it is as if within the belly of darkness; though its nature is that of supreme illumination, it has, as it were, reached a state of ultimate blindness.
The wicked play of saṃsāra has been blocked, the plague of the poison of desire has been destroyed;
the vampire of egoism has perished—he who possesses a body is yet bodiless.
This splendor of the world rests upon a single tip of one of his pores,
like a bee upon a flower somewhere on Mount Meru.
Within the hollow of the space of consciousness in every single atom, it sustains thousands of world-glories and, having created them, beholds them.

O Mahāmati, even by hundreds of thousands of millions of Hari, Hara, and Abjaja, the expansion of the heart of one who possesses liberation cannot be measured; alas, there is surely no such expansion for that which is non-existent.
The eighteenth canto, titled "Description of the Section," by Vasiṣṭha.
Within this very measure of consciousness, supreme awakening arises,
just as from a sown seed, a good fruit necessarily follows.
Even a human-authored treatise is to be accepted if it reveals logical reasoning;
conversely, even that which is of divine origin is to be rejected by one who adheres strictly to logic.
A statement endowed with reason is to be accepted even from a child;
anything else is to be rejected like a blade of grass—even if spoken by the Lotus-born Brahmā.
Who can instruct that passionate man who, thinking "this is my father's well," drinks the bitter water of a pit while abandoning the Ganges standing right before him?
Just as when the dawn has broken, light will inevitably arrive,
so too will self-discrimination arise within this measure of consciousness.
When [the teaching] has been heard from the mouth of a wise person or understood by oneself, and when an impression has gradually arisen in the intellect through repeated investigation; MU_2,18.6.
First, there arises within him a highly refined command of speech—
pure and lofty like a jasmine creeper— which serves as the ornament for the assembly hall.
Supreme detachment arises, endowed with the quality of greatness,
by which even kings and even pythons develop affection.
The person who knows what precedes and what follows becomes wise in all matters,
just as one with clear vision, holding a lamp in hand, perceives objects clearly at night.
The defects such as greed and delusion gradually diminish sufficiently,
just as the mists in the direction of the quarters fade away when autumn is near.
The intellects require only the practice of discernment;
no action whatsoever bears fruit without its own repeated practice.
The mind attains clarity like a great lake in autumn;
it achieves supreme equanimity like the ocean when Mount Mandara has ceased its churning.
Free from internal darkness, like a vajra-peak that has cast away the veil of gloom,
wisdom blazes forth intensely, discerning the true nature of all things.
Views such as wretchedness, poverty, and suffering, even when their inner nature has been revealed,
do not cut into one's vital points, just as arrows do not pierce one who is clad in armor.
The terrifying fears of cyclic existence do not tear at the heart of the wise man, even though they stand before him, just as rats cannot gnaw through a great boulder.
"How can there be a beginning for birth and action, which depend on fate and human effort?"—
such a multitude of doubts is extinguished just as darkness is dispelled by the sun.
In every way, attachment to all things indeed subsides when the light of wisdom has arisen, just as it does when the night has passed away.
Like the ocean, there arises in the one who investigates a depth of being; like Mount Meru, a steadfastness;
and like the moon, an inner coolness.
That state of liberation while living gradually reaches full maturity for that yogi who has stilled all mental constructs, having entered into it.
Cool toward all objects, pure, supremely illuminating, and wise,
it attains supreme radiance like the full moonlight of the moon.
In the stainless sky of the heart, where the sun of discernment shines with the light of tranquility,
the banners of strife that create a multitude of misfortunes do not rise.
The thirsts of those who are gentle subside, attain purity, and remain well-restrained; they become motionless and inert, like a mass of clouds in autumn.
Vulgar crudeness, which acts with such recklessness and cruelty,
ceases like the sport of ghosts when their faces turn pale at the break of day.
Mental anxieties do not ravage the intellect that is firmly fixed upon the foundation of Dharma and has ascended the yoke of fortitude, just as winds cannot uproot a painted creeper.
A living being does not fall into the pit that consists of attachment to sense objects; for who indeed, once he has learned the path, would run headlong into a chasm?

The intellect of those who follow true scriptures and virtuous conduct delights in action that is non-contradictory, as it arises spontaneously, like a virtuous woman in the courtyard of the inner apartments.
Within each and every one of the atoms found throughout millions of worlds, he whose intellect is free from the notion of creation beholds the worlds situated therein.
For a person whose inner organ has been purified by the realization of the means to liberation,
the flood of enjoyments neither causes distress nor brings delight at any time.
He perceives those multitudes of creations that fall and rise without obstruction in every single atom, like waves upon the water.
He feels no aversion toward things that have arisen, nor does he long for those that have ceased; though awakened, he performs his duties like a tree that is not yet awake.
He appears like an ordinary person in the world, following whatever comes to him;
yet, in the attainment of desired or undesired results, he remains unconquered in his heart.
Having studied and analyzed this entire treatise, one experiences this for oneself;
it is not merely a matter of hearsay like a boon or a curse.
This treatise is indeed easy to understand; it is a beautiful poem adorned with various ornaments, dense with aesthetic flavor (rasa), and elucidated through illustrative examples.
One who knows even a little of the words and their meanings understands this by himself;
however, he who does not know this by himself must hear it from a learned person.
Once this has been heard, reflected upon, and known, then for the attainment of liberation here, no further practice such as austerity, meditation, or recitation is of any use.
Indeed, for a person who has repeatedly examined this treatise through intense study,
preceded by scholarship and preceded by the purification of the mind, [the realization arises].
The mature [realization] that "I am the world"— this demon of the seer and the seen—
subsides of its own accord and without obstacle, just as a demon vanishes at the rising of the sun.
The delusion that "the world" and "I" exist ceases once it is truly understood;
like a dream-illusion fully recognized, it no longer delights us at all.
Just as joy or sorrow caused by an imaginary city does not afflict a person, so too the delusion of the world does not trouble one who has fully understood it within.
Just as a painted snake, once fully recognized, does not cause fear of a snake,
so too the perceived snake, once fully recognized, does not bestow pleasure or pain.
Just as the serpent-nature of a painted snake perishes through thorough knowledge,
so too does cyclic existence, though it remains present, become pacified.
O you who are impatient with the sprouts of the *sumana* flower, there might be some degree of conflict in [the pursuit of] worldly goals;
however, in the attainment of the state of ultimate reality, there is no conflict for us.
In the crushing of a flower petal, there is a movement of its parts;
however, in this case, there is only the cognition of the mere intellect, not the cognition of the limbs or their parts.
Seated on a comfortable seat, eating as is appropriate, and never remaining engaged in activities contrary to right conduct regarding the web of enjoyments; MU_2,18.44.
One should contemplate this treatise, as well as other subjects, at every opportunity and in every place with ease, according to the possibility of meeting with virtuous companions.
One attains the awakening of great wisdom, which brings peace to saṃsāra, and by means of that,
one never again undergoes the oppression of the machine of the womb.
Those beings who, having obtained enjoyments, remain attached to their flavor—even if they are worms in their own mother’s excrement—are not to be called base. (MU 2.18.47)
Listen now, O Rāghava, to this expansion of knowledge being told by me, which contains the most essential core of the intellect.
Listen now in detail to that [tradition] by which this scripture is heard,
and by which definition its true meaning is investigated.

The wise know that to be an example (dṛṣṭānta) by which, through a perceived object, there is the comprehension of an object not yet experienced here, yielding the fruit of assistance to understanding.
Without an illustration, O Rāma, a novel matter is not understood,
just as household goods and utensils in a house at night cannot be seen without a lamp.
O descendant of Kakutstha, whatever examples I have used here to awaken your understanding, all of them possess a specific cause; yet that which is to be attained is itself without cause.
The relationship of cause and effect between the objects of comparison and the things compared exists for all things whatsoever, with the exception of the Supreme Brahman.
For when an illustration from the instruction on Brahman is indeed cited here,
it is therefore understood as sharing the same properties in only one respect.
Whatever illustration is given here for the purpose of awakening to the reality of Brahman, each of them should be understood as being like the world perceived within a dream.
This being the case, how could there be an example possessing form within a formless Brahman? Thus, the conceptual objections of the foolish do not arise.
Any other [fault], such as the perception of a fallacy of contradiction with established facts (*siddhaviruddha*) and so forth, does not arise at all when refuting the example,
because the world is like a dream.

The unreal is that which, having been examined as present, does not exist in the past or the future; just as the waking state is established, so too is the dream state proven for everyone down to children, without exception.
Those objects which arise through dreams, mental constructs, meditation, boons, curses, medicinal herbs, and so forth,
serve as the analogies here, because the state of the world is of that same nature.
Whatever other treatises have been composed by the author for the sake of the means to liberation,
it is this very one alone that provides the systematic arrangement for the awakening to what is to be known.
And that the world has the nature of a dream will be understood from the sacred scripture;
it cannot be stated quickly, for speech indeed proceeds only step by step.
The world is like a dream, a mental construction, a city of the gods, and so forth;
since these alone are the illustrative examples, therefore they appear here and no others.
When that which lacks a cause is compared by its cause for the sake of awakening,
it is impossible for there to be complete similarity in those delusive comparisons.
The wise person, free from dispute, must accept that the subject of comparison shares a common property with the object of comparison in at least one respect, in order to achieve understanding.
Indeed, for the perception of an object, apart from mere light,
nothing else— such as the vessel, oil, or wick— is of any use.
O dear one, by virtue of sharing a common characteristic in one respect, the means of comparison brings about the cognition of the object compared,
just as a lamp reveals an object through its radiance.
When the awakening of understanding regarding that which is to be known arises through even a mere portion of an illustration,
the determination of the meaning of the great sentence (mahāvākya) should be grasped as something to be adopted.
One should not, by falling into the state of a fallacious logician, destroy awakened consciousness through those unholy conceptual constructions that deny direct experience.

Whether it be that which produces experience through investigation, having entered into the context of verbal discourse among people like us, or even another word spoken by a woman, or likewise a Vedic utterance— if it is merely a verbal prattle, it is not authoritative scripture.
O friend, our conviction is that all scriptures constitute a single unified statement;

for this reason, we hold that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for us other than direct experience (*saṃvedana*), which is nourished by its own internal limbs consisting of the meaning as it appears in the scriptures.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Means of Valid Cognition and Examples," by Vasiṣṭha.
In comparisons, it is the possession of common characteristics regarding specific parts that is apprehended;
for if there were complete similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, what difference would there be?
Through the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures on the realization of the one Self derived from the Buddha as an example,
and through the direct realization of the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), peace is called Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, enough with the proliferation of conceptual distinctions between the illustrative example and the subject illustrated;
by whatever means of reasoning possible, one should quickly take recourse in the meaning of the Great Sentence.
Know that peace is the supreme good; one should strive for its attainment. When the rice has been obtained, it is to be eaten—what is the use of speculations regarding its preparation?
Those who seek awakening employ non-causes as causes for the sake of understanding;
they do so by means of analogies that resemble the object of comparison only in certain respects.
One whose soul is devoid of discernment should not remain attached to worldly enjoyments here,
like a blind frog that has grown fat within the belly of a stone.
Through examples and reasonings, one should diligently abandon that which is contrary to what is desired; one who possesses discernment should become endowed with the meaning of the *Śāntiśāstra*.
Through the study of the scriptures, tranquility, gentleness, wisdom, and association with those who know them,
he intermittently engaged in the practice of acquiring wealth in accordance with the Dharma.
The wise person should investigate until he attains within himself that repose known as the fourth state (turya)— the peace from which there is no further destruction.
For one who is established in repose in the Fourth State (turya) and has crossed over the ocean of worldly existence—
whether living or dead, whether a householder or an ascetic— this [liberation] applies.
He has no concern for what is done or left undone, nor for the errors of the revealed and traditional scriptures;
like the ocean without Mount Mandara, he remains as he is.

The similarity between the objects of comparison and the subjects of comparison should be understood through a single aspect for the sake of awakening to what is to be known; one should not remain fickle in raising objections.
By whatever means possible, you must quickly realize that which is to be realized for the sake of liberation; those who are agitated and eager for debate do not perceive this.
When the Self has come to rest in the heart, in the space of consciousness, as the very nature of experience,
he who asks about what is not a real object is called one whose beak is intent on prattle.
The ignorant one, conceptualizing cognition through portions of conceited imagination,
defiles his inner awareness just as a snake defiles its own stainless mouth.
O Rāma, just as the ocean is the abode of all existing waters, so too is perception the sole authority here; listen to that.
The wise know that sensation is the direct perception of the essence of all objects;
indeed, that which is established in relation to it is declared to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That which is the experiencing, the feeling, and the comprehension of things as they truly are is given the name "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) here; and that very thing is the living soul (jīva).
That very consciousness is again of the nature of the notion of "I-ness" (ahantā);
that consciousness by which it arises is known as the "object" (padārtha).
Through delusions such as volitions and conceptual constructions, it manifests as the world with its various sequences, just as water appears as waves and the like.
Previously, at the beginning of creation, having first manifested as something causeless through the play of creation,
it itself became the manifest cause within its own self.
The causality of this living being (jīva), though non-existent, persists;
it has become manifest as if it were real within this attainment of the form of the world.
But inquiry itself, having destroyed its own form along with the notion of "I," quickly brings about the supreme state that is directly perceived.
When even the analytical inquiry, while investigating, does not perceive a self,
then that which remains is the supreme, beyond all description.

When the mind is desireless and tranquil, there is no purpose served here by those actions of the sense organs— neither by those performed nor by those unperformed, since there is an absence of mental cultivation.
When the mind is desireless and tranquil, those organs of action do not engage at all in action and the like, like a machine that is no longer being operated.
They know that sensation is the cause for the movement of the mental mechanism,
just as a rope is contained within the wooden frame of a ram.
The world, agitated by forms, light, mental attention, objects, and so forth,
exists within consciousness, just as movement exists within the wind.
When the pure awareness of the Self of all arises, it shines as that very essence,
manifesting in forms that extend beyond space and time, both external and internal, including the body.
The seer alone remains, maintaining his own nature while appearing as the object of sight;
just as it appears there in its own form, so indeed is it.
Just as the Self alone exists there, having as it were attained the state of volition,
so too does it quickly abide there and shine as if possessing that very form.
Because it consists of all things, it is logical that the object of vision appears as if it were the seer;
yet the state of being a seer exists only when there is a real seer, whereas for that which is non-existent, it does not exist.
Therefore, this world remains as the Brahma-cosmos without any other cause;
it is directly perceived as the Creator himself, while its constituent parts are free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhi).

O virtuous one, that supreme state which consists of nothing other than one's own effort— having cast far away the meaning of the word "fate"— is indeed attained internally by a hero through his own human exertion alone.
Reflect, for now, according to the truth and the white path of the succession of teachers,
until you yourself attain that supreme state which is pure, awakened, and of infinite forms.
The twentieth canto, titled "The Determination of the Means of Valid Cognition," by Vasiṣṭha.
Through association with the noble ones, through reasoning, and so forth, one should forcefully increase wisdom;
from that arises the state of a Great Being by means of the marks of a Great Being.
Whatever quality by which a person shines forth here,
one should quickly learn that very same quality from him for the sake of increasing one's own intelligence.
But this state of being a Great Person, O Rāma, which is endowed with qualities such as tranquility,
does not attain perfection for anyone without right knowledge.
Through knowledge, qualities such as tranquility increase by following the path of the virtuous;
they become praiseworthy through their inner fruit, like new sprouts from rain.
And from qualities such as tranquility, supreme knowledge increases,
just as an excellent rain of śāli rice grows from sacrifices consisting of food offerings.
Virtues such as tranquility arise from knowledge, and likewise, knowledge arises from tranquility and the other virtues; these two increase one another, just like a lake and its water.
Knowledge arises from the conduct of virtuous persons, and from knowledge comes the practice of virtuous persons;
thus, knowledge and the practice of virtuous persons increase through their mutual dependence.
Yet, even one of these two is not sufficient for a person to achieve success in this world.
Just as the joy of singing is accomplished by the female protector of the rice fields through her far-reaching, high-pitched song,
accompanied by the scaring away of the birds.
Through knowledge, the effort of a true person, and by means of that which is non-agent yet has the form of an agent,
the person who is likewise free from desire attains the supreme state.
O descendant of Raghu, this sequence of right conduct has been proclaimed by me;
now, this sequence of knowledge shall likewise be properly expounded.
This [work], which brings fame, prolongs life, and bestows the fruits of human goals,
should indeed be heard by a wise person from a trustworthy teacher who has mastered the meaning of the self-scriptures.
But having heard this, through the purity of your intellect, you will by force attain the state of the virtuous,
just as water inevitably attains clarity through contact with the *kataka* nut.
O Sage, once the knowable has been known, this mind indeed goes helplessly to the supreme state;
for that which is realized as the indivisible, supreme reality never again abandons the state of such realization.
The chapter titled "The Succession of the Wise Man of Knowledge" is concluded. Section 3: The Chapter on the Conduct of One Seeking Liberation.
Section 4: Origination.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Through the radiance of speech, the knower of Brahman perceives Brahman within himself as if in a dream;
let him who knows this very thing know it through its own words and meanings.
By this reasoning, when the entire creation exists within the ether of Brahman, the one who is eager to raise the objection, "What is this, and whose is it? is refuted.
I shall speak this according to my knowledge, according to the facts, according to their sequence, and according to their true nature; let all of it be heard, O wise ones.
One perceives the world as a dream— the sky of consciousness consisting of the body and the senses—
wherein the illustrations of the dream-like nature of saṃsāra are fully contained right here within this very life.
Following this treatise consisting of the discourse on the conduct of one seeking liberation,
I shall now fully expound this "Treatise on Origination."
This bondage is the existence of the visible; in the absence of the visible, there is no bondage.
Listen now in due order to how this visible object does not actually exist.
Whatever arises in the world, that indeed grows;
that very same thing attains liberation, or heaven, or even hell.
Therefore, for the sake of your own understanding, I shall first explain how and by what means one enters into the cycle of worldly existence.
O Rāghava, hear this meaning of the section in brief;
thereafter, I shall explain it to you in detail according to your desire.
All this world that is seen, both the stationary and the moving,
perishes at the end of the eon like a dream upon waking from deep sleep.
Then there remains something that is neither light nor darkness spread abroad, motionless and profound, ineffable and unmanifest.
"Ṛta," "Ātman," "Supreme Brahman," "Truth," and so forth— these are the names devised by the wise for the sake of conventional usage to designate that Great Self.
That very Self, though being such, shining forth as if it were something else,
seems to enter into the state of living beings, undergoing the various afflictions of future existence.
Then, having fallen into the agitation of conceptualizing the meaning of the term "jīva," it becomes the mind (manas), which is by nature silent but becomes sluggish through the act of thinking.
By that [mind], the mind becomes one with the Great Supreme Self;
it assumes an unstable form from that which is perfectly stable, like a wave from the ocean.
That [consciousness] itself constantly and spontaneously conceives [its objects] at will;
by that means, this splendor of a magical illusion is spread out as if it were extended.
Just as the referent of the word "bracelet" exists separately within gold, yet there is no such thing as a "bracelet" apart from it;
likewise, the referent of the word "world" does not exist apart from the Supreme.
This world exists as it is, non-different from Brahman alone;
there is no object corresponding to the word "world," just as there is no such thing as a bracelet apart from gold.
Just as a moving wave is nothing but the heat of the mirage-water,
so too this worldly splendor, like a magical illusion, is projected by the mind alone.
Ignorance, transmigratory existence, bondage, illusion, delusion, and the great darkness—
these are the names by which she is designated by those who know all things.
First, listen to this description of the nature of bondage being told;
thereafter, O moon-faced one, you shall understand the true nature of liberation.
The existence of the state of being an object for the seer is called bondage;
the seer is bound by virtue of the object, and is liberated through the absence of the object.
The world, "you," "I," and so forth—the nature of creation—is called the visible. As long as this exists, liberation is not found.
"This is not it, this is not it"—the disease of the visible world is not pacified by such futile lamentations that give rise to conceptual constructions; on the contrary, it increases.

Nor can the real, perceptible world be refuted by the grinding of logical arguments, nor by the observances of various religious orders and so forth; for these [latter] are merely investigators of that which already exists.
If this visible world were real, it could never cease to be;
for there is no coming into being for the non-existent, nor is there any passing away of the existent.
Wherever this Self, whose nature is neither consciousness nor unconsciousness, abides,
there the splendor of the visible world arises for it, even within the interior of an atom.
Therefore, this world of appearances exists; yet it has been wiped away by me through asceticism, meditation, and recitation, just as one is satisfied with a mere drop of sour gruel.
If indeed this visible world exists,
it is reflected without doubt in this mirror of consciousness, even within the interior of a single atom.
O Rāma, whatever is situated here or there— be it mountains, the sky, the earth, rivers, or oceans— is reflected in the mirror of consciousness (cid-ādarśa) in exactly that same way.
Then, there again arises suffering— old age and death, birth,
the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence, and that which is gross and subtle, moving and unmoving.
This visible world has been wiped away by me; I no longer abide within it.
This very state is the inexhaustible seed for the recollection of cyclic existence within meditative absorption.
But while this world of appearances exists, neither the state of imperishable deep sleep nor the fourth state (turya) is possible through non-conceptual meditative absorption.
For upon emerging from meditative absorptions, this entire world-suffering appears just as it is, unbroken, like the state immediately following deep sleep.
O Rāma, what indeed is gained by meditative absorptions? For even if there is a momentary state of equanimity, what happiness is there when one is again struck down by misfortune?
Or if one should attain stability in non-conceptual meditative absorption, that state resembles an imperishable deep sleep; I consider that to be the stainless state.
When this visible world exists, nothing at all is attained;
