for it is through the delusion of the mind that the error of the world wanders here and there.
If, moreover, the observer remains by force contemplating the state of being a stone,
even at the end of that [contemplation], the state of being an object of perception arises for him once again.
Furthermore, non-conceptual meditative absorptions do not remain as something comparable to a stone for everyone;
rather, this is experienced by some.
Yet these meditative absorptions do not become as firmly rooted as a stone;
they do not reach that supreme state which is peaceful, of the nature of consciousness, unborn, and undecaying.
Therefore, if this visible world were real, it could never cease;
that it might cease through austerity, recitation, and meditation is merely the imagination of the ignorant.
Just as the seed of a lotus dwells within the hollow of a lotus-pod in the form of a coiled sprout, so does the cognition of the visible object reside within the seer.
Just as flavor exists in substances, just as oil exists in sesame seeds and the like,
and just as fragrance exists in flowers, so does the cognition of the visible exist in the seer.
Just as the fragrance of camphor and other substances arises wherever they may be situated,
so too does the world arise within the belly of the element of consciousness.
Just as here your dream, mental construction, and thought-kingdom are seen through your own experience, so too the ground of the visible exists within the heart.
Therefore, just as a piśāca residing within a mental construction destroys a child,
so too does this [grasping] which takes the form of the visible destroy the internal observer.
Just as a sprout situated within a seed manifests its radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the cognition of the visible expand itself.
Just as the wonder of a gem is eternally manifest within its interior, which is devoid of rising or setting,
so too the existence of the world is the inherent nature within the interior of the substance whose body is pure consciousness.
The second canto, titled "Description of the Causes of Bondage," by Vasiṣṭha.
Listen to this narrative called "The Birth from Space," an ornament for the ears,
which is the section known as "The Origin," by means of which you shall understand, O Raghava.
There is here a twice-born man named Ākāśaja, who is supremely righteous,
constantly devoted solely to meditation, and ever intent on the welfare of all creatures.
When he lived for so long, Death thought to himself:
"I am indeed inexhaustible; I devour all beings one after another in due order."
In this way, why do I not devour the Brahmin born of space? Against him my power is blunted, like the edge of a sword on a stone.
Having reflected thus, he then went to that city to kill him;
for no one who has exerted effort ever abandons their undertaking.
Then, as soon as Death himself enters that abode,
fire— resembling the conflagration at the end of an aeon— burns him up.
Even though he had entered by tearing through the great mass of flames,
upon seeing the twice-born man, he strove diligently, desiring to seize him with his hand.
And though he was powerful, he was unable to seize the Brahmin even when seen before him at a distance of a hundred cubits, just as one cannot grasp a person created by mere thought.
Then Death, having approached Yama, the dispeller of doubts, asked:
"O Lord, why am I unable to consume that which is born of space?"
Yama said:
"O Death, you alone are not at all capable of slaying by force;
it is the actions of the one to be slain, and the agents of those actions here, that do so, and nothing else."
Therefore, diligently seek out the deeds of this Brahmin who is to be slain; with their assistance, you shall devour him.
Then Death wandered about, intent on searching for that deed,
through circles, the ends of the quarters, lakes, rivers, and all directions.
Forests, thickets, and groves; the slopes of mountains and oceans;
other continents, wild jungles, cities, and towns.
Having thus wandered over villages, entire kingdoms, and the deep recesses of distant regions,
he found nothing whatsoever anywhere on the circle of the earth.
Death exerted himself to obtain those actions born of space,
but like a wise man [seeking] the son of a barren woman, or another [seeking] a mountain of conceptual construction, he failed.
Then, having arrived, he questioned Yama, who is skilled in all matters;
for he is the ultimate refuge and the source of authority for those who live under his rule in times of doubt.
Mṛtyu said:
"O Lord, tell me, where do the karmas of one born of space reside?
Then Dharmarāja, having reflected for a very long time, spoke this.
The King of Dharma said:
"O Death, there are no actions whatsoever belonging to one born from space;
for this brahmin, Ākāśaja, was born solely from space itself."
He who is born from space alone must be as stainless as space itself;
there are no auxiliary causes whatsoever for him.
There is not even the slightest connection between this [present body] and past karma,
just as there is none for the son of a barren woman or for one who has never been born.
Therefore, this self-existent one is indeed unborn and truly unproduced;
he has no prior karma, just as there can be no great tree in the sky.
This mind of his is not subject to necessity because of the absence of prior karma;
for today, he has not accumulated any further karma whatsoever.
This Self, whose nature is the sheath of space, is eternally established in a meditative absorption that has the form of the clear sky; for it, there are no actions whatsoever.
It has no past actions, nor does it perform any action today;
thus, this [self] here consists of nothing but the space of consciousness.
The movement of the vital breath that is observed as its activity is perceived by us and others; yet we see this, while it has no conscious thought regarding that activity.
His body is seen by us, yet he does not perceive it as distinct from the supreme state,
just as one does not perceive a carved figure on a pillar of consciousness as separate from the pillar itself.
Just as an uncarved statue of a woman exists within a pillar,
so too, O twice-born one, does this Supreme Self abide within, having become one's own self.
Just as liquidity exists in water, emptiness in space,
and vibration in the wind, so does this [nature] exist in the supreme state.
For he has no actions accumulated today, nor any from the past; therefore, he has not fallen under the power of saṃsāra in this world.
That which arises in the absence of auxiliary causes is experienced as not being distinct from its own [material] cause.
This twice-born one is of the nature of the stainless space-receptacle, self-existent;
he was not the agent in the past, nor is he so today—tell me, how can he be overcome?
When he performs with his intellect that mental construction called death,
at that very moment, being devoid of that intellect, he himself will die.
He who possesses the firm conviction, "I am this [body] composed of earth and other elements," quickly becomes identified with the earth; and he can be grasped.
But this one, who lacks the form of an earthly king and possesses the nature of pure consciousness, is not at all fit to be grasped, just as the sky cannot be seized even with a strong rope.
Mṛtyu said: "O Blessed One, tell me how it is that one is born empty;
tell me also how the earth and the other elements exist, or how they do not exist."
Yama said:
This twice-born one was never born, nor is he ever non-existent;
he is solely the light of pure consciousness, and thus he remains.
Upon the occurrence of the great dissolution, nothing whatsoever remains;
only Brahman exists—peaceful, undecaying, the infinite Self, and absolute.
Know that pure consciousness, which is free from the object of thought, to be the subtlest of the subtle among atoms;
so subtle is it that, in its proximity, even the sky appears like a mountain.

Because its essential nature is pure consciousness, it perceives within the mind the form that appears as "I am the body" as something occurring by mere chance, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
This very Brahman, at the beginning of that creation within the belly of the sky,
self-luminous and having attained the state of the Self-born, shines forth, ageless and immortal.
He has no body, no actions, no agency, and no latent impressions;
he is the pure space of consciousness, an all-pervading mass of awareness.
No web of past latent impressions (vāsanā) exists for him at all,
for he is of the nature of space alone, like a light of the nature of radiance.
In this way, he is perceived solely through sensation alone;
yet when that mere sensation is completely stilled, even such a one is no longer seen.
Therefore, just as the space of consciousness is, so too are its perceptions;
for how indeed could there be the occurrence of earth and the like here, and in what manner?
Therefore, O Death, do not strive to seize me by this assault;
it is never possible for anyone at any time to grasp the sky.
Rāma said:
"O Brahman, you have described my great-grandfather as Brahmā himself;
it is my conviction that he is the Self-born, the Unborn, the One-Souled, the Self of Consciousness."
Vasiṣṭha said: "It is even so, O Rāma; this Brahman has been described by me to you.
It was on account of this that Death formerly engaged in a dispute with Yama."
During that Manvantara, when Death, devouring all beings, was carrying away the creatures,
he attained strength and himself undertook an effort to overcome the Lotus-born One.
Thus, having been swiftly exhorted by Yama, the King of Dharma,
one finds pleasure precisely in that which is performed constantly.
How indeed can Brahmā, whose body is the supreme ether,
devoid of mental constructs and lacking any form such as earth and the like, be ascended?
That which is indeed the wonder of consciousness, possessing the experience of space, is nothing but the sky of consciousness itself; it possesses neither causality nor the state of being an effect.
Just as the person of one's own imagination appears with a form shimmering in space,
though devoid of earth and other elements, so does the Self-existent One shine forth.
In the absolute, solitary Supreme Self, there is neither the visible object nor the seer;
nevertheless, because it is itself consciousness, this self-existent one shines forth as such.
This mind, which is nothing but volition, is called Brahman;
it is the person who is the ether of volition, and for him, earth and the other elements do not exist.
Just as a bodiless figurine situated within a painting appears,
even so does Brahma appear, a person born from the space of consciousness.
The self-existent one shines as Brahman—the mere, infinite, and beginningless-and-endless expanse of consciousness—by the power of his own mind;
though appearing as if possessing form due to its own essence, in reality he has no body, just like the son of a barren woman.
The third canto, titled "Description of the Original Creation," [from] the Rāmāyaṇa.
Thus it is: this pure mind, devoid of earth and the other elements, is like the sky;
O Sage, that which is devoid of earth and the rest is truly called Brahman.
In this regard, tell me: why is past memory not the cause?
For as it is for me, so it is for others and for all beings.
Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who possesses a prior body accompanied by past karma, memory arises; that is the cause for the persistence of transmigratory existence.
When no prior karma whatsoever exists for Brahmā,
how and from where could his recollection of the past arise?
Therefore, it appears either as causeless or as having its sole cause in its own consciousness;
being non-different from its own cause, it is self-existent and possesses its own nature by itself.
This body of the Self-existent One is indeed *ātivāhika*;
O Rāma, a material (*ādhibhautika*) body is not possible for the Unborn.
Rāma said:
Is there one subtle body (ātivāhika) and another material body (ādhibhautika)? Or is there for all classes of beings only one [body] from Brahman?
Vasiṣṭha said: For all beings whose nature is causal, there are indeed two bodies;
however, for the Unborn (Ātman), because of the non-existence of a cause, there is only the single subtle body (ativāhika).
The one Unborn is the supreme cause of all classes of beings;
there is no cause for the Unborn, and therefore he possesses a single body.
The body of the first Prajāpati is not composed of material elements at all;
consisting of a subtle, transportable body, he appears as one whose nature is space.
This first Lord of Creatures, whose body is mind alone and not composed of earth and the other elements, has space for his form and extends forth all creatures.
And those [causes], which are of the nature of nirvāṇa, exist without any other causes;
for it is experienced by everyone that whatever arises from whatever is indeed that very thing.
Nirvāṇa alone is the first; that very same thing is supreme awakening, and it is that alone which remains as mind-only; it does not undergo the state of being earth and so forth.
For all beings whose minds are engaged in the activities of saṃsāra,
this first reflected image is the mind-body that arises of its own accord.
Since this creation has issued forth from the prior prototype as non-different from its own nature, it is like the perception of movement arising from the wind.
Because this creation has the form of creative intuition (*pratibhāna*), it shines forth as consisting of nothing but intuition;
thus, this creation exists as if it were a real experience.
In this regard, the examples are a city in a dream and likewise sexual union with a woman in a dream;
though non-existent, they shine with the experience of reality through the fulfillment of their objects.
Not composed of earth or the other elements, appearing as the form of space and bodiless,
the Lord of Beings, who is his own self, shines in the form of a person as if he possessed a body.
Because it consists of the form of mental constructs, consciousness arises and then subsides;
because its own nature is self-dependent, it neither arises nor subsides.
Brahmā, free from volitional constructs and devoid of forms such as earth and the rest,
is the pure essence of consciousness alone, the cause for the existence of the three worlds.
Just as this very volition shines forth as its own arising under a particular name,
so too does it appear as having the nature of space, like a mountain born of your own volition.
Due to the firm-rooted and singular forgetfulness of its subtle nature,
it falsely appears like a ghost through the perception of it as a material body.
For one whose great consciousness has awakened through this first effort,
no forgetfulness of the subtle body arises, because of the purity of their awareness.
Therefore, the demonic spirit of materiality does not arise for him;
it is unreal, like a mirage, falsely producing the delusion of dullness.
When Brahmā consists of mind alone and is not composed of earth and the other elements, therefore the universe is mind alone; for whatever is that, it is indeed just that.
Since there are no cooperative causes for that which is unborn, there can likewise be none at all for that which is born from it; therefore, some [causes] do not exist.
The diversity of effects arises from the cause; therefore, there is nothing here [in the effect] that does not exist [in the cause].
Whatever the nature of the pure cause, such is the effect established here.
But here, the relationship of cause and effect is not at all tenable;
for exactly as is the Supreme Brahman, so too is the triple world.
The world is stretched out by Brahman as if it were the state of being mind,
non-different from the pure Self, just as fluidity is non-different from water.
Everything is stretched out by the mind; this entire expanse is indeed unreal, like a city of the imagination or a city of the Gandharvas.
There is no state of being a physical entity, just as there is no state of being a snake in a rope;
how then could those who are awakened, such as Brahmā and the others, remain therein?
For one whose mind is awakened, there is indeed only the subtle body (ātivāhika);
how and why could there even be any discussion here of a material body (ādhibhautika-deha)?
For the person named "mind," which assumes various forms,
the kingdom of the mind known as the world stands as if it were real.
Know that the mind alone is Viriñca, whose nature is volition;
having brought its own form to expansion, this universe is stretched out by the mind.
Virinca is the form of the mind, and the mind is the body of Virinca;
earth and the other elements do not exist here [in reality], and therefore earth and the rest are merely imagined.
Just as within a lotus there is a lotus-stalk, so too the mind exists within the field of vision;
yet the mind and the vision of what is seen are never, in any way, distinct from one another.

And thus, in this matter, your own dream and mental construction—the intellect that rules the mind—are themselves the examples seen through direct experience; therefore, the ground of the visible world exists within the heart.
Therefore, just as a piśāca dwelling within the mental constructions of a child destroys him,
so too does this [grasping] which takes the form of the visible destroy the internal observer.
Just as a sprout situated within a seed manifests a radiant body according to place and time, so indeed does the cognition of the visible expand itself.
If the suffering of the visible world does not subside at any time because the visible world itself does not subside, then there is no state of isolation for the knower.
However, when the visible world is impossible, the state of being a knower subsides even while the knower remains; indeed, they call that his liberation.
The Fourth Sarga, titled "The Cause of Bondage," by Vālmīki.
While the leader of sages was thus speaking these unrestrained words, the assembly became single-minded in their desire to hear, remaining silent and still.
The tinkling sounds of the networks of small bells were stilled, and even the hārītas and parrots within their cages had ceased their play, no longer fluttering about.
Even while the women remained with their amorous charms completely forgotten,
the entire royal assembly hall stood as if fixed upon a painted wall.
When only a single muhūrta remained of the day, its heat became mild;
all worldly activity, along with the rays of the sun, began to diminish.
Breezes blew, rich with the intoxication of clusters of blossoming lotuses, as if they had come to listen with sweetly trembling movements.
Like the sun abandoning its wandering through the arrangement of day and night to contemplate what it has heard, he left his solitude and went to the empty slope of the mountain of setting.
In the forest lands, the darkness produced by the onset of mist arose,
like the inner coolness of tranquility resulting from hearing the teachings on higher knowledge.
People in all ten directions became motionless,
as if they had abandoned all activity in order to listen with full attention.
The shadows grew long, as if they possessed elongated necks to hear the entire sequence of descriptions concerning the lineage of Vasiṣṭha.
The doorkeeper, bowing low before him, said to the lord of the earth:
"O King, the time for bathing and the worship of the twice-born has indeed passed by far."
Then the venerable Vasiṣṭha, withdrawing his sweet speech, said:
"O Great King, let what has been heard up to this point suffice for you today."
Having said, "We shall speak another [word] in the morning," he remained silent;
having heard this, the king said, "So be it," for the sake of increasing his prosperity.
With flowers, offerings of water for the hands (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), respectful honors, and the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
he reverently worshipped the gods, celestial sages, forest hermits, and brahmins.
Then the entire assembly rose, including the circle of kings and sages,
their faces surrounded by a halo from the mass of rays scattered by their earrings.
The armlets and bracelets jingled as they struck one another's shoulders, while the spaces between their breasts were covered by golden bands pressed down by the weight of their necklaces.
With the humming sounds of awakened bees resting upon the crests of their heads,
the upper parts of their heads seemed filled with a whirring noise, as if their hair were falling away.
The quarters of the sky were turned golden by the radiance of their golden ornaments,
while the activities of their senses were completely stilled through the meaning of the Sage’s words held in their minds.
The sky-dwellers went to the heavens and the earth-dwellers to the circle of the earth;
everyone performed their own daily routines in their respective homes.
In the meantime, the dark night appeared like a young woman in a house empty of the crowds of people.
The lord of the day departed to illuminate other lands;
for it is the very nature of a virtuous person to act as a light-giver everywhere.
The twilight arose on all sides, bearing a multitude of stars,
like the splendor of spring appearing with forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
Then, like mental states within the mind, birds settled upon the mango, nīpa, and kadamba trees, at the village shrines, and inside the houses.
Adorned with fragments of clouds tinted by the sun’s radiance as if with the hue of saffron,
the western mountain, clothed in yellow garments and joined by the sky adorned with the beauty of its necklace of stars, emerges from the ocean of darkness.
When Sandhyā had departed with the offerings as she had come,
the darknesses rose up like a circle of *vetālas*.
A cool breeze blew, soft and suggesting the lilies, dripping with drops of dew and shaking its sprouts with ease.
Even the quarters of the sky, though their stars were clearly visible, fell into utter darkness,
like widowed women with long, hanging locks of hair that are deep black.
The moon, an ocean of milk, arrived in the sky, filling the world with a flood of radiant milk and appearing as if composed of elixir.
Masses of darkness fled and vanished somewhere, becoming invisible,
like the ignorance of kings' minds fleeing upon hearing the words of wisdom.
The seers, the protectors of the earth, the sages, and likewise the brahmins,
rested in their own abodes with minds as if filled with diverse thoughts.
A dark twilight, thick with gloom like a twin-bodied woman, slowly approached them there; then the dawn arrived, appearing like a mist.
The bright stars in the sky became imperceptible,
like showers of saffron powder swept away by the morning breeze.
Behold, the faculty of discernment has arrived, its eyes opened by the light of the sun,
like a fresh sprout arising within the minds of the great.
Then the sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers returned to the assembly hall,
having performed their morning rites in the same manner as the previous day.
With her former arrangement, she entered the vast assembly hall;
she became motionless in appearance, like a lotus pond when the wind has ceased.
Then, seizing the opportunity, Rāma spoke in sweet tones to Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages and the best of speakers.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, tell me clearly what the nature of the mind is,
for by it this entire cluster of defects is spread forth.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, no form whatsoever is perceived of this mind,
other than its mere name, just as [no form is seen] of the sky, which is empty and insentient by nature.
The mind does not exist as a real entity either externally or within the heart;
know, O Rāma, that it is situated everywhere, just like space.
This form that has arisen for him is non-existent, resembling the water of a mirage;
now hear in brief about form, which is like the delusion of a second moon.
O virtuous one, know that this manifestation of an object which has come into public awareness—
whether it be real or unreal— is nothing other than the mind.
That which is the manifestation of objects is designated as "mind";
there is never anything else whatsoever that exists by the name of "mind."
Know that the mind is volition; it is not distinct from volition. Just as water is inseparable from its fluidity, so too is movement inseparable from the wind.
Where there is volition, O dear one, there the mind likewise resides;
volition and the mind are never, under any circumstances, distinct from one another.
Whether it be true or untrue, know that the mind is merely that which appears as an object; that is Brahman, this Grandfather.
The self consisting of the subtle body is designated as "mind" (manas); the intellect pertaining to the material realm is the constant thought, which is the long-enduring state.
Ignorance, transmigratory existence, mind, intellect, bondage, impurity, and darkness— these, the wise know, are synonyms for the visible world.
Indeed, there is no form of the mind apart from the perceptible;
and as for this perceptible, it has indeed arisen—this I shall state again.
Just as the lotus bud exists within the seed of the lotus,
so too does the visible world exist within the supreme atom of the Great Consciousness.
Just as light belongs to illumination, just as movement belongs to the wind,
and just as liquidity belongs to water, so too is visibility the nature of the Seer.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as water exists in a mirage,
and just as a wall exists in a dream-city, so too does the perception of the visible object exist in the seer.
In this way, that which exists as if non-different from the seer— the state of being an object of sight—
I shall quickly wipe away as a stain from the mirror of your mind.

Know that the state of being a solitary one (kevalībhāva) is that which, by force, becomes the non-seerhood of this seer when the visible object is absent; it is therefore [the state] of the existent arising from the non-existent.
When the state of reality has been attained, the latent impressions of passion, hatred, and the like subside,
just as the agitation caused by movement ceases when the wind is stilled.
When everything consisting of the directions, the earth, and space has become manifest,
the nature of the light becomes stainless, just as it is in its true form.
When the perceived world— including the three worlds, you, and me— has attained non-existence,
there arises for the pure-souled seer that state of absolute isolation (kaivalya).
For just as the nature of a mirror remains solely its own essential form, even when it contains the reflections of infinite mountains and all other things; ||| MU_3.4.56 |||
When the delusion of the visible world— such as "I," "you," and "the universe"— has subsided,
there arises that state of absolute oneness while the Seer remains established, no longer a beholder.
Rāma said: "If this [world] does not cease, or if there is no non-existence of that which exists,
then we do not perceive non-existence in this visible world which bestows defects."
Therefore, O Brahmin, how can this cholera of the visible world— arising from manifold things, causing delusion, and bestowing a continuous stream of suffering— be pacified?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to this mantra for the pacification of this visible piśāca,
by which Rāma will utterly meet his death and perish.
O Raghava, that which exists can never perish;
therefore, even when it has seemingly perished, it remains as a seed within the heart.
The perception of the visible world, arising once more from the seed of memory within the space of consciousness,
spreads forth a vast defect in the form of the worlds, mountains, and sky.
In this way, there would be the fault of the impossibility of liberation, nor could there be any possibility of its [liberation's] partial attainment;
for gods, sages, and seers are seen to be recipients of liberation.
If this world had a beginning, then liberation would not belong to anyone;
whether the visible world resides outside or within the heart, it serves only for destruction.
Therefore, O Rāma, listen to this most terrifying thesis,
which you will surely understand through the subsequent text.
This world, characterized as "I" and as having the form of space, the elements, and so forth—
surely there is no such thing as the referent of the word "world" at all.
Whatever web of visible objects is seen here before one,
all that is indeed the one Brahman alone— undecaying, immortal, and immutable.
In the full, the full expands; in the tranquil, the supreme tranquility abides.
Space has arisen in space alone; Brahman resides within Brahman.
There is neither the visible object nor the seeing, neither the seer nor the act of seeing;
it is neither empty, nor inert, nor consciousness—this all-pervading reality is simply peace.
Rāma:
A mountain is ground to powder by the son of a barren woman; a hare's horn is brought to life;
and a stone, stretching out its multitude of arms, performs the Tāṇḍava dance.
"Sands flow oil, stone statues recite,
and painted clouds thunder"— such, O Lord, is this very speech.
The world consists of the mountains of old age, death, suffering, and so forth, as well as space;
how is it that even you say to me, "This does not exist"? (MU 3.4.72)
O Brahman, explain to me how this universe is neither established, nor produced, nor existent, so that this may become certain for me.
Vasiṣṭha said: "I am not one whose speech is inconsistent; listen, O Rāghava, as I speak:
how this unreal appears as real, like the son of a barren woman appearing as a horse."
This was unoriginated in the beginning; therefore, it is not sufficient [to exist] at the start of creation.
For this shines forth by means of the mind, like a city in a dream and the like.
And at the beginning of creation, the mind itself was unarisen and of non-existent nature;
listen now as I shall explain how this is experienced.
The mind spreads this defect consisting of the visible world, which is by nature subject to decay;
it is indeed unreal, appearing in an unreal form, just as one dream follows another within a dream.
That [consciousness] itself spontaneously and swiftly conceives a body;
by that [conception], this splendor of a magical illusion is spread out through its expansion.
It throbs, it moves, it leaps, it begs, it exists, it sinks, and it withdraws by itself;
it even attains immortality, yet the mind merely flickers due to its fickle nature.
The fifth canto, titled "Description of the Occasion," ends with Rāma:
O Blessed One, tiger among sages, what indeed exists here in this mental delusion? How has the mind arisen, and from where does this mind consisting of illusion come?
"O Lord, tell me in brief about origination at the beginning;
thereafter, O best of speakers, you shall explain the remainder that is yet to be told."
Vasiṣṭha: When the great dissolution has occurred and the entire visible world has reached non-existence at the beginning of creation, only the tranquil remains.
The unborn, undecaying, and stainless Lord, the Sun, remains ever-risen;
he is the all-maker, the All, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord.
From which words turn back, which is realized by the liberated,
and for whom notions such as "self" and so forth are merely conceptual constructs and not born of intrinsic nature.
That person who [sees] the Sāṅkhya views, the Brahman of the Vedāntins,
and the purely stainless consciousness-only of the knowers of consciousness;
He who is the illuminator of emptiness for the proponents of emptiness, who possesses the brilliance of the sun,
who is the speaker, the rememberer, the knower of truth, the enjoyer, the seer, and the eternal agent.
Though existing, it is non-existent; though situated within the body, it is far away—this light of consciousness, for it is like the radiance of the sun.
From whom Viṣṇu and the other gods emerge like rays from the sun,
and from whom the infinite worlds arise like bubbles from the ocean.
Into whom all visible multitudes enter like waters into the great ocean,
and who illuminates both the self and objects like a lamp— [that is the Self].
He who is established in space and in the body, in stones, in waters, and in creepers; in dust, in mountains, in winds, and in the netherworlds.
He who drowns the agitated group of eight cities here and there,
by whom the deluded have been rendered mute, remaining as if fixed in meditation like stones.
By whom the sky was made empty, by whom the mountains were made solid, by whom the waters were made fluid, and by whose power the sun blazes; ||| MU_3,5.13 |||
From this [reality] flow forth the various views of the essence-less cycle of existence,
just as rains flow from a cloud filled with inexhaustible nectar.
In whom the waves of the three worlds, consisting of manifestation and disappearance,
vibrate incessantly like rays of light from the sun.
He whose nature is indestructible and whose essence is imperishable, who dwells within all things,
who is hidden though distinct, and who is established in all beings.
By which wind does that creeper of primordial nature dance— she who is born in the sky, whose fruit is the cosmic egg, whose roots are the mind, and whose petals are the senses?
That very jewel which shines within the casket of every body, in which moon these rays of the web of worlds quiver; //MU_3.5.18//
In that dense mass of tranquil consciousness, which rains down nectar,
living beings are the falling streams, and perceptions are the vivid flashes of lightning.
When objects cause one another to marvel by their appearance—
that through which the non-existent was born as non-existent, and through which the existent attained its state of being— [then they are truly perceived].
This body moves even against his will in the presence of him who is the supreme jewel, tranquil, and abiding within himself.
Fate, place, and time, as well as movement, vibration, and actions— by him, who approaches all beings, these have been brought into existence.
Because it consists of pure consciousness, that which is space becomes so through the cognition of space; yet, through the cognition of objects, it remains as the object itself, without being fixed.
Even while appearing to effect the infinite vibration of the great worlds, he never does anything at all;
having abandoned the notions of arising and abiding, he remains as the one alone within his own self, which is changeless consciousness that never sets.
The sixth canto, titled "Description of the Nature of the Deity who is the Root Cause," by Vasiṣṭha.
For this supreme Self, the God beyond gods,
supreme perfection comes from knowledge alone, and not from the exhaustion of ritual performance.
In this case, it is knowledge and its application that are required, and nothing else;
for it has the nature of perceiving the cessation of the delusion of water in a mirage.
This is neither far away, nor is it in space; it is not unattainable, nor is it difficult to reach.
Having the nature of the radiance of one's own bliss, it is obtained from one's very own body.
In this regard, asceticism, charity, vows, and the like do not provide any assistance;
there is no means of accomplishment here other than resting in the nature alone.
In this matter, the sole means for the genuine awakening that unravels the web of delusion is exclusively devotion to the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and true yogis.
Merely by the thorough recognition that "this is that God," suffering does not arise for a person, and he attains the state of liberation while living.
Rāma:
Merely by means of this self thoroughly knowing itself within itself,
faults such as death and the like shall never again cause affliction.
From where and from how far away can this great God of gods be reached?
By what intense austerity, or by how much suffering, is he attained?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, that Divine Being is known through the effort of one's own human exertion and through blossoming discernment; it is not known by means of austerities, ritual baths, or religious rites."
O Rāma, without the abandonment of passion, hatred, delusion, anger, pride, and envy, asceticism and charity are nothing but affliction; they are not real.
When the mind is afflicted by passion and the like, one acquires wealth by deceiving others;
therefore, the fruit of whatever gift is given from that wealth belongs to the one for whose sake it was acquired.
Whatever vow or other practice is performed when the mind is afflicted by passion and the like is called hypocrisy; its fruit is either slight or non-existent.
Therefore, by human effort, one should procure the primary medicine:
association with true scriptures and virtuous people, which destroys the disease of cyclic existence.
In this regard, apart from a single human effort,
no other means whatsoever is found to lead to the attainment of the destruction of all suffering.
Hear what that human effort is like for the attainment of self-knowledge,
by which the cholera-like afflictions of passion and hatred are entirely stilled.
With a livelihood as it may happen, not opposed to worldly custom or sacred scripture,
with a mind content through satisfaction, he should abandon greed for enjoyments.
According to one's capacity, through diligent effort and with a mind free from agitation,
one should first take recourse in devotion to the company of the virtuous and the study of the true scriptures.
He who is content with whatever he has obtained, who disregards what is censurable,
and who delights in the company of the virtuous and in the true scriptures, is swiftly liberated.
For the Great-Minded One who has fully understood the nature of reality through investigation,
these— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara— become objects of compassion.
He whom the world, consisting for the most part of good people, declares to be virtuous—he is distinguished; he would be a true saint. One should resort to him with diligent effort.

Among all branches of knowledge, the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā) is the foremost; they call that treatise which relies upon its discourse a "true scripture" (sacchāstra), and one who investigates it is liberated.
Impurities are forcibly destroyed by discriminations born from the study of true scriptures and the company of the virtuous,
just as the impurities of water vanish through contact with *kataka* nuts, or those of the dull-witted through the administration of poison.
The seventh canto, titled "Instruction on the Effort of One Seeking Liberation," [ends].
Rāma:
This god who has been described, by knowing whom one is liberated—
tell me, where does that god abide, and how may I attain him?
Vasiṣṭha:
This deity who has been described does not stand at a distance;
he is eternally established within the body, renowned as pure consciousness alone (cinmātra).
This [Self] is all this universe, yet it is not the universe; it is all-pervading.
For this alone exists as one, but there is no perception of anything designated as "the universe."
This moon-bearer is pure consciousness alone; the one whose banner is Garuḍa is pure consciousness alone;
the sun is indeed pure consciousness; and the lotus-born Brahmā is pure consciousness alone.
Rāma:
Even children say this: if the world is merely consciousness, what indeed could there be here called "instruction"?
Vasiṣṭha:
That which you have understood— that the entire universe is pure consciousness and sentient—
is not at all that knowledge which delivers one from worldly existence.
Volition is called saṃsāra; this living being is known as a bound soul (paśu).
From this very source emerge the waves of old age and death.

For the individual soul (paśu), though ignorant and formless, is indeed a vessel for suffering alone; because it possesses consciousness, it perceives this [suffering], and thus, remaining itself, it is established in extreme misfortune.
That state which is freedom from the object of thought, or rather, the orientation toward that which is beyond thought—that is its fullness; having known it, one does not grieve.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
Moreover, its tendency toward being oriented toward an object of thought cannot be restrained without the non-existence of that object;
for how indeed can the visible world, which is the object of thought, be stilled?
Rāma:
O Brahmin, tell me, what is that Supreme Self like which is seen through the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures as the one who carries us across the ocean of worldly existence?
Vasiṣṭha: Those who desire this conscious individual soul, which is shattered in the wilderness of birth, are ignorant, even though they are considered learned.
The living being (jīva) alone is the cycle of existence here, due to its consciousness and the continuity of suffering;
when this is known, there is nothing remaining unknown anywhere.
O Rāma, if the Supreme Self is known, then that succession of sufferings comes to an end,
just as cholera ceases when the influence of poison has subsided.
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, describe to me accurately the form of the Supreme Self,
by seeing which a person shall cross over all delusion entirely.
Vasiṣṭha said: That form which exists in the interval, in the mere twinkling of an eye, between consciousness that has reached one distant place from another, is the nature of the Supreme Self.
The absolute non-existence of the cycle of existence and the world's condition exists within that great ocean of awakening which is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That wherein the sequence of seer and seen, though present, has utterly set;
that which is not space yet is space—that is the form of the Supreme Self.
That which is empty yet as if non-empty, wherein the world remains as empty—
though the flood of creation exists— that which is empty is the form of the Supreme Self.
That which is composed of pure consciousness, though it remains like a massive stone and is seemingly inert, is in fact non-inert within; such is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That form of the Supreme Self, by attaining union with which everything— both external and internal— attains its own essential existence, is the true nature of the Supreme Self.
Just as light belongs to luminosity, and just as emptiness belongs to the sky,
so is this established wherein that form of the Supreme Self resides.
Rāma:
How indeed is this Supreme Self understood to be everywhere? From what cause is there the non-existence of this visible world called "the universe"?
Vasiṣṭha said: If there were a firm realization of the absolute non-existence of this worldly delusion— which has arisen like the color of the sky— that would be sufficient.
That form of Brahman is known through that [realization] and not by any other action;
for there is no other auspicious path except for the absolute non-existence of the visible world.
When this visible world has reached the state of absolute non-existence according to its true condition, that ultimate reality remains; it is then awakened to and known.
Nowhere does consciousness exist without a reflection, since there is no object of perception apart from it;
for where indeed does a mirror remain without a reflection?
Without the possibility of the existence of this visible world named "the universe," the supreme reality can never be understood by anyone at any time.
Rāma:
O Sage, how can there be non-existence for this entire web of the visible—the cosmic egg and the stability of the world? Where is Mount Meru within the interior of a mustard seed?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, if you remain for a few days with an undistracted mind,
intent upon the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures, then I shall [bring about] that [liberation] in an instant.
I wipe away for you the visible world, which is like a mirage in the state of awakening;
when the visible is absent, the state of being a seer also subsides, and pure awareness alone remains.
The state of being a seer exists when there is an object of sight; the state of being an object of sight exists when there is a beholder.
Indeed, unity exists when there is duality, and duality exists within the perception of unity.
Indeed, it is not the case here that the establishment of both occurs through the absence of one;
rather, when duality, unity, the seer, and the seen have ceased, the Real alone remains.
I cleanse for you the entire world-phenomenon of "I-ness" and so forth—
the impurity of the mind's ego from which it arises— by means of the realization of their absolute non-existence.
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being.
Since that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature cannot be found, what affliction is there to be wiped away?
This world, which is seen spread out and yet was unproduced in the beginning,
is Brahman itself, expanded by its own consciousness within its own stainless self.
That which is called the world has never arisen, does not exist, and is not perceived; it is like the nature of bracelets and such in gold. Why then this effort to polish it?
Thus, we shall explain this here in detail through many arguments,
so that it may indeed be experienced by oneself as something uncontradicted.
For how could there be existence here for that which was never produced in the first place?
How could there be a river of water in a desert, or a planet in the second moon?
Just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, just as there is no water in a desert,
and just as there is no tree in the sky, so too does the delusion of the world not exist.
O Rāma, that which is seen here is indeed Brahman itself, free from all affliction;
we shall explain this to you later through reasoning, and not merely by words.
O noble-minded one, it is improper for a person of exalted intellect to disregard that which those who know the truth proclaim here through reasonings;
for they know him alone as ignorant who, out of a deluded mind, holds in contempt what is consistent with reason, thereby bringing himself misery.
The eighth canto, titled "The Proposition that the World and All Perceptible Objects Lack Reality," [spoken by] Rāma.
How is this known through reasoning, and how is it established? Once this principle has been experienced, nothing remains to be known.
Vasiṣṭha:
This chronic cholera of false knowledge,
known by the name "the world," does not subside except through the mantra called inquiry.
O Rāma, I shall tell you these narratives for the sake of attaining awakening;
if you listen to them, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and wise.
If, due to a nature prone to agitation, you rise from the midst of it and depart, then nothing at all will be accomplished for you today, as you possess the character of a beast.
Whoever desires an object and strives for it in that manner will certainly attain it, provided they do not turn back out of exhaustion.
O Rāma, if you become devoted to the company of the virtuous and to the true scriptures,
then in mere days, and certainly not after months, you shall attain the supreme state.
Rāma:
O best among those who know the scriptures, what is the name of that preeminent scripture for the awakening of self-knowledge, by knowing which one no longer grieves?
Vasiṣṭha:
O Great-minded One, for those for whom the knowledge of the Self is paramount, this very work titled the Mahārāmāyaṇa is the supreme scripture among all scriptures.
From this supreme history, a higher understanding proceeds;
this is declared to be the essence of all histories.
Since the state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) arises spontaneously upon hearing this collection of words, therefore this alone is supremely purifying.
Through inquiry, the visible world, though it remains as it is, comes to its setting;
just as when a dream is fully recognized, the mental impression of the dream-objects vanishes.
"What exists here exists elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere else.
The wise know this to be the treasury of all the sciences of consciousness."
Whoever should hear this constantly, even a child, the intellect of that person of noble wonder will undoubtedly attain supreme awakening.
But for that unworthy person for whom this does not shine forth due to the arising of their own evil deeds,
let him investigate whatever scripture consists of mere intellectual words.
Upon hearing this, however, liberation while living (jīvanmuktatva) is experienced by oneself,
just as freedom from disease is felt when a potent medicine has been drunk.
For when this scripture is being heard, the listener understands it within himself:
"This has been stated by us exactly as it is, and not like a boon or a curse."
This suffering of saṃsāra is stilled for you by the great discourse of inquiry into one's own self alone;
it is not stilled by wealth, charity, austerity, sacred learning, or the Vedas, nor by hundreds of efforts devoid of that discourse.
The ninth canto, titled "The Determination of the True Scripture," by Vasiṣṭha.
With their minds fixed on that and their lives dedicated to it, awakening one another and constantly speaking of it, those who find contentment and delight therein— //MU 3.9.1//
For those who are solely devoted to knowledge, through the investigation of self-knowledge,
that state of liberation while living arises, which is indeed liberation from the body.
Rāma: O Brahmin, tell me the characteristics of one liberated while in the body and one liberated while living,
so that I may strive accordingly with an intellect guided by the vision of the scriptures.
Vasiṣṭha:
He for whom this world remains as it is, even while engaged in worldly affairs,
and who remains like the sky when the sun has set— he is called one liberated while living.
Having attained exclusive steadfastness in awakening, he remains truly awake even as if in deep sleep;
he who continues to engage in worldly affairs while thus abiding is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He whose facial radiance neither rises nor sets in the face of pleasure or pain,
remaining established exactly as it has come to be— he is called one liberated while living.
He who remains awake while established in deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists,
whose consciousness is free from latent impressions— he is called liberated while living.
Even while acting in accordance with passion, hatred, fear, and so forth,
he who is internally as utterly transparent as the sky is called one liberated while living.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, and whose intellect is not stained—
whether he is acting or not acting— he is called liberated while living.
He who perceives the dissolution and creation of the three worlds through his own opening and closing of the eyes, and who views them as equal to space, is called one liberated while living.
He who is neither an enjoyer nor a non-enjoyer, having attained oneness with pure consciousness,
remains within like one asleep— he is called liberated while living.

One who is always a seer yet appears as a non-seer, who is alive yet like one dead, and who engages in worldly affairs yet is like a mountain— such a person is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He from whom the world does not shrink away, and who does not shrink away from the world, being liberated from joy, envy, and fear— he is called one liberated while living.
He whose mental constructions regarding saṃsāra have been stilled, who, though possessing parts, is partless; he who, though possessing a mind, is mindless—he is called liberated while living.
He who, though engaged in all kinds of worldly affairs, remains cool as if toward the interests of others, and whose self is full— such a person is called liberated while living.
Having abandoned the state of liberation while living, when the body is destroyed by the power of time,
consciousness attains disembodied liberation, just as the wind reaches a state of motionlessness.
One liberated while in the disembodied state neither rises nor sets, nor does one cease to be;
one is neither existent nor non-existent, neither far away, nor "I," nor anything else.
Becoming the sun, Viṣṇu blazes;
as Rudra, he destroys all; and as the lotus-born Brahmā, he creates all.
Having become space, it supports the masses of wind along with the stars, gods, and asuras;
and having become the range of the principal mountains, it serves as the abode for the cities of the world-protectors.
Having become the earth, it sustains this unbroken stability of the world;
having become grass, shrubs, and creepers, it yields a continuous succession of fruits.
Bearing the forms of both water and fire, it blazes and flows when liquefied;
the moon produces nectar, yet it also brings death through the hālāhala poison.
Manifesting as fire, it illuminates the quarters; becoming darkness, it spreads blindness;
being empty, it attains the state of space; and being a mountain, it effectively obstructs all.
In its state as consciousness, it makes the moving immobile, and in the form of the immobile, it makes the immobile moving;
having become the ocean, it encircles the earth-woman like a bracelet.
Having assumed the form of the supreme sun, spreading its light within,
it remains utterly tranquil, pervading the multitude of motes in the three worlds.
Whatever appears here, whether it has already appeared,
is currently appearing, or will come to appear— whatever is visible throughout the three periods of time, all that is indeed he.
Rāma:
Why do you speak thus, O Brahmin? For my vision is indeed troubled; yet it is certain that this [vision] is difficult to attain and hard to traverse.
Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this is called liberation; this is declared to be Brahman;
this is described as Nirvāṇa. Listen now to how it is attained.
This visible world that is perceived, joined with the sense of "I-ness" and so forth,
is attained through the intellect by means of the non-arising of even this which exists.
Rāma said:

O best among those who know what is to be known, when those liberated while in the body (videhamukta) attain the three worlds, I consider that they have merely reached the state of being created objects.
Vasiṣṭha said:
If the three worlds exist, let them attain that state wherein not even the slightest meaning of the term "the three worlds" can possibly occur.

In that case, since [Brahman] has attained the state of the three worlds, how could there be an understanding of the meaning of the word "Brahman"? Therefore, no other conceptualization of the referent of the word "world" (jagat) is possible for us.
For one who has realized the truth, the truth is this: the world is indeed Brahman alone—non-dual, peaceful, a mere manifestation, and as pure as space.
For just as, even when examined, the state of being a bracelet is not seen anywhere within a golden bracelet apart from the stainless gold itself.
Apart from water, I do not perceive anything at all in the waves;
for that which is perceived as "waviness" by those like you does not exist there at all.
Vibration is never, at any time or place, anything other than wind;
wind is always vibration itself, and therefore the world does not exist apart from it.
Just as emptiness is the sky, and heat itself is water in the desert,
and just as light is itself fire, so too the triple world is Brahman alone.
Rāma:
O Sage, teach me that supreme method by which liberation from the world of appearances arises through the attainment of its absolute non-existence.
[Vasiṣṭha:
When the seer and the seen, which have come together, are both dissolved and reach a state of non-existence through the disappearance of one of the two, only nirvāṇa remains.
[Rāma:
Tell me how Brahman, which is thus established in its own nature, is understood as that from which this visible world never arises at all.
How is this known through reasoning, and how is it established? O Sage, once this is established, nothing remains to be proven.
Vasiṣṭha:
This cholera of false knowledge has been deeply rooted for a long time;
it will surely be eradicated by the mantra of inquiry.
It cannot be eradicated all at once in a single moment,
for ascending and descending a mountain requires equal effort.
Therefore, listen as this is explained so that the delusion of the world may be pacified through the yoga of practice, by means of reasoning, and through logical justifications. MU 3.9.43.
O Rāma, I shall tell you this narrative for the sake of attaining awakening;
if you listen to it, O virtuous one, you will indeed be liberated and wise.
Now, O Rāma, this section on origination is being told by me to you; for indeed, that which is produced becomes liberated by that very [production].
"This worldly delusion, though unborn and of the nature of space, appears in this manner"—
this is what is now being explained by me in this chapter on origination.
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving— everything, rich in all its various forms, including gods, asuras, and kinnaras.
When that great dissolution arrives, which results in the transformation of Rudra and the other deities, it becomes non-existent and invisible; it goes somewhere or perishes.
Then there remains something existent that is steady and profound, neither light nor pervasive darkness, indefinable and unmanifest.
It is neither empty nor space, neither the visible object nor the act of seeing;
nor is it a multitude of real entities, for it abides as the infinite.
It is something whose nature is indefinable, a form more full than the Full;
it is neither being, nor non-being, nor both being and non-being, nor absence, nor existence.
It is pure consciousness alone, devoid of any object of thought, infinite, undecaying, and auspicious;
it is without beginning, middle, or end, free from mental affliction, and beyond all disease.
In whom the world vibrates like a swan amidst pearls of vision—
he who is both this and not this, the God whose nature is both being and non-being.
Though without ears, tongue, nose, skin, or eyes, he everywhere and at all times hears, tastes, smells, touches, and sees.
That very light by which the form of existence and non-existence is perceived—
the variegated creation without beginning or end, as well as one's own nature which is unstained— [is that same light].
He who perceives the world—half-opened-eyed, with the pupils fixed between the eyebrows—as being of the nature of space itself, a constant manifestation that is his own true self; // MU 3.9.56 //
For that Lord, there is no other cause, just like the horn of a hare;
and this world is His effect, like a mass of waves arising from water.
The light of that lamp of pure consciousness, which blazes incessantly on all sides and abides within the vessels of the mind, illuminates the three worlds.
Without whom even these luminaries such as the sun would be like darkness;
and in whose presence the three worlds proceed like a mirage.

In that [consciousness] in which this splendor of the world arises as if throbbing when it is active, and subsides as if internalized when it is motionless— just like the circularity of a whirling firebrand.
The pervasive and great one, whose nature is stainless and imperishable, consists of both movement and stillness, and whose play is the creation and dissolution of the universe.
The existence of that [Self], which consists of both vibration and non-vibration and is all-pervading like the wind,
appears as if divided merely by name for the sake of conventional usage, but not in reality.
He who is always awakened, he who is always asleep,
and he who is neither asleep nor awakened, being everywhere and at all times.
That which is motionless is the peaceful Śiva; that which is its movement is the existence of the three worlds.
He who is the single one of full form, whose nature is the play of both movement and stillness.
Like fragrance in flowers that are destined for destruction, it does not perish;
though present before the eyes, it is nevertheless ungraspable, like the whiteness in white cloths.
He who speaks like one mute, he who thinks like a stone,
he who enjoys while remaining eternally satisfied, and he who acts while possessing nothing— [he is a sage].
He who, though without limbs, possesses all limbs; who has a thousand hands and eyes;
and by whom this entire world is pervaded, even though he abides as nothing at all.
He whose sensory functions are entirely complete even though he is devoid of sense faculties, and whose modes of mental emanation exist even though he is without a mind; //MU_3.9.68//
Because it is not contemplated, the fears of the serpent of saṃsāra appear;
when it is seen, all calamities flee in every way and at all times.
In that witness, which is a vast and stable manifestation like a lamp, all activities proceed, just as various movements are preceded by the flickering of a flame.
For from it arise hundreds of rows of objects in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth,
just as waves, droplets, surges, and billows arise from the ocean.
That very same entity arises through the delusions of hundreds of objects,
just as gold appears as bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, and anklets.
You who are of the nature of a single illumination, I who am such, and these people who exist;
and that which you are not, O one whose self is unawakened, and that which I am not, and those people who are not—[all are of this same nature].
In that [reality] in which the world of appearances manifests, it is both non-different and indeed different from that [reality], and it is transient— like a series of waves upon the water.
From which comes the reckoning of time, from which comes the visibility of the visible,
by which comes mental construction, and by which comes the shining forth of lights.
Action, form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and consciousness—whatever you perceive is that God; and that by which you perceive is also He.
O virtuous one, through focused attention, you shall realize your own self as that which exists as the act of seeing among the seer, the seeing, and the seen.

The unborn, undecaying, non-inert, eternal, and constant Brahman—ever-auspicious, stainless, and beginningless; beyond reproach by those who know only the barren objects of cognition; devoid of all mental constructions; the cause of causes; the internal experience that is itself unknowable, yet the very essence of knowing and consciousness.
The Tenth Sarga, titled "The Description of the Supreme Cause," [spoken by] Rāma.
Whatever remains at the occurrence of the great dissolution, let that be called "formless"; there is no doubt about this.
How could it not be empty? How could it not be luminous? How could it not be of the nature of darkness? Or how could it not be of the nature of space?

Or how could it not be of the nature of consciousness? Or how could it not be the individual soul (jīva)? How could it not be the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva)? Or how could it not be the mind (manas)?
Or how could there be nothing, or how could there be everything?
By this turn of phrase, a kind of delusion has arisen in me.
Vasiṣṭha said:
This question posed by you is exceedingly difficult;
yet I shall resolve it without effort, just as the sun dispels the darkness of night.
Listen as this is explained: that which remains as the existent at the conclusion of the great eon (mahākalpa) is indeed not empty in that sense. MU_3,10.6.
Just as a carved figure on a pillar remains uncarved [within it], so does the universe abide therein; therefore, that state is not empty.
This world, known as the "universe," appears here with such great abundance;
whether it be real or unreal, where could emptiness possibly reside within it?
Just as a pillar that has not been carved with a female figure is not empty of that figure, so too, my dear, the world is Brahman; therefore, that state is not empty of it.
Just as a wave in gentle water neither exists nor does not exist,
so this world within Brahman has reached the state of being both empty and non-empty.
Since space, time, and so forth are quiescent, the carving of a doll upon a tree is possible;
but in the unborn element, by what means could one not be deluded within?
Therefore, this [comparison] of the pillars, statues, and so forth, is an analogy that resembles the ultimate state of the world only in one respect, not in every way.
This never arises from another, nor does it ever cease;
being of such a nature, Brahman alone exists, established within its own self.
The conceptualization of the meaning of the word "empty" depends upon the non-empty;
since non-emptiness is impossible, how can there be emptiness or non-emptiness?
Indeed, this light in Brahman cannot arise from the elements;
for how could the sun, fire, moon, stars, and so forth exist there in that which is immutable?
The absence of the manifestations of the great elements is called darkness;
however, since that [darkness] arises from the absence of the great elements, there is no darkness anywhere in this [ultimate reality].
The manifestation of its own experience belongs solely to this [Self] whose nature is space;
that which exists within it is experienced by that alone, and not by anything else.
That which is liberated from both darkness and light— know this undecaying state to be the very sheath of space, the sheath that sustains the existence of the world.

Just as there is no difference whatsoever between a bilva fruit and that which is designated as "bilva," so too here, there is not even the slightest degree of difference between Brahman and the world.
Just as a wave exists within water, and just as a jar exists within clay,
so too, where the existence of the world resides, how could that [reality] be of the nature of space?
The beauty of analogies such as clay and water is not equal to that of this [world] which possesses form;
however, Brahman is as clear as space, and that [world] likewise exists within it.
Therefore, just as the space of consciousness is even more stainless than physical space,
so too is that which exists within it— the referent of the word "world"— exactly like that.
Just as pungency within a pepper is not perceived without a consumer,
so too is the state of pure consciousness in the supreme space not perceived without the element of the object of thought.
Therefore, even though consciousness is of the nature of the non-conscious, because it is not distinct from the object of cognition within itself,
this world-existence is exactly like that, by virtue of its being essentially composed of nothing but that.
Form, light, and mental attention consist of that alone and nothing else;
therefore, the universe as it truly exists is either deep sleep or the fourth state.
Therefore, the yogi, though engaged in worldly activity, remains with a tranquil mind as if in deep sleep;
he abides in Brahman, which is devoid of appearances and is the source-container of all manifestations.
Just as the process of fluidity resides in calm water that possesses form,
so too does the universe reside in the Supreme, which is formless and similar to it.
From the Full, the Full flows forth; from the formless, the formless. The universe has appeared from Brahman, yet it is devoid of any objective reality.
From the Full, the Full flows forth; that which is thus established is indeed the Full itself.
Therefore, the universe is unarisen; and whatever has arisen, that too is precisely that.
Since there is no cognizer in that state, what kind of object-nature could there be?
What kind of pungency could there be in a pepper if there were no one to taste it?
This [world] arises from the consciousness of the Supreme, which is truly real yet unreal;
since there is no reflection [of an external object], how can there be any capacity for being reflected?
It is subtler than even the subtlest atom,
purer, more refined, and more tranquil than even the interior of space.
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is exceedingly vast;
it is without beginning or end, a manifestation devoid of anything to be manifested.
Wherein only the nature of consciousness is found, how could there be a state of living,
or a latent impression in the form of the mind, which is like the wind?
Precisely because the nature of consciousness does not arise there, there is no state of being a living soul;
there is no state of intellect, no state of mind, no state of sense organs, and no latent impressions.
Thus abides this undecaying state, which, though full of the commencement of dissolution,
remains peaceful and empty according to our vision— surpassing even space.
Rāma:
What is the nature of that ultimate reality, which has the form of infinite consciousness?
Explain this again in detail for the sake of increasing my understanding.
Vasiṣṭha said: Listen as this supreme Brahman is described—that which remains as the cause of all causes when the great dissolution has occurred. MU 3.10.38.
Having destroyed one's own self through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind,
that which is the form, that which is inexpressible— that is the true nature of that reality.
There is no visible world and no seer; due to the absence of the visible, it is as if dissolved. That which appears as "it shines" is the very nature of that reality.
If that which is the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is oriented toward the object of cognition, it is the body;
whereas that which is pure consciousness alone, stainless and tranquil, is the cause of all causes.
When there is no sensation of wind or other elements through the thumb or a finger,
that which is the form of the mind of the living being is the supreme Self.
O sinless one, that form which remains after long contemplation— of that state which is dreamless, infinite, non-inert, and solid— is what is left.
That which is the heart of the sky, or of stone, or of the wind— that form of the supreme self, the inconceivable space of consciousness, is such.
The state of one who is without ego-conception, without mental activity, yet living and active—
that is the supreme, peaceful existence of that primordial reality.
That which is the center of the light of consciousness, or of dense light,
and that which is the center of vision— that is the form of the Supreme Self.
The experience of sensation, of light, of the visible, and likewise of darkness—
that which is without beginning or end is the nature of the Supreme Self.
That form of the Supreme Self, though eternally unarisen in nature, from which the world seems to arise as if distinct, though it is non-different—[that is the form]. (MU 3.10.48)
Even for one intent on worldly activity, that state of sitting like a stone,
which is the very nature of space though not space itself— that is the form of the supreme self.
Furthermore, that wherein these three forms— the object of knowledge, the act of knowing,
and the knower— arise and set, is the supreme and most excellent reality.
That in which this state of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower is reflected within the great mirror of the non-intellect and so forth— that is remembered as the supreme form.
That form of the Great Consciousness which is free from the six senses, including the mind—
whether in the moving or the stationary— remains at the end of creation.
If the form of immobile beings were indeed composed of consciousness,
being free from mind, intellect, and the like, it would be equal to the Supreme.
When Brahmā, Arka, Viṣṇu, Hara, Śakra, Sadāśiva, and the others have attained peace, this one supreme Śiva alone remains here.
He is the taught, the undecaying, the effortless, the desired; he is neither mixed nor unmixed, and he is not dependent upon the atom, nor is he dependent by anyone.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Description of the Ultimate Reality Remaining at the End of the Great Kalpa," [spoken by] Rāma.
O Brahmin, where does this radiant world, known as the visible universe of such a form, go when the great dissolution occurs?
Vasiṣṭha said:
From where does the son of a barren woman come, or what is he like, and where does he go?
Tell me, where does the forest of the sky go, and from where does it come?
Rāma:
The son of a barren woman and the forest of the sky neither exist nor will they ever exist.
What kind of visibility could there be for him, and what kind of non-existence?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as the son of a barren woman and the forest in the sky never exist at any time,
so too this entire visible world, beginning with the universe, never exists at any time.
That which neither arises nor perishes because it did not exist at the outset—what kind of arising could there be for such a thing? What talk can there be of the word "destruction"?
Rāma:
Indeed, the conceptualization of the son of a barren woman or a tree in the sky exists;
just as that [conceptualization] is devoid of destruction, birth, and so forth, why should this [world] not be the same?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O one of incomparable splendor, properly adorn yourself with blossoming locks of hair;
for the existence of the world is indeed just like a word that has no basis in reality.
Just as the state of being a bracelet, though clearly visible even while a golden bracelet is being perceived,
does not exist at all [as a substantial reality], so too is the state of being the world [non-existent] in the Supreme.
Just as emptiness does not exist in space as something distinct from it,
so too the state of being the world does not exist in Brahman, even though it is perceived there.
Just as blackness does not exist apart from collyrium, nor coldness apart from snow,
so too the world is perceived as distinct [from it], yet it does not exist in the supreme state.
And just as coolness is not distinct from the moon,
so too creation does not exist as something separate from Brahman.
Just as water in a mirage-river or moonhood in a second moon do not exist at all, so too the world does not exist, even though it is seen within the stainless Self.
This light of the eye of consciousness shines in the sky of consciousness,
within the stainless firmament called the world, like a string of pearls.
In the space of consciousness, that which shines by itself through its own consciousness is that very self-form which is perceived as the world.
For that which does not exist at the very beginning because its cause is absent by its own nature, does not exist even in the present; what kind of destruction could there be for it?
How could insentience, which is impossible in that which has arisen from the elements, be capable of being the cause of an insentient thing such as earth and so forth?
Just as sunlight cannot be the cause of shade.
Due to the absence of a cause, this effect has not arisen as anything at all;
that which exists is the cause itself, and it remains established in this very manner.
That which appears as unarisen is indeed the manifestation of consciousness;
that which is seen as the world in a dream is nothing but the radiance of consciousness.
Just as the delusion of the dream-world is nothing other than the internal manifestation of consciousness,
so too, at the beginning of creation, the manifestation of the world is extended within Brahman.
Whatever is seen here exists as reality alone, abiding within the Self;
this world never sets nor does it ever rise.
Just as liquidity is water, as movement is wind,
and as radiance is light, so too the three worlds are Brahman alone.
Just as the internal knower alone exists within the consciousness of a dream as if it were a city,
so too one's own self alone appears as the world within the Supreme Self.
Rāma:
If this is so, then tell me, O Brahmin, how can there be such firm conviction?
This poison of the visible world has arisen like the experience of an unreal dream.
[Vasiṣṭha:
When there is an object of sight, there is indeed a seer; when there is a seer, there is the state of being an object of sight.
When these two exist within a single reality, there is bondage; when one ceases, both are liberated.

As long as there is no absolute non-existence of the visible object— that is, as long as the Buddha is not perceived to be inexhaustible— so long is it impossible for the seer to attain the state of non-seeing that bestows liberation.
If the visible object exists at first and subsequently undergoes destruction,
then bondage— in the form of the useless recollection of that visible object— does not cease.
Wherever consciousness may be situated, just as in its own mirror, this reflection consisting of the memory of creation indeed adheres to it.
For if the visible world has never arisen from the very beginning and does not exist by itself,
then liberation is possible because of the absence of the delusion of the seer and the seen.
[Rāma:
Therefore, O best among the knowers of the Self, having logically dispelled my notion that liberation is impossible, please explain the absolute impossibility of the visible world.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāma, as I relate to you through this long discourse how the world, consisting of creation, appears though it is indeed non-existent.
As long as that [reality] has not been described through words of decisive discourse,
so long does it not rest within your heart, like dust in a lake.
Having realized the absolute non-existence of this delusive state of world-creation, you, with your self established in one-pointed meditation, will carry out your worldly activities.
Views characterized by grasping at existence and non-existence, by rejection, and by the gross, the subtle, the moving,
and the unmoving, will not pierce You, just as arrows do not pierce a great mountain.
This very Self is one alone; there is no second conceptualization.
O Rāghava, I shall explain to you how the world has arisen within this.

Therefore, all these manifestations have unfolded; for indeed, O dear one, this Great-Souled One, who is the entirety within the entirety, arises and dissolves by Himself as the locus of the treasury that illuminates the observation of forms and the mental reflection upon them.
The twelfth canto, titled "The Description of the Ultimate Reality," by Vasiṣṭha.
Listen with the highest intelligence to how this universe has arisen from this supreme, tranquil, and most holy state.
Deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears as if it were creation;
all is one and that is peaceful—listen now to the sequence regarding that.
Of that gem of consciousness, whose nature is infinite light and which is all-pervasive,
there is a manifestation consisting of pure existence alone, occurring incessantly by its very nature.
Therefore, within the Self, something itself appears as if it were an object of cognition;
though devoid of an external referent, it indicates the reflective awareness (*imarśana*) of consciousness in this state.
Through the mental constructions of future objects, its form is slightly inferred;
it is subtler than space, pure, and the awakening to all things within everything.
Then that supreme reality, Satī, becoming oriented toward consciousness,
becomes fit for the name "Citi" (Consciousness) by virtue of being slightly attainable through that [orientation].
After the dense perception [of the body],
when it departs from the supreme state, that mental construction of a self arises, which is designated as the "living being" (jīva) and so forth.
At that time, these [faculties], whose essence consists solely in the singular contemplation of the self and which are oriented toward the cycle of existence,
