remain subtle by virtue of the nature of reality.
Immediately following this, the emptiness of the space-being arises;
it is the seed of the qualities such as sound, and it bestows the designations and objects that are yet to come.
Thereafter, the sense of "I" arises together with the very existence of time;
for you, that is the primary seed for the future meaning of designation and for the persistence of the world.
Of that supreme power, however, there is only self-awareness;
this net, though unreal in nature, arises throbbing as if it were real.
Consciousness of this nature is the seed of the tree of volition;
therein, the sense of "I" (ahaṅkāra) is its sap, and the vital breath (marut) is its vibration.

The consciousness, possessing the nature of "I-ness," through the contemplation of the subtle element of sound within the ether, gradually solidifies by itself and becomes fully the subtle element of space.
That seed of the tree of the flood of words has the form of future objects; it is the transformative source of the multitude of Vedas, enriched with words, sentences, and means of valid cognition.
Therefore, the entire glory of the world will arise from that which has the nature of sound,
spreading forth through the transformation of the multitude of objects produced by the flood of sounds.
Consciousness, accompanied by such a retinue, is designated by the word "jīva";
it is the seed of the tree that is the flood of past existences, through the web of future words and objects.
Then, indeed, the fourteenfold collection of living beings, filling the expanse of the sky— the entire multitude of the world-machine— will come forth.
That very consciousness, whose essence has not yet reached the state of being named and which throbs as a living body due to its vitality,
becomes the subtle element of touch in an instant through the power of contemplation.
The seed of the tree that has contact as its sole branch is the expansion of the mass of wind;
from it, the vibration of the activity of all beings will spread forth.

In that regard, whatever light arises from experience through the play of consciousness is the subtle element of fire (*tejomātra*), which bestows its respective name and object for what is yet to come into being.
That seed of the tree of light, through the blossoming of the sun and other [luminaries],
will from that cause expand into the diversity of forms as saṃsāra.
Because it is the source of the four states of existence for both the existent and the non-existent,
the tasting of that Saṅgha is called the subtle element of taste.
That seed of the tree of aesthetic flavor (rasa), whose nature is the play of future emotions,
will cause this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) to expand through mutual relishing.
This [element], consisting of mental construction and named after the future scent, being of the nature of ideation,
bestows the state of the subtle element (tanmātra) of fragrance upon that which is of the nature of ideation.
From that seed of the tree of form, which is the soul of all supports and exists as the future terrestrial globe, this cycle of existence will expand forth.
The subtle elements (tanmātras), being clearly perceived as they mutually transform by themselves, are like waters within water, existing without any interval.
Likewise, these [elements], whether mixed or separate, are not found in their pure state; for indeed, they end in total destruction.
Existing within the interior of space as forms consisting of pure consciousness,
they become like the networks of a banyan tree within the interior of a tiny seed.
They behold the production [of worlds] with their hundred branches and they quiver;
they fit within a single atom and in an instant become kalpas.
They run toward mere illusory appearances, yet they are devoid of such appearances;
for all things known by consciousness indeed coalesce into a single mass in an instant.
At the time of perception, that Consciousness— remaining formless itself— beholds this group of subtle elements (tanmātra), which consists of its own volitions, as a multitude of atoms.
Indeed, the seed within the worlds is merely fivefold; its seed is the supreme, primordial power of consciousness, which is transcendent.
That which is born from it is always experienced as being that very same thing—therefore, the glory of the world is but the one, unborn, and primordial pure consciousness.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Seed of Saṃsāra," by Vasiṣṭha.
In the supreme Brahman, which is vast, equal, and established in absolute equanimity;
whose nature consists of non-arising, space, light, darkness, existence, and so forth.
First, the ideation of "the state of being an object of consciousness" arises from the consciousness of the objective portion of one's own consciousness;
subsequently, the ideation of "the state of being consciousness" arises from the consciousness of the power of consciousness itself.

From that arises the conception of being a living soul (*jīvatvakalana*) due to consciousness nourished by objects of thought; from that arises the conception of "I-ness" (*ahambhāvakalana*) through the power of exclusive devotion to those objects of thought.
Then, from the transformation of egoity (ahaṃtā), there arises the measurement of the intellect (buddhi);
this very [intellect] possesses the states of the mind (manas) and so forth, as well as the subtle elements of sound and the rest.
Through the contemplation of the void and the subsequent subtle elements,
this great thicket of the world, consisting of gross material forms, is perceived as having arisen in this manner from the primordial source.
In an instant, as if by a gradual process, like a city created in a dream,
it arises again and again and perishes within the great forest of the vast space.
This seed of the groves of the world-karañja trees does not depend upon anything at all, such as earth, water, wind, and so forth.
This [universe], consisting of consciousness, will subsequently manifest as the earth and other elements;
yet it is composed of pure consciousness alone, like a city within the perception of a dream.
The fivefold seed of the world, though situated anywhere, releases its sprout which is the beginning of the world; the imperishable consciousness is the seed of that fivefold group.
Know that whatever is the seed, that is the fruit; therefore, the world consists of Brahman.
Thus, at the beginning of creation, this group of five [elements] exists within the great space.
The self, having become the space of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is imagined and not real;
by means of this [imagined self], even though it attains swelling, this [universe] is spread out.
Even that [space] is not composed of reality because its nature consists of the conceptualization of the form of space;
indeed, nothing that is established by means of what is unestablished can ever be established anywhere.
How could that which is of the nature of conceptual construction, being the very form of the mind, attain reality?
Or if the fivefold world is Brahman by virtue of its being identical with Brahman— ||| MU_3,13.13 |||
That very Brahman, matured through the fivefold process, is the delusion of the three worlds;
just as it manifests at the beginning of creation, this arises from the fivefold [elements].
In the very same way, being itself here today becomes the cause by its own nature;
thus, nothing at all is born, yet the world is perceived as having been born.
Like a city of dreams or a city of creative imagination, the unreal appears as real;
the space of Brahman, the supreme space, exists within the self as the space of the individual soul.
Thus the one of pure nature knows [the self], because of the non-existence of earth and the other elements;
thus this living being is described as the space-self within the void, just as it has been explained.
Now hear how the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa) comes to occupy this body:
that space of the living soul is indeed the void itself within that supreme ether.
In this state, he perceives by his own thought, "I am a spark of light";
he then meditates upon that very [spark] within himself as if it were expanding in the sky.
Just as the moon of one's imagination perceives a hare where there is only non-existence,
so too, by contemplating that very [non-existent] thing as existing in the form of the seer and the seen,
the single entity itself attains duality, like one who perceives his own death in a dream.
Then, assuming as it were a slight degree of grossness, it perceives itself as a star; for in this state, its nature as consciousness manifests as the object according to how it has been cultivated.

Though this [Self] is eternally the void by nature of the void, it itself grasps the notion "I am that" due to its consciousness, just as you, O traveler, assume the state of being a traveler in a dream.
Then, by meditating on the form of the star as the form designated as the future body,
the mind attains that state, just as it [attains] the nature of the object of cognition.
Having seemingly cast off that external [world], it then shines within the hollow of the Tāraka,
even while remaining outside, just as a mountain appears within a mirror.
Just as one perceives a body situated in a well or contained within a casket,
so too does the individual soul perceive consciousness within the subtle body during dreams and mental constructions.

That which the individual soul (jīva), situated within the star-like essence of its own nature, perceives by itself— this is precisely what constitutes intellect (buddhi), mind (citta), and so forth, appearing in the form of a continuum of cognition.
Then the living space (jīvākāśa), situated within the treasury of the space of the stars, seems to expand into the sky with the thought "I shall see," as if to look.
Then, by means of the two apertures as it were, that pair of eyes by which one perceives what is to be called "external" shall come into existence by that name.
That by which it touches is its skin; that by which it hears is hearing;
that by which it smells is the nose; it perceives itself within itself.
That which later shall manifest as his tasting by the name of the tongue is that which vibrates;
it is the activity of the wind and the collection of the organs of action.
Meditating thus on that which is born from form, light, and mental attention,
one whose self is the subtle body remains in the sky within the sky.
Thus, while cultivating the notion of swelling within that spark of fire—
perceiving the unreal as if it were real— the Brahman dwells, bearing the designation "living being" (jīva).
Thus, having fallen into the confusion of conceptualizing the meaning of the word "jīva," he—
whose self is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) and whose form is the sky-like body of the mind (citta)— [remains].
Due to their own conceptualization, one perceives the form as situated within an egg;
another knows it as being in the water, and another as having the nature of a sovereign emperor.
One perceives and even experiences the manifestation of future universes from the mind,
which consists of one's own volitions, just as one experiences the inner chamber of the self.
Perceiving that [world] through the measurement of space, time, action, and substance,
the creator of sounds, while contemplating it, binds [beings] with imagined words.
In this unreal delusion of the world, this so-called "subtle body" appears as something unreal,
just like the act of flying in dreams.
Thus, this very primordial Lord and Progenitor, whose essence is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), arose spontaneously by himself as the Self-born One, even though he was previously unmanifest.
Even when this delusion, which takes the form of the cosmic egg, has come into being,
nothing at all has truly come into being, nor has anything been born, nor is it seen.
That Brahman-space remains as space itself, free from doubt;
though it has the form of a city of imagination, although it exists, it is not real at all.
This uncreated and bodiless painting has arisen in the sky;
it is unmade yet experienced, not real, yet standing as if it were real.

Because Brahmā and the others have been liberated since the beginning of the great aeon (mahākalpa), they undoubtedly possess no prior memory; thus, that [liberation] is the cause of their self-arising (svayambhū).
Therefore, this [world] arising from that is considered to be just as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū) is;
for such is the beginningless experience of the earth and the other elements.
Just as the earth and other elements experienced in a dream appear upon waking,
so too this entire world, when remembered, is always of the nature of mere space.
Just as fluidity exists in water wherever and in whatever manner, so too does no other creation exist within the Supreme Self.
Thus this mature creation exists, and thus this world-process stands; that which is called the "cosmic egg" shines forth as nothing but space itself, devoid of any constructed form.
Thus, this visible world is quiescent, of the nature of space, without foundation and without delusion;
it is without support and without anything to be supported, non-dual and devoid of unity.
Even when the perception of the world has arisen, nothing at all has been produced;
the supreme space remains as nothingness itself, utterly transparent.
In the state of universal withdrawal, that which remained was exactly as it was;
there was neither the object to be placed nor the locus, neither the visible nor the state of being a seer.
There is no cosmic egg, no Brahmā, and nowhere any belonging to the cosmic egg;
there is no world, nor is there a world-creature; everything exists as nothing but peace.
Thus, Brahman alone shines forth as the pure Self by means of the Self within the Self;
because of its consciousness, it appears within itself like water appearing as whirlpools due to its fluidity.
This world, though non-existent, appears here as if it were real;
at the end it perishes as something truly non-existent, just like one's own death in a dream.
Alternatively, because its nature is pure consciousness (*vāja*), this very reality is indeed free from affliction,
undivided, without beginning or end, and has the interior of the sky of pure knowledge as its belly.
In the supreme space itself, the first Lord of Creatures shines eternally by himself, identical with emptiness;
for he possesses a subtle, transportable body and not a form composed of the elements such as earth, since that which has not been born does not exist as a reality.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Self-Existent One," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, this entire world consisting of the "I," the "you," and so forth—the whole range of the visible—is nothing at all;
because it is unproduced, it does not exist, and that which does exist is the Supreme alone.
This very supreme space itself perceives within living beings,
like water moving within the belly of the motionless ocean.

Without ever abandoning its nature as space, let it be seen that the internal activity of consciousness perceives as if it were an object, just as in dreams, mental constructs, mountains, and the like.
That great body of the Virāj-self, which is devoid of earth and the other elements,
is indeed the subtle body (ātivāhika), consisting of pure consciousness and the ether of space.
It resembles a mountain appearing in an imperishable dream; it is like a city seen in a stable dream;
it has the appearance of an army situated within a painting, existing in a mind created by a painter.
It is like a multitude of statues on great pillars that have not been fixed in the ground;
one's own self, unfixed in the space of Brahman, is like a carved figure upon its own pillar.
In the beginning, the first Lord of Creatures was renowned as Svayambhū; because of the absence of his own prior effects, he was without a cause.
At the conclusion of the great dissolution, it is said that even the primordial Grandfathers are liberated; therefore, what prior karma could they possibly possess?
The very nature of the wall must be relinquished; it exists as both visible and invisible.
There is neither the visible, nor the seer, nor the creator, and indeed, nothing at all.
This very thing is the underlying desire for all objects; from it arises the series of living beings, just as a row of lamps arises from a single lamp.
Indeed, by its own volition alone, it departs from its volition, devoid of earth and the other elements,
yet appearing as if possessed of earth and the rest— like one who, without leaving his house, passes from one dream to another.
From this very reflection, these individual souls emanate;
and due to the absence of auxiliary causes, that [reflection] itself is what constitutes them.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, this cause of the effect is one;
therefore, there is no other delusion of creation apart from that.
Brahman alone is the primordial Virāṭ Self; the state of emanation is the Virāṭ Self itself.
That very one exists thus as the space of the individual soul (jīvākāśa), since the earth and other elements are unreal.
Rāma:
Is the mass of living beings finite, or is it infinite?
Or rather, is there an infinite self, a solid mass of souls as vast as a mountain?
Why do the living beings emerge like streams from a rain-cloud, like spray from the ocean, or like sparks from heated iron? MU_3,14.16//
Thus, O Blessed One, tell me the definitive determination regarding the net of living beings;
this has been mostly understood by me, so please reveal that very thing clearly.
Vasiṣṭha said: There is not even a single living being; how then can there be the arising of aggregates?
Your words are like saying that the horn of a hare has flown up into the sky.
There is no individual soul, O Raghava, nor are there multitudes of souls;
nor does there exist any single mass of soul resembling a mountain.

Let your firm conviction be that there are no such things as the conceptualization of the meaning of the word "jīva," nor any conceptualizations whatsoever, for all conceptualizations are devoid of reality.
Indeed, there exists here everywhere the pure, stainless Brahman, which is mere consciousness;
for, by virtue of its omnipotence, it assumes whatever aspect it wills of itself.
Indeed, by means of the very sequence of pure consciousness alone, one quickly beholds that [reality], whether embodied or formless, like a creeper in full bloom.
The individual soul, intellect, the vibration of activity, the mind, duality, and even unity—
all these direct that self-luminous existence toward cognition.
That very ignorance becomes awakened in this way; through awakening, it becomes Brahman itself.
Through discernment, ignorance goes to its destruction, yet that [ignorance] does not itself become aware.
Just as darkness perishes when observed by means of a lamp,
yet its true nature is not known [by the lamp itself], so indeed is it with that which is unawakened.
Thus, Brahman alone is the individual soul (jīvātman), undivided and continuous;
it possesses all powers, is without beginning or end, and assumes the form of the essence of the Great Consciousness.
But because it is entirely infinite, no conceptualization of difference exists within it; for whatever conceptualization there may be, that is itself experienced as that very [reality].
Rāma:
It is so, O Brahmin; how is it that all the living beings of the world do not act according to the will of a single life, under the influence of their unity with the Great Soul?
Vasiṣṭha said: That Great Soul, which is Brahman, consisting of all powers,
remains here exactly as it desires— undivided and without interval.
Whatever that great-souled one desires, that comes to him quickly;
however, if his desire first perishes, then duality arises from that.
Subsequently, for those powers that have been divided into pairs, a sequence of action is thus postulated by him: "By this, indeed, it becomes such."
That restriction which was established by that power of Brahmā and the others—without it, no other powers arise; it is only the will of Pradhāna that comes forth.
That power called the individual soul (jīva), whose will bears fruit,
does not do so without the performance of the regulation of the primary power (pradhāna-śakti).
If the regulation of the power of the Pradhāna were not firmly established,
then the fruit of undertakings would never occur anywhere, due to the presence or absence of that power.
Thus, the Great Soul (Mahājīva), which is Brahman, exists devoid of end, beginning, and middle; it becomes millions upon millions of individual souls, and yet it is nothing at all.
Through the perception of the object of thought, the living being comes into existence and enters the cycle of transmigration;
through the non-perception of that, form attains peace from transmigration.
Thus, through the sequence of activities of the elder souls, the state of being the primordial soul arises for the younger souls, just as the state of gold arises from copper.
In this infinite supreme space, even though this multitude is non-existent,
it arises as if existing, consisting of the wonder of consciousness, while being of the very nature of the void.
That wonder which is encountered by consciousness itself,
prior to the body and so forth that will come to be, the wise know as the contemplation of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāvanā).
That which is consciousness and the light of consciousness is infinite because it consists of that [consciousness];
this entire expanse of the worlds is its reflection.
By means of such terms as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and "modification" (vikāra), that very same immutable consciousness,
though indivisible due to its uniform nature, is awakened by its own power alone.
That which is the self-experience of consciousness, whose nature is uninterrupted play, is the very existence of the world— the luminosity that is devoid of any object of cognition.
This power of consciousness, which is more subtle than even space and is all-pervasive,
perceives this "I-ness" (ahantā) by its very nature.
That which manifests within this [Self] by the Self alone, like water,
as far as the end of the world— that very thing he perceives as the atom of egoity (ahantā).
Since this consciousness, which is beautiful and produces wonder,
manifests itself within its own self, it has thereby spread out that which is called the "world."
O Rāghava, the state of being a mind is the ego; that very thing is a mental construction.
Since even the subtle elements and so forth are consciousness alone, where can duality or unity reside?
If you do not renounce that which is the cause of life, then renounce both "you" and "I. Remain in the middle between existence and non-existence; thus you shall become the essence of reality.
Just as that existence was first conceived by consciousness, so it has arisen;
I perceive that existence and non-existence are non-different from space, and thus I know them.
The sky of consciousness, the void, the movements of the world, the void, the oceans, the gods, and the mountains—
because they are of the nature of the wonder of consciousness in the form of the void, there is indeed nothing else that exists.
Whatever is an ornament of something is never distinct from it;
this holds true even for that which possesses parts—what then need be said regarding that which is partless?
One should always cite that the Consciousness which is beyond thought has no form, for its manifestation is unimpeded;
whatever is the form of the world, that is the form of its own radiance.
Mind, intellect, ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions—
such is the arrangement of synonyms for consciousness (citta) as the reality from which the world exists.
Know that the world is the consciousness of consciousness; for there is no non-worldly consciousness.
Since it is non-worldly, consciousness would be non-consciousness; because there is no difference in being, how could there be a world?
The very same wondrous power that exists at the end of the seed-syllable *marīca* remains as this world, which is nothing more than the subtle element of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Because consciousness possesses the power of thought, that manifestation of its own power which is the conception of "I" within consciousness is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*); it consists of the activity of vibration and is designated as "that which is yet to be."

Whatever conceptualization occurs through the state of consciousness regarding its own produced objects of designation and so forth, that is differentiated by exclusions and modifications; therefore, it does not truly exist.
There is no difference between the agent and the action, for both consist of the vibration of consciousness;
the action is merely that vibration, and that itself is known as the Puruṣa.
The life-force (*jīva*) is the vibration within consciousness; for men, consciousness is that very same thing.
But the mind, taking the form of the senses, goes to various objects in manifold ways.
For the world is indeed a flash of the radiance of consciousness in which all particularity has been stilled;
therefore, nothing other than that exists, such as the relationship of cause and effect.
"I am indestructible, I am unburnable, I am indeed undampenable and un-dryable;
I am eternal, all-pervading, stable, and immovable"—thus it is established.
"Indeed, let them dispute here as they do with their delusions;
we, however, are no longer wandering, for we have become free from delusion."

In the visible, embodied form that is firmly rooted in ignorance, modifications and the like appear as distinct; but they do not exist in the formless consciousness of the knower, which is the sky of consciousness whose nature is both being and non-being.
The mind, which is the essence of the object of thought, expands its powers known as Time and the rest—
powers that are as clear as space— as its own blossoms, which possess the beauty of the honey of consciousness.
The unstruck bow of consciousness itself flashes forth in manifold variety; the jewel of consciousness itself gleams in manifold variety without any external cause.
The wind of consciousness, being non-inert by nature, possesses its own distinctive movement;
the water of consciousness, possessing its own diverse swirling, does not remain stagnant.
Itself fashioned as a lofty peak of consciousness from variegated elements,
it is itself the ever-risen moonlight of consciousness, radiant with the splendor of diverse aesthetic flavors.
The light of consciousness, which is pure by nature, is always manifest of its own accord; yet to the ignorant, it seems as if it has set, while to the wise, consciousness arises through knowledge.
By its own inertia, it has itself reached the state of deep sleep within inert things; likewise, by its own consciousness, the great sky of pure awareness is both vibrating and non-vibrating.
For the world exists and does not exist as the manifestation of the light of consciousness;
the world exists and does not exist as the singular voidness of the space of consciousness.
The world exists and does not exist as the great form of the light of consciousness;
the world exists and does not exist as the dense vibration of the wind of consciousness.
The world exists and does not exist as the blackness of the dense darkness of consciousness;
with the sunlight of the sun of consciousness, the day arrives when the world both exists and does not exist.
The delusion of the world is a particle of the mountain of consciousness-ink;
the world-lineament is the heat of the fire of consciousness; the world is the whiteness of the conch of consciousness.
The world is the interior of the mountain of consciousness; the world is the fluidity of the water of consciousness.
The world is the sweetness of the sugarcane of consciousness; the world is the richness of the milk of consciousness.
The world is the coolness of the frost of consciousness; the world is the blazing of the flame of consciousness.
The world is the oil within the ghee of consciousness; the world is the wave of the river of consciousness.

The world is the sweetness of the honey of consciousness; the world is the golden armlet of consciousness; the world is the fragrance of the flower of consciousness; the world is the fruit at the tip of the creeper of consciousness.
The existence of consciousness alone is the existence of the world, and the existence of the world alone is the body of consciousness;
herein, no distinction, modification, or the like exists, just as no impurity exists in the sky.
Thus, this triple world, being composed of Being, is both existent and non-existent;
or rather, because its nature is non-conceptual, it is that very same reality which is both existence and non-existence.

Where the world— including mountains, heaven, earth, and rivers— does not exist because of the oneness of consciousness, what occasion could there be for the delusion of anything else?
Although the consciousness is as solid as the heart of a stone, it is as clear as its own space;

In the space of the multitude of objects, you are like a mere fragment of space;

Like the arrangement of lines within a sprout, this consciousness, though pervasive,

Know that consciousness, by its very nature, is without cause; it is the primordial grandfather of the entire multitude of causes, established through direct experience.
Nor can the non-existence of consciousness, which is beyond thought, be established even by words;
for it is observed that only that which exists arises, like a sprout from a seed.
Like the sky, the three worlds exist within this Great Consciousness, O dear one, as a division of its perfect emptiness;
for you, through direct experience, have reached the certainty that all this which is visible consists of the Supreme State.

This world is indeed just like space; for just as a pearl shines within the pure sky, so does the world, whose nature is space, shine within the sky of consciousness.

Just as within the ocean, the waters remain motionless and do not deviate from their own nature, yet they seem to become objects of knowledge when known; so too are those who know the supreme reality distinct from those who know only the visible world.

Even though these things, such as earth and so forth, have been experienced in this world which is of the nature of space, they do not exist at all, just like those in dreams and mental constructions.

In this world, which lacks any substantial core and is like a city of Gandharvas,

Therefore, the world, being of the nature of non-consciousness and devoid of an object of cognition, is nothing but the void alone;

Seated before the Goddess who was upon her auspicious throne,

Līlā said:
O Goddess, the supreme ones do not feel agitation for one who is worthy of compassion;

Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, I ask you this which I have long desired;

[The Goddess:
There exists a mirror named "the World," clearer even than the sky,
of which tens of millions of millions of *yojanas* constitute but a minute fraction.
Without joints or bonds, without a head, soft, smooth, and cool; known by the name "the insentient consciousness" (acetyacid), it is without foundation and without grasping.
Space, time, the divisions of space, light, necessity, and succession—
these reflect within it, having attained a state of extreme limitation.
O Mother, the splendor of the reflection of the three worlds resides both outside and within; therein, which could be artificial, and which could be non-artificial? [Līlā]
The Goddess said: O beautiful one, tell me what the lack of artifice in creation is like;
what would constitute its artificiality? Explain this to me exactly as it is.
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, O Mother, just as I stand here and you are present,
O Sovereign of the Gods, I know that this creation is uncreated."
I consider that creation to be artificial wherein my husband now stands, because it is empty, lacking the fulfillment of space, time, and so forth.
The Goddess said:
An artificial creation never arises from that which is non-artificial;
for an effect dissimilar to its cause never emerges from it anywhere.
Līlā said:
O Mother, an effect is seen to be quite distinct from its cause;
water is unable to take up clay, yet the jar produced from it has that very clay as its substrate.
Devī: Indeed,
whatever effect is accomplished by means of auxiliary causes,
some diversity in its primary cause is observed therein.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, there is no cause such as earth or other elements for the creation of your husband;
nor was the earth produced from the terrestrial sphere in that case.
Even if it had flown away from here, how could it be on this earthly plane?
What indeed are the auxiliary factors, and what is the cause in this matter?
Even in the absence of [other] causes, that which arises from auxiliary conditions is experienced by everyone as being none other than the result of its preceding causes.
Līlā said:

and I know the cause of that memory to be this creation—this is my certainty."
The Goddess said:
"O gentle lady, just as memory is of the nature of space, so too is that which arises from it; for the creation of your husband was experienced by you as being nothing but space."
Līlā said:
Just as this creation consisting of the ether of memory has arisen from my Lord, even so do I consider it; that [other] creation is merely an illustration here.
The Goddess said: "So it is; this brilliant creation of your husband appears to you as unreal.
Just so does it appear here, O daughter; I see it thus."
Līlā said:
Just as from this formless Lord a creation consisting of delusion has arisen, so too has this [world] come into being; tell me this for the sake of removing the wall-like world.
The Goddess said: "Just as this creation arose from a mere delusion of prior memory, so too does it appear as consisting of dream-like error; listen as this is explained."
Somewhere within the space of consciousness, there exists a certain pavilion of saṃsāra,
having the form of a covering or a lack of covering, like a pane of glass in the sky.
With Mount Meru as its central pillar, the world-protectors as its statues,
the four continents as its inner chambers, the three realms as its courtyards, and the sun as its lamp.
Its corners were filled with mounds of earth and anthills,
its stones were covered by creeping plants, and it was the dwelling place of an aged Brahmin who had many sons and was the lord of his progeny.
The blackness upon the upper surface of the sky, rich with hosts of bears, cocoons, and spiders,
resounds with the humming produced by swarms of *maṣaka* insects— the Siddhas dwelling in the firmament.
Its corners were enveloped by fierce masses of smoke from houses of clouds;
it was a worm-like being dwelling within the great bamboo-pipes of the paths of the wind, amidst the celestial chariots.
It was filled with the tumultuous clamor of the playful antics of foolish gods, asuras, and others;
it was overflowing with the houses, villages, vessels, and utensils of other worlds.
Its surface was moistened by the waters of rivers, streams, oceans, and lakes;
its hollows shone with the vast expanse of the netherworld, the earth, and heaven.
There, in the interior of a certain corner-room,
upon a surface of stone and clods of earth, there was a single small pit belonging to a mountain village.

In this place, sheltered by rivers, mountains, and forests, that twice-born man became devoted to dharma, possessing fire, wife, and sons, free from disease, provided with cow's milk, and liberated from fear of kings, while being a host to all guests.
The nineteenth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Illusory Nature of the Entire Creation" within the Legend of Līlā. The Goddesses:
In wealth, dress, age, occupation, learning, power, and conduct,
he was like Vasiṣṭha, yet his consciousness was not that of Vasiṣṭha’s.
He was known by the name Vasiṣṭha; his wife was Indusundarī by name, who was Arundhatī on earth and Arundhatī in the sky.
She too was equal to Arundhatī in terms of wealth, dress, age, conduct, learning, power, and behavior, but not in the quality of her consciousness.
She, whose smile was like that of a white water-lily, who possessed the flavor of unfeigned love, and who moved with the languid grace of amorous play, was the very essence of his entire world.
Once, while that brahmin was seated upon a grassy meadow on the slope of that mountain, he saw the lord of the earth below.
Accompanied by his entire retinue, he went out with the desire for the hunt,
amidst the great roar of his army as if wishing to split Mount Meru.
With chowries scattering the rays of the moon, with banners creating a forest of creepers,
and with circles of white umbrellas making the sky appear like a silver-paved floor.
It possessed the color of clouds filled with the dust raised by throngs of cavalry and horses marked with fire-like spots;
it was protected by elephant-corps stationed within watchtowers and gateways with uplifted trunks.
A circle of spirits from all directions was being driven about in a great whirlpool of tumultuous clamor,
while necklaces, armlets, and earrings of shimmering gold and rubies were flying about.
Beholding that protector of the earth, he thought this:
"Oh, how delightful is sovereignty, illumined by every form of prosperity!"
"When shall I become a lord of the earth, filling the groves of the ten directions with foot-soldiers, chariots, elephants, horses, banners, parasols, and yak-tail whisks?"
When will the breezes, fragrant with the nectar of kunda flowers,
drink the perspiration born of the fatigue of love-play from the women of the inner apartments?
When shall I make the faces of noble women as bright as the rising moon, by scattering my fame throughout the quarters like camphor?
From that time forth, the brahmin remained thus resolved;
devoted to his own duty, he was ever diligent throughout his life until death.
Like a frost-bolt intent on shattering a lotus,
old age, accompanied by heartache, swiftly approached that twice-born man.
As he drew near to death, his wife fell into a state of withering,
like a creeper at the onset of summer that fades for fear of the heat when its flowering season has passed.
Then that woman propitiated me just as you have;
having realized that immortality is very difficult to attain, she chose this boon.
"O Queen, lest the life-force of my deceased husband depart from his very own pavilion,
I therefore accepted her."
Then, by the power of time, that brahmin passed away;
yet he remained in that very space of the house in the form of the vital breath (jīvākāśa).
By the power of his own numerous former resolutions,
that most powerful lord of the earth himself became one whose very body was like space.
The king was a conqueror of the three worlds: he had subdued the surface of the earth through his majesty, overwhelmed the heavens with his prowess, and protected the netherworld with his compassion.
He is the fire of time for the factions of his enemies, the god of love for women,
Mount Meru for the winds of sensory objects, and the sun for the lotuses of the virtuous.
He is the mirror of all scriptures, the wish-fulfilling tree for those who seek,
the footstool for the foremost of the twice-born, and the full moon for the nectar-like light of the Dharma.

When that twice-born man, whose body was composed of the elemental ether, had become a corpse within the space inside his own house— that space which is the self consisting of the ether of the mind— *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 3.19.24.
His Brahmin wife, utterly emaciated by grief,
split asunder in her heart like a parched bean pod.
Having become a corpse along with her husband and casting off her body far away,
she approached her husband by means of her subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*).
Following her husband like a river that has followed its channel,
she attained freedom from grief, just as a blossoming cluster of flowers does with the arrival of spring.
There, this brahmin possessed houses, land, immovable property, and great wealth;
yet today, on his eighth day since death was attained, his life-force remains within a temple in the village of Giri.
The twentieth canto, titled "The Death of the Brahmin," from the Līlopākhyāna; the goddesses said:
That husband of yours has today become a twice-born man who has attained the status of a king;
and she who was named Arundhatī, the Brāhmaṇī, you are she, O lady.
"May you two, a noble couple, rule this kingdom here like a pair of young cakravāka birds, or like Śiva and Umā born upon the earth."
Thus has been described to you in its entirety that former delusion of worldly existence;
it is mere illusion, like the sky itself, assuming the form of the individual soul.
This delusion has been reflected in the mirror of consciousness from that [prior] delusion;
though it is entirely unreal, arising from the unreal, it brings about the destruction of worldly existence for you both.
Therefore, who could consist of delusion, or who could be free from delusion? This creation is nothing other than the unfolding of unimpeded and vast consciousness.
