O Queen, how has your word come to be so false?
Where is the life of a brahmin in his own home, and where are we standing here?
How can such an intermediate world, that earth, those mountains, and those ten directions—
within which my husband resides— fit inside a single house?
The intoxicated Airāvaṇa was bound within the belly of a mustard seed;
a battle was fought by a gnat with swarms of lions inside the hollow of an atom.
Mount Meru was placed within a lotus seed and swallowed by a honey-drinker;
having heard the thundering of clouds in a dream, peacocks dance in a painting.
Just as it is inconsistent that you are the sovereign of all sovereigns,
so too is it inconsistent that the earth and mountains exist within your house.
O Goddess of gods, tell this as it truly is with an unsullied mind; for those of great power do not tremble when [the truth] is well-received through grace.
The Goddess said:
"I do not speak this falsely; listen to it exactly as it is, O beautiful one.
For the breaking of the laws of destiny is not performed by those such as myself."
I myself established that boundary which was being violated by another; once it has been breached by me, who else will uphold it?
The soul of the twice-born, while remaining in that very same abode of his,
perceives this entire realm of the earth within the sky itself, as one whose nature is space.
That former memory of yours has been lost and has arisen otherwise; O lady, this death is like the memory of waking that occurs in a dream.

Just as the three worlds appear in a dream, just as the triple universe appears through mental construction, just as there is a battle over the contents of a story, and just as there is water in a desert land; MU_3,20.17.
This earth, together with its mountains, forests, and cities, was situated within that brahmin’s house,
as if within a mental construction or a mirror.
This density of creation appears as if real, though it is unreal;
it exists within the hollow of the sheath of that sky of consciousness which manifests as unreal.
That which arises from the unreal—namely, "memory"—is itself unreal;
even a wave in the river of a mirage is not real.
Know that this dwelling of yours is situated within the space-receptacle of that house; know me, yourself, and everything else to be nothing but that void alone.
In this matter, dreams, associations, intentions, and the succession of one's own experiences are the primary means of valid cognition for awakening, like lamps.
The life-force of the twice-born remained within the house of the brahmin;
meanwhile, the earth with its oceans and forests stood like a bee upon a lotus.
Within a certain single, delicate hollow of that [tree],
this city appears like a tuft of hair in the sky.
O slender one, this abode of yours is situated within this very city;
therefore, why does it appear like a herd of elephants within even a minute atom?
"O child, within every single atom of the conscious Self there exist worlds within worlds; by whom can this even be numbered? (Muktikopaniṣad 3.20.26)
Līlā said: "O Supreme Goddess, that Brahmin died on the eighth day;
many years have passed for us since then, so how can this be?"
The Goddess said:
"Just as there is no length of space, so too there is no length of time. Listen as I explain, according to the proper method, how this is indeed not the case."
Just as this manifestation of the creation of the world is mere appearance,
so too is this manifestation of moments and eons mere appearance.
O child, listen to this sequence of how the manifestation of moments, kalpas, the creation of the world, and the births of beings occurs exactly as it is.

Having experienced for a moment the fainting of false death, the living soul, though its nature is space itself, at that very moment [returns] to the state of space by means of a mere opening of the eyes.
"I am that which is to be supported here in this support; I am situated here"—thus it perceives;
"this body, possessed of hands, feet, and so forth, is mine"—thus it views it.
Whenever he perceives his own body, at that very moment he perceives this:
"I am the son of this father; these many years are mine."
"These are my delightful kinsmen; this is my lovely dwelling.
I was born, I became a child, and I have grown to be such as I am now."
And all those kinsmen of his likewise continue to dwell there;
because of their identity with the single mass of the space of consciousness, they exist even within his own self.
Thus, even when this forest of saṃsāra has arisen within this consciousness, nothing at all has arisen or remains; it is just like the stainless sky.
Just as consciousness exists in the dreamer, so too does that same consciousness exist in the object seen;
because it is always one and the same, the seeing of the dreamer and the dream-object is therefore nothing but consciousness itself.
Just as consciousness arises in a dream, so it arises through the perception of the next world;
and just as it arises in the next world, so too does it arise here in this world.
Between those things that are non-existent and those that are existent in dreams, in the next world, and in this world,
there is not even the slightest difference, just as between waves in water.
Therefore, this entire universe is unborn, and because it is unborn, it is also undestructible;
and because its nature is that of the insentient, it does not exist at all—whatever appears is only consciousness.
Just as this [consciousness] is of the nature of the supreme ether even when not devoid of objects of thought,
so too it remains of the nature of the supreme ether even when accompanied by objects of thought.
Since that which is to be cognized is not other than this [consciousness], just as the state of being a wave is not other than water;
and yet, the state of being a wave does not exist at all, for it is just like the horn of a hare.

That very [consciousness], though never falling from its own nature, appears as if it has become the object of cognition; therefore, the visible object does not exist at all—how, then, could there be the notion of a seer and a seen?
In the mere twinkling of an eye, immediately after the living being's delusion of death,
the splendor of the visible creation of the three worlds arises as a mental representation.
According to the place, according to the time, according to the undertaking, according to the sequence,
according to the origin, according to the mother, according to the father, and according to the biological son.
According to age, according to agreement, according to station, according to desire;
according to kinship, according to service, and according to the rising and setting of one's efforts.
The one whose form is consciousness perceives that he is born even though unborn,
as well as space, time, action, substance, mind, intellect, and the senses.
In an instant, at the end of death, one perceives the body as youth,
thinking, "This is my mother, this is my father, and I was a child."
Whether it has been experienced or not experienced, that sequence consisting of memory which arises later is like the emergence of fruit from a flower.
It is experienced that everything passes away in the mere blink of an eye;
yet for Hariścandra, a single night became like twelve years.
For those separated from their beloveds, a single day becomes like a year;
and in the realm of dreams, one thinks, "I am dead," or "I am born," or "This is another father for me."

The notion that something yet to be enjoyed has already been enjoyed arises even when it has not been enjoyed; and the notion that something has been enjoyed arises when it has not been enjoyed—this is observed among gamblers and the like. Thus, enough with such examples.
In the consciousness of intoxication, sleep, and so forth, emptiness becomes crowded, misfortune is equal to festivals, and even separation is a gain.

Just as pungency resides within the tiny seed of a pepper, or as a network of carved figures exists within a pillar, so too does this visible world exist, non-different from the Unborn and quiescent; for whom, then, could there be the perception of bondage or liberation, and from what, or by what means?
In the *Maṇḍapopākhyāna*, also known as the *Līlopākhyāna*,
the twenty-first canto, titled "The Exposition of the Ultimate Reality of the World."
The Goddess said:
Immediately after the delusion of death, all worlds appear clearly to the living being, just as all forms appear fully to one whose eyes have opened.
And [these worlds] consist of space, time, the divisions of direction, ether, dharma, and karma;
they are expansive, infinite, and endure until the end of the aeon.
Even that which was neither experienced nor seen, such as "this was done by me," comes to be remembered at that very moment, just like one's own death in a dream.
Thus, this infinite delusion, radiant within the void of the sky of consciousness,
is a city-like conceptualization called "the world," which is devoid of walls.
"I am this world"— this very memory of creation expands,
producing only the confusion that results from the habitual reversal between the distant past and the present moment.

Thus, cognition is of two kinds: that which has experienced an object and that which has not; yet, even when previously appearing as if devoid of a cause, it proceeds as nothing other than the nature of consciousness itself.
Even in the case of what has not been experienced, the state of being experienced arises within consciousness;
it is not distinct from the dream-delusion, just as the memory of a father arises toward one who is not actually one's father.
At times, having abandoned the state of memory, it appears as mere intuition alone,
first in the form of the Lord of Creation, and thereafter in succession.

O slender one, this visible world, beginning with the three realms, exists for some in the memory of what has been experienced, but for others it does not exist in the memory of what has been experienced.
For this lordship over subjects appears to some atoms of consciousness even without memory, occurring by mere chance, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.
The visible world, when completely forgotten, is designated as liberation;
therein, there exist no desired or undesired objects for anyone whatsoever.
Without the attainment of absolute non-existence,
liberation— which consists of non-arising— cannot possibly emerge, for the state of "I" and the world persist.
The delusion of a snake in a rope does not occur without the presence of the referent for the word "snake";
likewise, although the world is eternally unarisen, peaceful, and quiescent, it does not cease to appear as such.
Being only half-pacified, he is not truly pacified, for he arises again through a different state;
even when one demon has ended, another demon arises for the one who is not wise.
And this worldly existence is merely an expansion;
such is the certainty that it appears as such due to the absence of a cause, and thus it comes to non-existence here.
Līlā:
In the creation consisting of the forms of the Brahmin and the Brahmin woman, what is the cause? How could that memory have arisen without something to be remembered?
The Goddess said:
"In that case, the cause is the memory of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
and his memory cannot possibly exist previously, because he was liberated from his prior birth."
Previously, the citi-consciousness itself could not possibly have been an object of memory;
for the state of being born from a lotus and so forth belongs to the conscious self as it exists in its own right.
Another being is born with the consciousness "I existed," while yet another arises by chance, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit, consisting merely of a flash of intuition.
Thus, when the world has arisen, there is nothing whatsoever that has ever arisen anywhere;
it is merely situated in the sky of consciousness.
The supreme state is the cause of this twofold mindfulness;
this relationship of cause and effect is but the single expanse of consciousness.
The existence of cause and effect [is established] through auxiliary causes;
the identity of cause and effect does not cease due to their absence.
Know that this very perception is nothing but the form of Great Consciousness (mahācidrūpa) due to recollection;
therefore, the relationship of cause and effect here is not real, and the word [denoting it] is not ultimate.
Thus, not even the slightest visible thing, such as the three worlds and so forth, has arisen;
it is only the sky of consciousness, abiding solely within itself, the sky of consciousness.
Līlā said:
"Oh, what a supreme vision has been shown to me by you, O Goddess!
The beauty of the world's forms is like the splendor of the morning light to the radiance of the eyes."
Now that my vision has reached such maturity in this regard, O Goddess, dispel this curiosity of mine without further delay through your practice.
Lead me to that mountain village, that place of creation, where that brahmin dwelt together with his brahmin wife.
The Goddess:
"By relying upon that supreme, purifying vision which consists of the nature of consciousness beyond the object of thought, and by casting off this [limited] form, you shall become stainless."

Then, like a man standing on the ground who perceives a city within the sky through his own mental resolve, you will undoubtedly attain the Self that is of the nature of space and abides in the ether.
We behold him thus situated, together with creation immediately following;
for in this way, through the gateway of that vision, the body is indeed the supreme bolt.
Līlā said:
O Goddess, by means of this very body, another world is attained; or is it not? Tell me the reasoning for this out of your grace.
The Goddess said:
"These worlds, which are formless, have been perceived by you as having form through a vain grasping, just as one might perceive a golden ring where there is only gold."
Just as the nature of a ring does not exist even in the forest of forms that constitute a ring,
so too the nature of the world does not exist within the state of consciousness that appears in the form of the world.
This world is indeed only space, and that very Brahman; it is not a visible object, for not even a speck of dust is seen here, like [a reflection] in the ocean.
Brahman alone sees Brahman; that which is not Brahman does not see Brahman.
Its very nature is such that it is celebrated by names such as "creation" and the like.
There is no arising of the relationship of cause and effect between Brahman and the world,
because of the absence of all auxiliary causes.
As long as the notion of duality is not stilled through the practice of cultivation,
you certainly do not perceive Brahman, which is not of that nature.
In this regard, those such as ourselves have attained proficiency;
for by means of the repeated practice of the realization of Brahman, we indeed perceive that state.
Like a city of imagination, my body is composed of space;
I perceive that state, which is Brahman itself, through this body as if it were the wind.
I am one whose body is pure knowledge, just like these beings born from lotuses;
O lady, this world beginning with Brahmā is my very limb.
Without practice in you, the ignorant one does not attain the nature of Brahman; remaining as a self whose form is conceptualization, he does not perceive that [Brahman].
Wherein one’s own city of mental construction is not perceived within one’s own body,
there the city of another’s mental construction is likewise not perceived within one’s own body.
Therefore, having abandoned this body, you who are of the nature of the space of consciousness—perceive that very [reality] immediately; do so, O best among those who know what must be done.
Just as a city of one's imagination is real for the one who imagines it—
whether with a body or without a body— it is nothing at all for anyone else.
Just as this delusion of the world came into its present state at the beginning of creation,
so too has destiny attained its full maturity from that very time onward.
Līlā said:
"O Goddess, you said, 'Let us go to the house of the Brahmin and his wife. How can this be accepted? O Mother, how should we proceed?"
"Having cast off this body here, with a mind following pure being, I shall go to that supreme world; you must tell me how."
The Goddess said:
Just as the tree of your mental construction, though it exists, is of the nature of space—
neither of the nature of a wall nor obstructed by a wall, nor is it destroyed by a wall.
That manifestation, it is said, belongs to one whose form is the mind of a single pure being; therefore, it differs only slightly from that supreme [state].
Such as this body is, I shall not depart leaving it behind;
by means of this very body, I shall reach that region, just as the wind carries fragrance.
Just as water mingles with waters, fire with fire, and wind with wind,
so too does the mind-body merge with other mind-made bodies.

For consciousness that is not of the nature of earth does not attain oneness with consciousness that is of the nature of earth; where, then, could there be a mutual collision between a mountain of conceptual construction and a real mountain?
This mental body of yours, like mine, is indeed purely subtle (ātivāhika);
yet, due to long-standing habitual tendencies, it has been grasped as a material (ādhibhautika) body through the intellect.
Just as in a dream, just as in long-term meditation, just as through delusions, just as in the imagination of one addicted to vice, and just as in a city of the Gandharvas; //MU_3,21.54//
When the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā) has indeed reached its firm state,
then the body returns no longer to the condition of being composed of material elements.
Līlā:

When the conviction that the body is merely a subtle, transportable vehicle (ātivāhika-deha) becomes firm, this [gross] body attains that state; it perishes when the delusion regarding its condition vanishes.
The Goddess said:
"If something truly exists, then this process of destruction and non-destruction might occur;
but if it does not exist in reality, what kind of destruction could there be?"
When the delusion of a snake in a rope has vanished due to the realization of its true nature, what talk can there be as to whether the son is destroyed or not destroyed?
For the snake itself was never there. Thus, what discussion can there be?
Just as the material body is no longer seen through the thorough knowledge of truth,
so too the material body is no longer seen through the knowledge of the subtle body (*ativāhika*).
If conceptual construction were constructed by anyone, it would cease; but that which never exists here has already been cast aside like a stone.
"O blessed lady, we see this body and so forth as existing, mutually filled with one another; this is the truth, yet you do not see it."
When, at the initial creation, consciousness becomes conceptualized through imagination,
from that point onward, a single sense of "self-ownership" is perceived as if it were an object of sight.
Līlā: When the supreme reality alone exists— tranquil, undivided by space, time, and so forth— whence can there be any occasion for conceptual construction?
The Goddess said:

Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, just as the state of being a wave exists in water, and just as reality exists in dreams, mental constructions, cities [of the Gandharvas], and so forth; //MU_3,21.64//

In the experience of truth there is indeed no such thing, nor is there any conceptualization in the state of consciousness; for that [consciousness] is by its very nature free from affliction and possesses no separate self.
Just as there is no dust in the sky, so too there is no part (kalā) in the Supreme;
this one, unborn reality is therefore peaceful, being beyond both parts and the perception of parts.
Whatever appears here is the stainless manifestation of that very [Self] alone,
like the radiance of a beautiful, supreme gem known as gold.
Līlā said:
O Goddess, tell us this: for how long a time have we been thus deluded by these conceptual constructions of duality and non-duality?
The Goddess said:
"O fickle one, you have long been deluded and distressed by non-investigation.
Non-investigation arises from one's own nature; it perishes through investigation."
Non-investigation perishes through investigation in a mere moment;
since this [non-investigation] is non-existent within it, this ignorance does not exist.
Therefore, there is neither non-investigation, nor ignorance, nor bondage;
there is no liberation either—this world is simply unimpeded, pure consciousness.
Since you did not investigate this for so long, you were not fully awakened; you were merely wandering, agitated like one in the ocean.
From this day forward, you have become awakened; you are liberated and discerning.
The seed has fallen into your mind, and the latent tendencies have been thinned away.
For when the drama of saṃsāra— the visible world— has never arisen from the very beginning,
then how, by what means, or even as what could there be any latent impression (*vāsanā*)?

Therefore, when the absolute non-existence [of the world] is accomplished, and when the supreme state is established in the single-pointed meditation of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing within non-conceptual samādhi;
When this seed for the destruction of latent impressions has sprouted even slightly within the heart,
the perceptions of passion, hatred, and the like will gradually cease to arise.
This origin of saṃsāra will reach a state of rootlessness;
it will find firm establishment in non-conceptual meditative absorption.
Free from the stain of temporal impurity, as pure as the expanse of the sky by its own power,
you shall exist within the totality of the instruments, effects, and causes, yet through the influence of only a few specific effects.
The twenty-second canto, titled "The Instruction on Rest," from the Narrative of Līlā.
The Goddess said:
Just as the dream-body is not real upon the full understanding of the dream,
so too this waking body, though experienced, is not real.
Just as the dream-body subsides through the full comprehension of the dream,
so too the waking body subsides through the thinning of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Just as this body is perceived at the end of a dream or a mental construction,
so too does the subtle body (ativāhika) arise within the state of waking imagination.
Just as the state of deep sleep arises in a dream when the seeds of latent impressions are absent,
so too does liberation arise in the waking state when the seeds of latent impressions are absent.
But that which is the latent impression (vāsanā) of those liberated while living is not a [binding] impression;
it is designated as pure being (śuddhasattva) and is called the universal existence (sattāsāmānya).
That sleep which possesses latent impressions is known as deep sleep (suṣupta);
that waking state which possesses latent impressions is called dense delusion (ghana-moha).
Sleep in which all latent impressions have been destroyed is called the fourth state (turya);
this occurs even while one is awake, once the supreme state has been realized.
The maintenance of life for those living here whose latent impressions have been exhausted,
yet which remains unrecognized by those who are not liberated, is called "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti).
The mind, having fallen under the influence of pure beings and having its latent impressions shattered,
attains a subtle, transportive state, like snow submerged in heat.
The mind, having become subtle and transportable, meets with other minds that have attained perfection through various births in creation, but not with anything else.
When this sense of "I" of yours comes to rest through your own practice, then,
at the end of the visible world, an expansive awareness will dawn for you of its own accord.
When that nature of yours is known as being of a subtle, transportive (ātivāhika) character, it attains an eternal state;
then, through the light of other mental constructs, it becomes intrinsically pure.
Therefore, O blameless one, exert effort toward the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā);
when that [attenuation] reaches full maturity, you will become liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
As long as this stainless moon of awakening has not been fulfilled,
let the body remain here while you look toward the other world.
A body of flesh enters into union with another body of flesh alone during worldly activities and actions, but not with a mental body.
This has been stated exactly as it exists, according to experience;
it is established even among children, being self-evident, and not like a boon or a curse.
Through the intense practice of awakening, the attenuation of the latent tendencies of saṃsāra arises for this very body; indeed, this is the state of the mind-body.
And this very [self], though about to arise here, is not perceived by anyone;
rather, people perceive only the body as it is dying.
This body neither dies nor does anything at all live;
for who indeed [is there] in the delusion of dreams and mental constructs, [to experience] death and life?
Just as life and death exist in a person created by imagination, so too,
O daughter, do these appear as unreal within this physical body.
Līlā said:
O Goddess, this stainless knowledge has been taught to me by you;
once it has entered my hearing, the cholera of the universe comes to rest.
For here, who indeed provides assistance, what is the practice, or of what kind is it?
How does it attain nourishment, and once it is nourished, what would come to pass?
The Goddess said: Whatever is done by whomever, whenever, and in whatever manner,
that never attains perfection here in this world without practice.
The wise know that contemplation upon That, discourse concerning That, mutual awakening to That, and the fixing of the vital breath and the mind upon That, constitute the practice of Brahman.
But those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end,
being liberated from the delusion of dualities, are to be known as the servants of Brahman.
Those whose nights pass in reflections on the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra),
intent upon the thinning of latent impressions (vāsanā), remain as practitioners of Brahman.

Those noble souls who, being dispassionate, cultivate within themselves the attenuation of the inclination toward enjoyments for the sake of non-becoming— they, the fortunate ones, are victorious on this earth.
Those whose minds are elevated by the beauty of nobility, colored by the essence of dispassion, and overflowing with bliss— they are the supreme practitioners.
Those who strive through reasoning and according to the scriptures to understand the absolute non-existence of any knowable object are established as practitioners of Brahman.
The visible world was never produced even at the beginning of creation; it does not exist at all, always.
"This world" and "I"—the wise know the practice of awakening to be the realization that these do not exist.
When passion, aversion, and the like have been attenuated through the realization of the impossibility of the perceptible [world],
that delight which arises from strength is declared to be the practice of Brahman.

The attenuation of passion, hatred, and the like through the realization of the impossibility of the perceptible world is called "austerity" (tapas) in the world; for the defect of the perceptible is the cause of suffering.
For when there is the realization of the impossibility of the visible [object], that is called the knowledge of the knowable;
through the cultivation of that, there is nirvāṇa—thus, this cultivation is of great benefit.

The profound sleep of existence, which has lasted through many nights, falls away from the mind— like a great frost in autumn— when it is intensely drenched by the waters of constant discernment, which are as cooling as ice.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. The assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the twenty-third canto, titled "The Description of the Practice of Higher Knowledge," Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus conversed that night with that beautiful woman, while the attendants were indeed asleep in the pavilion of the inner apartments; MU_3,23.1.
In that dwelling whose doors and windows were secured by firm bolts, and whose clever mind was languid with the thick, abundant fragrance of a profusion of flowers;
She stands beside a corpse adorned with unfading garlands and garments,
her abode illuminated by a face like the entire, stainless, full moon.
Having gone to the place of concentration, they stood with their limbs motionless,
as if carved from a jeweled pillar or placed upon a painted wall.
They both abandoned all their anxieties as contraction set in,
like two lotus plants at the end of the day when their streaks of fragrance have spread abroad.
The two became intensely tranquil, pure, and devoid of vibration,
like a pair of rain-clouds on a windless mountain in autumn.
Through their non-conceptual meditative absorption, they abandoned consciousness in the void,
just as two lovely wish-fulfilling creepers lose their full sap at the end of the season.

When, through those two [means of knowledge], it is understood that the error "I" and "the world"—that is, the visible object—has no origination from the very beginning, and that its nature is absolute non-existence; //MU_3,23.8//
Then, O sinless one, this visible demon has completely vanished for those two, and because of its very non-existence, it is like a hare's horn for us.
For that which does not exist at the very beginning likewise does not exist in the present; though it appears, it is as if unmanifest. Therefore, the world is like the water of a mirage.
The two women became nothing but their own inherently peaceful nature,
like the sky utterly free from the multitude of objects such as the moon and the sun.
By that very body of knowledge, the goddess of cognition crossed over;
but as a human being, she quickly crossed by means of the other [body], which corresponds to both knowledge and ignorance.
Having ascended just a span's height within the house itself, they indeed became two beings with the form of the ether of consciousness, possessing the appearance of sky-goers.
Then those two playful women, with their graceful eyes,
by the very nature of their consciousness of the object of thought, moved as if far away into the sky.
Remaining there, with a single movement of consciousness, they leaped across the expanse of the sky,
which was ten million yojanas wide, from one distant point to another even more distant.
Due to their inherent nature of perceiving what is seen, even though their bodies were like space, they became two companions here devoted to affection by gazing upon each other’s forms.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Traveling of Līlā and Prajñapti through the Body of Consciousness into Space," Vasiṣṭha says:
Having leaped from afar to even further, they slowly ascended to a high station;
placing hand in hand, they beheld the sky as they went.
It was swollen like a single vast ocean, deep and pure within,
soft, and bestowing the pleasant enjoyment of contact with the gentle breeze.
It is thoroughly delightful and serene, due to its immersion in the waters of emptiness; it is exceedingly pure and profound, like a virtuous person who is gracious.
They rested upon the pure, expansive nectar-filled interior of the peak-like clouds, as stainless as the belly of the full moon.
In that place, enchanting with the fragrance of the Mandāra garlands of the Siddhas and Gandharvas,
they took delight as the sweet breezes issued forth from the lunar orb.
At the end of the heat, they swam amidst a mass of clouds thick with water and slow-moving like a lake, crowded with red lotuses resembling flashes of lightning.
They wandered extensively through the quarters of the sky like two female bees among lotus ponds, upon the tips of the lotus-stalk sprouts that were the great mountains rising from the earth.
In that pavilion formed by the circles of clouds agitated by the wind, which bore downpours like the cascades of the Ganges, the wise ones dwelt with the thought that it was a shower-house.
Then Madhura and Kāminī, resting according to their strength,
beheld in the void of space a sky heavy with great agitation.
Never before seen, one another’s crowded hollows being filled and emptied even by hundreds of millions of worlds.
Higher and higher, ever more aloft, it was surrounded by various distinct celestial chariots of living beings, clouds, and rays of light, possessing diverse forms and coverings.
With the radiance from the ruby slopes of the principal mountains such as Meru, which completely filled the sky on all sides, it resembled the interior of the flames at the end of an aeon.
It was as beautiful as the slopes of the Himalayas with the floods of light from its pearl-like peaks, and it shone like a golden plateau with the radiance of the regions of the Golden Mountain.
The blueness of the meadows and grounds, through the luster of great emeralds,
[overcomes] the blackness arising from the darkness produced by the non-truth of the observer's failing vision.
With its multitude of celestial chariots having the *pārijāta* creeper as their fluttering banner,
the ground of lapis lazuli appeared as if its very form were blossoming with the clusters of enlightenment.
[He saw] the coming and going of those who had conquered the winds through the great siddhi of mental speed,
[a place] filled with the sounds of celestial chariots, houses, divine women, songs, and musical instruments.
The intervals between the movements of the multitudes of beings wandering through the three worlds were sparse;
it was crowded with hosts of gods and asuras whose paths were not seen by one another.
A circle of kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and guhyakas stationed at its perimeter;
a multitude of celestial chariots being carried along with great speed by the mass of wind.
It resounded with the deep roar of moving celestial chariots, its dense thunder capable of being grasped by the fist;
it possessed wind-machines that stirred from the movement of the hosts of planets and constellations.
The ground was abandoned by those who had achieved only minor accomplishments, scorched by the heat of the nearby sun;
the chariots of the deluded were burnt by the winds from the mouths of the Sun’s horses.
It was restless with the constant movement of throngs of world-protectors and celestial nymphs,
and shrouded in clouds of incense smoke rising from the burning of incense by the women of the divine inner apartments.
The ornaments fallen from the limbs of celestial women carried away by birds; the power of darkness consisting of a mass of fierce splendor that was unbearable even to ordinary Siddhas.
By the dense clouds, shaken by the coming and going of powerful throngs of *siddhas*,
the Himavat, Meru, and Mandara mountains stood with their flanks veiled in white.
It was surrounded by swarms of crows, owls, and vultures gathered together and moving about,
like the waves of the ocean filled with dancing *ḍākinīs*.
It was filled with throngs of dancing yoginīs who had faces like dogs, crows, camels,
and donkeys, coming and going for no purpose across a hundred yojanas.
A dwelling filled with clouds of incense smoke exhaled by the city guardians,
where pairs of siddhas and gandharvas had commenced the festival of love-making.
Its path was traversed by khadira trees intoxicated by hearing the songs of heaven,
and its wings were marked by hundreds of thousands of celestial chariots moving without ceasing.
The waters of the triple-pathed river flowed within the hollows dug out by the mass of winds,
while the children of the gods moved about, preoccupied with gazing at this marvel.
In some places it possessed thunderbolts, wheels, tridents, swords, and spears moving amidst clouds of doubt;
in others, it contained the tall Tumburu and Nārada dwelling in a home without walls.
In some places, it was agitated by the great onset of vast clouds upon the path of the clouds;
elsewhere, it resembled a painted depiction of a cloud from the end of an eon, rendered as if mute.
In some places it was like a cloud beautiful with a great mountain of rising wings and dark soot; in other places, it was like a rain-cloud lovely with a flowing stream of gold.
In some places, it is like a cloth of clouds—dumb and rained upon by the intense heat that resembles the moon;
in other places, it is the water of emptiness, utterly stilled within a windless ocean.
In some places, the grass-blades and shoots of its celestial chariots were tossed by the powerful rivers of wind;
in other places, it was stainless with the brilliance of the skin on the backs of swarms of moving bees.
In some places it was grey with the dust stirred up by winds in the caves of Mount Meru;
in other places its grounds were variegated by the splendors of celestial chariots and gods.
In some places it was garlanded by circles of naked, intoxicated mothers; in other places it was filled with hosts of female lords of yogis who were constantly laughing, shouting, and agitated.
In some places, the circle of sages rested in tranquil meditative absorption,
equally free from all agitation, enchanting the minds of the virtuous.
In some places there were circles of singing kinnaras, gandharvas, and celestial women;
in some places it was crowded with motionless cities; and in some places it carried the foremost of the gods.
In some places it was blocking the flow of cities, in some places it had besieged great cities;
in some places it was a city created by illusion, and in some places it was a city yet to come.
In some places there were lakes with wandering moons, and in others lakes with stagnant waters;
in some places there were throngs of Siddhas moving through the air, and in others the rising of the moon.

In some places it consists of the rising sun; in some places it is filled with the darkness of night; in some places it is tawny with the silken garment of twilight; and in some places it is grey with mist.
In some places white with celestial palaces, in others like a rain-cloud,
and in some places the sky itself appearing as if it were dry land where the guardians of the world have come to rest.
In some places, the hosts of gods and asuras were busily moving upward and downward;
in other places, they were agitated by their movements in the eastern, western, northern, and southern directions.
In some places, it extends for hundreds of thousands of yojanas where incense is difficult to obtain;
in other places, it is like the sky, filled with indestructible darkness, as if one were blind.

It is indestructible and vast splendor, resembling the sun or fire in some places, yet as cold as the interior of a mass of snow in others, such as in the abodes of the moon and other celestial bodies.
In some places there were forests of *kalpa* trees and creepers dancing within great cities;
in other places, there were divine cities with their lofty towers collapsing after being struck down by the Daityas.
In some places it was marked by streaks of fire from the falling of celestial chariots; in other places it was struck by the mutual clashing of hundreds of rising comets.
In some places, it was free from all inauspiciousness, being favored by a multitude of auspicious planets;
in some places, it was pervaded by the darkness of night, and in others, it was radiant with daylight.
In some places there were clouds thundering amidst difficult terrain, in others the moving clouds were silent;
in some places there was a profusion of flower-like fragments of white clouds scattered by the wind.
In some places it is utterly empty, pure, and boundless;
like the heart of a wise man, it is spread forth—blissful, soft, peaceful, and transparent.
In some places, the field of the sky-dwellers resounded with the cries of parrots, peacocks, and swarms of frogs from their throats, while being enveloped by the radiance of empty stars.
In some places it was covered by birds such as peacocks with golden crests,
and by the mounts of the goddesses and vidyādharīs which had taken up their positions there.
In some places there were circles of peacocks dancing amidst the clouds,
while in others the ground was darkened by fire-parrots as if it were a patch of green grass.
In some places, there were clouds in the form of the vehicle [of Yama], due to the majesty of the buffalo of the Lord of the Dead;
in other places, dark clouds were swallowed by horses out of a suspicion that they were mouthfuls of grass.

In some places it was pervaded by the cities of the gods, and in others accompanied by the cities of the Daityas; with cities that could not reach one another, it was formidable with the gaps between those cities.
In some places it was radiant with Bhairava dancing in the form of the Kulācala mountains; in other places it was the binding of hosts of celestial women from the city of the Gandharvas.
In some places, the ocean was sprinkled by hundreds of thousands of trees destroyed by trembling mountains;
in other places, it was cooled by the waters of a lotus-pond in the sky created by his illusory power.
In some places, the lordly mountains of the same class were dancing along with the Vināyakas;
in other places, mountains were being launched into the air by wings filled with gurgling winds.
In some places, there was a wind cooled and gladdening by a rain of moonbeams;
in other places, there were trees, mountains, and clouds scorched by the blazing fire.
In some places there was the absolute silence of winds that had utterly subsided;
in other places there arose a rising resembling the crests of flames from fires equal to mountains.
In some places it resounded with the gurgling roar of clouds intoxicated by the weight of the rainy season; in other places it was impassable due to battles waged by hosts of gods and asuras.
In one place, he saw his horse summoned by the voice of a female swan from the sky-lotus; in another, the wind plundering the lotuses on the banks of the Mandākinī.
Due to the proximity of embodied rivers such as the Gaṅgā,
its hollow interior was filled with leaping fish, crocodiles, and crabs.
In some regions, the earth-shadow produced by the sun reaching the netherworld was as black as a crow's beak;
in other circles, the disks of the moon and sun were swallowed whole.
In some places, there were forests of illusory flowers shaken by the breezes of heaven,
where the women of the celestial chariots were terrified by the heavy downpour of falling blossoms.
O beautiful lady, having crossed over that mass of beings contained within the three worlds— which move about like gnats inside the interior of a fig tree—
you are now prepared to leave the sky and return once more to the surface of the earth.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Sky," Vasiṣṭha says:
As the two women were traveling from the surface of the sky toward a mountain village, their minds having become aware of something, they beheld the surface of the earth.
The vast heart-lotus of the Cosmic Egg has the eight directions as its petals;
it is densely crowded with the mountains as its filaments and is beautiful with the fullness of its own fragrance.
It has the rivers for its filaments, the dewdrops for its pollen,
the night for its wandering bee, and is swarming with the mosquitoes of the multitudes of living beings.
It was filled with swarms of bees within, covered with beautiful hollows and perforations,
being carried by floods of water, and possessing a splendor like the light of day.
Moist with nectar, it was like a swan wandering in the sky, a vessel for the contraction of the night,
and like a lotus stalk whose lordly serpent is submerged in the mud of the underworld.
At times, its base causes the quarters of the sky to tremble with the shaking of the ocean,
while below it, the serpent Ananta bears the thorns of Daityas and Dānavas.
The heart, which is the great seed of the mountains, was pervaded by the creeper of the wounds of the Asuras— a seed-like entity that was delicate with the pleasure of enjoyment.
Therein, he made Jambudvīpa the vast pericarp,
with its rivers as the filaments of the lotus-stalk and its cities and villages as the filaments [of the flower].
Beautiful with seven lofty seed-syllables rising high above the principal mountain ranges,
it fills the expanse of the sky with the great Mount Meru as its central and elevated seed-syllable.
It was like a lake with drops of frost, or a forest of wild jasmine;
it was like a circle of people standing within the boundary of their own lines, appearing as a whirling mass.
It was pervaded by oceans that resembled bees, extending for hundreds of leagues, awakening at every new moon and lying across the four quarters of the sky.
She was like a humming bee upon a lotus resting on the eight petals of the directions,
divided into nine parts by her nine brothers who were kings.
It was a hundred thousand yojanas in extent, filled with particles of dust,
and steady with sprays of frost from the array of various inhabited lands.
Twice the size of the continent, it is encircled on the outside by the belt of the salt ocean, which, like the outer whorl of a conch shell, supports the Sāla forest.
Beyond that, she bears a body twice as large, shaped like a ring,
which is encircled by the world-tree branch known as the continent of Śāka.
She was further encircled by a band of the newly formed ocean of milk, which was twice as vast in form and possessed a sweet and cool nature.
It was further encircled by the coastal region of the island named Kuśa, which was twice as large in extent and adorned with various kinds of people.
Beyond that, it was encircled by a band of curd-ocean twice its size, which constantly gratified the hosts of gods.
Then, by that very strip of land called Krauñca-dvīpa, which was of such a measure,
[the earth] was encircled, like a new royal city surrounded by a moat dug out from its own heart.
Beyond that, there is a strip of the Ocean of Ghee of such a measure;
and beyond that, a strip of Śālmalidvīpa, filled with gods.
Then, with the line of the great ocean of wine, white as flowers,
she was like the form of Hari supported by the body of Śeṣa.
Then, with a line of gomedaka gems of such proportions, and likewise with a line of sugarcane stalks as pure as the slopes of the Himalayas; ||| MU_3,25.22 |||
Beyond that, it is surrounded by a ring of Puṣkaradvīpa twice its size,
and at the very edge by a ring of the Sweet-water Ocean (Svādūdakāmbhodhi) of the same dimensions.
In the southwestern direction, amidst the seven oceanic zones,
it is marked by sparks from the submarine fire of Vāḍava, which blazes with flames fueled by water.
Beyond that, he saw ten million [worlds] consisting of the earth, which possesses the luster of molten gold,
is graced with beautiful curves, is radiant with splendor, and is enjoyed by the gods.
Then, by way of measurement, it extends ten times further downward from the seven oceans, continents, and golden earth, reaching down to the surface of the netherworlds (pātāla).
It was encircled by a high, dug-out moat that appeared like a mass of chasms—
a terrifying path leading to the underworld.
Indeed, ten times greater than all this is that [suffering] which,
reaching to the very heavens in all four directions, is terrifying due to its accumulation of chasms.

On one side, she bore a garland of blue lotuses clinging to her form like withered darkness; on the other, she possessed the white water-lilies, night-lilies, and day-lotuses that were the peaks of various rubies.
It was encircled by the lofty and vast ramparts of the Lokāloka mountain,
appearing like the braided hair-tuft of the Fortune of the Three Worlds.
Then, from all this, she was protected by a forest ten times its size, known as Ajñātabhūtasañcāra.
Then, from all this, it became tenfold in nature,
pervading the four directions like the sky with pure water.
Then, from all this [universe], by means of a mass of flames ten times its size, which is intent on melting Mount Meru and the rest, [the yogin] is adorned with a garland.

Then, from all this [world], leading even Mount Meru and the other mountains—which are as immovable as a pillar—along with everything else, by means of a force ten times greater than that, as if they were blades of grass or dust; ||| MU_3,25.34 |||
It was surrounded on all sides by a wind that was silent due to its emptiness, yet which carried the fire from the wood of the enemy that had shattered the great mountains.
Then, from all this, by way of a tenfold increase,
it was surrounded on all sides by the void, which is of a single nature yet devoid of emptiness.

just as a ghost does not appear to a child when it is not perceived.
Just as the appearance of earth and so forth [in a dream] does not become actual earth and so forth in an instant,
so it is clearly evident even in the waking state through the thorough knowledge of the dream.
Earth and the other elements are perceived as space when they are cognized as such;
for indeed, even in a wall, those whose elements are agitated perceive an effort as if it were space.
In a dream, one perceives a city, the earth, a void, or a pit;
and even a woman in a dream performs causal functions for men, though she herself is empty.
When space is perceived as earth and so forth, earth and the other elements arise in an instant;
even the next world is directly experienced through a state of fainting.
The fool perceives a phantom in the sky, the dying man sees a forest in the atmosphere, one person sees a mass of hair in the void, while another perceives pearls in the sky.

Those who are terrified, intoxicated, or half-asleep, as well as those traveling by boat, always perceive trees and other objects in the sky, and they even experience them as if they were ghosts (vetāla).
This form of these categories has been previously cultivated; it is produced by habituation and will continue to exist, yet from the perspective of ultimate reality, not a single one of them exists.
But in play, as things truly are, earth and the other elements do not exist;

She was intent on extracting a worm from the root of a calf's ear,
and she was busy with household chores, such as watering the garden of domestic herbs.
Her calves were nourished by the grass moistened by the waves of the blue riverbank;
at every moment, she applied sandalwood paste as a cosmetic upon the door of her home.
For the sake of statecraft, she maintained the authority over household servants and cavalrymen;
through the regulation of boundaries, she was as constant as the shore of the ocean.
She was marked as if by a servant of life terrified by the agony of old age, mounted upon the swing of her ear which had the color of withered leaves.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, she herself showed [the place] to Sarasvatī as she was wandering within a hollow of Śikharin village.
This is my flower garden, adorned with groves of *pāṭala* trees;
this is my garden, featuring pavilions within its flowering orchards.
This is the lotus pond where the calves are tethered to the trees on the bank;
this is that cowherd girl named Karṇikā who has finished eating the leaves.
This is that wretched water-carrier, wasted away by fatness;
today, for the eighth day, she weeps with eyes filled with tears.
"O Goddess, here it was spoken by me; here I dwelt, here I stayed;
here I slept, here I passed away; this was given here, and this was brought here."
"This son of mine named Jyeṣṭhaśarman weeps in the house;
this milch cow of mine grazes on the lush grass in the forest."
Behold this body of mine here, known as the five [elements], which has settled in the house for its own burning— rough, as if covered in ash, and parched.
This kitchen area, entwined by fierce pumpkin vines as if by cravings,
is like another body of mine.
These kinsmen, their eyes copper-red from weeping, with rudrākṣa beads fastened upon their arms, carry fuel for the fire— themselves becoming a bond upon this earth.
With waves that incessantly snap at the clusters of moss upon the rocky shores, and which touch the leaves of the creepers on the banks with their towering forms;
With the meadows on their borders sprinkled by spray from the tossing of water,
and with droplets of foam leaping up as they strike against the surfaces of stone slabs;
The midday sunbeams were turned into frost by the mountain peaks,
whose trees were eager to bestow a shower of clusters of blossoming flowers.
It was filled with heaps of flowers that caused great splendor, appearing like coral through the reflected beauty of the blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
By the village stream, which was caught in a great whirlpool of tumultuous noise and whose village children were busily occupied with a flood of floating fruit; by that stream of the countryside.
It was encircled by trees whose trunks were washed by the waters tossed by the waves,
and it was perpetually cooled by the shade of the canopies of thick-leaved trees.
This palace pavilion is visible, beautiful with its winding flowering creepers, its windows concealed by swaying clusters of blossoms.
Here resides my husband, who is like a mere fragment of the space of life,
though he was once the lord of the earth girdled by the four oceans.
It is said that previously this one, whose nature was characterized by intense spiritual urgency, had desired: "May I quickly become a king."
In just eight days, O Supreme Goddess, he obtained that prosperous kingdom which provides security for a long time.
O King, that husband of mine, my very life, remains here in my house in the sky,
invisible like the wind in the atmosphere or like fragrance in the breeze.
Right here, at the tip of my thumb, that kingdom of my lord remains situated like a space; yet for me, it has become as vast as ten million yojanas.
O Sovereign Lady, both we two and that very sky, as well as my husband’s kingdom, are filled with thousands of mountains; oh, how vast this illusion is!
Therefore, O Queen, it is my desire to go once more to my husband's side;
come then, let us go there—for what distance is too great for those who are resolute?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the queen bowed to the Goddess and quickly entered the pavilion;
together with her, she flew like a bird into the sky that was dark as a sword-blade.
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, beautiful as a single peaceful ocean,
like the body of Nārāyaṇa, and possessing a spotless luster like the back of a bumblebee.
Having traversed the path of the clouds and likewise the realm of the winds,
he then ascends the path of the sun and passes beyond the path of the moon.
Having traveled beyond the path of the fixed stars and the very path of those in training (sādhya),
and having completely transcended the earth and leaped over the celestial sphere of the perfected ones (siddha);
Having gone to the interior of the Brahma-world and the realm of the Tuṣitas,
and having transcended Goloka, Śivaloka, and the world of the ancestors;
Having crossed far beyond the Videha gods and traveled a great distance,
she proceeded even further from afar until she was somewhat obstructed.
Afterwards, he looked back toward the sky that had passed away,
until not even a trace of the moon, sun, stars, or anything else was perceived below.
It remained motionless and profound with darkness, filling the hollows of the quarters; resembling the interior of a single ocean, it was as solid as the heart of a rock.
Līlā said: "O Goddess, tell me, where has the light of the sun and other luminaries gone?
Whence comes this darkness, motionless within the interior of stones, yet graspable by the fist?"
The Goddess said: "O sir,
you have come this far through the path of the sky,
from which even the lights such as the sun are no longer visible."
Just as a firefly is not seen from below within a great dark well,
so too, because one is behind it, the sun is not seen from below here on earth.
Līlā said:
"Oh, how far we have come upon this path!
Even the sun is not perceived in the slightest, appearing like a minute speck below."
"O Goddess, tell me this: what other path might there be beyond this one, and of what nature is it? Furthermore, how may it be traversed? Please explain."
Sarasvatī said: "Beyond this, ahead of you, is the shell of the vessel of the universe,
from which even the names of diamonds and other precious things have arisen as mere specks of dust."
Vasiṣṭha said:
As they were thus conversing, they reached the shell of the cosmic egg,
like two bees reaching the dense surface of a mountain cliff.
Therefore, you have emerged from that without any affliction, as if from the sky;
for that which is the state of certainty is the vajra-gone, and nothing else.
Then, her consciousness being free from obscuration, she beheld here and there,
beyond the veil of water and other elements, the exceedingly radiant regions at the edge of the cosmic egg.
The water-element is established as ten times the size of the Brahma-egg;
it stands enveloping that [egg], like the skin covering the back of a walnut.
Therefore, fire is ten times [greater] than that; wind is ten times greater than that;
space is ten times greater than that; and beyond that is the supreme ether.
In that supreme void, no conceptualizations of middle, beginning,
or end arise at all, just like talk of the son of a barren woman.
It is absolute, stainless, and peaceful; it is beginningless, free from delusion, and devoid of beginning, middle, and end—it abides within the Great Self.

If the Lord of Śivā, by means of his supreme power, were to forcibly cause the one whose banner is Garuḍa to fall from that [state] until the end of the kalpa; or even if the wind, moving with a single impulse, were to reach the limit of the stainless sky at the end of the kalpa through meditation upon Him—[even so, he would not fall].
The thirtieth canto in the Līlopākhyāna, titled "The Description of the Supreme Space," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this [process], having instantly transcended the veils of earth, water, fire, air, and ether— each ten times greater than the preceding one— MU_3,30.1.
He beheld that supreme space, devoid of all measurement;
this entire world was spread out therein such that it appeared there no larger than a mere atom.
She beheld such creations, veiled within cosmic eggs,
flashing by the millions in the sky like motes of dust in a sunbeam.
In the great ocean of space, within the waters of great emptiness,
there arise bubbles in the sequence of *arbuda*, born from the state of the fluidity of great consciousness.
Some he saw falling downward, some ascending upward,
others moving horizontally, and still others standing motionless through their own self-awareness.
Wherever consciousness has arisen for whomever and in whatever manner, there that very form has arisen for them in that very manner.
And there, indeed, there is no name, neither above nor below, nor any coming and going;
for that state is something entirely other than our body and its arrival.
There, consciousness arises by itself from its own nature again and again;
yet it comes to rest through one's own volitions, like the web of a child's imaginings.
Rāma:
What might be below? What might be above? And what might be across in that radiant [reality]?
Tell me this, O Brahmin, if there is no stability here.
Vasiṣṭha said: Here,
within this vast [space] devoid of end, all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) along with their coverings shine like a hair-net in the sky.
Since all things whatsoever run about lacking independence, the cosmic egg is but a portion of the earthly element; otherwise, it would be void below.
When ants move upon a round clod of earth in the sky,
it is said that for them the ten directions have their feet downward and their backs upward.
In the hearts of some, the surface of the earth is covered by a web of trees and anthills,
while the stainless sky is encompassed by the moon, the sun, the gods, and the demons.
This world, including its villages, cities, and mountains, was produced by Marubhūti,
just as a ripe walnut is produced from its skin without being cut.
Just as female elephants roam about within the expanse of the Vindhya forest,
so do the atoms of the cosmic egg exist within its vast interior.
In that [Brahman] everything exists; from it everything arises; it is everything and from everywhere it is;
and that eternal [Brahman] is likewise present within every atom.
Into that ocean of supreme light, which consists of pure consciousness,
the waves known as the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) come and go incessantly.
Some remain empty within, their nights of conceptualization having come to an end;
like waves in the ocean of water, they are carried along in the ocean of emptiness.
For some, the gurgling roar of the end of the eon has begun within;
it is neither heard nor known by others who are distracted by the flavors of their own inherent natures.
In others, at the very first beginnings, the desire to arise manifests,
just as the sprout-creeper unfolds within the seed-vessel that has been moistened by the creative impulse.
When the great dissolution occurs, some, their support melted by the sun's rays,
begin to fall away like drops of frost under the heat.
Some who have not yet attained the [spiritual] stages fall indeed until the end of the aeon;
it is said that they are born again only when their [bodies] dissolve, becoming composed of consciousness.
Some remain as if paralyzed, like a mass of hair in the sky;
those whose wealth has thus arisen appear like the vibrations of the wind.
According to the conduct prescribed by the Vedic scriptures, the undertaking for others is entirely different and described otherwise; it is extensive and its sequence is not established in that way.
Some are beings such as Brahmā and others; some are creators and protectors such as Viṣṇu and others;
some are other lords of creatures, and some are beings who have no protector at all.
Some are lords of manifold creations; some consist of the animal realm;
some are filled with the single ocean, devoid of anything other than water.
Some are crushed by the limbs of rocks; some are within the paths of worms;
some consist entirely of deities; and some consist entirely of humans.
Some are filled with eternal darkness, inhabited by creatures accustomed to such conditions; others are swarming with mosquitoes, resembling the appearance of the fruit of the udumbara tree.
Some beings, whose inner nature is eternally empty and who consist of the vibration of emptiness,
are filled here within our own minds by such a creation that they do not even enter the realm of conceptual thought, remaining like mutes or mountains in the sky.
Between these, there exists a vast space such that even Viṣṇu and the other gods, though they bestow life itself, cannot provide it.
Situated within each individual egg,
the earthly portion is by its very nature like a magnet, drawing forth the elements.
Since that manifestation of creation is beyond the scope of our intellects,
O Great-minded One, I have no power to describe that world.
Just as intoxicated yakṣas dance without seeing one another in a vast forest thick with terrifying darkness,
so do many great worlds flash forth within the far-extending supreme ether.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the thirty-first canto, titled "The Description of the Cosmic Egg," Vasiṣṭha said:
Reflecting thus, the two of them emerged from their own world and suddenly beheld the inner apartments as if they were fast asleep.
The great corpse of Mahārāja was filled with flowers standing upon it;
by the side of the corpse sat the body of Cittalīlā.
Crowded with people in deep sleep due to the dense darkness of night,
it was languid with the fragrance of incense, sandalwood, camphor, and saffron.
Beholding him again, Līlā, intent on returning to her husband’s world, fell from that very sky into this world by means of a body formed of volition.
Having pierced through the shell of the cosmic egg and repeatedly breaking through the veil of worldly existence, he entered a certain vast cycle of rebirth fashioned by the will of his master.
Together with that goddess, he reached once again the vast pavilion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which was surrounded by enclosures; having entered it, he proceeded with such speed.
That female swan beheld the world born of her husband’s volition as a mere puddle in the mud, with mountains for its lotuses and the clouds of darkness for its mire.
Those two goddesses entered that sky which is of the nature of space within the cosmic egg;
it was like a ripe clay bilva fruit inside an ant's nest.
There, having passed beyond other worlds, mountains, and the intermediate space,
they reached the surface of the earth, which was crowded with mountain ranges and oceans.
Jambudvīpa is adorned by Meru and has the interior of nine petals;
therein, in the region of Bhārata, is the mandala of Līlānātha.
In the meantime, on that adorned ground within that circle,
a certain king from a neighboring territory launched a sudden assault.
Because of those beings of the three worlds who had gathered there for the sake of witnessing the fury of the battle, that sky became exceedingly crowded.
Then those two queens, having arrived unexpectedly,
beheld the sky crowded with hosts of sky-dwellers, like a garland formed by clouds.
It was accompanied by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas,
and surrounded by Apsarases from the heavenly world who were eager to seize the heroes.
It was filled with spirits, *rakṣasas*, and *piśācas* dancing with mouths smeared with blood and flesh,
while the women of the *vidyādharas* held their hands full of flowers rained down from the sky.
It was surrounded by Vetālas, Yakṣas, and Kumbhāṇḍas, who were intent on watching the duel with eager attention,
holding mountain slopes as shields to protect themselves from the falling of weapons.
The circle of spirits fled from the region of the sky along the path of the missiles,
while it was illuminated by the soldiers of Indra, who were busily engaged in bringing forth heroes worthy of heaven.
It was adorned with the foremost elephants of the world-protectors, lofty and embellished for the sake of heroes;
it drew toward itself throngs of approaching heroes and charanas who were eager for the Gandharvas.
The noble warriors therein were gazed upon by the side-long glances of celestial women eager for battle,
while the spectators were formidable in their agitation as they jeered at those who boasted of their own prowess.
There, rumors of the imminent battle with Bhīma spread from one to another,
while beautiful women, eager for playful laughter and dalliance, waved their fly-whisks.

It is a supreme hymn of auspiciousness recited by those devoted to the side of Dharma and by the foremost sages; it is a hymn of praise offered by the many perfected goddesses of the lords of the world.
It was filled with throngs of women eager for the embrace of the circle of the heroes' arms;
by the white fame of the brave, it made the sun appear like the moon.
Rāma:
Venerable sir, what kind of warrior is designated by the word "hero"?
Who would be the ornament of heaven, and who would be one struck down like a mere child?
Vasiṣṭha: He who, for the sake of his lord who is endowed with conduct prescribed by the scriptures, dies or becomes victorious in battle, is a hero and partakes of the world of heroes.
But otherwise, the man who meets his death in battle with his limbs severed,
having been slain in a chaotic conflict, is said to be destined for hell.
The man who fights for wealth through conduct that deviates from the scriptures goes to the inexhaustible hell when he dies in battle.
One who fights while conforming to the meaning of the scriptures as far as possible and to worldly custom, and who does so out of devotion toward such a person alone, is called a hero.
For the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brahmin, and for the sake of a friend,
as well as through the effort to protect one who has come for refuge— one who dies thus becomes an ornament in heaven.
Having always protected the state of being governed solely by one's own country,
the king who dies for that purpose is a hero and partakes in the world of heroes.
Those who die in battle for the sake of a king or a lord who is intent upon the oppression of his subjects indeed go to hell.
If the battle were to be fought in accordance with dharma, however that might be, they—
being intoxicated and devoid of fear for the world— would utterly destroy this established order.
"Wherever a hero is slain, he goes to heaven"—such are the words of the base;
"A warrior who fights righteously is a hero"—this is the firm conclusion of the scriptures.
Those who endure the edge of a sword for the sake of those who possess virtuous conduct are called heroes; all others are merely struck down in a childish fray.
For their sake, celestial women stand in the sky of battle with longing hearts, sighing for the beloveds who were great beings now become goddesses.

Amidst the festival of the sky, the heavens shone forth as if they had been fashioned into a spectacle of beauty: filled with the sweet and languid songs of *vidyādharī* women; crowded with proud ladies entangled in garlands of *mandāra* flowers; and graced by rows of celestial chariots where lovely gods and *siddhas* rested.
The thirty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Sky Adorned with Spectators of the Battle of the Celestial Beings," from the *Līlopākhyāna*, by Vasiṣṭha.
Then Līlā, endowed with supernatural knowledge, stood upon the earth amidst the dancing Apsarases who were longing for Vīravara, and she gazed upon the sky.
In the region of Surāṣṭra, protected by his lord and adorned with groves of trees,
there was a certain vast forest as terrifying as a second sky.
The two armies were unshaken, resembling two tranquil oceans;
they were dense with great undertakings, intoxicated with vigor, steadfast, and accompanied by their two kings.
Fully equipped for battle and well-armored, it was like a consecrated sacrificial fire;
its target was fixed by eyes agitated with the anticipation of the first blow.
It was a place where people were being submerged by the torrential downpour of the edges of raised, stainless swords,
and it was crowded with the splendor of glittering battle-axes, spears, and slings.
It was shaken by the falling of forests agitated by the flapping wings of Garuḍa, and its golden armor shimmered with the light of the rising sun.
Their weapons were brandished in anger as they glared at one another's faces;
because their eyes were fixed upon each other, they appeared as if depicted upon a painted wall.
Its stability was established by long-established boundaries of writing;
it resounded with the roar of irresistible, great, and all-consuming destruction, a clamor never before heard.
Arrogant from previous blows, the drums had long since fallen silent;
the army was sluggish, its ranks rendered motionless by the fixed positions of the soldiers.
It was divided by a single bridge in its center, which was empty for a distance of two bow-lengths,
like a single ocean agitated by the winds at the end of an aeon.
The Lord was overcome by anxiety regarding the urgency of his duties,
while the interior of his heart was distressed and parched like the skin on the throat of a croaking frog.
An army of countless soldiers ready to sacrifice their very lives and all their possessions,
with bowmen whose bows were drawn back, intent on releasing floods of arrows fixed to the string at their ears.
Countless soldiers were rendered motionless by the sight of falling blows;
the scene was crowded with the frowns of warriors whose rigid bodies were locked in mutual combat.
The armor produced a harsh clanging sound as it struck against one another;
its hollows were abandoned by cowards, while it was unassailable by heroic warriors.
Human life is a flickering existence, a mere shadow of mutual form and light,
appearing like dust that has settled upon all the hairs of the body.
Because of her being preoccupied with watching for the first blow,
the city became like a seal of sleep, its tumultuous roar completely stilled.
The clamor of conchs, cymbals, and drums had completely subsided,
and all the clouds of dust on the surface of the earth had settled.
Abandoned inch by inch from behind by those intent on flight,
it shone like an ocean filled with fish in the form of a spreading array of *makara* monsters.
The trees were fanned by clusters of flower-stalks serving as banners, and the expanse of the sky was turned into a forest by the trunks of elephants raised high like pillars.
The entire expanse of the sky was filled with the sounds "dham-dham" arising from his breath, which accompanied the shimmering flood of his trembling gaze and all his weapons.
The wheel-array (cakravyūha) trampled the wicked Asura warriors,
while the host of serpents was made to flee by the fury of the eagle-array (garuḍavyūha).
The fierce formation, undivided like that of hawks, rose with a thundering roar; it was a mass of heroes falling upon one another, crushed by mutual explosions.
It was arranged with various arrays, terrifying with internal roars,
and a temple of mallets intoxicated by the brandishing of hands.
The sun was darkened by the web of rays from Kṛṣṇa’s weapons,
and the sound of his arrows resembled the whistling of *śalmali* trees shaken by the wind.
It stood as if possessing the same nature as the end of many kalpas,
like a single ocean arisen, agitated by the winds of universal dissolution.
Like darkness rising unagitated from the caverns of Pātāla,
like the Lokāloka mountain with its slopes shimmering and swaying from the wild dance of the intoxicated,
it rose as if bursting forth from the earth after shattering the mass of the great hells.
With the rays of their swaying spears, maces, swords, and axes, it seemed as if turning dark with showers of rain;
it was like the single ocean of the world-receptacle, prepared in an instant to become unfathomable through its infinite floods.
The thirty-third canto, titled "The Description of the Alteration at the Commencement of the Battle," from the Līlopākhyāna of the Rāmāyaṇa. Rāma:
O Blessed One, tell me briefly this battle in its essence;
for by these words of yours, the hearing of the listener is brought to delight.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then those two goddesses, having ascended a beautiful and steady celestial chariot prepared for that purpose, remained there in the sky to witness that battle.
In the meantime, there, being the adversary of Līleśa and unable to endure the onset of suffering in battle, he became distressed.
Like a formidable wave rising from the ocean of dissolution,
the fierce warrior hurled a mallet at the chest of the soldier, as one might cast a boulder down a mountain slope.
Then the clash of weapons between the two armies began violently, with the speed of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, scattering sparks of fire like lightning.
The surface of the sky was marked by lines at the tips of shimmering, trembling streams,
while the sound of "jhāṅ" was perceived amidst the ringing "jhaṇajhaṇa" noise.
He was a devourer whose roar was a mixture of heroic *huṃ* sounds and the gurgling twang of his bowstring;
he was a canopy of solar rays amidst the clouds of the flowing streams of arrows.
The fire of sparks flew up from the clanging of their armor,
while the sky was filled with fragments of weapons and shards of swords severed by mutual blows.

The sky was like a forest traversed by the movement of the tree-like arms of heroes; the courtyards of the celestial chariots were filled with the fleeing inhabitants, terrified by the twanging of bows and the clanging of discuses.
Making the sound of the clouds into the humming of bees with its great *halahala* roar,
it was as if established in non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) by virtue of its singular density.
The heads of heroes were severed by the foremost torrents of iron arrows,
while the field was crowded with armor clashing and rattling against one another’s shoulders.
Struck by the sound of "huṃ," it produced a harsh clashing noise from the impact of the foremost weapons;
its surging streams and waves were fierce and jagged, filling every quarter of the horizon.
It was filled with the clashing and agitation of weapons, the *jhaṇajjhaṇa* sound of fists being gripped,
and the crackling and *caṭacaṭa* noise of bursting and exploding projectiles.
The sound of the clashing of brandished swords resounded, mingled with the crackling noise of burning hemp;
it was filled with the moaning of corpses as they were vomited forth by the weight of autumnal arrows.
With blood from wounds rising from his severed throat— *dhag dhag dhag*—
and with his arms, head, and sword cut off, he filled the gaps in the sky with fragments.
His hair was scorched by the flickering flashes of fire arising from his armor,
while a thick *jhana-jhana* sound was produced by the multitude of swords clashing and falling in battle.
The blood surged forth from the waves of elephants struck by spears,
harsh with the *kreṅkāra* sounds produced by the crushing of tusks against tusks.
The air resounded with the loud cries of throngs crushed by the impact of great maces,
while the sky was covered by a profusion of lotus-like heads of brave warriors being carried away.
He was a cloud composed of the full dust raised by the lordly serpents whose coils were spread across the sky;
he brought about the counter-action for the hair-pulling struggle between Keśin and the man who had severed his head.
There was great terror as claws tore at eyes, ears, and noses;
the earth trembled under falling elephants in rut, and chariots rolled about.
Clad in the blood from wounds produced by the swift onset of battle, with his weapons gleaming as they flashed forth amidst the mist of rising dust; //MU_3,33.21//
Proud of his ocean-like army, which was a single mass of dense turbulence,
he was being devoured by Death with the playful laughter of a madman.
His thundering roar eclipsed the clouds, dwarfing the great mountain kings and lordly serpents;
at the base of the trees on the riverbanks lay his discus, spear, sword, and mallet.
The trees were covered by a dense mass of woolen threads,
and the fluttering banners, cloth streamers, and yak-tail fans were scattered by the confusion caused by the clouds.
The sky-dwellers were swiftly scattered by the flood of mechanical stones and wheels;
it was exceedingly gurgling with the cries of warriors whose limbs were severed while they were preoccupied with death.
His head was wounded by the massed blows of sharp axes;
the sky was made starry by the fragments of flashing swords that had flown far upward.
The earth was covered by a mass of spears released from pikes that were stuck in it,
while hammers were flung about by Vetālas who were leaping amidst the chaotic army.
The lofty archways of his heroic lances were raised high toward the sky,
while the rows of sword-fragments shattered by his *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons formed earrings for the heavens.
