The sky was filled with smoke from the thickets of *kunta* and *veṇu* forests, while the firebrands flickered;
the soldiers, honored by the king, were satisfied by the showers of sword-blades and spears.
The celestial nymphs were seized by the effort of grasping the true heroes who were swelling with pride;
the quarters of the sky were filled with the shimmering armlets falling away as they followed the mace.
He was fierce toward the warriors whose miserable efforts were crushed by the force of his spears;
he severed the four quarters of the unskilled enemies with the movement of the wind produced by the wheel of his discus.
Wild elephants fell, struck by the falling rain of axes;
soldiers leaped up and roared fiercely as they were tossed about by the whirling clubs.
The trees of chariots, their banners crushed by the falling of mechanical stones, were severed by swords;
the white lotuses of their lofty umbrellas lay scattered like fallen petals.
It was characterized by the earth strewn with soldiers whose lives were extinguished by the tossing and turmoil [of battle],
and its flanks were crushed by the falling of headless trunks and intoxicated elephants.
The brave warriors stationed on the conchs were fended off by those who mistook them for stakes;
the heroes, skilled in the specific application of nooses, lamented over their enemies.
The piercing of the belly by a razor-sharp blade causes the lotus-like heart to fall;
the noble Śiva dances with the trident as his face, amidst the falling [victims].
It resounded with the warbling of quivers filled by running archers, and it was a theater where the martial prowess of soldiers brandishing slings was performed.
The battlefield was crowded with great warriors whose backs were crushed by his adamantine fists;
with his spear raised high, he leaped into the path of the sky like a hawk.
His banner bore the great elephant and horse of Śakra, the lord of gods, trampled by his goad;
he who effortlessly crushed the mountain-like armies with the sound of "hālā-hala."
The surface of the earth was marked by pits dug by sharp-pointed spades,
and the rows of rocks in the world were shattered by weapons discharged from bows with double the usual force.
In this battle, intoxicated elephants were severed on both flanks like *krakaca* saws; it was a mortar filled with the rice-grains of the world’s people, where maces served as pestles;
and the birds that were the soldiers were bound by nets of chains resembling clouds.

The tumult of battle was like the end of an eon, with a flood of heroes like a rain-cloud pouring down showers of iron arrows, while headless trunks danced in agitation like peacocks amidst intoxicated clouds, and it was encircled by mountain-like elephants whirling about with great speed.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the First Clash of the Two Armies," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, among the kings eager for battle, the soldiers, the ministers,
and the impetuous spectators, these words arose:
Like a lake with swaying lotuses or like the sky filled with migrating birds,
the heavens, strewn with the heads of heroes, shine with the appearance of being starred.
Behold: even at midday, these clouds and sunbeams shine like the twilight, rendered crimson by the winds filled with floods of red-spotted drops of blood and vermilion.
"Sister, what is this? Is the sky filled with straw?
This is not straw; these are clouds of arrows for the heroes."
As many fine particles of dust as are pacified by the blood upon the earth,
for so many thousands of years shall the warriors have their dwelling in heaven.
"Do not fear; these are not swords with the luster of blue lotus petals;
these are the playful glances from the eyes of Lakṣmī, who gazes upon heroes."
The flower-weaponed god began to loosen the girdles upon the hips of the celestial women, who were eager for the embrace of their heroes.
With hands like trembling red sprouts on their swaying creeper-like arms,
with eyes intoxicated by the clusters of blossoms, they were fragrant with the scent of honey.
Entreatingly with their sweet voices, the deities of the Nandana grove have begun to dance, anticipating your arrival.
This army breaks its own ranks from within with harsh axes, like a rustic woman who, through her wicked behavior, destroys her beloved.
Alas! By my father’s broad-headed arrow, his head, adorned with flaming earrings, has been carried near the sun, like the eighth planet Rāhu by Time.
With his arms raised high, he whirled with speed the wheel called Citradaṇḍa, upon which two massive stones were mounted on an axle and rotated by means of a chain fixed to his feet.
Like Yama himself, this warrior approaches from the southern quarter, sweeping away the army from every side; come, let us go back the way we came.
Behold, on the battlefield, headless trunks— crowded with flocks of herons muddying the pits where heads have just been severed— are dancing as tall as palm trees.
A conversation has arisen among the assemblies of the hosts of gods;
tell me, O heroes, how will they go to the other world, who will go, and from where?
The armies that have arrived swallow [the enemy] like oceans swallowing rivers;
with their battle arrays of fish and crocodiles, oh, how formidable are these warriors!
Upon the temples of the elephants were scattered heaps of sharp iron arrows,
like full-fledged showers of rain fallen upon the clusters of mountain peaks.
As he was about to say, "Alas, my head has been carried away by the spear," the cry "The head has been brought! resounded in the sky like the call of a bird.
By means of a rain of mechanical stones with which he drenches us,
let a net of chains be forcibly cast upon this army.
"O lowest of men, lead all these deluded people who are half-dead together;
do not kill them with blows from your own feet."
While the throngs of celestial nymphs, filled with intense longing, were preoccupied with braiding their hair,
let it be seen that the soldier arrived at his side in a divine body.
Behold him who has come from afar upon the banks of the celestial river, where golden lotuses are in bloom and there are shadows, cool waters, and breezes.
With the sharp peaks of mountains shattered by the clashing of various weapons,
they moved through the sky with jangling sounds like scattered stars.
In the sky, where the river of emptiness flows with arrows for its water and whirlpools of discuses,
even mountains are reduced to the state of minute mud.
With the heads of heroic kings whirling in their orbits, the thorns of sword-blades became entangled in the stalks of the creepers that were the rays of their weapons.
With the banners serving as lotus stalks and the bees clinging to them,
and with the lotuses being the swaying creepers moved by the wind, the sky was turned into a lotus pond.
Like ants on a mountain where a herd of dead elephants lies,
the timid shrink away, just as women do from the chest of a man.
Winds that stir the tresses of the Vidyādhara women blow, heralding their union with a beloved whose unsurpassed beauty is unprecedented.
When the parasols had flown up and vanished, having been severed, the moon descended and,
assuming the form of his fame, rendered the sky white with the canopy of its radiance.
At the end of his swoon from death, the soldier, in the blink of an eye, attained an immortal body fashioned by the artisan of his own kalpa, as if reaching a city in a dream.
Showers of spears, javelins, double-edged swords, and discuses were released with clenched fists;
in the ocean of the sky, fish, crocodiles, and crabs stood like heroes.
The sky shone as if covered by hundreds of thousands of full moon discs gathered together, like swans falling from their umbrellas severed by arrows.
The sky is rendered beautiful by whisks that fly upward with pleasant gurgling sounds,
possessing the luster of a mass of waves tossed by the wind.
Those parasols, yak-tail whisks, and banners are seen utterly shattered,
like grains of rice of fame scattered across the field of the sky.
Behold, the shower of spears approaching like the beauty of a grain harvest is being brought to destruction by countless arrows flying through the sky, as if by locusts.
This clashing sound of the swords of soldiers with outstretched staff-like arms,
produced from their hard armor, is like the fierce roar of Death itself.
Shattered by the wind of sophistry and logic, with the streams of their tusks blocked,
they are like mountains whose elephants have perished during this age of humanity's destruction.
"Alas, alas! Woe! The city of chariots has been submerged, fallen, and destroyed in the great lake of blood from the battle-array—along with its lord of the discus, its horses, and its chariots!"
With the clanging sounds produced by the striking together of swords that sever tough armor, the battlefield is made to play like a lute as the Night of Doom dances there.
Behold how the quarters of the sky are reddened by the wind sprinkled with drops from those streams of blood that have gushed forth from men, elephants, horses, corpses, and mountains.
In the sky, she was dark as the hair of Kālī, appearing like a flash of lightning amidst the ocean of the rays of weapons, adorned with a garland of a multitude of arrow-buds.
With weapons whose blades were stained with fresh blood and which had dyed the earth,
the world shone like the turbulent realm of Agni, ablaze with excessive flames.
Showers of *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, spears, tridents, swords, clubs,
and javelins reached the state of a mass of sparks through their mutual cutting and piercing.

Because they strike with unshakeable singleness of purpose, the battle— whose wisdom seeks out the enemy's agitation— remains as if asleep while the movements of those other than Buddhas proceed against one another.
Resounding with the clanging of weapons struck by the unceasing sounds of other [bells],
the terrifying roar of battle, exulting in the agitation of destruction, seems to sing aloud.
The ocean of battle, filled with the powder from the tips of weapons struck against one another,
became as if composed entirely of sand, with severed umbrellas for its waves.

This mountain of battle, skilled in fierce wings and filling the world of the guardians of the quarters with the echoes of drums split open by the force of extreme impetuosity, seems to perform a widespread dance in the sky at the end of an eon.

Alas, alas! Fie upon these blazing iron arrows, which, like flashes of manifest lightning leaping forth from the stretching of formidable armor, resound as they are impelled by bowstrings vibrating with a twanging sound, and fly forth shattering the rocks of the mountain peaks.

Before these arrows, blazing with a fierce fire, can sever our desires with a "cham" sound and break our limbs, come quickly from here, O friend! Let us go; this fourth watch of the day is passing away.
The thirty-fifth canto in the *Līlopākhyāna*, titled "Description of the Words Spoken by the Spectators of the Battle," [ends]. Vasiṣṭha:
Then that ocean of battle became like one intoxicated in a wild dance, with its waves of horses intent on leaping upward.
The multitude of white arrows resting upon the handles of parasols were like schools of saphari fish;
the hollows [of the sky] were agitated by the surging waves of the cavalry and elephant forces leaping upward.
It possessed the swirling eddies of armies led by rivers of various weapons,
and was agitated by the masses of rutting elephants whose broad temples were trembling and restless.
With his head whirling from the revolutions of hundreds of whirling wheels, he was like a blade of grass;
the water-like luster of his brandishing sword was swallowed by the clouds of dust.
The fierce ship of the soldiers was shattered by the expansion of the crocodile-array;
the mountain caves resounded with the deep *guḍuguḍa* roar of the great whirlpools.
The mustard seeds were the mass of arrows discharged from the array of fish;
the circles of waves were the banners severed by the impact of the flood of weapons.
His earrings were like whirlpools in a sea wounded by weapons and water;
he was a vessel for the movement of dense fury, containing timi and timiṅgila fish.
Terror-inspiring with its army moving like water as it was clothed in black iron armor,
and terrifying with the mountains of troops caught within the lines of whirlpools formed by headless trunks;
The quarters of the sky were thick with the mist of arrow-spray,
and all sounds were reduced to a single, dense roar by the universal din.
The spray from the fragments of heads was agitated by falling and flying up;
within the circular array of whirlpools, the soldiers were whirling like pieces of wood.
Fierce with waves of spears, arrows, bows, and earrings,
it was like the ocean of rising soldiers emerging unexpectedly from the netherworld.
It was foamy with the parasols and banners of endless beings moving back and forth;
it carried away the trees that were chariots, swept along by the force of flowing rivers of blood.
It was filled with great bubbles of blood resembling elephants,
and its aquatic creatures were the horses and elephants tossing about in the surging flood of the army.
That battle was as wondrous to men as the city of Ambaragrāma;
it was as restless as mountains shaken by the earthquake at the time of universal dissolution.
With horses and birds galloping about, with the flanks of herds of elephants falling down, with throngs of timid deer wandering, and with the loud *ghur-ghur* sound resounding;
He was a lion among autumnal rows of arrows, the ground upon which the army of Śarabhaṅga was shattered;
he was a śarabha among leaping horses, and the earth that bore the burden of the śarabhas.

Resounding with the trumpeting of charging heroic elephants, its mountain caves serving as chambers for the musical instruments of battle, the army was like a cloud pouring forth rain, with the leaping warriors as its lions.
It was a cloud of spreading dust, a mountain of retreating troops,
rich with the falling limbs of excellent chariots, and filled with descending circles of swords.
Rich with fluttering silk flowers, bearing banners and parasols like clouds,
it possessed surging rivers of flowing blood and falling elephants trumpeting in distress.
That battle was like the end of an aeon, agitated by the devouring of the world,
with its standards, umbrellas, banners, chariots, and infantry scattered about.
He shone with the intense radiance of a multitude of falling, stainless weapons like the sun,
scorching all human beings who were already tormented by the heat of harsh life.
The sky was enveloped by a continuous downpour of arrows from the Puṣkarāvarta clouds of his bow,
while the atmosphere was encircled by flashes of lightning in the form of streaks drawn by the whirling sword-blades.
The mountain-like herds of elephants fell into the ocean of blood that surged like molasses;
the stars were the clusters of mechanical stones scattered and falling from the sky.
The sky was filled with clouds of arrows resembling the whirlpools of the ocean at the end of an eon,
while the intervals between the worlds were scorched by the fires of weapons like those at the dissolution of the universe.
The mountains upon the surface of the earth were shattered by the thunderbolt-like rain of arrows;
the multitudes of people were crushed by the falling mass of elephants, which resembled a range of great mountains.
The earth and sky were covered by clouds in the form of armies of rain-bearing chariots,
while a harsh roar arose from the collision and agitation of the great ocean of the massive host.
It was pervaded by water-monsters, serpents, fires, and mountains tossed up by fierce winds,
which arose as omens of weapons and were intent on crushing one another.
Piercing one another with spears, swords, discs, arrows, javelins, maces, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, lances, and other weapons, they resounded;
blazing and whirling by the hundreds, they assumed the appearance of objects tossed about by the winds at the end of an aeon, pervading the ten directions.
The thirty-sixth canto in the Līlopākhyāna, titled "Description of the Battle," by Vasiṣṭha:
Then, while the Śavaras and others stood there with their horns as their only comparison,
and rivers of flowing blood arose that were equal to the Gaṅgā;
While headless trunks with their limbs still attached danced with flailing arms,
and men, elephants, horses, and chariots sank into the waters of blood;
When all the armies had departed and become scattered,
when all the cowards were broken and fled in the ten directions;
Upon mountains of elephant carcasses where rows of clouds rest,
and in oceans of blood where yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas sport;
Of the great ones established in Dharma, endowed with virtue, splendor, and courage— pure lotuses of noble lineage, heroes who never turn back.
Duels broke out like the roaring of clouds,
eager to devour one another like the surging tides of the meeting oceans.
A multitude of elephants equipped with enclosures met by force a mass of elephants likewise equipped with enclosures; a mountain with its forests met as it were by a mountain with its forests.
A flood of horses met with a herd of horses possessing a roar and great speed,
like a mass of waves meeting another mass of waves in the terrible ocean.
One army of men fought another army of men with equal weapons,
like a flood of bamboos against a flood of bamboos, tossed by the wind and driven by the wind.
And one flood of chariots crushed the entire body of the other flood of chariots,
just as a city, driven by fate, might crush another city as it soars into the sky.
With its archers as its banners, the army fought, covering the sky with a previously unseen cloud formed by the showers of autumnal arrows.
When warriors of feeble resolve flee by some stratagem during battles with uneven weapons in that conflagration of war, then—
Wheel-bearers clashed with wheel-bearers, archers with archers,
swordsmen with sword-fighters, and those armed with *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles with those armed with *bhuśuṇḍīs*.
Musala-wielders were with musala-bearers; kunti-holders were with kunti-wielders;
those armed with double-edged spears were with spear-bearers; and those with darts in hand were with dart-wielders.
Those with mallets fought with mallet-wielders; those shining with clubs fought with those armed with clubs;
those skilled in the use of spears fought with spears; and those brandishing axes fought with battle-axes.

Those armed with clubs struck them with floods of clubs; those with stones attacked those whose weapons were stones; those with nooses were supreme at binding with nooses; and those bearing spikes struck with spikes.

Those bearing swords were [attacked] with swords, those with slings with slings; those wielding diamond-clubs were struck by those standing there with hooks, and those raised up by hooks were [struck] with hooks.
Those who wielded hammers were experts at grinding with hammers; those who bore tridents did so with tridents;
and those who possessed nets of chains did so with nets of soft, honey-colored chains.
The spear-wielders, skilled with spears, fought with spears like the surging masses of waves from an ocean agitated at the end of a kalpa.
Agitated by the whirlpools of wheel-like waters and by the winds of arrow-spray, with its tossing weapons as sea-monsters, the sky shone like a single vast ocean.
With the surging waves of leaping weapons and the aquatic creatures of the army-masses,
that ocean of the earth’s hollows became impossible for even the immortals to cross.
The army of the people from the eight directions was thus divided into two wings;
it stood there, split in half by each of the two kings.
Behold these provinces situated in the eastern direction according to their enumeration;
now hear of the districts belonging to the side of Padma, the Lord of Līlā.
In the east are Kāśī, Magadha, Kosala, Mithilā, and Utkalā;
Mekalā, Kavaṭa, Puṇḍra, as well as Auṇḍra and all the Gauḍakas.
The Drimiyas, Madras, Suhmas, and likewise the Tāmraliptas;
the Prāgjyotiṣas, Vājimukhas, Ambaṣṭhas, and the man-eaters.
There were those with ears for eyes but no ears, as well as eaters of raw fish;
there were those with tiger-like faces, Kirātas, Śavaras, and one-legged people.
There is the mountain named Mālyavat, as well as Śibi, Vān, Jñāna, Vṛṣabhadhvaja, Padma, and others, along with the mountain Udayakara.
Now, to the southeast, these inhabitants of the Vindhya mountains reside:
the Cedis, the Vatsas, the Daśārṇas, and the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Upavaṅgas.
The Kaliṅgas, Puṇḍras, Jaṭharas, Vidarbhas, Mekhalas,
as well as the Śavaras, Nagnaparṇas, and those who fill the three cities on their necks.
Those named Kaṇṭakasthala, the broad Pṛthudvīpaka,
the Komalas, the Kaṇṭhadrās, the Śoṇikas, and likewise the Carmaṇvatās.
The Kokakas, the Hemakuḍyas, and likewise the Śmaśrudharas;
the Baligrīvas, Mahāgrīvas, Kiṣkindhas, and Nārikelins.
Now, these are the mountains to the south of this Lord of Līlā:
Vindhya, Kusumāpīḍa, Mahendra, and likewise Dundura.
Malaya, Sūryavān, those consisting of oligarchies (gaṇarājya) and monarchies (nṛrājya), the region known as Avanti, and likewise Sāmbavatī; ||| MU_3,36.33 |||
Daśapura, Ekakaccha, the Ṛṣikas, the Turuṣkas, the Śakas, Vanavāsa, Upagiri, and likewise Bhadragiri; MU_3,36.34 //
The Nāgaras, the Daṇḍakas, the Gaṇarājyas, the Nṛrājyakas, the Sahārās, the Ṛṣyamūkas, the Kārkoṭas, and the Vanatimbilas.
The Padmanivāsins, the Caurakas, the Karkavīrakas,
the Vairikas, the Pāśikas, and the Dharmapattanapāṃśikas;
The Śākikas, Kṛṣṇacelūras, Nārmadas, Tāmraparṇakas, Gonandas, Kanakas, and those named after the city of Cīna; MU 3.36.37.
The Tālīkaṭas, Saritkīrṇas, Rahakas, Veṇukārhaṇas,
Vaivuṇḍakas, Tumbavanas, Lājinadvīpas, and Karṇakas.
The Karṇikāras, the Śivayas, the Kuṅkuṇas, the Citrakūṭakas, the Karṇāṭas, the Mañcakaṭakas, and likewise the Mahākaṭavikas;
The Āndhras, the Kollaśinas, the Śivātakas, the Cavarikas,
the Baladevas, the Pattanakas, the Krauñcas, and likewise the Ṭīvas.
Those peaks of Citrakūṭa, known as Nandana, Nandana, and Amala, where the hosts of Rākṣasas dwell, are carved from stone and chalk.
Then, in the south-east, there are the Mahārāṣṭras and Surāṣṭrakas,
as well as those called Sindhus, Sauvīras, and Śūdras, along with the Ābhīras and Dramiḍas.
There are the mountains known as Koṭaka, Ṣaṇḍa, and Sindhva, as well as Kali-ruha; here also is the Hemagiri mountain and the Raivataka mountain.
There is the land called Nabhu-kā, and the Yavanas are the creatures there;
also the Pahlavas, the Mārgaṇāvartas, and those named Dhūmras and Ambaṣṭhakas.
Likewise, the people of Lājakaṇa and those dwelling on Mount Āmrakīṭa—
these subjects of King Līlāpati were joined by the ocean and the submarine fire (aurvāgni).
Now hear of these regions situated as an antidote to that:
first, in the western direction, there are these great and majestic mountains.
The mountain king named Matimān, as well as Kṣurārpaṇagiri,
Vanaukahā, Meghavān, Cakravān, and Astaparvata.
The people known as the Pañcanadas, the Kāśas, the Brahmāvasātakas, as well as the Tārakṣatayas, the Pāravas, and the Śāntikas; ||| MU_3,36.48 |||
On the flanks of the Vātakapokras there are likewise the Girivānavas;
those lowest tribes of Mlecchas have abandoned the boundaries of dharma.
Beyond that is the Janapada land for two hundred yojanas;
beyond that is the peak of Mount Mahendra, with ground made of pearls and jewels.
Then there is the mountain named Āsta, surrounded by hundreds of peaks;
beyond that is the great ocean on the shore of the formidable Pāriyātra mountains.
In the northwestern direction lies the region of Girimati;
likewise Veṇumati, and beyond that the land of Turamati.
Likewise, there are the Phalgunakas, the Māṇḍavyas, the Ekanetrakas,
the Purukundas, the Tukhāras, and the Tālamallalahāvahas.
The Vandilas, Navilas, Vālas, those with long hair and long limbs,
the Raṅgas, the Khamūnikas, the Kampas, the Guruhās, and the Cāruhās;
Beyond that is the incomparable Strīrājya, where cows, bulls, and offspring abound;
then, in the north, there is Himavat, followed by the mountains Kāñcana and Madhumat.
Kailāsa, Vasumān, and Meru—these people dwell along those paths:
the Madras, Pauravas, Yaudheyas, Mālavas, and Śūrasenakas.
Likewise, the Rājanyas, the Aśvinīs, the descendants of Arjuna, the Trigartas, the Kekayas, the Kṣudrakas, the Mācellas, and those who dwell in Cūta.
The Ambalas, Prasthalas, Śākas, and Kṣemadhūrtis;
the Antaradvīpas, Gāndhāras, as well as the Vandivaṭas and Stavas.
Then there was the city named Takṣaśilā, and beyond that Lavaṇāvatī;
then the region of Puṣkalāvatī, and after that the land of Yaśovatī.
Then there were the Maṇimantīs, the Śyāmākas, the Khacarās,
the Dāśadānas, the Gavyasanas, and likewise the Daṇḍahavyasanas.
Dānadāś, Śūrakas, and likewise Vāṭādhāras;
Kohaka city and likewise Surabhūtipura.
Then indeed came Taṭakādarśa and Danturādarśa;
after them came those known as Piṇḍala, Mālavya, Ayana, and Āyaneya.
Mālahālā, Hūnahematālāśva, Svamukha, as well as Himavat, Vasumān, Kauñja, Kailāsa, and other mountains; MU_3,36.63.
Beyond that lies the land of Janapada, eighty hundred yojanas in extent;
now hear from me about these regions to the northeast.
The Kaulūtas, the Brahmaputras, the Kuvindas, the Dinādanās,
the Maḍavas whose kingdoms have perished, and likewise the Vanarāṣṭras.
The Kaiḍabhallas, the Siṃhapuras, as well as the Cāmavataṅgas,
the Sārpātakas, the Pārvatakas, the Kaśmīras, and the Daradas.
The Abhisāra, Jāda, and Ārva; the Pallola, Uka, and Ciroḍu; the Kirātas and Paśupālas; and then the Cīnas and the Land of Gold (Suvarṇabhūmi).
Following that was the ground of the divine groves, its splendor then surpassed by the palace of Viśvāvasu with its supreme opulence;
after that was the ground of Kailāsa, and then Mount Muñjavat, a realm for the pleasure-palaces of the Vidyādharas and immortals.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the thirty-seventh canto, titled "Description of the Country," Vasiṣṭha said:
In that battle, fierce with men and elephants violently torn apart, the throngs of warriors rushed forward, crying out, "I first! I first!"
These and many others there were reduced to ashes as they entered with great effort, like moths into a fire.
Other people from the Middle Country have not been cited by me here;
listen as I shall describe these followers of King Līlāvatī.
The Uddehikas, Śūrasenas, Guḍas, Aśvatthas, Nīpakas,
Uttamajyotikas, Drāṇis, Padakas, Madhyamikas, and others.
The Sālvakas, Ketakas, Matsyas, Dauleyakas, Kapiṣṭalas, Māṇḍavyas, Pāṇḍunagaras, Sauragrīvas, and Gurugrahas;
The Pāriyātras, the Kurāḍhyas, the Yāmuna-udumbaras,
the Gajāhvās, the Ujjihānas, the Kālakoṭikas, and the Māthuras.
And likewise the people of Kapila, Dharmāraṇya, Uttara, and Dakṣiṇa; the Pāñcālas, the Kurukṣetras, and the Sārasvata people.
Driven by the spears of Pañcanada, the ranks of the Avantī chariots,
streaming forth and fleeing in panic, fell into a great abyss.
The saffron robes and the garments of those dwelling in the Brahma-hermitage, torn by the people of Sāmbavatī,
fell to the ground and were trampled by rutting elephants.
The heroes of Daśapura, their noble necks severed by weapons,
were attacked by Tārakṣati and cast into the lake at Yojana.
And the marshes of Ṛṣyaka and Rukaca, marked by the hundreds of Śaivya’s arrows,
became mere mud on the ground through the crushing of the army.
Seeking shelter in the forest dwellings and mountain caves that offer no refuge,
they ran about on all sides and fell into the pool of the Yamunā.
With their entrails like strings protruding from their torn bellies,
the night-stalkers ceased their wandering and were devoured by piśācas in the night.
On the path of battle, the elephants, consecrated by auspicious mountains and trumpeting cries,
were cast into the pits of the earth like lotuses.
Like deer driven by a lion, the Haihayas fled like liquid blood, their great chariots shattered, as if blown away from Daṇḍaka by the wind.
Shattered by the tusks of elephants and crushed by the teeth of saws,
those enemies were carried away by the great river of blood like the sprouts of trees.
The Chinese, chewed by iron arrows and their lives worn out and shattered,
cast off their bodies— which had remained as a burden— into the ocean.
The brave Ābhīras, their mountain caves carved by the spears hurled by the Karṇāṭa warriors,
leaped into the sky like clusters of stars.
Struck by the force of the arrays of elephants and sea-monsters, their weapons shattered,
and engaged in hand-to-hand combat, the Daśakas and Śakas were routed.
From Daśārṇa, lightning bolts were released like fish with broken chains, terrified of the net, hiding in the blood-mud like ten-finger-long minnows.
By the destruction of the Gūrjara army, the plucking out of the hair of the Gūrjara women was accomplished by the sharp,
lofty spears of the Tāṅgaṇas in battle.
Emerging from the sky like flashes of lightning produced by the friction of weapons, they flowed forth in haste like torrents of arrows from a cloud that bestows fish as its weapons.
The enemies fell upon the Ābhīras— who were terrified by the ominous appearance of the dark sun and the flashing circles of the *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon— just as herds of cattle fall upon green pastures.
The river Taṅgaṇā, whose beautiful limbs possess the luster of fine gold, was stripped naked and enjoyed by the Gauḍa soldier through the dragging of her body, nails, and mass of hair.
By Rudra’s slicing of the wheels of the chariot yoked to the Gaganaga horses as they rattled in battle,
the Taṅgaṇas were scattered in pieces among the herons and vultures.
Hearing the loud *guḍaguḍa* sound of the Gaudas as they fled, leaping about while being beaten with clubs, the fierce Gāndhāra cattle ran away like those who are terrified.
Resembling the ocean of space and bearing a multitude of flowing weapons, it produced in the Pārasīkas the delusion of thick nocturnal darkness.
In that place as beautiful as the Milky Ocean, where the Mandara mountain had been uprooted and stood aloft,
the rows of forest trees became weapons upon the snowy peaks of the parasols.
When the sky was filled with swarms of weapons flying like clouds,
it appeared as if the firmament were being flooded by the restless circles of waves in the ocean.
The forest of the sky was seen filled with hundreds of moons by white parasols, dense with locusts by arrows, and thick with crows by spears.
The peacocks, huddling together and uttering long-drawn cries,
were driven away by herons that had swarmed in flocks, their heads tossed up toward the sky.
Having brought the daughters of the Himavat mountain to a state of passion by means of their tumultuous cries, they let out a roar as if with terrifying limbs that had been rendered bodiless by Love.
The *uddehaka* trees, overcome by the *kāśa* grasses, were rendered invisible by the birds out of compassion, as if by winds agitated and shaking their wings like gusts of dust.
Shaken by the weapons of the mad [demons], having abandoned their missiles on the battlefield,
they danced, laughed, and sang before the creator of Nandana and Ānanda.
The shower of spears,
accompanied by the tinkling of a multitude of small bells and driven by the wind of Śālva’s arrows, took on the appearance of a mist.
The Kauntas, mangled by Śaivya’s missiles and struck down by his whirling spears,
were seen as they turned to corpses and ascended to heaven like Vidyādharas.
By the steady Vīrasenā, whose nature is to support the earth,
the cities of Pāṇḍu were shaken by the mere thrill of her movement.
The Uddhekakas were crushed by the Pañcanadas,
who were like rutting elephants from Kāśī, their temples gored by the tips of spears as if they were lotuses.
Cut down by the hosts of Brahmā and Vāsantaka with their discuses,
they fell to the earth like flowering trees hewn down by a saw.
The Bhokkāṇa forest, being cut down by axes impelled from the bellies [of the demons],
was set ablaze by Bhadreśa as he stood nearby with the fire of his arrows.
The old elephants, their bodies smeared with the ichor of rutting temples,
met their destruction, just as fuel is consumed in a blazing fire.
Having wandered through the triple-gated whirlpools and pits, the Oṇḍras, who were like blades of grass,
fled with their heads scattered and entered the depths of Pātāla.
In the Magadhan army, which was radiant like the ocean stirred by a gentle breeze,
the sluggish Vandilas were submerged like old elephants in the mud.
Jahnu incited the fury of the Taṅgaṇas upon the battlefield,
just as the heat of the sun brings out the fragility of flowers crushed on a path.
Unable to endure the clamor of the Pauravas, the Kosalas— like children—
crossed over [the battle] while discharging showers of maces, spears, arrows, javelins, and double-edged swords.
With their limbs severed by broad-headed arrows, they shone like coral trees made of stone upon a mountain,
their forms drenched in streams of blood and thick with entrails flowing out.
The floods of iron arrows, their forms tossed by the winds of great weapons,
whirled about like swarms of bees shimmering upon the ocean.
Clouds like rain-bearing monsoon clouds, dark as if filled with black wool,
and trees covered with Śara reeds, roamed about swiftly while thundering loudly.
The forest kingdoms, worn out by speed, were the creatures of the camp-like terrain;
when violently pulled, they snapped like delicate threads.
Upon the chariots whose wheels stood upright and whose hubs were buried and then upturned,
throngs of people fell like clouds upon forested mountains.
Having reached a dense forest of *sāla* and *tāla* trees that was like a thick grove for people, there occurred the severing of arms, and the forest became filled with upright stumps.
Resplendent like the beauties of the Nandana grove, those excellent heroes, intoxicated with youth, rejoiced in the regions of the forests and gardens of Mount Meru.
The lofty forest of the army shone with the humming of crickets as long as it was not overrun by the opposing side, which possessed the splendor of the fire at the end of an aeon.
Though their weapons were snatched away by the Hūnas and they were beset by Piśācas,
the Daśārṇas fell upon Karṇa like young calves.
Their voices broken, they lost their luster through the power of the son of Tājika,
just as lotuses lose their beauty when their waters dry up due to the heat of the sun.
Covered with hunger, girdles, arrows, spears, double-edged swords, and mallets,
they fled and were cast into the hell named Kārkoṭasthala.
Surrounded by those from Kuru-kṣetra who are ascetics in appearance but fight with deceit,
they have clearly fallen into a state of powerlessness, like virtues overcome by the wicked.
Like bees taking the heads of banyan seeds in an instant,
they fled swiftly with their arrows, like lotus plants whose stalks have been severed.
The Mithas, Sārasvatas, Ādityas, and others, having achieved victory from beginning to end,
were like scholars in debates— neither agitated nor defeated.
The door-panels, turned back by the small, shallow pits dug by the mice,
attained a supreme brilliance, like fires extinguished by their fuel.
How much can be described of this place called Raṇavara, which is filled with streams of blood and where even Vāsuki would be unable to find words for it, despite his many tongues?
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Two Kingdoms," Vasiṣṭha said:

Thus, in that exceedingly tumultuous battle, crowded with warriors clapping their arms, where the beginning and end could not be discerned due to the lack of obstruction, and where hard armor resounded, [the combat continued].
While showers of stones were being carried along, leaping up, and falling, and while rivers arose from the tossing of projectiles with rows of lotuses in the form of fluttering banners; //MU_3,38.2//

While in the sky there arose streams of spray from the fires produced by the impact of the tips of their weapons against one another, and while rivers of arrows flowed far away, coming and falling; ||| MU_3,38.3 |||
When the ocean of the sky was filled with the whirlpools of the lotus-like heads of the Vahallūnas, surging like waves, and with the multitudes of weapons resembling the celestial Gaṅgā;
The doors rattled with the wind, and thick clouds of pulverized weapons fell; my limbs were constantly burning as they became infested with insects that caused the agony of *kapikacchu*.
With his splendor and sweet form, he, like a hero by the force of a weapon-strike, reduced the remainder of his ten-year period to one-eighth and became slender.
With their horses exhausted and the brilliance of their foremost weapons shattered by the impact,
the armies lost their luster along with the sun at midday.
Then, after the two generals had deliberated with their ministers,
they dispatched messengers to one another, saying, "Let the battle be withdrawn."
Then, due to exhaustion, with their leaves, weapons, and prowess all diminished,
everyone agreed at that time to cease the battle.
Then, one warrior from each of the two armies ascended to the tip of the lofty banner of his great chariot, like the Pole Star fixed in its place.
He brandished his silken garment, which was visible across the entire circle of the quarters,
like a long ray of the moon reaching toward the very heavens, as if to say, "Let the battle be concluded!"
Then the kettledrums resounded, their echoes filling the quarters of the sky,
like the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds at the subsiding of the great dissolution.
Just as the rivers of autumn, having set out upon the vast expanse of the sky,
proceed toward drying up, so too do the streams of the senses.
The movement of the soldiers' weapons gradually subsided,
like the trembling of trees at the end of an earthquake, or like the ocean when the wind has ceased.
The two armies set out to depart from the forest of battle,
like a flood of water flowing in four directions from the single ocean at the end of an aeon.
The army, agitated by the tossing of Mount Mandara in the churned ocean of milk, gradually attained a state of composure as its turbulent eddies subsided into tranquility.
Gradually, in a mere moment, the battlefield became as terrifying with its hideous corpses as it had been empty when the ocean was drunk by Agastya.
It was filled with a continuous succession of corpses and a great lake of flowing blood,
resembling a forest of reeds filled with the sounds of moaning and gurgling.
Resounding with the gurgling roar of waves from the currents of broad, crimson rivers,
it was filled with men agitated as they called out for protection, crying out in lamentation.
A torrential waterfall of blood flowed from the masses of corpses, some dead and others half-dead;
it struck terror with the quivering of the dead bodies still mounted upon the backs of living men.
There, fragments of clouds rested upon the peaks of the mountain-like heaps of lordly elephants;
the great forest of shattered masses of chariots surpassed even the splendor of a royal parasol.
The force of the flowing rivers of blood carried away chariots and elephants;
it was crowded with arrows, spears, double-edged swords, maces, clubs, darts, and scimitars.
The ground was covered with the saddles, the ends of the cloths, and the armor and mail;
the bodies of the young horses were protected by a multitude of banners, chowries, and silk ribbons.
The wind whistled through the groves of quivers with their wide-open leather straps,
while the Lord of the Dead lay asleep upon a bed of fallen leaves in the form of heaps of arrows.
It was surrounded by wheels and bows shining with crowns, necklaces, and armlets;
it had long ropes of thick entrails being dragged away by dogs, jackals, and birds.
The field of blood was jagged with the few remaining living beings shrieking,
while the living men were submerged in the mire of blood, uttering cries of distress.
He bore a hundred rivers of terrible red blood flowing from the multitude of his arms, which resembled a mass of wood, while hundreds of eyes protruded like heaps of cowrie shells.
It was filled with half-dead or dying men surrounded by their wailing kinsmen,
and its interior was crowded with all kinds of weapons, chariots, horses, and elephants, as well as those moving about.

The sky was turned into a forest by the multitude of trunk-like arms of dancing headless torsos, while the cavities of their nostrils were smeared with masses of the stench of rutting ichor, fat, and marrow.
Leaping horses and elephants were being struck down, their lives ebbing away; the drums were shattered by the blows of the waves of rivers of flowing blood.
It was a torrent of rivers of blood from the horses and elephants being carried away as they died,
with the thick wind of their blood stirred up by the hissing of the multitudes of men perishing.
With a voice marked by hiccups and a mouth filled with the arrows of a very short life,
he is afflicted by blood due to the wind arising from the smell of fat and marrow that must be consumed as a funeral offering.
Headless trunks were being trampled by the trunks of lordly elephants that had died from excessive trumpeting;
other headless trunks were falling as the elephants and horses they had been mounted upon collapsed.

It resounded with the cries of blood agitated by corpses abandoned by weeping kinsmen and friends; there, noble women whose husbands were dead cast away their weapons and gave up their lives at their lords' throats.
There, bodies were examined with necks upturned as they lay in their burial sites;
it was crowded with men mingled with those who dragged away corpses on donkeys.
With hair for its moss, the lotus-faces for its whirlpools, and the dancing of the turning of the eyes;
it was a great river of flowing blood, rich with surging, high waves.

It is called the "end of life," the "recollection of sons," the "desire for mother, gods, and wealth," and it is described as the "piercing of the vital organs" accompanied by cries of "Alas! Alas! and "O! O!"—a pain that cuts through the very marrow.
With half-dead men struggling to extract weapons stuck in their limbs, and with the Hūṇas,
Taṅgas, and Tājikas crying out in lamentation for those who have died in a foreign land.
He witnessed a battle of chariots that had begun between two who were mutually hostile and now dying;
he saw one who was incapable of fighting with tusks and remembered his beloved deity at home.
It is the flight of those who rely on the cowardice of the path of dying;
it is the longing for a place led by the whirlpools of unexpected blood.
It was filled with the sounds of "huṃ" uttered by those pained by the piercing of their vital organs by volleys of arrows,
and it bore the sequence of the writhing of vetālas that had begun upon seizing headless trunks.
With its rows of beautiful flags, umbrellas, and chowries being carried along,
it scattered the crimson glow of twilight in all directions like radiant red lotuses.
It was like an eighth ocean of blood, with the whirlpools of chariot wheels,
rich with masses of foam from the banners, and beautiful chowries for its bubbles.
With its chariots overturned, resembling a city destroyed by an earthquake,
it was like a vast forest whose trees have been blown down by a cataclysmic wind.
It resembled a world consumed by the fire at the end of an eon, like the ocean drunk up by a sage; it was like a region devastated by excessive rain, with its human inhabitants utterly exterminated.
It was entwined with black iron spears, crowded with circles of *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles,
shaped like the carcasses of rutting elephants, and filled with lowered *naracas*, *tomaras*, and clubs.
It was like an extended grove of palm trees growing on a rocky peak;
with spears rising like tall trees along the banks of flowing rivers of blood.
The sky was filled with trees of weapons entwined by serpents and covered in flowers of cloth,
while the atmosphere was webbed with masses of entrails used as girdles, dragged out by herons.
The multitude of lotuses in the form of banners was submerged in the lake of blood;
friends were summoned by men who were sinking in the mire of gore.
It was gazed upon by terrified people emerging from the dwellings of elephant corpses,
while its fierce headless trunks were suspected to be trees with creepers severed by weapons.
It was a place where herds of elephants served as rafts upon rivers of blood,
and where the foam of white garments shimmered amidst the currents of gore.
It was filled with men suddenly cut down by death as they wandered about,
and it was crowded with headless trunks falling here and there like headless corpses.
The people of the army fled, their ranks shattered by the flood of wheels whose targets were fixed high above;
there arose the sound of *bhāṅkāra* from the flow of blood, the sound of *hikkāra*, and the cries of those half-dead.
It was filled with silver-winged birds washed by streams of blood gushing from the openings of veins,
and rendered perilous by the frantic dancing of Vetālas to the loud clapping of their palms.
The wood of overturned chariots lay scattered within it, concealing brave warriors; with living soldiers stationed inside, it struck terror into the enemy's moving chariots.
Its mouth was filled with blood and mud, and it contained the moaning corpses of those barely alive;
dogs and crows were seen there, struggling in distress as they craned their necks toward the few remaining living men.
It was agitated by the clamor of battle among fierce carnivores competing for a single piece of meat;
it was crowded with immortal carnivores engaged in combat for the sake of that same morsel.

With countless horses, elephants, men, lords, and chariots overturned, and with rivers flowing with blood from the severed necks of the primary warriors, that battlefield became a garden of death; with its dryless creepers of weapons, it was like the entire world overturned at the end of an aeon, including its mountains.
The twenty-ninth canto, titled "Description of the Battle," from the Episode of Līlā;
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, like a hero, the sun—reddened by time—set;
its majesty and splendor forever withered, it was cast into the ocean.
Reflected in the mirror of the sky, which was reddened by the blood of battle,
the streak of twilight instantly appeared as if it were the severed head of the sun at the end of the day.
From the earth, the netherworld, the sky, and all directions, they arrived like the surging waters of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution—
dark as the night and resembling circles of vetālas.
It was seen: the cluster of stars, like pearls strewn about, reddened by the glow of twilight, upon the head of the lordly elephant of day, which had been split open by the blade of darkness.
In the lakes that were devoid of living beings, blinded by darkness, and lacking even a drop of water,
the lotuses withered away like the hearts of the dead.
In an instant, the birds fell asleep with their wings closed and their necks buried in the mud;
they lay within their nests like arrows embedded in every limb.
The rows of night-lotuses, blessed by the light of the nearby moon,
became radiant of heart, like the fortunes of heroes among the ranks of warriors.
The lotus pond became like the battlefield: filled with blood for its water, protected by arrows as its hidden bees, and its lotus-faces shriveled.
Above there was the sky-lake adorned with stars as its white lotuses;
below, however, was the water-sky with shimmering lotuses in the form of stars.
The darknesses, whose effects had not yet been consumed, and all living beings,
were thoroughly dispersed in every direction like waters spreading abroad.
The battlefield was crowded with throngs of singing vetālas,
where herons and ravens sported upon the throats of rattling skeletons.
It was radiant with the flames of the funeral pyre made of chariot-wood against the starry sky,
an inferno consisting of fat and flesh, resounding with the sounds of "paca-paca-paca."
The funeral pyres were obscured by the popping of cracking bones from corpses and by the torches rolling among the heaps of ashes,
while the water-sports commenced by the female Vetālas remained hidden from view.
It was intense with the clamor of dogs, crows, yakṣas, vetālas, and tālas; through the gathering of spirits, it resembled a forest where birds are taking flight.
He saw a *ḍākinī* busily extracting blood, flesh, fat, and marrow,
and a *piśāca* with blood, fat, and flesh trickling from its jaws as it chewed them.
The assembly hall was filled with a multitude of corpses and blood made manifest by the light of the fire-altars in its center;
great corpses were being cast down as horses led in by the *kharūpikas*.
Its belly was made terrifying by the frantic dance of a circle of fierce Kumbhāṇḍas;
it ended with the "chamacchami" sound of lamentation, and its clouds were composed of fat, blood, and tears.
It was filled with the forms of land-dwelling beings carried away by the swift currents of flowing rivers of blood;
it was crowded with vetālas and distracted by crows dragging along skeletons.
A young vetāla sleeping within the belly of a dead elephant like a casket;
a rākṣasa engaged in the sport of drinking at a secluded spot beneath a solitary tree.
In the tumult of the intoxicated vetālas, it was ablaze with funeral pyres and firebrands,
while the wind carried a heady scent mingled with flowing blood and fat.
In the jeweled casket, there was the tumultuous roar of the *vegaraṇa* and *duṭaruṭa* [beings],
while the *yakṣas*, excited by their greed for the taste of half-cooked corpses, were leaping about.
It was filled with birds perched on the limbs of the women from Tuṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Aṅga,
and Taṅga, and it bore the appearance of flames facing outward like the falling of stars.
In its midst stood a beautiful woman smeared with blood, amidst the joyous frolics of falling vetālas;
nearby, a host of yoginīs sang as they were overheard by the piśācas.
He played the great lute whose strings were his protruding intestines;
he was a man who had become a female demon through the influence of demonic impressions.

In some places, it was like a battlefield where brave warriors were half-dead from terror caused by the sight of the Rūpikā demoness, while in others, it was as if the day’s battle had been fought against Vetālas and Rākṣasas, with corpses rising up.
The night-stalkers were terrified by the corpse-like trunks and the shrouds of skin;
the sky was crowded with a multitude of previously unseen bags of elemental spirits gathered together.
[He saw] a heap of corpses scattered by the glances of hungry yakṣas looking for food, while the dying lords of men were being carried away with extreme effort.
With the fragments of the flames from the fire of Śiva’s mouth that fell during the night,
it was as if new clusters of *aśoka* flowers had been scattered all around and blown upward.
It had restless young vetālas bound to its neck by the trunks of headless corpses;
it was filled with yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and ajīvakas, who were like firebrands in the sky.
It was like a mass of darkness filling the hollows of mountain caves and the interior of space, resembling a vast expanse of water;
it was like a door-panel made of the world’s rays, shaken by the cosmic winds of the kalpa, which were agitated by the impetuous rush of wandering beings.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the fortieth canto, titled "The Description of the Battlefield at Night, Agitated by Night-Stalkers," Vasiṣṭha says:
Thus, on that battlefield long made terrible by the conduct of night-stalkers, amidst the rising shrieks of vetālas with their terrifying cries;
When the armies, having gazed upon the sky, had departed as they had come,
and the kings, along with their chariots and other vehicles, had rested in their own abodes as if weary;
While the people were visible on the field of battle like the waters of a great lake,
the conduct of the people remained as constant as the course of night.
In a house at night, where the walls are clearly visible even when a clod of earth is easily grasped by the hand,
the host of spirits dances with minds overflowing with the excitement of gain.
When the multitude of directions was sealed in sleep by a silent and peaceful movement,
the noble-souled Lord of Līlā appeared as if somewhat dejected in mind.
Having quickly deliberated upon the morning duties with his ministers, who were experts in counsel,
he lay down upon a bed as cool as snow and shaped like a long crescent moon.
In a bedchamber resembling the rising moon, within a cool inner chamber,
he fell asleep for a moment, his lotus-like eyes closed.
Then those two women, leaving that sky, entered that house through its openings, just as a gust of wind enters a lotus bud.
Rāma:
O best among those who know speech, how does this gross body, which is merely this much in size, enter through an opening as thin as a thread, O Lord?
Vasiṣṭha:
O sinless one, he whose deluded mind perceives this body as merely material cannot pass through the subtle apertures.
"One who possesses the thought, 'I have been obstructed by this,' or 'I am not intoxicated by this,' experiences it as something that has experienced what was previously experienced."
How can one who has experienced the thought "I am going to the first half" and is engaged in that action,
have a consciousness directed toward going to the second half?
Water does not rise upward, nor does fire go downward;
in whatever manner consciousness has proceeded, it remains exactly in that same way.
For one seated in the shade, how could there be experiences of heat?
An object perceived by one consciousness is not experienced by another.
In whatever manner the mind has proceeded, it remains fixed in that very state;
yet, through supreme effort, it is led once again to another condition.
The single cognition of a snake regarding a rope is forcibly removed by the cognition of its unreality;
otherwise, however, this [cognition] remains exactly as it was.
As is consciousness, so is the mind; as is the mind, so is its activity.
This is well-established even for a child; who does not experience it?
Furthermore, how and by whom can that which has the form of a mere void, appearing like the shape of a person imagined in a dream, be obstructed?
For indeed, the body of everything in every respect consists of mind alone; yet that which exists as sensation appears as if it were moving from within the heart to some external location.
Just as he desires, so does his setting and rising occur;
at the initial creation it arises from its own nature, and thereafter comes the contemplation of duality and unity.
Know that these three— the space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the third, the [outer] space— are indeed one, by virtue of their inseparable nature.
Know this to be the body of consciousness, which arises as all-pervading; for it arises according to the nature of its perceptions and according to the emergence of those perceptions.
He dwells within a mote of dust, he is led into the belly of the sky;
he merges into the buds of sprouts and becomes sap within the leaf.
It glimmers as the state of water-waves, it dances within the interior of stones;
having become a rain-cloud, it pours forth, and having become solidified, it remains still.
He travels through the sky at will, and even within the bellies of mountains;
possessing the form of space, he assumes the nature of the infinite, and then again the state of an infinitesimal atom.
He becomes the support for the best of mountains, with his seat firmly established at the summit of the sky; he possesses excellent body hair both within and without his body.
The ocean, being non-different from itself, assumes within its own self millions of abodes of the lotus-born Brahmā, just as it manifests the formation of whirlpools.
At the beginning of creation, this one—whose body is the mind—is unmanifest yet awakened;
having become the Great One whose nature is space, it perceives, having entered into the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Having realized that non-existence itself is the state of being obstructed, it arises as if it were real,
just as a man in a dream-delusion thinks, "I am the son of a barren woman."
Rāma said:
"What is this state of mind? Or how does it not exist for us?
And how is it that nothing other than this form exists even for a moment?"
Vasiṣṭha:
Each individual mind possesses such power; thus, the delusions of the world arise separately for each and every mind.
Through attachment to the world, moments and eons arise and dissolve; for some it is in a mere blink of an eye, for others it takes an eon—listen now to that sequence.
Immediately after death and the great delusion, this state arises—either instantly or after some time; hear now from me the sequence regarding that.
The fainting that consists of death and so forth is experienced by each individual;
know this, O wise one, to be the very night of the great dissolution.
At the end of that, everyone individually unfolds creation,
like the restless movement of mountains arising from the delusions of innate dreams and mental constructions.
Just as the Virāṭ Self, whose body is the mind, expands this universe at the end of the night of the great dissolution,
so too does it do so individually after each death.
Rāma:
Just as the creation after death is experienced through memory, so does the Virāṭ experience [the world]; therefore, the universe is not without a cause.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, during the great dissolution, all beings such as Hari, Hara, and others attain the state of disembodied liberation; what possibility, then, is there for memory?
One whose self is awakened like ours is indeed necessarily liberated;
how then could Brahmā and others be unliberated and bodiless?
For those living beings who exist at present, memory serves as the cause for their births and deaths here, due to the absence of liberation.
For that which exists within the living being, as if about to manifest, at the end of death and fainting,
yet remains unmanifested— that is designated as Pradhāna.
That void is called Prakṛti; it is the unmanifest (avyakta), both insentient and sentient.
This is the sequence for the arising of existence, due to both worldly transmigration and the lack of recollection [of one's true nature].
For when that which is oriented toward awakening becomes fully awakened, then from the void there arise the subtle elements, the directions, time, action, the gross elements, and so forth.
That very [subtle body] becomes swollen and awakened as the pentad of sense organs;
that alone perceives the body—it is this which is the *ātivāhika*.
Through long-standing conviction, this very [notion], thickened by conceptual construction,
brings about for you the perception of a material reality.
Then, the divisions of space and time, existing as its substratum,
arise while remaining unarisen, like the activity of vibration in the wind.
In this way, this wandering through the worlds has increased in vain;
though experienced by oneself, it is unreal, like union with a woman in a dream.
At the very moment a living being dies, he immediately perceives this entire expanse of the world situated exactly as it is right there.

Like the sky itself, the living being (jīva), whose nature is space, experiences the delusion that "I am the world," appearing as if it has become a self-possessing entity, though its true form is space.
It is jagged with cities, ports, mountains, suns, and clusters of stars;
its hollows are filled with the perils of old age, death, infirmity, and disease.
It is characterized by the intensity of the presence and absence of intrinsic nature, and is gross, subtle, moving, and unmoving;
it includes the mountains, the heavens, the earth, the rivers, the directions, day and night, and the destruction and arising of kalpas.
"I was born here by this father"—thus one forms a firm conviction;
"this is my mother, this is my wealth"—thus latent tendencies arise.
"I have done good deeds" and "I have done evil deeds"—such is the conceptual construction of "mine.
Yet today, I am a child, while [the other] sports in his heart thinking, "I am young."
Thus has this forest grove of saṃsāra been described in detail:
it is blossomed with the flowers of the stars, and its trembling shoots are like dark blue clouds.
Moving about with its herds of human deer, with gods, asuras, and birds as its inhabitants,
it has the pollen of the flowers of the worlds for its thickets and bowers of illusion.
The ocean is filled with lotus ponds, and Mount Meru and other mountains are like clods of earth;
within the seed of the lotus of the mind, the sprout of experience lies hidden.
Wherever this living being dies, there he sees in an instant; thus it is in each of the many world-systems that have arisen.

Tens of millions of Brahmās, Rudras, Indras, Maruts, Viṣṇus, and Vivasvats have passed away, their vision having extended across Meru, the oceans, the circles of the earth, the continents, and other worlds.

Those views that have passed, those that will pass, and those that are passing away— how could anyone be capable of counting them all within Brahman, who is rich in expansion and whose form is indestructible?
Thus, this universe consisting of walls does not exist at all apart from mental construction; and since mental construction is itself like space, reflect upon that now.
That which is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is remembered as the Supreme;
the act of thinking is the space of consciousness, and that alone is the supreme state.
That which is a whirlpool is indeed water, yet the whirlpool does not exist as a real entity;
it remains merely as something seen, like a visible object, yet it does not exist as a real entity.

Alternatively, because it is perishable at a later time, it does not exist as a real entity;
since all this is of such a nature, what room is there for the charge of nihilism?
In the waking state, the dream is unreal; in the dream, the waking state is unreal.
Death is unreal in birth, and birth is likewise composed of unreality in death.
O beautiful one, because it is fragile under investigation and because it is an experience, this world is thus neither existent nor non-existent; it appears as mere delusion.
Whether at the perfection of the end of a great aeon, or today, or in another age, that which is never subject to destruction is Brahman alone; that is this world.
In that [reality], these delusions called "creation" shine forth in the midst;
yet they do not shine forth in reality, like hairs in the sky.
Just as waves arise in the ocean, so do these creations in the Supreme;
rising again and again, they dissolve like dust in a great wind.
Therefore, since the appearance consisting of delusion is false in its very nature,
what reliance can there be on the ashes of creation, which are like the flow of water in a mirage?
And there are no other delusions therein; they themselves are the supreme state.
In dense darkness, the appearance of a yakṣa is merely darkness itself, not the yakṣas.
Therefore, birth, death, and delusion, as well as the sky, "I," "you," and this all-pervading universe— all that remains at the end of the great aeon of peace.
Therefore, this is seen as neither real nor ever unreal;
rather, both of these arise within that very Brahman.
Whether within the space of a single atom, or even within a subtle particle,
wherever there is a soul-atom, there it perceives this entire world as its own body.
Just as fire perceives its own heat arising from its inherent nature,
so too does the Self, which is pure consciousness, perceive this world as being one with itself.
Just as motes of dust dance in a house illuminated by the sun's rays,
so do these cosmic eggs appear as motes of dust in the supreme ether.
Just as vibration resides in the wind, fragrance in the air, and coolness in space,
so too does the universe abide in the Supreme, free from any grasping at solid form.
Existence and non-existence, grasping and abandoning, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving— Brahman is devoid of such constituent parts as these.
Now you must understand that for the sake of awakening,
they are non-different from your own self, just as the parts of a tree are not different from the tree itself.
This universe, as it exists, arises from the sequence of its own inherent nature;
empty of the referents of the word "universe," it abides as non-different from Brahman.
That is neither true nor untrue; it is like the delusion of a snake in a rope.
It is true from the perspective of false experience, but untrue upon investigation.
Having fully realized the supreme cause, one understands it sufficiently as if it were the state of being a living soul;
therefore, experiencing that very [cause], one clearly attains the state of being a living soul.
Whether real or unreal, this world that appears even in the sky truly delights the individual soul with its own arising experiences.
These experiences, however, are some derived from previous experience, while others are of unprecedented experience; they are both similar and dissimilar.
Sometimes and in some places those very same [experiences] appear, and sometimes even equal ones;
though unreal, they shine with the appearance of reality as experiences within the space of the living soul.
Those of the same lineage, the same conduct, born of the same stock, and sharing the same pursuits—
they alone shall be your ministers and citizens when you manifest your power.
And these [qualities] are truly sufficient within the self when they are equalized through place, time, and benefit;
such is the established state of intuition, which has the nature of all selves.
Just as a reflection consisting of pure being arises in the sky that is the Self of the King, so too does a truly real reflection arise in the luminous One who stands at the forefront of all things.
"Having your character, your conduct, your lineage, and your very form"—
thus does this play appear as a manifestation born of reflection.
In the mirror of all-pervasive consciousness, appearances reflect; whatever appears wherever it may be, it arises there in that very manner, without interruption.
That manifestation which resides within the inner space of the living soul shines forth by itself; it exists externally in the sky as a reflection from the mirror of consciousness.
This sky is you, and I am the world, the earth, and so forth; the king is all this, which is indeed unborn and a mere manifestation of light.
Know, my dear, that the firmament of consciousness is like the interior of a wood-apple fruit; understand this, and remain at peace, as you are, in this very state.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Burning by Fire, the Night Battle, and the World as Brahman," Sarasvatī said:
"This Vidūratha here is your husband; having cast off his body on the field of battle, he will reach that very inner apartment and become such a self once more."
Vasiṣṭha:
Having heard these words of the queen, Līlā, who had previously resided in that city,
stood again with her head bowed and, joining her palms in reverence, spoke these words.
The Second Līlā:
The Goddess, the Blessed Jñapti, is eternally worshipped by me;
O Goddess, she grants me her vision during the nights in dreams.
O Goddess of gods, O Mother, you are exactly as she is;
out of compassion for my wretched state, grant me a boon, O lady of lovely countenance.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus, that Jñapti then recalled her state of devotion and,
being pleased, spoke these words to Līlā, who was in her former abode.
The Goddess said:
"O child, I am well-pleased with you for your undistracted devotion that has remained unfailing throughout your life; accept the boon you desire."
The playfulness of that place:
"In the battle, having cast off my body, where my husband remains,
may I be there as his wife with this very same body."
The Goddess said:
"So be it! O daughter, you have been worshipped by me for a long time without obstacle, O Goddess, with your single-minded devotion through offerings of flowers and incense."
Vasiṣṭha said: Then,
when that local festival had blossomed due to the arrival of the bridegroom,
Pūrvalīlā, her heart agitated by doubt, spoke to the goddess.
The Previous Pastime: Those whose desires are true, whose resolutions are solely true, and who are of the nature of Brahman—
like you, everything they desire is swiftly accomplished for them.
O Sovereign Lady, why was I not led by that very body to another world, or to that mountain village?
The Goddess said:
"O woman of excellent complexion, I do nothing for anyone;
it is the individual soul itself that swiftly accomplishes all its own desires."
For I am the simple consciousness, the presiding deity of pure awareness;
I am the individual power of consciousness, existing in the form of the individual soul-power (jīva-śakti).
In whatever manner the power of "I" arises for any living being, that power always manifests its corresponding fruit for that very being in that very same way.
When they quickly propitiate me, the vital power (jīvaśakti) arises in such a way that,
while still within this body, it thinks for a long time, "I am liberated."
In various ways you have been fully awakened by me;
through that reasoning, O lady of excellent complexion, you have been led to a state of stainless being.
When I was awakened by this very cultivation for a long time,
I then attained that very goal through the power of my own consciousness.
Whatever effort of one's own mind arises for anyone over a long period, it yields its fruit in due time, exactly in accordance with that [effort].
Whether becoming austerity or even a deity, that very same immutable consciousness bestows the fruit at its own will, like the falling of fruit from the sky.
Since there is never anything other than the illumination of one's own self-awareness that constitutes the fruit, act quickly as you wish.
Indeed, the inner self is the very nature of consciousness, omnipresent; whatever it perceives and strives for, that it attains, and that is its glory.
Therefore, having deliberated as to whether something is pleasant or unpleasant, and having understood that which is purifying, abide within that.
In the Līlopākhyāna, the forty-sixth canto, titled "The Abiding of Satyakāma and Satyasaṅkalpa," Rāma said:
While they were conversing thus within that house,
what did Vidūratha do, having gone out from the house in anger?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Vidūratha, having emerged from his own palace,
was surrounded by a great retinue like the moon by a multitude of stars.
With all his limbs armored and adorned with clinging necklaces and ornaments, he went forth like the Lord of the Gods amidst great shouts of "Victory! Victory!"
Giving orders to the host of warriors, listening to the arrangement of the circles,
and surveying the heroic battlefields, the king ascended his chariot.
Resembling a celestial mansion, adorned with pearls and rubies,
and pervaded by clusters of banners, it was like a divine chariot descended from heaven.
With golden sprouts falling from the flowing streams along its moonstone walls, and with beautiful coral arches jingling with the sound of *jhaṇajhaṇa* from pearls;
With well-proportioned, auspicious, white, and lean horses, which,
by the speed that heightened their swiftness, seemed to be dripping from their hooves as if they were flowing with motion itself.
With their modes of progression that could not endure even their innate winds,
they seemed to cast off their hindquarters and drink up the sky.
It was harnessed by eight horses that seemed filled with joined moons due to the brilliance of their chowries, and whose neighing fulfilled all desires.
Then there arose the sound of kettledrums, filled with the roar of unrestrained elephants and clouds, made terrible by its echoes against the mountain walls.
It was filled with the clamor of cries let loose by the intoxicated soldiers,
with the tinkling of clusters of small bells, and with the clanging sounds produced by the collision of weapons.
With the crackling sounds of bows, the whistling songs of arrows,
and the jangling clatter of masses of armor crushed against one another's shoulders;
With the crackling sounds of blazing fires, with the cries of those suffering in pain,
with the mutual challenges of warriors, and with the agitated weeping of prisoners;
A sound that filled the hollows of the entire universe as if solidified into stone,
graspable by the hand, terrifying to you, and filling the groves of the ten directions.
Then it flew up toward the sky, as if intent on soaring into the heavens, while its dust-like form thickly obstructed the path of the sun and covered the surface of the earth.
Because of him, that great city became as if entered into a state of gestation;
darkness reached a density like the folly of youth.
Multitudes of lamps departed somewhere like stars with the day, while restless throngs of nocturnal spirits arrived with their forces.
She and the young maiden beheld that great battle with throbbing hearts, through the great vision granted by the Goddess.
Then, within their homes, the loud clattering sounds subsided,
like submarine fires in the waters of the single vast ocean.
Drawing his army along with his arrows, the king entered the midst of the enemy forces like Mount Meru, soaring on its wings into a single ocean.
Then there arose a clear, crackling sound of "caṭat-caṭat" from the discharge of arrows;
those who had created a cloud of their own bodies crossed over the succession of shafts.
Taking to the sky, birds with various weapons flew about;
the flashes of the weapons spread forth like mists throughout all directions.
Blazing with the friction of clashing weapons like the fire of a brand,
those heroic clouds roared while raining down torrents of arrow-showers.
Sharp weapons, cruel like herons, fell upon the limbs of the heroes with a *paṭapaṭa* sound as they struck one another in the sky.
The darkness quickly subsided by means of the lamps of weapons blazing like fire;
all the armies became as if covered with the hair of new iron arrows.
Rows of headless trunks rose up like dancers in a funeral procession; female goblins sang aloud the betrayal of battle, their voices shrieking.
In the strength of the elephants, there arose the "kreṅkāra" sounds from their intoxicated collisions;
like intoxicated rivers, they bore the stones of the catapults across the expanse of the sky.
Multitudes of chariots fell like the parched leaves of a forest,
and rivers of blood issued forth from the mountain of battle that was raining down death.
The dust was stilled by blood, the darkness by the fires of weapons,
the sounds by the single-minded concentration on battle, and the terrors by the certainty of death.
There occurred only a battle, tumultuous, incomparable, and bewildering, resounding with the gurgling of sword-waves that resembled undisturbed clouds.
With showers of arrows falling with a *ṣava-ṣava* sound, with *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles crashing down with a *kaṭakaṭa* noise,
and great weapons clashing with a *jhaṇajhaṇa* sound, that army lay like one asleep at night, its defenses newly shattered.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the forty-seventh canto, titled "The Departure of Vidūratha," Vasiṣṭha said:
While this terrible tumult of battle was thus proceeding,
the two Līlās spoke these words to the Blessed Jñapti standing before them:
The Two Līlās: "O Goddess, why does our lord suddenly conquer us in battle?
Tell us, for even though you are pleased, this elephant has fled."
Sarasvatī:
I have been propitiated for a long time by this King Vidūratha, the enemy of [your] king, for the sake of victory; I have not been so propitiated by King Vidūratha himself.
Therefore, he alone triumphs and Vidūratha is not defeated;
for this consciousness, which is internal awareness, is exactly as it is and whenever it arises.
Whatever he impels me toward quickly, that I accomplish for him at that time;
in whatever way he impels me, I abide as the fruit thereof for him.
"He does not possess this [victory] by nature, just as heat belongs to fire;
'May victory be mine in battle'—by this [thought], I have been honored."
Therefore, she attains such a fruit by means of the form of the image;
by Vidūratha, I have been awakened to this matter without having reflected upon it.
Thinking, "By this very means I shall be liberated," he became full of such conviction;
therefore, Vidūratha, having attained that body together with his wife, [attained liberation].
In time, O child, he shall be released by you and her;
for this king named Sindhu is his enemy,
and having slain him upon the surface of the earth, the victor will rule the kingdom.
Vasiṣṭha said:
While the queen was speaking thus and the two armies were engaged in combat,
the sun, as if to witness the marvel, ascended the mountain of sunrise.
At twilight, the clusters of stars in the sky were like corpses being created by the forces of darkness, which had assumed the form of bees.
Gradually, the mountainous terrains of the battlefield assumed a formidable appearance;
the world shone as if it had been cast up from an ocean of soot.
The rays of the sun, beautiful with their golden glow,
shone upon the mountains like streaks of blood from the battle among the preeminent heroes.
Then the sky and the surface of the battlefield appeared alike,
with arms whirling like serpents and strewn with splendors like scattered gold.
With their heads, it was strewn with heaps of jewels from their earrings; with its lotuses being the aged, it was filled with weapons as its dense foliage and bristling with arrows like śarabhas.
It was rich with red luster and unstable twilight, filled with perfected beings and corpses;
it was strewn with necklaces of sloughed snake skins and crowded with garments like rays of light.
With thighs that served as banners of victory over lassitude, it was adorned with archways;
with hands and feet, it was made to blossom, and with arrows, it resembled a forest of reeds.
Dark with the grassy meadows of sword-blades, possessing sandy banks of sword-grass,
strewn with garlands of weapons, it was as terrifying as if it were possessed by a mad spirit.
It had the appearance of a grove of blossoming *aśoka* trees due to the fires produced by the clashing of weapons;
it was filled with the tumultuous roar of great sounds, and the leaders of the *siddhas* were fleeing from it.
Its form was fashioned of gold, with weapons as bright as the rising sun;
its interior resounded with the clashing of spears, swords, discuses, pikes, double-edged blades, and mallets.
In the meantime, all the armies met their destruction;
the battlefield became as if empty, with only a few soldiers remaining on either side.
With men cut down, pierced, dead, destroyed, slain, or fleeing; with great heaps of falling corpses and streams of flowing blood like mud.
It was filled with a multitude of corpses being swept away by the force of flowing rivers of blood,
and crowded with *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, spears, lances, swords, and large stones.
It was filled with the falling of headless trunks severed by the blows of heroes' weapons,
and it resounded with the confused clamor raised by a multitude of vetālas performing a frantic palm-clapping dance.
