In the empty arena, those two moving chariots, drawn by lotuses and elephants and blazing with light,
appeared like the sun and moon in the sky, marked against the firmament.
Surrounded by thousands upon thousands of heroes, they were crowded with weapons such as discuses, spears, *bhuśuṇḍis*, double-edged swords, and javelins.
Wandering at will upon the ground spread out within the mandala,
they were both rendered simultaneously dead and immortal, crushed by the great wheel accompanied by the sound of hissing.
Crossing the rivers of blood with the grace of rutting elephants,
their wheels were shrouded by hair as if by water-weeds, and they were drenched in the crimson waters.
The elephants were thrown down in agitation by the shock of being struck by the revolving wheels,
while the hollows of the poles resounded with the jingling of gems and pearls.
The fluttering sound of the cloth at the tips of the banners struck by the wind was followed by many great heroes and numerous terrified soldiers.
They bore the weight of spears, arrows, and bows, as well as javelins,
spikes, and lances, which shone with a brilliant luster.
There, having whirled for a moment with numerous circular maneuvers, those two,
like clouds of weapons facing one another, engaged in combat.
With clouds of hailstones formed by the discharge of showers of iron arrows, they roared at one another like two intoxicated ocean-clouds.
As those two lions among men struck each other with arrows,
those shafts spread across the sky, appearing like stones and maces.
Some have sword-blades for fruits, others have mallets for faces;
some have sharp discuses for mouths, and others have axes for faces.
Some arrows had shafts like spears, some were razor-faced; some had points like spikes, axes, or crescent moons.
Some had faces like lions' stones, some had faces like the points of spears, and some had faces like tridents; they were as massive as great boulders.
Then the arrows coursed like masses of rocks cast down by the winds of cosmic dissolution;
at that moment, the encounter between the two became like the tumultuous agitation of the oceans at the time of universal destruction.
In the Līlopākhyāna, the forty-eighth canto, titled "The Meeting of Vidūratha and Sindhu," Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reached the city, King Sindhudvīpa, whose neck was held high,
became expanded with anger that resembled the heat of the midday sun.
He strung his bow, making the quarters of the sky resound,
like the slope of the mountain of the gods when struck by the winds at the end of an aeon.
The powerful king released a continuous succession of arrows fixed in his quiver overnight, like the rays of the sun at dawn.
From his excellence alone, a single great arrow emerges;
as it flies through the sky, it falls by the thousands and strikes its mark by the hundreds of thousands.
The power and dexterity of the Ocean were likewise the same;
indeed, the two of them possessed the skill with the bow that was equal to the face of Viṣṇu and the Sun.
Those arrows named musalas, shaped like musalas,
covered the sky with loud roars, like the mountains at the end of a kalpa.
Those rows of golden arrows of his shone in the sky like stars falling, distressed by the winds at the end of an eon.
From Vidūratha, showers of arrows issued forth incessantly,
like masses of water from the ocean or rays of light from the sun.
Like flowers shaken from a great tree by a fierce wind,
or like rows of sparks struck from a heated iron ball.
Like streams from a rain-cloud, like sprays from a waterfall,
or like brilliant sparks from the great conflagration of that city’s fire.
Hearing the crackling sound of the two bows snapping,
the two armies became as silent as a calm ocean, watching in stunned silence.
Floods of arrows flowed through the sky like the current of the Gaṅgā,
rushing toward the ocean with the gurgling roar of yakṣas.
From the cloud that was his bow, there issued forth incessant showers of whetted iron arrows,
accompanied by the "śava-śava" sound of falling corpses.
Seeing Bāṇa, who was like a flood of the Mandākinī, proceeding to fill the ocean, Līlā, a resident of that city, watched him from her window.
Fearing for her husband's victory because of that multitude of arrows,
she, whose lotus-like face was blossoming with joy, spoke these words:
Victory, O Goddess! Victory to this Lord of ours; look upon us!
For indeed, by this flood of arrows, even Mount Meru would be reduced to powder.
While she was speaking thus, the two goddesses— distraught by the sound of their deep affection, intent on watching her, and smiling in their hearts at her human nature— [listened].
The submarine fire of the ocean drank up that surging sea of arrows,
just as Jahnu swallowed the Mandākinī with its impassable heat of reeds.
Having pierced that entire mass of arrows with a shower of his own shafts,
he then cast them down and hurled them into the ocean of the sky.
Just as the movement of an extinguished lamp is not perceived,
so too the movement of that multitude of arrows was not discerned.
Having cut through that dense shower of arrows, which was like a thick cloud of his own shafts, he spread out in the sky a canopy accompanied by the howling of autumnal corpses.
Vidūratha also swiftly shattered him with his finest arrows,
just as the wind at the end of an aeon disperses an ordinary cloud.
Thus, with their showers of arrows rendered futile by counter-strikes, the two lords of the earth continued their attacks without ceasing.
Then Sindhu took up the deluding weapon (mohanāstra) obtained through his friendship with a Gandharva; by means of it, he caused all the worlds to fall into a state of delusion, except for Vidūratha.
With their weapons and garments cast aside, silent, and with dejected faces and eyes,
the warriors became like the dead, or as if they were figures depicted in a painting.
Just as King Vidūratha’s chariot was being brought to a standstill by delusion,
King Vidūratha took up the weapon of awakening.
Then, like a lotus-pond at dawn, the people regained their consciousness;
and Sindhu became as enraged toward Vidūratha as she had been toward the Rākṣasa.
He took up the terrifying Naga-weapon, which causes distress through the binding of nooses;
by it, the sky became filled with serpents resembling mountains.
The earth was entwined with serpents like a lake with lotus stalks; all the mountains became as if covered by blankets of black serpents.
All these objects, including the expanse of mountains and forests, were covered by the bodies of serpents, and the earth fell into a state of helplessness.
Scattered with sparks from the embers of the *dhūta* ascetic practices, signaling the onset of the poison's force,
winds blew carrying dust and flames like intensely hot frost.
Then Vidūratha, an expert in great weapons, discharged the Suparṇa missile;
by it, Garuḍas rose up like mountains made of gold.
They have made all directions golden and fulfill every desire;
they produce winds of universal destruction through the violent agitation of the mountain wings.
Circles of hissing serpents were drawn in by the movement of their nostrils,
and masses of clouds were filled with the sound of their great, rumbling roars.
Like Agastya drinking the ocean, that cloud-like Suparṇa drank up the flood of serpents that filled the earth, hissing as they were dragged along.
The circle of the earth, now freed from the serpent’s coils,
shone like a vast, dense, waterless expanse, or like a great heap of grain.
Then that host of Garuḍas vanished somewhere,
like a mass of lamps by the wind or a circle of clouds in autumn.
Furthermore, it was like a range of mountains rich in wings through sheer fear of the Vajra,
or like the world seen in a dream, or like a city of one's own mental construction.
Then Sindhu discharged the weapon of darkness, which produces blinding gloom;
by it, a darkness spread forth, resembling the interior of a black cloud.
Spreading across the cavity between heaven and earth, it became like a single vast ocean;
the mountains became like fish, and the stars became like jewels.
The darkness spread forth, resembling an ocean of ink-paste,
like a mass of collyrium-mountains shaken loose even by the end of kalpas.
All the subjects were as if fallen into a blind well;
all legal proceedings came to a standstill in every direction, like at the end of an eon.
Then Vidūratha, the best among those skilled in weapons, having performed the ritual procedures with potent mantras, bestowed the Mārtāṇḍa weapon within the pavilion of the universe.
Then the risen Agastya-like sun, with its rays, drank up the ocean of darkness, just as the stainless autumn season drinks up the black rain-cloud.
The stainless quarters of the sky, released from the garment of darkness,
shone forth like lovely women with beautiful breasts standing before the lord of the earth.
All the forest ranges within became visible,
like the intellects of the virtuous when they are freed from the soot-like net of greed.
Then Sindhur, agitated by anger, instantly unleashed the most terrifying Rākṣasa weapon, which, impelled by mantras, took the form of arrows.
The terrifying forest-rākṣasas rose up from all directions in a rage,
like the great oceans agitated by the *hūṃkāra* roars of the elephants of the underworld.
The fires, with their smoke-colored matted locks of Kapila hue, crackling with loud *caṭa-caṭa* sounds,
were like those with fierce, licking tongues and half-consumed fuel.
Moving in whirlpools across the sky, they let out terrifying, harsh cries like ḍakkās, resembling great fires with massive columns of smoke and flaming brands.
Their lotus-like faces and bodies were overrun by the sprouts of their fangs as venom,
appearing like matted locks of hair from which fierce flames issued forth from their bristling body hairs.
Swallowing [their prey], rushing forward, and roaring with threatening intentions,
they were like water-bearing clouds with masses of lightning flashing from their matted hair.
In the meantime, Vidūratha, the lord of Līlā,
bestowed upon him the Nārāyaṇa weapon, which wards off wicked beings.
As this king of weapons was being invoked,
the hosts of Rākṣasas were extinguished, like darkness at the rising of the sun.
The three worlds became cleansed of the hosts of Rākṣasas;
it shone forth stainless, like the sky in autumn when the clouds have departed.
Then Sindhu released the fiery weapon (*āgneya-astra*), which set the sky ablaze;
by it, the quarters of the world blazed as if enveloped by the fire of cosmic dissolution.
All the directions became shrouded by a mass of smoke and clouds,
as if agitated by the darkness rising from the netherworld and piercing through the sky.
They shone with a blazing appearance like mountains of gold,
resembling forests of dense, blossoming *caṃpaka* trees in full bloom.
The sky, mountains, and forest thickets took on the appearance of being matted with a mass of flames,
as if smeared with blood like saffron during the festival of Death.
Blazing with a single flame that touched the nearby sky,
they appeared like oceans encircled by the thousand-fold forms of the serpent-king.
Having conquered his enemy, Vidūratha, after paying homage, released the Vāruṇa weapon, striking back just as his opponent had struck him.
Floods of water, like floods of darkness, came from all sides— from below, from above, and from every direction— appearing like mountains in liquid form.
Like portions of the autumnal sky, like clouds with swift descent,
like great oceans standing upright, and like the rocks of the principal mountain ranges.
Like a mass of *tamāla* trees flying up, like nights gathered together,
like heaps of collyrium tossed upward, it was like the Lokāloka mountain reaching its peak.
Like the vast expanses of the caves of the netherworld (rasātala) desiring to behold the sky,
their forms were augmented by the force of a great, deep rumbling roar.
That mass of water swallowed the spreading line of heat from the fire,
just as the night swiftly swallows the evening twilight that pervades the world.
Having drunk that continuous stream of fire, the splendor of the waters filled the surface of the earth, her body having attained a manifest state of fluidity.
Those who are mutually hostile see and experience such delusions of weapons, which are composed of illusion, as being truly opposed and not otherwise.
Then the protectors of the wheels of the ocean, who bore the burden of its cause, were swept away by the waters like blades of grass; and his chariot was carried across.
In the meantime, Sindhu remembered the weapon Śoṣaṇa;
he gave it, which provides protection in times of distress, in the form of an arrow.
The water-based illusion was quelled by that very sun;
those who were dead remained indeed dead, and the earth became parched.
Then, equal in heat to the wrath of a fool, he tormented the subjects;
he yawned, as harsh as the vast expanse of a withered and decayed forest.
The complexion of her limbs, beautiful with the luster of refined gold, clung to every major and minor part of her body like that of the wives of the best of kings.
Because of that, those who were opposed to him fell into a swoon born of heat,
like tender sprouts scorched by a summer forest fire.
Vidūratha, having bent his bow whose long, tinkling stars were rattling in his mind,
then took up the Parjanya weapon.
The rows of clouds rose up like accumulated nights,
sluggish with the frantic onset of their flight through the tamāla groves.
With the surging flood of the waters of latent impressions, they move with a roar of unrestrained force,
their coils encircling the entire circle of the quarters, which are made sluggish by the mist.
Winds blew, swirling with showers of rain and shattering the mass of clouds, noble as they were with necklaces of scattered spray and mist.
The lightnings in the sky, quivering like the retreat of terrified golden serpents,
were like the flickering side-glances of the Daitya women.

The quarters of the sky, their mountain caves thick with echoes swollen by the roar [of the army], shook; the forests resounded with the gurgling cries of elephants, lions, and bears that had been set in motion.
Showers of rain fell in streams as thick as great clubs, harsh with the sound of painful *ṭāṅkāra* claps, like the glances of Death himself.
First, a very hot vapor rose from the earth like a mountain;
it was as if masses of clouds were emerging from the netherworld to engage in battle with the wandering clouds.
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, the mirages subsided,
just as the latent tendencies of saṃsāra are dispelled by the floods of the essence of supreme awakening.
The entire circle of the earth became marked with mud and impassable;
it was filled by full streams, just as the ocean is filled by water from rivers.
He discharged the Vāyavya weapon, which made the hollows of the sky whirl and was as terrifying as the roaring of Bhairava engaged in the dance at the end of an eon.
Winds blew from the quarters of the sky, their massed bodies condensed by the falling of thunderbolts and consisting of shattered fragments of rock;
signaling the time of universal dissolution, they struck terror into the warriors with their harsh and piercing whistling sounds.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the forty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Battle with Weapons," Vasiṣṭha said:
Winds blew, swirling with frost and scattering thick clusters of blossoms,
tossing masses of trees about, fierce in their uprooting and toppling.
Then, by that exceedingly terrifying wind, the groves of the dense forest were shattered and the walls of the chasms were torn asunder; even the chariot of Vidūratha was likewise [tossed about].
Then Vidūratha, though skilled in great weapons, cast away his mountain-weapon as he was being carried along by the river like a withered leaf.
By that blow from the mountain-weapon, the wind ceased as if it had exerted itself to condense even the sky into a state of density.
And by that wind which had become stilled,
the rows of trees situated in the sky moved toward tranquility and fell to the earth.
In that array where various people were eating, millions of crows,
uttering sounds of *śīt*, *ḍakka*, *bhākkāra*, and *ukkāra*, filled the directions.
Like the scattered fragments of the fame of reeds shaken by the wind,
they saw mountains falling from the sky like fallen leaves.
He discharged the blazing Vajra weapon against the Sindhus, who had arisen here and there like the Maināka and other mountains; consequently, they were overwhelmed by the thunderbolt-clouds.
Like fires consuming mountains due to the heat of a conflagration, they drank up the opposing mountains, shattering the peaks and fortresses with the tips of their beaks.
They lopped off their heads like fruits from a tree by means of violent winds;
then Vidūratha discharged the Brahmā-weapon to neutralize the Vajra-weapon.
Then, when the Brahmā weapon and the Vajra weapon had both been simultaneously neutralized,
the elephant urged forth the Piśāca weapon, dark as the color of a dark cloud.
Then rows of Piśācas, inspiring boundless terror, rose up;
as if out of fear, the day turned to darkness at twilight.
The piśācas carried off the world like masses of darkness;
resembling pillars of ash, they sported with the swiftness of palm trees.
Some appeared with massive forms yet were as nothing, graspable only by the fist;
some had hair standing erect, emaciated limbs, and even beards.
With emaciated and soiled bodies, these sky-dwellers appeared like common villagers; they were dull-witted in the assembly, acting like scoundrels who do whatever comes to mind.
Miserable, gluttonous, and cruel like vulgar folk,
they are fickle, dwelling in empty houses at the edges of roads, mud, and trees.
Licking their lips, appearing like hungry ghosts, with blackened limbs like outcaste dog-cookers,
they then, intoxicated, seized the remnants of the enemy's army that had survived the slaughter.
The soldiers stationed there, their minds terrified and agitated, abandoned their weapons and armor; with their lives trembling and their steps faltering, they fled.
With eyes, limbs, faces, and feet that inspired terror through their distortions,
they were stripped of their loincloths, utterly naked, and bursting with laughter.
Then the king of the Piśācas, while passing excrement and urine, began a steady dance before King Vidūratha.
As he was thus assailed, that wise king realized it was an illusion;
the ruler of the earth recognized that it was a magical conjuration intended to provoke a battle with the Piśācas.
She deployed that army of Piśācas against the enemy force;
consequently, her own soldiers remained healthy, while the enemy warriors were possessed by Piśācas.
Then, in anger, he gave her that Rūpikā weapon and another;
from the earth and from the sky, women with stiff hair rose up.
Naked, with hideous eyes, and with pendulous hips and breasts;
they were women who had reached the bloom of youth, yet were aged, stout-limbed, or decrepit.
With hips in the form of their own nature, with vulvas blooming from wicked dancing, with human lotuses for heads and hands, and with limbs crimson with blood; MU_3,49.25.
With their cheeks smeared by the flowing flesh and blood half-chewed,
they twisted and contorted their various limbs, raising and lowering their faces.
With veins standing out on their arms, faces, thighs, breasts, flanks, and hands,
they dragged out the entrails like ropes from the infants who had been beaten to death.
With faces like those of dogs, crows, and owls, and with sunken mouths, jaws, and bellies,
they seized those Piśācas as if they were weak, ill-nourished infants.
Then that army of female piśācas became a single mass;
they were naked, dancing with their faces, limbs, and eyes turned upward.
They were attacking one another and terrifying each other;
their great tongues were protruding, and they displayed various contortions of the face.
Laden with the weight of corpses, with the limbs of dead bodies being carried one after another,
it was sinking and emerging in a sea of blood, its shimmering forms bobbing up and down.
With a protruding belly, long arms, and pendulous ears, lips, and nose,
they wallowed together in the mire of blood, flesh, and fat.
Just as the ocean of milk, stirred by Mount Mandara, was filled with the shimmering sounds of churning,
so too was his illusory manifestation brought forth once again.
Having quickly perceived his agility, he likewise acted swiftly;
then the Vetāla weapon was discharged by him, and throngs of corpses rose up.
Headless trunks with heads restored, leaping as if possessed by *vetālas*,
and then appearing like throngs of *piśācas*, *vetālas*, and headless corpses (*kabandhas*).
A terrifying army, capable of swallowing the earth, arose;
then the other king also employed another illusion.
He swiftly discharged the Rākṣasa weapon, intent on overwhelming the three worlds;
from all sides, massive Rākṣasas rose up, resembling mountains in form.
Having emerged from their bodies like hells from the underworld (pātāla),
that army then became terrifying, striking fear even into the gods and asuras.
It was filled with roaring rakshasas like a great ocean, with dancing headless trunks,
the forms of female rākṣasīs, and the secure abodes of piśācas.
Rich with whistling flutes, its heads crowded with clusters of lotuses, encircled by dangling garlands of entrails, and sprinkled with the water of blood; MU_3,49.40.
It was a place where the piśācas shone with a brilliance enhanced by the rhythmic clapping of vetālas;
it was rich with fat, flesh, and marrow, made beautiful by the wine of blood,
and crowded with the frantic dancing of intoxicated vetālas, kumbhāṇḍas, and yakṣas.

A bridge was established by the spirits over the stream of blood, which was sprayed by waves tossed up by the blood stirred by their feet— the staff-like legs of the Kumbhāṇḍas performing a frantic dance— and which shone with the tips of droplets from the streams of twilight clouds.
In the narrative of Līlā, the fiftieth canto, titled "The Second Battle with the Astras," Vasiṣṭha said:
While that terrible state of violent agitation was then prevailing,
he alone acted for the sake of destroying the entire army of his enemies and for the pacification of his own forces.
The mindful one, possessing infinite and noble fortitude within, recalled the glorious Vaiṣṇava weapon, the lord of weapons, which was like Śaṅkara himself.
Then, from the tip of that arrow which had been consecrated with the Vaiṣṇava weapon when it was released,
sparks like firebrands issued forth.
The rows of their broad discuses made the horizons appear as if filled with hundreds of suns,
and the approaching maces turned the sky into a forest of hundreds of bamboo poles.
The sky was turned into a vast stream of thunderbolts, while the sky was turned into a row of trees by the broad-edged spears and the cloth-like banners.
Then the king, for the sake of pacifying the second Vaiṣṇava weapon,
discharged the Vaiṣṇava weapon itself, which was filled with the spitting of missiles.
Then rivers of weapons flowed forth from that [body], their own missiles destroyed by his weapons— rivers with currents of arrows, spears, maces, darts, axes, and so forth.
A battle took place in the sky between those rivers of missiles and weapons,
causing the destruction of the cavity between heaven and earth and splitting apart the lords of the great mountain ranges.
The spears were cut down by arrows, the axes shattered by swords,
the *paṭṭiśas* struck down by well-aimed *prāsas*, and the *śaktis* lopped off by spears.
He was like Mount Mandara intoxicated by the churning of the ocean of arrows,
and like a thunderbolt resembling an irresistible mountain intent on shattering with his mace.
The moon-like circle of spears whirled about, quelling the rain of swords;
the tridents, enraged as they swallowed [the enemy], became the risen Yama himself.

The mountain was shattered by half-moons and high peaks, its rocky surfaces rendered feverless by thunderbolts; the surface of its crags resounded with the *śūtkāra* hissing of spikes as fearful as stakes.
The circle of trees was struck by formidable *bhiṇḍipāla* slings hurled from *bhuśuṇḍī* engines,
while many men with axes and speers in their hands were mangled by the sharp edges of axes and spears.
The whirling chowries were severed by the sharp edges of the whirling discus,
while the triple-pathed river was shattered and split apart with a loud *caṭa-caṭa* sound.
A vast canopy of great clouds consisting of the mass of splinters from weapons,
with lightning flashing from the whirling sparks produced by the mutual clashing of arms.

As the two [warriors] fought with their weapons, the cosmic egg of Brahmā seemed to burst from the sound, and the principal mountain ranges were shattered by the blows, while the flood of missiles was severed by the [divine] streams.
The entire time of the powerful-souled one has been spent merely in warding off his weapons;
he now stands effortlessly upon the ocean to see for himself how much strength he truly possesses.
Vidūratha discharged the fiery weapon with a sound like a thunderbolt;
it set Sindhu’s chariot ablaze as if it were dry undergrowth.
In the meantime, within the hollow interior of that weapon in the sky,
it was like armor or like a mass of rain clouds in the monsoon.
Having engaged in an exceedingly fierce battle with the king of weapons as their witness,
they both, possessing great prowess, came to a mutual cessation like two noble warriors.
In the meantime, the fire of his weapons, having quickly reduced the chariot to ashes and consumed the forest,
reached the Sindhu river like a lion emerging from its mountain cave.
Sindhur, neutralizing the fire-weapon with the Varuṇa-weapon from close range,
abandoned his chariot, reached the ground, and was equipped with sword and shield.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, with his sword, he effortlessly severed the hooves of the enemy's chariot horses as if they were lotus stalks.
Vidūratha, too, became deprived of his chariot and took up shield and sword;
with equal weapons and equal zeal, they moved in circular maneuvers.
As those two struck each other, their swords became like saws; it was as if the row of teeth of Time itself were gnawing at living beings as they moved about.
Casting aside his sword, Vidūratha took up a spear and hurled it into the ocean with a roar like a thunderbolt during a great portent.
Arriving without interruption, she fell upon his chest,
like an unwilling mistress falling upon an unpleasant husband.
By that blow from the spear, he did not meet his death;
rather, the nāga simply shed a stream of blood like water.
Seeing that darkness shattered like the moon by its light, the playful grace of that region,
blossoming with intense bliss, spoke of her former play.
"O Goddess, behold! This husband of ours, the Daitya with his towering neck, has been slain by Nṛsiṃha with the tips of his millions of spike-like claws, like an elephant."
Like water driven by the *hūṃ* sounds of the lordly serpents dwelling at the bottom of a lake,
his blood gushes forth with cries of "śulu-śulu."
Alas, what a tragedy! Sindhu has brought forth a chariot and is intent on mounting it, like Puṣkarāvartaka ascending the golden peak of Mount Meru.
Behold, O Queen, this chariot of hers, crushed by the mallet as if it were a golden city by the falling of a revolving mountain.
"This husband of mine has set out to mount the chariot brought here;
alas, it is like a pestle hurled by Indra at Sindhunemi."
Having deceived [him] with her charm and swiftly mounted the chariot,
behold— this husband of mine shines exceedingly in battle!
Alas, what a tragedy! This elephant has forcibly mounted the chariot of the noble son, just as a monkey climbs a tree from a hole within it using a raft.
Behold, as he ascends with his sword, his master’s shoulder is severed;
he sheds blood like a mountain of rubies emitting its luster.
Alas, alas! Woe is me! By this sword-blade of Sindhu, my husband has been severed from his thighs, like a tree cut by a saw.
Alas, alas! I am struck down, I am consumed by fire, I am dead, and I am utterly ruined;
for both knees of my husband have been severed like lotus stalks.
Having spoken thus and beholding him, she, distressed by the fear of her husband's disposition,
fell to the ground in a swoon like a creeper severed by an axe.
Vidūratha too, his knees shattered while still striking the enemy,
fell swiftly from his chariot like a tree whose roots have been cut.
Just as he was falling, being carried away by his charioteer in the chariot,
the arrogant elephant struck him on the neck.
Then, with his throat half-choked by emotion, he was followed by Sindhudvīpa and entered the palace, just as Lakṣmī enters a lotus.
Due to the power of Sarasvatī, that intoxicated gnat was unable to enter that house,
just as one cannot enter the midst of a great conflagration.
With his garments and armor splattered by the streams of blood and froth flowing from the wound in his throat, which had been sliced open by a sword,
the charioteer entered the interior of the house and left him there upon the bed of death, his enemy having been slain.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the fifty-first canto, titled "The Death of Vidūratha," Vasiṣṭha says:
"The king is slain! The king is slain by a rival king in battle!"—when these words arose, the kingdom was overwhelmed with fear.
The entire population was fleeing, burdened with loads of household goods and utensils;
the city-dwellers were running away, accompanied by their wives who were crying out in distress, making the fortress difficult to traverse.
A great battle ensued, involving crowds of women who were being snatched away from their crying husbands as they fled, while the people remained preoccupied with plundering one another.
It resounded with the joyful clamor of the dancing armies of enemy nations,
where elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers moved about without being commanded.
Resounding with the *gharghara* sound of quivers flying up as door-panels were shattered,
it was formidable with enemy warriors clad in countless plundered silken garments.
The courtyard of Rājagṛha was filled with fresh entrails torn out by knives,
while heaps of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas rested within the king's inner apartments.
The common folk were intent on eating food and rice that had been stolen from their homes,
while the young trees were crushed by the feet of the throngs of thieves carrying loads of gold.
The women of the inner apartments were overtaken by youths such as they had never known before, while the paths and directions became bristling with priceless jewels fallen from the hands of thieves.
The circle of vassal kings was preoccupied with the crowding of horses, elephants, and chariots,
while the chief ministers stood at the forefront, intent on issuing the commands for the royal consecration.
The lord architect standing upon the ridge where the royal capital was being constructed,
with the king’s favorites falling into the wells, the windows, and the pits below.

It was filled with the roar of hundreds of shouts of victory from the kings of the Sindhu region, and it established its presence upon the Sindhu River, which was surrounded by countless throngs of his own royal kinsmen.
The royal favorites were fleeing, having been overtaken by the incursions of other villages; plundering of towns and villages had broken out within the various territories.
The path of coming and going was blocked by endless theft and loquacity;
the sunlight of the day was obscured by the mist of the absence of great-souled beings.
With the wailing of deceased kinsmen, the sounds of musical instruments heard [in the distance],
and the noise of horses, elephants, and chariots, the dense roar was grasped as a single mass.
"Sindhudeva is victorious, the sovereign of the earth under a single umbrella!"— thus,
immediately thereafter, kettledrums resounded in every city at that time.
Then Sindhu entered the capital with his neck held high,
like another Manu entering the world at the end of a Yuga to create new beings.
Then, from the ten directions, men set out to enter the city of Sindhunagara, like oceans filled with jewels entering the sea, accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots.
The ministers established for a moment the binding marks, signs, and instructions for each direction around the mandala.
In a very short time, in every land and in every city, there arose a restriction regarding life, death, and honor, just as if by the power of Yama.
Then, in the blink of an eye, the disturbances and upheavals of the land subsided, like the movements of objects when the winds of a portentous storm have calmed.
The entire region, encompassing the ten directions, quickly attained serenity,
like the Ocean of Milk when its churning whirlpools have subsided after Mount Mandara has been swiftly raised.

In an instant, winds that were everywhere fraught with inauspicious qualities blew, tossing the masses of hair and the lotus-like faces of the women of Sindhu, agitated by the swirling spray of water droplets.
In the narrative of Līlā, the canto titled "The Kingdom of Sindhu," the fifty-second canto;
Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, seeing that her husband was ahead of her and reduced to nothing but breath, Līlā spoke to Sarasvatī.
"O Mother, this husband of mine has set out here to cast off his body,
and Līlā remains as if dead, her limbs motionless."
"With this body and with this wife of a hero, we must go;
O Mother, how are we to reach that place?"
The motion: In such a great undertaking, in a battle, or in a national upheaval—
whether it has already occurred or is currently standing high, slow with its various undertakings.
Nothing at all has been accomplished—the kingdom, nor the surface of the earth;
for this world does not abide anywhere, since it is of the nature of a dream.
O sinless one, within that pavilion of yours, in the space near the corpse,
the earthly realm of your husband’s soul appears in this manner.
This palace of yours, with its inner apartments and the interior of the kingdom, stands within the house of the brahmin Vasiṣṭha; indeed, the entire world resides within the house of the dead.
Thus, this great undertaking, consisting of the three worlds, is a delusion joined by you, me, and her, along with the earth and its oceans.
Within the house of the village on the mountain, in the hollow of the sky, the self of space shines forth clearly, or perhaps it does not shine at all anywhere.
In the same way, within those two pavilions, though they are solidly constructed,
there exists only empty space in their interior, not the delusion of a world.
For in the absence of a deluded observer, what kind of delusion could there be in the delusion?
Indeed, the existence of delusion does not exist at all; that which exists is the unborn state.
In delusion, that which is seen is non-existent; for its seer, how can there be a state of seeing?
Since the sequence of seer and seen is absent here, that which remains is indeed the innate.
Know that supreme state to be devoid of destruction and origination;
it is one's own, self-luminous, unmanifest, peaceful, primordial, and free from ailment.
It is said that within the pavilion-house, people dwell there according to their own established conventions, as if in their own homes, within the Self that has arisen from its own inherent nature.
Neither the world nor any creation whatsoever is experienced by them;
therefore, I tell you that the world is space and unborn.
All consciousness of a self is empty, like the network of mountains such as Meru;
this is not anything composed of walls, just like a great city in a dream.
Even in a region the size of a span, there exist spaces composed of networks of mountains,
yet possessing the essence of adamant, in every single atom.
By means of the arrangement of the clusters of plantain leaves,
the three worlds exist extensively within the atom of consciousness, like a city in a dream.
Within that as well, by internal division, there is the world one by one in succession;
in that very world among them, King Padma Śava is situated.
"O auspicious one, your co-wife Līlā reached him even earlier;
as soon as this Līlā fell into a swoon before you, she was already standing near her husband Padma’s corpse."
Līlā said: O Goddess, how did she go there and become embodied?
And how, in what manner, did she attain the state of being his wife and remain there?
Tell me briefly: what form do those women dwelling in that excellent house see, and what do they say? Tell me this.
The Goddess said: Listen; I shall tell you everything in brief exactly as it was seen—O Līlā, the account of my own play, which brings an end to the difficult-to-perceive appearances.
"This very Padma is my husband"— thus he perceives this vast delusion,
consisting of the entire world, within his own abode alone.
This battle is a battle of delusion; these people are people born of delusion.
Through delusion alone does death exist here, and this very world is of the nature of delusion.
By this very process of delusion, his beloved Līlā remains;
both you and she, O beautiful woman, are merely a dream, O lady of excellent limbs.
Just as this husband of yours is, so too am I myself;
you are seen here as the very splendor of the world within saṃsāra, and thus it is said.
When this very thing is fully understood, one abandons the objects of perception and the meaning of words;
thus you are, and thus that king is, once this [realization] has been perfected.
And I, having attained the state of reality within the Self as the all-pervading Self—
here we have come together with one another like [the notes] produced by our own voice.
Thus, because she abides as a mass of great consciousness through her being the self of all,
this Queen remains in this manner, radiant with the play of a captivating smile.
Her eyes were playfully darting, she was endowed with fresh youth, sweet in her graceful conduct, and spoke with words that were both charming and noble.
Her voice resembled the song of the cuckoo; she was languid with intoxication and passion;
her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus; and her breasts were round and full.
With limbs as fair as lovely gold and lips like the ripe bimba fruit,
she is a portion of your husband’s mind, which consists of his own volition.
Then, at the moment immediately following the death of your husband, she stood there, possessing a form identical to yours, within the wondrous manifestation of consciousness.
This wife of yours was seen before you by the subtle atom that is your own volition;
for the mind itself experiences whatever objective state it encounters.
Therefore, one understands that the conception of a subtle body (*ātivāhika*) consists of unreality;
for when one perceives this material state (*ādhibhautika*), one knows it to be not composed of reality.
Then, through the consciousness of death, there arises in him the mental construction of another [body] within the delusion consisting of rebirth; this is the *ātivāhika* (transmigratory) intention.
For you have been recognized by him, and he has been understood by you;
thus he has seen you, and you have seen him.
You are established within the self because the conscious self is all-pervading;
for Brahman is omnipresent, and wherever and whenever it has arisen, it is so.
Thus it occurs swiftly; there, by its own power alone, it perceives whatever power it elevates, in whatever place, because it possesses all powers everywhere.
It remains there and shines forth in that manner due to the cause of intense spiritual urgency;
by the very moment of the delusion of death, this couple remains thus.
At that very moment, this was realized by us both in our hearts through the power of mental appearance:
"These two are our fathers, and these two are our mothers."
"This body, this wealth, and these past actions were such;
we two were married in this way, and thus have come to this state of oneness."
And people have come to regard these two as true;
likewise, there is an evident illustration for this case: the experience of a dream.
O Līlā, having meditated in this way, I was then worshipped by you with playfulness;
and I too granted him this boon: "May I not become a widow."
Thus, this young girl has indeed died here before you, like one who was seeking her goal;
for while you possess only portions of consciousness, I am of the very nature of consciousness.
"The family deity is always to be honored; therefore, I am doing this.
Then Jīvaka, assuming the form of the vital breath (prāṇa-māruta), departed from her body.
Having been drawn by the mind, he reached the tip of the mouth and abandoned his body;
then, at the end of the fainting spell of death, while still in this very house,
he was awakened by her, and the form was perceived by the living soul.
This fawn-eyed woman is perfected in beauty, her face possessing the splendor of the full moon; though proud and embraced by her lover, she desires to enjoy him further.

With her face turned forward in haste due to the memory of the past, yet restrained within by her own nature, she is like one in a dream, manifesting her natural majesty like a lotus-bearer risen at dawn.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the fifty-third canto, titled "The Manifestation of the Body Immediately Following Death," by Vasiṣṭha:
Now, having obtained this boon, I shall go by way of the sky to the celestial realm to obtain as my husband that lord of the earth with this very body.
Having reflected thus, she whose banner was the fierce god of love leaped joyfully into the sky like a graceful bird.
There, the maiden received that beneficial message sent by Jñapti,
as if it had emerged from before her very eyes from the great mirror of her own volition.
The maiden said: "I am your daughter, O friend Jñapti; welcome to you, O beautiful one!
I have been standing here on this path in the sky, waiting for you alone."
Līlā said:
"O Goddess with eyes like lotus petals, lead me to my husband;
for the sight of the great is never without fruit."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Come, let us go right there. Having spoken thus, that young maiden stood before him in the sky, intent on showing him the way.
Then, following after him, she reached the sky-cavity,
which was as stainless as the blade of a sword and marked with lines of auspicious signs.
Then, having crossed the path of the clouds, she rose up into the intermediate region of the winds;
having passed beyond the path of the sun, she reached the realm of the path of the stars.
Having leaped over the worlds of Vāyu, Indra, the Suras, and the Siddhas with ease,
he reached the shell of the cosmic egg belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Just as the coldness of frost situated within the wall of a jar manifests on the outside,
so too she, perfected by her own volition, emerged from the cosmic egg into the external world.
Having a body consisting of nothing but one's own mind, born from the power of one's own conceptualization,
one indeed experiences such a delusion within.
Then, having leaped over the nine coverings of water and the rest situated beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), he reached the vast expanse of the sky of great consciousness (mahācidgagana) ahead.
Even by a Garuḍa flying with extreme speed in every direction, its further limit and end cannot be seen even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Therein exist hundreds of thousands of Brahmā-eggs, innumerable and vast;
they are not seen by one another, like fruits in a great forest.
There, having pierced through a single city-like formation that was vast and possessed of enclosures,
he entered within like a worm entering its mouth.
Again, having transcended the radiant worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the others,
she reached the glorious orb of the earth from the path of the stars.
Having reached that mandala, entered that city and that pavilion,
she stood near the corpse hidden by flowers.
In the meantime, that beautiful-faced woman did not see the maiden there; she had vanished somewhere like an illusion once recognized.
Beholding the face of her own husband in the form of a Śava, she realized by herself,
through the power of intuition, that this was indeed the truth.
This is that husband of mine, slain in battle by the Sindhu;
having reached these worlds of heroes, he lies for a moment at his ease.
"By the grace of the Goddess, I, blessed as I am, have reached him here in such a state, with his very body; there is no one else besides me who has done so."
Having reflected thus, she took a beautiful fly-whisk in her hand and fanned him with it, as the sky fans the lunar orb or the circle of the earth.
Līlā said: O Goddess,
those servants or those maidservants, or that king who has awakened— what will they say, and with what kind of speech, by what words, and with what kind of intellect?
The Goddess said:
"That king, those servants of yours, and everyone else— through their union with the oneness of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) and by our power— all have become one with each other."
And through the great certainty of fixed destiny,
these manifestations of the Great Consciousness will thus recognize one another as mutually reflected.
"This is my co-born wife; this is my co-born friend;
this is my co-born queen; this is my co-born servant."
Only you, I, and she shall know this great wonder exactly as it happened in its entirety; no one else at all shall know it.
Līlā said:
"O lady of graceful speech, why did this Līlā not come to her husband with this very body, even though such an excellent opportunity had been obtained?"
The Goddess said:
Those of unawakened intellect are not capable of reaching the worlds of the Siddhas— which arise through the power of merit—
with their own bodies, just as shadows cannot reach those who stand in the sunlight.
For at the beginning of creation, Niyati was established by the enlightened ones:
that truth never mingles with falsehood in any way whatsoever.
As long as the conception of a ghost exists for a child, how and by what means could there be the arising of that [conception] for one whose mind is free from ghosts?
As long as the feverish heat born of non-discrimination exists within the self,
how can the coolness of the moon of discrimination sufficiently arise?
"How could one who internally possesses the conviction, 'I am the body composed of earth and other elements; I have no supreme movement through the sky,' ever possess a different conviction?"
Therefore, by means of the discernment of knowledge, or by merit, or by excellence,
they do not go to the other world with this body of merit.
Just as a dry leaf is instantly consumed by fire as soon as it falls upon glowing embers,
so too this body, once it has encountered the divine [fire], immediately perishes.
This much alone occurs through the expansion of the attainment of the supreme boon:
that consciousness is "I am He," and thus it is remembered; such is the established state.
How can that cognition of a snake with respect to a rope perform the function of a snake? For how can there be causal efficacy for that which does not exist even in its own right?
As for this false experience that "it is dead," this is merely the manifestation of previously cultivated habitual tendencies.
The delusion of worldly existence is easily traversed within the web of the universe when it is one's own direct experience;
such a habitual practice of creation and so forth does not exist in what is merely imagined by another.
The successions of births being experienced within [the self] are as far removed from those who perceive the external web of elements as the lunar orb is from men who do not know what is to be known.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Contemplation of Saṃsāra.
The Goddess said:
Therefore, those who are knowers of the object of knowledge, or those who have taken refuge in the supreme Dharma,
certainly attain the state of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), and no others.
The state of having a physical body is false and consists of delusion;
how could others remain [in it], and how could shadows exist in the sunlight?
Līlā, who knew all that is to be known, did not resort to the supreme dharma;
solely for that reason, she went to the city fashioned by her husband.
Līlā said:
"Behold my husband, O Mother, as he thus departs;
he has set out to relinquish his life-force. What should be done here now?"
How has the necessity of entities arisen regarding their existence and non-existence?
And how is it further indicated that there is no necessity in matters such as death and birth?
How is there the establishment of intrinsic nature? How does existence reside in categories of things?
How is there heat in fire and the like, and how is there stability in earth and the like?

How can there be coldness in snow and such things? What is existence in time, space, and so forth? How can there be the grasping and abandoning of being and non-being by those with gross and subtle vision?
How does grass, shrubs, sprouts, and so forth attain extreme height,
even though their own cause for height remains present and has not perished?
The Goddess said:
When the great dissolution has occurred and the state of creation has come to an end,
only the existent Brahman remains, as the infinite and tranquil space.
By virtue of its nature as consciousness, it perceives itself as "I am a spark of light," just as in a dream your consciousness perceives such things as traveling through the sky.
A spark of radiance attains a state of grossness within itself by itself;
this very thing is known as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is unreal yet appears as real.
Therein, within, he knows that Brahman, thinking "I am this Brahman";
then he creates a kingdom of the mind, for this very world is his own Self in the void.
In that first creation, whatever cognitions were described as occurring in whatever manner and wherever, they remain even today exactly so, unchanging.
In whatever manner consciousness manifests, in that very same way it becomes something else;
since it is itself unrestricted, there would be nothing here at all.
Moreover, "nothingness" (nakiñcittva) is not logically possible for that which has the nature of consciousness;
for having abandoned all structural forms, how indeed could it remain?
Just as at the beginning of creation, consciousness itself manifested within itself,
so even now it remains in that same state by its own inherent existence, appearing as snow, fire, and so forth.
Therefore, it is not logical for that which exists to abandon its own being;
since this is so for consciousness and the rest, this necessity does not perish.
Whatever has appeared in whatever manner, even though it is of the nature of space, it is as if it were earthly;
from the beginning of creation until this day, it has not been possible for that to move.
Whatever [conceptualization] manifests in whatever way, in the absence of one who knows the antidote,
it does not deviate from that state by itself through the force of habitual sensation.
That which is experienced here in the beginning of the world as unarisen is the manifestation of the sky of consciousness, like the sexual union with a woman in a dream.
It is established that what appears as true is indeed unreal;
thus, the cognition of intrinsic nature consists of such experiences of things as they have come to be.
In the beginning of creation, whatever continuous stream of consciousness arose in a certain manner, that very same thing remains even now as destiny (niyati), seen to be unmoved by anything else.
When consciousness has grasped the notion of space, the sky of consciousness becomes space;
when consciousness has grasped the notion of time, the ether of consciousness becomes time.
The consciousness-space, having taken on the cognition of water, exists as water;
for in a dream, a person likewise perceives the appearance of water within himself.
Through the consciousness of its own vital breaths, this [world] shines and exists just as it is; it conceals this unreal [appearance] by means of the skillful wonder of consciousness.
Even though it may be a bedstead, the wind, the earth, water, or fire,
consciousness itself knows its own internal state, just as in dreams, volitions, and meditations.
Listen to that which brings welfare— what has been heard regarding the sequence of experiencing the fruits of karma immediately after death, for the sake of pacifying all karma in this world.
In the primary creation (rūḍhasarga), the destiny (niyati) of men’s lifespan is fixed at one, two, three, or four [units]; now hear that destiny regarding their nourishment and so forth.
The purity or impurity of place, time, action, and substance regarding one's own deeds,
as well as their deficiency or excess, are the causes of the lifespan of human beings.
In this world, as the dharma of one's own actions diminishes, the lifespan of human beings diminishes;
when it increases, it attains increase, and when it is equal, it becomes equal accordingly.
Through actions that bring about the death of a child, a child meets death; through those that bring about the death of a youth, a youth meets death;
and through those that bring about the death of an old man, an old man meets death.
He who performs his own duty as it has been undertaken according to the scriptures becomes a glorious vessel for a lifespan in accordance with the scriptures.
Thus, according to their karma, a living being reaches its final state from this world,
with the power of speech ceased and suffering the agony of the vital organs being severed.
Līlā said:
"O moon-faced one, tell me briefly about death:
what is the pleasure in death, or what is the pain? And what happens after one has died?"
The Goddess said:
There are three kinds of persons who, at the end of the body, are about to die:
the fool, the one who practices concentration (dhāraṇā), and likewise the person possessed of yoga.

Having practiced the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) and performed the necessary activities, one who has mastered these concentrations and is likewise endowed with skillful means departs from the body at ease and proceeds accordingly.
He who has not attained the practice of *dhāraṇā* does not partake of liberation;
at the time of his own death, this fool meets with suffering, his mind being devoid of self-control.
Contemplating the helplessness brought about by the onset of latent impressions, one whose mind is intent on sense objects falls into a state of extreme wretchedness, like a lotus torn asunder.
One whose mind is not refined by the scriptures and who is devoted to wicked people experiences an internal burning at the time of death, like one fallen into fire.
When this one, whose nature is destruction, undergoes a hoarse throat and deformity arising from the loss of sight and complexion, then his mind becomes dejected.
The light was exceedingly dark, as if night had arisen during the day;
the expanse of the horizon swirled about, and the sky was as dense as a dark blue cloud.
Distraught by the agony of his vital wounds, he saw the circle of trees whirling about;
the earth seemed to have become the sky, and the expanse of the sky seemed to have become the earth.
The circle of the quarters having been overturned, he was as if being carried away upon the ocean,
as if being led through the sky, his heart awakening from its deep sleep.
As if fallen into a blind well, as if confined within a rock,
his tongue becoming numb of its own accord, he feels as if his very heart has been cut away.
It was as if falling from the path of the sky like a woodworm’s burrow carved into it,
or like a chariot rushing forward, having ascended toward the melting away of the Himalayas.
As if illuminating the cycle of existence, as if touching the midst of fire,
as if whirled about by a sling, he stands like a wind-machine.
He is whirled around like a spinning top, or dragged along as if by a rope;
he is as if revolving in a whirlpool of water, or as if fixed upon a mechanical device.
Like a blade of grass being swept away by the great wind of the ocean,
or like one cast far out by a flood of water as if falling into the submarine fire;
As if falling into the infinite sky, into a chasm, or into a whirlpool, he remains experiencing a state of upheaval in which the mountains, heavens, and earth are overturned.
As if falling incessantly or as if leaping up on all sides,
his entire collection of senses was bewildered by the hearing of the *ghūtkāra* sounds.
Gradually, all his cognitions of objects turn dark,
just as the directions fade away when the sun sets due to the diminishing light.
He no longer knows what is before or behind him, as his mindfulness has reached a state of attenuation;
it is like vision lost in the eight directions at the end of the western twilight.
One who is deluded abandons the capacity for mental conceptualization;
through that lack of discernment, he sinks into the great delusion.
When he takes up delusion, the wind does not take him up;
but when he does not take up delusion, then it fully takes up his life-breaths, and he falls into a state of extreme delusion.
Through the delusions of perception that have mutually attained solidity due to ignorance, a living being reaches the state of a stone; this has been established since the beginning of creation.
Līlā said:
"Why does this body undergo pain, delusion, fainting, dizziness, disease, and unconsciousness, even though its limbs are whole?"
The Goddess said:
Thus was this action, the vibration of consciousness, ordained at the beginning of creation;
for if such suffering had existed at this time, it would have been so for all this duration.
It may indeed shine forth like a cluster of blossoms on a branch, arising from its own nature;
it perceives that which arises from the expansion of consciousness, and there is no other cause here.
When, due to the force of agony, the channels abandon their contraction and expansion,
the vital breaths depart from the body and return to their own natural state.
When the winds enter but do not exit, or exit but do not enter,
due to their being obstructed by the *vināḍī*, then death occurs because of their lack of movement.
When the vital air neither enters nor indeed exits from the body due to the impairment of the channels, then one is said to be dead.
The consciousness that was previously informed— "I must go to destruction in such a time"— is impelled by that very [consciousness] to undergo death.
The consciousness born at the beginning of creation, which thinks, "I must become such a thing in this way," never undergoes the destruction of its seed-potency.
The very nature of consciousness is what is called "awareness," and it is inseparable from its own being;
therefore, birth and death are nothing other than the awareness of that very nature.
In some places this consciousness is turbulent like the eddies of a river, and in others it is as calm as the water of a stream;
thus it possesses the nature of living beings, being sometimes gentle and sometimes harsh.
Just as the nodes of a long creeper appear at regular intervals along its length,
so too do births and deaths occur within the continuum of conscious existence.
The conscious person is never born nor does he ever die;
this [world] is merely seen as a delusion, like the confusion of a dream.
If the person (puruṣa) is mere consciousness, when and how could it ever perish? And tell me, what else besides consciousness could the person be?
Tell me, up until today, who has died, what consciousness, and how?
Millions of bodies perish, yet consciousness remains imperishable.
If you were to die when even one person among them had died,
then all would have died here upon the death of that single individual.
Whatever variety of latent impressions (vāsanā) the individual soul (jīva) experiences by itself,
those alone are designated by the names "birth" and "death."
Thus, nothing whatsoever dies, nor is anything at all born;
the living being merely wallows in the pits of the whirlpool of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

And because that which is perceptible is absolutely impossible, this latent impression (vāsanā) is destroyed when there arises a firm knowledge through the investigation that it simply does not exist.

Having correctly perceived the continuous succession of the world—whether unarisen or arisen—as being full of calamities due to the fear of existence, the living being whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have ceased is indeed liberated; let this be the truth here.
The fifty-fifth canto, titled "Reflections on Death," from the *Līlopākhyāna*. Līlā:
O Goddess of the Gods, tell me how this living being dies and how it is born again, for the further increase of my understanding.
The Goddess said:
When the flow of the channels is disturbed and a person falls into a state of wind-disorder,
then indeed his consciousness seems to become stilled.
For pure consciousness is eternal; it neither arises nor ceases.
It abides in the stationary and the moving, in space, in the mountain, in fire, and in the wind.
When the movement [of the body] ceases solely due to the obstruction of the vital breath (vāyu),
then that body, known as "inert," is said to be dead.
When that body has become a corpse and the vital air has merged into the element of space,
the consciousness, joined with its latent impressions, remains right there as the ethereal self.
The name "jīva" is applied to that minute [entity] possessed of latent impressions (vāsanā);
yet it abides in that very place, like a corpse in a house, or likewise in the sky.
Therefore, it is designated by those engaged in worldly discourse with the word "preta" (departed spirit);
it is conscious, infused with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and exists like a fragrant breeze.
When one remains within another philosophical system after having renounced all this,
then that [system] appears in various forms, like a dream or a mental construction.
In that very same place, as before, there would be a portion of mindfulness;
then, at the end of the swoon following death, one perceives another body.
Within oneself, there is only the void, devoid of bones, jars, or nourishment;
whereas upon the supporting ground lies the world of space and its inhabitants, together with the sun.
Listen now to this classification of those who become such pretas:
there are those who are common sinners, those who are middling sinners, and those who are gross sinners.
One may possess ordinary qualities, intermediate qualities, or supreme qualities;
among these, some may have one, two, or even all three.
A certain person who has committed a great sin experiences for years a state of death-like fainting,
remaining inwardly stupefied like a heart of stone.
Then, after a long time, the Fully Awakened One experienced for a long duration the unimpaired suffering born of latent tendencies that had arisen from the womb of those very tendencies.
Having experienced hundreds of high births and passed from one misery to another,
one occasionally enters this delusion of the dream of saṃsāra.

Or else, at the end of the delusion of death, they experience that which resides in the heart as something insentient, agitated by hundreds of sufferings, and in an instant reduced to a mere tree or similar object.
Having experienced sufferings in hell that correspond to their own latent tendencies,
they are then born after a long time upon the earth in various wombs.
Now, he who is of middling evil, immediately after the delusion of death,
experiences for some time a state of dullness like the interior of a stone.
Then, having awakened after some time or in that very same way,
he will pass through the cycle of existence by entering wombs in the sequence beginning with the animal realm.
Even while dead, a certain person who has committed ordinary sins experiences a body that is complete and unimpaired, according to his own latent tendencies.
He perceives that [object] as if it were a mere mental construction; at that very moment, his memory arises in this way: MU_3,55.21.

But those who, due to the delusion of death, immediately after [their passing] perceive the highest great merit as the city of the Vidyādharas in heaven, they experience it through that very recollection.
Then, having experienced elsewhere the fruit of their own actions that resembles other deeds,
they are born in the world of humans, which is glorious and the abode of the virtuous.
Furthermore, those whose natures are middling, immediately after death and delusion,
while effecting their emergence here, perceive the body remaining.
Then those who possess common characteristics, immediately after death and delusion,
enveloped by space and wind, proceed toward the sprouts of medicinal herbs.
Having become a beautiful fruit there and having entered the hearts of men,
they then preside over her [the womb] in the embryo according to the sequence of births.
In accordance with their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), these hungry ghosts experience this state internally,
both gradually and all at once, upon emerging from their fainting spell.
At first they perceive, "We have died," and subsequently,
through the offering of funeral cakes and other rites by their kinsmen, they become aware that they have been reborn.
Then [he thinks]: "These are the servants of Yama, equipped with the nooses of Time;
being led away by them, I shall go in an instant to the city of Yama."
The merit-possessor repeatedly enjoys beautiful gardens and celestial palaces acquired through his own meritorious deeds; such indeed is the fruit of merit.
"These thorny pits and forests of sword-leaves have been reached by this sinner, arisen from his own evil deeds."
"This earth before me is pleasant to tread upon, with its cool grassy meadows, its glossy shadows, and its ponds; it lies ahead"—this is the intermediate [sign].
"This one has reached the city of Yama; this is that Lord of Beings;
here I have performed the examination of my karma"—thus he possesses direct experience.
Thus, this vast thicket of saṃsāra unfolds individually,
radiant with the conduct of all things exactly as they exist without exception.
In the utterly void space, the one who possesses such expansive awareness is himself of the nature of emptiness;
though radiant with the vastness of place, time, and action, he is nothing at all.
Commanded from here to experience the fruit of my own actions,
I shall go quickly— either to the auspicious heaven or indeed to hell.
"This heaven has been enjoyed by me, or this hell has been experienced;
these wombs have been abandoned, yet I am born again in the cycle of existence."
"This rice has been born as me; gradually, the fruit stands here"—thus will he come to understand through the awakening of his future state.
Thus, with its latent impressions (vāsanā) dormant, it attains the state of a seed within the man;
that seed, having fallen into the womb, becomes an embryo in the mother.
That embryo is born in the world according to its past karma;
whether it is destined for excellence or not, the infant appears with a graceful form.
Then, indeed, one experiences this youthfulness that is inclined toward passion;
thereafter, O lotus-faced one, one encounters old age as if a thunderbolt of frost had fallen.
From that too comes disease and death, and again the fainting of death; then, like a dream, there comes the assumption of a body through the collection of the elements.
He goes again to the world of Yama, and undergoes this cycle of wandering over and over again,
possessing a form of space within space itself.
Līlā said:
O Goddess, just as delusion alone proceeds at the time of the original creation,
tell me that again out of your grace, for the increase of my understanding.
The Goddess:
The mountains are the solid mass of ultimate reality; the trees are the solid mass of ultimate reality;
the earth is the solid mass of ultimate reality; the sky is the solid mass of ultimate reality.
Since that Lord of Consciousness, whose nature is the Self of all, arises in whatever manner, He becomes fully established as such within that [state], being the pure Self of the supreme ether.
At the beginning of creation, by the analogy of a person in a dream, the primordial Lord of Creatures manifested as he shines forth; even now, existence remains in that same manner.
This is the first *praticchanda*, for it is the original image (*bimbaka*) of all things;
that which is reflected from this remains established even today.
The wind situated within that hollow space of the bodies causes the movement of the limbs; therefore, one is said to "live."

Right at the beginning of creation, this state of being established within the moving world was ordained for me; therefore, even though they possess consciousness, those trees and such are motionless.
This very space of consciousness (cidākāśa), impelled by sentience, creates this portion; it alone becomes cognition (saṃvit), while the remainder is not that at all.
If a person perceives the tip of a hoof but does not perceive the eye-lid, then for him there is no life in the eye;
indeed, he is not alive at all in any respect.
Likewise, space is perceived as space, earth as earth, and water as water;
whatever one conceives of freely, one experiences it with a body corresponding to that very form.
Thus, with his entire body, the Self of all remains contemplating the moving as moving by its mobility and the stationary as stationary by its immobility.
Therefore, that which is called "mobile" possesses both existence and form;
it was perceived by the Buddha as such, and thus it remains exactly so even today.
Furthermore, that which is designated as "insentient"— the immobile—
understand that even today it remains insentient, such as stones, trees, grass, and so forth.
But there is no such thing as insentience existing separately, nor is there any sentience;
at the beginning of creation, there is no distinction here other than that of pure existence.
Whatever internal cognitions exist within trees and stones—such as the intellect and so forth—they are indeed merely intended [mental constructs]; such is their state here in this world.
For those [qualities] such as cognition (buddhi) and so forth which belong to that [Self], though they reside within [the Self], are indeed designated by other names;
they are established through other conventions with different referents.
For those such as worms, insects, and moths who possess internal self-awareness,
it is precisely their intellect and other faculties that serve the purpose of designating other objects.
Just as the people of the northern ocean know nothing at all of the state of those born by the southern ocean, except through their own individual experience.
Immersed in the experience of their own perceptions, all beings, both stationary and moving,
are mutually insentient, being solely intent upon their own conventional designations.

Just as there is no perception of the internal configuration or the external state of stones, and as frogs situated together do not perceive one another— being insentient and unattached— so it is with those who dwell within.
In that regard, that which was perceived by the sky of consciousness (cidvyoman) due to its all-pervasive nature,
and which at the beginning of creation was the impelling wind— that remains established here even today.

That which is known as "sauśirya" (hollowness) is space (*nabhas*); therein resides the wind (*māruta*), whose nature is vibration, and so forth; thus it is understood that [space] is a great entity among all things.
But consciousness, in the ultimate sense, resides in both the stationary and the moving;
it is only through the winds that bodies come into being and cease to be.
Thus, this entire universe, consisting of delusion, and these objects which are but fragments of consciousness,
remain even today exactly as they existed during the beginnings of creation and other such periods.
Just as the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of all diverse objects is unreal yet appears as real, so too has this been explained to you.
Behold, King Vidūratha has almost set;
he enters the secret cave of your heart, like a lotus garland for its master.
Līlā said:
"O Queen of the Gods, by what path do they go to the pavilion of the corpse?
O Excellent One, let us both go quickly so that we may see this very place."
The Goddess said:
"Abiding within the latent impressions of humanity, she proceeds by resorting to the path;
she thinks, 'I am this one going far to another world,' though she is composed of consciousness."
That which occurs through a path that is indeed without a dwelling place is approved by that very [path];
for mutual desire and consciousness do not constitute a bond of friendship.
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus,

when the sun of awakening had risen in the noble mind of the king’s excellent daughter— a process of pacification through the discourse thus prescribed— the aged Vidūratha became one whose ignorance had dissolved within the supreme vision.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the fifty-sixth canto, titled "The Movement of Saṃsāra and Death," Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, the king’s pupils rolled back,
his body became as if possessed by a single life-force alone, and his white lips instantly withered.
Having the luster of withered leaves, his facial complexion was wasted and pale;
his nostrils were contracted by the force of his breathing, which bore the resonance of the humming of bumblebees.
His mind has fallen into the dark well of the great swoon of death,
while the functions of all his sense organs, such as the eyes, remain withdrawn within.
Like a figure depicted in a painting, visible only in its outward form and devoid of consciousness,
he remains with all his limbs motionless, as if carved out of stone.
What need is there for much speaking here? His life-force abandoned him through the region of the palate, like a well-winged bird leaving a tree about to fall from the sky.
Those two children, possessing divine vision, beheld him situated in the sky—
the living soul composed of vital breath, like a trace of fragrance from consciousness carried by the wind.
That consciousness of the individual soul, being stirred by the wind of the sky and conforming to its latent impressions, began to travel far into the void.
Then he followed that very pair of women who were his own life-consciousness,
like a pair of bees following a drop of fragrance clinging to the wind.
Then, when the fainting fit of death had subsided in a mere moment,
consciousness awakened in the void like a scent upon a leaf, through its own inherent power.
He saw the messengers of Yama leading away his body, and he perceived that his own physical form had been produced through the offering of funeral cakes by his kinsmen.
On the path, which is filled with the manifestation of the fruits of karma, he stands far off,
having set out for the city of Vaivasvata, unable to be turned back.
The city of Vaivasvata has been reached, and it was then commanded that there are never any unwholesome deeds whatsoever belonging to him.
He is constantly the performer of pure and auspicious deeds;
he has been further empowered by the boon of the Blessed Sarasvatī.
"His former body, now become a corpse, lies there with its flowery garments;
let him go and enter it, and let this [body] be abandoned"—having observed this, he [did so].
Then, having abandoned the path of the sky, it leaped forth like a stone from a catapult;
thereafter, the triad consisting of Jīvakalā, Līlā, and Jñapti became the sky.
The streak of life, though formless, surged upward; it did not see them, yet those two followed that very streak, leaping across the expanse of the sky.
Then, having passed beyond other worlds and emerged from the house of the universe,
he reached a second world and arrived at its terrestrial sphere.
Having reached the city of Padmarāja and the pavilion of the Līlā harem, those two beloved ones, who were embodiments of resolve, united with the thread of life.
In an instant, they entered freely, like two streaks of wind into a cloud,
as sunlight enters a lotus, or as a fragrant breeze enters the air.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how did he reach that house near the corpse?
And how was the path recognized by him, whose body was dead?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, since all that resides within his own latent impressions (vāsanā) is necessarily present within his heart, how could he possibly fail to obtain it?"
Who indeed does not see that this immeasurable world, which is mere delusion, resides within the belly of a tiny living being, just as a banyan tree exists within its seed?
The collection of the three worlds is likewise of the nature of the atomic consciousness;
just as a person standing in one place perceives what is situated in a distant region.
He constantly perceives his own treasure with an unceasing mind,
just as one whose body is alive perceives the living sprout within the heart.
In the same way, even a living being who has passed through hundreds of births or is immersed in delusion perceives that which is desired, residing within its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Rāma:
O Blessed One, what kind of body does one become who is devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, and to whom no funeral cake is given?
Vasiṣṭha:

If the thought "Let a funeral cake be given to my mother" or "The funeral cake has been given to me" is firmly rooted in the heart as a latent impression (vāsanā), then that man partakes in the fruit of that funeral cake.
That a living being becomes identical with whatever its mind is directed toward is a matter of experience;
this occurs among both those with bodies and those without bodies, and never otherwise.

For by the realization "I am a sapinda," even one who is not a physical body-bearer becomes a possessor of the body; yet by the realization "I am not a sapinda," even one who is a sapinda does not possess the body.
For the reality of these objects consists in their being as they are meditated upon,
and meditation indeed arises from the objects themselves as its causes.
Just as poison becomes nectar for a living being through habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*),
so too does an unreal object attain the status of reality through intense contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
One never dispels anything for anyone by means of a cause;
therefore, O friend, be certain that there is no such thing as causality whatsoever.
Nowhere has an effect ever been seen or heard of without a cause until the great dissolution; nothing exists by itself in its own singularity apart from that [cause].
Indeed, it is latent impression alone that assumes the status of an object, as in a dream;
it enters into the relationship of cause and effect, yet it remains as something else entirely.
Rāma said:
"If a deceased person who, though possessed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), thinks 'I have no dharma,' is offered abundant merit by a friend after it has been performed for him— "
In this regard, would that dharma be lost here and now, or rather, would it be through cultivation?
And between cultivation based on a true object and cultivation based on an untrue object, which possesses greater power?
Vasiṣṭha:
Through the excellence of place, time, action, and materials, as well as through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
