wherever such [excellence] arises from equilibrium, that person is superior and victorious over the two [opposing sides].
If the latent impression (vāsanā) of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) has increased, then by that [impression] the mind of a hungry ghost is instantly filled;
if not, it is quickly filled by the cognition of a hungry ghost.
Thus, in this struggle between the two, the one of superior vigor triumphs;
therefore, with auspicious effort, one should cultivate the practice of the virtuous.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, if latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arise as superior to space and time,
then at the beginning of the creation of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), from what would the emergence of space and time itself arise?
By what auxiliary causes does this [impression] arise?
And in the absence of those auxiliary causes, from where could the latent impression (vāsanā) come?
Vasiṣṭha: It is so, O illustrious one; for one whose self is truth, there is never any such thing as space, time, or the like, even at the beginning of the creation following the great dissolution.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, this cognition of the perceptible does not exist;
it has not arisen, nor does anything whatsoever manifest.
Because the object of vision is impossible as a separate entity, whatever is seen here is in fact Brahman alone, abiding in this manner as the stainless radiance of its own nature.
We shall indeed explain this to you later with hundreds of arguments;
for that purpose, this effort is being made. Now, listen to the present narrative.
When they reached that palace with its beautiful interior, they beheld it strewn with offerings of flowers, cool as if it were springtime.
He stood together in the capital city of the essence of the morning rites,
his body shimmering with garments like clusters of garlands made of mandāra and kunda flowers.
There was the auspicious sight of full water-pots and other such items placed at the head of the beds for the dead;
meanwhile, the doors and windows of the houses remained unbolted with their hard bolts.
The light of the lamps was fading, leaving the pure walls darkened;
in one part of the house, the soft hissing of breath from those sleeping could be heard.
With a beauty as lovely as the luster within the crescent of the full moon, it surpassed the splendor of Indra’s palace;
possessing a charming radiance like that within the bud of Brahmā’s lotus, it was stainless like a silent rain-cloud or a moonstone.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the fifty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the State of the Deceased Immediately Following Death," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then they saw Līlā there, lying on one side of a funeral bier before Vidūratha, dead, she who had arrived first.
She possessed their former dress, former conduct, former bodies, and former latent impressions;
she was beautiful in every limb and form, resembling their previous appearance.
There she remained alone, her movements of limbs no longer guided by former memory, her face no longer turned toward the outside, and her body no longer covered by the weight of former ornaments.
She held a chowrie and gracefully fanned the lord of the earth;
observing a vow of silence, she was bent forward, her moon-like face resting upon her left hand.
She made the forest glade appear as if in full bloom with the flower-like rays of her ornaments,
while her glances rained down *mālatī* and blue lotuses in every direction.
She was creating from her own loveliness drops like rising moons,
appearing like Lakṣmī herself come together with Viṣṇu, the soul of the lord of men.
She appeared like the splendor of springtime arising from a mass of flowers,
as if she had moved her gaze to rest upon the face of her husband.
With her face somewhat withered like a night when the moon has faded,
that woman was seen by them, but they did not perceive her;
for since she was one whose resolve was true, she had not yet arisen in that manner.
Rāma said:
"In that region, having established her body in that former state of play, she departed through meditation accompanied by pure consciousness; thus it has been described."
O Lord, why is it that your divine play (līlā) has not been described here? Has it been completed, or where has it gone? Please tell me this.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Where is that body of play? For how can it have reality?
That was indeed merely an illusion, like the perception of water in a desert.
Just as this playfulness (līlā) gradually undergoes transformation within Awakening,
so too does its form melt away like snow into that Supreme Reality.
Through time, an illusion has arisen regarding the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha):
"I am the material body," just like [the perception of] a snake in a rope.

That which is conceived as the visible world, such as earth and so forth, by means of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) belongs to that very [subtle body]; it is designated as the "material" (ādhibhautika).
In its actual form, however, earth and the other elements consist of the physical body;
they exist neither as the word nor as the object, for both word and object are like the horn of a hare.
If a man has the thought in a dream, "I am a deer," would he search for a deer once his own state of being a deer has ceased?
Unreality arises quickly, and likewise unreality dissolves;
for it is like the grasping of a snake in a rope by one who is deluded.
This very perception has attained a false ascension through the delusion of some unawakened being born of the mind, which is entirely illusory.
Everyone remains experiencing their own perception of what is called creation as a dream,
with a self whose body has long been turned over, just like the shimmering of the earth's wheel.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, as a yogin proceeds toward his own destination while standing before the worlds,
what kind of body is this that is seen to be of a subtle, transportive nature?
Vasiṣṭha:

The transition from one body to another, which brings about the destruction of the previous body, occurs indeed within the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*), manifesting as it does in dreams. MU 3.57.21.
Just as a speck of frost in the heat, or a white cloud in the autumnal sky, though visible, attains invisibility— so too does the body of a yogi.
Or else, in an instant, the body of some yogi is no longer perceived by fellow practitioners,
like a bird that has suddenly flown up into the sky before their eyes with great speed.
Due to the sequence of their own latent impressions, some people at certain times perceive a particular yogi who has passed away as being "dead," while others see him as still present.
But their delusion that the body is the self subsides through the realization of truth, just as the notion of a snake in a rope subsides within oneself.
What is the body? Whose is its existence? Whose is its destruction? How and from where does it come?
That which has arisen is indeed stable; only ignorance has departed.
Rāma:
Does that which is purely material indeed attain the state of being "conveying beyond" (ātivāhika), or is it something else? Tell me this, O Lord, so that I may be carried across.
Vasiṣṭha:
Although I have said this many times, why do you not grasp my answer?
There exists only the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body; here, the *ādhibhautika* (gross) body does not exist at all.
Through the repeated practice of that very [meditation], the mind attains the state of being accompanied by the material elements;
when that [state] subsides, then his former [pure] state prevails.
Then heaviness, hardness, the state of having walls, and the stubborn grasping [of reality] would subside—
just as for a man in a dream— through the healthy awakening of the knower.
From that, the meditative attainment of lightness like cotton arises;
just as the body becomes light in a dream through the recognition of the dream as such.
Likewise, through such awakening, this body may become capable of leaping like a gross object for those whose minds have been transformed by the mental conception of a body sustained over many days.
When this corpse-like body has been burned, for those who remain right there,
the experience of a subtle body is indeed inevitable.
Due to the excellence of awakening, even for yogis who are still living,
when memory has arisen therein, the notion "I am the nature of volition" is completely gone.
Whatever that body may have been, such is this [body] of the awakened one.
This delusion appears just like the appearance of a snake in a rope;
when it has perished, what is lost? When it has arisen, what is produced?
Rāma:
O Lord, if those inhabitants there see you in your play, would they not perceive it as such by virtue of their power of true resolve? What of it?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The queens will perceive it thus: 'This woman standing here is distressed; she must be some other female companion who has come from somewhere to her.'"
What doubt could there be here regarding them? For they are like animals, lacking discrimination;
they act according to what they have perceived, so how could there be any deliberation for them?
Just as a clod of earth, rolling away from a tree, quickly escapes it,
so too does the ignorant populace unknowingly avoid the mountains, fire, deities, and the like.
Just as I know where the body of a dream goes upon waking, so too is this physical body unreal;
for it is exactly like that.
Rāma:
Venerable one, where does the mountain of a dream go upon waking?
Cut through this doubt of mine, as the wind disperses an autumnal cloud.
Vasiṣṭha said:
In dreams, in delusions, and in mental constructs, objects such as mountains and the like merge within consciousness, just as vibrations merge into the wind.
Just as the movement of the windless air enters fully within its own [subtle] vibration,
so too that which does not itself vibrate then attains oneness with it, becoming identical in nature.
The duality of consciousness and the object of a dream is never found,
just as [the duality] of liquidity and water, or of motion and wind.
But that which here is the non-realization of duality is unsurpassed ignorance;
this is said to be transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti), arisen as the nature of false knowledge.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, what indeed is the nature of consciousness? The duality of objects in dreams is devoid of reality.
As is a dream, so is this waking state; there is no doubt about this.
Just as an unreal city appears in a dream, so does the unreal world appear at the beginning of creation.
And an object presented in a dream is not capable of existing as real;
consciousness is eternally true, while dream-objects are unreal.
Just as a mountain in a dream becomes like space in an instant,
or gradually, so too does the material world become space upon awakening.
Those standing nearby wonder whether he has flown away or died,
because they are struck by their own nature which has become a vehicle for [limited] knowledge.
These creations are indeed false views, views born of delusion;
they appear as mere illusions, empty like the experiences of a dream.

These experiences of dreams— appearances of a clear creation that arise from the delusive vision of what is other than the awakening that shines within death— all of them, residing in the subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*), appear as false manifestations, like the sequence of a mirage at the sight of water.
The fifty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, Jñapti [spoke] before the living being Vaidūratha.
He quickly restrained the movement of his mind by means of volition, just as one restrains the flickering of a lamp with a cover.
Līlā said:
"Tell me, O Goddess, how much time has passed here in this palace while I was absorbed in samādhi and the corpse of the king lay there?"
The formal announcement:
"In this matter, one month has passed; here are these two female slaves, who remained awake for the sake of protection while [the king] slept in the bedchamber."
Listen, O woman of excellent complexion, to what has happened here to your body:
indeed, within a fortnight, your body has reached a state where its sinews are completely moistened with fluids.
Lifeless, fallen upon the ground like a withered leaf,
the corpse is as cold as frost, having become like mere wood or a wall.
Then the ministers, having arrived and determined for themselves from the sight of her moisture that she was indeed dead, cast her out of the house in fear.
What need is there for much speaking here? Having carried him away with sandalwood logs, they cast him upon the funeral pyre and, together with clarified butter, suddenly reduced him to ashes.
Then, when the king had died, your entire retinue, overwhelmed with grief, raised a loud wail and performed the funeral rites for him.
But now, seeing you here in this world with your physical body, it will be a great marvel that you have returned from the other world.
But you, by virtue of your power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*), are seen in that very same body as it was before; therefore, your mind is directed toward him.
O child, that very latent impression (vāsanā) which you had toward the body has now arisen as your form; therefore, it resembles what you previously were.
Indeed, everyone perceives everything according to their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*); the illustration for this, which is non-contradictory, is the vision of a child by a *vetāla*.
You have become a Siddha-Sundarī endowed with a transportive body;
that former body of yours has been forgotten, so lead it yourself.
For one who possesses the firm vision of the subtle body (*ativāhika*), the perception of the material world (*ādhibhautika*) subsides;
even while being perceived, it is like an autumn cloud in the sky for the awakened one.
The corpse becomes a body whose subtle, transportable state has become established;
it is like a cloud without water and resembles a flower devoid of fragrance.
From this day forward, once the consciousness of the subtle body has fully emerged, the physical body is forgotten, just as the embryo is forgotten during youth.
"Today is the thirty-first day since we arrived here in the sky;
at dawn, these two maidservants were stupefied by me with sleep."
Therefore come, O Līlā; by means of a creative will, let us both manifest ourselves to Līlā so that worldly interaction may proceed.
As soon as they thought, "Let Līlā see us two," the two goddesses, through their power of consciousness (jñapti), then became visible there in radiant splendor.
Then Vidūrathalīlā, her eyes agitated with emotion,
gazed upon that house, which was radiant with a mass of splendor.
As if carved out from the orb of the moon, as if washed with molten gold,
as if from a cool flame, it was like a wall possessing a beautiful center.
Having looked at the house and seeing Līlājñaptī before her,
she rose up in agitation and fell at their feet.
"O goddesses who grant life, victory to you both who have come to Majjayā! I have arrived here first to clear the path for you."
When she had spoken thus, those proud women, intoxicated by their youth, sat down upon the seats like creepers upon the peaks of Mount Meru.
The announcement:
"O daughter, tell me how you first came to this place;
what has happened to you, what have you seen on the road, or where?"
Vidūrathalīlā said:
O Queen, in that place, having fainted at that time,
I became like the crescent of the second moon enveloped by the flames at the end of an aeon.
I did not intend anything at all, whether fair or foul;
therefore, closing my eyes whose lashes were trembling, [I spoke].
Then, O Supreme Goddess, at the end of the fainting spell caused by death, I saw that as soon as I had quickly risen, I was leaping into the expanse of the sky.
Likewise, having mounted a chariot of wind upon the elemental ether,
I was brought to this abode by him like a streak of fragrance.
Here I see a dwelling adorned by its master,
with a radiant lamp, secluded, and furnished with a costly couch.
I shall look upon this husband as long as this Vidūratha lies here with his limbs covered in flowers, like the spring season in a flower grove.
"Moreover, he is exhausted by the fatigue of the fury of battle; let him sleep enough," thinking thus, O Goddess of the Gods, I did not prevent his sleep.
Immediately upon arriving at this place,
O benefactress, I told these two queens exactly as I had experienced it.
The motion:
"O you two who move with the gait of swan-stealers, O Līlā and Lalitalocanā,
let us raise this king from the surface of his bed of corpses!"
Having spoken thus, she released her life-force like a lotus releasing its fragrance;
taking the form of a gust of wind, it went near her nose.
He quickly entered the cavity of the nose like the wind entering the hollow of a bamboo flute,
carrying within him hundreds of his own latent impressions, as the ocean holds jewels.
His face, which contained the living soul within, attained its natural luster,
like a lotus entering the water when the drought has ceased.
Gradually, all his limbs shone with vitality,
like the clusters of creepers in a king’s spring garden.
Then he shone like the lord of stars on a full-moon night when his digits are complete, illuminating the palace profusely with the rays from the moon of his face.
He expanded his limbs, which were succulent and soft,
possessing a brilliance like shining gold, just as the spring season expands its sprouts.
He opened his eyes for the sake of pure light,
just as the moon and sun, beautiful and full of auspicious splendor, open their eyes for the world.
He rose up with his body radiant, like the Vindhya mountain increasing in height, and said:
"Who is this standing here, whose abode is reddened by the light?"
Then he said to the two Līlās standing before him, "Let it be commanded";
he saw the two Līlās standing there, bowing down before him.
Equal in concentration, equal in form, equal in appearance, and equal in stability; equal in speech, equal in exertion, equal in joy, and equal in attainment.
Looking at her, he asked, "Who are you? Who is she? And from where has she come?
To him, Līlā said, "O Lord, listen to what I have to say."
I am your former playmate, O Mahilā, who grew up with you;
like speech inseparably joined to its meaning, I remain here, full of affectionate attachment.
This second Līlā, this woman, was acquired by me with ease for your sake; I shall tell you such a thing.
Seated here upon this great golden throne at the head of the assembly is the goddess Sarasvatī, the auspicious mother of the three worlds.
Through the accumulation of our merit, you have appeared here in person;
by you, the lord of the earth has been brought here from the other world.
Having heard this, the lotus-eyed king rose up,
wearing hanging garlands and garments, and fell at the feet of Jñapti.
O Sarasvatī, salutations to you, the bestower of the welfare of all the worlds;
O granter of boons, grant me wisdom, long life, and riches.
When he had spoken thus, the deity of the formal motion (jñapti) touched him with her hand, accompanied by these words: "O son, may you be enriched with all desired objects."
Sarasvatī:

May all calamities and all views of evil deeds come to rest for you; may infinite happinesses arrive perfectly. May the people always be joyful, may they remain firm in the kingdom, and may fortunes always flourish.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the fifty-ninth canto, titled "The Revival of Padma," Vasiṣṭha says:
Having said, "Sarasvatī shall come there," she vanished on the spot;
at dawn, all the people awoke along with the lotuses.
Līlā embraced her lover Ghanavāhana in turn,
and the king experienced great bliss again and again, as if dead and restored to life.
Then the royal palace became languid with intoxication and passion,
its people intoxicated with joy, and filled with the sounds of musical instruments and song.
Resounding with the humming and gurgling sounds of the auspicious "Victory!
and "Meritorious Day" proclamations, its courtyards were filled with joyful and well-fed people and crowded with the royal retinue.
It was accompanied by the hissing sounds of flower-showers released by accomplished vidyādharas,
and the resonance of mṛdaṅgas, murajas, kāhalas, conchs, and dundubhi drums.
It was intense with the trumpeting of elephants whose massive trunks were raised aloft,
and it resounded with the cries of women engaged in a wildly exuberant dance.
It was rugged with various offerings falling and colliding with one another,
and beautiful with garlands and wreaths consisting of heaps of flower chaplets.

The sky was filled with land-lotuses in the form of the ministers, vassals, and citizens, who, with their hands dancing in the *tāṇḍava* gesture, scattered and tore their silken garments, drenching it with blood.
The earrings swayed playfully as they turned upon the necks of intoxicated women;
the mud of the flowers rose up with the stamping of feet by those who were dancing.
The courtyard of the palace was overspread with canopies of fine cloth, autumn clouds, and silken hangings; it was a place where the faces of beautiful women danced like a multitude of moons.
"The king has brought back his own self and his husband from the other world"—
thus did people in that foreign land sing in verses recounting these events.
Having heard the account of the events, King Padma briefly performed his ablutions with waters brought from the four oceans.
Then the brahmins, ministers, and one hundred kings consecrated him,
who had attained his rise and possessed infinite energy, just as the immortals consecrated Indra.
Then Līlā, Līlāca, and King Jīvanmukta, those of great intelligence,
took delight in recounting their former adventures as if they were acts of love.
By the grace of Sarasvatī and through his own human effort,
that king Padma attained the welfare of both worlds.
The perfectly awakened King Prajñaptijñāna, endowed with the two-fold play,
ruled there for eighty thousand years in an irreproachable kingdom.
Liberated while living, having conquered the mind and subdued the delusion of the five senses,
with an unattached mind, silent, and following whatever comes to him as it may.
He was like a drop drawn from that ocean of loveliness, appearing as the moon;
he was like a spark risen from that fire of majesty, appearing as the sun.
"Those are indeed the ones liberated while living"; having thus ruled the kingdom for eighty thousand years, they attained disembodied liberation, their consciousness perfected.

Having long protected their own kingdom— which was flourishing, brilliant, charming, noble, beneficial to themselves, and exquisite— the virtuous couple were liberated, bestowing satisfaction upon all people.
In the *Līlopākhyāna*, the sixtieth canto, titled "Nirvāṇa," Vasiṣṭha says:
This story of Līlā has been told to you, O sinless Rāma, for the purpose of removing the defects of the visible world; abandon the density of the universe.
The existence of the visible world is already quiescent; no further pacification of it is required.
For the cleansing of what exists is a hardship, but never so for that which does not exist.
Having perceived that the object of knowledge, which is of the nature of space through wisdom, is identical to the knower's own nature, the wise one remains like the sky, having become one with it.
That which has been established by the self-existent one— who is devoid of earth and the other elements and consists of nothing but the radiance of consciousness—
by means of that which is itself unestablished, is neither dual in nature nor truly established.
In whatever manner consciousness exerts itself, it appears as an external representation; it flows forth within the river of creative thought until it is awakened through effort.
This world is understood as the manifestation of the space of consciousness;
by the very sky of consciousness itself, within its own pure self, even down to the subtlest atomic particle.

Thus, regarding this vain delusion, tell me: what is its existence? What is its latent impression (*vāsanā*)? What is its duration? What is its necessity? What is its destiny? And what is said to be its inevitability?
All this remains exactly as it has been perceived, thus unimpaired;
it is simply this infinite illusion, yet there is no such thing as illusion at all.
Rāma:
Oh, how supreme a vision has been shown by you, O Blessed One!
It is like the lunar light for quenching the burning of those whose very layers are visible as forest fires.
Ah! After so long, this imperishable object of knowledge has been realized by me—just as it is, what it is, of what nature it is, from whence it comes, and when it occurs.
O best of the twice-born, I am as if stilled and as if extinguished, free from conceptual construction;
this is the wondrous narrative, the exposition within the perspectives of the scriptures.
O Blessed One, knower of all things, tell me this to dispel my doubt;
I am not yet satiated by drinking the nectar of your words with the vessels of my ears.
For that time of the Lord of Līlā, through his yogic power, spans three creations;
in one place it is a day and night, and in another it is merely a month.
In some cases, is it many years; for someone else, is it very subtle; for another, is it extremely long; and for yet another, does it last but a moment?
Thus, O Blessed One, please speak to me as it truly is out of your grace;
for what is heard but once does not remain, like water on a clod of earth.

Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, by whatever means, at whatever time, whatever thing, and in whatever manner it is perceived, by that very means, at that very time, that very thing is experienced in that very manner.
Poison always turns into nectar through the perception of it as nectar;
an enemy becomes a friend through the perception of him as a friend.
The very nature of these categories,
as it has been cultivated, comes under the sway of necessity through long-term practice.
In whatever manner this consciousness, which consists solely of luminosity,
manifests, so does that [object] immediately come to be there, because its sole cause is that very nature.
If one perceives a multitude of kalpas within a single moment and fully comprehends them, that very moment becomes a kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
If one perceives an eon as a mere blink of an eye, then even that eon quickly becomes a blink; for consciousness is of such a nature.
For one who suffers, a night is like an eon; for one who is happy, that very same night is but a moment.
In a dream, a moment may become an eon, and an eon may become a moment.
And likewise, one experiences: "Having died, I was born; I am young; I have remained here;
I have traveled a hundred yojanas"—all this is experienced as a dream.
Hariścandra experienced twelve years as a single night,
while Lavaṇa enjoyed a hundred years' lifespan in a single night.
That which is a single blink of the Lord of Creatures is the lifespan of the sage Manu;
that which is the lifespan of Viriñca is said to be a single day of the Discus-wielder (Viṣṇu).
For the yogi whose mind has been dissolved in meditative absorption, there are no days and no nights;
there are no objects, nor is the world real, nor even the self.
That which is sweet becomes bitter when contemplated with a sense of bitterness;
even that which is bitter attains sweetness when contemplated with a sense of sweetness.
O mighty-armed one, the world exists according to its perception: one who hates becomes a friend through the thought of friendship, and an enemy becomes a well-wisher through the thought of an enemy.
Those categories of things that have not been practiced— such as the study of scriptures, recitation, and so forth—
surely attain the state of being naturalized through the practice of their direct perception.
For those traveling by boat who are afflicted by delusion, the boat turns back because of their sensation;
for those who are afflicted by delusion but lack sensation, it does not turn back.
Through sensation, what is empty appears as if crowded, just as in the dreams of a dreamer;
through sensation, even that which is not blue is experienced as blue, or white as well.
To one who is utterly deluded, even a festival causes distress like a calamity;
the conduct of one whose elements are disordered is seen as empty space even within a wall.
The yakṣa of the present moment drags away even the lives of the deluded;
yet the woman of a dream provides pleasure, just like a woman who is awake.
Whatever has come about through repeated practice attains stability in that very way;
even that which is non-existent [appears] in the sky, and in the sky itself, it is but the sky within the self of consciousness.
Know that the world is like a dance performed by the shadows of a hundred elephants' hooves spread across the sky; it is a movement of the mind, not a substantial reality.
The manifestation of the demon of false knowledge is formless;
this body alone is merely a non-obstructing entity without a foundation.
The wise know this radiant manifestation, this vision of consciousness in sleep, to be something entirely unprecedented, like that which arises for a man who is fast asleep.
Just as a pillar carved in relief perceives the figures [it holds],
so does the Great Pillar of Ultimate Reality perceive the created worlds.
Just as a man sleeping at one's side may be agitated by great warriors in a dream, so too is the creation of Brahmā; it is only the Buddha who is like one in deep sleep.
Just as the sap at the end of winter, though present in the earth, is joined with grass, shrubs, and creepers,
so too does creation abide in the supreme state.
Just as liquidity remains latent within gold without manifesting,
so too does creation remain situated within the Supreme, like the space-nature leaping within every single atom.
Just as the arrangement of the limbs is not other than the self of the possessor of limbs,
so too the world is not other than the space-self of the bodiless one, the space-self of Brahman.
Just as a battle in a dream fought by one man against another man is of a nature both real and unreal, so too is this world, which moves through space, the very self of the void.

At the beginning of creation at the end of a great aeon, this body, whose nature is consciousness, perceives its own causality; subsequently, it perceives that which is mutually unreal, for it is not ultimately real.
If, when this Brahman is liberated, another Brahman were to arise born of memory,
then that memory would persist within the creation born of consciousness, by virtue of being mere consciousness itself.
Rāma:
How was the lineage of Vidūratha’s family perceived by all the leading ministers of the citizens there in exactly the same way?
Vasiṣṭha said: All cognitions follow along with the primary cognition,
just as ordinary gusts of wind follow a great whirlwind.
Through their mutual influence,
such perceptions arose among the protector of the people, the inhabitants, and the ministers.
"He is born from such a lineage; he is our king," so said the experts in local lore in the city of Vaidūrathe.
When the nature of something is already manifest, it is not logical to search for its cause,
just as one does not seek another cause for the radiance of a great jewel, which arises from its own inherent nature.
"I alone am the noble custom and the king of this earth"— such was the radiance of her inspired intuition, arising from the jewel of Vidūratha’s knowledge.
However many beings there may be in whatever creation at whatever time, they all,
due to the omnipresence of the element of consciousness, have come to perceive one another.
That consciousness which is free from conceptual construction and possesses an intense momentum attains supreme stability there, taking on the singular form of liberation itself.
By following after one another through the play of powerful forces,
inherent natures reflect off each other due to the nature of the mirror of consciousness.
There, with great effort, that consciousness conquers those other perceptions,
assimilating them to itself, just as a river flowing toward the ocean absorbs the smaller streams along its way.
Those who are in union here strive by virtue of their conscious nature until one prevails therein and the second sinks away.
Thus, throughout thousands of creations— as things are being born, perishing, and existing in great numbers— even down to every single atom— (it remains the same).
Nothing is pervaded by anything, nor does anything abide anywhere;
this entire world is the unborn, peaceful space of consciousness, devoid of any foundation.
This dream appears even when one is sleepless and devoid of a perceiver; though its awakening is inevitable, it consists of unreality even while being experienced.
Just as a single tree, though established as one, consists of the parts of flowers, leaves, and fruits,
so too the all-pervading Lord, though one, consists of infinite and all-encompassing powers.
The unborn state, which consists of the knower, the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and so forth,
is never forgotten by anyone at any time.
The reality of the arising and setting of emptiness, though possessing the nature of darkness, light, space, and time, is yet one, beginningless, and pure;
devoid of beginning, end, or middle, it remains as a single, transparent entity, like the ocean—rich with the rippling of waves—yet remaining one.
The world, consisting of "I," "you," and so forth, shines as the singular manifestation of pure consciousness;
in the expanse of the sky of the Self, there is only one's own emptiness—where, then, are the conceptual constructions of duality and unity?
The sixty-first canto, titled "Description of the Purpose" in the Līlopākhyāna,
[spoken by] Rāma:
O Brahman, please explain to me properly once more how this delusion that "I am the world" arises from something other than its own cause.
Vasiṣṭha:
Since one perceives all things simultaneously within consciousness,
therefore the unborn, all-pervading Self is in every way, at all times, and everything— entirely one.
All these parts of the meanings of words such as "all" (sarva) are Brahman alone and not separate from it;
for them, there exists no form consisting of the parts of the meanings of words like "all."
Just as the state of being a bracelet cannot exist separately from gold, nor the state of being a wave separately from water,
so too the world cannot exist separately from the Lord.
The Lord alone has the form of the world, but the world does not have the form of the Lord;
just as gold alone has the nature of being a bracelet and so forth, but the bracelet-ness is not the gold.
Just as the form of a whole consists of multiple parts,
so too the consciousness of the partless [Self] consists of all things, for consciousness is of the nature of all.
O Supreme One, that simultaneous perception of all the subtle elements (tanmātras),
which exists within, shines forth as this world, as "I," and even as "this."
Just as the arrangement of distinct lines of writing exists within the interior of a stone,
so too the world and "I" exist densely within the undifferentiated mass of consciousness.
Just as waves exist within water that is surging with ripples,
so too do creations exist within the Supreme, devoid of the words and meanings of "creation."
Neither the prior creation nor the subsequent creation remains;
for existence does not belong to either the whole or its parts, as these two are devoid of parts.
Through the consciousness-form of self-awareness, the subtle element of space is manifested as its own very nature or as the heart, just as vibration is manifested by the wind.
At that time, this atom of sound, assuming the form of the wonder of consciousness,
is perceived within by the ascetic alone, like a mental construction by the mind.
At that very moment, the wind itself knows its own nature as wind, which consists of its own existence and possesses the essence of internal vibration, just as it knows its state of blowing.
At that very moment, it manifests by itself its own nature as a mere appearance, like light within a sheath attaining the state of manifest radiance through a fragment of its own luster.
At that very moment, the Unborn perceives his own essence as the attained state,
consisting of the subtle element of taste residing within the heart, just as water perceives its own nature of fluidity.
At that very moment, the Unborn perceives the earth as being of one essence with his own mind,
containing within it the subtle element of smell, just as the earth possesses the quality of stability.
The perceptions [of the world] are a hundred-thousandth part of a moment’s duration;
they are the constant manifestation of consciousness, which is the succession of the floods of creation.
Thus, the stainless Brahman— whose internal nature is seen all at once, which is free from rising and setting, and which is unestablished— abides.
The Buddha is always with affliction, yet he is equal even when in association with it; the non-Buddha is of the nature of the form of affliction, yet he is always characterized by its absence.
In whatever way and by whatever means the conscious Brahman attains its own state within itself, it experiences all that accordingly; for it possesses all powers.

That [Reality] is true because it is devoid of the play of duality and consists of eternal experience; that [world] is untrue because it is comprised of the mind and the other five senses, being subject to all forms of ignorance.
Just as that mirage exists in the wind, so does creation abide in the Supreme;
though it is an unreal construction, it is an unreal construction within the Real, appearing as if it were real.
Just as light and heat, though appearing different, are non-different within fire,
so too the splendor of the universe exists within Brahman— the Self whose nature is both real and unreal.
Just as a figurine is uncarved in clay or wood,
and just as letters exist in a mass of ink, so do the creations abide in the Supreme.
In the desert of the reality of Brahman, which shines as nothing other than itself,
this triple world appears as a mirage— an unreal and impermanent existence.
By means of the Brahman consisting of consciousness, the Self alone is manifested as the creation;
yet, because of its non-duality, it is not manifested [as something separate], just as a tree is not [manifested] within its seed.
Just as sweetness belongs to milk, pungency to black pepper, liquidity to water, and internal motion to the wind; so too [is the nature of the self].
Whether non-different or indeed different, the creation—which is the nature of unrestrained consciousness—does not abide within itself;
thus the Supreme Self assumes the form of the self.
Since this world exists as nothing other than the golden jewel of Brahman,
it is therefore without a cause and is not distinct from it.

The perception of latent impressions, mind, the individual soul (jīva), and so forth, arises from sensation; it does not arise in the absence of sensation, for that which is devoid of sensation is not the human self at all.
Nothing ever sets nor does it rise anywhere at any time;
everything is the peaceful, unborn Brahman, a mass of consciousness as solid as a stone.
Toward every atom, floods of creations appear by the thousands due to its consciousness;
within each and every one of those atoms there are others—what counting could there be here, and how?
Just as the powers of waves and the like exist within water, both hidden and unhidden,
so do the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the rest reside within the individual soul (jīva).
If even the slightest aversion toward enjoyments has arisen, then by that much alone he has attained the highest state; such is the sacred tradition.
From whatever one is separated, from that one is liberated;
therefore, who would go toward the consciousness of birth, which is devoid of the consciousness of "I"?
Those who know the consciousness— which is both transcendent and immanent, unborn, formless, nameless, and consisting of the moving and the unmoving, as well as the earth— truly conquer.
Even though it exists within as something unmanifest and non-dual, like the circular ripples within the fluidity of water,
alas, by that [Self], the three worlds— which are neither existent nor non-existent and whose nature is the Supreme— are sustained.
The consciousness consisting of the self, through the differentiation of its volitions, expands the universe;
within itself, it experiences the infinite as if in vain, perceiving the end of an eon in the mere fraction of a ten-millionth of a blink.
The sixty-second canto, titled "The Description of the World's Appearance," by Vasiṣṭha.
Even when calculating a millionth part of an atom or a blink of an eye,
thousands of world-ages appear as if they were truly real.
Even within those [parts], there is likewise an end toward each infinitesimal atom;
thus, alas, this endless delusion appears.
These successions of creations, though existing as a supreme reality, have subsided;
they flow within like the liquid water of a river, with their whirlpools and eddies unmanifest.
In this great desert, the splendor of creation, being of a false nature, flows like a river whose waves carry flowers released from the trees and creepers on its banks.

Like a dream, a city of Indra’s illusion, or a city within a conversation; like a mountain of desire, or like a mere mental construction, the ground of the experience of creation appears as something entirely unreal.
Rāma said:
"O best among those possessed of perfect knowledge, when through such thorough investigation the knowledge of the non-conceptual Self arises as a single unity of oneness,"
For what reason do the bodies of even those who know the reality remain here?
They seem as if overcome by destiny; what, then, could "destiny" be in this case?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Here exists the divine destiny (niyati), whose form is the touch of the power of consciousness (cicchakti);
its sole reality is that which must necessarily come to pass, persisting throughout all kalpas.
For at the initial creation, destiny (niyati) establishes the inexhaustible variety of existents, such that it is accomplished: "By this, it must always be thus. || MU 3.62.9 ||
She is called the Great Being (Mahāsattā), known as the Great Consciousness (Mahāciti);
she is renowned as the Great Power (Mahāśakti) and established as the Great Vision (Mahādṛṣṭi).
She is proclaimed as Mahākriyā (the Great Action), heard of as Mahodbhavā (the Great Arising), matured as Mahāspandā (the Great Vibration), and arisen as the oneness with the Great Self.
"Grasses," "worlds," "demons," "gods," "serpents," "mountains"— such is the state of things until the end of the aeon.
Sometimes the deviation from the existence of Brahman is inferred, as if it were a painting in the expanse of space; otherwise, there would be no stability for the established order.
Because she causes those whose self is unknown to expand toward awakening through the Buddhas, beginning with Viriñca,
she herself is called "Necessity" (niyati), and this is described as "creation" (sarga).
The immovable Brahman, established among the noble ones, is seen as if moving;
it is without beginning, middle, or end, like a tree in the sky.

By means of Brahman abiding within itself— according to the analogy of lines carved on the interior of a stone— the creation of destiny is understood as if the sky were being awakened by that very Brahman.
Just as in the body the limbs and so forth are touched by the embodied soul due to its conscious nature, so too is the world,
with its constituent parts such as destiny, touched by Brahman through its state as the Lotus-born.
This is declared to be destiny (daiva), which pervades everything throughout all time;
having fully pervaded all objects, it abides as pure consciousness (śuddhā cit).
"The object must vibrate, or there must be the state of being an enjoyer;
'by this, it must be thus; by that, it must be thus'—such is the notion of destiny."
This alone is the entire world, including the movement of the person, the grass, the shrubs, and so forth;
this alone is all beings and the like, as well as the world, time, and their activities.
By this human existence and by its human nature,
these two— when they have entered into being— are perceived as having a single essence.
Both effects, which consist of existence, are brought about by human effort alone;
for such is destiny, and thus destiny and human effort are one.
"O Rāma, you must ask me about the determination of fate and human effort;
it is the fixed law that you must uphold the human effort I have described."
"Destiny will feed me"—thinking thus, one who is devoted to destiny remains inactive and silent; this is the certainty of necessity.
And when a man enjoys pleasures— ranging from sovereignty and so forth up to liberation— which he has acquired through human effort, this is the certainty of destiny (niyati).
Liberation from saṃsāra does not occur even through a multitude of kalpas for those wandering with a flood of bodies; this is the certainty of destiny.
She has no intellect, no actions, no transformations, and no form; rather, it is established that she exists solely in this manner through her persistence until the end of the kalpa.
For this established order— that "this must necessarily happen in this way"—
cannot be transgressed even by the intellects of Rudra and others.
A wise person, relying upon this [understanding], should not abandon human effort;
for it is through the very form of human effort that destiny exerts its regulating influence.
For destiny is indeed non-human, while that same destiny, when directed toward creation, is human;
it is fruitless when it takes a non-human form, but fruitful when its nature is human.
For one who remains inactive due to the cause of muteness imposed by destiny and the lack of human agency,
where does the vibration of the vital breath go?
Now, if one remains even after bringing about the cessation of the activity of the vital breaths and granting rest to them, then that virtuous person is indeed liberated; what more need be said?
The identity with the Supreme Spirit is the highest good; liberation is the absolute cessation of action.
But for great souls, a position that is a mixture of these two leads only to suffering.
Fate is the manifestation of the reality of Brahman; if one undergoes transformation within that which is supremely pure, then surely the supreme goal has been attained.
Through these great diversions of necessity and the like, Brahman alone, the soul of all, manifests;
just as existence resides within water, appearing as grass, creepers, trees, shrubs, and thickets upon the earth.
The sixty-third canto, titled "An Inquiry into the Meaning of the Word *Daiva*," by Vasiṣṭha:
This reality of Brahman is, in every way, at all times, and from every perspective, indeed everything—possessing all powers, all forms, the Lord of all, all-pervading, and the All itself.

Yet this Self, by virtue of its omnipotence and infinite power, manifests the power of consciousness in some places, the power of insentience in others; it manifests radiance in some places and tranquility in others; it manifests something in some places and nothing at all in others.
Whatever, wherever, whenever, and in whatever manner he contemplates, that very thing he perceives in that same way, at that time, and in that place.
For that which arises from the All-Powerful One in whatever manner, it is exactly so;
by its own nature, that power manifests as various forms at that time.

This web of conceptual constructions—such as "these are the powers" and "this is the self"—has been imagined by the wise for the sake of worldly convention; however, no such distinction exists within the Self itself.
Just as waves and ripples are not distinct from water, or as bracelets, armlets, and earrings are not distinct from gold, so too the consciousness of part and whole is merely conceptual and not real.
For whatever is perceived is exactly as it is; consciousness does not arise from either the external or the internal.

Because it is the self of all, Brahman—which consists of all forms—perceives its own manifestation as something or other in some place; for this entire world is Brahman alone. In that regard, those possessed of false knowledge imagine power and the possessor of power in the form of parts and the whole, though these are not ultimately real.
Whether [an object] be existent or non-existent, whatever the conscious [Self], being attached, conceives, it perceives all that very thing.
It appears as if it were a real entity.
This is the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Entry into the Mind."
Vasiṣṭha:
This God who is omnipresent— the Supreme Self, Maheśvara— is pure,
whose nature is the bliss of self-experience, and is devoid of end, beginning, or middle.
From this supreme bliss, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, the individual soul (jīva) is first born; from that arises the mind (citta), and from that, the world.
Rāma:
O Brahman, in this expansive Brahman, which is the means of knowledge through one's own direct experience and is devoid of duality, how does the individual soul (jīva) attain existence?
Vasiṣṭha:
Here, the inner self (adhyātma) appears as the unreal; yet there exists Brahman, magnified, whose body is the expanding Bhairava of consciousness, imperishable and named Bliss.
That which is even, fully filled, pure, and unmarked— a state that cannot be described even to those who know it— that is the peaceful, supreme state.
The very rising of that great tranquility, which is the reality whose nature is consciousness, is a vibration arising from its own essence; that is what is designated by the term "jīva."
Therein, within the supreme mirror of the sky of consciousness, these successions of the world-web— though unreal— appear as reflections consisting of experience.
O Raghava, know that whatever slight vibration of Brahman occurs, like that of a windless ocean or a windless lamp, is the individual soul (jīva).

O dear one, when that state of peace has departed, that natural vibration of the space of consciousness (cidvyoman), which consists of a subtle self-awareness within the pure [state], is the individual soul (jīvaka).
Just as movement belongs to the wind, heat to fire,
and coldness to frost, so too does the nature of being a living soul belong to the self.
That initial slight self-awareness which arises spontaneously by the power of the inherent nature of the reality of the Self, whose form is consciousness, is known as the *jīva*.
That very dense consciousness gradually attains the state of "I-ness," just as a minute spark of fire, through an abundance of its own fuel, reaches its own state of illumination.
Just as the blueness of the sky manifests when stars appear,
so too does the conception of "I-ness" arise within this living being, even though it is empty.
The living soul (jīva) assumes the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), ignited by the fluctuations of volition;
it does so either by its own density, just as the sky assumes the quality of blackness.
For the state of "I-ness" has a form marked by the limitations of space and time; though situated in the void, it vibrates through the power of volition like the movement of the wind.
Having turned toward volitional construction (saṅkalpa), it remains under the name of "I-consciousness" (ahaṅkāra);
it is designated by such names as mind (citta), the individual soul (jīva), intellect (manas), illusion (māyā), and primordial nature (prakṛti).

The mind, which consists of volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*), forms the conception of the subtle elements (*bhūtamātra*); by doing so, it truly attains that state, and through its own volition, it undergoes dissolution into the five elements.
The mind, taking the form of the five subtle elements, becomes a spark of fire,
like a delicate star in the sky where the world has not yet been born.
The mind assumes the state of a spark of fire through its conception of the subtle elements;
gradually, from its own vibration, it becomes like a seed turning into a sprout.
This spark of light, through the conceptualization of what is called an "egg," attains the state of an egg; with Brahma manifesting within it, it becomes like water that has been squeezed out.
Someone, through the sudden conceptualization of a body and so forth, assumes the state of a body—
a form that is neither that nor its opposite, arising from delusion— just as the Gandharvas imagine a city of splendor by their own will.
One attains the state of an immobile being, another even that of a mobile being; some attain the form of ether, water, and so forth—all arising from its own nature through volition.
At the beginning of creation, the body of the first-born is produced from the volition of the living being;
having gradually attained the state of Brahmā, it creates the world.
Whatever the self-born one, whose nature is conceptualization, conceives in an instant,
that very thing it perceives as already born, solely by the power of its own inherent nature.
The state of Brahman, which is the cause of all, has come forth from its own nature as consciousness;
subsequently, having fashioned karma, it remains as the cause within the cycle of transmigration.
The mind vibrates forth from its own nature, like foam from water;
it is subsequently bound by karmas, like curdled milk by ropes.
Volition is the seed of action; for that very self is indeed the living soul.
Having arisen, it subsequently expands action extensively, following a sequence that is ultimately free from action.
Having first embraced the sprout, the seed maintains its own nature as a seed;
later, it attains diversity through the various stages of leaves, sprouts, and fruits.
Other living beings who have assumed this very same form exist in the void itself;
once the world has arisen, they attain their station by depending upon the primary elements.
Then, by means of their own karmas which have become the cause of birth and death, beings go upwards or downwards; and karma is said to be the vibration of consciousness.
The vibration of consciousness becomes action; that itself is destiny, that is the mind, and that is the auspicious, the inauspicious, and so forth.
From that, the worlds and living beings arise instantly, like flowers from a tree at the very beginning.
The sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Determination of the Seed and the Sprout," by Vasiṣṭha:
For this very reason, the mind first arose in this way;
consisting of thought and seeking objects, it attained its state while remaining fixed right there.

Because of the oscillation between the existence and non-existence of phenomena, this creation is perceived as having the appearance of both being and non-being, just as a city appears by the power of a Gandharva’s will.
No distinction whatsoever exists, consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity,
between Brahman, the individual soul, the mind, māyā, the agent, action, and the perception of the world.
Through the surging waves of consciousness, which are boundless and vast, this very Self manifests as the single ocean of consciousness itself.
Though unreal due to its instability, it appears as real through its own manifestation;
just as in a dream, so too the world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, exists within the mind.
This delusion of the waking mind is neither existent nor non-existent;
it has arisen like a magical illusion produced by the combination of medicinal herbs.
This long dream called saṃsāra has persisted through the power of the mind;
due to incorrect vision, it is as futile as the false perception of a person in a tree stump.
Because it perceives what is not-self as self, the mind grieves for itself as a mind,
like a fool who fears a phantom conjured by his own imagination.

The state of being consciousness (*cittva*) arises from the orientation toward an object of cognition on the part of that ineffable essential nature which transcends all parts; and from that state of being consciousness, the conceptualization of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) occurs.
From the state of being a living being arises the sense of "I," and from the sense of "I" arises the nature of the mind;
from the nature of the mind arises the state of the senses and so forth, and from that comes the delusion of the body and other such things.
Due to delusion regarding the body and so forth, heaven and hell, as well as liberation and bondage, arise;
the commencement of the body and karma is firmly rooted like a seed and its sprout.
Just as there is no duality between consciousness and the reality of the Self, so too there is no difference between the individual soul and the mind;
and just as there is no difference between the individual soul and the mind, so too there is no difference between the body and karma.

Karma alone is the body, and indeed the body itself is the mind; that very thing, as "I," is the individual soul (jīva). That soul is the consciousness of the Lord, and that is the Self. All this arises from the single state of Śiva.
The sixty-sixth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Living Self," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, even though the supreme reality is one,
it is sufficient for its manifoldness to appear as if it were diverse, just as hundreds of lamps arise from a single lamp.
If one perceives with a discerning mind that the self is, in its true nature, non-existent, then being devoid of the sense of "I," one does not grieve.
When that [mind] is stilled, this world is stilled; for man, it is mind-only.
Is not the earth, for one whose feet are encased in shoes, indeed covered with leather?
Just as nothing exists for the plantain tree other than its mere leaves,
so too nothing exists for the worlds other than mere delusion.
It is born, it reaches childhood, youth, and likewise old age; through delusion, the mind dances, wandering toward death, heaven, and hell.

Just as the potency of wine resides within the wine itself, inseparable from it, even while its various bubbles surge forth, so too does the potency of the mind reside within the mind during the cycle of existence.
Just as one with eyes clouded by impurity perceives duality in the moon and such, so too does the consciousness, when overcome by the fraction of sentience, perceive it within the Supreme Self.
Just as a drunkard, deluded by the power of intoxication, perceives trees [as moving], so does consciousness, agitated by its own mentation, perceive the various states of cyclic existence.

Just as a child, due to the delusion of play, perceives the world as spinning like a potter’s wheel because of its own mental activity, so too does consciousness perceive the visible world. Indeed, consciousness itself is the visible.
When consciousness perceives duality, then there is the delusion of duality and unity;
when it does not perceive duality, then there is the cessation of both duality and unity.

Whatever is conceived is other than consciousness; there is nothing whatsoever apart from consciousness. Through the cessation of this [conception], the act of conceiving subsides within consciousness.
When you remain motionless, having attained oneness with the mass of consciousness (cidghana),
whether you are at peace or engaged in worldly activity, you are then said to be perfectly tranquil.
The subtle [mind] perceives the object of perception, whereas the dense [intellect], alas, does not perceive at all;
like one who has drunk little, it falls into agitation, for he who has drunk deeply indeed remains tranquil.
For one who has attained unity with the mass of consciousness and is firmly established in the supreme state,
there occurs a description by means of synonyms such as "selflessness" (nairātmya) and "the doctrine of emptiness" (śūnyavāda).
One perceives the error that "I am perceived by my own volition," [thinking] "I am born,
I live, I perish, I transmigrate"— all of which consists of unreality.
But apart from its own nature, there is no consciousness belonging to consciousness;
just as there is no movement in the wind apart from its own motion, therefore, what could be perceived by what?
But since no object of cognition whatsoever can actually be cognized by consciousness when such an object is impossible,
the wise know that appearance to be the delusion of ignorance, like the illusory perception of a snake in a rope.
O sinless one, why do you exert such effort against this disease called saṃsāra, which is to be treated by pure consciousness alone and is merely the vibration of the mind?
If you remain having renounced everything and transcended all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then at this very moment you are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Just as the fear of a snake in a rope vanishes in an instant without the movement of limbs,
so too does transmigratory existence perish through the mere unfolding of pure consciousness.
If one remains having truly renounced that which is the object of desire, then, my dear friend, liberation is already attained; what is difficult in this?
In this world, noble-minded people renounce even their lives like a blade of grass;
how then can there be any meanness in giving up merely that which one desires?

Having abandoned with a mind free from restraint whatever is the object of desire, remain, O friend, performing through the organs of action what is obtained, whether accepting or rejecting what is agreeable.
Just as a wood-apple on the palm of one's hand or a mountain standing before one is directly perceived, so too is the birthlessness of the Supreme Self manifest to him.

The Self alone shines as the world, like the immeasurable ocean appearing as waves at the end of an aeon; for when known, it indeed bestows the perfection of liberation, yet when unknown, it leads to long-term bondage through the mind.
The sixty-seventh canto, titled "The Yoga of the Cessation of Transmigration," [from] the Rāmāyaṇa.
This living being is unfit for the state of mind; how could it be the Supreme Self?
Or how has it arisen within this [body]? Tell me again, who indeed is this?
Vasiṣṭha: Brahman, the Lord of all, which is eternally radiant with its entire power,
perceives that very power by which it itself manifests.
That consciousness in the form of sentience which the Self, the soul of all, knows by itself, is designated by the word *jīva*; it is that very same [consciousness] which performs volition.
Having first conceived of itself as consciousness (cit) in its own nature as the cause of duality,
it subsequently assumes the state of manifold causes during birth, death, and persistence.
Rāma:
This being the case, O best of sages, what is that which is called "fate"? What is said to be "action," and what is said to be the "cause"?
Vasiṣṭha:
For here, only pure consciousness exists, whose very nature consists of both vibration and non-vibration;
through its vibration it is full of radiance, like the wind in the sky, and otherwise it is tranquil.

When the nature of consciousness has been cultivated, it is called "vibration" by the wise; when this same consciousness has not been cultivated due to its state of being an object of perception, it is traditionally known as "non-vibration."
When consciousness vibrates through pulsation, it is the creation; when it is without pulsation, it is the eternal Brahman.
The individual soul, the cause, karma, and so forth, are known as designations for the vibration of consciousness.
This very vibration of consciousness, which is of the nature of experience, is indeed what is called the soul, the cause, and karma; for this is the seed of transmigratory existence.
When the body has appeared through the power of the manifestation of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) which has undergone doubling (*dvitva*),
the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*), experiencing the state of various objects of volition (*saṅkalpa*), does so after a long time.
The vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*), having reached various states of causality, is liberated after a long time—
some after a thousand births, and some after a single birth.
Due to its inherent nature as a cause, consciousness, having come together as a duality,
gradually becomes the cause of bondage in heaven, liberation, or hell.
Just as gold exists in the form of bracelets and other ornaments,
so too does the state of manifoldness— born from the modifications of existence— reside within the inert body, which is essentially no different from wood or a clod of earth.

The mind perceives this delusion—that "I am born," "I am standing," or "I am dead"—as if it were real, though it is unborn and lacks any true form; it is like falling into the midst of another delusion.
Because it has not seen the ultimate reality, the mind— which exists under the sway of desire— perceives that which is truly unreal as "I" and "mine."
Just as the king, the lord of Mathurā, experienced agitation toward the outcaste,
so indeed does this state of the world flash forth within the mind.
All this is indeed the unfolding manifestation of the delusion of mind alone;
it vibrates as what is called "living being," like a ripple on water.
Prior to Śiva, the cause, consciousness arises first, intent upon the perception of objects of thought,
like a slight movement of water from a tranquil ocean.

Having attained the state of the living-cycle through its vibration, and having reached the condition of a wave of consciousness, the water of consciousness creates the bubble of creation within the ocean of Brahman.
That manifestation of consciousness belonging to Brahman, which is pure, gentle, equanimous, and slightly like the yawning of a lion, itself appears as if it were an object of cognition.

When consciousness (cit) is said to be "that which is conscious" (ceti), it becomes the individual soul (jīva); through volition (saṅkalpa), it becomes the mind (manas); as the intellect (buddhi), it is the object of consciousness; and from that, it receives such designations as the ego (ahaṅkāra) and illusion (māyā).
First, the mind, through the conceptualization of the subtle elements, spreads out this world—
which is unreal yet appears real— just like a city of the Gandharvas.
Just as one who perceives emptiness sees a string of pearls and the like,
and just as there is delusion in a dream, so too is the cyclic existence of the mind.
The pure self, as if eternally satisfied, tranquil, and established in equanimity, does not see, yet seems to see this delusion called the mind, which is like a dream.
Transmigration is said to be the waking state; they know the ego-sense to be the dream state;
the mind would be the state of deep sleep; and pure consciousness is called the fourth (turya).

That which is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), wherein there is for a long time a transformation into the absolutely pure consciousness alone— one who stands firm in that does not grieve again.
In that [Self] all this arises; in that very [Self] it is dissolved;
and in that very [Self] it expands, like a string of pearls appearing in one's vision.
Just as space, though not an agent, is the cause for the growth of trees because it does not obstruct them,
so too consciousness, though not an agent, is the cause for the existence of the world because it is conscious.
Just as a mirror, through its proximity, becomes the cause of a reflection, so too does this [consciousness], though consisting of pure spirit, become the cause for the cognition of objects.
Just as a seed becomes a fruit through the process of sprouts, leaves, and so forth,
so too does pure consciousness become the mind through the process of objects of thought, the individual soul, and the like.

Just as a seed, having cast off its fruit and so forth, becomes a seed once again from itself, so too the consciousness (citi), having abandoned the objects of thought, the mind, and the like, abides in its own natural state.
Just as there is no difference between the seed and the tree within the scope of ignorance and awakening,
so too there is no difference between the mind and the world-Brahman.
Nevertheless, when awakening occurs, the indivisible nature of the Self is manifested,
since it attains the light of pure consciousness just as the beauty of form is revealed by a lamp.
Whatever is dug out from the earth becomes just like that space;
likewise, whatever ignorance is investigated becomes just like that supreme reality.
Just as the arrangement of its own atoms within a crystal appears diverse even though it is pure because of perception, so too does the world appear manifold within the belly of Brahman.
The entire world, all existing things, is Brahman— a single, indivisible mass,
situated like a seed within its fruit, leaves, creepers, shrubs, and roots.
Rāma:
Oh, how wondrous is this world! Though unreal, it appears as if real.
Oh, how vast! Oh, how clear! Oh, how manifest! Oh, how subtle!

This world, which consists of the appearance within Brahman and is a sphere composed of the mere collection of subtle elements, shines forth like a drop of dew; this has been heard [in the scriptures].
O Lord, tell me how that [being] turns away from [the world], how it comes into existence as a self, and how its inherent nature is established.
Vasiṣṭha said:
That which is of an absolutely impossible nature, non-different from its own intrinsic being,
and never before experienced, appears as if it were directly experienced right before one's eyes.
Just as the words "hullas," "sabullo," and "ghullāṅgha" clearly arise in the mind of a child,
so does the state of being a living soul (jīvatā) arise within the Supreme Brahman.
Consisting of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge, it is indeed impure and unreal, yet it stands as if it were real;
though appearing as if divided, it is not different from this Brahman, whose nature is expansion.
Just as the individual soul, whose life consists of mental construction, quickly becomes Brahman,
so too the individual soul quickly becomes the mind, which is the experience of thinking.
The mind, consisting of mere mentation, quickly perceives itself as its own form;
this assembly, resembling a fragment of wind, vibrates within the void.
He experiences within himself a state of voidness, consisting of pure sensation, which lasts for only a moment and is like a drop of dew.
Perceiving the meaning of the word "I," as well as the sensation of the body and the awareness of objects,
the individual soul perceives the meaningful reality of words and their referents.
Then, that very cognition experiences the meaning of the word "taste" in an instant, as a partial experience of the object named "tongue" which is yet to come.
Through such a perception, the living being (jīva) becomes oriented toward the meaning of the word;
thus, there occurs an illumination within a portion of that which is to be called the "eye."
Then, that [subject] is such a consciousness because it perceives the functioning of that [nose];
as long as one remains in that state, the persistence of vision and the other [senses] will likewise persist.
In this manner, that individual soul, by chance as it were,
gradually perceives for itself the state of being a specific configuration once it has been brought into manifestation.
Through the act of hearing, he perceives that the nature of sound constitutes a single part of that mental construction, whether it exists or does not exist.
It perceives the nature of touch as a portion of the meaning of the word "skin," and it views the nature of taste as a portion of the form of the object of the tongue.
One perceives the portion of the nature of form as the shape of the object of the eye; one perceives the portion of the nature of odor as the nose.
Capable of manifesting this state consisting of such a nature,
she perceives within the body that cavity which will later be called the sense organ.
In this way, for the living being and for one such as Rāghava at the present time,
there arises the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*) itself, which consists of appearances.
The supreme reality is indeed inexpressible; though it does not move, it attains a state as if it were subtle and transportable, because its very nature consists of such power.

When the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, the knower, and so forth, are realized as Brahman alone through direct experience, then what occasion is there for the discourse on the subtle body (*ativāhika*); that very [Brahman] is it.
Rāma:

[The self] is other than the supreme because it is perceived as distinct; it is the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body. It is Brahman because it is perceived as Brahman; for that perception would otherwise not exist.
Because of its impossibility, or because of the lack of perception, or because of its nature as the Self that is Brahman—
what liberation could there be, and what inquiry? O Vasiṣṭha, enough with these conceptualizations of duality!
O Rāma, this question of yours is fitting only at the time of the final conclusion;
for even a garland of out-of-season flowers does not shine, however beautiful it may be.

Just as a garland of flowers that is out of season becomes useless even if it is meaningful, so too is untimely speech for a living being; indeed, everything is beautiful when done at the proper time.
It is observed that Time is the giver of obstructions and permissions;
indeed, all things attain their results through Time.
Thus this living self, having become a sleeping self, manifests;
in the course of time, it perceives within itself the state of being a grandfather, swollen with age.
He who, preceded by the consciousness of the utterance of "Oṃ," beholds the Vedas and creates a kingdom of the mind, quickly becomes one whose intellect is identical with that [of the Vedas].
Thus, perceiving this very non-existent as if it were existent— like a mass of mountains within one's own son who is but space— the world, which is itself space, expands within space.
Nothing is born here, and nothing perishes here;
the world, expanded by Brahman, has the form of a city of the Gandharvas.
Just as the existence of living beings, beginning with those born of Brahmā, consists of both being and non-being,
so too is it for all others, down to the crawling insects and the demons.
This is merely a delusion of consciousness; though it has thus arisen, it is unreal.
From the consciousness of Brahmā down to that of an insect, it is the cessation of correct cognition.
Just as one becomes a Brahmā, so too does one become a worm;
for the worm, due to its trivial karma, is driven by the surging flood of accumulated elements.
That very life which lives directed toward consciousness and is non-material—
that alone is human effort, that alone is its essence, and that alone is action.

O Brahman, at the end of the creation, even for a worm that has arisen from non-existence, there is this delusion consisting of nothing but mind; its destruction occurs simply through the act of discernment.
When the objects of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge are not other than pure consciousness alone,
then the meaning of doctrines concerning duality and unity is like a lotus growing from the horn of a hare.
The false cosmic egg of Brahman, consisting of the firmness of phenomenal existence,
is imagined by the Self alone, just as a silkworm imagines itself to be its cocoon made of saliva.
Whatever appears in whatever manner through the existence of Brahman, that is seen exactly so by those who know it; this is the certainty regarding its own nature.
Just as whatever object has arisen cannot exist without that very nature,
whether for a moment or an eon— this is the certainty regarding intrinsic nature.
This has arisen as false, and it grows as false;
it tastes as false, and likewise it dissolves as false.

Brahman is pure, all-pervading, infinite, and non-dual; yet, due to the power of difficult-to-comprehend ignorance, it is perceived as if impure, as if non-existent, as if manifold, and as if not all-pervading.

Just as the distinction that "the water is one thing and the wave another" is merely imagined through childish conceptualization and is not real, so too this appearance of duality is constructed solely by those who do not know reality, like the notion of a snake in a rope.

Thus, since the powers of difference and non-difference exist in Brahman alone as being truly non-different from it, duality is brought forth as if it were present by means of that very self which is non-dual— just as waves are imagined in water or bracelets are imagined in gold;
therefore, by its own nature, the Self perceives itself as if it were other than itself.
From this, conceptualization (kalanā) arose;

that very [conceptualization], having attained expansion, became the mind (manas). By means of that, the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) was imagined. That which is the first, consisting of non-conceptual direct perception (nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa), is the mind.
Therefore, through the cultivation of the meaning of the word "I" within the Lord,
memory is subsequently joined with the mind and the ego-sense;
by these three, the subtle elements (tanmātras) experienced therein are conceptualized.

When the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) exist, the individual soul (*jīva*), by its own nature as the mind (*cittātman*), perceives a configuration consisting of hands, feet, and so forth, fashioned as if by chance (*kākatālīya*); for whatever the mind imagines, that very thing it sees—whether it be real or unreal.
Whatever the mind, being attached, imagines, it sees that very thing as if it had attained the appearance of reality, just as in a dream. (MU 3.67–68)
The creation is within pure consciousness; pure consciousness is within all things.
Because it is the essence of the existence of everything, pure consciousness is indeed everything.
Pure consciousness alone, whether outside, inside, above, or below, assumes the state of the knower as both the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge;
thus, it is eternally quiescent—the single, perfectly equal, and peerless reality in which the existence of all things is eternally established.
The sixty-eighth canto, titled "The Instruction on Truth," by Vasiṣṭha:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history:
the entire web of great questions spoken by the Rākṣasī.
On the northern side of the Himavat mountain, there is a fierce Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī, like a statue carved from a mountain of collyrium paste.
The maiden named Viṣūcikā, who was an obstacle to justice,
has through her body attained emaciation by means of logic, like the Vindhya forest.
With eyes like a fire of great power, filling the cavity between heaven and earth,
clad in blue garments, she was dark as the night embodied.
Clad in a garment of frost, with a head-cloth of thick clouds,
her breasts are the hanging orbs of the clouds, and her upright hair is the perpetual upward-reaching darkness.
Her eyes are like steady streaks of lightning, her pupils are like *tāla* trees;
her nails at the tips of her toes are like *vaiḍūrya* cornucopias, and she smiles with ashes as if with frost.
Adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers formed from the mass of fleshless human bodies,
she is resplendent with a necklace of corpses whose limbs are all threaded together with entrails.
Her earrings were black skeletons trembling from the possession of *vetālas*;
her circle of fierce arms was as terrifying as blazing clouds eager to seize the sun.
