Because her body was so vast and because her own food was difficult to obtain,
the fire of her stomach remained unsatiated, like that of the ocean’s shore.

That large-bellied woman never attained satiety; like the tongue of the submarine fire, she once reflected thus: She never reached satisfaction; like the tongue of the subterranean fire (vaḍavānala), she thought one day:
Even if I were to swallow all the people dwelling in Jambudvīpa without ceasing and without breathing, like the ocean swallows masses of water.
Just as a mirage is quenched by a cloud, so is my hunger appeased;
for that method by which one lives in times of adversity is indeed not contradictory.
Who can oppress any person who is protected by mantras, medicines, asceticism, charity, worship of the gods, and so forth, and who is thus equally free from harm?
I perform supreme austerity with an entirely unwearied mind;
for by means of most formidable austerity, even that which is difficult to attain is achieved.
Having reflected thus, she, out of a desire to devour the entire multitude of living beings,
then called to mind a region inaccessible to other creatures for the sake of performing ascetic penance.
And she, whose eyes were steady flashes of lightning and who possessed a body with hands, feet, and other limbs, ascended that peak like a dark circle of clouds.
There, having settled to bathe and perform austerities, she who was clothed only in the sky stood on one foot, her eyes fixed motionlessly upon the moon and the sun.
In due course, the days, fortnights, months, and seasons passed for her,
who remained unmoved by cold and heat as if she had been carved from a mountain.
She became like a mass of clouds, her form paralyzed; with her black hair standing erect and her arms raised as if to seize the sky.

Beholding her— her skin and limbs shattered by the wind, rendered impotent by the groans and the rustling of the wind-shaken branches, and wearing a mass of upward-pointing hair like a veil of darkness that held a multitude of stars like pearls— the Moon approached her.
The sixty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Rākṣasī," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, after a thousand years, the Grandfather (Brahmā) approached him;
for even the fire of excrement, though it dispels the cold, becomes fierce when intent on the perfection of ascetic penance.
Having mentally bowed to him, that virtuous woman remained there, saying "So be it," and became filled with the thought: "What boon will suffice to destroy my hunger?"
May I become both non-metallic and metallic, a needle for living beings; having become two kinds of needles by her word, I shall enter invisibly.
Together with my vital breath, may my heart become as fragrant as a flower so that,
by means of this, I may devour all people according to my desire.
To her, who was reflecting, "The gradual destruction of hunger leads to the supreme happiness of the destruction of hunger," the Lotus-born One said:
She saw something never seen before, resembling the sun emerging from an immortal cloud.
Brahmā said:
"Daughter Karkaṭikā, you whose braid of hair is like a cloud on the mountain range of the Rākṣasa clan!"
"Arise! I am pleased with you; accept a desired boon.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, may I be a bringer of life to living beings."
"Consider for me the superior [nature] of that which is non-iron and that which is iron.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"So be it," and having spoken thus to her, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) once again—*Mokṣopāya* 3.69.8.
He said to Sūcikā: "In the future you shall become Viṣūcikā;
by means of subtle illusion, you will bring harm to the entire world."
You shall indeed inflict injury upon those who eat poorly, those who undertake evil deeds, the foolish, those of wicked conduct, those dwelling in improper places, and the arrogant.
Having entered the heart along with the vital breaths by piercing the lotus, the spleen, and other organs,
you shall become the disease known as *viṣūcikā*, consisting of streaks of wind.
You will encounter people who possess virtues as well as those who lack them;
however, this mantra is being spoken by me for the purpose of treating you in the presence of the virtuous.
Brahmā said:
On the northern side of the Himālaya mountains, there is a Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī;
she is the maiden called Viṣūcikā, who is an obstructer of justice.
Her mantra is:
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ rām / namaḥ to Viṣṇu’s Śakti.

O Blessed One, Viṣṇu-śakti, burn her, burn her! Cook her, cook her! Grind her, grind her! Slay her, slay her! Eradicate her, eradicate her! Drive her far away! Svāhā! O Viṣūcikā, rkhraḥ rkhraḥ rkhraḥ! Go to the Himavat mountains, go to the Himavat mountains; live!
Having placed the mantra, this great mantra— "saḥ saḥ saḥ candramaṇḍala gatāsi svāhā"— within the palm of the left hand;
Restrained, he should wipe away the appearance of the patient with that hand.
One should contemplate her as having fled toward the snowy mountains—
she who is like a crab, wailing harshly, and pulverized by the mallet of the mantra.
One should contemplate the patient as situated in a lake of elixir within the moon,
liberated from old age, death, and all delusions of mental and physical afflictions.
For the practitioner, having become pure, having sipped water for ritual purification, and being well-composed,
cuts through all colic pains by means of this sequence.
Thus the Lord of the Three Worlds, situated in the sky, his perfected mantra grasped by the sky-dwelling siddhas,
went to his own imperishable and foremost city of radiant splendor, while being venerated by Śakra and the lords of elephants.
The seventieth canto, titled "The Narration of the Sūcī-episode and the Recitation of the Viṣūcikā-mantra," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then that great black Rākṣasī, possessing the luster of a beryl horn,
was like a streak of collyrium upon a cloud as she prepared to depart.
Upon the abandonment of her cloud-like form, she took on the appearance of a tree;
from that state she became the size of a man, and thereafter she was only the size of a hand.
Then it became the size of a span, then the form of a finger; then it was equal to a masha and a shimī, and then it indeed became a needle.
Then she became a silken needle, beautiful with lotus filaments;
she took on the form of a mountain peak, as vast as a mountain of one's own resolve.
The black needle, made of smooth iron,
shone as it moved through the sky, enveloped by the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) and driven by the wind.
This needle is indeed seen, yet no such thing as "iron" exists;
this is merely a momentary error of consciousness, appearing like a needle in a dream.
Smooth like a jewel-needle, joined with the contemplation of the mind,
it is as beautiful as a streak of luster from lapis lazuli, lovely in its continuous succession.
Like a filament of the saffron of a collyrium-lotus carried by the wind,
the pupil of the eye is the clear sky visible through the minute aperture of the gaze.
With a thread held in her own mouth, which was as fine as the tip of a smooth tail-hair,
she became absorbed in the supreme vow of silence for the sake of pacifying the visible vastness [of the world].
Seen from afar like a lamp, it has reached a state of extreme subtlety;
even from a distance, it seems to belch out the sky with its beautiful face.
With her long eyes visible as they were slightly contracted, she was as delicate as a fine lamp-wick;
she was a playful girl with a forehead that appeared swollen from having just bathed.
Like a thread drawn out from lotus fibers, she has flown forth out of curiosity for external wandering;
like the Brahma-nāḍī, she is intent upon the outside, beautiful as a digit of the moon.
Its own power of the sense-faculties, though determined, is as if cast out by the *jīva*;
it remains unperceived, like the stream of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*) of the Buddhists and the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Like the tip of a hair from the doctrine of emptiness, or like a minute particle of air escaping through a hole, it is as sharp as the ray of a dying lamp, yet remains unperceivable.
She went forth, indicated for the sake of food, yet he was not of use to her;
she reflected on this: "Alas! This is but the manifestation of folly."
She reflected with focused intent that the needle was not a trivial thing;
seeing only the activity of the mind, she remained there at her ease.
Without any investigation, that person of deluded intellect requested the state of being a teacher;
for one whose mind is occupied with various objects, reflection upon what precedes and follows does not arise.

An object, possessing causal efficacy and supreme capacity, undergoes transformation through meditative cultivation into a state rich with the desired goal, just as a mirror [is transformed] by its own breath.
Even for this ogress, who has reached the state of a needle and is casting off her bulky body,
even a great death remains exceedingly pleasant.
Alas, how treacherous is the course of those who are devoted to a single object!
Even her own body was cast away like a blade of grass by the Rākṣasī according to her own will.
Indeed, other cognitions perish through excessive pride in a single object;
just as the Rākṣasī did not even perceive the destruction of her own body due to her pride in devouring [her prey].
Even destruction brings joy to the ignorant man who is excessively attached to a single object;
even when her body has become like a needle, the Rākṣasī is truly contented.
Another [power] arose, attached to that [Self], which is the indicator of the individual soul (jīva);
it is of the nature of space, formless, and has the functions of space as its body.
Having the appearance of a stream of threads of light, consisting of the threads of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
taking the form of the sensation of a trident, and beautiful with the rays of the sun through its central aperture— //MU 3.70.24//
It stands as if separate, like the edge of a sword, and like a series of atoms; it is like a streak of fragrance from flowers, having the nature of the perception of parts.
For that mental state of his was indeed evil in nature; it remained thus, intent upon the ultimate reality of piercing the vital breaths of others.
Thus her body was formed; for it consisted of two needles, slender like the awn of wild rice and as delicate as a thread of cotton.
Having entered the hearts of men with those two subtle bodies,
that cruel one then wandered through the ten directions, piercing them.
Everything becomes light or heavy by the power of one's own volition;
the karkaṭī plant, having cast off its fierce body, has assumed the state of a needle.
Even a trivial object becomes highly desirable for those of little strength;
thus, by means of asceticism, a rākṣasī acquired the form of a needle-bodied piśācī.
Even for those of meritorious bodies, the bond of birth does not cease;
for even Anusūcī acquired the state of a Piśācī through her association with a Rākṣasī.
While she was thus engaged in wandering to the ends of the earth along with the winds,
that very body of hers, having become gross, dissolved right there like an autumnal cloud.
When it enters the interior of someone whose limbs are powerless, who is intoxicated, or who is corpulent, it becomes a most severe piercing pain like a needle driven by the wind.
Even for someone who possesses a slender body, is pure, and is wise,
once they have entered into the state indicated by the vital breath (*jīva*), there arises an internal piercing pain.
Thus, in some cases, that [affliction] residing in the heart of the evil-minded finds satisfaction;
in other cases, it is eradicated by merits and by the application of mantras and medicinal herbs.
For many years she remained solely devoted to wandering,
traveling through both the sky and upon the surface of the earth with her two bodies.
On the ground she is concealed by dust; in the hand, she is concealed by the fingers;
in the sky, she is concealed by light; on a garment, she is concealed by thread.
Within the wretched river of sinews, white with dust, where the dry lines are like dried-up streams and the fine wrinkles are like withered grass; //MU_3,70.38//
Devoid of meaning, shorn of luster, empty, yet providing a means of breath;
it merely wards off flies and wind, being utterly bereft of the auspicious tree.
In this place, where the surface is covered with knots of thick bones and is constantly trembling and quivering,
there arises the delusion that it is a pure silken garment, as white as a cloudless mist, though it is not one's own.
Where flies, sparrows, and crows rest upon the tops of scars and stumps; where the branches of fingers quiver in the wind that carries the scent of dry, healed wounds.
In this saṃsāra, which is like a line of clouds of impurity, there are the hollows of wounds on one's own fingers;
it is fouled by the sweat and dew of perspiration, and its joints are like mountains of anthills.

In some places, there was the illusion of shimmering dust and water; in others, the ground was as rough as a *nakhājagaraka* (a type of lizard); and here and there, terrified lice and frightened travelers huddled together by the rivers.
In a place where there are few scattered, dried-up, and withered pools and puddles;
where the paths are marked by lines of dry ground amidst the flow of water; and which lies within the reach of cold winds.
When the world was everywhere overrun by the thumb-demon (Aṅguṣṭhayakṣa), who had long nails and mouths filled with the blood of swarms of men devoured by lice; //MU_3,70.45//
Adorned with various designs, she travels to the city of Citrapaṭa;
exhausted by her constant coming and going, she has long since become a mare there.
Carrying her bundle of thread and tools from city to city,
she arrived at Karatalāraṇya and there wandered about like a bull.
Having slipped from the hand for a moment's rest in a secluded place,
it falls apart somewhere, exhausted by the pulling of its face as it was threaded upon the loom.
Though it was hard, that [earring] did not cause pain when it was fastened to the ear;
for even a sharp thing does not abandon its lowliness in an external task.
With her iron needle-like mind fixed upon the needle of the intellect,
she moved about like a heavy stone boat in the waters, unable to turn its parts.
It spread out to the ends of the quarters along with the existence of the inner organ,
like a blade of grass by the power of the wind in the form of worldly existence.
With her face, she was casting aside the subtle thread of the end [of existence] while adorning her beautiful head;
through her effort to fill others, she seemed suddenly endowed with a heart.
Her heart was pierced by the needle of the essence of supreme fulfillment, as if it were being sewn together with fine thread while she incessantly vomited [her inner contents].
Even when worn out over a long time, it is filled up without deliberation even by sharp [objects];
the illustration for this is a tattered cloth that is filled in an instant by a needle.
The heart was pierced by the needle with rays of light emerging from the sutra,
and its splendor was instantly made manifest like the brilliance of the sun for the sake of filling others.
Suddenly, by that [sensation] which had arisen— consisting of a depletion followed by a filling—
she felt as if her heart were being tormented by the needle-work of a demoness.
Moving only slightly, she creates a piercing sound with the mere clatter of her hooves;
even her natural, ordinary gait causes distress.
The fourfold piercing passes the thread through the garments,
just as the long thread of latent tendencies (vāsanā) weaves through bodies like sensation (vedanā).
Moving with speed as if running when the eyes are cast about, wicked people pierce the vital spots while keeping their faces entirely hidden.
Threaded through the garments of the aggregates by the eye of the piercer, one beholds it with ease;
"How shall I pierce this?"—this is the desire of those who are sharp.
And yet, she is equally indifferent toward garments of silk and linen; for what dull-witted person indeed would overlook the difference between virtue and vice?
Holding a blazing thread pressed between her thumb and finger, she gazes as if vomiting forth an endless strand of entrails.
Because their mouths and hearts are sharp, the sluggish-moving [intellect], though prompted by the aphorisms, does not enter into any of the flavorful topics.
Even though her intellect was extremely sharp, it did not pierce the mouth of the donkey;
and even though she was the king’s daughter, she was heartless and ill-fated.
Without having harmed another, it seeks refuge in sharpness;
though pierced and obstructed, the needle dangles from the ear-ornament.
Moreover, why does this beautiful friend, like a grain of rice fallen from the hand onto the chaff, lie there?
To whom indeed would a friend who resembles one's own true nature not be pleasing?
Mingled with the mental fluctuations of the ignorant among common folk,
who indeed would wish to abandon association with those who are equal to oneself?
It becomes like a forge constructed by a blacksmith, abandoned and moving inward;
tossed by the blasts of the bellows, it is intent on soaring into the sky.
Abiding in the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, it enters within the heart-lotus;
it is an extremely terrible power of suffering, rising up like the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti).
By way of the opposite of *samāna*, it moves together with *samāna*;
by way of the opposite of *udāna*, it moves together with *udāna*.
Established in the vyāna [vital energy], it generates disease; it circulates through the essence of all the limbs and causes pain in the heart and throat, swelling, discoloration, and insanity.
She mostly delights in the hollow of a woolen ball held in the hand of a laundryman,
or in being pierced through the palm of a child’s hand as a toy.
Entering the feet and spreading across the courtyard of the blood-drinking [organs],
she who is satisfied by meager food is exceedingly pleased with those very meager foods.
She lies for a long time with her face downward, situated within a coating of mud;
having obtained a dwelling place according to her desire, who indeed would abandon it?
Through acts of violence, he reveals his own soul as plundered;
for even from a festival, quarrels bring pleasure to the base.
The Kapardika considers himself superior within the city of Valabhī;
for the wondrous manifestation of egoism is indeed difficult for living beings to eradicate.
By means of obtaining a pair of white garments and by taking [them] upon himself, he will bring about the death of men; for delusion does not arise regarding one's own purpose when it is variegated.
"By the separation of the threads of the cloth, 'this supreme atom quickly comes into being for me'— thus thinking, she becomes utterly pure."
When a needle, having been set aside, takes up dirt without being rubbed,
that disease of hers proceeds from the absence of piercing by another.
Subtle and piercing, it causes forgetfulness in an instant;
sharp, divisive, and cruel, it is like a divine needle.
One who has been harmed by a wicked person recognizes that person's malice only when that same person destroys another merely by pulling a thread.

It sinks in mud, it moves through the sky, it dwells amidst the winds of space; it lies on the edges of the horizon, in dust, on the ground, on the road, in a house, in a marketplace, in a forest, or in a harem;
it is in the hand, in the lotus of the ear, in soft woolen blankets, in holes, in wood, in clay, in veins, and in the heart—such is its existence as a substantial self.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The seventy-first canto, titled "The Description of the Needle’s Conduct," from the *Sūcyupākhyāna*, by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, after a long time, that rākṣasī named Karkaṭī surely attained satiety from all the human flesh.
It is said that she was satisfied by a single drop of blood on the previous day;
yet how can this needle of craving, which is so difficult to bear, ever find its end within the eye of a needle?
He thought: "Alas, what misery! Why has she come to this state?
I am subtle and my power is destroyed; yet the morsel does not fit within me."
O evil-minded one, where have those expansive limbs of mine gone?
They have withered like leaves in the forest, their splendor now like that of the clouds at the end of time.
Yet not even a slight portion of this— this morsel of savory meat-juice and this liquor scented with fat— finds room within me, who am so unfortunate.
I am sinking deep within the mud; I fall upon the surface of the earth;
I am struck down by the floods of the countryside and crushed by bandits.
Alas! I am ruined; I am without a protector, without comfort, and without refuge.
I sink from sorrow into further sorrow, and from calamity into further calamity.
I have no friend, no servant, no mother, no father;
I have no kinsman, no dependent, no brother, and no son.
I have no body, I have no place, and I have no refuge whatsoever;
finding no comfort in staying in one spot, I wander like a leaf in the forest.
I stand at the forefront of calamities; I am settled in a most dreadful state.
I long for non-existence, yet even that does not come to pass for me.
With a deluded mind, I have abandoned my own body,
like a fool who, through a mistaken perception, lets a wish-fulfilling gem fall from his hand.
Falling upon one, it first bestows delusion of mind; afterwards, it expands in the form of a proliferation of misfortunes.
I have slept among the dust and been tossed about upon the roads;
I have been thrust into wounds within—alas, what a succession of my miseries!
Constantly performing the service of others, always wandering on errands for others,
I have fallen into extreme wretchedness and have become subject to the will of others.
I perform this menial service, yet even that is merely the form of piercing;
alas, for me of such little fortune, even misfortune is difficult to obtain!
A massive vetāla has arisen; while I am performing a rite for peace, this total destruction has befallen me as I proceeded to seize the wealth.
Why was such a magnificent body abandoned by me, blinded as I am? Or rather, an inauspicious thought arises that it must surely meet with destruction.
Who indeed will rescue me, who am half-burnt and inferior even to a tiny insect,
lost amidst heaps of dust?
Where do those of ruined aspirations appear in the intellect of those with secluded minds?
They are like blades of grass on a village path to those dwelling upon a mountain.
For those who remain thus, how can there be any spiritual advancement toward awakening the ignorant?
Not even the slightest light arises for one who merely follows a firefly.
Therefore, I do not know for how long I shall have to wallow in the pits of the abyss of misfortune, my hopes destroyed.
When shall I become the form of the daughter of the great mountain Añjana,
supporting the sky and earth like pillars of lapis lazuli?
Her arms are like a mass of clouds, her eyes are flashes of steady lightning,
she is clothed in a garment of misty nets, and her hair rises high while her garment is black.
Her peacock-feather crown danced at the sight of the cloud-like belly of Lambodara;
her long, swaying breasts quivered as wine flowed from her dark body.
She veils the solar disc with a mass of laughing ashes,
assuming a singular form for the purpose of devouring those intent on destruction.
Carrying a *kuṇāla* bird, a mortar, a grass mat, a winnowing basket, and garlands of flowers,
she roamed from mountain peak to mountain peak, placing one foot upon each summit.
When shall that great belly of mine become radiant with its wide caverns? When shall my row of claws become thick as the clouds of a monsoon shelter?
When shall I have a smile that causes the great demons to flee? And when, intoxicated, shall I dance in the vast wilderness to the music of my own buttocks?
When shall I bring an end to the filling of my sweet stomach with large jars of fat and liquor, and with heaps of dead flesh and bones?
When, having drunk the blood of the great world,
shall I become intoxicated, rise up and dance, and then be sealed by sleep?
Having burned that radiant body in the fire of my own asceticism, I accepted its reduction to ashes,
just as gold accepts the state of being a ring.
Where, on one hand, is this body, resembling the Anjana mountain and filling the horizons;
and where, on the other, is this state of being as thin as a blade of grass, like the hoof-print of a mouse?
The ignorant man quickly casts away the earth even upon finding a golden bracelet;
thus, out of greed, I have cast away my radiant body as if it were mere soil.
Alas, Mahodara! You who resemble a cave of mist within the Vindhya mountains—how is it that today you do not bring an end to lions, deer, and elephants?
Alas, O arms, with tips curved by the weight of your burden and nails like the moon,
why do you not today rush toward the moon, mistaking it for a sacrificial cake?
Alas, O chest, as beautiful as the slopes of the great mountains of crystal and lapis lazuli!
Today you have abandoned that abode of lions and other beasts and instead held onto a forest of hair.
Alas, O eyes, radiant as the black night and glowing like a forest of parched wood,
why do you not adorn the quarters with the garland of flames from your gaze?
Alas, O bond of the aggregates, you are destroyed; you have fallen away from the surface of the earth. You have been cast down by Time; you have been ground upon the belly of a rock.

Alas, O moon-like face! Why do you not today perform penance with the rays from your teeth—[you who are] as enchanting as the lunar orb when it has been extinguished by the fire at the end of an aeon?
Alas, alas! Where have those two large hands of mine gone today?
Have I become like a needle, tossed about by flies and hooves?
"Alas, O beautiful Śvabhra, rich with Bhaga trees and fierce Karañjas, bestowing happiness!
O Vindhya mountain, you whose broad slopes are like a stainless orb, and whose forests are vast!"
Where is this form that fills the sky, and where is this body as thin as a needle? Where is the cavity of its mouth, equal to the space between heaven and earth, and where is this needle-like tip?

Where is the mouthful thick with a great mass of flesh, and where is the blocking by a single drop of water? Alas! This drama, leading to the destruction of my own self, has been composed by me alone.
The seventy-second canto, titled "The Lamentation of Viśvāmitra," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having reflected thus, that needle, possessing a voice capable of speech, conceived this thought:
"I shall quickly become an ascetic woman once more in order to regain that body."
Having reflected thus, he withdrew the power that causes the death of living beings while remaining established in goodness,
and went to that very peak of the Himalayas to practice steady austerity.
Thus she perceived her own mind within herself as having become a needle;
composed of the vital breaths, she entered through the life-forces and struck down the man.
Then, perceiving her own needle-form within herself, she, consisting of mind and having the vital breath for her body, went to the peak of the Himalayas.
There, in that place where a fierce forest fire raged, devoid of all living beings,
parched by the agitation of great rocky surfaces, and grey with dust;
She stood there, having risen up on a vast, grassless plain,
like a withered tuft of grass suddenly sprouted in a desert.
Having relied upon one subtle quarter with its own half,
she began to perform the ascetic penance of the single-quarter self of her own consciousness.
With the soles of her delicate feet, she has barely prevented the earth from being covered in dust; holding back her steps with great effort, she stands with her face turned upward.
With her body blackened, fierce, and sharp from subsisting on wind,
she strove with effort to set foot upon the ground, which was strewn with dust, grit, and pebbles.
In the forest, she imitated a female serpent agitated by fear, who had risen up to see from afar and was swaying her tail.
The ray of the sun emerging from the aperture of her mouth became her companion, appearing like a needle, guarding her from behind.
Even toward a lowly person who has become one's own kin, a person shows affection; even by a needle with its mere glint, the conduct of a female friend is indicated to one who has taken refuge in it.
She had a second companion, a pure female ascetic; she was left behind by her like a dark needle that reveals a hidden fault.
With her eyes narrowed in a smile as the rays of the sun emerging from the needle’s tip fell upon them,
she was seen later only as mere dust, her gaze having been drawn away by that smile.
Even those trees, creepers, and the like that are seen by her dust do not feel any longing to see that great ascetic needle.
The winds, with whistling sounds issuing from their mouths, agitated her who stood firm with her feet firmly planted and her disposition as noble as a flower.
"Having been swallowed by her, we shall soon be born again as the floral pollen within her"— thinking thus, they filled her mouth.
The dust, driven by the wind sent by Indra, carried away her ascetic merit;
yet she, under the pretext of not having eaten, did not swallow it even though it was in her mouth.
She did not swallow those dust particles, for her resolve was firm;
indeed, even small things achieve their purpose through internal strength.
Even the pollen of flowers did not enter their mouths;
the wind was struck with wonder greater than that of uprooting Mount Sumeru.
[The city] was sealed up to its very crest with mud, even though it was filled with great waters.
Though shaken by mighty winds, though terrified by the flickering of lightning, though covered in dust by the clouds, and though agitated by the thundering of the sky;
Even for thousands of years, that ascetic woman, her firm resolve fixed upon the mind, did not waver, like one asleep on a piece of fine cloth.
Then, when external movement had ceased and the proper time had not yet arrived,
she contemplated her own conscious self-nature.
The light of knowledge arose, which perceives both the higher and the lower;
it became the stainless needle of consciousness, the supreme purifier.
Once her evil deeds were exhausted through asceticism, she herself became born with that very intellect which had known what was to be known; she was like a needle that points out its own opening.
Thus, for thousands of years, she performed severe asceticism,
looking upward and causing distress to the seven great worlds.
By her ascetic power, which was as terrifying as the fire at the end of an eon, Mount Himavat became ablaze;
through that, the entire world seemed to burst into flames.
Then Vāsava asked Nārada, "Whose ascetic power has overcome the world? and he explained that to him.
For seven thousand years, this long-suffering needle remained within my body; since she was recognized by me as such, this world has been set ablaze.
The *nāgas* hiss, the mountains split asunder, the celestial chariots fall, and the clouds and oceans depart;
the quarters of the sky, together with the sun, go to desiccation and become darkened. O Indra, behold this destruction brought about by the power of asceticism alone!
The seventy-third canto, titled "The Power of the Needle-like Austerity," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having heard the entire account of Karkaṭīkaṭu, Vāsava,
his curiosity aroused once again, questioned Nārada.
Śakra:
O Sage, having acquired the state of a needle-bodied piśācī through ascetic penance, what kinds of riches were enjoyed by that karkaṭī in the interior of the Himalayas?
Nārada said:
That needle for the living which had become a female spirit (piśācī), as fragile as a stalk of śūkara-grass, was a needle of black iron; that was her own support.
Having abandoned that object of her own focus, she— seated upon a chariot of wind in the sky and having entered the body by way of the path of the vital breath (prāṇa)— [proceeded].
Within the openings of all the intestines, sinews, fat, marrow, and blood,
she of the soiled limbs is hidden like a bird within its nest.
In whichever channel a particular wind does not flow, that [wind], having entered it,
produces a sharp pain there, rooted and intense like the sprout of a banyan tree.
With those very bodies and senses, he likewise consumed many other human flesh-meat dishes that were his accustomed fare.
The young girl lay asleep, her many garlands slightly disheveled, her cheeks pressed against the leaf-designs sewn upon her lover’s chest.
She dwelt in forest groves free from sorrow, among birds,
amidst rows of clouds— twofold in volume— arising from the blossoms of the wish-fulfilling trees.
In the forests of the celestial mountains, there was the liquor-like nectar of the fragrant yellow mandāra flowers, with bees clinging to the swarms of bees.
The limbs of corpses were chewed by the vultures, who were swollen with pride,
as if they were the limbs of heroes in battle being devoured by swift horses urged on by the staff-like swords of warriors.
Like a streak of wind in all directions, it flew up and down through the channels of all the bodily cavities, like a crow through the paths of the sky.
Just as the vital breaths, which are the winds of the cosmic self (virāḍātman), flash forth in the sky within the heart,
so too does she flash forth within the house of the body.
Due to the corruption of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), it wanders through the bodies of all living beings,
just as the light of a lamp illuminates its own houses through a wife.
It has moved within the blood as if through liquid water,
and it has surged within the bellies like the turning of whirlpools in the oceans.
The fragrance of his own body was tasted within him as he slept upon his pure fat, like Viṣṇu sleeping on the serpent Śeṣa, or like nectar within the power of the wind.

Young trees, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and the like, having been enjoyed by the splendor of the forest breeze dwelling in his heart, were rendered incapable [of growth] merely by being looked upon with a harmful intent.
By the mere thought, "May I become a needle made of living soul," she became a mental needle— conscious, purifying, and sharp.
By her, who was invisible, who possessed horses as fierce as the wind,
and who dwelt within iron needles, he was pursued as she roamed through the directions, obstructing them.
Drinking, eating, sporting, laughing, giving, taking,
dancing, singing, and dwelling— all these have been performed by infinite embodied living beings.
Invisible, embodied, with a mind and body of wind,
and having the nature of space— there is nothing that she cannot accomplish.
Because she was intoxicated and unable to chew flavorful food, this young woman, clinging to her tethering post, has reeled about like a female elephant.
In rivers where the bodies of beings are diminished by the abundance of violent waves,
one has acted like a sea-monster with intoxicated speed that causes utter distress.
Unable to swallow the fat and flesh within her heart, she remained there for a long time, distressed by that thought, like an old woman whose intellect is impoverished despite being wealthy.
The elephant, camel, deer, elephant, horse, lion, and so forth, have long been made to dance within the heart,
like a dancer on a stage repeatedly swaying her limbs against one another.
By means of this [consciousness], which follows the unity of the winds both externally and internally,
and which is difficult to perceive as it abides within like a trace of fragrance, [the self is perceived].
Though beneficial through mantras, medicines, austerities, charity, worship of the gods, and so forth,
it is swept away like the high waves of a mountain river in full flood.
Like the flame of a lamp whose course is unknown, having gone, it quickly dissolves;
O Mother, it finds its cessation there, as if within an iron needle.
Everyone seeks a basis in accordance with their own latent tendencies; thus, the very state of being a Rakshasi was made into a basis by means of the state of being a Rakshasi.
Even after wandering through all directions, in times of distress, every dull-witted person returns to his own home, just as a living needle returns to its iron needle-case.
Exerting herself in this way as she dwells throughout the ten directions, she attains mental satisfaction, but never physical.
For properties exist here only when there is a substratum, not when it is absent;
it is said that the body of one who is seen is indeed satisfied by that [offering].
Then, through the recollection of her former body,
she became distressed, longing for the happiness of a belly full of sweet food.
Then, thinking to himself, "I shall perform extensive austerity for the sake of my former body," he determined a place for his asceticism by himself.
She entered the heart of the youthful sky-vulture through the path of the vital breath, like a doe moving through the air.
That vulture, directed by her, took up an iron needle that had settled upon some part of the funeral pyre, and with his beak he applied himself to it as the mind applies itself to its object.
Taking the needle, that vulture went to the mountain he had envisioned; driven swiftly by the Piśācī within him like a cloud by the wind, he departed.
There, in that desolate great forest, he established her in a state free from all conceptual constructions, just as a yogi establishes consciousness in the ground of reality.
Fainted by that single, minute tip of his foot,
she was like a goddess placed upon the summit of a mountain by a vulture.
With one foot, he stood with his neck uplifted upon a single grain of dust atop the great peak, like a crest of fire upon the summit of a mountain.
Seeing the life-thread, which had been raised and fixed like a needle within the vulture's belly,
it began to emerge from the bird's body.
With her consciousness directed upward, she emerged from the vulture's body like a needle,
just as a scent-streak emerges from the wind, drawn forward by the breeze of the nostrils.
The vulture went to his own place, like a porter who has laid down his burden;
free from disease, as it were, he became inwardly undisturbed.
A firm foundation has been prepared for his asceticism by means of iron;
indeed, the employment of resources befits one who is steadfast.

"For indeed, actions of that which is formless cannot be accomplished without a substratum," thinking thus, she remained engaged in asceticism, relying upon the necessity of abiding in a single substratum.
Like a whirlwind encircling a streak of fragrance, she surrounded the iron needle of the living soul— the Piśācī— on all sides, as if it were a śiṃśapā tree.
From that time forward, O Śakra, this long-suffering needle remained in the vast forest for many groups of years.
O you who are skilled in what must be done, exert yourself for the sake of obtaining her as a bride; for that ascetic power of hers, accumulated over a long time, is sufficient to consume the world.
Vasiṣṭha:
Having heard this from Nārada, Śakra then dispatched Māruta to the ten directions of the horizon to investigate the needle.
Then, having reached an understanding with the Maruts, he went forth to behold her;
releasing himself from the path of the sky, he moved along with great haste.
That consciousness of the wind, being indeed swift yet not all-pervading,
suddenly beheld [the object] without obstruction, like the supreme consciousness.
The earth, bound by the seven oceans at its edge upon a vast expanse,
has the Lokāloka mountain as its girdle and is composed of stones made of various jewels.
The circle of Puṣkara-dvīpa, surrounded by the ocean of sweet water, contains within it the range of mountains and the multitude of directions along with their interior cavities.
The surrounding ocean of wine contains aquatic creatures;
its coastal region is the Gomedha island, and within it lies a multitude of territories.
[He saw] the moat of the ocean of sugarcane juice, containing within it the ranges of mountains;
and the sacred seat of the region of Krauñcadvīpa, with its sequence of internal mountains.
The circle of the Ocean of Milk is like a pearl necklace with a central gem,
and the circle of the island named Śveta is like its corresponding pendant.
The submersion of the earth in the ocean of clarified butter, the abode of the gods situated within it,
the extent of the circumference of Kuśadvīpa, and the hollows of its vast great mountains.
It has the ocean of curds for its girdle, with the moving continents as its belly;
it has the land of Śākadvīpa as its form, with the intermediate regions as its internal organs.
[He beheld] Jambudvīpa with its great Mount Meru, surrounded by the salt-ocean moat and containing cities and mountains within it,
crowded with the principal mountain ranges.
At first, it falls from the masses of wind, tossed by the gusts;
in this sequence, at the end, it spreads forth here by that very same process.
Vāyu, looking thus and surveying Jambudvīpa,
reached that peak of the Himavat where the ascetic woman Sūci was.
Upon the great and formidable peak, he reached that vast wilderness which,
like a second expanse of space, was devoid of the activities of living beings.
Because of its proximity to the sun, it was devoid of any arrangement of grass and spread out entirely as dust, like the structure of saṃsāra.
It has attained the state of an ocean to be filled by the rivers of a mirage;
it possesses the nature of a mirage-river resembling the bow of Indra.
Extending to the very limits of the immeasurable, though watched over by the world-protectors,
it was filled solely with circles of dust stirred by the movement of the wind.
Smeared with the saffron of the sun’s rays and anointed with the sandalwood paste of the moon’s beams,
she was like a playful woman of the sky, singing the song of the wind’s whistling sighs.

Having wandered all around the surface of the earth—which rests upon a single swelling portion sealed by the seven islands and oceans—the wind, worn out by the long journey, reached that plateau of the foremost mountain; there, assuming the form of a bee as if clinging to the very edge of the sky, he rested with his vast body filling the infinite quarters of space.
The seventy-fourth canto, titled "Description of the Ripening of the Needle-like Austerity," by Vasiṣṭha.
There, upon that great forested summit of that upward-pointing peak,
he saw in its center that needle-like projection rising up like a crest of flame.

She was performing penance on one leg, withering away for a long time as she subsisted only on warm vapors; she was dried up by constant fasting, her skin shriveled over a belly that had become a mere lump.
Having seized that very wind with her mouth opened wide once for all,
she thereafter releases it while it remains incessantly within her heart.
She was withered by the rays of the fierce sun, worn out by the forest winds,
yet she did not move from her place, bathed by the beams of the moon.
Previously, it was occupied by a single atom of dust;
considering its purpose fulfilled, that atom gave no room for another.

She was like one who had been offered the guest-offering by the forest itself; she appeared as if her crest-lock had grown long ago, as if her life-breaths were established upon her head, and as if she were crowned with a mass of matted hair.
Beholding that needle, Pavana, his mind overwhelmed with wonder,
bowed down and gazed at her conduct before him as if trembling with fear.
"O great ascetic woman, Sūci, for what purpose do you perform this austerity?"— overwhelmed by her mass of splendor, he was unable to say "no."
"O wonderful is the great austerity of the Blessed One Mahāsūcī!"—
meditating thus alone, Māruta departed into the sky.
Having leaped across the path of the clouds, having passed beyond the layers of wind,
having left the hosts of perfected beings below, and having reached the path of the sun;
Having ascended above the realms of discursive thought, he reached the city of Śakra;
Purandara embraced him, who was meritorious enough to be seen even by a needle’s eye.
And when questioned, he said to Sahadeva and his host, who were dwelling in the abode of Śakra, "I have seen everything."
Vāyu said:
In Jambudvīpa there is a preeminent mountain king named Himavat,
whose son-in-law is the Blessed One, the wearer of the crescent moon himself.
To the north of that, on the back of the great peak, stands the ascetic Sūcī, possessed of supreme beauty, performing severe penance.
What need is there for much speaking here? To pacify her hunger for wind and other elements, she filled the cavity of her own belly and stilled it.
With its contraction stilled and its mouth opened wide by the particle of *rajas* for the sake of heat,
she has today covered herself with that [garment] to ward off the cold wind and hunger.
By means of her intense austerity, he abandoned his snowy form and assumed the form of fire; thus, as the Bull, he attained a state that is difficult even for the gods to approach.
Therefore, arise quickly; let us all go to the Grandfather for the sake of obtaining that boon.
Know that his asceticism is difficult to endure and leads to our misfortune.
Thus impelled by Vāyu, Śakra, together with the hosts of gods,
went to the world of Brahmā and petitioned that Lord.
"I shall go to the peak of the Himalayas to grant a boon," Brahmā promised; having said this, Śakra returned to heaven.
After such a length of time, she became a purifier,
her own heat of asceticism scorching the abodes of the immortals.
With her gaze fixed on the rays of the sun entering the cavity of her mouth, she was watched from beginning to end by her own clear reflection— a reflection that both caused wonder and turned away.

By means of the needle of his silken garment, Mount Meru was surpassed in stability as if it were a blade of grass; thus, by this skillful means, he was like a mother who submerges her child at both the beginning and end of the day through her own growth.
At midday, as if out of fear of the heat, she entered her mother’s interior; at other times, out of respect, she was watched from afar by her mother’s gaze.
When she gazes upon her with her eyes from nearby, she sinks into his limbs due to the heat [of passion];
for in a time of distress, a person forgets even the respect and hospitality shown to them.
With her shadow as the needle and her asceticism as the thread— thus, with herself as the third—
she made a triangle purified by austerity equal to Vārāṇasī.
Even those winds and dust particles that passed through that triangular [chariot] which had a moat of three colors attained supreme liberation.

O Rāghava, having personally realized the supreme cause and having reflected upon the consciousness of one's own volition, he alone—who follows the process of his own contemplation—is indeed the supreme Guru here; there is no other.
The seventy-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Manifestation of the Ripening of Austerities," by Vasiṣṭha:
Then, after a thousand years, the Grandfather arrived;
from the expanse of the sky, he spoke, saying, "Daughter, choose a boon."
Because she lacked the organs of action, Sūcī possessed only the subtle constituent of the individual soul;
she said nothing to him and reflected solely within herself.
I am fulfilled and my doubts have vanished; what need have I for a boon?
I am at peace, I am extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss alone.
Everything that was to be known has been known; the webs of doubt have been stilled;
one's own discernment has blossomed—what further need is there for anything else?
Just as this [reality] exists here, so indeed shall I abide;
having abandoned the very notion of truth and untruth, what need have I for anything else?
For all this time, I have been tormented by a lack of discernment,
like a young girl by a Vetāla spirit arisen from her own imagination.
Now he has become tranquil through his own investigation;
what use could there be for me in objects imagined as either desired or undesired?
Beholding that needle, which was endowed with such certainty, devoid of the organs of action, and remaining silent in its state of restraint, the Blessed One remained still.
Then Brahmā, his mind serene, spoke again to this woman free from passion:
"Daughter, choose a boon; remain upon the earth for some time."
"After enjoying worldly pleasures, you shall thereafter go to the supreme state;
this is the certainty of destiny, whose nature is irreversible."
"O most excellent one, by this asceticism, may your resolve bear fruit;
become once again that very same Rākṣasī of the snowy forest, full-bodied."
By that body in the form of a cloud with which you were previously separated,
O daughter, you are like a tree within a seed attaining the state of a great tree.
You shall again attain union with that body which has the form of its seed; by that very body you will take delight, O daughter, like a creeper established upon a sprout.
Because you have known all that is to be known, you will no longer experience affliction in this world;
you are inwardly pure, with the winds of passion stilled, like a circle of clouds in autumn.
If, at some time, you should cease internal meditation and emerge outwardly through play, you will become the embodiment of meditation upon the Self of all.
She is the embodiment of the support for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*), which are of the nature of worldly discourse;
she delights in the movement of the body, which has the wind as its inherent nature.
Then, O daughter, being opposed [to your desires] and obstructing the movement of your own karma,
you will righteously inflict suffering upon living beings for the sake of ending your hunger.

You shall become one who acts with justice in the world, yet you will be a subverter of injustice; while still embodied, through your liberation-in-life, you will be the sole protector of your own discernment.

Having spoken thus, the god departed from the expanse of the sky. Then, a slight reflection born of inner deliberation arose within her: "Let this needle be mine; what is the use of this dispassion, or even this passion, in upholding the meaning of the Lotus-Born One’s words?"

In an instant, it shone forth through the sequence of the seed-syllable of the wish-fulfilling tree: first as a mere span, then a cubit, then a fathom, then a spreading branch, then a wreath of clouds, and finally as a creeper with emerging parts.

Then, the subtle elements (tanmātras), possessing their full powers, emerged from the body along with the organs of action; these had previously remained latent within the seed, like the unmanifest flowers of the tree of volition.
The seventy-sixth canto, titled "The Attainment of the Body of a Needle," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then that needle-like female demon Karkaṭī became subtle once more, yet again attained bulkiness like an autumnal streak of cloud.
Having regained her own natural form, she became somewhat joyful;
through that awakening, she cast off the pride of the great Rākṣasa like a garment.
Right there she remained absorbed in meditation, established in the posture of the bound lotus; having taken hold of pure consciousness, she stood firm like a mountain peak.
Then, after six months, she attained awakening from meditation,
like a peahen in the rainy season at the roar of a great cloud.
Having awakened, her outward activity became devoted solely to hunger;
for as long as one lives, this nature of the body does not cease.
Then she reflected with this thought: "What shall I eat? And that which belongs to another must be consumed by me only through right means."
I consider death here better for embodied beings than that morsel of food which is censured by the noble or not acquired through righteous means.
If I must abandon this body, let it be so; yet I shall not consume anything that has not been acquired through righteous means, for wealth enjoyed through unrighteousness acts like poison.
What would it matter if one were to eat that which is not obtained through the worldly order?
For me, there is no concern whatsoever regarding life or death.
For I was indeed nothing but mind, consisting merely of the delusion of a body and so forth;
that [mind] has been stilled through self-awakening—whence, then, can there be a body or the perception of a body?
Remaining thus in silence, she heard a voice from the sky,
spoken by the wind-god who was pleased by her abandonment of the nature of a *rākṣasa*.
"Go, Karkaṭī; awaken the deluded quickly with knowledge, for it is the very nature of the great here to rescue the deluded."
Even if you try to awaken him, he who will not attain awakening is born for his own destruction; he should rightfully become your prey.
Having heard this, she said softly, "I have been favored by you," and rose from the mountain peak; then she descended gradually.
Having quickly crossed the plateau and descended from the edge of the valley,
he entered the settlement of the Kirātas situated at the foot of the mountain.
It contains abundant food, cattle, multitudes of people, wealth, crops, medicinal herbs, and meat;
it provides infinite roots, drinks, and grains, as well as wild animals, insects, birds, and so forth.

Thereafter, that night-stalker proceeded through a beautiful region frequented by the foothills of the Himālaya mountains, where the peaks resembled mountains of shifting, molten collyrium, traveling at night upon a path of thick and blinding darkness.
The seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Logic that Subverts Logic," by Vasiṣṭha.
In the meantime, there in that circle of Kirātas,
the dark night became like a mass of darkness so thick it could be grasped by the hand.
The expanse of the sky was covered by a cloth of blue clouds,
devoid of the moon, and scattered with masses of soot resembling thickets of *tāmāla* groves.
In that city, the thickets of creepers cause a blinding darkness within the hollows of the villages, while the narrowness of the house courtyards is like the confinement of youth in its prime.
At the four corners, the lamp-flame was dimmed by a mass of darkness,
while the line of hair on her body shone like a flame emerging from the keyhole of a door.
Like a female crab with her own mate, a dancing piśācī demoness stands amidst intoxicated skeletons and vetālas, as motionless as a wooden statue.
It was a time when the multitudes of living beings were as if in deep sleep or dead, a season that dispelled the thick mists like a dense fog,
and where the movement of the gentle breeze was like the spray of autumn frost.
In the lakes, it was filled with the waves of cranes, ducks, and frogs;
in the inner apartments, it resounded with the playful chatter of men and women.
In the forests, it blazes with fires whose tangled crests are flaming tongues;
in the fields, it meets with crops ripened by nourishment from the sprinkling of water.
In the sky, the circle of constellations shifted with imperceptible motion;
in the forests, the trees shed their flowers and fruits as the spreading winds blew.
In the ravines, there was the harsh sound of owls crying out as they were being seized by hawks, and the grating wails of villagers whose villages had been overrun by bandits.
In the villages, the villagers were unconscious; in the cities, the citizens were asleep;
in the forests, the winds were blowing; and in the nests, the birds were motionless.
In the caves, the pride of lions sleeps; in the thickets, the deer breathe freely; in the sky, there are clusters of frost; and in the forest, silence prevails.
Resembling the interior of a cloud of soot, like the belly of a mountain of glass,
dense within like a mass of mud, it is thick with the blindness that can be severed by a sword.
Agitated by the winds of cosmic dissolution, as flickering as a mountain of soot, it was thick with the belly of mountains and the great mire of the single universal ocean.
With claws like ten million glowing coals, beautiful in the state of deep sleep,
she is dense with the slumber of ignorance and possesses the hue of a bumblebee’s back.
On that terrible night, in the midst of the Kirāta people,
the king was then at that moment together with his minister.
The wise one named Vikrama departed from the city where the citizens were asleep,
entering the treacherous forest with the conduct of a hero.
In the forest, that cucumber saw those two— the king and the minister— wandering about, their portions of fortitude maintained as they gazed upward at the Vetāla.
Then she thought: "Ah, today I have found my prey!
These two are fools, ignorant of the self; their bodies are indeed a burden."
The fool lives for the sake of suffering, leading to ruin both in this world and the next;
he must be destroyed with effort, for no calamity should be nurtured.
For the fool who does not perceive his own self, death is life;
for through death there is his awakening, because it is the cause for the exhaustion of accumulated sins.
And at the beginning of creation, a rule was established by the Lotus-born One:
"The one who is deluded in soul, not self-possessed, exists for the sake of devouring the predatory."
Therefore, these two, having become my food, must be eaten by me this very day;
for one who is unworthy indeed neglects a faultless gain when it has been obtained.
May these two never become endowed with virtues and noble aspirations;
for such destruction of men is not pleasing to my very nature.
Therefore, I shall examine these two; if they are indeed endowed with virtues, then I will not eat them, for one should never harm those who possess virtue.
By one who desires unartificial happiness, fame, and long life,
those endowed with virtue should be honored by giving all that is desired.
If I should perish with this body, I shall not enjoy that which is endowed with [worldly] qualities;
for the virtuous bring more joy to the mind than even life itself.
One should protect a virtuous person even by the gift of one's own life;
for through the medicine of association with the virtuous, even death attains the state of a friend.
If even I, a Rākṣasī, protect one endowed with such virtues,
then another person might likewise follow that same stainless disposition of the heart.
Those embodied beings who dwell here endowed with noble qualities cool the surface of the earth intensely through their association, like moons upon the ground.
Death is the neglect of virtue; life is the reliance upon the virtuous.
From this reliance on the virtuous during one's life, there results the fruit of heaven, liberation, and so forth.
Therefore, I shall examine these two lotus-eyed ones at some point through the play of questioning, [to see] whether they possess the knowledge of measurement.
Having first investigated the presence of even a slight degree of virtue or vice, and having determined whether the offense is greater than the merit,
one should then impose a punishment upon the offender according to the circumstances— whether it be mild or severe— provided that wealth is available for its payment.
The seventy-eighth canto, titled "The Discourse on the Rākṣasīs," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then that ogress, a blossoming creeper in the forest of the Rākṣasa clan,
let out a deep roar in the very midst of the darkness, like a streak of cloud.
At the end of his roar, he spoke these words harsh with the syllable "Praiṅ," like the sound of thunderbolts and hail that follows a peal of thunder.
O you two, the moon and the sun, who traverse the path of the sky in this terrible forest; you are like insects dwelling within the hollows of the stone seats of the darkness of great illusion!
Who are you two, possessed of great intelligence or perhaps of wicked intellect, who have come together and fallen within the path of my grasp, destined to die in an instant?
The King said:
O Bhūtaka, who are you? And where do you dwell in this body?
Show yourself! Who would fear these words of yours, which sound like the humming of bees?
Those who seek their own interests fall upon their goal with all the speed of a lion;
you, however, imagine us to be equal to them in both appearance and word—why do you fear us?
For those who procrastinate, nothing is accomplished except for their own ruin.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the king had spoken thus, she reflected, "Well said," and for the sake of revealing their lack of composure, she both roared and laughed at the two of them.
Then the two of them beheld her, filling the quarters of the sky with sound,
her form made manifest by a mass of light emitted from her own loud laughter.
Resembling a mountain slope ground down by a fragment of a kalpa-ending cloud,
she set the sky ablaze with the circling flashes of lightning from her own eyes.
With her dark neck thickened by the swelling mass of roaring clouds, she was like the flickering flames of the submarine fire within the single ocean of darkness.

Before him appeared the city, where the night-stalkers were struck down with cries of "Hā! Hā! amidst the fury of their clashing faces, and which seemed to playfully serve as a pillar of soot for the two worlds, heaven and earth.
With hair standing erect, her body veined, with tawny eyes and composed of darkness,
she instills no small fear even in yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.

Her own mouth gleamed from the hollows of her cavernous ears; she was terrifying with the whistling of the wind, adorned with pestles, mortars, and firebrands, and crowned with ploughs and winnowing baskets.
Like the crest of a mountain of lapis lazuli quivering at the end of an aeon,
she was like the risen Night of Doom, whose laughter strikes terror into the Lord of the Universe.
She was like a forest of dense sky accompanied by clouds that had taken bodily form,
or like a fleshy night endowed with great clouds, come into being as a corporeal entity.
With the configuration of her body, she was like a pedestal of mud risen up,
as if her slender form had resorted to darkness for the battle between the moon and the sun.
She bears two dark breasts, resembling a pair of hanging clouds from a cleft in a sapphire mountain slope, and enriched with pestles and other farming implements.
Naked, her great body smeared with glowing embers,
her creeper-like arms swaying in the breeze from the footprints that resembled trees.
Beholding her, the two great heroes remained just as undisturbed as before;
for there is nothing that can cause delusion in one whose mind is detached.
The Minister:
O great Rākṣasī, what is this agitation of yours, manifesting as laughter? For women are indeed light-minded, and they are prone to excessive haste even in matters of triviality.
Abandon this agitation; this undertaking does not befit you.
For the wise, who accomplish their own goals, engage themselves within their proper sphere.
O frail one, thousands like you are like gnats;
for us, they are like blades of grass and leaves driven about by the whirlwind of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Having cast off the fever of agitation, that wise person accomplishes his goal with an even and healthy mind,
and through skillful worldly conduct.
Or rather, let the task be accomplished by its own worldly convention;
for what occasion is there for delusion when the principle of great destiny prevails?
Tell us what is desired by you; what do you seek as a petitioner? For one who comes before us as a seeker, even in a dream, never departs without having obtained their object.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by him at that time, the Rākṣasī reflected:
"Oh, how pure is the conduct of these two lions among men!"
I do not consider these two to be common; this is indeed a marvelous wonder.
Words, faces, and glances themselves reveal the internal certainty.
Through the doors of speech, expression, and glance, the intentions of the wise become unified with one another, just as the waters of rivers merge through their converging currents.
"By these two, my true nature has for the most part been fully understood;
neither of them shall be destroyed by me, nor indeed are they themselves subject to destruction."
I believe you two are knowers of the Self; for without the knowledge of the Self, the intellect—having its notions of existence and non-existence wiped away—does not become free from fear of death.
Therefore, I ask these two about a certain doubt that has arisen;
those who, having encountered what is to be attained, do not inquire about anything at all, are the lowest of men.
Having reflected thus, she restrained her laughter— which was like the sound of clouds at an untimely kalpa— and spoke in order to inquire about that matter spread across various occasions.
"Who are you two, O blameless heroes? Tell me this;
for from the mere sight of those with pure minds, friendship arises."
The minister said: "This king belongs to the Kirātas, and I have become his minister;
we are prepared to suppress people like you through a night-raid."
For a king, the duty day and night is the suppression of wicked beings;
however, those who abandon their own duty are fuel for the fire of destruction.
Rākṣasī:
You are the evil counselor of the king; because of this evil counsel, he has become a non-king (*arāḍ*).
A true king would have a minister, and by means of a good minister, he would become a true king.
At the outset, the king himself must be joined with discernment by his wise minister;
for as is the king, so are the subjects, and through that [discernment], he attains nobility.
Just as the supreme knowledge of the inner self belongs to those who possess the entire web of virtues,
so too should the king be such a king, and the minister likewise a knower of counsel.
Sovereignty and impartial vision—these arise through the royal science;
he who does not know that very science is neither a minister nor a ruler.
If you two are virtuous and possess knowledge of that [truth], you shall attain the highest good;
if not, you will bring about my own ruin, and I shall devour you both.
By a single means you two shall cross over from my side,
provided that you investigate with your intellect the essence of this cage of my questions.
O Lord of the Earth, O Minister, ask me questions; I am very eager for this. Fulfill my purpose! For who in this world, having promised a favor, does not incur the fault that brings about total ruin?
The seventy-ninth canto, titled "The Discourse on the Rākṣasīs," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having spoken thus, the Rākṣasī began to state the questions.
When the king said, "Let them be told," listen to these, O Rāghava.
Rākṣasī:
Within a single atom, which is yet composed of many parts, hundreds of thousands of world-systems dissolve like bubbles within the ocean.
Is space non-space? Is it nothingness or indeed something?
Who am I that has become thus, and who are you who stands as "I"?
Who is it that does not go even while going, and who is it that stands still even while standing?
Who is a conscious being yet a stone, and who is a painter in the sky?
And what is that which does not abandon its nature as fire, and what fire is not burning?
O King, how can fire arise from what is not fire, and why is there no interval between them?
Even though it is devoid of the moon, sun, fire, and stars, what indestructible entity is the illuminator?
And why does illumination proceed from that which cannot be apprehended by the eye?
What kind of supreme illumination could there be for creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and the like, as well as for those born blind and others who lack eyes? (MU 3.79.7)
Who is the creator of space and the other elements? Who is the giver of their intrinsic nature?
Who would be the treasury of the jewels of the world? And in whose treasury does the world reside like a gem?

What is the atom that is darkness and light? What is the atom that both exists and does not exist? What is the atom that is far away and yet not far away? What is the atom that is indeed a great mountain?
What is a kalpa but a mere blink of an eye, and what is a blink of an eye but a kalpa?
What is perception that lacks reality, and what is consciousness that is unconscious?
And what is non-wind and wind? What is sound and even the absence of sound?
What is everything and nothing at all? Who am I, and who might I not be?
What is there that, though attained through hundreds of efforts over many lifetimes, becomes nothing once obtained? Indeed, everything is eventually gained.
By whom, while living in health, has one’s own self been so highly betrayed?
By what minute thing is Mount Meru obstructed within, or the three worlds reduced to a blade of grass?
By what mere atom has a hundred leagues been filled?
And what is that very same atom which, being so small, does not fit even within hundreds of leagues?
By whose mere glance is the childish world made to dance?
Within the interior of which atom do the multitudes of mountain ranges exist?
Without abandoning its atomicity, what atom could have the form of something larger than Mount Meru?
What atom, whose nature is but a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, could be a towering mountain?
What is the atom that is the lamp providing illumination for light and darkness?
Within what atom do all atoms of experience reside?
What atom, though utterly tasteless, comes to be intensely savored?
By the relinquishing of what atom is everything abandoned, and by the retention of what atom is everything grasped?
By what atom, which lacks the power to conceal itself, is the universe concealed? And by whose logic does the existence of an atom depend upon the universe? MU 3.79.19.
What is that atom which has no parts? What is he whose eyes are the thousand rays [of the sun]? What is a moment, or a great eon, or even hundreds of great eons?
In what does the world abide within the atom, like trees in a seed—
manifest yet unarisen, from the seed-stage up to the fruit?
To what blink of an eye does an eon remain as an interval, like [the duration] of a living being? Who is an agent who acts even without resorting to the status of an instigating agent?
To achieve the perfection of the visible, the seer too should bring himself into the state of being visible;
for who, while seeing the visible, does not see their own self, just as one sees with the eyes?
And when all visible objects have been dissolved within, who, perceiving the indivisible Self,
would not see the visible object before them for the sake of the non-attainment of the visible?
Who illuminates the self, the seer, and the object of sight, as if they were objects themselves?
And by whom are these three swallowed up, just as bracelets and other ornaments are absorbed into gold?
Why does nothing exist separately, like waves and so forth from the great ocean?
And by whose will does anything exist separately, like a wave from the great ocean?
From that single non-existent which is existent and undivided by space, time, and so forth,
why does duality emerge as non-separate, like foam from the great ocean?
Who, having placed within himself— like a seed situated within a limb— the self, the seer, and the seen, both existent and non-existent, and extending through the three times, remains established?
The vast multitude of worlds, existing in the past, present, and future,
is eternally contained within [the Self], like a tree within its seed.
Just as a seed quickly becomes a tree, and a tree likewise [arises] from a seed,
what single thing could arise by itself, even though it has not yet arisen and lacks its own form?
O King, compared to which the great Mount Meru is but a spider's thread, within whose belly could there be millions of Merus and Mandaras?
By whom was this universe, consisting of many consciousnesses, stretched out? Of what essence are you that you thus leap about, strike, and protect?
By seeing what do you not exist, or rather, surely you truly exist? Speak that for the sake of the pacification of those who have unequal vision.
Let this great doubt of mine—the foul coating upon the mist of the face of the mind’s splendor—now dissolve;
for that doubt which does not dissolve before him never reaches the state of being called "learned," even when its roots are fully uprooted.
O wise ones, if you do not lead him to me through the gradual discourse that brings peace and resolves his slight doubts, then you will,
in an instant and without obstacle, swiftly become fuel for the fire in the belly of that Rākṣasa.
Afterwards, with my vast belly, I shall swallow that entire circle of your realm on all sides in an instant;
thus it occurs to you as if you were a good king, but I think that for fools, excessive indulgence leads only to their destruction.

Having spoken thus with a voice as deep and resonant as a vast thundercloud, that night-stalker, with words made manifest by her radiant splendor, remained silent; yet even in silence, she of exceedingly formidable form appeared like a circle of pure, autumnal clouds within the inner apartments.
The Eightieth Sarga, titled "The Question of the Rākṣasī," by Vasiṣṭha:
When this great question had been posed by the daughter of a great rākṣasa in the great forest at the dead of night, the great master of mantras gave his reply.
The minister said:
"Listen, O cloud-like one; I shall resolve this question of yours, just as a lion tears apart a rutting lordly elephant in due order."
"O lotus-eyed lady, you have described this Supreme Self through these very words, which are capable of awakening one who knows Brahman."
Because it is inexpressible and inaccessible, it is beyond the range of even the minds;
thus the atomic self is pure consciousness alone, subtler even than space.
Within the supreme, atomic consciousness, existence itself remains as if non-existent;
even this world, though it is pure being, manifests as if it were non-being.
Because it possesses some degree of experience, it exists as the nature of emanation;
having previously attained the existence of being through that very nature, so it is said.
Because it is beyond the senses, there is nothing [perceived]; that very atom is infinite.
And because it consists of all things, it enjoys everything, yet by that very fact, it enjoys nothing at all.
From the manifestation of the single consciousness, its manifoldness is proclaimed;
though it is unreal, it is as real as the state of being a bracelet in gold.
This is the subtle atom, the supreme ether, more minute than even space and unperceived;
it transcends the six senses including the mind, and remains as the self of all, even while existing.
If it were the self of all, it would never be empty;
one who says that what exists does not exist is considered a madman.
By no reasoning whatsoever is it logical here that what exists should be non-existent;
rather, its nature as the all-pervading self is revealed by one who remains hidden, like camphor in a hollowed-out pit.
That very same atom of pure consciousness exists here as everything whatsoever in its dense form;
yet it remains stainless, being nothing at all because its nature transcends the senses.
He alone is both one and many, because he is the self-experience of all beings;
he alone sustains this world, as well as millions of worlds.

These creatures are the waves of the water that is the triple world within the great ocean of your consciousness; they shimmer in those waters like the appearance of circularity arising from fluidity.
Because it cannot be apprehended by the mind, the senses, and so forth, it is subtle (*aṇu*), empty, and possesses a solid nature;
yet, because it can be apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), even though its form is like space (*vyoma*), it is non-empty.
Thus, O Lord, having emerged from existence itself due to the perception of duality,
I was born as you— possessing a body vastened by awakening— while you were becoming yourself.
Through the realization that swallows up everything consisting of "thou-ness" and "I-ness," there arises spontaneously neither "you," nor "I," nor "all," nor "not-all."
Though this atom has traversed a multitude of yojanas, it does not "go";
for by means of cognition, the state of being a multitude of yojanas resides within that very atom.
Though it has gone, it does not go; though it has arrived, it has not come, because it dwells within the treasury of its own being, beyond space and time.
Where indeed can he go whose destination resides within his own body? Is a son situated in the hollow of his mother's breast seen by her anywhere else?
For him whose great domain is accessible and remains inexhaustible as long as existence endures—
who dwells within and is the creator of all— how and where could he go?
Just as when a jar has reached another location with its opening well-sealed,
there is no coming or going of the space within it, so it is for the self.
When both consciousness and insentience exist within it as its internal states, characterized by experience, then it is indeed twofold: both conscious and insentient.
O Rākṣasī, when the sentient stone-being is of one essence with consciousness itself, then that very sentient being is like a stone.
In the supreme, beginningless and endless void, by means of the singular atom of pure consciousness,
this manifold and variegated triple world was created by that which is itself uncreated.

Through the cognition of that [fire], the existence of fire is established; thus, although it is omnipresent and the cooker of the substances of the world, it does not burn while retaining its fiery form.
Blazing forth from the stainless sky with a radiant form,
the fire, whose sole essence is consciousness, is born from that [space].
Because it is conscious, that [Self] is the illuminator within the Pradhāna;
its primordial nature as light does not perish even by the clouds at the end of a great aeon.
Unattainable by the eyes, consisting of pure experience, the lamp illuminating the chamber of the heart,
bestowing existence upon all, and infinite— that is remembered as the Supreme Light.
From this [reality], which transcends the six senses including the mind, light proceeds;
by means of it, there occurs within even among objects the wonder of the visible and the invisible.

That subtle atom [of consciousness], which consists of the nature of experience and is luminous, takes the form of the sensation of height (growth) even in non-sensory things such as creepers, shrubs, and sprouts.

Because time, space, action, existence, and intrinsic nature are self-cognized, [the Self] is the master, the agent, the father, and the enjoyer; yet, because its nature is space-like, it is nothing at all.
Without abandoning its atomicity, that atom is a casket for the jewels of the world;
within that cognition, the world exists as the nature of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
He alone shines clearly everywhere throughout the entire world;
when this world arises, he is then that supreme jewel.
Because it is difficult to perceive, that [self] is darkness; because it is pure consciousness, it is the seer of light.
It exists because its nature is awareness; yet it is non-existent insofar as it transcends the senses.
