It is distant because it cannot be grasped by the senses; yet, being of the nature of consciousness, it is not far away.
Because it perceives everything, it is the mountain; and though it is this very same [reality], it is indeed the atom.
That which appears as this world is merely that consciousness;
mountains and such things do not truly exist, and therefore the state of being Mount Meru exists only in the atom.
For the appearance of a momentary blink is called a "blink," and the appearance of an entire eon is expressed by the word "eon."
For the playful manifestation of the activities of an eon appears in a mere instant,
like a great city many yojanas wide appearing within the mind.
For within the hollow of a single blink of an eye, the tumultuous activity of an eon arises,
like the construction of a great city within a stainless mirror.
Where even millions of yojanas, kalpas, mountains, oceans, and cities exist within a single atom,
how can there be duality or unity there?
For the thought "I did this previously" arises in the mind;
in an instant, both the real and the unreal appear, as illustrated by the delusions of a dream.
For in suffering time is indeed very long, while in happiness it is always much shorter;
thus was the night of Hariścandra said to have lasted twelve years.
Whatever certainty arises within, whether it be true or even untrue,
shines forth like the nature of bracelets and other ornaments in gold, or like waves in the ocean.
There is no twinkling of an eye, nor is there a kalpa; there is no proximity, nor is there distance.
Thus, the manifestation of the atom of consciousness remains as neither different nor non-different entities.

Between light and darkness, between the distant and the near, between a moment and an eon— between these two which are but the single sheath of consciousness, there is not even the slightest difference.
Because it is the essence of the senses, it is direct perception; yet because it transcends them, it is not [merely] perceptible.
By virtue of its very visibility, it arises as consciousness, and as such, it is the Seer whose true nature is reality.
As long as there is the perception of a bracelet, there is no gold at all;
and as long as there is the occurrence of visibility, that subtle essence does not exist at all.
When the bracelet, which is perceived as an object, is destroyed, just as the nature of gold remains pervasive,
only the pure, awakened Brahman alone remains.
Because it is everything, this [Self] has the nature of existence; because it is difficult to perceive, it has the nature of non-existence.
It is conscious because its essence is consciousness, yet it is unconscious because there is no possibility of anything being cognized by it.

In this world, which consists of nothing but the wonder of consciousness and is of the nature of its own manifestation— resembling a tree moved by the wind— how can there be any differentiation between consciousness and the object of consciousness?
Just as the appearance of water in a mirage belongs to the heat of the sun,
so too the appearance of the world as a single, plump, non-dual entity is the manifestation of consciousness.
That which is free from affliction, fashioned from rays more subtle than the sun’s,
wherein existence and non-existence are absent— what thought could there be of it, such as one has for a wall or similar objects?
Just as gold shines in the sky marked by illusory particles of dust, so does this world appear; for where is there any distinction between consciousness and its objects?

Just as in a dream, a city of Gandharvas, or a city of one's imagination, there is no perception of walls— being neither existent nor non-existent— know the long-lasting delusion of the world to be likewise.
And thus, those who see things as they truly are, purified by the practice of cultivating such reasoning, emerge through the wall as if through space.
There is no difference between the wall and space except for firm perception;
whatever has become established from Brahma down to the individual soul (jīva), that remains firmly established as such.
In the stainless sky of appearances, emptiness— devoid of pillars and walls—
shines forth through its own density, like rays of light within a mass of radiance.
The appearance of distinctness arises through its connection with its own creative wonder;
for the supreme manifestation (pratibhā) is the soul of all things, like a seed that contains the essence of the tree.
Just as the potentiality of a tree within a seed is seen as manifold yet perceived as one,
so too is the world— though beyond counting— the peaceful Brahman, like the expanse of space.
Just as the state of non-duality with space exists within a tree that is contained inside a seed,
so too does the unagitated state of space exist within the world that is contained within Brahman.
All is peaceful, unborn, one, without beginning or middle; here there is no part whatsoever, nor any mental constructions in any way.
Remain established in that which is free from duality, tranquil, transcendent, manifold yet pure, appearing as form, and fully blossoming as the One.
The eighty-first canto, titled "The Differentiation of Questions," [concerning] the Rākṣasīs.
"Oh, how purifying is this speech on the ultimate truth from your minister!
Let this lotus-eyed king speak now."
The King said:
"This wind arises from subtle sensation, and the wind [itself] exists through the vision of delusion;
therefore, there is nothing such as wind and so forth—there is only pure consciousness."
Because sound is perceived [as such], it is a sound; and that [perception] is a mistaken vision.
Therefore, in this case, the view of the word and the meaning of the word has gone very far astray.
He is the atom, he is everything, and he is nothing; he is I, he is not I, and he is that very [Self].
For this Self, who possesses all powers, his own creative intuition alone is the cause here.
The self is to be attained through hundreds of efforts; yet once it is attained, nothing at all has been gained—except for that which is truly called "something supreme."
The creeper of worldly existence blossoms for a long time during the springs of birth only so long as awakening, which scrapes away the very roots, has not arisen.
By this subtle self-form, as if it were becoming visible, the mind— remaining in its own natural state— has, as it were, carried away the water by means of heat.

By means of this consciousness, having vomited out the diversity of Meru, the three worlds, and the grass-like [universe]— which exists both within and without and is composed of illusion— one beholds it as such.
Whatever exists within the atom of consciousness is seen outside;
for the example here is that of a person possessed by passion, such as the embracing of a desired woman in a state of mental construction.
At the initial creation, consciousness, possessing all powers, perceives everything instantly by itself according to its own impelled nature, just like a volition or a thought.
Whatever appears within the mind of one whose disposition is noble, that he perceives as if it were truly so; in this regard, the mind of a child serves as the illustration.
Even by this atom, which is pure consciousness alone,
and which is most extremely subtle, the entire universe is filled throughout its every part.
This very subtle [self] does not fit even within hundreds of leagues;
because it is omnipresent and possesses a form that is without beginning or end, its nature is that of pure sensation.
Just as a child is led astray by a rogue or a cheat through the movements of his eyes, the play of his eyebrows, and his various gestures; //MU_3,81.14//
Just as the world, including its mountains and grass, is incessantly enacted through the pure light of consciousness by constantly unfolding its dramatic gestures, so too is it always performed.
Just as by a minute cloth, because it possesses an infinite form,
one might imagine Mount Meru and other such things wrapped within it, so too does consciousness exist externally.
Because its nature is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is greater than Mount Meru;
yet, being composed of even a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, it is subtle, the supreme atom.

Indeed, a statement of equality between that which has the nature of the space of pure consciousness and an atom does not shine forth, just like [the comparison] between Mount Meru and a mustard seed.

The state of being a minute atom through the power of illusion (māyā) and the state of being the Supreme Self when free from illusion— there can be no equality between these two, just as there is none between gold and its form as a bracelet.
By this lamp, which consists of experience, illumination is made manifest;
for without it, that [illumination] would indeed exist preceded by the destruction of its own existence.
If the entire world, including the sun and so forth, were to become a single inert mass, then what would the self be? What would its form be? Where would light exist, or of what nature would it be?
That which is pure existence consisting of consciousness alone, established by itself within its own self—
that very same thing is seen by the individual soul as if it were a mass of light existing externally.
The radiances of the sun, the moon, and fire are not distinct from the mass of darkness;
the only difference here is that there is whiteness and blackness in their color.
Just as there is a distinction between collyrium and frost, or between clouds and mist,
such is the established difference between light and darkness.
It is said that when the sun of consciousness shines upon these two inert things so that they may be perceived, by that means they attain a state of identity with the existence [of consciousness].
The one Sun alone shines tirelessly day and night, both within and without, even inside stones and other such things, without setting or rising.
Because of that celebrated Self, this triple world appears as a hut for the living being—
a hut rich with various vessels of perception and possessing a hard interior.
By this [sun], which destroys the body of darkness, you are the darkness itself;
yet, through its radiant light, all darkness is illuminated.
Just as the lotus and the water-lily are manifested by the shining sun,
so too are existence and consciousness manifested by light and darkness respectively.
Just as the sun, by its daily revolution, reveals forms,
so too does consciousness, having fashioned both the existent and the non-existent, reveal form.
Within the atom of consciousness exist atoms of diverse experiences,
just as within a sweet mango fruit reside the splendors of its leaves, flowers, and fruits.
These atoms of complete experience arise from the atom of consciousness,
like various successions of flower-clusters from the essence of the spring season.
The supreme atom, being utterly devoid of flavor due to its subtlety,
yet being the sole generator of the existence of all flavors, tastes itself.
Whatever taste whatsoever, having established its existence within itself,
does not exist by its own nature apart from that [consciousness], just like a reflection in a mirror.
By that which consists of the supreme atom of pure consciousness, everything relied upon has been abandoned;
through non-perception the world was abandoned, and through perception everything has been embraced.
Even though it is incapable of protecting itself, consciousness has covered the entire world by spreading its own supreme atomicity like a canopy.
One whose nature is like the sky of the supreme self is unable to protect oneself,
even for a moment or in the slightest degree, just as an elephant cannot protect itself in a grove of durva grass.
Nevertheless, having pervaded the universe, he conceals his omniscience in an instant;
oh, how dense is the illusion of the Sustainer of the World, like a child!
This world lives by the subtle guidance of pure consciousness alone,
like a variegated forest row brought to life by the infusion of the essence of spring.
This very consciousness alone has arisen from itself as the entire world;
for a grove of trees is indeed diverse, vibrant with the essence of the spring season.
Know for certain that this world is indeed nothing but the reality consisting of consciousness;
know that these sprouts and shrubs are nothing but the very essence of the spring.
Because it is the essence of all composite parts, it possesses a thousand rays and eyes;
this very thing is the supreme atom, eternally arising without parts.
Since even within the perception of a fraction of a moment,
the atom of consciousness manifests a flood of thousands of kalpas, like the succession of childhood and old age in a dream.
Then even that atom of a moment expands sufficiently for hundreds of millions of eons through the play of all existence, for it is indeed a single intuition that unfolds.
Just as the conviction "I have eaten" arises even when one has not yet eaten,
so too does the determination of conceptual construction arise within a moment.
Those possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā) are seen to have the conviction, "I have eaten," even though they have not eaten, just as one perceives one's own death in a dream.
The worlds rest within the supreme atom, the conscious self;
for it is from that very source that the manifestations of the world proceed.
Whatever exists in something arises from that very thing; indeed, it is that [itself].
Modifications and the like are observed in that which possesses form, but not in the stainless sky.
All beings that exist now, and all those that will exist in the future, abide within consciousness, like trees within the seed of their potential power.
By this [consciousness], an eyelid's blink and an eon are rolled together like two grains of rice;
yet it is not constituted by these two, for it is an atom whose nature is its own self-awareness.
Sitting like one who is indifferent, this ethereal Self, though performing even the worlds, is not touched in the slightest by the states of being an enjoyer or a doer.
For this world arises from the atoms of pure consciousness; and as for the states of being an enjoyer and an agent, where indeed could they reside apart from that supreme atom?
Nothing whatsoever is ever created by anyone at any time, nor does anything whatsoever ever perish; this is the refutation of the primordial Māyā.
O Rākṣasī, know that all this which appears as the flavor of equanimity, contained within the treasury of space and designated by various synonymous terms for the world, is in fact nameless.
The atomic consciousness, for the sake of establishing the visible world, assumes an internal flash of consciousness—
which resides within itself by its own nature— in the form of an external appearance.

This [reality] exists both externally and internally; it resides in the word, not in the physical object, because the nature of consciousness pervades the three worlds for the sake of instructing sentient beings.
The seer, moving toward the state of the seen, perceives himself as if the eye were falling upon the visible; thus the existent appears as if it were non-existent.
The seer does not attain visibility, for he is non-existent and unreal;
since nothing whatsoever exists even within the self, how could it appear before one?
Vision itself is the eye, and that latent impression (vāsanā) is its own inherent form;
having manifested as the object of sight through its manifold forms, it arises as the seer.
The existence of the object of vision can never be without the state of being a seer,
just as there is no son without a father, nor unity without the state of duality.

The seer alone becomes the object of sight; there is no such thing as "seership" apart from that [object], just as there is no son without a father, nor any state of being an object of enjoyment without one who enjoys.
For the seer possesses the capacity to manifest the object of vision precisely because of its nature as consciousness,
just as pure gold has the capacity to take the form of a bracelet.
Since the object of perception is insentient, it lacks the capacity to create the perceiver,
just as the delusion of being a bracelet has no power in the creation of gold.
From volition, consciousness shines forth as the manifestation of the visible world, which is itself non-existent;
being without cause, it is the ground of delusion, just as gold appears in the illusory form of a bracelet.
For just as when there is the appearance of being a bracelet, the goldness of the gold does not cease to manifest as real,
so too the nature of the seer remains manifest even while the object of sight persists.
For the seer, abiding as the object of sight, seems to abandon its state of being a seer,
just as gold loses its appearance as a bracelet when there is the cognition of it as pure gold.
In a single manifestation, there is no existence of both the seer and the seen; when the cognition of the Puruṣa shines forth, where could the cognition of a bound soul (paśu) arise?
While perceiving the visible object, the seer does not perceive itself;
for when the seer falls into the state of being an object of sight, it remains as if its very existence were non-existent.
For the seer from whom the visible has dissolved through awakening, only pure existence shines forth,
just as gold remains gold even when it is not recognized as such in the form of a bracelet.
When the object of vision does not exist, the seer does not exist; when the seer does not exist, the object of vision does not exist.
Without these two, there is no unity, nor is there even non-unity between them.
Having understood everything as it truly is, for one whose self consists of pure consciousness,
there remains only a certain state of composure that is beyond the reach of words.
The self, the seer, and the seen are illuminated by it as if by a lamp;
everything is accomplished by this single atom of pure consciousness.
The triad known as the object, the means of knowledge, and the knower is swallowed up within the intellect,
just as the unreal forms of bracelets and other ornaments appear within gold.
Just as water is not even slightly separate from its waves and so forth,
so indeed nothing at all is separate from this atom of intrinsic nature.
Because its nature consists of the experience of all things, and because it takes the form of the experience of everything,
when the experience of oneness is established as logical, his identity with all things indeed becomes firm.
By his will, there is a distinctness [of objects] like that of waves from the great ocean,
for he has attained the fulfillment of his desires and possesses the singular realization of all things.
The Supreme Self alone exists, unconditioned by space, time, and so forth;
because it is the self of all, it is the universal self by virtue of its own inherent experience of all.
This [Self] is existent because its nature is consciousness, and non-existent because of the lack of awakening;
yet here, in the Great Self whose form is truth, neither duality nor unity exists.
If there were some second [to the one], then oneness would belong to that one;
for the establishment of duality and unity is mutually dependent, like sunlight and shadow.
For where there is no second, how can there be oneness for that which is one? If oneness is not established, duality itself does not exist.
This being the case, that which remains here would be empty because it lacks any stable existence;
therefore, its form is not distinct [from the mind], just as fluidity is not distinct from water.
Vast with its manifold undertakings, yet in its equilibrium of undisturbed form,
the world exists within Brahman like a tree within a seed.
Duality, too, is not separate from that [Reality], just as the state of being a bracelet is not separate from gold;
for when the cognition of identity is awakened, duality exists yet is not composed of reality.
Just as liquidity belongs to water, motion to the wind,
and emptiness to space, so indeed is duality not separate from the Lord.
For this perception of duality and non-duality leads to suffering for one whose nature is subject to decay;
however, those who are skillful know that the non-perception of these two is the supreme state.
The knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth—the seer, the seeing, and the seen:
this much is the world, and it all resides within the consciousness of a single atom.
How is it that this atom of a world is eternally held within its own body by this atom of Mount Sumeru, just as movement is sustained by the wind?
"Aha! Is this not a terrifying illusion, or rather, a supreme power of illusion, since the succession of the three worlds exists within a single atom?"
Moreover, this state of being like an illusion has always existed;
the world exists as nothing more than the subtlest atom of pure consciousness alone.
Although containing within itself the entire web of the world, this atom does not abandon its own size;
it remains as it is, like a seed containing a vast tree within the belly of a vessel.
Just as the expansion of a tree, complete with its fruits and shoots, exists within a seed,
so too does the world exist within the atom of consciousness when viewed with the supreme vision.

Just as a tree remains situated within the hollow of its seed without abandoning its nature as a tree with branches and fruit, so too does the world abide within the radiant atom of consciousness (cidaṇu).
He who perceives the world as existing within a single atom of consciousness— as a duality established [within it] like the seed-vessel of non-duality— he truly sees.
There is neither duality nor non-duality; neither seed nor sprout;
neither gross nor subtle; neither unborn nor indeed born.

This triple world exists neither as being nor as non-being, O gentle one; it is neither pleasant nor agitated. Within the atom of consciousness, there is either no sentient being at all, or nothing whatsoever.
Neither the world nor the non-world exists; there exists only the supreme atomic consciousness.
Since it is the self of all, whatever arises wherever and in whatever manner, it appears exactly as such.
Though unarisen, this supreme atomic self, which is the single essence manifested through self-awareness, arises as if it were the totality of all selves within the void.
Though it is without arising, the supreme reality emerges as if having become a tree, or as if becoming a seed,
through the dissolution of the world and the emergence of the destruction of the world.
Just as a tree does not quickly abandon its state of being a seed,
so too the supreme atom remains, having neither abandoned nor not abandoned its lack of motion.
The great Mount Meru is like a fiber of a lotus stalk when compared to the supreme atom;
for indeed, what is visible as a fiber in a lotus stalk is the state of being the supreme self to one whose eye is invisible.
It is said that the great Mount Meru is like a spider's thread within the atom of the Self;
indeed, millions of Merus and other such worlds reside within that very same dense mass.

By this and that great atom, the entire manifold array of the universe is pervaded, extended, fashioned, produced, and created; like space itself, the all-pervading emptiness is obtained as pure on every side.

As if not abandoning its own form— which is more beautiful through duality— yet having attained oneness with the Supreme Consciousness through a state resembling deep sleep, the world thus remains as the very essence of ultimate reality, free from coming, going, and staying.
The eighty-second canto, titled "The Compendium of the Ultimate Reality of the World," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having heard this from the mouth of the king, Karkaṭī, like a forest monkey, realized that the king was standing right at her feet and abandoned her jealousy and fickleness.
She attained inner coolness, contentment, rest, and freedom from distress,
like a peahen at the onset of the rainy season, or like a night-lotus under the moonlight.
By those words of the king, Ānanda was greatly moved within,
just as the embryo of a female crane is stirred within her by the roar of a rain-cloud in the sky.
Rākṣasī:
Oh, how pure this intellect of yours shines!
It is illuminated by the sun of awakening, whose essence has not yet set.
This pure, tranquil, and equanimous drop of discernment has been seen by us emerging from your hearts, like moonlight from the orb of the moon.
I consider those like you, who possess discernment and are honored by the world, to be worthy of service;
through association with you, I have blossomed like a night-lotus at the sight of the moon.
Just as fragrance arises from contact with flowers, so does auspiciousness arise from association with the virtuous;
it is like the blossoming of lotuses through contact with the sun.
Only through association with the great does suffering no longer afflict one;
for who indeed, with a lamp-flame in hand, can be overcome by darkness?
Since you two, who are like suns upon the earth, have arrived here in the forest, you are worthy of worship; therefore, let your auspicious desire be told quickly.
The King said:
"O Mañjarī of the Rakṣasa clan, in our kingdom you constantly afflict the people excessively, causing them a piercing pain in their hearts."
Since all people are now perpetually afflicted by severe cholera,
I have therefore departed tonight on my nocturnal journey from this circle of men.
When the piercing pains in the hearts of men do not subside through medicines,
then I emerge for the sake of mantras and other means taught by those such as you.
And my exertion for the sake of restraining people like you, who strike down the simple-minded, may it fully attain success.
O auspicious lady, you should indeed accept this much alone:
that henceforth you must not take the life of anyone at all.
The Rākṣasī said: "Certainly, my Lord; from this day forward, I shall act thus without fail.
This is the truth; indeed, nothing at all shall be harmed by me henceforth."
The King said:
"If this is so, O lotus-eyed one, who subsist solely upon the body of another, what would be the use of maintaining your own physical existence while remaining intent on my desire?"
Rākṣasī:
O King, after six hundred years, having awakened from my meditative absorption, the thought of food has arisen; this desire for food is mine today.
Now, having gone to the summit, she remains there at ease for as long as she desires, motionless in that very meditation like a living statue carved from a *sāla* tree.
Having bound the concentration on the nectar of immortality (*āmṛtī-dhāraṇā*), I maintain this little body;
it is my intention that I shall eventually cast it off at will.
O King, from this moment until the abandonment of my body, I must not harm the lives of others; therefore, listen to these words of mine.
There is a mountain named Himavat, pure as the rays of the moon in its luster, which,
at the heart of the northern quarter, has touched both the eastern and western oceans.
There I dwell in that formidable cave-house with golden peaks,
a Rākṣasī named Karkaṭī, like an iron pillar-line.
Brahmā was entreated by me through ascetic penance with the desire to bring about the destruction of living beings, [saying]: "May I become a life-taking cholera, yet remain subtle. (MU 3.82.23)
Therefore, having obtained this boon, for many groups of years I have existed as cholera, tormenting people by piercing their vital breaths.
"A great mantra was established for me by Brahmā with the purpose of restraint: 'You must not harm those who possess virtue. I remain standing, entirely dependent upon that."
Therefore, let this be accepted by him; by that, all the piercing pain in the hearts of this world will come to rest—what then need be said regarding the delusion caused by me?
Indeed, I have desisted from violence; because of that which was previously committed by me against people, my bodily channels have fallen into a state of distress.
Those people whom I abandoned after having harmed their blood and flesh— those who were born from the channels of Vidhura are also like that.
O King, this mantra for curing cholera has indeed been perfected by you;
for there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished by those possessed of courage.
Therefore, O King, quickly take up that mantra which has been proclaimed by the Brahmins for the complete pacification of pains within the sheaths of the bad channels.
"Come near the river, O King; let us go there. Once you have sipped water for purification and are self-restrained, I, who am firm in my vows, shall give [it] to you."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, during that night, those ministers of the Rākṣasa king,
having developed mutual affection for one another, went to the bank of the river.

Having thus ascertained the Rākṣasī’s friendship through both positive and negative concomitance, those two, who dwelt at the edge [of the forest], remained there after having sipped water for purification.
Instructed by her in this way, he was then given by those two,
out of affection, the mantra for cholera (viṣūcikā) in due order, which grants success through recitation.
Then, having developed mutual affection, when that night-stalker woman prepared to depart after taking her leave, the king spoke these words.
The King said:
"O Great Queen, you are our elder and our companion; may you be at ease.
O lotus-beautiful one, we both earnestly invite you."
You ought not to render our request in vain;
for the goodwill of virtuous people increases simply from the sight [of them].
Having assumed a charming form endowed with light splendor,
come to our house, O auspicious one, and stay there at your ease.
Rākṣasī:
"O you who can give food to one wearing the form of an innocent woman,
with what will you satisfy me, who am wearing the form of a rākṣasī?"
This food of mine is indeed for the satisfaction of a Rakshasa, not the meal of an ordinary person;
this innate nature, established from of old, increases until the end of the creation.
The King said:
"O blameless one, remain for some days in my house in the form of my wife, adorned with garlands of golden flowers, for as long as you desire."
Then, having brought from the districts hundreds of thousands of wicked thieves deserving of death, he gave them to you, O Subhojanā.
Having abandoned his beloved form and assumed the body of a rākṣasa,
he took up those hundreds of men whom he had previously gathered for slaughter.
"Lead me to a peak of the Himalayas; there, enjoy yourself as you please.
For the consumption of great quantities of food is indeed pleasant in solitude."
Having abandoned sleep while asleep, become once more possessed of meditative absorption;
having again desisted from absorption, come back once more at another time.
You will not desire to kill other men who are to be slain; for this violence is not in accordance with Dharma, and indeed, violence committed according to one's own duty is equal to great compassion.
And you shall certainly meet me again when you emerge from your meditative absorption;
for even among the wicked, a firmly rooted bond of friendship does not perish.
The Rākṣasī said: "O King, you have spoken rightly; O friend, I shall do exactly as you say.
Who would not welcome the words of one who acts out of friendship?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that playful Rākṣasī there became manifest,
wearing necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and garlands of woven flowers.
Having said, "O King, come, let us go," the king and his minister set out to walk ahead at night, while she followed behind them.
Then, having reached the king’s palace, they spent that night together in a delightful house, conversing with one another with great respect.
At dawn, he stayed within the inner apartments amidst the playful diversions of the women; meanwhile, the Rākṣasī and the minister-king each attended to their respective duties.
Then, over the course of six days, the king collected [wealth] from the inner palaces of other kings as well as from his own circle of territories.
He gave those three thousand condemned men to her;
at nightfall, she herself became that fierce, black Rākṣasī.
He took those thousands of victims upon his circle of arms,
just as a row of clouds holds masses of raindrops within its hollow.
Having taken leave of the king, she returned to that very peak of the Himalayas,
like a poor woman who has acquired gold returning to her home, though her body remained formidable.
There, having eaten her fill and slept happily for two days, she awoke again, exceedingly clear and once more possessed of meditative absorption.
In either five or three years, she fully awakens;
thereafter, she enters that mandala and is honored by that king.
There, having spent some time with them in conversations filled with confidence, she then took those condemned men and returned to her own abode.
Thus, as one liberated while living, that demoness remains even today in that very forest,
staying on that same mountain with her mind’s one-pointedness of meditation dissolved.
When that king had attained peace, having himself abandoned all desires,
she remained for a long time in that kingdom, enjoying her own portions through the affection of the ruler.
The eighty-third canto, titled "The Friendship with the Rākṣasīs," by Vasiṣṭha.
In that Kirāta region, whatever kings there may be,
with each and every one of them she develops the highest friendship.
There, that Rākṣasī, perfected in yoga, wards off all great portents, even the fears of Piśācas and the like, as well as diseases.
Having not ceased from meditation for many groups of years,
she comes there and devours the well-accumulated creatures she has slain.
Even today, those who are to be executed there are still offered by the king for that purpose; for who indeed would not be resolute in honoring a friend?
While she sat absorbed in meditation within that circle of Kirātas,
a long period of time passed without her returning, for the sake of pacifying the faults of the people.
That goddess, named Kandarā and known by other inauspicious names,
was driven far away into the depths of a dense forest within the city.
From that time forward, whichever ruler of the earth was there,
he himself would install the Blessed One Kandarā.
That base king who does not establish either caves or fortresses, his subjects will diligently strike him down with a multitude of calamities.
By worshipping that, a person obtains the desired fruit;
by not worshipping it, one incurs misfortune, as it swells with power through the force of its own inherent nature.
That goddess is worshipped with the customary rites of the world of the slayable;
even now, residing within the image, she bestows the fruits that reside in the mind.

Victorious is that supreme goddess of long standing, who brings auspiciousness to all the world, who has devoured all great beings worthy of slaughter, and who dwells here among the Kirāta people, possessed of ultimate awakening.
The story of Sūcī is concluded;
this is the eighty-fourth canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus has this entire, irreproachable narrative concerning the forest-dwelling ogress Karkaṭī been told to you exactly and in proper sequence.
Rāma said:
"O Lord, how did that black ogress come to be called Karkaṭī as described in the caves of the Himavat? Tell me this exactly as it happened."
Vasiṣṭha said:
There are many lineages of Rākṣasas by their very nature;
they are black, white, green, and brilliant.
A Rākṣasa named Karkaṭa, who resembled a crab, existed;
born of him, that Kṛṣṇā became a female crab (karkaṭī) with the form of a crab.
This has been told by me to you in connection with the inquiry concerning the Karkaṭī, within the context of spiritual discourse for the purpose of defining the nature of consciousness.
Thus, although it is incomplete in comparison to that which is complete, this world is clearly [manifest] from the single, supreme cause, the state that is without beginning or end.
Just as future waves exist in the water as both distinct from and non-distinct from it,
so too do other present creations exist [within the same substrate].
Just as fire, even while not burning within pieces of wood, performs a causal function—such as removing the cold—for monkeys and other creatures; ||| MU_3,84.8 |||
Without ever abandoning its equanimity and its state of eternal radiance,
Brahman thus creates this manifold world as if it were a diverse creator.
Has this very creation already arrived even before it has come to be?
O consciousness of the wooden statue, you have become as well-awakened as if you were made of wood!
Just as the fruit and so forth, though not different from the seed, arise as if they were different;
so too, the object of cognition, though not different from consciousness, arises as if it were different.

Because there is no severance of their single existence, there is no difference whatsoever between the fruit and the seed, nor between consciousness and its object, just as there is none between water and its waves in a single reality.
Without inquiry, no distinction between these two is possible;
whatever [distinction] has arisen from any cause whatsoever perishes through inquiry.
O scion of Raghu, let this delusion depart just as it came;
once awakened, you will understand this—simply let it go.
Once the knot of delusion has been severed by listening to my words,
you will yourself fully understand the reality behind the distinctions between knowledge, words, and their objects.
This misfortune and prosperity arise from the mind; and that mind, as well as this other [body], will undoubtedly attain peace simply by hearing my words.
"Everything has arisen from Brahman, and everything is indeed Brahman"— having been fully awakened by my words, you shall understand this thoroughly, O blameless one.
Rāma:
Therefore, O Brahmin, the ablative case here has the sense of distinction (*vyatireka*), as in "this [is] from that.
But why do you say that "everything is non-different from the Lord of Gods" as well?
Vasiṣṭha:
In the treatises, a word produced for the purpose of instruction arises either from a [conventional] meaning or from a [logical] object;
it possesses the exclusion of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogivyavaccheda*), as well as the properties of number and definition.
This distinction is indeed perceived through conventional usage, but it is not real;
it is merely imagined for the sake of practical action, like a ghost conjured up for a child.
In that state where things abide according to their true nature, there is neither duality nor unity;
how could such a corruption of conceptual construction exist therein?
For just as the relationship between cause and effect is characterized by that of property and owner,
so too is the sequence of the parts [of a syllogism] constituted by the reason and that which possesses the reason.
The delusion of transformation as either distinct or non-distinct,
as well as the modifications of existence, knowledge and ignorance, and pleasure and pain [arise from this].

Thus, this [world] consists of such things, woven together by the fabrication of false conceptualizations for the sake of awakening the ignorant; however, there is no actual division in the reality itself.
This distinction exists due to lack of realization; once known, duality is no longer found.
When known, all mental constructions are stilled, and only silence remains.
"At the time of attaining realization, having reached enlightenment, you will know it as the supreme, one, without beginning or end, undivided, and indivisible."
For those who have not awakened conceptualize through the manifestations of their own mental constructions;
this discourse exists because of instruction, but once [reality] is known, duality is no longer found.
The relationship between the signified and the signifier is not established without duality;
yet duality is not possible, whether there be silence or speech—enough of this!
O scion of Raghu’s line, having fixed your intellect upon the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) and disregarding the diversity of words, listen to that which I now say.
Having arisen from somewhere, the mind—like a city of the Gandharvas—is born;
it extends this mere illusion called the world as its own unfolding.
O sinless one, listen as I tell you this illustration for understanding creation: how the mind spreads out this world-illusion, just so it is. MU 3.84.31.
O Rāma, having heard this, you yourself will become certain that all this is merely illusion, and you will cast away latent tendencies far behind you.
The three worlds are nothing but a creation of mental ideation;
having relinquished everything, you, with a tranquil self, shall dwell in your own self alone.
Intent on grasping the meaning of my words, you shall also exert effort in treating the mental affliction by applying the medicinal ointment of discernment.
This being the case, it is the mind alone that expands here as the form of the world;
the body and so forth do not exist, like oil within sand.
Mind alone is saṃsāra when defiled by the afflictions such as passion; that very same mind, when freed from them, is called the end of existence.
The mind must be cultivated, protected, investigated, and acted upon like a noble person; it must be uplifted, engaged in worldly conduct, moved forward, and held with reverence.
In this way, the mind bears the manifold triple world within itself;
like a peacock’s egg, it unfolds in due time.
That which is this cognitive aspect of the mind is the seed-nature of all objects;
and that which is its insentient aspect, my friend, is this world—a delusion.
This earth and the rest did not exist at all at the beginning of creation;
like one seeing a formless dream, the unborn one does not see them as they appear.
Through the long-lasting consciousness of creation and so forth, and through the consciousness of insentient things such as mountains,
the knower of the subtle perceives the body as subtle, empty, and not real.
The mind, whose nature is its own object of cognition, is pervaded by the all-pervading Self;
it is as stainless as the netherworld (ātala) is by the light of the sun, O gentle one.
Due to a lack of awakening, the fool of a mind falsely perceives the world as a demon;
through awakening, he perceives his own supreme form, free from all affliction.
Listen as I shall explain to you how the Self comes to appear as an object of perception, giving rise to the delusion of duality and unity, through the sequence of stories that are about to be told.
For that which is spoken with words endowed with heart-touching analogies and sweet, charming meanings, O dear one,
spreads throughout the listener's heart and pervades it entirely, like oil upon water, without hesitation.

Devoid of comparison, containing unpleasant words, difficult in meaning, agitated, hurried, and with syllables swallowed up, such speech does not enter the heart of the listener; it goes only to destruction, like clarified butter poured into ashes.

O virtuous one, whatever narratives exist on earth, whatever stories there may be, and whatever object of knowledge has been declared, however subtle— through the presentation of illustrative examples, all that quickly attains clarity in the world, just as the world does by means of the white-rayed moon.
The eighty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Sprouting of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
O sinless Raghava, since you have asked, I shall relate to you that which was formerly told to me by Brahmā during his discourse on the creation.
Indeed, in the past, I questioned the Blessed One, the Lotus-born:
"O Brahmā, how do these multitudes of creations come into being?"
Brahmā said: "In this way, indeed, this very mind manifests as such a reality,
like the vast and variegated whirlpools of a moving body of water."
Listen, my dear, to what occurred long ago in a certain previous aeon, when at the beginning of the day, having fully awakened, He desired to create the world of transmigration.
Once, at the end of the day, having withdrawn the entire creation,
I alone, one-pointed and composed, passed my night.
Having fully awakened at the end of the night and performed the twilight rites according to the prescribed rule,
I directed my wide gaze toward the sky in order to behold the subjects.
I beheld the sky, neither pervaded by darkness nor by light,
utterly expansive, empty, and devoid of limits.
Having resolved, "I shall bring forth this creation," I began to gaze upon the sky itself with a mind that was pure and subtle.
Then, in that vast expanse of space, I beheld with my mind various great undertakings— creations whose stability was unimpeded.
And they saw Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, together with the gods, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, uragas, and humans, all invisible to one another.
He [saw] Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Mahendra, and Malaya, along with the mountains,
the earth, and the rivers— ten of them, radiant in their number.
Within them, appearing as reflections of that [Brahman], the ten lotus-born ones reside, dwelling within the calyxes of lotuses and mounted upon vehicles drawn by royal swans.
While those ten worlds stood separate, with their rows of rising beings,
long tongues of flame blazing within them, and their radiant splendors shining throughout the universe.
The great rivers flow, and likewise the oceans roar;
the suns scorch with heat, and the winds flash across the sky.
The gods sport in heaven, human beings sport on earth,
and the Dānavas as well as the serpents dwell happily in the netherworlds.
The six auspicious seasons, all together, impelled by the wheel of time, adorn the earth on every side, filled with fruit according to the season.
The states of conduct, both auspicious and inauspicious, directed toward every quarter of the sky, have everywhere attained maturity, yielding the fruits of hell and heaven.
All classes of living beings, desiring the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, strive for their respective goals at the proper time and in the proper order.
The seven worlds, as well as the continents, oceans, and mountains,
observing the end of the eon, quiver with a most tremendous roar.
In some places it has become night; in others it remains steady.
It rests within mountain thickets, where darkness is swiftly overcome by fragments of light.
Within the blue lotus of the sky, the swarms of bees that are the clouds wander about;
the shimmering clusters of stars have become a profusion of filaments.
The dense mist at the end of the eon settled within the groves of Mount Meru like the pure cotton-wool of the Śālmali tree inside the hollows of its seed-pods.
The girdle of the Lokāloka mountain resounded with the roar of the ocean of battle;
it was enriched by the sapphire-like fragments of darkness and adorned with its own jewels.
Bearing the earth, which resounded with the humming of living beings,
she remained within the expanse of the world like a woman in her inner apartments.
Resplendent with the glow of the night situated amidst the rows of white clouds, the beauties of the year appear like garlands of lotuses and water-lilies.
The worlds of beings situated within the various internal layers appear individually,
glowing with light like pomegranate seeds in a cluster.
Flowing in three currents, traversing the three paths, and moving upward, downward, and across,
she appears like the sacred thread of the universe, shimmering with the stainless beauty of the crescent moon.
Moving here and there, they wither away and spring up again;
like lightning-flower creepers of the quarters, they are cloud-sprouts at the end of the wind.
Adorned with rows of celestial chariots, gardens, and cities of the Gandharvas,
the path of the ocean, the earth, and the sky shines forth brilliantly.
In other worlds, gods, asuras, humans, and serpents stood buzzing around the Saṅgha like gnats around udumbara trees.
Time, marked by ages, kalpas, moments, lavas, kalās, and kāṣṭhās,
flows on unperceived, awaiting the destruction of all things.
Having thus beheld this with my own pure and supreme splendor, I was struck with great wonder, thinking, "What is this? How can this be?"
How is it that with my fleshly eye I do not see anything at all,
yet with my mind I behold this incomparable net of illusion in the sky?
Then, after gazing for a long time at the sun from the sky with my mind alone, I brought him forth from that web of the world and questioned him.
"Come, O Lord of the gods of gods! O Bhāskara of great splendor!
Welcome to you!"—thus was he addressed by me, even though he had already been told [to come].
Who are you? How was this world born—whether as a single world or as many worlds?
O Blessed One, O sinless one, if you know this, please explain it to me.
Having been addressed thus, Arka then recognized me; having paid homage, he spoke these words with a voice of irreproachable cadence:
Thus was he addressed by me, and then that Arka recognized me; having paid obeisance, he spoke this with a voice of blameless cadence.
Bhānu said:
"Why do you not know that I have always been the cause even for this visible piśāca? Why, O Lord, do you ask me?"
Now, O all-pervading one, if your play consists in the sequence of my words,
then listen as I speak that which has arisen from the inconceivable.

O Great-Souled One, the mind, which is the very self of the Lord, shines forth here, expanded by its parts into "existent" and "non-existent"— parts that, through their vast arrays of forms, bestow the delusion of the distinction between the weight of error and reality.
The eighty-sixth canto, titled "The Meeting of Brahmā and Āditya," Canto 86.
Bhānu said:
O Great God, on the day before yesterday, at the foot of Mount Kailāsa, in a single corner of Jambudvīpa, while you were in a state of mental construction—
The glorious mandala, beautiful with abundant happiness, which was established by your sons—who have produced offspring—under the name Suvarṇajaṭa; ||| MU_3,86.2 |||
There lived a Brāhmaṇa named Indu, born of the lineage of Kaśyapa, who was exceedingly righteous, the best among the knowers of Brahman, and possessed of an extremely tranquil soul.
While he was dwelling there at that time among his own circle of kinsmen,
no son was born to him, just as there is not even a blade of grass in a desert.
That wife did not shine for him, like a straight, fair, and perfectly pure bamboo stalk that has flowered but bears no fruit, being empty within.
Then that distressed couple, for the sake of a son, ascended a shoulder of Mount Kailāsa to perform austerities, appearing like two forest trees grown upon it.
In that empty grove of Kailāsa, unobstructed by living beings,
those two performed severe penance, subsisting on water alone while remaining among the trees.
Having drunk a single handful of water at the end of the day, they remained standing motionless, subsisting on the practice of living like trees.
Then those two remained there, devoted to the life of forest-dwellers,
until the two ages of Tretā and Dvāpara had passed away.
Then the god who bears the crescent moon became pleased with the two of them, just as the moon is pleased with two night-blooming lilies scorched by the heat of the day.
He came to that place where the brahmin couple were,
a region of trees entwined with creepers, like the Lord [Śiva] coming to a grove of blossoming flowers.
The couple beheld Soma mounted upon his bull, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel and a face in full bloom, like the moon reflected in a white water-lily.
They both bowed down before that god, the Lord, who was as stainless as snow,
appearing like the full moon risen over heaven and earth.
Then Śiva, threatening with a sound like that of a forest of fresh bamboo shaken by the wind— gentle yet powerful, and radiating smiles— spoke these words.
Īśvara said:
"O Brahmin, accept a boon quickly; I am pleased with your desire.
Be as delighted as a forest of trees overwhelmed by the essence of the spring month."
The Brahmin said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, may ten sons of great intelligence be born to me,
by whom my grief shall no longer be afflicted."
Bhānu said:
"Then, saying 'So be it,' the Lord vanished;
having made a roar in the sky and the ocean, he became a great-bodied wave of water."
Then that couple, having obtained the boon from Śiva, went home satisfied,
like Umā and Maheśvara, resembling the gods as they returned through the sky.
There, that brahmin woman became pregnant with a noble child in her home;
with her belly full, the dark-complexioned lady shone like a streak of cloud filled with rainwater.
In due time, that charming woman gave birth to ten sons as tender as the crescent moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, just as the earth in the springtime brings forth fresh sprouts.
Having received the sacraments of Brahmā, those of great luster attained growth in a very short time, like new clouds in the rainy season.
Having reached the age of seven years, they became masters of the sciences;
they shone there with splendor like spotless planets in the sky.
Then, after a long time, those two parents of theirs, being skilled in knowing their destination, abandoned their bodies and attained their own state.
Then those ten Brahmins, deprived of their mother and father,
abandoned their home far behind and went to the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
Thereupon, those kinsmen, being deeply distressed, reflected and said this to one another: "What might be the highest good in this situation?"
O brothers, what in this world would be appropriate? What would be free from suffering?
What constitutes greatness, great sovereignty, or auspicious and vast prosperity?
How insignificant is this lack of sovereignty, for vassals have long been lords; what indeed is the wealth of a vassal, for kings are truly great lords?
What indeed is the prosperity of kings? Here, the sovereign emperor is the Maheśvara. What indeed is the prosperity of empire? For here, Indra is the Maheśvara.

What indeed is that thing called sovereignty over Indra which perishes in a mere moment of Prajāpati? What could that be here that is truly auspicious, which does not perish even at the end of an eon?
Then, while they were thus speaking, the eldest brother, who was high-minded and possessed of profound speech, spoke these words like a deer among herds of deer:
"O brothers, among all forms of sovereignty, that which does not perish until the end of the kalpa— that state of Brahmahood is what pleases me here, and nothing else."
Then all those excellent sons of the twice-born praised him with words inspired by Indra, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! MU 3.86.32.
And they said this: "O Father, how may we attain the lotus-seat, which wipes away all suffering, is worshipped by the world, and is the state of Viriñca?"
Then that brother spoke again to his brothers of great splendor:
"May all of you fully carry out everything that I have said."
May there be for you long-lasting meditation: "Seated upon the lotus throne, radiant, with the thought 'I am Brahmā,' I create and I withdraw. MU 3.86.35.
When the elder brother had spoken thus, those excellent ones, saying "So be it," remained together with their superior out of devotion, their minds intent upon meditation.
Having assumed the forms created by the painter and absorbed in meditation, those ten,
with their minds fixed within, reflected with great reverence.
Seated upon the high throne of the center of a blooming lotus bud,
I am Brahmā, the creator of the world, the agent, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord.
These excellent Vedas, endowed with the sequence of sacrificial rites and possessing great power along with their primary and secondary limbs, are joined with Sarasvatī and Gāyatrī.
This heaven, adorned by the gods, possesses a circle of moving Siddhas who have entered the cities of the world-protectors; it is characterized by unrestrained good fortune.
Adorned with mountains, islands, oceans, and forests,
this dark-blue orb of the earth serves as the earring for the ear of the three worlds.
This is the cavernous hollow of Pātāla, the home of the Daityas, Dānavas, and serpents— a deep abyss filled with throngs of nectar-like women.
This Indra, mighty-armed, with his tree-like arms adorned by the thunderbolt,
alone protects the city of the three worlds— he who partakes in the purifying sacrifice.
As if restraining the multitude of directions with the leather thongs of their blazing nets,
these rays of the sun, possessing abundant light, shine forth in succession.
These world-protectors protect the world with unshakable conduct,
by means of their noble boundaries, just as cowherds guard a herd of cattle.
These living beings emerge and submerge, quiver and fall, like waves of water in every direction.
I create this creation and likewise withdraw it with due regard;
I abide within the Self and remain at peace as the Lord of the world.
This year has passed; this age has come to its end.
This is the process of creation, and now this is the time for dissolution.
This kalpa has passed today, and this is the night of Brahmā;
thus I abide within myself as the Supreme Lord, the perfect Self.
Thus, with their minds so cultivated, those ten sons of Indu remained with their activities turned inward, as if carved out of stone.
Having attained the sequence of the Lotus-Throne and having shed the net of all other trivial activities,
they shone for a long time upon the lotus-like creation of Brahmā, seated upon thrones worn out by constant use.
The seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Restoration of Aindava," Canto:
Bhānu.
Then, having fixed their devotion upon that ancestral lineage,
they remained attentive, their minds overcome by those very actions.
As long as their bodies remained, they withered away through that heat and those winds,
just like severed lotus shoots in the summer heat.
There, the flesh-eating forest-dwellers devoured those corpses,
rolling them here and there like monkeys among choice fruits.
Then, with external objects stilled and having cultivated the meditation upon Brahman,
they remained until the end of the four ages, when the kalpa came to its dissolution.
Then, as the eon wanes and the mass of suns blazes forth,
while the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds rain down with a loud and harsh roar;
While the winds of the kalpa blew and the great ocean remained as it was,
when the multitudes of beings had perished, they remained situated exactly as before.
Now that you have awakened and desire to see the cycle of existence,
they remain situated exactly as they were before, each according to its own course.
O Blessed One, O Brahman, these ten are the Brahmins of Brahmā;
these ten transmigrations are established within the void of the mind.
O Lord, among them, I am this Ākāśamandira;
I am the Sun on earth, appointed to the task of measuring the subtle divisions of time.
This creation of the ten Brahmās born from the lotus has been told to you, O lotus-born one; as for their manifestation in the sky, do as you wish.
This entire supreme world that has arisen, enveloped by various conceptual constructions and deluding by means of a web of rays— that is all a delusion within one's own mind.
The eighty-eighth canto, titled "The Determination of the Ten States of the World," by Brahmā.
"O Brahmin, [this is] the radiance of Brahmā," having said this to me, who am Brahmā, he, O Brahmin,
best among the knowers of Brahman, became silent.
Then, after reflecting for a long time in my mind, I said to him:
"O Bhānu, O Bhānu, tell me quickly—what else shall I create?"
"Since these ten worlds indeed exist there, O Bhāskara, tell me: what purpose would another creation serve for me?"
Bhānu said: "O Lord, what purpose is there for you, who are effortless and desireless, in creation?
O Master of the World, this creation of yours is merely for diversion."
O Lord, from you alone, who are free from desire, the creation comes into being,
just as the sun arises from water or as a reflection appears from a mirror.
When both aversion and attachment toward the configuration of the body have been abandoned,
O Blessed One, the state that is free from desire neither longs for nor relinquishes anything.
Then, O God, O Lord of Beings, you create this world merely for sport,
repeatedly withdrawing it again and again, just as the sun withdraws its light at the end of each day.
"This world must be created by you solely for the sake of your own eternal, unattached diversion, and not out of intense desire."
You do not perform creation, nor do you carry out the daily activities of the self;
by abandoning obligatory duties, what unprecedented result will you obtain?
Indeed, one should always perform whatever duty has arisen while remaining unattached,
just as a stainless mirror performs the function of reflecting images.
Just as there is no desire in the wise man for performing action,
so too there is no desire in the wise man for not performing action.
Therefore, by means of this desireless mental state which is like deep sleep,
perform your duties as they arise, remaining like one who has awakened from sleep.
O Lord, the world finds satisfaction through the creations of the sons of the Moon;
therefore, O Lord of the Gods, these creations will not satisfy you.
You perceive these creations with the eyes of the mind, not with the physical eye;
for who, not seeing a creation with the eye, could know that "it has been created"?
O Supreme Lord, he alone by whose mind this creation was fashioned beholds it with his own physical eyes, and no other.
And no one is able to destroy these ten transmigrations, which arise from the ten dustless qualities and have endured for a long time due to the firmness of consciousness.
It may indeed be possible to restrain that which is performed by the organs of action;
however, no one is capable of restraining that which is brought about by the resolve of the mind.
O Brahmin, that firm resolve which has become fixed in the mind of a living being cannot be turned back by anything other than that very [resolve] itself.
That which has been practiced for a long time with a firm resolve by the mind suffers no destruction even by a curse, nor when the body has perished.
Whatever has taken root in the mind as a firmly established seat, a person becomes that very form in this world and nothing else;
I consider any other means for awakening to that [reality] here to be utterly fruitless, like a mass of rocks.
The eighty-ninth canto, titled "The Declaration of Aindavan’s Resolve," Canto 89:
Bhānu.
For it is heard, O Lord, that in ancient times there was a sovereign in Magadha known as Indradyumna, who was like a second Indra.
He had a lotus-eyed wife named Ahalyā, who was like a reflection of the moon’s orb, just as Rohiṇī is to the Moon.
In that very city, it is said, there was a powerful eunuch;
and another, a certain illustrious young Brahmin named Indra.
Once, during the course of a conversation, the queen heard from Ahalyā that she had formerly been the beloved of Indra.
Having heard that, Ahalyā became enamored of Indra;
she grew full of longing, wondering, "Why does Śakra not come to me, Ahalyā?"
Upon beds of lotus stalks, pearl necklaces, and plantain leaves,
that young woman suffered intensely, like a creeper cut down in the forests.
He found weariness in all those royal splendors,
just as a fish scorched by the summer heat finds distress when tossed about on dry land.
"This is Indra, this is Indra"— with such idle chatter,
she who had already lost her self-control even abandoned her sense of shame.
Then, to her who was thus distressed with deep affection, her friend said:
"O friend, I shall bring even Indra here for you without any obstacle."
Hearing the words, "I am bringing Indra to you," her eyes blossomed wide,
and she fell at her friend's feet like one lotus falling upon another.
Then, when the day had passed and the arrival of night drew near,
that female companion went to that young Brahmin named Indra.
Having awakened that prince Indraka as was appropriate,
she quickly brought him to Ahalyā’s side during the night.
Then, adorned with many garlands and ointments, she took her pleasure with that Śiḍga Mahendra in a certain secret chamber.
Then that young woman was captivated by him, who was charming with necklaces and armlets,
just as a creeper is drawn by the juice of honey through its passion.
Then, being devoted to him and seeing the entire world as consisting of him alone,
she did not think much of her husband, who was filled with infinite virtues.
Then, after some time, that lion among kings discovered her devotion to Indra, she who was the moonlight in the sky of his face.
As long as she meditated upon Indra,
her face shone like the full moon or a blossomed white water-lily.
Thus, observing their mutual state of attachment, the king then issued a command against both of them with many punishments.
Both of them, being truly peaceful and having renounced everything while dwelling in that body of water, laughed there in contentment and did not fall into despair.

Then the king asked them, "Are you weary? Are you not well? They, having been pulled out from the body of water, replied to the protector of the earth: The king then asked them, "Are you exhausted? Are you not unwell, O evil-minded ones? They, having been raised up from the reservoir of water, spoke to the lord of the earth.

O protector of the earth, in this cycle of rebirth, we two have become so infatuated with each other’s irreproachable facial beauty that we would not be satiated even by our own limbs being cut to pieces.
Even when cast into the fire, they remained entirely untroubled;
with their hearts gladdened and their memories refreshed, they spoke thus to one another.
Entangled in the elephant's feet, remaining there with their claws unharmed,
they spoke thus to one another, their memories restored and filled with joy, to the king.
Though struck by the harshness [of the ordeal], they remained undaunted and spoke thus; though sunk in the mud, they remained undaunted and spoke thus.
Again and again, having been drawn forth from various other scriptural traditions and conceptual constructs,
they were questioned and spoke of that very same matter over and over.
Indra said, "O protector of the earth, this world is dear to me;
therefore, painful commands do not trouble me in the slightest."
And for this very reason, O King, the entire world is indeed composed of me;
therefore, no suffering arising from our command afflicts us in the slightest.
"O King, we call it 'mind'; for the mind is indeed remembered as the person (puruṣa). This body is seen to be merely a conceptual proliferation (prapañca)."
Even by a sudden mass of blows applied all at once,
it is not possible to pierce even slightly the steadfast mind.
O Great King, what indeed are they, of what nature are they, and whose powers are they,
by which even minds possessed of firm resolve are shattered?
Whether the body falls or rises, or whether it goes to dissolution,
the mind remains as before, having attained the object it has cultivated.
No states of being whatsoever residing within the body are capable of breaking my steadfast mind, which has long been established in its desired object.
O Lord of the Earth, that which has been cultivated by the mind with intense force,
that alone one perceives immovably, and not the movements of the body.
O King, no actions whatsoever— not even boons or curses—
are capable of shaking the mind of one who is possessed of intense spiritual urgency.
For men are indeed unable to move the mind— though it may be attached with intense force toward what they desire— just as deer cannot move a great mountain.
This dark-eyed woman is delightful, established within the treasury of my mind,
like the divine goddess in a lofty temple.
I do not experience suffering through the loss of my beloved life,
just as a mountain feels no heat from the summer season when it is enveloped by a mass of clouds.
O King, wherever and in whatever manner I stand or move forward,
there I experience nothing other than the attainment of my desired object.

This mind, though attached to the one named Ahalyā’s beloved, now approaches the one called Indra; this occurs through mental construction alone, and not by virtue of anything external to its own nature.
For the mind of a wise man, O King, when intent upon a single task,
cannot be shaken even by the power of the most formidable curses, just like Mount Meru.
For the body undergoes change through blessings and curses,
O King, but not the steadfast mind that has arisen with the desire for victory.
And these, O King, are not the causes of the minds here, for they are mere fragments of bodies that have not arisen from them;
rather, the mind is the cause within these little bodies, just as water is the cause in all the juices of the creepers and thickets in a forest.
Know that the mind here is the primary body, O Great-souled One; by it are fashioned the multitudes of bodies in this world.
Whichever primary body a person presides over, in that very one his actions bear abundant fruit, and not in any other.
O fortunate one, know that the mind is indeed the primary sprout of man; from it the bodies have spread forth like the shoots of a tree.
When the sprout is destroyed, the beauty of the shoots does not arise again, yet the sprout itself does not perish even when the leaves fall away.
Upon the destruction of the body, the mind quickly creates a multitude of various bodies, like a new forest appearing instantly upon the ground of a dream;
yet when the mind is destroyed, the body does nothing at all. Therefore, protect the jewel of the mind.
In every direction, O King, I see only the deer-eyed beloved; because my mind is fixed on her, I am constantly delighted.
I do not perceive any fruit whatsoever arising from your fluctuations of pleasure—whether it be painful for a moment or for a very long time.
The Ninetieth Sarga, titled "The Fabricated Speech of Indra," Chapter 90.
Bhānu:
Then, having been addressed thus by Indra, that lotus-eyed king spoke to the sage named Bharata, who was seated beside him.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, do you behold today the excessive audacity upon the face of this evil-souled man who has carried off my wife?"
O great sage, grant him a curse that is commensurate with his sin;
for the sin incurred by killing one who should not be killed is indeed equal to that incurred by abandoning the opportunity to kill.
Thus addressed by that lion among kings, Bharata, the best of sages,
quickly reflected upon the sin of that evil-minded man exactly as it was.
"O evil-minded one, go to your destruction along with this woman of wicked deeds, who has overcome you through her betrayal of her husband!"— thus he uttered a curse.
Bhānu said:
Then, their minds bound by affection, they both fell to the earth due to the curse, like two leaves fallen from a tree.
Then, having fallen into misfortune and entered the womb of deer,
they both subsequently became birds once again.
O Lord, today in this creation, we have become a most meritorious Brahmin couple, devoted to austerity and bound together by mutual affection.
For that curse of theirs,
O Lord, was indeed effective only in assailing their bodies, not in restraining their minds.
By that very cause which prepares the body until this day,
wherever you two are born, there you shall be husband and wife.
Beholding that lovely affection of theirs, permeated by the essence of unfeigned love,
even the trees became permeated by the essence of affection and agitated by gestures of passion.
The ninety-first canto:
Bhānu said:
"O Blessed One, O Sage, I speak this of the mind exactly as it has arisen."
It is unseizable and indivisible, even by difficult-to-withstand curses.
Therefore, O Brahmin, the destruction of the lineages of Aindavas created in this manner is not fitting; nor is it appropriate for such a high-souled being.
O Lord, what is there in this world, or even in the various worlds,
that could cause dejection even for you, the protector of the Great-Souled One?
For the mind is the creator of the worlds; for the mind is remembered as the person.
In this world, what is done by the mind is truly done; what is done by the body is not considered done.
That which is determined by the mind cannot be destroyed in a living being by means of physical substances, medicines, or punishments, just as the reflection in a gem cannot be removed.
Therefore, let these remain here with their radiant and tumultuous creations;
you, having brought forth creatures here, remain as the infinite one even within the space of the intellect.
The space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the third, the [outer] space—
these three alone are infinite, illuminated by the space of consciousness.
O Lord of Creatures, create one, two, or even many worlds;
abide in yourself according to your own will. What have you received from the sons of Indu?
Brahmā said:
O great sage, when the solar net of the world had been thus described by me, I reflected for a long time and spoke this.
O Bhānu, what you have said is indeed fitting: for the sky is indeed vast, the mind is vast, and the space of consciousness is expansive.
O Bhāskara, I perform my eternal duty according to my own will; I swiftly fashion many diverse networks of living beings.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you yourself quickly become the first Manu here;
urged by me, perform the work of creation as you desire.
Then that Prabhākara, of great splendor and best among those who practice austerity, having accepted my words, divided himself in two.
By means of that former body, having attained the state of the sun,
he spread a succession of days across the creation as it traveled through the path of the sky.
Having made me his second self by means of his own body in an instant,
he created the entire, expansive, and desired creation of mine.
Whatever indeed appears as a manifestation to this mind,
that very thing attains clarity, stability, and fruitfulness.
Having been ordinary Brahmins, it is said that by the power of their realization, the sons of Indu attained the state of Brahmā; behold the potency of the mind!
Just as those who lived in the city of Indra attained the state of Brahman through their state of consciousness,
so too have we, being of the nature of consciousness, attained the state of Brahman through our state of consciousness.
For the mind is of the nature of appearance, and that which is its appearing;
this appears as the semblance of the body and so forth, and therefore there is no perception of a body.
Consciousness is the wonder of the Self;
it wonders by itself, as far as possible, within its own self like the nature of a mirage.
This very thing, appearing as if endowed with consciousness and known as the *ātivāhika*,
is that same [reality] which, through delusion, they call by the name "body" when it has become solidified.
This mind, whose latent impressions have become attenuated, is called by the name "jīva"; know that the jīva is the tranquil wonder of the body, which gradually becomes the Supreme.
Neither I nor anything else exists here; this mind alone remains, like the consciousness of Vasiṣṭha and Indu, which, though unreal, has attained the appearance of existence.
Just as Brahmā is the mind of Indra, so too do I stand here;
and this world, created by me, shines forth as nothing other than my own volition.
Know that this play of the mind, which persists in the thought "I am Brahman," is merely the nature of the body and so forth, arising from the voidness of the self.

Through the contemplation that "pure consciousness is of the single form of the Supreme Self," [the self] becomes a living being and, having become the mind, falsely perceives itself as having the nature of a body.
All this world, which has the nature of consciousness, appears like the cycle of existence of Indra;
it is a long dream born of one's own power, appearing as a perfected reality due to a lack of awakening.

Having the form of the delusion of two moons, that delusion regarding the forms of the subtle elements (tanmātra) arises from the consciousness; the mind (manas) is the cognitive capacity (cittva) of the consciousness, established like the moon or a lotus.
The form of the "I" is neither existent nor non-existent, and likewise for existence and non-existence;
through perception it has the form of existence, yet it is unreal because of its contradiction [with reality].
Know that the mind, which has a vast form consisting of volition, is both inert and non-inert:
it is non-inert because its nature is Brahman, and it is inert because it assumes the nature of the visible object.

The nature of reality consists in the experience of the perceptible; in the absence of that [perception], it dissolves, just as the state of being a bracelet dissolves into gold, so too is it established within Brahman.
Because Brahman is everything, everything—from ourselves down to a stone—is either composed of consciousness or is indeed inert; yet, in its true nature, it is neither inert nor conscious.
Since wood and such things lack consciousness, the occurrence of perception is impossible;
for perception arises only from a connection with something similar.
Know that through perception everything is indeed conscious;
for perception arises from a connection, and that connection exists between two things of equal nature.
The splendor of the meanings of words such as "insentient," "sentient," or "peaceful" does not exist in the ineffable state, just as there are no leaves, creepers, or the like in the great desert.
That which is the conceptualization of an object within consciousness is declared to be the state of the mind (*manas*).
Here, the aspect of consciousness is the non-inert part, while the state of being an object is the inertness in this context.
"The conscious portion here is the aspect of awareness, while the insentient is the object of cognition, for that is its visibility.
Thus, the living being (jīva), perceiving the delusion of the world, falls into agitation.
This very being is consciousness itself; thus, by means of purity alone, it is made twofold.
Therefore, that same [consciousness] is the entire world, having acquired the portion known as duality.

Having perceived its own self as something else, consciousness—though partless—appears as if it were a single part, taking on the form of the visible object; thus, afflicted by delusion, it seems to wander.
There is no delusion, nor indeed is there anyone who experiences delusion; this is the certainty here.
Consciousness, resembling a full ocean, is established in this manner as consciousness.
Because it is all-pervasive, let there be insentience in this consciousness; yet you recognize its sentience.
Herein, the aspect of consciousness is the element of awakening, which arises from the non-arising of "I-ness" and insentience.

In the supreme reality, "I-ness" and so forth do not exist even in the slightest degree, just as waves and the like do not exist separately from water; for that [reality] has consciousness as its essence.
Know that the object of cognition, which appears as the notion of "I," has arisen like a mirage; therefore, it certainly does not exist at all.

Know that the state of the Self is free from the stain of "I-ness" (ahantā); the wise understand "I-ness" and the like to be nothing other than [the Self], just as they know coldness to be nothing other than snow.
