It is consciousness alone that perceives its own insentience, like one's own death in a dream;
by being the self of all and exercising all powers, it does not admit of any equal.
The mind unfolds as all forms, appearing as objects and the like;
this body of consciousness is not a manifold self, having a form as clear as space.
One who always abandons the body and so forth— which are of the nature of the self as a bodily appearance—
must clearly investigate the mind-ness (*cittva*) that is the nature of appearance by means of the mind itself.
When the copper of the mind has been purified and attained the state of the ultimate gold, there is uncontrived bliss; what is the use of fragments of stone that are bodies?
That which exists can be cleansed; but by whom can a tree in the sky be washed?
If ignorance regarding the body and so forth were real, then attachment toward it would be appropriate.
Those ignorant ones who, in this world, teach the existence of a self to those who are attached to what is unreal— such as the body and so forth— are indeed like rams among men.
Just as one contemplates this within one's own mind, so does it become in an instant;
the illustration for this is the certain conviction regarding the moon, the depth of the ocean, or an artificial Indra.
Whatever manifests in whatever manner as the mind, whose nature is one's own self-reflection, that very thing arises as the body;
having realized this single nature of pure consciousness—that "this body exists, yet I am not"—remain free from desire.
Thinking "this is the body" and "this indeed is I," one strives solely for the sake of the body due to its very nature; thus it goes to destruction.
Just as a child, through some reasoning, experiences fear caused by the imagination of a yakṣa or similar being even when he has gone to a place where no yakṣa exists.
The ninety-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence of the Descent of Living Beings," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having spoken thus to me, O descendant of Raghu, that Blessed One, the lotus-born creator and lord of beings, set aside his words and was questioned by me once again.
O Blessed One, you yourself have declared that the powers of curses, mantras, and so forth are unfailing; how then have those very same powers been rendered futile?
Indeed, it is said that among living beings, even the mind, intellect, and senses are all seen to be utterly deluded by a curse or by the power of a mantra.
Just as wind and its movement, or just as oil and ghee, so indeed are these two— the mind and the body— always inseparable.
Or perhaps the body does not exist at all, being merely beneficial to the mind;
it is experienced in vain, like a dream, a mirage, or a double moon.
In this case, the destruction of both is admitted upon the destruction of one;
for the dissolution of the body necessarily follows the destruction of the mind.
O Lord, how is it that the mind is not assailed by defects such as curses and the like?
Or how, indeed, is it assailed? Tell me this, O Supreme Lord.
Brahmā said:
There is nothing within the vessel of the world that cannot be attained by people through pure human effort, provided they pursue virtuous actions.
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, at all times and of every kind,
all embodied beings in this world indeed possess two bodies.
The one [body] is the mental body, which acts swiftly and remains both stable and mobile;
the other body, however, is composed of flesh and is incapable of action.
In this body composed of flesh, which has fallen entirely under the power of everyone, one will be assailed by all curses as well as by the multitude of mental and physical ailments.
For he is almost mute, incapable, wretched, and perishing in an instant; as fickle as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, his state is dependent upon the gods and other powers.
That which is called the mind is the second body here for those who possess a body; though dependent, it is not subject to the elements within the three worlds.
If, relying on his own manliness and maintaining constant fortitude,
he remains unassailable by sufferings, then he is beyond reproach.
In whatever way this mind-body of embodied beings exerts itself,
in that very way it becomes, reaping exclusively the fruit of its own resolve.
No human effort regarding the body of flesh bears fruit;
however, every action of the mental body is fruitful.
For one who remains with a mind fixed upon the sacred investigation through constant recollection,
curses and the like are as fruitless as arrows shot at a stone.
Let the body fall into water, or into fire, or into mud;
that which the mind contemplates, that alone it certainly attains.
O Sage, every excellence of human effort arises from the subduing of all mental states; for it is the mind that, through the mind, bestows its fruit without obstruction.
Having made his inner mind full of love through the power of his manly effort,
that artificial Indra did not experience even a pang of suffering, even while under instruction.
Having made the mind free from passion and devoid of fever through human effort,
Māṇḍavya conquered the afflictions even while remaining upon the tip of a stake.
Even while remaining in a blind well, the sage Dīrghatapas attained the city of the gods through mental accumulations of sacrifice.
Through meditation, the sons of Indu attained the state of Brahman by means of human resolve alone— a state which is not even contradicted by me.
Others too, who are vigilant— the steadfast gods and great seers—
do not abandon their own internal investigation even for a moment.
Mental anxieties, physical diseases, curses, and likewise the glances of the evil-eyed do not wound them, just as blows from a lotus leaf cannot affect a stone.
Moreover, as for those who have been shattered by curses and other such shafts of affliction,
I consider their minds— incapable of self-discrimination— to be devoid of manliness.
Never at any time in saṃsāra, even for a moment or in a dream, does anyone exist who is not utterly corrupted by the nets of defects.
Therefore, in this world, a person should, by means of the mind itself and through human effort, unite his own mind with its very self upon the path of purification.
O Sage, whatever appears to him becomes sufficient for that very purpose; in an instant, his mind becomes swollen with pride like a child’s ghost.
Immediately upon its manifestation, the appearance abandons its prior state,
just as a pot abandons its state as a lump of clay immediately after the potter's work.
O Sage, the mind attains the state of manifesting objects in an instant,
just as water, whose nature is mere vibration, assumes the form of lofty waves.
Merely by means of mental investigation, the mind with its impure senses perceives night even in the solar orb, just as it perceives duality in the lunar orb.
Whatever this mind perceives, that very thing quickly comes to fruition;
it experiences that together with joy and sorrow; therefore, that alone is real.
And even upon seeing a hundred flames of fire in the moon at every step of his inspired intuition, he experiences burning; and being burnt, he suffers intensely.
For the mind that follows every word of inspired eloquence is like an elixir even in the midst of bitterness;
having seen it and drunk it, it attains supreme satisfaction, leaps for joy, and exults.
Even in the sky, he perceives a vast forest at every step of his inspired eloquence;
having seen it, he cuts it down, and having cut it down, he plants it once again in abundance.
In this way, O dear one, the mind itself quickly perceives that very magical illusion which it imagines;
having understood that the world is neither non-existent nor existent, you must surely abandon this vision of manifold diversity.
The Ninety-third Sarga, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus was it previously spoken to me by the Blessed One;
that very thing has been told to you today.
Therefore, from this unmanifest, all-pervading Brahman, the subtle act of thinking (manana) arises first.

Having itself attained density, it becomes the mind (*manas*). That mind, preceded by the conceptualization of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), fashions a physical form. Thereupon, it becomes the luminous person (*taijasa-puruṣa*).
Thus, he gave the name "Brahmā" to this Self. Know that this Parameṣṭhin, by whom that name was given, is the principle of mind (manas-tattva).
That Blessed One Brahmā, being of the nature of the principle of mind, perceives exactly what he wills, because he consists of volition (saṅkalpa).
Therefore, this ignorance was conceived by him as consisting of the conceit of a self in that which is not-self;
by that Brahman, this world—composed of mountains, grass, and oceans—was gradually projected.
Thus, this creation has come forth from the reality of Brahman in a gradual sequence, yet it appears as if it had come from something else.
Therefore, O Rāma, the origin of all things existing within the belly of the three worlds is from Brahman, just as waves arise from the ocean.
Thus, when the world has arisen, that consciousness of Brahmā which consists of the nature of thinking, having fashioned the ego (ahaṅkāra), attains the state of Brahmā.

As for the other powers of consciousness—which are indeed non-different from all powers but are as if imagined to be different—they manifest through the mind in the form of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) once the world has been expanded.
These, revolving by the thousands, are called individual souls (jīvas).

Having risen from the sky and being enveloped by those subtle elements (tanmātra) in the atmosphere, they enter— by means of the vital power (prāṇa-śakti)— that very species among the fourteen kinds of elemental beings which exists in their vicinity, whether stationary or moving, and thus attain the state of seeds within the body.

Thereafter, they are born into the world from a womb; thereafter, they become partakers of the fruits of karma corresponding to the stream of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by chance, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.
Then, bound by the ropes of the fruits of karma entwined with latent impressions, these embodied beings wander, falling and rising again.
In this manner, these are the classes of living beings.
Some, enriched with thousands of births, fall like forest leaves;
whirled about by the whirlwind of karma, they roll in the hollows of mountains.
Some immeasurable beings, deluded by continuous ignorance,
have been wandering here for even many hundreds of kalpas since their birth.
Some, having passed through only a few previous delightful existences,
dwell in this world, devoted to virtuous deeds.
Some, having realized consciousness, have reached the supreme state,
like drops of ocean water tossed by the wind that vanish into the midst of the sea.
For from the state of Brahman arises the birth of all seeds; thus, existence, characterized by passion, is fragile due to its appearance and disappearance.
Latent impressions (vāsanā) sustain the fever of imbalance caused by the poison of worldly attachments; they bring about a chaotic mixture of endless, perilous, and harmful effects.
Wandering through various directions, lands, times, and the interiors of mountains and caves,
she has fashioned supreme variety and produced the whirlpools of her movement.
This withered creeper of the world’s wilderness, O Rāmabhadra, has been completely cut down by the axe of perfect discernment; its mind and body dissolved and agitated no longer sprout forth again.
The ninety-fourth canto, titled "The Vision of Origination," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
O Rāghava, listen as I explain this classification of the origins of superior, inferior, and middling objects scattered here and there.
For one who has arisen for the first time in this very birth,
that is accepted as the first sattvic manifestation of Brahmā.
This [faith] is called "the first," arising from the practice of virtue;
it is based on virtuous worlds and is followed by virtuous actions.
If that [intellect], which operates through the latent impressions of diverse saṃsāra,
were to attain liberation through a few [remaining] entities, it would be overflowing with qualities.
Because it infers what is to be done and what is not to be done solely through the granting of such results,
it is called "Rājasasattva" by those of perfected self.
Yet, if she is engaged in the worldly activities of the manifold latent impressions of saṃsāra and is extremely defiled, she may become a partaker of knowledge after thousands of births.
That [mind], which provides the inference of dharma and adharma solely through the granting of such fruits,
is called "the mind of inferior beings" by those of perfected self.
If that very state, following immediately after a multitude of births beyond numbering,
results in liberation being uncertain, it is called the most extreme darkness (atyantatāmasī).
O Rāma, that middling birth of a person which occurs within two or three lifetimes, arising from such causes, results in an intellect that has attained its end in this present life.
In the same way, O best of kings, the *rājasa* [nature] in this world follows after its effects;
it is described by those of perfected intellect as a path whose stages of rebirth are not far removed.
For she, by the mere fact of being born in that [family], is fit for liberation;
thus, through the inference from such effects, she is declared by those seeking liberation to be of rajasa-sattvika nature.
If that very same [disposition], through other minor births, becomes a partaker of liberation,
then such a state is described by those who know reality as *rājasarājasī* (the most excellent among the passionate).
If that same person, having sought liberation for hundreds of births, finally desires it after a long time,
she is then described by the virtuous as being of rajasic and tamasic nature, given such an undertaking.
If that very [action] results in liberation being doubtful even after thousands of births,
then such an undertaking is declared to be rajasic and extremely tamasic.
But that birth of men from Brahmā, which occurs after thousands of births have been experienced,
is indeed declared by the great seers to be a long-lasting liberation, characterized by darkness (tāmasī).
If it is said that one becomes a partaker of liberation by that very birth,
those who know reality call such a person "tāmasasattva," as it portends an undertaking of that nature.
If she is a partaker of liberation through only a few dispositions,
it is said that she possesses the nature of *tamas* and *rajas* due to such functions of the qualities (*guṇa*).
Having been enriched by thousands of previous births and even hundreds of prior births, she is then declared by those who know the truth to be fit for liberation; such is the *tāmasatāmasī* type.

But if one who was previously rich in hundreds of thousands of births, even if now before [the eyes of the teacher], has a doubtful liberation due to those hundreds of thousands of births, she is called "extremely dark" (atyantatāmasī).
All these classes of beings belonging to Brahmā come together,
slightly stirred from their state of enjoyment like waves from the mass of water.
All these multitudes of living beings have emerged from Brahman;
they are stirred by their own radiance for the sake of experience, like rays of light from a lamp.
All the multitudes of beings that have arisen from Brahmā are like sparks from a firebrand whirled by its own force.
Therefore, all classes of living beings have arisen from that Brahman,
like rays from the orb of the moon, appearing in the form of Mandāra flower clusters.
All perceptions of the visible world that have arisen from Brahman are like the diverse beauties of the branches of a tree, which possess the very form of that tree.
All the individual life-forces (jīva-śakti) have arisen from Brahman alone,
just as bracelets, armlets, and upper-arm ornaments are produced from gold.
O Rāma, all the multitudes of living beings have indeed arisen from Brahman,
like droplets of water from a fountain of pure radiance.
O Rāma, the entire conceptualization of the succession of beings belongs to the Unborn alone,
just as the spaces within jars, bowls, and holes belong to space itself.
All the mental constructions of the world have indeed arisen from the state of Brahman,
just as droplets, whirlpools, waves, and spray arise from water.
O Rāma, all these perceptions of the visible world arising from Brahman are like the waves of a mirage produced by the heat of the sun.
All perceptions of the visible are not distinct from the seer in their essential nature, just as moonlight is not distinct from the cool-rayed moon, or as light is not distinct from fire.
Thus indeed these various classes of beings in the worlds, having their diverse supports, emerge from that very source and enter back into that very same source.
Some [births] are long-lasting, extending over the end of thousands of lifetimes; others are established as having the form of only a few past births.
Thus, in these diverse worlds, by the will of that Blessed One, the splendors of beings— possessing various forms and engaged in worldly activity—
come and go, fall and likewise rise, like pots of sparks arising from a fire.
The ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Exposition that Everything is Produced from Brahman," by Vasiṣṭha:
The agent and the object are non-different;
they emerge simultaneously from the supreme state, just as the fragrance and the flower of a tree manifest together.
In the stainless Brahman, which is free from all conceptual constructions,
individual souls manifest like reflections of the blue sky in the vast expanse of space.
O Rāghava, wherever the conduct of unawakened people is observed,
there the assertions that "living beings are born from Brahman" remain established.
O Rāghava, it is not fitting for those who follow the conduct of the fully awakened ones to speak in this way: "Was this world born from Brahmā, or was it not?"
O Raghava, as long as even a slight conceptualization has not been brought to full manifestation,
the splendor of the teaching for the one to be instructed does not shine in the world.
Therefore, having provisionally accepted the miserable state of differentiation, it is taught that "this is Brahman" or "these are the individual souls"; such is the delusion of words.
Thus, through this perspective, the world arises from Brahman which is free from attachment;
yet that very reality born of it remains difficult to comprehend.
Many multitudes of living beings, resembling Mount Meru and Mount Mandara,
having risen up again and again, dissolve away into that very supreme state.
Others, without beginning or end, flash forth by the thousands as they are born,
like sprouts upon trees in various forest thickets.
Floods of living beings will arise like new sprouts in the spring,
and they will go to dissolution in that very same place, like honey-vines in the summer.
They remain eternally throughout the ages, and many others besides them are born and then dissolved again within that Supreme One; such are the multitudes of living beings.
O Raghava, the person and his action are inseparable like the flower and its fragrance; having emerged together from the Supreme Lord, they both gradually dissolve back into Him.
In this manner, these Daityas, Uragas, humans, and gods in this world flash forth again and again through appearances, disappearances, and non-existences.
O virtuous one, no other cause for their dwelling [in saṃsāra] is observed apart from the forgetting of the self; there is nothing else that yields the fruit of the path of birth.
Rāma:
That which has its meaning consistent with reality, which is established by those possessing the vision of valid cognition,
and which is determined by those free from passion— that is called a scripture (śāstra).
Those who are endowed with the qualities of great beings, who are steadfast and possess equal vision,
and whose instructions bear fruit— they are declared to be the virtuous ones.
But this entire view leads to the accomplishment of all actions;
by means of virtuous conduct, one always follows the scripture.
All people cast out that person who does not follow the scripture established in the conduct of the virtuous, and he sinks into suffering.
In this world and in the Veda, O Lord, the sacred tradition has always declared that action and the agent are joined here in a continuous succession.
The agent is produced by action, and the action is measured by the agent;
this traditional teaching found in the Vedas is like that of the seed and the sprout in the world.
A living being is born from karma, just as a new sprout arises from a seed;
from the living being, karma is produced again, just as a seed is produced from a sprout.
By whatever latent impression (vāsanā) an action is cast into the cage of existence,
a fruit corresponding to that very impression is experienced.
This being the case, how indeed can you claim that the arising of beings from the state of Brahman occurs without karma, which is the seed of birth?
By this position, O Blessed One, you have refuted the notion that the birth and activities of beings in the world are necessarily concomitant with one another.
O Brahmin, you have cleared away from the world the notion that there is a fruit for actions when those actions are performed without a motive, even regarding results such as birth and the like.
When confusion has arisen in the world and actions yield no fruit, while the "law of the fish" prevails, only destruction remains.
What indeed is that which has been done? O Blessed One, tell me this in truth;
O best among those who know the Vedas, dispel this vast doubt of mine.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Excellent, O Rāghava! I have been asked this auspicious question by you.
Listen, I shall speak to you so that there may arise a profound awakening of knowledge."
That which is the unfolding of the mind through the form of the manifestation and withdrawal of its parts—this is the seed of actions; of this alone does the fruit exist.
For that very reality which is the mind, having arisen from the state of Brahman,
is itself the karma of living beings, existing as the individual soul (jīva) within the body.
Just as there is no distinction here between the flower and its fragrance, even though they are distinct,
so too there is no distinction between karma and the mind, even though they are distinct.
In this world, the vibration of activity is called "karma" by the wise;
since its precursor is the body of the mind, karma is indeed the mind itself.
There is no mountain, no sky, no direction,
and no heaven where there is no fruit for the deeds one has performed oneself.
Whether it be an action performed in this life or one from the past that is clearly manifest,
this supreme human effort is never without fruit.
Know that the mind which has arisen from Brahman is action, and nothing else;
know that very thing, O Raghava, to be the seed of the people, and nothing else.
Because it proceeds from one place to another due to the cause of continuous connection, the mind is indeed the primary cause; therefore, the wise know the mind to be action (*karman*).

From Brahman, who resembles an unagitated ocean, there arises consciousness characterized by vibration; it is this consciousness that people call the mind, which has become the life-force of living beings.
The mind is action, the mind is the living being, and by that very mind the body is extended;
therefore, action and the agent are not distinct, like sesame seeds and their oil.
For the two entities consisting of the agent and the object are indeed eternally non-different;
they appear as distinct only due to a lack of understanding, and thus their conceptualization is entirely in vain.
O Rāma, there are two minds regarding action for the foolish, but not for the wise;
it is like the perception of difference among children between the water of the ocean and the water of its waves.
Know that these two are indeed synonymous terms for the activity of the mind;
they remain synonymous even when set aside, because [the nature of the mind] is difficult to comprehend.
The mind, whose nature is action, first proceeds from the Supreme,
just as a flower of various forms issues from a tree through its inherent fragrance.
In this world, the cognitions that denote the agent and the object proceed incessantly from the Supreme One,
like waves from the ocean.
But those very things designated as "living beings," having been extracted from that [source],
dissolve away after having vibrated, like waves in the ocean.
Whatever action is performed by the mind, that alone becomes fruitful;
it is in the mind alone, not that which arises from the body. Therefore, the agent of action is the mind.
In the mirror whose expanse is illumined by light,
the agency within the mind shines forth clearly once it has been touched by the reality of Brahman.
Just as a quality such as whiteness resides in a possessor of qualities such as a cloth,
so too does agency reside in the mind known as the individual soul (jīva).
Just as frost is not perceived when it is devoid of coldness and other qualities,
so too no mind whatsoever is perceived in the absence of karma.
Just as soot vanishes of its own accord when blackness is destroyed,
so too the mind perishes when the activity of vibration ceases.
The destruction of karma and the destruction of the mind— indeed, the state of non-action resulting from the destruction of the mind—
belong only to one who is liberated, never to one who is not liberated.
Just as fire and heat are always conjoined, so too are the mind and its activities;
in the absence of either one of these two, both simply dissolve away.
Know that this mind is always the play of vibration; indeed, know that action is of the very nature of vibration.
O Rāma, when the state of the possessor of attributes (dharmin) and the attributes themselves (dharma) have reached [this realization], the mind and action are indeed mutually one with each other.
The ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Identity of Karma and the Person," by Vasiṣṭha.
For the mind is merely a mental construction, and mental construction consists of vibration;
it is an activity, and its manifested form is the fruit that everyone pursues.
Rāma said: O Brahmin, you ought to describe in detail to me— though I am dull-witted yet possess an undull form— the nature of the mind when it has ascended to the level of conceptualization.
Vasiṣṭha said:
They know that form of the infinite reality of the Self, the omnipotent Great Soul, which is endowed with the power of volition, as the mind.
That reality which stands poised between the perception of the insentient and the sentient,
and which is grasped by both, is known as the nature of the mind.
The conviction that "I am not of the nature of the light of consciousness; I am miserable" is known by the wise as a state of the mind characterized by constant agitation.
Between existence and non-existence, being vibrates motionless within men; when it becomes intent upon conceptualization, the wise know that to be the form of the mind.
In this world, a mind devoid of the power of action, which consists of temporal succession, is not possible, just as a possessor of qualities cannot exist without those qualities.
Just as the existence of fire and heat is not possible if they were distinct,
so too it is with action and the mind, and likewise with the self and the mind.
By its own nature as consciousness, through its activity characterized by the quality of fruition,
having volition as its sole body, and possessing manifold expansions.
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) is planted by whom, where, and in what manner—like a creeper—it bears fruit accordingly for that person; thus, exactly that which was obtained is what is attained.
The vibration of the mind is said to be the seed of karma, and it is experienced as such;
its various activities are like the branches of a tree that bear manifold fruits.
Whatever the mind intends, all these functions of the organs of action accomplish; therefore, the mind is traditionally known as "action" (karman).
Mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, action, as well as imagination, transmigratory existence, latent impressions, ignorance, effort, and memory.
The senses, primordial nature, illusion, and action— these and many other diverse splendors of sound are the causes of the delusion of saṃsāra.

Through a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit, the various synonymous functions were attributed to the consciousness (cit), which has abandoned its expansive wonder and follows after the objects of thought (cetya).
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how have these various modes of the supreme consciousness come to be established as they are, assuming diverse objects that are merely being conceptualized?

Vasiṣṭha: When consciousness, which is essentially conceptualization, has as it were departed from its state of being stained by duality and has become manifest in the form of unfolding, at that very moment the state of the mind arises.
When the investigation of phenomena is established through certainty,
then this is called fixed intelligence, capable of apprehension.
When, through false conceit, it itself imagines its own existence,
it is called by the name "ego" (ahaṅkāra), which binds one to worldly existence.
When, like a child, she is fragile and abandons this to take up that,
completely forsaking discernment, then she is called "the mind" (citta).
When, because its sole characteristic is vibration, it rushes toward the fruit of vibration, then it is designated as "action" (karman), signifying both action and backbiting.

When, by a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit, one abandons the certainty regarding a single substance and conceives of a state of being as desired, that is what is meant here by "conceptual construction" (kalpanā).
When one forms a determination within this [mind] that "this was seen before" or "it was not seen," or "it was created previously," then that is declared to be memory (smṛti).
When the latent impressions (vāsanā) dwell within the potencies of objects as if they were already experienced, with all other thoughts subsided, it is then called "subsidence" (asta).
There exists the stainless reality of the Self, marked by the second vision;
for that which is unborn and non-existent is then called ignorance (avidyā).
It throbs toward its own destruction and causes one to forget that state;
through a web of false conceptualizations, that impurity is imagined.
Having heard, created, seen, tasted, smelled, and reflected, it gladdens Indra; therefore it is traditionally known as an *indriya*.
Since the entire web of the visible world is unperceived within the Supreme Self,
it is called "primordial nature" (prakṛti) because of its being the inherent source of all entities in the world.
It swiftly leads existence to non-existence, or non-existence directly to existence;
because it thus carries away the flood of conceptual constructions—whether existent or non-existent—it is called "illusion" (māyā).
Through the activities of seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and smelling,
that which has entered into the state of cause and effect is called "action" (kriyā) in the world.
These are the synonymous designations for the mind (citta), which follows after objects of thought, has fallen into a state of defilement, and possesses the nature of manifesting forms.
Having reached the state of pure consciousness and departed from the ordinary plane,
[these impressions] have attained full growth through their own hundreds of volitions.

The intellect (cit) is indeed agitated by its own conceptual constructions; it is marked by the stains of what is to be willed, follows the web of dullness, and is characterized by the divisions of enumeration.
In the world it is called the *jīva*, and it is also spoken of as the *manas*;
it is likewise called the *citta* and the *buddhi*.
The wise describe this defiled [intellect], which has fallen away from ultimate reality, as a collection of synonyms that is turbid with various conceptual constructions.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, knower of reality, the thought arises within me that there is no certainty regarding whether the mind might be insentient or indeed sentient. MU 3.96.36.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, the mind is indeed neither inert nor has it attained the state of pure consciousness;
it is called 'mind' because it is a vision that is both faded and neither-inert-nor-conscious."
O Rāma, that turbid form which appears in the midst of the existent and the non-existent as the cause of the world is called the mind (citta).
That which exists here without a permanent, uniform, and certain state is called "mind"; from that, this world has arisen.
That which, situated like a swing between the perception of the insentient and the sentient, is a mental construction of consciousness whose form has become withered— that is called the mind (manas).
O Rāma, that which is the impure outflow of consciousness, possessing an interior marred by blemish, is called the mind; it is neither inert nor composed of pure consciousness.
For that [Self], these various names have been fully assigned:
ego, mind, intellect, the individual soul (jīva), and others as well.
Just as an actor assumes various forms,
so indeed does the mind, O Rāma, undergo a change of identity as it moves from one action to another.
Just as a man goes according to the power of his various undertakings, so does the mind go according to the power of its diverse functions.
O Raghava, these very designations of the mind that I have described are explained otherwise by disputants through hundreds of conceptual constructions.
Having superimposed upon them a reasoning that is regarded as intrinsic nature,
various songs of names have been composed for the mind, the intellect, the sense faculties, and so forth.
For the mind of one person is inert, while that of another living being is distinct;
likewise, for one disputant there is egoity, while for another there is intellect.
O descendant of Raghu, the views concerning ego, mind, and intellect— which are conceptual constructions of what has been created— have been described by me as being of a single nature.
The Naiyāyikas have postulated such [categories] in one way,
while the Sāṅkhyas have postulated them otherwise, and the Cārvākas have likewise postulated them in yet another way.
By the followers of Jaimini, the Ārhats, the Buddhists, and likewise the Vaiśeṣikas,
as well as by others who are diverse, such as the Pāñcarātras and so forth.
For all must indeed go to that supreme state of the Self,
just as travelers from various places and times arrive at a single city.
Due to ignorance of the ultimate reality and because of their perverted understanding,
those who desire to ascend [to higher stages] merely engage in disputes through conceptual constructions.
Proponents praise their own paths with a variegated vision,
like travelers who, arising at various times and places, each extol their own route.
O Raghava, those whose minds are fixed on action have falsely spoken of their own respective diverse arguments by means of objects projected by their own conceptual constructions.
Just as a single person, while performing the acts of bathing, giving, taking, and eating,
assumes various roles as an agent, so too does this mind.
Due to the influence of various effects, the agency of the mind is described by different names— namely, as "living being" (jīva), "latent impressions" (vāsanā), and "karma."
This entire world is experienced as nothing but the mind; for a person in this world who is without mind does not see, even while seeing.
Having heard, touched, seen, smelled, or tasted what is pleasant or unpleasant,
one who possesses a mind indeed experiences internal joy or dejection.
The mind is the cause of objects, just as light is for forms;
for one whose mind is bound is indeed bound, while one whose mind is liberated is indeed liberated.
Know that to be the best among the dull-witted by whom the mind is called "dull";
and understand that mind to be dull for which there exists a conscious [self].
This mind that has arisen is neither conscious nor inert;
from it the world has emerged, with its manifold experiences of pleasure and pain.
For when the mind becomes uniform, saṃsāra dissolves;
the turbid cause of delusion has presented the world through delusion.
For that which is called the mind, if it were non-inert, would not be the cause of saṃsāra;
and that which is inert, even if possessing the nature of a stone, is likewise not the cause of saṃsāra.
The mind is the cause of objects, just as the appearance of forms [is the cause of their perception];
if there were anything other than the mind, what would that world be for one who is without a mind?
Therefore, O Rāghava, in this world, neither consciousness nor insentience remains;
for the entire aggregate of all created beings completely dissolves.
Just as time, through the seasons, attains variety, so the mind— having entered into the states of various karmas and assumed manifold designations— reaches a state of diversity despite being one.

If indeed the activities of the ego and the senses disturb the body even for those who are without mental attention (*amanaska*), then let there be other [principles] such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth.
However, those distinctions among the philosophical systems (darśanas) that have been proclaimed in the mind through reasoning— whether by proponents or indeed by critics— are found here and there.
O Rāma, these do not conflict with one another, nor are they ever distinguished [as superior],
because all powers indeed exist within the omnipresent Lord.
Indeed, when even a slight degree of consciousness arises from that which is thus pure,
then a power as if insentient has emerged, and diversity has come into being.
Just as a thread is produced from a spider, and the insentient from the sentient,
so too does primordial nature (prakṛti) arise eternally from the supreme, ever-awakened Brahman.
Under the influence of ignorance, various mental dispositions have come into existence;
therefore, in this world, the meanings of the words that are synonyms for "mind" differ among proponents.
Indeed, this impure consciousness (cit) has attained its manifestation as the living soul (jīva), the mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), and the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti);

it is this very same [consciousness] that is designated in the world by the multitude of terms such as "sentient being" (cetana), "mind" (citta), and "living soul" (jīva)—of this there is truly no dispute.
The ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Perception and Discernment of Mind," [from] Rāma.
O Brahmin, it is from the mind alone that this "outward display" (āḍambara) is said to arise;
for it is understood from the meaning of the statement that the mind itself is action.
His body, with its radiant covering, was embraced by the mind alone, which was colored by firm resolve, just as a bright cloak is enveloped by a fierce wind and scorching sun.
O Brahman, I consider that in this world it is the mind alone that has assumed form; in some places it is established in the state of a human, and in others it arises as a god.
In one place it shone forth as a Daitya, in another it arose as a Yakṣa;
in some places it attained the state of a Gandharva, and in others it took the form of a Kinnara.
In the form of various forests, mountains, expanses, cities, and towns,
I believe it is the mind alone that expands through its vast manifestations.
This being the case, the flood of bodies is comparable to bits of straw and wood;
what purpose is there in investigating them? For us, it is the mind alone that must be investigated.
Therefore, I believe that this entire expansive and deeply agitated world is spread out [as an illusion],
and that apart from it, only the Supreme Self remains.
The Self transcends all states, is omnipresent, and is the refuge of all;
by its grace, the mind runs and leaps about within saṃsāra.
Therefore, I consider that the mind is the agent and the cause within bodies; for it is the mind that is born and dies, since such a quality does not belong to the Self.
I think that by such reflection, the mind will surely reach dissolution; and through the mere dissolution of the mind, thereafter the highest good will come to pass.
When that which is called "mind" has been completely exhausted, and when action is devoid of harmful agitation, the living being is said to be liberated; indeed, he is not born again.
O Blessed One, you have described three types of births for human beings;
the primary cause of these is the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
How then can the mind— which is called pure consciousness (śuddhacit) yet is devoid of purity— arise from that reality and, expanding outward, become the creator of the manifold world?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, there exist three expanses spread throughout the intermediate space:
the expanse of the mind (cittākāśa), the expanse of consciousness (cidākāśa), and the third is the elemental expanse (bhūtākāśa).
For these are indeed common to all and are established everywhere;
yet, through the power of pure consciousness, they have attained a state of oneness with existence.
He who, abiding both within and without, is the knower and the awakener of existence,
pervading all beings— he is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).

The creator who is intent on the welfare of all beings, whose nature consists of the manifestation and withdrawal of all parts, by whom all this is pervaded— he is called the space of consciousness (cittākāśa).
For that which has an uninterrupted body extending throughout the expanse of the ten directions,
that elemental self is this space, the substratum of wind, water, and the rest.
The two—space and the space of consciousness—arise through the power of the space of consciousness;
for consciousness is indeed the cause of the entire flood of effects, just as the day [is the cause of all activities].
The conviction that "I am inert" or "I am not inert" is a defilement of the consciousness;
know that very thing to be the mind, by which space and the other elements are brought into being.
The conceptualization of the three spaces has the unawakened self as its object;
it is indeed imagined for the sake of instruction, but not for the awakened one.
There is only the one supreme Brahman, which is everything and fills all things; it is awakened, stainless, eternal, and devoid of parts or mental constructs.
Through the various distinctions between duality and non-duality, which are woven into the structure of the scriptures,
it is indeed the ignorant person who is instructed, and never the awakened one.
As long as there is the state of being unawakened to Rāma, so long is that conceptualization of the three spaces taught by me for the sake of awakening.
Space, the space of the mind, and so forth, have issued from the stained space of consciousness,
just as mirages arise from a forest fire in the desert.
For when the mind becomes defiled, it assumes the nature of form and weaves the illusory nets of the three worlds, which are of a chaotic nature.
Indeed, this state of being a mind is seen in this impure reality which is essentially consciousness by those devoid of awakening;
just as the nature of silver is perceived in mother-of-pearl, but not by those possessing awakening. Bondage here occurs through ignorance, while liberation occurs through the power of awakening.
The Ninety-Eighth Chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Consciousness-Sky," by Vasiṣṭha:
O sinless one, whatever mind arises from any source whatsoever always strives with effort for its own liberation.
There is indeed a vast, empty, and tranquil forest that is yet terrifying,
wherein the sky is visible as nothing more than a mere corner.
In that [city], there stood a single person with a thousand hands and eyes, of terrifying appearance and vast form, his mind utterly agitated.
Taking up many iron clubs with his thousand arms,
he strikes his own back and flees by his own self.
Striking himself with his own self by means of firm blows,
he, with a terrified soul, flees even for hundreds of leagues.
Crying out as he fled, having gone far away here and there,
he was exhausted, helpless in appearance, with his feet and limbs shattered.
Helpless indeed, he quickly fell into a great blind well—
a deep cavity within the sky of the night, terrifying with the darkness of the dark fortnight.
Then, after a long time, he emerged from that blind well;
striking again with blows, he fled from himself by means of himself.
Having gone even further, he entered a thicket of Karañja forest bushes covered in thorns, like a moth entering a flame.
Therefore, having emerged from that thicket of *karañja* trees as if in an instant,
he himself, striking with blows, flees from himself by means of himself.
Having gone even further, that blind man quickly entered that very same blind well, his limbs and form shattered.
Having emerged from the blind well, he enters a grove of plantain trees;
striking again with blows, he flees from himself by means of himself.
Having gone even further, he entered, as if smiling, a lovely grove of plantain trees, cool as the rays of the moon.
Emerging again from that grove of plantains in an instant,
he reached a bright thicket of *karañja* trees from the plantain forest.
Having entered from the Karañjaka grove into a well, and from the well into another part of a plantain grove, he continued striking while remaining established within himself.
Having observed his conduct of such a nature, I looked upon him with respect and,
having forcibly restrained him, awakened him for a moment.
And when asked: "Who are you? What is this? For what purpose do you perform it?
What might be your desired goal? Why do you delude yourself in vain?"
Thus questioned, O descendant of Raghu, he said this to me:
"I am nothing at all, nor do I perform anything whatsoever, O sage."
By you I have been broken; you are my enemy, O subduer of foes.
Seen by you, I am both destroyed and [subjected] to sorrow and joy.
Having said this to me, he looked at his own limbs and stood there;
miserable, he wept with a piteous cry like a cloud rumbling while raining.
In a mere moment, having ceased his weeping there and gazing upon his own limbs, he laughed with a whiteness like that of the moon's rays.
Then, at the conclusion of his loud laughter, that man gradually cast off his own limbs from all sides before me.
First his extremely dreadful head fell,
then his arms, followed by his chest, and after that his belly.
Then, in an instant, that man, those limbs, and the agitation—
all vanished, just as a dream disappears for one who has awakened.
Having reflected upon the power of destiny, I then prepared to depart; however, in a secluded spot, I saw yet another man in the same condition.
Even while striking out in all directions with his thick-set arms, he himself flees away.
He falls into a well, but rising from the well, he runs away;
again he falls into the midst of a thicket, and once more, afflicted, he flees.
Again he enters the clear, cool forest for a moment;
enraged again and again, yet pleased again, he strikes out by himself.
Having observed for a long time his conduct, which was generally of this nature, I gazed at him with wonder; then, having firmly restrained him, I questioned him in that very manner.
Then, in that very same sequence, having wept and having laughed,
he reached a state of bodily dissolution and became entirely invisible.
Having reflected upon the power of destiny, I then prepared to depart; however, in a secluded spot, I saw yet another man in that same state.
Striking them in that very same way, he himself flees;
while fleeing, he falls into a great, blind well.
There I dwelt for a very long time, waiting for him,
until that rogue finally emerged from the well after a great deal of time had passed.
Then, as I was preparing to depart, I saw once more a man of that same appearance and that same conduct, striving in exactly the same manner.
Having quickly taken hold [of him] in that very manner, I spoke to him again;
yet, O lotus-petal-eyed one, he did not understand it.
"Only this fool does not know anything at all about me!
Ah, you wicked, evil twice-born!"—having said this, he departed, having reached the end of his own business.
Then, while dwelling in that great forest in such a manner,
I beheld many such men who committed offenses.
Some who are questioned by me come to rest like the delusions of a dream;
others do not welcome what I have said, just like the barking of dogs.
Some, having fallen into the blind wells, have not risen again; others, from the grove of plantains, have not emerged even after a long time.
Some vanished within the vast grove of *karañja* trees; some found no place to stay, while others were intent on wandering.
O descendant of Raghu, such was that vast great forest which still exists even today, wherein those men remained in this manner.
And that forest was seen by you here, O Rāma, as you were engaged in worldly activity;
yet, O Rāghava, because of the immaturity of your intellect regarding reality, you do not remember it.

That terrifying forest, its body crowded with various perils and dense with thick darkness, is frequented by worldly people who are ruined by a lack of wisdom for their own peace, but not by those who know the truth; it is like a bower of flowering shrubs.
The ninety-ninth canto, named the Canto of the Discourse on the Mind;
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, what is that great forest? When and how was it seen by me?
Who were those men there, and what were they striving to do?
Vasiṣṭha:
O mighty-armed Raghunātha, listen; I shall tell you everything.
That place called the Great Forest is not far away, nor indeed are those men.
O Rāma, know this path of saṃsāra— deep, hollow, and decayed— to be a vast forest, empty yet abounding in transformations.
When she is filled by that single object alone which is attainable through the light of discernment,
and is not joined with anything else, then she is indeed absolute.
In that regard, know that those great-bodied beings who roam about are, in truth,
merely minds fallen utterly into suffering.
O Mahāmati, I am the discerning observer of them; O Rāghava, through discernment, I have seen those others as distinct.
For by means of discernment, those very minds are perceived by me through my own constant self-luminosity, just as lotuses are perceived by the sun.
Having attained awakening through me, O high-minded one, by my grace,
some minds have reached that which is beyond tranquility.
Some do not welcome me due to their delusion regarding solitude;
moreover, under the influence of their contempt for me, they fall right into wells.
O descendant of Raghu, those dark wells and dense hells are their very minds; they fall into them and leap out from within.

That thicket of *karañja* trees is known as the passion for one's wife; human existence, crowded with the thorns of suffering and characterized by the three kinds of craving, is likewise so described.
But those minds that have entered the thicket of the karañja tree are born again in the human state, finding their sole delight therein.
O scion of the Raghus, know that this grove of plantains, cool as the rays of the moon and bringing delight to the heart, is heaven itself.
You ought to know that the minds of those who have entered the plantain grove are solely intent upon heaven.
O Raghava, those minds which have entered into the depths of the blind well but have not emerged are possessed of great sins.
O descendant of Raghu, those minds born of the human race which have not yet emerged from the Karañja forest do not depart.
Some, fully awakened there, are released from their bonds;
others, assuming many forms, indeed pass from one womb into another.
Some maintain their bodies, which are well-sustained and appropriate, through penance purified by merit and characterized by a formidable nature.
By those foolish men who insulted me as a "wicked brahmin," they have,
by their own minds ignorant of the Self, insulted their own discernment.
"What was quickly said by you, 'I am ruined, you are my enemy,' was indeed a lamentation uttered with a faltering mind."
O Raghava, that great wailing and weeping with many tears which you have shed was the lamentation made by the mind as it renounced the web of worldly enjoyments.
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state,
there will be intense anguish as the mind abandons worldly enjoyments.
With compassion, he beheld their weeping limbs and thought in his mind: "Alas! Why should I depart, abandoning these?"
For one who has attained partial discernment but has not yet reached the stainless state,
anguish indeed increases as the mind abandons its limbs.
O Rāma, that laughter which was joyful for a person due to the awakening of intoxication becomes, however, a state of contentment for the mind when discernment has been fully attained.
For one who has attained solitude and abandoned the wandering of saṃsāra,
bliss indeed increases as the mind relinquishes form.
Those limbs which were seen by a man while he was laughing in derision are indeed seen by the mind as bestowing deception.
"I have long been deceived by things fashioned by false conceptualization"—
with this thought, he looked upon his own limbs with a sense of derision.
For the mind that has attained discernment and rests in the expansive state looks upon its former wretchedness from afar and laughs at it with steadfastness.
When he was firmly restrained and questioned by me with great effort,
it was shown that discrimination forcibly took hold of the mind.
That the limbs, having fallen apart, vanish before one's eyes,
demonstrates that the desire for objects ceases when they are separated from the mind.
That which has been described as the state of having a thousand eyes and hands for the person is indeed shown to be the infinite form of the mind.
When a person strikes himself with a torrent of blows,
it is his own mind that strikes him with the blows of its own evil imaginings.
When a person flees from striking himself,
it is his own mind that flees from the blows of its own latent tendencies.
It strikes its own mind by itself, according to its own will, and it flees away by itself; behold the manifestation of ignorance!
For all minds, scorched by their own latent impressions,
flee of their own accord when they long to go to that state.
This mind itself expands this widespread suffering;
yet, once its own self is excessively distressed, it flees from that very suffering of its own accord.
The mind comes to bind itself within the web of its own volitions and latent impressions,
just as a silkworm binds itself with threads made of saliva.
Just as a child, not foreseeing its own future suffering, plays restlessly with its own mischievous antics, so too does one act impulsively, meeting with misfortune.
Just as the monkey who pulls out a wedge suffers pain because he does not see how to step upon the testicles situated within the cleft of the wood, so too is this mind.
Through long-term protection of the mind and likewise through long-term cultivation,
having attained a state of natural composure through practice, one does not grieve again.
Through mental negligence, sufferings increase like mountain peaks;
yet by that very [mindfulness], they perish, just as frost before the sun.

O noble-minded one, for as long as life lasts, the mind should be protected by an irreproachable mental impression (*vāsanā*) born from the meaning of the scriptures; indeed, through silence like that of a sage, it should be guarded against passion and the like.
Afterwards, that cool, unborn state—the purifier of purifiers—is attained, abiding in which a person no longer grieves even amidst great calamities.
The hundredth canto, titled "The Narrative of Citta," is completed.
Vasiṣṭha said:
This mind has emerged from the supreme state of Brahman;
it is both non-identical with and identical to it, like a wave [arising] from the ocean.
O Rāma, for the awakened, the mind here is indeed Brahman and nothing else;
to those who perceive the commonality of water, a wave is not other than the ocean.
The mind of those who have not awakened to the beautiful [reality] is the cause of the delusion of saṃsāra,
just as one who does not perceive the commonality of water fails to see the difference between water and its waves.
For the sake of awakening those whose intellects are unawakened,
a distinction based on the relationship between the signified and the signifier is merely conceptualized.
The Supreme Brahman possesses all powers; it is eternal, ever-full, and imperishable.
There is nothing that does not exist within that pervasive Self, nor is there anything that exists apart from it.
For the Blessed One possesses all powers; whatever power pleases him, the omnipresent Lord manifests that very power extended throughout all things.
O Rāma, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is perceived within bodies,
the power of motion (spandaśakti) within the winds, and likewise the power of inertia (jaḍaśakti) within stones.
Furthermore, the power of fluidity resides in water, the power of fire in fire,
the power of emptiness in space, and the power of existence in the persistence of being.

For the power of destruction is seen in all things subject to destruction, and the power of grief in those who grieve; indeed, these belong to Brahman, who possesses all powers and extends in the ten directions.
The power of bliss resides in the Joyful state; the power of vigor resides in the Great Hero;
the power of emanation resides in the Emanations; and at the end of the aeon, there is the power of universal withdrawal.
Just as a tree exists within the seed of a tree— possessing fruit, flowers, creepers, leaves, branches, twigs, and joints— so too does this [universe] abide within Brahman.
By the power of appearance alone, the mind— which is situated between sentience and insentience and is designated as either the "living being" or "other"— is perceived within Brahman.
Just as the powers of various trees, creepers, shrubs, networks, sprouts, and grains exist according to the season, so too do all things abide within Brahman in this world.
Just as the earth, with all its seasonal flowers scattered according to the distinctions of region and method,
yields blossoms, so too does the Creator of the world yield various minds.
From that [source], certain powers emerge at certain times and in certain places;
due to the diversity of space and time, they appear just as rice crops arise from the surface of the earth.
O Rāghava, this—Brahman alone—is designated by the name "non-conceptual pure consciousness" when it is not perceived as a mental construction; it is I, you, the world, and the quarters of space.
O Rāma, that Self is all-pervading and possesses an eternally manifest great body;
when it assumes even a slight power of thinking, it is called the mind.
Just as there is the delusion of a peacock's tail-feather in the sky, or the perception of a whirlpool in water,
so too the mind and the individual soul (jīva) are merely a fraction of appearance within the Self.
O subduer of enemies, that which has been described as the form of the mind, consisting of the nature of thinking, is the power of Brahmā; therefore, it is indeed Brahman itself.
The distinction between "this" and "I am that" arises from appearance;
when the mind is perceived as other than Brahman, delusion is the ultimate cause.
Whatever this state of mentation may be, whether consisting of the existent or the non-existent, it is all designated by the All-Powerful One; that power is indeed Brahman—so they know it.
That which is called the "mind-being-self" (manassattātman), which resides within the mind,
is born through its own manifestation and perishes by that very same [manifestation], not by another.
And those things such as the exclusion of opposites, number, form, and so forth,
which are conceptualized by means of mental words— know them to be born of Brahman and to be Brahman itself.
In whatever manner an appearance arises for this mind, in that very same way it comes to be; in this regard, the lunar mansions (the stars) are indeed cited as an example.
Just as movement occurs in the great ocean, which is itself unmoving and pure,
so too does this individual soul (jīva) exist within the Supreme Self (paramātman), being the cause of saṃsāra.
O Rāma, for the knower, through all consciousness, Brahman alone perpetually revolves within itself, like the water of the ocean amidst its surges, waves, and billows.

There is no second [reality]; existence itself consists of the activity of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), just as the conceptualization of something other than water does not exist in the ocean, which is composed of various waves.
That which is born, perishes, goes, or remains—this very world is Brahman within Brahman; it is Brahman alone that manifests as this through its own power of illusory transformation (*vivarta*).
Just as the intense heat of the sun appears through a mirage within its own self,
so too does the Self, though devoid of diversity, manifest itself through its own nature in manifold variety.
Cause, action, and agent; birth, death, and duration—all this is Brahman alone; there is nothing else apart from it, for in reality, all is but a mental construction.
There is no greed, there is no delusion, and there is no thirst; they are stainless.
What greed, thirst, or delusion can there be for the Self within the Self, and from where could they arise?
This entire world is indeed the Self; the process of mental construction is indeed the Self. Just as gold arises in the form of a bracelet, so does this Self arise in the form of the mind.
O Rāma, that Brahman which is unawakened is called the mind and the individual soul (jīva);
when it remains unrecognized, it quickly turns from being a kinsman into a stranger.
By means of its own conscious self, though ignorant, life itself has manifested emptiness through its own volition, just as the sky manifests through space.
In this world, the Self alone shines as the living soul, appearing as if it were not the Self;
like the appearance of two moons due to a faulty vision, both the existent and the non-existent have arisen from it.
Since these two— the perception of the objects of words such as "delusion" and so forth— are utterly impossible,
and because the Self is indeed all-pervasive, where is the Self bound, and where is it liberated?
For one for whom bondage is eternally impossible, the notion that "bondage exists" is a false imagination;
for one whose liberation is merely imaginary, that liberation is false and not real.
Rāma:
Whatever the mind resolves upon, that it becomes, and not otherwise.
Therefore, O Lord, how could there be any bondage that is merely conceptual?
Vasiṣṭha:
This conception of bondage for fools is merely a false imagination;
their other conception of liberation has likewise arisen as a falsehood.
Thus, through the construction of ignorance, the notions of bondage and liberation are remembered;
but in reality, O Mahāmati, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
The unreality of conceptual construction is for one whose intellect is fully awakened, O wise one, like that of a snake in a rope; it is not so for one whose intellect is unawakened.
No delusion regarding bondage, liberation, and so forth exists at all for the wise man;
O Raghava, delusion concerning bondage, liberation, and so forth belongs only to the ignorant.

First is the mind, then the views of bondage and liberation, and afterwards the construction of conceptual proliferation known as the world; for this established order has become like a mere narrative suited for the understanding of the ignorant.
The one hundred and first canto, titled "The Description of the Arising of the Mind Preceded by the Treatment of the Mind," [spoken by] Rāma:
O best of sages, why is this sequence of stories called "The Boy" told?
Please explain this to me in due order, for it is the cause for describing the mind.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, this child, whose mind is utterly innocent, asks his nurse to describe some story that has reached the path of his ears."
O Great-Minded One, for the amusement of that child, his nurse told him a narrative composed of clear and sweet syllables.
In a certain vast and empty city, there were three auspicious high-souled princes, like brilliant stars in the sky.
Two were not born, and likewise one did not even remain in the womb;
they shine like moons, possessing auspicious conduct and auspicious forms.
Then, once, for the sake of obtaining the highest gain, they gathered together; persistent yet with dejected faces and minds struck by grief.
Emerging from that empty city with their faces distorted,
they appeared like Mercury, Venus, and Saturn clustered together in the sky.
With limbs as delicate as the śirīṣa flower, scorched from behind by the sun, they fell into exhaustion on the road like tender leaves withered by the heat of summer.
With their lotus-feet scorched by the heated sands of the path, they lament, "Alas, father! O mother! like deer strayed from the herd.
With their feet pierced by the tips of *darbha* grass and the joints of their limbs exhausted by ascetic toil,
they have traveled a long distance, their forms grey with dust.

On the way, they reached three trees whose branches were entangled with clusters of blossoms, whose foliage was covered with fruits and new shoots, and which served as a refuge for flocks of birds and deer.
Among those three trees, two have not grown even slightly;
as for the third, the self-climbing tree, its very seed does not exist.
Exhausted from their journey, they rested beneath a single tree on the banks of the Pārijāta, like Śakra, Vāyu, and Yama in heaven.
Having eaten the fruits produced from nectar and drunk their juice,
and having fashioned garlands from clusters of blossoms, they departed after resting for a long time.
Having gone even further, when midday had arrived,
they reached a triple river whose roar was tremulous with waves.
There, one river was completely dried up, and not even a trace of water remained in the other two; their appearance was like that of the eyes of a blind man.
In that very river which had become utterly parched, they bathed with great devotion,
like Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara, afflicted by the heat of the summer sun, bathing in the celestial Gaṅgā.
Having engaged for a long time in water-sports and having drunk water like nectar,
those princes departed happily with joyful minds.
Then, at the end of the day, as the sun was hanging low,
they approached the city that was to be newly constructed, which resembled a mountain.
The lake of the dark-blue sky was filled with the lotus-ponds of banners,
and the circle of the city was resonant with songs whose sound could be heard from afar.
There they beheld three delightful mansions of excellent splendor, made of jewels and gold, like the peaks of a great mountain.
There were two unconstructed dwellings there, one of which was indeed without walls;
those three men entered that beautiful, wallless mansion.
Having entered and quickly sat down, those fair-faced ones, dwelling there,
reached three vessels made of refined gold.
When two of them had turned into shards and one had been reduced to powder,
those long-sighted ones took up that pot in its powdered form.
With those ninety-nine *droṇas* of that [grain] and one *droṇa* of the food,
there was a deficiency of one hundred *droṇas* there, as they were consumed by those who eat much.
Then it was eaten by hundreds of people and likewise by hundreds of brahmins,
as well as by those three princes who had attained supreme peace.
O son, those three princes are currently staying happily in that city, occupied with the pursuit of hunting.
This delightful narrative has been told by me to you, O sinless one.
Keep it in your heart, O wise one; you shall thereby become refined.
"O Rāma, this auspicious narrative was told by the nurse to the child;
and the child attained satisfaction through this excellent story."
O lotus-eyed Rāma, this story of the boy has been told by me to you in connection with the narrative concerning the mind.
This construction of saṃsāra has come to such a state through fierce conceptualizations, falsely imagined like the tales told to children.
O sinless one, this very net of conceptual construction, whose nature is mere appearance,
unfolds in the form of the notions of bondage, liberation, and so forth.
Nothing else exists here apart from mere volition;
by the power of volition, something becomes either something, nothing, or indeed something else.
The sky, the earth, the wind, space, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—
all this is fashioned by the mental construction of the Self, like a dream.
The three princes, the rivers, and likewise the city—
just as they were fashioned by mental construction, so too is the existence of these three worlds.
Mere volition alone flashes forth tremulously on all sides,
like the ocean consisting of mere water within itself by means of itself.
At first, mere volition arose within the Supreme Self;
that very thing has expanded through its activities, just as the day expands through its various functions.
The entire world is merely the manifestation of the web of volition; know that the perceived object is indeed but a playful volition.
Abandoning this mere volition sufficiently, and taking refuge in the certainty of the thought-free state, O Rāma, attain peace.
The One Hundred and Second Chapter, titled "The Narrative of Bālaka," by Vasiṣṭha.
Under the influence of his own volitions, the fool falls into delusion, but the wise man does not;
for it is only like a child that one is deluded by the conception of a ghost where no ghost exists.
Rāma said:
O best among the knowers of Brahman, who is this yakṣa conceived by whom, and by what means,
does one indeed always seize the great delusion through that which is non-existent?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Through this attachment to the elements, the Yakṣa who assumes the form of the ego has been falsely imagined here,
just as a Vetāla is imagined by a child.
When the single supreme reality alone exists in its entirety,
from where does this thing called "I" come, and how indeed has it arisen?
In reality, there is no ego-sense in the Supreme Self due to its non-duality;
yet, through incorrect vision, it appears like a river on a path in the intense heat of the sun.
The mind-jewel, characterized by great activity, is perceived as saṃsāra;
resting upon itself through itself, it vibrates like water within water.
Therefore, O Rāma, abandon false vision, which is without support;
take refuge in right vision, which has a support, is true, and is blissful.
With an intellect characterized by discernment and free from the agitation of delusion,
investigate the truth now and completely abandon what is false.
Having said that the unbound is bound, why do you grieve in vain?
How, by what means, and in what manner can the infinite reality of the Self be bound?
In this entire reality of Brahman, which is undivided despite the mental constructions of various diversities, what is bound and what is liberated?
Even though you are not afflicted, why do you suffer when a limb is severed because of the reality of affliction?
No affliction whatsoever arising from the modifications of difference or non-difference exists in the Self.
When the body is destroyed, wounded, or wasted away, no injury comes to the Self; just as when a bellows is burnt, the gold situated within it is not destroyed.
Whether the body falls or rises, what loss has come to us? When a flower is destroyed, who is deprived of the fragrance that rests in the sky?
Let the glories of cold and heat, which are the joys and sorrows of the body-lotus, descend;
what harm has befallen us when they are like bees hovering in the sky?
Let the body fall, or rise up, or go to the ends of space;
what loss can that possibly be to you, whose nature is distinct from it?
O Raghava, just as there is a relationship between the cloud and the wind, and just as there is one between the bee and the lotus, such is the relationship between your body and your own self.
The mind is indeed the body of the entire world;
its essence is consciousness, which is the self, and it never perishes.
O one of great wisdom, as for that self which you perceive as perishing, it never perishes; why then do you grieve in vain?

Just as the wind goes to the infinite space when the cloud has dispersed, and just as the six-legged bee goes to the infinite space when the lotus is withered, so does the Self go to the infinite space upon the dissolution of the body.
For even the mind of a living being dwelling in this saṃsāra does not perish without the fire of knowledge; what then need be said regarding the destruction of the self?
The relationship between the perishable body and the imperishable self is exactly like the analogy of the jujube fruit in a bowl, or the sequence of the pot and the space within it.
Just as a jujube fruit falls into the hand when its bowl bursts open,
so does the self enter the sky when the body moves away.
Just as the space within a jar does not lose its nature as space when the jar moves,
so this embodied soul remains free from affliction even when the body perishes.
For the mind-body of living beings is concealed by space and time;
repeatedly covered by the shroud of death, it lies there—so why lament?
O mighty-armed one, when concealed by place and time, why does even a deluded man fear death? For here, no one at all perishes.
Therefore, O Rāma, abandon this latent impression that "I am" which exists as a mere falsehood,
just as the king of birds abandons his egg when he longs to travel through the sky.
For this mental power, which follows after the desirable and the undesirable—
by means of this, this world has been falsely imagined through delusion, like a dream.
This is ignorance; it is of evil end; indeed, it increases for the sake of suffering.
When not fully understood, it expands this world composed of the unreal.
This deluded person perceives space as if it were a wall, and fire as if it were frost, because of the inherent nature of their own form.
This expansive, imagined world, which is truly non-existent though it arises as if existent and appears sluggish at its inception, has been projected by this [avidyā] like a long dream.
Its very nature is mere mental construction that has attained the state of an agent;
it is like a confused eye of the worlds perceiving a peacock feather in the sky.
O Rāma, through inquiry, bring about the dissolution of its very nature,
just as the sun, the lord of day, dissolves a slab of snow.
Just as the sun, seeking the absence of cold, achieves its purpose through its own rising,
so too does the one who seeks the dissolution of the mind accomplish his desired goal through inquiry.
For ignorance has indeed set forth, spreading wide and difficult to traverse with its manifold evils; like a magical illusion or a sorceress's trick, it rains down gold.
The mind alone is fully capable of performing this act of its own destruction;
for the mind dances the drama known as "the slaughter of the self."
The mind perceives itself solely for its own destruction;
for the one of evil intellect does not realize that destruction is at hand.
By the mere absence of conceptualization, the mind quickly brings this state of its own discursive thought to completion; affliction is of no use here.
Having quickly conceptualized its own nature and then, through discernment, refined the mind,
it abandons that form and undertakes the realization of the Self.
The destruction of the mind is a great attainment, yet its arising is a great calamity;
therefore, apply yourself to the destruction of the mind, and not to the impetuous flow of the mind.

In this forest where dense groves of trees are the incessant cycle of pleasure and pain, and where the great serpent Kṛtānta lurks in wait, O fortunate one, this entire mind of ours, devoid of discernment, is the sole cause of our great calamities.
Vālmīki:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
The assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The one hundred and third canto.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The mind has arisen from that which is beyond, like a drop rising from the surging ocean.
Having attained expansion, it spreads this world here and there.

It quickly makes the short long, and brings the long to a state of shortness; it thoroughly transforms what is one's own into something else, and likewise transforms what belongs to another into one's own.
Even an object the size of a span,
by the very power of its own perfected cultivation, quickly becomes as radiant as the king of mountains.
The mind, having attained a firm foundation and surging forth from the supreme state,
in a mere moment both creates and does not create the worlds of saṃsāra.
Whatever is seen here— this world, both stationary and moving, all of it enriched with every variety— all this has arisen from the mind.
Agitated by the powers of place, time, action, and substance,
the mind moves from one state to another due to its fickleness, like an actor.
It quickly leads non-existence to existence, and fully leads existence to non-existence;
it takes on exactly such pleasures and pains as have been cultivated.
Just as the fickle mind resolves,
so does the aggregate of hands, feet, and other limbs always exert itself accordingly.
Then that very action bestows the fruit desired by the mind in its entirety in an instant, just as a creeper, when watered at the proper time, yields such a result.
Just as a child in a house makes a variety of toy-arrays out of mud,
even so, O Rāma, the mind creates the world through conceptual construction.
Therefore, among the objects of the world, what single form could possibly be conceived within those things which are like the soft exhalations of children’s play upon the mind?
Just as the time that brings about the seasons causes a change in the form of a tree,
so too does the mind here cause a change in those very objects.
In a mental wish, in a dream, and in the constructions of one's imagination,
the mind’s own playful activities are like a cow’s footprint compared to a vast array of leagues.
This [mind] turns an eon into a moment and brings a moment to the state of an eon;
since it is dependent upon that [mind], the wise know it to be the sequence of space and time.
Due to the intensity or mildness of spiritual urgency, and through the distinction of its abundance or scarcity,
the mind does not linger for long, nor does it fail due to incapacity.
Delusion, agitation, misfortune, and the coming and going of time and place—
all these arise from the mind like shoots from a tree.
Just as the ocean is nothing but water, and fire is nothing but heat,
so indeed this world, with its various agitations, is nothing but the mind.
This entire extended field of objects of cognition, along with its agents, actions, and instruments,
