and enriched by the seer, the seeing, and the seen— all that, according to you, is nothing but the mind.

The mind perceives itself as having arrived of its own accord in various forms— as worlds, universes, and forest regions— just as people perceive gold, which is essentially nothing other than that, through their notions of bracelets, crowns, and anklets, once they have abandoned the thought of it being a single piece of gold.
The One Hundred and Fourth Chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this regard, listen as I shall tell you this wonderful account of how the splendor of this world’s magic trick remains dependent upon the mind.
On this surface of the earth, there exists a great and prosperous country named Uttara-Pāṇḍava, filled with various cities and forests.
Where ascetics rest in groves of dense, fresh citron trees,
and where the city-gardens possess vine-swinging pleasure-grounds inhabited by Vidyādharīs.
The mountain was tawny with masses of lotus filaments stirred up by the wind,
and it was adorned with forest garlands consisting of shimmering clusters of flowers.
The surrounding wilderness was hidden by groves of *karañja* flower-clusters,
while the sky resounded with the humming of bees from villages nestled among date palms.
Tawny with fields of ripening rice where rows of ears were swaying,
it was adorned by forest circles resounding with the loud cries of peacocks.
The forest groves of lotuses resounded with the excited cries of cranes,
and the mountain villages were adorned with earrings of dark tamāla thickets.
The banks of the river were reddened by *pāribhadra* trees in full bloom, while the air was filled with the sweet warbling of flocks of various birds.
The god of love was summoned by the songs of the maidens in the rice fields;
the clouds of flowers were shaken down by the wind blowing over the flower-strewn grounds.
Having emerged from his cave-dwelling, he was praised by siddhas and cāraṇas;
it was as if beauty itself had been summoned from heaven and fashioned anew.
It was adorned with groves of plantain trees as far as the singing kinnaras,
and it was white with flower gardens shaken by the force of the gentle breeze.
There was a king named Lavaṇa, supremely righteous,
born of the lineage of Hariścandra, like a sun upon the earth.
There the mountains shine with their circular shoulders white with the flowers of fame as their crest-ornaments, appearing like Shiva with his matted hair tossed upward.
From him, who has completely cut down the entire circle of his enemies with fragments of his sword,
the world of his foes contracts fever merely by recollecting him.
People will long remember his conduct, characterized by noble undertakings and the protection of the world of the noble, just as they do that of Hari.
Upon the peaks of the king of mountains, in the abodes of the immortals, the songs of his virtues are sung by the Apsarases, accompanied by the thrill of blossoming horripilation.
The songs of his own Sundarī, long heard by the world-protectors,
resound as hymns of praise for his virtues through the swans of Brahmā, due to their own repeated practice.
O Rāma, for one of such noble wonder, not even in dreams have the rays of the defect of wretchedness ever been seen or heard.
He who does not recognize crookedness, by whom greed has never been seen, and by whom nobility is maintained like a rosary of beads by Brahmā; //MU_3,104.19//
When the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky,
he once sat upon his lion-throne in the assembly hall.
While the king sat there comfortably like the moon in the sky,
the armies of the vassal lords entered with great haste.
Then, while the beloved women were singing and the kings were well-seated,
the sound of the lutes, flutes, and cymbals captivated the mind with its joyful resonance.
While the king— resembling the preceptor of the gods and asuras— was resting with his circle of ministers, those women with graceful gestures held beautiful chowries in their hands.
When important state affairs have been presented by the ministers,
and when reports concerning the country have been delivered by skillful spies and secret agents;
While the sacred Itihāsa was being recited from the manuscript at the auspicious hour, and while the bards stood bowed before him chanting holy hymns of praise; //MU_3,104.25//
A certain magician entered that assembly with arrogance,
like a rain-cloud entering the earth with its burden of water, having aroused a storm of fury by raining down [its contents].
Having approached the feet of the protector of the earth, whose shoulders were as noble as mountain peaks, he bowed down like a fruit-bearing tree before a lovely mountain.
He sat down before the king— who possessed a fine luster, broad shoulders, and was laden with fruit and flowers— just as a monkey might settle upon the top of a tree.
Fickle and greedy for riches, he spoke with his neck outstretched to the king, who was like a lotus, as the breeze of pleasant fragrance [blows] upon him— just as a bee [sings] to a lotus.
O Lord, while remaining seated upon your throne, behold for a moment this single display of harshness here, which is as wondrous as the moon in the sky looking down upon the earth.
Having said this, he whirled his peacock-feather whisk, which caused them to spin like Māyā— the seed of various manifestations— whirling by the Supreme Self.
The protector of the earth beheld her, radiant with a streak of splendor,
like Śakra seated in his celestial chariot gazing upon the tendril of his own bow.
At that moment, the Saindhava vassal entered the assembly hall,
like a cloud entering the path of the sky strewn with the rays of the moon.
And that excellent horse, possessed of supreme speed, followed right after him,
looking up toward the world of the gods from the ocean like Uccaiḥśravas following Śakra.
Taking that horse, he spoke to the king,
just as the Ocean of Milk, possessing Ucchaiḥśravas, spoke to the Lord of the Maruts.
O Lord of the Earth, this jewel among horses is like Uccaiḥśravas;
in its speed and victorious nature, it is as if the Wind-god himself were incarnate.
"O Lord, this horse has been sent to you by our master;
for the auspicious splendor of an object truly shines when offered to the great."
When he had spoken thus, the magician replied to him,
like a *cātaka* bird toward a mountain when the thundering of the clouds has ceased.
Mounting this noble steed, O Lord, roam the world like the sun over the earth, which possesses no small splendor bestowed by its own majesty.
The king gazed at the horse, just as a peacock, eager with longing, looks toward a cloud signaled by its thundering roar; thus he spoke.
Then the king, whose form was like a painting, gazed at the horse with an unblinking eye, as if it were fixed in a work of art.
Having gazed for a moment at the peacock and the horse, he stood with his eyes closed,
like a timid man who has seen a turbulent ocean and mountains.
For two muhūrtas, however, the Buddha remained as if absorbed in meditation within himself,
like a passionless sage abiding in supreme bliss.
"He has not been awakened by anyone; rather, this king, having been conquered by his own majesty, is brooding over some anxiety out of fear."
There, the nights with their chowrie-wavers became motionless,
as if the rays of the moon had been paralyzed.
Those members of the assembly, filled with wonder, stood motionless,
like lotuses whose filaments and petals have become rigid as if formed from mud.
The clamor of the people in the assembly hall gradually subsided,
like the thundering of the sky with its clouds at the end of the rainy season.
Emerging from the ocean of doubt, the excellent ministers fell into anxiety,
like the gods when the king of the asuras wields his mace in hand.
As the king stood with eyes motionless, that multitude— seated in the delusion of worldly existence and distorted by widespread wonder— assumed the luster of a forest of closed lotuses.
In the narrative of Indrajāla, the hundred-and-fifth canto, titled "The Delusion of the King," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after two muhūrtas, the lord of the earth attained awakening,
like a magnificent lotus released from the waters of the rainy season.
Awakened from his seat, he, with his armlets and crest-jewel, trembled like a mountain whose peaks and ridges are covered by forests during an earthquake.
Half-awakened, he sat trembling upon his throne,
like Mount Mandara within the depths of the underworld when it is violently shaken.
The leaders held that king with their arms as he was falling,
just as the principal mountain ranges support Mount Meru when it is shaken at the time of universal dissolution.
Supported by those walking before him, the king, his mind deeply agitated,
bore upon his face the splendor of the moon tossed by the waves.
"Who is this? Whose assembly is this? the king asked slowly, like a bee dwelling within the heart of a lotus sinking beneath the water.
Then the assembly spoke respectfully to the god, "What is this?
like a lotus plant with humming bees upon it seeing the sun eclipsed by Rāhu.
Then his chief ministers questioned him, who was terrified by the onset of the dissolution, just as the gods once questioned Mārkaṇḍeya.
O Lord, while you remain in such a state, we are utterly distressed;
for groundless delusions shatter even the mind that is otherwise indivisible.
In which conceptual constructions has your mind wallowed— constructions that are delightful at first sight but bitter in their final outcome, much like sensual enjoyments?
Why does your mind, which has been cultivated through constant discourse on noble conduct, sink into states of agitation?
The mind that takes as its object what is hollow and fragmented within worldly affairs adopts delusion; it does not expand through greatness.
For whatever state of mind has arisen in him through constant practice,
he follows that very state even when intoxicated by the pride of his body.
For even your mind, though it has a non-empty object, is pure, awakened, and captivated by qualities, appears as if variegated and torn asunder.
For the mind that has not practiced discernment follows the influence of place and time; it falls under the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, but not one whose conduct is noble.
How can one who has constantly attained discernment suffer from being cut or shattered? His expansive mind is not distressed by it, just as the wind does not shake the mountain of the gods.
When these words had been uttered, the splendor of that king adorned his face,
just as fullness adorns the cool-rayed moon at the end of the month.
With his eyes wide open in wonder, the king shone like the month of Mādhava when the winter season has passed and a profusion of blossoms has burst forth.
Then, with a face marked by excessive agitation, wonder, and a weary smile,
he shone like the moon in the sky upon seeing Rāhu approaching death.
Having beheld the magical display, he then spoke as if laughing,
like Takṣaka in the form of a serpent upon seeing the predatory Babhru.
O fool! What is this net that has been cast by you, O matted-haired one?
The ocean, troubled by the movement of fish, returns to clarity in an instant.
How wonderful! For the hundredfold powers of the objects of the Divine are indeed marvelous;
though my mind is exceedingly powerful, it has been cast into delusion by these.
Where are we, lamenting over the vicissitudes and events of the world;
and where are these vast, common calamities that bring delusion to the mind?
Even when great knowledge has been practiced, the mind may at times remain within the body; even for the wise, it may occasionally succumb to delusion for a moment.
O members of the assembly, listen now to this wondrous narrative of what was displayed here by my illusionist in a mere moment.
In this place, I have witnessed many shifting states of affairs,
like the Creator Brahmā beholding the worlds at a single moment— just arisen and already destroyed, like the gods led by Śakra.
Having spoken thus, while the members of the assembly looked up with wide-eyed curiosity, the king, as if smiling, began to describe the wondrous account.

The King: Here, on this earth crowded with various objects, filled with lakes, rivers, mountains, and cities, and rendered perilous by great peaks and oceans, there is this region abounding in prosperity.
The one hundred and sixth canto, titled "The Awakening of the King," Canto 106:
The King.
There exists this region, endowed with various forests and rivers,
like a younger brother born of the same womb as this very circle of the earth.
And here I am, the king, conducting myself in accordance with the wishes of the citizens; today I am established in this assembly hall like Indra in heaven.
Meanwhile, a certain conjurer arrived from afar;
this magician had risen up from the subterranean realm like Maya himself.
By this [wind], the peacock-feather broom, adorned with rows of feathers,
has been whirled here like a streak of Indra’s bow by the clouds driven by the winds at the end of an aeon.
Beholding this restless [horse] standing before me,
I, alone and with a bewildered mind, mounted its back.
Then, as the Puṣkarāvartaka wind agitates the mountain at the time of universal dissolution,
I mounted my horse as it was trembling and shaking.
Then, setting out alone with great speed for the hunt,
I was like the wave of the ocean at the end of an aeon rushing to shatter the dry land.
By that horse, tossed by the wind, I was carried far away,
just as an ignorant and deluded man is led astray by his own mind, which has become dulled through the habitual pursuit of worldly enjoyments.
The mind is empty and devoid of anything, as unfortunate as the heart of a woman;
thereafter, it is as terrifying as the abode of the world when consumed by the fire of universal dissolution.
Exhausted by my journey, I reached a vast, boundless forest, devoid of birds, free from salt-mists and frost, without trees, and lacking water.
It was like a second sky, like an eighth ocean,
like a fifth sea that had completely dried up, a hollow void.
His mind was expanded like that of a wise man, yet his anger was as slow as that of a fool;
he had not seen the company of people, nor had any blades of grass or shoots grown there.
Having reached this vast wilderness, my mind has fallen into despair,
like a wanton woman who, having encountered poverty, finds herself without food, fruit, or kinsmen.
There, as the quarters of the sky were flooded by the mirage-waters of the desert sands, I spent the entire day until the sun’s end, sinking in exhaustion.
That forest was traversed by me with great hardship and exhaustion,
like the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) by one seeking solitude— a form that is hollow within and vast in extent.
Having passed that day, I reached a vast wilderness,
like the weary sun reaching the peak of the western mountain after wandering through the empty sky.
In those groves consisting mostly of *jambū* and *kadamba* trees, the birds warble sweetly,
appearing like kinsmen to travelers.
Where rows of young grass-tips appear densely upon the ground,
they are like the movements of joy within the heart of a crooked man who has attained the fortune of wealth.
For that which brings even a slight measure of pleasure is better than the flavorless wilderness of the past;
indeed, among living beings, illness is preferable to death, which is absolute suffering.
There I reached the base of a grove of jambīra trees, just as Mārkaṇḍeya reached the king of mountains after wandering through the single vast ocean.
There, scorched by the heat, I grasped a creeper clinging to the mountain, like a dark line of clouds by a king of mountains parched by the sun.
As I hung down from this branch, that horse galloped away,
just as the accumulation of evil deeds departs from a person clinging to the Ganges.
Exhausted from traveling a very long distance, I rested there like the sun upon the slope of the western mountain at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree.
Just as the sun has settled upon the lap of the western mountain as if for rest, together with the entire burden of worldly activities in saṃsāra.
When the entire interior of the world was gradually seized by darkness,
and the nocturnal activities had fully commenced in the forest;
I remained hidden within that slender, delicate thicket of grass,
free from all agitation, like a bird in its own nest.
For one whose discernment has fallen away due to calamity, whose hope is severed, and whose memory is fading— like one who is wretched as if sold into slavery, or as if submerged in a blind well.
There, a night equal to an eon passed for me, submerged in delusion,
like that of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya while being carried away upon the single ocean.
I did not bathe, nor did I stand [in prayer], nor did I eat then;
that night passed for me as I stood at the forefront of calamities.
Sleepless, devoid of fortitude, and trembling along with the sprouts,
that night passed for me in the extreme length of my sorrow.
Then, as the streaks of darkness, along with the stars, the moon, and the night-lotuses, fell into a state of fading, so too did those with dejected faces fall into a state of despondency toward me.
And as the shrieks of the vetālas subsided in that forest of human corpses,
there arose together with them the whistling and hissing sounds of rows of teeth shivering from the pain of the cold.
In the morning, I saw the eastern quarter as if it were flushed red from drinking honey-wine, appearing as though it were laughing at me as I sank within its depths.
In an instant, like an ignorant man perceiving knowledge, or a pauper perceiving gold,
I beheld the Sun ascending upon an elephant of the sky.
Then, having stood up, I slapped my arm-guard,
just as Hara, delighting in his twilight dance, slaps his elephant hide.
I set out to roam through that vast wilderness,
which was like the world-hut at the end of an aeon when its multitudes of beings have been consumed by fire.
Nothing real is seen there in that withered wilderness, just as not even a trace of virtue exists within the body of a fool.
Only the birds roam about, free from all fear, restless as they circle through the groves, uttering their cries of "cī-cī," "kū-cī," and "cī-va."
Then, when the lord of the day had reached the eighth part of the sky,
and the creepers were as if bathed, with every last drop of dew dried away;
While wandering here, I saw her carrying a vessel of boiled rice,
holding a fine jar of nectar like the Mādhavī creeper held by a Dānava.
With eyes like shimmering stars, dark-complexioned and clad in white garments, I approached her there as the moon approaches the night.
"O child, give me this rice quickly during this time of great distress;
for through the removal of the suffering of the wretched, riches attain expansion."
This hunger, having increased within me like a black female serpent dwelling in the hollow of an old tree that has given birth, burns me from within, O child.
Even through such begging, nothing at all was given to me in this manner,
just as wealth is not given by Fortune— even when entreated with effort— to one who has committed evil deeds.
Only after a long time, as you have been my constant companion,
falling from grove to grove while standing before me like a shadow, [have I come to this state].
Addressed by her, he said, "Know me to be a Caṇḍālī, adorned with necklaces and armlets—
extremely cruel like a Rākṣasī, with the faces of a man, a horse, and an elephant."
O King, you shall not obtain food from me by mere begging; rather, O handsome one, you shall receive it as a mark of kindness from this humble and unpretentious person.
When she had spoken thus, as she walked, stumbling at every step and sinking into the groves with her body gracefully bent, she said:
"I give you this food if you will become my husband;
for the world does not provide benefit to one who is merely common, without affection."
Here at Uḍḍāra, my father, a Pukkasa,
drives my oxen like a hungry Vetāla, grey with dust, in a cemetery.
This food belongs to him; it is given while he remains in the position of a protector, for beloved men are to be honored even with one's own life.
Then I said to her: "O lady of virtuous vows, I shall become your wife;
for in times of distress, who considers the constraints of caste, dharma, or family lineage?"
Then she offered half of that rice to me,
just as in ancient times Mādhavī offered half of her nectar to Indra, who was devoted to Agni.
I drank the juice of jambu fruits and ate the rice of the Pukkasa; there, with my mind carried away by delusion, I rested.
Like a pond filled to the brim, that dark rainy season has passed away,
as if it had seized with its hand my life-force standing outside and carried it off.
He approached his father, who was of hideous appearance, of evil intent, and inspiring fear, yet possessed of a massive form, as if approaching the Avīci hell by the command of Yama.
By her, who was attached to me, her own purpose was communicated to that Mātaṅga, just as a bee, clinging to a flower, communicates its intent through its humming sound.
Having said "Certainly" to her, when the end of the day had arrived,
he released the two tamed horses that were bound, like the servants of Kṛtānta.
When the quarters were as if ablaze with frost-clouds and seemed to be covered in rising dust,
we departed from that forest at the end of the day like Vetālas.
In an instant, at twilight, they reached the outcaste settlement from the Long Jungle,
like Vetālas emerging from one cemetery to enter another, vast cemetery.
It was strewn with mangled boars, horses, monkeys, cocks, and crows;
the ground was drenched with blood, and swarms of flies buzzed about the scattered fragments of flesh.
In the groves, the intestines were moistened by the discharge of wasting diseases, while birds fell exhausted from the nets of lassitude;
jackals clung to the clusters of jambīra trees standing in the pleasure gardens.
In the courtyard shone birds perched upon heaps of dried,
heavy fat, while drops of blood flowed from hides smeared with blood that had adhered to leather water-bags.
Where flies buzz around lumps of raw flesh held in the hands of children,
and where infants cry out as they are threatened by an aged and fierce Caṇḍāla.
We entered that terrifying settlement, strewn with heads and entrails,
like the attendants of Kṛtānta entering a world that has become as if dead at the end of a kalpa.
There, in my father-in-law’s new residence, I took my seat upon a large pedestal made of plantain leaves, which had been prepared with great haste.
My mother-in-law, who had squinting eyes, said with tears welling in her eyes, "This is my son-in-law," and she was delighted by that.
Then, having rested upon a seat of antelope skin, he consumed the food of the Caṇḍālas,
which had been gathered there in abundance like his own many misdeeds.
Those words of affection, though not at all pleasant to the ear, were heard as seeds of endless suffering and were truly inauspicious.
Then, on a certain day when the sky was cloudless and the stars were visible,
through various undertakings and efforts, and by the offering of their wealth in garments—
Then he gave that girl, who was terrifying, to me—
she who was as dark as a sinful decree by one of dark complexion.
There, the outcastes, having drunk great quantities of flowing liquor, roared impetuously on all sides;
like great heaps of their own misdeeds, they were full of merriment, beating their drums with a sharp *paṭa-paṭa* sound.
The one hundred and seventh canto, titled "The Marriage of Caṇḍālī," Canto 107.
The King:
What need is there for much speaking here? From that time forth, my mind being drawn by my own festival, I became a well-nourished Pukkasa there.
At the conclusion of the seven-night festival, eight months had passed in succession; she then became blooming with flowers, and thereafter she remained pregnant.
She gave birth to a daughter who brought sorrow, like a calamity that brings about suffering;
that girl grew up quickly, becoming stout like the swelling of a fool's thoughts.
Again, after three years, that woman of evil intellect gave birth to an unlovely son, who was like a calamity and a creator of the snares of hope.
Again she gave birth to a daughter, and then once more to a boy;
thus I became a man with a wife, an old outcaste in the forest.
Many years were spent by me there with her,
as if by a slayer of a Brahmin perishing in hell along with his remorse.
In the midst of the forest, rendered helpless by the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat,
he has long been tossed about like an old tortoise in a small pond.
With an intellect struck by anxiety for wife and family,
and being consumed by burning anguish, I beheld my arduous undertakings as if the very quarters of the sky were ablaze.
Wearing many worn-out pieces of linen cloth,
he carried a load of wood through the forest like his own misdeeds incarnate.
The rainy seasons were spent on the floors of the dwellings of the wealthy— floors strewn with husks, worn out, damp, and smelling of rags used as loincloths.
Like a frog in winter, eager to fill its belly yet worn out by the cold winds, it has hidden itself within the hollows of the forest.
Driven away by the spreading heat of the surging waves of various quarrels,
drops of blood have been released from the eyes under the guise of tears.
In the forest, the nights— drenched by the downpour of clouds— were spent by him in the corner of a cave-dwelling made of stone slabs, while he fed upon the flesh of a wet boar.
When the oil has run out in due time, when the wife has become unfaithful,
and when there is a lack of affection from kinsmen along with incessant quarrels;
With a heart full of apprehension at every turn, and with a mind rendered wretched by my son who was as talkative as a playful child, I have spent years in the houses of others.
His face has reached a state of decay through the threats of fierce outcastes agitated by quarrels with their Caṇḍālī wives, like the moon marked by the teeth of Rāhu.
The morsels of panther flesh were chewed by his thick-lipped mouth like the tongues of hell-beings, brought from hell and sold.
The fierce winter winds, blowing forth from the caves of the Himalayas,
struck his bare body like arrows released by Death itself.
By one who was utterly worn out by old age and delusion, the roots of many withered trees were uprooted all at once, as if they were the roots of his own virtuous deeds.
In forest huts and in earthen bowls,
raw meat was eaten with devotion by me, who possessed a wicked wife, along with people who were themselves unwashed.
With his many mouths contorted in transformation, he acted to destroy the splendor of the perceiver,
as if selling his own portion of fortune to another as a commodity.
Having repeatedly cut off the flesh from his own body, which was the form of a living being,
he sold it away throughout the lands of the Vindhya forest settlements for the sake of his livelihood.
Like one's own accumulated sin arising from thousands of previous births,
it was scattered and strewn across the grounds of the monastic circles and gardens.
Having seen the spade with a gaze that was straight and overflowing with affection,
that crow attained a state of tenderness, as if he had fallen into the Raurava hell.
As if entering into kinship with the thickets of the Vindhya caves, he—
possessing the form of a Pulinda— had leaf-patterns applied upon his body.
His wife and children were sustained on meager food obtained by begging from village folk, while his own speed was surpassed by dogs beaten with sticks.
Nights were spent with the forest monkeys, whose teeth chattered, beneath the dry palm leaves rustling in the downpour of rain.
When I am brushed by the cold wind upon my millions of hairs,
droplets of water are held by them like pearls during the rains.
With his belly emaciated by the agitation of hunger, he engaged in a tumultuous quarrel with his wife in the great forest for the sake of a piece of the root of an *ajājī* plant.
In the forest, with his teeth chattering and eyes squinting from the cold,
his body soiled by soot, he acted like a kinsman to the vetāla.
He wandered along the riverbanks carrying a hook for the sake of fish,
like Kṛtānta, the noose-wielder, wandering through the worlds at the end of an eon for the sake of all beings.
Having fasted for many days, he drank the blood of the deer,
freshly drawn and warm at that moment, as if it were the milk from his mother’s breast.
From me, who am intoxicated with blood and clad in red garments, the forest vetālas stationed in the cremation grounds have fled,
as if pursued by Caṇḍikā.
A snare is laid out in the forest for the purpose of binding deer and birds; likewise, those consisting of sons, wives, and kin are like a net spread for the sake of increasing one's desires.
By me, worlds were brought to ruin with illusions; birds with nets made of threads; and the quarters of those whose lives were well-spent with snares.
There, when the mind has been granted excessive freedom and evil deeds arise,
hope extends far away like a river in the rainy season.
Like a snake fleeing far away out of shame from its own trunk,
compassion was cast off from the body as if it were a slough by a serpent.
Cruel, noisy with the fury of its roar, raining arrows and thundering,
it was embraced by him like the dark cloud at the end of summer is embraced by the sky.
Though they were blooming and undamaged, they were avoided from afar by people, just as withered jasmine clusters are; likewise, calamities, though long endured, were cast away by me like a chasm.
In the cremation grounds of hell, whose corners are swarming with dogs and crows,
handfuls of the seeds of evil deeds have been sown by showers of delusion.
Like the merciless God of Death dwelling in the caves of the Vindhya mountains with snares and weapons,
he pounced upon the deer as if they were living beings.
With my head resting against the walls of the necks of commoners, I slept, devoid of discernment, like Śauri upon the remaining coils of the serpent Śeṣa.
With my body— its garment of trembling leaves and its rising smoke of falling arrows— I have become like a cave in the misty marshlands of the Vindhya mountains.
For a long time, I carried on my shoulder a patched cloak thick with lice,
produced by my own body during the summers, just as a boar carries upturned earth with its snout.
Many times have I been like Time itself, having followed its likeness by consuming multitudes of living beings with forest fires and devouring the world with the fire of the end of an aeon.
Just as iron fetters are difficult to grasp, so too my wife brought forth there diseases and misfortunes, as well as sorrows and even sons.
Then, as a son with three young wives and only one child, I spent sixty kalpas of years under the influence of incessant faults.

O members of the assembly, for a long duration I was there— afflicted by that, bound by the shackles of evil impressions, crying out when reviled, wailing in calamities, eating miserable food, and dwelling in wretched hamlets.
The one hundred and eighth canto, titled "The Description of Adversity," from the Episode of Indrajāla.
The King said:
Then, as time passed and my lifespan became worn out by old age,
I came to bear a beard like a mass of young grass covered in frost.
As the masses of days fall away— driven by the winds of karma, whether full of flavor or devoid of it— like heaps of withered leaves.
Like in a battle amidst showers of arrows, there is no rest in pleasures and pains, nor in quarrels, nor in affairs that come and go.
In the delusion of the world, which revolves like a whirlpool of conceptual constructions,
the mind wanders like an ocean amidst a mass of surging waves.
When the self has mounted the wheel of thought, which is ever-moving and accumulated by reflection,
it wanders like a blade of grass being swept away in the whirlpool of the ocean of time.

Thus, in this world, the lifespan of the two-armed donkey— who is like a worm in the wound of the Vindhya earth and whose sole refuge is a village— is exhausted when his years have thus run their course.
When my status as a king was forgotten, like a great fever in a corpse;
when my state as a Caṇḍāla became fixed, like a mountain whose wings have been clipped.
Like the end of an eon to the cycle of existence, like a forest fire to a grove,
like a wave of the ocean to its shore, and like a thunderbolt to a withered tree.

Then he went to the marshlands of the Vindhya mountains, where food, grass, leaves, and water were scarce, and which were filled with circles of fierce Caṇḍālas who had taken flight due to sudden death.
When the mass of clouds has ceased raining and vanished, and the wind blows carrying with it scattered particles of glowing embers, remaining stationary in some places; MU_3,108.10//
In the forest glades where the leaves were withered and rustling, and which were enveloped by forest fires, appearing empty as if long abandoned by those who had gone forth into homelessness.
Suddenly there occurred a terrifying fire of unrestrained fury,
which dried up every thicket and reduced all grass and shrubs to ashes.
With all its limbs grey with dust, with every man famished,
and regions where food, grass, and water were absent, it was like a circle of forest fires breaking out.
The region of the earth was submerged in the mirage-waters of the desert sands;
the sky was shrouded by clouds that were actually banks of sand raised by the wind.
A multitude of men, longing only to hear the sound of water,
with all their people utterly exhausted and perishing from the heat of the sun.
Intensely agitated by hunger and having abandoned all regard for life, he devoured his own son,
his circle of teeth rolling in fury as he gnawed upon his own limbs.
It swallowed a mass of fierce khadira-wood embers, mistaking them for meat;
it seized fragments of forest stones, hoping they were lizards or snakes.
A multitude of mothers, sons, and fathers were violently entangled with one another, while forest parrots, seized by the sharp beaks of vultures, shrieked from within their bellies.
The surface of the earth was drenched with blood from the mutual severing of limbs,
while the elephants were frantic and agitated, enraged by the devouring of lions.
It was terrifying with lions roaming about, intent on swallowing their prey;
it was a battle waged by world-athletes striving to devour one another.
The wind was filled with flying embers from trees stripped of their leaves;
the ground of the mineral-rich floor was licked by cats eager for the blood they had drunk.
The forest winds were adorned with the dense massing of thick flames,
and the wilderness was turned tawny by the heaps of blazing fire that fell everywhere.
The thickets were dense with smoke rising from the groves of scorched pythons;
the sky was enveloped by twilight clouds and flames tossed by the wind.
The circle of ash-pillars was whirled about by the fierce winds,
while the cries of children were raised as they were crushed by the tips of the tusks of screaming elephants.
It was filled with the great corpses of men whose teeth had been severed by throngs of bewildered beings,
while their own fingers were stained crimson, consumed by the force of their craving for flesh.
With the appearance of dark foliage, creepers, sounds, yellow smoke, and dense clouds; with vultures wheeling about as if swallowing the sky, mistaking it for the flesh of a blazing firebrand.
It was agitated by the fleeing of people whose limbs were mangled by one another,
and its hearts and bellies were torn asunder by the crackling sounds of blazing fires.
There was the leaping of forest fires, terrifying with the whistling sounds of the moving winds; there were trees whose branches fell like glowing embers due to the hissing of frightened pythons.
Suddenly encountering that [fire], that region with its parched hollows came to resemble the world consumed by the fire of twelve suns.
With its clusters of trees possessing matted locks of blazing fire, and with people driven away by the spreading force of the gusting winds,
that region came to resemble the pleasure-houses of the sons of Agni, Tapana, and Bhāskara.
In the *Indrajālopākhyāna*,
the chapter titled "The Description of the Sudden Occurrence," the one hundred and ninth chapter;
the King said:
While that painful reversal of fate was occurring,
at the end of an eon marked by untimely intensity, it produced extreme heat.
Some people, having departed together with their wives and kinsmen,
went to another land like clouds from the sky in autumn.
With their sons, wives, and foremost kinsmen clinging to the limbs of their bodies,
some lay there shattered, like trees cut down in a forest.
Some were devoured by tigers roaming the directions as they emerged from their own dwellings,
like fledglings that have not yet grown wings being carried off by hawks as they leave the nest.
Some entered the blazing fire like moths;
others fell into chasms like boulders fallen from a mountain.
But I, having abandoned those— my father-in-law and my own people— and taking only my wife, have emerged from that country with great difficulty.
Having deceived the fires, the winds, the guardians, and even the devourers,
I have emerged from the terrors of death together with my wife.
Having reached the edge of that region, he set down his sons from his shoulders at the foot of a palmyra tree, as if they were formidable calamities.
I am at rest, long-exhausted as if emerged from Raurava;
like a waterless lotus in summer, tormented by the heat of a forest fire in the hot season.
Then, while the Caṇḍāla girl rested at the foot of a tree,
she fell asleep in the cool shade, embracing her two children.
"My only son named Thutthaka stands before me;
he is our most beloved, the youngest, and full of charm."
With a distressed soul and eyes filled with tears, he said to me:
"O trusted one, quickly give me flesh and blood for a drink this very moment."
Speaking thus again and again, that foolish son of mine reached a life-ending state, crying out once more from hunger.
Indeed, I have told him many times, "O son, there is no meat," yet that evil-minded man continues to say, "Give me meat."
Then, deluded by affection and overwhelmed by excessive grief, I said to him: "My son, let my cooked flesh be eaten."
That too was accepted by him as he said "give," he whose livelihood was exhausted and whose skin was slackened, desiring to eat my flesh.
Deluded by affection and compassion for the sake of dispelling all suffering,
I then rose up suddenly toward my friend who had come to his death.
Having gathered wood from the forest scorched by the heat of summer,
I constructed a funeral pyre there for my own death.
Then that funeral pyre, blazing with the flickering flames of a leaping fire,
stood for a moment crackling and popping as it yearned for me.
I said: "From me, you must cut off flesh moment by moment and eat it from this son who has fallen upon the funeral pyre."
Having said this, just as I was about to throw myself upon the funeral pyre,
the king suddenly rolled away from this lion-throne with great speed.
Then, by the sound of trumpets and the shouts of "Victory! on all sides, I was fully awakened; and with mindfulness, I remained there, composed.
Thus, by this magician, delusion has been produced here within me,
just as ignorance produces hundreds of states for the living soul.
I have thus related this account of my own life to you,
just as Mārkaṇḍeya described the endless suffering of the kalpa to the virtuous kings.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When Lavaṇa, the lord of kings of immense splendor, had spoken thus,
that sorcerer vanished there in an instant.
Then those members of the assembly, their minds overwhelmed with wonder, spoke as follows,
their lotus-petal-like eyes busily glancing at one another.
"Aha! How truly marvelous is this illusion; it is indeed extraordinary!
Who could this Śāmbarika be, and where has he gone ahead?"
For the powers of the All-Powerful Ordainer are indeed manifold and hundreds-fold,
since even this discriminating mind is deluded by his illusory power (māyā).

Where on one hand is this lord of the earth, who has fully understood the ways of the world; and where, on the other, are these vast outbursts of agitation, which are suited only to the ordinary mind?
And this illusion, which deludes the mind, is not produced by a magician;
for these magicians are indeed always greedy for wealth.
"They strive for wealth with effort, yet they do not disappear"—
thus, caught upon the swing of doubt, we have been tossed about.
O Rāma, I indeed resided in that assembly hall at that time;
therefore, this was seen by me with my own eyes and not heard from another's report.
O Great-Souled One, lead this mind of yours—which has had its limbs nourished by excessive conceptualization—to tranquility;
when the intrinsic nature has reached supreme peace, you will attain that most holy state.
The hundred-and-tenth canto, titled "The Narrative of Śāmbarika," by Vasiṣṭha.

At first, due to an external cause, consciousness falls into the state of being an object; having reached the stage of mental construction, it undergoes further internal conceptualization and defilement.
O Rāma, when delusions of this kind— which are indeed non-existent—
become dense, one sinks for a long time into their utter emptiness.
The mental activity directed toward what is non-existent, though withered,
spreads suffering extensively through a thousand defects, just as a child spreads a vetāla spirit.
For indeed, even great suffering is brought to non-existence in an instant by a stainless mental state, just as the light of the sun dispels darkness.
Bringing the distant near and the near to a distance,
the mind flutters among beings like a foolish child among young birds.
Fearlessness appears as fear to the ignorant mind possessed of latent impressions;
to the deluded traveler from afar, even a tree stump takes on the nature of a demon.
A mind stained by suspicion suspects enmity even in a friend;
a creature whose intellect is possessed by intoxication sees the very ground as spinning.
For when the mind is agitated, lightning strikes from the moon;
nectar, when consumed with the nature of poison, undergoes the effects of poison.

Enveloped by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), the mind perceives the construction of cities and towns— which are non-existent— as if they were real, even while in the waking state, just like in a dream.
The intense latent impression (vāsanā) of the mind, which is the sole cause of a living being's delusion,
must be uprooted with effort by cutting it at its very root.
Drawn by the snare of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the deer-like mind of men falls into utter helplessness within the thicket of the forest of *saṃsāra*.
The light of that wise one shines forth, like the sun in a cloudless sky, since his latent impressions have been severed through inquiry into the nature of the living self.
Therefore, O mind, know that this person is the mind alone, not the body;
for the body is inert, whereas the wise know that the mind here is neither inert nor non-inert.
Whatever is done with the mind, O Rāma, know that to be truly done, O Rāghava; whatever is abandoned by the mind, O Rāma, know that to be truly abandoned, O Rāghava.
The entire world is mind alone; the circle of mountains is mind;
the sky is mind, the earth is mind, the wind is mind, and the Great One is mind.
If the mind did not indeed join the object with its own nature,
then even these things such as the sun would never be manifest.
The mind takes on delusion, because of which one is called "deluded";
when the body has fallen into delusion, it is not called "deluded" when it is a corpse.
The mind becomes the eye when seeing; it attains the state of hearing when listening;
it reaches the condition of touch through feeling; and it attains the state of smelling through sniffing.
Just as a taste becomes manifest through tasting, so too the mind alone moves within the body through these various functions, like an actor in a drama.
This [mind] makes the short long, and it goes from existence to non-existence;
it turns the sweet into bitterness, and it brings an enemy to the state of a friend.
Whatever appearance belongs to this mind as it functions,
that alone is indeed direct perception here, because it is the experience of that [appearance] itself.
By the power of mere appearance, for Hariścandra, whose mind was occupied with the objects of a dream, a single night became twelve years long.
By the power of the influence of his mind, a yuga became a mere moment for Indradyumna, who dwelt within the city of Brahmā.
Through a pleasant mental state, even the Raurava hell becomes a state of bliss,
like the imprisonment of one who has already obtained his own kingdom in the morning.
When the mind is conquered, the entire host of the senses is likewise conquered;
it perishes just as a string of pearls is destroyed when its thread is burnt.
By the power of consciousness, which is ever-present, transparent in nature, changeless, subtle, eternal, and acting as the witness; by that [power] which is the *samaya*. //MU_3,110.26//

Though it is insentient and like the body, even when it is mute within the reality of the Self of Rāma— which pervades all existents and is not distinct from the object of consciousness— [it functions as such].
The mind leaps within, its restless thoughts and desires stilled by vigor, while externally it sports with the playfulness of mountains, rivers, sky, oceans, and cities.
While awake, it turns a desired object into something as sweet as nectar,
yet it turns even nectar itself into poison for that which is undesired.
Having fully projected the self-manifestation (*ātmacamatkṛti*) of all existents,
the mind, however, creates within objects a form that corresponds to its own desired aspect.
In vibrations it attains the state of air, in luminous things the state of light,
and in fluids it attains the state of fluidity— the mind, suffused by the power of consciousness.
On earth, the mind—pervaded by the power of consciousness—attains solidity; in states of emptiness, it attains voidness; and wherever it abides through desire, it assumes that very form.
It turns white into black and leads the black to whiteness;
behold the power of this mind, which operates even without regard for place or time.
When the mind is attached elsewhere, even the taste of most delicious food that has been chewed by the tongue is not truly experienced.
That which is seen by the mind is not truly seen;
it is unobserved, like a form in darkness, for the sense-faculty is devoid of mind.
The mind dispels the senses, but the senseless mind does not dispel the senses;
the senses are produced from the mind, but the mind is not produced from the senses.
Those great-souled ones who have realized the knowable and are highly wise— those for whom there is the unity of the utterly distinct mind and body— are worthy of homage.
With her hair-knot radiant with flowers and her eyes cast down in playful languor,
the woman remained as if mindless, even though she was clinging to limbs that were like wood or a wall.
When the mind was distracted elsewhere in the forest by one free from passion,
he did not even notice his own hand on his limb being chewed by a carnivorous beast.
To make great sufferings into happiness and to make happiness into suffering, the extraordinary powers of the Sage’s mind are joined with ease and speed. (3,110.40)
Alas, when the mind is attached elsewhere, even a story being told with effort is cut short like a creeper severed by an axe.
When the mind has ascended to the mountain slopes [of the external world], even a living being who is a householder experiences the suffering of wandering through chasms, clouds, and caves.
When the mind is delighted in a dream, cities and mountains appear within the heart itself,
created in an instant like [objects] in the vast expanse of space.
The mind, agitated in a dream, projects a series of mountain cities within the heart itself,
just as the surging ocean projects a multitude of waves within itself.
Just as waves, crests, and ripples arise from within the water of the ocean,
so too do the rows of mountains and cities in dreams arise from the mind within the body.
Just as the splendor of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits arises from a sprout,
so too do the manifestations of the delusions of waking and dreaming arise from this mind.
Just as a golden woman is not distinct from gold,
so the splendor of the activities of waking and dreaming is not distinct from the mind.
Just as the beauty of the stream, droplets, waves, and foam is perceived in water,
so too this manifold diversity of various prosperities belongs indeed to the mind.
This very activity of one's own mind, arising as the states of waking and dreaming,
assumes various roles like an actor through its immersion in aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Just as the state of being a Caṇḍāla is [merely] due to the power of appearance,
so too this expansive world is nothing but the mental construction of the mind.
Whatever is perceived, by that very thing one quickly becomes;
it is a creation of the mind's own conceptualizing—do as you wish.
Having assumed the forms of various cities, rivers, and mountains for embodied beings,
the mind spreads this very delusion of waking and dreaming that resides within it.
Due to its nature as a spirit, it attains the state of a Daitya; due to its nature as a Naga, it also attains the state of a Naga.
By the power of mental appearance, the mind encounters calamity, just like Lavaṇa.

Just as an actor quickly assumes the state of a woman from the state of a man, or again the state of a son from the state of a father, so too does the mind [assume various forms] through its own volition.
Through volition one dies, and through volition one is born again;
the mind, having practiced for a very long time, attains the state of a living being, though it is formless.
The mind, deluded by its own thinking and driven by the wind of latent impressions,
enters the womb through volition, [experiencing] pleasure and pain, fear and fearlessness.
Pleasure and pain reside in the mind like oil in sesame seeds;
depending on place and time, they may become intense or slight.
Just as the oil of the sesame seed attains its eternal clarity through the process of churning,
so too do pleasure and pain become solidified through the mind's attachment to mental constructs.
O Rāma, it is indeed intention (*saṅkalpa*) itself that is designated by the terms "space" and "time," for it is under its influence that space and time maintain their existence.
When the conceptualization of the body bears fruit, the mind quiets down, exults, approaches, departs, rejoices, and leaps; yet it is not the physical body that does so.
By means of various surges of movement produced by its own volitions,
the mind gallops within this body like a horseman in an arena.
Therefore, one should restrain the mind so that it does not extend toward fickleness; thus it attains discipline, like an elephant tethered to a post.
He whose mind does not waver, like an excellent pillar of steel, is a man of the True Reality; all others are but worms in the mud.
He whose mind, having attained freedom from fickleness, is established in one place—
that sinless one has followed after the unsurpassed state through meditation.
Through the restraint of the mind, the turmoil of saṃsāra attains peace,
just as the great ocean of milk becomes still when Mount Mandara ceases its churning.
Whatever growths of the mind arise through the delusions of desire for enjoyment,
those alone are the sources of the sprouts of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra.
These fools, dull-witted and sluggish with intoxication and delusion, circle about like restless blue lotuses;
their minds torn asunder and shattered, these wretched human-bees fall into the whirling of the wheel within the eddying whirlpool.
The One Hundred and Eleventh Chapter, titled "Description of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha:

Listen to the excellent medicine for the treatment of this great disease of the mind: it is within one's own control, easily mastered by oneself through proper method, and resides within one's own self.
By one's own human effort, which is of the nature of self-awareness, the vampire of the mind is quickly conquered through exertion by abandoning desired objects.
He who remains free from affliction while renouncing even his most cherished object has truly conquered his mind, just as a well-tamed elephant subdues a wild one.
The infant-like mind is nurtured through the effort of self-reflexive awareness;
it is joined to the unreal and the real, and is likewise awakened.
O Sage, with a mind steady through engagement with the scriptures and free from distress, cut through the mind with the mind alone— like iron with iron— though it be heated by anxiety.
Just as a child exerts itself here and there without effort, why is it so very difficult for the worthy to likewise direct the mind within? MU 3.111.6.
One should direct the mind with conscious intent toward a noble deed that brings about a future rise of prosperity, by means of one's own manly effort alone.
Fie upon that worm of a man for whom the renunciation of his own cherished desires— which is within his own power and exclusively beneficial— has become difficult to perform!
Having contemplated the forest as something delightful through one's own self-awareness,
the mind is conquered without effort, just as a child is subdued by a wrestler.
By human effort, the mind is quickly conquered;
by means of that mindless state which is free from adversaries, one is established in the state of Brahman.
Fie upon those jackals among men who are unable to accomplish that which is within their own power, easily achieved, and requires nothing more than the conquest of their own minds!
Without the mantra of mental tranquility— which is to be accomplished solely through one's own effort and consists in the renunciation of what one desires— there is no auspicious state of existence.

By means of the object of accomplishment, which is the self-awareness of one's own nature, let that which is without rival, without beginning or end, and immovable be desired here through the mere slaying of the mind.
But when the beauty of the mind’s tranquility— which is the means for attaining what is desired—
is present, methods such as the teacher’s instruction, the meaning of the scriptures, and mantras are like mere straw.
When the disease of the mind has been severed by the weapon of non-conceptualization, then everything becomes the all-pervading, peaceful Brahman.
In this matter, which is to be accomplished through self-awareness, which destroys the miseries of conceptual construction,
and which possesses the nature of a peaceful, clear sky— what kind of affliction could there be for such a person?
Surely, disregarding destiny— which is fashioned by the deluded intentions of the mind—
bring the mind to the state of non-mind through human effort and self-awareness.
Following for a long time that singular and ineffable Great State,
having made the mind devoured by consciousness, become even beyond consciousness itself.
Liberated through the contemplation of existence and endowed with supreme intellect,
one should remain undistracted, holding the self within the consciousness that is beyond the mind and unswallowed by it.
Relying on supreme human effort and leading the mind to the state of non-mind,
come to that great station where you do not exist, nor does anything else.
O Rāma, just as a weak enemy is easily conquered by force, so too can the mind— which takes the form of the distortion of perception— be swiftly subdued through manly effort alone.

Freedom from agitation is the root of prosperity; from freedom from agitation arises the conquest of the mind by a living being, through which the conquest of the three worlds becomes as trivial as a blade of grass.
In that [state] where there is not even the slightest stroke of weapons, fire, or calamities,
what kind of torment could there be when only one's own nature has been set aside?
How will those lowest of men, who are incapable even of being overcome by their own sensations, conduct themselves in the circumstances of worldly affairs?
"I am a man," "I have been born," "I live"—such are the false views;
they are the flickering fluctuations of the mind, arising from what is unreal.
No one here dies, nor is anyone born here;
one perceives death within the body as the mind has gone to another world.
Having departed from here, the mind manifests in another form in the next world;
it does not perish until liberation. Therefore, whence can there be fear of death?
Wandering through this world and the next in the form of the body, the mind remains until liberation; no other form of it is found.
When a son, brother, servant, or the like suffers, it is men who experience the affliction;
it is not in their own minds, for my view is that [suffering] consists in the turning away from one's own consciousness.
Having investigated again and again in the horizontal, upward, and downward directions,
it was found that there is indeed no means other than the pacification of the mind.
When the path has been traversed, purified, and cleared, and when consciousness has arisen in the heart as awakened awareness, rest is produced merely through the dissolution of the mind.
One meditates upon consciousness within the space of the heart by means of the flow of the wheel of consciousness;
kill the mind without hesitation, and mental afflictions will no longer torment you.
If that which was delightful has been perceived by you as un-delightful through knowledge,
it is my conviction that the very limbs of the mind have been severed.
"This is that I am; this is mine; my mind is merely this much"—by the mere contemplation of its non-existence, it is cut away as if by a sickle.
Just as a cloudless sky is cleared of mist in the autumn,
so too the mind, free from latent tendencies, is purified within the supreme reality that is beyond conceptual construction.
Where weapons, fire, and wind blow, there fear may arise;
but when [the mind] is under one's own control, gentle, and clear, what fear can there be in the absence of conceptualization?
"This is better, this is not"—this conviction remains unimpaired even among children;
therefore, one should direct the mind toward the sublime good, as one would toward a beloved son.
Those who slay the five-sensed lion within the mind— which nourishes the cycle of worldly existence— triumph here and fall into the state of Nirvāṇa.
These terrifying calamities, which cause great agitation, are produced from the mental construction of conceptual thought,
just as mirages arise from the heat of a desert.
Let the winds blow at the end of the eon, let the oceans become one, and let the twelve suns blaze; yet for one who is free from the mind, there is no injury.
From the seed of the mind arise these thickets of saṃsāra, which yield the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and possess the seven worlds as their sprouts.
For the sake of accomplishing everything that is to be achieved solely through the single means of non-mental-construction,
remain intent on maintaining firm resolve within the sovereign empire of non-mental-construction.
The mind, as it gradually wanes, bestows supreme bliss,
just as a charcoal whose parts are nearly consumed grants joy to one seeking the extinction of that charcoal.
If the mind's desired object is even the peak of Brahma’s abode,
it is clearly perceived as distinct within the space of an atom.

Having conquered the mind through the power of mere resolve—which brings about great misfortune—and through the power of the pacification of resolve which accomplishes one's goals; having conquered it through the power of mere contentment, attain victory with effortless, ever-arising [wisdom].

May that unborn state which remains—transcending the minds of the knowers of the Self through supreme purity, dispassion, equanimity, and realization; and through tranquility, moderation, and the cessation of egoism—be my refuge.
The one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nature of the Power of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
For upon whatever object, by whatever means, and in whatever manner the mind—endowed with intense spiritual urgency—beholds that which it desires; //MU_3,112.1//
This intense agitation of the mind arises and perishes;
by its very nature, it is without cause, like a series of bubbles on calm water.
Coldness is like that of frost, and blackness is like that of collyrium;
restlessness is the form of the mind, which possesses a single nature ranging from intense to mild.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how can the movement of this exceedingly fickle mind— which has nothing but its own momentum as its cause— be forcibly restrained?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this world, a mind devoid of flickering restlessness is nowhere to be seen;
flickeringness is an inherent property of the mind, just as heat is a property of fire."
Know that this flickering power of vibration, which resides within the nature of consciousness, is the mental power whose essence is the phenomenal display of the world.
Just as the very existence of wind cannot be inferred apart from its vibration and touch,
so too the existence of the mind does not exist apart from its flickering movement.
That mind which is devoid of flickering is said to be dead;
and that very state is called liberation, as it is well-known from the scriptures on austerity.
By the mere dissolution of the mind, the cessation of suffering is attained;
by the mere arising of the mind, supreme suffering is attained.
The rakshasa of the mind, having risen up, produces intense suffering;
therefore, with effort, cast it down for the sake of infinite enjoyment of happiness.
This instability of his which is called ignorance (avidyā)—
known by the other name of latent impression (vāsanā)— destroy it through inquiry.
Through that ignorance and its latent impressions, which have dissolved within by means of the peace of the mind through the power of renunciation, the supreme good is attained.
That which is the middle between existence and non-existence, and the middle between consciousness and insentience—
that, O Rāma, is called the mind, its form oscillating between the two.
For the mind, when seized by the contemplation of dullness and kindled by its very nature as dullness,
indeed attains a state of dullness through the power of firm habituation.
Through the continuous contemplation of solitude, the mind, by virtue of its nature as a portion of consciousness,
attains stability and reaches oneness with consciousness through the power of firm practice.
By means of human effort, whatever state the mind is directed toward,
having reached that state, it becomes red-tinted by practice.
Therefore, relying on human effort and mastering the mind with the intellect,
take refuge in the sorrowless state and remain steadfast, free from doubt.
O Rāma, if the mind is not broken by the contemplation of worldly existence through the mind itself, it must be forcibly extracted; there is no other means.
The mind alone is indeed capable of firmly restraining the mind;
for who other than a king, O Raghava, would be capable of restraining a king?
For those seized by the grasp of craving, being carried away by the whirlpools in the swift current of the ocean of saṃsāra, one's own mind alone is the boat.
Having severed with the mind alone the mind— that bond which is the supreme fetter—
he by whom the self has not been liberated will not be liberated by any other means.

Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) called "mind" arises within one who has cultivated their inner being, the wise person should abandon each and every one of them; through that, the destruction of ignorance occurs.
Having abandoned the latent impression of the flood of enjoyments, abandon the latent impression of distress;
then, having abandoned both existence and non-existence, become blissful and free from conceptual construction.
The non-cultivation of cultivation—this much is the exhaustion of cultivation;
this alone is the dissolution of the mind, which is called the destruction of ignorance.
Whatever is perceived, it is better that there be no perception of it;
for non-perception is nirvāṇa, while suffering arises from perception.
By that very effort of one's own, a person attains it in an instant;
the non-contemplation of phenomena leads to prosperity, therefore one should constantly practice it.
Having understood that those things such as passion which are desired by the mind are each devoid of substantial reality, abandon them;
then, having uprooted the sprout of attachment along with its seed, you shall, being satisfied, no longer undergo joy or sorrow.
The one hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Portion of the Teaching by Means of the Sound of the Hoof," [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.
For this latent impression (vāsanā) has always arisen with respect to that which is unreal, like the delusion of two moons; therefore, O Rāghava, it is proper to abandon it.
Ignorance exists only for one whose wisdom is destroyed; it is accepted as non-existent by name alone. For one of right wisdom, how could it exist?
Do not be ignorant; be wise, O Rāma, and investigate correctly.
There is no second moon in the sky; it is perceived in vain through delusion.
Apart from the reality of the Self, nothing exists— neither a real entity nor a non-entity—
just as there is nothing apart from the mass of water in the vast ocean garlanded with waves.
Do not superimpose upon the self— eternal, pervasive, white, and pure— these notions of existence and non-existence created by your own conceptual construction, which are devoid of reality.
You are not the agent; why do you have this sense of "mine" regarding these actions?
For when there is only one [the Self], what is done by whom, and how?
O wise one, do not become a non-doer; for what is to be accomplished by you here through non-action?
There is something to be achieved and something to be attained; therefore, O sinless one, remain established in yourself.
O scion of Raghu, you are indeed an agent because of your non-attachment;
yet, being an agent through non-attachment, you remain a non-agent and may act with movement like one who is an agent.
If it were true, it should be accepted; if it were false, it should indeed be abandoned.
For attachment to action is appropriate because of one's exclusive attachment to what is to be accepted.
Where the entire world is a magical illusion, consisting of māyā and devoid of substantial reality—
there, O Rāma, what are those views of what is to be rejected or accepted, and how could they exist?
O scion of Raghu, this ignorance is the seed-grain of saṃsāra;
for though it is non-existent, it has attained expansion as if it were real.
This wheel of the cycle of existence, which consists of the essence of directed effort,
should be understood as this mental latent tendency that bestows delusion.
Like a beautiful bamboo stalk that is hollow and pithless within, or like a succession of river waves, it is impermanent and subject to destruction without interruption.
Even when grasped with the hand, it cannot be held;
though soft, its tip is exceedingly sharp, like a rising wave from a mountain torrent.
It appears with a manifest radiance, yet it is not employed for the sake of the real object;
it is like a river appearing as waves, though its form is not ultimately established.
In some places crooked, in others straight, long, short, stable, or moving—
whatever arises through its grace has thus attained a state of differentiation from it.
Though empty within, this beautiful essence is seen everywhere;
though not established anywhere here, it is perceived everywhere.
Though insentient, she appears as if composed of consciousness; subsisting on the vibration of another, she never remains still for even a moment, yet she inspires the hope of stability.
Though her complexion is pure like a flame, she has a hollow as dark as soot;
she leaps about by the favor of another, yet withers away when not looked upon by him.
Faded in pure light, it shines intensely in darkness;
like a vast mirage, it displays the play of various colors.
Crooked, uneven, slender, soft, yet rough with thorns;
fickle, hungry, and thirsty—the woman is like the tongue of a serpent.
Like the flame of a lamp itself, it quickly perishes when its oil is exhausted;
like a streak of vermilion powder, it does not glow without passion.
Momentarily flashing, flickering, and assuming forms within the dull-witted mind, she arises like a crooked lightning bolt, striking terror into the simple-minded.
Seized with effort, it burns; having come into being again and again, it dissolves away.
Though sought, it is not found; as fleeting as lightning, it is exceedingly fragile.
Though delightful, a thing that comes unbidden brings misfortune;
like a garland of flowers out of season, it should not be welcomed for the sake of one's welfare.
This [mind], which has been utterly forgotten for the sake of supreme bliss and which causes delusion,
has arisen only for misfortune, like the occurrence of a bad dream.
By the power of mere appearance alone, having produced the three great worlds in a mere moment, he sustains them and devours them.
By her, a single moment was made into a series of years for Lavaṇa,
and a night was fashioned as twelve years for Hariścandra.
Furthermore, for others who are separated from their beloveds and suffering the pangs of absence,
the night becomes as long as a year through her grace.
For one who is happy, time becomes short; for one who is suffering, it becomes long. Indeed, this is due to the influence of that [time] which is characterized solely by its reversals.
In these activities, its agency exists merely by virtue of its own existence;
it is not real in substance, just as a lamp is the cause of the effects of its light.

Just as a woman with breasts like ripe *śālī* grain, though adorned with variegated ornaments, is not truly a woman if she lacks her feminine nature, so too this [woman], though steady in appearance, is incapable of performing any action whatsoever.
Like a kingdom of the mind, though brilliant in form and possessing hundreds of thousands of branches, it is devoid of reality and is nothing at all from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Like a mirage in the forest, it is entirely false and full of ostentation;
it deceives only those deluded like deer, not human beings.
Like a mass of foam, it arises and perishes, devoid of continuity;
though perceived as something inert yet flickering in form, it is in truth nothing at all.
Though not different from consciousness, it is surely as if distinct and remains separate;
like a short silkworm’s thread, though inert, it rests upon that which is non-inert.
Turbid and violent in its activity, grey with the spreading of dust,
it is like the shifting wind at the end of an aeon, having pervaded the interior of the world.
Like a column of smoke clinging to the body, causing burning and perspiration,
it pervades the worlds, having internalized the sequence of the aesthetic flavors (rasa).
Like a very long stream from a cloud, it is composed of insentient matter; like a firm rope made from a collection of pithless things, it is constructed from bundles of straw.
Like a garland of water-lilies upon a wave, it is described as being mere imagination; like a lotus stalk, it is full of holes, matured in mud, and insentient by nature.
Like a flame, it appears intent on increasing, yet it does not truly grow;
like the taste of poison, sweet at first but extremely dreadful in the end.
Like the flame of a lamp that has gone out, I do not know where it goes here;
like a mist seen at close range, though grasped, it is nothing at all.
Spread out like a handful of dust,
this ultimate atomic state is seen as nothing more than the blueness of space, utterly devoid of causal characteristics.
Like the delusion of two moons, it has arisen; like a dream, it has produced error.
Just as a stationary post appears to move to one traveling by boat, so too has this [delusion] arisen here.
When the mind is afflicted by this [ignorance], the long delusion of the dream of saṃsāra appears to people as if it were enduring for a long time.
Even that which is pleasant and true is seen as non-existent;
and that which is unpleasant and untrue is seen as existent.
But when this mind is afflicted by this [ignorance], various delusions arise and perish, like waves of the ocean.
Mounted upon the chariot of objective entities, this powerful mental construction swiftly assails the mind, just as a snare catches a bird.
Out of compassion, he leads his mother— whose eyes tremble and whose breasts drip with drops of milk—
to the state of being his wife, filled with overflowing bliss.
The nectar of the full moon, though already moist, quickly turns the three worlds into poison by its overflowing abundance.
For even a stump, through its own mental conception, becomes agitated by the onset of the movements of a mad, supreme vetāla and approaches a mute man.
And during times such as the twilights, it is by her grace that clods of earth, stones, walls,
and serpents are perceived with the eyes in this world.
Just as a single thing appears as a pair when two moons are seen, or as being far away when it is near, or as crossing the ocean in a dream; so too does the one arise as a duality.
Time that is long becomes a mere moment when it is desired as night;
likewise, a single moment appears like a year to those separated from their beloveds.
There is nothing that this arrogant woman will not do;
yet behold, O Rāghava, the power of her who possesses nothing at all!
One should diligently restrain consciousness by means of consciousness itself;
by blocking the flow of consciousness, this river of the mind dries up.
By this very non-existent, fragile-limbed,
and utterly hollow thing called "false imagination," the world has been wonderfully blinded.
By means of this formless, shapeless, and charmingly devoid of consciousness,
which perishes instantly even while it exists, the world has been wonderfully blinded.
By the flickering light that perishes within the midst of darkness,
which possesses the nature of an owl's eye, the world has been wonderfully blinded.
The world has been wonderfully blinded by her who performs exclusively evil deeds, who cannot endure being looked upon, and who does not even recognize her own body.

The world is wonderfully blinded by that woman of noble intellect, who is ever devoted to the dharma of right conduct, yet who is naturally beautiful and perpetually setting [into the horizon of death].
Constantly held by this [ignorance], which is always agitated by endless suffering and devoid of true awakening— it is truly a marvel that it has blinded the world!
The world has been wonderfully blinded by this insentient-bodied woman, whose breasts are the thick clouds of desire and anger, and whose mouth is the spreading darkness.
By this inert [nature], which dwells in the blind well of the self, which is worn out by dullness,
and which utters long lamentations of suffering, the world has been wondrously blinded.
The world has been wonderfully blinded by Māyā, which shatters attachment to the person, is like a disease, remains unimpaired, evolves through various intentions, and is ever-shifting.
It is a marvel that a man has been blinded by a woman who is utterly incapable of even enduring his gaze, let alone resisting him.
A man is wonderfully blinded by that woman who is no man at all— a woman whose very consciousness does not exist, yet who perishes even while she has not perished.

O Lord, by what means does this latent impression (*vāsanā*) dissolve— this creator of infinite and difficult-to-restrain diversions, this bringer of pleasure and pain subject to rise and fall, which is bound to the state of being within the cave of the mind?
The One Hundred Fourteenth Chapter, titled "The Description of Ignorance. Rāma:
O Brahmin, how indeed can this great blindness of the world, or of the individual soul, which arises from the expansion of ignorance, be destroyed?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a frost-lotus perishes in an instant from the sight of the sun,
even so does this ignorance perish from the vision of the Self.
For so long does that [craving] cause the embodied being, together with its own self, to oscillate amidst the precipices of saṃsāra and within the thorny thickets of suffering.
As long as ignorance has not arisen within him— that which brings about its own destruction—
the desire for self-realization does not itself bestow the exhaustion of delusion.
O Rāghava, for her who perceives that which is beyond [this world], her own destruction proceeds, just like that of a shadow seeking to experience the sunlight.
When the all-pervading God is seen, [the individual self] dissolves of its own accord,
just as shadows vanish when the twelve suns have risen together.
In this world, ignorance is merely desire; its destruction is called liberation.
And that, O Rāghava, is accomplished simply by the absence of volitional thought.

When even the slightest darkness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is destroyed within the sky of the mind, that blackness becomes attenuated through the great rising of the sun of consciousness (*cid-āditya*).
Just as darkness vanishes somewhere when the sun has risen,
so too does ignorance dissolve somewhere when discernment has arisen.
Bondage of the mind reaches density through firm latent impressions (vāsanā),
just as the conceptualization of a restless spirit becomes solid for a child at twilight.
Rāma:
Whatever is seen here is ignorance (*avidyā*), and that ignorance is destroyed by the contemplation of the Self (*ātmabhāvanā*), O Brahmin. Of what nature is that Self said to be?
Vasiṣṭha: That which is the reality of consciousness (cittattva)— free from the pursuit of objects of thought, universal in its commonality, and inexpressible— is the Self, the Supreme Lord.
From Brahma down to a blade of grass, whatever constitutes this world—all that is at all times only the Self; O sinless one, ignorance does not exist.
Indeed, all this is Brahman—eternal, a mass of consciousness, and imperishable;
no other mental construction called "mind" exists at all.
Nothing whatsoever is born or dies in these three worlds;
nor does the existence of the modifications of being exist anywhere.
Only pure consciousness exists here— absolute, appearing as absolute, the universal whole that remains unimpaired, and free from the pursuit of objects of thought.
In this eternal, pervasive, pure, and untroubled state of pure consciousness alone;
in that which is peaceful, characterized by equal enjoyment, and whose self has arisen free from modification.

That which, having conceived of itself as having attained its own nature, runs forth— consciousness itself, the object of consciousness, inherently undecaying, yet appearing decayed— that is known as the mind (*manas*).
From that one, all-pervading, omnipotent Great Self,
the power of differentiation has arisen like a wave from water.
In that one, vast, and peaceful [reality] wherein nothing exists,
