she has attained perfection within the Supreme Self by means of mere volition.
Therefore, this which is accomplished by volition perishes by volition alone—
just as a flame of fire that was produced by it is extinguished by that very same wind.
That ignorance, which has taken the form of a desire for enjoyment accomplished through human effort and exertion, dissolves by the mere absence of conceptualization.
The mind is bound by the firm resolve that "I am not Brahman," but it is liberated again by the firm resolve that "all is Brahman."
Volition is the supreme bondage; non-volition is liberation. Having conquered volition within, do as you wish.
I have seen here in the sky a lotus pond with golden lotuses, where restless bees like lapis lazuli hover, its fragrance perfuming the very air.
With her circles of lotus-stalk arms, their stalks raised high and their fullness manifest,
she seemed to laugh at the orb of the moon’s rays.
In this way, the net of conceptual construction, though unreal and indeed non-existent, appears as if real;
it is imagined by the fool for the sake of destroying the mind's composure.
In the same way, this ignorance here, which binds one to existence through mental cultivation,
is imagined by the childish mind— fickle and leading only to suffering.
"I am emaciated," "I am extremely miserable," "I am bound," "I possess hands, feet, and so forth"— one is bound by such conventional usage that accords with these mental states.
"I am not suffering, nor do I have a body; what bondage can there be for this conscious Self?"—by such conduct that accords with this realization, one is liberated.
"I am neither flesh nor bones; for I am other than the body, the Supreme"—one who possesses such certainty within is said here to be one whose ignorance has been destroyed.
Then, the splendor of darkness stood above, possessing the luster of the top of the lofty divine mountain or of a peak of lapis lazuli, yet difficult to pierce even by the rays of the sun.
For just as blackness is imagined in the sky as something arising from its own nature by a person standing on the earth, impelled by his own conceptual construction; so too is this [imagined].
Thus, O Rāghava, this ignorance is merely imagined as the conception of a self in that which is not the self; it belongs to the unawakened person, not to the awakened one.
Rāma said:
"This is neither the luster of the sapphire of Mount Meru, nor is it the radiance of darkness.
O Brahmin, tell me: what is this blueness that has been produced in the sky?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, the blueness of the empty sky does not exist as a quality;
nor is this the radiance of another jewel here, for it is not of the nature of a sapphire."
Because the cosmic egg consists of light, because the perfected light is expansive,
and because there is luminosity beyond the limits of the egg, darkness cannot possibly exist here.
O fortunate one, this vast emptiness alone is perceived;
it is not composed of reality, but is like a companion to its corresponding ignorance.
When one's own false views have been destroyed, that very darkness which had arisen is seen to be non-existent by its very nature, like the blackness of the sky.
Just as, through such understanding, the blackness seen in the sky is not perceived as actual blackness,
so it is with the darkness of ignorance.
For the wise have declared that the absence of conceptualization is the restraint of ignorance; and this is itself exceedingly easy to accomplish, like [the non-existence] of a lotus in the sky.
O virtuous one, for this worldly delusion that has arisen like the color of the sky, I consider its non-recollection to be better than mere forgetting.
Just as one perishes through the mental conception "I am lost" by means of suffering,
so too does a person attain happiness through the mental conception "I am awakened."
Likewise, one whose resolve is deluded indeed returns again to a state of delusion;
yet, through a noble resolve for awakening, one pursues awakening.
From the mere recollection of these [objects], eternal ignorance arises;
through the effortful forgetting of them, the true goal perishes in reality.
She is the one who brings all states of being into manifestation and deludes all living beings;
she is the savior when one's own self is destroyed, yet she is the destroyer when that same self increases.
Whatever the mind intends to pursue, all the functions of the senses accomplish that in an instant, just as ministers carry out the command of a king.
Therefore, he who does not engage the mind in mental constructions regarding objects attains peace through internal conscious effort.
That which did not exist in the beginning does not exist even today;
that which appears here is Brahman—peaceful, one, and unmoving.
Since objects of thought and the mind itself are to be contemplated as such, for whom, how, and from where could they exist?
Remain free from constraint, established in that which is changeless, without beginning or end.
Relying on supreme human effort with the highest intelligence, one should thoroughly uproot from the mind the cultivation of hope for enjoyments, along with its very roots.
That supreme delusion which arises, the cause of old age and death,
in which hundreds of snares of hope flourish— that is the manifestation of latent impression (*vāsanā*).
"My sons, my wealth, I am he, this is mine"—
this single latent impression leaps about like a magical illusion.
In this very empty body, which is as flickering as the wind in an arjuna tree,
the serpent of egoism has been cast by ignorance and latent impressions.
For one who knows reality in the ultimate sense, the notions of "I," "mine," and "this" are quite enough;
I consider that apart from the reality of the Self, nothing ever exists at all.

Through the vision of creation, that very same ignorance— though appearing as something else entirely— revolves again and again over the range of mountains including the earth and its peaks, displaying manifold wonders.
It arises through mere ignorance and perishes through mere knowledge;
it is to be discerned as nothing but pure consciousness, like the serpent in the rope.
O Rāma, that which is ignorance for the ignorant becomes this very earth with its mountains and rivers for the knower;
for him there is no ignorance, as he is established in Brahman within his own majesty.
The two conceptualizations of the rope and the snake are both imagined solely through ignorance;
however, by the knower, only the single, uncreated vision of Brahman is determined.
Do not be ignorant; become wise. Abandon the latent impressions of saṃsāra. Why do you weep like another, by perceiving a self in that which is not-self?
O Rāghava, what is this dull and mute body of yours?
For its sake, you are helplessly deprived by pleasure and pain.
For just as there is no identity between wood and lacquer, or between a jujube fruit and its bowl, even though they are joined together, so it is with the body and the possessor of the body.
Just as when a bellows is burned, the fire does not burn the air contained within it,
so too, upon the destruction of the body, the self is not destroyed.
"O scion of the Raghus, the delusions that 'I am suffering' or 'I am rich in happiness'—
when the mind is afflicted by these, there is torment here in this world that is difficult to cross."
[She is] entirely false, causing harm, swollen with the mental brooding of the mind,
bestowing suffering, and blinded by the impurity of great delusion.
Even though the lunar orb is moist with nectar, by imagining it to be the Raurava hell,
one experiences the suffering of burning and desiccation characteristic of that hell.
In lakes whose cool waves are filled with water-lilies tossed by the play of the wind,
a greatness abounding in mirages is perceived.
In dreams and other such states, people experience the agitation of falling from or rising up into a city created in the sky, which bestows various kinds of pleasure and pain.
If the latent impressions of saṃsāra do not indeed fill the mind,
then what could the frenzied activities of waking and dreaming lead one to in this world?
When false knowledge has increased, the hells of Raurava and Avīci appear as places of misfortune and torment, while the grounds of the celestial groves appear as paradises.
Pierced by this [wisdom], the mind instantly perceives even within a lotus fiber the delusive whirlpools of the entire ocean of saṃsāra.
For when the mind is afflicted by this [passion], even while remaining established in a kingdom,
a person undergoes various states that are not fit even for a dog-cooker (outcaste).
Therefore, O Rāma, having abandoned the latent impressions that bind one to existence— which consist of all objective states— remain free from passion, like a crystal.
While you remain engaged in your duties, let there be no coloring by passion,
just as a crystal assumes various reflections while remaining itself unchanged.
If you always perform worldly activities with a mind fixed on the supreme goal, free from the attachment to curiosity and through effortless play, then by what could you, O Great One, be compared?
The one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Avoidance of the Faults as Previously Described," by Vālmīki.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, appeared as if awakened.
With his inner heart blossomed, he attained a perfect splendor,
like a lotus that has been refreshed when the darkness has faded and it is bathed in the light of the sun.
With his face brightened by a gentle smile born of the wonder of awakening,
he spoke these words, which were washed white by the nectar of the radiance from his teeth:
Rāma:
Oh, how wondrous! Mountains are bound by threads produced from lotuses;
by that ignorance which does not exist, everyone is brought under control.
This is that very form which has attained the state of the diamond (vajra) within these three worlds;
it is that which, though indeed existent, appears as if non-existent due to ignorance.
Out of compassion, tell me once more the true nature of this illusory drama of saṃsāra, which is performed upon the stage of the three worlds, so that there may be perfect awakening.
Moreover, O Great-Souled One, this doubt dwells within my heart:
what calamity did that illustrious Lavaṇa encounter?
O Brahman, when the two— body and embodied self— are closely joined and unharmed, who indeed therein is the transmigrating being that alone enjoys the fruits of good and evil?
Having thus inflicted that unsurpassed calamity upon Lavaṇa,
where has he gone with his fickle undertakings, and who was that magician?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, the body is like a wooden post or a wall; it is nothing at all, yet it is conceptualized by this mind as if it were a vision in a dream.
But know, O wise one, that the mind which has entered living beings— enveloped by the power of consciousness— is subject to saṃsāra and as flickering as a young monkey.
For the mind, which constitutes the active portion within the body and sustains the body in its various forms,
is designated by the names "ego," "mind," and "life."
O Rāghava, these endless pleasures and pains belong to that [Self] when it is unawakened and when it is well-awakened; they do not belong to the body at all.
The unawakened mind, constructing conceptualizations based on various perceptions,
follows its diverse fluctuations and assumes manifold forms.
For as long as one remains unawakened, until the very end of sleep, one perceives the confusion of a dream; once awakened, one never does so again.
As long as the living being, agitated by the sleep of ignorance, has not been awakened,
so long does he perceive the bewildering onset of saṃsāra, which is difficult to comprehend.
All darkness vanishes from the fully awakened mind,
just as the blindness of a lotus dissolves when it blooms at the light of day.
That which is designated by the self-realized as mind, ignorance, mental organ, life-force, and latent impression,
and which is called the "karmic self," is the embodied one who is skilled in suffering.
The body is inert and not deserving of suffering; it is the living soul (jīva) that suffers due to a lack of inquiry.
This lack of inquiry arises from dense ignorance, and ignorance is the cause of suffering.
The living soul has become an object for both auspicious and inauspicious phenomena;
due solely to the fault of lack of discernment, it does not reach this great state within the sheath.
Bound by the nature of non-discrimination, the mind, possessing various mental modifications,
wanders like a wheel through its various modes of activity.
It rises, it cries out, it kills, it eats, it moves, it leaps, and it rejoices;
it is the mind alone within this body, and never the body itself.
Just as a householder is in his home, or as a charioteer is in his chariot,
so is the mind in this body, like a serpent within its slough.
Just as the wind, though moving, appears motionless within a tree, so too the mind flickers within the body; the body is situated in the body, not in the mind.
In all pleasures and pains, and in all mental constructions,
know that the mind is the agent, the mind is the enjoyer, and the human being is of the nature of the mind.
In this regard, listen as I shall tell you this wonderful account of how that Lavaṇa fell into the state of a Caṇḍāla due to a delusion of mind.
The mind experiences the fruit of its actions, whether auspicious or indeed inauspicious;
since you have surely understood this, listen accordingly, O Raghava.
O sinless one, in former times, Lavaṇa, born of the lineage of Hariścandra,
sat alone in a secluded place and reflected for a long time within his mind.
My grandfather was a great officiating priest of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
born into his lineage, I worship that sacrifice mentally.
Having thus reflected in his mind and having made the necessary preparations from the very beginning,
that lord of the earth entered into the initiation for the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He honored and worshipped the officiating priests and the holy sages;
he paid homage to the deities and kindled the sacrificial fire.
While he was thus performing sacrifices, more than a year passed in his mind within the garden, spent in the worship of divine sages and brahmins.
Having given away all his possessions as a sacrificial fee to the beings, beginning with the twice-born,
the king awoke at the end of the day in his own grove.
Thus King Lavaṇa attained the Rājasūya sacrifice,
for he was endowed with a nourished mind and possessed of its fruit.
Therefore, know that the mind is the man who experiences pleasure and pain; O Rāghava, unite it with the truth that is beginningless and effortless.
When the mind is full, the person is complete; when it is lost, he perishes.
As for those who hold the conviction "I am the body," enough with such so-called wise men!
When the mind is full of discernment and fully awakened, all sufferings are utterly dissolved for one whose intellect has become detached;
indeed, when the cluster of lotuses is revealed by the rays of the sun, the dullness and darkness born of closing are long since dispelled.
The one hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Experiencer of Pleasure and Pain," [of] Rāma:
O Lord, Lavaṇa has obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
what indeed could serve as a standard of proof here amidst this illusory net of conceptual constructions?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"When the magician arrived at the assembly hall of Lāvaṇī at the proper time,
I was staying there and witnessed it with my own eyes."
Then, when Śambara’s creator had departed from there, I was questioned with effort by the members of the assembly and by Lavaṇa as well, asking, "What is this?"
Having reflected and seen what was said there, listen as I shall explain to you that which was intended by the practitioner of sorcery, O Rāma.
For those who perform the Rājasūya sacrifice undergo for twelve years the suffering of adversity, consisting of various forms of conditions.
Therefore, O Rāma, that divine messenger in the form of a juggler was sent by Śakra from the sky for the sake of Lavaṇa’s suffering.
Having bestowed the supreme station upon that performer of the Rājasūya sacrifice,
he departed by way of his own celestial path, frequented by gods and siddhas.
Therefore, O Rāma, this is indeed evident; there is no doubt in this matter.
For the mind is the agent and the enjoyer of diverse activities.
By rubbing and purifying that very jewel of the mind here, just as frost is dissolved by the heat of the sun, and by bringing it to dissolution through discernment, you will attain the supreme good.

Know that the mind alone is ignorance (*avidyā*), which creates the vast spectacle of the entire world and its inhabitants. Through the power of its manifold web of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), it brings this [world] into being.

Knowing that there is no difference between the words "ignorance," "mind" (*citta*), "living being" (*jīva*), and "intellect" (*buddhi*), just as there is none between the words "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and "sapling" (*taru*), you must dissolve the mind itself.
But when the sun-disk of the stainless mind has risen, O Rāghava— which dispels the fierce darkness of all conceptual constructions—

there is nothing that is not seen, nothing that is not attained, nothing that is not made one's own, nothing that is not abandoned, nothing that is not honored, and nothing that is neither one's own nor another's.
The ultimate truth is that everything, at all times, becomes everything. Thus, upon awakening, the entire mass of existing things attains the state of a single lump,
just as a collection of various clay vessels, once fired, becomes one when placed in water.
Rāma:
Thus it has been declared by the Blessed One that when the fluctuations of the mind are completely extinguished, the end of all pleasure and pain is attained.
Therefore, O Great-souled One, how can there be the existence of this mind, whose very nature is so exceedingly restless?
Vasiṣṭha:
O moon of the Raghu dynasty, listen to the method for the pacification of the mind;
having understood it, you will restrain the mind just as a groom restrains a vicious horse.
For here, it was previously stated that there is a threefold origination of all beings from Brahmā;
therein, first of all, the mental construction arises,
and that becomes Brahmā.
Having become of the nature of Brahman and consisting of volition (*saṅkalpa*), she sees exactly what she wills;
by that, she fashions this grand display of the worlds.

Therein, fashioning the cycle of transmigration—including birth, death, pleasure, pain, and delusion—she remains for many eons, slow in her undertakings, and then dissolves away of her own accord, like a drop of frost when the sun has risen.
By the power of intentions arising from time, it is born again in another form;
that too dissolves again,
and yet another arises— either the same or different— as one pursues the cycles of saṃsāra again and again.
Having himself brought about cessation, he becomes tranquil.
In this manner, infinite millions of Brahmās have passed away and will pass away in this cosmic egg and in others as well;
there exist other infinite ones whose number is simply not known. (MU 3.116.13)
In this regard, while abiding in this view, hear how the individual soul (jīva) comes forth from the Lord and how it is liberated:
the power of the mind of Brahman, having arisen and supported itself upon the power of space standing before it, follows the wind situated therein and attains the state of dense volition (saṅkalpa).

Then, having again attained the five subtle elements (tanmātra), it becomes the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti) known as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa); through contact with the sky and the wind, it takes the form of frost and [settles] within rice plants.
It enters; or living beings go into the state of the womb;
therefore, they are born from it.
Then he becomes a person (*puruṣa*).
By that very person, as soon as he is born, the acquisition of knowledge must be undertaken from childhood onwards,
and the gurus must be followed.
Then, in due course, a sense of wonder arises in you as a man;

in a person whose mental disposition resembles yours, the discernment between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted is born. When such a person—possessing that discrimination yet still harboring a sense of ego—stands within the foremost class consisting of pure *sattva*, the sevenfold stage of yoga, which brings about the illumination of the mind for the sake of auspiciousness, indeed descends upon him gradually.
The one hundred and seventeenth canto, titled "The Incarnation Born of Sattva," from the Rāmāyaṇa.
"O Blessed One, what are the seven stages of yoga that bestow the accomplishments? Tell me this in brief, O best among those who know all reality."
Vasiṣṭha said:
The ground of ignorance consists of seven stages, and the ground of knowledge likewise consists of seven stages;
however, between these two, there are countless other intermediate stages.
These two creepers, the Great Being and the Tree of Existence, having taken their own effort as their sap, bear their respective fruits at every step once they are firmly rooted.
In that regard, listen to the sevenfold nature of the stage of ignorance;
thereafter, you shall hear of the sevenfold nature born from the stage of knowledge.
Liberation is abiding in one's own true nature; its loss is the non-perception of "I-ness.
This has been stated in brief as the defining characteristic of knowledge and ignorance regarding that [Self].
For those who do not deviate from the essential nature of pure consciousness alone,
there is no possibility of ignorance, because of the absence of the arising of attachment and aversion.
That which is the loss of one's own true nature and the immersion in the objects of thought—
there has never been, nor will there ever be, another delusion greater than this.
When one object has passed from the mind and another has not yet arisen, that state which exists in the interval— devoid of the marks of mental reflection— is called abiding in one's own true nature.
That state which is like the interior of a stone— where all conceptual constructions have been completely stilled,
yet which is free from dullness, sleep, and the like— is known as abiding in one's own true nature.
When the ego-sense and the like have completely subsided, and duality has ceased,
that non-inert state of the mind which shines forth is remembered as one's own true nature (svarūpa).
The seed-awake, likewise the awake, and similarly the great-awake; the awake-dream, as well as the dream, the dream-awake, and deep sleep.
Thus, this sevenfold delusion further becomes interconnected with one another; hear now its definition under various names.
First, there is that which is consciousness, indefinable and stainless, the pure awareness of the *cit*;
it is the vessel for the future meanings of names and words such as "consciousness," "living being" (*jīva*), and so forth.
Existing in the form of a seed while awake is called "seed-awake" (bījajāgrat). This is the ninth state of consciousness; now hear from me about the state of established waking (jāgratsaṃsthiti).
For one who has arisen in this way, the clear conviction that "this is another," "this is I," and "this is mine"— that is the waking state, preceded by the absence of [such] conceptualization.
"This is that very person, this is mine"— such a thick conviction arising from previous births,
manifesting vividly, is called "great waking" (mahājāgrat).
Whether it has ascended [to a higher state] or not, whether it is without sleep or not externalized—
that kingdom of the mind which belongs to one who is awake is called waking-dream (jāgratsvapna).
Through various distinctions such as the double moon, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and the mirage, that state of waking, having reached its habitual repetition, becomes manifold.
"Even the cognition that arises at the end of sleep regarding an object experienced during the time of sleep— 'this was seen by me for only a short time, yet it is not real'— " ||| MU_3,117.19 |||
That dream was told to him; it remained in his heart as a great waking state, its vast form not yet fully blossomed due to the absence of long-term observation.
When a dream has ascended to the state of waking and reached the stage of the great waking—
that which occurs when the body is wounded or unwounded is indeed considered the dream-waking.
The state of the insentient living being when the six conditions have been abandoned,
which is rich with the awareness of future suffering, is called the state of deep sleep.
In that state, all these entities— grass, clods of earth, stones, and so forth, whether ancient, future, or recent— remain as they are.
"O Rāghava, these seven stages of ignorance have been described by me;
each one here has a hundred branches, appearing in various forms."
The waking dream, having long been firmly established, proceeds as if it were truly waking;
through the differentiation of various objects, it unfolds and expands.
And within her belly there exist those resembling the great waking state;
within them, too, there are others, and thus the cycle of rebirth is dense.
Even while remaining in these intermediate states of deep sleep and dreaming,
this entire delusion remains as solid as a stone.
From one dream to another, from one delusion to another, the world passes on through ignorance,
just as a whirlpool falling downward moves from one body of water to another.
Some transmigrations exist as being like waking from a long dream;
others, however, are repeated dreams, while still others are like dreams within waking.

"I have described this ground of ignorance in seven stages, distinguished by various internal divisions of changing states. You shall cross over it through beautiful investigations, once you have directly perceived your own Self, stainless with awakening."
The One Hundred and Eighteenth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Stage of Ignorance," by Vasiṣṭha:
Listen, O sinless one, to this sevenfold stage of knowledge,
by knowing which you shall not sink again into the mire of delusion.
Proponents of the stages of yoga speak in many different ways;
however, these very [stages] which bestow auspiciousness are surely what I favor.
They know that awakening is knowledge; this [knowledge] consists of seven stages.
Liberation is said to be that which follows beyond the seven stages.
The realization of truth and liberation are indeed synonymous terms;
through the awakening to truth, this living being does not sprout again in this world.
The first stage of knowledge is declared to be called "the desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā);
the second here is "investigation" (vicāraṇā), and the third is "the attenuation of the mind" (tanumānasā).
The fourth is the entry into existence; thereafter is that called non-attachment.
The sixth is the non-contemplation of the categories of existence, and the seventh is known as the state beyond the fourth.
Liberation stands at the end of these; in it, one no longer grieves.
Listen now to this definition of these stages.
"Am I truly a fool remaining here? I shall examine the scriptures and the company of the virtuous.
Desiring this with detachment is called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the good) by the wise.
That engagement in right conduct which is preceded by the study of the scriptures, association with virtuous people, and the practice of dispassion is called *vicāraṇā*.
Non-attachment toward the objects of the senses through investigation and virtuous aspiration,
wherein there is an absence of even slight suffering, is called *tanumānasā*.
Through the practice of the three stages, by virtue of the mind’s cessation of engagement with objects,
when it abides in the pure self of being, that is declared to be the attainment of being (*sattvāpatti*).
Through the practice of the four stages and by means of the fruit of non-attachment, that state in which the wonder of pure being has taken root is called "Non-attachment."
Through the firm practice of the five stages, by virtue of delighting in one's own self,
there arises the non-contemplation of internal and external objects.
Through long and diligent effort applied by another,
the sixth stage arises, known as the "cultivation of the meaning of words" (*padārthābhāvanā*).

That state of being established solely in one's own nature, resulting from long-term practice on the six stages and from the non-perception of duality, is to be known as the fourth stage of realization.
For this fourth state (turya) exists here among those liberated while living;
beyond that is the state transcending the fourth (turyātīta), which concerns those liberated after death (videhamukta).
For those highly fortunate ones who have reached the seventh stage— those great-souled ones who delight in the self— have attained the supreme state.
Those liberated while living do not sink into the state of the flavors of pleasure and pain;
they may perform ordinary or noble actions, or they may not perform anything at all.
Once awakened, those who have been standing by perform every traditional practice that has come down through succession;
uninjured, they act just like one who has woken from sleep.
Delighting only in the self, they bring no pleasure whatsoever to those various worldly activities, just as the beauty of visible forms brings no joy to those who are in deep sleep.
However, these seven stages are the domain of the wise alone;
they are not for animals, immobile beings, and the like, nor for the minds of barbarians and others.
Even those such as animals and barbarians who have attained this state of knowledge—whether they possess a body or are bodiless—are liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
For "cognition" (*jñapti*) is the severing of the knot; when that occurs, there is liberation.
This [liberation] consists essentially in the mere subsiding of such things as the cognition of water in a mirage.
But those who, having crossed over the thick cloud of delusion, have not yet reached the purifying state,
remain in these stages, intent upon the attainment of their own true self.
Some belong to all stages; some belong to only one final stage;
some belong to three stages; and some belong to five stages.
Some have reached six stages; some have reached one and a half stages;
some have reached four stages; and some abide in two stages.
Some are vessels for a portion of the earth; some consist of three and a half stages;
some consist of four and a half stages; and others consist of five and a half stages.
Discerning men move through the worlds upon these stages,
remaining amidst the various states of worldly existence that are like the heat of a dwelling-house.
For those wise and excellent kings conquer in these ten ways; indeed, the defeat of the enemy hosts of elephant-warriors appears to them as insignificant as a blade of grass.

Indeed, those great beings who conquer these stages are truly worthy of worship, for they have vanquished the enemies that are the senses; they instantly attain that vast state where even the status of a universal monarch (*samrāj*) or a sovereign ruler (*virāj*) is regarded as a mere blade of grass.
The one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Ground of Knowledge," by Vasiṣṭha.
Just as gold, through its consciousness as a ring, forgets its nature as gold and cries out in vain,
"I am not gold," due to a false sense of ego, so it is with the Self.
Rāma said:
O great sage, O Lord, tell me truly how the emergence of the consciousness of the ring arises from gold as being of the nature of the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva).
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Only for that which exists can coming and going be questioned, never for that which is non-existent.
The state of 'I' and the state of being a wave both exist, but [the underlying reality] is never non-existent."
If it is said, "Give gold; you are the one who gives the ring;
take it," and it is given by that very person with the ring, then that [gold] exists—of this there is no doubt.
Rāma:
If that is so, O Lord, then what would be the nature of being a mere finger-ring here?
Through this very distinction of meaning, I shall come to know the form of Brahman.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, if the formless nature of the non-existent is being described as having form,
then you must describe to me the features and qualities of the son of a barren woman.
The state of being a ring is a vain delusion, like an illusion whose nature is non-existent;
its true form is this very fact that it is no longer seen when scrutinized.
In the water of a mirage, in the double moon, in the ego-sense, in the circle of fire, and so forth—
the very nature of these things is such that, though they are being perceived, they are not apprehended as real.
He who perceives the form of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does not obtain even a single atom or a minute particle of silver anywhere.
Through a lack of thorough investigation alone, the unreal appears as if it were real,
just as the nature of silver appears in mother-of-pearl, or water in the mirages of the desert.
When that which does not exist is examined, its non-existence becomes manifest;
yet when it is not examined, it appears as water in a mirage.
And that which is non-existent indeed becomes a causal agent and appears stable;
it is like the meeting with the delusion of a vetāla, leading only to the death of fools.
Excluding the single state of being gold, nothing else exists within gold,
just as the forms of rings, bracelets, and so forth do not exist in sand, like oil [does not exist].
Here there is neither truth nor falsehood; whatever appears in a certain way, it performs its function in that very way, like the illusory transformation produced by a child’s yakṣa.
Whether it be real or even unreal, whatever is firmly established in the heart performs its purposeful function, just as [the thought of] nectar [performs] the function of neutralizing poison.
For that very ignorance is indeed Māyā, and this transmigratory existence is it;
it is the cultivation of a sense of "I-ness" toward that which is unreal and without foundation.
O King, the state of being a subject and so forth exists [in the ego], but the state of "I-ness" and so forth does not exist in the Self;
for it is precisely because of the absence of "I-ness" that the supreme reality is thus pure, tranquil, and equanimous.
There is no such thing as eternity, nor is there any state of being Viriñca; there is no state of being the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), nor any state of being a god and so forth.
There is no such thing as another world, nor is there anywhere any beginning of creation; there is no such thing as Mount Meru, nor the sky, nor the mind, nor the body.
There is no such thing as the nature of the great elements, nor is there any causality anywhere;
there is no reckoning of the seasons, nor any reality of existence or non-existence.
There is no such thing as "thou-ness," "I-ness," "selfhood," "that-ness," existence, or non-existence;
there is no conceptualization of difference anywhere, nor any coloring by being or non-being.
All is peaceful, without support, wise, clear, eternal, auspicious,
free from ailment, without appearance, nameless, and without cause.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither the middle nor the end, neither all nor indeed not-all;
it is ungraspable by mind or speech, both empty and non-empty, and perfectly eternal.
Rāma:
O Great Brahmin, all of this has now been understood by me;
nevertheless, tell me further—what is this creation that is being observed?
Vasiṣṭha said: Beyond is that which is called the Supreme, abiding as the Tranquil;
here there is never any creation, nor any designation of "creation" whatsoever at any time.
Like water situated within the waters of the great ocean,
the supreme state is motionless, though like water it seems to move due to its fluidity.
That state shines like the luminous Self, yet it does not shine at all;
it appears as the radiance of lights, but the wise know it to be beyond all appearance.

Just as water within the belly of the ocean surges both downward and upward, so too this world appears as if manifold due to the consciousness of the Supreme, though it is not different from that Supreme.
Knowing only slightly due to its own nature as consciousness, it perceives itself as if it were something else;
it awakens to the fact that this is merely creation, and through tranquility, it attains eternal peace.
But the determination is this: "creation" is merely a designation for the ultimate reality;
it neither exists nor does it not exist, just as space within space.
Due to the presence of consciousness, there is the manifestation of creation; due to the absence of consciousness, there is the dissolution of creation.
This occurs within the Supreme, which is supremely tranquil, just as the delusion of a bracelet exists within gold.
When the joy of the realization of consciousness arises, that which is truly existent becomes non-existent;
when self-awareness dawns, that which is non-existent attains existence.
Know that consciousness is the agitation arising from the emergence of the sense of "I" and its creations; know that non-consciousness is the supreme state of perfect peace, and it is not insentient.

By this [knowledge], one realizes that there is no creation and that this world is not manifold; it is of the nature of the one Self, which is Śiva, just as an army made of clay by craftsmen is produced through the action of books.
This is full, without beginning, infinite, and without rising;
within the Full, the Full remains as it was before, through the supreme fillings.
That which is perceived as this creation is Brahman abiding in Brahman;
like space resting in space, it is the peaceful in the peaceful, the auspicious in the auspicious.
Just as a city reflected in a mirror appears both distant and not distant from the city itself, so too does the Lord appear as both that and its opposite in succession.
The universe arises from the non-existent, yet it is always arisen from the existent;
though appearing as real due to its manifestation, it consists of non-existence because it lacks substantial reality.
In this creation, which has the form of a city in a mirror, which shines like the water of a mirage,
and which appears as the delusion of two moons— what reality can there possibly be?
Just as a city appears in the sky due to the scattering of magical powder,
so does the cycle of existence appear in consciousness— both as substantial and as insubstantial.
As long as ignorance— dense with its spreading branches— is not forcibly burnt away to its very roots by the fire of analytical investigation,
it continues to produce various dense forests of pleasure and pain.
The One Hundred and Twentieth Chapter, titled "Instruction on Liberation," by Vasiṣṭha.
O Rāghava, hear what kind of "I-ness" belongs to ignorance, which, like a false golden ring or similar object, is destined for destruction.
Then, having witnessed such a delusion, that king Lavaṇa set out on the second day to travel through that great forest.
I remember that forest where I experienced such suffering;
because it exists within the mirror of the mind, it may perhaps be found there through the power of the mind.
Having thus resolved with his ministers, he departed for the Deccan;
once again for the sake of world conquest, he reached the Vindhya mountain.
Out of curiosity, he wandered over the entire coastal land of the eastern, southern, and western great oceans, like the sun traversing the path of the sky.
Then, in one place, he beheld that formidable forest stretching out before him like a wall, resembling the earth of the world beyond.
Dwelling everywhere, he saw all those various events;
having seen them and indeed having understood them, he was filled with wonder.
Having recognized those hunters born of the Pukkasa caste before him,
he wandered about again in great agitation, his mind filled with wonder.
Then he reached, at the edge of the great forest, that very village where he had previously lived among the well-fed Pukkasas, grey with smoke.
There he saw various people, various women, various huts, those groves, those reservoirs of water, and those riverbanks of the earth.
And he [beheld] that untimely destruction of those trees, those enclosures and groves,
and likewise those very same landscapes, now marked solely by that tragic event.
To her other friends— elderly women with tearful eyes, overcome by grief— her companion recounted the countless sufferings of kinsmen scattered across untimely wildernesses.

An old woman, her eyes overflowing with blazing tears, her throat choked, her breasts withered, and her body emaciated, stands weeping there, utterly exhausted, like a region scorched by a fierce thunderbolt during a drought.
Alas, my son! Your entire body was once covered with hair; now, your limbs are withered from three days without food.
When the dog tore away your skin from your aged body, how and where were those vital breaths of yours released?

I remember how, in the presence of your own wife, you laughed with delight at the reason for her necklace of *guñjā* berries— those red, fine fruits resting between her teeth, which were moistened by water and resembled palm leaves.

When shall I ever again behold the terrifying leaps and bounds of my son, as he frolics within the groves of *kadamba*, *jambīra*, clove, and *guñjā* trees, while the hyenas crouch and dart about in fear?
Those graceful charms found upon the faces of women fond of betel-leaf are not present on the single region of the chin of my son, which is dark as a *tamāla* tree while he has meat in his mouth.

The daughter too was led away along with her husband Yama; she who was like the Yamunā river was carried off by him, just as a tamāla creeper, together with its clusters of flowers, is swept away by a forest-blowing wind.
Alas, my daughter, you who wear a necklace of *guñjā* berries, whose limbs are graced by full and swelling breasts,
whose complexion is like dark collyrium shimmering in the wind, and who possess cloud-like lips amidst garments of leaves!

"Alas, O Prince, as lovely as the moon! Having abandoned those playful women of the inner apartments, you have gone to find delight in my daughter; yet even she has not attained stability in your affection."
What trifling thing indeed has not been done by that king, who— amidst the mockeries enacted by the playful activities of the waves of the river of saṃsāra— was united with a Pukkasa maiden?
She, whose eyes were like those of a frightened deer, and he, whose prowess was like that of a satiated tiger—
both perished in a single step, just as hope perishes along with its object, or as gold [is lost] when it is not joined with its purpose.
I am one whose lord has died; I am one whose son has perished; I have traveled to a wretched land; I am fallen into misfortune;
I am born into a miserable birth; I am in great distress; or rather, I am one whose calamities have risen up before me of their own accord.

Women are always the sole abode of pride arising from lowly insults, of a husband prostrated by hunger, and of grief whose onset is irresistible and whose course is unceasing— women who are themselves without a protector.
For one tormented by fate, deprived of kinsmen, deluded, and rooted in a great field of mental anguish, that which is life is death; and that which would be death is the supreme life.
For one who is separated from his people and living in a foreign land, endless sorrows arise,
like the grass on a mountain during the rains, thick with sap and branching out in a thousand directions.
Having comforted his wife’s elderly nurse—who was thus lamenting—with female servants, the king asked that woman: "What has happened here? Who are you? Who is your daughter, and who is your husband?"
Then, with eyes full of tears, she said: "This village is named Pukkasaghoṣa;
here lived my husband, a Pukkasa, and he had one daughter who was like the moon."

By the turn of fate, that wretched woman found her husband— the king, who resembled the moon— arrived here by the power of destiny, like a solitary she-camel finding a broken jar of honey in a desolate forest.
Having enjoyed pleasures with him for a very long time, she gave birth to daughters and sons;
they grew up in this hollow of the forest, like a gourd vine entwined around a tree.
The one hundred and twenty-first canto, titled "The Lamentation of Caṇḍālī," Canto 121:
Caṇḍālī.
Then, after some time, O Lord of Men, there occurred in this village a terrifying suffering of drought that broke the spirit of the people.
Due to this great suffering, all those people from the village departed and went far away, where they met their death.
Therefore, O Lord, we here are partakers of suffering, empty, and pitiable;
with tears flowing and our vision blurred, we lament.
Having heard this from the mouth of the woman, the king was filled with wonder;
looking at the faces of his ministers, he became as if fixed in a painting.
He reflected further upon that unsurpassed marvel;
becoming filled with even greater wonder, he questioned him again and again.
Having brought about the destruction of their suffering through appropriate mental honors, he— pierced by compassion and having perceived the high and low states of the world— [acted].
Having stayed there for a long time and reflected upon the courses of destiny,
he returned to the city and entered it, being saluted by the citizens.
In the morning, in that assembly hall, that king asked me, filled with wonder: "O sage, how is it that this dream has become manifest?"
Just as it was according to the facts, that very doubt of his— such as it was— was driven from his heart by me through various arguments, like a rising cloud driven away by the wind.
Thus, O Raghava, this great ignorance is the giver of delusion;
it quickly brings the non-existent into the state of existence, and likewise reduces the existent to non-existence.
Rāma:
How can you speak thus, O Brahmin? A dream has attained the status of reality; this matter, like a burden of delusion, does not settle in my mind.
Vasiṣṭha:
All this is indeed possible within ignorance, O Rāghava,
just as the appearance of cloth is seen in jars, or as in the delusions of a dream.
The distant appears as if near, like a mountain within a mirror;
for the youth, the long night seems to pass with speed, as if it were his beloved.
The impossible becomes possible, just as one's own death occurs in a dream;
and the non-existent arises as if it were real, like traveling through the sky in dreams.
What was very stable moves excessively during a whirlwind, like the turning of the earth;
the weak gains strength, like a mind agitated by intoxication.
The mind, enveloped by latent impressions, intensely contemplates whatever in whatever manner;
it quickly experiences that very thing accordingly—neither as something existent nor as something non-existent.
The very moment that ignorance, consisting of the sense of "I" and so forth, has falsely arisen,
at that very moment the infinity of delusion— devoid of beginning, middle, or end— is said to have emerged.
By the power of mental appearance alone, everything revolves:
a moment becomes the duration of an eon, and an eon becomes a moment.
To what state would a being with a perverted mind not fall?
By the power of its own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), even a deer assumes the nature of a lion.
Poison, delusion, intoxication, ignorance, infatuation, egoism, and so forth are all equal;
through the perversion of the mind, they all become causes for the attainment of results.
Like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit, through the power of mental impressions (*cittavāsanā*),
great undertakings and worldly transactions proceed spontaneously and mutually.
Whatever occurred previously in the king Lavaṇa’s settlement— that which appeared to him, whether good or bad— has become manifest in his mind.
Just as the mind forgets even an extensive action it has performed,
so too it certainly remembers what was done as not having been done.
Nevertheless, one indeed perceives in a dream, "I have not eaten" or "I have eaten," and even the journey to another country, though it was not actually performed, is understood.
Such is the worldly convention of the village of the Vindhya Pukkasa,
appearing to him just like a previous narrative in a dream.
Or rather, that very same dream-delusion which was quickly witnessed by Lavaṇa became the consciousness of the Pukkasa of the Vindhya mountains.
The consciousness of the Vindhya Pukkasa has ascended into the mind of the king,
just as many people may share a similar speech, name, and appearance.
Likewise, even in a dream there exist time, place, and action;
yet, insofar as it pertains to worldly convention, its existence consists in its manifestation.
The existence of all things is nothing other than consciousness;
within consciousness, the manifold succession of creations appears.
Just as a tree exists within the seed of a tree as that which is past, present, and future,
so its existence and non-existence are established as being neither existent nor non-existent.
For that which is real is indeed real; it does not consist of unreality due to a lack of cognition.
Ignorance (avidyā) does not exist at all, just as oil and the like do not exist in sand.
What pungency could there be in gold? That would be something other than gold itself.
Likewise, a connection with ignorance is not possible for the pure Self.
That connection which exists between similar things is manifest and bestows experience;
therefore, the connection between lacquer and wood and the like is not [a case of] similarity.

When all this is composed of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), consisting solely of a single locus and not having the nature of mutual experience, then stones and other such things [are that very reality].
When all things within the world consist of pure consciousness and pure existence, they are perceived as equal through the power of their interconnection.
At that time, these entities shine forth mutually while established in their own individual experience;
for no continuous relationship is possible between dissimilar things.
Without mutual connection, there can be no reciprocal experience; for an object similar [to another] cannot sufficiently attain oneness with that which is similar to it in a single moment.
The form expands as one, precisely because of its oneness and not otherwise; consciousness, when joined with consciousness, arises as the perception of the nature of the visible.
When the insentient meets the insentient, it becomes a dense mass of insentience;
and the unification of consciousness and the insentient can never occur anywhere due to their essential difference.
If consciousness and insentience were to exist together in one place, they would never merge;
because it consists of consciousness, the trace of consciousness is experienced through the trace of consciousness.
For these [objects] such as wood and stone are not of the nature of consciousness;
indeed, one object is experienced by means of another object through transformation.
Like the tongue with regard to taste, that [perception] also arises from its own kind and is flickering;
know that identity is the relationship, for there is no connection between the insubstantial and the substantial.
Therefore, among the insentient and the sentient, the insentient—such as a stone—is not considered [to be consciousness];
rather, it is consciousness itself that has become conjoined with consciousness, appearing in the form of stones, walls, and so forth.
When everything— including wood, stones, and so forth— is composed of the ultimate reality, it becomes a single entity and produces the delusion of the seer, the seen, and the rest.
All that is extended as if infinite, rich in every variety, is perceived as an object of vision because it is internally connected with that Self.

"Know this entire universe to be nothing but pure Being (*sanmātra*), O best among the knowers of reality; for even though the universe is unreal, my dear, it appears through hundreds of delusions characterized as the universe."
The wonder of consciousness is full, yet nothing at all is filled;
it is like the cities of men's imagination, which do not perceive one another.
Creations do not exist in consciousness for the sake of perceiving space and time;
for the state of being a creation is indeed the perception of duality, which arises from the delusion of "I-ness" and so forth.
Just as there is the delusion of bracelets and so forth upon the relinquishing of gold-consciousness,
the delusion of bracelets and so forth would occur within the gold because of the presence of place and other factors.
But for one overwhelmed by the vision of You, there is no other ignorance remaining as something separate;
likewise, the stainless Brahman is the one reality, despite the great diversity of forms such as bracelets and the like.

Due to the oneness of consciousness, this creation—though appearing as existence—is in fact entirely non-existent; it is like an army made of clay, which, though variegated, is perceived through the cognition of clay and consists of nothing but clay.

Water is one, yet it appears as waves and the like; wood is one, yet it appears as carved figures; clay alone is one, yet it appears as jars and the like; Brahman is one, yet it is the delusion of the three worlds.
Regarding the relationship between the seer and the seen, that which is the true nature of the seer—
devoid of seer, seeing, and the seen— is this supreme reality.
When the mind moves from one state to another, that form of consciousness which exists in the interval—
the awareness and reflection that is not inert— become absorbed in that at all times.
That which is your eternal form—neither waking, nor dreaming, nor in deep sleep; neither insentient nor inert—be always absorbed in that.
O Rāghava, having abandoned all but one state of insentience— which is indeed the heart of a stone— become absorbed in that, whether you are unagitated or agitated.
For anyone here, nothing whatsoever arises or dissolves;
whether unagitated or agitated, remain at ease as you please.

The person does not desire nor does he hate anything whatsoever within the body at any time; remaining healthy and free from apprehension, abide as one who has entered into the functioning of the body.
Just as you do not remain occupied with the affairs of a village or its villagers that are yet to come, so too,
having attained the nature of reality, do not remain fixed within the fluctuations of the mind.
Just as a person from another land, just as a piece of wood, just as a stone—so too do you perceive the mind; it is indeed non-mind, just like the nature of the self.
Just as there is no water in a stone, and just as there is no fire in water, so too the mind does not exist within its own self; how then could it exist in the Supreme Self?
Considering that whatever is done anywhere by one who perceives nothing at all does not truly constitute an action, transcend the mind.
If you follow after a mind that is ultimately not your self,
why do you not follow a barbarian living on the frontier?
Disregarding the outcaste of the mind from afar and without delay, remain established in yourself, free from fear; you have been rendered as inert as mud.
"Indeed, my mind does not exist; it has truly perished this very day"—becoming thus resolved, remain as motionless as a stone statue.
In the state of discernment, our mind does not exist; you are therefore devoid of it in reality.
So why are you tormented by that which is useless for its sake?
For those of feeble intellect who have been utterly overpowered by the non-existent yakṣa of the mind, a thunderbolt has arisen from the moon.
Having cast the mind far away, remain firm as you truly are;
be liberated through meditative cultivation and endowed with the supreme reasoning.
Fie upon those who follow after what is non-existent— those mental states that lack the nature of reality, whose passage of time is driven solely by the actions of the sky-like forest!
With a mind completely dissolved, O great-souled one, become one whose self is stainless, having reached the further shore of existence.
Even after reflecting for a very long time, nothing at all has been found within the self by the self through the mind.
The one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
From the very moment of birth, a person whose intellect has just begun to blossom must be intent upon the company of the virtuous.
This torrent of the river of ignorance, which flows in an unceasing stream, cannot be crossed without contact with the scriptures that lead to tranquility and with holy men.
Consequently, in a person possessed of discernment, there arises an investigation into what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
By that means, he arrives at the stage of discernment called *śubhecchā*.

Then, through the power of discernment, by means of investigation and right knowledge, as he abandons improper latent impressions (*vāsanā*), his mind becomes attenuated with respect to the latent impressions of saṃsāra.
By that, he has descended into the stage of discernment known as *tanumānasī*.

At the very moment that right knowledge arises for the yogin, at that very moment there is the attainment of *sattva*. When, by virtue of that, his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have reached attenuation, then he is said to be "unattached," meaning he is not bound by the fruit of karma.
Then, he practices the attenuation of mental cultivation toward that which is non-existent,
until— though acting and though engaging in worldly affairs, and though remaining amidst the unreal entities of saṃsāra— he,
by virtue of his practice and because of the exhaustion of the mind within himself, does not act even while acting toward external objects, and does not see even while seeing, nor does he grasp them.
Therefore, he meditates intensely;
and because his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have become attenuated, he performs his duties like one who is half-asleep and half-awake, rather than with a mind actively cultivated in contemplation.

Thus, having ascended to the stage of yoga that is beyond cultivation, with his mind withdrawn within, he practices for several years until, even while performing all external activities, he completely abandons the mental cultivation of external objects.
He becomes the self of the fourth state (*turyātman*);
therefore, he is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*).
He does not rejoice in what has been attained, nor does he grieve for what has not been attained.
Being entirely free from doubt, he simply continues with what has been attained.

O Rāghava, you too have understood that which is to be known regarding the entirety of the inner self; I believe that, among all your activities, your latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have become attenuated.
Whether your activity transcends the body or you remain within the body, do not fall into grief or joy; you are the Self, free from all affliction.
O Rāma, while you— yourself, pure, all-pervading, and eternally risen— abide, whence can there be pleasure and pain, and whence birth and death?
Why do you, though yourself without kin, grieve for the sorrows of your relatives? For when this [Self] stands alone and without a second, what indeed are relatives to the Self?
Only a mere accumulation of the atoms of the body is perceived;
because it undergoes changes in place and time, the self neither arises nor perishes.
Since you are imperishable, why do you grieve, thinking "I am perishing"?
For what kind of destruction could there be in the pure Self, which is beyond the power of death?
Just as when a jar is reduced to shards, the space within the jar does not perish,
so too, when this body is destroyed, you do not perish.
Just as when the mirage-river has dried up, the heat [of the sun] does not perish,
so too, when the body is destroyed, the Self does not perish.
Why does this desire arise in you? This internal delusion is purposeless.
Since you are non-dual, what second entity could there be that your self might desire?
O Rāghava, there is nothing in the world— whether audible, tangible, visible, delightful, or olfactory— that exists apart from the Self.
All these powers reside entirely within that very Self, which possesses all power; they abide in the manifest and pervasive One, just as emptiness resides in space.
O Raghava, this triple world has arisen from the mind within the wombs of women;
by means of these three modes, it causes delusion among the people here.
When the pacification of the mind— known as the destruction of latent impressions and the destruction of karma— is accomplished,
this illusion utterly perishes.
O Rāghava, diligently sever this latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is the firm, mechanism-driven rope at this water-wheel of the fierce cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
When this [nature] is not fully understood, it bestows great delusion;
but when fully understood, it grants the bliss called "the infinite" and leads to Brahman.
Having come here to this world from Brahman and having experienced transmigratory existence as a play,
one remembers Brahman once again and dissolves into Brahman itself.
O Rāghava, from Śiva— who is formless, immeasurable, and free from affliction—
all beings were born, just as luminous objects arise from light.
Just as a multitude of lines appears on a leaf, as a network of ripples in water, as bracelets and the like in gold, and as heat and so forth in fire; //MU_3,122.21//
For this triple world consists of both that [Brahman] and its absence;
it is situated in that very [Brahman], born from that, and is indeed that itself.
This very Self of all beings is called Brahman;
when that is known, the entire world is known, and when it is unknown, it remains indeed unknown.

For the sake of conventional usage in the scriptures, names such as "Consciousness" (cit), "Brahman," and "Self" (ātman) have been devised for this [reality] of expansive form by those of perfected minds.
When there is contact between the sense objects and the senses, that pure experience which is free from joy and resentment is indeed this immutable Self, consciousness.
In that Self of Consciousness, which is clearer than the clearest ether,
the world is reflected as if separate, though it is merely its own manifestation.
If the Buddhas are distinct from them, then greed, delusion, and the rest would become enemies;
if they are not distinct, then those [defilements] would be the Buddhas at that very moment.
For you, who are indeed bodiless and whose form is non-conceptual consciousness, from where has this delusion arisen— this so-called shame, fear, and despondency?

O you who are not a body, why are you overcome by the defects born of the body— such as shame and the like— which are composed of unreality, like a fool of poor intellect with his conceptual constructions?

When fragmentation occurs within the body of that which is of the nature of indivisible consciousness, even for one of imperfect vision there is no destruction; how much less so for one of right understanding?
O Rāma, that which exists even on the path of the sun, which is not contradicted by scripture or tradition—that is to be known as consciousness (*cittva*); it is the Person (*puruṣa*), not the body.
Whether the body exists or not, O Rāma, this person—whether conscious or unconscious—abides throughout the three worlds; even when the body is destroyed, he does not perish.
All these various sufferings that you perceive belong to the body, not to the ungraspable Self which is pure consciousness.
Since it has transcended the path of the mind and remains as if empty,
how indeed can that consciousness be grasped by either sufferings or pleasures?
But from this distinguished cage of a body, the self consisting of consciousness departs with its habitual latent impressions, just as a bee leaves a lotus for the sky.
If the reality of the self does not exist, then what indeed would be lost when this cage of the body perishes, O Rāma, that you should grieve?
Cultivate truth; do not experience delusion through it. O you of faultless form, for the Self which is free from desire, there are no desires whatsoever.
Within the conscious Self— which is the witness, impartial, pure, and free from conceptual construction—
the worlds appear of their own accord, like rays of light within a precious gem.
Just as there is a connection between a mirror and its reflection that is devoid of desire,
so too is this relationship between consciousness and the world established by the power of their own nature.
Just as duality and unity are established between a mirror and its reflection,
so too here are difference and non-difference established between the self and the world.
Just as activity arises on earth merely through the proximity of the sun,
so too is this world brought forth by the mere existence of consciousness.
O Rāma, when the grasping of this world-existence as a solid mass has ceased,
it becomes space even within your own minds.
Just as the light of a lamp exists by its very nature through its mere presence,
so too does this activity of the world arise from the intrinsic nature of the reality of mind.
Formerly, the mind arose from the reality of the Supreme Self, and by it this world was spread out as a web of its own conceptual constructions;
just as the sky, though empty and stainless, appears blue and beautiful with lovely creepers.
But when the mind has dissolved through the destruction of volitional constructs (saṅkalpa), the mists of delusion regarding saṃsāra vanish.
Then, like the sky in autumn, the one, unborn, primordial, and infinite Pure Consciousness (cinmātra) shines forth clearly within.

At the very outset, the mind, whose nature is action, arises through volition; having assumed the form of the lotus-born Brahmā, it expands this infinite and manifold world, just as a deluded child imagines the body of a ghost.
Unreal yet appearing as if real, the mind is first perceived, then it comes into being, and then it dissolves again;
its own expansive body throbbing within consciousness, like a series of circles of water in the great ocean.
The One Hundred and Twenty-Third Chapter, titled "The Investigation of Ultimate Reality," by Vasiṣṭha:
In this way, understand that this visible world is established as such;
it is a mere illusion, devoid of form, consisting of "I" and so forth, and composed of unreality.
Without an agent and without a body, a painting has arisen in the sky;
it is without a viewer, yet accompanied by experience—a dream-vision occurring without sleep.
The construction of the future city appeared like a painting come to life;
it shone with the glow of a forest fire and was situated like a whirlpool in the water.
Though it possesses a real form, it is empty like solar radiance in the sky;
it is seen in the atmosphere like a net of jewel-reflections, yet without a foundation.
Like a city of one's imagination, it is maturely experienced yet composed of unreality;
consisting of the manifestation of the meaning of a narrative, it neither exists nor does it abide anywhere.
Though devoid of essence, it appears as if possessing an extreme internal essence; like a mountain in a dream, it is a mere emptiness, radiant with form like the elemental ether.
Like an autumn cloud situated before one's eyes, it is seen as something unsubstantial, appearing to be perishable yet actually indestructible, like a color in the expanse of the sky.
It has the form of dalliance with a woman in a dream; though it appears to have an object, it is devoid of any real purpose.
Like a garden in a painting in full bloom, it is sapless despite its appearance of being full of flavor.
It was like light devoid of radiance, like a painted sun or fire;
it was experienced as unreal and unsubstantial, like a kingdom of the mind.
Like a variegated lotus pond devoid of cranes and fragrance,
it shines forth in emptiness, possessing various colors and a nature composed of forms.
In the ultimate sense, it is spread out with elements that are dry and as fragile as sprouts;
it is inert, devoid of essence, and as hollow as the trunk of a plantain tree.
Pervaded like a circle of darkness visible to wide-open eyes,
that which is absolutely non-existent appeared as if it were directly perceived.
Like a water bubble, it is expansive yet empty within, its form quivering; though consisting of essence, it is devoid of true essence, with its arising and perishing occurring without interruption.
Like a spreading mist, though grasped it is nothing at all;
it is inert, its locus is empty, and it is empty—like an atom, according to some.
It is established that something consisting of the unreal exists as a void;
though being grasped, it is of a non-existent nature, like a sword-blade that has arisen [from its scabbard].
Rāma:
At the end of a great kalpa, the visible world remains like a sprout within a seed; tell me, how is it that this arises again from that very source?
Are those who have such an awakening ignorant, or are they knowers of that? O Blessed One, speak clearly and as it truly is, for the sake of pacifying all doubt.
Vasiṣṭha:
He who says that this visible world exists within the Great Destruction like a sprout within a seed, speaks out of extreme ignorance due to his great childishness.
In the case of contact, what is that which is unconnected? How can this be unreal?
This is a perverted cognition produced by the ignorance of both the speaker and the listener.
The notion that the world existed here like a sprout at the time of the seed is a deluded and meaningless prattle; hear now how this is so.
The seed itself would be visible as the object of the mind and the senses;
in this regard, the emergence of a sprout from things such as a banyan seed or grain is logical.
How could that which transcends the six senses, including the mind, and which is even more ethereal than space,
be capable of being the seed of the self-existent world?
How and in what manner can there be the state of being a seed for the Supreme Self, which is subtler than even space, transcendent, and unperceivable by any of the senses?
The existent is subtle and appears as non-existent, for it is indeed non-existent to those who do not see it as such.
What kind of seed-nature could there be therein? In the absence of a seed, whence can there be a sprout?
Even within that supreme state, which is clearer than the sky and empty,
how can there exist the world, Mount Meru, the oceans, the sky, and so forth?
How can that which is nothing whatsoever be something? What entity could exist there within what is non-existent? If it does exist there, why is it not seen while being present?
How or from where could something belonging to the self arise from that which belongs to the self?
Or rather, from where, when, or where could a mountain ever be born from the empty space within a jar?
How can anything exist within its opposite, as [darkness exists] in light or [heat] in shade?
How can darkness exist in the sun, or how can fire exist in ice?
How could Mount Meru reside within an atom? How could there be anything at all in that which is formless?
Where could there be a unity between that which possesses such a nature and that which does not, like shadow and sunlight?
It is logical that the sprout exists within the acorn and so forth when they possess form; it is illogical that the world, which has great form, exists within that which is formless.

That which is invisible due to the power of all the faculties, such as the intellect, in another place or in another person—indeed, that does not exist at all; and when there is no cognition of such a thing, it is said to be "nothing at all."
He whose understanding is utterly deluded claims that the effect has attained the state of being the cause;
by what means, then, could that effect arise from it, through its own multitude of causes in the form of auxiliary factors?
Having cast far away the notion of the relationship between cause and effect imagined by those of dull intellect,
know that this very world— which is without beginning or middle— is established as nothing other than that Reality itself.
The one hundred and twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Refutation of the Produced and the Producer," by Vasiṣṭha.
Now, O best among those who know what is to be known, I shall speak regarding this acceptance:
in the stainless, great space of consciousness, which transcends all mental constructs.
If the primordial sprout of the world exists therein, then tell me: by what auxiliary causes does it arise?
In the absence of auxiliary causes, the sprouting of a seed or the birth of a barren woman's daughter has never been seen by anyone at any time.
And that which has arisen in the absence of auxiliary causes is the very root cause, the Self; it remains thus established in its own nature.
At the beginning of creation, Brahman itself abides within itself in the form of creation; since it remains as it is, devoid of form, where is there any sequence of produced and producer?
If earth and the other elements, or something else, having come from somewhere,
act as auxiliary causes, then the same refutation applies here as before.
Therefore, the world remains quiescent beyond that [cause]; the claim that it spreads forth without its auxiliary causes belongs to the ignorant, not to the wise.
Therefore, O Rāma, the world never existed, does not exist, and will not exist; it is only the pure space of consciousness that shines forth in this manner within itself.
O Rāma, when the absolute non-existence of this world is realized, then all this is Brahman; it is not otherwise.
That which subsides through prior destruction, mutual non-existence, and so forth, is not actually pacified within the mind; for it does not truly cease to exist.
Therefore, for the complete destruction of the world of appearances, there is no other method whatsoever than the absolute non-existence [of that world].
This awareness of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) which exists as the world and so forth— this is that "I," and this too is form, light, mind, its subtle parts, and the rest.
This is the sun and so forth, this is the earth and so forth, and likewise this is the year and so forth;
this is the eon and this is the moment, and these are death and birth.
This is the agitation at the end of a kalpa; this is that very end of the great kalpa.
This is the commencement of creation; this is that sequence of existence and non-existence.
These millions of kalpas, these millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa),
these multitudes of Brahmās and Indras, and these powers of Viṣṇu and the others [are all within me].
These have been transformed, these have returned again;
these are the networks of celestial abodes, and these are the portions of space and time.
The great consciousness, the supreme space, unobstructed and infinite,
shines forth by itself as tranquil, just as it has always existed from the beginning.
These [appearances] are but a thousandth part of an atom of the Great Consciousness;
existing within it as its very nature, they neither come nor go.
That which is itself an internal wonder, when projected forth by consciousness, appears as this manifestation of creation; it is of the nature of light and possesses no supporting substrate.
They do not arise nor do they perish; they do not come nor do they go;
they are as immovable as the inscriptions within a great rock.
These creations flash forth spontaneously within the pure self by itself,
like portions of space within space, formless within the formless.
Like the fluidity of water, like the vibrations of the wind,
like the whirlpools of the ocean, or like the qualities of one who possesses them.
This entire world is established as a single mass of consciousness,
infinite, peaceful, and pervasive, including its beginning, its setting, and its rising.
"To claim that the world is empty due to the absence of causes such as auxiliary factors,
yet that the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) is born [from it], is indeed the babbling of a madman."
With all stains of the parts of objects completely stilled, with the bed of all conceptual constructions entirely cast away,
and having long since dispelled the deep sleep of ignorance, he is awakened— the fearless one who adorns the earth.
The one hundred and twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Presentation of the Seed of Memory," [spoken by] Rāma:

At the beginning of creation following the great dissolution, this first Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) is born as the very essence of memory; from that, the world likewise arises as the essence of memory.
Vasiṣṭha:
O scion of Raghu, it is exactly so at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution;
at first, that very first Prajāpati exists as the self of memory alone.
And since the world consists of that [Supreme Being's] volition, this [universe] likewise consists of memory;
it appears as a city of volition established by the former Lord of Creatures.
Even though this is the case, O Rāma, that stability of that former Prajāpati is simply not possible, just as a great tree cannot exist in the sky.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how is it that memory of the past does not exist at the beginning of creation?
How is it that prior memory is destroyed by the delusions of the great dissolution?
Vasiṣ�ṭha said: O wise one, prior to the great dissolution, Brahmā and the others of old indeed attained nirvāṇa; they necessarily reached the state of Brahman.
Who is the rememberer of that prior memory? Therefore, O observer of noble vows, explain this:
since the rememberer has attained liberation, the memory has become rootless.
Therefore, in the absence of a rememberer, how could that memory arise, and what or how?
For indeed, at the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), all beings necessarily become partakers of liberation alone.

The memory that arises within the sky of consciousness itself regarding both the experienced and the unexperienced is the matured glory of the world; for in the absence of the visible, it is indeed the radiance of consciousness.
It is the radiance of consciousness alone that shines, pure and illuminating without beginning or end;
that which is established as this "world" and as the "Self-existent" (Svayambhū).
That innate manifestation of Brahman, established from beginningless time,
is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) of Virāj, which has the form of the universe.
Within the atom, this entire world shines forth, together with the three realms,
endowed with the succession of space, time, action, substance, day, and night.
Then, within each atom, there likewise appears that very same [world],
shining with its radiant form and similarly enveloped by mountain ranges.
Even there, such a form, extending thus to every atom, appears as a visible object consisting of light; my friend, this is not real.
Thus, there is no end anywhere for either the view of existence or the view of non-existence;
but for this [view], O sinless one, awakening has arisen, whether with respect to the awakened or the unawakened.
For one who has awakened, this is indeed Brahman alone—tranquil and immutable;
