but for one who has not awakened, it appears as a dualistic manifestation accompanied by the worlds.
Just as this radiant world shines forth, expanded from an egg,
so too do thousands of millions of others shine within every single atom.
Just as there is a figurine at the end of a pillar, and a figurine on its limbs, and another figurine on that figurine’s limb, so too is the figurine of the three worlds.
Just as atoms on a mountain are neither distinct nor countable,
so too are the atoms of the three worlds upon the vast Mount Meru of Brahman.
The minute particles of light in the rays of the sun may be counted;
but the atoms of the three worlds, which have no beginning or end, cannot be counted within the sun of consciousness.
Just as atoms move within the rays of the sun, within waters,
and within dust, so do the atoms of the three worlds move within the space of consciousness.
Just as this element of space consists of the mere experience of emptiness,
so too does this space of consciousness consist of the mere experience of creation.

When "creation" (sarga) is understood as the meaning of the word *sarga*, it leads one downward; when it is understood as the meaning of the word *brahman*, it becomes a sufficient means for the highest good.
The conscious self, the ruler, the seed of the universe, is Brahman alone—the primordial, one's own, nothing but the sky of consciousness.
Know that whatever is born from that is indeed that very same thing; understand within yourself that it is nothing but the awakening of pure awareness.
The one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Infinite Description of the World," by Vasiṣṭha.
The ocean of existence is crossed by means of this bridge, which is the restraint of the collection of the senses;
it cannot be crossed by any other action whatsoever in this world.

Through the study of the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and constant practice, one who possesses discernment and has conquered the senses realizes the absolute non-existence of this flood of perceptible objects.
All this has been told to you, O best of embodied beings: the nature of how the successions of the ocean of saṃsāra come and go.
What need is there for much speaking here? The mind is the sprout of the tree of karma;
when that is severed, the tree of karma, with all its world-branches, becomes severed.
O Rāma, all this is within the mind; when that is treated, this entire existence consisting of the web of births is thereby cured.
Thus, this mind, agitated by a trace of impurity, arises in the world;
apart from the mind, where indeed is the body ever seen?
Without the absolute non-existence of the object of perception, the demon of the mind does not come to rest by any other cause, even in hundreds of eons.
And this is indeed possible for the treatment of mental disease;
it is the supreme, most excellent medicine, whose nature is the absolute non-existence of the perceptible.
The mind takes on delusion; the mind dies and is born again.
Yet, through the grace of someone, it is bound and then released once more.
Thus the entire world throbs within the mind that is agitated by conceptualization,
like the city of Gandharvas in the vast, empty sky.
This entire expansive universe exists and vibrates within the mind;
it is like fragrance residing within a cluster of flowers, being both identical to and distinct from it.
Just as oil exists in a sesame seed, or as a quality exists in that which possesses the quality,
or as a property exists in its substratum, so too is this [reality] established in the mind.
Just as a mass of waves arises in water, just as the delusion of two moons appears in the moon, and just as a mirage appears in the heat, so does cyclic existence appear within the mind.
Just as a network of rays exists in the sun, just as light exists in brilliance,
and just as heat exists in fire, so too does this world exist within the mind.
Just as coolness is in frost, as emptiness is in the sky,
and as flickering is in the wind, so is this world in the mind.
The mind is the world, and the entire world is likewise the mind; for these two are indeed always inseparable from one another.
When the mind is incessantly wounded, both of them are wounded, but when the world is wounded, the mind is not.
The one hundred and twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Discourse on the Seed of Stability," [spoken by] Rāma.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, supreme among those who understand the beginning and the end:
how does this vast cycle of existence abide within the mind?
O sinless one, tell me clearly how this expansive undertaking manifests vividly in the mind, by means of a clear illustration.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as the worlds of the sons of Indu,
though bodiless, remain firmly established in the minds of the wise, so too does this [universe] abide within the mind.
Just as King Lavaṇa attained the state of a Caṇḍāla when his form was confounded by Indra’s magical illusions, so too has this [illusion] remained fixed in the mind.
For a long time, Bhārgava’s mind remained fixed on this: the desire to enjoy the pleasures of heaven and the state of being the lord of all enjoyments.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, how did the son of Bhṛgu, through his desire to enjoy the pleasures of heaven,
come to possess lordship over those enjoyments and yet remain subject to worldly existence?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāma, to an ancient account, a dialogue between Bhṛgu and Kāla,
which took place on a ridge of Mount Mandara, thick with the branches of *tāla* and *tamāla* trees.
In ancient times, on a certain peak of Mount Mandara thick with blossoms,
the venerable Bhṛgu performed severe austerities.
The radiant and highly intelligent young son Śukra, who possessed the luster of the full moon, attended upon him just as light attends the sun.
In that excellent forest, Bhṛgu remained established in meditative absorption at all times, as if carved out from the surface of a forest rock.
The boy Śukra sported playfully upon beds of flowers, amidst lotus-pools of silver, and on swings made of *mandāra* trees.
At that time, it is said, Śukra remained between the two visions of knowledge and ignorance, like Triśaṅku suspended between heaven and earth, having not yet attained the great state.
Then, while his father was established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he remained undistracted in solitude, like a king who has conquered his enemies.
There he beheld an apsaras traveling along the path of the sky,
like Janārdana beholding Lakṣmī emerging from the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
She was adorned with garlands of *mandāra* flowers, her locks of hair were stirred by the gentle breeze,
her gait was as captivating as that of a swan, and she perfumed the air of the sky with her fragrance.
A creeper upon the tree of loveliness, with eyes rolling from intoxication,
she made that entire region nectarine with the moonlight-like splendor of her body.
Upon beholding his beloved, his mind became tremulous with joy,
like the body of the ocean when the stainless, full moon is seen.

Having restrained his mind within his heart, which was struck by hundreds of mental arrows, Uśanas thereafter became, through his own self, consisting entirely of celestial nymphs, as all other mental functions had dissolved.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the chapter titled "The Stumbling of Bhārgava," the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter; Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, meditating upon her with his mind, Uśanas alone, with eyes closed right there,
began this reign of the imagination.
For this woman is in the sky, the abode of the thousand-eyed one; I have now reached heaven, which is graced by the ever-tremulous celestial beauties.
These gods of yours are beautiful with crests of soft mandārava flowers,
their bodies radiant with the grace of molten gold.
These are those lovely ones with gazes like deer, playful with charming smiles, who rain down blue lotuses created by the delight of their eyes.
These Maruts, radiant with the Kaustubha gem and reflecting one another’s forms, possess appearances comparable to the Cosmic Form (Viśvarūpa) and look like those intoxicated by wine.
These are those songs of the hosts of gods, sung in sweet, falsetto tones, and heard by bees who have grown weary of the fragrance from the temples of Airāvaṇa.
This is that Mandākinī, where the female cranes of Brahmā wander among the golden lotuses,
and where the celestial consorts rest in the gardens upon its banks.
These are your world-protectors— Yama, Candra, Indra, Sūrya, Anila, Jala, and Anala— their bodies radiant with scattered, blazing, and intensely glowing rays of light.
This is that Airāvaṇa, whose face was scratched by the tips of the tusks of the gods’ prowess, and whose champing tusks pierced the circle of the lords of the Daityas.

These beings who were situated on the surface of the earth have now attained the state of stars in the sky; as celestial dwellers in their mansions, they wear shimmering, beautiful necklaces, chowries, and earrings.
These are those rows of celestial palaces, adorned with various gardens and jeweled mansions, possessing the splendor of beautiful golden light.
These are those waves of the Ganges' water, strewn with mandāra flowers, by which the deities are drenched with spray as they strike the surface of Mount Meru.
These are the avenues of Śakra’s grove, where rows of apsarases sway upon swings, rendered tawny by clusters of spreading mandāra blossoms.
These are the breezes from the Pārijāta tree, fragrant with the nectar of the kunda and mandāra flowers, resembling a mass of moonbeams.
This Nandana grove is filled with throngs of vine-like women who are eager for the battle of scattering flower-pollen as if it were a silken veil.
These two, Nārada and Tumburu, have voices as melodious as the lute and cause the celestial maidens to dance with joy through the sound of their lovely songs.
These performers of meritorious deeds, adorned with many ornaments,
dwell in happiness within celestial chariots soaring through the sky.
These celestial women, their limbs intoxicated by passion and love,
attend upon the Lord of the Gods like forest creepers in a grove.
These kalpa-trees, with their flower-clusters made of moonbeams and bunches of wish-fulfilling gems, are bristling with clusters of ripe jewels.
Here, first of all, I shall worship and salute this Śakra as he sits upon his throne, as if he were a second Lord of the Gods.
Having reflected thus, the Lord of Śacī, by means of his mind alone, greeted him there; he appeared like a second Bhṛgu.
Then Śukra, having been honored by Śakra, rose respectfully;
[Śakra] took him by the hand, led him forward, and seated him nearby.
"O Śukra, this heaven now shines with fortune because of your arrival;
O Śakra, please dwell here for a long time," he said to him in this manner.
Then, having sat down there, that descendant of Bhṛgu, his face radiant,
eclipsed the splendor of the entire stainless moon.

Worshipped by the entire host of gods and stationed at the side of Indra, that son of Bhṛgu attained incomparable satisfaction for a very long time; he abandoned his human mindset and became truly transcendent.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the one hundred and twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Mental Kingdom of Bhārgava," Vasiṣṭha says:
Thus Śukra, having reached the city of the gods with his own mind,
forgot his former nature and his previous calamity, except for his addiction.
Then, having rested for a moment at the side of the Lord of Śacī,
he set out to roam through heaven, urged by the inhabitants of the celestial realm.
Having beheld the splendor of heaven, marked by their tremulous eyes,
he went to gaze upon the women, as a crane goes toward a lotus pond.
There he beheld that beloved woman with eyes like a young fawn’s, who had arrived and stood at the edge of the forest, just as a bee finds a mango creeper.
Beholding her, whose form was graced by shimmering and restless charms,
his limbs began to melt away like a moonstone in the moonlight.
With all his limbs dissolving, he gazed upon that amorous woman,
as a moonstone gazes at the cool, playful moonlight in the sky.
Beheld by him, she too became intent upon him,
like a female cakravāka bird cooing at the end of the night when called by her mate.

Surely, the splendor that belongs to the sun and the lotus in the morning— when they have blossomed through their essence and are truly enamored of one another— that very same splendor belonged to those two.
Because that region grants whatever is desired,
she was rendered helpless in every limb by Madana and surrendered to Śukra alone.
The arrows of Love fell repeatedly upon her tender limbs,
like torrents from a fresh rain-cloud upon the petals of a lotus.
Shaken by love, with her curls like a swarm of restless bees,
she became the counterpart of a flower-cluster tossed by a gentle breeze.
Madana agitated her, who had eyes like blue lotuses and a gait like that of a swan or an elephant, just as a flood disturbs a bed of lotuses.
Then, seeing her in such a state, Śukra, who was intent upon his desired object, willed forth darkness, just as the Creator wills the dissolution of all beings.
That region of the triple heaven became shrouded in darkness,
like the shore of the Lokāloka mountain at the edge of the world, where the earthly realm is enveloped in blinding gloom.
When he— the sharp-rayed sun to the darkness of shame— had established himself within that circle of gloom, it was as if the god of love had taken his stand for that couple.
When all those beings had departed from that place toward their desired directions,
at the end of the day, they returned to the world of mortals like birds.
With her long, white-cornered eyes and her passion thus fully aroused,
she approached the son of Bhṛgu as a peahen approaches a rain-cloud.
On a couch prepared in the midst of a white chamber,
Bhārgava entered there like Mādhava into the Ocean of Milk.
Clinging to his feet like one helpless, that fair-faced woman shone like a lotus plant clinging to the foot of a divine elephant.
And she spoke these sweet, joy-bestowing words, flowing with playful syllables, in a voice radiant with overflowing affection.
O lady with a face like the full moon, behold: why does this bodiless one, having drawn his bow into a circle, pursue me, a weak woman?
Protect me, O Lord, for I am weak, distressed, and here take refuge in you;
know, O virtuous one, that consoling the miserable is the vow of your true conduct.
O Great-minded One, it is only by the foolish who do not understand the gaze of affection that endearments are disregarded; those who know the true flavor never do so.
The affection of two people who love one another, attained without hesitation,
surpasses even the tasted nectar of the moon, O beloved.
This sovereignty over the three worlds does not so gladden the mind as the mutual affection of two people who have first fallen in love.
O giver of honor, by the touch of your feet I have been comforted,
like a night-lotus at night touched by the rays of the moon.
O handsome one, I live by drinking the nectar of your touch,
just as the restless female cakora bird lives by drinking the essence of the moonbeams.
Embrace me, this bee clinging to your feet, with your sprout-like hands, and place me within your heart, which is like a true lotus filled with nectar.
Having spoken thus, she whose limbs were as soft as flowers fell upon his chest,
her bee-like eyes rolling like a flower-cluster on a tree.
There, that couple, radiant with amorous play, sported in those forest glades—
glades white with filaments and stirred by the breeze— like two intoxicated bees among lotus ponds.
The one hundred and thirtieth canto, titled "The Reunion," from the Bhārgava-episode,
[spoken by] Vasiṣṭha:
Thus, through those beloved advances imagined for a long time by the play of his mind,
the sage Bhārgava’s union with her was for his own satisfaction.
Then, with her who was adorned with garlands of *mandāra* flowers and intoxicated by the nectar of the gods, he was accompanied by that second [companion], the spotless moon.
He dwelt upon the golden lotus-beds where intoxicated swans roamed,
and on the banks of the celestial river together with the Kinnaras and Cāraṇas.
The playful lover, together with the gods, drank the yellow elixir flowing from the moon’s crescent while dwelling within the bowers of the *pārijāta* creeper.
He sported for a long time with playful ease upon the vine-swinging arbors of the beautiful Caitraratha grove, accompanied by groups of eager Vidyadhara maidens.
The expanse of the Nandana grove was violently tossed about by the attendants of Śambhu, just as the ocean is by Mount Mandara.
And he wandered through caves thick with networks of young golden creepers,
like one intoxicated by passion wandering among the lotus-beds of Mount Meru.
In the forest groves of Kailāsa, that playful lover spent the night— white as the moon’s rays— with her amidst the songs of the Gaṇas.
Having rested upon the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana,
she was adorned by him from head to foot with golden lotuses.
O Rāma, he sported with her, laughing, upon the shores of the Lokāloka mountain, which are captivating with their various wonders.
In the groves between the Mandara trees, together with the young fawns,
he dwelt for sixty years, having fashioned a celestial palace for himself.
On the shores of the Ocean of Milk, half of the Kṛta Yuga was spent by him in the company of his wives and the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa.
Through the playful creation of celestial cities and gardens,
he has come to imitate Time, which brings about the creation of infinite worlds.
Then that Śukra dwelt again in the city of Purandara for eight cycles of four yugas, happily together with the deer-eyed woman.
Due to the exhaustion of his merit,
he then fell upon the circle of the earth along with that proud woman, his form stripped away.
With all his limbs mangled by others, his chariot and its delights seized, overcome by anxiety and ruined, he was like a soldier struck down in the heat of battle.
As he lay fallen upon the earth, his body shattered into a hundred pieces by long anxiety, like a mountain torrent crashing against a rock.
When their two bodies had perished, those two minds, shrouded by latent impressions (vāsanā),
wandered in the sky like two birds without a nest.
There, those two entered the moon’s web of rays;
having quickly attained the state of frost, they then became rice.
That best of brahmins ate those cooked *śāli* rice grains in the Daśārṇa country,
and the king ate those born from the womb of Śukra’s wife in the Mālava country.
Formerly, Uśanas was born among the Daśārṇas from an excellent brahmin,
and his wife was born among the Mālavas from a king of supreme fortune.
There the boy grew, and there that woman grew;
they were like a former husband and wife born upon the earth after falling from heaven.
Then Śukra, bearing the name Sāraṅga, became sixteen years old;
a glorious young brahmin boy, endowed with youth, remained in his father’s house.
That maiden Mālā, the daughter of the asura, grew up in the king’s palace like a creeper with bee-like eyes in a choice forest.
Then the auspicious princess Mālā worshipped Śaṅkara incessantly, thinking, "May I obtain my former, perfected husband."
Then, at the sacrifice of the King of Mālava, she beheld Sāraṅga, who had arrived at the assembly of brahmins together with his father.
Seeing him, she of faultless limbs, permeated by former affection,
shone with her body moistened by love, like a moonstone that has seen the moon.
Then, in the midst of the sacrificial assembly, that garland, the daughter of the King of Mālava, chose the son of the twice-born from Daśārṇa as her husband.
When he had gradually completed his marriage, the lord of Mālava, worn out by old age, handed over the entire kingdom to him and departed for the forest.
Together with her, that Sāraṅga ruled the kingdom in that realm of Mālava for a hundred autumns, as exceedingly happy as Śakra himself.
Then, after a long time, due to the fickleness of the mind and by the power of destiny, those two, husband and wife, became mutually disagreeable.
But Sāraṅga, worn out by old age, his body ready to fall, assumed the color of withered leaves due to the weakness of his breath.
Due to his detachment from his wife and family, and because of his extreme old age,
he— devoid of desire and with all hesitation stilled— welcomed death.
Then, in that sapless kingdom which proclaimed an excess of suffering,
delusion reached an extreme density, like a vetāla spirit in a forest.
Falling incessantly into the blind well of delusion due to attachment to enjoyments,
he is undiscriminating, ignorant, and devoted to the company of the wicked.
Just as a frog seizes a helpless, crying moth that has swallowed a flame, so does Death seize this person whose heart is gripped by craving.
Then, having experienced the fruit of his own auspicious and inauspicious karma in the next world,
he was born as a fisherman among the limbs [of beings] due to the power of that evil disposition.
There, performing the work of a fisherman for a hundred autumns,
he attained a state of world-weariness because his mind was worn out by suffering.
Reflecting thus that "saṃsāra is suffering," he then leapt toward the sun;
by means of that [act], he was born as a great king in the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa).
Then, by the power of his virtuous state, he attained some degree of knowledge;
having cast off his royal body, he became a teacher, an instructor of all.
Having indeed attained success through the accomplishment of mantras, he then became a Vidyādhara;
for one kalpa, he enjoyed the city of the Vidyādharas.
Having brought about the time of the end of the eon with her body in the form of wind,
when creation had begun once more, the son of the Sage was born again.
Then, through contact with the sages, he established himself in fierce asceticism;
blameless, he dwelt in the depths of Mount Meru for the duration of a Manvantara.
There, a son of a deer in human form was born to him;
through affection for that child, he again fell into a state of extreme delusion in an instant.
"May this son have wealth, virtues, and eternal life for me"—
with such incessant anxieties, he abandoned his abiding in truth.
Because he had fallen away from reflection on the Dharma and was preoccupied with thoughts of wealth for the sake of his son,
Death carried him off as a serpent snatches the wind from one whose life is spent.
With his consciousness departed while occupied solely with thoughts of enjoyment,
he attained the status of the son of the Lord of Madra and became the sovereign of the Madra land.
Having ruled the kingdom in the land of Madra for a long time, with his enemies utterly destroyed,
he reached old age here like a frostbolt reaching a lotus.
But he cast off that body of the King of Madra along with the latent impressions of his asceticism; therefore, he was born as an ascetic, the son of a forest hermit.
Having reached the bank of the great river Samaṅgā,
O Rāma, that ascetic of great intelligence practiced austerities, free from all distress.
Having followed the succession of bodies with a mind rendered helpless by the various states of birth,
that son of Bhrigu remained happily on the bank of the excellent river like a firm tree.
The one hundred and thirty-first canto, titled "The Experience of Various Births" in the Bhārgava Episode, Canto 131; Vasiṣṭha said:
As Śukra was reflecting thus, a vast period of time consisting of many years passed before his father.
Then, after a long time, his body— withered by wind and sun— fell upon the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed.
But his mind, its range flickering, wandered through those various and most diverse states, like a deer among the rows of forest trees.
His mind— wandering, reeling, and agitated as if fixed upon a whirling wheel— found rest on the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
Śukra remained there, experiencing that state of worldly existence— which is both fragile and yet very firm, and dense with infinite occurrences— while being himself bodiless.
Standing upon the peak of Mount Mandara, the body of that wise one became withered by the spreading heat until it was reduced to mere skin.

Through the sound of hissing produced by the wind flowing through the apertures of his body, he seemed to sing a *kākali* melody born from the bliss of the cessation of the suffering of physical activity.
Like a sigh of breath through the recollection of life, it released its vapor as it was stirred by the play of fierce winds across the forest lands.
The wretched mind, wallowing in the pits of the realms of existence,
is as if laughing with its row of teeth, white as exceedingly bright clouds.
She revealed her own natural emptiness to the eyes through the beauty of the hollows of her mouth, which resembled the shape of an ancient well in a forest.
Scorched by the heat and drenched by a downpour of rain,
it was covered with dust raised by the wind, as if defiled by its own misdeeds.
Tossing like dry wood, making clattering sounds as it falls,
it is pierced by the falling torrent of rain at the onset of the clouds.
On the bank of a mountain river, drenched by the flood of a monsoon torrent,
she stood like a forest stone, her loud sighs sounding like the whistling of the wind.
Crooked, with strings of dried entrails, foul-smelling, and making a gurgling sound,
she was like the lute of the Goddess of the Forest, her belly made of empty skin.
Because that holy hermitage was free from passion and hatred,
and because Bhṛgu was engaged in great austerity, it was not consumed by beasts or birds.
The mind of that descendant of Bhṛgu, whose slender body had been emaciated by restraints and observances, was intent on asceticism;
meanwhile, his body, its blood drained away by the wind, lay for a long time upon the great rocks.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the chapter titled "The Description of Bhārgava’s Body," the one hundred and thirty-second chapter; Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after a thousand divine years,
Bhṛgu, the Supreme Lord, desisted from his meditative absorption due to his supreme awakening.
He did not see his son before him, whose face was bowed down in humility,
who stood like merit incarnate, and who was the very limit of all virtues.
He saw before him a great skeleton, appearing as pure Time alone,
like misfortune embodied or poverty personified.
Its body was withered by heat; partridges quivered within its skin-cavities, and frogs rested in the shadows of its dried-out internal organ-caverns.
It was like a forest of insects sleeping within the hollows of eyes,
or a swarm of silkworms pinned inside a cage of flies.

With a body washed by the stream [of tears] from the corners of his eyes, and with a garland of dry bones, he laughed at his former desire for enjoyment, which yields both desired and undesired fruits.
With his bright, well-formed skull, possessing the luster of the moon,
he mocked the beauty of a linga-head drenched in camphor.
With his neck straightened, completely withered and white, reduced to mere bones, and stretched out behind him, he seemed to lengthen his very form.
He bore a face whose boundaries were defined by the bridge of his nose, which was as pale as a lotus stalk and from which the flesh had been stripped away by the steady flow [of blood].
Surely, with her long neck extended and her face turned upward,
she was gazing as if at his life-breaths departing into the belly of the sky.
With his shanks, thighs, knees, and staff-like arms having attained double their length,
he seemed to be measuring out the boundless quarters out of fear of the exhaustion from the long journey.
With a belly deeply sunken, reduced to mere skin and withered,
it seemed to display the extreme emptiness of the ignorant man's heart.
Beholding that withered skeleton, which was like the hitching post of an elephant,
Bhṛgu rose up without reflecting on what had preceded or followed.
Simultaneously with the appearance of light, Bhṛgu’s intuition arose: "Has my son been dead for a long time, or has he returned in an instant?"
Even as he was thus reflecting, his power regarding the future then gave rise to an exceedingly terrible wrath directed toward time.
"Why has my son been taken away at such an untimely hour? Thus provoked to anger, the Blessed One began to cast a curse upon Time.
Then Kāla, having assumed a form and having swallowed the subjects,
approached the sage, taking on a physical body composed of material elements.
The glorious one, holding a sword and a noose, adorned with earrings and clad in armor,
possesses six arms and six faces, and is surrounded by a vast army of servants.
The sky bore the splendor of a mountain of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees by the leaping mass of flames arising from his body.
With the circles of fire spat forth from the tips of the tridents held in his hands,
the quarters of the sky shone as if with rising golden earrings.
By the wind of his noose, the mountain peaks were strained;
the mountains, as if mounted upon a swing, swayed, fell, and reeled.
The orb of the sun, darkened by the radiance of the circle of his sword,
appeared as if it were obscured by the smoke from the world consumed at the end of an aeon.
Approaching that great sage, who was as deep as the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, the mighty-armed one spoke to him with conciliatory words.
O Sage, those who have understood the nature of the world and have seen both the higher and the lower are not deluded even by a reason; how much less so, O Supreme One, without a reason?

"You are a brahmin of infinite austerity, while we are merely observers of destiny; therefore, O venerable one, you are honored by us as one worthy of worship, O holy man, and not according to our own will."
Do not exhaust your asceticism with these agitated fires that burn at the end of an aeon;
since I am one who has not been consumed by them, what can you possibly burn me with your curse?
Cycles of saṃsāra have been swallowed; tens of millions of Rudras have been devoured;
multitudes of Viṣṇus have been consumed—by whom, O Sage, have we been cursed?
"For we, O Brahmin, are the eaters, while you and others are the food. This is indeed the fixed law of destiny; it was not our own doing."
Fire ascends upward of its own accord; waters flow downward of their own accord;
food goes to the eater, and creation itself goes toward its end.
O Sage, this form of the Supreme Self is thus;
here, the Self itself manifests by its own power within its own self.
By the vision that has destroyed all taints, there is neither an agent nor an enjoyer here;
yet by the vision that has not destroyed its taints, there are many agents here.
O Brahman, agency and non-agency are merely imagined through incorrect vision alone,
and not through correct vision for you.
Flowers in groves of trees and living beings in the worlds come and go here of their own accord; yet the causality of a Creator is postulated.
Just as in the movement of the moon's reflection there is neither agency nor non-agency— being neither true nor false— so it is with time regarding the creations [of the world].
In this world, the mind, due to false delusion, creates the conceptualization consisting of agency and non-agency,
just as one with blurred vision perceives a snake in a rope.
Therefore, O Sage, do not give way to anger; such is the course of calamities. Let it be exactly as it is; look upon the truth without agitation.
We do not act out of a desire for power, nor are we overcome by pride;
rather, we abide solely in our destiny through the force of our own inherent disposition.
A wise person, under the influence of necessity, should follow the established course of worldly activity as determined by destiny, but should not be shrouded in the great darkness of egoism.
Only that which ought to be done is performed by those skilled in action,
having resorted to the state of deep sleep and being free from any desire whatsoever.
Where is that vision consisting of knowledge, where is your greatness, and where is your fortitude?
For since the path is well-known to all, why do you wander in delusion like a blind man?
Even while maintaining in your mind the stainless vision of the three times,
why do you become deluded like a fool, failing to investigate the course of the world?
O Omniscient One, why do you deserve to curse me in vain like a fool, without considering the state of my son, which has arisen from the ripening of his own karma?
O Sage, for all embodied beings here, the body is of two kinds;
do you not know this—the one being the physical body and the other called the mind?
In this regard, the body is utterly insentient and solely intent on destruction;
the mind, however, is constantly active, and whether it perishes through its afflictions or not remains uncertain.
O virtuous one, just as a chariot is driven by a skillful charioteer who exerts some effort here, so too is this body driven by the mind.
Having conceptualized what is unreal, the real body is destroyed in an instant by the mind, just as a clay figure is destroyed by a child.
In this world, the mind alone is the person; what is done by it is said to be "done.
Bound because of conceptualization, it is liberated when conceptualization ceases.
"This body, this eye, this limb, this head—
this [entirety] characterized by expansive modifications is designated as that very mind."
For it is the mind (*manas*) that lives as the so-called "living being," while the intellect (*dhī*) functions as the faculty of discernment;
the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) exists because of the sense of self-identification, and it is this [mind] that indeed undergoes manifoldness.
If the mind, through the latent impression of the body, imagines other things as its own,
it perceives them as if they were physical bodies made of earth.
If one perceives the truth, then the mind,
casting off its unreal conception of a body, attains supreme bliss.
While you were thus absorbed in meditative concentration, the mind of your son traveled further and further away along the path of its own desires.
Having abandoned this body in a cave of Mount Mandara,
he departed for the abode of the gods, like a bird flying up from its nest.
There, in groves of *mandāra* trees, in dwellings of *pārijāta* trees,
in the thickets of the Nandana garden, and in the cities of the world-protectors;
O Sage, for eight cycles of four ages, that one of great splendor attended upon Viśvācī, the celestial beauty, just as a bee attends a lotus.
Then, filled with intense spiritual urgency, when his own merit was exhausted— just like the mist of a winter night— he [vanished] from that place fashioned by his own imagination.
With his flower-ornament withered and his limbs perspiring, he became languid as he moved his bracelets;
he fell down along with her like a fruit ripened by time.
Having abandoned that divine body in the very sky,
and having reached the elemental ether, he was born upon the earth.
There was a twice-born man among the Daśārṇas, a lord of the earth among the Kosalas, a fisherman in the great forest of Aṅga, and a swan on the banks of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā).
The king of the Solar dynasty was Pauṇḍra; Saura was among the Sālvas; the glorious and wise Vidyādhara was the ruler of the Daśārṇas; and then there was the son of the sage.
Then the protector of the earth, that young ascetic,
known as Vāsudeva, remained on the bank of the Samaṅgā river.
Furthermore, by the power of his own diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
this son of yours wandered through infinite and perilous wombs.
There was a cowherd in the Vindhya forest, a hunter among the Kekayas, a local chieftain among the Sauvīras, and a guide from Traigarta.
The bamboo thicket among the Kirātas, the deer in the Cīra forest, the reptile beneath the palm tree, and the wild cock in the Tamāla grove.
This very son of yours, having become the best among those who know mantras,
formerly recited the lore that bestows the status of a Vidyadhara.
Therefore, O Blessed One, that great Vidyadhara Brahma moved through the sky,
adorned with necklaces, earrings, and armlets, dancing with a multitude of graceful gestures.
He was like another flower-bowed god to the lotus-like heroines,
the beloved of the Vidyadhara women, and the ornament of the city of the Gandharvas.
Having reached the end of the eon within the abode of the twelve suns,
he was reduced to ashes, like a moth in a fire.
Then, in the vast sky devoid of the creation of the world,
that latent impression of his wandered about like a bird without a nest.
Then, when time had arrived— initiating the manifold undertakings at the commencement of the cosmic display of saṃsāra, following the reversal of Brahmā’s night—
That mental impression of his, having been stirred by the wind,
attained the state of a brahmin upon being performed, and was thus born today on the surface of the earth.
O Sage, this young Brahmin named Vāsudeva was born among the wise, having studied the entirety of the Vedas.
"O Great Sage, having been a Vidyādhara for an eon, your son now practices austerities, standing on the bank of the river Samaṅgā."

Driven by the persistence of various uneven latent tendencies, he has entered into the world’s ancient wombs— caves as formidable as *khadira* and *karañja* trees— and into the most impenetrable forest regions.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the chapter titled "The Words of Kāla," the one hundred and thirty-third chapter; Kāla says:
Today, on the bank of the excellent river, where the wind resounds with the gurgling roar of a surging mass of wild waves,
your son performs austerities.
Wearing matted hair and a rosary of beads, having conquered the delusions of all his senses,
he remained there for eight hundred years, steadfast in his ascetic practice.
O Sage, if you wish to see that son who is but a delusion of the mind,
then quickly open the eye of discernment and look.
When this had been said by Jagadīśa, who looks upon all with equal vision,
the sage reflected with the eye of his knowledge upon what was intended for his son.
And in a moment, by the power of his intuition, he beheld the entire account of his son reflected upon the mirror of his intellect.
Then, having come from the bank of the Samaṅgā river, Bhṛgu entered his own body, which was situated on the slopes of Mount Mandara at the time when it stood at the peak of the dark fortnight.
Having looked at Kāla with a gaze smiling with wonder,
the passionless sage spoke these words to his beloved, who was herself free from passion.
Bhṛgu said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, we are but children and unsullied; O God, only those like you possess the intellect that perceives the three times without impurity.
Though it exists, this course of the world— rich in transformations, manifold in form, and appearing as something unreal— produces delusion even for the wise man.
O Lord, you alone know this form of the activity of her mind, which functions like a magical illusion, that resides within you.
"O Blessed One, it is said that death does not exist for this son of mine;
therefore, seeing him dead, I have become filled with agitation."
"O Lord, though my son's life was not yet exhausted, Time has carried him away;
by the power of destiny, the desire for your curse has arisen within me."
But we, who have understood the course of saṃsāra, do not fall under the sway of joy or resentment when encountering either misfortune or prosperity.
"Anger toward one who acts improperly and favor toward one who acts properly—
this worldly condition, O Blessed One, has become established as something that must be practiced."
"This must be done, this must not"—such is the course of the world for as long as one lives;
as long as fire persists, so long are its perceptions of heat, burning, and so forth observed.

O Teacher of the World, for one who regards the state of the world as something to be abandoned— thinking "this is to be done" and "this is not"— the total renunciation of that very [state] is itself what must be abandoned.
O Blessed One, since we became agitated by you without having considered that this was merely a mental fabrication, for that reason we deserve censure.
"O Lord, I have now been reminded by you of what was intended for my son;
therefore, this son of mine was seen by me on the bank of the Samaṅgā."
I believe, O omnipresent one, that among all beings in the world there are not two bodies;
for the mind alone is the body, by which this world is brought into being.
Kāla said:
"O Brahmin, you have spoken correctly; for us, the mind alone is the body.
Having formed a volitional conception, it creates the body, just as a potter fashions a jar."
Through delusion, the mind, by means of conceptual construction, creates an uncreated form and destroys one that has been created in an instant, just as a child [imagines] a Vetāla.
And likewise, during states of agitation, powerful forces resembling cities of the Gandharvas— manifesting as dreams, false cognitions, and the like— are observed within the mind.
But relying upon this coarse perspective, O great sage, it is said that for a person there are two bodies: the mind and the physical body.
O Sage, these three worlds are merely a manifestation of mental ideation; they have arisen as something vast that is neither existent nor non-existent, and nothing else.
Through the creeper-like limbs of the body of consciousness, fueled by the latent impression of duality,
this manifoldness has arisen from ignorance, like the appearance of two moons.
Due to the manifold latent impressions of differentiation, the mind perceives everywhere a diverse collection of objects, such as jars, huts, cloths, and so forth.
"Emaciated, extremely miserable, and deluded— I am such"— cultivating these and other such notions arising from its own conceptual constructions, the mind enters the state of saṃsāra.
"This mental fabrication is my assumed form; I do not fall [into it].
Through the abandonment of that, the mind becomes tranquil—the eternal Brahman.
Just as in the vast, expansive ocean, stretching out with its many waves, graced by a succession of numerous billows consisting of gentle vibrations; ||| MU_3,133.29 |||
In the Self, which is like water— equal, clear, pure, sweet, cool,
imperishable, vast, of great majesty, and manifest— //MU 3.133.30//
Meditating on its own form as a triangular wave, it, by its very nature,
creates its own conceptual construction through the discrimination, "I am triangular."
Thinking, "I am falling away and my form is utterly ruined," he goes to the *talātala* hell by means of that very mental disposition toward the surface of the earth.
And when it has been forcibly raised upward, one conceives "I have risen";
through various conceptual constructions, one conceptualizes that state along with its designation.
When reflected as the sun, it is cultivated as "I am light";
when struck by a mass of dust, it is cultivated as "I am impure."
Enveloped by a net of jewel-like rays, he shines with radiant splendor;
yet, pierced by a heavy burden of frost, he perceives himself as cold.
With its body blazing with the reflection of the ever-flowing forest fire, it trembles and cries out, "Alas, I am being burned! even as it swallows the fish.
With the reflections of its shores, mountains, birds, forests, and trees, it shines,
as if possessed of a great undertaking and intense activity, thinking, "I am here."
"Having destroyed my flickering body through the arising of stainless radiance, I have been reduced to pieces"— thus he cried out as if seized by a lamentation.
And those waves are not distinct from the water of the ocean;
nor is there any single form among them that, though existing, is composed of unreality.
Nor do those qualities such as deficiency or length reside in those various things;
they are not established in the ocean like waves, yet they are not unestablished there either.

Merely by being fragmented by their own volitions while remaining within their respective natures, they are lost and yet not lost; born again and again, and though born, they are repeatedly destroyed.
Through mutual contact, they attain a state of manifoldness;
yet, being composed of the single essence of water, they remain free from affliction.
In the very same way, within this vast, white, pure, and stainless Brahman— which has the singular form of Brahman alone and possesses a pervasive nature— [all things abide].
Within the all-powerful [Brahman], which is without beginning or end, various powers— distinct yet non-distinct, established as diverse and restless through manifold activities— reside.
For Brahman, abiding within its own form, attains multiplicity through its various powers; it expands within Brahman like a circle of waves in water.
Because it takes on various forms, destiny— which produces hundreds of diverse appearances—
presides over every object with its fixed form.

The power, which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), assumes insentience when it is inert, and attains the state of consciousness when it is composed of consciousness; this occurs for the Self that abides in its own true nature.
O sinless one, it is Brahman alone that expands in this vast form,
appearing as if filled with various shapes and movements, like the ocean.
It assumes diversity of its own accord through dwelling in various forms;
it is like the ocean water within itself by means of itself.
Just as various waves are not distinct from the water,
so all mental constructs are not distinct from the Lord of All.
Just as the stalks, flowers, creepers, leaves, fruits,
and buds reside within a single seed, so do all powers reside within Brahman.
Just as there is a multiplicity of powers in the Person (puruṣa) due to his being a manifold agent,
so too in the omniscient Self (ātman) there is always the possession of all powers.
Just as a variegated color is seen in the harsh sunlight,
so too does the Lord of Gods possess a manifold power consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
This world of diverse forms arises from the non-diverse Śiva,
just as a streak of lightning emerges from a cloud of uniform color.
From the non-inert, the state of inertness arises, caused by the contemplation of dullness,
just as a thread emerges from a spider or as deep sleep arises from a man.
The auspicious Śiva, though devoid of mind, extends his mental power for the sake of his own bondage at will,
just as a silkworm weaves a cocoon from its own fibers.
O Brahmin, by voluntarily contemplating its own form as the Self,
one attains liberation from saṃsāra, just as an elephant [is freed] from its tethering post.
Whatever the self constantly contemplates, once it has been cultivated by itself,
even the great [self] is swiftly filled with that very power.
Cultivated power brings the self to its true nature in an instant,
just as a great autumn mist [clears] the infinite sky.
The unborn power that has arisen quickly attains identity with that [state];
indeed, having reached that very state, the tree becomes identical with it.
There is no liberation for the Lord, nor is there bondage for the Self;
I do not know from where these notions of bondage and liberation have arisen in the world.
For him there is neither bondage nor liberation, and he is perceived as being composed of that very essence; alas, this world is illusory, eternally swallowed by the unreal!
And as soon as the mind is conceptualized by the non-temporal, afflicted self,
then this self is enveloped by it, like a silkworm in its cocoon.
Yet these powers of the mind, which are non-different in essence from it though their forms are imagined as distinct, issue forth from this [Self] by the millions.
Abiding in that and born from that, they appear as distinct forms like waves from the ocean; abiding in that and born from that, yet situated separately, they are like rays from the moon.

In this vast ocean of the Supreme Self, which consists of vibration, whose waters are consciousness, whose expansive expanse is spread out, and which abounds in the essence of pure consciousness alone; //MU_3,133.66//
Some of these surging waves, which exceed the power of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra,
manifest themselves through their own inherent nature.
Some, resembling Yama, Indra, the Sun, Fire, Vaiśravaṇa, and others, strike, act, and remain; these waves of restless craving [behave] in such ways.
Some Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Suras, and others—
fierce waves leaping and falling— dart up and down.
Some exist in a certain state of form, such as those born from lotuses and the like;
others have arisen and then perished, such as gods, humans, and so forth.
Worms, insects, moths, and the like, as well as pythons, cobras, and so forth—
some of these flash like mere droplets within that great ocean.
Some, such as the *calānana*, *mṛgagṛdhra*, and *vañjulaka* birds,
flutter about in the mountain thickets like those on the shores of the coastal forests.
Some have very long lives, while others have extremely short lives;
some have empty bodies due to their own empty mental cultivation.
In the turbulent dream of saṃsāra, some are imbued with a sense of stability,
while others, struck down by their own conceptual constructions, imagine the world to be firmly established.
Some cultivate only meager meditations, being overcome by the fault of dejection;
they are made firm in their sufferings by thinking, "I am emaciated, extremely miserable, and deluded."
Some have attained the state of stationary beings, some have reached the state of gods;
some have attained the state of men, and some have gone to the state of Dānavas.
Some remain in this world for many hundreds of kalpas, while others, being utterly pure, go to the Supreme Person;
for the cognitions of consciousness—which possess the other name "thinking"—arise from the ocean of Brahman, restless like waves.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the one hundred and thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction on Yoga for Demonstrating the Functioning of Saṃsāra. Time.
O Sage, these cognitions that take the forms of gods, asuras, and humans are non-different from the ocean of Brahman; this is the truth, and everything else is false.
O Brahman, those who are stained by their own conceptual constructions through false meditation have fallen downward because of the internal conviction: "We are not Brahman."
Even those who have entered the ocean of Brahman, conceiving themselves as distinct from Brahman,
become utterly deluded within the terrifying realms of worldly existence.
O Sage, these cognitions pertaining to Brahman, which are not stained by manifold defects—
know that this is the seed of actions, or rather, know it to be action itself.
O Sage, by this internal process of mental construction, which is itself the form of volition,
one holds a terrifying handful of seeds for the *karañja* trees of the web of karma.
In this vast world, these rows of stone-like bodies stand,
they leap about, they weep, and they laugh.
From the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass, they throb like the wind;
they exult, they restrain themselves, they wither, and they laugh.
Among these, some are exceedingly clear, such as Hari, Hara, and others;
some are situated in slight delusion, such as the uragas, naras, and amaras.
Some remain in a state of absolute delusion, such as trees, grass, and the like; others, utterly bewildered by ignorance, have come to the state of worms and insects.
Some are carried away like blades of grass far from the great ocean of Brahman;
these have not attained the [spiritual] stages, just like the serpent-demons and others.
Seeing only the riverbank, some have fallen into despair;
those both born and unborn are being buried by the old rat of Death.
Having reached the inner essence of the great ocean of the reality of Brahman, Viṣṇu,
Brahmā, Hara, and the others have attained that state for the sake of freedom from sorrow.
Some, possessed of little delusion, remain established by relying upon that very ocean of Brahman, in which the flood of the disease of passion has never been seen.
Some multitudes of births are yet to be experienced, while millions of multitudes of births have already been experienced;
such are the classes of beings existing as either manifest or obscure.
Some go from above to below, and likewise from below to the Great State;
some go from above to even higher, and others from below to even lower.

This activity, fraught with many joys and sorrows, has come about through the failure to remember the Supreme State; it perishes upon the realization of the Supreme State, just as the agony of poison vanishes from the remembrance of the Lord of Birds.
In the Bhārgava episode, the chapter titled "The Description of the Detailed Origin" is the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter; the time [is now].
Of these classes of beings, which are diverse and manifold like waves in the ocean, or like various kinds of creepers in the month of Mādhava—
Having conquered the delusion of the mind through the Middle Way, and having perceived the higher and lower worlds,
those liberated while living wander here as yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
But others, resembling wood or walls, have become deluded and attained the state of the immobile;
since their delusion is not yet exhausted, what is there to be deliberated regarding them?
In this world, for the sake of establishing the self of beings who are awakening,
treatises have been composed and circulated here by those who have attained fitness of soul.
But for those whose intentions are fully awakened through the exhaustion of misdeeds,
their intellect proceeds stainlessly in the investigations of the scriptures.
The delusion of the mind dissolves through the investigation of the true scriptures,
just as the darkness of night vanishes from the sky due to the movement of the sun.
For a mind that does not diminish leads only to delusion and not to accomplishment;
like a mist, it obscures one's vision, and like a Vetāla, it leaps about.
O Sage, for all beings in this world, it is the mind alone that is the vessel for pleasure and pain, not the body composed of flesh.
This collection of flesh and bones that is seen as the physical body—know it to be a mental construction; the body is not ultimately real.
O Sage, whatever your son has done with his mind and body, he alone has quickly reaped that result; we are not at fault in this matter.
Whatever action a person performs according to their own latent impressions (vāsanā), they obtain the corresponding result; here, no other has agency.
Who indeed exists in this world who has the power to do that which is not kept in mind within by one's own mental impressions?

Whatever enjoyments there are in heaven and hell, and whatever desires for heaven and hell there are, they are the outflow of the moon of one's own mental conceptualization, which bestows the suffering of dullness.
What is the use of much speaking here by one who merely composes strings of words?
Arise, O Blessed One; let us go to where your son resides.
Having consumed everything with his mental body, Śukra has here in an instant become a practitioner of austerity (tāpasa) who is equal to the moon through its contact with its rays.
That vital breath, joined with consciousness and moving through the lunar rays, having become the essence of nectar,
exists as a person by way of its potency.
Vālmīki:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Time, as if smiling at the courses of the world,
seized Bhṛgu with his hand from [Bhṛgu’s] hand, as the sun seizes the moon.
"Ah! How truly wonderful is the established order of destiny! saying this slowly, the venerable Bhṛgu rose up like the sun from the mountain of sunrise.
Then, in that excellent forest dense with *tāla* and *tamāla* trees, those two, arising from their perfectly harmonious union,
shone like the full moon and the sun, free from clouds, rising simultaneously in a cloudless sky to traverse it.
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites;
the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the chapter titled "Consolation," the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
Then the two gods, Kāla and Bhṛgu, set out from a cave in Mount Mandara to go upon the earth to the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
As they were descending from the mountain, those two of great splendor saw sky-dwellers sleeping in bowers formed by thickets of fresh golden creepers.
The celestial maidens were playing on swings formed by circles of creepers,
their gazes— so charmingly innocent like those of a doe— calling to mind the beauty of blue lotuses.
They sat upon high fragments of rock used as seats, which were like lions;
they seemed to embody their own vigor, having effortlessly surveyed the three worlds.
He saw the leaders of the elephant herds, their trunks resting upon *tāla* trees that swayed high above them,
drowsy from the pride of rut, appearing as if they were the personified embodiments of intoxication itself.
He saw the beautiful yak-tails, their bodies red as flower filaments and their tails crimson with the wind,
flickering and moved by the auspicious rites of the monarch.
The bees, having sought refuge in the branches of *sarja* and *kharjūra* trees, were submerged by the continuous downpour of streams of falling flowers.

[He saw] monkeys, fierce in their roaming, who had conquered the *kīcaka* reeds with their mutual blows and roars, whose beautiful faces were as pale-red as mineral ores (*dhātu*), and who were formidable in their movement.
They saw the perfected ones (siddhas) in grove-palaces whose roofs were covered by canopies of creepers,
being struck with mandāra flowers by the celestial women.
The riverbanks, covered by clouds of water reddened by mineral ores,
were devoid of human contact, appearing as if they had been ordained into the Buddhist order.
The rivers, with their masses of waves laden with *kunda* and *mandāra* flowers,
have assumed the adornments of the spring season as if out of longing for the ocean.
The trees, their limbs laden with a weight of flowers and shaken by the wind,
appeared like drunkards reeling upon attaining intoxication, with bees for their rolling eyes.
Beholding the vast splendor of the king of mountains here and there,
the two of them reached the earth adorned with cities and towns.
In an instant, they both reached there the river Samaṅgā, whose waves were shimmering with flowers, appearing as if it were composed entirely of blossoms.
Then, on a certain bank of that river, Bhṛgu beheld his son,
who had undergone a transformation of body and attained another state of being.
With his senses stilled and established in meditative absorption, the deer-like mind is no longer restless; it appears as if long rested after a long period of toil, for the sake of quelling fatigue.
He was as if contemplating the endless courses of the ocean of saṃsāra— long experienced and long abandoned, and characterized by an uninterrupted alternation of joy and sorrow.
Surely it has attained immobility, like a wheel that has spun excessively,
as if from the extreme exhaustion of revolving through the cycles of the infinite world.
Standing in solitude, lovely, relying on his own singular splendor,
he was intent on tranquility and had abandoned all mental agitation and attachment.
Established in non-conceptual samādhi, he had ceased from the activity of dualities,
laughing with a cool intellect at all the worldly destinies.
Having known the entire course of events, with all curiosity vanished,
the web of conceptual construction cast aside, and the great state of liberation attained.
In that state of infinite repose, one rests within the Self,
like a white jewel that remains without grasping at reflections.
Bhṛgu beheld his son, whose mind was perfectly awakened and steadfast, entirely free from the conceptual constructions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
Beholding that son of Bhṛgu, Kāla spoke these words to Bhṛgu, sounding like the roar of the ocean: "This one here is indeed your son."
With the words "Awake!", he emerged from his meditative absorption,
just as a peacock slowly rouses itself with the roar of thunderclouds.
Opening his eyes, he beheld before him the two powerful ones, Kāla and Bhṛgu, who appeared like the two gods, the Moon and the Sun, come together in their full splendor.
Then, rising from their seats of *kadamba* creepers, those two beloved brahmins, having come together, bowed down to each other like Hari and Hara.
Having performed their mutual greetings, they sat down upon the stone slab like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, who are worshipped by the world, upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Then that twice-born man named Śāntatapas, on the bank of the Samaṅgā,
spoke these peaceful words, beautiful as a flow of nectar, to them both:
By the sight of you both today, I have attained peace,
like the world when the cool-rayed and warm-rayed suns appear together.
That delusion of my mind, which could not be destroyed by scriptures, nor by austerity, nor by knowledge, nor by learning— that very thing has been exhausted by the vision of you two.
Showers of stainless nectar do not so gladden the heart as these visions of the great ones bring such supreme joy.
"O you two of immense splendor, who are you that have sanctified this region with your feet,
as the moon and sun sanctify the sky?"
When he had spoken thus, Bhṛgu said to his son from a previous birth:
"Remember yourself; you are awakened, O scion of Raghu, you are not ignorant."
Awakened by Bhṛgu, he remembered for a mere moment his own states from previous births, his eyes opened wide through meditation.
Then, his face smiling with wonder and his mind delighted,
that best of speakers uttered words slow with reflection:
Victorious is the destiny of the Supreme Self, whose undertakings are unceasing,
by whose power this expansive wheel of the universe revolves.
Indeed, my infinite past births remain unknown; yet, when remembered, they appear both appropriate and enriched by their respective conditions.
Many diverse and exceedingly vast karmas have been experienced,
as well as infinite fruits of various states of existence, occurring even unto the end of the aeon.
I have witnessed the intense struggles for power and the delusions of acquiring wealth;
and I have long dwelt upon the peaks of Mount Meru, free from all sorrow.
On the banks of the Mandākinī, by the mountain of the immortals, there is water colored by yellow, fragrant mandāraka flowers and white water-lilies.
I have wandered through groves of living beings filled with blossoming golden creepers,
and upon Mount Meru, where the peaks are beautiful with flowers in the shade of wish-fulfilling trees.
There is nothing that has not been experienced, there is nothing that has not been done,
and there is nothing that has not been seen among the various pleasant and unpleasant sights.
That which was to be known has now been known; that which was to be seen has been seen unimpaired. I am rested, having long been weary; all my delusion has come to an end.
"Arise, dear father, let us go; let us see that body situated on Mount Mandara, which has now become completely withered like a dried-up forest creeper."
There is nothing here that is unintended for me, nor is there anything intended;
I am merely wandering about to behold the fixed arrangement [of the world].
Why do I not follow that auspicious path frequented by the noble ones, which is steadfast, with the thought that my being is solely devoted to it?
Therefore, enough with these desired and undesired things; let them be, and I shall practice this very conduct.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the one hundred and thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Successive Births of Bhārgava," Vasiṣṭha said:
Reflecting thus upon the courses of worldly existence, those knowers of reality set out from that bank of the Samaṅgā river like rays of light in motion.
Gradually ascending into the sky and emerging from the hollows of the clouds,
they reached Mount Mandara with its golden caves by way of the path of the Siddhas.
On the plateau of that mountain, the descendant of Bhṛgu beheld his own body from a previous birth, now withered but still shrouded by fresh leaves.
And he said this: "O father, this body of hers is indeed slender—that very body which was formerly cherished by you with pleasant enjoyments."
This is that body of mine, for which cool beds were fashioned from heaps of mandāra flowers upon the grounds of Mount Meru’s groves.
Behold this very body of mine, once caressed by hosts of celestial women, now lying upon the surface of the earth, crushed by the mouths of crawling reptiles.
This very body of mine, by which I long sported in the groves of the Nandana garden,
has now become a withered skeleton.
Deprived of the mental state that delights in the lofty theater of passion through contact with the bodies of celestial nymphs, my body here withers away.
Having bound those very mental impressions to each of those various amorous sports and each of those various states, how is it that you remain at ease, O little body?
Alas, where have you been shattered? You have come to the withering of an ascetic; you have reached the state of a skeleton, yet you, O unfortunate one, still think of me!
I am now afraid of that very same body by which I was once delighted in its playful charms, for it has now become a mere skeleton.
Behold, where that necklace formerly appeared like a web of stars upon my chest, ants are now nesting there.
Behold: by that very body of mine which once captivated excellent women with its luster like molten gold, I am now dragged along by a garland of skeletons.
Behold these wild animals in the forest being terrified by my skull-frame with its gaping mouth, which, like that of an ascetic, is covered with dried-out skins.
Behold how the cave of my corpse’s belly, through its extreme dryness,
shines with the web of the sun’s rays as if with discernment.
With her body intoxicated yet now utterly parched, she lies supine upon the forest floor;
by the insignificance of her own self, she seems to lead even those dwelling in the sky toward dispassion.
On this mountain, my body is being emaciated by means of non-conceptual meditative absorption alone, which is liberated from attachment to sound, form, taste, touch, and smell.
When the vampire of the mind has been completely stilled, the state of bliss that the body attains is one that cannot be reached even by sovereignty over the entire world.
Behold: with all worldly exertion stilled, with every curiosity gone, and with the web of conceptual constructions cast aside, the body rests in bliss.
The tree of the body, agitated by the frantic agitation of the monkey-mind,
shakes with such force that it cuts away its very roots.
Free from the miseries of the mind, this body of mine— abiding like supreme bliss— no longer perceives the delusions of elephants, clouds, or lions upon the mountain.
I see no other source of welfare for living beings than mindlessness (acittatva), which is like the arrival of autumn to the mist of delusion caused by the fever of all desires.
Those of great intelligence and tranquil mind, who have reached a state of detachment, have indeed arrived at the very limit of the enjoyment of happiness.
"By good fortune, I behold this body of mine in the forest— freed from all states of suffering, perfectly tranquil, free from fever, and devoid of mental constructions."
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, it is said that at that time many bodies were consumed again and again by the descendant of Bhṛgu.
O Sage, since this body was produced by Bhṛgu, what great excellence has arisen in it, or is it merely a cause for lamentation?
Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, that very ideation of Śukra which had reached the state of a living being was born as the active principle of karma, taking the form of Bhārgava from Bhṛgu.
For that [vital breath], having first emerged from the supreme state and reached the state of elemental space (bhūtākāśa), becomes agitated by the movement of the wind.
Entering the heart of Bhṛgu by means of the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
they gradually attained virility and became endowed with the body of Uśanas.
Having received the sacred rites of initiation according to the Vedic tradition, she then went before her father;
and after a long time, she attained the state of a withered skeleton.
When that body of Brahmā first arrived,
Śukra then uttered that lamentation directed toward it.
Though free from passion and devoid of desire, Śukra, possessing a body of equal proportions, lamented for his own form; for such is the nature of that which is born of the physical body.
However, under the guise of grief, that wise one demonstrated for the sake of attaining detachment that very distinction between the body and the embodied soul.
For both the wise and the ignorant person, this is the rule for as long as life lasts:
that worldly conduct should always be carried out according to one's capacity or lack thereof, just like the common people.
Those who have fully understood the course of existence and those who are ignorant, following the nature of beasts, remain within worldly conventions like a forest thicket.
Just as the worldly practitioner is ignorant, so indeed is the wise man;
here, the difference lies merely in their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is the cause of bondage and liberation.
For as long as there is a body, so long is there suffering in suffering and pleasure in pleasure;
yet the wise, whose minds are unattached, demonstrate this as if they were unawakened.
Great-souled beings are always happy amidst pleasures and sorrowful amidst painful conditions; indeed, they are seen to be truly cool within.
The reflections of a pillar tremble, but its steady form does not;
likewise, for the wise man, it is only the organs of action that tremble, but his steady mind does not.
Through its state of being both moving and unmoving, the knower of that abides amidst worldly activities,
like the sun remaining below while appearing clearly in reflections.
One whose intellect is unawakened is indeed bound even if he has abandoned worldly actions; one whose intellect is awakened is indeed liberated even if he still indulges in the play of delusion.
For one whose faculty of intellect is liberated is liberated even if the faculty of action is bound;
likewise, one whose faculty of intellect is bound is bound even if the faculty of action is liberated.

In this world, the intellect and the senses alone are the cause for the perception of pleasure and pain, as well as for the perception of bondage and liberation, just as lights are the cause for illumination.
Outwardly, observe the conduct appropriate for the world, but inwardly, remain devoid of such conduct; remain as if you were non-existent, with all desires completely stilled.
Free from all desires, abiding in the Self by means of the Self, perform the actions that must be done; indeed, let your state be centered in the mind alone.
Do not fall into this pit on the path of saṃsāra, which is a great whirlpool of mental and physical ailments, and which yields only misery— an abyss of fierce "mine-ness."
You do not exist in things, nor do things exist in you, O lotus-eyed one;
you are of the nature of pure awakening—remain firm, established in the Self.

O Great-Souled One, if you have attained the stainless state free from longing, wherein the great darkness of the notion of "mine" has vanished, and thus prevail over the mind, then homage to you, the one of supreme wisdom and being!
The one hundred and thirty-eighth canto. Vasiṣṭha:
Then, having refuted those words of Bhrigu’s son, [Bhṛgu spoke].
The Blessed One Kāla spoke these words in a deep resonance.
Kāla said:
"O Bhārgava, having cast off this body of a female ascetic,
enter this body, O virtuous one, just as a king enters his city."
O sinless one, having performed penance with this body in a former birth, you must once again assume the leadership of the lords of the Asuras.
When the end of the great aeon has arrived, you must cast off this body of Bhārgava, like a withered flower, so that it is not taken up again.
Having attained the state of liberation while living, remain, O high-minded one, performing the role of preceptor to the great lords of the asuras with this body of your former form.
May it be well with you both; we shall go toward our desired direction.
There is not even the slightest thing that would not be desired by the mind.
Having spoken thus, as they were releasing the flower, he vanished from between them like the radiant sun with its rays from heaven and earth.
When the Blessed One had departed after speaking those words regarding what was destined to be,
Bhārgava reflected upon the unbreakable and fixed course of destiny.
Mādhava entered that youthful body— which was withered by the cause of Time yet destined for the future emergence of flowers and fruit— just as a bee enters a beautiful creeper.
That Brahmin’s body, with its face and limbs turned pale,
fell trembling quickly upon the ground like a creeper severed at its root.
When that body had been entered by a living soul, the great sage performed a nourishing rite with mantras and the water from his water-pot.
Then all the slender channels of that [body] shone,
filled as if they were rivers whose hollows are brimming with floods of water during the rainy season.
Like a lotus pond in the rainy season or a new creeper in spring, when she was full, her vital breaths blossomed like sprouts.
Then Śukra rose up, his vital breaths flowing forth,
like a cloud filled full through the union of moisture and wind.
He of pure appearance saluted his father from the front,
just as a first-risen cloud greets a mountain with its thundering.
Then his father embraced his body,
moist with affection, just as a cloud after a long time embraces the slope of a mountain.
Bhṛgu beheld his own former body with affection;
the conviction that "this one was born from me" carries away even a person of great intelligence.
At that time, the affection [born from the thought] "this is my son" even overcame Bhṛgu;
for this sense of "otherness" and "selfhood" persists as long as the physical form exists.
Then the father and son became mutually radiant,
like the sun and a lotus-pond at the break of dawn.
Like a pair of cakravāka birds joined after a long separation, or like a peacock and a cloud whose deep affection intensifies with the arrival of the rainy season.
Having stayed there for a moment with that conversation, which was suited to their long-standing and firm longing, those two great-minded ones then rose.
There they reduced that body of the twice-born Samaṅga to ashes;
for who indeed, born into this world, does not follow established custom?
Thus, in that sacred forest, those two— Bhṛgu and Bhārgava—
remained, blazing with ascetic power like the moon and the sun in the sky.
The two masters of the world, who have realized what is to be known and are liberated while living,
possess a penance that is easily accessible and firmly established amidst the floods of place, time, and circumstances.
Then, in the course of time, Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the Asuras,
while Bhṛgu likewise remained in his own appropriate and healthy position.
This Śukra was first born from this supreme state in due order;
thereafter, through his own swift wandering from the path of mindfulness, he became thus utterly agitated amidst various conditions.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the chapter titled "The Resuscitation of Śukra," the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter;
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, why is it that the inspired flash of insight belonging to the son of Bhṛgu arose together with its fruition for him alone, and not so for another?
Vasiṣṭha: At that time, this pure intellect of Bhārgava arose for the first time from the foot of Brahmā, unstained by any other birth.
That state of the mind which is pure upon the complete subsiding of all desires is called *sattva*; it is described as this very stainless consciousness (*cit*).
Whatever the mind— which is the essence of stainless beings— contemplates,
that very thing quickly comes to be, just like the swirling eddies of water in the ocean.
Just as this delusion arose spontaneously for the son of Bhṛgu,
so too is the son of Bhṛgu himself the illustrative example here for each individual case.
Just as a seed brings about its own wonder in the form of sprouts, leaves, and so forth,
even so does the thicket of delusion arise for all the multitudes of living beings.
This entire universe that is seen is exactly like that; for each individual thing arises falsely and likewise sets falsely.
Nothing in the world ever sets nor does it rise for anyone;
this is mere delusion, a magical illusion expanding in vain.
Just as this grove of saṃsāra exists within our own appearance,
so indeed do thousands of such worlds exist for them, mutually unseen by one another.
Just as the activities within a dream and an imagined city are not seen as distinct from one another, so too are these delusions of saṃsāra.
In this way, there exist multitudes of cities whose forms consist of mental constructs within the sky;
yet they are not seen by one another except through the vision of knowledge.
For there truly exist piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas of such a form;
their bodies consist of mere volition and are composed of pleasure and pain.
In this very way, O delight of the Raghus, we and these others are perfected,
having the nature of our own mental constructs, conditioned by the state of false reality.
For the cycle of creation and transmigration exists for others in exactly this manner;
yet in reality, it is not real, as it is established upon that which is non-substantial.
In this very way, the entire universe has arisen individually and is indeed in vain,
just as the essence of spring appears in the form of various flower-bushes.
This first [state], one's own volition, has thus come to great expansion,
such that it is conceptualized in this way through a firm and ultimate transcendence.
Each individual consciousness that arises, abiding within the womb of its own inherent nature,
perishes as it perceives this world as being thus commenced.
By the power of appearance there is existence, and by the observation of the actual thing there is non-existence;
the web of the world is a long dream, the tethering post for the elephant of the mind.
For the existence of the world is indeed the existence of the mind, and the existence of the mind is the existence of the world;
in the absence of one, both perish, and that occurs through the investigation of reality.
For the manifestation of a pure mind is indeed true;
for the dyeing with saffron adheres only to a stainless cloth.
The quality of one who is not brought low by another necessarily increases;
in one who is not assailed by discursive thoughts, the intuitive flash of insight arises in the mind.
Just as gold does not remain [pure] when it is in a soiled garment,
so too a single vision does not remain stable when the mind is withered.
Just as a gem is purified by polishing and copper by the application of a chemical agent,
so too does the purification of the mind arise from long-term, firm, and continuous practice.
Rāma:
