Since this world consists of mere appearances, how could these sequences of time and action,
along with their rising and setting, arise for the mind of Śukra?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as this world was seen by Śuka through his father and mother,
so did it remain established in his mind, like a peacock within a peacock's egg.
That which has been tasted from the treasury of intrinsic nature has arisen through this sequence,
just as a sprout, leaf, and so forth, a creeper, flower, and fruit arise from a seed.
The living being perceives within itself exactly that which is the essence of its own latent impressions;
in this regard, a dream is the illustration, while this world is a long-lasting dream.
O Rāma, surely this thicket of saṃsāra has arisen individually;
it is clearly manifest within one's own self, like the dream-network of soldiers at night.
Rāma:
This flood of worldly existence merges together of its own accord;
or if it does not, you ought to tell me that correctly.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"For a mind that is impure and lacking in vigor does not deserve union with another; it is like iron to unheated iron.
But when both are pure and heated, one merges into the other."
The pure principles of consciousness merge with one another;
for just as waters that are not turbid attain unity, they become of one form.
For the purity of the mind is a single state consisting of the absence of latent impressions and the non-perception of unreal objects;
having awakened from that state of deep sleep or the self-abiding stage, it attains union with the Supreme through the yoga of those subtle elements alone.
The one hundred and fortieth canto, titled "The Convergence of the Kingdom of Dreams," by Vasiṣṭha:
In all the groves of cyclic existence, for that which consists of the nature of the seed-form and its parts,
there is no difference in the manifestation of that which appears as the mere subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
Whether it be engagement or withdrawal, for every class of living beings, it occurs immediately after the state of deep sleep, preceded by the attainment of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
Those living beings who partake in active manifestation have reached the state of the subtle elements; through their oneness with those subtle elements, they perceive mutually imagined creations.
Through the single channel of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the variegated reservoirs of creation merge with one another and attain density on all sides.
Some have reached a separate existence and have likewise gone to a separate dissolution; some have been joined together with one another and established as world-systems.
Wherein thousands of world-systems, numbering beyond count, exist within every single atom without touching one another— that is the forest named Brahman.
Having attained density, it does not merge with anything else;
whatever has grown in whatever place and in whatever manner, that alone it perceives, and nothing other.
Due to the power of present-day mental constructions, the successions of living beings are mutually conjoined; such is the established conceptualization of the worlds.
The existence of the body has become deeply rooted, while the absence of the body is forgotten;
because of this deep-seated identification with the body, the sky of consciousness has forgotten its true self.
Just as the pure vital breath, through the piercing of another's vital breath,
perceives the kingdom of the mind of the one to be pierced, so too does the [mind] residing in a human perceive the worlds of creation.
For all multitudes of living beings, the Self rests in three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; in this regard, the body is not the cause.

Thus, within the Self—which consists of three other states—the state of being a living soul shines forth; and within that, corporeality shines forth, just as the state of being a wave appears within heated water.
Having reached the state of the power of consciousness (citkalā) and remaining in the state at the end of deep sleep,
the awakened individual soul (jīva) returns [to its source], while the deluded one proceeds toward creation.
For when there is purity of intrinsic nature, then loving-kindness proceeds;
it consists in the very oneness of the two, demonstrating one's own benevolence.
An ignorant individual soul (jīva) awakens from deep sleep and partakes in its own creation; yet, because consciousness is all-pervading, another [soul] may be led by the creation of another.
In each creation, there exist other creations with distinct forms;
within those as well, there are floods of further creations, like the layers of a plantain leaf-stalk.
In every creation, it possesses a thick, leaf-like expansion that fills the intervals between creations;
it is naturally cool, a pavilion made of the leaves of the plantain-tree of Brahman.
Just as there is no difference among even the hundreds of leaves of a plantain tree,
so too there is no difference within the reality of Brahman, even across hundreds of creations.
Just as a fruit arises from a seed and, through its juice, becomes a seed once again,
so too Brahman, having become the mind, becomes Brahman again through awakening.
The seed, having sap as its cause, unfolds into the state of fruit;
the individual soul, having Brahman as its cause, unfolds into the form of the world.
It is not appropriate to say what the cause of taste might be;
furthermore, because it is devoid of specific distinctions, it is not appropriate to speak of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Furthermore, it is impossible to assert non-existence anywhere in that which consists of all things;
nor can there be a cause or the like in that which is not a cause, or in the ultimate primal cause.
Just as a seed is seen to become its own fruit without abandoning its own form,
so too Brahman, without abandoning its own form, abides as both the fruit and the seed.
Everything possesses the form of a seed, whereas that state is formless; therefore, it is not possible to equate them. Consequently, there is no analogy for Śiva.
Space itself is born from the nature of space, yet it is not born as something perceived as other than that;
therefore, know, O Brahmin, that this world is neither unborn nor born, like the sky.
While perceiving the visible world, one does not perceive one's own self as the seer;
for whom, whose consciousness is overcome by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), does one's innate state arise?
When the delusion of water in a mirage exists, what cleverness is there? But when cleverness exists, what is this mirage?
The seer, as clear as space and all-pervading, does not see itself, even though it has become the act of seeing—like one's own eye; oh, what a delusion!
Brahman, which is as pure as space, is not attained even with effort;
if that which is visible is perceived as a visible object, its attainment is very far off indeed.
Where even something as gross as you cannot be seen without careful attention,
there the perceptibility of a subtle object for a perceiver is as if cast far away.
The seer remains only the seer and does not touch the state of being seen;
and while the object of sight is seen by him, O Rāma, the seer is not seen.
Only the seer exists as one; for here, the seen does not exist at all.
If the seer, who is the self of all, remains as the seen, then what is there that can be called "the seen"?
Whatever is accomplished by a king who possesses all powers, in whatever manner it is done, that very thing quickly comes to be exactly so; he himself arises in that very form.
Just as a grove of mango trees becomes radiant,
yet without ever ceasing its state of being flavorful, it remains exalted with fruits, flowers, and leaves.
Thus the radiance of consciousness, having become the individual soul (jīva), becomes the embodied being;
yet, without ever abandoning that state of pure consciousness, it consists of the vision of the Seer.
Just as the sap of the earth arises from its own self through thousands of diverse and peerless streams, so does consciousness arise through the delusions of "I-ness."
Of these trees of the radiance of consciousness, shining by themselves within the Self,
no end is perceived here, for they are rich with hundreds of branches of the visible world.
Just as a eunuch experiences the aesthetic wonder of flavors individually within himself, so too does this consciousness perceive the various states of worldly existence separately.

In whatever manner and by whatever means the life-force (jīva-śakti) generates its own cycle of manifestation, in that very same way, consciousness (cit), abiding within it, undergoes the existence of the elements and the worlds.
Certain streams of living beings meet one another;
having wandered through saṃsāra by themselves, they eventually come to rest after a long time.
In this same way, you perceive yourself with a subtle and supreme vision,
as well as thousands of world-nets even within the interior of a single atom.
The targets of worldly existence are present in a wall, in space, in stone, in flame, in wind, and in water; they exist in everything, like oil in sesame seeds.
When the mind attains purity, then the individual soul becomes consciousness;
and since that [consciousness] is pure and all-pervading, there is a mutual merging between them.
The long, great dream of the world, which fulfills the delusion of self-existence for all beings such as Padmajā and others, has itself arisen from within.
Certain successions of beings pass from one dream to another;
therefore, their perception of walls and such things remains most firm.
Whatever one intensely contemplates upon anything, that very thing quickly comes to be there;
even that which is seen by her in a dream is indeed real at that time.
Within the atom of consciousness exist all atoms of experience,
just as within a seed exist the atoms of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits.
The supreme atom of consciousness contains the entire universe within itself;
it holds the latent space within space—abandon the delusion of duality and unity.
The consciousness experiences the atoms within itself through its own constituent atoms— known as space, time, action, and so forth— since no other atom can exist [within it].
Itself manifesting as everything, this pure mass of atoms of consciousness is experienced through the perception of bodies, from Brahmā down to the smallest insect.
In reality, there is nothing at all here that has been manifested;
rather, the atoms of consciousness themselves experience duality as their own self-nature.
The cluster of atomic consciousnesses, possessing expansive bodies, shines forth by itself, emitting the fragrance of awareness through the flower-like gates of the eyes and other senses.
Someone perceives others as being composed of pure consciousness in their external form,
because consciousness— the seed of all that is visible— is omnipresent and indestructible.
Someone perceives the entire, undivided world within themselves;
therein, due to excessive mental construction, they rise up and sink down.
There, seeing one dream after another again and again,
he rolls about in false pits like a stone fallen from a mountain peak.
Some are closed in on themselves, while others remain in delusion within their own selves;
these multitudes of embodied beings are immersed in the nectar of their own consciousness, throbbing with life.
Those few who perceive within themselves the agitation of the world and its living beings—
by them that [world] is seen as such, based upon it as if it were an unreal dream.
Because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the self of all, that which is visible is real within the Self;
for wherever the All-pervading One is present, there indeed everything arises.
Within the manifestation of creation that exists inside the living being (jīva), a multitude of living beings arises once more; and within that, yet another [multitude] arises.
A living being is born from within a living being, and yet another living being is born within that one;
everywhere, like the core of a plantain leaf, the seed of life continues to live.

This infinite [reality], which is the transformation of the perception of the visible, is uniform; like the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments in gold, it perishes through mere thorough understanding.
For one in whom the inquiry "Who am I? and "What is this? does not arise, there persists this long delusion of the fever of existence, unreleased from its beginning and its end.
The discernment of that person of right understanding should be known as having borne fruit,
for whom the greed for enjoyments diminishes day by day.
Just as medicine administered to the body brings about health,
so too does discernment applied to the conquest of the senses bear fruit.
Discernment exists only in words, brilliant like a fire in a painting; by one who possesses such [verbal] discernment, that very state of being discerning leads only to suffering.
Just as the wind comes to existence through touch and not by means of speech,
so too is its discernment understood through the very attenuation of desire.
Know that the nectar in a painting is not truly nectar, and know that fire in a painting is not truly fire;
a woman in a painting is surely not a woman without a body, and verbal discernment is indeed no discernment at all.
First, through discernment, passion and enmity become attenuated and then are uprooted;
thereafter, they are utterly extinguished where such purification occurs—therein lies true discernment.
In the Bhārgava-episode, the chapter titled "The Incarnation as Jīvaṣaṇḍaka" is concluded.
The Fourth Section: Origination. Section Five: Persistence.
The First Chapter:
Vasiṣṭha says:
Now, immediately following the section on origination, hear this.
O Rāma, you have understood the section on stability, which brings about liberation.
The seed of the living soul is the Supreme Brahman, stable everywhere like space;
by that [Brahman], the living soul exists in manifold ways even within the world that is the belly of the living soul.

Because they consist of the single, solid mass of consciousness, the various classes of living beings exist within the individual soul like the layers of a plantain tree, or like insects in the belly of a man.
O Rāma, just as in the summer heat a worm may arise from bodily excrement and sweat,
so too, by virtue of its consciousness, the void itself spontaneously becomes a living being, each according to its name.
In whatever manner those Jīvakas strive for the realization of their own self,
in that very way they quickly become [perfected] through various methods of worship.
For those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; those who sacrifice to the Yakṣas go to the Yakṣas;
those who sacrifice to Brahman go to Brahman. One should therefore take refuge in that which is not vain.
For that Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, because of the purity of his own consciousness,
was quickly bound by nature by the object of perception seen for the first time.
When consciousness first reaches a newborn child who is of noble birth and unwithered, it assumes that very form; no other [form] whatsoever exists.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, you should explain the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming.
How is it that the waking state is waking, and how does the dream state become non-waking?
Vasiṣṭha said:
That which is endowed with stable cognition is called waking;
that which consists of unstable cognition is declared to be dreaming.
If that which is seen in a moment were waking, and the dream were to persist for a different duration of time,
then that waking would become a dream, and the dream would attain the state of waking.
The distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not exist without stability and instability;
for the experience of both is always and everywhere equal.
That which attains stability is called the waking state;
hear now how the dream state, characterized by momentary destruction, comes to be.
The life-element exists within the body by which one lives;
it is called "heat," "vitality," and "life-element"—know that, my dear, as such.
When the body, through mind, action, and speech, becomes engaged in worldly activity,
then that perfected vital element (jīvadhātu) flows forth.
As that [subtle body] spreads through the limbs, consciousness indeed arises from contact;
due to its fullness, it is called "mind" (citta), wherein the delusion of the world is internally dissolved.
Crawling through the apertures such as the eyes and so forth, it perceives within itself a form composed of external elements, rich with various shapes and transformations.
Because of its stability, that state is likewise understood as "waking"; this is called the sequence of waking. Now, hear the sequence beginning with deep sleep.
When one's body is not agitated by mind, action, or speech,
then this element of life remains tranquil and pure.
When the winds have become equalized, the heart within is no longer agitated,
just as a lamp in a windless chamber produces only light.
Consequently, consciousness does not move into the limbs, and for that reason it is not agitated;
it does not enter the eyes and other senses, nor does it go outside through the apertures.
The living soul vibrates within itself, just as the consciousness of oil is in the sesame seed,
the consciousness of coldness is in the frost, and the consciousness of fluidity is in clarified butter.
The individual soul, remaining for some portion of time within itself in a state of tranquility,
attains the state of deep sleep, which is serene and devoid of conscious thought.
Having known this, when the mind has ceased, one who remains tranquil even while engaged in worldly activity—
awake through the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— is said to possess the fourth state (turya).
When that vital element (jīvadhātu), having attained a state of softness from deep sleep, is set in motion by the vital breaths (prāṇas),
it then arises as consciousness (saṃvit) in the form of the mind (citta).
The web of the world, residing within one's own mind, quickly perceives itself within that very mind as an expansion through successive revolutions of its parts, like a tree from its seed.
When the element of life is slightly agitated by the vital winds, it then moves like the sky; one perceives within oneself a movement in the void.
When it is flooded by water, then it experiences within itself the agitation of the water and so forth,
just as a flower experiences its own fragrance.
When it is overcome by bile and the like, then it experiences within itself a vast delusion of the heat of fire and so forth, as if it were entirely external.
When one perceives external places and times as red in color and filled with blood, because that perception is of the nature of direct experience, one sinks right there [into that state].
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) it cultivates, that it perceives within while asleep,
just as [the mind] is agitated by winds through the apertures and perceived externally through the senses such as the eyes.
When one whose sensory vulnerabilities have not been assailed remains undisturbed within,
and experiences consciousness immediately, that is called a dream.
When one whose sensory apertures have been invaded becomes agitated by external perception and perceives [objects], the most wise call that "waking. (MU 4.1.33)
Thus, by you who have now understood this, O one of renowned great intelligence, let there be a firm abiding in truth within;
for in a world that is non-existent, one should not cultivate the contemplation of death, loss, and the defects of saṃsāra.
The Second Chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Nature of Waking, Dreaming, Deep Sleep, and the Fourth State," by Vasiṣṭha.
All this has been told to you by me, O Rāghava, for the purpose of defining the form of the mind, and not for any other reason whatsoever.
Whatever the mind, with firm resolve, contemplates repeatedly,
it becomes that very thing, just as a lump of iron attains the state of fire through contact with flame.
The views of grasping at existence and non-existence, or of rejecting them, are imagined by the mind;
they are neither unreal nor real, being merely the cause of the mind's restlessness.
For the mind is indeed the cause and the agent, and the instrument for the existence of the world;
it is the defiled mind that expands this [world] in its manifold forms.
For the mind, O Rāma, is the person; it must be directed onto the auspicious path, since all prosperities in the world are accomplished solely through its conquest.
If the body were indeed the body, how could the high-minded Śukra have undergone various forms of division arising from many different bodies?
Therefore, the mind is indeed the person and the mind is indeed the body;
whatever this [body] consists of, that it undoubtedly attains.
That which is non-empty, effortless, free from attributes, and beyond delusion—
strive with effort to contemplate that, and you shall attain its true nature.
The body falls toward the stability of the mind, but the mind does not go toward the physical form.
Therefore, O fortunate one, let your mind fall here upon the truth; let it abandon that which is otherwise unreal.
The third canto, titled "The Description of Manu’s Form," [ends with] Rāma:
O Blessed One, Knower of all Dharmas, this great doubt of mine,
restless like a wave upon the ocean, churns within my heart.
In that which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, all-pervading, eternal, and free from affliction—
whence has this withered consciousness called "mind" arisen?
Since there is no other name, no being that has been, and none that will be—
whence, of what kind, and how could its stain exist, and where?
Vasiṣṭha: Well said, Rāma! Your mind has become a partaker of liberation; it is the outpouring of the highest [wisdom], like a blossom on the Nandana tree.
This mind of yours, intent upon investigating what precedes and what follows,
will attain that exalted state which was reached by Śaṅkara and the others.
But for this question, O Rāma, the time is not yet right for you;
this question is addressed only when the final conclusion is being stated.

At the time of establishing the final conclusion (siddhānta), you should ask me about this point; by that means, the final conclusion will become as clear to you as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of your hand.
This question of yours shines forth at the time of the final conclusion;
for the cry of the peacock is appropriate only in the rainy season, while the song of the swan is fitting in autumn.
The innate blue hue shines in the sky at the end of the rainy season,
whereas during the rains it arises from thick, towering masses of clouds.
This supreme determination of the mind, which is the subject at hand and has been commenced, is that by virtue of which the birth of living beings occurs; listen to it, O you of noble vows.
Thus, O Rāma, it has been determined by all seekers of liberation that this very nature (prakṛti), characterized by the mental activity of thinking, is what constitutes action (karman).
Listen to how that [reality] has come to possess various names through the distinction of characteristics,
as eloquent speakers have proclaimed it with diverse philosophical perspectives.
Whatever state the mind, restless in its thinking, takes hold of,
it enters that very state, just as the wind, situated in the midst of a dense fragrance, becomes permeated by it.
Then, having determined that very [object] and conceptualizing it as such,
one colors one's own sense of ego with that same coloring.
Based on that certainty, one attains aesthetic flavor (rasa) in that very [object];
then, through identification with it, one experiences it in the body and subsequently even in the faculties of cognition.
For that which consists of the mind, O Rāma, the body follows accordingly through its power;
it attains the nature of that [mind], just as the wind within a flower attains the nature of fragrance.
When the sense organs are active, the group of action organs then vibrates spontaneously, like particles of dust on the earth tossed by the wind.
When the group of organs of action is agitated, it fully manifests its own power;
thus, extensive action is produced, like a mass of dust from the wind.
For thus the activity of the mind is known as the seed of action;
the existence of these two is non-different, just like that of a flower and its fragrance.
Whatever state the mind assumes through the power of firm habituation,
its vibration— known as action— manifests accordingly, and it thereby relinquishes its branches.
Likewise, he zealously performs an action that yields its fruit;
then, having quickly experienced the very taste of that [fruit], he is bound.
Whatever state he assumes, he perceives that very thing as the reality;
the conviction arises in him that "this alone is the highest good, and there is nothing else."
For they always strive for the sake of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation,
with minds of firm resolve through their very own practice.
But the followers of Kapila, having fully embraced their own position with their minds and having reached a conclusion, have fashioned scriptural perspectives [of their own].

But regarding liberation, they maintain that there is no other way to attain it; thus, with their minds conditioned in this way, they remain fixed in the delusions of their own restrictive rules while elaborating upon their own views.

The proponents of Vedānta, through their intellect, having ascertained by means of reasoning endowed with tranquility and self-control, and having conceptualized it, [declare]: "This is Brahman. (MU 4.3.26)
But for those whose minds are convinced that liberation cannot be attained otherwise,
they remain fixed in their own dogmatic delusions while elaborating upon their own views.
The proponents of consciousness (Vijñānavādins), by means of their intellect which flashes forth in the form of its own delusion,
reveal their own view through their very own arbitrary errors regarding restrictive rules.
By the Arhats and others, as well as by various other [teachers], diverse systems of scripture have been fashioned according to their own preferred inclinations and through their varied conduct.
Indeed, various literary styles arise through their own mature certainties, like a multitude of gentle water bubbles rising from a signless source.
O mighty-armed one, the mind alone is the single source of all these modes, just as the ocean is the source of jewels.
The neem and the sugarcane are neither bitter nor sweet; the moon and fire are neither cold nor hot.
Whatever is practiced by the mind is perceived exactly as it has been so cultivated.
One should indeed strive for that unconditioned bliss;
the mind must be led to consist of that, and by that means it is attained.
The mind that completely abandons the trivial objects of perception residing within the child of saṃsāra is not helplessly dragged away by the pleasure and pain born from them.
O sinless one, do not contemplate the visible world— which is impure, unreal in nature, delusive, a cause of fear, expansive, and a manifestation— as bondage.
This is indeed illusion, this is ignorance, this is a mental construction that brings fear;
the wise know that which consists of being absorbed in consciousness to be karma.
Know that the mind’s one-pointed concentration on the seer and the seen is delusive;
it is false and leads only to error, like the work of a mole digging in the earth.
This experience of identity with the visible world, which is the very nature [of the ignorant], is called "ignorance" (avidyā) by the wise; it is the intoxicant of saṃsāra.
Afflicted by this, the world does not attain what is auspicious,
just as one whose eyes are blinded by a cataract cannot perceive the brilliant light of the sun.
And that [mind] arises by itself from volition, like a tree in the sky;
by the mere absence of volition, it perishes by itself.
O Mahāmati, when meditation has been exhausted through mere non-conceptualization by means of one's own clarity and playful discernment, [the state of liberation is attained].
When stability has been attained regarding all objects as being non-attached, when the vision of truth has become clear, and when the unreal has come to an end; MU 4.3.42.
That Self, whose nature is non-conceptual and transparent consciousness, is fully attained;
it is that which has neither non-existence nor existence, neither pleasure nor suffering.
The state of absolute oneness alone is perceived within him,
not by means of unworthy contemplation, nor by the mind, the senses, or the intellect.
He who is abandoned by infinite latent impressions (vāsanās), though they are non-different from his own self, is like the sky freed from rows of clouds.
Just as the state of being a snake is imagined in a rope that is subject to doubt, even so,
bondage is imagined by the unbound Self through the nature of the space of consciousness.
An imagined object, through another successive imagination,
assumes a different state, just as the sky appears different by day and by night.
Whatever is not void, effortless, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of delusion— that very thing, when conceived as such, conduces solely to happiness.
Just as there is fear that a lion is inside an empty granary,
so too is there the fear that one is bound within this empty body.
Just as a lion is not found when one looks inside an empty granary,
so too, when examined, that which is fit to be bound by saṃsāra is not found.
"This world" and "this I"— this delusion has arisen among the ignorant,
like a phantom shadow during the dark of night.
Through the power of conceptual construction, for a living being, existents and non-existents, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
repeatedly pass from non-existence to existence and back again in an instant.
Like a mother, having assumed the state of a housewife and hanging from his neck,
she performs the duties of a wife, bestowing the bliss of sexual union.
Like a beloved embraced with maternal affection and held around the neck,
she utterly causes one to forget the state of intoxication caused by love.
And having observed the multitude of objects which yield results according to one's disposition,
the wise do not proclaim a single form for these objects here.
Through firm cultivation, whatever the mind intensely contemplates in such a way,
it perceives that very result, appearing in that form, for that duration of time.
There is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not false;
whatever is determined by someone in a certain way, it appears as such to them in that very way.
The mind, having cultivated the elephant of space,
pursues the female elephant of the forest of space who stands within that space, perceiving it as the elephant of the sky.
Therefore, O Rāghava, abandon volition itself, which consists of the nature of all things; being well-established, abide in the Self by means of the Self alone.
For a gem is indeed incapable of performing the act of negating reflections due to its insentient nature, O Rāma, but such is not the case for one like you.
O Rāma, whatever reflects here in the jewel of your mind,
having determined that it is not a real entity, do not allow yourself to be colored by it.
Or, considering that very [Self] to be the Truth and non-different from the Supreme Self,
contemplate the Self, which is without beginning or end, by means of the self.
O Rāghava, may those objects that reflect in your mind not color you— yourself being attached to something else— just as a crystal [is colored by the objects reflected in it].
Just as various new dyes enter a stainless crystal clearly and openly,
so indeed let the desires for the worlds enter you here clearly and openly, O Dispassionate One.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Doctrine of Consciousness," by Vasiṣṭha.

For a person who has performed inquiry, whose mind’s fluctuations have dissolved, who abandons discursive thought through the knowledge of the Self, and who has partially realized the Self; // MU 4.4.1 //
For one who has abandoned the visible as something to be discarded, who has attained that which is to be accepted,
who perceives the Seer, and who no longer perceives the visible as a seer— // MU 4.4.2 //
While remaining awake within the supreme reality,
yet living as if asleep upon the path of worldly existence, which consists of dense delusion.
Because of the ultimate and absolute lack of flavor even in flavors, he is devoid of taste even for enjoyments that are delightful when indulged; being without desire, he is without any longing.
When the dullness of the mind has fully worn away and attachment has dissolved, the self attains oneness with the waters,
just as a mass of snow melts in the heat of the sun.
And as their inner waves subside, like rivers whose turbulent currents of longing have calmed at the end of the rainy season; MU_4,4.6.
When the net of worldly tendencies has been torn asunder— like a bird’s web by a mouse—
with its knots loosened and rendered weak, and with the force of its bitterness spent;
Just as water becomes clear upon coming into contact with the kataka fruit,
so too does intrinsic nature become completely purified through the power of higher knowledge.
Free from passion, free from attachment, free from duality, and free from dependence,
the mind emerges from delusion like a bird from a cage.
With its wickedness and doubts stilled, and with its restless wandering and delusions gone,
the mind, its inner space completely full, shines like the full moon.
Having produced supreme beauty, and with its high and low points cast far away,
it rises everywhere as evenness, like a calm sea when the wind has subsided.
Consisting of darkness, deluded, and with its interior shattered by dullness,
it attains attenuation like the night at dawn, as if it were the latent impression of worldly existence.
The lotus-pond of wisdom, with its shoots of merit, having seen the sun of consciousness,
blossoms with stainless radiance like the sky at dawn in embodied form.
Wisdoms that captivate the heart and are capable of gladdening the world proceed from the glory of sentient beings like the rays of the full moon.

What need is there for much speaking here? The one of great intelligence, who has known that which is to be known, neither rises nor sets, being like the expanse of the sky which is not composed of elements.
For one whose own nature has been fully understood through inquiry and whose self has arisen,
even these— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara— become objects of compassion.
Even though its form is manifest, conceptual constructions do not reach that one whose inner mind is free from egoism, just as deer cannot reach the water of a mirage.
Like waves, these worlds come and go on all sides; do not embrace birth and death, which arise from the self, as if they were real for the wise man.
Manifestation and disappearance constitute transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), and no other sequence; one who rejoices in the equal vision of these two does not suffer.
Just as the space within a jar is neither born nor dies when the jar is decorated or defiled,
so it is with the self-possessed one here in this body, whether it is adorned or corrupted.
When the cool light of discernment has arisen, the latent impression born from the weight of false delusion perishes, like a mirage in the desert when the clouds have vanished.
As long as one has not investigated "Who am I? and "How is this? the grand spectacle of saṃsāra remains like darkness.
He truly sees who perceives this body— not a locus of calamities, but born from the weight of false delusion— as not being the self through the cultivation of the realization of the Self.
He who perceives the pleasures and pains of the body as arising from the influence of place and time, and as being "not mine," is free from delusion; he alone sees truly.
He truly sees who perceives both himself and everything else through a vision that is eternally undivided, seeing all as nothing but the light of consciousness.
He who perceives everywhere that "I alone am" the limitless sky and its boundaries, as well as space, time, and all activity— he truly sees.
He who perceives that "I am subtle" and all-pervading— though [the self] is imagined as being ten million times smaller than a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair— he truly sees.
He who perceives within that which is all-powerful, infinite in essence, abiding within all beings, and non-dual consciousness— he truly sees.
He who perceives "I am the body"—which is subject to mental and physical ailments, fear, old age, death, and birth—is not wise; he truly sees.
"My greatness pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
he who sees that 'there is no second to me'—he truly sees."
All this is strung upon me like clusters of gems on a thread;
he who sees that "I alone am the charioteer of the mind" truly sees.
Neither "I" nor anything else exists here; only Brahman exists, yet even that does not exist.
He who perceives the middle between existence and non-existence in this way—he truly sees.
Whatever exists in the three worlds, that is but a single limb of mine; he who perceives this within himself sees truly, like a wave in the ocean.
When the notions of "self" and "other," as well as "thine" and "mine," have ceased through the realization of the Great Self, he whose vision is clear beholds [reality].
"She is to be pitied and protected by me alone; she is my younger sister.
He who looks upon the three worlds as fragile in this way—he truly sees.
He who perceives the body consisting of the Bhairava of Consciousness— free from the pursuit of objects of thought and filling the entire web of the universe— he truly sees.

Whether one perceives pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, and whatever notions of lack of discrimination may arise, or whether one thinks "I do not know," one certainly does not fall away from the goal.

When the world is filled with the supreme reality of one's own self and devoid of anything else, the man of true vision perceives: "What is there for me to abandon? What is there to be accepted? (MU 4.38)
I bow to Him for whom the notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have utterly ceased— He who is beyond reasoning, devoid of appearance, and is pure Being alone.
He who, like space, is the single Self even while pervading all beings,
and yet does not undergo the coloring of existence— he is the Great-Souled One, Maheśvara.

O gentle one, I bow to that state which has been attained— you who are free from the perception of darkness and light, who have become the very nature of time, and who are perfectly equanimous and established in well-being.

Salutations to that Śiva, the possessor of supreme awakening, whose infinite and uniform activity— though directed toward the single goal of all— remains equal amidst the diverse and beautiful manifestations of the world's rising and setting.
The Fifth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Essential Nature Resting in the Supreme State," by Vasiṣṭha.
Taking hold of the supreme state, he remains like the whirling of a wheel;
even while exercising sovereignty over the city of the body, he is not defiled.
For one who knows that, this great city of his own body—resembling a pleasure grove—is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; it leads only to happiness, not to suffering.
Rāma said: O great sage, how indeed can the body possess the nature of a city,
and how can a yogin dwelling within it be solely devoted to the pleasures of sovereignty?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, this city of the body is delightful and endowed with all virtues;
for the knower, it is rich in infinite diversions and illuminated by the sun of self-perception."
With the light from the windows of her eyes illuminating the interior of the world,
she reached the lower regions with the expanse of her arms as broad highways.
Her line of body hair was like a creeping vine, her skin was garlanded with watchtowers,
and her circle of shanks and thighs rested upon pillars of guggulu resin at her ankles.
Its feet were first fashioned from formidable stones marked with lines;
it was beautiful with the boundaries of joints, the essence of veins, and the vital points of its skin.
With the opening of her private parts fashioned from the panels at the front of her two thighs,
she was covered by a veil of shimmering locks of hair like a covering of lotus petals.
Adorned by a garden-like face possessing the luster of her eyebrows, forehead, and mouth,
she has broad cheeks strewn with the blue lotuses of her glances.
The lake of her chest has the bud-like breasts sewn upon it;
the mountain for her playful climbing is her shoulder, covered by the dense line of body hair.
With the shards of her desired food cast into the cavity of her belly,
she makes a sound from the agitation of wind expelled through the long hollow of her throat.
Adorned with the objects obtained as they arise, determined at the marketplace of the heart,
the city of the vital breath flows incessantly through its nine gates.
Her mouth was wide open, filled with fragments of bone from teeth she had seen;
her tongue flickered like a flame within her gaping maw, chewing upon her food.
The hollows of her ear-cavities were covered with a mass of hairy grass;
the edges of her buttocks were bent by chains, and her broad back was like a vast wilderness.
The mud of endless [defilements] has been drawn up from within the water-wheel of the bowels;
the noble woman of self-reflection dances upon the garden-ground of the mind.
The restless monkeys of the sense-faculties are firmly bound by the ropes of wisdom;
she is delightful with the blossoming flowers of laughter in the garden of her face.
For the knower, his own body-city is the most beautiful of all auspicious things;
it leads only to happiness and not to suffering, and to the highest welfare.
For the ignorant, this [body] is the keeper of the treasury of infinite sufferings;
for the wise, however, it is the keeper of the treasury of infinite happiness.
O subduer of enemies, when this [intellect] is lost, nothing is lost for the wise man;
when it remains, everything remains established. Therefore, this [intellect] brings about the happiness of the wise man.

Since the wise one, having mounted this [chariot], traverses the cycle of existence sufficiently for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation without remainder, it is therefore known as the "chariot of the wise."
Since sound, form, taste, touch, smell, kinsmen,
and prosperity are indeed obtained through this very [wisdom], it bestows gain upon the wise man.
O Rāma, when this [intellect] itself bears the web of the activities of pleasure and pain, then it is capable of supporting the weight of all things everywhere.
For in that city of the body,
the Knower, free from delusion and devoid of agitation, dwells while exercising sovereignty, as Indra does in his own city.
He does not cast the wild horse of his mind into the pit of arrogance,
nor does he surrender the daughter of wisdom to the twin form of greed.
Furthermore, he does not perceive any vulnerability in the enemy kingdom of ignorance;
rather, within the midst of the fear of the enemy that is saṃsāra, he cuts away its very roots.
He does not sink into the whirlpool of craving’s essence, which is as difficult to grasp as the agitation of desire, nor into the dice-game of pleasure and pain that overturns all things.
Moving according to his desires, he incessantly performs ablutions both externally and internally in an instant at the confluences of rivers and sacred fords, proceeding in due order.
Invisible to all people, turning his back on the spectacles of the city,
he dwells constantly in bliss within the inner apartments under the name of meditation.
This divine city, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is eternally a source of happiness for those whose souls are ever-joyful, just like Amarāvatī belongs to Śakra.
Everything remains stable through that which is stable; nothing is destroyed by that which is destroyed.
How could that city of the king not bring happiness?
When the city of the body has perished, nothing at all is lost for the knower,
just as when a jar is destroyed, the space contained within it suffers no loss.
Just as the wind touches an existing jar but not one that is not present,
so too does the embodied soul touch this city of its own body.
Abiding here, this Blessed One, although omnipresent,
having experienced the state of being a person created by his own conceptualization, has attained the vision of the Self.
Even while acting, he does not act; though fully intent upon all activities, he sometimes presides over all the matters at hand.
Sometimes, with playful ease, his stainless mind ascends a lovely, unimpeded, and swaying celestial chariot to wander about.
Abiding there, he constantly delights with Lokasundarī, whose limbs are ever cool,
and with Maitrī, who is eternally established in his heart.
Two beloved ones stood at his sides, truth and solitude,
gladdening his heart like the two stars Viśākhā beside the moon.
The knower beholds all these worlds, torn asunder by the saw of suffering,
like one seated on a pedestal looking at anthills, or like the sun from behind its back.
Having long fulfilled all his hopes and being beautiful with every perfection,
he shines like the full-orbed moon, never again to suffer eclipse.
Even when enjoying a flood of pleasures, no weariness arises in him; indeed, the Kālakūṭa poison shines all the more upon the neck of one who has conquered his afflictions.
For when enjoyment is consumed with full understanding, it leads to contentment;
and when a thief is recognized and reassured, he attains friendliness rather than enmity.
In the midst of the tumultuous dance of the throngs of men and women, the wise man beholds the fortune of enjoyment as a mere spectacle, like a procession passing by at a distance.
Just as travelers on a road observe a village festival that has arrived unexpectedly,
so too do the wise observe the activity consisting of worldly transactions.
Just as the eye falls effortlessly upon objects within its range, such as the directions or things before it,
without any attachment, so too does the intellect of the steadfast fall upon its objects.
The senses never take away an object already attained, nor do they give it up once attained; thus, the wise man remains established in completeness.
Those who have not yet attained [the goal] but have attained equanimity do not cause the one of noble mind to waver, just as flickering blows from a peacock's tail feathers cannot move a mountain.
With all doubt completely stilled, with all curiosity dissolved,
and with the web of latent impressions (vāsanā) thoroughly exhausted, the knower shines like a sovereign emperor.
Not contained within itself, it expands by its own nature within itself;
like the ocean of milk, the self-possessed one is complete, without limit or end.
With a mind free from madness and tranquil, he laughs at those beings who are wretched in their craving for enjoyments, as well as at those whose senses are dejected, as if they were madmen.
Just as one who desires another's wife is ridiculed by others,
so too is the wise man ridiculed when his senses desire enjoyment.
One should bring the mind— which has abandoned its great happiness in equanimity and is distracted by sense objects—
back to tranquility through discernment, just as one restrains a lordly elephant with a goad.
That mental tendency which is allowed to flow toward sensual enjoyments must be destroyed at the very outset, just like the sprouting of a poison plant.
For even the honor shown after one has been struck is boundless;
like a field of rice scorched by the summer heat, even a small sprinkling of water acts as nectar.
For honor and great respect are not perceived by one who is not in need;
the slight rain of the monsoon flood shines forth only when the rivers are already full.
But one who is full, even when benefited by another, desires yet more;
even the single ocean takes up all the water for the sake of filling the world.
When the mind has been restrained, whatever subsequent embellishment of its state occurs,
one values that very thing highly because it is the attainment of what was previously unattained and has not yet expanded.
A king who is bound is satisfied with even a single village;
but one who is unbound by others and not oppressed does not hold sovereignty in high regard.
Pressing hand against hand and grinding tooth against tooth,
and as it were crushing limb with limb, conquer your own enemies— the senses.
By men who are resolute and desirous of rising above others,
the senses must first be thoroughly conquered, for they are enemies of the heart.

On this vast surface of the earth, those men are truly fortunate and possess virtuous intentions who are counted among the subjects of human discourse because they have not been conquered by their own minds.

I salute that subduer of enemies who has attained peace, in whose heart-cavern the serpent of the mind— with its earrings formed by the heart's core and its virulent poison of restless fancies— has been brought to rest.
The sixth chapter, titled "The Union with the Splendors of the City of the Body and Other Such," by Vasiṣṭha.
The great kings of hell are like rutting elephants of evil deeds;
they are difficult to conquer, for the enemies that are the sense faculties are bristling with the arrows and shafts of desire.
Those who, being ungrateful, destroy their own first refuge— the body—
are the enemies of one's own senses, which are difficult to conquer and serve as a vast treasury for evil deeds.
Having taken refuge in the physical body out of greed for the bait of sensory objects,
the vultures of the senses— those fierce birds whose wings are what ought and ought not to be done— flit about restlessly.
Those rogues who are caught in the net of the threads of discernment cannot harm his limbs, just as one cannot devour a mouthful of stone.
Those who delight in sense objects that are charming only at first sight fall into hells whose final end is utter desolation.
In this city of the wretched body, one who possesses the wealth of discernment is not helplessly overcome by the enemies that are the senses dwelling within.
Likewise, kings who dwell in formidable cities made of clay are not as happy as those who have mastered their own minds and are masters of the city of their own bodies.
For one who has brought his senses under control as servants and well subdued the enemy that is the mind,
the blossoms of awakened wisdom flourish like clusters of flowers in springtime.
For one whose pride of mind has perished and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses,
the latent impressions of worldly enjoyment wither away like lotus ponds in winter.
Vāsanās leap about in the heart like Vetālīs at night,
as long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice on the single reality.

I consider the mind of the discerning person to be a servant, because it performs what is desired; a minister, because it accomplishes what ought to be done; and a vassal, because its own senses are under its command.
I consider the mind of the wise to be a tender woman because of its fondling, a purifying father because of its protection, and a friend because of its supreme trustworthiness.
That which is personally observed through the vision of the scriptures, well-pondered, and fervently entreated,
bestows supreme accomplishment upon the father of the mind who has surrendered himself.
Well-polished, well-cleansed, well-sustained, and well-awakened,
this heart-pleasing jewel of the mind shines within the heart when joined with excellent qualities.
This counselor of the mind ordains for the doer of auspicious deeds those actions which serve as axes for the tree of birth and which result in future prosperity.
O Rāma, having thus cleansed the jewel of the mind— which is stained by much mud— with the water of discernment for the sake of perfection, become possessed of light.
Even though you are expanded by discernment, do not fall helplessly into the terrifying stages of existence,
which are full of calamities, like an ordinary person.
Do not disregard this mist of great delusion— this illusory cycle of existence that has arisen, crowded with hundreds of calamities.
Relying upon supreme solitude and perceiving the truth with your intellect,
having thoroughly conquered the enemies that are the senses, cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
O Rāghava, let not the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa occur to you, even though this body does not truly exist and pleasure and pain do not truly exist.

O Great-minded One, having thoroughly cast aside with a noble intellect that vain certainty of "this is I," resort to that other state; drink, eat, and enjoy, for being without a mind, you are not bound.
The seventh canto, titled "Demonstrating the Trustworthiness of the Mind," [begins]:
While this wise one was dwelling in the world, taking delight in the world, [he thought:]...
For one who stands for the sake of the highest good and is intent upon the supreme goal, effort must be exerted for the sake of further excellence.
O Rāghava, let not the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours; through the state of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa, may you possess complete freedom from sorrow.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, you who remove the torment of worldly existence, why have you cited the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa? Let it not be so."
Awaken me, who am pure, with this noble speech that removes the thick heat of suffering, as the rainy season awakens the peacock.
Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, having heard the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the state of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa, do thereafter whatever you desire.
In the cavern of the netherworld (pātāla), which was enchanting with every wonder,
there lived a lord of the Daityas named Śambara, a great ocean of the jewels of illusion (māyā).
He has constructed the palaces of the asuras within gardens in a city of the sky;
his own realm is adorned with artificial, supreme suns and moons.
The delightful mountain of Ramanācala is enriched with lotuses born from fragments of stone;
it fulfills the desires of the dānavas through the commencement of its infinite splendor.
The sound of the songs sung by the women in his jewel-adorned mansions surpassed the voices of the celestial nymphs;
and the trees in his pleasure groves were filled with fruits as large as the orb of the moon.
Its delightful abodes were dense with clusters of blooming blue lotuses;
its golden lotuses were frequented by cranes summoned there like jeweled swans.
He formed lotus buds upon the tips of the branches of his golden trees,
and produced a profusion of mandāra flowers from the clusters of karañja blossoms.
There, Indra was defeated by infinite Daityas who were like machines made of jewels;
there, garden pavilions were constructed from the flames of fires as cold as snow.
He surpassed the Nandana grove with its gardens of flowers blooming in every season;
he removed the serpents from the Malaya mountains by means of his illusory snake.
The splendor of his inner apartments eclipsed the loveliness of the world of golden women;
there, the Lord, for the sake of sport, competed with the wielder of the discus and mace.
The sky of his own city was enriched by stars that were a continuous stream of soaring jewels,
while its courtyards were filled with heaps of various flowers reaching up to the knees.
During the nights, he was like a hundred moons for the entire expanse of the netherworld,
while the excellence of his virtues was sung in songs by the gazes of the female statues carved upon his palace walls.
The lordly elephant of the gods was put to flight by the illusory Airāvaṇa,
and the interior of his harem was filled with the excellence of the splendors of the three worlds.
He was blessed with every prosperity and endowed with all sovereignty;
his supreme commands were honored by all the Daitya vassals.
The assembly of asuras rested in the shade of his great forest-like arms;
he was adorned with earrings made of the essence of jewels from the caves of all the oceans.
That Asura, who had destroyed the gods and possessed a harsh and terrifying form, came to have a vast army that brought ruin upon the deities.
When that Māyābala was asleep and had likewise departed for another land, the gods, having found a vulnerability, indeed entered his army.
Then, for the sake of protection, the Daitya Śambara appointed his own vassals, such as Dudrika, Hava, and Drumā, over his various armies.
Having reached their midst, the leaders of the gods struck them down,
like hawks moving through the sky attacking agitated sparrows.
Furthermore, the best of the asuras appointed other generals who were restless and loud in their cries,
like the waves of the ocean.
The gods quickly slew even them; therefore, filled with rage, he went to the celestial realm (*triviṣṭapa*) to destroy the immortals.
There, terrified by his illusory power, those gods vanished,
like deer into the groves of Meru’s forest at the sight of the teacher of Gaurī.
He beheld heaven empty, like a world exhausted at the end of an eon, with the hosts of minor gods wailing and the faces of the goddesses drenched in tears.
Having stayed there in anger and having seized what he had obtained, Śambara burned the cities of the world-protectors and went to his own abode.
When enmity had thus become more intense between the Dānavas and the gods,
the gods abandoned heaven and vanished from sight in all directions.
Then, whichever commanders of the army were appointed with great effort by the Daitya Śambara, those very ones the gods, intent on their own exertion, slew.
Then Śambara, overcome with agitation and filled with intense rage,
blazed up like a grass-fed fire fanned by the wind, heaving deep sighs.
Then, even after searching throughout the three worlds, he did not find the gods,
despite his supreme effort, just as a wrongdoer fails to find his own good deeds.
By means of his illusory power (māyā), he created three terrible and exceedingly powerful Asuras,
who arose for the sake of protecting Bala like Time itself embodied in form.
Created by magic, those terrifying beings with arms like wish-fulfilling trees rose up,
their massive bodies resembling mountains shaken by the wings of great birds.
Marked by the names Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa,
they are each the sole agent of whatever occurs to them, possessing the property of mere consciousness.
Due to the absence of karmas, they are devoid of past latent impressions (vāsanās);
their sole activity consists in the vibration of pure, non-conceptual consciousness alone.
Bearing within themselves a slender, artificial, and unripened seed of karma consisting of mental ideation, they have come into manifestation.
For there, those soldiers, having abandoned their latent tendencies, follow the action at hand by tradition, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
Just as children who are half-asleep move only their own limbs,
so too are those [liberated ones] indeed devoid of both latent impressions (vāsanā) and the conceit of selfhood (ātmābhimāna).
They know neither retreat nor flight, nor do they know life or death, nor battle, victory, or defeat.
Seeing only the soldiers before them intent on striking,
those whose mountains were shattered by blows struck down their enemies in battle.
Śambara, his mind fully satisfied, thought within the city:
"My army, well-protected by the illusory asuras, shall indeed be victorious."
For these [beings] are utterly freed from the latent impressions of the desirable and the undesirable;
therefore, they do not fear in battle, nor do they flee, remaining steadfast.
Since these do not flee even when struck by the gods,
this exceedingly powerful army of mine now stands firm.
Protected by the tree-like arms of the exceedingly powerful Asuras, my army will attain great stability,
just as the golden ground of the celestial mountain remains firm during the collisions of the tusks of the gods' elephants.
The eighth canto, titled "The Origin of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having thus resolved, the lord of the Daityas dispatched his army, accompanied by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, to the surface of the earth to destroy the gods.
From the groves along the ocean, from the mountain caves, and from the divine mountain, the Daityas rose up with terrifying roars, like winged mountains in flight.
Urged on by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭi, the Dānavas filled the hollow of the two worlds (heaven and earth), striking down the sun with blows from their hands.
Then, from the groves and from the caves of the mountain of the gods, the hosts of celestial dwellers arose,
agitated like at the end of a cosmic dissolution, terrified by the inhabitants of heaven.
Then that battle between those two, who bore the banners of the gods and the asuras,
took place within the world, terrifying like a premature and violent dissolution of the kalpa.
From the sky, heads fell downward like mountains with the sun and moon overturned at the time of universal dissolution; their earrings vomited forth splendor that swallowed the darkness.
Resounding with the lion-roars emitted by the warriors, they reeled like mountains filled with the blasts of the dissolution-wind and accompanied by loud peals of laughter.

The slopes of the great boundary mountains trembled, their movements pained by the falling of weapons that were like the very rocks of their own substance, while the circles of lions wandered about in fear.
The flickering sparks of fire arising from weapons struck down by one another were like stars scattered at the end of a kalpa.
On the shores of a single vast ocean filled with floods of blood and flesh,
there were Vetālas as tall as the *kalpa* trees, with bodies like palm trunks, clapping their hands loudly.
In the sky, where the clouds of dust were stilled by the downpour of gushing blood,
the tips of the earrings from the heads crushed and struck by weapons [were visible].

The quarters of the sky became devoid of any gaps, filled by the Daityas whose arms were like wish-fulfilling trees and whose forms resembled the sun, as they crushed the great lords of mountains with their blows.
With their walls shattered by the impact of the mass of blazing missiles,
the mountains were reduced to a shower of fragments, as if enveloped by the fire at the end of an aeon.
The gods gathered together their splendor, like those invigorated by the horse-sacrifice;
they pursued the Asuras, just as winds follow the clouds.
Then, having attacked them, the gods seized those [demons] as lions seize old rats; the gods and asuras trembled in heaven like mountains swaying in a forest of blossoming trees.
They filled one another and the ten directions with showers of weapons,
just as the winds fill the forests of Mount Sumeru with masses of blossoms.
A terrible battle took place between the armies of the gods and the dānavas,
like that of two great swarms of gnats within the hollow of the space between heaven and earth.
Then, with the circles of world-protectors raising their trunks like clouds at the end of an aeon, the sky was filled by the terrible roar of battle as they rushed forward.
As if it were a paved courtyard on the surface of the earth within the sky, it was grasped as a single mass;
thick and heavy, its belly moving slowly like a great cloud, it could be seized by the fist.
Its slopes resounded with the clashing of weapons and rocks crushed at the initial impact; it was filled with the harsh, gurgling cries of the lifeless as their hearts burst apart.
It is nourished by the roar of the clouds of the kalpa arising from the dissolution-consciousness,
and resembles molten gold produced by the friction of the twelve suns.
Having turned back from the impact against the wall of the cosmic egg and returned to the earth,
it was like the floodwaters of a great river struck by a dam, as it rushed toward its source.
It possessed the forceful roar of the winds from the wings of the moving king of mountains;
it filled the caverns of the mountain kings with its hardness and caused them to burst open as they were blown apart.
The garment [of the wind] resembles the agitation of the Milk Ocean when churned by Mount Mandara;
it causes the creatures of the islands to tremble with echoes, roars, and thumping sounds.
Between the two enraged armies there occurred a battle marked by the upheaval of dānavas,
in which cities, villages, mountains, forests, and men were crushed to dust.

The quarters were filled with the mountain-like Dānavas cut down by hundreds of great weapons, while the interior of the sky was filled with the dust of mountains formed by weapons struck against one another.
The hundreds of peaks of Mount Meru were shattered by the striking of the circle of his *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons;
the lotuses that were the Daityas, Devas, and Asuras were cut down by the wind of his arrows.
The old grass of gods and demons was whirled about by hundreds of revolutions of the whirlpools,
while the sky was enveloped by the surging waves of the flowing torrent of the army.
The multitude of celestial chariots fell, crushed by the falling mountain of Hetya;
the city in the sky was flooded by the mass of ocean waters brought down by his hand.
Carrying hundreds of rivers of great missiles— swords, spears, and pikes—
it rendered the pavilion of the universe inert by the violent crashing of mountain wings.
The city of the world-protectors collapsed under the torrent of blows from the Daitya’s heels,
while the golden palace shrieked with the tumultuous cries of women.
The mountain-like Daityas rolled about, stirring up the waters of the intoxicated ocean;
with those waters as their mountains, they washed away the dust raised by the warriors in the blood-stained sky, while the sound of their cries caused the cowherd settlement to flee.
It was covered again and again by the clouds that were the guardians of the world,
yet it was filled with the hosts of armies seen through the splendors of the gods and asuras.

It was terrifying with the loud clanging of many *bhāṅ* sounds produced by the flapping wings of the birds as they flew back and forth over the mountain-like bodies of the Dānavas, which resembled mountains of similar form.
The entire earth, oceans, and mountains were reddened with blood from the mountain-like Daityas, whose peaks had been split by weapons, flowing down like mountain torrents.
It was filled with countless asuras, elephants, horses, men, chariots, and mountains, amidst ruined kingdoms, cities, forests, villages, and mountain caves.
In that arena where iron arrows were scattered like a shower of rain from clouds at the end of an eon, the celestial bards were driven away by the clashing of swords and spears;
the mountains were shattered by the torrential downpour of the clouds of the kalpa.
The elephant Airāvaṇa had its shoulder crushed by the blow of his fist,
while Mount Kulācala was pulverized and cast up into the air by the impact of his great thunderbolt-like strike.
The Dānava was set ablaze by the masses of flames leaping from his provoked fire,
yet he extinguished that fire by pouring out the ocean brought forth in a single hollowed palm.
The great mass of water was solidified by the accumulation of lunar coldness and other factors,
while the mountain ranges were melted by the flames of the fire fueled by the forest thickets.
It was a night of the end of the aeon, with darkness as difficult to dispel as that created by weapons;
yet the mass of illusory suns shone forth, stripping away the vast veil of gloom.
It was like the raining down of a mass of fires at the end of an eon, with illusory showers falling;
it was the dragging forth of a collision between the wind, fire, and a multitude of weapons acting in concert.
It arises from the weapons of the rain of vajras and the rain of mountains,
abounding in the battle of the weapons of awakening from sleep, and possessing the weapon of the restraint of rain.
It bore trees as weapons with moving saws, was equipped with missiles of water and fire,
was as fierce in battle as the Brahma-weapon, and was variegated by the weapons of darkness and light.
The entire sky was rendered dense with hosts of weapons disgorged by the stars,
enveloped by showers of stones and missiles, and blazing with showers of fire-missiles.
In a mere moment, the chariots— whose banners brushed against the moon and whose wheels roared like thunder— leaped over both the mountains of sunrise and sunset.
The great asura who dies without ceasing from the blow of the vajra;
the other asura who is born through the great vidyā of the immortal semen.
With its neck uplifted by battles against the floods of ill-omened portents arising here and there, which were protected by the great comet Śubhagraha; MU_4,8.48.
Due to his irresistible enmity, he made the earth, the oceans, and the heavens resemble a forest of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees with the waters of blood from the world.
A great ocean filled with corpses as numerous as mountains,
with massive, dangling corpses hanging from the branches of entire trees.
The surface of the sky was filled with forests of arrow-clusters as tall as palm trees, being carried along, moistened by their own wind, and adorned with the flowers and fruits of their feathers.
With the forest-arms of headless trunks as numerous as mountains,
they were dancing, while fallen clouds, celestial chariots, and the stars of the gods lay scattered about.
Mountains were pierced by arrows, spears, maces, darts, and axes;
the sky was covered with fragments of walls fallen from the seven worlds.
The thundering sound from the back [of the chariot] was like the incessant roar of clouds intoxicated with rain,
and it caused the elephants at the bottom of the netherworld to trumpet aloud.
The long mountain of Dānavas was drawn forth by the hand of Vināyaka, while the hosts of Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Maruts were rendered motionless on the edge of the horizon.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, gods, and Cāraṇas fled in all directions;
the leaders of the Gandharvas lay dead, mangled, emaciated, and falling down.
The host of Daityas and Dānavas had for the most part achieved a slight victory;
the army of the gods was suffering, and Indra was utterly despondent.
It possessed the great radiance of red weapons like fire arising from the northern quarter; at every moment, it was intense with the light of blazing heat and darkness.
Winds blew from the quarters of the sky, their limbs massed with falling thunderbolts and fragments of shattered rock;
signaling the time of universal dissolution for the gods, they were terrifying with their immense, gurgling roar.
The Ninth Sarga: The Description of the Battle between Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; by Vasiṣṭha.
While that terrible tumult of battle was then occurring,
the bodies of gods and asuras fell like fragments of mountains.
While streams of blood flowed like the floods of the Gaṅgā descending from the sky,
and while the multitude of gods was bound by the tethering rope amidst the thick roar of their released war-cries;
Upon a tiger that had crushed all the celestial abodes by the drawing back of its own claws, and upon a mountain peak where the gods were overwhelmed in a battle of fierce fury;
When Airāvaṇa’s rut had faded and he was intent on flight,
the army of the Dānavas surged forward like the sun at midday.
With their weapons and limbs fallen away and blood streaming forth,
the divine armies fled like waters whose banks have been breached.
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa followed those [demons], even though they had long since vanished,
with loud shouts, just as fires follow their fuel.
Although they searched with great effort, the Asuras did not find the gods,
just as lions do not find deer that have flown up into a forest thick with nets of clouds.
When the hosts of immortals had not been captured, Dāma, Vyāla,
and Kaṭa then went with joyful hearts to their lord residing in the treasury of Pātāla.
Then the gods, having become despondent, recovered for a moment and went to the infinitely powerful Brahmā in order to find a means of victory after being defeated.
To them, whose faces possessed the splendor of deep redness, Brahmā appeared,
like the moon appearing over oceans whose waters have been turned crimson at twilight.
Having prostrated before him, those gods fully explained to him that matter uttered by Śambara— the sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.

Having heard all that and having reflected upon it, Brahmā, the discerning one, spoke these words of consolation to the host of gods: tam ākarṇyākhilaṃ brahmā vicārya ca vicāravit / uvācedaṃ surānīkam āśvāsanakaraṃ vacaḥ //MU_4,9.12//
Brahmā said:
"Alas! At the end of a thousand years, Śambara must by turns slay Hari, the Lord of the Immortals; therefore, let that time be awaited."
"O best of the immortals, today you must fight these Dānavas— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa— and put them to flight by means of illusory warfare."
Through the power of habitual practice in battle, the wondrous manifestation of egoism will enter into the hearts of these [warriors] like a reflection in a mirror.
But these gods Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, having taken up latent impressions,
will be easily conquered by you, like birds caught in a net.
But today, being free from latent desires and devoid of pleasure and pain, these [monkeys],
slaying their enemies with fortitude, have attained invincibility even against the gods.
Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions (vāsanā) and brought under control by the snares of desire fall into subjection in this world, like birds tied with ropes.
For those wise ones who are free from latent tendencies, whose intellects are unattached to anything, and who neither rejoice nor feel anger— they are the great-minded ones, difficult to conquer.
He whose internal bondage of knots is formed by the rope of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*),
though he be great and possessed of vast knowledge, is overcome even by a child.
One who forms conceptual constructions such as "this is I" or "this is mine" becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters.
He by whom the self has been cultivated as limited to this much alone—
even if he were omniscient— has everywhere fallen into a state of supreme wretchedness.
He by whom the limit of the infinite and immeasurable reality of the Self has been conceived,
by him the Self has been brought under control through his own self.
Whatever exists in the three worlds that is distinct from the self, toward that one becomes bound by the notion of it being something to be grasped.
They know that mere attachment is the cause of endless sufferings;
they know that mere non-attachment is the cause of all happiness.

As long as you maintain a lack of attachment toward the persistence of existence— just as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa did— then indeed you shall not be conquered by them, any more than mosquitoes are by the winds.
A living being is overcome by a lowly state when pursued by internal latent impressions; otherwise, even a mosquito would be like the immovable mountain Meru.
Wherever there is latent impression (*vāsanā*), there too comes wretchedness;
for it is observed that being permeated by qualities and defects belongs to what exists, not to what does not exist.
O Śakra, act in such a way that they cultivate within themselves the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of "this is I" and "this is mine," just as Dāma and the others did.
Whatever misfortunes people encounter and whatever states of existence and non-existence they experience,
these are the pungent yet tender blossoms of the thorny *karañja* creeper of craving.

Bound by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), this world revolves; when those [impressions] have fully increased, they lead to extreme suffering, yet when they have been eradicated, they lead to happiness.
Even one who is steadfast, even one who possesses vast knowledge, even one born of noble lineage, and even one who is great—
a living being is bound by craving, just as a lion is bound by a chain.
For this bird of the mind that dwells within the tree of the body and rests in the abode of the heart, craving has been fashioned as a snare.
The world, wretched with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is dragged away by the End-maker (*kṛtānta*), like a helpless bird incessantly gasping, pulled by a rope by a child.
Enough with the burden of weapons and with wandering through battles;
by means of reasoning alone, you should dispel the enemy’s latent tendencies along with their misconceptions.
When the enemy's fortitude is shaken from within, neither your weapons, nor your treatises, nor your missiles can conquer you, O leaders of the immortals.
But these— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa— by virtue of their practice in combat,
will seize within themselves a latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of egoism.
If those mechanical men created by Śambara do not rely upon latent impressions (vāsanā), they will attain invincibility.
O gods, let them first awaken those [beings] through battle by means of reasoning,
until they come to possess the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by virtue of repeated practice.
Then those whose minds are bound by worldly existence will become objects of slaughter for you; in this world, there are none who are not pierced by the arrow of craving, nor any who are not tender.
This entire world, both even and uneven, has attained stability through its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
yet it moves like the mass of waves in the ocean. Therefore, it is that very [impression] which must be treated here.
The Tenth Sarga, titled "The Words of the Grandfather" in the Narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord vanished on the spot,
like a wave of water that has made its sound upon the shore at the edge of the tide.
But the gods, having heard those words, departed toward their own respective quarters,
carrying with them the fragrance of the lotuses, like breezes bearing a forest garland.
For some days, they rested in their own lovely palaces, which possessed enduring splendor, just as bees rest within lotuses.
Having attained for a short time that auspicious state which brings about their own exaltation,
they raised a roar like the sound of kettledrums, resembling the thundering of clouds at the dissolution of the world.
Then, a terrible battle ensued in the sky with those Daityas who had risen from the depths of the netherworld, causing a long delay.

Multitudes of swords, arrows, spears, and mallets; hammers, clubs, axes, and throngs of fierce discuses; thunderbolts, mountain rocks, fires, and trees; and weapons with the faces of serpents, Garuḍas, and others, blew forth.
A river created by magic, with a torrent of great waters and weapons, swiftly surged forth in every direction;
it was a river possessing a deep roar like the flood of agitated waters that tosses millions of rocks, mountains, riverbanks, and trees. MU 4.10.7.

With mountain-like spears, lances, swords, darts, arrows, and javelins carried in the middle of the current, with celestial palaces surrounded by waters like the Ganges, and with the drawing in of rainfalls of thunderbolts in all directions; //MU_4,10.8//
