That army of gods, asuras, and siddhas—which consists of bodies as harsh as earth and other elements when striking or being struck, yet is like a body of light rays in the sky—subsides; however, that very same army, created by illusion, arises again through its own inherent power.

Then the faces of the quarters became like great oceans filled with floods of blood from mountains shattered by weapons as hard as rock, where the forests of *kunta* and *tālī* trees grew upon the divine mountain-like bodies of the lords of the gods and the asuras.

Then there fell a rain of iron lions, alive and possessing rows of fierce teeth and claws that were like saws creaking as they ground; they vomited forth spears, arrows, pikes, maces, swords, and discs, and playfully swallowed the mountains hurled by the gods and Dānavas.

The line of venomous serpents surged forth like a drunken ocean; with their blazing eyes, they were like a host of suns at the end of an eon causing a world-conflagration, while the long-stretched earth and mountains seemed to fly upward.

The entire world became a body of extreme distress, surrounded by mountain ranges and the surging waves of the ocean-like sky filled with the clattering sounds of loud-roaring vajras and makaras, as it was whirled about by the swirling currents of rivers of various weapons.

The sky was filled for a moment with mountains, missiles, weapons, Garuḍas, mountains, and garlands; for a moment with lofty female nāgas and hosts of celestial nymphs; for a moment it was full of oceans, for a moment of masses of fire, for a moment of suns, and for a moment of darkness.
With floods of mountain-like fires from weapons spread through the sky, agitated by the whirring of Garuḍas,
the world became like the space between the earth and the celestial abodes blazing at the unbearable time of the end of an eon.
The asuras leapt up from the surface of the earth like birds from a mountain slope into the sky;
the gods fell to the ground by their own great force, like boulders from a mountain shaken by the dissolution of the world.

Then, engulfed by the great conflagration clinging to the forest-like rows of trees formed by the lofty weapons fixed upon their bodies, the gods and demons assumed the appearance of mountains tossed about by the winds at the end of an eon within the expanse of the sky.

The ocean of the sky, filled on all sides by streams of blood flowing from the bodies of the lords of the gods and asuras as they whirled about, bore the appearance of its own body being bathed by hundreds of rising Gaṅgās reddened by twilight.
They brought to rest the raining down of mountains, the raining down of water, the raining down of various fierce weapons,
the raining down of terrible thunderbolts, and likewise the mutual raining down of fire.
Those experts in the path of right conduct, who had shattered the walls of all the great mountains,
simultaneously showered down a rain of flowers upon every limb of the quarters of the sky.
The gods and asuras, distressed by the agitation of their tumultuous battle, with weapons in their hands busily crushing one another’s limbs,
and burning like masses of fire, wandered through the sky, scattering blood from their broad seats and hurling insults.
Then, with severed heads, hands, arms, and thighs— inauspicious, wandering like locusts through the expanse of the sky—
the interior of the world became filled from the horizon to the sun with fierce masses that obscured the mountain ranges at the edges of the quarters, as if with clouds.

The world-egg became as terrifying as an untimely dissolution at the end of an aeon: its fires were intoxicated, its waters agitated by the wind, its sun blazed, its forests withered, the hosts of gods and demons perished, and its walls and corners were shattered to pieces.
He was utterly bewildered, his sense of direction completely lost by the mountain peaks that struck him with massive weapons and rang out,
as if with cries of distress from the fierce winds in the mountain caves, and as if with the loud, incessant roars of lions descending upon him.

It wandered within the sky like forest leaves scattered by the wind—amidst illusions, rivers, oceans, clouds, and conflagrations; amidst trees, the corpses of gods and asuras, mountains, and floods of rocks; and amidst the whirling heads, arrows, spears, maces, and various weapons.
By the fierce blows from the palms of his hands, which were as irresistible as the movement of the wings of the Lord of Mountains,
there suddenly arose an ocean-like flood of celestial cities— filled with the falling bodies of warriors and shattered by the impact of those mountain-kings.

Then that cave-like expanse of the world became filled with a dense, humming roar; its interior of mountains was washed by blood, and it was crowded with those moving about the banks of lakes of gore.

Then, indeed, that battle became like this very cycle of existence (saṃsṛti): it caused transformations extending through infinite directions; it bestowed pleasure and pain oriented toward decline and rise; and it was crowded with hosts of gods and asuras engaged in the act of combat.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Description of the Battle Again," from the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, with such tumultuous undertakings, the life-taking Asuras,
impelled by great recklessness, engaged in battles where death was the only outcome.
By means of illusion, as well as through dispute, alliance, and war;
by flight, by fortitude, by deception, and by stratagem.
That battle was waged by the gods for thirty-five years through acts of treachery, combat with missiles, and frequent instances of their own invisibility.
For eight, five, seven, and ten years, for days, months, and years,
there fell rains of trees, fire-arms, water, thunderbolts, and mountains.
But after such a length of time, through the firm habituation of egoism,
Dāma and the others, their minds being swallowed up by it, grasped at the notion "I am."
Just as a mirror becomes like the reflected image due to the excellence of its proximity,
so too have they attained the state of egoism through the excellence of their practice.
Just as an object that is too distant does not reflect in a mirror,
so too the latent impression of an object does not arise from a lack of repeated practice.
When Dāma and the others were born, their latent impressions of egoism arose;
then they fell into wretchedness, thinking, "This is my life," and "This is my wealth."
Seized by the latent impression of fear, struck down by the latent impression of delusion,
and bound by the snares of hope, they have consequently fallen into a state of wretchedness.
For indeed, by those who are free from egoism, the sense of "mine-ness" has been constructed in vain,
just as the state of being a serpent is [superimposed] upon a rope by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
"May this vine of my body, from head to foot, remain firm"—
thus did they, wretched with craving for "mine," fall into a state of misery.
"May my body be firm; may my wealth lead to happiness"—the fortitude of those whose minds were thus bound vanished within.
Because their bodies were devoid of latent impressions (*avāsana*) and because the enemies of the gods were free from attachment (*anāsthā*),
that state of being intent on striking them was instantly wiped away.
Thinking, "How may we become stable in this world?",
they fell into dejection, like lotuses deprived of water.
But for those who possessed the ego-conception regarding food and drink, their delight—
rooted in worldly existence, terrifying, and sharing in the nature of *bhava*— came to pass.
Then, in that battle, out of fear they became full of hesitation,
like young deer agitated by a herd of rutting elephants in the forest.
"Shall we die? Shall we die?"—with their hearts struck by such thoughts, they indeed wandered very slowly in the battle against the enraged Rāvaṇa.
For those who seek only their own bodies and are terrified of death,
they have placed their feet upon my head out of weakness of character, even though it brings them calamity.
Then, their courage failing, they were unable to strike the soldier standing before them, just as fires whose fuel is exhausted cannot burn the oblation.
As the gods struck, they became easy prey;
with all their limbs mangled and wounded, they stood like ordinary soldiers.
What need is there for much speaking here? With their minds terrified of death, the Daityas fled from the field of battle as the gods surged forward.
While all those famous mountain-like Dānavas known as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa were fleeing in every direction from the abode of the Asuras, [the Lord acted].
That army of Daityas fell from the sky, fleeing hither and thither like the host of stars shaken on all sides by the winds at the end of an aeon.
In the groves of the Immortal Mountain, upon the rocks of its peaks,
on the shores of the oceans, and amidst the masses of clouds;
In the whirlpools and abysses of the ocean, in chasms and rivers,
in wildernesses, at the ends of the quarters, and in forests ablaze;
In villages and cities whose treasuries were devastated by that war,
in forests inhabited by fierce yakṣas, and in deserts where forest fires were breaking out;
On the mountains at the edge of the Lokāloka range and in the lakes,
as well as in the cities of Andhra, Dramiḍa, Kaśmīra, and Pārasīka.
In the waves of various oceans, in the masses of Ganges waters,
in distant other continents, and in the Jambu-tree thickets and creepers;
Those enemies of the gods fell from all sides with the forms of mountains;
their limbs and feet were shattered, and their hands and arms were torn asunder.
With entrails like strings clinging to the branches, shedding streams of flowing blood,
their limbs, hooves, and heads scattered about, they emerged with eyes full of rage.
The armor and weapons were shattered by the force of the whirling of their own arms;
various garments fell, scattered and overturned by the long-distance flight [of the arrows].
Terrified by the harsh clatter of helmets striking against necks,
they hang with their bodies pierced by sword-blades sharpened on stone.
The spikes of their armor were pierced by the forceful impact of the tips of *śālmali* thorns,
and their heads were shattered into a hundred pieces by the striking of well-hewn stone slabs.
Immediately upon their mere fall, all those lords of the asuras, though fully equipped with weapons, met their destruction in every direction, like dust particles entering the waters of the ocean.
The twelfth canto, titled "The Fall of the Asuras," in the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, while the gods were gratified and the Dānavas were slain,
Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others became distressed and overwhelmed with fear.
Enraged, Śambara— whose army had been destroyed— blazed like the fire at the end of an aeon, burning against Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Then, out of fear of Śambara, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa abandoned the circle of the Dānavas and went to the seventh netherworld (pātāla), where they remained.
There stand the servants of Yama, capable of terrifying with vetālas,
known as Kukuhās, who are the guardians of that ocean of hell.
But they gave their daughters in turn, who were like anxieties personified in dense form.
Together with them, Dāma and the others brought that period there to its limit of ten thousand years, having taken hold of endless evil predispositions.
"This woman is mine, delightful; she is my sovereign"—for those bound by such hollow affection, time passed away.
Then, on one occasion, Dharmarāja arrived at that place by chance,
for the purpose of investigating the affairs of the great hells.
Not recognizing him as the King of Dharma, three asuras did not bow down to him for their own destruction, treating him like an ordinary servant.
Then, by the command of Vaivasvata, they were cast into the grounds of blazing chasms, where their eyebrows were made to twitch.
There, you, along with your friends, wives, and kinsmen, cried out in piteous lamentation as you were consumed like trees with their leaves and branches by forest fires.
Likewise, by their own cruel latent tendencies (*vāsanā*),
the Kirātas and the king’s servants are born with the very appearance of executioners.
Then, having abandoned that birth, they were born as crows among the Suhmas;
at the end of that, they became vultures, and from there they passed into the state of cranes.
Those of crooked intellect caused me to become a Śavara among the Trigartas, a sheep among the Barbaras, and then an insect among the Magadhas.
Having experienced a most varied succession of births here,
O Rāma, today we fish dwell in a pond within the forest of Kaśmīra.
Consuming the thin, boiling mud-paste of the forest fire,
they neither die nor live, being worn out by the old silt.
Having repeatedly experienced the agitation of various wombs,
and having come into being again and again, they perish once more like waves in the ocean.
Driven by the winds of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), those who have entered the ocean of existence have long been carried like straw by the waves in the form of bodies;
they have not yet attained peace, O Rāma. Consider, therefore, the endless and terrible magnitude of latent tendencies.
The thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Previous Births of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, O high-minded Rāma, I speak this for your awakening; it is not said in jest, lest you fall into the error of the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Due to a lack of discernment, the mind effortlessly embraces such a calamity for the sake of endless suffering.
Where, on one hand, is the lordship over Śambara’s host that destroys the immortals;
and where, on the other, is the state of being a fish withered by the mud of waters heated by the sun’s glare?
Where is that great fortitude capable of routing the hosts of the immortals,
and where is this state of being a lowly servant to the Kirāta king?
Where, indeed, is the noble fortitude of the pure consciousness that is free from egoism,
and where is the wicked conceptualization of egoism arising from the influence of false latent impressions?
This vast and spreading cluster of the miseries of saṃsāra, dense with its branches and tendrils,
arises precisely from the sprout of egoism.
Therefore, O Rāma, diligently cleanse the ego within;
having cleansed it by realizing "I am truly nothing at all," become happy.
The orb of the moon of ultimate reality, consisting of elixir and cool, has become invisible, shrouded by the cloud of egoism.
Devoured by the demon of egoism, the three— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—
though non-existent, attained existence as demons through the greatness of Māyā.
O Rāma, today the fish dwelling in the small pool on the shore of the Great Lotus Lake in Kaśmīra are greedily longing for bits of moss.
Rāma:
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being.
Tell me, how did those who were non-existent become existent? MU 4.13.11.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"It is so, O mighty-armed one; for that which is non-existent never comes into being anywhere.
At some time, this may become something vast, or it may become minute."
Tell me, how can that which is non-existent be established as existent, or how can that which is existent be established as non-existent?
By this very illustration, I shall bring about your awakening.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, it is indeed true that we who are here—Dāma and the others—are virtuous; yet you say that even though they are not virtuous, they stand as virtuous."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, just as Dāma and the others exist here as products of illusion,
they are indeed unreal though appearing real, like the mass of water in a mirage."
In the very same way, we too— along with the gods, asuras, and dānavas—
are entirely unreal, yet we move about, go, and come.
Your existence is indeed false, and my existence is likewise false;
though experienced, it is unreal in nature, just like one's own death in a dream.
Just as a deceased kinsman experienced even in a dream is composed of unreality, so too is this world, for there arises the cognition that "this one has died. MU_4,13.18//
For this statement, which pertains to the realm of the deluded, does not shine at all;
it vanishes through practice, for there can be no denial of direct experience.
A conviction that has taken deep root within never perishes for anyone in this world at any time, even without the effort of repeated practice.
Those who are insane laugh excessively at that person who says, "This world is unreal; Brahman alone is real," just as the insane laugh at another insane man.
Where indeed could there be unity between one who is ignorant and one who knows the truth, or between the blind and the enlightened? It would be like the union of shadow and sunlight.
Even with effort, neither one who knows nor one who does not know is able to deny an object that has been experienced as real, just as a corpse cannot resist being stepped upon.
It is appropriate for one who knows that [Brahman] to say "the entire world is Brahman," because in the absence of the experience of ignorance, he has experienced nothing other than That.
For this speech, O Rāma, shines forth only within the domain of the awakened;
in the form of "I am the Awakened One," there is indeed nothing at all.
For the wise one who experiences that "this supreme Brahman alone is peace," how could it be appropriate for him to perform a negation of his own direct experience?
Apart from the other, there is no "I" whatsoever within the Self; just as a ring or such cannot exist apart from gold, so too the state of being Vasiṣṭha does not exist within me.

Apart from its true nature, the deluded person perceives nothing at all within the self; for the ignorant one, there is no ultimate reality, just as there is no gold in the perception of a wave or similar forms.
The deluded person consists of the disease of false ego, while the wise person consists of the one true Self;
indeed, there can never be a denial of the inherent nature of these two.
How could the denial of that which consists of something be appropriate with respect to that very thing?
For the statement "I am a jar" on the part of a person is indeed mere madness.
Therefore, neither we nor Dāma and the others are real anywhere;
they and we are unreal, for indeed there is no origination of us.
The pure realization of truth is the stainless sky of awakening;
it is the truth that is all-pervading, peaceful, and neither sets nor rises.
Everything that exists is empty and void, established as if it were nothing at all;
within that space, O dear one, these perceptions shine forth as its own inherent radiance.
Just as to one with cataracted eyes, innate visual perceptions appear as clusters of hair and the like, so too do these creations appear therein.
He experiences himself in an instant exactly as he perceives it;
therefore, the sky of consciousness, though unreal, becomes real through that perception.
Therefore, in this world and throughout the three realms, there is neither truth nor falsehood;
whatever form of consciousness perceives a thing, that very thing arises exactly as it is perceived, without a doubt.
Just as Dāma and the others were, so too have we arisen;
whether real or unreal, my friend, what room is there here for conceptualization regarding them?
In this infinite, all-pervading, and formless sky of consciousness, consciousness arises in whatever manner; thus it shines forth there in its fullness.
Wherever consciousness itself manifests in the form of a rope or the like,
it is established as being exactly that, through the experience of its having that particular form.
The world is designated as the manifestation of one's own dream, just as the sky-like void of consciousness— though its nature is space— is [erroneously perceived] as a mirage by a traveler.
Where the sky of consciousness is awakened, there the designation "the visible" is applied;
where it is asleep by that very same [consciousness], there the designation "liberation" is applied.
And that never sleeps anywhere, nor is it ever awakened;
let it be understood that the visible world is merely the sky of consciousness.
Nirvāṇa itself is the glory of creation, and the glory of creation is itself nirvāṇa;
there is no difference in meaning between these two words, just as there is none between synonyms.
In ultimate reality, one perceives the world as one's own form by oneself,
just as a person with cataracts sees a mass of hair where none exists.
That is not a hair-net at all; rather, that vision remains as it is.
This visible world is nothing whatsoever; thus the sky of consciousness is established.
Everything exists everywhere exactly as it is experienced; nothing whatsoever exists here that has not been experienced.
This peaceful, existent, and singular reality remains thus, pervasive and free from division; therefore, remain without fear.
This clear sky is the form of the great consciousness, dense with the appearance of a cave of rock and profoundly tranquil;
the two views that "it exists" or "it does not exist" do not apply anywhere, for whatever exists shines forth as that very reality alone.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Chapter on Nirvana," [spoken by] Rāma:
How could there be an end to the suffering of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others— who, though they were virtuous, were treated as if they were non-existent like children, yakṣas, and piśācas?
Vasiṣṭha said: O descendant of Raghu, listen to this which was spoken by Yama when he was requested by those very servants of Yama for the sake of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa at that very time.
When Dāma and the others shall experience separation and hear their own story, they will undoubtedly become liberated.
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, where, when, and how will they hear this account of my own life? By whom will this sequence of stories be narrated?
Vasiṣṭha said:
In a small pool on the shore of the Great Lotus Lake in Kaśmīra,
these two repeatedly experienced a succession of births as fish.
With their intentions fettered and fickle, they will meet their end in time;
right there in that lotus pond, they will become cranes.
There, amidst garlands of white water-lilies and clusters of lotuses,
among the excellent creeping vines of moss and the undulations of the waves;
Upon swings of blooming white lotuses and upon creepers of blue water-lilies, amidst streaks of clouds formed by masses of spray, and within the movements of cool whirlpools;
Having enjoyed the pleasures of Lake Sarasa, those ornaments of the world,
after sporting there for a very long time, have now sufficiently attained purity.
Having attained the proper means for liberation, they will become dissociated from it,
just as the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas are separated by chance through their attainment of distinct states.
Within the region of Kaśmīra, there will be a city adorned with mountains,
a glorious place known by the name Adhiṣṭhāna.
In its center there will be a peak named Pradyumnaśikhara,
like the small bud of a lotus within its calyx.
On that summit of the mountain, some king will build a palace,
a great sala tree reaching to the clouds, like another peak upon a peak.
In the interior of a breach in the wall at the northeast corner of the house, marked by grasses tossed incessantly and without rest by the wind; MU 4,14.14.
In the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya), there will be a demon, a serpent, and a sparrow;
like a student who has heard little at the outset, it chirps meaninglessly.
At that very time, there will be a king there named Śrī Yaśaskaradeva, like another Śakra in heaven.
Within the house of the Dānava named Dāma, there will be a mosquito;
with a soft sound, it will dwell in a hole on the back of a large pillar.
At that time, in that very city called Adhiṣṭhāna,
there will also be a monastery known as the Ratnāvalī Monastery.
In that place, there will be a minister of that land known as Narasiṃha,
who will perceive bondage and liberation as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
In his house there shall be a bird that acts as a plaything—
a magical demon named Kaṭa, who has fashioned a cage for himself.
That lion among men, the king’s minister, will relate this narrative composed in verses concerning Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others.
Having heard that story, Kaṭa Krakara will remember his own true nature; with the false sense of "I" stilled within, he will attain supreme Nirvāṇa.
The sparrow dwelling on the edge of the Pradyumna peak,
having likewise approached and heard this discourse of his own, will attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Even a mosquito, having come to dwell within a wound inside the wood of the royal palace,
will attain peace through that very circumstance upon hearing [the teaching].
O Rāghava, the sparrow from Pradyumna’s horn, the mosquito from the royal palace, and the cricket from the monastery— all these shall attain liberation.
This entire sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and Krama has been told to you;
this very world-process is but an illusion, empty and yet exceedingly radiant.
When not fully understood, it causes one to wander like a mirage mistaken for an ocean;
when fully understood, it subsides like a mirage mistaken for an ocean.
Thus, even from a high position,
deluded fools fall downward through the power of ignorance regarding the True Self, just like Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Where is the capacity to endure the crushing of Mount Meru and Mandara by the knitting of eyebrows,
and where is the state of being a mere mole within a wound inside the wood of the Rājagṛha palace?
Where is the state of having the orbs of the sun and moon felled by a mere slap of the hand,
and where is the state of being a bird in a hole in the wall of a house on Mount Pradyumna?
Where is the lifting of Mount Meru with a hand trembling in the play of plucking flowers, and where is the state of being a mere young parrot in the house of Nṛsiṃha at Āṣyaśṛṅga?
For the space of consciousness, though its radiance is falsely colored by passion (rajas),
perceives itself as if it were deformed, even while not abandoning its own true nature.
By its own delusion of latent impressions— which, though unreal, appears as if real— a living being passes from one state to another, like the perception of water in a mirage.

Those who, through the very intellect of their own natural flow, remain free from latent impressions, having realized by means of the scripture that "this visible world is unreal," cross over the ocean of existence.
Those who cause the dry arguments of false doctrines to resound with cries of distress quickly go to the waters of the abyss; they do not destroy their own misfortune.
O dear one, for those who proceed by the path established through one's own experience and in accordance with the scriptures,
there is no destruction, just as there is none for those who are falling [toward the earth].
"The thought of the wise is: 'May this be mine, may that be mine';
yet because of their own wretchedness and misfortune, not even ashes remain for them."
All calamities abandon that noble-souled one who always regards even the three worlds as a blade of grass, just as moisture leaves withered grass.
The lords of the world protect him in whom the wonder of pure being constantly vibrates within, like the indivisible cosmic egg of Brahmā.
Even in the face of a terminal calamity, one must never take pleasure in what is contrary to the proper order;
for even Rāhu died while drinking the nectar in violation of the proper order.
Those who take refuge in the sun of contact with true scriptures and holy beings, which bestows fierce illumination,
do not again fall under the power of the blindness of delusion.
All calamities inevitably come to an end and pass away;
prosperity inevitably comes to one whose fame is to be purchased by their virtues.
Those who are dissatisfied with virtues, those who lack passion for learning, and those who are addicted to falsehoods—these men are beasts; all others are different.
Hari surely resides in the embodied form of those oceans of milk, whose moonlight-like fame illuminates the sky of the hearts of people.
Everything that was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed, and all sights to be seen have been seen; what else remains but non-attachment to further enjoyments for the sake of shattering worldly existence?
Abide according to the sequence, according to the scriptures, according to custom, and according to established order; let the unreal greed for enjoyments within you be released.
Let your fame be cultivated through virtues that reach the heavens;
for objects of enjoyment never protect one who has encountered death.
Those whose moon-white fame is sung by beautiful Siddha women with melodies throughout the expanse of the sky—they truly live; all others are dead.
Who, applying the supreme human effort and undertaking excellent exertion, would not partake in success through conduct that is free from agitation and in accordance with the scriptures? MU 4.14.49.
One who dwells according to the scriptures should not be in haste for the attainments;
an attainment that has ripened over a long period of time will be more robust.
Let legal proceedings be conducted according to the scriptures— free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue, and devoid of greed and constraint— so that they do not come to ruin.
The living soul has gone into concealment within the decaying blind wells of worldly existences;
let it now be drawn out from there by you, who possess abundant power.
From this point forward, do not go further down and down again;
let this scripture be mastered as a weapon for warding off calamities.
In battle, where elephants are violently torn asunder and lives are cast away, what need have noble men for mere wealth? Let them look instead to the sacred scriptures.
Reflect with the thought, "This is a mango tree; this is a neem tree.
Whether by yourself or prompted by another, do not proceed like cattle.
Bestowing misfortune, wretched, devoid of virtue, and lacking discernment—this dense and long-lasting great sleep must be abandoned; awaken!
Do not remain asleep like an old, sluggish tortoise; slowly rise up and accept exertion for the sake of pacifying old age and death.
The attainment of wealth leads to misfortune; a flood of enjoyments brings about the disease of existence;
all prosperities result in calamity; and victory everywhere is a lack of self-respect.

For those engaged in worldly affairs, happiness is achieved through action that accords with the ways of the world, proceeds from rational deliberation, and is not in conflict with the conduct prescribed by the scriptures.
For one whose conduct is beautiful through good behavior, whose life is lived in seclusion, and who does not crave even the slightest pleasure amidst the sufferings of saṃsāra,
his lifespan, fame, virtues, and prosperity flourish together for the sake of the noble fruit, like a spring creeper in full bloom.
In the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," Vasiṣṭha said:
Because every excellence bears fruit, everything is indeed possible everywhere and at all times; therefore, one should never abandon one's own virtuous exertion.
By propitiating the Lord of the Lake, who bestows joy and delight upon friends, kinsmen, and relatives, even death was utterly conquered.
Even the gods exist in a state of total inferiority, being crushed by the Dānavas—
who are rich in noble Dānava power— just as lotus ponds are trampled by elephants.
At the sacrifice of King Marutta,
the great seer Saṃvarta fashioned another creation, including gods and asuras, like Brahmā himself.
The brahminhood attained through asceticism— which is difficult to reach— was repeatedly sought by Viśvāmitra, who was endowed with great excellence.
By such an unfortunate man as Upamanyu, who consumed the water of the *piṣṭātaka*— as difficult to obtain as a life-prolonging elixir (*rasāyana*)— the Ocean of Milk was won over.
Striking down Trailokyamalla, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others like blades of grass through the firmness of his superior skill, Kāla was himself struck down by Śveta.
Having won over Yama through her affection and having made a verbal agreement with him,
Sāvitrī brought back her husband Satyavān from the other world.
There is no excellence in this world that does not have a manifest fruit;
therefore, one who possesses every excellence must be investigated.
Self-knowledge is that which eradicates the root of all perceptions of states of pleasure and pain; therefore, one should cultivate excellence in it.
By this extremely corrupt vision, which seeks its objects through such a distorted perspective,
no happiness free from affliction can be attained, except for suffering.
Non-quiescence is the supreme Brahman, and quiescence is the supreme state;
even though this is so, nevertheless, know this tranquility to be Śaṅkara.
Having abandoned conceit and resorted to eternal tranquility,
one should cultivate noble qualities through wisdom and attend upon virtuous people.
Neither austerities, nor sacred fords, nor scriptures conquer you in crossing the ocean of saṃsāra as effectively as the service of the virtuous.
He whose greed, delusion, and anger diminish day by day as he conducts his own duties according to the scriptures— he is a virtuous person.
Through association with one who knows the inner self, his intellect proceeds in such a way that he perceives the absolute non-existence of the visible world.
But because of the absolute non-existence of the visible world, only the Supreme remains;
through the power of the absence of anything else, the individual soul quickly dissolves right there.
The visible object has not arisen, nor did it exist, nor will it ever be;
even in the present it does not exist at all, for only the supreme, which is beyond being known, exists.
This has been demonstrated by a thousand arguments and is being demonstrated even now;
for what is experienced by everyone, I shall indeed demonstrate at this moment.
Just as this entire triple world is peaceful, being the sky of consciousness, so too is this reality;
how and in what way could non-existence or the like possibly exist here?
The beautiful, flickering mind experiences wonder within its own restless nature;
that by which it does so is itself understood to be this very world.

Experience, which takes the form of the three worlds, is the orb of rays from the sun of consciousness; O you who are free from boastfulness, tell me, where is the difference between the moon and its rays? MU 4.15.22.
The opening and closing of this consciousness-vision by its very nature are these two:
the setting and the rising of the experience of the world-form.
The referent of "I," when not fully understood, is a stain upon the sky of ultimate reality;
but the referent of "I," when fully understood, becomes the very sky of ultimate reality.
When the sense of "I" is fully understood, it no longer exists as "I";
it becomes one with the self of the consciousness-ether, just as water merges with water.
The world of perception, beginning with the "I," does not exist at all in reality;
why, then, must it necessarily remain for one who investigates the "I"?
Even among those of dull intellect, the notion of a ghost arises toward one who is not a ghost;
yet this does not occur in children whose inner faculties are pure, because of their capacity for discernment.
As long as the moonlight of consciousness remains shrouded within by the thick clouds of egoism,
the night-lily of ultimate reality does not attain its full bloom.
When this word "I," along with its referent, has been wiped away by consciousness itself,
what room is there for the mere conceptualization of craving for hell, heaven, liberation, and the like?
As long as the cloud of egoism expands within the heart,
so long does the cluster of *kuṭaja* blossoms of craving continue to bloom.
When the sun of consciousness has been eclipsed and the cloud of egoism stands in its place, only dullness persists; it never attains luminosity in any way whatsoever.
This ego-sense, falsely imagined by itself, is close at hand;
it leads only to suffering and not to joy, like a yakṣa conjured by a child's delusion.
The sense of "I," which is falsely imagined through delusion, bestows further ignorance,
producing an endless cycle of saṃsāra, just as in the case of a wicked-minded person regarding a rope and similar objects.
There is no greater darkness in this world than the expansive delusion of thinking "I am this [body]";
such a source of misfortune has never existed in saṃsāra, nor will it ever exist.
Whatever comes here, whether pleasure or pain, like a whirling firebrand, that is the unfolding manifestation of the wheel of egoism.
For him who has planted in his heart the painful sprout of egoism,
the forest of saṃsāra— with its thousand branches and difficult to cut— has taken root.
The sense of "I" is the sprout of the trees of birth, which are inexhaustible by nature;
"this is mine" are their branches, spreading out in thousands.

Objects arising from latent impressions appear like the crackling of wood being split or like the succession of the roar of waves— such as the sounds *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha* produced by the bursting of wind-blown sores.
You, being free from the sense of "I," should bring to a halt the wheel of saṃsāra, which has the great navel of egoism, by restraining yourself.
As long as the darkness of the sense of "I" expands within the forest of the person,
so long do these female demons of thought-intoxication prowl about.
For that lowest of men who is seized by the demon of egoism,
neither tantras nor mantras can bring peace to him, for he is without a protector.
Rāma:
When the pure Self, which is consciousness alone and resembles a mirror, remains stainless, the ego-sense appears as its reflection; therefore, what room is there here for verbal designation?
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāghava, this wondrous manifestation of egoism is not an inherent property of the object;
it is a matter produced by latent impressions (vāsanā) and is pacified through human effort.
"I am not, nor does the glory of wealth belong to me; where do pleasure and pain abide?"—from such contemplation of the nature of things, the ego-sense does not arise.
"This splendor of Indra’s net is false; what use have I for attachment or aversion?"—through such internal inquiry, the ego-sense does not arise.
Thinking, "I am not in the self, nor does this visible splendor belong to me," through such peaceful conduct, the ego-sense does not increase.
For when the view of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted regarding "I" and "the world" has ceased within,
and equanimity has become serene, the ego-sense no longer functions.
Rāma:
What is the form of egoism, O Lord, and how is it abandoned?
Whether it possesses a body or is bodiless, what becomes of one when it has been cast off?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, there are three kinds of egoism (ahaṅkāra) here in the three worlds;
two are excellent and the other is to be abandoned. Listen, I shall tell you.
"I am this entire universe; I am the Supreme Self, the Infallible One.
That supreme consciousness which realizes "there is nothing else" is indeed the true ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti).
For one who is liberated while living, this [state] leads to liberation and not to bondage;
its designation as "ego" (ahaṃkāra) is merely imagined and not real.
I am distinct from everything, conceived as even a hundredth part of the tip of a hair;
or else, this supreme second egoity is simply consciousness itself.
For one who is liberated while living, this [state] exists for liberation and not for bondage;
its designation as "ego" (ahaṃkāra) is imagined, not real.
"This [body], consisting merely of hands, feet, and so forth, is I"—
this very conviction is the third, worldly ego (ahaṅkāra), and it is indeed trivial.
This evil-minded one is to be avoided; he is known as the supreme enemy.
A living being struck by him does not grow again.
With their minds dwarfed by this powerful enemy who inflicts manifold calamities, people sink into nothing but distress.
By long abandoning this wicked egoism through its very existence,
the living being, possessing the refined ego, attains the state of liberation as the Blessed One.
Having determined that "I am not this body," which is the very form of the fault of worldly egoism, its abandonment is the teaching of the great ones.
Even if one accepts the first two forms of ego as being extraordinary, the third form of ego must be abandoned; it is worldly and brings about suffering.
"Indeed, through this wicked pride, Dāma, Vyāla,
and Kaṭa have reached that state which is painful even to mention in stories."
Rāma:
O Brahmin, having abandoned this third worldly egoity from his mind, what state must a person attain to obtain what is beneficial for the self?
Vasiṣṭha:
This [woman] must indeed be abandoned; having renounced her who brings only suffering, in whatever manner a man remains established, to that same extent he attains the Supreme.
If a person free from sin remains contemplating these [elements] within the previously mentioned state of egoity, he attains that supreme state.
Then, having abandoned even those [notions] and being devoid of all ego-conceit, he remains established;
nevertheless, he ascends to the highest state.
At all times and with every effort, worldly conceit must be abandoned by one of great intelligence for the sake of awakening to supreme bliss.
By abandoning the diseases residing in the body, demerit, and the wicked ego, there is no higher good than this;
this alone is the supreme state.
Having abandoned this gross worldly sense of "I" through the realization of true being, a person does not fall downward, whether remaining still or engaged in worldly activity.
For a person of great intelligence whose egoism has been completely stilled, the diseases of worldly enjoyments do not taste sweet,
just as the juices of potent poisons do not appeal to one who is well-satiated.
When sensual enjoyments no longer provide satisfaction, what else indeed can the mind of a man turn toward, when the darkness has been dispelled and the supreme good lies before him?
O Rāghava, by the mere abandonment of the pursuit of egoism,
which arises solely from human effort, one crosses the ocean of worldly existence.
Thinking, "I am not, nor indeed is there anything that is mine," and "all this, in its entirety, is indeed I alone"—
having thus established in his mind that venerable consciousness which has found its firm footing, the great-souled one attains the supreme state.
In the narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, the sixteenth canto, titled "The Examination of Egoism," Vasiṣṭha says:
In this regard, listen as I tell you what occurred in the city of Śambara— which was like a mountain— after Dāma and the others had departed.
Thus, when the entire army of Śambara had fallen from the sky, its established order destroyed and utterly perished like a mass of clouds in autumn.

Having spent several years with his army conquered by the gods, that Dānava, intent on slaying the gods once again, reflected: He, whose army had been defeated by the gods, having spent several years [in exile], the Dānava, once more intent on slaying the gods, reflected.
Those Asuras, Dāma and the others, whom I created through my illusory power (māyā),
conceived a false sense of ego within themselves due to their folly regarding the battle.
Now I shall create other Dānavas, arisen through my illusory power;
moreover, I make them knowers of their own scriptures and endowed with discernment.
Then, through the thorough knowledge of reality, they will abandon the egoism that arose from false contemplation, and they will conquer those gods.
Having reflected thus, the lord of the Daityas created such lords of the Dānavas through his illusory power (*māyā*), just as the ocean produces bubbles.
All-knowing, knowers of the objects of knowledge, free from passion, and devoid of sin; acting solely according to what has been attained, these supreme ones have cultivated their selves.
Marked by the names Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa,
they possess purified minds and regard the entire world as if it were a blade of grass.
Having reached the earth, those Daityas covered the sky,
roaring with weapons for lightning, like clouds in the rainy season.
They fought equally even against the gods for many groups of years;
yet, through the power of discernment, they never succumbed to egoism.
As long as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) "this is mine" arises within them, so long does [the ego] go toward unreality through the inquiry, "Who is this? What am I? (MU 4.16.12).
"The body is non-existent, the consciousness is pure; who am I?"—through such inquiry, these [fears and other afflictions] did not arise for them. (MU 4.16.13)
"The body is unreal and does not exist; pure consciousness alone abides in the Self.
There is no such thing as 'I' nor anything else. Having thus resolved, the Asuras became [liberated].
Then, by those heroes who were free from egoism, fearless of old age and death, who imitated what had been attained and followed the path currently trodden—

By those whose intellects are eternally unattached, who have destroyed all [defilements] yet do not consider themselves destroyers, who are liberated from the net of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and who, having accomplished their task, are non-doers; // MU 4.16.16 //
"Thinking, 'This is the work of the Lord; this must be done,' they are intent upon their vow, free from passion, devoid of hatred, and always possessed of an even vision."
That divine army was struck down, devoured, wounded, and scorched by the Dānavas, Bhīma, Bhāsa, Druta, and others, just as the beauty of one's own entrails is consumed by those who eat.
Then the army of the gods, crushed by Bhīma,
Bāṣpa, and Druha, fled with great speed like the Gaṅgā falling from the Himavat.
That army of the Asuras went for refuge to the god who reclines upon the ocean of milk, just as a garland of clouds driven by the wind seeks shelter on a mountain.
Viṣṇu comforted that terrified army of the gods,
like a leader consoles a solitary woman pursued by serpents.
Then that host of gods dwelt in the cavern of the Ocean of Milk for as long as the Blessed One did not set out for the sake of destroying the enemy.
Then a fierce battle took place between Śauri and Śambara,
like an untimely dissolution of the world in which the great mountain ranges were cast up into the sky.
In that battle, the Daitya Śambara, along with his army and mounts, was subdued;
struck down by Nārāyaṇa, he departed for the city of Viṣṇu.
But Bhīma, Bāṣkala, and Druhyu were brought to rest by Viṣṇu himself in that treacherous battle, like lamps extinguished by the wind.
For when they have indeed reached peace, being entirely free from latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), then their course becomes like that of lamps going out.
Therefore, O Rāma, the mind is bound by latent impressions and liberated when free from them; quickly attain the state of being free from impressions through discernment.
Through the correct perception of reality, latent impressions dissolve;
and with the dissolution of latent impressions, the mind attains tranquility like a lamp [when its fuel is exhausted].
There is nothing whatsoever here that truly exists which one can cultivate;
therefore, the realization that "cultivation itself does not exist" is right vision.
Where the two words "vāsanā" (latent impression) and "citta" (mind), which are endowed with their respective meanings,
dissolve through the vision of reality— that is the supreme state.
This entire world is indeed the Self; who could conceptualize what, or where?
Conceptualization itself does not exist at all—this is the correct vision.
The mind, enveloped by latent impressions, attains its state here; that very same mind, when liberated from them, is called "liberated."
When the mind has become settled in various forms such as jars and cloths,
that very mind should be quickly brought to peace, like a false yakṣa that has arisen.
Just as the mind was transformed by the forms of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa,
so too was the mind transformed by the forms of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa.
O Raghava, may the principle of Bhima, Bhasa, and Druta be yours;
O Raghava, let not the principle of Dama, Vyala, and Kata be yours.
O Rāma, this was formerly told to me by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā;
today it has been told by me to you, my disciple who is exceedingly wise.
Therefore, O Rāghava, let not the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours;
O sinless one, let the logic of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Druṭa be yours forever.
This path of worldly existence, having arrived at the contemplation of phenomenal becoming, is a thicket of incessant pleasure and pain;
yet for one engaged in worldly activity, it perishes through constant non-attachment toward the elements of existence.
The seventeenth canto, named "The Narrative of Dāma and Others," is completed. Vasiṣṭha:
Victorious are those ever-brave and virtuous ones by whom their own mind— intoxicated by the wine of ignorance and ever-outward toward sense objects— has been utterly conquered.
For this saṃsāra, which bestows all manner of afflictions and suffering, there is only one means: the restraint of one's own mind.
Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped:
bondage consists solely in the desire for enjoyment; its abandonment is called liberation.
What is the use of other collections of treatises? Listen to this alone: whatever is pleasant, my dear, let all that be regarded as poison or fire.
Sense objects are like poisonous enjoyments; they must be investigated again and again.
For they are undesirable when abandoned, yet they bring happiness when cultivated [with discernment].
A mind perfumed by latent impressions (vāsanā) gives rise to expansive defects,
just as ground strewn with thorn-seeds produces a proliferation of thorns.
The intellect, whose womb contains no latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and which is devoid of mental proliferation,
having seen neither passion nor hatred, gradually attains supreme tranquility.
The intellect, containing within it pure latent impressions, always gives birth to excellent qualities,
just as the earth containing superior seeds produces fruit-bearing sprouts in due time.
Through the continuous cultivation of virtuous states, when the mind has become serene and the dense cloud of false knowledge has gradually subsided; MU 4.17.9.
When kindness had increased like the moon in the bright fortnight,
and when merit had spread through discernment like the radiance of the sun over the world;
When her inner fortitude had grown strong, she remained as if liberated from Kīcaka,
like the luster of the moon established within after it has emerged from a cloud.
When the cool-shaded tree of association with the virtuous has borne fruit,
and the straight-trunked tree of meditative absorption drips with the excellent nectar of bliss;
The mind becomes free from dualities, devoid of desire, and untroubled; its restlessness is stilled, and it is free from purposeless striving, greed, delusion, fear, and disease.
One whose doubts regarding the meaning of the scriptures have perished, from whom all curiosity has vanished,
who has cast off the web of conceptual constructions, is liberated while living and remains untainted.
It is effortless, free from reproach, indifferent, and devoid of mental anguish;
it is with sorrow and mist thoroughly stilled, unattached, and liberated from knots.
Having destroyed his own son born of his senses— the charioteer who is the cage of his thirsty wife—
he accomplishes his own self, which is the supreme goal.
One spontaneously abandons the conceptual constructions that cause the body's plumpness; like a loyal servant, one casts off the body like a blade of grass for the sake of the master’s tasks.
The rise of the mind is its destruction; the destruction of the mind is the great awakening.
The mind of the wise man goes toward destruction, while the mind of the ignorant man increases.
The wheel of the world is mind alone; the circle of mountains is the mind.
The sky is the mind, the body is the mind; the friend is the mind, and the enemy is the mind.

That forgetfulness of the self-nature of the mind-essence which is turbid with conceptual construction is called the "mind" (manas); this is the latent impression (vāsanā) that partakes in cyclic existence.

The reality of consciousness (cittattva), when affected by the descent of the object of thought, when its name has been slightly impaired as being "mere consciousness" (cinmātra), and when it is somewhat turbid with conceptualization, is called the individual soul (jīva).
That which has fallen into the state of being an object of thought, having become established as a notion and arrived at a state of ignorance,
is itself imagined with further expansion through the nature of that mind.
The transmigrating person is not the self, nor is it the body, nor the blood;
everything such as the body is inert, while the embodied one is like space, untainted.
When the body is cut into pieces, nothing remains other than blood and such;
when the trunk of a plantain tree is split open, nothing remains other than its sheaths.
Know that the mind is the living person; it has assumed that very form.
By means of itself, it grasps itself as something fashioned by the fragments of its own conceptual constructions.
A person spreads out the threads of his own conceptual constructions and weaves them extensively,
just as a silkworm creates a cocoon for its own confinement.
Having abandoned this wandering through bodies, it again assumes another body in another place and time, just as a sprout attains the state of a leaf.
Whatever kind of latent impression this mind possesses, such it becomes;
with whatever state of mind a person sleeps, that he sees in a dream at night.
A seed that is sour, sprinkled with a sour juice, sweet, and colored with honey, yet sprinkled with the paste of *prativiṣā*, becomes pungent.
Through a great and auspicious latent impression, the mind becomes great;
by means of Indra’s mental kingdom, a person becomes an experiencer of the dream-state of Indrahood.
Through base latent impressions, the mind attains a fragile state of baseness;
like one healthy who, due to the delusion of a demon, sees demons at night.
When the mind is expansive in its purity, turbidity finds no footing;
likewise, when it is expansive in its turbidity, clarity finds no footing.
When there is extensive turbidity in the mind, a fruit of that same nature arises;
likewise, when there is extensive purity, a fruit of that same nature arises.
Even when exhausted, the most excellent person does not abandon the noble path;
like the moon striving unceasingly to fulfill its course, he persists with effort.
Here there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither one to be bound nor any binding;
this is merely an illusion arisen from delusion, like a creeper of Indra’s net.
This saṃsāra, consisting of what is unreal, has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas, arises from the sequence of a mirage, and manifests like the optical illusion of two moons.
The false conviction that arises as "I am not infinite" or "I am miserable" dissolves through the certainty: "I am infinite; I am supreme."
This cultivation of the notion of a cognizer within one's own all-pervading and pure self—
this is that bondage in the world, fashioned by one's own conceptual construction.
Devoid of the states of bondage and liberation, and free from duality and unity—this entire reality is the existence of Brahman; such is the ultimate truth.
When the mind has attained purity and is unattached to all views, it perceives Brahman as if it had reached a state beyond the mind; it is not otherwise.
The mind, having attained purity through the waters of the auspicious continuum,
takes on the vision of Brahma, just as a white cloth takes on the dye.

O sinless one, when the duality of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has been destroyed through the true contemplation that "everything indeed is my self," what can be said of bondage and liberation?
For one whose mind has been purified by the teachings, dispassion, and wisdom, the body—
like a noble gem— melts away and spiritual luster emerges.
Know that the one-pointedness of the mind which arises from attaining oneness with an object is a vision of imperfect knowledge, perishing in an instant.
When the mind remains completely dissolved, having abandoned all perceptions of the visible, both external and internal, then that state has been attained.
This clear perception of the visible object is necessarily composed of unreality;
know that being composed of that [unreality] is the very nature of the mind, and nothing else.
Because it is perishable at its beginning and end, it is likewise unreal in the middle;
therefore, those with ignorant minds suffer even though [the treasure] is held in their own hands.
Without the realization that "this world is indeed the Self," the splendor of the visible world bestows suffering; otherwise, however, it is the sole giver of both enjoyment and liberation.

The notion that "the water is one thing and the wave another" is ignorance due to perceived multiplicity; whereas the realization that "this wave is indeed the water" is true knowledge due to perceived unity.
From ignorance arises suffering, which consists of that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted;
however, through the absence of that [ignorance] by virtue of knowledge, infinity alone remains.
And because it is fashioned by conceptual construction, the form of the mind is composed of unreality;
tell me, O Rāghava, what affliction can there be when that which is unreal is destroyed?
Just as a kinsman who is not affectionate is seen with a mind free from attachment and aversion, so too do you see the cage of your own perceptions.

Just as one is not stained by pleasure and pain due to a relative who is not affectionate, so too is one not stained by them due to the thorough realization of the "otherness" of the collection of principles that constitute the self.
That beginningless, auspicious knowledge which lies between the seer and the seen—
in that truth, the mind becomes tranquil, just as dust settles when the wind has ceased.
When the wind of the mind has been stilled, the dust of the body subsides;
once again, the mist of cyclic existence does not arise in the city of saṃsāra.

When the rainy season of latent impressions has ended and their persistence has ceased, when dullness has come to rest and produced a trembling in the heart, and when the mud has reached a state of drying; MU 4.17.56.

Within the great forest of the heart, where the creepers of dry craving grow, where the clusters of sense-faculties are unexhausted, and where the dense clouds of false knowledge have been pierced; MU_4,17.57.
The mist of delusion is dissipated like the night at dawn;
that dullness departs somewhere, just as poison destroyed by a mantra.
On the mountain of the body, the rivers from the nine apertures do not flow forth;
the peacocks of fierce volitions do not emerge with their radiant wings outspread.
The hollow of its own consciousness-sky attains supreme purity;
the sun of the living soul (jīvāditya), exceedingly clear and of great glory, shines forth intensely.
Freed from the heavy burden of delusion and having attained supreme solitude,
the great quarters of space, cleansed and having reached tranquility, shine with exceeding beauty.
The stainless Mañjarī of Joy shines intensely,
cooling the circle of the quarters like moonlight in the autumnal sky.
The ground of discernment, when thoroughly secluded, attains a state of intense fruitfulness, abounding in supreme bliss through the manifestation of all perfections.
The interior of the world becomes exceedingly beautiful with its supreme light, encompassing mountains and forests, and possesses a very clear and cool shade.
The lake of the heart, its clear and stainless lotus-bud interior expanded by excellent tranquility and broadened by crystal-like purity, attains its true state.
The restless bee of one's own impure ego-sense departs from the calyx of the heart-lotus to some unknown place, never to be seen again.
He becomes free from attachment, all-pervading, and the leader of all;
devoid of latent impressions, with a tranquil mind, he is the sovereign in the city of his own body.

When the mind has become a lamp for the self through the attainment of discernment and is entirely free from defilement, the one of steady intellect, beholding the states of existence as tasteless and fraught with the fear of decay, dwells joyfully within the city of the body, free from all feverish distress.
The eighteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of Quiescence," [spoken by] Rāma:
O Brahman, tell me again for the sake of increasing my understanding how this universe is situated within the conscious Self that transcends the universe.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as waves exist in water in a latent state, unmanifest yet destined to arise,
so too do creations exist within the essence of consciousness, neither truly existing nor non-existing due to their imperceptibility.
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not perceived due to its subtlety, so too the part consisting of consciousness, though all-pervading, is not observed because it is without parts.
Just as a female image within a gem is neither non-existent nor existent, so too this creation exists within the Self— neither abiding nor not abiding.
Just as the sky is not touched by clouds that rest in the sky and have the sky as their support,
so too the supreme consciousness is not touched by creations that reside within consciousness and have consciousness as their support.
Just as fire is reflected in the oceans but not on the earth,
so too consciousness is perceived only within the subtle bodies (puryaṣṭakas) and not in the gross physical bodies.
Free from all conceptual constructions and devoid of all perceptions,
this very consciousness is designated by such terms as "the indestructible self" and "ultimate reality."
Subtler than a hundredth part of the space within an atom, she is of an undivided form;
she perceives the single Self whose nature is the entire, stainless cycle of existence.
Just as the vast diversity consisting of waves and so forth in the ocean of water does not manifest apart from the water itself,
so too [the world] does not manifest apart from pure consciousness alone.
Because it accumulates (*cinoti*) that which is accumulated (*cita*) and that which is to be accumulated (*cetya*), this world remains within the Self.
However, in the Knower (*jña*) and the ignorant (*ajña*), a state of difference arises from the conceptualization that "there is something else."
Among the ignorant, she takes the form of the multitude of the insubstantial and fierce cycle of existence;
among the wise, she is of the nature of pure light alone, being the single essence of all.
By virtue of experience, she is eternally the illuminator of the sun and other luminaries;
she is the taster of all existents, and the creative contemplation for those who bring about worldly existence.
It neither sets nor rises, it neither arises nor stands still;
it neither goes nor comes, it is neither here nor not here, yet it is consciousness (cit).
This very consciousness, pure in form, established within itself by its own nature,
O Rāghava, thus unfolds as the manifold world called the universe.
Just as light radiates through masses of light and water through surges of water, so does consciousness manifest through the vibrant activities of creation.
By its own nature, it is named Consciousness; it is all-pervading, arisen as the Self, manifest yet unmanifest, partless yet bearing parts.
Abandoning the infinite state by failing to employ one's own power of self-turning,
one proceeds slowly toward the state of command with the thought, "I am he."
When this manifoldness has taken root through the process of cyclic existence,
one comes to abide in the state of grasping at existence and non-existence, and of accepting and rejecting.
The subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) performs hundreds of vibrations, yet it neither acts nor does not act;
it attains growth like a mass of sprouts situated within the hollow of the earth's womb.
Space assumes the quality of vacuity, which is not in conflict with any form;
wind possesses the sole property of motion; and water has the nature of taste. MU 4.18.20.
The earth is firm, the worlds abide in manifest splendor,
and time exists through its reckoning to impose both obstruction and permission.
The flower, with its gathered filaments, slowly reaches the end of the creeper;
the joy of the sap within the hollow of the earth returns to the state of grass upon the ground.
The delicate sprouts at their base yield fruit, consisting of mere traces of sap;
these lines take on the arrangement of rows of young shoots.
The atoms sustain their arrangement upon Indra’s bow;
through this configuration, there is a yoga that is ever new and uninterrupted.
Heaps of flowers and sprouts wait upon the spring; the manifestations of forest fires arrive as the rule of summer.
The dark lines of clouds long for the rainy season,
and all the masses of fruit pursue the autumn.
In the winter, the ten directions become laughing with snow; in the cold season, winds chilled by frost reduce the water to the state of ice.
Time does not abandon its own boundary consisting of these ages;
creations pass away with the playful motion of a river's flood of waves.
Necessity attains its established state, acting with the skill of stability;
the earth, whose nature is to support, remains steadfast until the dissolution of all things.
Within this world-system, there are fourteen kinds of beings,
possessing various modes of conduct and dwellings, and various forms of manifestation.
Again and again they dissolve, and again and again they are born,
like bubbles in water that falls in a continuous succession of streams.

It comes, it goes, it stands still, it cries out loudly, it acquires its own objects, and it runs about within the mass of births; like one driven mad, with its mental formations fixed and its efforts exerted, the wretched multitude of beings is rendered helpless by Kṛtānta (Death).
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Sun of Consciousness," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, all these series of transmigrations, consisting of both the stable and the moving,
come forth from and return again to Brahman by its very nature.
All this has arisen from itself and functions as mutual causes;
perishing through mutual interaction, it dissolves back into itself alone.
Just as a vibration appearing like a pillar occurs within the depths of unfathomable water by itself,
so too this world— both unreal and real— is perceived as consciousness alone.
Just as rivers are seen to vanish from the heat into the sky itself, which is devoid of appearance,
even so these perceptions of creation are perceived within the reality of consciousness.
Just as, under the influence of intoxication, one's own self appears as if it were another,
so too, due to its nature as consciousness, the element of consciousness itself remains as if it were non-existent.
This consciousness is neither existent nor non-existent, for it does not stand by being located therein;
it is neither distinct nor non-distinct, just as the nature of gold remains the same in bracelets and other ornaments.
O Raghava, that by which you perceive sound, taste, form, and smell—
this is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, which exists pervading all things.
Since the stainless Self is all-pervading and transcends both difference and identity, no second conceptualization exists for it; otherwise, there is none whatsoever anywhere.

Due to the absence of any other aggregate, the auspicious and inauspicious states of existence and non-existence are conceptually constructed; they do not arise from the Self by means of the Self, nor within the Self.
Because desire arises only when an object distinct from oneself is established;
where nothing whatsoever exists apart from one's own self, what indeed could the self desire there? What could it pursue?
What could it approach?
Thus, conceptual constructions such as "this is desired" or "this is undesired" do not touch the Self.
Therefore, by virtue of being desireless, this Self performs nothing at all, because of the identity of the agent, the instrument, and the object.

It does not abide anywhere because the support and the supported are one. Nor is inaction intended for a self devoid of desire, because a second [entity] is impossible under that conception. Therefore, O Rāma! (MU 4.19.10)
You are neither Rāma nor Ārāma; this is the established state of Brahman. Completely liberated from all dualities, become the agent free from the fever of anxiety.
Moreover, O Rāghava:
having performed this various kind of action with vigor, what is it that you must now attain? Tell me, for what is appropriate to be gained from the multitude of beings?
Let there be for you no reliance on the state of being an agent; do not harbor desires in your mind. Be healthy and clear, with a most steady intellect, an ocean of fortitude.

Thinking that even by a person striving and traveling very far, that by which this world is fully satisfied cannot be found here, you should abandon the multitude of objects with your intellect; for you yourself are the Reality, the conscious Self, in the sense of the ultimate truth.
The twentieth canto, titled "The Giving of Instruction," by Vasiṣṭha.
This being the case, that agency which is observed among those who possess such knowledge—whether in sacrifices and the like, or in acts of killing and the like—is unreal;
it does not belong to the ignorant.
For what indeed is called "agency"?

For that determination or conviction regarding acceptability which arises from the intermediate state of mental activity and is designated as "latent impression" (*vāsanā*), is expressed by the term "agency.
Because of such effort, there is the state of being the enjoyer of a corresponding fruit;
for due to agency, a person vibrates in accordance with their latent impressions, and they experience a fruit in accordance with that vibration.
The established doctrine is that the state of being an enjoyer of the fruit is indeed agency (*kartṛtā*). And thus:
whether one acts or does not act, [the result occurs] either in heaven or even in hell.
Whatever kind of latent impression this mind may have, that very thing is experienced by it.
Therefore, agency belongs to those persons who do not know reality, whether they act or do not act;
but it does not belong to those who have known reality, because they are free from latent impressions (*avāsanatva*).
For one who has known reality, whose latent impressions have become slackened, does not pursue the fruits even while acting.
One whose intellect is unattached performs merely the movement of the limbs;
even when a result is attained, one does not experience it, thinking, "All this is indeed the Self. For what distinct thing could be experienced by whom?
Therefore, the knower of reality, even while acting, does nothing at all;
whereas the ignorant person, though not performing the movement of the limbs, experiences the entire fruit of action consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Even without acting, he acts with a submerged mind.
Whatever the mind does, that becomes done;
whatever it does not do, that remains undone.
Therefore, the mind alone is the agent, not the body.
This saṃsāra has come from the mind alone;
it exists as consisting of mind, as nothing but mind.
But for the wise, everything is utterly tranquil.
"It is not that it was non-existent;
rather, the Knower alone exists here.
For those who possess the Self, that mind has attained supreme tranquility, like the water of a mirage when the rain-cloud pours down.
Like a drop of dew melted by the fierce heat of the sun,
it remains having reached the fourth state;
it is neither bliss nor the absence of bliss, neither moving nor unmoving, but steadfast.
The wise know that the knowing of these is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor even something between them.
The knower of reality does not sink into the savor of vibration consisting of latent impressions, like an elephant in a small pond;
the mind of the fool perceives only the land of enjoyment and not the true essence of existence.
And thus, there is this further illustration here.

Even without falling into a pit, a person who has fallen into the mental habituation (*vāsanā*) of falling into a pit experiences the suffering of falling into a pit while lying on a bed or sitting in a seat.
Conversely, even while actually falling into a pit, one whose mind has attained supreme tranquility (*upaśama*) experiences the bliss of lying on a bed or sitting in a seat.
Thus, between two people occupying the same bed or seat, one who did not perform the act of falling becomes effectively the performer of it.
The second person, though the agent of falling into a pit, becomes a non-agent through the power of the mind;
therefore, the established conclusion is that a person consists of whatever his mind is.
Consequently, let your mind remain eternally unattached, whether you are an agent or a non-agent.
Let there be nothing apart from the reality of the Self upon which attachment could be conceived.
Understand that whatever exists in this world, all of it is merely the manifestation of the pure reality of consciousness (*śuddha-cittattva*).
When a person has thus realized the nature of being and known what is to be known, the certainty arises that "this Self is not an object accessible to pleasures and pains."
When the certainty arises that there exist no perceptions of a container and its contents distinct from the self;
when the certainty arises that there are seen no seer, seeing, or object of sight distinct from the self;
and when the certainty arises that there exists nothing—whether active or inactive—distinct from the self.
When the certainty arises that "I am not the body";
when the certainty arises that "I am distinct from all objects, even as much as a thousandth part of the tip of a hair";
and when the certainty arises that "whatever exists here, all that is indeed I."
When the certainty arises— "I am indeed the all-pervading light of consciousness that illumines all reality"—

and when the certainty arises— "I am not an object accessible to pleasure and pain," then for the wise one who remains amidst worldly affairs with a mental state free from feverish distress, joy alone— like moonlight adorning the regions of the world— ornaments him effortlessly in both times of crisis and times of ease.
There is no thought.
Therefore, even while acting, the Knower has become a non-doer,
because the mind is unstained.
He does not experience the fruit of action, even that which is produced by effort such as the movement of hands and feet.
This mind is the seed of all actions, all desires, all states of being, all worlds, and all destinies.
When it is abandoned, all actions are abandoned.
All sufferings are exhausted;
all joys arrive.

Even by mental action, even by that which is performed with effort, the Knower is not assailed, is not rendered helpless, and does not fall into passion, because he is non-different [from the ultimate reality].

Just as a child, while mentally constructing and destroying a city, experiences the mental construction of that city as something uncreated, as if in play, and does not regard it as something to be grasped;
he sees this as uncontrived happiness. And seeing the destruction of the city as if it were uncreated, even while experiencing the suffering as if in play, he does not see it as suffering.
Thus, one who knows the ultimate truth is not defiled even while acting.
Since the quality of being "acceptable" (*upādeyatā*) in all things is wasting away in this world, what could be the cause of suffering?
Furthermore, nothing whatsoever that is acceptable can possibly exist—whether it be indestructible or distinct from the self.

Therefore, this Self is in reality both an agent and a non-agent, both an enjoyer and a non-enjoyer. This agency and enjoyment which are superimposed upon it must necessarily be due to the delusion of incorrect vision (*asamyag-darśana*), and not due to its actual nature.
Through the investigation of things as they truly are, the states of being an agent and an enjoyer do not exist.
Views such as aversion toward or desire for the senses and their objects are seen by those who hold such views, but not by those who do not hold them.
For those whose minds are unattached, there is neither liberation nor saṃsāra in this world.
But for those whose minds are attached, everything exists within as it truly is.
For the knower, only the reality of the self shines forth;
he does not establish duality or unity once duality and unity have been resolved,
nor does he posit the two— existence and non-existence.
And it demonstrates that the state of possessing all powers is non-different from the web of powers.
Therefore:
"There is no bondage, there is no liberation; there is no one to be bound, nor is there a binder."
This suffering arises from lack of awakening; through awakening, it dissolves away.

The notion of bondage in this world is conceived in vain; the notion of liberation in this world is likewise conceived in vain. O Rāma, having renounced everything, free from egoism, established in the Self, and acting upon the earth with wisdom, remain steadfast as a wise man.
The twenty-first canto, titled "The Giving of Instruction," [from] the Rāmāyaṇa:

"O Blessed One, since such a supreme Brahman, distinguished by these qualities, exists, from where could the origin of this creation—variegated in form through ignorance—come? Tell me, O Great-Souled One!
Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Prince, it is this very reality of Brahman that revolves."
Because it possesses all powers, therefore all powers are seen in Brahman: existence and non-existence, duality and unity, beginning and end;
and beyond that, there is nothing else.
Just as masses of water within a great body of water attain manifestation, displaying various forms through successive surges and counter-surges,
so too the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*) itself, gathering consciousness, gathers, sustains, generates, and dissolves all powers— whether consisting of action, speech, or mind.
[This applies] to all individual souls (*jīva*) and all perceptions on every side.
The constant arising of all constituent entities from Brahman occurs perpetually.
The worlds emerge from that Supreme and, remaining within it, they fully dissolve;
they are constantly composed of that very essence, like waves in the ocean.
Rāma:
Venerable sir, this expression of yours is exceedingly profound;
indeed, I do not comprehend the meaning of the sentence.
Where, indeed, is the reality of Brahman, whose mental and sixfold sensory functions have passed away;
and where is this fragile splendor of objects born from it? Such is the construction of the statement.
And if this undertaking has fallen upon Brahman, then it must be of a nature similar to that very Brahman.
Whatever is born from something becomes similar to it;
as, for example, a person from a person,
or a lamp from a lamp.
