From grain comes grain;
therefore, that which has arisen from the changeless must itself be changeless. Now, if this [body] were distinct from the Self, then how could this stain accrue to that stainless one? (MU 4.21.7)
Having heard this, the venerable Brahmarṣi Vasiṣṭha said:
"O sinless one, this world exists as Brahman alone; there is no impurity here."
In the ocean of water, amidst the multitude of waves and ripples, not even a speck of dust is stirred.
O scion of Raghu, no second conceptualization exists here apart from Brahman alone, just as there is no heat apart from fire alone.
Rāma said:
"Brahman is free from suffering, and this world born of it is devoid of dharma;
O Brahman, the meaning of these words of yours is unclear, for I do not understand them."
Vālmīki:
When Rāma had spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha, that tiger among sages, reflected in his mind upon how to instruct the descendant of Raghu.
Yet this understanding of his has not reached its full development;
having attained only a slight degree of clarity, it is still being carried forward here regarding this subject.
But for that wise one whose mind is fully developed, who has known what is to be known,
and who has reached the further shore of the words concerning the means to liberation through discernment;
"No one has any fault; ignorance does not exist within the Self"—when this is said, O Rāghava, one attains rest only when [this truth] has been fully expressed.
But for one whose intellect is only half-developed, it is certainly not fitting to say this;
for by cultivating the state of enjoyment through this view, he perishes.
For one who has attained the supreme vision, the desire for enjoyments no longer arises;
this was appropriate for Rāma at the time when he had established the conclusion that "all is Brahman."
In the beginning, one should purify the disciple through qualities consisting primarily of tranquility and self-restraint;
afterwards, being purified, one should awaken him to the realization: "All this is Brahman; you are that."
He who says "everything is Brahman" to one who is ignorant or only half-awakened casts that person into the snares of the great hells.
For that great-souled one whose awakening is fully realized, whose desire for enjoyment has perished, and who is free from longing, it is right to say that the stain of ignorance no longer exists.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the best of sages, Vasiṣṭha— the sun to the earth who dispels the darkness of ignorance— spoke.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, whether the attribution of a stain exists or does not exist in Brahman—this must be stated at the time of reaching the final conclusion; you yourself will understand it, O sinless one."
But Brahman is all-powerful, all-pervasive, omnipresent, the self of all, and everything itself.
Just as you see a magician performing various deeds that bring the existent into non-existence and the non-existent into existence, so too does He act.
In the same way, the Self is not composed of illusion, yet it appears as if composed of illusion;
just as a supreme magician turns a jar into a cloth.
He makes a cart out of a pit;
he produces a creeper upon a stone,
like the Nandana grove on the golden slopes of Mount Meru.
He produces a stone upon a creeper,
like a cluster of jewels on wish-fulfilling trees;
he superimposes a forest upon the sky.
The grove, like a celestial garden of the Gandharvas,
reaches toward the sky;
it is as if the people have lost their shadows.
He brings the sky down to the surface of the earth,
as if it were the vast courtyard of a royal palace in a city of the Gandharvas;
he establishes the sky upon the ground.
Like a reflection of the sky upon a jeweled floor,
what is there in the world— whether it has existed, exists, or will exist— that the Lord, though possessing an unmanifest form, does not display by assuming the state of mind?
Everything indeed occurs in every way, everywhere, and at all times.
"In this world, there exists only one single reality.
Therefore, O Rāma, what occasion is there for joy, resentment, or wonder?
A wise person should always abide in equanimity alone. (MU 4.21.27)
The knower of reality never undergoes any transformation caused by pride, wonder, delusion, joy, or indignation, for he remains unshaken in equanimity.
For in this world, diverse patterns are seen to exist throughout space and time without end;
yet the Self does not laboriously construct these patterns,
for the ocean does not exert effort to produce its waves.
And it does not reject those things that have arisen, just as the ocean [does not reject] its waves;
rather, it is like clarified butter in milk,
or like atoms in a jar.

Like threads in a cloth, or like banyan trees within a banyan seed, these powers reside within the Self alone; having come into manifestation, they are carried away incessantly like waves. Herein there is no agent, no enjoyer, and no destroyer.

When the Self alone— the witness of the reality of the Self, free from affliction, and eternally unshakable— abides in equanimity, then the world comes into being by itself, just as light exists when there is a lamp, as day exists when there is the sun, and as fragrance exists when there is a flower. (MU 4.21.31–32)
This which is perceived is merely a manifestation;
it is like the vibration of the wind, existing neither as being nor as non-being.
In the ultimate sense, the Blessed One is not the creator of any worldly views that have perished, nor is he the destroyer of those already made;
rather, they are merely sometimes manifest, sometimes slightly manifest, and sometimes very manifest, like heaps of flowers in a forest.
For in this world, that thing which is not one's own self perishes, whereas that which is one's own self does not.
How can that object which is one's own self perish from oneself?
Therefore, by the power of incorrect knowledge, all things arise from Brahman;
and for those who have descended, ignorance arises at the very moment of their descent,
through which that lack of knowledge becomes firm.

Therefore, from this [ignorance], the tree of saṃsāra expands, possessing a trunk of a hundred thousand [elements] and entwined with various auspicious and inauspicious [states]; it has vast branches that are the worlds. Its form is clustered with the blossoms of hope; it is curled around by the terrible serpents of suffering; it has sprouted with enjoyments; it has flowered with old age; and it is radiant with the creepers of craving. Having cut down this poisonous tree of saṃsāra—which is a shackle for the self—with the sword of discernment, you, being liberated, may wander here like a lordly elephant released from its post.
The twenty-second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Teaching of Universal Unity," [spoken by] Rāma:
O Lord, tell me in detail: how does the birth of these living beings from the state of Brahman occur; what is its extent, and of what nature is it?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as the various classes of beings arise from Brahman, just as they go to their destruction, and just as they become liberated; 4.22.2.
And how they increase, how they endure, and how they disappear— listen, O mighty-armed and sinless one, as I shall explain this to you in due order.
The stainless power of consciousness belonging to Brahman,
possessing all powers, by its own will and through the act of perceiving, becomes the object of perception itself, which consists of that very act of perception.
Having attained density through its own ideation, whatever even that [mind] subsequently conceives, it comes to possess that very reality, reaching the state of the mind.
By the mere volition of the mind, it instantly expands this unreal visible world like a city of Gandharvas, provided it abandons the vision of Brahman.
The nature of consciousness, though shining forth, remains as nothingness alone;
therefore, that which exists as the visible world is, for us, nothing but space.
Having formed the intention to become a lotus-born being, he perceives his own form as that of the Lotus-born; thereafter, he fashions the world, beginning with his own Prajāpati.
O Rāma, this very notification (jñapti), having emerged from the mind, has become a creation teeming with fourteen kinds of infinite elemental beings.
Consisting of mind alone, it is empty, having a body that is mere space;
it is a city of mere conceptualization, unreal in nature, consisting of nothing but delusion.
In this world, some species of beings exist in a state of great delusion;
some have awakened knowledge, while others indeed falter midway.
Among all the various classes of beings on earth who are awakening and proceeding toward the state of being taught, these human births are [the most excellent].
For those [women] are full of many anxieties and consist of suffering, being afflicted by hatred and fear;
from among them, I shall first describe the one characterized by passion and goodness (rājasasāttvikī).
That which exists is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction;
it is the manifestation of consciousness, called the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion.
From a single portion of the existence of vibration within that motionless body,
it attains density in the gentle ocean, like the state of being a whirlpool due to its movement.
Rāma:
What is said to be a single part of the infinite reality of the Self?
How could there be any modification, and how could there be a succession of parts?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The construction of words such as 'born from that' or 'born from him' is for the sake of conventional usage in the scriptures, O Rāma, and not in the ultimate sense."

Transformation, having parts, possession of spatial directions, and being taught [as such], as well as succession— none of these are possible in the Lord, even though they are seen to arise [in other things].
Apart from that [non-conceptual cognition], there is no other conceptualization, nor will there ever be;
how then could there be the sequential word and meaning, or the expressions born of worldly convention?
Whatever conceptualization, whatever object, whatever word, and whatever group of embodied beings there may be—
because they are born from that and because they consist of that, each is held to be composed of that.

That very [cognition] arises from that [object], just as fire arises from fire; the conceptualization of difference—such as "this is the produced" and "this is the producer"—is merely a verbal designation.
"This has arisen from that"—this is the established order of the world;
that which possesses a superior capacity for action is the produced, and that alone is the producer.

The confusion regarding the meaning of words—thinking "this is one thing" and "that is another"—occurs only when [the object] has been expressed; for once it has been cognized, there is no duality in the deity.
By that very power of the mind, cognition arises spontaneously;
through firm cultivation, its desired object is attained.
That one flame of fire has a second as its producer—this is merely a verbal artifice; there is no truth here in the meaning of the statement.
For those other [opponents], such expressions as "the produced" and "the producer" do not occur;
for how could that which is one and infinite ever be born?
This is the inherent nature of a statement: that as soon as it is uttered, it is immediately joined with meanings such as the exclusion of its counter-correlate, number, and so forth.
That which appears in the Supreme like a network of waves in the ocean,
taking the form of the conceptualization of words and meanings— that the wise know to be Brahman alone.
Brahman is consciousness, and Brahman is the mind; Brahman is knowledge and the non-substantial;
Brahman is the object, Brahman is the word, Brahman is the direction, and Brahman is the elements.
"This is one, this is another, this is a portion"—
when such words are spoken through the conceptual constructions of false knowledge regarding the two internal selves, what truthfulness can there be in them?
This so-called "flame" arises from the flame of fire; for that splendor of conceptual construction which arises from the fickleness of the mind is not established in reality.
The expression of conceptual construction, though unreal, is imagined to have the nature of reality because one's vision is impaired by delusion, like the defect of the cognition of two moons.
From that all-pervading, infinite Brahman, which is the supreme state, nothing else whatsoever can arise; what has been described is indeed that very reality itself.
Nothing whatsoever here is possible apart from the reality of Brahman;
indeed, all this is Brahman—this alone is the ultimate truth.
O wise one, such will be your established conclusion (siddhānta).
Right here we shall set forth the cage of words explaining the meaning of that conclusion.
In this case, certain sequences such as ignorance and the rest exist, but no others;
you will understand the entirety of these matters sufficiently once this ignorance has been destroyed.
When the accumulation of non-entities is exhausted, the real entity becomes clear as it truly is;
the world, which is the object of perception, is seen exactly as it is upon the destruction of the darkness of night.

O Rāma, this entire world which has been spread out by false views will, through your stainless splendor and your vision of infallible boons, become truly free from falsehood; there is no doubt whatsoever in this matter.
The twenty-third chapter, titled "The Instruction Establishing that This Entire World is Indeed Brahman," [ends].
Rāma:
By your various and profound utterances here, which are cool, pure, and radiant like the waters of the Ocean of Milk, [the world is filled on all sides].
For a moment I fall as if into blindness, and for a moment I attain clarity; like a day in the rainy season when the power of the sun is stilled by shifting clouds, I fluctuate.
How has the conceptualization of that which is infinite, immeasurable, all-encompassing, singular, luminous, and whose essence never sets come to be?
Vasiṣṭha:

All my utterances have as their meaning the reality of things as they truly are; they are never ineffective or contradictory in meaning, nor do they produce contradictions between what precedes and what follows.
When the vision of knowledge has become clear and awakening has arisen extensively, you will,
established in yourself, fully understand this perspective of my words as they truly are.
This arrangement of words and sentences for the sake of instruction, for the purpose of teaching, and for the comprehension of the meaning of the treatise, may lead you into error for a moment.
When you shall now know that truth which is utterly stainless,
then indeed you will understand the distinction between the signified and the signifying, and between word and meaning.
This proliferation of speech that creates distinctions is imagined for those who are to be instructed;
it exists only among the ignorant, but among the wise, it does not exist in an ultimate sense.
Not even the slightest impurity of conceptualization, such as volitional effort and the like, exists within the Self;
that very Brahman, free from passion and beyond dualities, stands as this world.
O sinless one, this must be explained at length once again, with many varied expressions, on the occasion of the final conclusion.
However, without the elaboration of speech, it is impossible to make an effort to break through this incomparable darkness of ignorance, which has arisen as a mutual interplay.
O Rāma, it is through ignorance itself— when it is most excellent and intent upon the destruction of its own self—
that knowledge, which removes all defects, is attained.
For a weapon is quelled by a weapon, impurity is washed away by impurity;
poison is neutralized by poison, and an enemy is slain by an enemy.
Such is this illusion of existence (*bhūtamāyā*), which bestows joy through its own destruction;
its true nature is not perceived, for it perishes the very moment it is observed.
It veils discernment and produces the worlds in abundance;
yet it is not recognized—behold this great wonder!
When not being observed, it throbs; when observed, it perishes.
This illusion dances about only as long as its true nature remains unrecognized.
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion that binds one to saṃsāra!
Though it is utterly unreal, it appears so very real that it destroys even the wise.
He by whom the illusion of saṃsāra— which spreads out extensive differentiation within that single, undivided word— is fully understood, is the Supreme Person.

"By means of cultivation [based on] the thought that 'this does not exist in the ultimate sense,' having become a knower through the attainment of the object of knowledge, you will understand its intention."
But as long as you have not yet awakened, let your conviction remain firm and unrestrained through my words alone: that ignorance does not exist.
That great mental activity of the mind which has come into the state of being an object of perception—
when one has the internal certainty that "this is unreal," such a person partakes in liberation.
Whatever has come into the range of vision is but the manifestation of the mind alone;
he who possesses the internal certainty that "that which is real is Brahman" is also a partaker of liberation.
The third view, which is flickering yet bound by cultivation,
is a snare that binds all beings and birds in the entire world.
He who, with a mind free from attachment, perceives the world as illusory— like a dream or a delusion— and is certain that it is neither real nor unreal, does not sink into suffering.
For one whose nature consists of these very mental constructs regarding their own forms,
and who thus lacks the true nature of his own being, it is ignorance alone that exists.
No defects whatsoever, such as mutability and the like, exist in the Great Self; in the Supreme Self, they are not found, just as dust is not found in water.
This cultivation, which consists of the coloring of words and their meanings, pervades the world;
it has arisen for the sake of conventional usage, yet it is not distinct from the Self.
Without this conventional usage, these perspectives of the scriptures do not attain stability, just as cloth does not exist without its threads.
For the self, being carried along on the path of ignorance, is not perceived here;
yet that [perception] is attained through the knowledge of the self, which is acquired from the meaning of the scriptures.
O Rāma, it is said that the further shore of the river of ignorance cannot be reached except through the attainment of the Self; for that indeed is the imperishable and immutable state.
Since this ignorance, which causes delusion, has arisen from somewhere or other,
it has surely attained a state of existence by remaining after having completely veiled the true state.
O Rāma, let there be no deliberation for you as to "whence has this been born?"; let your deliberation be only this: "How shall I slay her? MU 4.23.32.
O Raghava, when this [ignorance] has set and been destroyed, you will know from where it came,
what it is, and how it was lost, without exception.
In reality, this [duality] does not exist; it merely appears when not investigated.
Who could know the form of that which is non-existent yet appears through delusion, and from where?
Once this [intellect] has been born and has reached maturity, it leads only to harm because of its expanded form;
you will indeed come to understand this only after you have forcibly destroyed it.
There are no such heroes nor such wise men in the three worlds who have not indeed been rendered helpless by ignorance.
Therefore, exert yourself in providing medical treatment for her in this infirmary,
so that she shall not again subject you to the suffering of childbirth.
Completely uproot ignorance— the sole companion of all calamities, the blossom of the tree of nescience, and the mother of a multitude of misfortunes.

Having forcefully cast aside this false view— which bestows fear, despair, and unbearable calamity, and which is clouded by the great cataract that deludes the heart— may you reach the further shore of the ocean of existence.
The twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Discourse on Ignorance," from the Vasiṣṭha [Yoga-vāsiṣṭha].
O Rāghava, hear now the medicine for this disease spread by ignorance— a disease which, though it belongs to one who is agitated and non-existent, is destroyed by mere observation.
O Rāma, listen to that birth which is both rajasic and sattvic, concerning which I have begun to speak for the purpose of examining the power of the mind.
That which exists is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction;
it is the manifestation of consciousness, called the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion.
For the vibration of that [Reality], whose body is the pulsation of consciousness,
arises from a certain point alone and attains density, like the movement from a gentle ocean.
Just as the water within the ocean, though motionless, appears to move through its own vibration,
so too does the All-Powerful One, when focused in one place, attain the state of the power of vibration.
Just as the wind moves within the sky by itself through its own power,
so too does the self here experience agitation within its own self by means of its own power alone.
Just as a lamp, by the power of its own flickering flame, attains a state of height that is lunar in nature, so too does this Self sport within its own body.
Just as within the waters of the ocean there is shimmering water that moves here and there,
so too within the body of all-pervading power (sarvaśakti) there is a playful vibration.
Just as an ocean of molten gold shines forth with its radiant circles of light,
so does the ocean of consciousness manifest within the Self through its pure vibrations.
Just as the movement of a pearl is perceived in the sky by the eye,
so does the radiant power of the consciousness of Brahman arise.
That power of consciousness, slightly agitated in the great ocean of consciousness,
vibrates as something composed of that very essence, pure like a wave upon the ocean.
Though non-different from the Self, it remains as if distinct,
like the splendor of light within the hollow of a light-source, having attained density.
For a moment, that Goddess, throbbing with her universal power,
gathers her own power by herself, just as the moon-gem gathers its coolness.
This power of consciousness (cicchakti) of the Supreme Self, called "the Manifest" (prakāśa), having arisen, draws forth its companions— the powers of space, time, and action.
Not knowing its own nature, it remains pervading the infinite state;
though undifferentiated, it conceives of form as if it were limited.
At the very moment that form was contemplated by her, most beautiful one,
at that very moment followed perceptions such as names, numbers, and so forth.
Then, while remaining in this very state, consciousness— distinct from the Self that has become established—
emerges instantly as an infinite [expansion] inherent within it, like a wave from the great ocean.
Just as there is no distinct difference in nature between bracelets and armlets and the gold [from which they are made],
so too the mind, while manifesting its own partial form as the nature of the Self, is not different from it.
Just as a lamp [illuminates] lamps that have already arisen by itself, so too is one's own nature cultivated by consciousness, with the distinction consisting merely of place, time, and degree.
Then consciousness, ignited by the power of the vibration of space and time, pursues its own volition and enters the state of conceptualization.

O mighty-armed one, the form of consciousness, which takes on shapes imagined by conceptual thought and serves as the locus for space, time, and action, is called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
They say that the "field" (kṣetra) is the body; he knows that field in its entirety, both internally and externally, and for that reason he is called the "Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña).
Even while conceptualizing latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that [mind] again attains the state of egoism (*ahaṅkāratā*);
this egoism, when fully determined, is called the temporal intellect (*kālikī buddhi*).
The intellect (buddhi), fashioned by conceptualization (saṅkalpa), proceeds to the domain of reflection (manana);
then the mind (manas), characterized by dense discursive thought (vikalpa), gradually attains the state of the senses (indriya).
The wise know that this body consists of hands and feet, along with the sense organs;
it is this body that is born in the world, dies, and lives.
Thus, the individual soul (jīva), bound by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā) and consisting of volition (saṅkalpa),
its self enveloped in a web of suffering, gradually attains the state of the mind (citta).
Just as a fruit gradually attains a different state through the process of ripening,
so too does the individual soul (jīva) undergo change through its own condition due to the influence of impurity, and not by its essential nature.
The individual soul (jīva) attains the state of ego (ahaṅkāra), and the ego attains the state of intellect (buddhi);
the intellect, enveloped by the web of volitions (saṅkalpa), arrives at the state of mind (manas).
For the mind consists of volition and is intent upon grasping at forms;
it is delimited by its counter-correlates and is pursued even by others.
The powers beginning with desire, like intoxicated cows, run after me who am like a rutting bull for my own ruin, just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
Thus, the mind, consisting of creative power (*śakti*), having attained the state of dense egoity (*ahaṅkāra*),
enters into bondage by its own will, like a silkworm in its cocoon.
Because of his pursuit of his own volitions, his body is encircled by fetters;
he suffers with intense anguish, thinking, "Alas, I am bound by myself."
Perceiving "I am bound," the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), gradually abandoning [its true nature],
generates within ignorance the demoness of the world-jungle.
And dwelling within the net of those very elements imagined by its own volition,
it falls into a state of supreme helplessness, like a lion bound by chains.
Under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it assumes the agency of performing diverse actions,
and it continuously undergoes ever-new states fashioned by its own mere will.
In some places it is called the mind (*manas*), in some the intellect (*buddhi*), in some knowledge (*jñāna*), and in some action (*kriyā*);
in some it is this ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and in some it is known as the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
In some places it is called *prakṛti*, in others it is conceived as *māyā*;
in some places it is declared to be the *manas*, and in others it is established as *karman*.
In some places it is clearly known as "bondage," in others it is explicitly called "mind";
in some places it is declared to be "ignorance," and in others it is appropriately termed "desire."
Therefore, O Rāghava, this mind here is bound, suffering,
possessed by craving and grief, a dwelling place of disease, and afflicted.
Afflicted by old age, death, and delusion, struck down by the contemplation of worldly existence, seized by what is desired and undesired, and stained by ignorance and passion.
Its form is contracted by desire, it is the fresh sprout of the tree of karma; it has utterly forgotten its place of origin and imagines imagined misfortunes.
Bound like a silkworm that has entered its cocoon,
it consists of a multitude of mere aggregates, [exposed] to the heat of infinite hells.
Though invisible, it bears a weight as massive as the king of mountains;
it is the poisonous, wretched tree of saṃsāra, richly branched with old age and death.
Just as a banyan seed contains within itself a banyan tree that is devoid of fruit, so too does one maintain this entire cycle of existence, which produces the bonds of hope.
Burnt by the flames of the fire of anxiety, chewed by the python of anger,
struck by the waves of the ocean of desire, it has forgotten its own grandfather.
Like a deer strayed from its herd with its mind struck by grief,
he was like a moth burnt in the blazing fire of sense-objects.
Like a lotus whose roots have been severed, he has reached a state of supreme witheredness;
his hope for himself is cut off, and he is ill at ease, having lost his place and become attached to a foreign land.
He has wallowed in endless hardships amidst enemies disguised as friends, and in the midst of those who are neither friends nor foes,
within the infinite and extremely perilous states of existence.
Like a bird fallen into a terrible snare,
the world is bound within the net of existence— an empty city of Gandharvas.
O you who resemble the Immortal One, rescue my mind— which is being swept away in the ocean of misfortune and distracted by sense objects— just as one might pull an elephant from the mud.
O Rāma, forcibly extract your mind from the pond of thought, which is submerged like a bull and whose limbs are torn and shattered.

O Rāma, he in whose human form no compassion arises for this world— toward one whose appearance is struck down by the expansion of the auspicious and inauspicious, and who is fainting from the despair of blazing old age and death— is a demon in the world.
The twenty-fifth canto, named "The Descent of the Living Being," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, due to the state of being conscious, living beings are struck down by the contemplation of worldly existence;
from Brahman, whose form is unmeasured, they arise by the hundreds of thousands and even by the millions.
Innumerable beings have been born in the past, are being born even now on all sides,
and others will continue to be born, like showers of spray from a mountain torrent.

Under the influence of the obsession of their own latent tendencies, they have fallen into a state of helplessness driven by hope; with their intentions bound by themselves, they find themselves in most diverse circumstances.
Without ceasing, in every direction and in every region, upon water and on land,
beings are born and die like bubbles in water.
Some have taken only one birth; some have transcended the power of birth;
some have undergone countless births; and some have had hundreds of births as their interval.
Some belong to future births, some have experienced great existences in the past; some possess present existences, and some have gone to the state of non-existence.
Some, being born again and again for thousands of eons, have resorted to only a single womb; others have resorted to different wombs.
Some are struck by great suffering; some are still young;
some have risen to the highest degree; and some have arisen like the sun.
Some were kinnaras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas; some were Arka, Indra, Varuṇa, Tryakṣa, Adhokṣaja, and Padmaja.
Some are known as kumbhāṇḍas, vetālas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas;
others are recorded as groups of brahmins, kings, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
Some became Śvapacas, Caṇḍālas, Kirātas, Khaśas, and Pukkasas;
others took refuge in grass, herbs, leaves, fruits, and roots.
Some were parched by forest creepers, thickets, grass, and stones;
others were [sheltered] by *kadamba*, *jambīra*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees.
Some were lords of the earth, intoxicated by the accumulation of great wealth; others were clothed in rags, having adopted the silence of the sages.
Some are serpents, oxen, worms, insects, and ants;
others are lions, buffaloes, deer, bears, yaks, and antelopes.
Some became cranes, ruddy geese, herons, ducks, and cuckoos;
others attained the state of lotuses, white lotuses, water lilies, and blue lotuses.
Some are born as young elephants, great elephants, moths, bulls, or donkeys; others are born as bees, mosquitoes, ants, gadflies, or bamboo.
Some are overcome by the force of calamity, some have attained prosperity;
some dwell in the city of heaven, and some reside in hell.
Some are situated within the circle of the stars, others are within the hollows of trees;
some abide in the form of the wind, and some abide in the realm of space.
Some abide in the rays of the sun; some abide in the rays of the moon;
and some abide in the sweet essences of grasses, creepers, and shrubs.
Some wander here as liberated while living, vessels of auspiciousness;
some remain as those long-liberated, and others are surely fully matured.
Some, being deceitful, will attain liberation only after a long time;
others, possessing evil dispositions, hate their own state of isolation (kaivalya).
Some are born in this world, some are situated elsewhere;
some are neither here nor elsewhere, being established in the supreme state alone.
Some are Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Mandara, and Meru;
others are the oceans of salt water, curd, milk, clarified butter, and sugarcane juice.
Some were vast quarters of the sky, some were rivers of great velocity,
some were women with lovely eyes, and some were fierce eunuchs.
Some possess awakened intellects, while others have extremely dull dispositions;
some are instructors of knowledge, while others have attained meditative absorption.
Living beings, rendered helpless by the onset of their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
remain in these various states, fixed in their habitual conceptions (*bhāvanā*).
They dwell within the treasury of the world, falling and rising like balls struck incessantly by the hand of Death.
Bound by hundreds of snares of desire and bearing the burden of latent impressions,
they pass from one body to another, like birds flying from tree to tree.

By means of the illusory power that causes the upheaval of infinite and endless conceptual constructions, she spreads out this great world-maya, which consists of the universe, like a magician’s trick.
The deluded wander in saṃsāra like masses of whirlpools in water, as long as they do not perceive their own blameless self.
Having seen the unreal self and abandoned it, and having attained true consciousness,
they reach the supreme state in due time and are not born here again.
Having experienced thousands of births, and then through knowledge or austerity,
some reach the state of Parameṣṭhin and go to the supreme station.

Some, even after attaining the high status of Śakra, return again to the state of an animal due to the meanness of their intellect; and from the state of an animal, they may even attain the state of a human being.
Some of great intelligence, having arisen from the state of Brahmā,
enter fully into that very [state] at that very moment through that single birth alone.
In other cosmic eggs, by that same process,
these multitudes of living beings attain the state of being born from a lotus, while others likewise attain the state of being absorbed by Hari.
Some go to the state of animals, others even to the state of gods, and others again to the state of serpents, O Rāma; for it is exactly as it is here [in this world].
For just as this vast world exists, so indeed do other worlds exist—
those that have passed away and those that will come to be in great numbers.
Through various diverse sequences and by different causes,
their manifold creations arise and fall away.
Some attain the state of Gandharvas, some go to the state of Yakṣas;
some proceed to the state of Suras, and some come to the state of Daityas.
By the very same conventions by which people exist in this universe,
they likewise exist in others, their arrangements being indistinguishable.
Driven by the force of their own inherent natures and through mutual collisions,
creations revolve like the waves of a river.
Through manifestations and disappearances, through emergences and submergences,
creations revolve like the waves of a river.
From that which is ineffable and self-cognizable, multitudes of living beings emerge incessantly from the other [world], and they flash forth rapidly right back there.
Like visions of light from a lamp, like rays from the sun,
like sparks from heated iron, or like scintillations from a fire.
Like the various seasons from time, like fragrances from a flower,
like droplets from a downpour of rain, and like waves from the ocean.
Rising up again and again over time, having cast off a succession of bodies,
the multitudes of living beings reach dissolution in their own very state.
This dense, vast, and lofty array of the three worlds exists, perishes, and grows in vain;
it is the delusive illusion of the world's construction, like a wave in the ocean within the supreme state.
The twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Structure of the Aggregate of Living Beings," [spoken by] Rāma.
By what sequence, O Blessed One, does the living being (jīva), having attained its own state through this process, take on a body— a mere cage of bones?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, why do you not understand what I have already told you?
Where has your intellect gone, which ought to be capable of discerning the sequence of cause and effect?
For this world, beginning with the body and including all things mobile and immobile, is merely a manifestation; it is unreal, having arisen like a dream.
O sinless Rāma, this is indeed a long dream that appears as something entirely false;
it has the appearance of the delusion of two moons, like a mountain seen by one afflicted by vertigo.
With the sleep of ignorance completely stilled and all mental constructions dissolved,
he whose mind is awakened does not perceive the dream of saṃsāra while looking upon it.

O Rāma, for all living beings, the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is imagined through the notion of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), exists within the self until the attainment of the state of liberation.
The imagined nature always exists within the self of everyone;
the body of the living being is flickering, like a whirlpool in water.

Just as the expansive sprout arises from the seed, just as the leaf arises from the sprout, just as the flower arises from the leaf, and just as the fruit arises within the calyx of the flower; //MU_4,26.8//
And since there exists within the mind a body consisting of conceptual construction,
O Rāma, it therefore clearly exists here in the form of external appearance.
Whatever manifestation indeed arises for this mind,
that very thing quickly becomes [the external object], just as a lump of clay becomes a jar.
O Rāghava, this world appears as nothing more than a mental construction; it is not real, just like the water of a mirage.
And by means of this appearance, this body is seen before one,
just as a child, terrified and deluded, sees a Vetāla standing in front of him.
In the beginning of creation, that very manifestation of his body which was his mind became the all-pervading Brahmā, dwelling within the abode of the lotus bud.
Through the very sequence of that [Supreme Being’s] volition,
this infinite creation has come into existence from Him, like an illusion produced by a master illusionist.
Rāma said:
"O Brahman, tell me quickly and in detail how the individual soul (jīva), having attained the state of the mind (manas), reaches the state of Brahmā (vairiñca), and how it becomes everything."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, hear the process by which the body is assumed according to the Vedic tradition;
through that very illustration, you shall understand the state of the world.
The reality of the Self, unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, assumes through its own power a body delimited by space and time, solely as a matter of sport.

Thus, this mind— which is intent on the immersion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), characterized by the states of the individual soul (*jīva-paryāya*), and restless— becomes oriented toward both conceptualization and its cessation.
First, the power of the mind, while impelling [the senses], instantly contemplates a pure meditation on space,
which is oriented toward the essence of the seed-syllable of sound.
Then, having attained that density, the mind gradually contemplates its own dense vibration as the vibration of the wind, becoming intent upon the flavor of the seed of tactile sensation.
From the friction of those two— space and wind— which are perceived by the mind's eye and consist of the natures of sound and touch, fire is produced.
The mind, having attained a state of density, then in an instant brings about luminosity with its stainless light; by that, the light increases.
The mind, possessing such a multitude of qualities and perceiving the subtle element of taste, instantly grasps the coldness of water; from that, the cognition of water arises.
Then, in an instant, the mind, through its mass of such qualities,
manifests its own nature as gross like fragrance, by which the earth shall emerge.
Then, this body, enveloped by the elements and subtle essences (tanmātras), casting off its thinness, appears as a flickering spark of fire in the sky.

Endowed with the subtle element of egoity (ahaṅkāra-kalā), and accompanied by the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva), that is called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); it is the bee within the lotus-heart of living beings.
By cultivating that [meditation] upon it with intense urgency, the mind attains a radiant form through its maturation, just as a mango fruit reaches fullness when ripened.
Then that light, shining like molten gold in a crucible within the stainless sky, assumes its own natural configuration by its very nature.
Then, within that vast mass of light which constitutes its own abode, the mind spontaneously cultivates a firm and expansive contemplation.
Above, she consists of the seat of the head; likewise below, she consists of the feet;
on the sides, she takes the form of the hands; and in the middle, she possesses the nature of the belly.
Then that child remains with his limbs manifest, his pure form appearing like a mass of flames,
having assumed a body through the power of his mental resolve.
In this way, O Sage, the mind— its limbs being imagined through the influence of its own latent impressions—
causes its own body to increase, just as the season causes its own natural characteristics to flourish.
In time, having attained full manifestation, he becomes one of stainless form,
established in intelligence, purity of being, strength, energy, discernment, and sovereignty.
This very Blessed One is Brahmā, the sovereign leader of all worlds;
he resembles molten gold and is born from the supreme ether.
Then, abiding in the supreme ether and possessing a supreme form,
he fashions his own dwelling while remaining within himself through the play of the mind.
At times it is merely the sky, supreme and devoid of boundaries;
at times it is stainless water, without beginning, middle, or end.
At times it was adorned with the blazing flames of the fire at the end of an eon;
at other times, the lovely forest appeared like the bud of the navel-lotus.
In each successive birth, this Lord effortlessly fashions various and manifold seats of different forms until the end of his reign.
In this regard, when he first descended from the station of Brahmā,
he was then considered to be in a state of perfect equanimity through that very knowledge.
Upon the departure of the sleep of the womb, one perceives a radiant body,
rich with the flow of prāṇa and apāna, as if constructed from material substances alone.
It is covered with millions of pores, endowed with thirty-two teeth,
possessing three pillars, five deities, and marked by a footprint below.
It has five parts and nine openings, with skin as its smooth covering;
it is endowed with twenty fingers and marked by twenty nails.
Having two arms, two breasts, and two eyes— or indeed many eyes and arms—
it is the nest of the bird of the mind and the lair of the serpent of passion.
It is the abode of the ogress of craving, a cave for the lion of life, a tethering post for the elephant of pride, yet adorned with the lotus of its face.
Beholding his own most excellent and beautiful form, the Blessed Brahmā, whose vision is stainless regarding the three periods of time, reflected.
In this vast hollow of space, marked by me,
whose further limits are unseen and whose boundaries are unknown, what was there first?
Having thought thus, Brahmā, newly born and possessing the vision of the stainless Self,
beheld the multitudes of creations that had passed away in great number.
Then he recalled all the sequences of virtuous qualities,
just as a spring season recalls flowers, together with the Vedas and their associated branches of knowledge.
In sport, he fashioned diverse beings born of his volition,
engaged in various activities and undertakings, just as a Gandharva creates a city.
For their sake, for the purpose of attaining heaven and liberation, and for the accomplishment of dharma, desire, and wealth,
he composed infinite and diverse treatises.
Thus, O Rāma, this creation has attained stability within this world-process,
like the beauty of flowers arising from the mind of Viriñca, as from the springtime.

O son of Raghu, by means of his mind alone— which assumes the form of Brahmā through various compositions and playful creative acts— the splendor of creation has been brought to an incomparable state in this world.
The twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Means for Entering into Saṃsāra," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, this which is so accomplished is not established as anything at all;
it is merely empty space, the supreme play of the mind.
Space and time are nowhere obstructed by this cosmic egg,
even though it possesses a vast form, for it is itself of the nature of space.
This world, whose nature consists of mere conceptualization, is like a city seen in a dream;
wherever this exists, there is only the void, established as pure space.
Even though it is not made of material substance and lacks the application of pigment to a wall, this wondrous painting is seen in the sky as if it were actually created.
Everything from the body to the three worlds is imagined by the mind;
this is the cause of transmigration, just as the eye is the cause of seeing light.
For the world, consisting of the sequence of jars, huts, and cloths, is a mere appearance;
it revolves, yet it does not exist as a real entity, for walls and other such things do not stand apart from it.
For this body has been fashioned by the mind for the purpose of habitation,
just as a silkworm creates its own cocoon for itself.
There is nothing that the mind does not accomplish when it is slowed by its own volitions; nor is there any place difficult to reach, however exceedingly hard to attain, that it does not achieve.
In the supreme deity who possesses all power, what indeed are those powers by which [the Self] is not manifested, being concealed within the cave of the mind?
For indeed, O mighty-armed one, the existence and non-existence of all things at all times are possible only when the omnipresent Lord, who possesses all powers, exists.
Behold, through meditative cultivation, the lotus-born form was attained by the mind;
therefore, O Rāma, they know that its creative power is endowed with all potencies.
In the process of creation, gods, asuras, humans, and moving and non-moving beings are produced by one's own volitions; when those volitions subside, they are extinguished like a lamp without oil.
O one of great intelligence, behold the entire world as resembling space, manifested solely through conceptual construction, like a very long dream that has arisen.
No one whatsoever is ever born or dies here in this world from the perspective of ultimate reality, O wise one; everything proceeds as a mere illusion.
In that forest of trees marked by lines, where nothing ever undergoes increase or destruction, who indeed could suffer any injury?
Not seeing your own body, which is but a delusion, with a discerning eye, why do you speak like an ignorant man, O Rāghava, your mind struck down by sin?
Just as a mirage appears due to heat and an excess of mental activity,
so too all these beings, beginning with Brahmā, though non-existent, are perceived.
All the multitudes of forms in the world are composed of false cognition; they arise like a wishful thought and resemble the illusion of seeing two moons.
Just as the perception of the movement of a post by those traveling in a boat is false,
so too this constant succession of mental images has arisen as something unreal.
Know this to be a magical illusion, a cage constructed by *māyā*;
it is a creation of the mind's own thinking, existing as neither real nor unreal.
This entire world is indeed Brahman; how, then, can there be any otherness? What kind of consequence would that entail, what would it be, and where would it abide?
"This is a mountain, this is a post"—such is the delusion of mental inflation;
through the firmness of mental cultivation, the unreal appears as if real.

O Rāma, having abandoned this world— which begins with the fourfold proliferation of conceptual elaboration, which is empty within, and which consists of the mental activity of desire and craving— meditate upon that which is other.
Just as a grand undertaking in a dream is merely an illusion and not substantially real,
know that this long dream is likewise constructed by the mind.
Abandon this ostentation of saṃsāra— the treasury of the serpent-like cravings— which appears as great enjoyment yet, when grasped, is devoid of substance.
Knowing that this is non-existent, do not fix your mind upon its existence; for what wise person, having recognized a mirage, would pursue it?
The deluded soul who pursues a woman composed of mere desires, rich with forms born of his own imagination, becomes a vessel for nothing but suffering.
If the real does not exist, let this world go as it wishes toward the unreal;
but he who abandons the real and goes toward the unreal perishes.
This world is merely a delusion of the mind, like the fear of a snake in a rope; through the diversity of mental cultivation alone, it revolves for a long time.
In this world, only the fool is deceived by unreal entities that arise like the shimmering moon reflected in water; one such as you, who knows reality, is not so deceived.
That fool who, while cultivating this collection of virtues, seeks happiness,
merely wipes away his own dullness upon a fire that does not reflect it.
This entire visible cage of objects appears though it is truly non-existent; it is a construction of the mind's own thinking, like a city within the heart.
This arises by the will of the mind and dissolves by its will;
it is seen falsely as something vast, like a city of Gandharvas.
O Rāma, when this world perishes, nothing at all perishes;
and even when this world is joined [with its constituents], nothing at all is truly joined.
When the city of the heart, constructed by the mind, is either broken or has grown expansive, tell me: what has increased, and what of whom has been destroyed?
Just as a city arises in the hearts of children for the sake of play,
so too does this world arise incessantly within the mind.
Nothing belonging to anyone has been lost, just as in the waters of a magician's illusion; likewise, when this worldly existence arising from power has fallen away or perished, nothing is truly lost.
If that which is non-existent were to remain non-existent, then what indeed would be lost for whom?
Therefore, this so-called saṃsāra finds no footing in either joy or despair.
Since that which is absolutely non-existent cannot possibly perish,
O Mahāmati, in the absence of destruction, what occasion is there for suffering?
Or rather, what indeed can perish of that which is absolutely real?
This entire world is Brahman alone; how then could pleasure and pain arise?
In this entire cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is unreal and exclusively productive of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), what is there for a wise person to accept that they might desire?
Since this entire threefold world is everywhere real and consists of the essence of Brahman, what is there that should be abandoned? Let the wise discern that which is to be avoided.
Whether the world be unreal or real, for the knower it is thus; therefore, he is inaccessible to pleasure and pain, whereas the fool is afflicted by a third part [of them].
That which does not exist in the beginning and does not exist at the end, does not exist even in the present.
O Rāma, for one who desires what is non-existent, only non-existence remains.
That which is real in the beginning and at the end is indeed real in the present as well;
for one to whom everything is indeed real, only reality itself remains.
Only the foolish, not the excellent ones, long for things such as the moon, the sky, or a lotus stalk within the water— things that are unreal— out of mental delusion.
For the fool finds satisfaction in objects that are empty of substance despite their expansive forms; this leads to endless suffering, not to happiness.
Therefore, O lotus-eyed Rāma, do not be a fool;
having perceived the impermanence in this world, take refuge in that which is eternal and steadfast.

Do not fall into despondency by calculating that "all this, including myself, is non-existent"; rather, do not fall into despondency by perceiving that "all this, including myself, is indeed existent. MU 4.27.49.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. The assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Application of Reality as It Is," by Vasiṣṭha.
When wealth, wife, and so forth have perished, what occasion is there here for grief?
What lamentation can there be for that which was seen for a moment like a magical illusion and then vanished?
Whether half of a city of the Gandharvas is adorned or defiled,
or whether it pertains to a portion of ignorance such as a son and so forth, what sequence of pleasure and pain could there be?
When wealth, wife, and so forth have already been attained, what occasion indeed is there for joy? When a mirage has vanished, can one who seeks water find any delight?
When wealth and wives have grown old, sorrow is appropriate, not contentment;
when delusion and illusion have grown old, who here can find consolation?
By those very objects of enjoyment which, when excessively pursued, give rise to passion in the fool,
it is by those same objects that detachment arises in the wise man.
The deluded, who do not perceive the further shore, attain satisfaction through enjoyments;
but the virtuous, who behold the further shore, attain detachment through them.
Therefore, O Raghava, you who know the truth regarding the worldly affairs of saṃsāra,
disregard what is lost as it is lost, and accept what is obtained as it is obtained.
Not desiring future enjoyments and the unartificial enjoyment of those that have arrived— this is the characteristic of a wise person.
In this turmoil of saṃsāra, where the self is concealed and acts like a predator,
conduct yourself as a perfectly awakened one (saṃbuddha) so that you do not fall into delusion.
Those of perverted intellect who do not see correctly and with equanimity this sequence of the display of the cosmic manifestation of saṃsāra are ruined.
Whosoever, by whatever means, finds aversion for the realm of the visible here, their stainless intellect is nowhere immersed.
For one whose reliance on the notion "this is real" has ceased with respect to all things,
that unreal ignorance does not embrace the Omniscient One.
He whose mind is established in the realization that "I and this entire world are one," having abandoned both attachment and non-attachment, does not sink.
Having grasped with the intellect that pure state which is the middle between existence and non-existence, do not grasp at nor release the universe, including all that is external and internal.
Extremely expansive, pure, possessing all yet devoid of all,
remain passionless like the sky, O Rāma, even while performing your duties.
For the wise person who stands in action without desire and without aversion,
his discernment is not defiled, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Whether your group of sense organs performs acts such as seeing and touching or does not perform them, you remain the master of yourself, free from desire; these organs are merely secondary to you.
Let the mind, which conceives "this is mine" regarding sense objects that do not truly exist, not sink; being unimmersed, let it not act—or let it act.
O Rāghava, if the splendor of the objects of the senses does not please your heart,
then you have realized true knowledge and have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
For you, whether possessing a body or being bodiless, liberation has been accomplished by the power of reality itself, even though you have not tasted the objects of the senses and do not desire it.
O Rāma, by means of supreme wisdom, separate the mind from the multitude of latent impressions for the sake of the highest state, just as one extracts noble fragrance from a flower.
In this ocean of saṃsāra, which is flooded with the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā), those who have boarded the boat of wisdom have crossed over; others have drowned.
Having investigated the reality of the self with an intellect that is supremely steady and sharpened like the edge of a razor, enter your own true state.
O Rāma, one should conduct oneself just as the wise who know reality do— their minds nourished by knowledge— and not like a fool.
The great-souled ones who are liberated while living, ever-contented and noble-minded, are to be followed by their conduct; not those who are deceitful and miserly in their enjoyments.
Those people who know the higher and the lower neither reject nor desire the worldly affairs occurring in the world; they simply conform to everything.
In this world, those great ones who perceive reality never become wretched, whether in the face of power, pride, virtues, fame, or fortune.
Even in complete solitude they do not grow weary, for they are unattached even in celestial gardens;
like suns, the great do not abandon their destined course.
Free from desire, following the conventional usage as it has been attained, they move about without arrogance, established in their own nature, situated within the chariot of the body.
O Rāma, you too have attained this discernment that has come to you;
by the power of this wisdom, I know you are at ease, O handsome one.
Maintaining a clear vision, free from pride and devoid of envy, dwell upon this seat of the earth; you shall attain supreme accomplishment.
Established in yourself, renouncing all that is beneficial [to worldly ends], and desiring only what is seen from afar,
dwell, O sinless one, having taken up supreme coolness within.
Vālmīki:
Thus, by the pure speech of the sage of pure intent, Rāma appeared as if polished;
filled within by the sweet, radiant nectar of knowledge, he attained a coolness like that of the moon.
The twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Application of Conventional Usage Based on the Comprehension of Reality as it Is," [ends with] Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, master of the Vedas and Vedānta,
I stand as one who has found rest through your pure words.
I do not reach satiety in hearing your words as you speak— words that are sublime, dispassionate, elegant, and appropriate.
O Blessed One, on another occasion during our discourse, you described the birth of the lotus-born Brahmā from a *rājasasāttvika* womb.
O Great-Souled One, this doubt dwells within my heart;
O Destroyer of All Doubts, let it be explained quickly.
How is the diverse origin of the lotus-born Brahmā described in the scripture— sometimes from a lotus, sometimes from space, sometimes from the cosmic egg, and sometimes from water?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, many hundreds of Brahmas, Śivas, and Indras, as well as thousands of Nārāyaṇas, have passed away."
Today, in many other diverse universes,
thousands wander about, engaging in various modes of conduct and pastimes.
Simultaneously, in infinite worlds throughout the succession of time, many other [Buddhas] will arise in great numbers.
O mighty-armed one, the various births of those celestial beings, such as the lotus-born Brahmā and others, within those eggs have been described in heaven.
Sometimes the creations belong to Śarva, sometimes they arise from the lotus-born [Brahmā],
sometimes they belong to Viṣṇu, and sometimes they are fashioned by the Sage [Nārada].
Sometimes he is the lotus-born Brahmā, sometimes he is born from the waters;
sometimes he is born from an egg, and sometimes he is born from the sky.
In one egg there is the three-eyed Arka; in another, Vāsava;
in another, Puṇḍarīkākṣa; and indeed, in another, the three-eyed one alone.
In one creation, the earth was densely crowded with trees;
in another, it was packed with men; and in yet another, it was covered by mountains.
One [earth] was made of clay, another was made of stone;
one was made of gold, and likewise another was made of flesh.
In this very world, some of those other worlds exist in a different manner; some consist of mutually exclusive single worlds, while others are even entirely devoid of penetration.
In this great sky of the reality of Brahman, infinite worlds sink down and emerge again, like the multitude of waves in the ocean.
Just as waves are in the ocean, as a mirage is in the desert,
and as flowers are on the mango tree, so too are the glories of the universe in the Supreme.
The motes of dust within the rays of the sun may be counted,
but the multitudes of worlds cannot be numbered within the reality of Brahman, whose form is ever-shifting.
Just as swarms of mosquitoes in sugar-cane groves during the rains fly up again and again only to perish, so too do these creations of the world.
Nor is it known from what time they have come;
these successions of creations are characterized by constant arrival and departure.
Beginningless and incessant, they flash forth like waves;
indeed, each preceding one arose from what went before it, and that in turn from what was even earlier.
Having come into being again and again, the gods, asuras, humans, and other such beings—
all these classes of living creatures— dissolve away like the breaking of waves upon a river.
Just as this egg of Brahmā, so too have thousands of series of cosmic eggs perished, like the hollow stalks of a lotus at the end of the years.
Others currently exist, possessing present bodies,
beyond this city of Brahmā, in the vast domain of Brahman.
There will be many other splendors of the city of Brahmā;
yet they too will perish in the future, having come into being again and again, just like spoken words.
Other successions of creations will exist within Brahman,
like jars in a heap of clay, or like sprouts in a seedling.
Just as the currents and waves of water extend as far as the ocean,
so too do the splendors of the three worlds extend within the space of consciousness, as far as Brahman.
Rich with vast forms and transformations, when scrutinized they are nothing at all; rising up and sinking down, these glories are neither real nor unreal.
Inert yet imbued with flavor, slender like creeping moss, they share the nature of waves, their forms appearing and vanishing in an instant.
Of all the millions of creations, there are diverse conducts and activities,
diverse forms and transformations, and creations of diverse appearances.
O Rāma, all perceptions of creation are not separate from the Lord of All; they are objects for the knower of reality, just as raindrops are not separate from water.
Creations emerge from the Lord like rains from a cloud;
from Him alone they are all born, just as visual perceptions arise from light.
All perceptions of creation are not distinct from the Lord of All;
they appear as if distinct, like the thorny excrescences on a silk-cotton tree.
O Raghava, here, within these created worlds— whether flourishing or degraded—
the Supreme [Self] is garlanded by the subtle elements (tanmātra) born from the ether.
Sometimes, first, space attains a state of stability;
from that, Brahmā is born—that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) who is born from space.
Sometimes first the wind attains its foundation;
from that, Brahmā is born—that Prajāpati who is born of the wind.
Sometimes, first the water attains expansion;
from that, Brahmā is born, that Lord of Creatures who arose from the waters.
Sometimes first the earth attains expansion;
from that, Brahmā is born, he who is the terrestrial Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati).
Thus, when the fifth [element] increases by compressing the four,
then the Lord performs the activities of the world through that very birth.
Sometimes a certain person, by virtue of their innate nature, manifests spontaneously within water, air, or even in a vast expanse of fire.
Then, from the mouth of that man it sometimes arises, or from his feet;
sometimes from his shoulder, or from his back, or sometimes from his eye or his hand.
Sometimes a lotus is produced from the navel of this Puruṣa;
Brahmā moves within it, and he is celebrated as the "Lotus-born."
This is an illusion, a delusion like a dream, a false cycle of constructs;
it is as fleeting as a kingdom of the mind and as beautiful as ripples on water.
Tell me, how could this cognition possibly exist here for us?
Unless, of course, this is being questioned as a mere whim of a child’s imagination.
Sometimes, within the pure ether, through the coloring of the principle of the mind,
a golden cosmic egg containing Brahman manifests of its own accord.
At times this Person emits vigor into the water;
from that a lotus is born, or else the great cosmic egg.
From him Brahmā is born; at times he is indeed the Sun, at times Varuṇa, and at times Brahmā or Vāyu, the lotus-born.
Thus, O Rāma, within these diverse creations that are devoid of internal reality, various and manifold origins have proceeded from Brahman.
O sinless one, this origin has been told to you for the sake of illustration regarding the creation of a single Prajāpati; it applies equally to any other as well.
O you of noble mind, this sequence of creation has been described for your enlightenment, [showing] that this saṃsāra is but a manifestation of the mind.
Thus have the classes, beginning with the *sāttvikī*, come into being;
this sequence of creation has been described to you for the sake of explanation.
Again there is creation, again destruction; again suffering, again happiness;
again the ignorant, again the knowers of that; and again the views of bondage and liberation.
Again and again creating [the world], bearing the state of being soaked with oil, like lamps that have provided light, they are extinguished and arise once more.
In the arising and destruction of both lamps and Brahmas,
once one has abandoned the distinction of duration based on time, there is no difference whatsoever in their destruction.
Again the Kṛta age, again the Tretā, again the Dvāpara and the Kali;
everything revolves once more through the turning of the wheel of time.
Again and again begin the periods of the Manvantaras, again and again the successions of Kalpas,
and again and again the states of activity, just as every morning begins the day.
This entire world, whose interior is fashioned by the divisions of light and darkness and by time,
is again and again nothing at all, again and again.
Like sparks from fire falling upon a heated iron ball,
these phenomena always abide by their very nature within the space of consciousness.
Sometimes unmanifest and sometimes having come into manifestation,
all this exists within the supreme reality, like the seasonal growth on a tree.
The vibration of consciousness alone is the self of all, always possessing such a form;
from it arises the world-creation, just as the appearance of two moons arises from a single eye.
All accumulated tendencies and continuous perceptions of creation converge;
though they abide within that [Reality], they appear as if not abiding there, like rays from the moon.
Indeed, this so-called saṃsāra never exists at all,
because within the power of the All, there exists the power of non-saṃsāra.
And yet, O virtuous one, this world has never been otherwise than it is now;
for within the All-Powerful One, the power of the cycle of existence is ever-present.
If one were to think that cyclic existence will not exist now because it has been burned away by the fire of meditation for a duration of time as long as a great kalpa, that would be logical.
O Great-minded One, through the vision of knowledge that "all this is indeed Brahman alone," our position that "there is no saṃsāra" is indeed logically established.
But from the perspective of the ignorant, because the state of transmigratory existence is uninterrupted,
it is only for such a person that this illusion of saṃsāra is appropriately regarded as eternal.
And because he has contemplated this again and again, O descendant of Raghu, even that statement— "the world is never otherwise than this"— is not false.
Seeing the quarters of the sky filled with beings falling incessantly and destined for destruction,
how could it not be established that this entire world is subject to perishing?

Seeing the quarters of the sky where the sun and moon have forever risen, and [seeing] the mountains as stable and immovable, one perceives that the entire world is indestructible; this too is an unfailing analogy.
There is nothing that does not exist within that one, expansive Self;
for in that which is beyond description, the entire web of conceptual constructions and mental fabrications is not possible.
Again and again all this occurs: again death and birth;
again pleasure and again pain; again the instruments and the actions.
Again the quarters, again the sky, again the oceans and the mountains;
creation arises again and again, just like the light of the sun eternally.
Again the Daityas, again the gods, again the succession of other worlds;
again the desire for heaven and liberation, again Indra, and again the Moon.
Again there is the god Nārāyaṇa, again the sons of Manu and others;
again there are the quarters of space, along with the moving and beautiful moon, sun, Varuṇa, and Vāyu.
With Mount Sumeru as its pericarp, beautiful with the thorny bristles of bears for its filaments,
and its vast interior blossoming wide, the lotus of the two worlds rises up once again.
Having ascended the forest of the sky, the lion that is the sun leaps once more with the multitude of its rays as claws, in order to tear apart the herd of elephants that is darkness.
Furthermore, the moon, with rays as beautiful as swaying mango blossoms,
produces nectar-like delight and serves as an adornment for the faces of the quarters, who are like brides.
Furthermore, those who were the guardians of the fruits produced by merit fall here with their limbs shattered, driven by the wind of the exhaustion of their merit from the tree of heaven.
Furthermore, having made some rustling sound with its various functional activities, the partridge of time departs, bearing the name "the commencement of saṃsāra."
Furthermore, O Indra-like one, having tasted the filaments of sovereignty,
the bee that is the other lord of gods returns to the lotus of heaven.
Furthermore, the Kali age defiles even that which has been purified by time,
just as a violent wind of refuse defiles the ocean even when it contains the Discus-bearer.
Furthermore, the wheel named Time, fashioned by the potter Time, revolves with force and without ceasing, having created the earthen vessels that are living beings.
Furthermore, the world, its auspicious stability destroyed, returns to a state of saplessness,
like a forest withered by the approaching end of an aeon.
Furthermore, when the bodies of infinite beings have been consumed by the fires of the sun,
the world— filled with the bones of all creatures— attains the state of a cremation ground.
Again, by the rains of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, which take the form of the great boundary mountains,
the world attains the state of a single ocean, with dancing ashes for its massive foam.
Furthermore, when wind and water have subsided and the world is empty of all things,
it returns to a state of emptiness like that unprecedented space.
Furthermore, having consumed a few more years with an evenness of taste toward all things,
he— his life spent in his worn-out body— is absorbed into the Brahman within the self.
Again, at another time, he likewise expands the multitude of worlds within the void with his mind, just as a gandharva creates a city in the air.
Again there is the commencement of creation, again the occurrence of dissolution;
all this, O Rāma, revolves like a wheel.
O Rāma, having determined what is true and what is false in this long deception of great illusion, let that which is said here be declared.
O Rāma, this wheel of saṃsāra is like the story of Dāśūra;
its form is constructed by conceptualization, yet it is empty of reality in actual fact.

This world is spread out densely with conceptual constructions that arise from the unreal and possess forms like those of a second moon; since it is fashioned by what is non-existent and is not real, how could such delusion possibly arise here?
The thirtieth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Method for Determining the Existence and Non-existence of the World," by Vasiṣṭha.
When those who are intent on various ritual actions and whose intentions are destroyed by enjoyments and power do not regard the Truth, then the deceitful do not see it.
But those who have gone beyond the intellect and are not mastered by the senses,
they see this worldly illusion as clearly as a wood-apple fruit in the palm of their hand.
Indeed, having perceived that worldly illusion,
the discerning living being abandons its reliance on the ego, just as a snake sheds its skin.
Having thereafter attained non-attachment, one is not born again,
even if remaining for a very long time in a field, like a seed scorched by fire.
Fools strive for the benefit of the body— which is beset by mental and physical ailments and destined to perish this very day— but not for the sake of the self.
You too, like an ignorant man, should not fulfill the desires of this ignorant body for the sake of suffering; rather, be solely devoted to the Self, which is your true nature.
Rāma said: "O Lord,
is this wheel of worldly existence merely like the story of Dāśūra—
a form constructed by imagination, devoid of any real substance?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, listen as I relate the narrative of Dāśūra, which is presented by way of describing the true nature of the world-illusion (jaganmāyā).
Upon this surface of the earth, there exists a great and glorious region known as Magadha, abounding with trees of various flowers.
Spreading through groves of *kadamba* trees, with its forests lined by rows of palm trees,
it was filled with flocks of diverse birds and was enchanting with every kind of wonder.
Its boundaries were crowded with crops, it was adorned with city groves,
and the banks of all its rivers were filled with lotuses, blue water-lilies, and white lilies.
The night resounded with the humming songs of women sporting on garden swings, while the ground of the path was densely covered with flowers gathered during the night.
There, on a certain mountain slope thick with *karṇikāra* flowers,
dense with groves of plantain trees, and adorned with clusters of *nīpa* shrubs, [he dwelt].

Where chakora birds and yak-tailed oxen warble, where the waters of the mountain torrents resound, where the thickets of blossoming mango creepers abound, and where the sweet-voiced cuckoos sing their songs.
In that place where the sky was covered by palm trees swaying with the play of Pulindas, and which was the very life of the jīvañjīvaka birds, abounding with blossoming lotus ponds; MU_4,30.15.
In the wind shimmering with a flood of flowers and reddened by the pollen of filaments,
where the *kāraṇḍava* ducks raised their cries and the cranes moved gracefully through the lakes.
In that meritorious, excellent mountain, where the trees were filled with various birds,
there lived a certain sage of great asceticism whose soul was devoted to the supreme Dharma.
Named Dāśūra, he was endowed with great power of austerity;
residing on the slopes of Mount Kadamba, he was free from passion and possessed of great intelligence.
Rāma:
O venerable one, for what reason did the ascetic seer dwell upon the back of the great kadamba tree in the forest, and how did he live there?
Vasiṣṭha said:
His father was renowned as Śaraloman;
he lived on that very same mountain like another Brahmā by name.
He had an only son named Kaca, like that of the preceptor of the gods;
together with that son, he spent his life in the forest.
Then, having eaten only a single blade of grass, he went through a multitude of ages;
having abandoned his body, he entered the abode of the gods like a bird that has left its nest.
In that very forest, Dāśūra, deprived of his father by fate, wept piteously all alone like a kurara bird.
With his heart tormented by grief due to the separation from his parents,
he surely succumbed to withering, like a lotus in the winter season.
Then, O Rāma, that boy, dejected in spirit, was thus consoled in the forest by a forest deity whose body remained invisible.
O son of a seer, possessed of great wisdom, why do you weep like one ignorant?
Why do you not understand the flickering nature of saṃsāra?
O virtuous one, such is the nature of this world at all times: the cycle of existence is unstable;
one is born, lives, and afterwards inevitably perishes.
O Sage, whatever is visible to the eyes, from Brahmā downwards—all that must go to destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, do not indulge in futile despair over your father’s death;
the setting of one who has been born is inevitable, like that of the sun at the end of the day.
Hearing those bodiless words, Śikhaṇḍin, his eyes reddened,
regained his composure as if at the sound of thunder.
Having risen and performed his necessary duties, he, out of reverence for his father,
set his mind firmly upon austerity for the sake of attaining the highest perfection.
As he practiced austerities in the forest through brahminical rites,
his status as a learned Vedic scholar became characterized by infinite resolve.
But because his intellect still sought to know what was yet unknown, despite his profound erudition,
his mind found no rest even upon that sacred ground.
Seeing even this entire surface of the earth as pure, yet as if it were impure, he indeed found no delight anywhere at all.
Then, by his own volition alone, he resolved:
"The very top of the tree is pure; my staying here is appropriate."
Therefore, I shall now perform such austerity by which I may attain,
like a bird, the ability to remain upon the branches, the twigs, and the leaves of trees.
Having reflected thus, he kindled an exceedingly brilliant fire and,
having cut his own flesh from the surface of his shoulder, offered it as an oblation into it.
Furthermore, let not the entire throats of the host of gods be reduced to ashes by the Brahmin flesh held in my mouth.
Having reflected thus, the seven-rayed Lord, assuming a physical form, appeared before him with blazing splendor, like the sun appearing before the Lord of Speech.
He spoke these words, which were agreeable to the heroic prince:
