"O virtuous one, take this boon that has been set aside for you, like a jewel from the depths of a treasury."
When Anala had spoken thus, the young Brahmin, having honored him with words of praise and with an offering of water and flowers adorned with blossoms, addressed him.
O Blessed One, I do not attain that sacred place on earth which has been purified by the perfected ones; therefore, let my dwelling be upon the trees.
When the son of the sage had spoken thus, the Fire-god, the mouth of all the gods,
said to him, "So be it," and the Lord vanished from sight.
When that god had vanished in an instant like an evening cloud,
the prince, his desires fulfilled, shone like the full moon.

Possessing joy, he laughed with the speed of the splendor from the faces of his beloveds that he had attained; he surpassed the moon, though it was surrounded by its full digits, and the blooming white lotus by means of his smile.
The thirty-first canto in the narrative of Dāśūra, titled "The Granting of Boons to Dāśūra," by Vasiṣṭha:
Then [he saw] a pavilion situated in the middle of a forest, which kissed the circle of the clouds and whose central courtyard was frequented by the horses of the sun, exhausted at midday.
As if measuring the belly of the quarters with his long, branch-like arms,
he gazes upon the directions with eyes that are blossoming flowers.
With his hair like a swarm of bees fluttering profusely, tossed by the wind,
he seemed to be wiping the faces of the quarters with his hands of tender sprouts.
He was laughing with his groves, which were tawny with masses of bright flower-clusters and possessed of large stalks, appearing like mouths filled with betel and garlanded by bees.
With the pollen from the filaments of flowers blooming in the playful grace of creepers,
it formed a circular expanse like the full moon with its radiance.
The world was crowded by the high rows of branches where cakora birds warbled in the bowers,
and where kinnaras sang, like a lofty path of perfected beings.
The sky was adorned by the plumage of peacocks hanging down from those seated on vine-seats, as if by clouds accompanied by rainbows.
It was illuminated by white chowries, raised and lowered on every shoulder,
appearing like full moons followed by *cakora* birds for an entire year.
With the sweet warbling of kapiñjala birds, the melodious cooing of cuckoos, and the cries of jīvajīvaka birds, he seemed to be singing with powerful strains.
With flocks of *kādamba* geese sporting in their nests,
and with *siddhas* resting within the hollows of the heavens, the world seemed as if it were entirely covered.
It was frequented here and there by clusters of blossoms with hands as red as coral and eyes like bees, resembling the celestial nymphs inhabiting heaven.
With its dark form turned tawny by the swaying pollen of a mass of flowers, it was like a cloud accompanied by lightning and a rainbow.
Rich with a thousand branching arms, filling the hollow of the sky,
it was like the Universal Form dancing, with the moon and sun as its earrings.
Seated upon that lord of serpents, he appeared like another orb of the earth in the midst of the sky, which was crowded with hosts of stars and composed of creepers and flowers.
Like the grandfather of all mountains, forests, and trees,
he was like a single treasure-trove upon the earth for fruits, shoots, and flowers.
Bearing a mass of buds veiled by the pollen of flowers,
it resembled the sky at dawn when the network of stars is obscured by the rays of the sun upon the marshy banks.
The surface of the earth was encircled by tree trunks crowded with flocks of nests and swarming with restless birds,
like the countryside surrounded by fickle people.
It was enriched with flower-clusters and beautiful banners, adorned with bowers of creepers,
white as *makkola* flowers, and strewn with heaps of blossoms.
It resounded with the warbling of cakoras, camaras, parrots, cuckoos, and śārikas,
while its arched windows were formed by the crevices covered with dense clusters of blossoms.
With flocks of birds moving about and hollows sluggish with the intoxication [of spring],
it was like the supreme inner apartment of all the forest goddesses.
It was resplendent with masses of flower filaments in which swarms of bees were submerged like waves,
appearing like a mountain with rivers cascading down it.
Its trunk was covered by masses of whirling flower petals, tossed playfully by the gentle breeze,
appearing like a mountain shrouded by swelling white clouds.
With his pillar-like knees rubbed by the frontal globes of elephants,
he stood with firm footing upon his broad base, like a great mountain upon its slope.
It was surrounded by a multitude of birds with variegated colored wings, moving within the hollows of their shoulders, like a horned creature surrounded by a swarm of living beings.
With his trembling web of fingers formed by clusters of blossoms, he seemed to be demonstrating the art of dramatic gesture for the forest creepers dancing in the woodland breezes.
Only some who were once hopeless and no longer seeking anything from me depart with contentment,
as if dancing amidst the swaying circles of flowering creepers.
Because it was the sole beloved of the creepers, it was overflowing with the aesthetic sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
as if singing in a low, sweet falsetto through the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees.
With flowers scattered far and wide by the sky-dwelling Siddhas,
it seemed as though it were offering a welcome with the warbling of cuckoos and the humming of swarms of bees.
With the splendor of its fruits, flowers, and creepers, and the height of its trees,
it seemed to laugh with the brilliant radiance of its blossoming buds.
With its upward-reaching circles of trunks, it seemed as if it were striving to conquer the *pārijāta* tree, rushing through the midst of the sky with its necks held high.
With clusters of flowers having thick filaments and bees shimmering upon their centers,
it seemed as if it were striving to surpass Indra’s thousand eyes with its peerless beauty.
Covered by a multitude of gems upon its hoods, which were like shimmering clusters of flowers, it was like the serpent Śeṣa rising from the netherworld with a desire to behold the sky.
His form was covered with dust like a second Śaṅkara,
yet he brought joy to all the sages through his shadow, which was laden with fruit.

He beheld the *kadamba* tree in the sky, which was like a city, provided with new pavilions of flowering creepers whose walls were formed by densely packed leaves, and crowded with flocks of birds as its citizens.
The thirty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Kadamba Tree," from the narrative of Dāśūra; Vasiṣṭha said:
Then that one of great intelligence, his mind slow with joy, beheld him who was adorned with fruits and shoots, resembling a mountain composed of flowers.
Śauri ascended the kadamba tree standing in the forest, which acted as a pillar for heaven and earth,
like a lofty wish-fulfilling tree situated in the single ocean.
There, having reached the sky, he entered the tip of a sprout on the end of a branch suspended in the air, like a Buddha entering the edge of a reed-thicket.
Then, having sat down upon a soft seat of fresh sprouts,
he gazed for a moment at the quarters of the sky with eyes languid with curiosity.
The mountains, beautiful with their single-string pearl necklaces of rivers, have the peaks of the lord of mountains for their budding breasts;
they possess the stainless sky as their braided hair and the moving blue clouds for their locks.
Clad in garments of green grass, their bodies white with the pollen of flowers,
they carried full jars of ocean water as ornaments for the city.
They possess blooming lotuses, the fragrance of their breath,
the humming of crickets in the villages, and the sound of waterfalls for their anklets.
The heavens are their heads, the great earth their feet, the rows of forests their lines of body hair,
the jungles their thighs and hips, and the sun and moon their earrings.
Marked by rice-paddies traversed by water-buffaloes and by sandalwood trees serving as footstools,
they have the white clouds— clinging to their peaks like breasts— as their snowy silken garments.
The full waters of the great ocean were their newly adorned mirrors;
the masses of trees were the horripilation of their heat; and the interior of the world was their inner apartment.
Wearing garments dyed with menstrual blood, they were stained by the rays of the sun and saffron;
adorned with various flowers, they were anointed with sandalwood paste as white as moonbeams.

Seated upon a leaf of the creeper in the expanse of the sky, he joyfully beheld the ten directions— adorned without interval with flowers— which appeared like the waters of rivers flowing from the rows of forests spread out below.
In the narrative of Dāśūra, the thirty-third canto, titled "Dāśūra’s Survey of the Directions," Vasiṣṭha says:
From that time forward, he became famous in that ascetic hermitage as Kadambadāśūra, a hero in his rigorous asceticism.
Standing upon that lotus leaf and gazing at the quarters for a moment,
he firmly assumed the lotus posture, withdrawing his mind from all directions.
Not knowing the ultimate truth, abiding in mere ritual action,
and with a mind possessed by a craving for results, he performed that sacrifice.
In the midst of the forest, seated upon the leaf of a creeper suspended in the sky,
he performed all the sacrificial rites in their proper sequence within his own mind.
There, for ten years, he worshipped the gods with his mind alone through sacrifices such as those involving cows, horses, and human beings, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
When his expansive mind had attained purity over time, knowledge born of self-serenity descended within him by its own power.
Then, with his veils shattered, the stains of latent tendencies washed away,
and all impurities gone, the sage dwelt upon that sprout.
Once, he beheld a forest goddess standing before that creeper, large-eyed and clad in garments of swaying blossoms.
She possessed a face as lovely as that of a passionate woman, with eyes rolling from intoxication;
she was endowed with the fragrance of blue lotuses and was exceedingly captivating to the mind.
The sage spoke to that woman of faultless limbs, whose face was cast down like a forest creeper bent with the weight of its blossoms and the song of the cuckoo.
Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, who agitate the god of love?
Why do you stand there like a flowering creeper beside its companion?
Having been addressed thus, Gaurī, whose eyes were like those of a young fawn and whose breasts were full,
spoke these charming words in innocent accents to the sage.
Whatever things on the surface of the earth are difficult to obtain, yet desired,
all those are quickly attained through the very petitioning of the great.
"O Brahmin, in this forest, which is thick with creepers and adorned by your *kadamba* tree, I am a forest deity whose abode is the playful sport of the vines."
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, during the festival of Smara,
an assembly of forest goddesses took place in the Nandana grove.
O Lord, I went there— to that assembly hall of the beauties of the three worlds— where fragrant flowers and bees were present, and which was adorned with cuckoos and bees.
Then, during the festival of love, I saw all my friends accompanied by their sons;
being childless myself, I was therefore deeply distressed.
While you, the great wish-granting tree, stand as the caravan-leader for the multitude of all seekers,
O Protector, how indeed can I— though not truly childless— be pitiable like one who is orphaned?
"Give me a son, O Blessed One; otherwise, I shall offer my own body here as an oblation into the fire to pacify the burning pain caused by the loss of a son."
When the slender lady had spoken thus, the bull among sages smiled and,
filled with compassion, gave her a flower from his hand and said:
"Go, O slender-limbed one; in a month you shall give birth to a beloved son worthy of worship, whose eyes are like those of a deer, just as a fine creeper produces a flower."
However, because he was entreated by you while under the influence of death— a state characterized by sin— he will possess knowledge that is attained with great difficulty.
Having spoken thus, the sage dismissed the slender woman, whose countenance was bright with joy and who was eager with the prayer, "May I perform service for you."
She went to her own abode, and he remained with his own self;
time passed in due order, marked by seasons and years.
Then, after a long time, that very same lotus-eyed woman approached the sage with her son, who was now twelve years old.
Having prostrated and sat before the Sage,
she whose face was like the moon spoke with gentle words, like a female bee to a mango tree.
"O Blessed One, this is that worthy prince, our son;
indeed, I have made him proficient in all the arts."
O Lord, he has merely not attained that auspicious knowledge by which one is no longer tormented within this machine of saṃsāra.
O Lord, you alone must now compassionately teach him this knowledge;
for who indeed would consign a son born into a noble family to a state of ignorance?
To her who was speaking thus, the sage said, "O weak woman, leave this son of mine right here," and having spoken, he dismissed her.
When she had departed, that wise one remained restrained as an attendant to his father, like Aruṇa standing before the Sun.
Then, for a long time, that sage enlightened his son there with various eloquent expressions concerning the wisdom to be attained through diligent effort.
Through a constant and detailed sequence of discourses that inspire no weariness,
[the truth] is established in the intellect of those of superior wisdom, having ascended to the level of direct experience.

By virtue of his own experience, the great-souled Maharṣi had no need for a multitude of words whose meaning was already appropriate; like a cloud awakening a peacock standing before him in the sky, he enlightened his son.
The thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Awakening of the Son of Daśūra," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then once, while traveling along that path by way of the sky, I went to the river flowing from Kailāsa to bathe, my form invisible.
Having emerged from the hollow of the circle of the seven sages in the sky,
O Sumati, I reached the space above the Dāśūra tree during the night.
I heard from the hollow of a bough in the forest a voice,
like the humming of a bee trapped within a lotus bud.
Listen, O son of great intelligence, to this marvelous account concerning the nature of this reality;
I shall relate to you this single, most wondrous narrative.
There is a king of great heroism, renowned throughout the three worlds, the illustrious one named Svottha, who is capable of subduing the world.
The instruction of whom all leaders throughout the worlds bear upon their heads with uplifted crowns, like a supreme crest-jewel.
This Great Soul, whose sole delight is in daring feats and who dwells in manifold wonders— by whom in the three worlds has he not been brought under control?
He whose thousands of undertakings, which bestow both pleasure and pain,
cannot at all be numbered, like the waves of the ocean.
The prowess of that one of great valor could not be overcome by anyone in the world with weapons or missiles, nor even by fires, just as the sky cannot be grasped with a fist.
Even Śakra, Upendra, and Hara do not imitate even slightly his playful activity, which is vast in its undertaking and radiant with creative manifestation.
O mighty-armed one, his three bodies, capable of pervading the directions,
remain having drawn in the world— consisting of the superior, the inferior, and the middling.
Born within that very vast sky as one possessing three bodies,
he attained his station right there, like sound, wind, or a bird.
Right there in the boundless sky, he created a city with fourteen great streets, adorned with three distinct divisions.
Abounding with groves and orchards, beautiful with pleasure-mountains,
encircled by strings of pearls, and adorned with seven ponds;
It was illuminated by two lamps whose nature was both cool and warm and which were never exhausted;
it was crowded with a merchant's path consisting of upward and downward movements.
In that very same vast city, the king established wandering groups of simple-minded people who lived in small huts.
Some are stationed above, some below, and some in the middle;
some perish after a long time, while others are quickly destroyed.
Covered with dark roofing, adorned with nine doors,
with winds blowing incessantly, they are provided with many windows.
Illuminated by five lamps, they have three pillars made of white wood;
they are smooth, plastered, and soft, and are crowded with rows of gateways.
O Mahāmati, by that king, great yakṣas who were created through illusion and who were constantly afraid of light were appointed as guardians over them.
Then, as the crowds of people moved through the lower rooms, that lord of the earth engaged in various sports, like a bird in its nests.
O son, having dwelt for a short while with those yakṣas within that triple-bodied city, he quickly emerges and departs again.
O child, at times a firm desire arises in that one of restless mind: "I shall go to construct some city that is yet to be."
As if possessed by a spirit, he rises up in agitation and runs;
he reaches even that city, which is like one constructed by the Gandharvas.
Sometimes a desire arises in that dull-witted one, thinking,
"I shall go to destruction," and because of that, he quickly perishes.
It arises again swiftly, like a great wave from the water;
it expands worldly activity intensely, yet again becomes sluggish in its undertaking.
Then, at some point, one is distressed by that very same worldly activity;
one grieves, thinking, "What shall I do? I am ignorant, I am suffering."
And sometimes, having attained joy, it returns of its own accord to fullness,
like the current of a river swelling with the flood of monsoon rains.
The son of that lord of great majesty drinks, leaps, walks, yawns, quivers, shines, and does not shine; he is radiant like the lord of waters agitated by the force of the wind.
The thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Manifestation Arising from One's Own Self," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, during the deep night in Jambudvīpa, the son of pure intent questioned his father, who was seated upon the crest of a kadamba tree.
The son said: "Who is this king known as Svottha, whose form is like that of my father?
And what was it that you told me? Tell me this in accordance with the truth."
Where will the emanation be? Where can one go while it is present?
Since it contradicts both purposes, your speech is for the sake of delusion.
Dāśūra said:
Listen, my son; I shall tell you this exactly as it is, so that you may realize the true nature of this wheel of saṃsāra.
Thus have I described this structure of saṃsāra, which arises from what is non-existent, is devoid of substantial reality, and is pervasive.
The volition born from the supreme ether is said to arise from itself;
it is born by itself alone and dissolves by itself alone.
This entire expansive world exists as that very nature;
by its birth it is born, and when it is destroyed, it perishes within it.
They know Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others to be merely his limbs,
like the branches of a tree or the peaks of a mountain.
In the empty sky, he fashioned this city of the three worlds;
by the mere continuity of appearances, he attained the state of Viriñca.
In this [world] are spread out the fourteen world-enclosures with their vast light, where there are forests, groves, and protected lands, and where there are successions of pleasure gardens.
Where Sahya, Mandara, and Meru serve as pleasure-mountains;
where the moon and sun, with their cool and hot radiance, are like lamps; and where wind remains unexhausted.
Where the rivers flow with moving, excellent pearl necklaces— tall pearls upon trembling waves that resemble the rays of the sun.
Where the seven great oceans exist as lotus ponds, with waters of sugarcane juice, milk, and so forth, and where the submarine fire is a lotus and the jewels are its sprouts.
Furthermore, in the vast expanse above and in the sky, there is the wealth and splendor of merit and demerit,
where men, gods, and kirātas engage in the buying and selling of themselves.
In this very world, within this city, the king Saṅkalpa has constructed various bodily dwellings for his own sport.
Some, known by the name of gods (gīrvāṇa), were appointed only above;
others, such as humans, serpents, and so forth, were established only below.
Moving by the force of wind-machines, they are made of flesh and clay, with white bones for wood; they are variegated, smooth from the application of skin, and stainless.
Some perish after a long time, while others are quickly destroyed;
they possess the beauty of a covering fashioned from the dark hair-like grasses of the *kacaka* and the swelling *ulapa*.
Possessing nine openings, foremost among them the ears, eyes, and nose,
they [the breaths] are warmed and cooled by the vital air (prāṇa) that flows without ceasing.
Equipped with a multitude of windows such as the ears, nose, mouth, and palate,
with the arms and other limbs serving as its gateways, it has the five sense organs as its small lamps.
O Great-minded One, within those [elements] fashioned by illusion,
the great yakṣas of egoism— those who are terrified of the supreme light— arise through conceptual construction.
Within the hollows of the body, he indeed sports excessively with the great yakṣas of egoism, which are entirely unreal and arisen from the unreal.
Just as a cat is in a granary, as a snake is in a bellows,
and as a pearl is within a bamboo stalk, so is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) within the body.
In the houses of bodies, volition rises for a moment and subsides for a moment like a lamp, like a wave in oceans.
Then he attains even the creation of a new city,
when he perceives the intended object as if it were already present before him.
By the mere absence of conceptualization, it perishes quickly by itself;
for its own destruction leads to its supreme welfare, whereas its arising does not.
It arises from one's own mere conceptualization, like a child’s imaginary ghost;
it leads only to endless personal suffering and never to bliss.
This vast suffering of the world expands through the existence of the self;
through its non-existence, it is destroyed in an instant, just as darkness is dispelled by the absence of blindness.
He wails because of his own actions which bring him suffering,
like the monkey who pulled out the wedge while his testicles were pinned between two pieces of wood.
He remains with his neck held high, possessing only a tiny fragment of the bliss he had imagined,
like a young camel suddenly tasting a drop of honey fallen from the sky.
Like an unworthy child, conceptual thought itself undergoes cessation for a moment, finds delight for a moment, and undergoes transformation for a moment.
Having diligently rendered this [self] stainless from all phenomenal states, the wise have attained the supreme state; act accordingly, my son.
However, this Intellect has three bodies— superior, inferior,
and intermediate— known as Tamas, Sattva, and Rajas, which are the cause for the persistence of the world.
For volition, being of the nature of darkness, through constant worldly activity,
falls into supreme wretchedness and descends to the state of worms and insects.
For volition, whose nature is pure being and which is devoted to the knowledge of reality,
presides over sovereignty when it is not far from the state of absolute liberation.
For volition, which is of the nature of passion, exists within worldly activity;
it persists in saṃsāra, enamored with children and wife.
But having abandoned these three kinds of form, O Mahāmati,
conceptual construction reaches the supreme state upon the cessation of the self.
Having abandoned all views and restrained the mind with the mind, bring about the destruction of conceptualization regarding both external and internal objects.
Even if you perform severe austerities for a thousand years,
or if you were to grind yourself to dust with a stone as if in play, it would be enough.
Whether you enter the ocean or even the submarine fire, or whether you fall into a chasm or into the water on the edge of a sword-blade; MU_4,35.40//
Whether Hara be your teacher, or Hari, or even the lotus-born Brahmā,
or the Lord of the World, Bṛhaspati, who is overcome with supreme compassion;
Whether you reside in the netherworld, on earth, or even in heaven,
there is no other means for you than the cessation of mental constructs.
Exert yourself to the utmost through human effort toward the cessation of mental constructs within that bliss which is beginningless, immutable, supremely purifying, and most holy.
O sinless one, it is said that all states of being are woven upon the thread of volition;
when that thread is broken, I know not where those fragile things go.
The non-existent, the existent, and both the existent and non-existent—all this arises from volition alone and from nothing else.
Since both the existent and the non-existent proceed from volition in this way, what can be called "truth" here?
Whatever is conceptualized in whatever manner, that becomes exactly so in an instant;
therefore, O knower of reality, never form any conceptualization whatsoever.

Become free from conceptual construction and devoted to worldly activity as it naturally arises; for when conceptual construction is utterly destroyed, consciousness indeed turns toward the unthinkable.
Having arisen in an unreal form,
by which this world— unreal in its very nature— is pervaded, this suffering is thus futile, being like the self itself.
Therefore, O sinless one, what is the use of resorting to that which leads to great suffering?
The wise in this world resort to that which leads to the absence of suffering, and nothing else.
Having attained the state of ultimate reality and having forcefully cast aside the web of conceptual constructions,
realize that peerless state for the sake of expansive bliss, with the activities of the mind stilled as in deep sleep.
The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Inquiry into Saṃsāra and Conceptualization," is concluded. Chapter Thirty-Six.
The Son.
"O Father, what is the nature of this volition? How, O Lord, does it arise?
How does it increase, and how indeed does it perish?"
Dāśūra says:

They know that the mind's orientation toward an object of cognition— which belongs to the infinite reality of the self, whose nature is universal existence— is the sprout of volitional construction (saṅkalpa).
Having attained a slight degree of existence, that very mind becomes dense;
filling the sky, it proceeds toward solid inertia like a cloud.
The consciousness, while contemplating the object of thought as if it were distinct from itself,
attains the state of volition here, just as a seed attains the state of a sprout.
For volition is indeed volition; it arises by itself and grows rapidly of its own accord, leading only to suffering and not to happiness.
For you are indeed nothing but volition, just as the ocean is nothing but water;
apart from volition, no other state of transmigratory existence truly exists for you.
Indeed, you have arisen in vain through a chance occurrence like that of the crow and the palm fruit;
and like a mirage or the appearance of two moons, you increase though you are unreal.
Just as the perception of gold in one who has swallowed a mātuluṅga fruit is false,
so too shall your own internal conceptualization become unreal upon its own arrival.
You were born as nothing but unreality; you grow as unreality;
and when this consciousness arises, being unreal, you dissolve away.
"This is I," "these entities consisting of pleasure and pain are mine"—thinking thus, you are filled with hope; it is for this very reason that you suffer within.
You are indeed non-existent and unborn; how could there be birth for one who is inert?
You are deluded in vain by your own power of conceptual construction.
Do not form a volitional construction; do not dwell upon existence while remaining in this state.
By this very disposition, you shall become fit for ultimate well-being.
No great effort is required from you to destroy conceptual construction;
conceptual construction perishes within the heart merely through the absence of mental cultivation.
In the crushing of a *sumana* flower, there might be some degree of physical contact;
however, in the destruction of conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*), which is easily accomplished through mere non-existence, there is none.
The effort of moving the hand when picking flowers is useful for the son;
yet even that does not assist him once his conceptual constructions have ceased.
By one who must destroy conceptual construction (saṅkalpa),
it is effortlessly destroyed even in half a moment through the reversal of the perception of existence.

When one remains established in one's own self, wherein even the mere state of being has been stilled, what could there be that is unattainable? For whom, then, would it be unattainable, and how could it be so for one who is not deluded?
O sage, having pierced through thought with thought and the mind with your own mind, abide within your own self; what is so difficult in this?
For when conceptual construction is stilled,
O Mahāmati, this incomparable suffering of saṃsāra becomes stilled at its very root.
For volition, mind, the individual soul, consciousness, intellect, and latent impression—
O best of those who know the meaning, these differ only in name, not in their actual substance.
Apart from a portion of volition, there is nothing whatsoever existing anywhere here;
cut that very [volition] out from your heart—why do you grieve for anything else?
Just as this sky is empty, so indeed is the world empty;
for both of these are extended from conceptual constructions consisting of what is non-existent.

All this that has been established by means of what is unestablished is itself unestablished; therefore, since the world is a mere mental construction, where can meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) find a footing?
But if there is no firm conviction in truth, upon what could latent impressions (vāsanā) be grounded?
Since perfection is attained through the exhaustion of latent impressions, nothing remains to be acquired thereafter.
Therefore, all this should be viewed as non-existent with a sense of detachment, and not through meditative cultivation; by that means, one is not smeared by pleasures or pains.
Having determined that "this is not a real entity," no further attachment arises here;
when attachment is exhausted, joy and resentment, as well as existence and non-existence, are no longer born.
The mind falsely creates this delusion of clouds of pleasure and pain;
the mind is the living soul that vibrates intensely as the mental city of the world.
Transforming the future, the present, and the past,
the mind remains in the world with its powers flashing forth under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The impure and fickle living being, like a monkey in the forest of the heart, establishes this unstable arrangement according to its own disposition, in accordance with its own nature.
Having assumed a long form, they become short in the blink of an eye;
these volitions, like dull waves, cannot be grasped.
When even slightly observed, they increase and consume everything along with its surroundings;
like the remnants of a fire, these volitions blaze up from a mere blade of grass.
Manifesting the world, blazing, momentary, causing delusion, and consisting of insentient forms— such are volitions, like flashes of fire from lightning.
As soon as this son was near, he could have been treated immediately;
there is no doubt in this matter—that what is non-existent never becomes existent anywhere.
If that conceptualization were truly established, it would then be difficult to cure; however, since this is indeed unreal, it is very easy to cure.
If this impurity of saṃsāra were innate, like the blackness of charcoal,
then what wise person, O virtuous one, would ever set about to wash it away?
However, this [defilement] remains within it like the husk, the chaff, and the inner skin of a grain of rice;
when that is so, it is destroyed through human effort.
O son, although it is uncreated, this pervasive impurity of saṃsāra appears utterly artificial to the wise man because it is so easily destroyed by happiness.
Just as the husk of rice or the blackness of copper is destroyed by processing, my son, so too is the impurity of a person removed through spiritual practice.
Just as the husk of a grain of rice, even though it is innate, is surely destroyed, so too is the impurity of the living being;
of this there is no doubt. Therefore, be one who possesses effort.
This samsara, which has been produced in vain by conceptual constructions based on the unreal, comes to dissolution with little effort; for how indeed can an unreal thing be stable?
For one who investigates its own true nature, saṃsāra comes to non-existence,
just as blindness vanishes from the light of a lamp, or the appearance of two moons from one’s own correct vision.
"This is not yours, nor do you belong to this; O son, abandon delusion!
Do not fixate upon what is unreal as if it were real."
Let there be no vain delusion within you that "these playful manifestations are the glorious power of my guru";
for while you exist, those manifestations are extended, and this entire world shines as that very reality of the Self.
In the narrative of Dāśūra, the thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Treatment of Volition," Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard that conversation between the two of them there at night, [he said]:
"O descendant of Raghu, moon in the sky of the Raghu clan! (Raghuvamśa 4.37.1)
He fell from the sky onto the summit of a kadamba tree, thick with leaves, flowers, and creepers;
silent and motionless like a raincloud atop a mountain peak.
There I saw Dāśūra, a hero in the restraint of his senses,
endowed with supreme austerity like a fire with its brilliance.
With his splendors issuing forth from his body, turning the trees to gold,
he was heating that region like the sun heating the world.
Then, seeing that I had arrived, the fisherman honored me with the offering of guest-water and,
having provided a seat of leaves, worshipped me with supreme devotion.
Then, he engaged in conversation with that radiant fisherman,
discussing stories related to his son which were capable of delivering one across the cycle of existence.
I saw that tree, its hollows thick with flower buds,
appearing as if it were smiling with its blossoming teeth, its petals quivering in the wind.
By the will of Dāśūra, it was frequented by all the beasts and birds that had descended there,
like a forest adorned with bowers of creepers.
With yak-tail fans as beautiful as the moon, fluttering against the edges of the creepers,
it was covered like the autumn sky by clusters of fragments of white clouds.
Every limb was adorned with a string of pearls in the form of a succession of frost-drops,
and it was completely filled with an abundance of clear blossoms.
Anointed with saffron and sandalwood paste, it was unblemished and adorned with vast,
pure, and expansive red garments.
It was an endeavor undertaken by a city-dweller who, with his attire suited for marriage and carrying a burden of flowers and other offerings, was attached to a creeper-like woman.
Adorned with circles of creepers in the form of well-bound matted locks,
and furnished with flower-clusters as banners, it was like a city during a festival.
Dusty with the pollen of flowers shaken off by deer scratching themselves,
it stood like a champion tree that had driven back the forest from its borders.
With its peacocks, pale-red with the pollen exhaled from their plumage,
the mountain appeared as if it were scattering the clouds of twilight upon its young *sāla* trees.
With hands as red as coral, reclining in cool shade,
reeling with wine, and possessing a brilliance like the shimmering of frost.
With a dense mass of flowers swaying in the forest breezes,
it possessed eyes in the form of sleepy buds and bore breasts in the form of flower-clusters.
Clad in garments as red as saffron, gathered from heaps of pollen from clusters of flowers,
he leaned against a window that served as a dwelling within a canopy of creeping vines.
With the playful grace of a swing made of fresh flowering creepers,
he sported from the top of his head down to the soles of his feet, together with the entire grove of creepers.

Accompanied by a multitude of forest goddesses who were skilled in the warbling of cuckoos, whose clusters of blossoms were in doubt [of their identity], whose eyes were bees, and who were full of smiles; MU_4,37.20.
Their fatigue from pleasure was allayed by the morning dew;
languid with intoxication, they were closely embraced by one another, covered in the pollen of flowers.
It was surrounded on all sides by pairs of intoxicated bees dwelling within the interior of the flowers, humming something appropriate for their affection, and appearing utterly transparent.
With a desire to hear the humming from the cities on the outskirts of the forest,
they momentarily pricked up their ears with beautiful chewing-sounds that filled the quarters.
For a moment, they gazed upon the ocean-girdled earth, which appeared like a mass of water due to the moon’s rays, while their heads rested charmingly upon the tips of the petals.

The interior of the śāra-reeds was filled with deer sleeping within their leafy nests, appearing as if they were the personified offspring of the forest regions abiding there in accordance with the principles of policy.
It was a place where birds slept confidently with their young in their nests,
and where circles of hanging creepers swayed at the edges of trees from which ripe fruits had fallen.
The bees were rendered hesitant and silent among the flower clusters by the rosaries of lotus seeds,
while the edges [of the forest] were darkened by circles of blue sprouts.
Its entire forest was made fragrant, with clouds of flowers formed like rain-clouds;
it was variegated with *kadamba* trees covered in pollen, and its base was crowded with those seeking fruit.
What is the use of saying more here? There is not even a single leaf on that tree which is not eaten or consumed.
In every leaf of that sovereign of trees, deer slept, having found rest in the thick foliage;
in every thicket, birds were hidden.
As I gazed upon that tree distinguished by such qualities,
that night became like a great festival.
Then, by means of other discourses delightful with the light of higher knowledge, I led his son once again to supreme awakening.
There, with various conversations between one another,
that night passed for us like a single moment, as it does for two lovers.
At dawn, as the web of water-born lotuses of the day’s heat gradually spreads wide, and as the cluster of stars slowly emits the sprouts of the forest of the sky; MU_4,37.34.
Having bid farewell to Dāśūra, who was accompanied by his son and had followed me as far as the region of the sky where the Kadamba trees grow, I went to the river on Mount Harācala.
There, having attained his desired goal and reached the vault of the sky,
he entered the atmosphere and stood composedly in the midst of the sages.
O descendant of Raghu, this story of Dāśūra has been told to you;
it is like a reflection of the world, appearing real in form yet composed of unreality.
O Raghava, I have related this very story of Dāśūra to you for the purpose of discerning the form of the world as a formidable mass of evil.
Therefore, having abandoned both unreal and even real passion,
remain ever noble and self-possessed through the wisdom of the Dāśūra doctrine.
By this chariot of the story of Kadamba and Dāśūraka, which is as beautiful as the immortal gods, let us go;
you shall soon reach that city, by means of which you will become a lord over the worlds.
The thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Meeting of Vasiṣṭha and Dāśūra. Vasiṣṭha said:
Having determined that "this does not exist," abandon attachment to everything;
for what reliance can there be here for those who investigate upon that which does not exist?
If this which is being perceived exists, then what of yours has passed away?
Let it remain; why indeed do you attribute the nature of a self to it?
Even if you possess the certainty that "this exists" or "this does not exist," how can attachment to meditative cultivation be appropriate for one who is both moving and unmoving?
This world does not exist, O Rāma, nor is it non-existent, O Great-minded One;
it is merely this kind of appearance arising solely from itself in this manner.
This is not created by an agent, nor does it follow a sequence uncreated by an agent;
yet, having reached the state of being both agent and non-agent, this manifests of its own accord.
Whether the web of the world be without a creator or have a creator,
O sinless one, do not entertain any connection with this in your mind.

In this world, that self which is devoid of all sense-faculties is like an insentient object; I consider it to be truly a non-agent, and thus the universe arises by mere chance, like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence.
Whatever occurs by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence,
only the fool, and no one else, fixates upon it with a sense of personal involvement.
O Rāma, this world is never peaceful, nor is it subject to destruction;
for it is perceived incessantly and it arises again and again.
O Rāma, this world never exists, nor is it indestructible;
for by inference, it is seen to be constantly wasting away and is subject to destruction.
When the agent here has transcended the domain of all the senses and is free from fever,
then, while acting, he never experiences weariness.
Therefore, this mature destiny, consisting of the states of existence and non-existence,
remains just such— stable and long-lasting— and does not perish even when it has arisen from the mind.
In the midst of infinite time, a hundred autumns is but a small fraction;
how can one who possesses such a brief lifespan still pursue worldly attachments?
If worldly phenomena were stable, then attachment to them would not be improper;
for how indeed could there be a mutual union between the insentient and the sentient?
If the phenomena of the world are unstable, then even attachment to them is not fitting; for this attachment, being as unstable as water-foam, will yield you only suffering at its end.
O mighty-armed one, the bond of attachment between the world and the self—
which are respectively unstable and stable— does not shine forth, like that between foam and a mountain.
Although it is the creator of all, the Self does nothing at all;
it remains perfectly indifferent, like a lamp with respect to its light.
While acting, he does nothing at all, like the sun performing its daily task;
while moving, he does not move, remaining established in his own state just as the sun stays fixed in its own station.
This world appears as if produced from some unknown source,
spreading out like the wind from Arjuna or like a whirlpool in a flood of water.
If this has been discerned by you, O Rāma, with skill, and investigated with a mind purified by valid means of knowledge; MU_4,38.20.
Therefore, O virtuous one, cultivation (bhāvanā) is not capable of establishing the reality of an object;
for what kind of cultivation could there be regarding a fire-brand circle, a dream, or an illusion?
A creature who has arrived by chance is not a fit vessel for affection;
and this web of the world, which is but a delusion, is likewise not a fit object for reliance.
Just as you do not conceive a firm conviction in a hot moon, a cool sun, or the water of a mirage, so too do not conceive a conviction in this [worldly] existence.
Just as you perceive a person created by imagination, a person in a dream, or the delusion of two moons,
so too should you perceive this entire collection of existing things.
Having completely abandoned internal attachment consisting of the cultivation of the splendor of worldly existence, remain as you are in this world; sport here at your ease, O sinless one.
Of the Self who stands in the state of non-agency even while performing agency, who dwells within all beings and yet transcends everything; //MU_4,38.26//
This necessity unfolds merely through proximity,
just as luminosity appears without any desire simply through the presence of a lamp.
Just as *kuṭaja* trees [blossom] by the mere presence of clouds,
so too do the three worlds [arise] by the mere presence of the Self.
Just as the glory of worldly activity arises when the sun remains in the sky, free from all desire, so too does ritual action arise when the Lord exists.
Just as light proceeds from a jewel that remains without desire,
so too does this multitude of worlds proceed by the mere existence of the Divine.
Therefore, both agency and non-agency reside in the Self;
because it is devoid of desire, it is a non-agent, yet it is an agent by virtue of its mere presence.
Because it transcends all the senses, the Lord of Beings is neither agent nor enjoyer;
yet, because He is contained within the senses, He alone is indeed the agent and the enjoyer.
O sinless one, two states indeed exist within the self: agency and non-agency.
Relying upon whichever of these you perceive as conducive to your highest good, remain steadfast.
By means of this firm cultivation that "I am the non-doer in all things," you are not tainted even while performing actions that have entered the stream of worldly life.
When a living being realizes through direct awareness that "I am the non-doer" in all circumstances, the desire for enjoyment becomes flavorless due to the non-engagement of one's own mind.
Where there is the firm conviction, "I do nothing at all here," who could either entertain a desire for a flood of enjoyments or abandon it?
Therefore, through meditation kindled by the thought "I am eternally a non-doer," that very equanimity known as the supreme nectar remains.
Furthermore, O Rāma, if you desire that state which consists in the thought "I do everything," then by virtue of this great agency, they know that too to be the highest state.
Wherever I produce this entire delusion of the world, how could there be a sequence of passion and hatred there? For it is impossible for anything else to exist.
Since my body was burned by one and cherished by another, it is simply a manifestation of my own activity; therefore, what room is there for either grief or joy?
When my own happiness and suffering expand, and when the world-web undergoes its rise and fall,
what internal sequence of distress or elation can there be for one who thinks, "I am the doer"?
But when the play of exhaustion and exhilaration has itself dissolved through the single agency of one's own self, only equanimity remains.
That which is equanimity toward all things is the supreme, true state;
the mind established in that state shall no longer experience suffering.

Or else, O Rāghava, having abandoned everything— both the state of being the doer of all and the state of being a non-doer— and having drunk in [the essence of] the mind, remain firm as you truly are.
"This is I," "this is not I," "I do this," or "this is not [done by me]"—
a view consisting of such mental constructions does not lead to contentment.
That which is the path of the Kālasūtra hell, that which is the snare of the Mahāvīci hell,
and that which is the row of sword-leaf forests— all these are the state of abiding in the thought, "I am the body."
She should be abandoned with every effort, even when total ruin is imminent;
a noble person must not touch her, any more than a Pukkasi woman carrying dog-meat.
When that streak of redness has been cast far away from the sight,
the supreme vision arises like moonlight when the clouds have vanished.

Having clearly realized within yourself that "I am not the doer, nor is this [body] I," or having reached the certainty that "I alone am the doer, I am everything," or having concluded that "I am some indescribable being, or perhaps nothing at all"— abide in your own supreme state, where the best of men, the virtuous knowers of the path, are established.
The thirty-ninth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Investigating Agency," [spoken by] Rāma.
O Brahmin, what you have spoken is true and beautiful in its expression:
the Self is indeed a non-doer yet the doer, and though it is a non-enjoyer, it is the sustainer of all beings.
The Lord of all, consisting of all, pure consciousness alone, the stainless state,
the God whose body is self-experience, abides within all beings.
O Lord, through your words, the Brahman has now reached my heart,
just as the cool water of a mountain reaches it through its streams.
Due to indifference and lack of desire, he neither enjoys nor acts;
yet, because he brings about the welfare of the entire world, the Lord both enjoys and acts.
But, O Blessed One, this vast doubt remains within my heart;
O Brahman, sever it with your word, as the moon dispels darkness with its rays.
"This is real and this is unreal; I am that one, and you are this one;
this is one and this is a second"—such impurities of conceptual construction [are cast off].
How is this [world] situated for the first time within the pure Self, which is as vast and tranquil as the sun amidst the mist?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, I shall explain the establishment of the answer to this excellent question only at the time of the final conclusion; you will understand it then indeed."
O Raghava, having attained the established doctrine of the means to liberation,
you will become fully qualified to hear these questions and answers.
O Rāma, just as a youth is the recipient of beloved songs to be sung,
so too is one who has attained insight the recipient of questions and sublime utterances.
Just as a discourse filled with passion becomes useless for children,
so too does a discourse arising from noble inspiration become fruitless for those of meager understanding.
At a particular time only does something shine forth for a man;
the fruit of a tree appears only in autumn, not in the month of Mādhava.
The words of instruction take hold in an elder, as dye does on a clean cloth;
and discourses on sublime wisdom take hold in one who has realized the self.
The answer to this question was previously stated by me in brief; because it was not given in detail, it has not been clearly understood by you.
If you perceive the self by means of the self, then you yourself, O virtuous one, know this answer to the question; of this there is no doubt.
But when you have attained awakening at the time of the final conclusion, O virtuous one, this sequence of questions and answers shall be explained by me in detail.
The self alone knows the self, for it has been fashioned by the self through itself;
being perfectly serene, the self indeed attains the self.
O Rāma, I have thus related this investigation into the agent and the non-agent;
for the destruction of the substrate of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the knower of that [truth] becomes free from such impressions.
For bondage is indeed the bondage of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), while liberation is the destruction of latent impressions.
Having abandoned the latent impressions, abandon even the desire for liberation.
Having first abandoned the tamasic tendencies perfumed by sense objects,
take up the pure tendencies known as the cultivation of friendliness and the other [divine abodes].
Having abandoned those [external objects] internally while interacting with them externally,
become one whose internal attachment is entirely stilled, with consciousness alone as your latent impression.
Then, having abandoned even that [mind] along with the intellect,
remaining firm in your concentration, abandon that by which you abandon.
The mind, the intellect, the notions of time, light, darkness, and so forth;
the latent impressions and the one who is impressed—all these are preceded by the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa).

O one of noble intellect, you who have abandoned everything along with its very root, whose mind is tranquil and who are as serene as the moon in the sky— you shall indeed become that [liberated state] without delay.
Having completely renounced everything from the heart, the one of great intelligence who remains free from agitation is liberated; he is the Supreme Lord.
Whether he practices meditative concentration or performs actions— or whether he does not—
such a person, whose heart has relinquished all objects of desire and who possesses the supreme intention, is indeed liberated.

For one whose mind is free from latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no need for inaction (naiṣkarmya), nor is there any need for ritual acts; nor is there any need for meditative concentration (samādhi) or the chanting of prayers (japya).
The scriptures have been sufficiently investigated and long deliberated upon among one another;
for those who have abandoned all latent impressions, there is no higher state than silence.
Having wandered through the ten directions, all that is to be seen has been seen;
yet only a few people truly perceive things as they really are.
Whatever is perceived, wherever one goes,
and whatever is other than the desired or undesired— toward that, people do not strive.
Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever sequences of actions people perform—all of these are for the sake of the body alone; nothing at all is for the sake of the self.
In Pātāla, in the world of Brahmā, in heaven, and on the surface of the earth,
only a few virtuous ones are seen who have perceived the ultimate vision.
That wise one for whom the certainties— "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted"— have dissolved because they arose from what is unreal, is exceedingly rare to find.
Let him rule the world, or enter into fire or water;
no living being attains rest except through the attainment of the Self.
Those of great intelligence who are heroes against the enemies of their own senses, and who strive for the destruction of the fever of birth— those of vast wisdom are to be venerated.
Everywhere there are only the five elements; no sixth thing exists.
Where, then, can one of steady intellect find delight—in the netherworld, on the surface of the earth, or in the sky?
For the wise one who crosses over by means of reasoning, cyclic existence is like the footprint of a cow;
but for one who has abandoned reasoning from afar, it is like a vast, intoxicated ocean.
For one whose consciousness is expansive, what can the universe— which is as clear as a *kadamba* flower bud—
bestow, and what can it consume, even when this entire world has been attained?
For this reason, O Rāma, I consider those great acts of war undertaken by the ignorant to be like begging for alms that results in the destruction of hundreds of thousands of lives.
In a mere moment of time, O you of delicate belly,
that which is destruction even for this [body] is like a great thunderbolt to a creeper.

Since there is nothing in the three worlds superior even to a blade of grass for one who regards a portion of the Self as being everything, what could there be for such a person of self-possession that remains unattained?
On one side it is covered with hundreds of mountains, and likewise on this side with masses of water;
how small is the body of this earth that it might fill [the universe] so magnificently?
There is nothing whatsoever in this world, including the netherworlds and the oceans,
that can cause any effect for the self-possessed one who knows the truth.
For the wise one who has attained oneness, who is as pervasive as space, who is self-abiding and possesses the Self, and who remains established in the Self beyond the mind; MU 4.39.44.
The three worlds are a vast wilderness, grey with the misty nets of bodies, hollow within, and beautiful in their stillness.
All the great mountain ranges are but foam upon the vast and stainless ocean of Brahman;
the splendors of the world are a mirage within the great radiance of the sun of consciousness.
The successions of creations are the waves of the great ocean of the reality of the Self;
the perspectives of the scriptures are the rains from the ocean of the unsurpassed state.
The lights of the moon, sun, and fire are like a jar, a piece of wood, or other such objects; likewise, the hosts of living beings are illuminated by the radiance of the lamp of consciousness.
For a long time, men, gods, and asuras have been like deer wandering in the forest of saṃsāra with their true selves hidden, devouring the grass of sensual pleasures.
The bodies of the world are door-bolts of bone-fragments with heads as covers and tendons as chains; they are the caskets of flesh containing the jewel of the world’s living beings.
To amuse their childish intellects, they kept leather dolls— charming like young forest does— that moved at the command of others.
A person of such noble mind and great intelligence does not waver even slightly before floods of enjoyments, just as a mountain is unmoved by gusts of wind from the mouth.
O Rāma, it is said that the Knower of the Self abides in that most exalted state,
from which even the regions of the moon and sun appear to us as if they were the netherworld.
Having become possessed of light, those who possess true knowledge behold these worlds— which were once without light—
as if they were crawling reptiles submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
None of these worldly phenomena can delight one who knows reality, just as the courtesans of a wretched village cannot please a refined city man.
No worldly phenomena whatsoever can please one who knows reality,
even when they are close at hand, just as clouds cannot color the vast sky of his heart.
None of these worldly phenomena can delight one who knows reality, just as dancing female monkeys cannot please Hara, who seeks the graceful dance of Gaurī.
None of these worldly phenomena can delight one who knows reality, just as the beauty of a reflection from the past cannot delight a jewel placed inside a jar.
Beholding the world as resembling a wheel upon which one is mounted, as consisting of nothingness, and as a reflection formed by waves tossing upon the surface of water,
the knower of that reality finds no delight in the pleasures sought by it, just as a royal swan finds no pleasure in mere blades of kusha grass.
The fortieth canto, titled "Description of the Form of the Fulfilled Intention," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this very matter, O Rāghava, listen to those purifying verses sung by Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, which were appropriate for his ancestors.
Once, while staying in a certain thicket of Mount Meru, the son of the preceptor of the gods attained rest within his own self through the power of practice.
His mind, filled with the nectar of right knowledge,
found no delight in this visible world, which consists of the five elements, is withered, and is of a fragile nature.

As if despondent because he saw nothing beyond the reality of the Self, he spoke these words alone in a faltering voice: tena nirviṇṇa iva sa ātmatattvād ṛte param / apaśyan samuvācedam eko gadgadayā girā //MU_4,40.4//
What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I grasp? What shall I abandon?
The entire universe is filled by the Self, just as it is by the waters at the end of a great aeon.
Suffering, the self, pleasure, space, hope, you, and likewise I—all this has arisen as consisting of the self; alas, I have been lost through the self!

Within bodies, both externally and internally, below and above, and in all directions—from here the Self, and likewise from there the Self; there is nowhere anything that does not consist of the Self.
For the Self indeed abides everywhere, and everything is established within the Self;
all this is the Self alone—thus, I bow down to the Self within the Self.
There is nothing where I am not, and there is nothing that is not in me;
what else could I desire? I simply abide in tranquility.
By means of that [state] through which I bow within myself to the Self by the Self,
and by which my inner self is filled and I become tranquil— where else could I possibly go?
I am fire, I am wind, I am the earth, I am the sky;
whatever does not exist apart from me is nothing at all—I alone pervade everything.
Possessing a form as vast and terrifying as the infinite sky,
consisting of all consciousness and full, I abide like a single, universal ocean.
Thus meditating upon this state within a bower of the Golden Mountain,
he then gradually utters the syllable Oṃ, like the sound of a bell.
Meditating neither within nor without upon the final half-measure of the syllable *oṃ*, which is as tender as a young shoot, one should contemplate it in the supreme heart.

Pure, with the stain of the divisions of time removed, his mental fluctuations dissolved within his heart, he remained like the cloudless autumn sky; Kaca stood there, possessing a form as solid as a mountain of stone.
The Forty-first Sarga, titled "Kaca-gāthā," from the Vasiṣṭha [section].
Apart from attachment to food, drink, and women, there is nothing here in this world that is auspicious or reliable; what then would a great man desire?
How can the virtuous find delight in those enjoyments and the like by which the base, the beasts, and the deluded are satisfied?
Enough with those human donkeys in this world who place their trust in enjoyments— the entire property of the wretched, which is fragile in its beginning, middle, and end.
"Here are the hair, there is the blood"—this is the body of a woman;
with this, dogs find satisfaction, not human beings.
The earth is clay, trees are wood, the body is flesh, and the mountain is stone;
the ground is beneath and the sky is behind—what in this is unprecedented for the sake of happiness?
All worldly cognitions follow upon contact with sense-objects and are fragile at the stage of discernment; when grasped, they lead only to delusion.
At the very end of every state of existence, even that which is auspicious,
there is indeed defiled suffering, just as soot exists within a flame.
The activities of the six faculties, including the mind, are impermanent due to their coming and going;
like a creeper clinging to a lordly elephant, they do not support a state of being.
"This daughter is the beloved of my blood and flesh"—with such affection, she clings to that heap of bones which she calls her own body; what logic is there in this?
O Rāma, all this is real and stable for the sake of the ignorant;
but for the knower, O Rāma, the world is unstable and unreal, and thus does not bring satisfaction.
Even when poison has not been consumed, that which brings about the stupor of poison—
abandoning that attachment to existence, attain the state of knowing through the oneness of the Self.
When the mind has attained stability by perceiving a self in what is not-self,
then this world-web, consisting of unreality, comes into being.
By the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), a body is imagined by the mind of Brahmā,
just as the brilliance of gold appears upon a wall that has been infused with light.
Rāma:
O Brahmin of great intelligence, having reached the state of Brahmā,
how does the mind gradually bring this world to a state of solid density?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having arisen from his bed in the lotus as a newborn infant, he first uttered the word "Brahman"; therefore, he is called Brahmā.
Then, within him, the Fortune of Resolve established a firm footing for that mind, which consists of a web of volitions and assumes imagined forms.
Then he first willed forth a great, blazing radiance, a circle of flickering fire-tendrils that bent the very horizons.
The sky was filled with a mass of harsh sparks from fire spat out like stars,
while its borders were turned into golden forests, tawny as *muñja* grass.
His own mandala was dense with a mass of flames and golden creepers, adorned with shimmering,
spreading, and fiercely radiant armlets and earrings.
Within that radiant splendor, the mind residing in his body fashioned the sun,
which bore the very form of the Self.
Then, from that splendor, the sun rises,
situated in the midst of a circle of flames, with his golden earrings blazing.
Bearing a mass of matted locks of flames, vomiting forth spreading fire,
with limbs that are the play of flames, he fills the entire circle of space.
Then Brahmā, possessed of great intelligence, [beheld] those other particles of splendor,
suddenly appearing as beautiful celestial chariots through his inspired intuition.
In an instant he formed a mental resolve and beheld those very things,
just as a wise man perceives the multitude of sounds arising immediately after his intention.
O mighty-armed one, this is the established order of the Self-existent One at every re-creation: for each day and for each world, the gods and asuras are ordained by his volition.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, the islands, the directions, the mountains, and the earth.
This Brahmā fashioned the gods, Daityas, humans, Nāgas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, just as the ocean produces waves.
The Lotus-born One ordained their countries, mountains, and supreme celestial mansions, as well as their distinct functions.
They too, having attained success through their mere volition and possessing all powers,
beheld the object exactly as they had intended it, appearing before them in an instant.
Then they imagine many other diverse hosts of beings; those [beings] imagine others there, and those others imagine yet others, even of various kinds.
Having recollected the Vedas, which are endowed with the qualities of the sequence of sacrifices,
Brahmā then established the boundaries for the wife of the world-household.
Assuming a Brahmanic form, the mind, possessing a great illusory body,
thus expands this creation, which is crowded with a continuous succession of beings.
[He saw] the earth, rich with oceans, mountains, and trees, which had established the sequence of the various worlds,
and whose interior was a mass of matted locks consisting of Mount Meru, the surface of the earth, the quarters, and the forest thickets.
Pierced by pleasure, pain, old age, birth, death, and disease;
struck by passion, hatred, and fear; and consisting of the nature of the three qualities (guṇas).
Whatever was previously imagined by those minds born of Viriñca,
all that is seen exactly as it was, even today, through illusion.
Thus, in all creations— or in some of them— the Unborn One conceives the cycle of existence and beholds it as stable.
Thus this delusion has falsely attained stability in the world;
it is itself incessantly imagined by the mind through its own conceptualization.
By the power of volition, all the activities of the world proceed;
by the power of volition, O Goddess, destiny remains fixed and established.
When the creation had been established by the Lords of Creatures, that Lord Brahmā, born from the lotus,
sat upon his lotus-throne and reflected.
By the mere vibration of the mind, this wondrous creation has arisen—
vast, expansive, and subject to the transformations of worldly activity.
It is enriched by Indra, Upendra, and Narendras; it is crowded with mountains and oceans;
and its hollows are congested with the netherworld, the earth, the quarters, and the various paths.
This entire web of mental constructs has been spread out by me as something harmful;
now I shall desist from this process of manifesting such constructs.
Having thus resolved, having desisted from the perilous thicket of conceptual constructions,
he remembers the beginningless, supreme Brahman as the Self by means of the self.
Having reached that state which appears as such, with his mind dissolved therein,
he remains happily with a tranquil self, like one weary from a journey resting upon a couch.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, having attained supreme peace,
he abides within himself by means of the self, like an undisturbed ocean.
At times, the Lord, the Master, withdraws from meditation of his own accord,
by the power of consciousness, like the ocean ceasing its movement of water due to its inherent gentleness.
He contemplates saṃsāra as endowed with pleasure and pain,
bound by hundreds of snares of hope, and afflicted by passion, hatred, and fear.
Then, his mind overcome with compassion, he composes here various treatises of great significance for the sake of the manifestation of reality.
The Purāṇas and other such works, which contain the inner essence of knowledge and the Vedas and Vedāntas, lead all embodied beings to liberation.
Again, having taken that supreme state as his object— a state free from calamity—
he remains established in himself, his soul at peace, like the ocean without Mount Mandara.
Having observed the activities of the world and having established them within the bounds of moral order,
Brahmā, seated upon his lotus throne, abides once more within his own self.
His body, by virtue of the impressions of birth alone,
persists like the whirling of a potter's wheel, solely for the sake of no further rebirth.
To him, neither the renunciation nor the grasping of the body is pleasing;
neither self nor other exists here, nor likewise does persistence or non-persistence.
The undertaking of all states of being is equal in all modes of conduct;
like the form of a full ocean, he remains truly liberated.
Sometimes, being entirely free from all conceptual constructions,
he awakens by chance for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
O Mahāmati, know that this meritorious state of Brahmā which I have described is the sattvic state among the hosts of gods.
In the supreme space of emission, that portion of the mind of Brahman which first arises— this very [portion] attains the state of Brahman.
But when the state of persistence has occurred during creation, another supreme ideation arises;
that, having taken recourse in space and wind, enters into the sprouts of medicinal herbs.
One attains the state of a woman, another the state of a man;
one attains the state of an animal, and another the state of a yakṣa.
Having taken the sprouts of medicinal herbs through the conduit of the moonbeams,
whatever being she approaches quickly becomes that very same being.
Indeed, having been born in that very life by virtue of association,
one is either bound or liberated according to the distinction of one's own wondrous power.

Thus, O Rāmabhadra, this creation has indeed reached such a state; clearly bound by the fetters of karma that manifest as dire calamities, it is distressed by the intensity of the burden of various appearing forms, activities, and pastimes, through the misfortune of its own conceptual constructions.
The forty-second canto, titled "The Conduct of Kamalaja," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
O mighty-armed one, while this blessed and holy Grandfather, who has established the order of creation, was stationed in his stainless state;
In this world, which is like a dilapidated water-wheel, the thirst for life functions according to its own mechanism,
using as its rope the cord of craving for existence and the buckets of living beings.
And when living beings have arisen as Brahman and enter the cage of worldly existence,
their latent impressions (vāsanās) being cut away and withered, they dissolve like water into a mass of water.
When other minds have arrived from the Lord, wandering amidst the wind of the sky, they are like sparks flickering from the end of a whirling firebrand.
O Rāma, streams of living beings emerge incessantly from the Brahman and likewise enter it from all sides, like waves in the ocean.
Born from the state that is without beginning or end, others have entered the realm of conceptualization; they enter the elemental ether like the beauty of smoke entering a cloud.
There they attain oneness with the spheres of the elements and subtle essences,
just as the fragrance of mandāra flowers merges with sweet breezes.
But they, being assailed by that fierce wind of the subtle elements which has attained the state of their vital breath, are overcome like the immortals by a host of Daityas.
By that wind arising from the vital breaths of living beings,
those odors are deposited within bodies, like scents in the cavities of the nostrils.
Into those bodies of the elements, living beings enter as vital energy;
from that they are born in the world and become manifest living creatures.

Others, by way of the path beginning with smoke, enter the state of an embryo within embodied beings and attain the state of being a living creature, or they remain for a long time in the state of an immobile being.
Some, entering the path of the wind and dwelling within the hollows of *śālī* trees, attain virility and are born as various beings possessing the nature of living creatures.
O Rāma, some lineage of living beings, as soon as it has arisen,
remains for a while within the hollow of the sky, enveloped by those subtle elements alone.
The Blessed One rises like the moon with its full orb,
flooding the world with rays that are like shimmering waves of milk.
Then, among those exceedingly beautiful moonbeams, she, like a restless female bird, set her foot upon one after another, as if moving from tree to tree.
From those moonbeams as well, she drew forth the sprouts of medicinal herbs,
just as a female bee draws [honey] from a fresh cluster of night-lotuses from day-lotuses.
The fruits of those medicinal plants become exceedingly sweet within;
they even attain fullness, just as stalks of sugarcane do through their juice.
Upon those fruits, the row of living beings sets foot, like a line of insects upon the weight of a mother’s breasts filled with milk, as they drip with the rays of the moon.
When those circles of fruits are eaten ripe by embodied beings,
the potency enters into them and remains there, unawakened.
The splendor of the individual soul (*jīvaśrī*), with its web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dormant, presides over the cage of the womb,
just as the splendor of the seed (*bījaśrī*) with its leaves folded sleeps within a jar.
Just as fire resides in wood, just as a jar resides in clay,
and just as clarified butter resides in milk, so does the living soul reside within vitality.
By this sequential yoga, having attained the supreme state from Maheśvara,
that man who is born on earth becomes one whose bodily splendor is unseen by others.
For he would belong to the sattvic class and possess noble conduct;
if, by that very [nature], he is a partaker of liberation from birth, then he is a sattvic person.
Then, having entered this womb and experienced a succession of births,
if one has attained a birth for the sake of liberation, that person is characterized by both the qualities of passion (rajas) and goodness (sattva).
O Rāma, I shall now describe to you the sequence for a man of rajasic temperament in his final birth, and how he attains liberation.
He who has come for the first time, being exceedingly pure in nature, is someone who occasionally arises somewhere within this cycle of existence, O sinless one.
O Rāma, men who are characterized by both passion and goodness arise here;
therefore, they alone should be investigated, and one should proceed in this world according to their perspective.
O Rāma, those men who first emerged from the Supreme Self are endowed with great qualities and are difficult to find.
And as for others who are variously mute, deluded, and of a tamasic nature—
those who are like stationary objects— what is there to deliberate upon regarding them, O Rāma?

Having experienced only a few other births and having attained great fortune in his present life, this man has indeed reached a state of fitness for profound inquiry; he is one whose nature is both passionate and pure.
The forty-third canto, titled "The Incarnation of the Living Soul," taught in connection with the determination of the person to be investigated; by Vasiṣṭha.
For those who abide in the quality of passion (rājasa) yet possess these great virtues on this earth,
they are always joyful and exalted, like moons in the sky.
They do not undergo exhaustion, just as the regions of space do not become soiled; they do not wither in adversity, just as golden lotuses do not fade at night.

They do not desire anything other than their own nature, just as the sun does not desire anything other than the day; they always delight in their own right conduct, just as trees delight in their own seasonal flowering.
They never abandon their internal state of constant fullness and imperturbability, which is as beautiful as the moon, even in times of adversity, just as the moon does not lose its coolness.
By the very form of their beauty, which is lovely with virtues such as loving-kindness, they shine forth like great trees graced by a creeper smiling with clusters of fresh blossoms.
Those who are even-tempered, full of the essence of battle, gentle, and always virtuous toward the good, remain steadfast in their boundaries like the ocean, possessing expansive minds.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, their state, which is the removal of all calamities, should always be followed; it should not be plunged into the ocean of misfortune.
In this world, one should wander without weariness in such a manner that those characterized by passion and goodness act for their own upliftment.
Having mastered the noble and authentic treatises and having investigated them again and again,
one should swiftly cultivate the perception of impermanence with a mind that is secluded and inwardly focused.
One should quickly meditate upon that very form which is eternal at the beginning and at the end of all things existing within the three worlds; one should not meditate on anything else in vain.
Having abandoned false vision, which is futile and finite, one should remember this alone: that which is correct, which possesses the essence of knowledge, and which is infinite.
"Who am I? How is this? What is this extended cycle of existence?"—this should be investigated with effort by one who is wise and in the company of the virtuous.
One should not immerse oneself in improper actions, nor should one dwell with the ignoble;
one should regard the destroyer of all as death itself, never treating it with contempt.
One who occupies a high position, who possesses great coolness of disposition, and who is wise,
should be followed by the virtuous alone, just as the peacock follows the cloud.
Having performed pure inquiry into egoism, the body, and the arising of saṃsāra, a person should take refuge in reality alone.
Having abandoned the body— along with its bones and flesh, and the impure elements such as blood—
one should behold pure consciousness alone, like a thread upon which a string of pearls is strung.
In Truth— which is eternal, pervasive, pure, all-pervading, the source of all existence, and auspicious—
all this is strung together like a multitude of gems upon a thread.
That very same consciousness which exists in the sun, the ornament of the expanse of the worlds in the sky,
is that same consciousness within the belly of an insect dwelling in a crevice of the earth.
