Just as there is no difference between jars and space in the ultimate sense,
O sinless one, so too there is no difference among the consciousnesses residing within bodies.
For all beings, the bitter and the pungent are no different;
indeed, because experience is one, there can be no distinction based on the individual self alone.
Since the reality that is pure consciousness alone remains eternally as one,
what is this delusion of yours that thinks, "this has arisen," or "this has perished"?
There is no such thing here that, having not existed, is born;
nor is there any such thing that, having existed, perishes.
O Rāghava, this is merely a mental appearance; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Due to the mind being agitated and unpeaceful, it stands as if it were real.

Let there be delusion and confusion for you because of your ignorance that "this which perishes is not real," and let there be firm certainty for you that "it is not unreal"; thus, may you be free from sorrow.
If the world does not exist, what indeed is there here for delusion? And if it does exist, what indeed could be the cause of such delusion?
Therefore, amidst the conditions of birth and death, remain ever-peaceful and as utterly equanimous as space.
The forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Reflection on Delusion," by Vasiṣṭha.
A wise person who possesses discernment should, from the very beginning,
dwell together with a noble person of great intelligence who knows the meaning of the scriptures and is possessed of wisdom.
Whatever sublime insights that destroy suffering exist,
they flourish among virtuous people like creepers in the springtime.
O mighty-armed one, by deliberating with a virtuous, dispassionate, amiable, and great soul, the supreme state is attained.
O Rāma, a person who is refined by study of the scriptures, association with virtuous people, detachment, and practice shines like you— a fit vessel for higher knowledge.
But you, whose own conduct is noble, steadfast, and an ocean of a multitude of virtues,
abide in a birth that is free from suffering, characterized by the qualities of passion and goodness.
No longer in this burnt-out cycle of existence are you a vessel for suffering;
you are one who has reached his final birth, O Sage, and you run toward your true nature.
The reality of the world has become manifest to you through your own stainless vision, exactly as it is, by its very radiance, like that of the sun.
Now, with the impurities burnt away by the fire of the poison of my words, you shall surely become stainless, like the autumnal sky when the clouds have been dispelled.
Make the mind— liberated from the contemplation of worldly existence, joined with supreme consciousness, and like a cluster of liberated pearls— utterly transparent within your heart.
When the mind is freed from the calculation that "this is mine" and "this belongs to another," and is devoid of all distinctions, it is undoubtedly liberated.
Those men on earth who shall now follow the conduct of your supreme majesty will also attain the state free from sorrow.
Those men who shall sport according to the conduct of Rāghava will cross over the ocean of existence by means of the small boat of their own minds.
That virtuous person who possesses a mind equal to yours and views all things with equanimity is fit for the visions of knowledge, just as the full moon is fit for its radiant beams.
You have reached the state free from sorrow, following the course as it has come to pass;
remain with your intellect as long as the body lasts, devoid of passion and hatred.
Outwardly, observe the conduct appropriate for the world, but inwardly, having abandoned all desires; having attained supreme coolness, remain like the orb of the full moon.
But those born in other births who lack virtuous qualities are not to be considered; for they possess the nature of jackal cubs.
O mighty-armed one, by cultivating those qualities that belong to men born with a *sāttvika* nature, a person attains a noble birth in a future life.
Whatever caste and qualities a person constantly cultivates in this world,
even if born into another caste, they attain that very state of being in an instant.
All previous states of being, which follow the influence of birth and karma,
are overcome by the courageous through human effort, just as brave men conquer their enemies.
One should rescue the intellect with fortitude, even when it is distressed by the defects of karma belonging to a previous birth of impure nature, just as one rescues a bewildered doe from the mud.
Even those who have taken birth in other classes, whether tāmasa or rājasa,
attain the state of a sāttvika birth through the power of their own discernment.
O Rāghava, whatever is directed within the clear jewel of the mind, the self becomes composed of that; therefore, human effort triumphs.
Through human effort characterized by highly precious virtues,
those of later auspicious births in this world become seekers of liberation.
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere,
that a person endowed with virtue cannot attain through human effort.
Endowed with undecaying fortitude, the impetus of excellent dispassion,
and wisdom firmly rooted, what desired goal do you not attain?
Having secured your own welfare through the state of a Great Being by means of your wisdom, become free from sorrow;
then, by your very example, these people on earth shall likewise become entirely free from sorrow.

O Rāma, O Rāma! Since you are endowed with the great majesty of discernment in this final birth, and are delightful through the quality of *sattva* that has spread within you, surely let this deluded anxiety regarding the bonds of worldly existence not take root in you as you perform actions established in *sattva*.
The Chapter on Abiding is completed.
Chapter Five: Peace; First Sarga.
Now, immediately following the section on "Abiding," hear this section on "Quiescence," which, when understood, brings about Nirvana.
Vālmīki:
While Vasiṣṭha was thus speaking these delightful and purifying words in that well-ordered assembly, which was as still as the autumn sky studded with stars—
And for the sake of hearing [the teaching], while the king remained silent within the assembly,
he was like a lotus-pond where the lotuses are motionless due to the absence of wind.
And among the wanton women, whose power of passion and delusion had been stilled,
an inner tranquility arose as if they had been long ordained for the life of a wandering ascetic.
As if from hearing [the news], the swans in his lotus-like hands had vanished; and as if through paralysis, the fly-whisks with their silent, low-hanging bells lay still.
While those kings who knew the truth were examining the subtle portion of consciousness with the tips of their index fingers resting upon the ends of their noses, [the sage spoke].
When Rāma had blossomed like a lotus at dawn,
he was like the rising of the sun in a sky where the seat of darkness has been abandoned.
Daśaratha listened with delight to the words of Vasiṣṭha’s daughter,
as a peahen listens to the thundering of a cloud that rains down heavily.
Having withdrawn his mind, which is as restless as a monkey, from all enjoyments,
he applies it with effort toward listening while the minister remains present.
When his own Self, as stainless as a digit of the moon, was fully realized through the words of Vasiṣṭha,
Lakṣmaṇa shone forth, his aim clearly perceived and distinguished by the power of his training.
When Śatrughna, the crusher of enemies, had attained fullness of mind,
he remained like the full moon of the Rākā night, having reached a state of sufficient bliss.
When Sumantra had attained a state of friendship, his mind became as cool as the rays of the moon,
and his heart blossomed like a lotus at that very moment.
Then, while those other sages and kings remained there,
their jewels of minds were washed clean and their hearts seemed to breathe a sigh of relief.
Then there arose the sound of midday conch shells, filling the quarters of the sky and deep as the roar of clouds at the end of an aeon, resembling the thundering of the ocean.
By that great sound, the words of the sage were eclipsed,
just as the cries of cuckoos are drowned out by the roar of a thundercloud.
Then the sage interrupted his own speech in the assembly:
"By what great person can a virtue whose essence has been overcome be proclaimed?"
Then, after hearing that midday clamor for just a moment,
when the dense tumult had subsided, the sage spoke to Rāma.
O crusher of enemies, I have thus described to you this much of Rāma’s daily routine for today; tomorrow morning I shall explain the rest that remains to be told.
This midday libation is that which must necessarily be performed by the twice-born; it is our duty, yet it is falling into neglect, O Noble One.
You too, O fortunate one, skilled in proper conduct, arise and perform the entire ritual of the sacrifice, including the bathing, giving of gifts, worship, and so forth.
Having spoken thus, the sage rose together with Daśaratha,
like the sun rising from the slope of the eastern mountain along with the moon and its assembly of stars.
When those two rose, the entire assembly trembled to rise as well,
like a lotus pond with eyes like blue lotuses when touched by a gentle breeze.
Adorned by a swarm of bees arising from her ear-ornaments,
she rose up like the army of elephants on Mount Vindhya, with their trunks swaying like lotuses.
With the circles of their armlets pulverized by the mutual friction of their shoulders,
she indicated the time of twilight with clouds reddened by the dust of jewels.
The humming of bees wandering about her falling ear-ornaments filled the air,
while the sky was turned into a rainbow by the brilliant radiance of her magnificent crown.
With the hands of lovely creepers as moving chowries of flower-clusters,
she was like a forest line agitated by a herd of noble elephants.
With their garments mutually drawn by the brilliance of the jewels in their glittering bracelets,
they were like a garland from the Mandara forest whose flowers are shaken by the wind.
With pure clouds formed from the frost-like particles of musk,
she spread across all the lands like an autumnal garland along the slopes of the quarters.
With the cavities of the sky made crimson by the mass of jewels on the playful crowns [of the gods],
she was like the twilight that brings about the dissolution of the activities of the restless and trembling lotuses.

Filled with water in the form of the rays of jewels, with lotus-faces in close succession, encircled by swarms of bees, and possessing the essence of the sound of tinkling anklets— she was like a lotus pond.
That assembly, crowded with hundreds of kings and filled with a continuous succession of beings,
arose like a newly arisen creation.
Then, having bowed to the king, the princes departed from the royal palace like waves of the ocean made into rainbows by jewels.
Then the neighboring kings and ministers, experts in statesmanship and discernment, bowed down to Vasiṣṭha and the lord of the earth and departed to bathe.
Vāmadeva and others, as well as Viśvāmitra and the rest,
stood with Vasiṣṭha at their head, intent upon the ritual bath.
Having honored the assembly of sages there, King Daśaratha,
the subduer of enemies, was dismissed by them and then departed for his own purpose.
Those who dwell in the forest went to the forest; those who dwell in the sky went to the sky;
and the city-dwellers likewise departed for their morning arrival at the city.
Requested out of affection by both the lord of the earth and Vasiṣṭha,
the powerful Viśvāmitra spent the night in the residence of Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha was being attended by the foremost of brahmins, by kings, and likewise by sages,
as well as by all the sons of Daśaratha, headed by Rāma.
The glorious one, honored by all the worlds, went to his own hermitage,
followed by a multitude of gods, like the Lotus-born Brahmā proceeding to the world of Brahmā.
From that place, the sage dismissed all those sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and the others, who were bowing at his feet.
Having dismissed those who move through the sky, those who move upon the earth, and those who move in the water— all of whom were within the range of his praised virtues—
he performed, in due order, those daily rites for the twice-born in his own home before the noble sage.
The Second Sarga, titled "Description of the First Day," by Vālmīki:
Having gathered at the house, those heroic princes, radiant as the moon, performed the entire sequence of daily rites in their own dwellings without exception.
Vasiṣṭha, Rāghava, the kings, the sages, and the twice-born—
all performed their respective duties then within the courtyards of their own homes.
They bathed in reservoirs that captivated with lotuses, white lilies, night-blooming water-lilies, and blue lotuses,
and resounded with the cries of ruddy geese, swans, and cranes.
They gave gifts to the brahmins consisting of cattle, land, sesame seeds, gold, beds, seats, food, and fine garments.
In their own palaces, variegated with gold and jewels,
they worshipped the gods beginning with Acyuta, Īśāna, Hutāśa, and Arka.
Together with their sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen, and circles of companions,
they then partook of their appropriate meals.
And at that time, it was day in this city; because only an eighth part remained, the sun was mild and charming with its gentle breeze.
Together with his kinsmen, he performed the evening rites according to their respective desires appropriate for that time, until the sun went to its setting.
They performed the twilight devotions thoroughly, recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn,
chanted sacred praises, and sang delightful verses.
Then, as the moon that dispels the sorrow of the night-lily rose from the Milky Ocean, bestowing its dew like the daughter of Indra;
The descendants of Raghu rested upon couches that were strewn slowly with flowers, sprinkled with handfuls of camphor, and as delightful as the long orb of the moon.
Then, in the absence of Rāma, that beautiful woman passed the night there slowly, occupied with those activities, like a single auspicious moment (muhūrta).
Rāma remained there, reflecting upon those very words of Vasiṣṭha— sweet and noble— which he had previously drunk in, just as a young elephant recalls the milk it has drunk before.
What indeed is this wandering in saṃsāra? Who are these people? What are these various beings here that come and go? MU_5,2.14.
What is the nature of the mind, and how is it projected?
From what does this illusion arise, and how is it brought to an end?
And what benefit or what fault could there be from its cessation?
Furthermore, how has this contraction come upon the Self, which is all-pervading?
What was said by the Blessed One, the Sage, regarding the destruction of the mind?
What was proclaimed concerning the mastery of the senses? And what was said regarding the self?

Through its pervasive forms such as the individual soul (jīva), the intellect (citta), the mind (manas), and illusion (māyā)— though these are composed of unreality— it is the Self alone that expands this cycle of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).
When these very things, bound by the threads of mind alone, have come to an end, there is the cessation of suffering; how then are they not easily cured for us?
How can I separate this female crane of my intellect from the swirling mass of clouds that are enjoyments, just as a swan separates a stream of milk from water?
Enjoyments cannot be abandoned, yet without abandoning them, our intellects have no power over calamities; alas, a dire crisis has arrived!
This very purpose, which is to be attained by the conquest of the mind alone, has been fully accomplished for me; yet it remains as heavy as a mountain due to my folly, like a yakṣa to a child.
When will our mind, having attained its own peace and being freed from the agitation of saṃsāra,
find happiness like a young woman who has found her beloved?
May my mind become purified— its agitation stilled, all curiosity vanished, and resting in the shoreless state.
When shall I laugh at the world, having well-rested in that state which is cooler even than the moon, though it be full of all its digits?
When will the mind, having abandoned its form that is delicate through conceptualization and having dissolved within itself, attain peace, like a wave in water?
When, having crossed the ocean of saṃsāra— turbulent with the waves of craving and garlanded with the crocodiles of illusion— shall I become free from the fever of suffering?
When the paths have become pure through the subsiding of all faults, we, the wise ones who perceive with equanimity, shall dwell without sorrow among those seeking liberation.
When will our mind, which has scorched every limb, which causes fear to all the elements, and which is the long-lasting fever of saṃsāra, finally be stilled?
O Buddha, like the trace of a lamp in a windless place, having burned away all defects and abandoned delusion, you shall attain peace immediately following self-illumination.
When will you, whose bodies have been scorched by evil desires, easily cross over from sufferings, like Garuḍas emerging from the ocean?
"This is he," "I am this," "this is mine"— this delusion arising from manifest [ignorance],
like a dark cloud in autumn, when will it ever subside?
The delight we once found in the rows of Mandāra groves now seems like a blade of grass compared to that state which we shall one day attain as our own.
Tell me this: will the stainless visions of knowledge proclaimed by those free from passion ever take up residence within you?
"O father! O mother! O son!"—may I never again be the vessel for such words, O mind, my own kinsman, nor the recipient of those who consume suffering.
O sister, quickly fulfill my request regarding the Buddha; for the sake of our liberation from suffering, reflect upon the words of the Sage.
Calamity falls upon you with affection, like a daughter, as long as existence persists;
therefore, O fortunate one, remain steadfast for the sake of the destruction of existence.
First, the words concerning dispassion were spoken by the sage Vasiṣṭha;
then followed the conduct of one seeking liberation, and after that, the sequence of the births.
Then, O Mind, remember in its entirety and exactly as it is the chapter on Stability, which is beautiful with various illustrations and contains the essence of consciousness.

Even that which has been performed and deliberated upon a hundred times, if it does not reach the intellect of a human being, becomes fruitless like an autumn cloud; therefore, the intellect alone is the essence of action.
The third canto, titled "The Hearing of the Instruction," by Vālmīki.
Thus, with such extensive and noble thoughts,
that night passed for him like a day for a lotus longing for the sun.
Then, as the quarters of the sky— reddened by the glow of twilight and tinged slightly with dawn— became pale like Rāma’s complexion, the stars grew sparse.
Simultaneously with the sound of the morning trumpets,
the illustrious Rāghava, whose face resembles the moon, arose like a lotus from a bed of lotuses.
Having performed the entire morning ritual together with his brother,
and accompanied by a limited retinue, he went to the residence of Vasiṣṭha.
Seeing the sage established in meditative concentration, dwelling in solitude and devoted to the Self,
Rāma bowed from afar with his neck bent low.
Having prostrated before him, they stood in that courtyard full of humility,
until the darkness was completely torn asunder and destroyed from the circle of the quarters.
Kings and princes, as well as sages and Brahmins,
came to Mauna’s abode like the immortals to the world of Brahmā.
That residence of Vasiṣṭha became crowded with people,
thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, and beautified by the palaces of kings.
In an instant, the venerable Vasiṣṭha emerged from his meditative absorption;
with appropriate conduct, he received the people who stood before him in prostration.
Then, followed by the sages, the illustrious sage, accompanied by Viśvāmitra,
suddenly ascended the chariot like the lotus-born Brahmā ascending his lotus-throne.
Surrounded by a vast army, he went to the home of Daśaratha,
just as Brahmā, adorned by all the gods, went to the city of Śakra.
He entered the spacious and beautiful assembly hall of Daśaratha’s son,
like a royal swan surrounded by a flock of swans entering a lotus pond.
Then, at those three words, King Daśaratha, endowed with great heroism, rose from his lion-throne and quickly went forth.
There, all those kings headed by Daśaratha, as well as the sages, seers, and brahmins headed by Vasiṣṭha, entered.
And there were the ministers, headed by Sumantra; the wise priests, headed by Dhaumya;
the princes, headed by Rāma; and the sons of the ministers, headed by Suhotra.
The subjects, beginning with the vassals; the citizens, beginning with Suhotra; likewise the servants, beginning with Mālava; and the attendants, beginning with Paura.
When they had all sat down in their respective places and upon their respective seats, with their gazes fixed intently upon Vasiṣṭha.

When the clamor of the assembly had subsided and the bards were established in silence, and when inquiries concerning their welfare had been made in that gentle inner chamber of the assembly; MU_5,3.18.
In the sunlight of the day, which resembles a mass of vermilion dust, resting beneath a canopy and shimmering upon a circular mirror, the young girl shines.
It flickers among the fringes of her garments, enters the hollows of lotuses, and flutters over the ruby-studded necklaces and strings of pearls.
As the sweet breezes blow, carrying a thick fragrance from the large flower-swinging platforms that extend out in every direction.
While the matrons sat upon couches by the gentle windows, their feet resting on floors strewn with flowers, they gazed [at him].

The fickle women holding white whisks stood in silence, having abandoned even a trace of their restlessness; their eyes trembled at the rays of the sun entering through the lattice, and they were turned tawny by the mass of light from the jewels upon the whisks.
And upon the courtyard grounds, whose surfaces were beautiful with the rays of the sun reflected in pearl ornaments, a swarm of bees did not savor the abundance of *caṃpaka* flowers;
through delusion, they wandered as if perceiving them to be drops of fresh sunlight, like a flight of insects in a cloud in the sky.
May that meritorious flow of Vasiṣṭha’s speech, which is heard and praised with spreading wonder by the noble world,
be yours— speech consisting of soft words and syllables, charming, spoken amidst an assembly with mutual smiles, and delightful through its many virtues.

From all directions, from the cities, and from the sky, a distinguished assembly of royal sages, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, noble Munis, and hosts of Brahmins entered silently and without sound, approaching with silent salutations and profound reverence, while the words of those present were hushed.

When the breeze blew—reddish-brown with the golden pollen of swarms of intoxicated bees drawn from the soft buds of blossoming *kokanada* lotuses; resonant with the song of clanging bells set in motion; and cool with the waters of the night it had drunk—it was as follows.

When the smoke of aloe and tagara, mingled with the fragrance of sandalwood, perfumes the clouds; when the breeze blows, marked by the intense scent of fresh flower-garlands and bearing whorls of white canopies and lotuses, stained with the pollen of drifting blossoms and the sound of bees discerned by their humming; [then let him enter].
The Fourth Sarga, titled "Description of the Assembly Hall," by Vālmīki.
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, Daśaratha spoke these words, beautiful in their confident phrasing, to the leader of sages.
"O Blessed One, I hope that you have been relieved of the exhaustion born from yesterday's composition of words— an exhaustion exceeding even the emaciation caused by your asceticism."
Today, we have been comforted here by that collection of words which you spoke— blissful and solitary—
which was like a rain of nectar.
Like moonbeams made of nectar that dispel darkness,
these pure words of the great ones cool the inner self.
Bestowing unprecedented joy, resting upon the highest state,
and removing extreme delusion— these well-spoken words are showers of nectar.
He from whom the creeper of eloquent speech arises— the ultimate lamp that illuminates the jewel of the self— is that tree of the virtuous who is worthy of veneration.
The well-spoken words of the virtuous wipe away every ill-deed and ill-performed act,
just as the rays of the moon dispel a mass of darkness.
O Sage, our thirst, greed, and other such fetters of saṃsāra have been thinned by your teaching, like dark clouds in autumn.
We have set out to behold our own self free from stain,
like those born blind who, having received eyes through the ointment of mercury, seek to see gold.
The mist called the latent impressions of saṃsāra has arisen in the sky of our hearts;
O Autumn of Your Speech, may it now begin to thin away for us.
O Sage, neither the blossoms of the Mandāra tree nor the waves of the nectar-water delight the inner self as much as the words of those possessed of noble intellect.
O Raghava, whichever day passes while being honored by the great multitude, that day alone here possesses light; all other days are blind.
O Rāma, lotus-petal-eyed one, desiring to see the true nature of the matter at hand,
you again awakened the sage who was established in a state of serene grace.

When the king had spoken thus, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, noble-souled, stood facing Rāma and said this: *ity ukte bhūbhṛtā tatra rāmābhimukham āsthitaḥ / uvācedam udārātmā vasiṣṭho bhagavān muniḥ //* MU_5,4.14 *//* When the king had spoken thus, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha, noble-souled, stood facing Rāma and said this.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, sole moon of your lineage, O high-minded one, do you perhaps remember the meaning of what was spoken by me, having considered it from beginning to end?
O crusher of enemies, do you perhaps remember the classification of all those diverse births according to the distinctions of the qualities such as *sattva*?
Do you remember the form of the God, the Pure Supreme Self, which is both the whole and the partless, both being and non-being, and eternally manifest?
O virtuous one, sole recipient of praise for your goodness, do you remember how this entire universe was manifested from the Lord of Lords, the Ruler of all? (MU 5.4.18)
O one of noble mind, do you correctly remember that form which is the hollow and fragile expansion of ignorance—both infinite and yet finite? MU 5.4.19
That it has been established through the investigation of salt and other examples that "the person is nothing but the mind and not something else"—do you remember that well? MU 5.4.20.
O Rāma, have you reflected upon the entire meaning of the statement? Has that which was examined yesterday been retained within your heart during the night?
When repeatedly examined and firmly established in the heart, the purpose bears fruit abundantly; it does not remain if its stability is struck down by negligence.
O giver of honor, you are a vessel for words that are solitary and pure,
for your own heart is solitary, like a bamboo flute for pearls.
Vālmīki:
Having been thus granted the opportunity by the sage of great luster, the son of Kamalāsana,
Rāma spoke these words.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this is indeed the manifestation of your own power, that I have understood your most noble speech.
"Everything that you have commanded is exactly so and not otherwise;
the meaning of your words was contemplated by me throughout the night while I was free from sleep."
O Lord, yesterday you, the sun for the world, extended a delightful mass of rays of speech to destroy the darkness of existence.
O one whose self is undepressed, all that is delightful, meritorious, and diverse has been taken up by me within, just as the ocean takes up a multitude of jewels.
Whose head would not bear upon its crown your instruction— for the sake of attaining perfection— since it is beneficial in its consequences, heart-pleasing, meritorious, and a means to bliss?
With the veil of the frost of saṃsāra dissolving away,
we have become clear through your grace, like days at the end of the rainy season.
Your holy instruction has a beginning sweet at its onset, increases one's good fortune in the middle,
and results in unsurpassed fruit at the end.
May the flower of your speech— blooming, white, unfading, delightful, and gladdening the heart— be for us eternally auspicious and bestowing its fruit.
O you who are expert in all the eternal scriptures, a single great lake for the spreading waters of merit;
O you of extensive vows, now show great favor toward me, whose sins have been destroyed.
The fifth canto, titled "The Question of Rāghava," by Vasiṣṭha:
O you of beautiful form, listen attentively to this beneficial Chapter on Quiescence, which is beautiful as the supreme philosophical conclusion.
O Rāma, this long-lasting illusion of saṃsāra is perpetually sustained by men of rajasic and tamasic nature, just as a pavilion is supported by sturdy pillars.
By heroes like you, who are established in purity and enriched by virtues,
this mature illusion is cast off with ease, just as snakes shed their skin.
O virtuous one, those classes of beings who are wise— whether characterized by passion (rājasa) or goodness (sāttvika)—
they investigate the world in its prior and subsequent states, as well as the Supreme.
For those whose debts have been cleared through association with the study of scriptures and the company of the virtuous,
an intellect arises that resembles a lamp, beholding the essential core of reality.
By means of one's own self, through inquiry itself, one must investigate the Self;
as long as the object of knowledge has not been realized, it is not attained.

O delighter of your lineage, you are the foremost among those who possess wisdom, who follow the right path, who are steadfast, who are illustrious by birth, and who are noble beings fit for kingship.
O wise one, examine for yourself the views regarding the commencement of saṃsāra;
what is real and what is unreal? Become devoted to the Real.
What reality can there be in that which does not exist at the beginning and at the end?
O Rāma, that alone is real which is eternal in the beginning and at the end; nothing else.
For that deluded beast of a creature whose mind is attached to an object that is unreal from beginning to end, by what means can discernment be produced?
In this world, it is the mind alone that is born; it is the mind alone that grows;
but through the vision of right insight, it is the mind alone that dissolves.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, this has been understood by me: that in these three worlds, it is indeed the mind alone that wanders through saṃsāra and is the vessel for old age and death.
Tell me with certainty that means for crossing over it;
by you, the sun, the darkness within the hearts of the Raghavas shall be destroyed.
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāghava, first the mind is led toward purity by means of the scriptures, by dispassion, by the [right] choice, and likewise by association with the virtuous.
When the mind, nourished by goodness, has attained detachment,
then one should follow those gurus who are indeed masters of realized knowledge.
Then, having performed meditation, worship, and so forth as instructed by him,
one gradually attains that state which is supremely purifying.
Through pure discernment, one perceives the Self by means of the self,
just as one sees one's own reflection within through the cool light of the moon.
In the great ocean of existence, a person is carried away like a blade of grass until,
through the mind, they attain rest upon the shore of discernment.
The intellect of this person, who has thoroughly understood reality through investigation,
casts all mental afflictions beneath it, just as water washes away grains of sand.
"Just as a goldsmith clearly recognizes, 'This is the gold leaf, this is the ash,' so too there is no delusion for one who has known the Self."
When it is realized for a long time that "this is the inexhaustible, indestructible self,
my very own self," then what delusion could remain here, and from where could it arise?
For when the essence of a gem is not fully understood, one is bewildered regarding its value;
but when its essence is known and its value is beyond doubt, where indeed could there be delusion?
O people, the self unknown leads you to the accomplishment of suffering;
but when fully known, it leads to infinite happiness and tranquility.
Having separated your own self from this body which has afflicted it as if by mingling with it, become established in yourselves without delay.

O humans, there is not even the slightest connection between this body and the stainless Self, just as there is no connection between gold and a speck of mud, even when that gold is situated within it.
The self is distinct from the body; they are like a lotus leaf and water. With arms upraised, I cry out, yet no one listens to me.
As long as the mind remains inert by nature, like a tortoise in a pit—
stupid, its body sluggish in enjoyment, and having forgotten the inquiry into the Self.
For that long, the darkness of saṃsāra is not pierced even slightly, even by the moon together with the fire, nor even by twelve suns.
For when the mind is fully awakened, it discerns its own state;
like the rising of the sun, the darkness within the heart flees away.

One should constantly awaken the mind, which is lying upon the bed of worldly enjoyment, for the sake of supreme enlightenment; for existence brings about the cycle of rebirth and is indeed the giver of ultimate suffering.
Just as the sky is not defiled by dust and just as a lotus is not defiled by water, even though they are in contact with them, so too is the Self of yours, though it is joined with bodies.
Just as dross and the like, though adhering to gold,
remain distinct and do not undergo internal transformation, so too does the inert body [remain distinct] from the Self.
One perceives that the experience of pleasure and pain belongs to the self,
just as one perceives the duality of moons or the yellowness [of a conch] in the sky, though these are non-existent.
For pleasure and pain belong to the body, not to the Self which transcends everything;
these indeed pertain only to the ignorant one, and when that [ignorance] is destroyed, they belong to no one.
There is no happiness for anyone, nor is there any suffering for anyone;
behold everything as consisting of the Self, peaceful and infinite, O Rāghava.
These expansive perceptions of creation that are seen here are like waves in water; they are like peacock feathers in the sky, or rather, in the Self.
Just as a gem spontaneously emits its own luminous reflections without external cause,
even so does this Self project the worlds of creation.
O wise one, the self and the world are neither one, nor two, nor even non-existent;
this entire manifestation merely appears in this manner as it unfolds at present.
All this is indeed Brahman; this entire world is pervaded by the Self.
O sinless one, abandon the delusion that "I am one thing" and "this is another."
O Rāma, within that eternal, dense mass of Brahman, no conceptual constructions arise; they are like waves in the ocean of water, for there is nothing other than water.
When the entire universe is expanded within the one Supreme Self alone,
no second conceptualization exists, just as there is no particle of frost in fire.
Meditating upon himself by means of his own self as consisting of consciousness alone,
this very Self indeed expands the web of the universe within itself.
There is no sorrow, there is no delusion, there is no birth, and there is no one who is born;
whatever exists here exists as that alone—be free from the fever of anxiety, O Rāghava.
O Rāghava, become equanimous, self-abiding, steady-minded, tranquil, peaceful in spirit, silent, pure as a precious gem, and free from the fever of passion.
Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, devoid of the pursuit of acquisition and preservation, self-possessed, peerless, sorrowless in nature, and free from fever— be thus, O Rāghava.
Solitary, with thoughts stilled, firm-minded, and resolute in purpose, following whatever comes to you, be free from the fever of passion, O Raghava.
Free from passion, free from exertion, free from dejection, and cleansed of all impurity; neither a taker nor a renouncer—be free from feverish distress, O Rāghava.
Having attained the state that transcends all, filled with everything that is to be attained,
remain free from feverish anxiety and unagitated like the full ocean, O Rāghava.
Freed from the web of conceptual constructions and devoid of the ointment of illusion,
with your soul satisfied within the Self by the Self, become free from the fever of worldly existence, O Rāghava.

O Rāghava, best among the knowers of the Self, you whose form is infinite, shoreless, and boundless, and who are as steadfast as the peak of the earth-supporting mountain— be free from feverish distress.
Cultivate magnanimity within yourself by means of yourself alone, like the full ocean;
cultivate joy within yourself by means of yourself alone, like the orb of the full moon.
This construction of the manifold universe is unreal in nature; one who knows that does not pursue what is unreal by name.
You are a knower of that, you are one whose mental fluctuations have ceased, you are free from affliction, and you are eternally risen. O beautiful one, remain with your sorrow stilled.
Instructed by your father, rule for a long time over this earth under a single umbrella, protecting it properly with a vision consistent with the sacred law;
let the world of kings be delighted by all your virtues—neither renunciation is appropriate here, nor attachment to worldly activities.
The sixth canto, named "The First Instruction," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
It is my conviction that he who engages in activities without the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of thinking "I am performing such an exertion" is liberated.
Resorting to the human body, some of these, devoted to ritual actions,
go from heaven to hell, and again from hell to heaven.
Some, devoted to evil deeds and devoid of self-discernment,
go from hell to hell, from suffering to suffering, and from fear to fear.
Some, bound by the threads of their own latent impressions and agitated by karma,
go from the state of an animal to the body of an immobile being, and from there to the body of another animal.
Certain fortunate knowers of the Self, whose vision of the mind has been scrutinized and whose fetters of craving have been severed, proceed to the state that is exclusively free [from suffering].
O Raghava, having experienced only a few births in the past,
he who attains liberation in this very birth is one characterized by both the rajasic and sattvic qualities.
Once born, he attains growth like the moon on the day of the full moon;
prosperity follows him as the beauty of the *kuṭaja* flower does in the rainy season.
O Great-minded One, pure branches of knowledge enter that person for whom this is the final birth, just as pearls enter an excellent bamboo tube.
Nobility, amiability, loving-kindness, gentleness, liberation, and wisdom always attend him, just as women attend upon the inner apartments.
He who performs all actions while remaining equanimous whether they succeed or fail, and likewise regarding their fruits at all times, neither rejoices nor grieves.
Just as darknesses vanish by day, so do dualities reach their end there;
just as clouds in autumn, so do the qualities attain purity there.
All people desire one whose conduct is gentle and sweet,
just as herds of deer in the forest long for the bamboo that produces a sweet sound.
Such splendors of virtue pursue a man of his final birth from the moment he is born, just as cranes follow a rain-cloud.
Then, filled with virtues, he follows the teacher alone; the teacher enjoins him to that solitary, purifying practice of seclusion.
With a mind endowed with virtue and free from the passion for discursive thought,
he then beholds the Lord, or rather the Self, as a single form, free from all ailment.
Therefore, O Rāma, with a beautiful inquiry and a tranquil mind, one must first awaken the mind that is sluggish in its mental reflections.
For those of great virtue who are born later awaken the sleeping deer of the mind first with songs of their own excellences.
Having diligently served teachers of renowned virtue and having investigated the jewel of the mind with a stainless intellect,
a person attains the stainless state after beholding for a long time the light within this world.
The seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence," from the *Vasiṣṭha*.
This general sequence has been declared for all living beings;
now hear from me this other specific detail, O lotus-eyed one.
O Rāma, for those embodied beings born into this turmoil of saṃsāra, there are these two supreme methods for attaining liberation.
First, that which bestows perfection is said to arise gradually from the practice taught by the Guru, either within a single lifetime or over the course of many births.
But for another whose mind has attained some degree of proficiency through his own effort, the attainment of knowledge occurs swiftly, like the falling of a fruit from the sky.
In order to understand the falling of fruits from the sky,
listen here to this ancient account which I shall relate to you.

Listen, O fortunate one, how those of great majesty— having cast off the flood of the fetters of former good and evil deeds— attain the stainless, supreme solitude of their final existence, like a fruit that has fallen from the sky.
The eighth canto, titled "The Indication of the Sequence," by Vasiṣṭha.
There is a powerful king of the Videhas named Janaka, whose intellect is noble, who has brought all calamities to an end, and in whom prosperity is ever-rising.
He was a wish-fulfilling tree for the multitudes of supplicants, a sun for the lotuses that were his friends,
a spring for the flowers that were his kinsmen, and a god of love for women.
A cool-rayed moon to the night-lotuses of the twice-born, a sun to the darkness of his enemies,
and an ocean of the jewels of goodness, he dwelt upon the earth like Viṣṇu.
Once, during the spring season, when the young creepers were in full bloom, tawny with clusters of blossoms, and shimmering with the joyful songs of intoxicated cuckoos; MU_5,8.4.
He proceeded to the lovely pleasure grove, its expanse filled with blossoming trees and its graceful vine-like women, just as Indra goes to the Nandana garden.
In that delightful choice forest, where the breeze was fragrant with the scent of *kesara* flowers,
he wandered through the beautiful groves, accompanied by his followers stationed at a distance.
Then, in a certain thicket of *tamāla* trees, he heard words uttered in the course of their own conversation by invisible perfected beings (*siddhas*).
O lotus-petal-eyed one, these songs, which take the form of meditation on the Self, belong to those whose minds are eternally dispassionate and who dwell in mountain caves.
We worship that outflow arising from the reality of one's own Self, which is the certainty of the bliss of consciousness resulting from the union of the seer and the seen.
Having abandoned the seer, the seeing, and the seen, along with all latent impressions,
we worship the Self as the first manifestation of vision.
We ever worship the Self, which is like a mental image, appearing as a mental creation; it is the effortless cultivation of non-existence.
We worship that Self which is eternally situated between the two positions of "it exists" and "it does not exist," and which is the illumination of all illuminations.
We worship that Self of ours, which shines like the letter *ha* without its head (*aśiraska*), which is established in all forms, and which is uttered incessantly.
Those who, having abandoned the Lord who dwells in the cave of the heart, go to another deity,
are like those who desire a jewel while having discarded the Kaustubha gem held in their own hand.
Indeed, by renouncing all desires, this fruit is obtained,
whereby the entire root-stalk of the poisonous creepers of desire is severed.
Even after perceiving the utter distaste for all objects of experience, that dull-witted man who again forms attachments to them is no mere donkey; he is a human being [acting like one].
Again and again, one should strike down these senses— whether they have arisen or not—
with the thunderbolt of solitude, just as Indra strikes mountains with his thunderbolt.
The pure mind of the virtuous person attains tranquility through the power of peace and brings about the bliss of serenity;
for one whose mind is fully calmed, there arises a supreme and enduring abiding in the happiness of its own true nature.
The Ninth Chapter, titled "The Song of the Siddhas," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having heard these songs sung by the hosts of Siddhas, the lord of the earth immediately fell into despondency, like a coward at the sound of battle.
He went toward his own home, drawing along his retinue,
like the flood of the rainy season following the trees on its banks as it flows toward the ocean.
Having dismissed his entire retinue there to their own abodes,
he ascended alone to the highest palace, like the sun ascending a mountain peak.

Then, observing the courses of the worlds, which were as flickering as the wings of birds eager to fly upward, he lamented thus in his distress: * *tataḥ proḍḍayanālolakhagapakṣaticañcalāḥ / ālokayaṃl lokagatīr vilalāpedam āturaḥ //* 5.9.4 Then, observing the courses of the worlds, which were as flickering as the wings of birds eager to fly upward, he lamented thus in his distress.
Alas, what misery! Amidst these most wretched and fickle conditions of the world, I am forced to wallow helplessly like one stone against other stones.
I live but some infinitesimal fraction of infinite time;
yet I fix my attachment upon it—shame on me, of such base intellect!
How small indeed is this kingdom of mine, lasting only as long as my life!
What sorrow is there without it, that I remain like one whose intellect is destroyed?
I am infinite at the beginning and at the end, yet in the middle my life is fragile;
like a child gazing at a painted moon, why do I remain here so stubbornly in vain?
"Alas, what a pity! I am utterly bewildered by this ensnaring net of illusion fashioned through conceptual proliferation; by whom have I been so completely deluded?"
Whatever object there may be, whatever is delightful, whatever is noble or unartificial—none of that exists here at all; upon what, then, is this resolve of mine based?
"Even that which is far away is not far for me, since it dwells within my mind"— having thus resolved, I abandon all mental cultivation directed toward external objects.
The state of coming and going in this world is as fragile as the ripples in a whirlpool;
though seen even now to lead only to suffering, why do you still maintain such attachment toward pleasure?
Year by year, month by month, day by day, and moment by moment,
pleasures are pierced by sufferings, while sufferings, however, recur again and again.
Repeatedly examined, scrutinized, questioned, and observed—
there is nothing here that is not trivial wherein the steadfast may find their abiding place.
Those who today stand at the head of the great will, in a few days, fall low;
O ruined mind, what kind of confidence is this of yours in greatness?
I am bound even without a rope; I am defiled even though I am free from mud; I have fallen even while standing on high—alas, O my soul, your stability is destroyed!
Why has this delusion come upon me all of a sudden, even though I am wise?
It is like a dark cloud that obscures the light, appearing before the sun.
"What are these great riches of mine? Who are these kinsmen of mine?
Like a fool terrified by a ghost, I suspect for what reason I am so agitated."
Why do I myself bind upon myself this very resolve regarding worldly objects— a resolve that brings about old age and death and is laden with anxiety?
Whether it remains or departs, what concern is mine regarding its perfection?
For this, like the beauty of a bubble, has appeared thus as something entirely false.
Those great riches and enjoyments, those virtuous and affectionate kinsmen—all have come within the range of memory; since even that which is present has vanished, what stability can there be?
Where are the riches of kings, or where are the worlds of the Brahmins? Those of former times have passed away; what is this confidence of mine?
Millions of Indras have fallen away like bubbles upon the water;
the virtuous will laugh at me, who still cling to the hope for life.
Tens of millions of Brahmās have passed away, and successions of creations have gone by; kings have vanished like dust—what stability is there in my life?
If I continue to maintain attachment toward this void delusion consisting of the body— a nightmare in the night of saṃsāra— then let me be cursed for such a lack of steadfastness.
Why am I, like an ignorant person, struck down by this demon of egoism— which arises in vain from that which is essentially non-existent— thinking "I am this"?
"Carried away, carried away is this life by this long-drawn-out, subtle line of time; though I see it, I do not truly perceive it."
Those for whom Īśāna was made a footstool and Śārṅgin was a play-ball have been swallowed by Kālakāpālin; why do you prance about me, who am such a person?
These days come and go incessantly even now;
yet not even a single day has been seen to pass away, for the one true reality remains undestroyed.

Just as cranes [do not appear] in a lake that is devoid of water, so too within every human heart it is only enjoyments that flash forth internally, and never those whose vision is fixed upon the Void.
Having reached what is more miserable than misery, having gone to what is more painful than pain, even now I am not dispassionate; alas, shame on me, whose resolve is base!
In whatever firm objects one's intense mental cultivation is firmly bound, those very things are seen to perish; what, then, is supreme in this world?
Whatever is pleasing in the middle, whatever is pleasing at the end, and whatever is pleasing at the first sight—
all that is indeed impure, defiled by destruction and filth.
In whatever objects a person fixes his attachment, in those very things a great arising of suffering is seen to occur for him swiftly.
Day by day, the dull-witted person here reaches a state that is ever more wretched, ever more cruel, and ever more distressing.
Afflicted by ignorance in childhood, struck by passion in youth, and tormented by worries for his wife in the end— when and what can this dull-witted man do?
Why does my mind not perceive this saṃsāra— which is devoid of essence yet seemingly full of essence, bitter with coming and going, and corrupted by the inequality of its various states?
Even by performing hundreds of sacrifices such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha,
one attains heaven for some portion of a great kalpa, but no more.
What region is there— whether in heaven, on earth, or in the underworld—
where these calamities do not rush upon one like ill-behaved female bees?
How indeed can these mental anxieties and physical ailments— which are wild beasts within the cave of one's own mind and sprouts upon the ground of the body— be warded off?
Non-existence resides at the pinnacle of truth; lack of delight at the pinnacle of delights;
and sufferings at the pinnacle of pleasures. Which one of these shall I take refuge in?
Ordinary, lowly creatures are born and die;
by them alone the earth is packed without gaps, yet truly virtuous people are difficult to find.
With eyes like rows of blue lotuses and adorned with supreme love,
these playful women exist merely for the sake of laughter, due to their momentary nature.
Those men by whose closing and opening of their eyes the dissolution and creation of the worlds occur—such as they have passed away; what need is there to count those like me?
There are things more beautiful than the beautiful and more stable than the stable; why then is the splendor of material objects such that it ends in mere anxiety?
And as for those various prosperities which are approved by the mind,
I consider them surely to be great calamities, despite their grand undertakings.
If even those various calamities are regarded as agreeable in the mind,
then I consider them too, when undertaken on a grand scale, to be complete successes.
In this world, which is a mere manifestation of mind and as fragile as a drop of water, how could there be for me this unprecedented string of syllables: "This is mine"?
When the stability of the world has come about by way of a chance occurrence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow,
the notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have been fruitlessly devised by a rogue.
To what limited perceptions, defined by specific forms and called "pleasure," am I attached, like a moth to the flames of a fire?
It is better to wallow in the fires of Raurava, where there is constant burning,
than to remain within the cycles of saṃsāra, which are torn and shattered.
Samsara itself is said to be the very limit of sufferings;
how, then, can happiness be found by one who has fallen into its midst?
Those who are situated in this cycle of existence, which is characterized by uncreated great suffering,
perceive other sufferings as being quite sweet.

I too have become like those ignorant people who, having failed to realize the true nature of reality, stand as motionless as wood or clods of earth— alas, I have reached a state of equality with them.
Of this tree of saṃsāra, which abounds in thousands of sprouts, branches, trunks, fruits,
and shoots, the sprout consists of the mind as its root.
I consider that [tree] to be nothing but volition; by the cessation of volition, I shall wither it away so that the tree of saṃsāra reaches its end.
In these mental fluctuations of the monkey-like mind, which are charming only in their outward form,
I shall no longer take delight even today once they have been fully understood as being devoid of essence.
I have experienced the cycles of saṃsāra, which are pierced by hundreds of snares of desire and bring the affliction of repeated falls and rises; now I shall desist.
"Alas, I am struck down! I am ruined! I am dead!"—thus I lamented again and again;
yet now that I have departed, I no longer weep.
I am awakened; I am delighted, for I have seen the thief of my own self.
This one named "mind" I shall slay, for I have long been struck down by the mind.
For all this time, this pearl of my mind remained unpierced;
now, however, it has been pierced and is worthy of the thread.
The frost-flake of my mind will surely soon dissolve through the heat of the sun of discernment, leading to my long-lasting liberation.
I have been well enlightened by the wise, the virtuous, and the perfected ones;
I follow after the Self, which is the means to supreme bliss.
Having found the jewel of the Self in solitude and beholding it with joy,
I remain here, free from all other things, like a cloudless sky in autumn.

Having forcibly cast out from within the false flickering of "I am this" and "this is mine," I slay the exceedingly defiled enemy that is the mind; I attain tranquility—homage be to you, O Discrimination!
The tenth canto, titled "Janaka’s Reflection," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
As he was reflecting thus, the doorkeeper entered before him at dawn, like Aruṇa ascending the front of the chariot of the Sun.
The doorkeeper:
O King, upon whom rests the entire burden of the earth supported by the pillars of your arms,
arise and perform the daily duties befitting a monarch.
These women, carrying jars filled with water scented with flowers, camphor, and saffron,
stood ready in the bathing area like personified rivers.
This lotus pond, where bees wander through groves of day-lotuses and night-lotuses,
has been created for the sake of women, with its pavilions fashioned from woven cloth.
These shores of the lotus ponds are filled with parasols belonging to those attending the occasion of the royal bath, along with fly-whisks, chariots, elephants, and horses.
The grounds for your worship of the gods have been prepared with baskets filled with various flowers and overflowing with jewels and medicinal herbs.
Having bathed, with purifying grass in hand and having recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn,
this assembly of twice-born men worthy of sacrificial gifts gazes upon you alone, O God.
O Supreme Lord, the cool dining areas have been prepared by beautiful women with fly-whisks waving in their hands.
Arise quickly, may prosperity be yours; perform your duty with resolve.
Great men do not let the proper time for their own tasks pass by.
When the lord of the gatekeepers had spoken thus,
the king then reflected in the same way upon the wondrous nature of worldly existence.
How small indeed is this so-called happiness of sovereignty!
It is established that I have no need here for this which perishes in an instant.
Having completely abandoned all false pomp and agitation,
I abide in solitude alone, like a perfectly tranquil ocean.
Enough with these manifestations of enjoyment of mine, which consist mostly of what is unreal;
having abandoned all activities, I shall remain happily in solitude.
Therefore, O mind, abandon this cleverness born from the agitation of habitual attachment to enjoyments,
for the sake of pacifying the mire of the snare of birth, old age, and dullness.
O mind, from whichever conditions you perceive agitation,
from those very same conditions you shall attain supreme happiness by becoming utterly detached.
Whether engaged in activity or withdrawn from it, again and again, for a long time and ever longer,
O mind, you find no satisfaction amidst all the realms of sensory enjoyment.
Therefore, enough of this trivial concern for enjoyments;
rather, attain that pervasive [state] by which unartificial contentment arises.
Having reflected thus, Janaka became silent;
with his restless mind stilled, he was like a figure depicted in a painting.
Out of both respect and fear, the doorkeeper did not speak further words,
for the mental dispositions of kings are difficult to fathom.
Then, having remained silent for a moment, Janaka again reflected in his mind, which was characterized by tranquility, upon the life of living beings.
What is there to be accepted here that I should strive to accomplish?
Upon what object, free from destruction, shall I fix my steadfastness?
What is the use of being intent on action, or even what is the use of inaction?
For there is nothing that has been spoken which is not subject to destruction.
Whether this body be active or inactive, it has arisen from what is unreal;
what loss indeed can there be for me, who am real, stable, and pure consciousness?
I do not long for what has not been attained, nor do I abandon what has been attained; I abide established in the self as it truly is—let whatever belongs to me remain mine.
I have no purpose here with what is done, nor any with what is not done;
for that which is to be attained by action or non-action is neither real nor unreal for one who exists.
Whether I am acting or not acting, my deeds— whether appropriate or inappropriate—
have no desired object here that has attained the status of being worth adopting.
Therefore, having risen, let this body perform its natural activity as it has sequentially arrived;
for what will it accomplish while its limbs remain motionless?
When the mind is steady, free from desire, equanimous, and devoid of passion,
the activity and inactivity of the limbs of the body produce equal results.
Regarding the fruits of prosperity born of karma, the mind is both the agent and the enjoyer;
when that [mind] has attained tranquility, even what was done by men is as if undone.
Whatever firm resolve has taken root within a person regarding their actions attains the state of being identical with that;
my intellect has reached the state free from affliction, so I shall completely abandon inner instability.
The eleventh canto, titled "Janaka’s Resolve," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having reflected thus, Janaka rose to perform the duties as they presented themselves,
remaining unattached like the sun at the beginning of the day.
Having himself abandoned all mental impressions regarding the desirable and the undesirable,
he acted according to whatever came to him, remaining awake yet as if in deep sleep.
Having completed those daily duties preceded by winning over his noble elders,
he spent that night alone in the very same manner, absorbed in the play of meditation.
Having made the mind equanimous and stilled the wandering toward sense objects,
he thus awakened his consciousness as the night was fading away.
The restless expansion of your mind is not for your own happiness;
come to peace, my dear, for from peace you shall obtain the essential happiness.
O mind, in whatever measure you effortlessly conceive a flood of conceptual constructions, in that same measure does this cycle of existence expand for you.
Just as a tree attains a hundred branches through watering, so too,
O rogue, do you attain endless mental anguish through the desire for enjoyments.
These creations of saṃsāra arise from the play of the web of thought;
therefore, abandoning this manifold thinking, attain tranquility.
O handsome one, weigh this flickering creation of saṃsāra;
if you find its essence, then take refuge in it alone.
Abandoning attachment to this visible world, O you who long for the vision [of reality], do not grasp at this [world] nor let it go; wander with pure desire.
Whether this visible world arises or sets, whether it be unreal or real, O virtuous one, fall into a state of detachment; do not be affected by its qualities or defects.
There is not even the slightest connection between you and an object perceived by the senses;
for what kind of connection can there possibly be with that which has no existing form?
This non-existence is not real, nor is it real for both the non-existent and the existent; to say there is a relation between them is a truly wondrous and unprecedented string of syllables.
If this non-existent becomes existent, even so, O handsome one, tell me: what kind of association can there be between the existent and the non-existent, like that between the dead and the living?
If both the mind and the object of perception were truly existent and eternally established, then from what source would the outflow of joy and sorrow arise?
Therefore, O fortunate one, do not be deluded, do not give way to exultation;
maintain an undisturbed intellect and abandon the state of worldly existence.
Like the fruit of the *tinduka* tree, it burns uselessly within yourself alone;
O evil-minded one, do not fall into dullness by contracting the impurity of delusion!
There is nothing here that is so exalted or supreme by which you might attain ultimate perfection; therefore, O rogue mind, relying with force upon extreme fortitude, abandon your fickleness!
The twelfth canto, titled "Instruction on the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
Reflecting thus in his own kingdom, King Janaka performed all his duties and, being firm-minded, was not deluded.
His mind did not leap forth toward any objects of joyful experience;
rather, it remained at all times perfectly equanimous and pure.
From that time forward, he neither grasped at nor rejected the visible world;
rather, he remained established in the present, free from all doubt.
Then, by that mind which was through unceasing solitude,
no further stain was ever again taken up, just as the sky does not take on the darkness of night.
Through the pursuit of his own discernment, that lord of the earth attained perfect knowledge of infinite luster, and his mind reached a state of purity.
The conscious self, free from disease and untouched by any portion of conceptual construction,
arose in the space of his heart like the sun in the sky.
He, the infinite self, who knows the self of all beings, beheld all phenomena spread out like jewels upon the loom of the mind, as being identical with his own self.
He was never elated, nor was he ever distressed; because he engaged in worldly affairs as they naturally occurred, his mind was always equanimous.
From that time forward, O giver of honor, Janaka became liberated while living; his knowledge had matured, and he knew the higher and lower realms of the world.
While ruling the kingdom of the Videhas, Janaka, the life of his people,
was not at all distressed by joy or sorrow, even though he was subject to them.
Free from both virtues and faults, it neither sets nor rises;
through gains and losses arising from its own sovereignty, it neither desponds nor exults.
Even while acting, he does nothing at all anywhere,
because he always remains established in the state of one liberated while living.
Like that of King Janaka while he was in the state of deep sleep,
all mental constructions had completely set for him with respect to all existing things.
He does not pursue the future, nor does he dwell on the past;
he remains in the present moment, even while laughing.
O lotus-eyed Rāma, by the power of his own inquiry alone, he has attained everything that is to be attained; it was not through any other desire.
To whatever extent the limits of discursive investigations are reached, to that same extent one investigates by means of one's own mind alone.

That state which is attained from the heart through association with the virtuous— made clear by the inquiry arising therefrom— is not obtained from a teacher, nor from the meaning of the scriptures, nor from merit.
O Rāma, the state [of liberation] is attained through one's own innate wisdom alone— which is affectionate and straightforward— and not indeed by any other action.
For one whose flame of wisdom— sharp-tipped and wandering through the past and the future— is ever ablaze, darkness never follows after him.
O Mahāmati, those calamities which are difficult to cross over and are crowded with waves of suffering are crossed by means of wisdom, just as one crosses waters by means of a boat.
Even a slight misfortune afflicts a fool who is devoid of wisdom,
just as a mere breath of wind destroys a sapless blade of grass.
O Rāma, even one who is without a companion, without a teacher, and without attendants, crosses over the ocean of saṃsāra by means of wisdom alone, just like a boat.
One who possesses wisdom reaches the successful conclusion of his task even when lacking companions;
whereas one of poor wisdom perishes, even when undertaking a primary enterprise.

One should first increase one's wisdom through the study of scriptures and association with virtuous people, just as one nurtures a creeper for the attainment of fruit by means of watering, protection, and cultivation.
The tree of right action, with its vast root of the power of wisdom,
bears fruit that is exceedingly sweet in due time, like the lunar disc in the month of Māsa.
The very same effort that men exert in acquiring external objects should first be applied to the increase of wisdom.
One should avoid dullness of wisdom, which is the boundary of all sufferings, the supreme treasury of calamities, and the seed of the trees of saṃsāra.
O Great-minded One, whatever is obtained from heaven, from the netherworld, or from sovereignty— all that is attained from the treasury of wisdom.
O Rāghava, one crosses over this terrible ocean of saṃsāra through wisdom; not by means of conduct, nor by sacred fords, nor by austerity.
That even men who walk upon the earth have attained divine prosperity is the sweet fruit that has arisen from the flowering creeper of wisdom.
Lions, whose mouths were stained with the blood of wild elephants torn by their claws through wisdom,
were defeated by jackals, just as deer are overcome by lions.
Even by men who were once commoners, kingship has been attained through the power of wisdom;
it is observed here that the fitness for heaven and liberation belongs only to the wise man.
Through wisdom, all speakers— who are but the playful manifestations of their own conceptual constructions—
conquer those who resemble the Sugata, like the roars of the ocean against the thunder of clouds.
This wisdom, like a wish-fulfilling gem, resides within the heart-casket of the discerning person;
like a celestial kalpa-tree, it bestows the very fruit one has contemplated.
The capable one crosses the cycle of existence; the inferior one is carried away by it.
The trained one reaches the further shore; the untrained one perishes with the boat.
Wisdom, when rightly applied, leads a person to the further shore; when wrongly applied, it carries him through the cycle of existence like a boat drifting on the ocean.
Faults arising from the multitude of desires do not afflict the discerning man who is undeluded and wise, just as arrows do not strike one who is well-armored.
Through wisdom, my dear friend, this entire world is seen exactly as it is;
for one who sees correctly, neither calamities nor prosperities arise.
The dark, expansive, and inert cloud of egoism, which conceals the supreme sun,
is torn asunder by me through the wind of wisdom.
By one who desires to attain that incomparable state, this very mind must first be nurtured;
for surely, by a farmer seeking the fruit, the earth itself is tilled first.
The thirteenth canto, named "The Greatness of Wisdom," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, O Rāma, having investigated the self by means of the self like Janaka,
you will before long attain the state of those who have known what is to be known.
For those wise men of kingly birth who are born later attain by themselves that which is to be attained, just like Janaka.
One should strive to conquer those enemies known as the senses to such an extent that this Self, by means of the self alone, becomes serene within the self.
When the all-pervading God, the Lord of gods, the Supreme Self,
is pleased and beholds one personally, all perceptions of suffering come to an end.
When that which is both supreme and inferior is seen, the fists of the seeds of delusion, the showers of various calamities, and false views all go to destruction.
O Rāma, like Janaka, always with an intent soul engaged in all undertakings,
having discerned the self through wisdom, become one who possesses glory and is supreme.
For one who constantly maintains discernment and observes people as fickle,
the self becomes serene of its own accord in the course of time, just as it did for Janaka.
Neither fate, nor actions, nor wealth, nor kinsmen provide refuge for those terrified by worldly existence, except for their own personal effort.
O dear one, those who are devoted to fate and intent upon such false conceptualizations as ritual action— their intellect is dull and perishable, and it cannot lead them to liberation.
Relying upon supreme solitude and beholding the Self by means of the self,
one should cross the ocean of saṃsāra with an intellect intensified by dispassion.
This, O Rāma, has been described as the attainment of knowledge, which bestows happiness and fells the tree of ignorance, like the falling of fruit from the sky.
Like that of Janaka, the wise and discerning one, this embodied being— who is himself a god— attains full expansion by his own accord, like a lotus at dawn.
The mind, its mentation completely stilled, dissolves through discernment,
just as snow— with its color, form, and touch melting away— is dissolved by the heat of the sun.
On this night, when destruction has dawned, the thought "I am indeed this" gives rise to its own expansive light, which is all-pervading and self-manifesting.
When this contraction of "I am this very [person]" has dissolved,
an expansion that pervades infinite worlds arises.
Just as Janaka abandoned the latent impression of egoism,
so too, O one of noble intellect, having investigated within yourself, you should abandon it.
When the cloud of egoism has been dissipated, the stainless supreme sun of one’s own light truly becomes manifest in the pure sky of consciousness.
The cultivation of the sense of "I" is nothing but profound darkness;
when that ceases, illumination arises.
When it has been cultivated that "I am not, nor is there another, nor is there non-existence," the mind attains tranquility and does not sink into things to be grasped.
O Rāma, know that the mind’s pursuit of what is to be accepted and its absolute avoidance of what is to be rejected— this alone is bondage, and nothing else.
Do not indulge in grief regarding things to be abandoned; do not be intent on things to be accepted.
Having relinquished the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, abide in the remainder and attain self-composure.

Those for whom there is the settled conviction that "this is to be accepted" and "this is to be rejected" have dissolved [into the Self]; they neither desire nor renounce anything here, and no others do so.
As long as the mental calculation of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has not ceased within the mind,
so long does equanimity not shine forth, like moonlight in a cloudy sky.
For one whose mind is agitated by the thought "this is non-existent" and "this is existent," equanimity does not arise, just as a flower cluster does not appear on a withered tree.
Where there is the pursuit of what is appropriate and inappropriate, delighting in gain and loss, how can there be the clarity of equanimity that laughs with hopelessness?
Since this single, stainless reality of Brahman exists,
how can there ever be irrationality or rationality in the perception of constant multiplicity within that which is non-dual?
I suspect that on the tree of the mind there are two restless female monkeys, the one desirous and the other undesirous;
since they leap about therein, how can there be any gentleness in it?
Hopelessness, fearlessness, permanence, equanimity, knowledge, effortlessness, actionlessness, gentleness, and non-conceptuality.
Firmness, friendliness, mindfulness, contentment, joy, and gentle speech—
women who are devoted approach the wise man who is free from attachment to what is to be rejected or accepted.
One should forcibly withdraw the mind as it runs downward toward sense-objects by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*),
just as water falling downward is held back by a dam.
Having abandoned these external objects, whether standing, walking, sleeping, or breathing,
one should at all times and in every way restrain all internal [states].
The turbid water of saṃsāra has spread forth, its net of latent impressions (vāsanā) caught by the fish of craving, and it is stretched out with the threads of anxious thought.
O dear one, with this sharp probe of wisdom,
cut through [your doubts] as the wind, blowing across the vast expanse, disperses a cloud.
One should uproot the root of this tree of saṃsāra— the seat of the sprouts of defects—
with a resolute intellect and through a steadfast fortitude that is firm.
Having severed the mind with the mind itself, having forgotten the final mind,
and having severed even the present mind, attain the state of one whose cycle of existence is severed.
When delusion has been forgotten, saṃsāra no longer sprouts forth.
Whether standing, walking, breathing, O Rāma, dwelling, rising, or falling,
having internally resolved that "this [world] is indeed unreal," abandon all attachment.
Relying fully on equanimity, performing the duties that have come to you,
and not thinking of those not yet attained, dwell here indeed, O Rāghava.
Just as the sky bears all the signs of the seasons and yet bears none,
so too, O sinless one, perform actions here or do not perform them.
You alone are the Knower, you are the Unborn, you are the Self, you are Maheśvara;
this reality, which is non-different from the Self, is spread out and pervaded by you.
He who has abandoned all mental cultivation regarding this entire mass of visible objects is not seized by defects born of joy, resentment, or despondency.
Freed from passion and hatred, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal,
the yogi who has abandoned the latent impressions of saṃsāra is called "liberated."
Whatever he does, whatever he eats, whatever he gives, or whatever he destroys— in all that,
his mind being liberated, there is equanimity toward pleasure and pain.
Having abandoned the cultivation of likes and dislikes with the thought that "only what has arisen must be done," he who engages in his duties does not sink anywhere.
O Mahāmati, the mind that possesses the certainty that "this is merely the existence of consciousness," having abandoned the conceit of enjoyment, attains tranquility.
The mind, being insentient by its very nature, pursues the principle of consciousness,
just as a cat in the forest follows the lord of beasts out of a craving for meat.
Just as a jackal eats meat obtained through the power of a lion’s prowess,
so does the mind resort to the visible world attained through the power of the vigor of consciousness.
The mind, though thus unreal in its conceptualization, lives by the grace of consciousness;
by contemplating consciousness alone, it attains the state of pure thought, and from that, even consciousness itself [is transcended].
That which is indeed inert, devoid [of consciousness], and abandoned by the lamp of the intellect— that mind, resembling a corpse, being insentient, how could it arise?
The power of vibration, consisting of vital breath and touched by the nature of consciousness,
is called "citta" through the term "kalana" (the act of forming) by those who perceive the scriptures.
That very form which is accumulated and agitated is called "mental construction" (kalana).
Having realized that "I am consciousness alone," it goes toward pure consciousness itself.
That consciousness which is devoid of an object of thought is the eternal Brahman;
that same consciousness, when accompanied by an object of thought, is called mental construction (kalana).
That Brahman which exists in an indistinct form is the mind;
having attained an unreal state of conceptualization, it appears as if real within the heart.
When the conceptualization of consciousness as "mind" (citta) becomes established here, at that very moment, having forgotten its true nature as consciousness, it remains as if inert.

Having become perfected, it is named "discrimination" (kalanā); it follows after conceptual construction (saṅkalpa), possesses the faculty of differentiation, and is characterized by that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted.
This very consciousness, as it were, having become inert through its own power,
does not perceive its true form as long as it has not been fully awakened.
Therefore, through inquiry into the scriptures, through supreme detachment,
and through the restraint of the senses, one should personally awaken from conceptual construction.
The differentiation of all beings occurs through consciousness and its cessation;
one who is awakened attains the state of Brahman, whereas otherwise the world wanders in delusion.
