One should awaken that mental construction which is intoxicated by the wine of delusion, which wallows in the pit of sense objects,
and which is fast asleep regarding the realization of the Self.
For this [intellect] is unawakened and inert; it perceives nothing at all.
Like a creeper of mental construction within, though appearing, it is composed of unreality.
By means of that supreme vision abiding within, this mental construction shines forth among all objects, just as the fragrance-potency shines within a flower-cluster.
But this "calculation" (kalanā) which has been conceived in the three worlds is not [the Self],
for it perceives only something [external] and possesses the sole characteristic of eternal insentience.
How could that which is inert, consisting of the nature of a stone of mental construction, ever perceive?
Like a lotus-pond by the heat [of the sun], it is awakened only by the Supreme.
Just as a maiden made of stone does not dance even when urged,
so this mental construction within the body perceives nothing at all.
Where was a battle with a gurgling roar ever fought by kings who were mere painters?
And where were medicinal herbs ever awakened by the rays of variegated moonbeams?
Where could there be the tossing about of corpses whose limbs are possessed by non-existent spirits?
And where could there be sweet-sounding song from circles of forest stones?
Where is the darkness of night dispelled by suns fashioned from books?
Where are shadows created by forests of the sky consisting of mere mental constructs?
Where can any action be performed by these minds— which are as inert as stones, arisen from a mass of false delusions, and consisting of nothing but a mirage?
Just as a river of mirages appears when a vast expanse of heat stands present,
even so this mental construction flashes forth within the Self, though it is entirely real.
O Rāma, know that this subtle vibration of the mind which has been gradually attained is the power of the vital breaths residing within embodied beings.
This consciousness which is unassailed by even the slightest fragments of volitional determination,
and whose aesthetic flavor and form are not projected outward— this is the radiance of the supreme Self.
The conceptualization that persists as "I am this" and "this is mine" with respect to the vital breath (prāṇa) and the principle of the self (ātmatattva) is called by the name "living being" (jīva).

"Intellect, mind, and the individual soul—these are designations conceived by those who know that [reality], O Rāma, for the sake of the unreal volition; they do not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth."
Neither the mind, nor the intellect, nor the individual soul, nor even the body exists here in the ultimate sense; only one's own Self exists here at all times.
The Self alone is this entire world, and the Self likewise is the progression of time;
it is clearer than eternal space, neither non-existent nor existent, and is stainless.
Because it is transparent, it appears as non-existent; yet, by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness, it is existent.
The Self, which transcends all categories, is experienced through one's own direct experience.
Where the consciousness of the Supreme Self has reached its complete exhaustion, there the mind is utterly spent;
where darkness comes to an end, there light prevails.
Where there is even a slight inclination toward volition within the pure radiance of self-awareness,
there occurs the forgetting of the Self and the recollection of the birth of the mind.
The mind of another person is said to consist of volition;
through the absence of volition, the state of being "mindless" arises, which is known by the name liberation.
This much indeed is the birth of the mind— the seed of the tree of saṃsāra— namely,
that the consciousness of the self is directed toward conceptual construction.
The existence of the non-conceptual mind, when stained by the mark of conceptualization, is called "mental construction" (kalanā); here, the mind does not exist as a separate entity like a jar.
When the power of prāṇa is restrained, that which is called the mind dissolves;
for when it abides as a substance, that mental [entity] indeed takes the form of prāṇa.
The vital breath (prāṇa), situated within the heart, perceives the experience of other places;
that which arises from the sensation of its vibration is designated as the mind (manas).
Through dispassion, through the practice of the instruments, through right method, through the exhaustion of latent impressions,
and through the realization of the ultimate reality, the vital energies are restrained.
A stone may perhaps possess the power to taste food,
but the mind has no power whatsoever to perceive motion.

Vibration is the power of the vital breath and the winds; it is of a fluctuating nature and insentient. Consciousness, however, is consciousness itself, established in its own self, and it is always all-pervasive.
The mind is conceived as the connection between the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) and the power of vibration (spanda-śakti);
that which has thus arisen is indeed false, and it is called false knowledge (mithyājñāna).
For this is indeed called ignorance; it is described as illusion (māyā).
This is that supreme nescience which bestows the poison of the higher worldly existence (saṃsāra).

If the conceptualization of mental constructs is not performed through union with the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) and the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), then these fears of worldly existence are utterly destroyed.
When the power of vibration belonging to the wind is perceived by consciousness,
then that consciousness, together with its object of perception, attains the state of "mind" (citta) internally through volitional construction (saṅkalpa).
This "cittatā" (the state of being mind) is falsely imagined by consciousness, like a ghost conjured by children;
for that which exists as the reality of vibration, in the form of an unbroken circle, is consciousness itself.
Since consciousness is all-pervading, with what indeed could it be connected?
With what could Indra, whose power is indivisible, have any conflict?
Therefore, due to the absence of related entities, no relation exists here;
without a relation, for whom is that mind established, and of what nature is it?
When consciousness and its vibration are one, what indeed can be called the mind?
What is an army without the clashing together of a multitude of horses and elephants?
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "corrupt self-mind" within the three worlds;
it is through the correct thorough knowledge of this that the destruction of the mind occurs.
O sinless one, do not thus conceive such thoughts in your mind to no purpose;
the mind that has arisen falsely does not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality.
O great-minded one, do not form any conceptualization whatsoever within;
for that which is called the "conceptualizing mind" does not exist anywhere here.
O Sage, through your perfect vision, the mirage of conceptual construction— which arises from incorrect knowledge— has been completely stilled within the desert of your heart.
Because it is insentient and devoid of its own essential nature, the mind is always dead;
yet by that which is dead, the world is slain—wondrous indeed is this wheel of folly!
He who has neither self nor body, neither support nor even form—he by him all this is consumed; wonderful indeed is this snare of folly!
If one who is devoid of all spiritual equipment is struck even by the mind alone,
I believe his head would shatter from blows as light as lotus petals.
I consider that fool to be burnt by the rays of the full moon who is struck even mentally by one who is dull-witted, mute, and blind.
For a hero who exists is overcome by the world;
this [world], however, destroys that which does not exist at all. Therefore, it is said to arise from delusion.
Formed by false conceptualization and existing only falsely, it is not seen even when sought; what power, indeed, can it possibly possess?
Oh, how truly wondrous is this creator of illusory forms,
by whom the world is overwhelmed even with a mind that is exceedingly fickle!
Folly is the ultimate source of all calamities; for what misfortune does not befall the ignorant?
Behold: by folly alone is this creation brought forth even by one who is unborn.
Alas, what a pity! This creation is exceedingly naive, having fallen under the sway of folly, in that it is tormented even by this unreal living self.
I believe this creation, consisting of fools, is exceedingly fragile;
it is shattered into fragments by the blow of a sword-like wave.
It is torn asunder, as if by a machine, by the fall of the stalk of a blue lotus;
it faints at the touch of the rays of the full-orbed moon.
He is bound by the enemy-like threads of sight released from the eyes,
and he is overcome by the army of his own volitions.
For it is said that this [mind] is not troubled by anything that remains fixed anywhere,
but rather by another— something imagined, futile, and miserable.
This creation, consisting of a world of fools, arises from the mind itself as something unreal;
that which one is unable to bring under control is not taught by Rāma.
This [intellect] possesses a noble nature, yet it is not capable of piercing through the subtle points of wisdom;
it is not fit for the words of instruction, remaining as if entirely complete unto itself.
For she fears the thin sound of the strings of the lute;
she even fears the radiance of the face of her sleeping kinsman.
Even when people laugh loudly, she flees in utter terror;
this ignorant woman has indeed been rendered helpless by her own mind alone.

Overpowered by a mere fragment of pleasure, as if scorched by her own heart dwelling within her like an enemy, her intellect is impaired; utterly deluded, she falsely perceives that which is truly real.
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Warding Off of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
By that person who has conquered their own mind— which was being carried away by the worthless waves of the ocean of saṃsāra— the mind itself is no longer mute.
In this treatise, I have not taught these discursive explanations, which yield the noble fruit consisting in the attainment of the Self.
For what person of evil intellect indeed would show a forest variegated with diverse clusters of blossoms to one who is blind and does not see at all?
What person of little intelligence, whose nose is wheezing from leprosy, would take as an authority a fool in the investigation of various fragrances or in self-instruction?

Who, being himself devoid of wisdom, would accept as authoritative for the determination of the Dharma a person whose senses are perverted, who is intoxicated, and whose eyes roll from the effects of liquor?
What rogue would ask a corpse lying in a cemetery about the method of attaining liberation?
And who indeed instructs a fool when there is doubt?
How indeed can that evil-minded one be called a teacher, by whom even the serpent of the mind— dwelling within the cave of his intentions and remaining mute and blind— has not been conquered?
Know that the mind is indeed conquered in reality because it does not exist;
that stone which does not exist at all is already destroyed even before one approaches it.
O Rāma, he who has not conquered his mind— which, though possessing nothing, is yet wicked—
is killed by the fainting fit of poison, as if by having swallowed venom itself.
The Knower always perceives the Self; it is the powers of knowledge that vibrate through the senses in their respective functions. What, then, is called "mind"? MU_5,14.10
The power that causes the vital breaths to vibrate is the power of knowledge belonging to the Supreme Self;
it is simply the innate power of the senses—so who here is bound?
And since all powers belong to that Self who is indeed omnipotent,
from what source could this distinction or otherness possibly arise?
What indeed is called the "living soul" (jīva), by which this world is blinded? Know that it is merely the mind and is non-existent; what power can it possibly have?
O Rāma, seeing the succession of sufferings of those whose vision has been consumed by their own minds, my intellect, overcome with compassion, suffers as if it were deluded.
Who indeed here, and from what cause, would feel distress? For it is only the fool who suffers; for common people and young camels are born solely for the sake of suffering.
The unintelligent are born within inert bodies solely for destruction,
rising and falling incessantly like bubbles in the oceans.
Behold, how many animals are slaughtered every day in every slaughterhouse by those who act like butchers! What lamentation can there be in this?
The wind daily destroys tumors in the thickets of shrubs; so too does it destroy gadflies and mosquitoes—what lamentation can there be in this?
In every direction, upon the lords of mountains and in forest after forest, throngs of Pulindas slaughter hundreds of thousands of living beings; what lamentation can there be in this?
In the water, a large fish tears apart its body from the swarm of aquatic creatures for its daily meal; what lamentation can there be in this?
Vultures, hawks, and other birds of prey incessantly plunder the flocks of winged creatures in the sky; what lamentation can there be in this?
A fly, tormented by hunger, eats a nit as small as a speck of dust;
a hungry spider eats that fly, and a restless gnat eats even the spider.
The frog eats that gadfly, and the serpent eats that frog;
the fierce donkey kills the serpent, and the mongoose tears that donkey apart.
The cat kills the mongoose; the dog tears apart the cat;
the bear kills the dog; and the tiger tears apart the bear.
The lion overcomes the tiger, and the *śarabha* devours the lion;
yet the *śarabha* comes to destruction when it attempts to leap over a thundering cloud.
The clouds are scattered by the winds; the winds are overcome by the mountains;
the mountains are crushed by the thunderbolt; and the thunderbolt is subject to the will of Śakra.
Indra is supported by Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu undergoes the state of a living being,
garlanded with the succession of pleasure and pain, and the cycle of old age and death.
Even creatures of massive bodies, even those equipped with the weapons of magic spells,
are indeed subsisted upon by lice clinging to their limbs.
Thus, this forest of living beings is constantly torn asunder and shattered;
out of delusion, they devour and protect one another to their heart's content.
Various kinds of living beings perish incessantly,
and diverse beings are born incessantly in every direction.
In the reservoirs of water, fish, elephants, sea-monsters, and the like are born;
within the earth, swarms of insects, scorpions, and so forth are produced.
In the intermediate space as well, birds and the like are born in the sky;
in the forest paths, lions, tigers, deer, and so forth are born.
Even within the limbs of living beings, lice, bugs, and ants are born;
and among stationary things, species such as wood-boring insects and pythons are born.
Within stones, insects, frogs, woodworms, and the like are born;
likewise, various swarms of insects are born even within excrement.
Thus, throughout countless other births,
whether in states of decline or prosperity, may those possessed of compassion rejoice or weep incessantly.
In this turmoil of saṃsāra, which is incessant and arises without end, one who is engaged [in its nature] experiences neither contentment nor suffering.
In this very same way, these rows of beings, arising in great numbers, fly up together with the multitudes of leaves from the trees and dissolve away again and again.
He who, being compassionate, has set out to wipe away the suffering of the wicked-minded,
undergoes great exhaustion, like one who rubs the rays of the sun with his hand as if they were a parasol.
Men on this earth do not possess the same nature as animals;
what purpose is there in speaking words to one who is like a monstrous tree-stump in the forest?
What indeed is the distinction between those whose minds leap with excitement and the beasts?
Beasts are led by a rope; those of deluded mind are led by their own thoughts.
Seeing the calamity of fools who are submerged in the mud of their own minds and whose nature is fashioned from the fragments of their own desires, even stones weep.
For those who have not conquered their own minds, there are infinite heaps of suffering;
therefore, one whose wisdom is perfected does not apply himself to wiping them away.
O descendant of Raghu, for those who have completely conquered their own minds, sorrows are easily warded off; therefore, let one who has known what is to be known proceed in this world.
The mind does not exist, O mighty-armed one; do not deludedly imagine this.
By such an imagination, you will be destroyed as if by a Vetāla spirit.
As long as you, being deluded, had forgotten the reality of the self,
for that long the serpent of your mind remained aroused.
Now you have understood it as it truly is, O subduer of enemies: the mind grows from conceptual construction; therefore, abandon that very thing immediately.
If you rely upon this visible world, then you possess a mind and are bound;
if you utterly abandon this visible world, then you are without mind and have attained liberation.
This collection of qualities, when relied upon, leads only to bondage; it is only when completely renounced that it leads to liberation. Do as you wish.
Meditating that "I am not this" and "this is not I," remain immovable like a mountain; with a heart resembling the infinite sky, you are the Lord of the Heart.
O Rāma, having abandoned the impurity of conceptualizing a distinction between yourself and the world— the duality consisting of "I" and "the other"— remain steadfastly established in what remains.
Always contemplate your own self as the act of seeing—the distinction between the seer and the seen—within yourself and within the world; thus remain.

Meditating constantly on that which is abandoned by both the object of taste and the taster, which dwells between the object of taste and the taster, and which stands at the end of the act of tasting— become one with the Self.
Today, having taken hold of the middle path— which is itself without support— remain steadfast as the object of Rāma’s experience and likewise as the experiencer himself.
Having thus meditated upon the self as devoid of the contemplation of becoming and free from the state of existence and non-existence, remain established in the self and become that yourself.
O Rāma, when you abandon this existence of the self and yourself conceive of it as an object of thought, then you fall into the state of the mind, which brings extreme suffering.
O mighty-armed one, having forcibly severed this chain of the mind by means of the reasoning of knowledge of one's own true nature, liberate the lion that is your own self.
When you abandon the state of the Supreme Self and fall into the impurity of the object of thought,
you then proceed toward conceptualization and become that very object of thought.
Through the awareness of the limbs that there is an object of consciousness existing as distinct from the self, the mind becomes miserable; by abandoning that awareness, it is destroyed.
When the internal dawn of consciousness arises that "this entire world is indeed the Self," where is the knower,
where is the mind, what is the object of thought, and what is the act of thinking?
"‘I am the self,’ ‘I am a living being’—the wise know that this much alone constitutes the mind;
by this, O Rāghava, is this beginningless and endless suffering extended."
"I am the Self, not that which is called the individual soul (jīva); there are no other existences anywhere"—this very stilling of the mind is said to be supreme bliss.
O Rāghava, when the certainty arises that "this world is indeed the Self," the non-existence of the mind is born; of this there is no doubt.
When, through the realization of truth, it is established that "this is indeed one's own self," know, O mind, that you have completely dissolved, just as darkness does before the light of the sun.
As long as the serpent of the mind remains within the body, there is great fear;
once it has been driven out through yoga, whence can there be any occasion for fear?
O sinless one, let this vampire of the mind, which has arisen from mere delusion,
be forcibly cast down by you through the mantra of perfect knowledge.
O best among the powerful, when the yakṣa of the mind has departed from the house of the body, remain free from mental anguish and devoid of agitation; there is no fear for you.
"Thinking, 'I am indeed free from passion and indeed free from all taints,' by this much alone the existence of your mind has dissolved.
You have reached the supreme state, the highest station, which is devoid of suffering; remain thus within, with all desires completely stilled."
The fifteenth canto, titled "Description of the True Nature of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
Following this impure mental state, O Rāma,
which is the seed-grain of saṃsāra and the snare that binds the individual soul.
The Self, having abandoned its own true nature and fallen into a state of impurity, pursues anxious thoughts and assumes the stain of mental constructs.
Fainting, bestowing great delusion,
and causing fear, craving— in the form of a poisonous creeper— brings about nothing but fainting.
Whenever it arises, this craving— which bestows great delusion and causes the affliction of infinite blindness— is like the dark night.
Hara and the other gods are capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon;
but no one at all is capable of enduring the burning of the flames of the fire of craving.
Sharp, black, and very long, this terrible sword of craving always flows within one's own body; though it feels cool, it results in unhappiness.
O Rāghava, those things which are terminal, difficult to restrain, and arrogant are the fruits of the creeper of craving; they are the sufferings here in this world.
Invisible, this hound of craving, lurking within the cave of the human mind, devours the flesh, bones, blood, and other parts of the body.
The river of craving, its rainy season in full flow, quickly shatters the dull-witted; at one moment it attains exhilaration, and at another it falls into emptiness.
Seeing his own wretchedness, his heart struck down and his vigor destroyed, a person succumbs to baseness;
overcome by craving, he becomes deluded, cries out, and falls.
The vital breaths moving within the cavity of the heart remain healthy for that man in whom the black female serpent of craving does not dwell in its hollow.
Surely, wherever the dark night of craving has set,
there meritorious deeds increase like moons in the bright fortnight.
That tree of a man which has not been gnawed by the woodworm of craving always shines forth with the ever-blossoming flower of merit.
In the forest of the mental disposition, the river of craving and delusion flows for men— endless, agitated by waves, and crowded with eddies and whirlpools.
Driven by craving, all these people are carried away, shattered, and repeatedly gathered together, like the birds on a stringed puppet-machine.
Even the very subtle roots, though as hard and rough as iron,
are cut away by craving as it strikes them like the edge of an axe.
The deluded person, pursuing craving, falls into a pit,
just as a young deer, following a dark trail of grass and branches, falls into a chasm.
Neither old age, nor hunger, nor even decrepitude consumes one so swiftly as does craving— that which wears away the heart like a leprosy.
Through the root of craving, which is like the river Kauśikī and is inauspicious within the heart,
this Blessed One Viṣṇu has assumed the state of a dwarf.
Indeed, by this craving, which is somehow knotted within the heart by fate, one is made to wander through the sky day after day, as if by a rope attached to the sun.
Avoid from afar this cruel craving, which dwells within living beings in this world and takes the form of all suffering, as one would avoid a venomous female serpent.
By craving the winds blow; by craving the mountains stand firm;
by craving alone the earth supports all; the three worlds are enveloped by craving.
This entire course of worldly existence is strung together by the cord of craving;
those bound by the rope are released, but none who are bound by craving are ever liberated.
Therefore, O Raghava, abandon craving by relinquishing mental constructs;
for it has been determined through reasoning that the mind does not exist as a constructor of thoughts.
"First of all, do not entertain that dark-minded, evil desire within your heart, O mighty-armed one, thinking 'I am this name'."
O Rāma, if you do not cultivate this notion of self in what is not-self— which gives rise to suffering— then you may be counted among the truly wise.
O fortunate one, having severed this unwholesome state consisting of the sense of "I" with the very probe of self-arisen being,
you shall attain the power that overcomes all fear born of worldly existence on the ground that marks the end of becoming.
The sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of Craving," Canto 16;
Rāma:
O Blessed One, these words of yours are exceedingly profound, in that you say to me: "Do not grasp at egoism and craving."
If I am to abandon egoism, O Lord,
then I shall completely cast off this structure known as the body.
Just as a great tree is supported by its massive trunk,
so indeed is this body supported by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
Upon the destruction of the ego-sense, the body indeed necessarily perishes,
like a great tree when its root is cut by a saw.
Therefore, O Sage, best among speakers, having determined this single matter, tell me: how may I abandon this, and how may I live? MU 5.16.5
Vasiṣṭha:
O lotus-eyed Rāma, the renunciation of latent impressions (vāsanā) in all circumstances is said by those who know reality to be of two kinds, known by the names *dhyeya* and *neya*.
"I belong to these objects, and these belong to me as my very life;
I am nothing without them, and they, it is said, are nothing without me."
Thus, having abandoned internal certainty and reflected with the mind, one contemplates:
"I am not the object, nor does the object belong to me."

That which is indeed the abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) by one who performs actions with ease through an intellect that is inwardly cooled— that is proclaimed as "the object of meditation" (dhyeya).

Having brought about the destruction of latent impressions through an all-encompassing cognition of everything, he who, being free from mental constructs, abandons the body— that is to be understood as the destruction of latent impressions.
He who, having effortlessly abandoned the latent impression consisting of egoism,
remains as one who has renounced all objects of meditation, is called liberated while living.
O descendant of Raghu, know that he who has brought his latent impressions (vāsanā) to an end by uprooting all mental constructions is liberated; he does not depend on the scriptures.
Having abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), those great-souled and noble people remain in a state of effortless ease as those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), like Janaka.
But those who have attained peace by completely abandoning these latent impressions remain as Videhamuktas (bodilessly liberated) in Brahman itself, both the higher and the lower.
"O Raghava, these two types of renunciation are equal and established in the state of liberation;
both have attained the nature of Brahman, and both are free from the fever of worldly distress."
O sinless one, when supreme faith has been attained in liberation, there remains only the pure [state]:
one stands with a throbbing body, while the other stands with a tranquil body.
One remains with the body, liberated and free from fever;
the other, having cast off the body, exists as one who is emancipated and whose latent tendencies are no longer led [by karma].
He who neither rejoices nor desponds when pleasure and pain fall upon him incessantly and in due course is said here to be liberated.
He for whom neither the desired nor the undesired exists within his perceptions of objects,
who moves like one in deep sleep— he is said to be liberated.
He whose internal sense of "mine," "I," and "here" regarding the calculation of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has completely perished is called one liberated while living.
He who is not internally affected by joy, resentment, fear, anger, desire, miserliness, or [wrong] views is said to be liberated while living.
He who always remains awake with a mind whose mental fluctuations have been stilled as if in deep sleep,
and who is ever attended by joy like the moon joined with its digits— he is remembered here as one who is liberated.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The seventeenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Treatment of Thirst," by Vasiṣṭha.

O Rāma, those who are liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamuktas) do not at all remain within the range of speech here; therefore, listen to these [others] who are liberated while living (jīvanmuktas).
They know that state of liberation while living to be that by which these very activities of one's nature are performed with a clear mind, free from craving.
The teachers say that the state of a living being who, through craving fixed upon external objects, remains attached to them, is bondage— the firm fetter of saṃsāra.
Surely that latent impression which, having abandoned its conceptual construction in the heart, wanders externally,
is here called the "embodied one liberated while living."
"O Rāghava, craving that is swollen by the misfortune of external objects is called 'bound';
craving that is liberated from the misfortune of all objects is called 'liberated'."
But that craving which previously existed and persists even now as eternal freedom from suffering and partlessness is considered by the wise to be liberation itself.
"O Raghava, O high-minded one, know that this internal notion, 'let this be mine,' is craving, a fetter, and a mental construction."
Having forever abandoned this [notion] regarding all things, whether they exist or do not exist, the high-minded one attains the most exalted state.

Having abandoned the hope for bondage and the hope for liberation, as well as the states of pleasure and pain, and even the hope for existence and non-existence, remain like the unagitated great ocean.
O best among the wise, having realized the Self to be ageless and immortal,
do not let your mind become turbid with fears of old age and death.
This collection of objects does not belong to you, nor are you this [collection], O Rāghava;
this is something else entirely, and you are another, the eternal one.
Whether the universe has arisen from the non-existent or is eternally established in reality,
since you have attained that very state, whence can there be any union with craving?
Furthermore, O virtuous Rāma, a fourfold conviction of vast scope arises in the mind of a discerning person. (MU 5.17.13)
"From head to foot, I am created by my mother and father"— this is the single conviction, O Rāma, which leads to bondage through the perception of what is unreal.
"I am subtler than even the tip of a hair, transcending all existing things"—
this second conviction arises in the wise for the sake of liberation.
"I am always the undecaying Self of all things in the web of the universe"—
if this third conviction is established in such a way, O scion of Raghu, it leads indeed to liberation.
"I and this world are non-existent, eternally empty and like space"—
this is the fourth certainty for the attainment of liberation.
Thus, among the four certainties, the first is said to lead to bondage; the other three, when interwoven with pure contemplation, are declared to lead to liberation.
Among these, the first is bound by craving that is fit for bondage;
the other three, whose cravings are pure and clear, are liberated while living and full of grace.
O Mahāmati, having taken up that conviction that "I alone am everything," your mind shall no longer fall into despondency.
The greatness of the Self pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
therefore, by the internal certainty that "all is the Self," you are not bound.
The Void, Nature, Illusion, Brahman, Consciousness,
Śiva, Puruṣa, and Īśa— these are eternally said to be the Self alone.
All this is always indeed existent; here, duality or anything else is never found anywhere.
The world is pervaded by true knowledge, not by the other, which is blinding ignorance.
The ocean, whose self is infinite, has filled the depths of the underworld with its waters;
the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is filled by the Self.
All this is eternally the Truth; falsehood exists nowhere at all.
Just as the entire ocean is nothing but water, and not waves and such things separately.
Bracelets, armlets, anklets, and so forth are not separate from gold;
likewise, the millions of forms of trees and grasses are not distinct from the Self.
Through the playful manifestation of the world via the emergence of both duality and non-duality,
the power consisting of the Supreme Self unfolds as nothing but non-duality.

Regarding all things, whether belonging to oneself or to another, at all times— whether they have perished or increased, and whether they are effects, pleasures, or pains— do not grasp them as "mine."
Relying upon the non-duality of existence and having as your essence the non-duality of being, disregard the non-duality of action and become one who embodies both duality and non-duality.
Do not fall, through this worldly contemplation, into the terrifying stages of existence which are full of calamities, like a blind elephant in rivers.
Duality is not possible in the Great Self who is omnipresent; nor is unity possible in that Self whose nature is manifested as both.
They say that non-duality is devoid of unity, eternally manifest, and that everything is nothing other than its own essential nature.
Neither do I exist, nor indeed do the worlds exist; yet all this that appears is surely the unchanging.
It is mere consciousness alone that shines forth, peaceful; know that the world, "I," and "existence" are neither non-existent nor existent.
The supreme nectar, primordial, the illumination of all illuminations, unborn, undecaying, inconceivable, without exit, and changeless;
free from the web of the senses, the life-force of the vital power, devoid of all mental constructs, the cause of all causes.

May you have this firm conviction within: that this entire reality—this Brahman—is eternally risen as the Lord, situated within the expansive light of consciousness; it is the seed of experience, to be pointed out as one's own self-nature, and the tasting of which occurs within the intellect; it is always "all this," "you," "I," and "the world. MU 5.17.34.
The eighteenth canto, titled "The Severance of Thirst," by Vasiṣṭha.
O mighty-armed one, this is the natural disposition of great beings who are free from attachment and unassailed by false views, as they move about here in this world with effortless ease.
Even while dwelling in saṃsāra, the sage, whose mind is liberated while living,
laughs at the worldly states of existence, which are tasteless in their beginning, middle, and end.
Established in all his natural duties, impartial toward all modes of conduct,
he remains steadfast by relying on the relinquishment of latent impressions (vāsanā), which is the object of meditation.
Free from agitation in all circumstances, nourishing all goals,
his soul delighted in the garden of solitude, he dwells in the grove of awakening.
Taking as his object the state that transcends all things, with a mind as cool as the full moon,
neither agitated nor complacent, he does not sink in saṃsāra.
Remaining impartial toward all enemies, endowed with compassion and courtesy,
and acting appropriately toward those who are superior, one does not perish in saṃsāra.
He neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires;
established in silence, engaged in his natural activity, he does not sink in the cycle of existence.
When questioned, he speaks of the subject at hand; when not questioned, he remains like a pillar.
Free from likes and dislikes, he does not sink in the cycle of existence.
One who speaks what is pleasing to all, who is eloquent when exhorted,
and who understands the intentions of living beings, does not perish in saṃsāra.
He knows the affairs of the world— seized by the states of right and wrong, and with its activities impaired by craving— as clearly as a wood-apple fruit within the hollow of his hand.
Having ascended to the supreme state, he gazes upon the fragile condition of the world as if laughing, with an intellect that is inwardly cooled.
O Rāghava, you have described to me the very nature of those great-souled ones who have conquered their minds and have seen both the higher and the lower.
But we do not know the intended doctrine of those fools whose own minds are unsubdued and who are submerged in the mire of worldly enjoyments, even though they wish to speak.
The women they desire, adorned with gestures and expressions of love,
are actually the flames of the fires of hell appearing as the luster of gold.
Meanings are dense with what is useless, consisting of the torment of pursuing empty objects; they point toward the onset of suffering and bring about calamities.
We are unable to describe those actions that bind one to fruits, which consist of various modes of conduct and are filled with pleasure and pain.

Firmly grasping the perfect vision that delights in the relinquishment of all objects of meditation, remain established in yourself through the state of liberation while living, O Rāghava, and move about in the world.
Internally having abandoned all expectations, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions,
yet externally maintaining all conventional conduct, wander in the world, O Raghava.
Noble, of refined conduct, and following all proper behavior,
yet inwardly renouncing everything— wander thus in the world, O Raghava.
Having investigated all the stages, O Rāghava, dwell in this world by taking as your object of devotion that very state which is most sublime.
Carrying inner despair while outwardly acting with a desire for hope,
scorched on the outside yet cooled within, wander through the world, O Rāghava.
Displaying outwardly a feigned agitation while being inwardly free from all agitation, act as an agent on the outside but a non-agent within; thus, O Raghava, move about in the world.
You have understood the true inner nature of all things;
therefore, O Rāghava, wander in the world according to your will with that vision.
Abiding in feigned exultation and joy, with feigned agitation and censure,
and with feigned zeal in your undertakings, move about in the world, O Rāghava.
Having abandoned egoism, with a mind at peace and as radiant as the sky,
wander through the world, O Rāghava, free from the mark of blemish.
Freed from hundreds of bonds of desire, equanimous toward all modes of livelihood,
and engaged in your natural duties outwardly, wander in the world, O Rāghava.
In the ultimate sense, there is neither bondage nor liberation for the embodied being;
this revolving cycle of saṃsāra is a false splendor, like a magical illusion.
O Rāghava, this world is seen as mere delusion due to ignorance,
producing conviction in its vastness, just like water [appearing] in intense sunlight.
How could there be bondage for the Self, which is unbound, uniform, and all-pervading? And in the absence of that [bondage], for whom is liberation prescribed?
This pervasive delusion of the transmigratory world arises from the lack of knowledge of reality;
it comes to an end through the knowledge of reality, just as the perception of a snake in a rope vanishes.
You have realized your own true nature through this subtle intellect;
you have become free from egoism, so remain stainless like the sky.
If you do not exist, then all those notions of friends and kinsmen must be abandoned;
for what indeed can be the notion regarding that which is of the nature of non-existence?
If you are such a one, you are inferred to be possessed of supreme goodness;
for you have emerged as the very first from the Supreme Cause.
The self has no connection with enjoyments, kinsmen, or worldly states, nor with auspicious or inauspicious actions; why then do you grieve for it?

For you whose mind has arisen with the realization "I am that whose sole essence is the reality of the Self," there is no connection with worldly existences; O Rāma, why do you fear the delusion of the world?
O Rāghava, since your kinsman is unborn, what connection do you have with the succession of his joys and sorrows, that you should mourn for him?
If you existed in the past, you will exist just so now;
if you are standing here, you have understood this with certainty.
Why then do you not grieve for those many other kinsmen who have passed away, who were even more numerous and who were celebrated as belonging to your previous lineages?
As you were before, as you are today, and as you will be hereafter— O Rāma, if you are thus of an eternal nature, why do you become deluded?
If you did not exist in the past, do not exist today, and will not exist again in the future,
then even so, since saṃsāra has been exhausted, why do you grieve?
Therefore, it is not fitting to be sorrowful regarding the natural course of worldly existence, nor is it fitting to be joyful; rather, it is proper to act in accordance with one's duty.
Do not go to sorrow, O Rāma, nor even to happiness;
attain equanimity toward all things, for you are the omnipresent Supreme Self.
You are infinite and of a transparent nature, with an interior as utterly pervasive as the sky;
you are eternally pure and luminous, like the hollow core of a flame.
Your body is subtler than the invisible atoms of all worldly objects;
though residing within the heart, you are spread throughout like the single thread of a pearl necklace.
This very persistence of saṃsāra consists in being born again after having been; it occurs only for the ignorant, not for the wise. O Rāma, you are wise; remain steadfast.
For this very nature of this continuous cycle of worldly existence expands through ignorance; yet you, O noble-minded one, are possessed of knowledge.
What else could form be but mere delusion, apart from delusion? For what other sequence could there be in a dream, apart from the dream itself?
This power of the All-Powerful is considered to consist of mere delusion;
established as the so-called "world-process," it is neither unreal nor composed of reality.
O Rāma, solely due to the deformity of knowledge and a lack of discernment, this exceedingly radiant manifestation is perceived in such a manner.
In this world, no one is anyone's relative, nor is anyone anyone's enemy;
at all times, everything belongs to everyone, according to the will of the Lord of All.
This entire world, torn asunder and shattered, yet intermingled with one another, flows incessantly like a torrent of waves from water.
Just as the rim of a wheel moves all around, so too does this unstable cycle of worldly existence move upward and downward, and likewise from the high state it goes to the low.
Those dwelling in heaven go to hell, and those in hell go to the celestial realm;
people pass from one womb to another, and from one continent to another.
The wise fall into wretchedness, while the wretched attain wisdom;
living beings flutter about in the confusion of hundreds of falls and rises.
Nothing uniform, stable, self-abiding, pure, and free from distress can be found here, just as a particle of frost cannot remain in fire.
O Rāma, whichever highly fortunate ones there may be— whether many or few—
they are all seen here to have perished within just a few days.
O mighty-armed one, conceptions such as otherness, selfhood, difference, yours, mine, and so forth, are not real here, just like the vision of two moons and the like.
"This one is a kinsman and that one is a stranger; this is I and this is you"—O Rāma, may these false views now fall away from you.
Remaining engaged in worldly affairs for the sake of play with these [senses] whose vision has been destroyed—
whose roots are severed from within— move about externally with ease.
O observer of noble vows, conduct yourself in this ocean of saṃsāra in such a way that you do not undergo weariness or become exhausted by the burden of latent impressions (vāsanā).
In whatever measure this auspicious investigation of yours arises, which brings about the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), in that same measure you become tranquil.
"This one is a kinsman, this one is not"—such is the calculation of those with narrow minds;
but for those of noble conduct, the intellect is indeed free from all such limitations.
"There is nothing where I am not, and there is nothing that is not mine"—
for those who have thus determined the essential truth, the intellect is indeed free from all obscuration.
He who is as vast as space neither sets nor rises; established in his own self, he perceives everything, just as one standing in the sky sees the surface of the earth.
For indeed, O Rāma, all these classes of beings are your kinsmen;
none of them are truly strangers to you.

In this world, where confusion has been accumulated through hundreds of diverse births, the state of delusion alone leaps about for a moment, thinking "this is a kinsman" or "this is not a kinsman"; yet in reality, the three worlds are eternally kin, even though they are not kin.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Description of the Nature of Liberation while Living," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history:
the conversation between two sons of sages on the banks of the triple-pathed river.
"‘This one is a kinsman, this one is not’—it was remembered from such a discourse.
O Rāghava, listen to this meritorious and wonderful history."
In a certain corner of this Jambudvīpa,
there is a mountain named Mahendra, the great crest-ornament of the forest array.
Where gods and kinnaras rested in the shade of groves of wish-fulfilling trees,
he conquered the sky itself with his lofty peaks that seemed to stretch across it.
He seems to sing the Sāmaveda with the deep, humming echoes of those who have reached the realms of Brahmā and roam among his peaks and caves.
He who shines with clouds thick with water, tossed against the tips of his peaks and entwined with creepers and flowers, as if with locks of hair.
On its slopes, it resounds through the mouths of its caves with the yawns of śarabhas eager to leap upward, as if laughing at the clouds of the cosmic dissolution.
By means of the roar of its waterfalls flowing through the interior of the caves,
it has completely surpassed the playful splendor of the waves of the ocean's waters.
On a delightful, expansive jeweled plateau of that mountain,
the celestial Gaṅgā was brought down by sages for the purpose of bathing and drinking.
On the bank of that river which flows through the three worlds, where the trees were in full bloom,
and where golden lotuses shone like the glittering slopes of a mountain of jewels.
There was a sage named Dīrghatapas, whose wisdom had fully dawned, who was a mass of asceticism and possessed noble intellect; he stood as if he were the very embodiment of austerity.
To that sage were born two sons, as beautiful as the moon,
named Puṇya and Pāvana, like the two hairs on the head of Bṛhaspati.
Together with those two sons and his wife,
he dwelt on the bank of that river, which was lined with fruit-bearing trees.
Then, in the course of time, one of those two sons became possessed of wisdom; O Rāghava, he was named Puṇya, the elder by age and the most excellent in virtues.
Pāvana became half-awakened, like a lotus at the dawn twilight;
having transcended ignorance, he remained as if established in a state that was not yet fully stable.
Then, when immeasurable time has passed, when the causes of death have been gathered, when the multitude of years has dwindled away, and when the wretched body’s life-force has departed;
Abandoning attachment to this cycle of existence— which is rich with fragile beings and terrifying with its burden of events— he, whose life was worn out by old age, departed from it.
The sage Dīrghatapas abandoned his body— the nest of the bird of Time—
within his mountain cave-dwelling, just as a porter casts off a burden.

He attained that passionless state, the abode of consciousness devoid of objects of thought, wherein the onset of all mental constructions has been stilled, just as the fragrance of flowers pervades the sky.
Then the sage’s wife, seeing his body— devoid of the vital breaths of prāṇa and apāna— rolling upon the ground like a lotus severed from its stalk, [was overcome with grief].
Through the practice of yoga long cultivated and perfected by her husband,
she cast off her unfading body, just as a female bee leaves a lotus.
She followed her husband alone as he vanished from the sight of the people,
like the moon that has set, having reached the expanse of the sky of its own radiance.
When his parents had passed away and the funeral rites were completed,
while Puṇya remained undistracted, Pāvana arrived with sorrow.
With his mind struck by grief, wandering through the forest paths and not seeing his elder brother, Pāvana lamented.
Then, having performed the funeral rites for his parents, the noble-minded and virtuous one went to the sacred forest, which was purifying yet filled with the intensity of grief.
Puṇya said:
"My son, why do you bring your grief to such intensity— a cause solely for blindness,
a terrible producer of streams of tears like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season?"
O one of great wisdom, your father has departed together with your mother to his own supreme state, which is called liberation.
That is the station of all beings, that is the form of those who have realized the Self;
since you have attained your own true nature, why do you grieve for your father?
What kind of delusion-born conception has been formed by you here,
that even though your father is not to be mourned, he is being mourned by you in this cycle of existence?
She alone was not your mother, nor was he alone your father;
nor were you alone the son of those two, who had countless sons.
O son, thousands of mothers and fathers have passed away for you,
like many watercourses flowing down through forest after forest.
Of those two who have countless sons, you alone are not their son;
O son, the multitudes of sons of men pass away like the waves of a river.
Countless hundreds of thousands of sons have passed away from our parents,
like clusters of leaf-buds from creepers and trees.
In birth after birth, the multitudes of friends and kinsmen pass away for a living being,
just as the fruits of a great tree fall season after season.
O son, if parents and children are to be pitied because of affection,
then why are those who have passed away— not being pitied— though they number in the thousands and are constant?
O illustrious one, this worldly delusion is seen as a conceptual proliferation;
but in the ultimate sense, O wise one, there is neither friend nor kinsman.
For here, O brother, not even the slightest thing exists in the ultimate sense,
just as there is not even a drop of water in a vast desert that has been scorched for a long time.
O one of great intelligence, these splendors that you behold, flickering like parasols and yak-tail fans, are merely a dream for three or five days.
But with the ultimate vision, my son, investigate the truth:
you are not here, nor is this yours; abandon the delusion within.
These views—that "this person has died" or "I have departed"—arise again from the fever of one's own conceptual constructions; they are seen, but not in reality.
In the vast desert of ignorance, this world of manifold forms flashes forth as water in the mirage of its own latent impressions, consisting of the shimmering waves of fluctuating merit and demerit.
The twentieth meritorious canto, named "The Purification and Enlightenment."
Who is the father, what is a friend, who is the mother, and who are kinsmen?
By one's own intelligence alone they are shaken off, just as the dust of the earth is blown away by a whirlwind.
This conceptual proliferation is extended merely by the notion of "self," consisting as it does of the states of affection, hatred, and delusion toward kinsmen, friends, and sons.
When cultivated as a kinsman, one becomes a kinsman; when cultivated as a stranger, one becomes a stranger.
This state of affairs is bound by mental cultivation, like the condition of poison or nectar.
For the all-pervading Self that exists as a single unity,
how can there be the false conceptualization that "this one is a kinsman" and "that one is a stranger"?
"O son, investigate for yourself with your own mind: 'Who am I?'—in relation to this body, which is a mere heap of blood, flesh, and bones, a skeleton of bone."
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither you nor even I;
it is only false cognition that prances about, thinking "this is merit" and "this is purifying."
Who is your father, who is your friend, who is your mother, or who is your enemy?
For you whose play is infinite within the void, tell me: what is yours and what is not yours?
If you were such [a person], then when those other many births had passed away,
why do you not grieve for those who were your kinsmen and those who were your riches?
They were many fortunate kinsmen who lived upon flower-laden plains and among the wild beasts; why do you not mourn for them?
Those swans, the kinsmen of Haṃsa, dwelt upon the lotus-filled banks of the rivers of the ocean; how is it that you do not grieve for them?
They became many kinsmen—trees with shimmering leaves amidst the variegated forest groves; how is it that you do not grieve for them?
They were many lions among kinsmen upon the great-peaked summits of mountains; why do you not grieve for them?
They became many kinsmen, fish, in rivers, lakes, and lotus ponds; do you not grieve for them as well?
In the Daśārṇas you became a brown forest monkey;
among the Tukhāras you were a prince, and in Puṇḍra you were a wild crow.
Among the Hehayas he was Mātaṅga; among the Trigartas, Gardabha; among the Śālvas, Saramāputra; and on the Śavara tree, Patatrī.
Having become a *pippala* tree on the Vindhya mountain, having become a wood-worm in a great banyan tree,
and having become a monkey on Mount Mandara, you were born as a brahmin in a mountain cave.
Having been a twice-born man among the Kosalas, having been a partridge among the Vaṅgas,
and having been born as a horse among the Tukhāras, you were born from a Brāhmaṇa in the forest.
He who was a biting insect within the heart of a palm tree, he who was [a worm] in an udumbara tree, and he who was a bird in the Vindhya forest— that very person is you, my younger son.
That very ant which was in the hollow of a hole in the bark of a birch tree in a cave of the Himalayas for six months— that is you, my younger brother.
O virtuous one, that scorpion which lived for a full year upon the cow dung in a wretched village on the border of Suhma— that very one is you, my younger brother.
He who once lay nestled upon the breasts of Pulinda women in the forest, like a bee among lotuses— that very person is you, my younger brother.
In these and many other various wombs of beings,
you were born previously in this Jambudvīpa hundreds of thousands of times.
Thus, with a subtle intellect purified by right vision, I perceive the sequence of your own past latent impressions.
Many diverse wombs of mine, slowed by delusion, have also passed away;
today I remember them with a vision arisen from knowledge.
Having been a parrot among the Trigartas, having been a swan on the riverbank,
and having been a crow in a hamlet, I have now been born here in this forest.
Having experienced the state of a Pulinda in the Vindhya mountains, having become a tree among the Vaṅgas,
and having passed through the state of a camel on a mountain, I have now been born here in this forest.
He who was a Cātaka bird on the Snowy Mountain, he who was a king in the region of Puṇḍra,
and he who was a tiger in the thickets of the Sahya mountains— he is indeed your elder brother here.
He who was a vulture for ten years, he who was a deer for five months,
and he who was a lion for a hundred years— he is indeed your elder brother here.
This is being told to you by me, the Cakora bird of the Andhra village, the steed of the Tukhāra king, and the son of the teacher of Śrīśaila.
O brother, I remember all my former births, with their various agitations, their diverse modes of conduct and actions, and their playful diversions.
This being the case, hundreds of fathers, mothers, brothers, and likewise friends have passed away for both of us throughout the births of the world.
Whom do we both lament together, and whom do we not lament at all?
Whom indeed do we grieve for among our kinsmen? Such is the very nature of the world's condition.
Infinite fathers pass away, and infinite mothers pass away,
for men wandering in this cycle of existence, like the leaves of a forest tree.
Therefore, my son, what measure can there be here for either suffering or happiness?
Consequently, having abandoned everything and attained a state of well-being, let us remain thus.
Having abandoned the mental cultivation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and the "I" that resides in the mind,
go to that state— may you be blessed— to which those skilled in the goal proceed.
In this world, the wise do not grieve over the state of constant flux, consisting of falling and rising; they simply apply themselves to the remedy.
Free from existence and non-existence, devoid of old age and death—remember your true self with an undistracted mind; do not let your mind become deluded.
For you there is no suffering, no birth, no mother, and no father;
you are the Self alone, O wise one, for you are indeed none other than that.
O virtuous one, in this journey of saṃsāra, it is only the ignorant who act as actors, presenting various performances and endowed with aesthetic flavors and emotional states.
Those with impartial vision are composed and see things as they are obtained;
but those who know that [reality] are merely observers, established in the duty of witnesses.
Even those who act are not truly agents, just as lamps at the onset of night;
such is the knowledge of that [reality] regarding the activities of illumination here in the world.
Just as mirrors, gems, and the like are not defiled by reflections— even those reflected within their own surfaces— so too are those of great intelligence unaffected by their effects.

In the center of the lotus of the heart, by means of this very great jewel— the self which is free from the stain of all the diseases of craving and endowed with a pure nature— cast aside all agitation within yourself, O son, and attain complete satisfaction.
The twenty-first canto, titled "The Attainment of Purifying Consciousness," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus awakened by that Puṇya, Pāvana then attained enlightenment and clarity, like the surface of the earth at dawn.
Then, both of them, having attained perfection and having reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, wandered at will through that forest, blameless in conduct.
Then, after some time, those two from Videha, having reached the state of nirvana, became free from attachment and attained tranquility like extinguished lamps.
In this way, for those who have previously experienced bodies, there are infinite hopes born of wealth and kin; O sinless one, what is to be grasped from them, or what is to be abandoned?
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, for these endless cravings, the only remedy is their abandonment; certainly not their preservation.
Thought increases through thinking, just as fire increases with fuel;
it perishes through non-thinking alone, like a flame without fuel.
Mounted upon the chariot of abandoning all objects of meditation, beholding with a gaze vast with compassion the world in its misery, do not remain; arise, O Rāghava!
This is the pure state of Brahman—free from desire and devoid of affliction;
having attained it, O mighty-armed one, even one who was deluded is no longer bewildered.
Taking solitude as your friend and a mature intellect as your companion, you will not be deluded even in times of distress while wandering in this manner.
When all resources have been blocked and kinsmen cast aside,
no one can rescue one from such a crisis except through one's own fortitude.
Then, through dispassion, by means of the scriptures, and also by qualities such as greatness,
one should with effort uplift one's own mind for the sake of warding off calamities.
Neither from sovereignty over the three worlds, nor from a treasury filled with jewels,
is that fruit obtained which is attained from a mind augmented by greatness.
In this belly of the world, men continue to fall through the oscillations of calamities and portents only so long as their minds have not become free from fever.
When the mind is full, the entire world is filled with the flow of nectar;
indeed, for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth itself is as if covered with leather.
The mind that follows the power of desirelessness attains fullness through hopelessness;
yet the mind that follows the power of hope reaches emptiness, like a lake in autumn.
The heart of those whose minds are helpless before their desires becomes empty, its core laid bare, like the ocean swallowed by Agastya.
In whose expansive mind-tree the restless monkey of craving does not leap, for him the great inner forest of the heart shines resplendent.
To those whose minds are free from craving, the three worlds are like the calyx of a lotus seed, a league's distance is like a cow’s footprint, and a great eon is but half a blink of an eye.
That coolness is not found in the moon, nor in the caves of the Himalayas, nor in rows of plantain trees or sandalwood; it resides only in minds free from desire.
Neither does the full moon shine thus, nor the full ocean of milk,
nor the lovely face of Lakṣmī, as this mind shines when it is free from longing.
Just as a streak of cloud defiles the moon, or as ink defiles a plaster of nectar,
so does this demoness of hope corrupt a man from within.
The branches of the tree of the mind, known as hopes, cover the horizons;
when these are severed, the great tree of the mind attains formlessness.
When the mind, having become a trunk with its great branches of craving severed,
comes to rest, fortitude— though previously of a single form— attains a hundredfold branching.
O Rāma, when the mind has reached its dissolution through that unsurpassed fortitude, that state is attained wherein no destruction exists.
O Rāghava, if you do not allow these mental fluctuations— the various hopes— to take root within your noble disposition, then you truly exist.
When your mind, devoid of fluctuations, has reached the state of non-mind,
then you attain that pervasive internal existence which consists of liberation.
O Rāghava, when the mind is agitated within by craving— which is like the wing of a peacock— it brings about an abundance of inauspicious things.
It is said that "subsistence" (vartana) means "conduct" (vṛtti); the mind subsists through its underlying disposition (āśaya).
Therefore, having abandoned the disposition that is the movement of the mind, proceed to the state of mindlessness (niścittatā).
Whatever mode of existence one lives by, that very mode perishes without it;
therefore, for the sake of the mind's tranquility, one should bring that mode of activity to its cessation.
O Great-Souled One, having cast off the bonds of worldly existence, become one whose mind is liberated, with all desires completely stilled.
When the ropes of the fetters of the mind—those wretched hopes—have fallen away, who is not liberated?
The twenty-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Application of the Treatment for Thirst," by Vasiṣṭha.
Or else, O full moon of the sky known as the lineage of Raghu,
may you attain stainless knowledge through the differentiation of the intellect, like a firebrand.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, through your grace, everything that was to be attained has been attained by me within my heart; I have found rest in the stainless state.
O All-pervading Lord Kṛṣṇa, like a vast cloud from the sky in autumn, the entire great darkness of delusion, which was black, has departed from my mind.
Filled with nectar, clear, cool-souled, and of great luster,
I abide within, full of bliss, like the full moon at evening.
O autumn season for the clouds of all my doubts,
yet I do not reach satiety with these words as you speak.
Furthermore, O All-pervading Lord, tell me how to attain the wisdom of the Vedas for the further increase of my own understanding; for the virtuous do not grow weary of one who is humble.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāghava, I shall tell you the supreme account of Bāli;
by hearing it, you will attain eternal awakening.
Within this treasury of the world, at some distant edge of the quarters,
there exists a realm situated beneath the earth, renowned as Pātāla.
In some places, its interior is filled without gaps by the daughters of the Dānavas, who are smeared with the nectar-water produced from the Ocean of Milk; thus it shines.
In some places it was filled with serpents possessing hundreds of heads, whose tongues were fierce and darting, and who bore the weight of poison as their weapons.
In some places it was filled with the sons of Danu, who, devouring the entire universe as they sportively turned it over, were like moving Mount Merus.

In some places, it was resorted to by the elephants of the quarters, whose mountain-like tusks rested upon the peaks of its ramparts and walls, while their massive bodies supported the circle of the earth.
In some places, the quarters of space were filled with foul odors as the circles of hell resounded with a succession of spirits being consumed by the great *kaṭakaṭa* crackling sound.
Reaching down to the surface of the earth and extending through the seven desired circles of the netherworlds (pātāla),
it was in some places filled with oceans of jewels, as if by other netherworlds themselves.
In some places, it was sanctified by that Blessed One Kapila, whose lotus feet rest upon the heads of both gods and asuras.
In one place, he was protected by that Lord Hāṭakeśa, who desires the play of worshiping with infinite offerings gathered by the Asurīs.
While that great burden was being sustained by the pillar of the Asura’s arm,
there arose a Dānava king named Bali, the son of Virocana.
He whose massaging of the feet was desired by the king of the gods, together with all the gods, vidyādharas, and nāgas, as he sat upon his own throne.
He is the treasury of the jewels of the three worlds, the protector of all embodied beings, and the upholder of the laws of the universe— to him Hari has bowed down.
At the mere mention of Airāvaṇa’s name, the temples [of the elephants] became parched, and like the cries of a peacock, the veins in the hearts of serpents underwent a state of distress.
By the fierce heat of his majesty, the seven oceans— as if at the time of universal dissolution— reached a state of boiling, on the verge of drying up, as he assumed a wrathful form.
The rows of clouds formed from the smoke of the clarified butter of his sacrifices,
enveloping the mountains, have always served as armor for this hollow of the cosmic egg.
By the forceful fall of whose gaze all the quarters of space, including the Kulaparvata mountains, bow down like creepers bent by fruit.
Having effortlessly conquered the entire expanse of the world and adorned it,
that Daitya ruled the kingdom for ten crores of years.
Then, as many ages passed away in their cyclical revolutions,
and as the great floods of gods and demons rose up and fell back again;
Even as he continuously enjoyed the pleasures existing within the belly of the three worlds,
Baḍi, the leader of the Dānavas, felt a sense of revulsion.
Once, standing at a window smeared with the tips of Meru’s peaks,
he himself reflected upon the nature of worldly existence.
To what end should this empire now be ruled by me, whose power remains unimpaired, and through whom I am to sport within the three worlds?
Of what use is this great kingdom of mine, which causes wonder throughout the three worlds, or even its enjoyment, which is burdened by an abundance of pleasures?
What indeed can this mere enjoyment and consumption of objects bring me as happiness— sweet only at the first moment, yet inevitably leading to exhaustion?
Again there is the passing of a single day, again the persistence of the night, and again those very same activities; this leads only to shame, not to contentment.
The beloved is embraced again and indeed enjoyed once more;
this is like the play of children, which brings great shame here to the wise.
Why is it that a wise person does not feel shame when, day after day, they repeatedly engage in that very same stream of activity which is as tasteless as stale food?
Again a day, again a night, again a succession of tasks;
again and again, I consider this to be the mockery of even a wise man.
Having again encountered the state of being wavy, one returns once more to the state of being waveless;
just as water does, so too does this person undergo various activities.
This repeated action, appearing like the behavior of a madman,
repeatedly causes even the wise person to laugh, as it is constantly comparable to the play of a child.
Even if this ritual action were performed constantly until its task was completed,
what purpose would there be such that one would no longer undergo further rebirth?
Furthermore, for how long must this great ostentation be practiced by us here, and until what point is it to be attained?
This endless play of children is in reality devoid of substance;
it is performed in vain through repetition by those who seek the production of misfortune.
I do not perceive here any single fruit that is truly magnificent; there is only another task to be performed upon reaching which nothing at all remains.
"Without enjoyment, what could be both extremely delightful and imperishable?
I shall reflect upon this immediately. Having thought thus, that Baḍi meditated.
Then the king of the Asuras, reflecting upon the matter within his own mind with a frown, said in an instant, "It is remembered."
Long ago, it is said, the Blessed One Virocana was questioned here by me,
his father— he who knew the reality of the self and had perceived the higher and lower worlds.
O Mahāmati, where all delusions regarding both all sufferings and all pleasures are stilled—what is that called the ultimate limit? MU_5,22.44
Where has the delusion of the mind been stilled? Where have all desires passed away? O Father, where is that long rest, free from cessation?
Having obtained what here among all things already acquired does a person become satisfied?
Having seen what, O Father, does one’s vision no longer suffice to further benefit [the soul]?
For even these extremely abundant enjoyments do not bring happiness;
they agitate the mind and cause even the virtuous to fall into delusion.
Therefore, dear father, tell me something of that very nature— beautiful with expansive bliss— abiding in which I may attain long-lasting rest.

Having heard this in the past, spoken by my father—who had been carried off to heaven—beneath a *sāgara* tree planted in his courtyard, which served as a veil for his blossoming flowers that vied with the rays of the moon, words equal to a potent elixir of vast form for the pacification of my delusion: *ity ākarṇya purā niśākarakaraspardhāparārdhyollasatpuṣpāpūrakṛtāvaguṇṭhanapaṭasyoktaṃ tale tena me / pitrā svargahṛtasya sāgarataros saṃropitasyājire sphārākārarasāyanāsavasamaṃ mohopaśāntyai vacaḥ //* 5.22.49 "Having heard this in the past, spoken by my father—who had been carried off to heaven—beneath a *sāgara* tree planted in his courtyard, which served as a veil for his blossoming flowers that vied with the rays of the moon, words equal to a potent elixir of vast form for the pacification of my delusion."
The twenty-third canto, titled "The Words of Virocana," Canto Twenty-three:
Virocana.
O sons, there exists an exceedingly vast region with a wide hollow,
wherein even many thousands of triple-world systems find room.
Where there are neither clouds nor oceans, nor mountains;
neither forests nor sacred fords, nor rivers nor lakes.
Neither the earth nor space, neither the sky nor the winds and so forth;
neither the moon and sun, nor the lords of the world, nor the gods, nor the dānavas.
Neither spirits, yakṣas, nor rākṣasas; neither shrubs nor the splendors of the forest;
neither things consisting of wood or grass, nor anything stationary or moving.
Neither water, nor fire, nor space; neither above, nor below, nor the earth;
neither light, nor darkness, nor the "I," nor Indra, Hara, and the rest.
There is only one great king there, possessed of immense splendor;
he is the doer of all, the all-pervading, the all, and he remains established in silence.
The minister, directed by him, intent upon all counsel,
quickly brings about what was impossible and thoroughly dismantles what was already established.
He is unable to enjoy anything and knows nothing at all;
yet, though he is ignorant, he always performs everything solely for the sake of the king.
He alone was the sole performer of all the king's duties;
the monarch himself remained entirely at ease in private.
O Lord, what is that land of great splendor, free from mental and physical afflictions? How is it reached, and by whom has it been attained?
Who is that such-like minister or even that king of great power,
by whom we have not been conquered, even though he treats the nets of the world as if they were mere playthings?
This narrative is unprecedented and strikes fear into the hearts of the immortals;
dispel for us the cloud of doubt from the sky of our hearts by recounting it.
There, that Blessed One, the Mantra-holder, cannot be overcome in the slightest even by the hosts of gods and asuras gathered together, even if they were multiplied a hundred thousand times.
He is neither the thousand-eyed Indra, nor Yama, nor the Lord of Wealth;
he is neither a god nor even an asura, if my son is defeated.
There, weapons such as swords, clubs, javelins, vajras, discuses,
and maces become blunted, like the striking of a lotus against a stone.
He is not within the reach of missiles or weapons, nor of the fierce deeds of warriors;
by him all the gods and asuras have been brought under control at all times.
Even without Viṣṇu, by that very [wind], the asuras such as Hiraṇyākṣa were cast down,
like the wish-fulfilling trees of Mount Meru by the wind at the end of an eon.
Even the gods, beginning with Nārāyaṇa, though they were all-knowing,
were overcome by him and cast into pits according to his will.
By his grace, Smara, possessing five arrows,
strides with pride through these three worlds, having conquered them like a sovereign emperor.
Though censured by the hosts of gods and asuras, though devoid of virtue, foolish,
and even ill-formed, it is through his grace that Wrath flourishes.
The repeated conflict between the hosts of gods and asuras is but the sport of that counselor who possesses the power of mantras.
O son, if that minister is conquered by that lord alone, then he is easily subdued; otherwise, however, he is as immovable as a mountain.
When that very lord develops the desire to conquer his own minister at the proper time, he is conquered by him without effort.
If you have the power to conquer the wrestler who churns the three worlds and who has caused the three realms to tremble, then you are truly a man of valor.
When that sun has risen, these lotus-pools of the three worlds come into bloom;
when it has set, they dissolve away.
If you are able, O steadfast one, to conquer that single [mind] with a singular intellect free from delusion, then you are truly one of noble vows.
When that is conquered, the worlds are conquered even if they were previously unconquered;
but if it remains unconquered, these remain unconquered even after being held for a long time.
Therefore, for the sake of infinite accomplishment and for eternal happiness,
apply yourself to the conquest of that [mind], even through arduous exertion.

Indeed, by that exceedingly powerful one, even the three worlds— including the Asuras, Nāgas, Yakṣas, humans, Mahoragas, and Kinnaras, together with their fathers-in-law— were brought under control on all sides as if in mere play.
The twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Verses of Virocana," in the account of Bāli. Bāli.
"By what means, dear father, is that powerful one completely overcome?
Who is he? O you of great heroism, tell me everything quickly."
Virocana said:
"O son, listen as I speak of the ease with which even that minister of firm and ever-conquering resolve can be overcome."
O son, when this [mind] is grasped through skillful means, it comes under control in an instant;
without skillful means, it burns like a fierce, venomous serpent.
Those who, having fondled him like a child, restrain the king through skillful means,
attain their goal upon beholding that monarch.
When that protector of the earth is seen, that minister comes under your control;
and when that minister is overcome, that king is seen once again.
As long as that king is not seen, the minister is not conquered;
and as long as the minister is not defeated, the king is not seen.
When the king is not seen, that evil counselor leaps about excessively for his own suffering;
when the counselor is not subdued, the king goes to utter invisibility.
Therefore, through practice, one should bring about both results equally:
the audience with the king and the defeat of his minister.
Gradually accomplishing these two through human effort and one's own practice, he attains this auspicious state.
O Lord of Daityas, if you do not grieve even slightly once that practice has borne fruit and you have reached that state, then you shall attain it.
There dwell the virtuous, whose every exertion has been stilled, whose intentions are eternally joyful, and whose doubts have all been completely pacified.
Listen, my son; I shall reveal everything to you. That which I have described to you by the name of a "country" is liberation, the destroyer of all suffering.
But there, O Mahāmati, the Blessed One— the Self who transcends all states— made the wise one named Manas his minister.
The mind, through its universal nature, has undergone this universal transformation,
just as a lump of clay becomes a pot, or as smoke becomes a cloud.
When that is conquered, everything is conquered and everything is attained;
one should know that it is difficult to conquer, yet it is thoroughly mastered through skillful means alone.
Bāḍi said:
