"O Blessed One, tell me clearly that method for the conquest of his mind, O Father, by which I shall conquer this terrible one."
Virocana said:
"O son, that supreme lack of reliance toward all sense objects in every respect is indeed the method for the conquest of the mind."
This alone is the supreme method; by this very means, the great rutting elephant of one's own mind is instantly brought under control.
For this, O Mahāmati, is extremely difficult to attain and yet easily attained;
for it is difficult to attain if not practiced, but it is attained with ease when well-practiced.
O son, this detachment from sense objects, when practiced gradually,
attains full manifestation in every respect, just like a creeper watered by irrigation.
For even one of deceitful nature who desires it cannot attain that which has not been practiced, just as rice that has not been sown, my son; therefore, one should cultivate it.
So long do these embodied beings wander through sufferings, dwelling in the wilderness of saṃsāra, until they attain detachment from sense objects.
Without practice, no embodied being can attain detachment from sense objects,
even one who has reached the very end [of life], just as one cannot reach another country without travel.
Therefore, by one who bears a body and constantly meditates on the abandonment of objects of thought,
a lack of interest in enjoyments should be brought to growth through practice, just like a creeper.
O son, without human effort, nothing auspicious is attained here;
indeed, the fruit of all undertakings is obtained through human exertion alone.
Just as when the fruit of an action has been attained, people in the world speak of "fate" (daiva) due to joy, resentment, and so forth; yet fate never exists anywhere as a physical body.
That which is called "inevitable destiny" or "necessity" is expressed by the word *daiva* (fate) by humans alone, and not by others.
That which is always present here, wherever it has reached fruition,
and which serves to destroy both joy and resentment— that is called destiny (daiva).
Fate, which takes the form of destiny, is overcome by human effort,
just as the delusion of a mirage is dispelled by the play of correct knowledge.
Whatever is conceived through human effort, that very thing comes to pass; just as the sky, when perceived as having a surface, bestows the pleasure of that surface-experience.
Therefore, the mind alone is the agent here; whatever it conceives, that becomes so.
Whatever kind of destiny it resolves upon, that becomes exactly so.
The mind makes certain phenomena determinate, others indeterminate, and some even non-determinate;
therefore, this mind is that which joins [beings] to their destinies.
Establishing a fixed destiny that is sometimes true to its name,
the individual soul vibrates within this sheath of the world like the wind in the sky.
Sometimes the mind, making destiny devoid of necessity, flashes forth like the wind, using the word "destiny" (niyati) in the sense of the conventional term "necessity."
Therefore, as long as the mind exists, there is neither destiny nor necessity;
O virtuous one, once the mind has set, let whatever happens be so.
For the living being is born as a person; whatever he intends in this world according to his human effort, that it becomes for him exactly so, and not otherwise.
"O son, nothing exists here apart from human effort;
relying on supreme manly exertion, one should cultivate detachment toward worldly enjoyments."
As long as there is no weariness with enjoyments, which bestows victory over this world,
so long is that supreme bliss, which destroys cyclic existence, not attained.
As long as attachment to sense objects, which causes delusion, persists,
so long does the swinging of the hammock of the states of existence continue.
O son, without practice, this wretched hope— arisen from the weight of enjoying worldly pleasures— never ceases to cause suffering.
Bali said:
O Lord of all Asuras, how does this internal lack of attachment toward enjoyments come to abide within the living being, bestowing upon it long life?
Virocana:
For one who beholds the Self, the fruit clearly bears further fruit:
the soul's aversion to worldly enjoyments, like a great creeper in autumn.
Through the contemplation of the Self, this detachment from sense objects takes its place in the supreme heart, like the goddess Śrī within the hollow of a lotus.
Therefore, with the most exquisite investigation using the whetstone of wisdom,
one should view the deity and simultaneously strip away both enjoyment and passion.
One who has not yet attained proficiency in the noble method should fill two parts of the mind with enjoyments, one part with the study of the scriptures, and one part with service to the guru.
One who possesses some degree of proficiency should fill one part with enjoyments,
one part with service to the guru, and one part with reflection on the meaning of the scriptures.
For one who pursues thorough understanding, he should daily fill his mind such that two parts are devoted to the scriptures and dispassion, and two parts to meditation and the worship of the Guru.
When the living soul has attained goodness, it becomes fit for the sequence of discourse on knowledge;
with its form purified, it receives the supreme dye, just as a cloth does.
One should protect the child-like mind by means of gentle nurturing, through skillful methods and purifying words, and by the gradual internalization of the meaning of the scriptures.
When others have reached maturity in knowledge and their stubborn grasping has become relaxed,
their mind shines coolly, like crystal pierced by moonlight.
Then, with supreme and straightforward wisdom, one should immediately observe the form of the body as being exactly the same as that of enjoyments and the lord of wealth.
O son, by means of the power of wisdom and investigation, one should always maintain an equal balance,
bringing about both the observation of the self and the relinquishing of craving.
When the other is seen, there is freedom from thirst; and when thirst is destroyed, there is the supreme vision.
These two visions support each other, like a boat and its helmsman.
When the multitude of enjoyments has lost its relish and the supreme and non-supreme deity has been seen,
an eternal and infinite repose arises in the Supreme Brahman.
For those living beings, infinite bliss arises after long-standing fruition; it never occurs except through resting in the Self.
Neither by austerities, nor by charity, nor even by visiting sacred fords,
does a living being attain detachment from enjoyments, except through the contemplation of the true nature of reality.
By no means of reasoning whatsoever does the intellect proceed toward the vision of the Self for the sake of a person's welfare, except through the person's own effort.
O son, apart from the attainment of the ultimate truth through the renunciation of enjoyments,
the supreme bliss of resting in the state of Brahman is not reached.
O virtuous one, nowhere in this world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass,
is there any such consolation as that which is found in the Supreme Cause.
Relying on human effort and casting destiny far behind,
the wise man should despise enjoyments, which are the firm bolts barring the path to the highest good.
When the censure of worldly enjoyment has matured, discernment arises,
just as the glorious and stainless autumn season appears when the rainy season has grown old.
Discernment arises from the censure of enjoyments, and the censure of enjoyments arises from discernment;
these two fulfill one another like the ocean and the rain-cloud.
Censure of enjoyments, discernment, and the eternal light of one's own self mutually accomplish their purpose, just like very affectionate friends.
Having previously disregarded destiny and attained human effort through exertion,
one should press the teeth against the teeth and cultivate a lack of delight in worldly enjoyments.
In the beginning, one should acquire wealth through manly effort that is not contrary to local customs and which is beneficial to one's kinsmen.
One should win over noble and virtuous people with wealth;
through association with them, one's attachment to enjoyments comes to an end.
Then comes investigation, followed by the compendium of the meaning of the scriptures of knowledge;
from that, the attainment of the supreme state arises in due order.
O Lord of Asuras, when in due time you cease from the objects of the senses,
then, through the power of discernment, you shall attain the supreme state.
You will rightly attain rest within the self, which is utterly pure;
you shall not again cast yourself into the mire of mental constructs to suffer.
O dear one, acquire wealth through gradual means and with little reproach, and thereby win over virtuous people with honor;
for by disregarding the objects of the senses arising from that association, through the power of right reflection, you shall attain the realization of the Self.
The twenty-fifth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Healing the Mind," is concluded.
This was previously told to me by my father, who possesses beautiful discernment;
now, by good fortune, it has been remembered, and I have attained full awakening.
Today, this clear distaste for enjoyments has truly arisen within me;
by good fortune, I enter the pure bliss of tranquility, cool as nectar.
Filling the quarters once more, gathering wealth again,
and winning over beloved women once more— I am weary of this state of worldly prosperity.
Ah, how truly delightful is this ground of tranquility, so cool within!
For all perceptions of pleasure and pain come to rest in tranquility.
I am stilled, I am completely extinguished; established in tranquility, I dwell in happiness.
In this state I rejoice, like the reflection of the moon set within [a vessel].
Alas, the acquisition of wealth is suffering: its vast physical form is nourished by the impetuous force of frantic dancing, and it is characterized by incessant agitation.
That I was formerly delighted by pressing limb against limb and flesh against the flesh of a woman— that was merely the manifestation of delusion.
Examples have been seen, and what was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed unimpaired;
the entire multitude of living beings has been traversed—what, indeed, could be more auspicious than this?
Again, those very same things, here and there, elsewhere and in this place,
moving from here and there— there is nothing at all that is called "new."
Having mentally renounced and cast aside everything by myself,
I remain purely within my own self, full like the ocean.
In the netherworld, on the earth, and in heaven, there are women, jewels, precious stones, and the like;
yet even that essence is swiftly swallowed up by worthless time.
For so long a time in the past, I was utterly childish,
harboring hatred toward the immortals for the sake of this trivial worldly desire.
What noble purpose could there be for the Great-Souled One in merely creating through his mind that which is called the world— whether it be abandoned or taken up?
Alas! For a very long time, like a child intoxicated by the pride of ignorance, I have pursued what is harmful with the thought that it was beneficial, just as a dog [pursues a bone].
What indeed have I, ignorant as I am and driven by ever-increasing thirst, not done in these three worlds to increase my future remorse?
Therefore, let me have done with this trivial former reflection;
human effort achieves its fruit through treatment directed toward the present.
Today, through the oneness of my own self with the cause that possesses infinite forms,
I attain happiness from every side, as if entering the ocean for the sake of an elixir.
"Who indeed is this 'I,' and what might the self be?"—this is my contemplation upon the self.
O Lord, I ask Uśanas for the sake of surely pacifying ignorance.

I contemplate the Supreme Lord, who swiftly bestows pure grace; then, instructed by His word, I abide by myself within my own self in that state of infinite splendor, for the words of instruction bear fruit as an inexhaustible goal.
The twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Instruction on Yoga According to the Siddhānta of Baḍi’s Mind," within the narrative of Baḍi; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, with eyes half-closed like a *baḍi* flower,
meditated upon Śukra, whose eyes were like lotus petals and whose abode was the sky.
Then Bhārgava, whose meditation was infinite and eternal upon the all-pervading Consciousness,
recognized his disciple Baḍi as being conscious in the city and seeking the Guru.
Then the lord Bhārgava, whose self is all-pervading and infinite consciousness,
brought his own body into the jeweled window of Baḍi’s palace.
His body touched by the mass of light radiating from his guru’s form, Bāḍi awoke at dawn like a lotus awakened by the rays of the sun.
There, he honored that descendant of Bhṛgu by offering precious gems as a gift, by scattering heaps of mandāraka flowers, and by prostrating at his feet.
Then Baḍi spoke to his preceptor, whose limbs were strewn with precious gems, who wore a crown of mandāra flowers, and who was resting upon a costly throne.
Bāḍi: O Blessed One, this intuition arising from your grace impels me to speak before you, just as the rays of the sun urge one to perform their task.
I am dispassionate toward enjoyments, which bestow great delusion;
I desire to know that reality which removes great delusion.
"What is here? How much is there? Or what is it made of?
Who am I? Who are you? And what are these worlds? Tell me this quickly."
Śukra said: What is the use of speaking much here? I am striving to go to the sky;
O Indra among the lords of the Dānavas, hear the essence of everything in brief.
For here, there is only consciousness; this is indeed composed of consciousness alone.
You are consciousness, I am consciousness, and these worlds are consciousness—this is the summary.
Taking hold of this firm resolve, look with an illumined intellect;
by yourself, through the self, you shall attain the infinite state.
If you are capable, then by this [teaching] you will certainly attain everything;
if not, then even though much has been spoken to you, it is as if an oblation were poured onto ashes.
The cognition of that which is not to be cognized is bondage; its liberation is called liberation.
"Consciousness is the non-object of cognition, for it is the Self"—this is the summary of all established doctrines.
Adopting this certainty, look with an illumined intellect;
you shall yourself, by means of the self, attain the infinite state.
"I am going into the sky here, where these seven sages have gathered; I must remain there in the air for some mission of the gods."
O King, as long as this body exists, even for those whose minds are liberated,
the renunciation of objects as they happen to be encountered does not occur by their very nature.

When Bhārgava had thus spoken, he then leaped with great speed along the path of the clearly visible ocean of stars into the midst of the sky, which was variegated with bees [or dark clouds] and agitated by the multitude of planets like restless waves.
The twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Body," by Vasiṣṭha.
When that son of Bhṛgu, who is honored in the assemblies of both gods and asuras, had departed, Bāli, the best among the powerful, reflected in his mind: MU_5,27.1//
It was rightly said by the Blessed One: "This triple world is indeed consciousness alone;
I am consciousness, these worlds are consciousness, the quarters are consciousness, and this action is consciousness."
In ultimate reality, everything—both external and internal—is consciousness alone;
apart from consciousness, there is nothing whatsoever here or anywhere else.
If this sun is not perceived as "this is the sun" due to lack of awareness, then what distinction between the sun and darkness could possibly be apprehended here?
"This is earth"—if this earth is not perceived as such, what indeed would be the "earth-ness" of the earth? That [nature] would have become something that has ceased to exist.

If these directions are not perceived as "this is the direction" or "that is the direction," then what indeed constitutes the directional nature of the directions, or the mountain-nature of the mountains?
If this world is not perceived as a world by consciousness,
then what constitutes the "world-ness" of the world, and what constitutes the "sky-ness" of the sky?
If this body, which has the form of a mountain, is not cremated upon a funeral pyre,
then what indeed is the "bodiness" of the bodies of embodied beings?
Consciousness is the senses, consciousness is the body, consciousness is the mind, and consciousness is that seeking;
consciousness is within, consciousness is without, consciousness is space, consciousness is existence, and consciousness is the persistence of becoming.
I am indeed consciousness alone, the one who performs everything preceded by the desire for touch;
yet through the body, I do not experience even the slightest contact with objects.
What is the use of this body of mine, which is equal to wood or a clod of earth?
I am consciousness itself, the singular Self of the entire world, whose nature is pure awareness.
I am indeed consciousness in the sun within the sky; I am indeed consciousness in the cage of the elements;
I am consciousness among gods and demons, and in all things both stationary and moving.
Indeed, there is only consciousness here; for no second conceptualization exists.
Since duality is impossible in the world, who is an enemy and who is a friend?
When the radiant head of the body named Baḍi was severed,
what part of the consciousness would have been severed, given that it pervades all the worlds?
Hatred that is accumulated and conceptualized becomes hatred, and not otherwise;
therefore, all states such as hatred, whether existent or non-existent, have consciousness as their essence.
Even when thoroughly investigated, nothing whatsoever other than consciousness is found apart from this vast interior of the three worlds.
There is no hatred, there is no passion, nor does he possess a mind or its fluctuations;
for pure consciousness, which is utterly stainless, how could there be any conceptual construction?
I am indeed consciousness, all-pervading and omnipresent, consisting of eternal bliss;
I transcend the fabrication of conceptual thought and am devoid of even a fragment of conceptualization.
That which is called "consciousness" (cit) is not a name for that which is nameless;
this all-pervading power of consciousness, whose essence is sound, vibrates everywhere.
Freed from the seen and the seeing, possessing a purely stainless form,
eternally risen and free from appearance, I am the Seer, the Supreme Lord.
I am neither the doer nor the enjoyer; I am the stainless witness alone, consisting of the beautiful digits of time whose forms are devoid of conceptual construction.
Arising as mere appearance, eternally devoid of that which is manifested, I am of the singular nature of pure light; by my own true nature, I triumph.
Salutations to me, who am my own true nature— the Great Soul, free from the stain of the objectified world, liberated, and whose form is inward consciousness.

Salutations again and again to me alone, who am consciousness, who am liberated from the object of consciousness, who am joined with the appropriate method, and whose form is the manifestation of all things.

I am that pervasive pure consciousness alone— free from the object of thought, the very form of consciousness, filling the entirety of the universe in every direction, and with all objects of perception completely stilled.
I am infinite like space, yet more subtle than the atom and all-pervading;
these various states of pleasure and pain do not reach me.
That pervasive consciousness is itself unperceivable and beyond the reach of thought;
neither the existence nor the non-existence of things within the world is capable of defining me.
Or rather, let these states of the world define me as they please, for they are indeed not distinct from me.
If an entity is measured by another entity that is its very own nature,
then when it is taken away or given, what loss indeed has occurred for whom?
At all times, I am indeed everything; I am the doer of all and associated with all.
This which is to be perceived is only myself; not even the slightest thing has been produced.
What is the use of volitions and mental constructs? I am the single radiance of both consciousness and the unconscious.
Why then do I agitate myself? I shall instead find peace within the purifying Self.
While reflecting thus, the highly wise Baḍi remained established in meditation, contemplating the meaning of the half-and-half-mātrā of the letter *a*.
With all volitional constructs completely stilled and the multitude of mental fluctuations pacified,
he remains free from doubt, with the thoughts of the thinker and the objects of thought cast far away.
Devoid of the meditator, the object of meditation, and the act of meditating, with his mind extinguished and his latent impressions stilled,
Baḍi became like a lamp in a windless place, having attained the Great State.
With his mind tranquil, Baḍi dwelt for a long time in that jeweled window, as if carved out of stone.
With his desires stilled, his accumulation of thought-faults abandoned, and his being perfected by stainless purity, Bāḍi shone like the autumn sky, which is free from clouds due to its clarity.
The twenty-eighth canto, titled "Resting from the World," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then those Dānavas, the followers of Baḍi,
instantly ascended that high crystal palace.
The mantrins such as Ḍimba and others are the heroes; the vassals such as Kukuha and others; the kings such as Sura and others; and those who seize strength, such as Vṛtra and others.
Hayagrīva and others were his courtiers; Śukunda and others were his kinsmen;
Luḍaṅga and others were his friends; and Palmūla and others were his attendants.
The gods, beginning with Kubera, Yama, and Śakra, brought offerings;
the yakṣas, vidyādharas, and nāgas waited, longing for the opportunity to serve him.
And Rambhā, Tilottamā, and other excellent women who wield yak-tail whisks;
likewise the rivers, oceans, mountains, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions.
Then, for the sake of serving him, many other perfected ones (siddhas) dwelling within the belly of the three worlds came to that region of Baḍi.
The rows of crowns bowed down as they beheld Bāli with reverence, standing motionless in meditative silence and absorption, like a figure depicted in a painting.
Seeing him, those great asuras, having accomplished what was to be done, bowed down;
they became faltering with despondency, wonder, joy, and fear.
Then the ministers, the Dānavas, having deliberated on what was to be done,
thought of Bhārgava, their preceptor and the best among all who know.
Immediately after this thought, the Daityas beheld the radiant Bhārgava before them,
appearing like a conjured city of the Gandharvas that had suddenly come into existence.
Being honored by the hosts of asuras and seated upon a venerable throne,
Bhārgava beheld the lord of the Dānavas, who was established in the silence of meditation.
Having rested for a moment as it were, he looked with affection upon Badi,
whose delusion regarding worldly existence had been exhausted, while contemplating him with his gaze.
As if casting the assembly into the Ocean of Milk with hundreds of rays from his body and the brilliance of his teeth, the Guru smiled and spoke these words.
Śukra said:
"O Daityas, how wonderful this is! By his own discernment alone, this venerable Baḍi has attained pure vision and become perfected."
O best of Dānavas, let him, remaining right here in this very state,
attain stability within his own self and behold the state that is free from affliction.
Exhausted, having attained rest, with the wandering burden of thoughts diminished and the mist of saṃsāra stilled— he is not to be awakened, O Dānavas.
Upon the destruction of ignorance, he has attained his own very light,
just as the sun’s mass of rays does when the agitation caused by clouds has subsided during the day.
For in due time, this [intellect] will awaken by itself,
through its own self-awareness, like a sprout emerging from its seed-capsule after being dormant.
"Perform your respective duties, all you leaders of the Dānavas;
Bāṇa will emerge from his meditative absorption after a thousand years."
When this was said by the Guru, the Daityas abandoned the anxiety born of fear, joy, and despair, just as trees cast off their withered blossoms.
Having assumed the form of Vairocana’s radiance according to the previously established arrangement,
all the asuras then remained intent upon their respective duties.

Men went to the earth; the lords of serpents to the subterranean realm; the planets to the sky; the hosts of gods to the celestial abode; the quarters, the mountains, and the lords of waters to the caves; and those who roam the forests and those who roam the heavens departed for the firmament.
The twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Fish-Hook Samādhi," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, after a thousand divine years, the blessed Baḍi, the best of asuras,
was awakened by the sounds of celestial drums.
When Baḍa had awakened, that city then shone intensely,
like a bed of lotuses when the mass of sunbeams has risen from Brahmā.
He was indeed already awakened; until the Dānavas arrived, he reflected for a moment in his meditation chamber.
"Oh, how delightful is this ultimate path, so cool!
Having stood upon it for but a moment, I have attained supreme rest."
Therefore, following this very path, I shall dwell here;
what need have I for external luxuries enjoyed by you?
Even from the lunar orbs, the waves of bliss do not so satisfy me within as do these stages of the manifestation of pure consciousness.
Thus, as his mind again became slackened in its effort to find rest,
the Daityas obstructed its progress, just as clouds block the moon.
Beholding them, his eyes agitated by the desire to bow before them, he reflected once more;
his body was then surrounded by those [beings] who resembled great mountain ranges.

For me, whose mind is gathered and whose conceptual constructions have been exhausted, what is there to be grasped? Let that mind, because it has fallen away [from its objects], go sufficiently to the state of being mere flavor (rasatā).
"I desire liberation; why am I bound? By whom was I bound in the past?
Being unbound, I desire liberation—what kind of childish mockery is this?"
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; my ignorance has come to an end. What use have I for the play of meditation, or what would come to me through meditation?
I desire neither meditative absorption nor lack of absorption, neither enjoyments nor the state of non-enjoyment; free from all feverish distress, I remain in equanimity.
I have no desire for the supreme reality, nor do I have any desire for the maintenance of the world;
I have no need for the vision of meditation, nor have I any need for worldly power.
I am neither dead nor do I live; I am neither existent nor non-existent, but equal.
This is not mine, nor is it not mine, nor is there anything other than me; salutations to me, for I am indeed the Self.
"Let this kingdom of the world remain; I shall stay here established in my own nature.
Or rather, let there be no kingdom of the world at all; I shall remain coolly within the Self."
What need have I for the vision of meditative absorption, or for the splendor of royal power and wealth?
Let that which comes come; I desire nothing, nor do I belong to anything anywhere.
"If indeed there is nothing at all to be done by me now,
then why do I not perform here some action that is appropriate to my nature?"
Having thus resolved, Bāṇa, the perfect soul and best among the powerful,
gazed upon the Daityas as the sun gazes upon lotuses.
By the power of his glance, he received the prostrations of all the sons of Danu, just as the wind gathers the fragrances of flowers.
Then Vairocana,
there, with a mind consisting of the relinquishment of objects of meditation, performed all the duties of the king.
He honored the gods, the twice-born, and his gurus with worship,
and he paid due respect to his friends, kinsmen, vassals, and virtuous men.
He satisfied his servants and groups of supplicants with wealth, and he cherished the women by bestowing upon them various riches.
Thus he dwelt in that kingdom under complete dominion;
then, at one time, his mind became inclined toward sacrifice.
Having gratified the entire world and being honored by the hosts of gods and sages,
he performed a great sacrifice together with Śukra and other eminent figures.
Having determined that Baḍi was not seeking the burden of enjoyments, Mādhava,
the bestower of success, went to his sacrifice for the sake of fulfilling Baḍi’s desired goal.
Knowing what must be done, he gave this forest tract of the world to Śakra, who was the eldest by age and worthy of it, yet solely miserly for the sake of enjoyments.
There, having deceived Bāli by the mere pretext of a step, Hari bound the monkey at the bottom of the netherworld (pātāla), as if he were a house situated within the earth.
Today, O Rāma, he has been established once more for the sake of the state of Indra;
possessing the body of one liberated while living, he remains composed, his intellect eternally seated in meditation.
Remaining in the cavernous depths of the netherworld, the fish whose mind is liberated while living views both calamity and prosperity with an equal eye.
That wisdom neither sets nor rises amidst pleasure and pain;
it is even and of a most stable form, like a row of variegated suns.
Having long observed the thousands of appearances and disappearances of living beings here, his mind has attained detachment from enjoyments.
Having ruled over the three worlds for ten billion years,
he finally attained detachment, and his mind became perfectly stilled like a fire that has gone out.
Having examined thousands of arguments for and against, and hundreds of instances of existence and non-existence, where could he find any consolation?
Having completely abandoned the desire for enjoyments, Bāḍi, his mind fulfilled,
remains eternally established as one who delights in the Self within the cavern of Pātāla.
Furthermore, O Rāma, by means of this Baḍi, this entire world was to be governed as its Indra here for many groups of years.
No satisfaction arises in him from attaining the station of Indra,
nor does any agitation arise in him from falling from his own station.
He is equanimous toward all things, his disposition always uplifted; taking what comes to him, established in himself, he remains like space.
This attainment of the supreme knowledge has been declared to you by me;
having firmly grasped this view, may you also rise up.
O Rāghava, through your own discernment, by the certainty that "I am eternal," you shall attain the state free from duality solely through human effort.
Having enjoyed the three worlds for eighteen crores of years,
even Bāḍi, the best of asuras, eventually fell into a state of weariness.
Therefore, O subduer of enemies, having utterly renounced the multitude of enjoyments that inevitably lead to bitterness,
proceed toward the state free from bitterness, which is perpetual bliss.
O Rāma, these perceptions of the visible world, which produce various forms and transformations, are none of them yours; they are like rocks on a distant mountain.
Bind this mind that runs here and there, wallowing in worldly activities, and establish it within the hollow of the heart.
You alone are the sun of consciousness, situated everywhere in the universe;
who is another to you, and who is your own? Why do you stumble in vain?
You are Ananta, the mighty-armed; you are the primordial Puruṣottama;
as the embodiment of consciousness, you manifest through hundreds of forms of objective reality.
All this world, both stationary and moving, is strung upon you,
who are eternally awakened and pure, like a multitude of gems upon a thread.
You are not born, nor do you die; you are the unborn, sovereign Puruṣa. Pure consciousness—may the delusions of birth and death not befall you.
Having deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness of all the diseases of birth,
abandon craving for enjoyments and become merely an enjoyer.
While you, the Lord of the World, the sun of consciousness ever-risen, abide,
this entire mandala of the dream of saṃsāra appears.
Do not indulge in vain despondency; this longing for pleasure and pain is not yours.
You are pure consciousness, the self of all, the illuminator of all things.
Having first conceptualized that what was desired was undesired and that what was undesired was desired, abandon both of those as well through the practice of that [equanimity].
Upon abandoning the perception of the desirable and the undesirable, eternal equanimity arises;
by means of that which dwells within the heart, a living being is not born again.
From whatever objects the mind sinks, like a child, one should indeed withdraw it from each of those and establish it in reality.
In this way, having bound with one's entire being the wild elephant of the mind through the practice of constant application, the supreme good is attained.
Do not fall into equality with the deceitful, those who know things as they are not, whose intentions are destroyed by false views, who are deluded fools sold out by their own crafty designs.
In this world, there is nothing more painful than the state of one who possesses nothing yet remains undecided within himself, while hanging upon the words of others out of ignorance.
O high-minded one, quickly drive far away this delusion born of non-discrimination that has arisen in the sky of your heart by means of the wind of discrimination.
As long as one does not bestow favor upon oneself through one's own effort for the sake of self-observation, so long will there be no arising of discernment.
Even through the Vedas, the Vedānta scriptures, the meaning of the treatises, and the perspectives of logic,
this Self does not become manifest until one's own direct perception occurs.
O Rāma, established in serenity within yourself by means of your own self,
you have attained expansive awakening and now comprehend my words.
This pervasive pervasion of the supreme self, the sun of consciousness, which is devoid of all parts of conceptual construction, has been grasped by you as I have described it.
With all mental constructs dissolved, with doubts and delusions stilled,
and with the mist of curiosity exhausted, you have become one who is free from the fever of worldly existence.
Whatever you approach, protect, destroy, drink, leap, or grow through—
by that very fact, O Great Sage, may you be free from the suspicion of any stain upon your awakening.
The thirtieth canto, titled "The Attainment of the Knowledge of the Flame," by Vasiṣṭha.
Now, O Rāma, listen to this further sequence for the attainment of realization, just as Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas, attained perfection through his own self.
In the depths of Pātāla there was an asura named Hiraṇyakaśipu, who had routed the gods and possessed the prowess of Nārāyaṇa.
Having pervaded the entire expanse of the world, he seized the universe from Hari,
just as a royal swan plucks a lotus with its large petals from a six-legged bee.
Having overwhelmed both gods and asuras, he ruled over the worlds,
just as a tusker, having driven away the swarms of swans, rules over the bees in a lotus pond.
Then that lord of the Asuras, exercising sovereignty over the three worlds,
in the course of time begot sons, just as the springtime tree produces sprouts.
They grew in no time at all, their brilliance outshining the stars,
like a thousand rays of ten suns sporting as they pervaded the sky.
Among those most worthy ones, there was indeed a venerable one named Prahlāda, who was the very soul of their preeminence, like the Kaustubha gem among precious jewels.
With that son, who was endowed with every beauty, Hiraṇyakaśipu shone intensely, like the year with the spring season.
Then that Daitya Mada, accompanied by his sons and endowed with an army and a treasury, arrived at Trigaṇḍa, where the elephants were dripping with rut.
With the very splendor of his rays, which was ever-expanding, he scorched the three worlds with the heat of his advancing strides, like the multitude of suns at the end of an eon.
Then the gods, headed by the Sun and the Moon, were not distressed by him,
just as kinsmen are not troubled by a child who is restless with wicked playfulness.
They entreated Śauri for the slaying of the lordly elephant of the Daitya kings;
for even the great do not tolerate repeated wrongdoing.
Then there was the roar of the world being overturned at the time of dissolution,
and it was bristling with the points of diamond-like claws resembling the tusks of the elephants of the quarters.
The circle of his upward-pointing crest-jewel blazes with a network of steady lightning-flashes,
while flaming earrings are emitted from the hollows of the ten directions.
Its vast belly was formed from the massed bulk of all the great mountain ranges,
and it shattered the shell of the cosmic egg by the violent shaking of its tree-like arms.
He was one who had driven away mountains with the wind issuing from his mouth and belly,
and who was proud of the fire of the world-ending kalpa, which he was intent on burning the three worlds.
The sun was driven away by the movement of his thick, formidable shoulders covered in hair;
the mountains were turned tawny by the masses of fire blazing from the pores of his skin.
His eye-sockets were fierce from pounding the great walls of the mountain ranges,
and he spat out from all his limbs pattisas, prāsas, and tomara spears.
Assuming the form of a man-lion, Mādhava slew the great asura,
who let out a terrifying *kaṭakaṭa* sound, just as an elephant slays a horse.
With the flames vomited from his eyes, he consumed the Asura city along with all its inhabitants,
just as fire at the end of an eon consumes the entire web of the world.
When that Nṛsiṃha-māruta had become violently agitated,
it thundered with the slapping of clouds, like a single turbulent ocean.
Those hosts of Dānavas fled in all directions like swarms of gnats;
they vanished from sight like lamps whose light has faded.
Then, with the lords of the Daityas having fled and the circles of the inner apartments burnt,
the surface of Pātāla became like the world crushed at the end of an eon.
When the Lord, who had been honored by the frantic efforts of the gods, had gradually quelled the ritual of the untimely dissolution of the world and departed for some unknown place; MU_5,30.24.
The surviving sons of Danu, protected by Prahlāda,
returned to their burnt land like birds to a dried-up lake.
There, having performed lamentations for their own destruction as was appropriate for the occasion,
they paid the funeral honors to their lords and kinsmen.
They slowly consoled their own people who had survived the slaughter, whose captives had been carried off and whose circle of kinsmen and relatives had been consumed by fire.
With forms as wretched as figures depicted in a painting, devoid of effort, and with hearts as dejected as lotuses struck by frost,
those leaders of the asuras, their minds tormented by grief, became like burnt trees, stripped of all vitality.
The thirty-first canto, titled "The Slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu," from the *Prahlādaviśrānti* of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, his soul overwhelmed with grief because the Dānavas had been slain by Hari,
Prahlāda, observing a vow of silence, reflected within the cavern of Pātāla.
"What means might we have whereby this very sprout of the Asuras, which grows here with a sharp point, might be consumed by that monkey, Hari? (5.31.2)
Never did the Daityas, though possessing arms as sturdy as staffs, remain stable in the netherworld; they were shattered like lotuses upon the Himalayas.
Leaping up again and again, they vanish— resounding with gurgling sounds and possessing radiant forms— like the waves of the ocean that flash forth for a moment before their onset.
The enemies, who rob the entire world of its light and cause unprecedented delusions of darkness, have reached full maturity, bringing suffering both within and without.
With their hearts filled with darkness and their wealth of petals closing up,
they experienced distress like lotus-pools at night.
The realm of my father has been overrun by the gods, who act as sweepers of the footstools in his Malinīvyūha palace, just as wild beasts overrun a great forest.
Devoid of effort, their prosperity departed, wretched and with their inner intentions laid bare,
kinsmen do not shine, like lotuses whose petals have been scorched.
In the houses of the asura heroes,
grey clouds of ash and frost swirl incessantly with the winds, like dense masses of incense smoke.
Upon the walls of the Daityas' inner apartments, where the door-panels had been torn away,
new sprouts of barley appeared like the luster of emerald.
Even the Dānavas, who were like intoxicated elephants in the lotus-pond of the three worlds, fell into a state of wretchedness like gods; alas, what is impossible for Fate?
Even at the slightest movement of a leaf, the wives, terrified by the fear of their enemies,
tremble in disarray like does that have strayed into a village.
The trees, whose clusters of blossoming jewels had served as ear-ornaments for the Asura women,
were felled by the hand of Narasiṃha and attained the state of mere stumps.
There, in the Nandana grove, the wish-fulfilling trees were replanted, possessing leaves that were celestial garments and creepers, and bristling with clusters of jewels for blossoms.
Formerly, the faces of the captive goddesses were gazed upon by the Daityas;
today, however, the faces of the captive Asuras are gazed upon by the gods.
I believe that the great rivers of my gifts will flow forth upon the flanks of the celestial elephants' temples like streams cascading down mountain ridges.
The ashes from the forest fires upon our temples shine like dust in parched desert thickets.
Those plateaus on the peaks of Mount Meru, where the winds are reddened by the nectar of blooming white mandāra flowers, have become inaccessible to the Daityas.
The beauties of the gods and gandharvas, who had dwelt within the inner apartments of the dānavas,
returned once more to Mount Meru like blossoms upon a tree.
Alas! The graceful charms of my father’s wives, now withered like waterless lotuses, are mocked in playful laughter by the celestial nymphs.
Alas, O my father, by those very same chowries with which the thousand-eyed Indra was formerly fanned in heaven, he is now being fanned.
This other calamity has come upon us, bringing us wretchedness,
solely through the favor of that one Hari, who possesses such wicked manliness.
Having found rest in the dense shade of the forest of their arms,
the gods are never tormented, just like the peaks of the Snowy Mountain.
Resorting to the fierce peaks of Śauri’s valor, they have seized our prosperity;
like monkeys, they now torment us sages.
Thus, the tears shed upon the lotus-faces of the wives of the asuras— who were ever adorned with auspicious ornaments— were like frost falling upon lotus plants.
This crumbling pavilion of the world, with its walls decayed, broken, and falling,
is supported solely by those very arms, which serve as pillars of sapphire.
He is the upholder of the celestial army as it sinks in the ocean of calamity,
like the tortoise supporting Mount Mandara when it was submerged in the depths of the Ocean of Milk.
All these, beginning with his father, were struck down by him alone— those foremost of asuras— like the great boundary mountains by the agitated wind at the end of an aeon.
This very Madhusūdana, whose rows of arms are capable of such acts of destruction,
is the illustrious and formidable friend of the host of gods.
By the prowess of that one who is an axe to the staff-like arms of the Daityas,
the heroic Śakra torments the Dānavas as a monkey harasses young children.
Difficult to conquer is the lotus-eyed one; even when his weapons have been cast aside, he—whose essence is like a diamond—is not shattered by the severing of missiles and arms.
By him, many terrifying battles were practiced together with our grandfathers, in which mountains were hurled at one another in the fervor of combat.
In those various and most terrible battles of the Asuras that have been waged,
he who was not afraid even now— what need is there to speak of his fear [in this]?
I consider this alone to be the clear and singular means for attacking Hari; apart from that, I believe there exists no remedy.
With one's whole being, with every faculty of the intellect, and with the full force of all one's exertion—that Lord alone is the refuge and the goal here; it cannot be otherwise.
There is no one superior to him within the three worlds;
Hari has become the cause of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.
Therefore, from this very moment onward, I have forever taken refuge in the unborn Nārāyaṇa; for everywhere, I am permeated by Nārāyaṇa.
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all purposes;
it does not depart from the treasury of my heart, just as the wind does not depart from the sky.
Hari is the quarters, Hari is the sky, Hari is the earth, and Hari is the world;
this immeasurable Self is Hari, for I am indeed composed of Hari.
One who worships Viṣṇu while not being Viṣṇu shall not partake in the fruit of that worship;
having become Viṣṇu, one should worship Viṣṇu, [realizing]: "I am this Viṣṇu who stands here."
Having filled this infinite space, the son of Vinatā,
with his golden limbs, has become the seat for my own limbs.
His hands were like great emerald trees, upon which all weapons rested as solitary birds, and which were strewn with the blossoms of the rays from his fingernails.
These are my four arms, their shoulders bound with garlands of soft *mandāra* flowers, and their armlets rubbed by Mount Mandara.
This Lakṣmī, born from the depths of the Ocean of Milk, stands by my side, holding beautiful chowries that shimmer like the flowing rays of the moving moon.
This Fame of mine, who has effortlessly won over the world, who is like a blossoming cluster on the tree of the three realms, and who smiles with pure whiteness, stands by my side.
This illusion, which ceaselessly creates the ever-new net of the world and sports with its own magical displays, stands by my side.
This is she, who effortlessly overcomes the groves of trees that are the three worlds;
she, Jayā, shines at my side like a creeper upon the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
These two gods, the Moon and the Sun, who are eternally cold and hot respectively, have manifested the nature of saṃsāra as my eyes within my mouth.
This radiance of my body, dark as a blue lotus and beautiful like a full rain-cloud, spreads abroad and turns the circle of the quarters dark blue.
This conch Pāñcajanya in my hand, with its throbbing sound,
is like the sky personified as the essence of sound, as if established within the Ocean of Milk itself.
This glorious lotus, born from the hollow of my own navel, rests upon the palm of my hand; within its pericarp-cup dwells the bee that is Brahmā.
This heavy mace of mine, adorned with jewels, resembling the peak of Mount Sumeru,
encased in golden bands, is the crusher of Daityas and Dānavas.
This form of mine is radiant, pleasant to behold, and beautiful to see;
its edges are matted with flames, turning the quarters of the sky a deep crimson.
This dark, blazing sword Nandaka stands ready, beautiful as a flaming banner-bearing fire, a battle-axe for the trees that are the Daityas, bringing joy to its wielder.
This is the Puṣkarāvartaka cloud for the showers of my envy;
it is the Śārṅga bow, possessing the luster of the lord of serpents and as beautiful as Indra’s rainbow.
Within my belly, I have long borne these infinite worlds— those already born and destroyed, and those existing now in their manifold varieties.
These two, the earth, are my feet; this, the sky, is my head;
this, the three worlds, is my body; and these, the quarters of space, are my bellies.
"I am this very Viṣṇu himself, with the luster of the interior of a dark blue cloud,
mounted upon the mountain Garuḍa, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace."
All these evil-minded ones are fleeing from me,
like heaps of straw with flickering movements scattered by the wind.
This very person, dark as a blue lotus, clad in yellow garments,
bearing a mace, endowed with splendor, and mounted upon Garuḍa, am I myself, Acyuta.

Who is this person of hostile nature who comes toward me, capable as I am of burning the three worlds— a moth approaching the fire at the end of an aeon, agitated by the wind, for its own destruction?
These gods and asuras standing before me are unable to endure your fiery gaze, just as those with weak eyes cannot bear the brilliance of light.
These beings— Brahmā, Indra, Agni, Hara, and the others— praise me, Viṣṇu, the Lord, with infinite speech issuing from their many mouths.
I have become one whose sovereignty is fully manifested, possessing an unconquerable form; indeed, by my supreme majesty, I have transcended all states of duality.
I bow to that singular form which fills the interior of the three worlds, which forcibly destroys all wicked beings,
and which, though dwelling within dense mountains, grass, and forests, removes every fear.
The thirty-second canto, titled "The Transformation into Nārāyaṇa at the Nirvāṇa of Prahlāda," by Vasiṣṭha:
Having reflected thus and assumed the form of Nārāyaṇī, he named him Prahlāda and then further contemplated [a means] for the worship of the enemy of the asuras.
From this body of Viṣṇu, this other one— the supreme and yet lower form consisting of the Maruts—
stands outside through the flow of the vital breath.
Mounted upon Vainateya, with his fourfold power clearly manifest,
holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, he has four arms and a dark-complexioned body.
The glorious one, whose eyes are the moon and the sun; the delighter of Kānta, Nandaka, and Nandana; lotus-handed, large-eyed, wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and possessed of great splendor.
Therefore, I shall quickly worship him, together with his retinue,
with a mental worship that is delightful through all its constituent offerings.
Therefore, I shall worship this Mahādeva once again with a great external offering of abundant jewels and enjoyments.
Thinking "This is Prahlāda," he worshipped Mādhava, the husband of Kamalā, with a mind bearing the weight of his accumulated spiritual provisions.
With arrays of jewel-filled offering bowls, with ointments such as sandalwood, with incenses and various lamps, and with diverse ornaments of manifold wealth;
With garlands of *mandāra* flowers, clusters of golden lotuses,
thickets of *kalpavṛkṣa* creepers, and circles of jewel-like blossoms;
With the sprouts of celestial trees, with garlands of various flowers—
kiṅkirātas, bukas, kunda, campakas, and blue lotuses— ...
With *kalhāra* lilies, water-lilies, *kāśa* grass, date palms, mangoes, *kiṃśuka* trees, *aśoka*, *madana*, *bilva*, *karṇikāra*, and *kirātaka* trees;
With *kadamba*, *kukura*, *nīpa*, *sindhuvāra*, and *sayūthika* trees; with *pāribhadra*, *guggulu*, *vidula*, and clusters of *kuyyaka*.
With clusters of *priyaṅgu*, with trumpet-flowers (*pāṭala*), with red ochre-colored flowers,
with mangoes, hog-plums (*āmra-taka*), *bhavya* fruits, and yellow myrobalans (*harītakī*) and beleric myrobalans (*vibhītaka*).
With the tender creepers, flowers, and shoots of *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees; with clusters of buds; and with *sahakāra* mangoes mixed with saffron.
With *ketaka* flowers, *saptaparṇa* trees, and clusters of *erā* blossoms, as well as with various *pālīvata* plants and diverse species of *ṭaṅka* trees.
With clusters of *mālatī* and *mādhavī* flowers blooming from the heart-stealing *ruka*,
and with masses of fresh *śephālikā* blossoms as beautiful as gold.
With various kinds of foods to be chewed, those to be eaten, as well as drinks, things to be licked, things to be sipped, and thick liquids;
with juices, fruits, and sprouts of diverse flavors and varieties.
With silken garments, beds, and costly vehicles; with golden seats, songs, dances, and instrumental music; and with throngs of highly precious women.
By offering the entirety of their wealth— including gardens, groves, and pleasure-parks—
by honoring all forms of beauty, and even by personally surrendering their very selves.
With supreme devotion toward Hari, which was as magnificent as the splendor of the universe,
Prahlāda mentally worshipped his Lord within the inner apartments.
Then, in that temple, the lord of the Dānavas worshipped Janārdana with an offering complete with external ritual requisites.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord again and again with that very same external object in that same sequence, the Dānava became filled with satisfaction.
From that time forward, Prahlāda worshipped the Supreme Lord every day with the same complete devotion.
Then, from that time forward, all the Daityas in that city became devoted to Viṣṇu; indeed, they all became auspicious, for the king is the cause of conduct.
The news went to the sky, to the world of the gods, and then to Hari:
that the Daityas, having abandoned their hatred for Viṣṇu, remained as his devotees.
O Rāghava, Śakra and the other gods, together with the hosts of Maruts, were filled with wonder: "How is it that the Daityas have indeed taken up devotion to Viṣṇu? (5.32.26)
In the Ocean of Milk, the gods, filled with wonder,
left the sky and went toward Hari, who was reclining upon the coils of the serpent and was radiant in battle.
There, they related this account of the Daityas to him and,
out of wonder at such an unprecedented marvel, questioned him as he sat there.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, why is it that these Daityas, who have always been your adversaries, have now attained identity with you? This must surely be an illusion."
Where, indeed, are the utterly wicked Dānavas who have shattered the mountains,
and where is devotion to Janārdana, which is obtainable only through a great birth in the West?
"O Blessed One, this talk that 'an ordinary person has become virtuous' is like a garland of out-of-season flowers: pleasant at first, yet leading to distress."
For that which is not appropriate in a certain place does not shine there,
just like a highly precious gem in the midst of a heap of glass trinkets.
Whatever kind of qualities a living being possesses, he attains that very same state;
for I do not think a dog finds pleasure anywhere even among those who are equal to the Unborn.
Diamond needles, even when plunged into the body, do not cause such pain as these views of substantiality, which are bound together by their dissimilarity [to reality].
Whatever is appropriate, consistent with the sequence, and irreproachable in a particular place, that alone shines there— just as a lotus shines in water, but not on dry land.
Where is that base, vulgar, and wretched Dānava, always delighting in inferior deeds and lowly undertakings; and where indeed is Vaiṣṇava devotion?
Just as a lotus plant growing in harsh, saline soil does not bring happiness here because it has taken refuge in a poor environment,
so too, O Lord, the story that even the son of Danu was devoted to Mādhava does not bring us such joy.
The thirty-third canto, titled "The Speculations of the Gods," in the Legend of Prahlāda; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.

Then Mādhava, the slayer of enemies, spoke these words to the one roaring with great fury, just as a cloud speaks to a flock of peacocks: The slayer of enemies, Mādhava, addressed the one who was roaring and exceedingly enraged, just as a rain-cloud speaks to a flock of peacocks.
The Blessed One said:
"O wise ones, do not be despondent because Prahlāda was devoted;
this is his final birth, for that subduer of enemies is worthy of liberation."
From this point forward, this son of Danu,
having been utterly consumed, must no longer perform the function of an embryo, just as a burnt seed cannot produce a sprout.
The wise know that "the virtuous has become devoid of virtue" is a sequence of misfortune;
they say that "the one devoid of virtue has become virtuous" is the sequence that bestows success.

O best of immortals, depart to your own various worlds; this daughter of Prahlāda has not been obtained by you here for the sake of unhappiness, but rather for the sake of your delight through her virtues.
Vasiṣṭha:
Having spoken thus to the gods there amidst the waves of the Ocean of Milk,
the Lord vanished like a cluster of blue lotuses on the shore.
That host of gods, having worshipped Hari,
ascended into the sky like a mass of spray from the ocean tossed by the Mandara mountain.
Then the gods felt affection toward Prahlāda;
for where the great are not agitated, there the mind becomes full of trust.
The devoted Prahlāda worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, every day with his mind, his actions, and his speech.
Then, as he was devoted to worship, over the course of time, his virtues— foremost among them the power of discernment, bliss, and dispassion— increased.
He did not delight in the multitude of enjoyments, like a tree withered of its sap;
nor did he find pleasure in his beloveds, like a deer in the parched lands of a desert.
He took no delight in worldly discourses except for the exposition of the meaning of the scriptures;
he found no pleasure in visible objects, just as a lotus finds none on dry land.
His mind found no rest in the attachment to the diseases of worldly enjoyments,
like a pearl unattached to the surface of the earth.
His mind, having abandoned the pursuit of enjoyments yet not having attained rest, remained merely suspended as if fixed upon a swing.
From the hollow of the ocean of milk, he whose body was Kṛṣṇa perceived that state belonging to Prahlāda through that all-pervading and supremely beautiful [consciousness].
Then Viṣṇu, his vanguard gladdened, arrived at Prahlāda’s temple of worship by way of the path to Pātāla.
Having recognized that the god had arrived, the lord of the Daityas honored the lotus-eyed one with a twofold-intensified worship, paying him homage with great reverence.
Prahlāda, filled with supreme joy, praised with nourishing words Lord Hari, who was present in person within the sanctuary of worship.

Prahlāda said: I take refuge in Hari, the unborn Lord and Sovereign, the imperishable, the worthy refuge, the protector of the helpless, the supreme light that removes all blemish, and the treasure-house beautiful within the abode of the three worlds.
I take refuge in Him who resembles a mountain of blue lotus petals, who is like the hollow of the cloudless autumn sky,
who has the luster of bees, darkness, and kohl-like collyrium, and who bears the lotus, the discus, and the mace.

I take refuge in that lake of water which is my own heart-lotus, whose tender limbs are like a swarm of trembling bees, whose conch-shell possesses the luster of a white lotus bud, and where the bee that is Brahmā hums with the sound of the Vedas.

I take refuge in the expansive autumnal sky of Hari, strewn with the stars of his clusters of white jewels, possessing the full orb of the moon of his broad face brightened by a smile, and containing the Gaṅgā of the radiating rays from the jewel upon his chest.

I take refuge in Hari, the white lotus of the lily-pond of the three worlds, the foremost lamp that dispels the delusion equal to darkness, the conscious essence who is himself unclouded though others are most dull-witted, and the remover of all the world's afflictions.
I take refuge in Him who is fair as the pollen of a newly blossomed lotus, whose limbs are adorned by the form of a radiant lotus,
who resembles the crimson sky at the time of day’s departure, and who is beautiful in garments resembling gold.

I take refuge in that Child who lies at the foot of a tree—whose play consists of the continuous creation, destruction, and re-creation of the universe; who is eternally unborn, unchanging, and vast; and whose noble body has been worn out by hundreds of ages.

I take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, who is the frost-fall for the lotus-pond of Diti’s sons (the Daityas), the ever-rising solar disc for the lotus-pond of the gods, the flood of water for the lotus-pond of Brahmā, and whose abode is the heart-lotus.
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus honored with words full of many virtues, that Hari— the destroyer of demons, whose shoulder-region is graced by the presence of Śrī,
and whose body is like the petals of a blue lotus— replied with joy to the joyful lord of the Asuras, just as a cloud responds to a peacock.
The thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Arrival of Nārāyaṇa," in the Legend of Prahlāda.
The Blessed One said:
O treasure-house of virtues, great crest-jewel of the Daitya lineage, please accept a boon as you desire for the further pacification of the suffering of rebirth.
Prahlāda said:
O bestower of the fruits of all intentions, who dwells within all worlds,
O God, instruct me in that which you know to be the most sublime.
The Blessed One said:
"O sinless one, may there be for you a state of solitude that culminates in the repose of Brahman, for the sake of pacifying all agitation and for the sake of the supreme fruit."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to Indra, the son of Diti, Viṣṇu vanished like a wave of the ocean that has produced a gurgling roar.
When the god Viṣṇu had vanished, the Dānava cast aside the final handful of flowers from his worship, which was adorned with jewels and gems.
Then, seated in the lotus posture upon a soft and excellent seat,
he reflected with his mind upon the procedure for reciting the hymn of praise.
"I have been told by the Lord, the enemy of worldly existence, 'May you indeed be possessed of discernment';
therefore, I shall quickly perform this internal investigation."
What indeed am I in this grand display of the world,
such that I say, "I go," "I stay," "I exert myself," or "I take"?
This world—including trees, forests, and mountains—is not "I";
since that which is external and utterly insentient could it possibly be me? MU_5,34.9
Non-existent, yet arisen, mute, it quivers for a moment due to the vital winds;
in a short time the body dissolves. I am not this insentient thing.
Sound, which is insubstantial in form and born from emptiness, is fashioned by the inert auditory canal that lasts but a moment; it is not I, for it is unconscious.

By means of the skin, which perishes in an instant, that which is to be attained is not attained; otherwise, having realized the Self through the clarity of consciousness, there is no contact with the insentient, for I am not insentient.
I am not the insentient taste, which gains its existence through the tongue, which is trivial, restless by nature, characterized by slight vibration, and dependent upon material substances.
The form that is dissolved in the seen and the seer—both of which are perishable and subject to momentary destruction—is extinguished when only the Seer remains; I am not that insentient form.
I am not the insentient fragrance, which is imagined by the utterly dull and decaying nose, and which is fragile and rests upon no fixed support.
Free from "mine-ness," free from mentation, peaceful, with the delusion of the five senses gone, I am pure consciousness alone, devoid of all parts and their perceptions.
I am this pure consciousness alone, devoid of the object of thought, the illuminator that pervades both the external and the internal, partless, stainless, and composed of bliss.
Now I have remembered all this truth:
I am this all-pervading Self, the manifestation of non-conceptual consciousness.
By this consciousness, all these things, from jars and cloths up to the sun, are illuminated by it as if by a lamp of supreme brilliance.
By this [Self], these flickering activities of the diverse senses are set in motion here through its internal radiance, just as rows of sparks are produced by the heat of a fire.
By this, these powers of mental reflection flash within,
just as mirages do by the all-pervading heat of the summer sun.
By this, the substantiality of these categories is established,
just as the possession of qualities such as whiteness is [revealed] by a lamp for garments.
For that very Self alone, among all beings who are awake,
is the experiencer of everything on earth, situated like a mirror.
By the grace of this non-conceptual lamp of consciousness,
the sun is warm, the moon is cool, the mountain is solid, and water is liquid.
By means of this [cognition], the status of being an object arises with great force for those things experienced continuously,
just as the state of being heated arises through intense heat.
This is the primordial cause of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra—the causes for the maintenance of the world; yet there exists no cause for this [Supreme Cause].
From that which is causeless, from that which does not act, and from the cause of all causes— this world has arisen from this, just as coldness arises from ice.
Salutations again and again to this Self of mine, which is devoid of names such as "the knower" and "the known," and which is eternally manifest.
Within this Lord of Beings, the non-conceptual Self of Consciousness, all beings abide and enter as subordinate qualities.
Whatever indeed is conceived by this conscious inner self, that alone comes to be everywhere; nothing else occurs, even though it may exist.
Whatever is perceived by consciousness attains its own true state;
whatever is not perceived by consciousness here has set, even though it exists.
These hundreds of rows of worldly objects, appearing in the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth, are indeed reflected in this vast mirror of space.
Invisible to all beings, yet attainable by those whose minds have dissolved,
this supreme space is perceived by the virtuous who are absorbed in it.
This world, both existent and non-existent, remains like the reflection of the sun within an object that is increasing when it increases and diminishing when it diminishes.
This diversity of visible clusters of blossoms attains prosperity,
for it is rich with the bees of right conduct from this tree of causes.
From this arises that unstable structure of saṃsāra,
lofty and rich with diverse trees and shrubs, like a forest range rising from a mountain.
This self of consciousness, which illumines all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass existing within the belly of the three worlds, is undivided.
This is that very I, devoid of beginning and end, possessing all forms; I abide as my own direct experience within the moving and unmoving beings.
Of me, who am that very [Self], these many bodies— both stationary and moving— are beyond all calculation.
This very I am that single Self, manifesting by the power of my own experience; because I am the seer of all seeing and the seen, I possess a thousand hands and eyes.
This is that very I who dwells in the sky with the beautiful body of the sun,
and also with another, the moving body of the wind.
This body of mine is dark-blue, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
for it moves about in this world as the very pinnacle of all good fortune.
I am born here, always seated upon the lotus throne,
established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, and have attained supreme bliss.
In the form of the Three-eyed One, a bee at the lotus-face of Gaurī, I withdraw this universe at the end of creation, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
In the form of Indra, I protect this monastery of the three worlds,
which has come to me by succession, just as an ascetic protects his own small hut.
I abide as the sap within the network of grasses, creepers, and shrubs;
from the soil of consciousness, I cause them to rise up like a vast creeper from a well.
For the sake of my own play, this beautiful and vast display of the world was spread out by me when I was a noble child, like a toy made of mud.
All this is offered to me; having reached me, it attains its true being.
And that which is abandoned by me, even though it exists, is truly nothing at all.
Whatever reflection has appeared in me, the expansive mirror of consciousness, that alone exists and nothing else; therefore, nothing other than me is found here.
Among flowers, I am the fragrance; among lotus petals, I am the luster;
among lusters, I am the art of form; and among forms, I am the experience itself.
Whatever is seen here as this world, whether stationary or moving,
that which is devoid of all conceptual construction— that supreme reality of consciousness am I.
The power consisting of rasa, which is watery and whose arising is manifested through the subtle flow [of breath], is just as it is in wood and walls; so am I in all things.
Having attained that supreme state of existing within all other objects, I manifest the diversity of consciousness by my own will.
Just as ghee exists within milk, and just as the power of taste exists within water,
so too do I abide within all beings as the power of consciousness.
This world, existing throughout the three periods of time, is situated within me alone, who am consciousness;
it is devoid of the mental constructs of the objectified, like a collection of objects resting upon the earth.
Having filled the interior of all directions, having abandoned the delusion of limitation,
I stand as the Virāj and the Samrāj, present everywhere and the sustainer of all.
This vast sovereignty over the world has come to me unbidden— an unprecedented state where Indra is no longer bound and the gods are crushed by weapons.
"Alas! I am indeed expanded; I do not measure myself by means of my own self within the Self, like the single ocean swollen by the winds at the end of a kalpa."
I find no end within myself, though I am clear and have arisen by myself within; I am like a crawling cripple quivering within the ocean of milk.
This small Brahma-cottage named Jagat is very cramped;
my vast body does not fit within it, like an elephant in a wood-apple.
Beyond the abode of Viriñca, even at the end of the principles (tattvas), he seized my station;
yet my form continues to spread forth even now and does not turn back.
"How could this internal notion 'I am named so-and-so' be without support?
Indeed, for me, who am of infinite form, this [notion] was but a mere trifle."
The delusion that "this is you" and "this is I" is entirely false; for consciousness, whose form is boundless, what is the body and what is the non-body?
Wretched and of feeble intellect were my grandfathers,
who abandoned this empire and took delight in the splendors of wealth.
Where indeed is this great vision, filled and expanded by Brahman;
and where are the pleasures of royal splendors, which are as terrifying as crawling serpents?
Infinite and infinite in its enjoyment, characterized by supreme tranquility,
this pure vision consisting of consciousness triumphs among all visions.
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am the inner witness, whose nature is consciousness, the self of pure awareness free from objects of thought, and who dwells within all beings.
I am victorious; I have been born, having worn out the cycle of worldly existence.
This Self has been attained by me again and again; I live, and I am victorious.
Having abandoned this supreme, eternal sovereignty of awakening, I find no delight in the unenjoyable splendors of kingship, which are nothing but suffering.
Fie on that wretched worm of the Grandfather, ignorant of the self, who lusted for this earth which consists of nothing more than wood, water, and stone!

What indeed has been accomplished by that ignorant preceptor, who, with substances whose sole nature is ignorance, satisfies the consumer of the clarified butter (the fire) which consists of ignorance?
Having spent only a few years in this village of the world,
what indeed did Hiraṇyakaśipu obtain that was truly fitting for him?
Without having tasted the bliss of tranquility, even one who tastes hundreds of kingdoms of the world would have tasted nothing at all in this life.
Nothing has been attained by that through which this supreme nectar is attained;
for one who has attained it and is filled within, everything is attained in its entirety.
The fool who has abandoned the immeasurable attains the measurable, but the wise man does not;
for the camel, having abandoned the excellent grass, goes toward the thorn, but no other animal does.
Having abandoned this supreme vision, who would delight in a kingdom that is like ashes?
What wise man, having discarded sugarcane juice, would drink the bitter decoction of neem?
Indeed, all those ancestors of mine were fools,
for they abandoned this vision and took delight in the perils of kingship.
Where are the blossoming groves of Nandana, and where are these parched desert lands?
Where are these peaceful visions of awakening, and where is the notion of a self in sensual enjoyments?
There is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that is desired as a kingdom;
yet all of it exists indeed within the nature of the mind—why then is it not experienced?
By means of that consciousness which abides in all things, which is pure by its very nature, and which is changeless,
everything is perfectly attained in every way, at all times, and from all sources.
The solar power is radiant, the lunar power flows with nectar;
the power of Brahmā is great majesty, and that of Śakra is sovereignty over the three worlds.
The supreme fullness belongs to Śarva, and the fortune of victory belongs to Viṣṇu;
mental power moves swiftly, while the power of Vāyu is strength.
The Āgneyī is the power of burning; the Pāyasī is the fulfillment of taste;
the Maunī is the perfection of great austerity; and likewise, the Vidyā is that of Bṛhaspati.
She is the celestial splendor of the gods in their mansions, the stability of the sky, and the firmness of the mountains;
she is the profundity of the oceans and the great height of Mount Meru.

The splendor of the Sugatas is equal to the beauty of the autumn season: it is gentle, intoxicating, and trembling with passion; it is composed of the *mādhavī* flowers and possesses the abundance of thick crops.
There is the illusory nature of a yakṣī, the stainlessness of the etherial,
the coolness of frost, and the heat-tormented state of summer.
These and many other [states], consisting of place, time, and action,
arising from various forms and transformations, are situated within the womb of the three times.
The various powers are produced by consciousness through its own pure commitment, which is changeless,
supreme, and free from the differentiation of parts.
Free from conceptual construction, consciousness rushes equally toward the perception of hundreds of all objects, just as light radiates from a luminous source.
Just as the earth experiences in an instant the entire multitude of objects— resting within the treasury of all hopes and encompassed by the activity of the three times— so too does [the yogi].

In the same way, the stainless consciousness, being of the nature of that [expansive reality], gathers the splendor of the vast state of the entire objective world throughout the three periods of time.
Pure consciousness is indeed complete, encompassing the infinite expanse of experience and the perception of hundreds of calculations regarding the three times simultaneously grasped.
For consciousness, which has grasped the three times and whose vision perceives the infinite,
only fullness remains— fullness being synonymous with equanimity.
When perceived simultaneously by a mind that is either gentle or harsh,
the mind attains equanimity through that which is equal, just like the experience of honey at the end [of a meal].
By means of that subtle state of consciousness, which has abandoned all mental constructs, which pervades all beings, and whose sole nature is the non-duality of existence; //MU 5.34.95//
Even the diverse splendor of objects, though their internal natures are intertwined with one another,
is experienced as if in a state of equality because they are experienced at the same time.
By relying on existence through existence, existence abandons its state of suffering;
but by perceiving existence through non-existence, existence abandons its state of contentment.
When the mind has disregarded the three times and is free from the bonds of the inferior,
and when the object of thought has been disregarded by the mind, only equanimity remains.
Because it is inaccessible to words, it goes, as it were, into a state of eternal non-existence;
it remains as if it has attained the stage of the established doctrine of selflessness.
The self likewise becomes Brahman—either as nothingness or as the whole;
merged in supreme tranquility, it is designated by the name "liberation" (mokṣa).
But this consciousness, being fashioned by conceptual construction and possessing a dim appearance,
does not perceive this world correctly, just as a cataract-afflicted vision does not see clearly.
That consciousness which is internally coiled by impurities consisting of both effort and non-effort is indeed unable to fly up, like a bird bound by a snare.
By the very act of conceptualizing, these various people have fallen into the snares of delusion, like birds caught by a hunter.
Enmeshed in the web of volitions and falling into the pits of sensory objects,
this path free from affliction was not seen even by my grandfathers.
Within just a few days, having quivered upon the surface of the earth,
those wretched ones were destroyed by him like mosquitoes in their burrows.
If they had known the truth, then those of ruined hopes, who seek only the pleasures of enjoyment,
would not have fallen into the blind wells of existence and non-existence.
Driven by the delusion of dualities arising from desire and aversion,
living beings have become equal to worms submerged in the crevices of the earth.
He who has stilled the mirage of conceptualization— which takes the forms of the desired and the undesired—
by means of the cloud of the realization of truth, he truly lives.
For how could there be any perception of a spot upon this pure moonlight, which possesses an uninterrupted and stainless form, and whose radiance is only slightly warm?
Salutation to myself, to me who am the uninterrupted conscious self;
O God, jewel illuminating the worlds, alas, you have been attained by me only after a long time!
You have been grasped, you have been found, and after a long time you have arisen;
you have been lifted out from conceptual constructions. Whatever you are, you are that—homage be to you!
Salutation to me and to you, the infinite; salutation to you and to me, whose nature is auspiciousness; salutation to the God beyond gods, the supreme, the Supreme Self.
Like the full orb of the moon from which the clouds have vanished, I bow to my own true nature, which is free from the veil of mental constructs;
I bow to that which rejoices in its own body, established in itself, arisen by itself, and whose essence is self-manifested.
The thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Yoga of Prahlāda’s Instruction," begins with Prahlāda:
"Om"—this form, whose nature is thus manifested, is free from all modification;
this very Self is all this, whatever exists within the world.
