Although this conscious being has transcended fat, bone, flesh, marrow, and blood,
it illuminates the sun and other luminaries like a lamp situated within.
It makes the burning heat cool, it tastes the nectar-like flavor,
and it experiences the sensations of the senses, just as a sovereign king enjoys his pleasures.
For even while standing, he is not seated; even while walking, he does not walk.
Though established in worldly activity, he is peaceful; even while acting, he is not defiled.
As it was formerly, so it is today, and likewise now— both here and in the hereafter—
this [Self] remains equal in all states of existence, whether concealed or unconcealed.
He remains here, causing the world— from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— to revolve through various states of manifestation, concealment, and non-existence.
Though he is eternally composed of constant vibration because he is the ever-moving Deity,
he is eternally inactive even as a pillar, and he is eternally untainted even as space.
He agitates the minds as the wind stirs the sprouts;
he drives the row of senses as a charioteer guides his team of horses.
Always like a laborer within the house of the body, which is exceedingly miserable,
he is like a sovereign king, established in his own well-being, the all-pervading enjoyer of experience.
This very one is always to be sought, praised, and meditated upon;
by means of this, one transcends old age, death, and delusion and proceeds [to liberation].
This [Self] is exceedingly easy to attain and easy to know, like a trusted kinsman;
it is the six-legged bee within the lotus-cavity of the body for everyone.
Even without being drawn or summoned, he is obtained from his own very body;
even when merely slightly invoked, he appears face-to-face in an instant.
Even when being attended upon, he who possesses every prosperity will have neither pride nor arrogance, like a lord of wealth.
As fragrance resides in flowers, as oil in sesame seeds,
and as flavor in juices, so does the Divine abide within bodies.
Due to the lack of inquiry, this conscious being, though residing within the heart,
is not recognized for a long time, like a beloved kinsman standing before one who has not been seen for a long while.
When this Supreme Lord is fully known through investigation,
supreme bliss arises, just as it does upon finding a beloved person.
When this supreme kinsman, who bestows unrestrained bliss, is seen,
those various perspectives arrive by which bondage dissolves.
The bonds snap apart on all sides, and all enemies are destroyed;
desires do not cut through the minds, just as wicked rats cannot destroy houses.
When this is seen, the world is seen; when this is heard, everything is heard; when this is touched, the world is touched; and when this is established, the world is established.
This one keeps watch over those who sleep; he strikes down the undiscriminating;
he removes the calamity of the afflicted; and he bestows [virtue] upon those who are not high-souled.
He wanders through the worlds like a lamp for the stability of the universe; he sports in enjoyments and he shines forth among all things.
Experiencing the self by means of the very self within through tranquility,
the living being remains present in all bodies, just as pungency resides within black peppers.
Consisting of volition and the faculty of cognition, formless, and resting upon both the external and the internal,
it abides as the universal existence of the entire mass of objects in the world.
This is emptiness in space; this is the movement in the wind;
this is the luminosity in the fires; and this is the supreme essence in water.
He is the hardness in the earth, the heat in the fire,
the coolness in the moon, and the very existence in the multitude of worlds.
Just as blackness is in a mass of ink, whiteness in a particle of snow,
and fragrance in flowers, so does the master of the body abide within the body.
Just as existence is all-pervading, just as time is all-pervading,
and just as space is all-pervading, so too is the Lord all-pervading.
Just as the sovereign power of a monarch extends to all lands,
so too does the being of the self extend beyond the perception of forms and mental attention.
This very one is the eternal God, the awakener of the gods;
I am myself the Self, and for me there is indeed no other conceptualization whatsoever.
Just as the sky is not affected by a particle of dust, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water,
and as a stone is not moved by agitation, so too there is no connection between me and sin.
Let happiness, suffering, and prosperity fall upon the body or not;
what loss have we sustained by the showers falling upon a gourd?
Just as light reaching the wick of a lamp is not bound by the wick,
even so am I unbound, transcending the entire multitude of existent things.
What connection indeed do we have with desires, with existence and non-existence, or with the senses?
By what is space bound, or by what is the mind grasped?
When the body is shattered into a hundred pieces, what injury is there for the embodied self?
When a jar is broken, pierced, or worn away, what loss is there for the space within the jar?
Like an invisible piśāca, the mind has arisen in vain;
when that inert thing is destroyed through awakening, what loss has befallen us?
That mind of mine which formerly consisted of the latent impressions of pleasure and pain has today become one; is this not indeed liberation?
One eats, another takes [the food], yet the calamity of misfortune belongs to someone else; one person watches—oh, what folly! To whom indeed does this cycle belong?
Nature eats and the mind experiences the afflictions of the body;
the witnessing Self is merely a witness. Since there is no ignorance here, what loss is there for me?
I have no desire for the maintenance of enjoyments, nor for their abandonment;
let that which comes come, and let that which departs depart.
I have no longing for pleasures, nor do I have indifference toward states of suffering;
let pleasures and pains come or go—they are but means, and who am I in relation to them?
Let the various latent impressions (vāsanās) in the body go to their setting or to their rising; I am not among them, nor do any of them belong to me.
For all this time, I have been robbed of my entire treasure of discernment by the great enemy of ignorance and utterly crushed into solitude.
Through the beautiful grace of Viṣṇu arising from within himself,
and having now recognized his own true nature, he has been utterly crushed by me.
This demon of egoism, which dwelt within the hollow of the tree of the body,
has now been driven away by me with the mantra of supreme awakening.
This great tree that is my body, from which the yakṣa of ego has departed,
has attained a state of perfect merit and shines as if in full bloom.
With the poverty of delusion pacified and the fault of evil desires destroyed, I stand as the Supreme Lord through the accumulation of the wealth of discernment.
All that is to be known has been known, and all sights to be seen have been seen;
that which was to be attained has now been attained, such that nothing remains here to be attained.
By good fortune, [I have reached this state] which has cast far away all misfortunes, from which the serpents of the sense-objects have departed,
from which the mist of delusion has been stilled, and in which the mirage of desire has become calm.
I have reached the vast and exalted ultimate ground, which is free from all dust and desire, and where the tree of cool tranquility stands.
Through praise, prostration, petition, tranquility, and self-restraint, this Blessed One has been obtained as one's very self; He has been clearly seen and realized.
The Lord, the Self, Viṣṇu, the eternal Brahman— the very nature [of all things]— having long transcended the state of egoism, has now come back into my memory.
In the pits of the serpents that are the sense-faculties, on the ground of the abysses of death,
in the thickets of the *karañja* trees of craving, and amidst the clamor of sensual desires;

Within the nets of the forest of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), amidst the interior wells of rebirth, in the burning of the forest fire of suffering, and bearing the coals of evil deeds; //MU_5,35.53//
Through hundreds of thousands of omens of fall and rise, through the delusions of sinking and surfacing,
through appearances and disappearances, and through the entanglements of the snares of hope;
For a long time, I have been utterly crushed by the enemy that is egoism,
like a man of little fortitude in the night being tormented by a piśāca in the jungle.
Indeed, by your own power of action,
you yourself have now awakened the splendor of discernment under the guise of Śauri’s words.
O Lord, when the Sovereign has awakened, I no longer see that demon of egoism, just as one sees no darkness when a lamp is lit, O All-pervading One.
O Lord, I do not know the destination of that yakṣa of egoism, which dwells in the cavity of the mind and has been extinguished like a lamp.
O Lord, as soon as you were seen, my state of pride and arrogance, which was intent on flight, vanished like a thief at the rising of the sun.
When that demon of egoism, which had arisen from what is non-existent,
has been stilled, I remain perfectly at ease, like a tree from which all serpents have departed.
I am at peace; I have attained final nirvana; I am awake and possessed of awakening. I have been released from the thief; after a long time, I am now at rest.
I have attained inner coolness, with the mirage of desire extinguished; I am like a mountain bathed by the heavy rains of the monsoon, its forest fires stilled.
When this significant term "I" has been thoroughly cleansed through inquiry,
what delusion remains, what sorrows, what evil desires, and what scorching heat?
Delusions such as hell, heaven, and liberation proceed only when there is the sense of "I," just as a painting proceeds only on a wall and not in the sky.
When the mind is swollen with the mass of egoism, the wondrous essence does not shine forth,
just as the coloring of saffron does not shine upon a faded garment.
In the autumnal sky of the mind, which is free from the clouds of egoism and devoid of the showers of craving, there shines a clarity endowed with radiant beauty.
Salutations again and again to you, my own Self, who are a lake of bliss for me, whose inner being is perfectly serene, and who are free from the mire of egoism.
Salutations again and again to me, who am like a mountain of bliss, resting in peace, for whom the clouds of ego have vanished and the forest fire of desire has been extinguished.
Salutations again and again to You, my own Self— the one whose fierce crocodiles are the senses stilled, whose submarine fire of the mind has been extinguished, and who is an ocean of bliss.
Salutations again and again to you, my own self, who are like a lake of blossoming lotuses of bliss, whose great waves are peaceful thoughts, and who transcend the mind within.
Salutations again and again to my own inner self, who dwells within the hollow of the lotus, who is the side of the manifestation of consciousness, and who is the swan of the entire mind.
Salutations again and again to You, whose form is fashioned by the creative arts yet who is partless; to the immeasurable Self, the moon of the eternally risen and perfectly full Atman.
Salutations again and again to the sun of consciousness, which is ever-risen, cool, the dispeller of the great darkness of the heart, all-pervading, yet invisible.
Salutations again and again to the lamp of consciousness, which is ignited by the oil of its own essence, which has transcended the wick, and which is steadfast in its natural substrate.
My mind, heated by the fire of reflection, has been forcibly severed within me by my cool mind, just as red-hot iron is cut from iron.
Having cut the senses with the senses, and having repeatedly cut the mind with the mind, and having cut egoism with the realization of non-egoism, I remain as the Residue; thus do I conquer.
Having crushed existence with non-existence and severed craving with non-craving,
having crushed ignorance with wisdom, the Knower has joined the ignorant to me.
When the mind has been severed within the mind and egolessness has been attained;
when existence has dissolved through being, I remain established in my own self, absolute.
Free from objective manifestation, free from ego, without mind, and without desire,
my body remains as a machine consisting solely of pure vibration and the self.
This liberation of mine has arisen, which is endowed with supreme tranquility and is the sole resolve for the infinite universe fashioned by ease.
With the vampire of delusion pacified and the rakshasa of egoism departed,
freed from the lecherous woman of desire, I have become one whose fever has vanished.
Having severed the multitude of the ropes of craving from the cage of my own body,
I know not where the bird of wicked egoism has flown away.
In this tree of the body, whose nest of dense ignorance has been shaken loose,
I know not where the bird of egoity has flown away.
By good fortune, our companion— desire, which is long-suffering through wicked longing, grey with the ashes of enjoyments, and destroyed by fear and worldly pleasures— has died.
For how long a time have I been such a mind,
by which I myself have falsely fallen into a state of firm egoism?
Today I am truly born; today I have become one of great intelligence, for I have been completely released from the great cloud of egoism by Kṛṣṇa.
This Blessed One, the Self, has been seen by me; He has been realized within, grasped, experienced in my very limbs, and I have been joined with that experience.

This mind has reached tranquility: it has lost its foothold, ceased its thinking, and abandoned its desires; it has cast aside the delusion of egoism, become skillful, free from effort, devoid of the coloring of passion, and stripped of curiosity.

The great calamities—difficult to cross, alternating between even and uneven, hard to endure, and productive of long-lasting faults—have come to an end; the immutable Consciousness, the Great Lord, has been attained within, free from the fluctuations of the mind.
The thirty-sixth canto, titled "Prahlāda’s Reflection on the Attainment of His True Self.
Prahlāda said:
O Self, who has transcended all states, you have returned to memory after a long time;
by good fortune you have been found, O Blessed One! Salutations be to you, the conscious Self.
Having saluted you and gazed upon you, enough now with embracing me;
O Blessed One, who else in the three worlds could be a kinsman other than you?
You kill, you protect, you give; you praise, you go, you leap about.
You have arrived here, you are seen—what are you doing, where are you going?
O you who fill the entire universe with your own existence, O friend of all people!
You are perceived everywhere at all times; where can you flee now?
The vast interval between our two births has today been bridged; by good fortune you have been seen, O kinsman! It is not far away now that it has come to pass.
Homage to you who have accomplished all that was to be done; homage be to you, the creator and the destroyer!
Homage to the dance of saṃsāra, the eternal one, the pure-souled!
Homage to the one who holds a discus and a lotus in his hands; homage to the wearer of the crescent moon;
homage to the lord of the wise; homage to you, the one born from the lotus.
This distinction between us here, which arises solely from the perspective of the signified and the signifier,
is a false conceptual construction, like that between a wave and the water of the wave.
You alone manifest here through this eternal power, which takes the form of an infinite variety of endless objects and delights in the play of existence and non-existence.
Homage to the Seer, homage to Tvaṣṭṛ, homage to the one of infinite expansion;
homage to the one whose nature is all things, homage to you who go everywhere.
Throughout many successive births, for a long time, I have been possessed by great sin, scorched by your illusion and smeared with foulness, enduring manifold and protracted sufferings.
The conditions of the world have been observed by you, and various perspectives have been seen; yet you have not attained that by which anything at all could be acquired.
This entire world consists of nothing but earth, wood, stone, and water;
O Lord, there is nothing here apart from you that, once attained, is not desired.
O God, today you have been found; you have been seen and you have been attained.
You have been reached and you have been seized; homage be to you, for you shall not be released.
How is it that the Lord, whose body is pervaded by a network of rays from the pupils of his eyes,
and who exists in the form of vision, is not seen within?
Just as one touching the flower of the *tvak* tree perceives its scent within the oil in the sesame seed, how is it that this [scent] which exists internally is not experienced?
How could that [Supreme Reality] be far away, when it brings horripilation upon one's body by causing one to inwardly perceive its supreme power upon hearing its sound?
To whom would he not be pleasing— he from whose limbs even the objects that cling to the sprout of his tongue taste so sweet?
Who would not have a place in the mouth of that person who, out of affection, takes flowers and perfumes and anoints their body with the hand of the nose?
How indeed can that Self, which is sung of through the Vedas, the Vedānta doctrines, logic, the Purāṇas, and sacred songs, once it is known, ever go to oblivion?
O Lord, that very same row of enjoyments which was so delightful to me today no longer tastes sweet within me now that you, the supreme and the non-supreme, have been seen by me in your pure essence.
Through you, the stainless lamp, the sun has attained its brilliance;
through you, the cool frost, the moon has attained its chill.
By you these mountains, the gurus, were held; by you these sky-dwellers were supported;
by you alone this earth was made firm, and by you alone the sky was covered.
By good fortune you have attained me, and by good fortune I have come to you;
I am you, O Lord, and you are I—by good fortune there is no difference between us.
O virtuous one, salutations again and again to you, the Great Soul, through the two synonymous words "I" and "you," whether they refer to me or to you, as they are merged together.
Homage to me, the infinite one, whose nature is free from ego;
homage to me, the formless one; homage to the abode of peace.
One remains here in one's very own Self— within me, the Self, which is equanimous, pure, the witness, devoid of attributes, and unconditioned by space, time, and the like.
The mind undergoes agitation as the perceptions of the senses quiver;
the expansive power that flows through the prāṇa and apāna breaths comes forth.
The bodily machines, smeared with skin, flesh, and bone, and possessing the mind as their charioteer, are drawn along by the reins of desire.
I am this very embodiment of consciousness, which has established no abode anywhere;
let the body fall or rise according to its own desired will.
After a long time, I have become "I"; after a long time, this attainment of my own self has occurred;
after a long time, I go to peace, just as the world does at the end of a kalpa.
Having traveled for a long time along the long path of saṃsāra, I am weary from long exhaustion; I have come to rest like the wind at the end of a kalpa.
Homage again and again to you who transcend all and who are everything;
and let there also be homage to those who speak of you as "I" or as "me."
Victorious is the witness-nature of the Supreme Self, which possesses all infinite enjoyments yet remains untouched by the perceptions of defects, and for which no karmic accumulation has been made.
O Self, you abide everywhere within this body, like fragrance in a flower, like fire in a mass of fuel, and like oil in a sesame seed.
You laugh, you watch, you give, you thunder forth, and you leap;
though you are devoid of the form of egoism, this illusory power of yours is truly wondrous.
Victory to you, O Lord, with your blazing radiance who causes the entire world to open its eyes;
victory to you who once again causes the world to close its eyes, free from all activity.
Within a single atom of yours alone is this entire circle of saṃsāra; and just as the banyan tree exists within the banyan seed, so it has been, it is, and it will be.
Just as a cloud in the sky appears in the form of horses, elephants, and chariots,
so too, O Lord, are you perceived through the delusions of hundreds of objects.
O Lord of Existence, for the sake of the cessation of the manifold states of existence,
become one whose self is liberated from becoming and who stands beyond both existence and non-existence.
Having abandoned pride, intoxication, anger, turbidity, and likewise cruelty,
the great do not sink into the common mire of worldly qualities.
Remembering again and again those former states of long-standing wickedness, laugh with a white burst of laughter like a shower of pearls, thinking: "Who am I? What was that which occurred?"
Those undertakings have departed;
those wasted days are gone, in which you were withered by the mass of flames from the fire of anxiety.
Today you are the king in the city of the body with expansive desires;
you are seized neither by sorrows nor by pleasures, just as the sky cannot be grasped by hands.

Having today conquered the wild horses of the senses and subdued the elephant of the mind, you stand presiding over sovereignty after having utterly crushed the enemies of worldly enjoyment on all sides.
You are the traveler in the boundless sky, eternally rising and setting;
you are the sun that constantly bestows light both externally and internally.
O All-pervading Lord, you are always in a state of deep sleep, yet you are made aware by your own power for the sake of the play of observing enjoyments, just as a lover is awakened by his beloved.
The honey of form, brought from afar by the small bees of sight, is drunk by you after being taken possession of through the power residing in the window of the eyes.
The vital breaths (prāṇa) and downward breaths (apāna), which move within the hollow of the cosmic egg, are observed by you every moment as they go and come within the city of Brahmā.
In the flower of the body you are the fragrance; in the moon of the body you are the nectar of immortality; in the tree of the body you are the sap; and in the ice of the body you are the coolness.
In you there exists an affection consisting of consciousness, like clarified butter within the milk of the body;
you abide within this body like fire within wood.
You are the supreme taste of the waters; you are the luminosity even of the radiant energies; you are the knower of all objects; and you are the illuminator of all lights.
You are the vibration of all the winds; you are the rut of the elephant of the mind;
you are the radiance and the very sharpness of the flame of the fire of wisdom.
By your power, illusion dissolves away somewhere like a lamp;
yet, like a lamp, it arises again from somewhere else.
Likewise, the cycles of objects existing within the realm of saṃsāra reside in you,
just as the forms of bracelets, armlets, and upper-arm ornaments exist in gold.
By means of such words as "you," "this one," "I," and "thou," you yourself playfully praise and speak of the Self by means of the Self.
Just as a cloud driven by a gentle breeze is perceived in the sky by the gaze of elephants, horses, and men,
so too are you perceived by the gaze of all beings.
Just as fire glows with flames in the forms of horses and elephants,
even so do you dwell within creations through the objects of perception, though you are not distinct from them.
You are the unbroken thread stretched across the pearls of the cosmic eggs;
you are the field for the crops of living beings, who are nourished by the elixir of consciousness.
That which was non-existent and unmanifest among objects is revealed by you as reality, just as the taste of meats is perceived by a cook.
Even though the splendor of an object exists, it does not abide in you when you are not present, just as the beauty and charm of a woman's form does not exist for one whose eyes have departed.
Even though it exists here, an object that has not been perceived by you does not lead to satisfaction,
just as one's own beauty, when not reflected in a mirror, does not bring joy.
Without you, this body rolls upon the ground like a piece of wood or a clod of earth;
though it exists, it is seized by non-existence itself, like the night without the sun.
The sequence of pleasure and pain, having reached you, perishes,
just as darkness, heat, or cold vanishes upon encountering light.
These states, such as pleasure and the rest, attain their existence solely through your perception,
just as colors like white and others appear in the morning through the light of the sun.
Having attained their own nature, they perish at the very moment of their connection;
like darkness before a lamp, they utterly vanish as soon as they are seen.
Darkness is clearly perceived as the absence of a lamp;
yet at the very moment of connection with the lamp, that darkness arises and perishes.
In the very same way, the fortune of pleasure and pain, upon seeing you who are free from affliction,
arises the moment it is born and perishes through total destruction.
Because of its fragility, it is not capable of remaining here for even an atom of time,
just like a subtle fraction of time known as a *nimeṣalakṣabhāga*.
The fleeting, perishable, and subtle conception of pleasure, pain, and so forth,
manifests by your grace, yet dissolves once you are seen.
Born at the very moment of beholding you, and perishing at the very moment of beholding you—
by whom could she be perceived as being born already dead, or as being dead even while born?
How could an object that is unstable even for a moment perform a function?
How, indeed, can a garland be woven from waves that have the form of blue lotuses?
If an action were to produce a real entity that perishes as soon as it is born,
then people would begin to fashion garlands out of flashes of lightning.
Abiding in the mind of a person of discernment, you neither grasp nor abandon this fortune consisting of pleasure and the like, remaining equanimous.
O Soul of Existence, you who are undiscriminating, enough of this description of your nature by chance; O abode of the stainless word, [be as you are].
By you— who are effortless, partless, and free from egoism—
agency has been accepted, whether as being or even as non-being.
Victory to you of formidable form! Victory to you who are devoted to peace!
Victory to you who transcend all scriptures! Victory to you who are the foundation of all scriptures!
Victory to you who are born, victory to you who are unborn; victory to you who are wounded, victory to you who are unwounded!
Victory to you who are existence, victory to you who are non-existence; victory to you who are the conquerable, victory to you who are unconquerable!
I exult, I am pacified, I abide, and I have transcended;
I am victorious, I conquer, I live—homage to me, homage be to you!

While you abide in me—my self free from affliction, established in its own nature, and untainted by the dye of passion—where are my kinsmen, where are calamities, and where are prosperities? Where are existence and non-existence? I attain eternal peace.
The thirty-seventh canto in the *Prahlāda-upākhyāna*, titled "Self-Praise," by Vasiṣṭha.
While reflecting thus, Prahlāda, the slayer of enemy heroes,
attained the state of non-conceptual absorption in supreme bliss.
Established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, motionless as if depicted in a painting,
he shone while abiding in his own state, as if carved out of a mountain.
Thus, as he remained in his own home while dwelling in the world, a very long period of time passed for him, like that of the enemy of the gods (Rāhu) staying upon Mount Meru.
Even though he was awakened by the lords of the asuras, the one of great intelligence did not wake up,
just as a sprout does not emerge from its seed-vessel despite abundant watering at the wrong time.
For five thousand years, with broad shoulders and fixed gaze,
he remained perfectly tranquil in the city of the Asuras, like a stone in a turbulent ocean.
Through that state which is exclusively transformed into the condition of supreme bliss,
he has reached the station of manifestation as if it were without manifestation and devoid of bliss.
After such a length of time, that realm of Rasātala became kingless and was tormented by the harsh law of the fishes.
When Hiraṇyakaśipu had perished and his son remained absorbed in meditation,
there was no other king left in the abode of the sons of Danu.
Despite the efforts of those lords of the Asuras seeking him out,
Prahlāda did not wake from his meditative absorption, even with the greatest exertion.
There, the enemies of the gods did not attain their lord, who had assumed a blossoming form,
just as bees at night cannot find a lotus whose mass of luster from its petals is shining.
No wind of consciousness was perceived within that one who had lost his senses,
just as the human effort of movement is no longer felt in the earth when its light has departed.
Then, while the Daityas were agitated and had departed in their desired directions,
they wandered at will through city after city, which was left without a king.
Due to that absence of kings, the circle of the netherworld became overturned by the law of the fishes, and the succession of virtues came to an end.
The city of the weak was devoured by the strong, devoid of all order and restraint;
every woman was possessed by everyone, and they struck one another down.
The interior of the city was distorted and filled with harsh lamentation and wailing; its gardens and palaces lay overturned, tormented by futile calamities.
The hosts of gods were overcome with anxiety, their kinsmen deprived of food and fruit;
helpless before an untimely calamity, the entire circle of the quarters was cast down.
It was humiliated by the sons of the gods, overrun by other spirits, emptied of living beings,
devoid of prosperity, and its hollows were almost entirely ruined.

That host of asuras became utterly distraught— engaged in a battle intoxicated by the pursuit of uncertain women, crying out on all sides because their wealth and wives had been seized, and resembling the gaping bellies of the fierce spirits of the Kali Yuga era.
The thirty-eighth canto, titled "Description of the Destruction of the Asura City," in the *Prahlāda-episode* (from the *Vasiṣṭha*). Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Hari, who delights in protecting the order of the entire web of worlds,
was reclining upon his bed of Śeṣa in the city of the Milk Ocean.
When the sleep of the rainy season had ended, the destroyer of enemies occasionally surveyed the condition of the world with his intellect for the sake of the gods.
Having mentally surveyed both the realm of the gods and the earthly kingdom,
he swiftly proceeded to Pātāla, which was protected by his enemies.
There, while Prahlāda the Dānava remained established in steady concentration, he beheld the calamity that had befallen the lord of his enemies as it reached its full maturity within the city.
By one who moves within the body of Him who rests upon the serpent-couch, reclining on the ocean of milk, and who holds the conch, discus, and mace in His hands.
Seated in the lotus posture, with a mind and body exceedingly radiant, he who was like a great bee to the lotus of the three worlds reflected as follows:
Now that Prahlāda has found rest in his station and the leader has gone to the netherworld (pātāla),
alas, this creation has for the most part become devoid of Daityas.
In the absence of the Daityas, the host of gods will reach a state free from the desire for conquest and will come to rest,
like a great river when the mass of clouds has vanished.
Then, with pride extinguished and devoid of passion, it will reach that state called liberation, which is free from duality, becoming like a withered vine that has reached total desiccation.
When the flood of gods has attained peace, all sacrificial and ascetic acts on earth,
which otherwise bear the fruit of divinity, will undoubtedly come to rest.
Furthermore, when all activities have been stilled, the world of mortals will come to its end;
thereafter, there will be no further involvement in saṃsāra, and only the ultimate goal will remain.
This triple world, which was created by me to endure until the end of the kalpa,
shall go to destruction prematurely through that heat, like a drop of frost.
What is achieved by me here, who have brought about the destruction of my own play, when this manifestation has thus dissolved and come to an end?
Then, in this void where the moon, sun, and stars have perished, I too,
having attained the tranquility of the body, shall abide in that state.
For when the world has thus come to such a state of destruction so unexpectedly, I see no good in this; I think it better that the Dānavas should live.
Then, due to the agitation caused by the Daityas, the gods' performance of sacrifices and austerities was disrupted;
because of that, the established order of the world was altered, and the process of worldly existence became otherwise.
Therefore, having gone to Rasātala, I shall restore the lord of the Dānavas to his own station in due order, just as the season restores the tree.
If, however, I were to kill any other lord of the Dānavas instead of Prahlāda, I think he would then utterly destroy the gods.
But this final body of Prahlāda is great and purifying;
he shall dwell here with this very body until the end of the kalpa.
For such is the divine destiny, certain and ordained by the Supreme Lord:
that an embodied being must abide here according to its own lot, just as Prahlāda did.
Therefore, having gone quickly to that very lord of the Daityas, I shall awaken him,
just as a rain-cloud awakens a peacock sleeping in a mountain cave by its thundering.
Established in the samādhi of one liberated while living, let him exercise lordship over the asuras,
just as a gem, free from mental activity, produces a reflection.
This creation, along with the gods and asuras, shall not perish;
nor shall it exist without duality, for that will be my play.
Although these two—the destruction and the arising of creation—are perfectly equal to me, nevertheless, let this world remain as it is; what does it matter to me otherwise?
That effort which, due to a corrupted intellect, is applied equally toward existence and non-existence, or toward their destruction or their persistence, would be like striking at empty space.
Therefore, I am going to Pātāla to awaken the lord of the Asuras;
I shall bring stability to the cycle of existence and accomplish my divine play.
Having reached the city of the Asuras, which is terrible with its arrogant conduct, I awaken the Daitya as the sun awakens the lotus;
I bring stability to this entire world resting upon me, just as the cloud-season brings steadiness to the mountain by settling the flickering mass of clouds.
The thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Inquiry into the Supreme Lord," from the Narrative of Prahlāda;
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, O Rāma, the Soul of All moved from the Ocean of Milk toward that city,
together with his retinue, like a mountain accompanied by clouds.
Through that very opening at the surface of the Ocean of Milk, whose waters were solidified,
he reached the city of Prahlāda, which was like another realm of Śakra.
Then Hari saw the Asura situated within the treasury of the golden palace,
like the lotus-born Brahmā reclining in a mountain cave, absorbed in meditative concentration.
There, shaken by that Vaiṣṇava splendor, those various Daityas fled far away,
like owls terrified by the rays of the sun.
Accompanied by two or three principal Asuras and surrounded by his retinue,
Hari entered the abode of the Asura, just as the moon with its stars enters the sky.
Seated upon the vehicle of Vainateya, with Lakṣmī waving a chowrie for him,
surrounded by his own weapons and attendants, he is saluted by divine sages.
"O Great-Souled One, awaken!"— uttering these words, Viṣṇu blew his conch Pāñcajanya, making the quarters of the sky resound.
By that great sound, born from the vital breath of Viṣṇu,
which at the same time possessed the force of the ocean and clouds agitated at the end of an eon;
The demonic host fell to the ground in utter confusion,
like a row of royal swans at the roar of a dark, intoxicated cloud.
The assembly of people, filled with joy and free from agitation, rejoiced like a row of *kuṭaja* trees blossoming at the roar of a rain cloud.
The lord of the Dānavas gradually regained his full consciousness,
like a kadamba tree in the forest whose blossoms shine with the roar of clouds.
Then the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), having risen from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), gradually overwhelmed the demon, just as the Gaṅgā overwhelms the entire ocean.
In an instant, the splendor of his vital breath assailed the asura from all sides,
just as the solar radiance, immediately upon its rising, pervades the interior of the world.
Then, as the nine apertures of his vital breaths began to function,
his consciousness became oriented toward objects of thought within, reflected upon the mirror of the vital breath.
When the consciousness was oriented toward volition, *cit* attained the state of *manas*,
O Rāghava, like the beauty of a face reflected in a mirror appears as a duality.
When his mind had slightly sprouted and his eyes were about to open,
they gradually became like two blue lotuses at dawn.
As his consciousness moved through the hollows of the channels touched by the inward and outward breaths,
a throbbing arose within him, like that of a lotus afflicted by the wind.
In merely the blink of an eye, the mind attained fullness,
as it were a wave in water when the breath has become complete within it.
Then, with his eyes, mind, breath, and body blossoming,
he shone like a lake of lotuses when the sun has half-risen.
At that moment, as soon as the Lord said, "Awake!",
he became fully conscious, like a peacock at the sound of thunder.
To him, whose eyes were blossoming, whose mind was awakened, and whose memory was robust,
the Lord of the Three Worlds spoke as he had formerly spoken to the one born from the navel-lotus.
O virtuous one, remember Mahālakṣmī; remember your own form.
Why do you bring about the cessation of the body so abruptly?
For you who are devoid of the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted, what purpose can there be in the presence or absence of states belonging to the body? Arise now! Arise!
"O blameless one, you must remain here with this body for as long as this kalpa lasts; for we know destiny exactly as it is."
Remaining here in this very kingdom as one liberated while living,
you must preserve this body, free from agitation, until the end of the kalpa.
O sinless one, when your body has perished at the end of the aeon, you must abide in your own majesty,
just as the space within a jar remains in the sky when the jar has been shattered.
Abiding until the end of the aeon, pure, and having perceived the higher and lower worlds,
this body of yours has become a playful manifestation of liberation while living.
The twelve suns have not risen, nor have the mountains melted;
the world has not been consumed by fire, O virtuous one—why do you abandon your body in vain?
The wind blows, not mad, grey with the ashes of the three worlds;
marked by the skulls of fickle gods, why do you abandon your body in vain?
Like blossoms on an aśoka tree or lightning from the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, they do not flicker within the vessel of the world; why do you abandon your body in vain?
The quarters of the sky, with mountains resounding under torrential rains and blazing with flaming fires, do not crumble; why then do you abandon your body in vain?
This world does not remain as a residue consisting solely of the triad known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
it stands like a withered cloud—why do you abandon your body in vain?
The clouds of the kalpa do not roar in the sky with a sound as terrifying as the crashing of the great mountain peaks; why then do you abandon your body in vain?
I, whose banner is the bird, dwell with light amidst the beings scattered throughout the ten directions; do not disregard my body.
"We are these, these are the mountains, these are living beings, this is your lordship, this is the world, and this is the sky; do not disregard the body."
For one whose mind is agitated by the application of intense ignorance, sufferings cut him to pieces; for such a person, death is a joy.
"I am emaciated, exceedingly miserable, and deluded"—these and other such thoughts rob one's mind; for such a person, death is a blessing.
One who is bound within by the snares of hope is led here and there by the restless movement of the mind; for such a person, death alone shines forth as the best option.
For one whose heart is shattered by cravings that have carried away his cultivation of mindfulness—
just as sea-monsters destroy a wretched house— for him death is glorious.
For him in whose forest of the mind the creeper of mental fluctuations has grown as high as a palm tree and borne fruit through pleasure and pain, death shines with splendor.
Death shines forth as the great flood of calamities that sweeps away this tree of a body, which possesses the net of the row of body hairs as its foliage.

For him whose forest of his own body is being consumed by the forest fires of mental anguish and physical disease, and whose trembling creeper-like limbs are scorched, death shines as a welcome prospect.
For him in whose body the serpent consisting of desire and anger writhes,
death shines forth as if within a withered tree.
This abandonment of the body is known in the world as death;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, and for those who know the object of knowledge, it is not a cause [of bondage].
The life of that wise person shines, who, seeing things as they truly are, does not turn his mind away from the contemplation of the reality of his own self.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled,
and who is equal toward all things— for him life is truly radiant.
He who, with an inner mind cooled and free from passion and hatred,
beholds this life like a witness— his life indeed shines.
For one who, having correctly understood through thorough discernment what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted,
has placed the mind within the mind— that person’s life shines with splendor.
When the mind is absorbed in that reality which resembles a non-entity and is stainless through the absence of conceptual construction, his life shines forth.
Firmly grasping the true vision, this activity of the world is performed by him as a mere play; his life shines forth, being free from latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).

The life of one who does not feel satisfaction at the end nor undergoes agitation even while living, and who remains equanimous upon encountering what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, is truly radiant.
Just as a flock of swans from a lake belongs to the bright fortnight and is pure,
so too does his life shine forth, from which a flood of virtues flows out.
When he has come within the range of hearing, been seen, or has entered the memory, living beings attain joy; his life is truly radiant.

O Lord of the Danavas, long life shines forth in him—like the fullness of the imperishable moon—by whose rising all the lotuses of people’s hearts, possessing swarms of living beings, blossom; it does not shine for anyone else.
The fortieth canto in the *Prahlāda-upākhyāna*, titled "The Application of the Presentation of the Words of Nārāyaṇa," [spoken by] the Blessed One:
The stability of the perceived body is called "life" by the wise;
the abandonment of the body for the sake of another body is known as "death."
O Mahāmati, you are liberated from both these two sides;
what death is there for you here, or what life do you possess?
This was spoken by me for the sake of illustration, O crusher of enemies;
you do not die, O All-Knowing One, for you never perish.
Though abiding in the body, you are bodiless because you are devoid of embodiment; you possess the vision of the disembodied.
Though abiding in space, you are indeed not space, for like the wind, you are unattached.
O you of noble vows, you are indeed the body because you cause the perception of touch;
and space is the cause of extension by virtue of its obstructing that extension.
Because you have awakened through the knowledge of reality, you both exist and do not exist;
for those who are ignorant, form is limited by finitude and is characterized by suffering.
At all times, you are entirely the singular consciousness whose nature is the light of the Intellect (citprakāśa).
What is this body, or what is this non-body, that you either grasp or abandon?
Whether spring arises or the wind of dissolution blows,
what has come to the Self, which is devoid of both existence and non-existence?
Even when mountains are crumbling, even when the fires at the end of an aeon are burning,
and even when cataclysmic winds are blowing, the self remains established solely within itself.
Let all beings remain, or let them go forth together;
let them perish or let them flourish—the Self remains established in the Self alone.
The supreme Person does not perish when [the body] reaches destruction, nor does he increase when it increases;
he does not quiver even while this body is quivering.
Even when the delusion that "I am the body" or "the body is I" has perished, why does this false conceptualization arise: "I shall abandon it" or "I shall not abandon it"?
"Having done this, I shall do that; having abandoned this, I shall take that"—such volitions, my dear, have come to an end for those who know reality.
Once awakened, being the makers of all things, what indeed will they do anew? Since there is nothing new to be made, they have eternally attained the state of non-agency.
From the absence of agency, the absence of being an enjoyer follows by implication;
indeed, who in these three worlds has ever gathered what was never sown?
When agency and enjoyership have been stilled, indeed only peace remains;
when that very peace has reached full maturity, it is called liberation by the wise.
Awakened, consisting of consciousness, and pure, they abide pervading everything;
what is there to be abandoned that they should take up, or what is there to be grasped that they should abandon?

The relationship between the grasped and the grasper, which constitutes the sequence of the parts of valid cognition, is itself devoid of the parts of the object to be cognized; what, then, could it grasp, and what could it abandon?
When the relationship between the grasped and the grasper has utterly ceased, peace arises fully;
having attained stability within that, it is designated by the name "liberation."
Established therein, the virtuous ones such as you, O Supreme Persons,
always move about indeed by virtue of a similarity to the movement of limbs during deep sleep.
Those whose latent impressions have come to rest through the awakening of others perceive this worldly condition with a mind established in the Self, as if they were half-asleep.
For those whose intentions are focused solely on their own inner self do not take delight in pleasant things,
nor do they tremble at sufferings, because they find a single flavor within their own self.
Ever awakened and free from attachment, they undertake these activities just as they arise, without desire, like mirrors reflecting images.

Established in their own self, they are awake; yet established in the state of worldly existence, they are as if asleep. They act like children, while their inner disposition is like that of deep sleep.
Having reached the state of the Unconquered, having enjoyed for but a single day the splendor of the Lotus-born One,
O Great-Souled One, go now to the supreme abode of Acyuta, which is endowed with a multitude of virtues.
In the *Prahlādopākhyāna*, the forty-first canto, titled "The Instruction of Prahlāda," Vasiṣṭha says:
When Padmanābha, who is like an ocean of jewels for the world and whose sight is a marvel to the three realms, had spoken thus with a voice as cool as moonlight:
That body named Prahlāda, with his lotus-eyes blossoming,
spoke these words gently and firmly, having adopted a course of reflection.
Prahlāda said:
O Lord, for a long time you have been seen by me within with a pure intellect;
by good fortune, O Lord of gods, you are now seen again by my external vision.
O Maheśvara, I existed within this infinite vision,
which is free from all conceptual constructions, like space within pure space.
Neither by grief, nor by delusion, nor by thoughts of dispassion,
nor by the act of abandoning the body, nor by fear of saṃsāra.
For when that One alone exists, whence can there be sorrow? Whence can there be injury?
Whence the body? Where is saṃsāra? Where is stability? And where are fear and fearlessness?
Thus, O Lord, I have dwelt in this vast and pure state solely by my own stainless will.
"Alas, I am dispassionate; I shall renounce saṃsāra"—O Lord, such is the thought of those with unawakened intellects, which brings about the fluctuations of joy and sorrow.
"When there is no body, there are no sufferings; when my body exists, there are sufferings"—this serpent of poisonous thought devours only the fool.
"This is happiness, this is suffering; this does not exist for me, this exists"—a mind thus oscillating is indeed deluded, not wise.
The latent impressions of ignorance that cause one to think "I am indeed different from another" are cast far away by those of superior intellect, just as the nights are dispelled by the suns.
The false delusion of the mind that "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted" does not lead to madness within one who knows, as it does the ignorant person of wicked intellect.
O lotus-eyed one, when you have pervaded the entire self,
how can there be a second conceptualization consisting of the categories of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted?
The entire world appears as consciousness, existing as both being and non-being;
what is there to be rejected and what is there to be accepted, such that it is either abandoned or not?
Investigating the seer and the seen solely through their own intrinsic natures,
I rested for a moment within myself, by means of the self, in the Self.
Freed from existence and non-existence, devoid of that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted—
thus was I previously, and now I am established in this state.
O Great God, since you have attained peace within yourself and have reached the state of all-pervading being that belongs to the virtuous, I shall do whatever pleases you.
O lotus-eyed one, you are indeed worthy of worship throughout the three worlds;
therefore, you ought to accept from me this honor which has come to you as is fitting.

Having spoken thus before the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, the lord of the Dānavas presented a vessel for the guest-offering (argha-pātra), like a king of mountains offering the full moon.
Then he worshipped Govinda, who was at the forefront of the three worlds, together with his weapons, the host of Apsarases, the gods, and the lord of birds.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Worlds, who has pervaded all worlds both external and internal, the Lord of Kamalā spoke to him as he sat there.
The Blessed One said:
"Arise, O Lord of the Dānavas, take your place upon the lion-throne;
I myself shall soon bestow the consecration upon you."
May those Siddhas, Sādhyas, and hosts of gods who have assembled here upon hearing the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, bring you auspiciousness.
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one joined the Dānava upon the lion-throne at the conclusion of his yoga, like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Then Hari [honored him] with the great oceans, such as the Kṣīroda and others, summoned there;
likewise with the floods of rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and with the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
Accompanied by all the assemblies of brahmin seers and likewise by all the hosts of siddhas,
joined by sages and vidyādharas, and attended by the world-protectors.
The immeasurable-souled one consecrated the great asura in the sovereignty of the Daityas,
while he was being praised by the hosts of Maruts, just as Hari had been in a previous creation.
While being praised by the gods and asuras, Madhusūdana spoke these words to Prahlāda, who was himself being praised by the gods and asuras at his consecration.

The Blessed One said: "O sinless one, as long as Mount Meru endures, as long as the earth remains, and as long as the orbs of the moon and sun exist, so long shall you remain a king, praised for your unimpaired virtues."
Having abandoned the fruits of the desirable and the undesirable with a mind of equanimous vision,
protect the kingdom, free from passion, fear, and anger.
In this kingdom, which is filled with enjoyments and where the supreme ground has been seen,
you should not feel agitation whether regarding heaven or hell.
O friend, remaining established in the task at hand according to the views obtained through place, time, and action, abide with all latent tendencies abandoned.
That which is not taken because it is utterly fit to be abandoned, and from which the sense of "mine" has been completely relinquished—
performing actions here with equanimity toward both existence and non-existence, you are not bound.
Having seen the full extent of saṃsāra and having weighed the incomparable state of the Tathāgata, you know everything everywhere; what else remains to be taught?
While you, free from passion, fear, and anger, reign as king,
the earth shall no longer drink the blood of demons, as it did when she was ruled by the greedily grasping Durgṛdhri.
The beauty of his tears will not fail to captivate the ears of the Asuras,
just as a river with its rising current and lofty waves sweeps away a row of forest trees.
From this day forward, the world shall remain at peace, with the conflict between Dānavas and gods completely stilled, like the ocean when Mount Mandara is no longer used as a churning-stick.
Let the wives of the gods and asuras, brought together within their own harems and among their husbands, place their mutual trust in one another.
O son of Danu, having dispelled the darkness of the deep sleep of existence through many nights, and possessing the splendor of a mind ever-risen [in virtue],
enjoy for a long time the unconquered royal fortune, which is as delightful as the amorous play of celestial damsels.
The forty-second canto, titled "The Coronation of Prahlāda," in the *Prahlāda-episode* of Vasiṣṭha’s work.
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one, together with men, gods, and kinnaras,
moved from the abode of the asuras like a second cycle of worldly existence.
Afterwards, the mass of feathers on the back of the Lord of Birds was filled with handfuls of flowers offered by Prahlāda and others who had been liberated.
Having reached the Ocean of Milk in due course and dismissed the celestial river,
he sat upon the seat of the serpent's coils like a bee upon a white lotus.
Viṣṇu sat upon the seat of the serpent’s coils, Śakra remained in heaven with the immortals, and the lord of the Dānavas stayed in the netherworld; thus they all remained, free from anxiety.
O Rāma, this attainment of awakening, which destroys all impurities without exception, which belongs to Prahlāda, and which is as cooling as the liquid moon, has been told to you.
For those humans in this world who, even though they have committed many evil deeds,
shall contemplate this with their intellect, they will attain the state before long.
Through general inquiry, evil karma comes to an end;
through inquiry into the words of yoga, who would not attain the supreme state?
Ignorance is said to be evil, and it perishes through inquiry;
therefore, one should not abandon inquiry, for it cuts away the very root of evil.
For those men who contemplate this perfection of Prahlāda,
the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes undoubtedly reach their destruction.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, how was the mind of the high-souled Prahlāda awakened when it had become absorbed in the supreme state through the sounds of the Pāñcajanya conch?
Vasiṣṭha:
O sinless one, two kinds of liberation are possible in this world. One is with the body, the other is without the body; hear now this distinction between them.
Know that the state of one whose mind is unattached to the taking up and casting off of actions, and who is free from longing, is liberation while living in this world.
O Rāma, that very state, when the body has perished and is free from rebirth, is called Videhamukti; established in that, they do not come within the range of the visible world.
Like parched seeds, devoid of the sprouts of future birth,
the pure latent impression (vāsanā) of those liberated while living resides in the heart.
Purifying, supremely noble, and following after the mere essence of being,
she who consists of meditation on the Self remains eternally as if in a state of deep sleep.
O scion of Raghu’s line, even at the end of a thousand years, those who are liberated while living awaken within that very body which remains as an intermediate state.
O mighty-armed one, Prahlāda attained awakening through his own internal, pure sattvic impression, awakened by the sound of a conch shell.
For Hari is indeed the self of all beings; whatever manifests to him becomes exactly so immediately, since the self alone is the cause in all things.
As soon as Vāsudeva thought, "May Prahlāda attain awakening," at that very moment it occurred within the blink of an eye.
Without cause for himself, yet as the cause of all beings, he has assumed that body by his own self for the purpose of creation; that is the nature of Vāsudeva.
Through the contemplation of the Self, Mādhava is quickly perceived;
through the propitiation of Mādhava, the Self itself is quickly beheld.
Firmly grasping this view, quickly sport as the Virāj-self in the perception of the Self of Rāghava; you shall attain the eternal state.
O Rāma, this vast rainy season of worldly existence, filled with the showers of pleasure,
bestows supreme dullness upon one who does not behold the sun of discernment.
By the grace of Viṣṇu himself, this exceedingly radiant illusion does not afflict the wise, just as a female spirit does not affect one who possesses the protective mantra.

O sinless one, this infinite illusion that weaves the net of saṃsāra attains density within by its own will, and in time, it reaches thinness by its own will, just as the flame of a fire does through the movement of the wind.
The forty-third canto, titled "The Consolation of Prahlāda," [from] Rāmāyaṇa:
O Blessed One, Knower of all phenomena, we have been brought to fulfillment by the pure rays of your words,
just as medicinal herbs are by the rays of the moon.
Your words, which are soft, pure, and longed for by the ears, adorn those who receive them like flowers held in the hand.
If everything is attained through human effort,
O Prahlāda, then why was he not enlightened without the grace of Mādhava?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever was attained by the high-souled Prahlāda, O Rāghava, all that was achieved by him through manly effort alone, and not otherwise.
The Self and Nārāyaṇa are indeed not distinct, like sesame seeds and their oil;
likewise, they are like whiteness and a cloth, or like a flower and its fragrance.
For he who is Viṣṇu is indeed the Self, and he who is the Self is Janārdana;
the words "Viṣṇu" and "Self" are synonyms, just as "tree" and "woodland plant" are.
First, by his own self through his own supreme power, he himself was appointed to devotion toward Viṣṇu under the name Prahlāda.
For Prahlāda himself acquired this boon by his own effort;
he himself performed the deliberation and he himself conquered his mind.
Sometimes the Self awakens itself by its own power;
sometimes it is awakened by the body of Viṣṇu, which is attainable through devotion.
Even though he has been propitiated for a long time and is supremely pleased,
Mādhava is unable to bestow knowledge upon one who lacks discernment.
In the vision of one's own Self, inquiry arising from human effort is primary;
causes such as divine grace are secondary. Be intent upon the primary cause.
Therefore, having first forcibly subdued the five senses,
make the mind possessed of discernment through practice and every effort.
Whatever is encountered by anyone anywhere indeed results from the operation of one's own power; it is never obtained from any other source.
Relying on human effort and having leaped over the mountain of the senses,
cross the ocean of saṃsāra and go to the further shore, the supreme state.
If Janārdana were perceived without human effort,
why does that Unborn One not rescue the multitude of beasts and birds?
If the Guru rescues the ignorant man even without his own human effort,
why does he not likewise rescue camels, tamed oxen, and bulls?
Nothing great is obtained from Hari, nor from the Guru, nor from wealth,
for one whose mind is overcome by oneself— that which is not attained from the Self.
That which is attained from the Self— when it is joined with practice and dispassion and the serpent of the senses has been subdued— is not attained even from the three worlds.
Propitiate the Self by means of the self; worship the Self by means of the self.
Beholding the Self by means of the self, abide in the Self by means of your own self.
For fools who flee from the study of scriptures, effort, and inquiry,
devotion to Viṣṇu has been fashioned as a means for engaging them in virtuous conduct.
First, the primary method is said to consist of practice and effort;
in its absence, however, there is the secondary method, which is the sequence consisting of the worship of the worshipful.
If there is no mastery over the senses, what is the use of worship, the worshipper, and the object of worship?
If there is no mastery over the senses, what is the use of worship, the worshipper, and the object of worship?
For without inquiry and tranquility, Hari is not attained;
and for one endowed with both inquiry and tranquility, what need is there for the lotus-handed Lord?
Cultivate your own mind so that it is endowed with discernment and tranquility;
when that is accomplished, you are accomplished, otherwise you are but a wild donkey in the forest.
Since devotion and entreaty are directed toward Mādhava and others for the sake of a request, why is that same devotion not directed toward one's own mind?
Viṣṇu resides within every single person;
those who go outside, abandoning Him, are not wise.
The reality of consciousness (cittattva) dwelling in the cave of the heart is the primary, eternal body;
the form with conch, discus, and mace in hand is merely a secondary manifestation of the Self.
For he who, abandoning the primary, pursues the secondary, is like one who,
having rejected a perfected elixir, strives instead to achieve something that must still be accomplished.
But he who does not attain stability in this wondrous state of self-knowledge, O descendant of Raghu, remains one whose mind is intoxicated by delusion.
One who has not attained discrimination regarding the self, being ignorant within and enslaved by the mind,
worships the Lord of the Immortals, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands.
O Raghava, through the worship of that [deity] and through arduous austerity,
his mind attains purity in due time by means of the water of dispassion.
Through constant practice and discernment, the mind quickly becomes serene;
it gradually reaches the state of the mango tree itself, which possesses the sahakāra fruit.
O destroyer of enemies, even this fruit, which has been cultivated by the self itself, is obtained by the self through the instrumental cause known as the sequence of worshiping Hari.
Even he who obtains a boon from Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor has thereby obtained the fruit of his own tree of practice.
The restraint of one's own mind is the ground for all supreme goals and for all long-enduring prosperities, just as the soil is the ground for the beauty of the harvest.
Even for one who digs into the earth or scrapes away at a mountain,
there is no means here for destroying suffering other than the restraint of one's own mind.
Human beings wander upon this earth for thousands of births as long as the great ocean of the intoxicated mind does not reach stillness.
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others, though worshipped for a long time and being full of affection, cannot protect one from the mental affliction that has overwhelmed the mind.
Abandoning both the external and the internal— which shine with various forms— and which are unborn,
quickly practice the contemplation of pure consciousness alone for the sake of the destruction of birth.

Taste that which consists solely of the one, stainless consciousness, free from all objects of perception, infinite in form, and the pure essence of existence; you shall reach the further shore of the river of birth.
In the *Prahlādopākhyāna*, the chapter titled "The Conclusion of Prahlāda’s Rest" is the forty-fourth chapter. Vasiṣṭha said:
This illusion called saṃsāra is endless;
it comes to an end only through the conquest of one's own mind, and not otherwise.
O sinless one, listen attentively as I relate this history for the purpose of understanding the manifold variety of the world’s illusory expansion.
On this surface of the earth, there is a province named Kosala, which,
like the forest of the wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru, is a source of multitudes of jewels.
There lived a certain virtuous Brahmin known as Gādhi,
a supreme master of the Vedas and wise, who was like the Veda itself incarnate.
From his childhood, he shone with a mind utterly detached,
just as the world is illuminated by a stainless and pure sky.
Having set aside some cherished undertaking in his mind,
he departed from his circle of kinsmen and went to the forest to practice austerities.
There, that king of brahmins reached a lake filled with blossoming lotuses,
like the moon reaching the sky, which is bright, stainless, and studded with stars.
To behold Āśauṣi, the twice-born dwelt at that lake for the sake of asceticism,
submerged up to his neck in water like a lotus in the rainy season.
Eight months passed for him as he remained submerged in the waters of the lake,
his facial complexion shattered by bees that had been drawn to the lotus-like flesh and were now clinging to the tips of his protruding bones.
Then, once, Hari approached him who was heated by his asceticism,
just as a dark cloud approaches the earth's surface when it is distressed by the summer heat during the rainy season.
The Blessed One said:
"Arise from the midst of the milk; take the boon you desire.
The tree of your self-restraint has borne the fruit you wished for."
The Brahmin said:
Homage to Viṣṇu, the bee within the hollow of the heart-lotuses of the countless beings of the world, and the lake for the single lotus-pond of the three worlds.
O Blessed One, I desire to behold this supreme illusion arising from you, which is wondrous and known by the name of saṃsāra.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"When you see this as an illusion, then you shall abandon it," and having spoken thus, the Unborn vanished from sight like a city of the Gandharvas.
When Viṣṇu had departed, that lordly Brāhmaṇa rose up from the water,
like the moon emerging from the waters of the Milky Ocean due to his cool and stainless form.
His soul became completely satisfied by the sight of the Lord of the World,
like a night-lotus blossoming at the sight and touch of the moon.
Then, some days passed for him in that forest,
filled with the joy of beholding the monkey and engaged in the duties of a brahmin.
Once, he began his bath in a lake where lotuses had blossomed,
reflecting upon the words of Viṣṇu within his mind like a great ṛṣi.
Then, during the ritual of bathing, he performed a circumambulation within the water for the sake of destroying all his sins.

During that rite performed within the water, having forgotten his meditation, mantras, and intellect, and with the expansion of his consciousness overturned, he, situated in the midst of the water, saw this:
He saw himself dead, having become devoid of gentleness in his own home,
fallen by the force of the wind like a tree into the interior of a mountain cave.
Released by the flow of inhalation and exhalation, it has reached its end;
the vibration of its limbs is completely stilled, like a grove in a windless place.
With a pale face, withered like a sapless leaf from a tree,
he had become a corpse, devoid of joy, like a lotus whose stalk has been severed.
In the morning, the sky appeared as if its vision were inverted, like one sinking into it;
the village seemed as if under a drought, grey with dust on all sides.
It was surrounded by distressed kinsmen, their faces drenched with tears, wailing piteously like ospreys surrounding a tree.
He was attended at his feet by his wife, who resembled a lotus pond whose lotus faces were withering as water flowed away from the breach of the dam.
His mother, bewildered by wailing, crying, weeping, lamenting, and talking,
seized him by the chin, which was marked with fresh signs.
He was surrounded by other wretched people standing at his side with tear-streaming faces,
clinging to him like trees with withered leaves from which the dew is dripping.
It was covered by limbs stretched out far away, as if they were not their own, as though intent on avoiding union out of fear of separation.
With their lips not touching one another, they smiled slowly with teeth that seemed to have lost their luster, as if laughing at their own lives.
He was as if entered into silent meditation, as if carved from the mud;
he was slumbering for the sake of awakening, as if resting profoundly.
He seemed to listen with effort to the cries uttered amidst the tumultuous clamor of his kinsmen’s lamentation, as if to discern the nature of their affection.
Then, with gestures agitated by wailing like the waves of that moment,
they beat their breasts and were drenched in tears from their swollen eyes.
Gradually, by his own kinsmen who were agitated and making hoarse cries like those of female ospreys,
that inauspicious one was driven out so as never to be seen again.
It was led to the cremation ground, stained with the mire of congealed fat,
and crowded with hundreds of skeletons— some dry, some half-dry, and others decayed and putrid.

The sun’s rays were shrouded by vultures like clouds; the darkness was dispelled by the blazing of the funeral pyre; and the earth was made to sprout with a network of flames from the mouths of hundreds of jackals.
It was bathed in flowing rivers of blood, where cormorants, herons, vultures, and fierce crows were swimming;
there, aged birds were caught in a web-like net formed by the spreading of strings still wet with blood.
There, in that blazing fire, his kinsmen reduced the corpse to ashes, just as the oceans do with the submarine fire by pouring forth floods of water.
And the funeral pyre, possessing a mass of swelling flames like tangled roots, quickly consumed that corpse with crackling and popping sounds, as if it were dry fuel.
The fire, pervading the mass of clouds with its intensely crackling roar and spreading fragrance,
shattered the heap of bones on all sides, like an elephant crushing a bamboo grove from which its thick sap has been vomited out through the hollows.
In the account of Gādhi, the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Destruction of Gādhi," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Gādhi, with a mind made clear by his own intense concentration, beheld [him] within his own stainless self while still standing within the water.
The women of the outcaste Śvapacas, who dwell on the outskirts of villages as far as the Hūna territories, perceived themselves agitated while still within the womb.
Overcome by the fear of dwelling in the womb, its delicate limbs tormented,
it lies within the heart of a dog-cooker like a sprout in dog-dung.
In due time, through gradual ripening, she gave birth to one of dark complexion, as a dog-cooker woman might give birth to a cloud in the rainy season— dark-hued and covered with impurities.
In the house of a dog-cooker (śvapaca), he saw the child, beloved by the dog-cookers,
moving here and there like the overflowing waters of the Yamunā.
He had reached the age of twelve, yet remained fixed at sixteen;
with broad shoulders and noble limbs, he was as full-bodied as a rain cloud.
Accompanied by a retinue of dogs, he roamed from forest to forest,
slaughtering hundreds of thousands of deer and maintaining the lifestyle of a Paulinda hunter.
Then he was approached by the beloved of a dog-cooker (śvapaca), who resembled a creeper clinging to a tamāla tree, adorned with clusters of breasts and hands like fresh sprouts.
With his dark-complexioned new beloved, whose pure garland was a network of budding sprouts, and whose limbs were agitated by abundant amorous play; MU_5,45.9.
He was sporting at the edges of the forests with that ever-new bride,
like a dark bee with a female bee amidst the abundance of flowers.
Clad in garments of fresh leaves from the creepers, it appeared like the formidable Vindhya forest itself, having arrived in personified form to bring about another calamity.
Resting in forest thickets, sleeping in mountain caves,
hidden in leafy bowers, and making its home among the shrubs.
Abounding with *kiṅkirāta* flowers as ear-ornaments, adorned with garlands of jasmine,
made beautiful by *ketaka* flowers worn as crests, and filled with garlands of mango blossoms.
He had sported upon beds of flowers and wandered along the shores of the ocean;
he was an expert in the bowers of the forest and highly skilled in the killing of deer.
Then, upon the mountains, he brought forth sons who were the sprouts of his own lineage,
yet whose final results were exceedingly harsh, like thorns on a *khadira* tree.
Though he possesses a wife and is prosperous, he stands with his youth exhausted,
gradually falling into decrepitude like a dry land deprived of rain.
Then, having gone to his birthplace, the village of Hūṇahata,
he stayed there like a lord of sages, having constructed a small hut from leaves at a distance.
Having reached a state of extreme decrepitude through old age, one's own body and children become like a withered *tāla* tree in a ravine whose sap has almost entirely dried up.
The household life of the outcaste had become mature, possessing many kinsmen,
and had reached a state of supreme growth like a forest thicket of *karañja* trees.
Then Gādhi beheld all those wives of his,
who were like aged dog-cookers, causing delusion even to himself.
That wife was carried away entirely by him, who was filled with intense passion,
just as a mass of forest leaves is swiftly swept away by a driving gale.
Alone in the forest, emaciated by suffering, he laments like a deer separated from its herd— despairing and with eyes full of tears.
Having spent some days there with a mind overwhelmed by grief,
he abandoned his own country, just as a bird leaves a lake whose lotuses have withered.
Free from attachment yet filled with reflection, he wandered through many lands,
as if impelled by another, like a cloud driven by the wind.
Once, while wandering through the empty sky like an immortal in his celestial chariot, he reached the glorious city of Kīra in the region of the parrots.
With its paths covered by dancing jewel-garments, its trees and creepers like women,
strewn with flowers up to the ankles, it was as beautiful as the interior of the Nandana grove.
In that city, he reached the royal highway, which was crowded with vassals, women, and citizens, and resembled the path to heaven.
There he beheld the auspicious elephant, its stable constructed of precious gems, moving restlessly like a stainless king of mountains.
When the king had died, he wandered here and there for the sake of the kingdom,
like a connoisseur of jewels on earth seeking the wish-fulfilling gem.
That outcaste gazed for a long time at that naga with eyes wide with curiosity, seeing him motionless like a mountain, yet possessed of subtle movement.
Taking him who was looking on with his trunk,
that elephant respectfully placed him upon its own shoulder, just as Mount Meru places the sun upon its slope.
When he had ascended the palanquin, victory drums resounded on all sides,
like the great oceans roaring when the clouds of the end of the eon have risen into the sky.
The king shone with his desires fulfilled, while the sound of the people crying "Victory!
was like the warbling of birds awakened in a garden.
Then there arose from the throngs of bards a dense clamor,
like the roar of oceans whose waters are tossed by the shore.
There, beautiful women restrained him for the sake of adornment,
just as waves rising from the Ocean of Milk restrain Mount Mandara with the jewels they have brought up.
The proud women filled him with various jewels strung with threads of virtue,
just as the shorelines, rich in the power of diverse lusters, fill the coastal mountains.
With necklaces that had the cool touch of frost, those dark-complexioned women adorned him, as autumnal rains adorn a lofty mountain peak with the surges of new rivers.
With their sprout-like hands trembling, the women surrounded him with flowers of various colors and fragrances, as if they were the very splendor of spring adorning the forest.
With ointments of various colors, tastes, and fragrances, they quickly anointed him with masses of luster,
just as mountain slopes are covered by clouds born of mineral ores.
Beautiful as a jewel and gold, he took up the extended parasol;
like Mount Meru filling the sky with twilight clouds, stars, the moon, and rivers, he filled the heavens.
Adorned with playful young creepers and covered with flowers of jewels and silken garments, he shone like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
All the subjects, accompanied by their retinues, approached him who was in such a state, just as travelers approach a blossoming tree by the roadside.
Having reached that lion-throne in due order, they consecrated him upon that very elephant, just as the immortals consecrated Śakra upon Airāvaṇa.
Thus that outcaste obtained the kingdom within the city of Kīra,
just as a crow seizes a plump deer in the forest that has lost its life-breath.
His lotus-feet were rubbed by the lotus-palms of Kīrī,
and with saffron unguents applied to all his limbs, he was as beautiful as an evening cloud.
In the city of Kīra, that king, surrounded by the women of the city, blazed like a lion accompanied by a pride of lionesses in a forest in full bloom.
With his body adorned by clusters of pearls from the necklaces of women whose passion had been destroyed by Hari, and with his anxiety and dejection stilled,
he took delight there in great pleasures, like an elephant scorched by the heat of the sun’s rays finding relief in the full waters of a lake.
