With his royal majesty spread abroad and his commands established in every direction, having within a few days secured the administration of the country,
he became the king there by the name of Gavala, having fully assumed the entire burden of sovereignty by the subjects.
The forty-sixth canto, titled "The Attainment of the Kingdom," in the account of Gādhi; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.
Surrounded by playful women, honored by the circle of ministers, saluted by all the vassal lords, and adorned with the royal parasol and fly-whisks; //MU_5,46.1//
There, beloved by the teachings of the perfected ones, having understood the sequence of the qualities of sovereignty,
he attained the great station, free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue.
Having forgotten his own power, he was constantly [absorbed] by hymns of praise and auspicious rites,
as if utterly intoxicated by liquors through a state of being completely filled with bliss.
The outcaste ruled the kingdom among the parrots for eight years;
during that time, he maintained the conduct of an Arya in its entirety.
Then, on one occasion, he stood by chance with his ornaments cast aside,
like the sky when it is free from darkness and filled with the light of the stars, the moon, and the sun, as well as with clouds.
He considered his many necklaces, armlets, garments, and so forth as nothing;
a mind fortified by sovereignty does not delight in external acquisitions.
Wearing that same attire, he alone went out to the outer courtyard,
like the sun moving toward the horizon from the highest part of the sky.
There he saw a group of outcaste dog-cookers, dark as clouds and stout,
singing softly like a flock of cuckoos at the onset of spring.
With the playful movement of his sprout-like hands, he shook the cymbals and lute strings,
just as a tree shakes a swarm of bees that hum sweetly.
Then, from that [place], the leader of the outcasts rose up, aged and with bloodshot eyes,
like a horn of glass filled with snow.
Uttering "Just as you wish! suddenly, out of joy, he placed his hand upon the tip of the king's knee, like a crow alighting on a creeper.
And he said this to the lord of the parrots: "O friend, O Kaṭañjaka!
Where have you been? By good fortune you are seen today, after such a long time, my kinsman!"
Where have you rested for so long a time in the midst of the forest,
abandoned by your circle of kinsmen, all alone like a cuckoo?
In this world, does the king perhaps honor you, who are skilled in the art of song and possess a melodious voice,
as one full of passion honors the cuckoo?
Or does he perhaps fill [me] with gifts of houses, clothes, and food,
as the spring fills the tamāla branch with the juices of its fruits and leaves?
By the sight of you today, I have attained supreme bliss,
like a lotus at sunrise, or like the ocean at the rising of the moon.
The sight of a kinsman is the ultimate limit of all joys without exception, of all great gains, and of all infinite rests.
While the dog-cooker was speaking thus, the king, for his part,
showed his disregard by means of various gestures appropriate to the occasion.
Meanwhile, the beloved women at the windows,
as well as the subjects, having realized that he was a dog-cooker (śvapaca), fell into a state of profound despondency.
The citizens did not shine, like lotuses under a shower of frost, like villages beset by drought, or like great mountains engulfed by forest fires.
The king disregarded that conversation concerning his own kinsmen,
just as a lion ignores the yowling of a cat perched on the top of a tree.
He quickly entered the inner apartments, which were filled with dejected people,
just as a royal swan enters a lake whose lotuses have withered from lack of rain.
He reached a state of exhaustion pervading every limb,
like a tree whose great hollow within its trunk is filled with fire.
There he saw all the people with dejected faces,
like a cluster of saffron flowers whose roots have been gnawed away by a rat.
Then the ministers, the citizens, and the women did not even look upon that lord of the earth as he stood there, as if he were a corpse in his very home.
And his servants, though bound by deep affection, abandoned him from afar without offering him respect,
like one distressed by a child’s corpse.
Those who were not agitated thought much of him as one whose face was joyless, whose body was dark, who was bereft of splendor, and who resembled a scorched wasteland.
As his body was emitting smoke,
the people, overcome by a state of distress, did not approach his side, as if he were a mountain of fire.
Arising from a lack of vigor and devoid of collective strength,
these commands of his reached their end like drops of water upon ashes.
Because he had the appearance of one who performs cruel deeds and because his company bestowed inauspiciousness,
people fled from him in particular, as if from a *rākṣasa*.
Even while situated in the midst of people, he remained all alone,
devoid of wealth and other such qualities, like a traveler in a foreign land.
Even though he cried out loudly, the city-dwellers gave him no reply,
just as travelers ignore a whistling bamboo flute, even though it is adorned with a lattice of pearls.
Now, having been defiled by our association with the dog-cookers for a long time, we have not been purified by expiatory rites; therefore, we shall enter the fire.
Having thus resolved, the citizens and ministers in the city set ablaze hundreds of thousands of funeral pyres on all sides.
Then, as those [fires] blazed on all sides like stars in the sky,
the entire city became filled with men who were nothing but wailing.
The multitude of people ready to leap into the blazing pit was held back by their wives, who were crying out piteously and shedding streams of tears.
With the wailing of the attendants for the ministers who had entered the fire-pits,
the streets resounded with cries and the pits echoed with noise, like a forest stirred by the winds.
The air was thick with the scent of the flesh of eminent Brahmins roasted on funeral pyres, while a portentous whirlwind shook up clouds of ashes that appeared like falling frost.
The sky was covered by entrails wafted along by the wind, smelling of long-standing fat and filled with birds, appearing like clouds obscuring the sun.
The circle of cities blazed with funeral pyres fanned by the wind,
while the quarters of space were overspread by stars that were swarms of flying sparks of fire.
With heedlessness as its thief, with weeping children and slain youths, with terrified citizens who have abandoned all hope for life, it is a state of total disorder.
The city was filled with unprotected homes whose entire stores had been plundered by thieves,
and its citizens were distracted by death, having abandoned their sons and wives.
While that painful reversal of destiny was thus occurring—
a state resembling the end of an aeon, bringing about the destruction of all living beings—
Gavala, his intellect purified by contact with virtuous people in the kingdom,
reflected while his mind was agitated by grief.
For my sake, this great calamity has come to pass in this land—
an untimely event equal to the end of an aeon, which shall destroy all its leaders.
What is the use of my miserable life? Death is a great festival for me;
for a wretched creature condemned by the world, death is better than life.
Having thus resolved, Gavala, before the blazing fire,
offered his body as a libation without agitation, like a moth.

When that body named Gavala had fallen by force into the mass of fire and reached a state of being overwhelmed by its various parts, Gādhi suddenly regained consciousness within the water, following the throbbing sensation of the burning fire that was scorching his own limbs.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The forty-seventh canto, titled "The Loss of the Kingdom," in the narrative of Gādhi; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha:
Then, after two moments, Gādhi’s agitation caused by the weight of his mental anguish subsided,
like the swelling of the ocean at the shore.
Due to his confusion regarding the creation of milk, he desisted from that,
just as Brahmā desists from the fashioning of the world at the time of the end of a kalpa.
Having become tranquil, he gradually attained awakening, his intellect now alert and steady,
just as one whose life-force has matured does when intoxication has subsided.
He perceived: "This is I," "This is the task," and "This is not [the task]," just as people see when the night has passed and the veil of darkness has been destroyed.
Having regained his natural state, he raised his face from within the water,
like the spring month of Mādhava raising a lotus when its soul has awakened at the end of winter.
Beholding this earth, which possessed forests, rivers, and the sky, as if it were something entirely different before him, he was filled with supreme wonder.
"Who am I? What do I see? What indeed have I done?"—reflecting thus upon the painting, he remained for a moment with his eyebrows knitted.
"Having perceived this agitation in just a moment,
and having thus understood, he rose from the water like the rising sun."
And he thought upon the bank: "Where is my mother? Where is my beloved, since I have met my death in the midst of both my mother and my wife?"
Indeed, both parents of me, the ignorant child, have perished—
like a leaf carried away by the wind, with its creeper and tree consumed by fire.
I am unmarried and I do not even know the true nature of women,
who are as corrupting and agitating as wine, like a twice-born man [who has renounced].
Therefore, what indeed have I seen that is unreal—
this flurry of various undertakings, like a city of the Gandharvas?
Let this matter rest; for this state of existence, though surrounded by kinsmen, is indeed death itself.
In this slight delusion of *māyā*, not even a trace of reality is perceived.
Thus, the mind of embodied beings perpetually wanders among infinite false perceptions, like a frenzied tiger roaming through forest thickets.
Disregarding that delusion of the mind, Gādhi then led him for several days to his own hermitage.
Once, a certain guest fond of food came to Gādhi;
like Durvāsas coming to Brahmā, he rested there, weary from his journey.
That guest was brought to the highest satisfaction by Gādhi with the juices of fruits and flowers, just as a tree is nourished by spring.
Then, having performed their twilight devotions and completed their prayers, both of them reached their beds in due order and lay upon soft sprouts.
Then a conversation appropriate to their own duties proceeded between those two ascetics,
like the beauty of flowers belonging to two seasons of their respective months.
Then Gādhi questioned his guest with words that arose from the context:
"O Brahmin, why are you so emaciated in body, and why are you so full of fatigue?"
The guest said: "O Blessed One, hear the cause of my extreme emaciation and fatigue;
I shall tell you the truth, for we are not speakers of untruth."
On this surface of the earth, in a bower of the northern quarter,
there is a great and glorious country, highly renowned by the name of Kīra.
There I dwelt for a month, being honored by the people in the city, while my own mind-vetāla was deluded by its craving for infinite flavors.
Once, on a certain occasion during the course of a conversation there, one person said:
"O twice-born, it has been told to me that there was once a king here who was a dog-eater (śvapaca) for eight years."
Then, when I questioned them, all the inhabitants of the villages told me:
"A dog-eater became king here for eight years."
Having fully understood that very [truth], he entered the fire with speed;
thereafter, hundreds of brahmins here likewise entered the sacrificial fire.
Having heard this from their mouths, O twice-born one, I emerged from that circle and performed an expiatory rite at Prayāga for the sake of purification.
Having performed the breaking of my fast today on the third day at the conclusion of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, I have come here; because of that, I am exhausted and exceedingly emaciated.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this, Gādhi then questioned that twice-born man again, and he told him exactly the same thing, not otherwise.
Then Gādhi, filled with wonder, spent that night there;
and when the sun, the great lamp of the world-house, had reached its rising, he departed.

When the morning rites had been performed and the guest, having taken his leave, had departed quickly, he reflected upon this with a mind uplifted by wonder: *idaṃ sañcintayām āsa vismayoddhurayā dhiyā //* (MU 5.47.31)
"That which was seen by me in my agitation is indeed the truth and the reality; it was told to me by the twice-born one. What indeed could this be other than the method of Māyāśambara?"
That death of my own which I witnessed in the midst of my kinsmen was surely an illusion; there is no doubt of this, for I now perceive the truth in what remains.
Therefore, with an undaunted mind, I shall go quickly to the village on the border of the Hūna region in order to see that account of the Ātmaśvapaca.
Reflecting thus, he rose with reverence to depart for another mandala,
as if the sun were preparing to behold the side of Mount Meru.
Having set out on his path, he traversed many lands with the speed of a monsoon torrent, like a wave driven by the wind.
The young camel, seeking a multitude of thorns, entered the Hūṇa territory— a land of the customs of hollow people— just as one enters a forest of *kārañja* trees.
There, with his very consciousness remaining steady, he beheld before him a certain village, like a city of the Gandharvas.
At its edge, he beheld that very same dwelling of the outcaste,
like a multitude of hells in the netherworld beneath the three worlds.
Like a Gandharva city, he beheld that city of the Lord of the Śvapacas, which consisted of a vast array of variegated mental constructions.
In that very same configuration, he beheld the dwelling place of the outcaste as seen before;
it led his mind to an indescribable state of detachment.
It was battered by the downpours of the rainy season, with barley sprouts growing from its walls,
its roof partially collapsed, and some of its interior caves barely visible.
Poverty was as if crushed like stubborn misfortune;
wickedness was as if its limbs had fallen away; and instability was as if shattered to pieces.
Its outskirts were covered with the white bones of cows, horses, and buffaloes, crushed by the teeth of Gādhi,
which stood there as if to bear witness.
It was covered with those skull-bowls, once filled and now utterly filthy, in which he had previously eaten and drunk.
It is completely encircled by those very strings of entrails, dried up season after season, like long-reaching thirsts.
With a smile, he gazed for a long time upon that former house of his, as a self-possessed man might look upon his own body that has become a withered corpse.
Then, filled with wonder, he approached the village,
just as a traveler might reach the land of the Āryas after crossing through a city of Mlecchas.
There he questioned the people: "O good sirs, do you perhaps remember the former conduct of this village—the succession of the outcaste dog-cookers?"
For I have heard from virtuous people that all who possess wisdom clearly perceive even what occurred long ago as if it were held in the palm of their hand.
There he saw an old, noble outcaste living in solitude,
who was indeed like a singular physical embodiment of the sorrows of darkness.
"O good man, if you know that person, tell it to me;
for it is taught that in dispelling the doubts of a traveler, there is a great fruit of merit."
Thus asked repeatedly by the twice-born Gādhi, the villagers,
with no small measure of smiles and agitation, responded like physicians to a distressed man.
The villagers said: "O Brahmin, it is exactly as you say; it is not otherwise.
There was here a dog-eater named Kaṭaṅkaṭa, who was of a cruel appearance."
His retinue of sons, grandsons, friends, servants, kinsmen,
and relatives was exceedingly vast, like the mass of leaves upon a tree.
Death snatched away that entire family of the old man,
just as the wind sweeps away a great forest filled with flowers and fruits from a mountain.
Leaving that region, he went to the interior of Kīra’s city,
where he became king for eight years without any agitation.
Then, having recognized him there, he was shunned from afar by the people,
like a heap of filth or like a poisonous tree in a village.
Then, when the people entered the fire, he himself entered the consumer of oblations;
through association with the noble, that nobility indeed entered him from the noble ones.
Why, O Lord, do you so diligently question this single outcaste?
Is he some kinsman of yours, or perhaps someone with whom you have been acquainted?
As he questioned the villagers thus again and again,
Gādhi dwelt there in all those villages for one month.
Just as he himself had experienced that state of being a dog-cooker (outcaste), so too was it described by all those villagers to him exactly as it was, without any omission.
Then, having heard this from the mouth of Sakala without contradiction and having carefully observed it exactly as it had been experienced,
Gādhi— his form concealed— felt supreme astonishment, like the moon having taken root within his heart.
The forty-eighth canto, titled "Direct Observation in the Account of Gādhi," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having seen the house of the outcaste (śvapaca) overturned, Gādhi went away again filled with wonder; for the mind never reaches satiety in beholding marvels.
There he surveyed the sites and dwellings,
which appeared like worlds overturned by the upheaval at the end of an aeon, as the Lotus-born Creator surveys them.
He spoke thus to himself in that forest where his dwelling lay in ruins,
wandering like a ghost amidst a garland of dry bones.
These rows of ivory from dead elephants, which were fashioned as enclosures,
remain even today like the peaks of Mount Meru for an entire kalpa.
Here, that monkey meat, cooked together with bamboo shoots,
was eaten by those intoxicated with liquor and spirits along with their outcaste kinsmen.
Having embraced a dark-skinned outcaste woman here upon a lion-skin,
he sleeps while drinking sweet liquor mixed with the fresh, pungent ichor of elephants.
The female dogs of the household, nourished on oil-cake,
are tied here with leather thongs to a wooden post for dead elephants.
Here, those three baskets of elephant tusks were fastened with the fierce hide of a buffalo, which was as beautiful as a dark cloud.
In these various places here, he played for a long time with the children of the outcaste dog-cookers, like cuckoos sporting amidst a heap of mango leaves.
The song, which followed the resonance of flutes blown by the breath of their grown-up children, was drunk by those gratified by the liquor prepared with the blood of dogs.
There, together with his family members at the wedding festivities, that householder performed a dance accompanied by loud clamor, like the waves upon the ocean.
Here, a bamboo cage has been constructed and secured for the purpose of striking down others those crows, vultures, and birds that are eager to fly up.
Thus reflecting on his former deeds as a dog-cooker,
Gādhi’s head trembled with wonder as he contemplated the workings of the Creator.
Knowing his duty, he departed from that vast region after some time;
leaving the Hūna territories behind, he reached another land by degrees.
Having crossed the continuous succession of rivers, mountains, regions, and forests,
he reached the abode of the parrots situated on the Snowy Mountain.
There, his soul weary from wandering through the world, he reached the city of Mahīpāla, which resembled a mountain, just as Nārada reaches the realm of the gods.
Then, seeing places in the city that he himself had previously experienced, seen, and frequented, he respectfully questioned the people.
O virtuous one, do you perhaps remember the outcaste lord here?
If you know him, then tell me about him quickly and according to the facts.
The Nāgara said:
"O twice-born one, for eight years here a Śvapaca was the lord of the earth,
to whom sovereignty had been entrusted by Navamaṅgala-hastin."
Having fully understood this, he entered the fire;
twelve years have passed here, O ascetic.
Whatever Gādhi, filled with curiosity, asked people,
he heard from each of their mouths and experienced it accordingly.
Then he saw in that city the king, together with his army and vehicles,
having gone outside from the palace to behold the god who wields the discus.
Seeing that the sky was shrouded by the clouds of dust from his army,
he remembered his former royal status and spoke, utterly amazed.
These are those Kīra women, whose skin resembles the interior of a lotus,
who possess the hue of molten gold and eyes like trembling blue lotuses.
These multitudes of yak-tail whisks, white as the gathered rays of the moon,
resemble steady waterfalls or heaps of kāśa flowers.
Fans made of yak-tail hair are being waved by beautiful women;
these are like the flourishing growths of flowers from fresh creepers.
These are those hordes of rutting elephants, their temples joined together to form dwellings; with their wish-fulfilling trees, they resemble the successive peaks of Mount Meru.
These kings, whose power is equal to that of Yama, Śiva, Indra, and Kubera,
are like the world-protectors (lokapālas) surrounding Vāsava.
These are those rows of houses, rich with every kind of jewel, extending far and granting all desires, as beautiful as groves of wish-fulfilling trees and creepers.
This very kingdom of the Kīra people, which was enjoyed by me in the past, has today become manifest to me like the conduct of my own previous birth.
Like a true dream, this stands before me even as I am awake;
I do not know what has arisen, for this illusion unfolds before me.
"Alas! Indeed, by this long-expanding delusion of the mind, I have been brought to a state of helplessness, like a small bird caught in a net."
Alas, what a pity! My mind, unawakened and struck down by latent impressions, spreads out webs of delusion even as it observes, like that of a child.
"For this great illusion has now been shown to me by that wielder of the discus; thus, at this moment, I have rightly remembered it in its entirety."
Therefore, I shall now apply such effort in a mountain cave that I may know the true state of the vital point of this extreme agitation.
Having reflected thus, Gādhi departed from the city to perform austerities;
reaching a cave in the mountain, he stood like a weary lion.
There, for a year and a half, subsisting on a single handful of milk,
the one of great splendor performed austerities for the gratification of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then the lotus-eyed one, whose form was like water, approached him— dark as a blue lotus, like a great lake in autumn becoming clear.
He went to that cave in the king of mountains, the abode of the twice-born;
then he dwelt in the sky, his complexion as white as a cloud.
The Blessed One said:
"Gādhi, have you seen my most profound illusion?
Have you seen the activity of the snare of the world, which is of a binding nature?"
Now that this state, so cherished by the mind and perfectly blameless,
has been attained while practicing austerities on the mountain slope, what else do you desire?
Vasiṣṭha:
Seeing Hari speaking thus, Gādhi, the best of the twice-born,
worshipped his feet with a profusion of flowers from his own worship.
Having offered the guest-water, scattered flowers, and quickly bowed with circumambulations,
the twice-born spoke these words to Viṣṇu, like a cātaka bird to a cloud.
Gādhi said:
"O Lord, may you reveal to me that illusion of profound darkness which was displayed by you,
just as the sun reveals the earth at dawn."
O Lord, how is it that the mind, when garlanded with the impurity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), perceives delusion even while awake,
just as it does in a dream?

O you whose abode is the stainless state, how did this delusion of a dream within the water, which was perceived for only a moment as having a self-nature, come to possess direct perceptibility for me?
Given the vastness and brevity of time, and the coming into being and passing away of the body,
how could my delusion regarding the outcaste remain established here?
The Blessed One said:
This is the form born of the self of one who is shaken by his own mental afflictions;
it is that which sees vast delusions because the mind has not perceived reality.
Nothing exists at all externally—neither sky, mountains, earth, nor the directions;
all this exists within one's own mind, just as a cluster of leaves exists within a sprout.
Just as fruits and the like expand outward from a sprout,
so too do the earth and other elements manifest externally from the mind.
It is true that earth and the other elements reside within the mind and never exist externally;
for the fruit exists within the sprout, since it is from that [sprout] that the splendor of the fruit arises.
Just as a potter [produces] a jar, the mind destroys and creates forms, light, mental attention, existence, time, and action.
This is experienced by all men, even down to children,
in their perceptions of agitation, passion, disease, and so forth, which are like dreams and delusions.
Within the mind, which is permeated by latent impressions, millions of mental modifications reside,
just as fruits and flowers exist upon a tree rooted in the earth.
Just as a tree that has lost its earth does not grow leaves again,
so too for the soul that has been expelled [from the body], there is no further birth and so forth.
Since the entire infinite web of the world is established within that mind,
what cause for wonder is there if the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste) is manifested by it?
You have realized that the state of being a dog-cooker (outcaste) exists only by the power of appearance,
just as various intense afflictions, though diverse, produce transformation [only through such appearances].
In that very same way, you have witnessed the delusion of a twice-born guest who arrived, ate, slept, and told a story.
Rising up in that very same way, I go; "I have reached the realm of the Hūnas;
these are the Hūnas, these are the villages"—thus you experience delusion.
In the very same way, this former house of Kaṭañja was seen rolling about by people; and Kaṭañja, being told [this], perceived it as a delusion.
In that very same way, I arrived at the city of Kīra, and the Kīras told me:
"You have seen the king of the Śvapacas; this is a delusion."
Thus, O best of the twice-born, you have seen this entire web of delusion—
both that which you perceive as real and that which you understand to be unreal.
What indeed does the mind, enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), not perceive?
Even a purpose that requires a year to accomplish is seen accomplished in a dream.
O one of great intelligence, you did not see the guest, nor those Hūnas, nor those Kīras, nor that city; you saw all of this only through delusion.
O Brahmin, while traveling as a traveler to the land of the Hūnas, you rested in a certain cave, like a deer in a forest.
In that very way, due to being deluded by fatigue, one perceives this circle of smoke as "this is that" and "this is the house of the dog-cookers," yet it is not seen as such in reality.
In that very same way you saw the city of Kīra;
it was exactly so and not otherwise, for you, O twice-born one, were seeking an illusory object.

O Sage, though you have always dwelt amidst all things in their completeness, you have nonetheless perceived a delusion within the mind, like one who is deranged wandering through the quarters of the world.
Therefore, arise and remain performing your own duty with a tranquil mind;
for in this world, human beings do not attain the highest good without performing their own duty.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that Padmanābha, being honored by throngs of ascetics dwelling in the forest and surrounded by hosts of gods and sages with purified hands, went to his own abode, the ocean.
The forty-ninth canto, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Māyā within the Account of Gādhi," by Vasiṣṭha:
Then, after Viṣṇu had departed, Gādhi wandered again among the Hunas and other peoples like a cloud in the sky, in order to investigate his own delusion.
Having thus learned of his own situation from the people,
he once again went to a mountain cave and propitiated Hari.
Then, after a short time, Janārdana arrived;
for Mādhava becomes a kinsman simply through a single act of propitiation.
The Blessed One, being gracious, spoke to Gādhi like a cloud to a peacock: "What further do you seek through this asceticism? (MU 5.49.4)
Gādhi said:
"O Lord, I have been deluded for six months while staying among the lands of the Hunas and Kiras;
there, my account is contradicted even in their stories."
"O Lord, have you seen the land of the Huns through illusion? Thus was I addressed.
"The words of the great are for the destruction of delusion, not for its increase."
The Blessed One said:
"By a chance occurrence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow, the state of being an outcaste was reflected in the minds of all the Hūnas and Kiras in that very same way."
Therefore, my dear friend, that which they tell you regarding your own story is the truth;
for a manifestation once it has appeared does not again return to non-manifestation.
A certain dog-cooker (outcaste) had built a house on the outskirts of the village; that very house which was seen by you has now been reduced to fragments of brick.
Sometimes a single intuition arises even for many people;
for the movement of the mind is as diverse as the occurrence of the "crow and the palm fruit" (a chance coincidence).
For instance, many people may see the same dream,
like those whose minds are sluggish from sleep, delusion, or intoxication by liquor.
Just as deer in a single forest glade during a single play.
And many people strive at the same time through their manifested actions, just as trees do in the season through the ripening of their own fruit.
O Brahmin, that scriptural injunction which states "the time for prohibitions and permissions is the giver" is merely a mental construction; for time exists only within the Self.
The Blessed Time is formless; they know it to be Brahman itself, unborn.
It neither relinquishes nor takes anything from anyone at all.
This worldly time, which consists of years, kalpas, and yugas,
is conceptualized by means of the multitude of objects, and those multitudes of objects are [conceptualized] by it.
With their minds bewildered by the confusion arising from the appearance of identical forms,
those multitudes of Hūṇa and Kīra people perceived it in that manner.
Devoted to your own duty and investigating the self with your intellect, O virtuous one, remain right here once the delusion of the mind has departed; I am departing.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, vanished;
Gādhi remained in the cave with a mind made heavy by anxiety.
Then, after several months had passed on that mountain,
that twice-born man once again propitiated the one who holds the lotus in his hand.
And one day he saw his Lord arrive; he prostrated before him, honored him in his mind with deep longing, and spoke to the Lord.
Gādhi said: "O Blessed One, as I recall that wondrous situation of my own existence among the Śvapacas,
and this illusion of saṃsāra, my mind is utterly bewildered."
Having quickly spoken that according to the facts for the sake of dispelling great delusion,
employ me in this very pure action.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmā, this world is the grand display of the great illusion of Māyā;
all manner of wonders arise here within its vast expanse."
"You saw that in Hūnakīrapura out of delusion"—
this is indeed possible, for such an illusion is seen by people.
The Hūnas and Kīras, like you, have likewise experienced such delusion; though it appears real, it is in vain, arising simultaneously with other perceptions.
But listen to this which I shall speak to you as it truly is, O blameless one, by which your anxiety will become thin, like a creeper in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
He who was formerly that outcaste named Kaṭañjaka in the Hūna region became exactly like that again through that very same disposition.
In that very same way, having become one whose vows were impaired and having gone to another land, he became King Kīra; thereafter, he entered the fire.
At that time, such a state of conduct as that of Kaṭañja appeared to you alone within your mind, like something existing within water.
That which has been seen and experienced is sometimes completely forgotten;
yet sometimes the mind perceives even that which has never been seen, as if it were actually seen.
Just as there is delusion regarding the existence of realms in dreams and mental fantasies,
so too, my dear, is it seen by the mind itself even while awake.
Just as one who perceives the three times sees that which resides in the future and the past, so too does the life-story of Kaṭañja appear as a clear intuition within your profound mind.
The one who possesses a self-sense does not sink [in the world] thinking, "This is that I am; this is mine";
whereas the one who lacks a self-sense perceives it as, "This is that I am; this is mine."
The knower of reality does not despair, thinking "I am indeed everything";
he does not conceive of distinctions among objects as being meaningful.
Therefore, even though he is immersed in delusions and confusions that revel in pleasure and pain,
he does not sink, like a gourd vessel in water.

For your part, your mind is seized by the web of latent impressions (vāsanā) and you are devoid of discernment; like one suffering from a great disease with only a little remaining, you have not attained well-being.
Because your knowledge is incomplete, you are unable to ward off the delusion of the mind,
just as one who possesses incorrect mantras cannot dispel a cloud.
Whatever appears suddenly as a mere reflection in your mind,
by that very thing you are overcome in an instant, like a tree by the force of a torrent.

If one stands having ascended here upon the wheel of illusion (māyācakra), which has the mind as its navel and consists of all the constituent parts (kalās), then nothing whatsoever can obstruct that.
Arise! Practice austerities for ten years with an unwearied mind in a bower of the mountain; thereafter, you shall attain knowledge and the state of infinite being.
Having spoken thus, the lotus-eyed one vanished on the spot,
like a wind-blown cloud, like a lamp, or like a sudden surge of the Yamunā, in an instant.
Gādhi attained the highest dispassion born of discernment,
just as a tree reaches a state of withered sap at the end of the autumn season.
With his mind released from the burden of great delusion, he slowly censured the manifold and inconsistent activities of the Creator that had spread abroad.
With his soul moistened by compassion, he went toward the supreme glory of ascetic discipline,
like a cloud whose rain has ceased proceeding toward a mountain for rest.
Having cast off all mental constructs, he performed austerities there for ten years; by that means, he attained self-knowledge.
Thereafter, having regained his own true nature, the Great-Souled One— free from fear and delusion, devoid of desire for the realm of enjoyment,
possessing the ever-joyful form of one liberated while living, and profoundly tranquil like the full moon— remained with a mind that was no longer agitated or incomplete.
The fiftieth canto, titled "The Conclusion of the Account of Gādhi," ends; [then begins] the canto of Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, O descendant of Raghu, this illusion of the Supreme Self is exceedingly vast, difficult to comprehend, a source of great delusion, and treacherous.
On one hand, there is the vision seen in the confusion of a dream lasting but two moments; on the other, the delusion of being a king among the Śvapacas experienced for many years.
Where is there the state of being perceived in agitation? Where is direct perception? Where is the unmistakable unreality? And where is the transformation into reality?
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say: enough with this notion that "this is an illusion";
it casts the heedless mind into extreme peril.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, how can we stop this wheel of illusion,
which is so powerful that by its force it causes the severing of all our limbs?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, know that the mind is the great hub of this wheel of illusion that constitutes the form of saṃsāra, which, as it revolves, causes others to revolve as well.
When that [wheel] has indeed been firmly grasped through wisdom and human effort,
the wheel of illusion, its hub seized, comes to a halt.
When the navel of the mind is firmly grasped, the wheel of delusion does not turn,
just as a peg wrapped with a rope remains stationary when the rope is held fast.

O sinless one, why do you not know that even one who is solely skilled in the art of wheel-warfare understands that the wheel comes under control only when it is firmly fixed at the hub, and not otherwise?
Therefore, O Rāghava, having firmly grasped the non-existence of the mind, strive with effort to block the wheel of saṃsāra by restraining the self.
Without this reasoning, this suffering of yours is endless;
but observe that within this very reasoning, it reaches its end in an instant.
Without the supreme medicine known as the mere conquest of the mind,
the great disease of saṃsāra is not pacified, even with great effort.
Therefore, O Raghava, having abandoned the performance of pilgrimages, charity, and austerities,
bring the mind itself under control for the sake of the supreme good.
Samsara exists only within the mind, just as the space within a jar exists within the jar;
when the mind is destroyed, there is no samsara, just as when the jar is destroyed, there is no space within the jar.
Having destroyed the hollow of the sky that is the wandering of the mind— the space of the mental jar— enter your own form, which is like the incomparable, undestroyed sky.
The mind, by momentarily engaging with the present that has arrived in its natural sequence through external cognition,
while not engaging with the past or the future, attains the state of non-mind.
If you abandon all mental constructs along with their underlying tendencies at every moment,
then you have indeed attained that purifying state of mindlessness.
As long as there is the mental construction of conceptualization, so long do the manifestations of the mind persist;
as long as the expanse of the clouds remains, so long do droplets of water exist in the sky.
As long as there is a conscious mind and volition, so long will there be conceptualization and imagination;
as long as the world exists with its moonbeams, so long will there be fragments of frost.

If the mind is devoid of volition and has been cultivated for the sake of transcending worldly existence, know that the roots [of rebirth] have been burnt away from their very foundation; this is success.

Indeed, consciousness devoid of the mind is called "direct consciousness" (pratyak-cetana); it has the nature of being without the thinking faculty (nirmanaska), and therein no stain of conceptualization exists.
That is truth, that is auspiciousness, that is the supreme reality;
that is omniscience, that is contentment—indeed, that wherein the mind is extinguished.
But wherever the mind is established, there suffering and happiness always come into its presence, like crows to a cremation ground.
Through the realization that all things lack substantial reality,
the seed of the tree of cyclic existence no longer arises within conceptual construction.
Through the practice of continuous association with the scriptures and virtuous people,
the unreality of worldly phenomena is realized.
Having withdrawn the mind from its lack of discernment by means of one's own efforts and resolutions, it should be forcibly joined to the path of the scriptures and the conduct of the virtuous.
The self alone is the primary cause for the vision of the Supreme Self;
a jewel fallen into the deep is drawn out only by means of another jewel.
Only one's own self is capable of abandoning the sufferings experienced by oneself;
therefore, the self alone is traditionally held to be the sole cause for the knowledge of the self.
Whether speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, or even closing them,
remain intent solely upon infinite pure consciousness, free from all mental constructions.
Abandoning the latent impressions of "this is mine," "that," and "I am this," become intent solely upon the pure consciousness residing within, through one-pointed devotion.
Maintaining a single-minded focus throughout the present and future durations of your existence until the body's end,
remain intent on meditative absorption through the continuous integration of self-awareness.
In flightings and in battles, in sorrows and in joys,
in waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, remain intent upon your own self-awareness.
Having cast off the impurity that is to be experienced, having thoroughly churned the sluggish mind,
and having completely severed the bonds of hope, become intent upon your own self-awareness.
With the conventions of "pure" and "impure" stilled, the poison of desire extinguished,
and views regarding the desirable and undesirable destroyed, become intent upon the essence of pure consciousness.
Not touching your own internal sensations— which possess agents, objects, and instruments— remain intent upon pure self-consciousness alone, free from conceptual construction and without support.
Indeed, while remaining awake, contemplate that stable state which belongs to deep sleep; reflecting that "everything exists," become one whose body is the single essence of pure being.
Freed from the various states of the ten directions, and joined with liberation within the inner disposition,
become intent upon pure consciousness alone— the lamp that illumines everything in its entirety.
Having abandoned the notions of self and other, and being undifferentiated within the state of the world,
remain steadfast by supporting yourself like a diamond pillar.
Having severed the inner mental fetters in the form of worldly expectations with a noble intellect that possesses singular steadfastness, proceed to the state beyond both merit and demerit.
For one who attains reality as self-awareness, enough said:
even the most virulent *hālāhala* poison will become nectar for you.
Then arises the great delusion, which is the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra,
when there occurs a fall from one's own consciousness, which is stainless and partless.
Then delusion, the cause of the wandering in saṃsāra,
is utterly destroyed when one abides in stainless and partless self-awareness.
For you who have followed your true nature and crossed the great ocean of desire,
your consciousness will expand in every direction like the rays of the sun.
O Rāma, for one who beholds their own true nature and abides in the state of bliss, even a delicious elixir acts like a potent poison.
We feel no shame before those men who have attained their true nature;
the rest, though possessing long arms, are merely donkeys bearing the name of "men."
Mountains become as small as mounds before one who has reached the supreme pinnacle and stands elevated by self-awareness, just as elephants appear small before a mountain.
Within the boundary between the seen and the seer, even all the lights such as the sun do not assist one who possesses the divine eye of self-awareness.
These [senses] become non-entities, like lamps at midday for one who has attained the Self through the great illumination of the sun and other lights.
Among those possessing splendor, radiance, power, and even very great strength—
among all who are endowed with loftiness— the knower of reality is supremely exalted.
Just as the sun, fire, the moon, gems, and stars shine with light, so do those supreme among men, who have known all that is to be known, resplend in the world.
O Rāma, those men who do not know the ultimate reality are considered more insignificant than insects in the crevices of the earth, even than donkeys, and even than animals.
As long as one lacks the realization of the Self, the body remains a vampire of delusion;
but those who know that truth maintain that it is only the knower of the Self who is truly united with consciousness.
For he who does not know the Self is a wretched body; though moving about on the surface of the earth, he wanders like a corpse. But he who knows the Self is truly conscious.
When the mind has become thick with ignorance, self-knowledge recedes far away;
it is like the stainless splendor of light when a great cloud has arisen.
The mind should be gradually emaciated by the rejection of enjoyments and non-enjoyments,
by one who knows the truth, through the removal of their flavor over time, like a withered leaf.
Through this attachment to the mere body as a self where there is no self,
and through [attachment to] children, wife, and family, the mind becomes stout with craving.
Through the transformation of egoism, by the effortless stain of "mine-ness," and through the notion that "this is mine," the mind becomes swollen with attachment.
The mind grows fat with the suffering of old age and death, which leads to futile exaltation, and with the treasury of venomous serpents that are the mental afflictions.
By drinking the milk of false hopes, by the force of the wind of enjoyments,
and by this grasping at existence, the serpent of the mind grows fat.
Through the indulgence in mental and physical afflictions, through finding solace in the cycle of existence,
and through the effort of accepting and rejecting, the mind grows fat.
The serpent of the mind attains fullness through the swelling of enjoyments, which possess the nature of coming and going and indicate the instability of poison.
The body is a deep abyss where [sorrows] have long grown; it possesses clusters of blossoms formed by the towering heaps of anxiety;
it is bent down by the fruits of old age, death, and disease; and its flowers are in full bloom through the floods of sensual enjoyment.

O you who are like the moon, swiftly cut down with the saw of the essence of investigation the poisonous tree of the mind— its great branches being hopes, its fresh leaves being wavering thoughts— without hesitation and by force.

Fierce and incapable of resting even for a moment in the pleasure of sitting upon a single bank, it is intensely eager to churn the lotus-thicket of the feet of the virtuous; it is a boil of intense suffering amidst fleeting pleasures.

O Rāghava, lion among kings, tear apart with the row of sharp claws of your wisdom the elephant of the mind that dwells in the forest of the body— its long tusks being the chronic distortions— and make it perform its proper task.
It constantly finds delight in improper places, nourished by devouring the garland of bodies;
it is audacious, harsh in its actions, fierce with its beak, one-eyed, exceedingly fat, and blacker than the darkest part of the night.

Drive far away from the nest of your body that crow of your own mind—its wicked conduct harsh and screeching, arrogant and puffed up with pride—in order to pacify its faults. This is the very essence of what must be done.

Attended by the ogress of craving, it has rested in the great pits of ignorance and wandered for a long time through hundreds of bodies in the forest of its own cycle of existence, which is devoid of true consciousness.

As long as this demon of the mind has not been expelled from the house of one's own conscious self by means of discernment, dispassion, effort toward the guru, and independent mantras, how can there be any realization of the Self in this world?

It destroys the flood of pride through auspicious and inauspicious blessings; it is the constant antidote to the poison of anxiety and the armor of bodily ailments; it is the food for pure breath, and it is the destroyer of fear for all beings.

O Rāma, having brought the great serpent of the mind to rest within the hollow of the lotus-heart by means of the power of the mantra that censures the flood of enjoyments, and having utterly cast off fear, become one whose nature is fearless of worldly existence.
Bearing an inauspicious appearance due to his constant attendance upon rows of corpses,
weary from the exhaustion of wandering through the quarters of the sky, the cemetery-dweller has a body scarred by wounds.

If the vulture of the mind, with neck outstretched and its pride swelling as it runs toward the quarters of sensory enjoyments, flies away from the tree of the body— if that happens, then your victory is truly skillful.

I have been mocking the traveler on the path of saṃsāra— a person wandering through forest edges and distant quarters, restless and with agitated limbs, seeking fruits, and traveling from the land of birth back to the land of birth.

O dear one, for the sake of accomplishment, thoroughly subdue this great monkey of the mind as it frolics upon the tree whose trunk is the eyes and nose, whose branches are the arms and so forth, and whose leaves are the webbed fingers.

It has arisen for the destruction of the fruits of good deeds, flashing with the lightning of attachment to radiant pleasures; it rains down a torrent of a multitude of misfortunes, tossed within by the whirlwind of latent tendencies.

By the power of the formidable mantra that abandons both conceptualization and non-conceptualization, you must energetically dispel the cloud of the mind from the sky of the heart; having attained the great fruit, become wealthy and established in the Self.
Knotted by karmas created by itself, impenetrable by weapons and unburned by fires,
it inflicts supreme suffering upon itself, a long cord binding all successive births.

O Rāghava, having yourself severed with the weapons of mere non-visualization this multitude of bodies— numberless and interwoven— which are but the snares of the mind, roam at your pleasure, free from fear.
It scorches all people on the path with its hissing breath; it is utterly difficult for others to awaken to;
it withers the grove of living beings with the poison of desire; and its staff-like bodies are swollen like carrion by the wind.
Having swiftly burned with the power of the great fire of desirelessness that sluggish serpent of volition— which slumbers within the cave of the body— you shall become free from fear.

O virtuous one, having swiftly brought the mind to tranquility by means of the pure mind— just as one neutralizes a terrible weapon through the application of another weapon— abandon your long-standing restlessness, like a tree free from monkeys whose splendor remains unimpaired.

Having resolved "enough, enough" with your mind, free from fear and with inner impurities stilled, perceive everything—even this very body—as light as a blade of grass; having reached the further shore of saṃsāra, drink, sport, and rejoice with ease through the vision of what is to be abandoned.
The fifty-first canto, titled "The Application of Rāghava’s Intentions," by Vasiṣṭha.
Do not abide in mental fluctuations that are long-lasting, subtle, shimmering, dark, and like the edge of a razor.
O you who are skilled in policy, since this creeper of intelligence has grown in the great field at the right time, lead it to increase by watering it with discernment.
As long as this bud-like body does not wither from the ashes of the Kali age,
lift it up and preserve it before it falls upon the ground.
O you who know the single reality of the meaning of my words, through the contemplation of that single meaning of my words,
you attain happiness, just as the enemy of serpents [Garuda] does through the contemplation of the sound of clouds.
O wise one, having repeatedly torn apart and scattered the five elements like the flower of the *uddālaka* tree, investigate them within with a steady mind.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, in what sequence did the sage Uddālaka cut through those five elements and investigate them within?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, Rāma, to how in former times Uddālaka attained the supreme, unimpaired vision through the investigation of the multitude of beings.
In a certain corner of this dilapidated house of the world,
situated on a plot of land named after the wind and the directions, crowded with the burden of mountain-vessels;
It is said that there exists a certain plateau named Gandhamādana, the king of mountains,
strewn with flowers and grey with the scent of camphor trees.
It was filled with birds of variegated colors, sporting in various groves;
its banks were occupied by forest-dwellers, and it smiled with the filaments of its flowers.

In some places it possessed great jewels set within it; in some places it was like blue clouds or blue lotuses; in some places it had mists for its beautiful hair; and in some places it was like a lake serving as a mirror.
There, on a certain rising slope covered with fruit-bearing trees,
where flowers were strewn up to the ankles and great trees provided lush shade;
A sage named Uddālaka, who was observant of silence, self-respecting, and highly intelligent,
lived formerly as a fierce ascetic before he had even reached youth.
At first, however, he was one whose wisdom and discernment were slight;
he had not yet attained rest in the [highest] state, nor was his virtuous intention awakened.
Then, through the gradual practice of austerity, the study of the meaning of the scriptures, observances, and restraints,
discernment came to him just as autumn comes to the earth.
Then, dwelling in solitude, his mind once weary and terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, he reflected as follows.
What could that primary goal to be attained be, upon reaching which one no longer grieves,
and having reached which, no further connection with birth arises?
When, having abandoned all mental constructs, shall I find long-lasting rest in the supremely pure state, like a cloud upon the peak of Mount Meru?
When will the latent tendencies toward enjoyment within me reach pacification,
like the waves of the ocean roaring with the sound of restless billows?
When, with a mind resting in the ultimate state, shall I laugh at the inner thought that "having done this, that other thing must also be done"?
When will the web of conceptual construction no longer cling to my mind,
remaining there without attachment, just as water remains on a lotus leaf?
When shall I have crossed over, by means of the supreme vessel of wisdom, the river of craving with its surging, tumultuous waves?
I shall mock this action, which is composed of unreality and performed by beings belonging to the world of the Jāgata, like the fruitless play of a child.
When will the swinging of my mind, tossed by the fluctuations of conceptual construction, come to rest— like the dizziness of one whose strength has been drained by drinking wine?
With my body radiant as the sun that has risen, laughing at the worldly courses of existence,
I shall attain inner contentment like the Virāṭ-self whose intellect is full.
Peaceful, of even conduct, gentle, and free from longing for all objects of desire—
when shall I attain tranquility, like a great ocean freed from agitation?
Beholding this entire visible splendor, which consists of hundreds of desires,
as if in deep sleep, I shall become inwardly expanded.
When shall I perceive everything— both external and internal— as pure consciousness alone, by means of an intellect whose conceptual constructions have been stilled?
When my mind and self have become tranquil and have attained supreme consciousness,
I shall reach the highest light, as if through the disappearance of congenital blindness.
When shall I behold from afar this slender digit of Time with the beautiful light of consciousness attained through long practice?
Freed from both the desired and the undesired, devoid of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted,
when shall I attain contentment, established in the state of self-luminous reality?
When will this night of my delusion—strewn with the owls of false hopes, its lotus-heart withered by dullness—come to an end, O Kṛṣṇa? When will it perish?
With my mind stilled of all agitation, in a mountain cave, I shall attain equality with a stone through non-conceptual meditative absorption.
When will my elephant-like mind, intoxicated by the great pride of self-conceit,
meet its destruction, slain by the deer of the realization of reality?
When will forest bees build their nest upon my ear— the ear of me who am rendered silent by resting in partless meditation?
When will birds, their minds absorbed in meditation, come to rest fearlessly upon my chest as I remain like a stone pillar on the mountain?
When shall I depart, having abandoned the path through the forest of saṃsāra, which is entangled with the thorny bushes of craving and overgrown with the shrubs of birth?
Thus, overcome by anxiety in the forest, the twice-born Uddālaka sat down again and again and practiced meditation.
But when his mind, as fickle as a monkey, was being led away by sense objects, he did not attain that state of meditative composure which bestows joy.
Sometimes, immediately after abandoning external contacts,
the monkey of his mind experiences agitation regarding the abiding nature of reality.
Sometimes, having abandoned internal contacts, the monkey of the mind,
out of fickleness, wanders toward external objects like one greedy for poison.
O lotus-eyed one, at one time, having seen within his mind a radiance resembling the sun, it turned toward the objects of the senses.
Having abandoned the inner darkness of ignorance, the mind of one who is greedy for sense objects sometimes flies away like a frightened bird.
Having abandoned external and internal objects of touch as well as sleep, his mind never again experienced darkness or light, but attained a state of eternal stability.
Thus, with his internal meditative states agitated,
he wallowed day after day in fierce caverns like a tree broken by the wind.
With his mind healed from its wounds, he stood amidst the perils of mental reflection,
like a blade of grass with a swaying body upon a wave at the shore.
Then, with his mind distracted and devoid of delight, he dwelt alone on the mountain day after day, like the lord of the day upon Mount Mahāmeru.
Once, the sage reached a cave that was difficult for any being to attain in its entirety,
where all movement had been completely stilled, as if it were the state of liberation itself.
Unperturbed by winds, unattainable to beasts and birds,
unseen by gods and gandharvas, it possesses the supreme splendor of space.
It was covered with a profusion of flowers, soft as tender grass,
and appeared as if it were fashioned from emeralds set within crystals of *jyotīrasa*.
It possessed the beautiful luster of the songs of the Siddhas, was illuminated by manifest jewel-lamps,
and was as well-guarded as the inner apartments of the forest goddesses.
Neither too hot nor too cold, it was like the golden-white radiance of the autumn sun when it has just risen, which does not cause pain to the eyes.
She was not withered by the meager light, nor was she disturbed by the gentle sound of the wind;
her borders were entangled with flower-clusters, like a young girl wearing a garland.
She was, as it were, the very path of tranquility embodied, a form worthy for the repose of the Lotus-born;
she was beautiful on all sides, tender and delightful with clusters of flowers, like a lovely maiden within the hollow of a lotus.
The fifty-second canto, titled "The Aspiration of Uddālaka," by Vasiṣṭha.
That righteous-souled one entered that cave of Gandhamādana,
which he had reached after wandering for a long time, just as a bee enters a lotus-bud.
Entering with an inclination toward meditative absorption, he shone like the lotus-born Brahmā in his city of the self when he has ceased from the activity of creation.
There, that gentle creator of clouds fashioned a seat from dark blue leaves, with clusters of blossoms situated within, like a mass of rain-clouds.
Upon his back he spread a beautiful deer-skin,
like the sky studded with stars against the slope of a blue jewel on Mount Meru.
There he sat down, causing his mental absorption to diminish,
like a rain-cloud that has become silent after pouring its rain upon a mountain peak, his inner body now purified.
Like a Buddha, having firmly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) facing north,
he pressed his heels against his testicles and formed the Brahma-añjali gesture.
Having withdrawn [the mind] from the habitual tendencies that cause it to wander like a deer,
he undertook this investigation for the sake of non-conceptual meditative absorption.
O foolish mind, what purpose is there for you in the activities of worldly existence?
The wise do not practice actions that yield only suffering in the end.
He who pursues enjoyments after abandoning the elixir of tranquility is like one who leaves a grove of mandāra trees and enters a poisonous jungle.
Even if you go to the hollow of the earth or even to the world of Brahmā,
you will not find peace there without the nectar of tranquility.
Abandon this state of having hundreds of hopes unfulfilled, which bestows all suffering; go instead to the supreme, most beautiful state of ultimate bliss.
These various mental constructions, consisting of existence and non-existence,
lead only to your own fierce suffering and never to happiness.
O fool, what is the use of these [objects] such as sound, which have destroyed your faculties?
You wander incessantly and in vain, just like a female frog.
O mind-frog, what have you gained by wandering aimlessly through the world for so long in blindness?
O fool, why do you not fix your mind upon that state of tranquility from which you obtain whatever you desire and in which you find peace? Why do you not bind yourself to that very ground?
O fool, having come to the state of being a listener, do not go to ruin like a deer by means of an intellect that merely follows sounds— an intellect nourished by futile exertions.
O fool, do not become bound by this [body] which has come to the state of skin and is intent on touch for the sake of suffering, like a lordly elephant lusting after a female elephant.
O blind one, blinded by greed, having come into the presence of the tongue,
do not meet your destruction like a fish greedy for the baited hook.
Relying on the visual function directed toward the forms of women and the like,
O simple-minded one, do not meet with destruction like a moth greedy for light.
Resorting to the path of the nose within the hollow of the lotus-body,
do not seek bondage by being intent on fragrance, like a bee.
The deer, the bee, the moth, the elephant, and the fish are each destroyed by one [of these five];
but for the ignorant man who is beset by all these misfortunes, how can there be happiness?
This net of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) woven for the sake of bondage is innate to one's own self, like a web of foam spun by a silkworm.
If, having arrived like an autumn cloud, you attain purity free from the affliction of impurity and are extinguished without a trace, then your victories shall be infinite.
Even though you know that the worldly views give rise to the states of decline and prosperity and cause torment at their conclusion, if you do not abandon them, you will perish.
Or for what purpose do I perform this service of yours?
For, O sinless one, the mind of a man who possesses discernment does not exist [in such a state].
As long as there is density of ignorance, so long is there density of mind;
as long as the rainy season is powerful, so long is there an abundance of mist.
As long as there is a thinning of ignorance, so long is there a thinning of the mind;
as long as the rainy season has not ended, so long does the mist persist.
As long as the pure mind, accompanied by investigation, has reached a state of attenuation,
I consider that [mind] to be already exhausted, like an autumnal cloud.
This is the instruction: whatever is done for one who is non-existent or perishing is like striking the water, the wind, or the sky.
Therefore, I abandon you, who are wasting away and composed of unreality; for they say that the highest folly is to disregard the instruction one has been given.
I am the non-conceptual lamp of consciousness, free from the latent impressions of egoism;
I am not bound by you, the seed of egoism, for I am composed of unreality.
"‘This is that very me’—thus you have grasped a false view in vain, O fool; it is a cholera-like poison of doubt leading to your destruction."
The subtle and intelligent abiding of the infinite reality of the Self is not possible within the body,
just as the scent of a musk deer is not possible inside a wood-apple fruit.
O Mahāskandha, this [path] is profound, painful, and dependent on latent tendencies;
therefore, it is a fall into the unreal, and I shall not follow it.
What indeed is this vain delusion, like that of a child who does not investigate? It is a construction based on the continuous fabric of the error "I am he."
From the big toe up to the head, he analyzed [the body] bit by bit;
he did not find that which is called "I," and thus he remained [realizing], "Who am I?"
I behold that one [reality] in the three worlds, which fills every corner of the directions— an awareness that is itself beyond being perceived, its self-nature extended everywhere.
Its measure is not perceived, nor indeed is there any conceptualization of it;
it is neither unity nor multiplicity, neither greatness nor minuteness.
If you consider feeling— which is not to be felt by me— to be the cause of suffering,
then this very feeling shall be destroyed by me through the distinction born of discernment.
"This is flesh, this is blood, these are the bones in the body;
these are your breath-winds—where does that 'I' stand? (MU 5.52.40)
O mind, flesh is one thing, blood another, and bones yet others;
awakening is one thing, and movement is another—so who am I that stands [here]?
"This is the nose, this is the tongue, this is the skin, these are the two ears, this is the eye, and this is the movement; who is this that stands [within] as 'I'? (MU 5.52.42)
In its state of being as it truly is, there is no "I," no "you," and no latent impressions;
this pure Self, a mere manifestation of consciousness, shines forth in its absolute solitude.
"I alone am everywhere here, or else I am nothing at all here"—this is the vision consisting of pure Being; no other sequence exists.
For a long time I have been tormented by the rogue of ignorance and by extreme egoism,
like a young animal caught in the forest by a proud wolf.
By good fortune, this thief of ignorance has now been fully recognized by me;
I shall never again take refuge in it, for it robs one of the true nature of reality.
Free from suffering, I am not one who is subject to suffering; he does not belong to me, nor do I belong to him—just as a cloud remains distinct from the mountain upon which it rests.
"I am not one who, having come into being, says 'I' while standing, sitting, or walking;
through the vision of the Self, I have attained a state free from egoism."
Surely these others, the eyes and so forth, are distinct from me and ignorant; whether they go or remain in the body, they are none of mine at all.
Alas! Who is this so-called "I," and how was it fashioned by whom—this world-ghoul with a form as towering and incomparable as a palm tree?
For so long a time I have wallowed in vain within this pit,
like a deer upon a rugged mountain devoid of water and grass.
If the eye has turned upward toward the vision of one's own true interest,
then who could that "I" be, who am thus deluded by suffering?
If the sense of touch has turned its face toward its own true nature called "contact," then what is this that arises as the so-called "I," like a wretched ghost?
While this gustatory faculty is settled upon its own sequence of tastes,
from where does this contemptible delusion arise, namely, "I am an eater of delicacies"?
When the ear has resorted to the power of sound and is preoccupied with its own object,
what source can there be for that seedless suffering of egoism?
When the nose, filled with its own self-centeredness, encounters its own scent,
I do not recognize that thief who thinks, "I am the smeller."
This cultivation of objects is also like the sequence of a mirage;
when that [cultivation] is unreal, the existence of that [object] is likewise a delusion.
Even though this sense-faculty, such as the eye, is devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), it functions by itself toward its own external object; latent impressions are not the cause here.
O mind, surely action is performed free from latent impressions;
here, those perceptions of pleasure and pain are experienced only as mere appearances.
Therefore, O all you people, having abandoned the foolish senses and your own internal latent tendencies, perform every action; thus you shall not encounter suffering.
It was you yourselves who vainly cultivated habitual tendencies that lead to suffering;
like children distressed by the destruction of their playthings made of mud.

O sinless one, all perceptions such as latent impressions (vāsanā) and the like are distinct from the Self, just as waves are distinct from water; this is true for the ignorant person, but not for the knower.
You have been destroyed by craving alone, you who fruitlessly wander among the objects of the senses,
like silkworms bound by their own thread.
It is through craving alone that you wallow here in the peril of old age and death,
like travelers on a mountain path with blurred vision stumbling into the depths of ravines.
In this world, latent impression alone is the cause of your bondage in one place,
just as a string threaded through an empty space serves as the tether for pearls that have been strung.
For this [world] is not real in reality, being constructed by mere conceptualization;
it is severed by the mere absence of conceptualization, as if by a sickle.
For this [doctrine] leads only to your own delusion and destruction,
like a gust of wind to lamps flickering even with their own brilliance.
O mind, since you are the treasury of all the senses, you must surely attain unity with all the senses;
then, beholding the self as being of an unreal nature, abide in the nirvana that is singular, stainless, and awakened.
Having skillfully cast off the endless cholera of the poison of sense-objects and the latent impressions of worldly existence,
O Blessed One, through the application of means that avoid what is undesirable, become one who is free from fear and no longer a ground for terrors.
The fifty-third canto, titled "The Inquiry of Uddālaka," begins with Uddālaka:

Whether its body has no limit or end, or whether it is as subtle as an atom, consciousness is beyond being an object of thought; thus, latent impressions and the like have no power over its pervasion.
Arising from latent impressions, this female vampire of emptiness— provoked by the mind, intellect, ego, and the deceitful senses— is intent on causing terror.
May those very transformations produced by that [mind] experience fear from it again and again in abundance; for I am consciousness, entirely untainted within.
Since consciousness is indeed omnipresent, there is neither birth nor death for it;
tell me, what is it that dies, or by whom is anything ever killed?
There is no purpose in life for one who is merely conscious; that very consciousness is life itself.
What will this soul gain by living, if it has already died before?
The notions that "one lives" and "one dies" belong only to the minds characterized by a multitude of false conceptualizations; they do not pertain to the Self, whose nature is all-pervasive.
For he who has attained the state of "I-ness" is grasped by means of existence and non-existence;
but for the Self there is no "I-ness," so how could it have those states of existence and non-existence?
The sense of "I" is a vain delusion, and the mind is a mirage;
the entire collection of material objects is inert—so for whom could there be the cultivation of the notion of "I"?
The body consists of blood and flesh; the mind has perished through inquiry.
Since the intellect and all other faculties are inert, whence can there be the cultivation of the sense of "I"?
Since the senses are constantly and sufficiently occupied with maintaining themselves, and since objects remain as mere objects, how can there be any cultivation of the sense of "I"?
The qualities (guṇas) abide in the qualities; nature (prakṛti) is established in nature.
Reality alone rests in reality—whence, then, can there be the conception of "I"?
All-pervading, residing in all bodies, consisting of all time, and great— the pure,
supreme light is indeed established as the very self of consciousness alone.
Thus, what is my form, who am I, what is to be grasped, and by what am I made?
What is my nature, what am I composed of, who am I, what do I grasp, and what do I abandon?
Therefore, that which is called "I" does not exist here as something subject to the arising of being or non-being;
for one whose nature is free from egoism, how and with what could there be any connection?
When egoism is non-existent, what relation can there be, for whom, or of what kind?
When the absence of relation is established, the conceptualization of duality dissolves.
Thus, whatever exists in this world has Brahman as its self;
it is Brahman alone that exists, and I am that very same Brahman—why then do I grieve in vain?
When one remains in that single, stainless, and all-pervading state, how could there even be the name of the stain of egoism, and from where could it arise?
For there is no such thing as the splendor of objects; only the Self exists here, all-pervading.
And even if the splendor of objects were real, there would be no connection whatsoever for anyone.
When the senses play among the senses and the limbs, and the mind plays within the mind, by what is consciousness—whose form is never lost—bound; to whom does it belong; what is it; and how?
Just as there is no mutual connection between pebbles and counting-sticks,
so too there is no such connection among the body, the senses, the mind, and consciousness, even when they are perceived together in one place.
In this great delusion of egoism, which arises from what is non-existent and is thus futile,
this world is perverted by the notions of "this is mine" and "this is I."
This wondrous manifestation of egoism arises from the absence of the light of reality;
it dissolves through the light of reality, just as a streak of frost vanishes through heat.
Apart from the Self, nothing at all exists;
that reality is the Śabdabrahman—this I meditate upon fully.
I consider the non-recollection of this arisen delusion of egoism—which is like the color of the sky—to be truly better than its remembrance; indeed, forgetting it is preferable.
Having completely forgotten the long-standing delusion of egoism along with its very root,
I abide as the true Self within myself, like the autumn sky in the autumnal firmament.
The sense of "I," when pursued, bestows a mass of misfortune, causes evil deeds to flourish,
and spreads intense suffering.
When the dense cloud of egoism throbs within the watery space of the heart,
the cluster of vices blossoms everywhere upon the kadamba tree of the body.
Death is the end of life, and life ends in death;
existence is cut short by non-existence—how bitter is this sensation of suffering!
"This has been gained; this I shall obtain"—this [thought] causes internal burning and does not subside for the foolish, like the radiance of sun-gems in the summer heat.
The thought "this does not exist" or "this exists" runs toward the ego-sense,
just as a dull-witted person, with a dull mind, pursues a mass of clouds as if it were a range of mountains.
When the ego-sense has been completely exhausted, the tree of cyclic existence withers;
being sapless, it never again produces a sprout, just like a stone.
The black female serpents of craving for sense-objects, which have made their dwelling in the tree of the body,
flee somewhere when the son of Vinatā— the discerning self— has arrived.
When the universe has arisen from the non-existent, we who are born from it are likewise composed of the non-existent;
when the vibration of the non-existent occurs, what sequence can there be for "you" and "I"?
This world arises first from a causeless [source] as something causeless;
how can that which is causeless and swollen [with existence] be called "being" (sat)?
For an infinite time in the past, this body was fashioned like a jar from clay; it has existed thus now, and so too will it be at the end.
In the interim, for a certain period, it is merely the age of manhood and is flickering; having abandoned its initial and final states of serenity, it is like water taking the form of waves.
Those who have fixed their attachment upon this body, which is a flicker of a moment and prone to dissolution— like a wave— they are ruined, for they possess false views.
All things exist before, behind, and on all sides;
when their very center is indistinct, what reliance can there be on that which has lost its form?
O Videha, your mind was previously and is now peaceful;
whether existent or non-existent, it is dissolved into space—what ferocity can there be for you in this middle state?
Just as in dream-visions, just as in perceptions during a state of agitation, just as in the playfulness of intoxication, or just as in the disorientation caused by traveling in a boat.

Just as in cases of bodily humors being disturbed, or as in the impairment of the sense faculties, and just as under the influence of extreme agitation, joy, or the onset of a morbid affliction; //MU_5,53.41//
Form is seen and indeed perishes, being unstable as both existent and non-existent;
likewise, this very [form] undergoes deficiency and excess in the course of time.
And that [state] has been constantly produced by you, O mind, through the arising of suffering and happiness,
just as it is for lovers during the nights of separation and union.
You too appear as something unreal, falsely perceived as real;
since you are like a mirage, how could that which is produced by you be real?
Whatever has an objective extension, all that is the circle of the visible;
having determined it to be without substance, let the mind proceed to the state beyond the mind.
When the firm conviction has taken root in the mind that "this is a non-entity," the latent tendencies toward enjoyment wither away like lotuses in winter.
Surely, when the mind has seen the Self and is freed from its lack of vigor,
it becomes itself established in its own state through a passionless mind.
When the mind has its constituent parts of consciousness cast into the fire of the Supreme Self, it is itself completely consumed; thus, having its nature burnt away, it attains eternal purity.
Having perceived the body as something other [than the self], having abandoned the latent impressions of sense objects,
and having accepted its perishability, one conquers the mind like a hero.
The mind is the enemy of the body, and the body is the enemy of the mind;
