through a state of oneness they perish, like the relationship between a container and its contents.
For those who possess passion and hatred, which are eternally and utterly opposed to one another,
their destruction by the very root is the supreme happiness.
Any talk of taking pleasure in the union of these two is equal to the story of the earth being devoured by a woman made of iron in the sky.
Where both [passion and aversion] are joined together in a state of natural opposition,
there the successions of misfortunes fall like torrents of rain.
For that base person who finds delight in the association of mutually contradictory things should be abandoned, like a house of falling doors or a fire-pit without water.
Having touched the body with the mind through volition, like a child-demon,
he offers his own sufferings to it as one gives wealth to a worthy recipient.
Afflicted by those sufferings, the body then desires to destroy the mind;
even a son kills his father when the latter has become an assailant.
There is no one who is an enemy by nature, nor is there anyone who is ever a friend;
a friend is said to be one who bestows happiness, while those who cause suffering are known as enemies.
Experiencing sufferings, the body desires to destroy its own mind;
yet the mind instantly makes the body a secure fortress for its own sorrows.
Thus, when suffering and its cause are intertwined with one another, how can there be the arrival of happiness?
For this body and mind are, by their very nature, mutually piercing.
When the mind alone is completely exhausted, the body is no longer a vessel for suffering;
yet, out of an intense longing for that exhaustion, the body itself constantly runs about.
Lost again and again for one's own ruin, this body— the very seat of calamities—
is swiftly censured by a mind that has failed to attain self-discrimination.
For these two— the mind and the body— have indeed grown mutually thickened,
being insentient by nature, like a cloud and a lake during the rainy season.
Though they are essentially one and the same, having come together for mutual suffering and remaining in two forms,
they are intent on worldly transaction with each other like wind and fire.
When the mind is diminished, the body becomes utterly exhausted at its very root;
when it increases, the body grows with a hundred branches like a tree.
When the mind is destroyed, the body, with its latent impressions exhausted, perishes;
yet the mind is not destroyed when the body perishes—therefore, one should destroy the mind.
Having cut down the forest of the mind— the wish-fulfilling tree of volition and the creeper of craving—
I have reached the vast expanse of the earth and dwell there at ease.
I believe this mind of mine remains in a state of constant depletion;
the web of its latent impressions is subsiding like a cloud at the end of the rainy season.
This arrangement of the elements, known as the body and called "my" form,
should remain even as it dissolves while the mind is being extinguished.
That body for whose sake the glory of enjoyments is indeed desired—neither it belongs to me, nor do I belong to it; what purpose, then, have I in a mere fragment of pleasure?
Listen now to the reasoning in this sequence regarding the thought "I am not the body":
even though all the limbs are present, why does a corpse not move?
Therefore, I am beyond this body, eternal, and of undiminished luster;
having attained union with the Radiant One, I perceive the Sun within the sky.
"I am a knower; I have no concern for pleasure, nor do I suffer over what is not beneficial.
Let the body remain or let it cease to be; I stand free from all fever."
Where the Self is, there is neither mind, nor senses, nor latent impressions;
the vulgar do not remain in the vicinity of such a mountain-like being.
I have followed that path; I am alone, I am victorious.
I am free from longing, I am without parts, I am effortless, and I am without desire.
Now I have no connection with the mind, body, senses, and so forth,
just as there is no connection between crushed sesame seeds and the oil extracted from them.
For as I move playfully downward from this supreme state of my own,
this auspicious retinue indeed follows along.
It is self-abiding, vigorous, existent, heart-pleasing, true, and knowing;
it is considered to be blissful and tranquilized, as well as joyful and arisen.
Fullness, magnanimity, truthfulness, radiant beauty, one-pointedness, the oneness of all things, fearlessness, and the state in which the conceptualization of duality has perished.
These [energies], eternally risen, established in their own nature, beautiful, and the source of auspicious fortune,
are my beloveds, ever dear to my heart as I delight in the one Self.
Since everything is possible in every way, at all times, and for everyone,
in relation to everything, my desire and lack of desire, as well as pleasure and pain, have come to an end.
Free from delusion, free from dejection, and with a mind devoid of conceptual construction, I clearly bring myself to rest within my own cool self, like a fragment of cloud in the autumnal sky.
The fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Playful Deliberation of Uddālaka," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having thus resolved with that expanded and pure intellect, the sage sat in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana) with his eyes half-closed.
He uttered the syllable *oṃ* with a piercing sound that rose upward,
its resonance like the ringing of a bell whose handle has been struck correctly.
As he utters "Om," while his consciousness is directed toward that [reality],
it extends as far as the syllable Om situated above, within the vast and stainless Self.
In the first of the three and a half measures of the *praṇava*, when its sound is clear, the body resounds with the breath slightly agitated.
The process known as *recaka*, by which the vital breath exits from the entire body,
emptied him just as Agastya, having drunk its waters, emptied the ocean.
Having abandoned his body, he remained in the sky filled with the essence of consciousness, like a bird that has left its nest remaining in the air, his vital breath suspended.
The blazing fire of his heart, its flames flaring up, consumed his defiled body, just as a forest fire, swollen by a calamitous wind, burns a withered tree.
This state occurs as far as desired in the first stage of the *praṇava*;
it does not happen through force, for *haṭhayoga* indeed causes suffering.
Then, at the time of the other two parts [of the breath], when the *praṇava* was in a state of perfect equilibrium,
there occurred a sequence of the vital breaths known as the motionless *kumbhaka*.
Neither outside nor within, neither below nor above, nor in the cardinal directions—
there your vital breaths did not experience agitation, as if they were half-paralyzed.
The fire that had consumed the body was instantly extinguished like a meal;
only white ashes, as pale as snow, were seen remaining from the body.
Where the white, motionless bones of the body appear as if they had been comfortably asleep upon a bed of camphor.
The wind, having shaken that ash along with the bones,
deposited it within its own body, which was greatly swollen, as if it were observing the vow of the Three-Eyed One.
And that [destruction], stirred up by a fierce wind, having covered the sky in an instant,
vanished somewhere like autumnal mist and clouds, consisting of ashes and bones.
This state continues for as long as desired in the subsequent stage of the *praṇava*;
it does not occur through force, for *haṭhayoga* is indeed a source of suffering.
Then, on the third occasion, there arose the process known as "filling" (pūraka) of the vital breaths, which brings peace through the syllable *praṇava*.
At this moment, the vital breaths, dwelling within the nectar of consciousness,
attained a coolness in the sky as beautiful as the touch of snow.
Gradually, situated in the midst of the sky, they attained the state of lunar discs,
like smoke within the expanse of the sky attaining the nature of cool clouds.
In that lunar orb, which was complete with its full collection of digits, like a mass of merit or a great ocean of elixir, [he entered].
The vital breaths, endowed with great streams of elixir,
take the form of jeweled pillars, like the rays of the moon in the waters.
That stream fell from the sky onto the remaining ashes of Śarīra’s body,
like the river of the gods falling upon the head of Hara when it had been turned into an elixir.
With her four-armed body, which shone like the orb of the moon,
she emerged from the ocean like the Pārijāta tree rising from Mount Mandara.
That body of Uddālaka, having arisen as Nārāyaṇa,
shone beautifully and splendidly with radiance, like a blossoming mango tree.
Life-breaths consisting of elixirs filled his body,
just as the currents of rivers fill a lake, or as sweet juices fill a tree.
Within, the vital breaths, filled with reverence, filled the Kuṇḍalinī,
spreading out in curves and sub-curves like rivers filling lakes and ponds.
The body of that twice-born man returned to its natural state,
like the surface of the earth washed clean at the end of the monsoon's fury.
Then, seated in the lotus posture and having established a firm stability within the body,
he should bind the five senses as one ties an elephant to its tethering post.
He applied his resolve toward the goal of non-conceptual meditative absorption,
just as the stainless autumn season strives to bring its own nature to a state of clarity.
With his thought, he drew his heart from afar, like a tethering post pulled by a rope, for that deer of the vital breath which wanders through the various directions of the quarters.
He forcibly restrained his mind— which was running downward, intoxicated, turbid, and agitated— just as a dam holds back rushing water.
She half-closed her eyes, which were fringed with thick lashes,
like a lotus at twilight when the honey-bees have become motionless within.
The silent sage brought the force of the prāṇa and apāna breaths within his mouth to a state of gentleness,
like a favorable season bringing a wind that is auspicious for a desired region.
He diligently separated the senses from the objects of the senses, just as one extracts oil from sesame seeds, or as a tortoise withdraws its limbs.
He gradually abandoned external objects of touch without exception, casting them far away like an enemy;
just as a gem covered by its setting suddenly casts its radiance far into the distance.
He caused the internal sensations of touch to dissolve, devoid of their visual counterparts,
just as a tree in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa sheds its sap that remains within the hollows of its branches.
Then, by contracting the anus, he obstructed the winds of the nine gates,
just as one might block the other apertures of a jar by sealing its mouth.
The steadfast one bore his neck— richly illuminated by the jewel of his own body, clearly marked with flowers— like Mount Meru bearing the peak of its summit.
He held the mind, which had attained self-restraint, within the space of his heart,
like a mad elephant subdued by skillful means and confined within the Vindhya chasm.
Having attained a stainless and exceedingly gentle state like the autumn sky, she carried away the unshakable splendor of both the full ocean and Mount Meru.
Then he shook off the floods of conceptual constructions that had come into appearance before him,
just as the wind blows away gnats shimmering in front of one's face.
As the appearances repeatedly arose according to his desire as he was coming,
the hero severed them with his mind, just as one cuts arrows with a sword in battle.
When the flood of conceptual constructions had been completely cut away, he beheld within the sky of his heart a darkness that veiled the sun of discernment, black as flickering lampblack.
He also dispelled that [ignorance] by means of the sun of his own mind,
which had arisen through perfect knowledge, just as soot is quickly blown away by the wind.
When the darkness had ceased, he beheld that lovely mass of light,
like the evening cloud at dawn when the nocturnal gloom has subsided.
Like a young elephant, he trampled the grove of land-lotuses;
and like a vetāla, he drank the flood of blood with great speed.
When his vital heat had subsided, the mind of that sage,
reeling like a night-lotus, fell into sleep as unsteady as that of a drunkard.
Just as the wind scatters a mass of clouds, as the sun destroys the night-lotus, or as the sun of sharp rays dispels the night, he swiftly shattered her as well.
When his sleep had subsided, that creature with dark eyes directed his mind toward the sky, like a peacock looking for its crest in the heavens.
Just as a cloud [cleanses] the *tāpiñcha* tree, as the wind [dispels] the mist,
and as a lamp [removes] darkness, that pure Self quickly wiped away even that [impurity].
When the consciousness of the void was shattered, his mind became deluded,
like one intoxicated by liquor when sleep has dissolved away.
That noble-minded one also wiped away that delusion of his mind,
just as the sun removes the dullness produced by the night from the world.
Then, having reached an indescribable state free from light, darkness, sleep, delusion, and the like,
his mind rested for a moment.
Having quickly rested, he fell into a consciousness of his own limbs, which is the very nature of consciousness—
like the water of a lake dammed by a bridge, flowing back toward its own source.
Through the power of long-term investigation and from the tasting of its own self-awareness,
it then attained the state of pure consciousness, just as gold attains the form of an anklet.
Then, having abandoned its state as mind, the mind reached an expanded state of pure consciousness; it quickly became something entirely different, like mud remaining within a jar.
Having abandoned the object of consciousness, the pure consciousness attained the state of universal consciousness,
just as the singular awareness of the ocean remains when the distinctions of waves and the like have been cast away.
Having abandoned the mentalization of the flood of elements, he then became the vast sustainer of the universe—
the pure, pervasive sky of consciousness— and thus attained awakening.
There he attained great bliss, devoid of both the seen and the seeing—
an infinite, supreme savor, like an ocean of elixir.
Having completely transcended the body, he arrived at a certain state;
being of the nature of the universal essence of existence, he became an ocean of bliss.
This swan of the consciousness of the twice-born remained steady in the lake of bliss, like the full moon in the cloudless autumn sky.
He became like a lamp in a windless place, resembling a figure depicted in a painting; he was like an ocean whose tides have ceased, remaining still like a rain-cloud that has become silent.
Then, while staying in that great world for a long time, Uddālaka beheld numerous Siddhas moving through the sky, like immortals.
Various nets of perfected beings arrived from all sides, bestowing the stations of Śakra and Arka, and were densely crowded with throngs of Apsarases.
That twice-born man of profound intellect, remaining unperturbed, paid no heed to those throngs of perfected beings, just as one disregards the playful antics of childhood.
Then, disregarding the company of the Siddhas, he remained for six months in that temple of his own bliss, like the sun upon the northern horizon.
That state of liberation while living which that twice-born man attained is the very place where the Siddhas,
Suras, Sādhyas, Brahmā, Hara, and the others reside.
Because they have been transformed by bliss, they have gone to the state beyond bliss;
therefore, their consciousness shone forth neither in bliss nor in the absence of bliss.
Having found stability there for either a moment or a thousand years, the mind finds no pleasure in a flood of enjoyments, like one who has seen heaven and is now back on earth.
That is the state, that is the peaceful goal; it is the supreme good, eternal, and auspicious.
For one who has attained rest therein, no further weariness arises.
Having attained that state, the virtuous do not return again to this perception of the visible world,
just as those who have reached the Caitraratha grove do not go back to a garden of khadira trees.
Having attained that state of great bliss, the minds of embodied beings no longer value the visible world, just as kings disregard wretchedness.

O sinless one, when the mind has come to rest in that state, it perceives the Buddha regarding the realm of the visible; it either attains a realization free from purposeful striving, or else it does not depart at all.
Then Uddālaka, having dwelt for six months in a place far removed from the realm of the Siddhas,
emerged like the sun from the womb of the clouds at the beginning of spring.
With his self fully awakened, he again beheld the Siddhas of supreme splendor,
who bore bodies like the orb of the moon and were longing to offer their salutations.
The rows of celestial chariots were beautiful, with fly-whisks whirling amidst the pollen of white mandāra flowers, and possessed fluttering clusters of banners.
[He saw] sages such as ourselves, whose lotus-hands were marked by the purifying *darbha* grass,
as well as lords of the *vidyādharas* surrounded by *vidyādharī* maidens.
Then they said to that high-souled sage Uddālaka:
"O Blessed One, look upon us with favor through our prostrations."
"Ascend this celestial chariot and come to the city of the Thirty-three;
for heaven indeed is the ultimate limit of the abundance of worldly enjoyments."
O Lord, enjoy for an eon the desired pleasures that are appropriate;
indeed, all the practices of austerity are solely for the sake of enjoying the fruits such as heaven.
Behold these excellent women of the Vidyādharas, bearing necklaces and yak-tail whisks, as they wait upon you like female elephants attending a male elephant.
Sensual pleasure is the essence of both dharma and artha; those women of pure smiles, whose essence is sensual pleasure, become like heaven itself, just as blossoms are to spring.
Having thus addressed the perfected ones who had arrived as guests, that sage, having honored them according to the rule, remained composed and free from agitation.
That man of steady intellect neither rejoiced in nor abandoned that prosperity;
saying, "O Siddhas, go," he became intent on his own duties.
Then, after attending upon him— who was devoted to his own duty and had become indifferent to enjoyments— the Siddhas themselves departed within a few days.
And that sage, liberated while living, wandered at his pleasure as long as he desired through the forest edges and the hermitages of the sages.
Upon the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, and Vindhya;
and upon the islands, groves, cardinal directions, thickets, jungles, and forest lands.
From that time forth, the twice-born Uddālaka, having attained his goal,
dwelt in the caves within the recesses of the mountains, absorbed in the play of meditation.
Sometimes after a day, sometimes after a month, sometimes after a year,
and sometimes after a multitude of years, he, absorbed in meditation, awoke.
From that time forward, although Uddālaka was engaged in worldly affairs,
he remained perfectly composed, having attained oneness with the nature of consciousness.
Through the intensive practice of the singular mass of the reality of consciousness, he attained the state of the Great Consciousness;
in this visible world, like the sun in a painting, he neither set nor rose.
With his mind stilled by the attainment of the supreme state, the bonds of birth shattered, and the oscillations of doubt extinguished,
he bore his own body— beautiful as the autumnal sky, expansive, majestic, manifest, stainless, and beyond description.
The fifty-fifth canto, titled "Resting at Uddālaka," [ends]. Rāma:

O Lord, the sole sun for the day of self-knowledge, the fire that consumes the grass of my doubts, and the moon that cools the burning of ignorance—what is this "universal existence" (sattāsāmānya)? MU 5.55.1.
Vasiṣṭha:
When the mind is completely dissolved through the contemplation of absolute non-existence,
then there arises the state of being the universal existence of the nature of universal consciousness.
When consciousness, devoid of the aspect of "this-ness," dissolves into itself,
it then becomes like the utterly transparent generality of existence (sattāsāmānya), appearing as if it were non-existent in form.
When all objects of perception have subsided and there is no mutual cognition,
when they are realized as being of the nature of one's own essence and appearing as that very essence, then there is equanimity.
When unmeditated-upon objects, like the limbs of a tortoise, are seen to dissolve into the Self by means of the Self,
that is the state of pure Being-in-general.
For this supreme vision indeed always exists, whether one possesses a body or is bodiless;
it certainly arises in both states of liberation, resembling the state that transcends the fourth.
O sinless one, this [state] arises for both the one who has emerged from meditation and the one established in samādhi;
it belongs solely to the knower, and it never arises at all in the ignorant person born of awakening.
Abiding in this vision, all those noble-minded ones who are liberated while living are like perfected alchemical elixirs upon the earth, or like winds in the path of the sky.
O Raghava, all of us beginning with myself, as well as Narada and others,
and Brahma, Vishnu, Ishvara, and the rest, have been seen established within this [body].
Having taken hold of this path that destroys all fear,
Uddālaka dwelt in the house of the world for as long as he desired.
Then, after a long time, his intellect became firm and unwavering, resolving: "I shall remain liberated from the body once I have cast off this physical form."
Thus resolved, he remained in a mountain cave upon a seat of young leaves,
sitting in the bound lotus posture with his eyes closed.

Having restrained the nine gates of the mind by the suppression of the anus, and no longer heeding the contact of sensory objects, one becomes a solid mass of consciousness within one's own cultivated limbs.
With the vital breath restrained and the neck held in a straight posture,
his face shines as the root of the tongue touches the surface at the base of the palate.
With his mental vision concentrated, neither externally nor internally, neither below nor above, neither on an object nor in emptiness, he should keep his teeth from touching one another.
With the complexion of his face becoming clear as the flow of the vital breath is restrained,
the consciousness of awareness within his limbs arises, causing the hair on his body to stand erect.
Through the practice of the consciousness of the limbs, one attains the universal consciousness;
through that practice, one subsequently obtains the supreme flow of bliss.
Then, through the relishing of that [bliss], the sequence of the state of the commonality of the contracted mind reached the universal sustainer,
the infinite self, the commonality of pure existence.
Abiding therein, with an even and equal enjoyment, he has attained supreme repose; the radiance of his face is charmingly and utterly innocent, a bliss that is not merely ordinary joy.
With his hair standing on end from the bliss of perfect tranquility, he has fully attained the state and is liberated,
his worldly delusion consisting of thought-constructs and the like having been utterly exhausted over a long period of time.
That Great Being became like a figure fixed in a painting;
he was equal to the stainless autumnal moon when it is one digit short of fullness.
In a few days, he gradually became tranquil within his own stainless self,
having transcended the state of birth, like the sap of a tree in the spotless heat of the sun's rays at the end of autumn.
With all conceptual constructions gone, changeless, and delightful, his form was liberated from the adjuncts of all impure manifestations;
he attained that primordial bliss in which the splendor of Indra is carried away like a blade of grass in a mass of water.

Pervading the infinite expanse of the sky and spreading through all directions, full, having the nature of sustaining the world, and to be served by those of great fortune—he, who transcends description and qualities, became that Brahman: the Truth, the primordial bliss, the happiness that is not of the senses, the infinite.
Once her mind had entered its own primordial nature, the body of the twice-born, after six months of sitting there,
scorched by the rays of the sun and delightful with the whistling of the wind, became a mountain lute with very thin and numerous strings.
Then, after a considerable time, the Mothers, accompanied by the daughters of the mountain, emerged from the sky toward that ground of the mountain;
for the sake of accomplishing their desired fruits, they all descended together, like rows of flames with tawny hair falling toward a fire.
That heap of human skeletons, dried by the rays of the sun, was suddenly brought into contact with the tip of her skull-topped staff;
the goddess of gods, the consort of Śiva, who is worshipped by all the deities, having performed a dance with nine jewels during the night, imparted a glass-like luster to them.

Thus, today the corpse of Uddālaka lies within a cluster of creepers—a plaything of the great goddess Khinkhinikā—amidst a mass of peacock feathers shimmering like a fresh fragment of cloud, entwined with clusters of mandāra garlands; he lies there like a bee within the interior of a flower-cluster as the sun descends behind him.

This creeper of the mental fluctuations of Uddālaka, bearing blossoms that shine with the expansion of the self-bliss flashing through discernment, has taken root in his vast forest of the heart; once it has grown, he never again suffers separation from its radiant and beautiful splendor, and he attains a most exalted union with its fruit.
The fifty-sixth canto, titled "The Nirvāṇa of Uddālaka," by Vasiṣṭha:
O lotus-eyed slayer of enemies, having thus examined the self by means of the self through this sequence, one attains rest in the vast state.
One should investigate the meaning of the scriptures with a mind focused on the Guru,
continuing this practice until the supreme state is attained through the repeated dissolution of all that is perceived.
The meritorious state is attained through detachment, practice, the meaning of the scriptures, wisdom, and the sequence of preceptors and restraints; or else, it is attained by wisdom alone.
The intellect that possesses full awakening, is sharp, and free from blemish,
attains the eternal goal even when deprived of all other favorable conditions.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, is there anyone who, having mastered samādhi and being awakened,
remains at rest even while engaged in worldly activity?
Someone else, having resorted to solitude, remains fixed in meditative concentration;
O Blessed One, tell me which of these two is superior.
Vasiṣṭha:
For one who perceives this collection of qualities as not being the self,
that inner coolness which arises is called samādhi.
Having ascertained that "I have no connection with visible objects," one becomes cool;
such a person may remain engaged in worldly affairs, or may be established in meditative absorption.
These two, O Rāma, are perfectly equal when they are thoroughly cooled within;
that which is this inner coolness is true wealth, it is the fruit of austerity.
If the mind of one established in the state of meditative concentration is still flickering in its activity,
then that concentration of his is equal to the frantic dancing of a madman.
If the mind of one engaged in the frantic dance of madness has its latent tendencies exhausted,
then that frantic dance is equal to the meditative absorption of a Buddha.
The worldly man who is awakened and the one who is awakened while dwelling in the forest—
both these men have surely reached the state beyond doubt.
Even while performing an action, this mind with its attenuated latent impressions is a non-agent, just as a living being whose mind has gone far away is a non-agent when listening to a story.
Even though it performs no action, the mind is indeed the agent,
as when one stands on the brink of a precipice in a dream, even while the limbs are motionless.
That which is the state of the mind being a non-doer is the supreme concentration;
know that to be the state of absolute oneness, that auspicious and highest liberation.
For the flickering and unsteadiness of the mind is the supreme cause of forgetfulness;
therefore, through meditation and the vision of meditation, make that very mind free from the sprout of passion.
That very mind, when free from latent impressions (avāsana) and steady, is declared to be meditation (dhyāna);
that itself is the state of absolute liberation (kevalībhāva), for therein it is eternally at peace.
Even a slight residual impression is said to be striving for a high state;
therefore, the mind that is free from impressions attains the state of non-doership.
This mind, however, possesses dense latent impressions consisting of the notion of agency;
it bestows all suffering. Therefore, one should bring those latent impressions to a state of attenuation.
When one stands within with the world stilled before them, free from sorrow, fear, and desire,
and by which the self becomes established in its own nature— that is known as *samādhi*.
Having mentally renounced all things, including their conceptual constructs,
remain as you are— whether on a mountain or in a house.
For householders whose minds are well-composed and whose faults of egoism have been stilled, the home itself is like solitary forest lands.
For those whose vision is concentrated by the mind, a dwelling in the forest is equal [to other places],
just as for great beings here, all beings are equal to the great.
O Prince, even the cities, though radiant with throngs of people, become as empty as forests when the great cloud of the mind has subsided.
O slayer of enemy heroes, even desolate forests appear as cities filled with great crowds to one whose mind is intoxicated by its own habitual tendencies.
The mind that has emerged from meditation enters into the delusion of deep sleep when the wandering ceases;
it attains Nirvana—do as you wish regarding that Nirvana.
He who always perceives the Self as transcending all states of being, yet as the essence of all states of being, is said to be composed in meditative absorption.
O Lord of Men, this mind never perceives this world by itself, just as it does not in a dream; it is exactly the same even while one is awake.
Just as people living in a forest are considered non-existent even while they dwell there because of their lack of connection [to it], so too for the wise man, even a village is like a forest.
With his mind constantly turned inward, whether sleeping, waking, walking, or reading,
he perceives a city, a country, or a village as if it were a forest.
Everything becomes like space through constant inward abiding; for this world, agitated by the elements, is in every way useless [to one so situated].
But once inner coolness has been attained, the world becomes cool for those free from the fever of passion, as long as they remain alive, just like men who have recovered from a high fever.
For all living beings tormented by internal thirst, this world consists of a forest fire; that which is within exists externally.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers,
and the directions are the external manifestations of the reality of the internal organ.
Just as within the hollow of a banyan seed, that which belongs to its own self shines forth externally in splendor, like the fragrance of a blossoming flower.
Neither externality nor internality exists anywhere as anything whatsoever;
whatever is manifested according to its nature through the power of consciousness arises as such, in accordance with reality.
The interior of the reality of the Self shines forth externally as the world;
like camphor with its fragrance, it is both contracted and expanded.
This Self vibrates as this expansive universe, both as the "I" and as the "not-I," as external and as internal; yet it is neither non-existent nor existent, for it is all-pervading.
This Self perceives its own nature as it is known: that which is situated externally as external, and that which exists internally as internal.
The world, including all that is external and internal, is essentially non-different from the Self and is peaceful;
yet, as long as the sense of "I" and so forth persists within the body, there exists a great fear characterized by manifold suffering.
For one whose soul is struck by mental anguish, heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the quarters of the sky— all seem ablaze as if by the fire at the end of an aeon.
But he who, finding delight only in the Self within, performs actions with his organs of action,
and is not subject to joy or sorrow— he is said to be composed.
He who, seeing the Self as all-pervading, has a thoroughly pacified intellect, neither grieves nor broods; he is said to be composed in meditation.
He who, seeing the worldly courses of existence with their prior and subsequent limits,
laughs at these views— he is called one who is composed in meditation.
In others there is no "I," nor am I the cause of the world's birth;
just as there is no water in a mass of waves, nor do the elements of foam exist upon their destruction.
He within whom there is no sense of "I," nor division and the like, nor "mine," nor consciousness and unconsciousness—he exists; other people do not.
He who, being as pure as the sky, conducts himself here properly according to his own inclination,
remains like a piece of wood or a clod of earth amidst the transformations of joy and anger.
He truly sees who, by his very nature and not out of fear, regards all beings as himself and the property of others as a clod of earth.
An object, whether large or small, is not perceived as having the nature of non-existence;
nor is it experienced by a knower as having the nature of existence in the same way it is by one who does not know.
Endowed with such an intention, having attained the state of a Great Being (mahāsattva),
let him remain, arise, go, meet death, or strike down [others].
One may dwell either in one's own home, which is rich with the highest enjoyments and crowded with people,
or else in a vast forest, devoid of all enjoyments and free from activity.
Let him dance, intent on drinking while beating a drum wildly;
or let him attain peace on the mountain, having renounced all attachments.
Let him anoint his body with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor,
or else let him fall into a fire spreading with a mass of tangled flames.
Whether he commits a very great evil or abundant merit,
let him meet death this very day, or at the end of a multitude of kalpas.
There is nothing that he does not know, nor is anything left undone by that Great-Souled One;
he incurs no stain, just as gold remains untainted even when it has fallen into mud.
The consciousness is stained by the objects denoted by the words "person" (*puruṣa*) and so forth,
which are accompanied by blemish and consist of the latent impressions of the sense of "I," resembling silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
The pacification of all things occurs through right knowledge according to reality;
for it is that very [knowledge] which, by virtue of the non-existence [of objects], is its internal tranquility and its end.
The evil habit-energy of "I-ness" produces for the person whose nature is consciousness various pleasures and pains, which are the birthplace [of further existence].
Just as a householder finds relief when the delusion of a snake in a rope has subsided,
so too is internal equanimity considered to arise when the notion of "I-ness" has been completely stilled.
Whatever one does, whatever one eats, whatever one gives, or whatever one offers in sacrifice—that does not belong to the Knower, nor is the Knower therein; let him not act, or let him act.
He has no purpose through action, nor does he have any purpose through inaction;
the Blessed One abides in himself alone, according to his own nature.
From that, desires arise— not like sprouts from a stone—
but all those that do arise are that very [Self], just as waves are water.
This entire world, both this and that, is all one; there is no division whatsoever here.
He, whose singular form is the purifier, the Supreme Person, is "Being" (Sat); and that which is "Being" is indeed nothing at all.
The fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Contemplation on Meditation," by Vasiṣṭha.
Just as the sensation of sharpness is experienced within a mirage of the self because it possesses the nature of consciousness,
so too does this [consciousness] know non-selfhood, differentiation, space, time, and so forth.
That which is the perception of the saltiness within a minute particle of salt, due to its being consciousness,
exists as possessing distinctions such as "I-ness," as well as space, time, and so forth.
That which is experienced by the inner self as sweetness due to its own consciousness— namely,
the notions of "I-ness" and so forth, as well as the distinctions and the world— is what has unfolded from that [consciousness].

That which is the perception of hardness by the stone of the self through its own consciousness, having attained the states of "I-ness" and so forth, as well as distinctions such as space and time; [this is the nature of the self].
That experience of insentience which arises from the self’s own cognition of itself as a mountain and so forth is established as the "I-ness" (ahantva), duality, the world, and so on.
That which is the manifestation of the water of the Self from itself, due to the fluidity of consciousness, takes the form of whirlpools and the like,
as well as "I-ness" and the like, duality and the like, and the appearance of forms and the like.
The perception of that which belongs to the tree of the Self— its own branches and so forth—
is clearly manifest as "I-ness" (ahantā) and its various divisions, just like the world and its contents.
When the realization of emptiness occurs through the consciousness of the inner space of the Self,
that is cultivated as the meditation on the distinctions such as "I-ness" and so forth.
Since the interior of the sky of the self possesses consciousness,
its perception of emptiness is illuminated as "I-ness" and so forth, as well as "mind" and so forth, just like the body and so forth.
That which is the internal continuity of the self-wall by its own nature exists as if external due to the distinctions of "I-ness" and so forth, because of its consciousness.

Since it is by its own nature the knower of its own existence, that which is the singular awareness of being—whether it be established as "I-ness" and so forth, or as "difference" and so forth, or as "consciousness" and so forth—is [the self]. MU 5.57.11.
That which is the self-manifestation of the inner self’s own light— consisting of "I-ness" and so forth, as well as "cognition-ness" and so forth— it is this very thing that he knows as the *jīva*.
Within [the Self] there exists that which is the lunar essence of the Self, the elixir of consciousness;
because it is tasted by itself, it gives rise to the sense of "I" and so forth.
That which exists within the sugar-candy of the Supreme Self— consisting of the arising of the sweetness of consciousness—
is itself tasted by that [Self] through its own inherent "I-ness" and so forth within.
Because the jewel of the supreme Self possesses consciousness, that which is its own internal manifestation is itself of the nature of consciousness;
thus, within, it perceives itself as "I" and so forth.
And he knows nothing within, because here there is no object of knowledge;
nor does he savor any flavor, for there is simply no object to be savored.
And since there is nothing to be accumulated within, that [agent] does not exist;
nor is anything experienced, because of the non-existence of that which is to be experienced.
The Self, appearing as non-existent, is infinite and full in form;
it remains forever as a single solid mass within itself, like a great mountain.

But by this turn of phrase, O descendant of Raghu, I have demonstrated to you that there is no distinction between the non-existence of the "I" and so forth, and the non-existence of the world and so forth.
There is no mind, nor a thinker, nor the delusion of a world and so forth;
like the sky upon a stone, it is therefore peaceful and becomes utterly stilled.
Just as water attains the state of whirlpools and the like due to its fluidity within water,
so too does the knower attain the state of "I-ness" and so forth within the Self, which is consciousness, due to its nature as knowing.
Just as liquidity exists in water and motion in the wind,
so do egoity, space, time, and the like exist within the Knower, who is pure consciousness alone.
For that knowledge which the Knower knows in the state of knowing through the expansion of knowledge—
that is known as "I-ness" and so forth, and even as the "living self" (jīva) and so on, by means of the vital functions.
Just as the cognition of the knower arises through knowledge in whatever manner,
so does that [cognition] expand when it perceives its own non-difference from the object, despite the appearance of difference.

Knowledge is the life of the living being; when there is knowledge, there is the living of the living being. There is not even an atom’s worth of difference between the knower and the living being, nor any disparity in their nature.
Just as there is no difference between the Knower and the individual soul, O Rāma, so too there is no difference between the Knower and the world; know it to be peaceful and indivisible.
Everything is utterly tranquil, unborn, one, without beginning or middle, a mere manifestation consisting of self-experience, beyond thought and without signs.
Everything is utterly tranquil; yet this vision composed of words is for the sake of awakening alone—it is truly in vain, for that is simply "Om."
The fifty-eighth canto, titled "The Dispelling of Duality," by Vasiṣṭha:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
the wondrous account of the lord of the Kirātas, who was like a god.
It is the fat of the northern direction, a mass of camphor from the earth;
it is the laughter gathered from Śiva, or the white radiance of the moon.
On this Himālaya mountain there is a peak, a mountain named Kailāsa,
which is like the central gem of a cluster of pearls formed by the mass of other peaks.
His home was like the ocean of milk for Viṣṇu, like heaven for the Lord of the Gods, and like the navel-lotus of the Lotus-born Brahmā, as well as that of the Moon-crested Śiva.
He shines with the swaying clusters of rudrākṣa beads along with the celestial nymphs,
like the ocean with its waves of shimmering jeweled rods.
There, the *aśoka* trees, blooming in full splendor, shine like *aśoka* (griefless) beings, having been struck by the feet of the intoxicated women of the retinue who dance incessantly.
Where, as the quarters resound with the movement of the Bhrigus, waterfalls flow forth and ceaselessly return, moistening the ground with the liquid essence of moonstones.
That which is here enveloped by masses of creepers, shrubs, and trees, by ponds, lakes, rivers, and streams,
and by terrified herds of beasts and flocks of birds, like the cosmic egg.
At his base dwell the Kirātas named Hemajaṭas,
like ants gathered in the hollow at the root of an excellent tree.
In the forests at the foot of Mount Kailāsa, in Jaṭālā,
those base people who live near Sugulmaka dwell like crows.
Among them there was a noble-souled king, a conqueror of enemy cities,
who was like the right arm of both the Goddess of Victory and his subjects.
Named Suraghu, he was powerful, the destroyer of the pride of his formidable enemies; he was like valor incarnate, or like the wind embodied.

The Jina [is superior] through the riches of the power of dispassion; the leader of the Guhyakas through his wealth; the preceptor of Indra through his awakenings; and the teacher of the Asuras through his poetic compositions.
With an unwearied soul, he performed his royal duties through the sequence of punishments and favors, just as the sun traverses the days as they arrive.
Then he was overwhelmed by the pleasure and pain born from that,
just as a bird whose neck is caught in the snares of a net.
"Why do I afflict this suffering being with my power, as if he were a sesame-press?
For every living being, suffering arises just as it does for me."
"I bestow wealth upon him; through wealth, every person becomes possessed of joy, just as I am. Therefore, enough of my restraints!"
Or rather, I shall bring about the destruction of this world without him;
for without him, this creation cannot endure, just as a river cannot flow without water.
"Alas, what misery! This one was to be punished, yet by good fortune he is to be favored by me;
by good fortune I am happy today, yet by misery I am miserable today."
Thus the king’s mind, swinging to and fro, found no rest;
it wandered for a long time like a blade of grass caught in a great whirlpool of water.
Then one day, the sage Māṇḍavya came to his house,
having wandered through every corner of the quarters of the earth, like Nārada to the abode of Vāsava.
He honored that great sage, who was an axe to the stubborn tree-stump of the forest of doubt, and being skilled in all things, he questioned him.
Suraghu said:
"O Sage, by your arrival I have attained supreme bliss,
like one who has reached the surface of the earth during the month of Mādhava."
Today, O Lord, I stand at the forefront of the blessed by virtue of the Dharma,
since I have been beheld by you as a lotus is by the radiant sun.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, you have long been at rest;
therefore, sever this doubt of mine as the sun dispels the darkness.
Through association with the great, whose suffering indeed does not perish?
Yet those who know suffering say that doubt is the highest form of suffering.
Arising from the restraint and favor [of others], these anxieties, residing within the bodies of my servants,
torment me excessively, like the claws of a lion upon an elephant.
O Sage, O Honorable One, act with compassion so that it may arise within my mind in a manner that is all-pervading, like the rays of the rising sun.
Māṇḍavya said:
O King, this lightness of mind dissolves like snow through one's own means, established within oneself and dependent only on oneself.
The fever of the mind within is quickly pacified by one's own inquiry alone,
just as a great mist vanishes at the mere arrival of autumn.
With one's own mind, one should examine within oneself one's own sense faculties as they reside in one's body: what are they like, and what indeed are they?
"Who am I? How did this come to be? Or what is it, and how do birth and death occur?"—by investigating these matters within yourself, you will surely attain greatness.
For you, whose true nature has been fully understood through investigation,
the mental states of joy and resentment shall not cause your mind to waver from its immovability.
Having cast off its own form, the mind will attain peace and freedom from fever,
becoming as it was before, like a wave returning to the water.
O sinless one, even as the mind remains, it will abandon its form, just as time, when another season has arrived, sheds that which is devoid of blemish.
All those illustrious people will be objects of compassion for him who has seen reality and is content, just as subjects on earth are for their father.
O King, with the self perceived by the lamp of discernment, you will surpass even the greatness of Mount Meru, the oceans, and the sky, which bestows the supreme goal.
O virtuous one, your mind, having attained greatness amidst the cycles of worldly existence,
shall not sink down, like an elephant in the puddles of a cow's footprint.
But the wretched mind, O King, sinks even into a trivial matter,
just as an aged mosquito sinks into the water of a cow's footprint.
Through the mental impression of its own wretchedness, which clings to mere appearances, the mind sinks as if into mud like a worm.
To that same extent, O mighty-armed one, everything is surrendered by itself,
until only the Supreme Self remains as the supreme realm.
The ore is washed away until only the gold remains;
likewise, everything is scrutinized until only the Self is perceived.
Having completely renounced everything— in every way, everywhere, and at all times— by means of a universalizing intellect, one perceives the Self by means of the self.
As long as everything has not been relinquished, the Self is not attained;
when all things have been abandoned, that which remains is called the Self.

O virtuous one, as long as something else has not been relinquished, the thing-in-itself is indeed never apprehended as a universal; what then can be said regarding its attainment of its own self-nature?
O King, that alone— and nothing else— is truly attained where one, having abandoned all other activities, falls of one's own accord with one's whole being for the sake of attaining one's true self.
Therefore, for the sake of beholding the Self, one should renounce everything;
having renounced all things whatsoever, that which remains is the supreme state.

Having completely cast aside from the mind the expansion of all things existing within the world— which consists of the entire succession of causes and effects— and having utterly severed that [identification] from its own body, whatever remains is auspicious.
The fifty-ninth canto, titled "The Instruction of Māṇḍavya," within the narrative of Suraghu; Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to Suraghu, O descendant of Raghu, the Blessed One Māṇḍavya, adorned with silence, departed for his own quarter.
When the supreme sage had departed, the king went to a secluded and blameless place and reflected within his own mind: "Who indeed am I?"
I am not Meru, nor is Meru mine; I am not the world, nor is the world mine.
I am not the mountains, nor are the mountains mine; I am not the earth, nor is the earth mine.
"This Kirāta territory is not mine, nor am I the territory;
this region belongs to me solely by virtue of my own convention."
This convention has been abandoned by me; neither am I a country, nor is this [country] mine.
Now, only the city remains—this is the certain conclusion here.
A city rich with banners, city-gates, and palaces, crowded with servants and pleasure gardens, and filled with elephants, horses, and vassal lords— neither am I that city, nor is the city mine.
The multitude of enjoyments and the wife are bound by a useless convention; when that convention ceases, they are destroyed. Neither am I these, nor is all this mine.
Thus, along with my servants, my army, my vehicles, and my city, there is neither kingdom for me nor is the kingdom mine; for this worldly convention is but a source of confusion.
I consider myself to be nothing more than the body, joined with hands, feet, and so forth;
therefore, for now, I shall thoroughly examine this very thing within.
Therefore, in this regard, I am not this flesh and bone, which are insentient;
nor do they enter into union with me, just as water does not unite with a lotus.
Flesh is inert; it is not I, nor is blood sufficient to be I.
The bones are inert; they are certainly not I, nor do they ever belong to me.
I am not the organs of action, nor do the organs of action belong to me;
for that which is indeed insentient in this body, I am not that, as I am consciousness.
I am not the objects of enjoyment, nor do I possess objects of enjoyment, nor do I possess the sense organs;
for they are inert and of an unreal nature, and I am not the sense organs.
The mind is the root of the defect of transmigratory existence, for it is not the "I," which is indeed inert.
Furthermore, the views that "this is the intellect" or "this is the ego" are merely products of the mind.
That body consists of the sheath of the elements, ending with the mind, intellect, and senses;
I am not such a thing as the body and so forth—I perceive myself as distinct from that.

But the remainder is the living being consisting of consciousness, and it perceives by means of that which is perceived; when this [consciousness] is awakened by something else, it would not possess the nature of the reality of the Self.
Thus I renounce all that is experienced and all that is thought, for indeed I am not that; remaining free from conceptual construction, I abide as the residual, pure consciousness.
It is wonderful that I have attained my self and been born in time as one who knows what must be done;
yet I am that very Self which is infinite—wherein could there be an end for this Supreme Self?
In Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Vāyu, and likewise in the hosts of all beings,
this very Blessed One, the Self, exists like a thread running through pearls.
This very power of consciousness is stainless, free from the disease of the objectified world,
filling every corner of the quarters of space, and assuming the form of Bhairava.
Pervading all states of being, subtle, and free from both existence and non-existence;
it abides as far as the realm of Brahmā and is the source-casket of all powers.
She is the most beautiful and auspicious of all, the lamp illuminating all that is manifest;
she is the thread in the form of an extended cord for all those liberated from saṃsāra.
Rich in all forms of transformation, yet devoid of all forms;
she has become the flood of all beings, and at all times she has attained the state of being everything.
Within the belly of the world, these elements are of fourteen kinds;
this worldly conceptualization, consisting of them, is of the nature of sensation.
The entire course of all states of suffering is merely a false appearance;
the supreme consciousness itself, though appearing as various forms, is everything and is the Self alone.
This very [consciousness] is my all-pervading self; this is my awakening;
this, having assumed a bodily form, creates the delusion of being a king.
By the grace of this very [intellect], the mind, situated upon the chariot of the body,
gallops, leaps, and dances amidst the playful diversions of the web of saṃsāra.
This mind, body, and so forth are not anything at all in reality;
when this fragile [complex] perishes, nothing whatsoever perishes.
This dance, consisting of the web of the world, is performed by the actors that are the minds;
it is perceived as a single line by this streak of light.
"Alas, my concern regarding the state of restraint and favor was in vain;
it was centered solely on the body, yet the body itself is nothing at all."
Ah, how wonderful! I have now fully awakened; my false vision has vanished. That which was to be seen has been seen in its entirety, and that which was to be attained has been attained by me.
Whatever is seen here as this visible world, it is merely a portion of the outflow of consciousness; nothing else exists there that is eternal.
Where do those two exist, or of what nature are they, or upon what are they based, or what is their essence?
Likewise, [where do] restraint and favor, as well as the sequences of joy and resentment, exist in the world?
What is pleasure and what is pain? All this is the pervasive Brahman.
I was deluded in vain; by good fortune, I have now become un-deluded and remain established [in that truth].
In this light, why is there lamentation? Why is there delusion? What is being observed? What is being done? Where is one staying? Where is one going?
Something here shines forth as this very appearance of consciousness;
salutations, salutations to You, O One beyond all principles (nistattva), for You are both the seen and the seer, O Beautiful One!
Aha! I have indeed awakened; I have fully understood enough.
Homage to me, the infinite, and to the arising of perfect knowledge!

Free from passion, abiding in the objectless state, with the delusion of existence gone and devoid of striving, having transcended the state of stable deep sleep, I therefore dwell in the Self as the perfectly equal.
The sixtieth canto, titled "The Resting Place of Suraghu," by Vasiṣṭha:
Thus Hemajaṭādhīśa attained the unsurpassed state,
just as the son of Gadhi (Viśvāmitra) attained the status of a Brahmin through discernment and resolute effort.
He felt no weariness in his activities, which involved endless forms of action,
even as they were performed again and again, like a lord throughout a succession of days.
From that time forth, he remained free from the fever of all worldly desires,
intent upon his own duty as a mass of water flows toward a lower level.
Free from both joy and resentment, performing his natural duty, he—
possessing a noble and profound form— seized the splendor of the ocean.
He shone with a mental state possessing the quality of deep sleep—
unwavering yet luminous— just as a lamp shines by its own flame.
He was neither pitiless nor compassionate, neither subject to dualities nor free from envy; he was neither happy nor unhappy, neither desiring gain nor desiring loss.
With a constant vision of equanimity and a conduct characterized by stainless intellect,
he shone with inner coolness like the orb of the full moon.
Perceiving that the entire world is the manifestation of the essence of consciousness,
her intellect shone forth in its fullness, with the splendor of both pleasure and pain completely stilled.
Exulting, sporting, reeling, standing, walking, breathing, and sleeping,
he remained established in his own samādhi, awakened and absorbed in consciousness.
Then, ruling his kingdom free from attachment, that lotus-eyed one remained with his form unimpaired for many hundreds of years.
Thereupon, overcome by that splendor, he himself abandoned this bodily configuration called "the body," just as a drop of frost vanishes.
He entered that supreme, primordial cause, the Lord of Causes,
as a flood of water enters the full ocean by means of wisdom.

Having attained the stainless radiance of the singular form and reached the state of the sky, that Great-Souled One, with his sorrow stilled, became fully one with his supreme true nature, like a jar becoming one with the space within it when joined with the atmosphere.
The sixty-first canto, titled "The Conclusion of the Story of Suraghu," ends. Vasiṣṭha:
Holding fast to this view, the mind does not suffer,
like a child who has found a lamp while submerged in a terrible darkness.
Through the state of discernment, the mind attains tranquility by means of its very subtle form,
just as a bird in a chasm does so by clinging to a dense mass of firm grass.
Having understood this purifying vision and having cultivated it, speak [of it];
remain constantly in one-pointed concentration, adorning the surface of the earth.
Rāma:
O Lord of Sages, how can there be a single-pointed concentration, or of what nature is it? For the mind is as restless as the plumage of a peacock struck by the wind.
Vasiṣṭha said: Listen now to this wonderful dialogue between Suraghu, who was then awakened, and the royal sage Parṇāda.
I shall reveal to you this mutual conversation between the two whose souls have arisen awakened by the singular concentration on Rāghava.
There was a king of the Pārasīkas, a slayer of enemy heroes,
renowned by the name Parigha, who was like an iron bar upon his chariot.
O descendant of Raghu, Suraghu became his supreme friend,
just as Mādhava is to Madana when he dwells in the Nandana grove.
Once, there suddenly occurred a great upheaval in Parigha’s realm,
like the dissolution of the world at the end of an eon, born from the fault of the people's evil deeds.
There, many people perished, their lives destroyed by hunger,
like successions of living beings in a forest blazing with fire.
Seeing that suffering, Parigha fell into incomparable despondency;
he abandoned his entire kingdom like a traveler leaving a burnt village.
Unable to provide a remedy for the destruction of his subjects, yet free from passion,
he went to the forest to perform austerities like the Lord of the Jinas.
Unrecognized by the townspeople in a certain distant forest,
he dwelt there with a detached mind, as if in another world.
Practicing austerities with a tranquil mind and self-restrained, dwelling in a mountain cave,
he consumed there only dry leaves that had fallen of their own accord.
Then, for a long time consuming only withered leaves like a fire,
he acquired the name Parṇāda among the ascetics.
From that time forward, this best of royal sages became known as Parṇāda throughout Jambudvīpa and among the abodes of the munis.
Then, after a thousand years of asceticism performed with a resolute mind, he attained through the power of practice that knowledge born of self-purification.
He became free from dualities, devoid of passion, possessing equal vision;
effortless, beyond compassion, liberated while living, and awakened in intellect.
O virtuous one, he wandered at will through this monastery of the three worlds together with the Siddhas and Sādhyas, like a swan among lotuses.
Once, he reached the palace of King Hemacūḍa, which was constructed of jewels and resembled another peak of Mount Meru.
Having emerged from the pit of folly and having realized what is to be known, they both performed full mutual honors there toward their former friend.
"Ah! How indeed my auspicious and purifying deeds have borne fruit, since I have attained you!"—thus they spoke to one another.
With their bodies embraced, those two of irreproachable form sat together upon a single seat, like the moon and the sun upon a mountain.
Parigha said: "O my mind, through the sight of you, supreme bliss has arrived;
like the orb of the moon emerging from the water, it has attained inner coolness."
Natural affection for a friend, upon separation, branches out into a hundred shoots,
like a tree that has been cut down and regrown on the bank of a pond.
O virtuous one, remembering those confidential conversations, those playful gestures, and those actions from the past, I rejoice again and again.
O sinless one, this knowledge has been attained by me through the grace of Māṇḍavya— knowledge which arises from the grace of the Supreme Self, just as it was attained by you.
O lord of the earth, are you today free from suffering? Have you found rest upon the supreme cause, like Mount Meru above the circle of the earth?
O most auspicious one, does clarity arise in your mind through delight in your own self, like the water in a lake during the autumn?
O fortunate lord of men, do you perform all necessary duties with a gaze that is both very gracious and profound? MU_5,61.30.
Are the wise people in your lands free from mental and physical ailments, possessing abundant rice harvests, and dwelling without the fever of distress?
I trust that the earth, bending under the weight of your abundant harvests like a *phalinī* creeper laden with fruit, sustains your subjects most excellently.
I trust that your purifying fame has spread throughout the ends of the quarters like a cage of moonbeams, taking the form of a mass of frost.
O friend, have these quarters been made free of gaps by you through hundreds of virtues, just as the walls of a lotus stalk are filled with the water of a lake?
I hope that in every village, joyful young maidens sing your fame, which bestows bliss, even upon the stumps standing in the corners of the black-soil fields.
Is all well with your grain, your wealth, and your possessions; and is it well with your servants, your wives, your sons, and your cities?
Is this vine of your body free from mental and physical ailments,
so that it may bear the fruit known as merit, as described for both this world and the next?
Is your mind free from attachment toward the serpents of the sense-objects, which are pleasant at first sight but ultimately and utterly hostile?
"Alas! For a very long time we have been separated;
by the power of time we are joined together once more, like a spring day and a mountain slope."
O friend, those states of happiness and suffering born of union and separation, which are not witnessed by living beings, do not exist in this world.
In this same way, having reached a state of difference during these exceedingly long lifespans, we have once again become united; for the destiny of fate is indeed manifold.
Suraghu said:
"O Blessed One, who indeed can understand the course of this destiny governed by divine power— deep and causing wonder— any more than one can understand the movement of a lamp's flame?"
Having been separated from one another and cast far away into distant conditions, we have today once again been united; oh, what is impossible for Fate?
But we today, O Great Being, stand exceedingly well;
through the merit of your arrival, we have attained supreme purity.
For us, whose sins have been somewhat diminished by the arrival of Your teaching, the trees of merit have borne fruit in such a way that we are no longer distressed.
O royal sage, all the prosperities that were established in our city have today,
through your arrival, branched out into a hundredfold variety.
O one of great majesty, your sweet speech scatters about like a heap of elixirs; your glance is meritorious, for association with the virtuous is indeed equal to the supreme state.
The sixty-second canto, titled "The Encounter with Suraghu and Parigha," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, after staying for a long time engaged in such confidential conversation,
which was imbued with their former affection, the one named Ayudha spoke.
Parigha said:
"O King, whatever action is performed within this web of saṃsāra leads to happiness for one whose mind is concentrated, but not for another, O sinless one."
I hope you practice that supreme meditative absorption, which is free from conceptual construction, the ultimate place of rest, and the highest good of supreme tranquility.
Suraghu said:
"O Blessed One, tell me this which is free from all conceptual constructions:
what indeed is called that samādhi which is the supreme excellence of ultimate tranquility?"
O Great-souled One, who indeed is that wise person who, while constantly acting in silence or even in speech,
is never with an unconcentrated mind? Who, forsooth, is such a one?
But those whose minds are perpetually awakened, even while performing worldly activities,
remain always in perfect meditative absorption, being established in that single reality which is the Self.
Even for one who has assumed the lotus posture and joined his palms in the *brahmāñjali* gesture,
how can there be samādhi, or of what nature, for one whose own being is never at rest?
[Suraghu:
"O Blessed One, it is said that the realization of reality— which is a fire consuming the grass of all desires—
is attained through a specific kind of meditative absorption (samādhi), and not by remaining in silence."
O virtuous one, that which is concentrated, eternally satisfied, and perceives the object as it truly is,
is called supreme wisdom by the wise under the term "samādhi."
Unshaken, free from egoism, and not falling under the sway of dualities— the state that is firmer than Mount Meru— is designated by the term "samādhi."
Free from anxiety, devoid of longing, and abandoned of both the rejectable and the acceptable,
the perfectly fulfilled movement of the mind is designated by the term "samādhi."
From the moment his mind became endowed with ultimate awakening,
the concentration of that Great-Souled One remained uninterrupted from then on.
For once the mind has become awakened, meditative absorption is never again severed,
just as a lotus fiber drawn out by a child cannot be pulled back.
Just as the eye does not cease from seeing until the end of the day,
so too my wisdom shall not cease from beholding reality until the end of my life.
Just as a river is not obstructed by its constant flow of water,
so the vision of wisdom is not obstructed for even a moment through awakening.
Just as the movement of every fraction of time is never forgotten,
so too the intellect of the wise man never forgets its own self.
Just as the ever-moving wind does not forget its course anywhere,
so the intellect of the wise man does not forget the pure consciousness that has been ascertained.
Just as the movement of the divisions of time remains fixed while searching for its own course,
so too, O dear one, does the consciousness remain, searching for a long time that which is devoid of any object of thought.
Just as an object devoid of existence is not perceived,
so for the knower, time devoid of the knowledge of the Self is not found.
Just as one who possesses qualities cannot exist in saṃsāra while devoid of those qualities,
so too one who possesses a self cannot exist while being destitute of self-awareness.
I am always fully awakened; I am always stainless;
I am always peaceful in nature; I am always in a state of meditative composure.
By what means is a disruption of my meditative absorption produced, and how could it possibly be brought about by something distinct from the self, which is eternally of the nature of non-existence?
Therefore, my mind has never at any time been composed of meditative absorption,
nor has it ever been unconcentrated, because it arises solely from the reality of the Self.
The Self is all-pervading, eternal, and indeed everything in every way;
for what could possibly be non-concentration, and what is traditionally known as concentration?
The great ones, whose intellects are eternally concentrated and who possess perfect tranquility, abide free from the distinctions of the transformation of effects;
therefore, my supreme verbal exposition is not falsely proclaimed through the breaking down of the distinction between the unconcentrated and the concentrated.
The sixty-third canto, titled "The Determination of Samādhi," is concluded.
O King, you have surely awakened; you have attained that state.
With your inner self cooled, you shine like the full moon.
Filled with the honey of bliss and attended by supreme Lakṣmī,
you shine like a lotus— cool, smooth, and sweet.
Stainless, expansive, full, profound, and with your intentions made manifest,
you shine like the ocean when it is released from the agitation caused by the force of the winds at the shore.
Transparent, filled with your own bliss, with the clouds of egoism departed,
you shine clearly, vast and profound like the autumnal sky.
Everywhere you appear composed; everywhere you are fully content;
everywhere you are free from passion, O King, and everywhere you shine.
Having reached the further shore of discerning the essential from the non-essential through your great intelligence,
you know all this exactly as it is, without exception.
O Knower of the reality that distinguishes between existence and non-existence, O one of joyful disposition, your body remains free from the agitation of the states of equanimity and inequality.
O handsome one, you are completely satisfied with the non-substantiality of all things, as the ocean is by nectar, so that there shall be no further depletion.
Suraghu said:
"O Sage, there is no entity whatsoever in which we find anything to be accepted; for as far as this visible world extends, it is nothing at all."
Since there is nothing to be acquired, what indeed could there be that is to be abandoned?
Without the exclusion of its opposite, how can something be called "to be abandoned"?
Because all things are empty, yet because time is not empty,
my states of mind— both the empty and the non-empty— have long since been utterly exhausted.
Having observed here, through the influence of place and time, that the empty becomes non-empty and the non-empty becomes empty,
the wise should avoid both censure and praise.
In this world, praise and blame arise from passion; and passion arises from longing.
And that which is longed for is a magnificent object by one who possesses a beautiful intellect.
In the three worlds, women, mountains, oceans, rows of forests, and all living beings are utterly empty; there is no essence superior to that.
In this dilapidated world, which consists of soft tissues resembling tumors of flesh, and which is empty and devoid of anything desirable— what indeed is there to be desired?
When desire has ceased, there is the destruction of hatred and attachment,
just as light and heat vanish when the splendor of day has passed.
Enough with these excessively prolix elaborations of speech; here, this single vision is sufficient for happiness.
For if the mind within is joyful, its latent tendencies having been completely stilled, that indeed is the supreme state of stability.
The sixty-fourth canto, titled "The Firm Resolve of Suraghu," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having thus reflected upon the delusion of the world, Suraghu and Parigha honored one another; satisfied, they each returned to their respective duties.
O Raghava, having heard that very [teaching] which is the supreme cause of awakening,
become clearly established in this very awakening.
O steadfast one, when the dark cloud of egoism has completely dissolved in the sky of the heart by means of supreme wisdom, which is sharp through the extension of discernment, it is enough.
When the autumn season has arrived— agreeable to all the world, fruitful, joy-bestowing, pure, and expansive within the mind.
One abides in the supreme Self, the sky of consciousness— worthy of meditation, the refuge, perfectly equanimous, endowed with the wealth of all bliss, and most highly praised.
He who is eternally absorbed in the inner self, eternally turned inward and happy,
and eternally engaged in the contemplation of consciousness, is not afflicted by sorrow.
Even while deeply engaged in worldly affairs and even while filled with passion and hatred,
he does not take on internal stain, just as a lotus does not take on a drop of water.
The sage who possesses right discernment, having understood and whose mind is inwardly at peace,
is not afflicted by the mind, just as the lord of beasts is not harassed by an elephant.
The mind of the wise person never finds refuge solely in enjoyments nor becomes dejected;
like a tree in the Nandana grove, the mind of the wise remains as firm as the body of the Himalayas.
Just as a man is not pained by the death of a wife who has lost her passion for him,
so too the mind that has fully understood all ignorance does not give rise to suffering.
One who has fully understood the delusion of the mind through the nature of the arising light of the world is not touched by sin, just as the surface of the sky is not touched by dust.
The thorough comprehension of ignorance alone is the great medicine;
it is like a lamp for the darkness of the disease spread by ignorance.
For as soon as ignorance is thoroughly understood, it is then utterly exhausted; moreover, the realm of enjoyment no longer yields any pleasure.
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, the virtuous person whose inner mind is unattached and whose intellect is one-pointed is not touched by sin, just as a fish’s eye is not wetted by water.
When the light of the sun of consciousness has dawned and the night of ignorance has perished,
the ground of the mind of the knower reaches supreme bliss and shines forth.
When the sleep of ignorance has been stilled, a person awakened by the sun of knowledge attains that enlightenment by which one is never again deluded.
Those days are lived joyfully, and those sequences of action are truly fruitful,
in which the moonlight of consciousness, arisen from contemplation of the Self, shines within the sky of the heart.
A person who has crossed over delusion through constant reflection on the self attains an inner coolness, just as the moon does by means of its own nectar.
Those friends, those scriptures,
and those days by which the arising of self-reflection, radiant with the splendor of dispassion, becomes manifest.
Those wretched ones, who have incurred sin and are negligent in the contemplation of the self, grieve for a long time like creepers in the wilderness of rebirth.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, greedily longing for the bait of enjoyments,
its form worn out by old age, and tormented by sighs of grief.
One who carries the heavy burden of suffering, who lives in the wilderness of birth,
who is smeared with the mud of evil deeds, and who lies in the pond of delusion.
Bitten by the swarm of disease-stinging insects, dragged by the excellent rope of craving,
the horse of the mind is bound fast by the tether of kinsmen.
Worn out by children, wife, and poverty, sinking and surfacing in the mire of sin,
exhausted and deprived of rest, one is broken upon the long and arduous path.
Exhausted by coming and going, wandering through the forest of saṃsāra,
it has not found the cool shade and is tormented by intense heat.
Radiant in form yet wretched, overcome by the senses as if by draft animals,
and exhausted by the lashings of his own evil deeds, he is driven along in the carriage of karma.
[The mind] rolls about in the vast forest of ignorance with its limbs broken, difficult to bear as it revolves in the cycle of manifestation and disappearance.
Sinking into the pit of his own misfortune, perishing, destitute,
with limbs failing under the weight of karma, and uttering piteous cries;
O Rāma, exerting the greatest effort, one should by force for a long time rescue this bull of a living being from the pond of saṃsāra.
When the mind has been exhausted through the contemplation of reality, the individual soul is never born again;
at that time, it becomes one who has crossed the ocean of existence.
O Rāma, through contact with one of great power, the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra is obtained,
just as a firm boat is obtained from a navigator.
O Rāma, that desert-like land in which there is no tree of a virtuous person—
bearing fruit and providing cool shade— a wise man should not dwell there.
O Rāma, one finds great rest for a moment in the grove of the virtuous, which has leaves of smooth and cooling speech, is shaded by integrity, and is in bloom with smiles.
In the absence of that [discrimination], which bestows a continuous burning of great delusion,
a wise person should not sleep here with only a slight degree of discernment born.
For the self alone is the friend of the self; one should uplift the self by means of the self.
One should not cast the self into the mire-pit of rebirth through arrogance.
"What is this? How has it come to be? What is its root? What is its end?"—thus should the wise examine the suffering of the body with diligent effort.
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor scriptures, nor kinsmen can assist men when they have sunk and must be raised up by their own selves.
Having reflected upon something together with the mind alone— his constant companion and friend— the self becomes fully uplifted.
By means of the boat of the light of reality, which arises from self-reflection through the efforts of detachment and practice, one crosses the ocean of existence.
Though constantly pitied by people and burned by evil desires, one should not despise oneself; rather, one should lift oneself up with diligence.
One should lift up the elephant of the living being, which is submerged in the mire of birth, by using the great tethering post of ego-identity, the rope of craving, and the intoxication of the mind.
O Raghava, by this much alone the self becomes saved:
