that one casts aside delusion and wipes away the ego-sense.
By this much alone, the true path becomes fully manifest:
that the sense of "I" dissolves once the delusion of the mind has been cast aside.
By this much alone, O Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self is understood:
when the body is viewed as being equal to wood or a clod of earth.
When the cloud of egoism has perished, the sun of consciousness is seen;
thereafter, through its transformation, that state is attained.
Just as there is the perception of light itself when darkness is completely dispelled,
so too is there the self-perception of the Self when the ego-sense is severed.
That state which arises from the complete eradication of egoism, which is a source of perfect bliss,
is the supreme, full-formed consciousness that pervades all.
Resembling the full ocean, it does not enter the range of our speech;
it admits no comparison and does not pursue worldly passion.
If the fourth state (turyā) is attained as a vision characterized solely by the aspect of the light of consciousness and having reached stability, then it is compared to that [state].
Not far removed from similarity [to the waking state], this state of deep sleep is perceived as full in form, like the splendor of the sky reflected in the ocean.
When the mind and ego dissolve, there arises that supreme bliss, the body of the Supreme Lord, which abides within all states of being.
O Rāma, that state, which occurs through the perfection of yoga and arises immediately after deep sleep, is beyond the reach of words; it is experienced here only within the heart.
When this entire infinite reality of the Self is established within the mind that has attained firm transformation,
and when all external things have subsided, the God of gods, who is the soul of all moving and unmoving beings, is indeed experienced by oneself.
Following that, there is the destruction of the latent impressions of sense objects; following that, the auspicious and supremely lucid light [of consciousness];
and following that, by virtue of equanimity, there is the transformation into one’s own true nature, which is of an inconceivable form for the great-souled ones.
The sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Compassion," by Vasiṣṭha:
If the Self is not beheld even after cutting through the mind with the mind itself, having abandoned the notions of "mine" and "I," O lotus-eyed one; MU_5,65.1.
Worldly suffering does not set, like the sun depicted in a painting;
calamity arrives in endlessness, as vast as the great ocean.
Again and again approaches the agitated rainy season of worldly existence, dark as a cloud and like a tree, creating dull, surging waves.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between two friends, Bhāsa and Vilāsa, on the ridge of the Sahya mountain.
There is a mountain that has conquered the sky with its height, the surface of the earth with its plateau, and the netherworld with its base; it is a conqueror of the three worlds.
The Sahya mountain possesses an unbearable abundance of flowers, unbearable pure waterfalls,
treasures guarded by Guhyakas, and an irresistible luster.
Resplendent with golden slopes filled with layers of pearls and walls of reddish minerals, it was like the flank of a celestial elephant.

In some places it was strewn with a profusion of flowers; in others, it was more intensely variegated with mineral pigments; in some places it was scattered with blossoming lotuses; and in other parts, its surface was variegated with precious gems.
Here the mountain torrents roar; here the kīcaka reeds resound;
here the winds from the caves howl; and here the bees hum.
On the mountain peaks there were throngs of singing apsarases; in the forests, the soft warbling of birds; on the plateaus, intoxicated clouds; and in the thickets, the cries of wild beasts.
Guha was sung of by the Vidyādharas; the lotus-pond was sung of by the bees;
the Kirātas sang of its borders; and the forest trees were sung of by the birds.
Enveloped by the gods in its upper parts, enveloped by men at its feet,
and enveloped by the nāgas in the underworld, it was like another house for the world.
It was inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas) in its caves, by treasures hidden within it,
by elephants dwelling among its sandalwood trees, and by lions upon the peaks of its summits.
The wind had its body enveloped by clouds of flowers, was dusty with the pollen of flower-clouds,
bore clouds of flower-leaves, and was as pale-white as a flowering tree.
Tawny like a cloud of dust from the earth’s elements, standing upon a surface of precious stones, he was fully attended by throngs of celestial women as if they were carved from wood.
Where the mountain peaks, draped in garments of cloud-blue and adorned with ornaments of silent jewels, are as beautiful as women going to meet their lovers.
There, on the northern slope where the trees bent with fruit and where the waters of cascading torrents flowed into a network of jewel-pools;
Where the slopes of the quarters were thick with vidula, aṅkola, punnāga, and nīpa trees, bristling with clusters of blossoms shed from mango trees and creepers;
Where the sun was screened by a canopy of creeping vines, radiant with the mass of light from jewels,
where the ground was moistened by the flowing juice of the jambu fruit, and which brought delight to the celestial realm.
Equal to the world of Brahmā, as delightful as heaven, and comparable to the city of Śiva,
there is the glorious and great hermitage of Atri, which removes the fatigue of those who have attained perfection.
In that great hermitage of Atri, there were two ascetics who appeared like Śukra and Bṛhaspati in the path of the sky.
Then, from those two who shared a single dwelling, there were born two sons,
both sprouts of their lineage with pure bodies, like two lotuses from the goddess Sarasvatī.
Vilāsa and Bhāsa gradually attained growth,
like two young shoots on a creeper and a tree belonging to their parents.
Let them remain mutual friends, deeply affectionate and dear to one another;
they stand embraced like sesame seeds and their oil, or like a flower and its fragrance.
Those two were never separated, like a deeply devoted couple; their minds were so perfectly one that it was as if a single being had attained duality.
Thus, those two of most enchanting form, rejoicing in one another,
remained silent in their own hermitage like two bees upon a lotus.
Abandoning childhood, those two, beloved by the people, attained youth in a very short time, like the sun and moon risen together.
Then those two parents, afflicted by old age, abandoned their bodies and departed for heaven, like two birds flying up from their nest.
When their parents had passed away, the two of them became dejected in countenance,
with drooping limbs and devoid of energy, like two lotuses plucked from the water.
Having performed the funeral rites there, they both lamented;
for the way of the world is indeed inviolable, O giver of honor, even for the great.

Having performed the funeral rites for their deceased relative, they were then overcome by the pain arising from grief; having lamented piteously with voices of distress, they remained until the end of the day with hearts utterly vacant and devoid of all movement, like figures depicted in a painting.
In the account of Bhāsa’s playful adventures, the sixty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Sahya Mountain," Vasiṣṭha said:
Then those two firm ascetics stood overcome by grief,
all their limbs withered by penance like two trees in the forest.
Free from passion, the two twice-born ones spent their time in the forest,
having reached a state of supreme detachment like two deer separated from their herd.
Then days, months, and years passed for the two of them;
gradually, they both reached old age, like two trees growing from the edge of a chasm.
Having failed to attain pure knowledge, those two ascetics, long grown old,
once met together and spoke thus to one another:
Vilāsa:
O Bāṣa, great kinsman of this world, you who are the fruit of the fierce tree of life, the ocean of the nectar of consolation—welcome to you! MU_5,66.5//
"O virtuous one, tell me, where have all these days been spent by you who are separated from me? Is your ascetic practice perhaps free from blemish?"
Is your intellect free from fever? Have you become self-possessed?
Has your knowledge borne fruit? Are you well?
Vasiṣṭha:
To him who had spoken thus, being distressed by the ocean of saṃsāra and having not yet attained great wisdom, his friend then spoke with affection to that friend.
Bhāsa said:
"O virtuous one, welcome! Indeed, it is by good fortune that you are seen today, O giver of honor.
But how can there be well-being for us who remain here in this cycle of existence?"
As long as the knowable has not been realized, as long as the ground of the mind has not been exhausted,
and as long as one has not crossed over from saṃsāra, how can there be any virtue for me?
As long as wisdom has not been attained, as long as equanimity has not arisen,
and as long as awakening has not dawned, how can there be any well-being for us?
As long as the creepers of hope arising from the mind have not been cut down entirely,
like weeds by a sickle, how can there be well-being for us?
O virtuous one, without the attainment of the Self and without the great medicine of knowledge,
this cholera of miserable transmigration arises once again.
The wicked tree of saṃsāra approaches again: its growth sprouted in childhood, its foliage is fresh youth, and it is now flowering with old age.
From this body, which is like a decaying tree with its kinsmen as the humming bees,
there arises once more the cluster of blossoms that is death, white with the flowers of old age.

The series of years, having become insipid like food that has been eaten and turned sour with time, and having been woven together by many days, is led back again, consisting for the most part of dryness.
Furthermore, within the great caves of the mountain of the body, which are intensely bristling with the thorns of craving,
one is utterly destroyed by activities that are as effortless as playful serpents.

Nights pass and return, consisting mostly of unceasing arrivals and departures, long and long indeed, composed of both auspicious and inauspicious moments that take the form of fragments of pleasure amidst sufferings.
Life is wasted by base actions that fail to achieve their intended purpose— actions which are mere sprouts of the obsession with wicked desires and whose agents are themselves destroyed.
The intoxicated elephant of the mind, its tethering post of latent tendencies uprooted and prodded by the female elephant of craving, runs far astray.
Attached to the palate, which is like a petal on the tongue, within the cave-dwelling of the tree of the body,
the greedy vulture grows ever stronger upon that wish-fulfilling gem.
Lacking moisture, devoid of joy, and light, with limbs as fragile as falling petals and the color of withered leaves, this succession of days is wasting away.
Defiled by the dust of insult and with the beauty of its form vanished,
the face turns ashen, like a lotus struck by frost.
As the lake of the body dries up and the waters of youth flow away,
the royal swan of life, never to return, flees in an instant.
From the tree of life, shattered and shaken by the force of the wind of time,
the flowers of enjoyments and the leaves of days fall downward.
The mind sinks far away into the dark wells of delusion— waters filled with the croaking frogs of internal suffering, where those who indulge in enjoyments take refuge.
Diverse, manifest, and flickeringly delicate, craving ascends far aloft like a banner on a temple spire caught in the wind.
The hooves of Death clip away the life-hoping threads of this worldly system, which is rooted in the vast cavern of time.
The treacherous river of life flows on, with the surging waves of youth, foaming with intense exuberance, and possessing great whirlpools of recurring reversals.
The river of action flows boundlessly, its vast hollows agitated, crowded with a multitude of waves consisting of the shimmering effects of the various arts and powers.
Infinite rivers of kinsmen fall incessantly into the vast ocean of time, which has a deep abyss.
O Father, this jewel of a body is lost within the belly of the ocean of the mire of destruction;
it is not known where it has gone from birth to birth.
In the wheel of thought, which is ever-active with the movement of its revolving parts,
the mind wanders like a blade of grass in a whirlpool in the depths of the ocean.
Carried away by the great waves of mental activity within the infinite [ocean of existence],
the mind— its inner disposition dancing with anxiety— finds no rest for even a moment.
"This has been done, I am doing this, I shall do that"—enough!
Ensnared by the web of such mental constructions, the bird of the intellect swoons away.
This great malady of duality— “this is a friend, this is an enemy”—
cuts into my vital organs as if they were fresh lotuses.
Moving within the single mass of waves that are the whirlpools of intoxication, the fish of pride swells in an instant and in an instant suffers destruction through the spear of thought.
There are many such sufferings that belong to no self;
yet, by searching for them with the notion of a self, people fall into a state of wretchedness.
Falling into various kinds of pleasure and pain, shattered by the vast precipice of old age and death,
this worldling rolls upon the mountain of the belly of the universe and, like a sapless leaf, comes to a state of decay.
The sixty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition of Impermanence," by Vasiṣṭha:
Thus they exchanged inquiries regarding their welfare;
in time, having attained stainless knowledge, they then went to liberation.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, I say that for a mind bound by its fetters, there is no way to cross the ocean of saṃsāra other than through knowledge.
For one of noble intellect, even this infinite suffering is but a trifle; to a base bird, the ocean is like a mere puddle for the enemy of serpents (the peacock).
The great-souled ones, having transcended the body, abide in their own self which is pure consciousness;
seeing their own bodies from afar, they laugh at them as the sun laughs at the common folk.
When the body is suffering and agitated, what injury has befallen us? What loss is there for the charioteer when the chariot is overturned or broken?
When agitation arises in the mind, what has come upon the consciousness, my dear? When a wave is soiled by dust, does the ocean itself undergo any change?
What are swans made of iron? What are stones in the midst of milk? What indeed are rocks to wood? And what are enjoyments to the Supreme Self?
What kind of connection could there be between the eastern mountain of sunrise and the western ocean?
And what connection could there be between the nature of consciousness and bondage, which are separated by such vast distance and obstruction?
Even pieces of wood being carried along in the current of a river are eventually cast up;
what then can be said of the bodies of living beings in this world?
Just as from the friction of wood and water, sparks and the like arise,
so too do these fluctuations of the mind arise from the conjunction of the body and the self.
Just as reflections of wood and water are perceived from the wood in the water, so too are bodies perceived within the Self due to their connection with it.
Just as reflections in a mirror, water, and so forth are neither unreal nor real in reality, so too are bodies in relation to the Self.
Just as one is never distressed by the clashing of wood,
water, or stones, so too there is no injury to the five [aggregates] whether they are joined together or separated.
Just as trembling, sound, and other phenomena arise from water agitated by wood,
so too do they arise from this body when it is awakened by consciousness.
These cognitions do not belong to the Buddha or to the dull-witted, for they have consciousness as their body;
rather, these belong solely to ignorance, and when that [ignorance] is destroyed, they themselves cease to exist.
Just as there are no experiences of anyone regarding the contact between wood and water,
so too there are no experiences of anyone regarding the union of the body and the embodied self.
Just as this saṃsāra appears to have attained reality for the ignorant,
so too does this saṃsāra vanish and attain unreality for the knower of that.
Just as moisture on the surface of a stone is devoid of internal attachment,
so too are the experiences of external enjoyments when the activity of the mind is unattached.
Just as there is no internal attachment between water and wood,
even though they are in contact, so too is there no internal attachment between the body and the embodied self.
The connection between water and wood is devoid of internal attachment;
so too is the relationship between the body and the embodied soul, as well as between a reflection and the water [in which it appears].
Pure consciousness exists everywhere, devoid of any object of cognition;
other than that which is marked by duality, no difficult-to-perceive consciousness exists.
That which is not suffering becomes suffering through internal perception; clearly, a post becomes a ghost when it is conceptualized as a ghost.
For a non-connection indeed becomes a connection through internal determination,
like sexual union with a woman in a dream, or like the dissolution of a post or a ghost.
For a connection that is essentially unreal is like that between water and wood;
in the same way, the connection between the body and the Supreme Self is false.
Without internal attachment, water is not agitated by blows from wood;
the self, free from internal attachment, is not burned by the sufferings of the body.
The wise know that by the very cultivation of the body, the self remains under the sway of bodily suffering; therefore, through its abandonment, it becomes liberated.

Because they lack internal attachment, our limbs do not experience suffering even when joined together, just as leaves, water, stones, and pieces of wood do not suffer despite being in contact with one another.
Free from internal attachment, they attain supreme freedom from suffering;
likewise, the self is entirely unattached even when joined with the body, senses, and mind.
For internal attachment in saṃsāra is indeed the seed-cause of the trees that are old age, death, and delusion for all embodied beings.
A living being possessed of internal attachment is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
but one liberated from internal attachment has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra.
The mind that possesses internal attachment is said here to have a hundred branches;
the mind free from internal attachment is said to be dissolved.
Know that the mind attached [to objects] is impure, like a broken crystal;
know indeed that the unattached mind has the appearance of an unbroken crystal.
A mind that is unattached and stainless is clearly liberated even while wandering in saṃsāra; but one that is attached, even if engaged in long-term asceticism, remains bound by intense fetters.
The mind bound by internal attachment is liberated when freed from that attachment;
indeed, internal attachment alone is the sole cause of bondage and liberation.
For one who is liberated from internal attachment, there is no sense of agency even while acting,
just as there is no sense of being agitated by pleasure or pain in a dream.
Even for one who is bodiless, agency exists in the mind as the agent,
consisting of states of agitation, pleasure, and pain, just as in dreams and the like.
Within the mind, which is not the agent, the state of non-agency becomes clear;
for a person whose mind is empty does not perceive even while acting.
You experience what is done by the mind, but not what is not done by the mind;
nowhere indeed is the body the cause, nor is the mind the agent.
The wise know the mind to be unattached and indeed a non-doer while yet acting;
being unattached, it does not assume the state of being an enjoyer of the fruits of action.
One who is unattached is not tainted by the killing of a Brahmin or by the horse-sacrifice,
just as one whose mind is fixed on a beloved woman far away is untouched by the duties that lie before him.
The living being, liberated from internal attachment and possessing a sweet disposition,
is never truly an agent or an enjoyer, whether it is performing actions externally or not.
That mind which is liberated from internal attachment is without an agent;
it is disjoined, it is tranquil, it is united, and it is untainted.
Therefore, one should certainly avoid that cruel internal attachment which, though firmly established externally for all interconnected objects, causes all suffering.

The mind, freed from the fault of internal attachment and having attained peace, becomes like the primordial sky, possessing a stainless luster; it reaches a state of stable oneness with the Self, which is liberated from all mental constructs, just as a dark bee becomes one with the water that is as dark as a swarm of bees.
The sixty-eighth canto, titled "Reflection on Internal Attachment," [spoken by] Rāma:
O Blessed One, what kind of attachment is it that leads to bondage for men?
What is said to lead to liberation, and how is this [bondage] to be treated?

Vasiṣṭha: When the distinction between the body and the embodied self is entirely abandoned, there is no mental conception [of duality]. However, placing one's trust in the body alone is called attachment, which leads to bondage.
When there is a determination of limits regarding the infinite reality of the Self,
that desire for happiness which arises within it is called attachment, which is fit for bondage.
"All this is the Self alone; what do I desire, or what shall I renounce?"—know this to be the state of non-attachment residing in the body of one liberated while living.
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; let there be happiness or let there be none"—the man who is thus unattached within is said to be a possessor of liberation.
He does not delight in inaction, nor is he intent on the nature of action;
he who is perfectly equanimous and renounces the fruits of action is known as one who is unattached.
He whose mind does not fall under the sway of joy or anger, being solely established in the reality of the Self and free from attachment, is called one liberated while living.
The skillful renunciation of all fruits of action and the like by means of the mind alone, and not by means of physical action,
is known as non-attachment.
O dear one, when all activities manifested in various ways are performed without attachment,
they become a form of healing and bring about the highest good.
Under the influence of attachment, all these vast heaps of suffering branch out into a hundred directions, like a thorny tree in a ravine.
When a donkey on the road, its nose pulled tight by a rope,
carries a load with a terrified soul, that is the manifestation of attachment.
That a tree endures the affliction of cold, wind, and heat while remaining fixed in one spot with its body— that is the manifestation of attachment.
That a worm, its body tormented and crippled, wastes away its time submerged in a fissure in the earth— that is the manifestation of harmful association.
That a deer gives up its body due to the pain of a hunter’s arrow while feeding on dūrvā grass and shoots is the manifestation of attachment.
That they have become like creepers and grass, being mown down again and again,
and that their various movements have ceased— that is the manifestation of attachment.
Because of the union with the essence of the netherworld (rasātala-rasa), grasses, shrubs, creepers, and the like produce a certain form; that is the manifestation of attachment (saṃsakti).
Arising again and again, they dissolve like waves in a river;
that these infinite beings exist is the manifestation of attachment.
That the river of saṃsāra— which is inherently tranquil, yet appears infinite and crowded with hundreds of objects— is in such a state of intoxication, is the manifestation of attachment.
For attachment, O Raghava, is said to be of two kinds: barren and venerable.
The barren is everywhere that of the deluded; the venerable is one's own [attachment] for those who know reality.
Attachment born of objects such as the body, which is devoid of the realization of the reality of the Self, is called "barren" because it is a firm attachment that yields further saṃsāra.
Indeed, that attachment born of discernment, which has become true through the realization of the reality of the Self and is free from further saṃsāra, is said to be worthy of reverence.
With conch, discus, and mace in hand, his body manifesting through various modes of movement,
he protects the three worlds by virtue of his attachment to those worthy of worship.
Day after day, the sun makes the journey as a traveler upon the supportless path of the sky, due to its attachment to that which is worthy of reverence.
Through the power of devotion to the venerable one, the Brahmanic body indeed manifests, fashioned by a steady mind that maintains the composure of a great eon.
The body of Śaṅkara stands there, adorned with ashes, resting playfully upon the face of a woman, and rendered venerable by virtue of his attachment to her.
The perfected ones who have realized the course of consciousness, as well as the world-protectors and others,
abide within the multitude of worlds through the power of their attachment to those worthy of worship.
This other continuum of elements maintains the multitude of bodily mechanisms,
revolving through old age and death due to the power of fruitless attachment.
The mind falls upon sense-objects like a vulture upon scraps of meat,
solely under the power of a futile attachment born from the vain suspicion that they are delicious.
By the power of attachment, the wind blows within the hollow of the world;
the five elements abide, and this is the sustenance of the world.
In heaven are the gods, on earth are men, and in the netherworld are the serpents and asuras;
they all exist within the udumbara fruit of the cosmic egg like shimmering gnats.
Beings are born and die, they fall and they rise, incessantly and repeatedly, like droplets of water from a waterfall.
O dear one, the multitude of people, their limbs swallowed up by one another and shattered by dullness,
wanders about in confusion like a withered leaf in the sky.
The circle of constellations in the sky, densely covered by the swarm of gnats that is the earth,
vibrates with a whirling motion like the flood of water from the elephants of the underworld.
Even today, the moon does not abandon its soiled body, which— due to its dullness— is like a ball for the child of Time, marked by eclipses, portents, and indigestion.
The assembly of gods in heaven does not cut down the thicket of the mind, which is hardened by the sight of the suffering of various cycles of aeons.
"O Rāghava, behold this wonderful and variegated painting created by someone in the supreme ether, solely through the power of latent impressions."
This variegated painting of the world, fashioned within the void of the mind— the sole stage for its attachment— is never real at all.
For those whose minds are attached to this worldly existence and who are engaged in its affairs,
craving devours their bodies just as a flame of fire consumes blades of grass.

Who is able to enumerate the number of atoms in the bodies of the Lord of Waters, which are as numerous as grains of sand? Likewise, who is able to enumerate the multitude of atoms for one whose mind is thus distracted?
From the foot to the summit of Mount Meru, the waves of the Ganges—
like strings of pearls— are counted, but not the bodies of those whose minds are attached.
All successions of suffering come upon one whose mind is attached,
like great rivers surging with dull waves flow into the ocean.
For those whose minds are attached, these rows of beautiful inner apartments are fashioned as the hells named Raurava, Avīci, Kālasūtra, and so forth.
Know that people with attached minds are a dry heap of fuel for the blazing fires of hell; it is because of them that those fires burn.
O Rāma, whatever web of suffering exists within this world is all imagined for the sake of those whose minds are attached.
Everything is pervaded by ignorance, which is characterized by mental attachment, which is a burden to the body, and which seeks the states of both decay and arising.
O Rāma, through non-attachment to enjoyments, all prosperities reach their highest expansion,
like great rivers in the rainy season.
Know, O Raghava, that the attachment of the limbs to the internal self is like glowing embers;
know, O Rama, that the detachment of the limbs from the infinite is the elixir of immortality.
By the internal attachment, nature itself is consumed,
just as a medicinal herb is burned by the fire produced from its own fruit, like the woolly-ox-eye plant.
Unattached everywhere yet attached, abiding as if infinite, free from volitional construction and ever-luminous— the mind thus becomes conducive to happiness alone.
He who abides with his own mind free from all attachment— having attained the arising of the vision of wisdom, yet having reached the cessation of the domain of ignorance— is liberated.
The sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Discerning Attachment," by Vasiṣṭha.
At all times, with everyone, in every situation,
and even while engaged in all activities, the mind should be kept alert by one who possesses discernment.
It is not attached here to thoughts, nor to activities, nor to objects;
neither in space, nor in the region below, nor in the directions, nor in the creepers.
It is not outside in the vast expanse, nor indeed in the functions of the senses;
it is not within, nor in the vital breath, nor in the head, nor in the palate.
It is not between the eyebrows, nor at the tip of the nose, nor in the mouth, nor in the hollow of the eyes;
it is not in darkness, nor in light, nor in this sky of the heart.
It is not in the waking state, nor in the dream, nor in deep sleep, nor in the pure;
it is not in the black, nor in the yellow, nor in the red and other colors, nor even in the variegated.
It is neither in the stable nor in the moving, neither in the beginning nor in the middle nor elsewhere;
it is neither far nor near, neither in the limbs nor in objects nor in the self.
Neither in sound, touch, or form; nor in states of delusion or bliss;
nor in the activities of going and coming, nor in the reckoning of time.
Having rested solely in pure consciousness, let the mind— though still slightly supported by objects of thought— abide everywhere as if devoid of flavor, finding its only true relish in the Self.
Abiding there, free from attachment, the living soul has attained the state of the non-living;
let it perform all this worldly activity, or let it not.
Whether not performing or indeed performing the activity of delighting in its own self,
the living being does not incur a connection with the fruits of action, just as the sky is unaffected by clouds.
Or else, having abandoned even that objective aspect, let the living being remain as a mass of tranquil consciousness, perfectly stilled within itself like a glowing gem.

O Rāmabhadra, the living soul (*jīva*), having attained the self that is eternally manifest as nirvāṇa, does not incur attachment even while engaged in worldly affairs on earth; by virtue of being free from attachment, it remains aloof from the fruits arising from karma and, as it were, smiles at the body from afar.
The seventieth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Practice of Constant Conduct," by Vasiṣṭha.
Established in meditative absorption on the bliss of non-attachment, those who have realized the Self remain inwardly free from sorrow even while engaged in worldly affairs.
In the face of one whose body is both agitated and unagitated, whose consciousness is free from sensation,
and who is full within, glory is perceived like that of the moon.
He whose mind, free from fever, takes as its support the consciousness that is devoid of the object of thought— by him the world is made serene, just as water is clarified by *kataka* nut.
Constantly absorbed in the vision of the Self, the knower remains established in his own nature; even though he is fickle, he appears agitated only in vain, like the reflection of the sun in water.
The great-souled ones, delighting in the Self, awakened and possessing supreme exaltation,
are as flickering as the tips of peacock feathers on the outside, yet as immovable as Mount Meru within.
The mind, having attained the nature of a self through its coloring by pleasure and pain,
does not undergo that coloring, just as a smooth crystal [does not take on the hue] from contact with a dye.
The view of cyclic existence has arisen for one who knows the higher and lower worlds;
it does not stain his true mind, just as a streak of water does not stain a lotus.
One who consists of meditation on the self, having attained supreme awakening and being liberated from the impurity of conceptualization, is called "unattached."
Through delighting in the Self, the living being attains non-attachment here;
through knowledge of the Self, attachment comes to attenuation, and not otherwise.
O Rāghava, while still awake, the living being becomes as if in deep sleep;
in this vision, it is free from duality and is eternally beyond both setting and rising.
Here, having attained maturity, it reaches the purifying state of the fourth (turya),
just as the moon, by the power of its transformation, reaches the state of the sun on the new-moon day.

That state of one whose mind is exhausted, wherein the condition of being a "thinker" and the objects of thought have vanished, is called the cessation of mental construction; it is a state of deep sleep even while awake.
And having entered that state of sleep, a man who lives and conducts himself is never dragged about by the thongs of pleasure and pain.
He who, while remaining in the state of deep sleep even while awake, performs the activities of the world,
does not experience pleasure or pain, being like a mechanical puppet.
Attachment that causes affliction to the mind brings the torment of existence and non-existence;
when the mind has attained the state of selflessness, what can afflict whom, and how?

Performing actions with the intellect of one who is in deep sleep, as if by the effortless play of a former deity, the living being is not bound, remaining established in the state of liberation while alive.
O sinless one, relying upon the state of deep sleep, perform or do not perform your own action as it comes to you through the impulse of your innate nature.
Neither the undertaking nor the abandoning of action is pleasing to the one who knows;
those who have realized the Self remain, following whatever has come to them.
Even while acting, you are not an agent through the intellect that abides solely in deep sleep;
and even as a non-agent, you are an agent—act as you wish.
Just as an infant on its cradle does not stir, conceiving no thought of anything,
so too, O Rāghava, perform your actions without conceiving of fruits and the like.
Because he abides in the state that is both unconditioned and consciousness, he possesses the intellect of deep sleep even while awake;
whatever he performs once he has attained his true self, in that he has no sense of agency.
Having reached the state of deep sleep, the knower who has dispelled all mental impressions through self-knowledge alone attains an inner coolness, just as the moon does by its essence.
Abiding in deep sleep, the one of great splendor rolls like the orb of the full moon;
he remains the same in all states, just as a mountain remains constant through the seasons.
The wise-souled one, though established in deep sleep, emerges externally into a state of agitation;
yet he does not waver within during his activities, like a mountain trembling from an earthquake.
Having become established in the state of deep sleep, with the body free from all taints,
either cause it to perish quickly or sustain it for a long time like a mountain.
O Rāma, this very state of deep sleep, when it becomes mature through the practice of yoga,
is called the "Fourth" (turya) by those who are skilled in the principles of reality.
In this state, the knower of the Great Awakening becomes one consisting of bliss alone, with all afflictions completely destroyed and the mind utterly set at rest.
Abiding here, the knower is delighted and reeling with supreme bliss;
he regards this worldly construction as if it were a mere play.
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, with the agitation of saṃsāra gone,
the self-possessed one who has ascended to the fourth state (turya) does not fall again.
The man of steady intellect looks upon this person who strives to attain his own holy state as one standing on a mountain looks down at those below, smiling.
But having attained an imperishable state in this fourth stage,
one has reached the state beyond bliss because of being entirely absorbed in bliss alone.
Beyond even that state of great bliss which is devoid of worldly joy, and transcending all parts (kalās), the yogi who has reached the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is called "liberated."
Having dissolved all the bonds of birth and being entirely devoid of the mental conceit of egoism,
the great-souled one attains an existence consisting of the supreme essence, like a fragment of rock salt dissolved in water.
The seventy-first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Treatment of Attachment," by Vasiṣṭha.

O descendant of Raghu, as long as there is the reflective awareness of the Fourth (turya), so long is there the state of absolute oneness, which is the domain of the living-liberated (jīvanmukta) and of words.
Beyond this, O mighty-armed one, there is no sphere for those who are liberated while still in the body, nor for their words, just as the sky is not the domain of ordinary men.
For that state of rest is more distant even than the farthest distance;
it is reachable only by those liberated while in the body-less state (videhamukta), like the path of the wind through the sky.
Having enjoyed the maintenance of the world for some time through the state of deep sleep,
they thereafter attain the fourth state (turya), reeling with supreme bliss.
O scion of Raghu’s lineage, just as those who know that [reality] and are skilled in the Self reach the state beyond the fourth, so too do you attain that state free from dualities.
O Rāma, subduer of enemies, engage in worldly affairs with the state of deep sleep; like the moon of the mind, you shall have neither waning nor agitation.
Do not grasp at consciousness as being the body, whether in its dissolution or its stability;
for this is an error that expands, thinking "this is the body."
What purpose do you have for the destruction of the body? What purpose do you have for the preservation of the body? Engage yourself in your natural activities; let this [body] remain as it is.
You have known that truth; you have awakened to that state;
you have attained your own true nature. Be free from sorrow for the sake of your well-being.
Having abandoned what is desired, undesired, and neutral through the splendor of your cool radiance,
you shine like the sky freed from darkness, heat, and clouds.
The mind is your self; when perfected, it does not run after lower things.
A person accomplished through yoga, mantra, and austerity descends from the sky as if onto the earth.
Here, there exists only pure consciousness, devoid of near and far; let there be no delusion in you such as "this is that," "I am this," or "this is mine."
The designation "Self" is merely a conceptual construct for the sake of conventional usage applied to the All-pervading Lord;
distinctions such as name and form have long since departed far from Him.
Just as the ocean is nothing but water and not separate from its waves and so forth,
so too all this is only the Self and not separate from the multitude of elements and the rest.
Just as nothing other than the water of the entire ocean can be found,
so too, within the vastness of the world, nothing other than the Self can be found.
O wise one, where do you establish the notion "this is I"?
What is that "you," and what would belong to you? What is not you, and what would not belong to you?
There is no duality, nor a body, nor any connection with those [objects] for the stainless consciousness; it is impossible, just as darkness cannot affect the sun.
O Slayer of Enemies, even if one were to concede the existence of duality,
the omnipresent Lord could have no connection with the body and other such things, even if they were real.
Just as no connection is possible between the spreading of shadow and sunlight, or between light and darkness, so indeed it is with the body and the embodied self.
Just as there can never be a connection between cold and heat, which are eternally opposed to one another, O Rāma, so it is with the body and the self.
But how can a relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) be experienced between these two—
the insentient body and the sentient embodied self?
The claim that the body is connected to the Self, which is pure consciousness alone,
arises from a misconception as difficult to comprehend as the notion of water in a forest fire.
Through the contemplation of truth, this false view perishes,
just as a mirage in the heat vanishes upon the correct observation of it.
The conscious self is stainless, eternal, self-luminous, and free from affliction;
the body, however, is impermanent and impure—how could it be connected with that?
The body undergoes vibration through the wind and is made full by the elements;
therefore, there is not even the slightest connection between that body and the Great Self.
Even if duality were established for the body, a connection [to it] would not be possible;
but since duality is not established, O wise one, how could such a calculation even exist?
This alone is the truth; therefore, my dear, establish yourself in this very state.
There is neither bondage nor liberation for anyone, at any time, or anywhere.
O Rāma, bring to firmness everywhere, both internally and externally, this clear conviction that everything is composed of the Self and is peaceful.
"I am happy," "I am suffering," and "I am deluded"—these are known as false views.
If you maintain the notion of a real entity in these states, you will experience long-lasting suffering.
The same sequence that is stated regarding the equality between a mountain and a blade of grass, or between silk and a stone, applies likewise to the Supreme Self and the body.
Just as the unity of cold and heat is not seen even in mere discourse, so too there is no union between the insentient and light; such is the case for the self and the body.
Just as there is no connection nor any similarity between light and darkness,
O Rāma, so indeed it is with the absolute difference between the self and the body.
The body moves by means of that wind; by that very same [wind] it comes and goes, and it produces sound through that which sports within the channels of the body.
Just as sound consisting mostly of the letters ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa manifests within the internal wind,
so indeed does it arise from the hollows of the body, like that from a bamboo flute.
The twinkling of the pupils and the movement of the eyes are due to the vital air (māruta);
likewise, the throbbing of the sense organs is merely the consciousness of the Self.
The state of the Self resides everywhere—in space, stones, walls, and so forth;
it is perceived within the mind alone, like a reflection in a mirror.
Having abandoned the abode of the body, wherever the bird of the mind goes by the power of its own latent impressions, there alone the Self is experienced.
Just as where there is a flower, there the perception of its fragrance is established,
so too where there is the mind, there the perception of a self is established.
Just as space, which is omnipresent, is reflected in a mirror,
so too the Self, though omnipresent, is perceived within the mind.
Just as the downward-sloping place on the surface of the earth is the locus of waters,
so too the internal organ alone is the locus of the self's cognitions.
The self-consciousness, reflected within the internal organ, spreads out this form of the world— both real and unreal—
just as the light of the sun spreads out illumination.
Therefore, it is the internal organ alone that is the cause in the evolution of the elements;
but the Self, because it transcends everything, is the ever-existent cause that is itself no cause.
The great-minded say that lack of inquiry is ignorance, which is folly;
it is the essence of wandering through the cycle of saṃsāra and the cause of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Due to improper perception and delusion, the mind has grasped at existence,
like a tiny seed-particle of total confusion that is dissolved by the sun of wisdom.
O Rāghava, through the thorough knowledge of the single reality of the self as it truly is,
the mind reaches a state of non-existence in an instant, like darkness before a lamp.
Therefore, due to a lack of inquiry, the mind itself is the cause of saṃsāra;
it is known by such names as the living soul (jīva), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), consciousness (citta), and the intellect (manas).
Rāma said:
O Lord, these numerous designations have become firmly rooted in the mind;
tell me how this is so, O giver of honor, for the sake of my spiritual perfection.
Vasiṣṭha:
All these phenomena are eternally of the single nature of the reality of the Self,
just as various waves and droplets are nothing but water.
The Self, whose nature is solely vibration, resides here and there within them,
just as pure water or the stainless sky exists within restless waves.
In some cases, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) remains within them as one whose nature is motionless,
just as the state of water persists in waters that have not yet attained the condition of waves.
In that regard, entities such as stones are motionless and remain fixed in themselves;
however, beings such as humans are restless, quivering like the foam upon wine.
There, within those bodies, by means of the Self through its omnipotence, it assumes the mental construction of ignorance; thus, it has resorted to that ignorance.
That ignorance, veiled by the infinite Self, is called the *jīva*;
it is the transmigrating being, an elephant trapped within the cage of the great delusion of *māyā*.
It is called "jīva" because of its vitalizing function; the ego-sense is so named through its state of "I-ness";
the intellect (buddhi) is defined by its capacity for ascertainment, and the mind (manas) by its faculty of conceptualization and volition.

The body exists as *prakṛti* by virtue of its being the manifest nature, while the conscious self exists as *cetana* by virtue of its own essential being; the former is inert through its state of materiality, whereas the latter is conscious through its own existence.
That supreme reality which exists between the perception of the inert and the non-inert is this very same thing that has arrived as manifoldness through various designations.
Thus, O sinless one, the true nature of the individual soul has indeed been proclaimed in many ways across numerous Vedānta texts, such as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and others.
But by other deluded and false-imagining sophists, these designations have been fruitlessly conceptualized for the sake of mere delusion.
Thus, O mighty-armed one, this soul is the cause of saṃsāra;
what has been done here by this mute and most wretched body?
Just as the destruction of one of the two— the container or the contained— implies the destruction of the other, so too,
upon the destruction of the body and such, there is no destruction of the self.
Just as when the sap of a single leaf has been exhausted, the essence does not undergo further decay, and the leaf-sap enters into the midst of the network of the sun's rays; //MU_5.71.61//
Upon the dissolution of the body, the embodied soul does not undergo destruction for anyone;
if it is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), it likewise abides in the space of the self.
I think that for one whose ignorance is such that they have the delusion, "I am destroyed when the body is destroyed," a vampire has risen from the slope of his mother's breast.
For that whose destruction is absolute is known as "arisen";
indeed, the destruction of the mind would be its destruction, and that is called liberation.
When others say "he is dead" or "he is lost," that is false and not true;
having been separated by space and time, he is experienced once again.
It is perceived by people as if it were grass caught within the waves of a flood,
merely under the designation of "death," while [the body] remains concealed by place and time.
Driven by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the living being (*jīva*) departs, casting off its body,
just as a monkey leaves one forest tree and takes its stand upon another.
Furthermore, O Rāghava, having abandoned even that, it departs for yet another place in an instant, at another time and in another vast region.
Driven here and there by their own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), living beings are led for a long time by that which they subsist upon, just as children are led by a cunning nursemaid.
Ensnared by the rope of latent impressions and aged within the mountain clefts,
the jīvajīvaka birds waste away their lives with extreme suffering.

Bearing the heavy burden of suffering brought upon them by an aged world, their lives worn out by advanced decay and gasping for breath, multitudes of people fall for a long time into the weight of hell through the persistence of latent impressions produced in the heart.
Vālmīki:

When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites. The assembly, having offered their salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The seventy-second chapter, titled "Instruction on Saṃsāra," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
When the body is born, you are not born; when the body is destroyed, you are not destroyed.
You are the Self, the stainless Self; the body is nothing at all to you.

The analogy of the jujube fruit in a bowl, or the existence of space within a jar— when one of these two is damaged or destroyed, the notion that both are [likewise] destroyed is a futile conceptualization.
When this perishable body has been destroyed and has returned to its own state,
fie on that blind-minded person who grieves, thinking, "I am perishing."
Just as the connection between two chariots and their reins is devoid of affection or agitation,
so too is the relationship between the body, the mind, the senses, and pleasures perceived by consciousness.
O Rāghava, just as the relationship between a lake, mud, stones, and water exists through mutual dependence, so too is the relationship between the body, the senses, and the self.
Just as the union and separation of the ocean, the earth, and other such elements occur without longing or lamentation, so too are the union and separation of the body and the embodied soul.
Just as those terrified by the transformations of an imagined vetāla are themselves falsely imagined, so too are affection, pleasure, and the like.
The various classes of beings are fashioned from the aggregate of the five elements, just as diverse figurines are carved from a single block of wood.
In a wooden man, nothing other than wood exists;
in the body, nothing other than a mass of elements exists.
O people, when the five elements are agitated, destroyed, or produced,
why have you fallen under the sway of joy, resentment, and despair?
What excellence indeed is there in men, whether their name be "woman" or some other,
who have arisen as mere aggregates of elements, like a whirlwind of dust?
The diversity of arrangements and parts serves only for the satisfaction of the ignorant; but for those who know that, there is the vision of the five elements as they truly are.
Just as there is no passion between two stone statues situated upon the same rock, even though they are joined together, so it is with the mind and the body.
May there be for you, in the union of the intellect, the senses, the self, and the mind, that same kind of mutual disposition which occurs when clay figures meet.
The statues of stone do not possess the bond of mutual affection;
so too with the body, the senses, the self, and the vital breaths—who here is there to lament?
Just as a wave thoroughly brings together masses of grass that have drifted hither and thither, so does the Creator bring together all beings.

Just as blades of grass in the waters of the ocean are joined together and then separated, so indeed do the elements that constitute the body unite and disunite within the Self, once internal conceptualization has ceased.
The Self remains embracing the elements that constitute the body by means of its nature as consciousness,
like water that has turned back from its flow and is free from internal movement, though it still clings to the blades of grass.
Through awakening, having abandoned the state of being the mind, the self itself attains its own true nature,
just as water, by the power of its own movement, abandons its whirlpool and becomes transparent.
Then, situated within the mass of wind, the living being perceives the multitude of elements as something separate from it,
like one sees the circle of the earth from afar.
Having abandoned the collection of separate elements, he becomes unborn and transcends the body;
he attains supreme light, like a sun-crystal in the day.
Then he knows himself by himself, freed from the maladies of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge;
like one released from intoxication, he internally recollects his own consciousness.
The Self alone vibrates in the sky of consciousness, appearing as if arisen through the networks of objects,
just as the infinite waters of the ocean appear as waves, droplets, and surges.
Possessing such great awakening, free from passion and devoid of sin,
those liberated while living move about here in this world, having attained the state of a great being.
Just as great waves shine with various precious gems,
so do the best of men shine through diverse worldly activities, being free from all latent tendencies.
The ocean is not exhausted by the erosion of its shores, nor the sky by dust;
likewise, the self-possessed person here does not wither through his own worldly activities.

Whether by those who have departed or those who have arrived, whether they are pure or impure, fickle or dull-witted— the ocean feels neither passion nor aversion toward enjoyments once it has attained its own nature.
Whatever mental cogitation exists anywhere in the entire world,
the wise know that to be the radiant play of the nature of consciousness as it is oriented toward an object of thought.
That which I am, that which is the primordial being and so forth, and that which exists throughout the three periods of time—
the expansion of the relationship between the seer and the seen— that alone unfolds.
Whatever is perceived is either non-existent or existent, yet it relies upon a single perception;
since the other [the perceiver] is untainted by that, how can there be the states of joy or sorrow?
The unreal is indeed unreal, for the real is always real;
know that the real-unreal is non-existent—why then are you bewildered by its meaning?
Abandoning false vision, see correctly, O one with beautiful eyes;
the mature person who possesses right vision is never deluded here in this world.
That ultimate happiness which exists in the relationship between the seen and the seeing,
and which consists of pure experience, is therefore called the Supreme Brahman.

The unsurpassed consciousness of bliss arising from the relationship between the seen and the seeing bestows saṃsāra upon the ignorant and liberation upon the wise, bringing about the emergence of happiness.
The wise know the happiness of the relationship between the seen and the seer to be the very nature of the self;
when that [self] is enveloped by the seen, it is bound, and when free from it, it is said to be liberated.

If the experience of bliss arising from the relationship between the seen and the seeing is free from affliction and liberated from both decay and excess, that is declared by the wise to be liberation.
In the relationship between the visible object and the act of seeing, there is an experience whose own domain is [the object];
having taken as its support that [experience] which is free from both the visible and the seeing, one becomes neither existent nor non-existent.
For this very vision of deep sleep thus attains full illumination;
and thus it attains the state of the Fourth (turya), which is traditionally known as liberation.

O Rāghava, when the perception of the visible has been relinquished through the application of supreme intellect, yet this consciousness of the connection between the visible and the seer still persists; MU_5,72.39.
The self is neither gross nor subtle; it is neither perceptible nor conscious;
it is neither unconscious nor inert; it is neither non-existent nor composed of existence.
I am not "I," nor another, neither one, nor many, nor possessing many; I am neither standing near, nor standing far, neither existing, nor non-existing.
It is neither unattainable nor attainable; it is neither non-omnipresent nor omnipresent;
it is neither a category of existence nor a non-category; it is neither not fivefold in nature nor fivefold.
That which has come within the range of vision, the domain of the six senses with the mind as the sixth—
whatever state may transcend that is, as it were, nothing at all.
O wise one, for the knower who perceives this world correctly as it truly is, everything consists of the Self; there is nothing anywhere that does not consist of the Self.
In hardness, fluidity, motion, space, and vision,
the Self alone is everything within all things— earth, water, air, ether, and fire.
There exists only consciousness, without which there are no objects;
know that to say anything exists as something separate from that is the prattle of a madman.

O Great-Souled One, you have transcended worldly existence; for you possess this realization: "I am the Self alone, which has traversed all worlds throughout the entire succession of kalpas and their cycles of coming and going; there is no other conceptualization whatsoever. MU 5.72.47.
The seventy-third chapter, titled "Instruction on the Essential Nature," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
O Raghava, by such a perspective that abandons duality,
one's own true nature is attained by the knowers of reality, just as the wish-fulfilling gem is obtained by those who know it.
Now hear this other vision, O Rāma,
by means of which you shall behold the self as immovable and become possessed of divine sight.
I am the sky, I am the sun, I am the quarters; I am also that which is below.
I am the Daityas, I am the gods, I am the mountains, and I am the great light.
I am darkness, I am the clouds, and I am the earth, the oceans, and so forth;
I am dust, wind, and fire—indeed, I am this entire universe.
In all three worlds, everywhere, it is indeed that very Self alone that abides;
who am I, and what is "other" here? For how can there be duality for that which is one?
Thus, one who possesses such certainty within, perceiving the world as truly being the Self, is certainly not helplessly overcome by joy or sorrow.
O sinless one, since this entire world is indeed established as consisting of the Self (manmaya), tell me, O lotus-eyed one: what could be one's own and what could be another's? MU 5,73.7.
Apart from that Knower, what exists which,
upon its appearance, could cause joy, or upon its destruction, cause dejection, for the Knower who is identical with the universe?
These two pure forms of ego-perception belong to the quality of goodness (sattva);
they proceed from the knowledge of reality, are ultimate in nature, and bestow liberation.
"Another is the subtle ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*) which thinks, 'I am beyond all forms';
the first, O scion of Raghu, is described by others as 'I am everything.'"
But there exists, O sinless one, a third view of the ego, namely "I am the body"; know that this leads only to suffering and not to peace.
Alternatively, having abandoned even these three for the sake of attaining all perfections,
remain firmly established in that state, resorting to whatever support you desire.
Although its nature transcends all things and it surpasses all existence,
the Self, the illuminator, truly exists, filling the entire world with its own being.
Behold quickly through your own direct experience that you are indeed that which is eternally arisen;
O best among the knowers of reality, abandon doubt and the knot of the heart.
O Rāma, there is no self to be known through inference, nor through the words of authoritative persons and the like;
for he [the Lord] perceives everything, in every way and at all times, through direct perception.
Whatever this vision is— whether it be vibration or even the slightest consciousness—
all that is the Lord, the Self, who is devoid of both the seen and the seeing.
That deity is neither existent nor non-existent; he is neither atomic nor is he great.
He is not even the middle between these two states of perception, yet he alone is all this in every respect.
He speaks this very thing, yet it is not fitting for him to speak;
this is neither different from that, nor is it that—behold the faultless illusion!
"This is not the self; this too is the self"—this distinction of designations is imagined within one's own self by that very omnipresent power.
For it is established everywhere, radiant throughout the three times;
yet, because of its subtlety and its extreme greatness, it is not perceived as a mere [object].
While infinite objects exist,
the Self naturally reflects as a living being within the mirror of the *puryaṣṭaka* by its own inherent nature.

Through the very emergence of the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), the Self is experienced by itself at all times and in all states, just as the wind in the sky is perceived through the movement of clouds.
The conscious self is all-pervading and omnipresent; it does not abide anywhere as a localized entity.
Just as existence (sattā) belongs to all things, so too is Maheśvara.
When that subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) exists, the individual soul (jīva) manifests, but not as a stone;
just as dust appears when there is wind, or as sight appears when there is a lamp.
This desire of the city-of-eight arises only when one is established in the Self alone,
just as the worldly craving of people manifests when the sun has risen.
If, while the sun remains in the sky, this worldly activity perishes because its established order has arisen under its influence, what has happened to the sun itself?
If, while the Divine remains within the self, the body— whose very existence is sustained by the presence of that [Divine]— should meet its destruction, what of the self has been lost?
This Self of everyone, at all times, is neither born nor does it die; it neither desires nor abandons; it is neither liberated nor bound.
Arising from the awakening to the self, yet occurring in that which is selfless,
this delusion— taking the form of the error of mistaking a rope for a snake— leads only to suffering.
Because it is beginningless, this Self is not born; because it is unborn, it does not perish.
Furthermore, it does not desire anything distinct from itself, for such a thing is impossible.
Because it is not delimited by space, time, and so forth, this [Self] is never bound;
even in the absence of bondage, there is no liberation, and for that reason it is traditionally known as "non-liberation" (amokṣa).
O Rāghava, this Self is distinguished by such qualities as these for everyone;
yet, under the sway of lack of inquiry, this deluded world weeps.
O wise one, you who have correctly perceived the entire sequence of the world throughout its past and future— do not succumb to grief like those people afflicted by ignorance.
Always having abandoned the two very notions of liberation and bondage,
the wise person should conduct themselves like a machine, remaining silent within the self.
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor upon the surface of the earth;
for liberation is indeed the stainless mind awakened by perfect knowledge.
The spontaneous dissolution of the mind through non-attachment to all desires is what has been called "liberation" by the knowers of reality who perceive the Self.
O Rāma, as long as pure awakening has not arisen, so long is liberation desired through devotion born of the wretchedness of ignorance.
Having attained awakening for a long time and the mind having reached a state of non-extension,
even the ten liberations are not desired, let alone a single liberation.
This is liberation, but this is bondage; having abandoned this fragile conceptualization, you, the great renouncer, are yourself both existence and non-existence.

Having attained a state where conceptual constructions have completely dissolved, and with all attachments cast away within, may you long protect the circle of the earth— which bears the girdle of the ocean dug by the sons of Sagara— possessing glory that is ever-risen.
The seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Inquiry into the Self," by Vasiṣṭha.
Through the play of conceptualization, one perceives a body, and it arises within the self; just as in one who does not see the face of a beautiful woman, the notion of ugliness arises in the heart.
Under its influence, this great illusion— whose belly is full and whose power is intoxication— has arrived, as if from a mere taste of wine.
By this very [nature], which is subject to change and consists of both that and its opposite,
all this has come to be, just as water appears in a desert due to the heat.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the latent impressions, and even the senses—
thus marked by imagined names— the ocean of the Self surges with its waters.
The duality of mind and ego exists in words, not in reality;
for that which is the mind is indeed the ego, and that which is the ego is the mental faculty.
Just as whiteness is conceived as distinct from snow,
so too is the distinction between the mind and the ego falsely imagined.
When one of the two— mind and ego— is destroyed within,
both are indeed destroyed, just as when a cloth is destroyed, its whiteness is also destroyed.
Having abandoned the empty notion of liberation, as well as the idea of bondage and worldly desires,
one should solely exhaust the mind through excellent dispassion and discernment.
If the thought "May there be liberation for me" has arisen, then the mind has emerged from its state;
when the mind is intensely intent on such thinking, the body serves only as a source of affliction.
When the self has transcended everything, or when it is extended in every form, what is bondage and what is liberation? How can there be rootless mental construction?
Since the wind has the nature of vibration, when it strikes the body,
then the series of sprout-like fingers, limbs, and tongue quivers.
Just as the wind causes a row of sprouts on a tree to tremble,
even so the vital air (vāyu) thoroughly moves the series of limbs within the body.
It is all-pervading, subtle, unmoving, and cannot be moved;
it does not undergo vibration of its own accord, like the divine mountain [Meru] by the winds.
Reflecting all objects while abiding solely within itself,
it illuminates these worlds through its own consciousness, like a lamp.
In this regard, what is this vain delusion of yours that brings such extreme suffering?
It is the notion of "this is I," "these are my limbs," and "this is mine," which belongs only to those of perverted intellect.
Due to its flickering nature, like a mass of stones tossed by the wind,
the activities of knowing, acting, and enjoying are perceived [as belonging to the Self].
In that regard, this notion of a self as a thinker, an enjoyer, and an agent arises;
it is a mere delusion born from the heat of ignorance, like a mirage produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Unrecognized, this [illusion], though unreal, yet appearing real like a mirage, drags away the wild deer of the mind that is parched by thirst for sense objects.
Once this [nature] has been recognized as being of the form of truth, it perishes or flees,
just as a Caṇḍāla girl flees when she is recognized in the midst of Brahmins.
When ignorance is fully understood, it no longer drags the mind away;
when a mirage is fully understood, it no longer draws one who is thirsty.
O Rāma, through the realization of the ultimate truth, latent impressions fall away along with their very roots,
just as the mass of darkness vanishes when light arrives like a lamp.
When the certainty that "ignorance does not exist" has arisen through the scriptures and reasoning,
ignorance dissolves like a drop of frost under the heat.
Having resolved that "what is the use of enjoyments for the sake of this inert body," the man of knowledge shatters the cage consisting of hope, just as a lion tears apart its enclosure.
O Rāma, when the surrounding encampment of hope has truly been abandoned by the heart,
a person attains beauty and experiences joy like the moon.
He attains supreme coolness like a mountain washed by rain;
he maintains the highest bliss like a pauper who has obtained a kingdom.
He shines with stainless splendor like the vault of the sky in autumn;
yet he cannot be contained within himself, as the ocean cannot be contained at the end of an eon.
Free from agitation, he becomes like a cloud that has ceased raining;
the knower abides within himself, as tranquil as a calm ocean.
He assumes supreme fortitude and remains as steady as the immovable Mount Meru;
he shines with a composed splendor like a fire whose fuel has been extinguished.
He becomes extinguished within himself like a lamp that has been stilled;
the man attains the supreme vision, as if he had drunk the nectar of immortality.
Like a lamp within a jar, like a fire with its flame in the center,
or like a gem of shimmering luster, it attains internal luminosity.
He beholds his own self as the essence of all, omnipresent, the lord of all, the leader of all, possessing all forms yet devoid of form.
Enough of laughing; those delicate successions of days have passed away, during which my mind was as fickle as a volley of Cupid’s arrows.
Having withdrawn from the arena of worldly strife, with the fever of his mind and pride stilled,
he sat delighting in the inner self, his mind completely purified.
Having wiped away the stain of the mire of desire, having severed the bond of birth,
liberated from the fear of the defects of dualities, he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having attained supreme rest, having reached the station of the unattainable, he has arrived at the state from which there is no returning; he has come to the end of all karmas.
He who undertakes every desired undertaking desires nothing at all;
he who rejoices in everything rejoices in nothing at all.
He neither gives nor takes, neither praises nor blames;
he neither sets nor rises, neither rejoices nor grieves.
One who renounces the fruits of all undertakings, who is free from all limiting adjuncts,
and who has completely abandoned all desires, is known as one liberated while living.
Having abandoned all desires, become silent in mind,
just as a cloud ceases its downpour when it has completely exhausted its water.
Likewise, a woman of beautiful complexion clinging to one's limbs does not bring such pleasure as the coolness of the moon— the state of hopelessness— brings to the inner heart.
O Rāghava, even the moon, though pressed against the neck, does not bring such happiness as the all-pervading coolness of hopelessness brings within.
Spring does not shine as much with its swaying, pollen-dust-covered trees as does one of noble mind who observes silence and whose heart is equanimous through freedom from desire.
Neither from the Himalayas, nor from pearls, nor from plantain trees, nor from sandalwood,
nor even from the moon is that coolness obtained which is attained through hopelessness.
Even more than sovereignty, even more than heaven, even more than the moon, even more than Mādhava,
and even more than union with a beloved, the absence of desire is the supreme happiness.
O virtuous one, that supreme bliss which renders the splendors of the three worlds as insignificant as a blade of grass is obtained through the absence of desire.
Take hold of hopelessness— the axe for the *karanja* tree of desire, the station of supreme bliss, and the cluster of blossoms from the tree of tranquility.
O Rāma, for one whose form is adorned with hopelessness, the earth is but a cow’s footprint, Mount Meru a mere post, the quarters of space small caskets, and the three worlds a blade of grass.
In this world, actions such as giving, taking, gathering, dwelling,
and possessing are ridiculed by the best of men who are free from desire.
By whom can he be compared— he who has rendered the three worlds as mere straw, and in whose heart conceptualization never takes root?
"How can people weigh that Lord of the Self, in whose heart there is no attachment such as 'let this be mine' or 'let this not be mine'?"
Free from all distress, stainless, and blissful;
the supreme good fortune of the intellect—let hopelessness be embraced.
O Teacher, know that this world is a false delusion of hopes;
it has arisen like the turning of the rim of a wheel on a moving chariot.
Why do you, O mighty-armed one, though being wise, delude yourself like a fool with a distracted mind, thinking "this is mine," "that is this," and "I am he"?
"This entire world is indeed the Self; no diversity exists here. Having realized that the world is of a single form, O Rāma, the wise do not suffer."
O Rāghava, it is precisely through the vision of the flood of objects as they truly are that the supreme consolation of the intellect— hopelessness— is attained.
Taking as your support that nature which is free from contradiction regarding existence and non-existence and remains constant at the beginning and the end, establish the stability of all things.
This most delusive illusion flees away from the one whose mind is steadfast through despair,
just as a doe flees from a lion.
A man of steady intellect regards equally his beloved— intoxicated by unrestrained passion and fickle— and a wild forest creeper, as well as a row of weathered stones.
Enjoyments do not gladden the heart within, nor do calamities distress it;
O dear one, the splendors of the visible world do not carry away the wise man, just as winds cannot move a mountain.
Even for a sage of noble intellect who has become like a young woman flushed with passion,
the arrows of Love are shattered into fragments within his mind.
One who knows his own true nature is not helplessly dragged away by passion and hatred;
for him, there is merely contact with these two, so how much less could there be their overcoming?

He does not delight in sensual enjoyments— such as women swaying like creepers upon mountain rocks— even when they are present before his eyes, just as a traveler finds no pleasure in the desert lands.
The wise man, his mind liberated, enjoys the entire abundance of enjoyments that come to him effortlessly and with ease, just as the eye perceives light.

O dear one, a succession of enjoyments such as women and the like may arrive by chance, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow; yet even when indulged, they lead neither to suffering nor to satisfaction for the steadfast man.
The two states of pleasure and pain are unable to disturb even slightly the knower who has correctly perceived the nature of reality,
just as two waves cannot shake the king of mountains.
Looking upon enjoyments with detachment, gentle, self-controlled, and free from feverish anxiety,
he takes refuge in his own state which abides within all beings.
The Knower remains free from agitation even while possessed by agitation,
creating the worlds as if he were Brahmā himself, solely intent upon the Self.
As pleasure and pain descend upon him according to their desire, their time, and their sequence, he does not undergo agitation, just as a mountain remains unmoved by the changing seasons.
O Rāma, even though one who possesses great knowledge may sink through the activities of the organs of action,
he whose mind is eternally unattached does not sink at all.
Gold is said to be stained by an internal impurity, and not otherwise;
indeed, a living being is said to be attached due to attachment to worldly existence, and not otherwise.
For the discerning one who perceives his own self as distinct from the body,
nothing at all is cut away even when his limbs are being severed.
That which is known once as pure and radiant remains known forever;
for a kinsman who has been fully recognized does not again fall into a state of being unknown.
Just as when the delusion of a snake has ceased, the perception of a snake no longer returns to the rope—
unlike a mountain torrent that, once released from its slope, flows on during the rainy season.
Gold whose form has been purified by heating, though it has attained its own natural luster,
does not again take on impurity even when submerged in mud.
When the knot of one's own heart is destroyed, there is no further bondage by the qualities (guṇas).
Once a fruit has fallen from its stalk, by whom can it be bound again, even with effort?
Who has the power to join together again a stone and the mind, both of which have been broken into pieces on all sides by the blows of ill-repute and discursive thought?
Once ignorance has been fully understood, who would plunge back into it?
Having thoroughly comprehended the livelihood of outcaste dog-cookers, what twice-born man would look upon it with favor?
Just as the ocean of milk ceases its churning when it is in the water of nectar,
so too the latent impression of saṃsāra ceases its mental deliberations.
Poisonous water is drunk under the suspicion that it is honeyed water;
as long as it is not fully recognized, but once it is recognized, it is abandoned.
Even a passionate woman, though endowed with beauty and charm, is perceived by those who know reality as being like a painted beauty, consisting merely of material substances.
Just as soot, saffron, and the like appear on a woman in a painting, so too do hair and lips appear even on one who is living; why indeed should anyone have attachment toward her?
Just as sugar, though experienced as sweet, cannot be made otherwise by burns or cuts, so too the light of reality regarding the self cannot be altered.
A woman who is devoted to another man, even while busily engaged in household chores,
savors within herself that very elixir of the new union.
Thus, when the wise man has attained rest in the supreme, pure reality,
he cannot be shaken even by the gods together with the asuras.
By what powerful husband was a woman, devoted to another,
made to forget the great festival of union with the lover of her own imagination?
