By what means can the intellect of a great-souled knower of reality be made to forget its support— the infinite light of consciousness, which is the same in flavor as the entire world?
Dependent on his elders and vexed by his husband and father-in-law, he conducts his worldly affairs with unimpaired integrity amidst all manner of pleasure and pain.
Just as the world of brides, languid with bliss through the beloved of their own imagination, is not distressed by the nets of suffering even when beset by calamity; so too is the yogin.
Likewise, one whose ignorance has dissolved, even while engaged in worldly activity,
attains joy within the self through right vision and right conduct.

Though his limbs are severed, he does not cry out; though his eyes stream with tears, he does not weep; though he is burned, even when consumed by fire, he is not destroyed; and though he has perished, he does not cease to exist.
With the union of pleasure and pain departed, and undaunted even by calamities that thwart one's plans,
may he dwell in the palace of the supreme city, or on the vast mountain, or in the forest, or in the grove of asceticism.
The seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Teaching on Hopelessness," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
Janaka remained established in his kingdom, and though he was occupied with affairs of state,
he was always free from inner fever, his mind ever undisturbed.
Your grandfather Dilīpa, though fully devoted to all worldly undertakings,
enjoyed the earth for a long time solely through his inner state of freedom from passion.
Having the appearance of one liberated while living, the unborn one constantly protected the kingdom.
Though Māndhātṛ remained for a very long time engaged in various battles with armies and numerous worldly affairs, he did not abandon the supreme state.
Bāḍi, established on the seat of Pātāla, maintains his own daily existence;
ever-renouncing and ever-attached, he stands in the state of one liberated while living.
Namuci, the sovereign lord of the Dānavas, was always intent on provoking conflict with the gods;
amidst his various activities and diversions, he never felt any inner remorse.
In the battle with Vāsava, the proud Vṛtra, who was prepared to sacrifice his body and possessed a vast mind,
engaged in combat with the gods with a heart that was cool within.
Performing the duties of a Dānava as the protector of the netherworld,
Prahlāda attained joy that was free from harm and devoid of reproach.
O Rāma, although Śambara was solely intent on the art of illusion, he ultimately emerged through his singular focus on that very art; thus Śambara abandoned this illusory cycle of worldly existence.
With an unattached intellect, Hari, while engaged in combat with the Dānavas,
attained supreme consciousness and cast off his body with the mace.
The fire, though intent upon the entire network of ritual actions and the faces of all the immortals,
remains here as if liberated, in order to enjoy the prosperity of sacrifice for a long time.
The Soma, whose essence is uniform, being drunk by all the gods,
does not undergo any attachment anywhere, just as the sky remains untouched even when pervaded.
Even Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, though capable of conquering the Moon for the sake of a wife,
remained unreleased while performing his divine sport in the sky.
Śukra, who illuminates the expanse of the sky, who protects all goals once they are attained,
and whose mind is free from transformation, passes his time as the preceptor of the asuras.
Even though it has long been causing the limbs of the multitude of beings in the world to move,
the wind, which always moves through everything, remains truly liberated.
O Rāma, though he is worthy of agitation by the state of worldly flux and transmigration, Brahmā remains undaunted in intellect; with an even mind, he exhausts his long life.
Even though he is liberated, the Blessed Lord Hari wanders here for a long time through the play of the cage of dualities, such as the battle between old age and death.
Even by the liberated Three-eyed One, Gaurī— like a cluster of blossoms on the tree of beauty— is borne upon half his body, as if he were a lover carrying his beloved.
Even by Muktā, the three-eyed Gaurī was embraced around the neck with a white pearl necklace,
which was as pure as a cluster of pearls and as stainless as a digit of the moon.
The hero Guha, though liberated, being profound in intellect and a unique ocean of the jewels of all knowledge, undertook the sequence of battles against Tāraka and the others.
O Rāma, Bhṛṅgīśa offered his own blood and flesh to his mother with a mind that was resolute, purified by meditation, and liberated from all conceptual thought.
Although the sage Nārada is by nature liberated, he wandered through this forest tract of the world as if in play, out of his habitual inclination toward purposeful activity.
The self-controlled Viśvāmitra, though a master who considers himself liberated while living,
personally presides over the performance of the sacrifice prescribed by the Vedas.
Śeṣa supports the earth, the sun creates the succession of days,
and Yama performs his duty as the Restrainer— all this indeed occurs through the state of being liberated while living.
Moreover, in this triple world, hundreds of others— yakṣas, gods, humans, and asuras— who have attained liberation remain as virtuous beings within the cycle of existence.
Established in worldly affairs among those who maintain various modes of conduct,
some are cool within, while others are dull-witted like stones.
Having attained supreme awakening, some have come to the forest,
such as Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Sahadeva, and others.
Some remain in royal kingdoms, adorned with parasols, yak-tail whisks, and garlands, such as Janaka, Śaryāti, Māndhātṛ, Magadha, and others.
Some abide in the sky, situated within the circle of celestial mansions,
such as Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Candra, Sūrya, and the lords of sages.
Some have gone to the realm of the gods, seated in rows of celestial chariots,
such as Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Yama, Tumburu, and Nārada.
Some, liberated while living, reside in the depths of the netherworld (pātāla),
such as Baḍi, Suhotra, Andha, Prahlāda, Hlāda, and others.
O wise one, those of cultivated intellect always exist even among the animal births,
while those of foolish intellect exist even among the divine births.
For indeed, everything, by everything, everywhere, in every way, and at all times,
truly exists within the Self of all, which has the nature of both self and non-self.
The destiny of the Creator is manifold and slow to manifest its infinite undertakings;
yet, due to the variety of its structural components, everything is seen everywhere.
"Vidhi, Daiva, Vibhu, Dhātṛ, Sarveśa, Śiva, and Īśvara"—
by these names the inner Self, the inwardly conscious one, is designated.
Within a non-entity there exists an entity, like gold within sands;
within an entity there exists a non-entity, like impurity within grains of gold.
When examined through reasoning, the state of being "proper" in what is improper is clearly seen;
for it is out of fear of evil, O Rāma, that people engage in dharma.
O virtuous one, eternal truth is perceived within the unreal;
through the practice of meditation on emptiness, the eternal state is attained.
That which does not exist arises quickly through the play of place and time;
indeed, even horned rabbits are seen when Śambara is present.
Those things seen to be as firm as the essence of a diamond have gone to destruction at the end of a kalpa, just like the moon, the sun, the earth, the oceans, the gods, and the mountains.
Seeing thus, O mighty-armed one, the sequence of existence arising from being and non-being, abandon joy, resentment, dejection, and pride, and attain equanimity.
In this world, the non-existent appears as existent, and the existent is also seen as non-existent;
therefore, having abandoned both reliance and non-reliance, quickly attain equanimity.

O Rāghava, in this world, the attainment of liberation is not at all possible without the practice of discernment; indeed, millions of people remain submerged in saṃsāra because they lack such discernment.
O Rāghava, in this world, liberation is indeed always attainable through the practice of discernment; for by such discernment, millions of people have become liberated.
Liberation becomes easy to attain through solitude and difficult to attain through lack of solitude; since it is reached by the dissolution of the mind, therefore, kindle solitude.
One who desires prosperity should make an effort toward self-observation;
through the light of the Self, the severing of the head of all suffering occurs.
Free from passion, free from attachment, liberated while living, and possessed of great intelligence—
many such as Suhotra and Janaka arise here in this world.
Therefore, O Rāma, you too, with a mind made steady by the dawning of discernment,
roam as one liberated while living, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Two kinds of liberation exist in this world for those who possess a body: one is with the body, the other is without the body; hear now this distinction between them.
Indeed, the peace of mind resulting from non-attachment to objects is liberation;
O sinless one, that state is possible even while the body exists or has ceased to exist.
O dear one, the supreme sages know that the exhaustion of attachment alone is absolute liberation;
that occurs both when the body exists and when it no longer exists.
He who lives having abandoned all attachment is called liberated while living;
he who lives with attachment is bound, while the third is indeed liberated.
Effort for the sake of liberation should be exerted with diligence and according to the proper method; for one devoid of effort and method, even a cow’s footprint becomes difficult to cross.
But one should not, out of mere delusion, allow oneself to fall under the power of another for the sake of suffering that is vast in its nature, which arises from a lack of firm resolve.
Resorting to great fortitude with a resolute mind,
one should investigate the self by means of the self for the sake of one's own long-term perfection.
For one whose resolve is expansive, the world becomes like the hoofprint of a cow; for one whose resolve is shattered, even the hoofprint of a cow becomes the world.
That which the Sugata has attained is the supreme excellence; that which some king has attained is steadfastness;
and that which the great have attained is the highest state—that is the great fruit of the tree of the labor of effort.
The seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Inquiry into the Liberated and the Unliberated," by Vasiṣṭha.
O Raghava, these worlds emerge from Brahman;
they attain stability through lack of discernment, my dear, and they come to rest through discernment.
Who is able to count the movements of the whirlpools of the water of the world-web within the ocean of Brahman, or the motes of dust in its rays?
Know that incorrect perception is the cause for the persistence of the world;
correct perception is the sole cause for the cessation of saṃsāra.
For this terrible ocean of saṃsāra, O Rāma, is indeed difficult to cross;
it cannot be crossed by us without both the application of reason and effort.
For this ocean is full, filled with a mass of the waters of delusion; it has unfathomable whirlpools of death and its hollows are agitated by waves.
The foam of its merit is scattered abroad; it is the blazing Vāḍava fire of hell;
its restless waves are craving; and it is the elephant within the waters of the mind.

The river of life is constricted; it is a casket for the jewels of enjoyments, yet it is infested with the serpents of angry diseases and resounds with the gurgling of the crocodiles that are the sense-faculties.
Behold, O Rāma, these waves spreading forth, beautiful and flickering;
they are known as the lovely women, capable of drawing one toward their peaks.
Rich with the lotus-gem of the smile’s splendor, filled with the blue-lotus eyes, strewn with the pearl-like teeth, and graced by the foam of the smile; //MU_5,76.9//
With their hair like a circle of sapphire, rippling with the playfulness of their eyebrows,
expansive with the sandy banks of their hips, and adorned with conch-like necks;

Rich with the jeweled plaques on their foreheads, teeming with crocodiles in the form of playful gestures, filled with darting minnows in the form of sidelong glances, and possessing golden sands in the form of cosmetic pigments; //MU_5,76.11//
If one who is submerged can cross over this ocean of saṃsāra, which is so terrifying with its restless waves, that would indeed be the supreme human effort.
When the great ship of wisdom exists and the navigator of discernment is present, fie upon him who has not crossed over this ocean of saṃsāra!
He who, having traversed from the near shore to the far shore and having measured it on all sides,
plunges into the ocean of saṃsāra— he alone is known as a true person (puruṣa).
O Rāma, after the noble ones have reflected upon and surveyed this ocean of saṃsāra with their intellect, only then does play appear beautiful; not otherwise.
In this matter, O virtuous one, you are capable; for with a mind intent on inquiry, even as a youth, you investigate this cycle of existence.
He who, like you, first reflects upon the world with an exceptionally refined intellect and then enters into it, does not sink away in this worldly existence.
O Rāma, having first reflected with wisdom that these enjoyments bring fear even to the serpents themselves, they should be enjoyed only at the very end, like serpents by Garuḍa.
Those powers that are cultivated after one has reflected upon reality and perceived it are productive of a favorable result for a living being;
all others lead only to suffering.
The strength, intellect, and splendor of one who has perceived reality increase,
just as the beauty and other qualities of a tree flourish during the springtime.

O descendant of Raghu, with a mind that is constantly pure, equanimous, and cooled by the filling of profound alchemy, you shine forth intensely like the moon, having realized the bliss of the knowable.
The seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition of the Similarity between Saṃsāra and the Ocean," [from] the Rāmāyaṇa.
O Sage, tell me once more in brief of the marvel of perceiving reality within this noble narrative; for who could ever be satiated by your words?
Vasiṣṭha said: "The characteristics of one liberated while living have been described by me in many ways;
yet again, O mighty-armed one, listen to this which is being told."
Free from desire, the self-possessed one constantly perceives all this as if in deep sleep; unattached, he views everything everywhere as if it were unreal.
Having attained the vision of the Self, he remains as if having reached isolation (kaivalya), as if his mind were fast asleep, or as if reeling with bliss.
Even that which has been given he does not take up, nor even that which is held in his hand;
for with an equanimous mind, noble in its inward-turned nature, he remains detached.
Beholding this succession of people, like the movement of puppets on a machine, with a gaze withdrawn within, he of tranquil intellect smiles.
He does not look toward the future, nor does he abide in the present;
he does not dwell upon the past, yet he performs every action.
Though asleep, he is awake; though awake, he is as if asleep.
Though performing all actions, within he does nothing at all.
Internally renouncing everything and always internally free from seeking,
he remains established in that very state even while performing all external activities.
Externally, he continues with all worldly activities as they have been undertaken, intent on performing whatever actions come his way,
following the course of dualistic duties obtained through the sequence of his own karma.
Having his nature as the enjoyer of complete happiness, as if established within all hopes,
he performs all actions, having abandoned the delusion of agency.
Remaining as if indifferent toward the activities of the natural order,
he neither desires nor hates, neither grieves nor rejoices.
Devoted to the welfare of living beings with an unattached mind,
he behaves toward a devotee like a devotee and stands toward a rogue like a rogue.
Among the foolish he is a fool, among the aged he is aged, among the heroic he is full of valor;
among those engaged in the ways of youth he is young, and among the suffering he is suffering.
His speech was occupied with meritorious discourse; his disposition was free from dejection;
he was firm-minded, filled with rising joy, gentle, and one whose fame was rooted in virtue.
He is wise, serene, and sweet; full and possessed of the arising of excellent intuition; free from weariness and misfortune; and a loving kinsman to everyone.
With the appearance of noble conduct, he was an ocean of equal happiness;
most affectionate and cool to the touch, he was like the full moon risen.
For him there is no need for good deeds, nor for enjoyments, nor for ritual acts;
neither for evil deeds, nor for the renunciation of enjoyments, nor for kinsmen.
Neither by the undertaking of actions nor by inactivity,
neither by bondage nor by liberation, neither by the netherworld nor by heaven.
When the world is seen as it truly is, as consisting of a single self,
then the mind never becomes distressed for the sake of bondage or liberation.
For one whose web of doubt has been burnt away by the fire of right knowledge,
the bird of the mind soars forth freely and without fear.
He whose mind is free from delusion and abides in equanimity neither sets nor rises; like space, it remains so amidst all mental fluctuations.
Just as a child seated within a chest moves about,
so indeed does the limb-series of the wise man, devoid of any sequential connection.
Reeling like one intoxicated with bliss, having rendered rebirth powerless,
he— through the realization that nothing is to be grasped— remembers neither what was undone nor what was done.
He grasps and abandons everything in every way; having no purpose for anything that is not to be taken up, he acts like a child.
Even while engaged in activities according to the sequence of place, time, and action,
he is not affected in the slightest by the pleasure or pain arising from those activities.
Although externally engaged with all objects, within he remains free from effort; he does not attribute existence to objects, nor does he pursue their fruits.
He does not disregard the state of suffering, nor does he depend upon the hope for pleasure;
he feels no joy at the arising of success, nor does he grieve at the failure of his undertakings.
Even if the sun were cool-rayed, even if the lunar disc were pitch black,
and even if fire were to spread downward, no wonder would arise in him.
"These powers of the conscious self manifest here in this manner"— having realized this, no curiosity arises regarding its wondrous webs.
He does not adopt the wretchedness of pity, nor does he pursue cruelty;
he does not cultivate shame, nor does he fall into shamelessness.
Never dejected in spirit, never arrogant in spirit; never negligent, never weary of soul, neither agitated nor filled with joy.
In his mind, which is vast and as stainless as the autumnal sky, anger and other such passions do not arise, just as new sprouts do not grow in the sky.
In this world-process, which arises and falls incessantly,
where, how, or indeed for whom could there be happiness or even suffering?

In this state of constant flux like the movement of foam upon the water of the succession of beings, where indeed is there anything here, from whence does it come, and what is the end? What connection can there be with pleasure and pain?
Those men who have perceived the process of creation do not despair nor do they exult amidst the endless and incessant arising of living beings through existence and non-existence.
Just as other dream-visions occur every moment during the night,
so too these worldly perceptions arise and perish in that same manner.
In this world, which is consumed by saṃsāra— where things arise incessantly and perish incessantly— what room is there for both compassion and joy?
Since the pleasant has ceased to exist due to the absence of the beautiful, and [the mind] has come to abide in the absence of pleasure,
what are these extraordinary perceptions of suffering like, how have they arisen, or what indeed are they?
That state of suffering which, arising at the end of pleasure, spreads its own seed at the conclusion of that pleasure— how can it be "peaceful" when pleasure has been interrupted?

When pleasure and pain have been exhausted, and with their exhaustion the objects to be rejected and accepted [are gone], where do the desired and undesired remain? Furthermore, when the auspicious and inauspicious have dissolved, where are they?
When the desire for enjoyments has been stilled through the destruction of the perception of both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
and when the continuity of hopelessness has become fully matured, the mind melts away like snow.
When the mind has been destroyed at its very root, what talk can there be of volition?
When sesame seeds are completely burnt, how can there be any notion of oil?
Through the cultivation of the density of non-existence regarding all phenomena, the great-souled one remains like the sky, free from mental construction;
established in his own mind, joyful, knowing the single form, the wise one stays, sleeps, and lives, eternally satisfied.
The seventy-eighth canto, titled "The Description of Liberation while Living," by Vasiṣṭha.
Just as a circle of fire arises from the whirling of a firebrand,
appearing as something real though it is unreal, so too does the world arise from the vibration of the mind.
Just as a circular whirlpool appears as if distinct from the water due to the movement of the water,
so does the world appear due to the movement of the mind.
Just as a circle of peacock feathers or pearls is seen in the sky as if real due to the movement of the eye,
though it is unreal, so too is the world seen due to the movement of the mind.
Rāma said:
O Brahmin, tell me that by which the mind either vibrates or does not vibrate, for that alone must indeed be treated.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as whiteness is in snow, O Rāma, as oil is in sesame seeds, as fragrance is in flowers, and as heat is in fire; [so is the Self in the body].
O delight of the Raghus, the two movements of the mind are likewise joined together;
they are non-different, and the distinction between them is merely a false mental construction.
When one of the two sides— the mind or the movement of the mind— is destroyed,
both perish without a doubt, as they abide together by the nature of quality and the possessor of quality.
O Rāghava, there are two methods for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge.
Yoga is indeed the restraint of its fluctuations, while knowledge is correct discernment.
Rāma:
By what kind of practice, bound to the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
does the mind attain peace through that which is called yoga, which bestows infinite bliss?
Vasiṣṭha:
That wind which vibrates throughout this body and within the channels of the body,
like water flowing through the streams of the earth, is celebrated as *prāṇa*.
Due to its vibration, as it undergoes a variety of internal activities,
the names "apāna" and so forth have been conceptually assigned by those of perfected self.
Just as a flower is the support for fragrance, and snow is the support for whiteness,
so too this chariot has become inseparable from the mind as its substratum.
O Rāghava, know that this consciousness which arises from the internal vibration of the vital breath and is oriented toward the formation of volitions— that is the mind.

The wise know that vibration is the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa); from that very vibration arise the consciousnesses that produce the turning of the wheels, just as waves arise from the vibration of water.
Those adorned by the scriptures say that the mind is the vibration of the vital breath;
when that is restrained, the mind will surely become tranquil.
Through the subsiding of the vibration of the mind, this saṃsāra dissolves,
just as worldly activity ceases when the movement of sunlight comes to rest.
Rāma: How can the movement of the vital airs— such as the prāṇa and others— which move incessantly within the body-cave and travel through its depths, be obstructed?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Through contact with the scriptures and virtuous people, and by means of the yoga of practicing detachment,
one first develops a lack of reliance toward worldly activities and a firm reliance [upon the Self].
Through the long-term practice of a single-pointed meditation on the desired object,
and through the intensive cultivation of this very reality, the vibration of the vital breath is arrested.
Through firm practice of one's own [breath-control] techniques such as *pūraka* and others, performed without causing fatigue,
and through union with solitary meditation, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained.
By pursuing the reality of sound at the limit of the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*,
when consciousness becomes as if in deep sleep, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained.
When exhalation has certainly been practiced and the vital breath has entered the vast space,
the vibration of the breath no longer touches the openings of the limbs and is restrained.
In the state of retention (kumbhaka), as before, one remains for an infinite time;
through practice, when the vital breath is arrested, the vibration of the breath ceases.
Having diligently pressed the uvula with the tongue so that it reaches the root of the palate,
when the vital breath has entered the upper aperture, the vibration of the breath is obstructed.
When consciousness has dissolved through meditation into the subtle ether— which is named "nothingness" and is free from all temporal divisions— the vibration of the vital breath is arrested.
When the gaze is perfectly stilled upon the tip of the nose— twelve finger-breadths away in the stainless space— the vibration of the vital breath is obstructed.
Through practice, when the vital breath has reached the upper limit of twelve finger-breadths above the palate via the cranial aperture,
and when consciousness has dissolved, the vibration of the breath is arrested.
When the light of the star [of consciousness] has subsided and come to rest between the eyebrows,
the vibration of the vital breath ceases within the conscious abode of the intellect.

For the sage who has meditated with a mind free of latent impressions (*avāsana*) for a long time through the exclusive perception of the void within the heart, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is brought to cessation.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, what is that which is called the heart of all beings in the world,
in which this entire universe is reflected like in a great mirror?
Vasiṣṭha said: "O virtuous one, in this world, the heart of living beings exists in two ways:
that which is to be accepted and that which is to be rejected. Listen now to the distinction between these two."
Know that within the body, which is limited by such dimensions, that which is situated on one side of the trunk between the chest and the heart is the *hṛdaya*, which is to be abandoned.
Pure consciousness alone is remembered as the heart to be accepted by men;
it is both within and without, yet neither without nor within.
That heart is the preeminent essence; therein all this is established. It is the mirror of all objects and the treasury of all prosperity.
For all living beings, consciousness alone is called the heart;
it is not a mere physical part of the body, inert like a worn-out stone.
Therefore, when the mind is forcibly directed toward this pure heart consisting of consciousness, so that it is free from latent impressions, the vibration of the vital breath is arrested.
By these methods, as well as others devised through various intentions and residing in the mouths of various teachers, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.
Through practice, these methods of yoga become effortless;
for one who is capable, they serve as the means for shattering cyclic existence.
When [the practice] has attained firmness through repetition and is marked by dispassion,
the retention of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) according to one's latent impressions is considered fruitful.

When the vital breath is brought to rest through practice at the twelve finger-breadths located at the eyebrows, the nose, and the palate, it becomes tranquil like a mountain river far in the distance.
By repeatedly practicing for a long time, the uvula is touched with the tip of the tongue against the palate, whereby the vital breaths flow sufficiently upward.
Yet these meditative concentrations, though abounding in conceptual construction, quickly attain a state free from conceptualization for the sake of supreme tranquility through constant practice.
A person who delights in the Self becomes free from sorrow and finds inner happiness;
this comes only from practice and from nothing else. Therefore, be devoted to practice.
Through practice, when the vibration of the vital breaths has come to an end, the mind attains tranquility; only nirvāṇa remains.
Birth is enveloped by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), while liberation is a mind free of such impressions;
and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) takes hold [of them], O Rāma—do as you wish.
The vibration of the vital breath takes the form of the mind; from that arises the delusion of worldly existence.
When that very vibration comes to rest, the fever of worldly existence is extinguished.
When conceptual construction has been utterly exhausted for a person, that state remains,
from which all words, along with every form of mental fabrication, turn back.
That in which all is, from which all comes, that which is all, and from which all;
that wherein this is not, from whence this is not, that which is not this, and that which is not of such a nature.
Because it is subject to destruction, because it is conceptualized, and because it possesses qualities,
there is indeed no example whatsoever to be found among visible things for that which is the self devoid of qualities.
She is the relisher of all grains of rice, the illuminator of all splendors,
and the fashioner of all desires, from whom the moonlight of consciousness has arisen.
From the wish-fulfilling tree of volition, the numerous rows of fruits that are worldly existence arise incessantly and fall away, possessing manifold flavors.
The one of great intelligence who, having taken hold of that state which is the ultimate limit of all things,
remains with a steady mind as a knower of that reality, is called liberated while living.
Free from all longing and curiosity, with the conceptualization of the beneficial and the harmful completely stilled,
the Supreme Person, whose mind is liberated, remains intent upon all worldly activities.
The seventy-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Bondage of the Species of Those Liberated while Living," [spoken by] Rāma.
Thus has the pacification of this mind been described through the application of yoga;
now, O Lord, out of your grace, tell me of right knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha: "The Supreme Self exists here as the essence of light, without beginning or end"—
the wise know that such a broad and firm conviction is right knowledge.
The firm conviction that these hundreds of potencies which take the form of objects such as jars and cloths are the Self alone and nothing else is right vision.
Birth arises from incorrect perception, while liberation comes from correct observation;
from incorrect observation a rope appears as a snake, but not from correct observation.

Consciousness, when entirely free from the component of volition and devoid of any object of cognition, exists here as nothing other than what is designated by these primordial names; there is indeed nothing else.
When that [nature] is known in its pure form, it is called the Supreme Self (paramātman);
but when it is perceived in its impure form, it is termed ignorance (avidyā) by the wise.
Consciousness alone is the object of consciousness; there is no conceptualization of duality between these two.
O Rāma, the Self itself accumulates its own nature; indeed, nothing else exists.
The vision of reality as it truly is within these three worlds consists in this much:
the perfection that comes from the certain realization that the self alone is the entire universe.
Everything is indeed the Self; upon what are existence and non-existence based, or where do they reside?
Where is the conceptualization of bondage and liberation? O Rāma, what else is there to be grieved for?
There is neither mind nor anything to be thought; this Brahman alone expands as everything.
It is the one, supreme void; where is liberation, and for whom is there bondage?
This Brahman, whose form is expanded, vast, and established as the Great, has transcended all duality;
you yourself are that very Self through your own self.
When form is correctly observed, there is not even the slightest difference between wood, stone, and cloth; nowhere is there anything inclined toward conceptual construction.
That which is peaceful at the beginning and at the end, the indestructible essential nature of both things and the self— become absorbed in that, O Rāghava.
Through the delusions of old age and death arising from duality and non-duality,
the Self alone manifests as various selves, like water appearing as waves.
For one who remains established by taking refuge in the pure self with an intellect constantly situated within,
what enjoyment is capable of deluding that Lord of the Self?
For one who has cultivated expansive discernment, the enemies such as sensual enjoyments do not pierce the mind even in the slightest, just as gentle breezes cannot shatter a mountain.
In this world, sorrows swallow up the undiscerning, the ignorant, the deluded, and those devoted to hope, just as herons devour fish that are out of water.
"The entire world is indeed the Self alone; ignorance exists nowhere"—firmly grasping this correct view, remain steadfast.
There is no diversity in conceptual constructions in reality, just as there is no difference from the water in various kinds of lakes;
thus, the person who consists of this single certainty, having perceived the true meaning correctly, is said to be liberated.
The Eightieth Chapter, titled "The Characteristic of Right Knowledge," by Vasiṣṭha.
O dear one, for the discerning person who contemplates these internal enjoyments,
no longing ever arises even toward those that stand before them.
The eye exists for the purpose of seeing; the living soul, however, exists for pleasure and pain.
Like an ox is for the burden, the enjoyer is the leader of material things.
When the eyes are immersed in forms, what agitation can there be for the embodied being?
What loss is there to a general when his donkey plunges into a pond?
O base one, do not relish this mire of form; do not honor it.
For it perishes in the blink of an eye and indeed brings harm even to you.
A wise man, even if he is a hero, is quickly bound by the very actions of that person with whom he forms a friendship and whom he follows.

O eye, do not take refuge in form—which arises and perishes, which is pleasing only for a moment, and which consists of unreality—for the sake of your own destruction; rather, seek that which is indestructible.
Like a witness, you, the eye, remain; form resides within the self.
Light exists by the power of time; why do you alone suffer?
Like the ripple of water or a peacock feather rising from the sky, why does your mind, bound by its own kind, vibrate? What has come upon you?
O egoism, when the mind— which is characterized by flickering— vibrates of its own accord like a minnow in a tiny pool of water, from where has this "this-ness" arisen?
O mind, since light and form are both eternally insentient and flash forth in mutual dependence as support and supported, your agitation is in vain.
Form, light, and mental attention are not attached to one another;
yet they appear as if joined together, like a face and its reflection in a mirror.
For these [elements] have become closely joined and continuous by the ignorant creature;
when ignorance is dissolved by knowledge, they remain separate and composed of unreality.
For these— form, light, and mental attention— are closely bound together by the activity of the mind, just as pieces of wood are held together by lac.
When the thread of one's own mental conceit is severed through diligent practice of the mind and through inquiry, the latent impression of ignorance is indeed cut asunder.
When the mind has been exhausted through the destruction of ignorance,
none of these— form, light, and mental attention— ever again come together with one another.
The mind alone is the awakener of all the internal senses; therefore, that very mind must be eradicated from within, like a demon from a house.
O mind, you prance about in vain; the end of you has been seen by me.
You are utterly insignificant at the beginning and at the end, for you do not exist even in the present.
Why do you prance about within in vain through these five modes?
This prancing belongs only to one who perceives you as "this" or "that."
Your leaping about does not bring even the slightest satisfaction to my troubled mind;
like the movement of a phantom man, you burn in vain amidst your various activities.
Stay or go, O mind; you do not live for me, O rogue.
By nature you are eternally dead, and through inquiry you remain perfectly dead.
"O brother, you are devoid of reality, inert, and eternally dead in form; O rogue, only the fool who lacks discernment is deceived by you, not the one possessed of inquiry."
We have recognized you; it must have been through sheer folly that we followed you. Today you are as dead to us as darkness is to lamps.
In the past, for a long time, this house of my body was obstructed by you, the deceitful one, and deprived of association with the virtuous.
Now that you, who are insentient, resemble a ghost, and are a rogue of the mind, have departed,
this house of the body remains, fit to be inhabited by all virtuous people.
You were already dull and deceitful before, and you remain so even now;
if you do not change at this moment, O Vetāla, are you not ashamed?
Depart from this dwelling of my body, O mind-vampire, together with the ogresses of craving and the guhyakas of anger and the rest!
By good fortune, through the mantra of discernment, the vampire of the heedless mind has emerged from the temple of the body, like a wild wolf from its cave.
Oh, how truly strange and immense is this: by the dull, momentary, and treacherous mind, all these people have been rendered helpless!
What is your prowess? What is your strength? What is your support, that you leap about and thus harass these people?
You are indeed treacherous by nature; O base-minded one, you are not being killed by me.
O ignorant one, today you have merely realized that you are dead!
For so long a time, knowing you to have remained alive,
I have been afflicted for a long duration through the nights of saṃsāra, which are subject to many breakages.
"For it has been understood by me today that the mind, once dead, does not exist here;
therefore, having abandoned hope in you, I remain alone in the Self."
By good fortune, I have myself realized today that the mind is dead;
my entire life has not been led away by a rogue.
Having driven out the deceitful mind from the abode of the body in an instant, I now remain established within myself, healthy and free from the inner demon.
For a long time, having gained mastery over the vampire of the mind, I have produced various transformations; now that I have created them myself, I laugh at them.
By good fortune, the mind-ghoul— long since fallen from its perch, marked by the excellent sword of discernment,
and towering as high as a palm tree— is driven out from the chamber of the heart.
Now that the vetāla of the mind has been stilled and has entered the sacred path,
by good fortune I dwell happily and alone within the city of the body.
The mind is dead, thoughts are dead, and the demon of egoism is dead;
through the mantra of inquiry, I remain equanimous, healthy, and alone.
What is my mind? What are my hopes? Who might be my sense of ego?
By good fortune, this wife of mine has been entirely lost and rendered useless.
Salutations again and again to me alone, who am the one who has accomplished all that was to be done, who am eternal, whose nature is stainless, and who am known as non-conceptual consciousness.
I have no hope, no actions, no transmigratory existence, and no agency;
I have no state of being an enjoyer, nor do I have a body—salutations again and again to Me alone!
I am not the self, nor am I space, nor indeed am I this "I" myself;
there is no separation from me—homage, homage to me alone!
Salutations again and again to me alone— who am formless, beyond description, luminous, of stainless nature, and who abide solely as the Self by myself.
Salutations again and again to me alone—who am changeless, eternal, partless, and without a self; who am everything, and the cause of all effects.
I have attained that Being which is equal, all-pervading, subtle, and the sole illuminator of the universe; salutations again and again to that very Self within me.

Neither the earth with its mountains, nor the rivers, nor the limbs of the world, nor even I myself, nor indeed anything else—this entire universe, rich with all objects, belongs to me alone; salutations, salutations unto me!

I bow to the sovereign form of the Infallible One— devoid of mental construction, delightful through tranquility, manifesting the universe yet transcending it, infinite, itself unborn and undecaying, and beyond all qualities.
The eighty-first chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Relationship between the Perceived and the Perception," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having reflected thus within with the intellect, O mighty-armed one, the knowers of reality further reflect in this way: "The Self is to be known by the great-souled ones."
The truth that "this world is indeed the Self alone" has been cleansed by the mind;
from where, then, could the mind have arisen? Oh, how wondrous is that which is non-existent!
Because it is ignorance, because it is not mind, and because it is always characterized by equality,
the mind that is other than the delusion does not exist at all— like a flower in the sky.
Just as the movement of a pillar appears to a child on a boat,
so does the unreal mind appear to the unawakened, but not to the awakened.

When the delusion of ignorance and confusion has subsided, we no longer perceive the mind, just as one no longer perceives the shaking of a mountain once the illusion of riding on a spinning wheel has ceased.
For in this way, the mind does not exist at all; only Brahman exists, whose nature is that expansion.
The various mental constructions of objects are therefore unreal, as they are devoid of me.
I am born with my doubts stilled; I stand free from the fever of passion.
Just as I remain, so I remain—thus indeed am I devoid of longing.
In the absence of the mind, the qualities such as craving and the rest are forcibly exhausted,
just as various descriptions of colors vanish when the light has ceased.
The mind is dead, craving has departed, and the cage of delusion is destroyed;
selflessness has arisen, and I have awakened in this world.
The entire world is indeed one and peaceful; even multiplicity is not real.
What else shall I contemplate within? Enough with this discourse!
Having attained the stainless state, which is without beginning or end and purifying,
I am the eternal Self— gentle, all-pervading, and subtle— firmly established.
Whatever exists here and whatever does not exist— whether it be mind and so forth, the self and so forth, or even non-entities—
that is more transparent than space, peaceful, infinite, ungraspable, and all-pervading.
Whether the mind exists or not, whether it attains a fixed mindfulness or not— what need have I for deliberation, since my self has arisen as partless?
It was through ignorance that I existed as an investigator, thinking "I am";
now that investigation has assumed immeasurable forms, where is this "I" who was the investigator?
Even though this mind of mine has died, this glory of conceptual construction remains useless;
for what purpose does it arise, merely to serve the activity of the mind-demon?
Therefore, having thoroughly determined "this is it," I completely abandon this internal fabrication of conceptualization; with a tranquil self, I abide in silence within the Self.
O Raghava, whether eating, walking, sleeping, or standing, one who knows that [reality] should daily investigate it everywhere with wisdom and the mind.
Having investigated with their own minds, which are established in themselves and self-abiding,
the virtuous remain free from agitation amidst their natural duties.
Free from pride and intoxication, with joyful intentions and a radiance equal to the autumnal moon,
those of great intelligence dwell here in happiness, engaged in their natural worldly activities.
The eighty-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
Such was the reflection made in former times by the wise Saṃvarta;
it was told to me on the Vindhya mountain by him, the knower of the Self.
Grasping this view with an intellect intent on discernment,
cross over this ocean of saṃsāra by degrees.
Now, O Rāma, hear this other vision that bestows the [highest] state,
just as it was established without hesitation by the sage Vītahavya.
In ancient times, the immensely radiant Vītahavya wandered about, his garments like clouds,
through the long caves of the Vindhya mountains as the sun wanders through the caves of Mount Meru.
From this sequence of actions, which produces the wandering of saṃsāra and consists of the forms of mental and physical afflictions, he eventually came to feel revulsion.
Out of a desire for the sublime state attainable through a portion of non-conceptual meditative absorption,
he, worn out by old age, withdrew his own succession of activities.
He entered his own leaf-hut, which had been fashioned by Rambhā,
as a blue bee enters a fragrant, mango-colored blue lotus.
There, upon a seat that was level, pure, and well-spread with a deerskin,
he rested on the immovable and tranquil ground, like a cloud that has shed its rain.
Having assumed the lotus posture and placed his joined palms upon his heels,
he stood with a steady neck and motionless like a mountain peak.
Gradually, as evening approached, he withdrew his light scattered across the quarters of the sky,
like the sun entering a cave of Mount Meru while withdrawing its mass of radiance.
Gradually avoiding both external and internal objects of touch,
he reflected upon this with a mind free from sin.
Alas! This mind is indeed so fickle that, even when withdrawn, it does not attain stability for even a moment, like a leaf tossed by powerful waves.
Agitated by unrestrained forms perceived through the eyes and other senses, the mind leaps up incessantly like a ball struck by the palm of the hand.
Even as it quickly abandons one thing, it grasps at modes of existence increased by the senses; from whatever it is restrained, toward that very thing it rushes like one who is mad.
From a pot it goes to a cloth, from a cloth to a formidable cart;
the mind roams among objects like a monkey among trees.
I shall now examine these five gates of the mind, beginning with the eye, which are fully capable of being designated as "burnt faculties."
O you who have conquered the host of senses, why is this restlessness of yours here?
It is as fleeting as the surging waves of the oceans with their agitated waters.
O you of flickering intent, do not act with rashness for your own ruin;
remember the vast webs of suffering that have occurred in the past.
O forms, you are indeed merely inert and base to the mind;
through this inertia, an excessive longing leaps forth like a mirage.
This arrogance of those who are always blind, lacking vision, and whose very nature is devoid of essence, serves only to provoke laughter.
The unborn Lord, whose essence is consciousness, acts as the witness of everything;
you, whose faculties have been destroyed, why have you come here in vain?
These [senses], such as the eyes and so forth, are formless and yet they falsely dart about;
they are like a firebrand’s circle, resembling the delusion of a snake in a rope.
Therefore, by that self which possesses vast knowledge, the eyes and other senses are entirely devoid of cognition;
they are not connected even in the slightest degree, like the heavens, the depths of Pātāla, and the mountains.
Like a traveler afraid of snakes or a twice-born man afraid of outcasts,
pure consciousness— untainted and free from disease— remains far removed from the senses.
This mutual agitation of yours exists merely by the presence of consciousness,
like those engaged in their daily tasks while the sun remains at its ease.
O Cārvāka who wanders through the mind, you who beg from the bellies of the four quarters—
like a dog, roam this world in vain for your own ruin.
"‘I am like consciousness’—this is futile, for your latent impression is untrue;
O rogue, there can be no identity between consciousness and the mind, which are utterly distinct."
"I indeed live"—this is your drum of egoism;
it has arisen in vain for the sake of suffering, being false, devoid of truth, and lacking reality.
Abandon this agitation born of egoism, thinking "I am that";
O fool, there is nothing at all [to grasp], so why do you tremble in vain?
Consciousness is the mind, without beginning or end; nothing other than consciousness exists.
O great fool, what else could that which is called "mind" be in this body?
O mind, this suspicion of being an enjoyer and an agent, which has arisen like an elixir, ends in poison; indeed, it is entirely in vain.
O foolish aggregate of sense-faculties, do not become an object of derision;
you are neither the agent nor the enjoyer, for you are insentient and are awakened by another.
Who are you to these enjoyments, or what are these enjoyments to you?
For one who is dull-witted, even a self does not exist; how then can there be relatives, friends, and the like?

For that which is insentient does not exist at all; it is only the existent that is associated with non-existence, because [in the case of the insentient] the states of being a knower, an agent, an enjoyer, and a thinker are impossible.
If you are of the nature of immediate consciousness, then that alone is your true self;
O mind, what kind of existence, consisting of being and non-being, could possibly cause you suffering?
Or rather, since you have falsely apprehended the states of being an agent and an enjoyer,
listen, O rogue, as to how I shall wipe them away through reasoning.
First of all, you yourself are insentient; of this there is no doubt.
What kind of agency can an insentient thing possess? For how could stones ever dance?
Having long depended upon that pure, divine portion of His,
you live, you desire, you kill, you float, you go, and you leap about.
Whatever is performed by means of one's own power is considered to have been done by that [power] itself;
for example, when a sickle cuts by means of a man's power, it is the man who is said to be the cutter.
Whatever is drunk by means of one's own power, that remains drunk by that very [power];
the drink is drunk by the vessel, yet it is the man who is called the "drinker."
By your very nature you are utterly dull-witted and are awakened to knowledge repeatedly by the Knower;
therefore, it is indeed the Self that, by means of the Self, gathers this [knowledge] for itself. This is our position.
The Supreme Lord, your very Self, awakens you incessantly;
yet the ignorant must indeed be awakened by the wise through hundreds of repetitions.
For here it is the very existence of the Self that manifests, having the singular form of pure consciousness;
and by means of that alone, the mind quickly remains established, assuming the objects denoted by words.
Thus, O mind, you have come under the sway of your own power through ignorance;
but today, upon the dawn of knowledge, you have dissolved like snow in the intense heat of the sun.
Therefore, you are dead, you are deluded, and you do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Let there be no vain conceit that "I am that very same person," for it will lead only to your unhappiness.
The mental constructions of the unreal are like the creepers of Indra’s net; O dear one, here it is consciousness alone that expands as the state of Brahman.
The power of Brahmā arises fully in the forms of the world of men and gods;
like the ocean shore, it surges with a mass of waves born from the spray of the sea.
O deluded one, since you are composed of consciousness and are consciousness itself, and are eternally non-different from that supreme state, why do you grieve for anything else?
For that state is all-pervading, abiding in all things, and indeed possessing all forms;
upon its attainment, everything is always swiftly attained.
Neither you exist nor does the body exist; here, only the Great Brahman exists, vibrating.
Through the outpourings of "I" and "you," suffering indeed manifests—of whom, then, could it be, and for what?
If you are the Self, then the all-pervading Self alone exists here and nothing else;
if you are something other than the Self, then you are inert matter, and that which is non-conscious has no form of yours.
The self alone is the entirety of the three worlds; there is nothing else besides it.
That which is other than the self is nothing at all; if that "other" were you, then you would be nothing.
"Why do you strive in vain, thinking 'this is mine' or 'that is mine'?
Does a non-existent form manifest, and who has ever been killed by the horn of a hare?"
O fool, there is no third conceptualization other than the conscious and the insentient parts;
it is like a third coloring between shadow and sunlight.
O ignorant one, that which arises from the contemplation of truth and results from the destruction of the perception of mental activity and inertia is indeed nothing but self-awareness alone.
Therefore, O deluded one, you possess neither agency nor even the state of being an enjoyer;
you are that very Supreme Brahman itself. Abandon this ignorance consisting of the notion of a self.
However, solely for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of instruction regarding the domain of the ignorant,
it is said that "the Self acts" by means of you acting as an instrument.
The instrument, being insubstantial in nature, inert, and without support,
neither vibrates nor moves without the awakening of an agent.
O ignorant one, no power whatsoever exists in an instrument that lacks an agent;
what capacity could a sickle have to cut in the absence of a reaper?
The capacity for the action of severing by a sword-strike resides in the person,
not in the utterly insentient sword, even when all its parts have been cut away.
Therefore, my friend, do not be an agent; do not become a partaker of suffering in vain.
O fool, being afflicted for the sake of others does not look well among common people.
A lord such as this is not to be pitied, even if he should be one who has rendered you assistance;
for there is no purpose whatsoever for him in what is done here, nor any in what is left undone.
"The person of small intellect merely thinks, 'I shall serve him in every way,' yet while he suffers, no benefit at all accrues to the virtuous."
If you thus follow the will of the Creator, the Lord of enjoyment,
then he would have no desire whatsoever here, for he is eternally satisfied.
This entire world is filled by the one, all-pervading conscious self, which shines with an uncreated radiance; there is nothing else but mere conceptual construction.

By means of its own self, through the manifestation of the one and the many, as a totality whose nature is thatness, what is it that is made to cease within itself by itself? What is desired [as an object]?
But for one such as you, agitation arises in vain merely by seeing [an object],
just as the mind becomes intoxicated upon beholding a queen.
If there were a connection between you and the self, then you would be its agent, O handsome one;
however, you have no such connection with it, just as a stone has none with a flower.

That identity which exists equally with the second, being oneness through the state of that [second], is declared to be the apprehension of relation; it is oneness now, whereas previously there was duality.
Consisting of various types of arrangements and manifesting through various forms and actions,
it is known to be manifold, serving as the cause for states of pleasure and pain.
A relationship is observed between two equal things, as well as between two halves;
and when that [relationship] exists, there is another [distinct thing] in the three worlds, even between those that are very different.
Many substances are fully capable of supporting the qualities of another substance,
just as medicinal herbs [support] the coolness of the moon, or as great rocks [support] heat.
If, however, there is such a connection with the Supreme Self for you,
then let that mutual confusion of qualities be the seed of transmigratory existence.
By your own self, which transcends the power of mental construction and conceptualization,
there exists no such connection between you and the subtle atoms of the sensory faculties.
Moreover, another clear relationship based on convention is observed in the world,
such as the identity between two flames of fire, or even between two bodies of water.
Even for you, who are an atom whose self transcends the power of mental ideation and creative manifestation,
there can be no such connection with that which consists of the collection of sense organs.
Moreover, a relationship of thief and victim is observed even between two halves [of a single object],
due to the diversity of their respective parts, just as in the case of a man and a woman here in this world.
And by way of some slight difference, as between water and milk,
or else as between water and honey, or two kinds of honey that are distinct;
or even as between white and reddish light, such as the light of the dawn and the sun.
By your very self, which transcends the power of mental construction and conceptualization, there is no such connection between you and the subtle atoms of the sensory faculties.
There is another kind of causal relationship between two things that are utterly distinct,
just as there is here between wood and fire, so too between a man and an elephant.

Even such a connection as that does not exist for you with the subtle collection of sense organs, nor with the Self whose nature transcends the portion fashioned by the mental reflections of the mind.

Furthermore, for you, there can be no relationship consisting of cause and effect— whether according to the principle of the seed and the sprout or in the sequence of father and son— with respect to the self.
Even another person might be constructed by the mere convention of mental designation;
for indeed, between two people, there is the internal certainty: "I am yours" and "you are mine."
Furthermore, many other relations, such as that of the container and the contained, exist here in the world for those who skillfully establish relations.
Even so, there is no connection for you with the collection of sense organs, since your self is an atom that transcends the power of mental construction and conceptualization.
What kind of connection could there be between you and this terrible cycle of existence that causes suffering, which has never been seen by us before, nor is it being seen now? Tell us.
This connection is neither a creation of perfect similarity, nor a creation of partial similarity, nor a creation of dissimilar characteristics; what indeed could such a thing be?
O virtuous one, how can the moon, which consists of elixir, ever truly unite with the horn of a rabbit’s head, for it is said that the existent cannot eternally join with the non-existent?

O fool, how can there ever be a unity between existence and non-existence, between the group of sense organs and the self, between the luminous and the insentient, or between that which is stained and that which is stainless?
If both [the self and the object] are likewise non-existent, what attachment could possibly arise here?
It would be like that between the horn on a rabbit's head and a fragment of rock from the mountain.
Listen to this certainty, O mind; I speak only the truth:
no connection between you and the self exists even in dreams.
That which is not composed of the self cannot exist anywhere, because the self possesses all forms; therefore, you do not exist, O Citta.

This consciousness, though liberated from the objects of thought, manifests as the expansion of the web of the world; consisting of "I," "you," and so forth, it is the very being of Brahman that dances.
Although surrounded on all sides by every kind of mental construction arising from yourself,
O one of deceitful appearance and ruined mind, the All-pervading Lord, whose vision is entirely stainless, does not enter into association with you.
The eighty-third canto, titled "Instruction on the Mind," from the Narrative of Vītahavya; [spoken by] Vasiṣṭha.

The highly intelligent Vītahavya, on a mountain slope within a cave of the Vindhya range, further reflected upon this with an intellect as sharp as the edge of a razor: vītahavyo mahābuddhir vindhyādrau kandarodare / kṣurāgraśitayā buddhyā bhūyaś cedaṃ vyacārayat //MU_5,83.1//
In that which is devoid of the entire multitude of foolish sense-faculties, yet endowed with a complete arrangement;
enveloped by all volitional constructions, yet transcending all sprouts [of rebirth].
When this total destruction has arisen for you along with your entire retinue,
surely your soul emerges like the sun from darkness upon a wound.
O Supreme Lord, although You are eternally risen, You do not rise for one whose self is enveloped by latent impressions, just as the sun does not rise for one who is blind.
When the impurity of latent impressions (vāsanā) is completely stilled, you perish along with your very root;
thereafter, the dense mass of consciousness expanded by Brahman becomes manifest.
For bondage is merely latent impression (vāsanā); its destruction is called liberation.
Arise through the joyful severing of the rope of latent impressions!
When the all-pervading Lord is seen, the sensory faculties along with their latent impressions perish,
just as the perception of blindness vanishes when the sun has risen.
Upon attaining the Self, the row of the six senses, with the mind as the sixth, comes to an end;
and upon the destruction of the row of the senses, the Self is perceived by the self.
Therefore, for the sake of constant spiritual welfare, one should practice these two alone;
mastery over the self and the senses is achieved through practice alone.
The accumulation of qualities within oneself is seen to perish when the Self is realized,
just as the nocturnal agitation of beings ceases when the sun has risen.
When that [self] which perishes upon seeing [the truth] is itself non-existent,
how can that which is insentient by nature enter into a relationship with consciousness?
Just as it is impossible for light to unite with darkness, or for one who is hot by nature to unite with that which is cool, so too there can be no union between the living and the dead.
Where is he who has transcended all parts, and where is he endowed with all parts?
Where is the eternal one whose nature is pure light, and where is the impermanent one whose form is like darkness?
Where is the eternally risen form of consciousness, which never sets?
And where is that which is non-existent, inert, mute, and blind? Where is the dense mass of consciousness that illumines everything?
The conviction that the self is joined with the collection of senses leads to misfortune,
as long as ignorance alone dances within the minds of the foolish.
When it is established that the attachment belongs to the knower of that [Self] through the Self and not to the senses,
the world becomes identical with the Supreme Self once the collection of sense organs has reached its dissolution.
By that same reasoning through which this thick suspicion of yours—
that the self is stained— foolishly arises, that ignorance has now been destroyed.
That fool, having allowed himself to be entered by those who are treacherous toward the self and the senses, has swallowed poison and fallen into a swoon. (5.83.18)
When those who are suffering have their senses dulled, or when pleasures are destroyed,
what has happened to the Self— the witness whose virtuous conduct is undiminished?
The conjunction of the mind, the sense-faculties, and the self is not possible for us;
once the absence of any connection is established, how can there be the states of being an enjoyer and a doer?
Therefore, I am neither the agent nor the enjoyer; there is neither liberation nor bondage.
I do not exist, nor does another exist; there is only the stainless Self of pure consciousness.
"I am that very one; you are that very one; the world is that; the sky is that; the earth is that.
Since it has been determined that everything is indeed that alone, why do you become bewildered?"
The falling away from consciousness is suffering; do not fall away from consciousness.
By this much alone through one-pointed meditation, become one whose meditation is constant and who perceives the Self.

Know that when there is an absence of any internal object— whether visible or invisible— that bestows suffering, the mind's tendency toward conceptual construction is a fall from consciousness that brings suffering.
O mind, what kind of agency can there be in insentient objects of perception, such as the body and the senses? How could a forest exist in the sky?
In the Self, which has cast off the mire of temporal succession and whose nature is the destruction of mental construction, agency is not possible, just as it is not in the expanse of the sky.
This world is merely the Self alone, which manifests within itself through various forms of multiplicity; yet people are needlessly tormented by it, as if by the waters of the ocean.
When all this shines forth as mere appearance within this Self that is consciousness,
there is no second conceptualization, just as there is no [second] heated coal in the ocean.
In the God who is free from temporal succession, or in the body or the insentient mind, consciousness—when liberated from the object of cognition—is the essence, O beautiful one; it is nothing else.
"There is this other thing, and that is yet another— whether auspicious or indeed inauspicious"—
such conceptualization does not exist, just as a forest does not exist in the sky.
This entire expanse is nothing but pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra), devoid of anything to be perceived;
how, then, can there be the conceptual construction that "this is I" or "this is another"?
In that which is beginningless, formless, all-pervading, and the expansive Self—who could attribute conceptual constructs to it? Who could write the Ṛgveda in the sky?
While the Lord— who is the essence of all things and objects, eternally risen, and who stands filling the vast quarters to their fullness—
abides within the Self, and while the notions of "you" and "I" have rightly departed due to its stainlessness, the fragments of pleasure and pain have indeed perished for me, along with my delusion.
The eighty-fourth canto in the *Vītahavyopākhyāna*, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Controlling the Senses," by Vasiṣṭha.
Furthermore, the steadfast and excellent sage, with his pure intellect, properly awakened his own group of senses, which had been kept guarded. MU 5.84.1.
O assembly of sense-faculties, listen for your own sake; I shall speak most clearly.
Having heard this and attained its true nature, proceed to supreme freedom from suffering.
Your singular existence as a self leads only to suffering and is never-ending;
therefore, you should abandon that existence of a self when it is non-existent.
"By my instruction, this existence of yours has clearly come to an end;
for you have indeed arisen from ignorance."
O little mind, the very manifestation of your own existence leads to extreme suffering;
it is like the swelling of lac in a boiling cauldron, which only serves to burn both its sides.
Behold, O brother, while you exist, the multitudes of the rivers of saṃsāra— agitated by dull waves— enter the ocean of time.
Successions of sorrows fall from somewhere, like torrents of rain in a downpour, as they grapple with one another in a frantic "I first, I first" struggle.
The cruel, wailing cholera of existence and non-existence throbbs boundlessly, intent upon uprooting the heart.
While the tree of the body is withered by coughing, asthma, and trembling bees, the blossom-cluster of old age and death unfolds with its stainless radiance.
In this cave-like hollow of the body, which is coiled by the serpents of turbulent waves,
the pitiless whirlpool of anxiety digs its own trench.
The greedy fly, with its flapping wings and sharp pair of beaks,
plucks the lotuses of virtue from this withered tree of the body.
The harsh, impure, and arrogant cock of desire scatters its droppings upon the heart, here and there.
In the great night of delusion, the fierce owl of ignorance flits about like a vetāla in a cremation ground within the tree of the heart.
These and many other misfortunes, like malevolent spirits in the night, prowl about you as long as this collection of sense-faculties exists.
But if you were not present, O virtuous one, all auspicious glories would indeed blossom fully with light, like lotus ponds at dawn.
The sky of the heart shines here, its mist of delusion stilled;
it is free from dust, pervaded by stainless light, and vast within.
Like a sudden flood of stones fallen from the vault of the sky,
the surges of conceptual construction do not fall for long, causing such distress.
Loving-kindness, which gladdens all, is cool and supremely purifying; it arises from the heart, as delightful as a cluster of blossoms from a fine tree.
Full of internal flaws, joined with dullness, and its own virtues concealed,
anxiety withers away like a lotus plant scorched by frost.
Upon the destruction of ignorance, light enters into clarity within;
it is like the orb of the sun in the autumn sky when the clouds have subsided.
Clear, expansive, and profound, unagitated and unassailable,
the heart attains equanimity like an ocean when the wind has stilled.
The Person dwells within, filled with a flood of nectar and consisting of eternal bliss, like the cool moon.
The entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is meditated upon as resting solely within a single portion of consciousness; it is visualized as a full-bodied form, languid with bliss.
For those who are attached to the eight worldly concerns and bound by the snares of hope, there is no returning to birth, just as there is no regrowth of leaves that have been burnt.
By a man who has traversed the great path of worldly existence, old age, and birth,
rest is found for a long time within the tree of the self, so that there is no further wandering.
Such qualities as these, and others like them, exist as perfections;
yet they would not exist if you, the all-consuming one who destroys the night of all desires, did not exist.
Between these two positions— the mind having the nature of existence or non-existence—
whichever you perceive to be the better, accept that very one at once.
O best among men, I consider the absence of your own self to be happiness;
cultivate that very absence, for the abandonment of happiness is indeed folly.
If, however, there exists a reality that truly contains consciousness within it,
who would ever desire the absolute non-existence of you while you are still living?
But there is no sword; I tell you this truly, O handsome one.
Therefore, do not be unhappy with the conviction that "I live only by falsehood."
Either you do not exist at all from the very beginning, or that existence of yours which arose through delusion has now, by means of inquiry, utterly come to an end.
O virtuous one, your form is only this much: that which is beyond investigation.
When thorough investigation is performed, you are established as formless and non-existent.
Without investigation, you are born like darkness from the absence of light;
through investigation, you are stilled like darkness by light.
"O friend, for all this time my lack of discernment has persisted;
by that very fact, I have become excessively bloated, which is the sole cause of my suffering."
Through the mere power of deluded imagination, you became like a child’s phantom;
yet when that intense imagination was exhausted, you remained as you truly are.
Now that the eternal has arisen and your former form has passed away through the clarity of discernment, homage again and again to discernment!
Through the ultimate awakening of the mind, you have become unawakened;
when the state of mind has perished, you abide as the Supreme Lord.
Your former play of individual nature has now come to rest in the highest good;
liberated from all latent impressions, you are now the Great Lord.
That which arises from a lack of discernment perishes through discernment;
just as darkness born of the absence of light comes to an end through light.
O virtuous one, even though you do not desire it, when analysis reaches its conclusion,
this destruction— attained through this very means— is in fact for the sake of achieving happiness.

Therefore, by means of the logical arguments of our established doctrine, it has been determined that the sword does not exist; O Lord of the Senses, may it be well with you, for it has come to its end.
"May there be well-being for your own mind, which was eternally non-existent in the past, is currently of a non-existent nature, and will have no future consequence."
I am attaining final nirvāṇa; I am at peace; by good fortune I am free from the fever of passion.
Abiding in the state of the fourth form (*turya*), I remain established in my own self alone.
Therefore, there is indeed no transmigrating being, nor is there any state of mind;
yet the Self truly exists, for nothing else is found to exist.

I believe that the conceptualization "this is the self" does not belong to one whose inner being is stainless; for how could there be a conceptualization of a single entity through the exclusion of its opposites?
Not uttering the conceptualization "this is my self" because of that [realization],
I, as a silent sage, am extinguished within my own self, like a wave in water.

Having attained that state of perfect consciousness which is free from latent impressions, devoid of any support for the intellect, where the movement of vital breath ceases, and from which the defects of birth and destruction have vanished— being devoid of all objects of perception— I am stilled within this very silence, free from desire.
The eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Non-existence of the Mind through the Story of Vītahavya," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having thus resolved, that sage Vītahavya,
free from all mental impressions, remained motionless in meditative absorption within a cave of the Vindhya mountains.
With all movement stilled, beautiful with the bliss of motionlessness, his mind set at rest, he became as magnificent as the tranquil ocean.
Gradually, the continuity of his vital breaths subsided within him,
like the flickering of a mass of flames when the fuel has been consumed by fire.
When the external object has ceased to exist internally and no longer persists externally,
and when only the remainder remains established, his two eyelashes begin to throb.
Like two eyes with a very slight glimmer reaching to the edges of the nostrils,
they attained an equal beauty with their lotuses half-closed like buds.
With his body, head, and neck held perfectly erect, that one of great intelligence sat as if carved from a rock or as if depicted in a painting.
As he remained thus established, three hundred years passed within a hollow of the Vindhya marshes as if they were half a muhūrta.
It is said that for all this time, that self-possessed one did not wake up;
yet, being liberated while living and absorbed in meditation, he did not abandon that body.
For that duration, that fortunate one, the knower of yoga, did not wake up,
despite the unrestrained roars of thunderclouds and the gurgling sounds of heavy downpours.
[The quarters were filled] with the cries of the lords of the surrounding regions as they hunted,
with the roars of bears and monkeys, and with the sounds of elephants slapping their trunks.
With the roaring of lions in their fury, the thundering rumbles of waterfalls,
the crashing of fierce thunderbolts, and the dense clamor of elephants;
By the leaps of intoxicated śarabhas, by the crashing of mountain slopes during earthquakes, by the roaring sounds of forest fires, and by the surging and tossing of floodwaters;
By the blows from the great surface of boulders, by sinkings into the surface of the earth, by the surging and falling of floods of water, and by heats as harsh as fire;
It flows freely at its own will when the time for its cause has arrived,
like waves in water as the rainy seasons pass away.
In a very short time, he was turned into mud on the surface of the earth within that mountain cave by the floodwaters of the rainy season.
There he dwelt within a narrow cavity of the earth,
his body caked with mud like a stone deep within a mountain.
Then, when three hundred years had passed, the Lord himself,
whose nature is the Self, awoke while still confined within the hollow of the earth.
Consciousness alone seized that body of his as it was pressed down by the earth;
for the vibration consisting of the vital breath does not exist without the movement of the vital breath.
Having flown up and attained maturity within the sky of his heart,
that [vision], taking the form of his own mind, was experienced by him right there in his heart.
In the lovely Kailāsa forest, at the foot of a kadamba tree,
he remained for a hundred years as a stainless sage whose self was liberated while living.

For a hundred years, one shall possess the state of a Vidyādhara, free from all mental afflictions; for five yugas, one shall hold the sovereignty of Indra, bowed down to by gods and celestial musicians.
Rāma:
O Sage, regarding these manifestations of his such as his state of being a sage and so forth,
how can there be both restriction and non-restriction of the constraints of space and time?
Vasiṣṭha:
This power of consciousness, which is the self of all, becomes whatever it arises as, in whatever manner,
because its sole inherent nature is that very essence.
In whatever place, at whatever time, and in whatever manner the Buddha is determined [to appear], he remains established in that way,
because his nature consists of those very sequences of determination regarding place, time, and so forth.
