Thus, having been freed from latent impressions and devoid of mental afflictions, Vītahavya beheld these various worlds within the space of consciousness in his heart.
For those who possess right awakening, this very latent impression (*vāsanā*) is no longer a latent impression;
it has been burnt by the fire of knowledge. What seed-nature can there be for a seed that has already been burnt?
For one kalpa, he served as an attendant to the Moon-crested Lord,
having mastered all branches of knowledge and possessing stainless vision of the three periods of time.
Whatever kind of firm mental impression one possesses, that is exactly what one perceives;
Vītahavya experienced this very state through the condition of liberation while living.
Rāma:
Such being the case, O best of sages, even for one whose mind is liberated while living,
there exist perceptions of bondage and liberation, just as they did for Vītahavya.
Vasiṣṭha said:
This entire universe, as it exists, is tranquil and as pure as space; it is Brahman alone. For those liberated while living, how can there be any perception of bondage or liberation?
In whatever manner and wherever consciousness shines forth, in that very place and to that same extent, it perceives itself as extended.
O Rāghava, by him many worlds have been experienced and are indeed being experienced as the Self of all, in the form of Brahman.
In those countless worlds, which are formless and consist of the great-souled ones whose conscious selves are the fire of Vitahavya submerged within the cavities of the earth; MU 5.85.33.
He who was Śakra, unaware of his true nature, is today the king among the Cīnas;
at this very moment, he has set out on a hunt in the Nīpa grove.
He who was once a swan, his true self unawakened, dwelling upon the lotus of Brahmā,
is now this very lord of fishermen in a forest bower of Mount Kailāsa.
That king who, unaware of his true self, was once upon the earth in the region of Saurāṣṭra,
is indeed this very tree with its vast branches standing here in the village of the Andhras.
Rāma said:
It is said that this was the mental creation of Vītahavya; how then can those embodied beings therein be anything other than mere illusion? For they were merely the forms of his body.
Vasiṣṭha:
If that world of Vītahavya consists solely of a single delusion, then what is the nature of this which now appears before us? Of what is it composed?
This, my dear, consists solely of consciousness and mind alone, and is of the nature of delusion.
In reality, however, that is not the world, nor is this something other than it;
yet it is not that the existence of the world does not exist, for this Brahman alone shines forth.
The past, the present, and the future— this world and that which is other than it,
this entire visible universe— is composed solely of mind and is nothing but pure consciousness.
As long as this reality of such a nature has not been fully understood,
even though it is as firm as the essence of a diamond, it remains merely a supreme void.
For the ignorant, this mind alone expands in this manner,
characterized by the play of recurring manifestations, like water in the ocean.
The designation "mind" (manas) is simply one's own consciousness (svacitta), which is nothing other than the sky of consciousness (cidambara) as it truly exists.
By that [consciousness], the world and the visible universe are expanded; thus, while everything is pervaded, nothing at all has been pervaded.
The eighty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of Vītahavya’s Mind-Journey," Canto 86.
Rāma said:
Now, what was the state of Vītahavya while he remained within that forest interior?
How did he extract his body, and how did he become perfected?
Vasiṣṭha:
Immediately thereafter, the mind named Vītahavya, whose nature is infinite, realized its own self-manifestation in this manner: MU 5.86.2.
Once, a desire arose within this entire assembly to spontaneously recollect their past lives and to behold all their previous births.
Then he saw all his own bodies, one after another, perishing; from among those that had not yet perished, he [saw] him situated within a cavity of the earth.
By mere chance, the thought arose in him to uplift that body known as Vītahavya, which was being crushed within the hollow of the earth.
The mass of mud brought by the monsoon flood resting upon his own back,
as well as the earth on the surface of his body covered with a network of grass.
Having seen this, the one of great splendor, constrained within the cavity of the earth,
reflected once more with a mind directed toward supreme awakening.
Because my body is a composite of all its parts, it is rendered mute and, though overcome by the vital breaths, is unable to move even in the slightest degree.
Therefore, having gone there, I shall quickly enter this body of Vivasvat;
thereafter, his attendant Piṅgala will extract my soul from it.
Or rather, what need have I for this? I shall find peace without obstacle; I shall be extinguished and go to my own state—what use have I for the play of the body?
Having reflected thus in his mind, O high-minded one, Vītahavya remained silent for a moment and then further pondered upon the ground.
For me, there is nothing to be gained from either abandoning or clinging to the body;
as is the abandonment of the body, so too is the clinging to it.
Therefore, as long as this body exists and has not yet reached dissolution into atoms,
I shall mount it and wander about for a while.
Like a reflection entering a mirror situated in the sky, I enter my own body, the glowing form, by means of Piṅgala, in order to uplift it.
Thus that sage, assuming the form of the wind, entered the sun,
having become the body of the eightfold city, like fire entering a mass of metal.
The Lord Ravi, too, having seen that leader of sages within his heart,
reflected upon the sequence of duties to be performed, he of noble intellect.
He beheld the supreme body of the sage in a region of the Vindhya caves, covered with grass and stones, and devoid of consciousness.
Knowing what the sage intended to do, Bhānu, situated in the midst of the sky,
commanded his foremost host to lift the muni from the earth.
The consciousness of the sage Vītahavya, in the form of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka),
quickly bowed with its mind to the worshipful Sun, who consists of wind.
Permitted with due honor by Bhānunātha, he entered the leader of the group,
who had a tawny appearance and was heading toward the caves of the Vindhya mountains.
Leaving the sky, which was as beautiful as a forest elephant, that tawny one reached the Vindhya forest, resplendent with clouds intoxicated by the rainy season like garments in the heavens.
With the mountains uprooted by his claws, he drew the treasures of the earth from her womb,
just as a swan draws a lotus stalk from the mud.
Then, like a bird exhausted from wandering through the sky entering its nest, he entered his own body, the city of eight, in silence.
Having quickly bowed to one another, Vītahavya and the sky-dweller,
both repositories of splendor, became intent solely upon their respective tasks.
Piṅgala went through the sky, and the sage went to the stainless lake,
which was like a night-lotus with stars for its blossoms and possessed a form shimmering like the rays of the sun.
Vītahavya quickly sank into the lake of blooming lotuses,
like a young elephant in a forest at the edge of a muddy pool.
Having bathed there, performed his recitations, and worshipped the Sun,
he shone forth once again with a body adorned by asceticism, just as before.

Endowed with that loving-kindness, supreme equanimity, and profound peace, as well as true wisdom, sympathetic joy, compassion, and glory— the Sage, whose mind was liberated from all attachments, spent the day in delight upon the bank of a river in the Vindhya mountains.
The eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Samādhi by Vītahavya," from the [Yoga]vāsiṣṭha.
At the end of the day, that sage entered once again a certain vast and solitary cave in the Vindhya mountains in order to compose his mind.
Then, having seen the higher and lower worlds, he spoke with his mind while maintaining that very same composure toward the objects of the senses and without abandoning his continuous contemplation.
The collection of my senses has already been clearly restrained by me;
now there is no further need for my extensive reflection.
Having shattered the conceptualization of "it exists" or "it does not exist," like a tender creeper,
I remain in the remaining state, fixed in its form like an immovable mountain peak.
Like the risen [sun] having set, and like the set [sun] having risen;
equal, appearing as the same flavor, I remain, having attained self-abidingness.
Though awakened, I remain as if in deep sleep; though situated in deep sleep, I am awake.
Taking hold of the Fourth State (turya), I abide until the end of my task, with my state rendered motionless.
Steady as a pillar in solitude, with my mind established in all things, I abide free from affliction in the equanimity that is common to all beings.
Having reflected thus, he remained again in meditation for six days;
then he attained awakening, like a traveler who has slept for a moment.
Thus perfected, the Blessed One Vītahavya, a man of great austerity,
dwelt for a long time in that state of liberation while living.
He neither took delight in things nor ever censured them;
likewise, he experienced neither agitation nor did he attain joy.
Whether walking or standing still, this discourse arose in his heart with his own mind for the sake of diverting his thoughts.
O Lord of the group of unchanging senses, look: what kind of pervasive blissful happiness has been attained by you, who possess such tranquility of mind?
Therefore, O best among the fickle, you must constantly maintain this very state of passionlessness and abandon all restlessness.
O you thieves of the senses! O you of ruined hopes and ruined names!
This self does not belong to you, nor do you exist within the self.
Go quickly to the end of destruction; your hopes have been rendered fruitless.
You, whose very foundations are fragile, are not capable of overcoming it.
This latent impression (vāsanā) of yours that "I am the self" indeed arises from the forgetting of reality, like the perception of a snake in a rope that has been seen.
This notion of self in what is not-self, and this notion of reality in what is unreal, arose here through a lack of inquiry; through inquiry, it has come to an end.
"O sirs, you are one thing and we are another; Brahmā is distinct, and agency is something else.
The enjoyer is one thing and that which takes [the action] is another—what fault is there, and for whom, and of what kind?"
Wood is produced from forests; ropes, bamboo, and hides, as well as adzes and iron tools—thus the carpenter exerts himself for the sake of his livelihood.

Thus, just as here in this world, by means of a causal complex consisting of entities established by their own inherent capacities, a chariot in the form of a mere house is produced through a chance occurrence (*kākatālīya*).
Just as one who has attained perfection through a chance occurrence remains with senses stilled by his own power, so too indeed is this body; what destruction can there be here, and for whom?

Forgetfulness has been forgotten far away; mindfulness has been clearly recollected. What was existent has become non-existent, and what was non-existent has become non-existent; that which was perishable has perished, and that which was stable has remained.
In this manner, that tiger among sages, a great ascetic, remained here for many groups of years engaged in such contemplation.
Wherein thought has reached its end for the sake of non-rebirth,
and delusion remains far removed— there he dwelt forever.
Relying upon the infinite consolation of meditative absorption, which arises from seeing the flood of phenomena as they truly are, that man dwelt forever.
Upon the destruction of the dualistic views of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, and of attachment and grasping,
he dwelt in that state which is the supremely full Self and the peace of his own inner being.
Hear how that venerable son of Agastya, Vītahavya, who was free from all worldly attachments, attained the state of liberation while still embodied over the course of time.
Having dwelt here at this meritorious hermitage for thirty thousand and seven hundred years, as well as on Mount Meru, the abode of the gods;
The sage Vītahavya, whose mind was free from desire and aversion,
attained the state of absolute liberation (kevalībhāva) at Videha, the frontier limit of birth and karma.
Out of a desire for the supreme nectar of the flavor of renouncing attachment to saṃsāra,
he entered a golden cave on the Vindhya mountain with her in solitude.
Quickly perceiving the net of the world as something not to be encountered again,
he sat down there in the bound lotus posture and spoke within himself to himself.
O passion, go to passionlessness; O hatred, proceed to freedom from hatred.
For a very long time, I have sported here with you both.
"O enjoyments, homage be to you! For hundreds of millions of births, I have been cherished by you in this world like a child by its caregivers."
Homage again and again to that bliss which has caused me to forget even this supreme, meritorious path to the state of Nirvāṇa.
O Suffering, my self was earnestly sought by me through that which was heated by you;
therefore, this path has been taught to me by you—homage be to you!
"By your grace, this cool state has been attained by me; that which is called suffering is indeed suffering. O you whose very nature is the giver of happiness, homage be to you!"
May it be well with you, O friend, from this life which is as essence-less as the cycle of existence; we shall depart from this bodily state for our own abode.
Alas, how truly miserable is the fate of dull-witted beings!
Even after having undergone hundreds of births, I might yet be separated from my very body.
O friend, you who have been my companion for so long, I do not abandon you;
it is you yourself who have brought this injury upon yourself through the power of your own lack of self-knowledge.
Having attained self-knowledge, you have brought about the destruction of the self;
you are not broken by another within the body, for this was cultivated by you alone.
O Mother Thirst, you who have withered me while I was alone and I was at peace, you must not cause me further suffering; I am departing. MU 5.87.41.
O Blessed One, these faults born of perverse offenses must be forgiven; I seek only absolute tranquility—grant me leave, for I have had enough.
O Mother Tṛṣṇā, after a very long time, this separation from us has now occurred due to the fault of our union; this is our final salutation.
Salutations be to you, who are to be served by those of virtuous deeds; for in the past, having been rescued from the hells by you, I was established in heaven.

Homage to the tree of evil deeds, which has taken root in the field of bad actions, which carries the trunk of hell, which bears the weight of flowers that are the [Buddha’s] teachings, and which possesses branches of misdeeds.
Salutations to that Delusion, with whom you have long shared many births in evil wombs; from this day forward, salutations to you who are invisible.
Homage to her who dwells in the cave as an ascetic, whose speech is as sweet as a sounding flute, who is clothed in leaves, and who is my companion during meditative absorptions.
For one weary on the path of saṃsāra, you were the cause of consolation;
you were a most affectionate companion, the remover of all sorrow.
Distressed by every kind of peril and fleeing from my faults,
I have sought refuge in you alone, my supreme friend, for the sake of destroying my grief.
Salutations to you, the staff of wood, the exclusive friend of old age.
O body, having grasped this alone as your essential core— the skeletal frame belonging to you, likewise composed of threads of blood and entrails— depart!
Salutations again and again to the various ways of agitating the milk for the sake of ritual baths;
salutations be to worldly transactions, and salutations be to you, the cycles of transmigration!
These noble ones were my innate and ancient friends; I have now gradually cast them off as mere breaths of life. May it be well with you; I am departing.
Together with you, I have rested in many diverse wombs and wandered through mountain thickets as well as through other worlds.
He has sported within the inner courtyards of cities, dwelt upon the mountains, remained amidst the play of worldly affairs, and set out upon various paths.
There is nothing within the treasury of the world that has not been created, taken away, consumed, given, or grasped by me in your company.
Now, dear ones, you may go to your own directions, for I am departing;
for all unions on the path of saṃsāra end in separation.
May this visual light enter the orb of the sun;
may the forest flowers enter into the consciousness of the bliss of their fragrance.
Let the vital breaths and likewise the tactile sensations enter today into the wind;
let the successions of sounds to be heard enter the hollow of space.
Like clarified butter poured into a blazing fire, the mind, its form withered, dissolves into the moon.
May all things such as pleasure and pain return to their own natural state;
may craving, along with its undertakings, wither away like a lotus pond in winter.
Like a flaming fire whose fuel is consumed, like a lamp devoid of oil,
like the ocean without Mount Mandara, like a day when the sun has set.

Like a cloud in autumn, having reached the end of its course at will like the dissolution at the end of an eon, I become tranquil within myself by means of the self, coming to rest at the conclusion of the syllable Om.
With the entire succession of activities vanished, my state transcends all conditions of the perceptible;
with a mind stilled by following the peace of the *praṇava*, I stand here, free from the stain of delusion.
The eighty-eighth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Dissolving the Grouping of the Senses," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus reflecting within himself, with his mental seeking stilled,
he softly uttered the beautiful syllable *praṇava*, having attained the stage of its realization.
Having abandoned all volitions fashioned by the imagination— whether external or internal, subtle or even gross— which pertain to the three worlds.
Standing with an unshakable form within himself like a wish-fulfilling gem,
he was like the full moon or Mount Mandara at rest.
Like a potter’s wheel brought to a halt despite its momentum,
he was like the ocean at full tide— stilled, vast, and pure.
With its mass of light, darkness, and gloom stilled, and devoid of sun, moon, and stars, it is as clear, infinite, and free from smoke, clouds, and dust as the autumnal sky.
Together with the long-sounding thread that culminates in the *praṇava*,
he cast off the web of the senses and their subtle elements, just as the wind disperses a fragrance.
Then he abandoned that state of pure darkness which had appeared within him,
just as a wise man rises up from a trace of anger, his form now radiant.
Then, having reflected for half a moment upon that radiance which had appeared to him, he abandoned it; and at that time, there was neither darkness nor light.
Then, having reached that state, he mentally destroyed that mind— which was like a blade of grass— so that it did not even flicker for half a moment.
Then, the consciousness of the limbs, established in its own state and having attained manifestation,
is like the cognition of a newborn infant— free from conceptualization and stainless.
In a duration of time less than half of a half-nimēṣa, the Lord, who is beyond all calculation,
abandoned the state of being an object of consciousness within consciousness, just as the wind abandons its power of vibration.
Then, having reached the state of *paśyantī*, which consists of pure existence alone,
he attained the state of deep sleep and remained as immovable as Mount Meru.
Then the All-pervading Lord, having remained for a moment in the state of deep sleep,
and having attained stability within that deep sleep, entered the form of the Fourth (turya).
There he was both without joy and with joy, both being and non-being;
he was both nothing and something, as were light and darkness.
That which is said to be "not this, not this"— neither consisting of consciousness nor consisting of consciousness— He arose from that, He who is beyond even the range of my words.
Thus, that most excellent state, the supremely purifying station,
which has entered into the interior of all existents, became devoid of all [dualistic] things.
That which is the Void for the proponents of the Void, the Supreme Brahman for the best of the knowers of Brahman,
and that which is pure consciousness for the knowers of consciousness— [that is] the stainless Self.
To those who hold the Sāṅkhya view, he is the Puruṣa; to the proponents of Yoga, he is Īśvara; to the followers of the Śaśikalā school, he is Śiva; and to those who propound Kālakavāda, he is Kāla.

For those who know the Self, there is the Self; for those whose selves are such, there is freedom from desire; and for the Mādhyamikas, whose minds are perfectly tranquil, everything is the Middle Way.
That which is the established conclusion of all scriptures, that which conforms to the heart of all,
that which is everything, always, and for everyone— that which is real, he stands as that reality.
That which is the unsurpassed outflow, that which is the lamp even for lights,
and that which has self-experience as its sole measure— that very thing, that very thing, that very thing, he remains as that.
That which is both one and many, both with taint and without taint,
that which is both all and not-all— that very thing, that indeed, remains as it is.

Then, in an instant, that Lord— whose state is even more stainless than the nature of the sky— remained as the unborn, undecaying, beginningless, primordial, single reality, both with parts and without parts, and partless.
The eighty-ninth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Nirvāṇa for Vītahavya," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having reached the very limit of cyclic existence and arrived at the further shore of the ocean of suffering,
the sage Vītahavya thus became tranquil, his mind free from rebirth.
For when he has thus become tranquil and attained supreme peace,
he is like a drop of water in the ocean, merged into his own transforming state.
Remaining thus motionless, that body fell into a state of withering;
having reached an inner state of desolation, it was like a leaf at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Leaving the nest of his heart which resided within the tree of his body,
the birds of his vital breaths flew up into the sky like stones released from a machine.
All the elements have fully entered into the elements themselves; yet the body, a mere machine of flesh and bone, dwells upon the surface of the forest and the earth.
Consciousness has entered the ocean of consciousness; the elements abide within the elements;
everything remains in its own essential nature once the sage has attained tranquility.
This rest of Vītahavya, rich with hundreds of reflections, has been told to you, O Rāma; discern it through your own wisdom.
O Rāghava, having perceived the reality by means of such reasoning kindled by your own inquiry, arise and abide in that essence.
O Rāma, all this that has been described by me to you,
as well as what I am now describing, and what I shall describe hereafter— [all this is the nature of the Self].
"By me, who perceives the three times, who lives eternally and for a long duration, all of that has indeed been personally investigated and seen."
Therefore, O Mahāmati, relying upon this stainless vision, attain supreme knowledge; for liberation is indeed obtained through knowledge.
From knowledge arises freedom from suffering; from knowledge comes the destruction of ignorance.
From knowledge alone, O Rāma, comes supreme perfection, and not from anything else in reality.
Having completely severed all bonds on every side through knowledge,
the lord of sages Vītahavya has shattered the entire mountain of his mind.
Consciousness, whose essence is Vītahavya, is the world born of volition;
it has experienced this very universe, and that universe is itself [consciousness].
Vītahavya said: "The mind alone is everything; I am the mind, you are the mind, and these mountains are the mind.
This entire world is the mind; what room is there here for difference or non-difference?"
Having realized the ultimate truth, with defects such as passion extinguished, he has transcended all impurities, transformations, and limiting adjuncts through their destruction;
having long followed his own nature, the discerning one has attained the stainless and infinite state, his sorrow stilled.
The ninety-first canto, "The Resting of Vītahavya," is concluded. Vasiṣṭha said:
O Raghava, like Vitahavya, having led yourself to the state of one who has known what is to be known, remain engaged in actions, free from passion, fear, and hatred.
For thirty thousand years Vītahavya lived as a sage, free from sorrow; O Rāghava, live in that same manner.
Other sages of royal lineage, who have known what is to be known and possess great intelligence, dwell in their own kingdoms; O high-minded one, dwell in the same manner.
The self is never perceived through the sequences of pleasure and pain;
though it is all-pervading, O mighty-armed one, why do you grieve in vain?
Many who have realized the self dwell here upon this earth;
none have fallen under the power of suffering, my dear friend, like you.
Be established in yourself; be equanimous toward the vastness of existence; be happy.
You are all-pervading, you are the Self itself; for you, there is no further rebirth.
Those like you, who are liberated while living, do not fall under the sway of the transformations of joy and resentment,
just as lions do not fall under the control of the trees.
Rāma:
It is through this very occasion that this doubt has arisen within me;
may you dispel it for me, just as the autumn season disperses the clouds.
O best among the knowers of the Self, why are powers such as traveling through the sky not seen here in the bodies of those who are liberated while living?
Vasiṣṭha:
O descendant of Raghu, these deeds such as traveling through the sky and so forth are indeed the innate powers of those entities.
O Rāma, that manifold web of actions which is displayed and then concealed is merely the nature of objective phenomena; it is not the view of those who know the Self.
O Rāghava, even one who does not know the Self and is not liberated certainly attains such powers as moving through the sky by virtue of the potency of substances, actions, rituals, and time.
This is not the domain of one who knows the Self; for the knower of the Self is himself possessed of the Self.
Satisfied by the Self through the Self, he does not pursue ignorance.
Whatever worldly phenomena there may be, they know them to be created by ignorance;
how indeed could one who knows the Self and has abandoned ignorance sink into them?

Those who, by means of reasoning, establish even ignorance as being of the nature of happiness—they are indeed products of ignorance themselves; they are not knowers of the Self, nor do they follow that [right] sequence.
Whether one knows the truth or does not know the truth, for whoever exerts effort in accordance with time, substances, and actions, the attainment of Indra’s status and so forth is accomplished.
But the knower of the Self here transcends everything, free from desire;
satisfied in the Self alone, he neither acts nor strives.
He has no interest in traveling through the sky, nor in supernatural accomplishments, nor in enjoyments;
neither in power, nor in honors, nor in hope, death, or life.
Ever-satisfied, with a tranquil self, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions,
the knower of that reality abides in the Self, possessing a form like space.
Free from attachment, he is satisfied with both suffering and happiness that arrive unexpectedly, and with both life and death.
By means of whatever object has been obtained through the gradual descent of the waters of the oceans and rivers—
whether even or uneven— he remains, honoring his own self.
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object.
But he who, even though his self is cultivated, desires the networks of supernatural powers, accomplishes them in due order by means of the substances that achieve those powers.
"This is established by reasoning alone; such is the sequence of necessity, which cannot be rendered futile even by the best of gods, such as the Three-Eyed One."
This is the very nature of things, established by itself and not from another;
it never abandons its fixed character, just as the moon does not abandon its coolness.
For indeed, neither the Omniscient One, nor Śiva, nor even Viṣṇu, despite their power, is able to alter destiny in any other way.
O Rāma, those powers such as traveling through the sky and so forth are born from the inherent nature of substances, time, actions, and the application of mantras.
Just as poisons destroy, honey intoxicates, and the fruits of the *madana* tree cause vomiting when consumed; [so too does this knowledge act].
Likewise, by the power of their intrinsic nature, substances, time, and the sequence of actions— when joined with proper reasoning— swiftly and certainly accomplish the application.
O Raghava, for one who has transcended this [world] and is established in reason,
there is neither agency nor non-agency regarding self-knowledge.
Substances, mantras, rituals, times, and logical methods grant excellent accomplishments;
yet none of these assist at all in attaining the state of the Supreme Self.
Whoever possesses any desire at all can indeed accomplish spiritual success;
however, because of the perfection of self-knowledge, no desire whatsoever arises anywhere.
O sinless one, since the attainment of the Self arises only when the entire web of desires has been stilled, how could a desire— which is the opposite of that state— possibly arise from it?
Whoever has a desire arises, he strives accordingly by means of that desire;
thus he attains it in due time, whether he be wise or even otherwise ignorant.
Vītahavya strove for nothing while desire was not yet born;
once desire had arisen, he strove swiftly, just as a tree springs up from the forest soil.
Thus, the various accomplishments (siddhis), born of time, substances, ritual action, application, and intrinsic nature,
are achieved according to one's desire, having been acquired through successive stages.
O Rāma, those series of fruits known as the spiritual attainments (*siddhi*), which were obtained by someone, were acquired by him from the tree of his own diligent effort.
For the great ones who are eternally contented, who possess that knowledge, whose selves are purified,
and who have reached the end of their desires, the supernatural powers (siddhis) do not provide any assistance.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, this is my doubt: why was that body of Vītahavya not devoured by carnivorous beasts, and why did it not rot upon the surface of the earth?
O Lord, tell me exactly how it was that at that very moment Vītahavya did not immediately attain the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti).
Vasiṣṭha:
O virtuous one, that consciousness which is entwined by the thread of the impurity of latent impressions becomes,
in this world, a partaker in the burning of the states of pleasure and pain.
But that body which remains, consisting solely of pure consciousness from which all latent impressions have been liberated— no one here indeed has the power to sever it.
Listen, O mighty-armed one, to the reasoning by which the body of a yogi cannot be overcome by errors such as being cut or pierced, even over many hundreds of years.
Whenever and upon whatever object the mind falls,
it quickly becomes absorbed in that very thing at that very moment.
For in this way, upon seeing an enemy, the mind undergoes a transformation;
and upon seeing a friend, it spontaneously attains a state of affection.
But when a traveler encounters a tree or a mountain that is devoid of passion and hatred, he experiences for himself a state free from passion and hatred; this is how it is experienced.
One develops greed for what is delicious, feels no desire for what is unpalatable, and experiences a sense of distaste for what is pungent;
this is experienced by oneself.
Whenever and wherever a violent mind falls upon the body of a yogi, which is enriched by the play of equanimous consciousness, it immediately attains equanimity.

Because it is equally liberated from existence, it does not engage in cutting or other such acts; just as a traveler on a road does not engage in village work in a village, which would be useless for him.
Having gone near the body of the yogin, it indeed attains a predatory nature;
whatever occurs there quickly takes on that very form—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, by predatory beasts— tigers, lions, insects, and reptiles—
the body of Vītahavya, as it lay upon the surface of the earth, was not torn apart.
Consciousness exists everywhere, even in wood, clods of earth, stones, and the like; it abides in the form of the universal property of existence, like that of an infant or a mute.
The slender one is seen only as something flickering and floating,
like a reflection in waters, within the subtle bodies (puryaṣṭakas).
O Rāghava, because of that equal perception of earth, water, air, and fire, Vītahavya’s body was not subjected to any transformation.
And hear this further, O Rāma: in the maintenance of the world, vibration is the cause of destruction; and that which arises from the mind or from the vital air is the cause of transformation.
The vitality of the vital breaths arises from their vibration; when that ceases, they become like stones.
Since they remain steady through concentration (*dhāraṇā*), his body is not destroyed.
For one in whom no vibration of the mind exists— whether external or internal, and whether born of wind or otherwise— both transformation and destruction remain far away.
O best among the knowers of reality, within the tranquil vibration that encompasses both the external and internal,
the elements never abandon their established state in the body.
When the vibration of both the mind and the vital breath, which resides within the house of the body, has been completely stilled, the bodily constituents,
their nature now firmly stabilized, attain the immovable steadfastness of Mount Meru.
And so it is observed in the world that when vibration ceases, there is a firm stability; for the wise, just as in the case of pieces of wood, there is an absence of agitation in all their limbs.
Thus, for thousands of years, the bodies of yogins in this world neither decay nor disintegrate, remaining like fragments of indestructible diamond.
At that very moment, listen, did not that Vītahavya,
the knower of reality who had realized what is to be known, attain supreme peace by casting off his body?
For those who have understood what is to be known, who are free from passion, and possess great intelligence— all of them, having severed their fetters, remain independent while abiding in the body.
Likewise, neither past actions nor those of this life,
nor even their latent impressions (vāsanās), are at all capable of restraining that mind.
Therefore, O dear one, the mind of those who know reality, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit,
quickly brings about whatever it contemplates with complete efficacy.
By a chance occurrence like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, through his meeting with Vītahavya,
his life was now recognized and immediately made firm.
But when his creative intuition turned toward the state of being bodiless,
then he became liberated while in the body (videhamukta), established in absolute freedom.
The mind, freed from latent impressions and swiftly attained to liberation, arises as the Self;
whatever it desires comes to pass in an instant, for Maheśvara is composed of all powers.
The Ninety-first Chapter, titled "Instruction on the Contemplation of Attaining Siddhi," [Vasiṣṭha said:]
For when his mind had become almost entirely subsided through investigation,
then the qualities such as loving-kindness arose in this Vitahavya.
[Rāma:

O Sage, O Lord, you have said that when the true nature of the mind has vanished due to the dawning of discernment (*viveka*), qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arise. How can this be so? MU_5,91.2//
O Brahmin, best among speakers, tell me: when the mind has set, to whom do virtues such as loving-kindness belong, or where do they manifest?
Vasiṣṭha: There are two kinds of dissolution of the mind: with form and indeed without form.
That which is with form belongs to one liberated while living; that which is without form arises from one liberated after the body has fallen away.
In this world, the existence of the mind leads to suffering, while the destruction of the mind leads to happiness;
therefore, having brought the existence of the mind to an end, one should achieve the destruction of the mind.
Know that the mind, which is the cause of birth and is pervaded by the dark nets of latent impressions (vāsanā), exists solely for the sake of suffering.
That mind which, ignorant of reality, highly esteems the accumulation of natural qualities as "mine" and is thereby afflicted with suffering, is called the *jīva*.
As long as the mind exists, so long does endless suffering persist;
when the mind has set for a living being, saṃsāra has reached its end.
Know that the mind which exists as suffering, deluded, and constrained by the conviction "I am," is the fresh sprout of the tree of suffering.
Rāma said: O Brahmin, whose mind is lost? Or what would that which is lost be like?
What would its destruction be like, and what would its mode of existence be like?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O scion of Raghu’s lineage, I have described the existence of the mind;
now, O best among those who know how to inquire, hear from me concerning its destruction.
They know the mind of that steadfast person to be "dead" whom the states of pleasure and pain do not dislodge from equanimity, just as breaths do not move the king of mountains.
The thought "this is I" or "this is not I" humbles even the best of men;
they know that the mind of one who has no such [dualistic] end is dead.
O virtuous one, this is the destruction of the mind;
if the mind were thus destroyed, that would be the state of the destruction of the citta, which belongs to the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
O sinless one, know that state of mind to be delusion; when that perishes, then the pure being (sattva) called "the destruction of the mind" fully arises.
O Rāghava, some have given the name "mind" to that playfulness of being, which is the destruction of the mind and the very nature of one liberated while living.
O sinless one, the mind that is endowed with qualities such as loving-kindness possesses the highest latent impression; it is liberated from further rebirth and is liberated while living.
O Rāma, that mind which is pervaded by latent impressions that lead to further birth, yet remains unattached, is called *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living). This is what is known as *sattva*.
Because it has been experienced right now, and because it is endowed with reality through the attainment of existence,
this dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), possessing its own form, belongs to one who is liberated while living.
Loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy remain at all times and in every way within the one liberated while living who has dissolved the mind, like the radiance of the moon.
In the Himalayan mountain named Sattva— the dissolution of the mind of one liberated while living—
the riches of virtues blossom like flower clusters in spring.
But that formless dissolution of the mind, O scion of Raghu, which I have described,
exists only in the state of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), being of an undivided nature.
Even a being endowed with all the foremost virtues dissolves into the stainless, supremely purifying state of disembodied liberation.
In that state of disembodied liberation, which consists of the dissolution of the *sattva* and is called the destruction of the mind (*cittanāśa*), nothing whatsoever exists.
Therein, there are neither virtues nor vices, neither prosperity nor adversity, nor fickleness;
there is neither rising nor setting, nor the perceptions of joy or resentment.
There is neither light nor darkness, nor anything such as twilight, day, or night;
there are not the ten directions, nor space, nor the nature of benefit, nor the nature of harm.
There is no latent impression, no construction, neither effort nor lack of effort here, no passion;
there is neither existence nor non-existence, nor even that middle state—such is the ultimate reality.
It was like the sky, free from darkness by its radiance, with its canopy of clouds,
moon, sun, and rain-bearing clouds, clear as autumn and shining without the dust of twilight.
For those who have reached the further shore of both wisdom and the tumultuous display of saṃsāra,
that vast abode is like the sky for the winds.

In that state dwell the great ones, whose bodies are the expanse of space yet who are bodiless, in whom every fragment of the mind has dissolved; they abide where suffering is utterly stilled, whose nature is non-inert, who sleep in oneness, who are languid with bliss, and who are suns that have dispelled the darkness of *rajas* and *tamas*.
The ninety-second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Mental Discernment," Canto Ninety-Two:
Rāma said:
The tree of the other world is rooted upon the mountain of the treasury of supreme space;
it is variegated with the flowers of stars and has gods and asuras for its birds.
Its blue clouds, with their edges garlanded by lightning, are like sprouts;
its shores shine, delightful in every season and beautiful with the multitude of suns and moons.
It is encircled by seven oceans and ponds, filled with hundreds of rivers,
and it is the sustenance for an infinite variety of fourteen kinds of living beings.
O Brahmin, it belongs to the sprawling vine of worldly existence, which has spread its net and taken root by invading the forest of the universe.
Of this series of sufferings whose fruits are the various forms of suffering such as old age and death—
a series with deeply rooted roots, for which the water of delusion serves as a sprinkling—
What is the seed? And what is said to be the seed of that seed?
Furthermore, what is the seed of that [seed], and what would be the seed of that as well?
O best among speakers, tell me once more in brief all this for the further increase of awakening and for the accomplishment of the essence of gnosis.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, know the body to be the seed of the creeper of worldly existence, in which the great sprouts of good and evil are contained within as a dense internal inception."
With its dense thicket of spreading branches and shimmering with fruits and tender shoots,
this earth has become flourishing through him, like the earth in autumn.
The mind, which follows the dictates of desire, is the seed of this body— the treasury of the states of existence and non-existence, and the casket for the jewels of suffering.
From the mind this entire network of limbs arises—both real and unreal;
likewise, this is experienced by oneself in the delusions of dreams.
Just as a city arises from the conceptualization of a gandharva, so too does a body— resplendent in form and complete with windows— arise from the mind.
Whatever worldly object there is that possesses extension and has come within the range of vision—
that form is an expansion of the mind, just as the state of being a jar and so forth is an expansion of clay.
There are two seeds for the tree of the mind, which bears the creepers of its activities:
one is the movement of the vital breath, and the second is firm mental cultivation.
When the vital breath vibrates, intent upon touching the channels,
then the mind consisting of pure awareness is swiftly produced.
When the vital breath does not vibrate within the hollows of the channels of the veins due to the power of non-perception, the mind is not born within.
This very vibration of the vital breath is perceived through the gateway of the mind;
it has attained the state of the world within the void, just as blueness and other qualities appear to the sight within the sky.
The vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) constitutes masculinity; its cessation is called peace.
Through the vibration of the vital breath, consciousness moves like a ball set in motion.
Consciousness, awakened by the vibration of the vital breath, flashes within bodies like a ball struck by the hands, moving through the limbs with the revolutions of wheels.
The existent, all-pervading consciousness is awakened by the vibration of the vital breath,
assuming a form subtler than the subtlest, like a trace of fragrance carried by the wind.
Know, O Rāghava, that the restraint of consciousness is the supreme good;
it is the cause of equanimity, for no agitation exists therein.
Consciousness, as soon as it arises, quickly moves toward an object of perception with intensity;
from that perception, endless sufferings arise for the mind.
When consciousness, having fallen asleep, remains in a state of non-awakening,
then that stainless state— the goal to be attained— has been attained.
Therefore, if you do not cause consciousness to swell through the vibrations of the vital breaths and the impelling of latent impressions,
then you are unborn.
Know that the mind is the swelling of consciousness;
by it this web of misfortune is spread out, which cuts and destroys the lives of people.
For the sake of pacifying the mind, yogis practice the restraint of the vital breath through breath-control exercises, meditations, and applications devised by skillful means.
The wise know that the restraint of the vital breath bestows the fruit of the tranquility of the mind, is the supreme cause of equanimity, and brings about auspicious well-being of consciousness.
O Raghava, hear now this other [account] regarding the arising of the mind from latent impressions (vāsanā), as it has been revealed and experienced by those possessed of knowledge.
The grasping of an object with firm conviction, having abandoned prior and subsequent deliberation— that is proclaimed as *vāsanā*.
O mighty-armed one, that very state which has been cultivated by oneself through intense spiritual urgency quickly becomes his own, as all other memories vanish.
For such a person, rendered helpless by latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
becomes deluded, thinking that whatever he perceives is a real entity.
Due to the helplessness caused by the onset of latent impressions (vāsanā), one abandons one's true nature;
with faulty vision, one perceives delusion, just as everyone does under the influence of intoxication.
One who possesses incorrect knowledge alone becomes overwhelmed by mental distress,
being brought under control by an internal latent impression, like a fatal cholera infection.
Know that to be the mind, O Rāghava, which is wrong vision, which is the cultivation of the notion of self in what is not-self, and which perceives substantiality in what is unsubstantial.
Due to the cultivation of the notion that objects of firm habitual practice are real,
the extremely flickering mind arises as the cause of birth, old age, and death.
When nothing whatsoever— whether in the form of that which is to be abandoned or that which is to be adopted— is projected,
and one remains having relinquished everything, then the mind is not born.
When the mind does not think at all because it is perpetually free from latent impressions (vāsanā), then the state of no-mind (amanas-tā) arises,
which bestows supreme tranquility.
When nothing whatsoever flashes within consciousness, like a cloud in the sky,
then the mind is not born within, like a lotus in the ether.
When no state of being is cultivated toward any object whatsoever in the world,
then, in the empty sky of the heart, the demon of the mind does not arise.
O Rāghava, I consider this alone to be the nature of the mind:
the conceptualization of an object through passion and attachment.
For one who does not conceive of any perception whatsoever that is capable of being conceptualized,
and who is as pure as the expanse of space, how could the arising of the mind occur?
That which consists in not cultivating anything, that which consists in the cultivation of non-existence,
and that which is the seeing of things as they truly are— that is called "no-mind."
That mind which, having completely renounced everything within, abides in a state of coolness— even while engaged in activity— is declared to be of the nature of non-existence.
When one has no attachment due to the non-appropriation of the flavor within latent impressions (vāsanā), his mind has reached the state of non-mind; that is called a "being" (sattva).
He whose dense latent impressions (vāsanā) no longer cause rebirth is liberated while living; established in the state of pure being (sattva), he remains like the whirling of a potter’s wheel.
Those whose latent impressions (vāsanā) are like parched seeds— devoid of further rebirth and lacking the power to sprout— are indeed known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Having attained minds whose nature is pure being (*sattva*), they have reached the further shore of knowledge;
at the end of the body, they take the form of space and are said to be "mindless" (*acitta*).
O Rāma, there are two seeds of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath and mental impressions.
When one of these two is exhausted, both quickly perish.
For these two are mutual causes for the birth of the mind, O Rāma, just as water and a dense cloud are for the acceptance of water by a plant.
For these two are always inseparable, like the seed and the sprout, and like the sesame seed and its oil; they exist together in a sequence that depends upon time.
But they both produce simultaneously a mental state consisting of consciousness,
just as both the fragrance and the breeze together produce the pleasure of the sense of smell.
When these two arise together with the production of the mind, they are then established as being equal, like a flower and its fragrance, or like sesame seeds and their oil.
The vibration of the vital breath arises from the force of latent impressions, and by that [vibration], latent impressions are produced;
thus occurs the sequence of seed and sprout for the seed of the mind.

Because consciousness is set in motion by the activity of agitation through latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it awakens the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by that means, the mind (*citta*) is born.
Because its nature is vibration, the vital breath vibrates when it touches the cave of the heart;
by awakening consciousness through that, the child-mind is born.

For thus, O sinless one, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) are the causes of the mind; when either of these two is destroyed, there is the destruction of both and of the mind as well.
It has pleasure and pain as its great trunk, the body as its great fruit, the various activities as its budding form, and is entwined by the creepers of conduct and vows.
Enveloped by the black serpent of craving, it is the dwelling place for the cranes of passion and disease;
its root of ignorance is very firm, and the birds of the sense-faculties dwell within it.

Indeed, like a torrent of wind felling a fruit ripened by time, this gale of [right] understanding brings down in an instant the tree of the mind, known as the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā).
It has turned all directions white, veiled all vision, and takes on the form of tossing clouds; it has arisen from the pit of ignorance.
Having reached a mere blade of straw in the form of craving, his body takes the shape of a pillar;
trembling with its slight frame agitated, he is greedy for leaping upward.
O Rāma, one who perceives the great light abiding within dissolves; and by the cessation of the movement of the vital breath, the dust of the mind is instantly extinguished.
It is said that the seed of these two— the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*)— is that which is to be experienced, since from it those two manifest.
In the heart, through the craving for objects of perception, there arises the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) as well as latent impressions (vāsanā);
therefore, the object of perception is said to be the seed of these two.

Through the complete renunciation of the object of experience, the vibration of the vital breath and its latent impressions are swiftly destroyed along with their roots, like two trees when their roots are cut.
O Hero, know that consciousness is the seed of the object of consciousness;
without it, the object of consciousness cannot exist, just as a sesame seed cannot exist without oil.
Nothing whatsoever exists as a separate object of cognition, whether externally or internally;
consciousness itself, throbbing, manifests by its own power as the imagined object of cognition.
Just as one's own death or staying in another land is experienced in a dream,
so too is the experience of consciousness through the application of its own wondrous power.
O descendant of Raghu, that which proceeds from consciousness due to its own volition attains the state of being the web of the world; this is it.
Just as a child might perceive a phantom arisen from its own imagination,
or as one perceives a human being in a tree stump, so too does consciousness perceive [objects].
They know this false knowledge to be dissolved by right knowledge,
just as the state of being a snake in a rope [vanishes] upon seeing it clearly, or as the appearance of two moons [vanishes] through self-inspection.
"Pure consciousness alone is the three worlds; there is nothing else to be perceived"—when such a firm conviction has taken root within, the wise know that to be right knowledge.
Whatever appears to this consciousness, whether previously seen or unseen, that must be diligently cleansed away by one who possesses discernment.
For that very [ignorance], when merely uncleansed, has become the great cycle of existence;
its mere cleansing, however, is designated as liberation.
Consciousness leads to infinite suffering because it is of the nature of birth;
lack of consciousness, being established in non-inertness, leads to happiness because it is of the nature of non-birth.
Become non-inert, with bliss dissolved and sensation abandoned;
O scion of Raghu, you are that very one who is the awakened self, beyond all perception.
Rāma:
O Lord, what kind of being is one who is non-inert yet lacks consciousness?
Furthermore, since that inertness exists in the absence of consciousness, how can it be warded off?
Vasiṣṭha:
He who is established in non-abiding everywhere, yet finds rest nowhere at all;
that living being perceives nothing, for he is indeed consciousness-less and not insentient.

He for whom no objective support consisting of the state of conscious objects exists here is called "unconscious" (asaṃvit), yet he is declared to be non-inert even while performing hundreds of actions.
The space of the heart is not tainted even slightly by that which is to be experienced;
he who possesses this is called the non-inert, the one beyond perception, and the liberated while living.
When nothing at all is cultivated within oneself due to the absence of latent tendencies (nirvāsana),
one remains steadfast, like the consciousness of an infant, a mute, or the like.
Then, O wise one, that which is free from dullness and devoid of [dualistic] perception becomes pervasive and takes refuge [in its own nature], because of which it is no longer stained.
Through the abandonment of all latent impressions by means of non-conceptual meditative absorption,
a pervasive bliss proceeds forth, just as blueness [appears] from the sky.
When the yogin is absorbed therein, his consciousness becomes devoid of objective perception;
because he has become identical with that, even that [consciousness] dissolves within, being without beginning or end.
Whether walking, standing, touching, or even smelling, he is called by that [name]:
non-dull, with bliss dissolved, having abandoned all sensation, and happy.
Grasping this view with a painful and ruined effort,
cross to the further shore of the ocean of suffering— you who are an ocean of boundless virtues.
Just as from a seed a great tree arises and in time pervades the sky,
even so this world of objects of perception has arisen from consciousness through its own volition.
When consciousness, having formed an intention, perceives a body,
then that very consciousness becomes the seed of this web of births.
Having produced itself from itself and deluding itself again and again,
consciousness at the end leads itself to liberation everywhere, O Rāghava.
Whatever this [consciousness] contemplates, that very thing it becomes in an instant;
like an actor, having abandoned its role, it returns after a long time to its own body.
God, nāga, asura, yakṣa, rākṇasa, kinnara, and elephant—
it is her very self that dances within this playful dance of the world.
Just as the silkworm, having bound itself and wept,
eventually attains its solitary state after a long time, so too consciousness, by its own nature, attains its absolute isolation.
The consciousness of the nets of the world-oceans is likewise an abundant water;
having reached the state of mountains and so forth, it vibrates, filling the entire circle of the quarters.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—
these are said to be the waves of this continuous stream of the water of consciousness.
"The entire world is mere consciousness; there is no second conceptualization.
By such right knowledge, consciousness does not become anything else.
When it perceives nothing at all, neither throbbing nor moving,
consciousness comes to rest in its own self and is no longer defiled.
Now, O Rāma, it is said that the seed of this consciousness is pure being alone;
from pure existence alone does this arise, just as luminosity arises from light.
Therein, existence has two forms: one abides in various shapes, while the second is of a single form; hear now this distinction between the two.
The nature of existence (sattā) is described as potness, clothness, thatness, yours-ness, and mine-ness; yet it remains manifold in form through its various divisions.
But having set aside its divisions, existence, which is extended through its nature as a single essence,
is declared to have one form by way of its universal alone.
Having completely abandoned all distinctions, that which is pure existence alone, untainted, uniform, and the great form— that they know to be the supreme state of Being.
Form, by virtue of its manifold shapes, can never exist as something that is not perceived; therefore, this [notion of a universal] is without a real basis.
But that form which is of a single nature, whose essence is the stainlessness of existence,
never undergoes destruction nor does it ever become forgotten.
Whether it be the existence of time, the existence of parts, or this existence of objects—
having abandoned the mental calculation that differentiates them, become intent solely upon pure Being.
Although she is the supreme reality, being the existence of time and the existence of space, free from all conceptualization, nevertheless, she is not ultimately real.
How could that which is seen to be the cause of manifoldness— wherein the calculation of divisions produces divergent opinions— be purifying?
Cultivating only the singular commonality of existence as your sole form,
remain full, supremely blissful, and filling the expanse of all directions.
O Lord of the Wise, that which is the limit of mere universal existence (sattāsāmānya) has itself become the seed-state of this [world]; from that, it proceeds.
That which extends to the limit of universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), being free from conceptual construction (*kalanā*), is the primordial state without beginning or end; for it, no seed exists.
Consciousness dissolves therein and remains changeless;
having attained that state, she does not return again to suffering.
That is the cause of all causes, yet no cause for it is found;
it is the essence of all essences, yet no essence beyond it is found.
Within that expansive mirror of consciousness, all these perceptions of objects are reflected, just as trees on a riverbank are mirrored in a lake.
In that holder of taste, all these entities find their flavor;
they manifest there just as the six tastes do upon the tongue.
Therefore, that is indeed the state of the sky of consciousness, which is even clearer than the clear;
and it is the sufficient savoring of all those things born of its own sweetness.
In that, my dear, the multitude of worlds is born, exists, grows, is perceived, remains stable, and finally dissolves.
That is heavy among the heaviest, that is light among the lightest;
that is gross among the grossest, and that is subtle among the subtlest.
It is the most distant of the distant, yet it is the nearest of the near;
it is the smallest of the small, and it is the greatest even among the great.
O dear one, it is the light even among lights, the darkness even among darknesses;
it is the reality even among realities, and the supreme vision even among visions.
This and that is something and nothing; this and that exists and does not exist;
this and that is visible and invisible; this and that I am, and yet I am not.
O sinless Rāma, act in such a way that you may attain a firm standing in that most purifying state through every possible effort.
That is stainless, that is undecaying; that is the reality of the Self. Upon the realization of that, the mind attains peace.
Having realized the nature of that vast oneness, become one who is liberated from worldly existence, eternally arisen, for all time.
The ninety-third canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Examining the Seed of Saṃsāra," Canto 93.
Rāma:
"These seeds have been proclaimed by you, O giver of honor;
by the application of which one quickly attains that state?"
Vasiṣṭha:
By applying each of those remedies which I have declared for these seeds of suffering, the state [of liberation] is swiftly attained.

If, by means of human effort, one forcibly abandons latent impressions (vāsanās) and [rests] instantly upon that state which stands at the pinnacle of universal existence (sattāsāmānya), //MU_5,93.3//
O knower of reality, you establish a state that is imperishable even for a moment;
at this very moment, you shall fully attain that auspicious state.
Or if, my dear, you establish yourself in the form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya),
then you will attain that state here with only a slight additional effort.
O sinless one, if you abide with realized knowledge in the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva),
then through great and intense effort, you shall attain that supreme state.
O Rāghava, meditation is not possible upon a solitary object of perception,
because this consciousness is always present everywhere.
Whatever you think, whatever you go toward, whatever you stand upon, or whatever you do—
in each and every instance, it is consciousness that abides there, or else it is that very consciousness itself.
If you exert effort in the complete relinquishing of latent impressions (vāsanā),
then all mental and physical afflictions will instantly become weakened for you.
For this abandonment of latent impressions is considered more difficult than all previous efforts; indeed, it is harder to achieve than even uprooting Mount Sumeru.
As long as the mind has not dissolved, so long is there no destruction of latent impressions.
Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—
having become mutual causes for one another, these remain difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, O Rāghava, having abandoned the desire for enjoyment from afar, one should with effort and discernment take refuge in this triad through human exertion.
All these [factors] are equal; as long as they have not been repeatedly practiced again and again, the attainment of the state does not occur even in hundreds of aeons.

O Mahāmati, for the Sage who has practiced for a long time, the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the destruction of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the dissolution of the mind (*manas*) become fruit-bearing simultaneously.
Even if these are practiced individually for a long time,
they do not bestow accomplishment, just like mantras that have been broken.
Even though these have been practiced for a long time and even though they are wise, they are not able to attain the Supreme One individually, like soldiers [acting alone].
For when these are brought into balanced exertion by the wise man,
they cut down the enemy that is saṃsāra from its very roots, like soldiers.

The exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the dissolution of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the destruction of the mind (*manas*) must be cultivated with effort and for a long time; by doing so, my dear, you shall not suffer.
When these three are practiced for a long time, the firm knots of the heart are severed without remainder, just as fibers are cut from a lotus stalk.
O Rāma, this state of worldly existence has been practiced through hundreds of previous births;
it is never extinguished except through the practice of long-term cultivation.
Whether walking, hearing, touching, smelling, standing, waking, or sleeping,
always practice these three for the sake of your supreme welfare.
The wise who know reality understand that the restraint of the vital breaths is equal to the complete abandonment of latent impressions; therefore, one should practice that in this very manner.
Through the complete abandonment of latent impressions, the mind attains the state of non-mind;
through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, do as you wish.

Through firm practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the guru, and through the yoga of postures and their mastery, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspanda) is restrained.
Through the play of right knowledge and through lack of attachment to the objects of the world,
because of seeing things as they truly are, latent tendencies do not arise.
That stable form which is non-contradictory regarding things at their beginning and end— by seeing that, knowledge arises and through it, latent predispositions are exhausted.
Because one conducts oneself without attachment, because one has abandoned the cultivation of worldly existence,
and because one perceives the destruction of the body, latent tendencies do not arise.
Just as dust in the expanse of the sky ceases when the movement of the wind has subsided,
so too the mind does not arise when the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has perished.
For that which is the vibration of the vital breath is indeed the vibration of the mind;
from that, the worlds are born like dust from refuse.
The wise person should exert great effort to conquer the vibration of the vital breath,
sitting again and again with a one-pointed mind, repeatedly.
Or, if you prefer this very method of mental conquest, setting aside the sequential path, then you shall attain that state after a long time.
O blameless one, it is not possible to conquer the mind without a method,
just as it is impossible to subdue a wild, intoxicated elephant without a goad.
The attainment of inner knowledge, association with the virtuous,
the complete relinquishing of latent impressions, and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath;
These, indeed, are the well-nourished methods for the conquest of the mind,
by which it is swiftly subdued, just as the dust of the earth is settled by showers of rain.
Those who, despite these existing methods, attempt to restrain the mind by force,
are like those who cast away a lamp and try to destroy the darkness with eye-salves.
Those deluded ones who strive to achieve mastery over the mind through forceful effort bind the intoxicated king of elephants with lotus fibers.
Those who, having abandoned the method of yoga, purify their own bodies— which have long remained in a state of mental dullness— know them to be destroyed.
From fear they go to further fear; from affliction they proceed to further affliction.
Like wretched beings, they do not attain final peace.
For a long time, those possessed by hundreds of mental anxieties waste away their lives through delusions regarding sacred sites, austerities, charity, sacrifices, and the worship of gods, like deer.
Subsisting on fruits and sprouts, they wander among the mountain peaks like wretched deer— timid and possessed of most simple minds.
Her delicate-limbed mind, with its limbs lacerated and shattered,
finds no confidence anywhere, like a doe that has entered a village.
Their minds, tossed by violent waves and carried away by the force of delusion,
are swept far along, falling like grass in mountain torrents.
By the power of fate, at some time or other, those who are smeared by the conditions of suffering and defects may, to a small extent, know or not know the reality of the self.
Constantly coming and going through hells, heavens, and human realms,
beings are tossed up and down like balls.
From there they go to hell, and from there to heaven, or even right here;
they revolve through cycles of rebirth like ripples upon a river.
Therefore, O descendant of Raghu, having abandoned these false views and relying upon pure consciousness, remain steadfast, free from passion.
Only the wise man possesses happiness; only the wise man truly lives;
only the wise man is strong. Therefore, become one who consists of wisdom.

O Great-souled One, perceiving the single, supreme, primordial state of pure consciousness which is devoid of all that is to be perceived, remain within your own heart free from conceptualization; and while performing actions, attain the state of the non-doer, endowed with a glory that has never arisen before.
The ninety-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Sequence for Eliminating the Seed of Saṃsāra," by Vasiṣṭha.
He by whom even a slight restraint of his own mind has been achieved through even a moment of reflection has attained the fruit of birth.
In those whose hearts the delicate spark of inquiry vibrates,
that very spark, through the practice of yoga, comes to branch out in a hundred directions.
But when a man possesses somewhat mature discernment and is preceded by dispassion,
the bright qualities resort to him, just as birds flock to a full lake.
Even vast manifestations of ignorance do not greatly affect the wise person who investigates correctly and perceives things as they truly are.
What do sense objects, as well as mental fluctuations, anxieties, or even physical ailments, do here to one whose mind is firmly established in right vision?
The Puṣkarāvarta clouds, filled with winds that blow in all directions and reddish-brown with lightning,
were seized by his hands as if they were handfuls of a net.
"O charming girl, where is the moon situated in the midst of the sky? It has been placed by you, O lovely woman, inside this jewel-casket, mistaking it for a beautiful blue lotus."
Where are those elephants, their heads crowned with lotuses and swarms of bees rising from the straw mats, now tormented by gnats as sweet as the breath of lovely women?
Lions, enraged in the heat of battle, had their rows of claws flashing as they struck elephants' pearls; yet they were torn apart by deer.
Where are those agitated pythons, whose breaths— blazing with poison— once scorched the towering forest trees, yet who, now famished, have been swallowed whole by young frogs?

How could a steadfast man who has attained the stages, who knows what is to be known, and who possesses discernment, be overcome—so they say—by the bandits of the sense objects and the senses? He is, indeed, courageous.
The enemies that are the sense-objects carry away the immature intellect,
just as fierce winds blow away a tender creeper whose stem has been severed.

Mental anxieties are not able to shatter one who is matured by the power of discernment, just as gentle breezes cannot move a steadfast mountain that withstands the turbulence of the cosmic dissolution.

The whirlwind of anxiety cannot shake one who is firmly established in a stable state, whose mind is like a tree of flowers of discernment that has not yet taken root in the expanse of worldly existence.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
he whose mind is not intent on discernment is said to be dead.
One should constantly and gradually investigate with the vision of the inner self, either by oneself or together with virtuous people, "What might this world be? What might I be? MU 5.94.16.
By means of swift investigation beyond darkness, the supreme state is seen,
like a stainless jewel by a radiant lamp.
Through knowledge, the destruction of all sufferings arises,
just as darkness is dispelled by the sun through the play of its light.
When knowledge has become manifest, the object of knowledge arises by itself sufficiently,
just as pure light appears on the earth when the sun has risen.
That investigation of the scriptures by which the reality of Brahman is awakened is called knowledge; it stands as if non-different from the object of knowledge.
The wise know that reflection upon the inner sciences is the limb of knowledge;
its object of knowledge exists within itself, just as sweetness exists within milk.
A person, consisting of the knowable itself, becomes filled with the light of right knowledge,
just as one who has drunk *maireya* liquor becomes filled with the bliss of intoxication.
The wise know the supreme Brahman to be stainless, whose nature is both being and non-being;
by the mere attainment of knowledge, it becomes manifest of itself.
Possessing knowledge and with joy arisen, he does not sink anywhere;
liberated while living, free from attachment, he remains as the sovereign Self alone.
The wise man finds delight in pleasant sounds such as those of the lute and the flute, in the amorous songs of a beloved woman, and in her cooing during sexual union.
And amidst the humming of bees intoxicated by the springtime's passion,
and amidst the thundering of clouds nourished by the onset of the rainy season;
Amidst peacocks with their crests dancing wildly and uttering soft cries,
and amidst the rustling of clusters of lotuses and the warbling of cranes;

Amidst the sounds of hand-drums and other instruments ending with the *karatāla*, and amidst the deep tones of the *muraja* drums, as well as the sounds of various stringed, percussion, and wind instruments; //MU_5,94.28//
O Rāma, he does not fix his attachment to harsh sounds nor to sweet ones, nor to clamorous noises, just as the moon does not cling to lotuses.
The wise man [finds no delight] in the hands of young plantain-tree shoots,
nor in the dwellings of sandalwood, agallochum, and mandāra creeper clusters.

Upon the hips, breasts, and arms— which possess the luster of molten gold and serve as the ground for silken garments, pearl necklaces, jasmine, the moon, and white and blue lotuses— [the dust settled].

Upon her thighs, which shone like golden archways at the abode of the Bodiless One (Kāma), and which were the source of joyful dalliance for the vine-like limbs of the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas; //MU_5,94.32//
O Rāma, the wise man, whose intellect is unattached even to things within his own power, does not bind himself to the pleasure of touch, just as a swan finds no delight in the desert sands.
One who possesses knowledge [discerns] among dates, *piṇḍakharjūra*, *kadamba*, *panasa*, and so forth;
among grapes, *ikṣvāruka*, *kākṣoṭa*, lotus-stalks, *jambīra*, and *jāti* flowers.
In wines such as madirā, madhu, maireya, and mārdvīka, as well as in liquors made from molasses;
and in curd, milk, ghee, inspissated milk (āmikṣā), fresh butter, and boiled rice.
Among the six diverse flavors— whether in things to be licked or drunk, in luxuries, or even in fruits, grains, roots, vegetables, and meats— [he remains indifferent].
With his form satisfied and his intellect unattached,
the Brahmin does not bind himself to the pleasure of tasting [sensual objects], just as one would not to the scraps of meat on a dog's body.
The wise one [resides] among Yama, Candra, Indra, Rudra, Viṣṇu, the Lotus-born (Brahmā), and others,
as well as upon the peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Sahya, and Dardura.
Upon nets of silken leaves, upon fruits such as the lunar orb,
and within groves of wish-fulfilling trees where goddesses sport upon swings;
Upon walls of precious gold and those made of jewels and pearls,
and upon the vine-like limbs of Tilottamā, Urvaśī, Rambhā, and Menakā;
The illustrious one, whose intellect is unattached, does not desire to see anyone; with a perfectly fulfilled mind, he remains silent and self-respecting, like a weak man in the presence of enemies.
The wise man [discerns] among the kunda, mandāra, kalhāra, and kumuda flowers;
and among the kamala, utpala, punnāga, ketaka, aguru, and jāti.
Upon the *kadamba*, mango, citron, *kiṃśuka*, and *aśoka* trees;
and upon the *japā*, *atimukta*, *sauvīra*, neem, and *pāṭala* garlands.
And among sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and musk; and among saffron, water-lily, clove, cardamom, kakkola, tagara, and so forth.
With a single-minded focus on the delight in fragrance, he does not become attached to any particular scent;
possessing equanimity and remaining unshaken, he is like a bird amidst the various odors of honey.
He is not disturbed even in the slightest by the gurgling roar in the ocean, the sound of echoes in the mountains, or the roars of the lions, the kings of beasts.
He does not tremble in the slightest, even amidst the trumpeting of rutting elephants, the writhing of vetālas, or the shrieks of piśācas and yakṣas.
He does not tremble from the roar of thunderclaps, the sound of crashing mountains, or the trumpeting of Airāvaṇa, because he is absorbed in meditative concentration.
Though subjected to the friction of a whirling saw, the slicing of a sharp sword,
and the falling of a thunderbolt from a rock, it does not tremble in its essential nature.
He finds neither joy in the grove nor does he experience weariness;
he experiences neither weariness in the deserts nor does he find joy there.
Among enemies and kinsmen alike— who are like heaps of glowing embers amidst scanty sand—
and upon soft, grassy grounds covered with scattered flowers;
Upon beds of sharp razor-edges and fresh blue lotuses,
upon the heights of lofty mountains and within the depths of well-pits;
Upon sun-heated rocks and upon soft women;
amidst prosperity and fierce calamities; and in deaths as well as in festivals.
Even while dwelling [in the world], he experiences neither agitation nor joy;
