with his mind eternally inwardly liberated, he remains perfectly equanimous.
In the wilderness regions of hell, where bodies are pierced by iron spikes,
and where endless showers of spears and lances are hurled at one another;
He fears nothing, nor does he succumb to helplessness or dejection;
equanimous, with a healthy mind, silent and steadfast, he stands like a mountain.
Even that which is impure, unwholesome, or even poison, mud, and artificial poison, he digests quickly after eating; and what is moist or decomposed, he consumes as if it were delicious food.
One whose intellect is unattached and who knows the reality remains equanimous toward the tasting of the paste of nimba and prativiṣā, milk, sugarcane juice, water, or food.
He is neither delighted nor provoked by liquor, wine, milk, blood, fat, oil, spirits, husks, bones, grass, hair, or food.
He looks upon even the slayer of his life and the giver with an equal gaze, one endowed with serenity and sweetness.
Toward stable or unstable bodies, and toward objects that are beautiful or unattractive,
he neither rejoices nor desponds, being always kindled by equanimity.
Because of his renunciation of attachment to the world's existence, because of its ungraspable nature,
because he has surely realized all that is to be known, and because of the passionlessness of his own mind.
The virtuous person, with a mind freed from the sense of ownership, does not grant any scope for the activity of any sense organ toward any object whatsoever.
Swallowing quickly the senses— which do not know reality, which find no rest, which have not attained their true self, and which are unstable— just as deer swallow a sprout.
Being carried away in the ocean of existence, tossed by the waves of latent impressions, and crying out "Alas! Alas! in utter distress, it is swallowed by the crocodiles of the sense organs.
For one whose mind has found rest in the Self through inquiry and has attained its firm footing,
the floods of conceptual constructions cannot carry it away, just as torrents of water cannot sweep away a mountain.
For those who have come to rest in the supreme state at the limit of all conceptual constructions,
and who have realized their true nature, even Mount Meru is regarded as a mere blade of grass.
The world is like a withered blade of grass, and poison is indeed nectar;
for those whose minds are expanded, a single moment and a thousand eons are equal.
Realizing that the world is nothing but pure consciousness, those of joyful intellect dwell with their minds filled with joy,
for they perceive the entire universe as existing within themselves due to its being composed of consciousness.
Within this cage of worldly objects, which is but the vibration of pure consciousness,
what is there to be rejected and what to be accepted for the sage who knows reality?
All this is indeed consciousness alone; abandon other delusions, O sinless one.
You whose expansive body consists of consciousness—what do you abandon, and what do you strive for?
That which arises from the earth as a future, delicate sprout is nothing but consciousness manifesting in that way; there is no such thing as a sprout.
That which does not exist in the beginning or at the end, even if it is seen to have existence for some brief moment in the present— that existence of consciousness is an illusion.
Thinking thus, abandon the intellect that follows after existence and non-existence;
having reached the end of all becoming, become one whose form is the light of unattached consciousness.
Whether performing action with the body, mind, intellect, or even with the senses alone,
you are not tainted, being free from attachment whether acting or not acting.
O mighty-armed one, even while acting with a mind free from attachment, you are not stained by pleasures and pains, as if they were merely the states of a mental wish.
One whose mind is free from attachment, even while performing actions with the limbs of the body, is not tainted by pleasures or pains, as if they were mere fragments of a mental fantasy.
One whose mind is free from attachment does not see even while looking with the eyes;
this is experienced even by a child because the mind is fixed elsewhere.
The mind of a living being, when free from attachment, does not see even while seeing;
it does not hear even while hearing, nor does it touch even while touching.
Even while smelling, he does not smell; even while opening his eyes, he does not open them;
he does not fall at all upon an object, nor is he overcome even when forcibly cast down.
This is experienced even by those of immature intellect— by fools, indeed— even when their minds are fixed on another country while they themselves remain in their own home.
Attachment is the cause of worldly objects; attachment is the cause of saṃsāra.
Attachment is the cause of hopes; attachment is the cause of calamities.
They know that liberation is the renunciation of attachment; from the renunciation of attachment comes freedom from rebirth.
O sinless one, by completely abandoning attachment to all things, you shall become liberated while living.
Rāma:
O Sage, you who are like an autumnal wind that dispels the mist of all doubts, tell me briefly, O Lord: what is meant by "attachment"? MU 5.94.84.
Vasiṣṭha:
That impure latent impression (*vāsanā*) which, through the presence or absence of objects, produces the fluctuations of joy and resentment, is called attachment (*saṅga*).
For those whose bodies are liberated while living, their latent impression (vāsanā) becomes pure, free from joy and sorrow, and brings about the state of no further rebirth.
Know that to be called "non-attachment," which persists as long as the body exists;
whatever action is performed by means of it leads only to bondage.
Having thus abandoned such attachment that causes the distortion of one's own limbs,
if you remain unperturbed even while acting, then you have truly mastered it.
If you do not undergo any change of state due to the fluctuations of joy and resentment,
then, O Rāghava, being free from passion, fear, and anger, you are unattached.
O sinless one, having taken hold of that steady state of liberation while living— which is unattached and effortless— you have become equanimous, self-abiding, and free from passion.
With a mind liberated while living, silent, having restrained the grasp of the senses,
free from pride, intoxication, and envy, the noble one remains free from the fever of passion.
For although his disposition is always equal toward the entire range of things,
this one of undaunted being performs nothing else whatsoever than that which arises spontaneously from mere activity established in its proper sequence.
Whatever task belongs to him that is to be done according to the established order of nature, he performs that very thing;
remaining free from attachment and worldly ties, he takes delight with an untiring mind within.

Whether encountering misfortune or great prosperity, the one of great intelligence does not abandon his own natural disposition, even when tossed by a gentle breeze, just as the great ocean of milk does not lose its whiteness.
Having attained either universal sovereignty or calamity, or the state of a crawling creature or the lordship of the gods,
he remains without the arising of distress and with joy extinguished, uniform in nature amidst both decline and prosperity, like the moon.
With all agitation cast aside and all sense of duality discarded, with your various fruitless and trivial activities stilled,
you of undaunted spirit should investigate the Self, so that you may become established in the highest goal of life.
Thus, with a mind purified by the play of the expansion [of consciousness] as it has arisen, behold the stainless state free from fever;
so that, having attained the vision of the Self, you are no longer bound here by the fetters of rebirth through your enlightened intellect.
The chapter titled "The Further Giving of Instruction" is completed.
Chapter Six: Peace. Chapter: Nirvāṇa.
Immediately after the section on tranquility, listen to this section on nirvana, which, when understood, brings about liberation.
Vālmīki:
While the leader of sages was speaking such unrestrained words, and while the prince remained silent, his sole delight being in listening; MU_6,1.2.
While the assembly of kings remained motionless, as if depicted in a painting, their minds fixed on the meaning of the Sage’s words and all other activities ceased.
While the assembly of sages, with their eyebrows quivering and their fingers twitching, respectfully deliberated upon the meaning of Vasiṣṭha’s words, [the king remained silent].
When the group of matrons, their eyes like bees blossoming with the joy of a wondrous gaze, had become like clusters of flowers upon the tree of their uplifted necks; ||| MU_6,1.5 |||
When the sun was situated in the fourth part of the day in the sky, and having become gentle through the acquisition of scriptural knowledge, had attained a slight degree of tranquility; MU_6.1.6.
While the wind, bestowing the sweet fragrance of the Mandāra flowers, remained silent, its expansive movement completely stilled as if merely to listen.
While the swarms of bees slept upon the flower-garlands out of intoxication,
they were surely like those possessed of right meditation, having realized that which is to be known.
Likewise, within the lattices, pearl necklaces, and on the surfaces of mirrors,
everything shines without vibration, as if standing still to listen to the heat.
When the rays had entered deep within the houses through the windows,
they became cool, as if seeking rest after their long journey through the sky.
The sunlight, its own body having subsided as it were, with its self dusted by the ashes of the mass of light from the lattice of pearls, seems to proclaim tranquility.
In the lotuses of his hands and on the crests of the mountains,
[the waters] dried up due to the evaporation of their essence, as if in minds deprived of their livelihood.
While children, ignorant folk, and pet birds were crying out incessantly for food, obstructing the group of young women.
When the pollen from the flowers had settled completely upon the fly-whisks—which were like eyelashes—and was stirred by the wind arising from the wings of wandering bees; MU_6.1.14.
As if out of fear of the web of shadows arising from grasping at the foremost rays,
they flew up through the windows and other openings and entered the interior of the house.
There arose a sound of kettledrums, small drums, and conchs that filled the quarters of the sky, intent on announcing the presence of the fourth part of the day.
By that, his voice, though loud, quickly vanished,
like the cry of a peacock at the roar of a thundercloud.
The row of birds staying in their cage was agitated,
like a forest line with shimmering *tāla* leaves during an earthquake that disturbs the flocks of birds.
Terrified by fear, the children fled into the hollows between their nurses' breasts,
crying out like clouds in the rainy season rushing toward the deep cavities of lofty mountain peaks.
Swarms of bees flew out from the crest-ornaments of the kings,
like droplets of water from rivers with stony, jagged currents.
Thus, while that house of the son of Daśaratha was then thrown into agitation,
the sound of the conch gradually subsided as the designated day for the elder’s passing arrived.
Withdrawing his discourse on the subject at hand, that tiger among sages spoke in sweet verse to the scion of Raghu in the midst of the assembly.
[Vasiṣṭha:
O sinless descendant of Raghu, this web of words has been spread out by me;
having bound the bird of the mind with it, take hold of it and lead it to the state of the Self.
Have you grasped the meaning of my words in this way—
having abandoned what is difficult to understand, like a swan extracting milk from water?
Having reflected upon this in its entirety again and again by means of your own intellect,
O virtuous one, you must now proceed along this very path.
O Rāma, by sporting with this very wisdom you will not be bound;
otherwise, you would quickly fall downward, like an elephant into the pit of the Vindhya mountains.
O Rāma, if you do not act upon my words which have been well-grasped by your intellect,
then you will fall into a pit like a traveler at night who has abandoned his lamp.
"Conventional usage, as it has been attained, functions without attachment for its own establishment"— taking up this very established doctrine of the scriptures, may you be successful.
"O members of the assembly, O Great King, O Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and you rulers of the earth—
all of you, for now, attend to your daily duties."
Let them do so, for this day has mostly reached its conclusion;
we shall deliberate on what remains once we have returned in the morning.
Vālmīki:
When that sage had spoken thus, the entire assembly then rose up,
their lotus-like faces blossoming like a blooming lotus pond.
The kings, having praised the king, performed their salutations to Rāghava,
and after honoring Vasiṣṭha, they departed for their own dwellings.
Accompanied by Viśvāmitra, the illustrious Vasiṣṭha rose from his seat to go to the hermitage, having paid homage to the sky-dwellers.
Kings beginning with Daśaratha and likewise sages followed that sage for a long time, attending upon him as was appropriate for each.
Having taken their leave, some went to the sky, some to the interior of the forest,
and some to Rājagṛha— those virtuous ones, like bees rising from a lotus.
Having offered a pure handful of flowers at the feet of Vasiṣṭha,
the king, followed by the citizens, entered his inner apartments.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, having arrived at their guru’s hermitage,
devotedly worshipped his feet and then returned to the royal palace.
Having reached their respective dwellings, all those listeners quickly bathed and offered worship to the gods, the brahmins, and likewise to the ancestors.
And in due order, together with their retinues beginning with the Brahmins and ending with the servants, they partook of the food appropriate to the sequence of the duties of their respective castes.
When the sun had set along with the activities of the day,
and the moon-maker had arrived together with the activities of the night.
The kings of sages who roam the earth, as well as princes and great seers, were seated upon couches, silken beds, and thrones.
With single-minded attention and reverence, they reflected exactly as instructed upon the means for crossing over saṃsāra, as proclaimed in the words of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, after only a single watch of the night, with their faces sealed in sleep,
they went to that beautiful woman of their dreams, like lotuses seeking the day.
For three watches of the night, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa,
and Śatrughna contemplated that unimpaired instruction of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, for half a watch, with their eyes closed,
they fell into that sleep which dispels fatigue in an instant— the sleep of dreams.
Thus, for those of pure mind who possessed discernment and whose intentions were elevated by having attained the essence [of the teachings], the night then reached its end;
the three watches passed away, and the moon, like a face, assumed a darkened aspect.
The Second Sarga, titled "Description of the Day's Activities," by Vālmīki.
Then, with her moon-like face dejected and the veil of dense darkness agitated,
the dark night appeared like a latent impression (vāsanā) being worn away by discernment (viveka).
In the east, appearing as if destroyed by the light, and in the western mountain,
the cluster of stars assumed the luster of *śephālikā* flowers used as ear-ornaments.
Drawing in droplets of dew, having touched the orb of the moon,
and eager to swallow the moonlight, the morning breeze blew.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, having risen together with their attendants and performed their salutations to the twilight, went to the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
There, having first offered a continuous stream of arghya water, they paid homage at the feet of the sage who had performed his twilight devotions and emerged from the fire-sanctuary.
In an instant, that palace, which had been silent with sages, brahmins, and kings, as well as elephants,
horses, chariots, and vehicles, became densely crowded in a moment.
Then that tiger among sages, followed by Rāma and the others, went with that very army to the house of Daśaratha at dawn.
There, the king, who had already performed his morning devotions, went forward a long distance and honored him with great respect.
Having entered the assembly hall, which was further adorned with multitudes of flowers, pearls, and gems, they all took their seats upon the thrones and other furnishings.
Then, at that very moment, all those listeners from the previous day— both those who move through the sky and those who move upon the earth— arrived together.
Having entered that assembly, which was pleasant and characterized by mutual greetings,
it shone with its perfectly even expanse like a lotus pond when the wind has subsided.
When those brahmin-sages, royal seers, and great munis had quickly settled according to their respective places, at ease and in accordance with the suitability of that region, [the Lord spoke].
When the soft sound of "welcome" had gradually subsided,
and the bards seated in the corners of the assembly hall had become silent, [he spoke].
As if hurriedly arisen to hear [the news], as if having arrived quickly,
and as if born from the windows, the rays of the sun entered [the palace].
The tinkling sound of the pearl necklace, produced by the force of the listener's hand as it quickly enters [the chest], subsides like the sacred syllable *oṃ*.
He was like Kumāra to Śaṅkara, like Kaca to Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, like Prahlāda to Śukra, and like Suparṇa to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Rāma slowly cast his wandering gaze upon the face of Vasiṣṭha,
as the wind casts a bee toward a full-blown lotus in the sky.
Then the sage, skilled in speech, spoke in due order to the descendant of Raghu— who was himself an expert in the meaning of words— using those very same words that had been left unsaid.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Do you remember, O delighter of the Raghus, the words spoken by me yesterday, which were of exceedingly profound meaning and which reveal the ultimate truth?
Now, O crusher of enemies, listen to this other matter being spoken by me for the sake of awakening and for the attainment of eternal perfection.
Through the power of the practice of dispassion and likewise through the vision of reality, one crosses over from saṃsāra; therefore, apply yourself to the practice of those very things.
When difficult-to-understand [objects] have come to an end through the correct awakening to reality,
and when the immersion in latent impressions has dissolved, one attains the sorrowless state.
Unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, and transcending both ends of the unseen (the seen and the unseen),
the one Brahman alone exists as the world, having come, as it were, to a state of duality.
Where Brahman alone exists, unconditioned by any entities,
peaceful and appearing as an absolute equality— how could anything else exist there?
Thinking thus, having internally abandoned the notion of "I," you, the great one whose body is liberated,
uniform, with a tranquil self, silent, and absorbed in your own Self— become so.
There is no mind, nor ignorance, nor the intellect, nor the individual soul;
these conceptual constructions, O Rāma, are created by Brahman alone.
Whatever prosperities, whatever perceptions, whatever thoughts, and whatever desires there may be—all that is indeed Brahman, without beginning or end; here, nothing exists that is not Brahman.

Whatever is seen—from the netherworld, the earth, and heaven, down to the three-eyed Lord Śiva and up to a blade of grass—that is indeed the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness; for there is nothing else at all.
Relatives, wealth, and the body—these must be disregarded, abandoned, or accepted as circumstances;
yet Brahman alone, devoid of beginning and end, expands like the ocean.
As long as there is the calculation of ignorance, as long as there is the latent impression of non-Brahman,
and as long as there is attachment to the web of the world, so long does the conceptualization of the mind and its derivatives persist.
As long as there is the sense of "I" in the body, as long as there is the notion of "self" in this visible world,
and as long as there is the attachment that "this is mine," so long does the delusion of the mind and its derivatives persist.
As long as the height [of the mind] has not been raised by association with the virtuous,
and as long as folly has not been completely exhausted, so long will there remain the downward inclination toward the mind and its objects.
As long as this world-creator has not reached a state of looseness through the power of right vision, so long does the arising of the mind remain manifest.

As long as there is ignorance, blindness, lack of self-mastery through longing for sense objects, and the intensification of fainting and delusion, so long does the conceptualization of the mind and its derivatives persist.
As long as the fragrance of the serpent of hope vibrates within the forest of the heart,
the cakora bird of discernment does not enter there at all.
For one whose mind has no attachment to enjoyments, who is cooled by pure bliss,
and whose web of bonds of hope has been severed, the delusion of the mind perishes.
For that man who has abandoned craving and delusion, whose consciousness is eternally cool,
whose mind is perfectly stilled, and who is awakened— where can there be a ground for the mind?
For one who perceives his own body as something unfamiliar, unsubstantial, and unreal—as if it were standing at a distance—how can there be a world of the mind? MU 6.2.38.
For one whose self has become the nature of infinite consciousness through the transformation of form and formlessness,
and for whom the world is dissolved within the parts of his own limbs, the delusion regarding the individual soul and so forth is stilled.
When false vision has been stilled—its nature being a mass of erroneous delusions—and the supreme sun, the vision of ultimate reality alone, has arisen; MU 6.2.40.
Know that the mind has dissolved like a drop of ghee in fire, burnt away like a withered leaf so as never to be seen again.
The path of the mind belonging to those great-souled ones who are liberated while living and who perceive the higher and the lower is called *sattva*.
In the bodies of those liberated while living, the latent impression that engages in worldly activity no longer exists under the name of "mind," for it has reached the state of pure being (sattva).
For those who know reality are mindless and always established in the state of pure being;
they wander here at their ease, with the effortless play of abiding in pure being.

Though engaged in worldly affairs, those who are peaceful, established in being, and have their senses restrained, constantly behold the light of consciousness; for them there is neither duality nor unity, nor any latent impressions.
For one who, through inward-turned awareness, offers the entire three worlds like blades of grass into the fire of consciousness,
those with cool dispositions continue to act within as if they were fools.
The mind purified by discernment is called *sattva*;
it no longer bears fruit in delusion, like a burnt seed that cannot sprout.
That latent impression (vāsanā) within the deluded interior which is subject to rebirth is designated by the word "mind" (citta); it ceases through awakening.
O Rāma, you have attained what was to be attained; having reached the state of pure being, your mind—consumed by the fire of knowledge—shall not sprout again.
A wound pierced by an arrow, or likewise by an axe or fire, heals;
but the mind, once clearly awakened and consumed by the fire of knowledge, does not [heal].
For the world is indeed the expansion of Brahman, and the world exists through the expansion of Brahman;
thus, there is no difference here between these two—the world and Brahman, who is a mass of consciousness.
The three worlds exist within consciousness, just as bitterness exists within a mirage;
therefore, consciousness and the world are not distinct, and thus existence and non-existence are vainly imagined.
Since you are not composed of consciousness, you are not the self; why then do you weep?
Since the worlds are not composed of consciousness, how can there be mental constructions in their absence?
If you are composed of consciousness, then investigate that entire nature of consciousness:
since it is pure being, without beginning or end, my dear, how could there be any conceptual constructions therein?
You are the conscious self, you are partless, and you are devoid of near and far shores;
remember your own expansive form, and do not become limited by forgetfulness.
Having attained that own-being, you are everything or nothing at all, the source of the arising of existence;
you are of such a nature, you are peaceful, you are consciousness, you are the form of Brahman.
You are indeed the belly of the sword; you are not, nor are you not-not;
you are below. Whatever you are, that you are; yet you are not even that. You are being, you are non-being, and you are self-luminous.
That specific entity which is within you is neither you nor another; it does not exist apart from you.
You are that, yet you are not that, O you whose nature is a mass of pure consciousness! Homage be to you!
You, whose body is the dense mass of consciousness, swelling within the vast expanse of a stone-like interior devoid of beginning or end, are as pure as the sky;
established in your own nature, free from decay, you abide with the playful grace of the bud of a fresh sprout within the ocean of the entire universe—victory to you!
The third canto, named "The Consolidation of Rest," by Vasiṣṭha.
O sinless one, you are that consciousness which, like a mass of water containing within it a multitude of future waves, carries along infinite worlds.
O Self of Consciousness, liberated through contemplation and devoid of both existence and non-existence, tell me: where indeed could impressions and the like remain?
This living soul shines forth by itself as "this" through latent impressions;
tell me, what relevance can there be here for the meaning of another's speech? MU 6.3.3.
O ocean of consciousness, whose nature is great, tremulous, profound, and radiant—you are named Rāma; you are motionless, equanimous, and as gentle as the moon.
Just as heat is not distinct from fire, fragrance from the lotus, blackness from soot, whiteness from snow, and sweetness from sugarcane; ||| MU_6,3.5 |||
Just as light arises from the luminous part of the sun, so does experience arise from consciousness;
O friend, just as waves arise from water, so does the world arise from the nature of consciousness, which is the self of pure awareness.
Experience is not different from consciousness, nor am I different from experience;
the individual soul (jīva) is not different from me, and the mind is not different from the individual soul.
The sense organ is not distinct from the mind, nor is the body separate from the sense organ;
the world is not distinct from the body, for there is indeed nothing other than the world.
Thus, this great wheel appears as if it has been set in motion for a long time;
yet nothing at all has been set in motion, neither swiftly nor for a long duration.
This is not manifold; indeed, everything is the one undivided whole.
It exists as space within space, neither in anything nor as anything at all.
In the void, the void is fully expanded; Brahman is magnified within Brahman. Truth unfolds within truth; the full resides within the full.
Even while performing the acts of seeing forms, attending to light, and mental attention, the wise one does nothing at all; for agency exists only with respect to that which is to be appropriated.
Whatever is grasped with the thought that it is to be accepted leads either to suffering or to pleasure;
but that which is not to be accepted through notions of existence or non-existence is a non-agent regarding pleasure and pain.
Just as space is neither manifold nor non-manifold, and as a mass of water is like water within space,
so too is the sequence of the self and the world essentially empty, even while possessing its own meaningful function.
Pure within like the inner sky, and proficient in right conduct externally,
he remains as steady as a piece of wood or a clod of earth amidst the fluctuations of joy and anger.
He who perceives that very person who is an extreme enemy, envious, and intent on killing, as an unfeigned friend— he truly sees.
He who scrapes away both friendship and envy, root and all, like the current of a river uproots a tree— he is the destroyer of the faults of joy and resentment.
If the true nature of the transformations of passion and hatred is not contemplated, then even though they exist, they are as if non-existent; even when cultivated, they remain uncultivated.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, and whose intellect is not tainted—
even by slaying these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
Regarding that which does not exist, the realization of its existence has been described;
through thorough understanding alone, that [realization] undoubtedly perishes, just like an illusion.
Like a lamp devoid of oil, he whose internal essence of latent tendencies has been stilled has not truly created anything at all; even though he is wise, he is no longer an agent.
He for whom this entire collection of objects, whether existent or non-existent, is not to be grasped in any state—
neither for the sake of suffering nor for the sake of pleasure— is indeed liberated here, even while still alive.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman," by Vasiṣṭha.

O sinless one, since the mind, intellect, ego, the senses, and so forth are all composed of pure consciousness and are themselves devoid of objective thought, where can things such as the individual soul (jīva) reside?
Know that the multiplicity bestowed by the Great Self through its very own nature is, in truth, non-multiplicity— just as the state of being a bracelet is not distinct from the gold itself.
As long as there is delusion through ignorance, so long does the mind of saṃsāra exist;
once the destruction of ignorance has occurred, where could there be either the object of thought or the mind?
Through the practice of inner science, dullness likewise comes to an end,
just as the internal chill caused by water is dispelled by attending a fire.
As soon as the possession by the poison of craving for enjoyments has come to rest,
ignorance is destroyed at that very moment, like blindness resulting from the destruction of darkness.
Through the internalization of the mantra of the inner science, the cholera-like poison of craving is destroyed within,
just as mist is dissipated by autumn.
Know, O Rāma, that when folly is destroyed, the mind along with its kin is likewise destroyed;
for when the cloud has dissolved in the sky, the dullness subsides without obstruction.
When the mind has reached the state of non-mindfulness, the delusion of latent impressions perishes,
O sinless one, like the scattering of pearls from a necklace once the string has been severed.
Those who do not contemplate the meaning of the scriptures for the sake of destroying the dense mass of afflictions,
they unite their minds only for the experience of being worms and insects.
O you whose lovely eyes are like the red lotus,
let the restlessness born of ignorance be stilled, just as the trembling of a lake caused by the wind ceases.
You have attained stability in that state which is devoid of existence and non-existence and is supremely expansive,
like a wind within the sky.
I believe, O scion of Raghu, that you have been awakened by my words,
as one who was asleep in the sleep of widespread ignorance is roused from slumber by drums.
I believe that the words of a family preceptor carry weight even with one who is ordinary;
O Rāma, how could they not carry weight with you, whose intellect is so exceedingly noble?
Wherever the quality of having acceptable speech has been cultivated by one's own mind,
those words enter deeply within, just as water enters a heated field.
"O Great-Souled One, we are indeed the eternal family preceptors and teachers of the scions of Raghu.
Therefore, O Noble One, these words spoken by us should be taken to heart by you immediately, like a necklace."
The fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of the Mind," [ends].
Rāma:
Oh, how truly wonderful! Through the contemplation of the meaning of your words, O Lord, this entire web of the world has become peaceful for me, even though it stands right before my eyes.
I have personally entered into supreme peace within my own self,
just as the surface of the earth, scorched by a long drought, is refreshed by rain.
I am stilled, O cool-natured one; I abide in pure bliss. I have attained serenity, like a lake free from agitation.
O Sage, this entire circle of the quarters now appears to me perfectly clear and serene; I perceive it as it truly is, as if free from all mist.
I am born, my doubts have vanished, and the mirage of desire has been stilled; freed from the mist of passion, I am cooled like a desert after rain.
Within myself, I have attained that bliss which is devoid of end;
wherein, O Lord, even the taste of the elixir of immortality seems like a blade of grass.
Today I abide in my true nature; I am well, and I am joyful.
I delight in the world, yet I am Rāma. Homage to me, and homage be to you!
Those doubts and those mental constructions have all set for me,
like the roaming of night-vampires at dawn when the sun shines bright.
In my heart, which is stainless, expansive, lotus-adorned, and cool as snow,
my mind has attained tranquility like a female swan in a lake.
Doubts such as "Why is this a blemish on my soul? or "How so? have surely been uprooted, just as darkness vanishes before the sun.
Everything everywhere and at all times is indeed the Self alone, whose form is ever-manifested;
how then can there be the false conceptualizations that "this is one thing" and "that is another"?
"Who was I in the past, such as I was, bound by the shackles of craving?"— thus I laugh, full of blossoming joy, at my very inner self.
Ah! Now I have rightly remembered:
this one is indeed I, the Unborn, who stands here having been bathed by the flood of the nectar of your speech.
"Oh! How wonderful that, while remaining right here, I have ascended to the vast, purifying earth where the sun appears to us as if it were situated in the netherworld!"
Salutations to the one who is eternally worthy of homage; I, having attained my true being and departed from the ocean of existence, conquer myself by means of the Self within the Self.

O Lord, by the power of experience, having clearly become like a bee within the calyx of my heart-lotus through your excellent words, I have attained here a state of my own that is long since arisen, free from sorrow.
The sixth canto, named "The Resting of Rāghava," by Vasiṣṭha.
Furthermore, O mighty-armed one, listen again to my supreme word,
which I shall speak to you, who are pleased with me, out of a desire for your welfare.
Even though you have already accepted awakening, listen further for the sake of increasing that awakening,
so that even those who are only slightly awakened may become free from suffering.
The ignorant man who, not knowing the Self, identifies the body alone as the Self,
is overcome by the arrows of the senses, which rise up like a surge of pain caused by anger.
For that wise one who has known the Self and whose firm abiding is in the true Self, no afflictions strike that blameless person, just as enemies do not harm one who is content with his own senses.
For what reason does that embodied being, who shines for the sake of others, undergo the flood of bodily suffering, unless it be through censure?
The self is not connected to the body, nor is the body in the self;
these two are mutually distinct, like light and darkness.
The Blessed One is eternally free from all modifications of existence and remains untainted; the Self does not set, for it is ever-risen and never ceases to be.
Let that which happens to this body— insentient, ignorant, trivial, ungrateful, perishable, and full of anger— be so.
And when the Self is scrutinized, nothing whatsoever exists as separate from it;
for how could anything possibly belong to that which is insentient and whose nature is non-existent?
That which was spoken for the sake of subtle realization is now being made known to Rāghava again and again through various and most diverse methods.
If the self were, in the ultimate sense, to assume the qualities of the body, then why does it not take on the insentience of a corpse? MU 6.6.11.
If, in the ultimate sense, the body were to grasp the qualities of the self,
then how could it not also take up the mental factors (caitta), which consist of consciousness and are ever-arisen?
Tell me, what kind of equality in pleasure and pain can there be between those two, when the full comprehension of one results in sheer dullness for the other?
How could those two, who are equal and perform identical actions, ever—
being both non-existent— enter into a mutual relationship with one another?
How could the gross be of the nature of the subtle, and how could the subtle become gross?
When one arises, there is no existence of the second, like day and night.
Knowledge does not become ignorance, nor does shadow turn into heat;
the existent Brahman never becomes non-existent, even amidst diverse perspectives.
There is not even the slightest attachment for the all-pervading embodied soul,
even though it resides within the body, just as a lotus is unattached to the water.

There is not even the slightest contact between Brahman and the existence of the body; for although it resides within that body, it does not participate in its functions, just as the sky is unaffected by the wind.
There is nothing whatsoever in the Self, nor in the non-existent body;
therefore, O Rāghava, this delusion of pleasure and pain is entirely in vain—whence could it arise?
Old age, death, misfortune, pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence—none of these exist here even in the slightest; O Nirvāṇa, be at peace!
The delusion consisting of rising and falling, which exists as the body, is seen to be situated extremely high within Brahman alone, just as the state of waves is seen within water.
For here, the self indeed arises from the existence of the Self;
the bodily machine has emerged like a wave from the mere existence of water.
Just as, my dear, the states of agitation, existence, and non-existence arise through the vibration of the support,
so too do they arise for the embodied soul through the body, like the reflection of the sun and other luminaries.
O one of right vision, when the self is perceived as it truly is,
the delusion of ignorance consisting of the body comes to rest and dissolves away.
Through the knowledge of the body and the embodied as they truly are, their existence arises— consisting of both being and non-being— just as the manifestation of two objects arises from a lamp.

Those who lack right knowledge, who flutter here within this world through their own cycles of birth and death, are empty at their core; they are merely the winds of delusion that fan the fire of worldly existence.
Those of deluded intellect, who have not reflected upon their own true welfare and have not realized consciousness, move about like grass caught and released by a whirlwind.
Those whose nature of mind has not been tasted are insentient; impelled by their own winds as if by threads, they move and quiver like machines set in motion.
They bring forth and cast away everything, such as grass and wood;
possessing sound, touch, form, and the rest, their limbs are as tremulous as waves.

Though insentient, these beings possess a flickering form; they are filled with intense and vast currents of passion, subject to coming and going like pleasure-gardens, resembling great floods—such are those of dull intellect.
Indeed, this immutable consciousness remains present in all of these;
however, due to the power of ignorance regarding it, they have fallen into a state of extreme wretchedness.
For the successions of breaths of the ignorant are seen to be merely for the sake of movement, like the bellows of a blacksmith; they quickly appear to be so, but they do not accomplish any purpose.
Like the twang of a bowstring from a fool, a threatening roar is heard for the very purpose of killing— a sound utterly devoid of conscious awareness.
Even the fruit obtained from a fool is like that of a wild forest tree;
resting upon him is like resting on a stone slab.
Therefore, whatever union there might be even with a tree stump in the forest,
for that purpose whatever has been done is like striking empty space with clubs.
Whatever is given to that lowest of men is like casting it into putrid mud;
and whatever conversation one has with him is like summoning a dog to a sacrifice.
Ignorance is the ultimate source of calamities; for what misfortune does not befall the ignorant?
This path of saṃsāra flows by the power of the ignorant.
For the ignorant, fierce sufferings and even firm pleasures recur again and again with each new age, like immovable mountains.
For the ignorant person who remains attached to the body, wealth, wife, and so forth, this terrible suffering never ceases.
For one who has conceived the notion of a self in this corpse-like body which is devoid of self,
how indeed can this illusion consisting of unreal cognition ever perish?

For one of evil disposition whose intellect is stunted, who is blind regarding reality and possesses a corrupt mind, and for one who possesses eyes yet stumbles at every step regarding what is not real; MU_6,6.41.
Poison arises from the moon as fragrance does from a flower;
even a thorn emerges from milk as a blade of durva grass does from dry land.
For the ignorant person, desires are born like rice crops after a good rain; they are the female serpents that coil around the body-palm tree and the chains for the elephant of the mind.
The splendor of hell, guarded by the serpents of evil deeds, joyfully protects one who does not know the self, just as a peahen welcomes a rain-cloud.
With eyes flickering like restless bees and sprout-like lips quivering,
this poisonous creeper that is a woman blossoms only for the sake of fools.
Upon the ground of the heart of the ocean of the ignorant,
the coral-tree of passion grows with trembling as its sprouts, yet it is devoid of luster.

The forest fire of hatred blazes in the desert of the ignorant's hearts, with the skin of the body as its smoke, weapons as its flames, and the soldiers as its torches; it is a calamity born of anger.
In the lake of ignorance and stinginess, with the slander of others as its lotus leaves,
the lotus-plant of envy flourishes fully, with anxiety as its bees.
In every birth, the submarine fire of death again assails the insentient body with the agitation of waves of most intense suffering.
Birth inevitably passes into childhood, youth moves toward old age, and old age approaches death; this cycle repeats again and again for the deluded man alone.
In this ancient water-wheel of the world, the ignorant have been reduced to fragments by rising and sinking within the machine of saṃsāra, using the rope that is worldly existence itself.
That very world which is as fragile as a cow’s footprint and distant from the intellect of the wise, becomes for one who lacks greatness an unfathomable abyss without end or limit.
Like birds from a cage, the thoughts of the ignorant do not reach the further shore, as if they were confined within the hollow interior of the sky of consciousness.
The rims of the wheel of birth cannot be made manifest, for they consist of nothing but mental states and have their origin solely in latent tendencies.
By the ignorant one, for the sake of the bed of the senses, the body— red with the blood of passion—
is spread out in the forest of saṃsāra like a lump of raw meat.
This creation, composed of the mountain of elements, consists of nothing more than a mere fragment of clay and flesh;
yet, through delusion, it appears as the coloring of the mind's objects and misfortunes.
Victorious is the wish-fulfilling tree of the imagination of the vast conceptualization,
from which spreads forth for the ignorant a continuous succession of leaves that are the worlds.
In which [palaces] they dwell, shine, gleam, and sport,
endowed with various artistic arrangements and abounding in enjoyments and birds.
In this [tree], births are the joints, the web of karma is the buds,
merits and sins are the fruits, and the splendor of worldly power is the flower-clusters.
Due to the rising of the moon of ignorance, these women have clearly attained supreme splendor as medicinal herbs within this forest grove of saṃsāra.
Victorious is the moon of ignorance: thick with dullness, full of its digits, rising at the time of darkness, appearing as a self within the void, and the lord of all defects.

By the grace of the moon of ignorance— which is filled with the nectar of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which satiates the *cakora* birds of the quarters of hope, and which seeks the essence of the jewel of the mind— *MU_6,6.62*
The lovely women, sporting like royal swans with limbs as cool as frost,
shine like night-lotuses whose bees are their tremulous eyes.
That women— who possess breasts as pale as the moon— shine with the splendor of dark tresses like the night, is merely the manifestation of the moon of ignorance.

O Rāma, these are the various and abundant fruits that have spread forth from the tree of ignorance: sweetness that lasts only at first sight, fruitlessness, having a beginning and an end, and fragility in all states of existence.
The seventh canto, titled "The Greatness of Delusion," by Vasiṣṭha.
The women, adorned with strings of pearls and jewels,
shine like the waves of the churned ocean of the milk of desire when the moon of intoxication has risen.
The glances of the women, flickering upon the petals of their cheeks, bear the beauty of swarms of bees hovering over the interior of golden lotuses.
In the groves of garden forests, having set foot upon the ground in springtime,
the charming *sumanas* flowers shine like the smiles of the Mind-born God (Kāmadeva).
Flesh-eating vultures, jackals, dogs, ravens,
and crows are compared by women to the moon, sandalwood, and lotuses.
The row of a woman’s breasts appears like a golden jar with high lotus buds, resembling a linga adorned with red cloth-wrappings.
The fleshy fragment called the lip, moistened with saliva, is compared to the liquid of honey-wine flowing from the moon of elixir.
Arms shaped like *śālmali* thorns and cruel bone-stakes are described by auspicious poets using such terms as "arms" and "creepers."
Lovely as a mass of plantain trunks, she delights in beauty;
the splendor of the archway of the God of Love has arisen from the grace of her thighs.
Even prosperity— which is sweet only at the first encounter, followed by the onset of dualities in its midst,
and utterly tasteless at its swift conclusion— is ardently desired.
The mind encounters suffering, and suffering branches out into a hundred directions;
upon these branches of suffering, the splendors of the fruits of various karmas are born.
In the rainy season, the creepers stand thick with spreading tendrils like ropes for the purpose of binding, appearing as if they were dense nets enveloping the quarters of the sky.
The mist of delusion, which distorts what ought to be done from what ought not to be done, approaches its essence like the Yamunā river in the rainy season, dark as the gloom of twilight.
With his inner heart made bitter by the end of life, and experiencing various forms of transformation, he tastes the poison-like flavor of rebirth, devoid of all affection.
The winds of one's own karma blow, scattering various golden dusts from the rows of withered, decayed, and aged leaves that are the masses of living beings.
This Time, though it has swallowed the infinite worlds like ripe fruits, and possesses a voracious, boundless belly, is not satiated even by kalpas.
Intoxicated by the wind of delusion and transformed by the poison of haste, these powerful calamities, like hissing serpents, quiver within the cave of the mind.
Afflicted by the demoness of anxiety and lacking the rising moon of discernment,
the night of youth passes away in total darkness, devoid of light.
The tongue falls into a state of decay through the fevers of vulgar flattery,
just as even a lotus petal situated within the hollow of its bud withers from the frosts.
The firm *śalmali* tree of poverty, with its great trunk of a miserable life and crowded with the thorns of hardships, spreads out a thousand branches.
In the night of excessive begging, the owl of greed flutters about, having made its dwelling in the temple of the mind that is inwardly empty, puffed up, and ruined.
Having long ago seized with both ears the quivering mouse of youth, old age now tears it apart as a decrepit female cat.
This creation, devoid of essence and having gradually surpassed the loftiness of the mountains,
comes to fullness like a mass of foam.
The creeper of existence has blossomed, white with the flowers of radiance, adorned with the sprouts of the world,
and bearing the fruits of dharma and artha.
The beautiful house of the three worlds is supported, with Mount Meru as its great pillar, the moon and sun as its windows, and the sky as its roof.
In the vast lake of saṃsāra, the bees that are living beings move about within the lotuses that are bodies, drinking the nectar of the nature of consciousness.
Within the interior of the world-egg, the sun-lamp shines with radiant beauty upon the great sapphire mosaic of the path of the sky.
The multitude of people is like an aged bird, its limbs bound by the thread of hope,
trapped within the cage of the senses fastened to the end of the peg of its own latent tendencies.
The creeping vine of saṃsāra, whose succession of leaves consists of beings born from incessant falling [into rebirth],
has long been quivering, touched by the python of worldly existence.
For some time on our backs, we were unseen by the net of Time;
for a moment, we cast down the mire of the fierce hells and were freed from all anxiety.
In the lake of the path to heaven, where the crescent moon is the lotus stalk and the dark clouds are the water-moss,
the celestial swans flash within.
The lotus-pond of action is abundant, possessing rows of various fruits, garlanded by the water of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), filled with the fragrance of vibration, and blossomed by ritual acts.
The wretched fish of worldly existence, quivering in the pond of saṃsāra,
is swallowed by the crafty, aged vulture that is Death.
Like a line of waves and foam, it is both the same and yet different, fragile;
day after day, a variety of forms arises like the crescent of another moon.
This wheel is spun around by the potter Time, who fashions momentary clay vessels out of the abundant elements.
Innumerable and not a few networks of worldly thickets have arisen in the immovable state, yet they have been consumed by the fire of the cosmic age.
Through endless existence and non-existence, and through hundreds of states of pleasure and pain, this worldly condition perpetually undergoes transformation.
The steadfastness of their intellect was not shattered by the upheavals of the turning of the ages, nor by the chains of latent impressions, nor by the falling thunderbolts of delusion.
Vāsanā bears the body of Indra, which has been pursued by hundreds of the lords of enemies— the sons of Danu— and whose modesty has been shattered and broken.
This constant whirlwind of destiny incessantly enters the throat of the serpent of time, carrying a continuous succession of the dust of created beings shaken loose.
All the waters of objective entities, with their fruits as foam, fall incessantly from every side into the mouth of the submarine fire of non-existence.
The diverse powers of substances, endowed with their mere intrinsic nature, quiver when suddenly arisen, like the splendor of the movement of waters.
The lion of Death, with its mane bristling, devours even the many great world-cubs, though they be filled with the pearls of living beings.
The world-birds, which produce water from their wings like clouds and bear fruit in the form of great mountains,
are born, they die, and they fly about.
Upon the wall of consciousness, which is bright with vibration, the painter of destiny unfolds the paintings of saṃsāra using the five colors of the senses.
It is constantly moving, the cause of all activity,
possessing parts each equal to a hundredth of a blink of an eye, transparent, and sprouting with stimulated vitality.
Steadfast beings of the stationary class perceive, as if through meditation, the subtle movement of time that brings about their own arising.
All classes of living beings are worn out by old age, death, and delusion, which arise from passion and hatred and consist of existence and non-existence.
On the surface of the earth, rows of insects— upholding their own particular meditations through their past misdeeds— are inevitably tormented for a fixed period of time by the power of destiny.
In an instant, this serpent of Time— whose hole is extremely difficult to perceive, who possesses vast coils, and who is blissful— swallows everything while remaining invisible.
From the moment of a single instant up to the end of an eon, due to the coloring by light and darkness,
one's own body is perceived as something over time and is thus accepted [as real].
In this world, the six seasonal planets move through the sky of time, powerful with cold, wind, and heat, radiant with the splendor of blooming flowers, and bestowing their fruits.
In the alms-bowl of the universe, the Goddess Kālī, who is Action itself,
repeatedly gives and then seeks to take up the alms of all beings.
Within the hollow of the lotus of the three worlds, which rests upon a mass of milk,
the swarm of bees that are living beings produces a great humming sound.
Her dark-blue hair is like darkness, her eyes are as flickering as the sun and moon,
and she has the earth, Brahmā, Upendra, Hara, Indra, and other gods as the limbs of her excellent mountain-like body.
She has the reality of Brahman as her sole father; she is one whose breasts hang down;
she has the power of consciousness (cicchakti) as her mother; she is gross, tremulous, and possesses dense lightning.
Her teeth are a lattice of stars, her lower lip is reddened by the twilight;
she holds all the lotus-ponds in her hands, and her face is the city of Indra.
The seven oceans are her pearl necklace, the dark-blue sky is her garment,
Jambudvīpa is her great navel, and the beauty of the forests is the line of hair on her body.
Having come into being again and again, the aged mistress of the three worlds perishes;
having been destroyed, she is born repeatedly, causing manifold delusions.
Then, others were submerged in the great, terrifying ocean of time,
where the bursting bubbles of world-systems perish at every moment of an eon.
But having repeatedly paused again and again at the lake that is time’s unfathomable depth,
the cranes of worldly existence have flown away in the mere blink of an eon.
Arising again and again, these continuous flashes of creation,
which are as delightful as the light of consciousness, flicker within the cloud of time.
With birds that are spirits crying out, the guardians of the fruit of the cosmic egg fall down incessantly and swiftly from the exceedingly high *kālatāla* tree.
There are certain leaders of gods somewhere who perform the creation of Brahmā with their opening of an eye,
and who perform the dissolution with their closing of an eye.
In a certain supreme city, there exist some Rudras by the thousands, for whom the entire web of kalpas is exhausted in a mere blink of an eye.
Even he by whose mere blink they come into being or cease to be—such indeed is the Lord of Gods; for this state of activity is infinite.
In the void state of Brahman, which consists of infinite volitions,
what powers or diverse arrangements could possibly exist?
Thus, this worldly conceptualization, which shines with the burden of the objects of thought and mental constructions that are never exhausted, is the manifestation of ignorance.
That which consists of prosperity and likewise constant adversity; that which consists of the afflictions of childhood, youth, old age, and death;
and that which is immersion in the succession of pleasure and pain—these are the manifestations of the intense darkness of ignorance.
The eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ignorance," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this forest grove of saṃsāra, situated on the slopes of the mountain of consciousness,
what kind of creeper indeed has blossomed and spread forth, known as ignorance?
This slender body-staff, which possesses joints as massive as great mountains, is encased in the skin of the cosmic egg; it is she who makes the three worlds beautiful.
Pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, knowledge, and ignorance—
these are the roots and fruits that have wide-ranging functions here.
From pleasure, ignorance arises intensely, and it yields that very same thing in the end;
from pain, ignorance arises intensely, and it ripens fully as that very same thing in the end.
From existence this ignorance arises; it clearly bears fruit for that very existence.
From existence it attains being; in an instant, it bears fruit for that very existence.
Through ignorance it increases; that indeed is remembered as its fruit.
Through knowledge it attains true consciousness; that very same thing bestows [liberation] at the end.
Her body unfolds, possessing manifold splendors, bestowing the fragrance of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and covered with a dense mass of young sprouts.
This [world-tree] has the day as its arrayed flowers, the restless night as its bees,
and it is constantly trembling, with living beings falling from it like leaves.
Having arrived again and again with force, it is at times shaken off by the discerning one;
though its spreading dust is cleared away, it returns once more.
Abounding with emerging coral shoots, bristling with newly sprouted buds,
endowed with the flowers of every season, and rich in all essential juices.
The river of births is densely crowded with whirlpools, leaking through the fissures of destruction;
it is filled with the essence of the expansion of enjoyments, yet it is gnawed by the woodworm of solitary inquiry.
Indeed, those circles of the moon and sun which blossom day by day in the sky are, it is said,
merely her flowers, tossed about by the wind.
O descendant of Raghu, those stars which have filled the hollow of the sky have now reached the state of buds, their forms quivering.
The light of the moon, the sun, and fire is merely her flowery pollen;
for it is by this that she, fair-limbed as a woman, draws away the hearts of men.
Enveloped by the elephant of the mind, with the warbling cuckoo of conceptualization,
variegated by the serpents of the senses, and stained by the skin of craving.
Resorting to the dark-blue body of the Tamāla tree against the blue sky, she has attained great height;
with the two worlds as her excellent pillars, she stands upon the ground of the garden of the universe.
With the lower portion of the cosmic egg as its own basin,
it possesses a net-like structure through which the waters of all the oceans, milk, and other liquids are provided as irrigation.
The three Vedas are like restless bees, colored by the flowers of beautiful women;
consciousness is stirred by the wind of its own vibration, bearing the broad leaves of ritual action.
The floral pavilion of the splendor of heaven is pervaded by the python of evil deeds; it is densely packed with jīvajīvaka birds and bestows various intoxications of joy.
Consisting of various flavors, variegated, smiling with various flowers,
pervaded by rows of various fruits, and blossoming in various colors.
It possesses circles of various flower-beds, it supports various kinds of birds,
it is rough with various pollens, and it is marked by fragments of various clouds.
It was covered with various blossoming creepers, rising from various forest groves,
climbing upon various mountain slopes, and spreading continuously across various peaks.
Born and being born, dying and likewise dead; unsevered as well as severed, it is eternally indestructible.
Both past and present, she is the locus for both existence and non-existence;
eternally and utterly youthful, she has forever attained tranquility.
For this is indeed a great poisonous creeper; when embraced, it swiftly bestows the fainting fit of the poison of saṃsāra, and when touched, one perishes.
From here it is vast, from there it has flowed away; from here it is rooted, from there it is firmly established.
Here is water, there are mountains, here are the Nāgas, and there are the gods.
From here she has come to the state of the earth, and from here she remains as radiance;
from here she has attained the nature of the moon and sun, and likewise from here the form of the stars.
From here is darkness, from here is light, from here is the sky, and from here is fertile earth;
from here is the scripture, from here are the Vedas, and from here is that which is free from duality.
From this [path] comes merit, from that demerit; from this comes the delusion of fixity, while from knowledge and the cultivation of wisdom, these are utterly exhausted.
On one side, she remains through the gradual depletion of her merit, asceticism, and gifts;
on the other, she has surely come to exhaustion through the play of yoga.
In one place she flew as a bird, in another she remained as a deity; in one place she stood firm as a pillar, and in another she attained the state of the wind.
In one place she is merged in hell, in another she dwells in heaven;
in one place she has attained the state of a god, and in another she exists as a worm.
In one place Viṣṇu, in another Brahmā, in another Rudra, in another the Sun;
in one place Fire, in another Wind, in another the Moon, and in another Yama.
Whatever exists in the worlds, O dear one—whether it be pervaded by great majesty or reduced to the state of withered straw;
whether it be visible, shimmering, or even subtle like Śiva and the rest—know that to be ignorance (avidyā). The attainment of the Self occurs through the transcendence of that.
The ninth canto, named "The Play of the Creeper of Ignorance," ends.
Rama.
O Brahmin, having heard that even Hari, Hara, and the others— who have arisen as a multitude of forms— are nothing but ignorance, I have fallen into a state of confusion.

Vasiṣṭha: That which is untouched by anything perceivable, which is tranquil, which is the self of all, and which is devoid of conceptualization— exists here as being, consciousness, and even as appearance.
From that, therefore, arises the *kalā*, whose nature is to differentiate; it emerges as a throbbing form, like a whirlpool arising from water.
It is conceived as threefold— subtle, intermediate, and gross—
and then again, by means of its own very form which has attained the state of mind (manas).
In these three states, when differentiated, the designations "sattva," "rajas," and "tamas" are conceptually constructed; this very [state] is clearly Nature (prakṛti).
Know that ignorance (avidyā) is primordial nature (prakṛti), characterized by the three qualities (guṇas);
this alone is the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti) for a living being, and its further shore is the supreme state.
In this regard, these three qualities that have been mentioned are also traditionally held to be threefold;
each quality—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is divided individually.
This ignorance is divided into nine kinds according to the distinction of its qualities;
whatever is seen here is entirely dependent upon it.
The seers, the sages, the perfected ones, the nāgas, the knowledge-holders, and the gods—
know these, O Rāghava, to be the portion of ignorance that is characterized by goodness (sattva).
Of this sattvic portion, the Nāgas and Vidyādharas are Tamas;
the Munis and Sādhyas are Rajas; and the gods, Hara and the others, are Sattva.
In the divine womb born of the essence of beings, within the quality of the nature of ignorance,
the pure state has arrived as the essence known as Hari, Hara, and the others.
O Rāma, he who becomes a knower of that which is the sattvic portion of nature is no longer deluded; therefore, he is called liberated.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, these beings such as Rudra and others remain as portions of *sattva* for as long as the world endures, until their bodies are released from the person (*puruṣa*).
As long as they possess a body, these great-souled ones remain liberated while living;
at the end of the body, they will abide as supreme lords, liberated beyond the body.
This portion belongs to ignorance alone, yet it has attained the status of knowledge;
the seed becomes the fruit, and the fruit attains the state of the seed.
Ignorance arises from knowledge like a bubble from water;
ignorance dissolves into knowledge just as a bubble dissolves into water.
Just as the difference between milk and its waves arises solely from the perception of duality,
so too the difference between knowledge and ignorance arises solely from the perception of distinction.
Just as the identity of water and its waves exists from the perspective of ultimate reality,
so too does the identity of knowledge and ignorance exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Neither the state of ignorance nor the state of knowledge exists here as anything at all;
having abandoned the views of knowledge and ignorance, that which truly exists here is indeed what remains.
O scion of the Raghus, these two views of knowledge and ignorance do not exist by virtue of the exclusion of their respective opposites; remain firmly established in that which remains.
Neither ignorance exists nor knowledge exists; nothing whatsoever is established by this conceptual construction.
That which is called consciousness and awareness remains as neither something nor nothing.
That very [reality], when its manifestation is unknown, is designated as "ignorance" (avidyā);
that same reality, when known, is termed the "destruction of ignorance."
Due to the absence of true knowledge, a false conceptualization called ignorance arises;
at the end, the mutual existence of these two is like that of a shadow and its bearer.
But when ignorance has dissolved, O Rāghava, in an instant these two very conceptions dissolve; that which is inexpressible remains.
O Rāghava, when ignorance has been destroyed and even the side of knowledge has perished,
that which remains is either nothing at all, or it is this very expanse that is spread out.
In this regard, it is seen that everything is seen, yet nothing at all is seen;
just as a banyan tree, though possessing flowers, fruits, and so forth, exists within its own banyan seed.
That is manifested as all powers and is the casket of all powers;
it is emptier even than space, unknowable, and of the nature of consciousness.
Just as fire exists within a sun-crystal, and just as clarified butter exists within milk,
so too does all this— the sequential arising of space and time— reside therein.
Just as sparks issue from fire, and as rays from the sun,
so do these flickering cognitions emerge from that which remains.
Just as the ocean is the constant repository for waves, and a flawless gem for its radiance,
so too is that [reality] the constant repository for the radiances of infinite cognitions.
It remains external and internal to all things at all times, being by nature indestructible, just as space is to jars.
Just as a magnet is considered the agent of the movements of iron, even though it is itself inactive,
so too is agency attributed to that [Self], though it is indeed non-agent.
Just as inert iron vibrates by the mere proximity of a magnet,
so too does this body, though insentient in nature, move by the very presence of that [Self].
Therein rests this entire world within the single seed of the universe, that which is named Consciousness (*citi*), and within the conceptualization of "awareness" (*saṃvit*).
Like a mass of restless waves upon the water, the nature of consciousness is formless even more than space; therein, nothing at all exists.
The Tenth Chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Ignorance," by Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, know this: this entire world, both stationary and moving, is truly nothing at all; know, O dear one, that not even the slightest thing has ever attained the state of being.

In that state, there is no conceptualization whatsoever consisting of existence or non-existence; therefore, O Rāma, all this beginning with the individual soul (jīva) is vain—why do you strive for it?
This one who is designated as "the wise one within" is not found,
just as one does not find the snake [there] due to the delusion of a rope-snake.
The very self, when not fully known, becomes the source of delusion for those who wander;
when known, it attains the state of selfhood, which is the ultimate limit of all consciousness.
In the world, that which is called ignorance is consciousness when it is adorned with the impurity of the object of thought;
when it transcends the object of thought, it attains purity, being freed from all limiting adjuncts.
For the person is indeed mind-only; when that [mind] is destroyed, he is not destroyed.
While it remains, he remains, just as this self [remains] like space when a jar exists.
Just as a child, while walking, sees one who is walking, and while standing, sees one who is standing,
so too this mind perceives itself as agitated, just as it perceives the sun.
Like a silkworm, one who wraps oneself within the mind with the manifold threads of latent tendencies does not realize this due to ignorance.
Rāma:
O Lord, what is the nature of that which has reached the state of extreme density through ignorance, which remains as it is, and has assumed the bodies of immobile beings and so forth?
Vasiṣṹṭha:
Having attained neither the state of non-mind nor having fallen away from the state of mind,
this consciousness remains among immobile beings by resorting to a neutral form.
Where the eightfold city of dreams, which causes suffering, remains dormant,
there [the Self] abides by its mere existence, like one who is mute, blind, or inert.
Rāma:
O best among those who know what is to be known, I consider liberation to be not far off for one in whom consciousness, abiding as the non-duality of existence, is present even in stationary things.

Vasiṣṭha: If that which consists of the awakening to the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), arising from investigating this through prior intelligence and perceiving things as they truly are, were liberation, then it would be eternal.

The supreme abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanās) through thorough comprehension— that which is the state of being the universal form of pure existence (sattāsāmānyarūpatva)— the wise know that to be the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya).

Having reflected and investigated the scriptures together with the noble ones through the cultivation of inner self-knowledge, they know that which abides in the universal reality of existence to be the supreme Brahman.
Know that state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatva*) to be the latent impression (*vāsanā*) wherein one remains internally asleep and dull, like a sprout within a seed, which bestows birth once again.
With its mental activity withdrawn within and its latent tendencies asleep on all sides,
deep sleep is insentient by nature, yet it bestows hundreds of sorrows of rebirth.
For all these beings, beginning with the immobile, possess the nature of insentience;
having ascended to the state of deep sleep, they are fit for birth again and again.
Just as flowers reside within seeds and pots within a heap of clay,
so too, O virtuous one, do their own latent impressions (vāsanās) reside within stationary beings.
That state where the seed of latent impressions (vāsanā) still exists is not true deep sleep (suṣupta);
that state where latent impressions are seedless is known as the Fourth (turya), which bestows perfection.
Likewise, even a small remnant of latent impressions, fire, debt, disease, enemies, oil, enmity, or poison causes affliction.
One whose seeds of latent impressions have been burnt away, possessing the nature of pure universal existence— whether still embodied or disembodied— shall never again be a partaker of suffering.
The power of consciousness, whose nature consists of the seeds of latent impressions and which possesses the character of sleep,
eternally exists in the form of sapidity within all things, from stationary objects onwards.
In seeds, it exists as radiance; in inert things, as inertia;
in fluids, as fluidity; and in others, as solidity.
Then she was like the radiance of the sun in ashes, like minute particles in dust,
by her position at the base in dark objects, and by her sharp edge in swords.
The power of the Self abides in all things— such as jars, huts, and cloths— by relying everywhere upon the form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya).
Thus, having taken up the entire state of the visible, she remains established just as the rainy season, with its thick clouds, rests upon the sky.
And its very nature has thus been declared and investigated:
it is non-universal, yet all-pervading; it appears as if existent, though its essence consists of non-existence.
This view of a self is a non-vision that bestows the wandering of saṃsāra;
yet when it is seen [for what it is], it brings about the destruction of all sufferings.
The non-perception of this [Self], however, is called ignorance by the wise;
for ignorance is the cause of the world, and from it everything proceeds.
As soon as ignorance is perceived to be devoid of form,
it dissolves instantly, like a particle of frost in the heat of the sun.
Just as when a man whose sleep is fading reflects upon his own state with even a slight degree of conceptualization, his sleep dissolves away.
In this way, as long as one conceptualizes what this non-entity is like,
ignorance is exhausted, just as blindness is dispelled by light.
When one approaches with a lamp in hand, desiring to see that which is of the nature of darkness,
then all that darkness melts away, just as clarified butter does in heat.
But by means of lamps, the determination of the form of darkness is not perceived;
rather, there arises only the destruction of gloom, which possesses a stainless form.
When observed in this way, it flees and goes somewhere;
for through investigation, its lack of substantiality is seen, as it is of an unreal nature.
Just as whatever is seen appears in such a way when light has arrived, so too,
since ignorance is a non-entity, its lack of substantiality is perceived.
As long as it is not illuminated, nothing at all is perceived;
in whatever manner and whatever thing is illuminated, in that very manner is it apprehended.
As soon as one reflects for oneself, "Who am I in this machine of blood, flesh, and bone?", everything quickly dissolves away.
When that which is of the nature of non-existence has certainly been discarded from both the beginning and the end of the heart,
they know that which remains as the total destruction of ignorance.
That which is both nothing and something, that which is real, is the eternal Brahman;
that is the reality, that is to be accepted, and that is the cessation of ignorance.
The very nature of this name is known to be devoid of intrinsic being;
for the taste of sugar residing on the tongue is not perceived through anything else.
Ignorance does not exist anywhere; this is the indivisible Brahman alone, by which the entire expansion of the manifestations of existence and non-existence is adorned.
Ignorance is precisely this: the certainty that "this is not Brahman.
Its destruction is precisely this: the certainty that "this is Brahman."
If it is asserted here that "the web of appearances consisting of jars, cloths, and carts is not the All-pervading One," that is indeed ignorance;
but if it is held that "the web of appearances consisting of jars, cloths, and carts is the All-pervading One," then that ignorance has utterly dissolved.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Ignorance," by Vasiṣṭha.
Again and again, O Rāma, this is spoken by me for the sake of awakening:
without practice, O virtuous one, the realization of the Self does not arise.
This powerful ignorance, known by other names such as "avidyā," has surely reached its full maturity after developing over hundreds of previous births.
It is experienced by all the senses both externally and internally;
because of this, the body has attained an extreme density amidst both existence and non-existence.
But self-knowledge is beyond the range of all the senses;
it attains its mere existence when the six senses, including the mind, have ceased.
How indeed can that which remains transcending the powers born of the senses,
and whose mode of being lies beyond perception, ever come within the range of direct perception for a living being?
Therefore, O sinless one, ignorance alone is constantly and thoroughly practiced by all embodied beings; true knowledge never arises for them, either in this world or in the next.
Therefore, one should burn the other with the primary portion of ignorance until,
through mutual friction, it subsides of its own accord and becomes auspicious.
For nothing whatsoever anywhere yields fruit without practice;
whatever is attained in any field is the fruit of the tree of practice.

One should, through the firm practice of self-knowledge and without agitation, bring to rest even ignorance that has been practiced for a very long time and has taken deep root, by means of diligent effort.
Cut down this creeper of ignorance that has grown upon the tree of your heart with the stroke of the sword of the playful practice of knowledge, for the sake of spiritual perfection.
O Rāghava, dwell in that same manner as King Janaka, who had known all that is to be known, through the intense practice of self-knowledge.
The certainty that Marutta possesses regarding the discernment of what ought and ought not to be done, whether he is awake or standing still—that is knowledge; through that, there is truth.
It is certainly because Hari descends upon the earth into various wombs for the sake of diverse modes of conduct that his omniscience is proclaimed.
O Rāghava, may that certainty which belongs to the three-eyed Lord as he dwells with his beloved, or even to Brahmā who is free from passion, be yours.
That which is the certainty of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, and of Bhārgava;
and that of the Sun, the Moon, Wind, and Fire.
[The teachings] of Nārada, Pulastya, and myself, as well as those of Aṅgiras, Pracetas, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Atri, and Śuka.
O Raghava, may that same certainty which belongs to other gods, chief brahmins, and royal sages who are liberated while living, be yours as well.
Rāma said:
