O Blessed One, O Brahmin, tell me truly that by which these heroes of great intellect remain established, free from sorrow, through their firm resolve.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O prince of mighty arms, you who have known all that is to be known, listen clearly to what has been asked; this is the certain conclusion regarding these matters.
Whatever web of the world appears here that has any capacity for experience—all that is the stainless Brahman; it is established in this manner as its own expansion.
The quarters are Brahman, the world of Brahmā is Brahman, and the succession of beings is Brahman;
I am Brahman, my enemy is Brahman, and my friends and kinsmen are Brahman.
Brahman is ether, air, and fire; Brahman is earth, water, and so forth;
Brahman is the three divisions of time, and all that is established in Brahman alone.
Just as the ocean increases within itself by means of a series of waves,
so does this Brahman increase through the splendor of objects in this manner.
Brahman is grasped by Brahman; Brahman is enjoyed by Brahman;
Brahman expands within Brahman through its own expansions, namely by the power of Brahman itself.
If Brahman is the form of my enemy, and if Brahman is the doer of what is dear to me, then that Brahman is merged in Brahman; what else is there, and who has done what?
Since desire and the other afflictions are non-entities, merely imagined like trees in the sky,
and are destroyed by the absence of conceptualization, what possibility is there here for their increase?
For within Brahman alone does all movement, vibration, and so forth manifest;
since the entire universe is Brahman, how can there be happiness or suffering?
Brahman is the knower within Brahman; Brahman is established in Brahman.
Brahman vibrates within Brahman; there is no other self-existent entity besides it.
The pot is Brahman, the cloth is Brahman; I am Brahman, this all-pervading reality.
Therefore, what is the use of the futile conceptualization of passion and dispassion?
When the Brahman of death has freely united with the Brahman of the body, what could that which is called "suffering" possibly be? It is like the delusion of a snake in a rope.

When one is established in the bliss of the *sambhoga* and other states within the Brahman that is the body, this [bliss] is already perfected as "I"; whence could there be any vain conceptualization?
Just as the notions of "you" and "I" do not exist in the moving waters of a wave,
so too the states of "thou-ness" and "I-ness" do not exist in Brahman, whose nature is vibration.
Just as nothing whatsoever dies when the water in a whirlpool has perished,
so indeed does nothing die when the Brahman-body (dehabrahman) has reached the state of Brahman.
Just as the notions of "this" and "that" do not persist in water that is both moving and still,
so too the forms of the inert and the non-inert do not abide in the Supreme Self.
Just as the state of being a bracelet belongs to gold, and as a whirlpool belongs to water,
so too does this nature belong to the Self, consisting of both that and its opposite.
"This element is indeed the living self, and this [body] must be of an insentient nature"—
such is the delusion of one who has not known the Self, but never that of one who has known the Self.
To the ignorant, the world consists of a flood of suffering; to the wise, it consists of bliss.
To the blind, the world is darkness; but to the one with sight, it is light.
To the knower, the world is of a single nature; to the ignorant, it yields the suffering of duality.
It is like a night in which a yakṣa appears to a child, whereas for an adult, it is merely the darkness itself.
In this single, eternal, and all-pervading mass of Brahman,
O Rāma, nothing whatsoever dies, nor does anything whatsoever live.
Just as waves and the like in the great ocean neither perish nor are born during its surges and play, so too is the multitude of beings within the Self.
"This does not exist, this exists"— thus, within the Self, by means of the Self,
a power that is truly without cause flashes forth internally like a fragment of crystal.
The Self alone, as the essence of the power of the universe, is Brahman abiding within itself,
just as a mass of water exists within the spray and waves of water.
How could there be the notion of death regarding Brahman through the destruction of the body?
For nothing such as the body exists as distinct from Brahman,
just as waves and the like do not exist apart from the water in the ocean.
Whatever is a drop or a small droplet, whatever is a ripple or a wave,
whatever is foam or a surge— that is just as water is within water.

Whatever body, whatever mental construction, whatever visible object, whatever the perishable and the imperishable, whatever efforts, whatever arrangement, and whatever purpose— each of those is Brahman within Brahman.
The diverse arrangement of forms belongs to Brahman, like [ornaments] from gold; it is not of a different nature. For the deluded, however, there is only the vain conception of duality.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the subtle elements, and the senses—all this is Brahman alone; there is no other self, nor do pleasure, pain, and so forth exist.
Through speech arising from such meanings as "this is I" and "this is you," the Word unfolds within itself, like an echo on a mountain.
Brahman itself, when unknown, remains as if it has attained a state of ignorance;
for indeed, one's own self is seen by the dreaming mind as if it were dead.
That which is not cultivated as Brahman becomes consisting of the ignorance of Brahman;
just as gold that is not refined as gold becomes mere clay.
When Brahman is known as Brahman, it becomes Brahman itself in an instant;
when gold is known as gold, it becomes gold itself in an instant.
For Brahman is the Self, possessing all powers; whatever it intensely contemplates, that it immediately perceives in that very way, spontaneously and by its own power, without external cause.
Those who know Brahman know this Brahman to be without action, agent, or instrument; without cause, free from affliction, self-luminous, and the Great Self.
Ignorance that is not fully understood is called "ignorance";
when it is fully understood, it becomes knowledge, which brings about the complete destruction of ignorance.
Indeed, a kinsman who is not recognized is called a non-kinsman;
once recognized, he becomes a kinsman by destroying the delusion of being a stranger.
But when one internally realizes that "this is improper," the cultivation [of detachment] arises;
through that distaste for what is improper, one indeed becomes dispassionate.
But when it is realized within that duality is unreal, this realization arises;
through that intense distaste for duality, one indeed becomes dispassionate.
When it is clearly known that "this is not I," meditation arises vividly;
through this, one certainly becomes dispassionate due to the dissolution of identity with false egoism.
When it is known that "I am indeed Brahman," that true contemplation arises by which one is completely absorbed within that own true nature.
When it is known that "all this here is indeed Brahman," only Brahman remains; for when the nectar has been drunk, who indeed would not become composed of nectar?
Whatever the mind grasps, that alone quickly becomes sufficient for it;
by taking Brahman as its sole nourishment, it becomes Brahman itself in an instant.
When it is known that what is false is indeed in vain,
this realization arises by which all false perception is surely wiped away.
When it is known that "all is indeed Being," there arises the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) within that vast expanse of Truth, by which one attains a state of stability.
O dear one, cultivation reaches its stable state only when directed toward that which is as it truly is, according to reality, according to its form, and according to how it exists; never otherwise.
Even when one's own kin have passed away for a hundred years and are forgotten, even though they remain as if unrelated, the mind nonetheless feels affection for them by its own force.
For even when the delusion of worldly existence, practiced through hundreds of previous births, persists,
the Self finds supreme bliss within the stainless Self alone.
Even when one's own kinsman is constantly by one's side, as if dependent like another relative, the mind does not attain peace within, for it still perceives him as a stranger.

Indeed, even when poison is present in food and remains utterly concealed, the memory of it certainly flashes forth— whether it has ceased or whether it has begun to act— just like the eye of the *cakora* bird.
Even when supreme friendship arises through practice over hundreds of other births,
this Self does not find peace in this visible world, which is not the Self.
Indeed, even when the nectar of immortality is kept in a completely hidden place during a meal, mindfulness shines forth,
just as the moon shines even when shrouded by clouds on a night.
When the Self is eternal, true, and such as it is, it rejoices in itself alone,
even when the impurities of conceptualization have been obscured for a time or have been utterly destroyed.
One should diligently wash away this impurity with impurities by means of the self;
it must be purified by the scriptures until it becomes white, being freed from the impurity of evil thoughts.
When the mind is free from evil inclinations, knowledge and merit adhere to it,
just as the coloring of saffron adheres to a stainless white cloth.
The firm conviction is that all of creation, existing throughout the three periods of time,
is eternally one, equal, and pure Brahman alone.
In every way, at all times, this entire universe—everything including pots, cloths, and so forth, which has expanded through birth—is Brahman; thus do I know it.
For me there is no suffering, no karmas, no "mine," nor any desire;
I am equanimous, established in well-being, and free from sorrow—I am Brahman. This is the truth.
"I am the blood, I am the flesh, I am the bones, I am the body;
I am consciousness and I am the power of cognition; I am Brahman"—this is the truth.
"I am the grass, I am the creeper, I am the shrub, I am the forests;
I am the mountains, the oceans, and the caravans—thus indeed Brahman alone exists."
The elemental powers are preceded by taking, giving, and contraction;
I am indeed the all-pervading Brahman, whose nature is consciousness and who assumes an expanded form.
I am the manifestation and the desire for the growth of creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and so forth;
I am the Supreme Brahman, the essence of bliss, peaceful and residing within the conscious self.
"In that which all exists, from which all proceeds, who is all, and who is everywhere—that is this very Consciousness, the one Self, the Supreme Brahman; such is the certainty."
The all-pervading reality, which is pure consciousness devoid of any object of thought, is designated by such names as Cit, Ātman, Brahma, Sat, Satya, Ṛta, and Jña. (MU 6.11.82)
It is experienced as the stainless mere appearance that awakens one to all beings,
which is omnipresent and tranquil— the Brahman of consciousness.
Having abandoned all distinctions accumulated by the entire collection of mind, intellect, and the senses, I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, my own self-luminous manifestation.
I am the pure Brahman-consciousness, the illuminator of reality for all causes—the world, sound, and so forth—by which the universe exists; I am without decay.
I am the supreme immortal Brahman-consciousness, whose nature is the flow of a stream of pure consciousness falling incessantly; I am the light, the silence beyond the mind.
I am the Brahman-consciousness, unstained, whose form flows incessantly and who eternally experiences the nectar of bliss; day and night my splendor shines forth.
I am the Brahman of consciousness, free from all latent impressions— tranquil like deep sleep, pure in nature like light, and appearing as the ultimate limit of the enjoyment-body (sambhogakāya).
That consciousness which persists even slightly in the perception of the sweetness of sugar-candy and the like,
even within the unawakened mind and its functions— that I am, the immutable Brahman of Consciousness.
When the moon has risen for one whose mind is attached to his beloved, [he realizes]:
"I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, whose very self is the existence of the cognition of the moon."

When the moon is situated in the sky, the power of those standing on the ground who gaze at it and whose eyes are fixed upon it is like a thread suspended in the air; I am that stainless Consciousness-Brahman.
Devoid of the conceptualization of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and likewise without mind;
whose nature is the experience of reality—eternally, I am the Self, the Consciousness-Brahman.
When the traveler is seen as a stranger and the mind is fixed elsewhere,
that innocent perception— "I am the all-pervading Brahman, which is consciousness"— is the truth.
In the relationship between the elements of earth, water, air, and the seed regarding the activities of the sprout,
that power which emerges until the end— that pervasive Consciousness-Brahman, I am.
That existence of taste which remains latent within dates, nimba fruits, and bimba fruits, while they themselves abide within me— that Brahman-consciousness am I, equal [to all].
Consciousness, which is free from the internal states of sorrow and joy, arises as pure manifestation; equal in the occurrence of gain and loss, I am the stainless Brahman, the Intellect.
As far as the earth extends from the Pole Star, so far is the line of vision stretched;
within that, I am the pervasive Consciousness—tranquil, stainless, and resembling the center of it all.
Whether in the waking state, in deep sleep, or even in dreaming, I am the ever-arisen, beginningless and endless Brahman-consciousness, the Turiya, free from all affliction.
Like the uniform sweetness found within all the sugarcanes grown from hundreds of fields,
I am the one and the same Consciousness-Brahman, abiding equally within all.
Pervading all, subtle in form like the radiance of the sun, illuminating and lovely, this consciousness-Brahman is the "I" that has expanded everywhere.
Like a mere fragment of the bliss of enjoyment, or like the power of tasting nectar;
measured solely by my own inner experience, I am the eternal and imperishable Brahman-consciousness.
Like a fiber within a lotus stalk, I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, whose form vibrates even when the body is cut or split, though it remains hidden within its every limb.
Though pervading the entire world like a mass of clouds, yet possessing movement,
I am the pervasive power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), whose form consists of imperceptible atoms.
I am consciousness, devoid of decay, characterized solely by the oil of affection residing within experience, like the essence of ghee within milk.
The arrangement of bracelets, armlets, and earrings is not composed of those [ornaments] themselves; rather, it exists within gold.
Likewise, consciousness (cit) resides within the body as the all-pervading Self of Brahman; I am that.

I am that untainted Consciousness which exists both externally and internally within the flood of objects, such as mountains and the like, in the form of the universal essence of Being (sattāsāmānya).
That which is the uncontrived mirror of all experiences, inaccessible to the traces of impurity— that is the Great Reality of Mind (cittattva), which I am.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which bestows the fruit of all volitions, illuminates all splendors, and is the ultimate limit of everything worthy of being attained.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which rests within all its parts yet transcends all parts, and whose form shines incessantly.
We worship the conscious Self, which always tastes its own sweetness within the pot, the cloth, the bank, the wall, and the body, remaining in deep sleep even while one is awake.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which is hot in fire, cold in ice, sweet in food, sharp in a razor, black in darkness, and white in the moon.
We worship the conscious Self, who has entered into sweetness within sweet things and pungency within pungent things for the sake of the power inherent in objects.
In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as in the fourth state (turiya) and the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta),
we ever worship the conscious Self (cidātman) as the same everywhere.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, in whom all volitions are stilled, in whom all curiosity has vanished, and from whom every agitation has ceased.
We worship the self of consciousness, which is entirely free from curiosity, free from support, free from effort, partless, and devoid of egoism.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which stands at the end of all things, which is itself everything, whose singular form is boundless, and which is the infinite manifestation of consciousness.
We worship the conscious self, the supreme thread stretched out for those liberated from the body of the three worlds, which effects both expansion and contraction.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which, like a wondrous and vast net, encompasses within itself the bird of the universe— both the internal and the external, both tranquil and fierce.
We worship that single Self of Consciousness, wherein all this exists and yet does not exist even in the slightest degree, being both existent and non-existent.
We worship the conscious Self, the supreme condition, the full foundation of all cognitions, who abides in every mode of existence.
We worship the conscious self, the support of all, which is timeless, yet drives the wretched machine of the body bound together by skin, vital points, and veins.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which is partless yet possesses sixteen parts, devoid of the forms of mental construction, possessing all forms yet nothing at all.

We worship the Self of Consciousness, which resides in the heart, throat, and palate, reaches the tips of the eyebrows and nostrils, and abides in the vital breath characterized by its constant coming and going.
We worship the conscious self, which resides within the hollow of the heart-lotus, which encompasses the sheaths of all limbs, and which is the mirror for the spectacle of the worlds.
We worship the self of consciousness, which is without head, ends with the letter *ha*, is luminous, indivisible, and the ornament of all beings.

We worship the lamp of consciousness, which is both joined with and liberated from the flickering caused by the impact of the winds at the mouth of the channel that is the support for the oil of attachment, occurring within and without.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), which is the root-fiber of the lotus in the lake of the heart, which colors every limb, and which is the means of sustenance for all living beings.
We worship the Self of Consciousness— the nectar that is not to be taken away, which arose from the milk-ocean, which dwells within the heart of the moonless [sky], and which is Truth.
We worship the tranquil Self of consciousness, which has appeared through sound, form, taste, touch, and smell, yet is entirely devoid of those very things.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), which possesses great majesty, is unassailable by all creators, and, despite being the agent, is yet a non-agent in its true nature as an agent.
"All this is mine alone; everything is mine, yet I am not even 'I,' nor is anything else 'I.
For one who has realized this, the world is destroyed for me, or rather, it remains steadfast; thus, free from fever, I become."
The twelfth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Certainty regarding Liberation while Living," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus resolved, those great ones,
free from sin, abide happily in the state of peace where truth and untruth are equal.
Thus, the wise ones of perfected intellect, whose minds are equanimous and free from passion, neither deplore life nor rejoice in death.
Thus, possessing an inviolable charm like the arms of Nārāyaṇa,
they shone with unswerving forms like other Meru mountains.
They gazed upon the forest groves, islands, and cities,
as well as the rows of celestial gardens and the heavens, like gods.
They wandered upon the stone slabs of Mount Meru’s peaks, which were filled with flowers, delightful with the play of swings, and adorned with various forest groves.
They established kingdoms that had conquered their enemies, possessed fly-whisks and parasols, contained diverse wealth, and were characterized by wonderful conduct.
All these followed her in this world— this course of action characterized by various tastes and activities, whose undertakings are prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Adorned with enjoyments and luxuries, they sported in delightful groves that captivated the dances of women and were charming for recreation and dining.
And they roamed through the grounds of the Nandana grove, which were filled with beautiful mango trees, entwined with mandāra blossoms, and resounded with the songs of apsarases.
They dwelt, in due order, in household lives purified by right conduct, where all beings found rest and which were made formidable through the performance of sacrificial rites.
In those waves of the ocean of battle, where lordly elephants were being slaughtered, where countless arrows were whirling about, and which were terrifying with the booming roar of kettledrums.
They remained amidst all dualistic doctrines— those characterized by human anxieties, those that agitate the mind, and those that are fierce with the turbulence of passion.
But their minds are free from passion, devoid of limiting adjuncts, free from delusion,
unattached, supreme, peaceful, and have reached the highest state of pure being.
Today, even though great perils have repeatedly approached me from every side, I am not shaken at all,
like the principal mountain ranges amidst the lakes.
O scion of the Raghus, he shone with the most lovely Śrī, who sported like a playful woman, as the mass of waters does with the beauty of the full moon.
He did not wither under the parching heat of suffering, like a forest glade in summer;
nor did he rejoice in floods of enjoyments, like a medicinal herb at the touch of dewdrops.
For they, O Rāma, acting solely with undistracted focus within the cage of their duties, neither clung to nor abandoned the fruits of their actions, whether desired or undesired.
They did not rejoice upon the accomplishment of their tasks, nor did they sink when overcome by them; they did not exult at the attainment of happiness, nor did they wither even in times of distress.
They did not falter in delusions, nor did they sink into a succession of calamities;
they did not grieve with sorrow, nor did they weep like you in your grief.
Performing only those actions obtained through their natural conduct,
they remain free from agitation, like other Meru mountains.
Adopting that vision which destroys the sins of the descendants of Raghu,
and adorned by the absence of egoism, dwell here at your ease.
Seeing this succession of creations exactly as it truly is, remain steady like Mount Meru, deep as the ocean, and free from delusion.
All this is indeed pure consciousness alone, having come to appear in this manner;
here there exists nothing whatsoever, whether real or unreal, anywhere at all.

Relying fully upon this greatness and casting aside this world with indifference, O noble one, become one whose intellect is unattached everywhere and who brings about the destruction of worldly existence.
"Why do you weep with such intense agitation and grieve like a fool? You wander with a bewildered mind, O gentle one, like a blade of grass caught in a whirlpool."
Rāma: Oh, venerable one! Indeed, I perceive the true form [of reality] correctly. Through your grace, I am awakened, like a lotus by the contact of the sun.
My delusion has surely vanished like mist in autumn;
with all my doubts completely stilled, I shall carry out your word.

O virtuous one, since you have long since risen above yourself—having cast off intoxication and delusion, being freed from pride and envy, and having stilled your sorrow—you now speak with a clear and resolute mind that does not waver toward suffering; I shall do what you say without hesitation.
The thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Certainty of Liberation while Living," [spoken by] Rāma:
O Brahmin, when the dissolution of latent impressions arises through the play of right knowledge, tell me: how does one rest in the state of liberation while living?
Vasiṣṭha said:
The method for crossing over the cycle of existence is expressed by the word "yoga.
Know that it is of two kinds, characterized by the pacification of the mind.
Self-knowledge is declared to be one method for this [attainment] on earth;
the second is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa)—listen, as it is being described by me.
Rāma:
Because one is easy to attain and the other is free from suffering, which of these two is superior—
the knowledge of which, as soon as it is understood, prevents further agitation from afflicting me?
Vasiṣṭha:
Although both modes have been declared by the word "yoga," nevertheless, that which is conjoined with breath has attained a very firm conventional usage for this term.
Thus, yoga as well as knowledge are declared to be the two equal means for the process of crossing over saṃsāra,
both of which grant the same fruit.
For some, yoga is unattainable; for others, the certainty of knowledge.
But for me, O virtuous one, easy to discipline, the sequence born of knowledge is what is intended.
That which is known cannot become unknown again, even in dreams;
knowledge proceeds eternally in all states of being.

"Or perhaps yoga does not attain ease of practice because it must be accomplished through the locations for the seats of concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth; however, this alternative is not tenable."
"O descendant of Raghu, it is said that there are indeed only two types of yoga arising from effort—knowledge and action.
Of these, knowledge has been described to you as stainless, with the object of knowledge situated within."
Mounted upon the chariot of prāṇa and apāna, dwelling in the secret cave of the hidden body,
and bestowing infinite perfection— O virtuous one, listen, this is what is called yoga.
O Prince, when the cessation of the fluctuations caused by the breath of the mouth has occurred and the mind has reached its dissolution,
you shall dwell here in the supreme state, established in meditative absorption through the practice of yoga, with all fear dissolved.
The fourteenth canto, titled "An Inquiry into the Yoga of Knowledge," by Vasiṣṭha.
Indeed, within the infinite sky, there is supposedly this vibration in the form of the world, like a mirage in a desert.
There, Brahmā, born from the lotus, became the cause; he remained as the Grandfather, his mind reeling from the weight of the created beings.
I am his mind-born son, Vasiṣṭha, whose conduct is preeminent;
I dwell for each Yuga within the circle of the stars that revolves around the Pole Star.
Once, while I was staying in the assembly hall of Śatakratu in heaven,
I heard from Nārada and others the story of those who have lived for a very long time.
Then, during the course of a certain conversation,
a sage named Śātātapa— silent, dignified, and high-minded— spoke there.
In the sky situated in the northeast corner of Meru, upon a peak made of ruby,
there is a glorious wish-fulfilling tree known as Cūḍa.
At the top of that wish-fulfilling tree, within the hollow of its southern branch,
upon the tip of a golden creeper, there exists a bird's nest.
In that vast hollow dwelt a glorious crow named Bhusuṇḍa,
free from passion, like Brahmā in his own lotus.
Just as he lives here for a long time within the treasury of the world, so shall that long-lived one dwell in heaven; no such person has ever existed before, nor will there ever be again.
He is long-lived, he is free from disease, he is glorious, and he is of great intelligence; he is one whose mind is rested, he is peaceful, he is beloved, and he is skilled in the knowledge of time.
If one lives here as that bird lives,
then that life of men would be both long and truly inviolable.
Thus was that Bhusuṇḍa described in due detail by him, whose form is truth, when questioned again in the assembly of the gods.
Then, when the assembly of gods had departed and the occasion for conversation had subsided,
I went out of curiosity to see the bird Bhusuṇḍa.
Where Bhusuṇḍa was situated, there I reached in an instant that lofty peak of Meru, vast and composed of rubies.
With a brilliance like molten red chalk and the splendor of fire,
he colored the quarters of the sky as if with the essence of honeyed wine.
It was like a mountain massed with the flaming tongues of fire at the end of an eon,
with the smoke of sapphire stones darkening it and the sky reddened by its light.
He stood like a mountain for the mass of all passions,
and like a single dense mine for the entire web of twilight clouds.
As Meru undergoes its upward departure, the beautiful submarine fire— the digestive heat of the stomach— emerges through the Brahma-nāḍī and reaches his head.
Like a goddess of the Sumeru forest, she playfully extended her hand— its fingers like a crest— with its nails stained by fresh lac, as if to grasp the moon in the sky.
With garlands of reddish clouds like tongues of flame,
the sky seemed to throb as if it were about to depart, appearing like the submarine fire (vāḍava) situated upon a mountain.
With its rays like fingers, the stars seemed to touch the sky,
and with the tips of their shimmering rays as if they were fingernails, they seemed to kiss the heights.
With its chasms of shimmering jewel-stones and its golden caves radiant with light,
it was filled with the clouds of autumnal flower-pollen and the wandering Vidyādharas and immortals.
The mountain was a theater for a dance, where the wind blew through the sounding bamboos, the jeweled creepers were the dancing girls, and the thundering clouds served as the drums.
Rich with clusters of blossoming flowers and swarms of humming bees, it clearly appeared as if laughing aloud through its rows of petals, using its teeth as cymbals.
Where throngs of celestial nymphs sway like cradles, where passion and intoxication run wild,
where gods rest upon the rocks, and where mountain caves are occupied by pairs of lovers.
Wearing a bright garment of deerskin and the sacred thread of the Gaṅgā,
he stood like a tawny ascetic holding a bamboo staff.

Resounding with the roar of the Ganges' cascades, it contained celestial beings within its bower-like creepers; it was made beautiful by the songs of Gandharvas and sweetened by fragrant, pleasant breezes.
The tawny head of Maira, adorned with a crest of full-blown golden lotuses and decorated with stars like jewels, appeared as if it had reached the very limit of the sky.
With heaps of jewels and flowers in white, green, yellow, pale red, and white— the nine fresh colors—
it was fashioned by the Creator as a spotless, variegated pleasure-mountain for the world of celestial maidens.
In the Bhuśuṇḍa-episode, the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Summit of Mount Meru," Vasiṣṭha said:
Upon his head, whose locks of hair were like clouds filled with blossoms,
I beheld the arrival of the Kalpa standing like a circle of crests.
Enveloped by clouds of flower-pollen and bristling with clusters of jewels,
its height surpassing the sky, it was like one peak placed upon another.
With a flood of flowers twice as vast as the stars, with sprouts twice as abundant as clouds,
with dust twice as thick as the rays of light, and twice as golden as lightning.
In its peaks, it possessed the sound of bees doubled by the songs of *kiṃnarīs*,
and its beautiful creepers were made to double their swaying by the world of *apsarases* swinging on their swings.
It was filled with flocks of birds that surpassed even the hosts of Siddhas and Gandharvas;
its bark-garment was doubled by a clear frost that possessed the luster of jewels.
Its supreme and vast fruit is doubled by its embrace of the lunar orb;
its joints are doubled by clouds that are as silent and withdrawn as if they were in a state of meditative absorption.
Its trunks were entwined with fragrant creepers, kinnaras rested upon its leaves,
clouds cooed within its bowers, and the children of the gods slept by its marshy banks.
Having driven away the large bees that resembled her own form with the sounds of her bracelets,
she was surrounded by celestial nymphs who resembled female bees, holding flowers within their hands.
Accompanied by the foremost of the *suras*, *kinnaras*, *gandharvas*, and *vidyādharas*,
he reached a state that filled the sky like a forest pervading the world.
It possesses a dense network of buds, dense and tender shoots,
dense blossoming flowers, and is garlanded with dense fruits.
It was a dense mass of flower clusters, a thick cluster of jewels,
rich with garments and gems that were without gaps, and agitated by the blossoming of creepers.
Filled with flowers of every season, with fruits and sprouts of every season,
and with heaps of pollen from every fragrance, it has attained a state of supreme variety.
In its marshy banks, in its groves, in the leaves of its creepers, at its joints,
and upon its flowers, I saw birds nestled within their dwellings.
They were nourished by fragments of lotus stalks as delicate as portions of the moon, the lord of the night;
they were Brahman-swan-like beings whose food consisted of the roots of the lotuses growing in the navel of the Unborn.
They were the young swans for the chariot of Brahmā, singers of the Sāman chants, friends of the syllable Om and the Vedas, and consumers of the lotus-fibers of the Brahman-lake.
They vomited forth a multitude of mantras with the natural sound of the utterance "svāhā," resembling dark clouds composed of a dense mass of steady lightning.
Like gods who constantly drink clarified butter, they were like the shoots of the sacrificial altar; they were parrots, dark as the fire, young with crests as bright as the tips of peacock plumes.
The excellent peacocks of Kumāra, whose plumage was protected by Gaurī,
were experts in all the Śaiva sciences imparted by Skanda.
He saw the kinsmen of the great sky-birds, born and perished within the very heavens, who had built their nests there and possessed forms like autumnal clouds.
Others were born from the swan of Viriñca, others from Agniśuka,
others from the peacock of Kumāra, and others from the bird of Ambara.
Then there were two-beaked *bhāruṇḍa* birds, golden-crested birds,
sparrows, cranes, vultures, cuckoos, curlews, and roosters.
O Raghava, I saw there many other birds as well— peacocks, blue jays, cranes, and the like— as well as multitudes of living beings, like those upon the earth.
Then, while standing in the sky, I beheld from afar the southern branch of the tree, its leaves fully grown, as it remained suspended in the air.
With its circle of black crows and garlanded with clusters of blossoms,
it stood like a mass of clouds at the end of an eon in the forest of the Lokāloka mountain.
There, I saw as far as a single hollow in a tree trunk,
strewn with various flowers and filled with manifold fragrances.
Those who subsist on the offerings made to the dwellings of Śakra, Vāyu, Yama, Arka, and Indu, and those who utter auspicious cries at the women of the merit-makers in heaven; MU_6,15.26.
The crows stood in the assembly with undisturbed appearance,
like clouds dispersed by the wind that has been leveled by a gentle breeze.
Standing in their midst was the illustrious Bhusuṇḍa, of lofty form,
like a towering sapphire set in the center of pieces of fine glass.
With a fulfilled mind, free from pride, and beautiful in all his limbs,
he remains constantly inward-turned and happy through the focused observation of the movement of the vital breath.
Renowned as "Long-lived" because of that long life of his,
he was known throughout the world by the name Bhusuṇḍa, whose longevity was well-known to all.
His mind was matured by witnessing the conditions of the coming and passing away of the ages;
and he grew weary, counting the succession of Indras throughout every kalpa.
He is the rememberer of the past births of the world-protectors, of Viṣṇu, Indra, and Garuḍa, as well as of the gods, the asuras, and the kings.
With a serene and profound mind, his speech was elegant, gentle, and charming; he spoke without crookedness, was wise, free from possessiveness, and devoid of egoism.
A friend, one who is self-controlled, a companion, a servant, a son, a teacher, and a master— at all times, in every way, and eternally— all these are to be praised by everyone.
He is gentle, serene, sweet, flavorful, and great-souled; he is heart-pleasing, like a lake with unbroken coolness within.
He knows the workings within the hollow of the heart-lotus, never forsaking his transparent profundity, and possesses the glory of a manifest intention.
The sixteenth canto, named "The Vision of Bhusuṇḍa," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, with my body blazing, I descended before him,
causing a slight agitation in the assembly like a star falling from the sky onto a mountain.
The lake of blue lotuses at Vāyasa-āsthāna was agitated for a moment by the gentle breeze of my descent, like the ocean by an earthquake.
Immediately upon seeing him arrive unexpectedly,
Bhusuṇḍa realized, "This is Vasiṣṭha who has arrived."
He rose up from the heap of leaves like a young cloud from a mountain;
"O Sage, welcome," he said in sweet syllables.
With his two hands, which were produced by mere volition, the young cloud quickly offered me a handful of flowers, like a heap of gold.
When the leader of the crows had abandoned his attendants and, having said "This is the seat," brought forward a fresh garment from the wish-fulfilling tree; ||| MU_6,16.6 |||
When the birds had risen from the *bhuśuṇḍa* tree with their wings slightly fluttering,
they saw the sage seated there, his gaze directed toward his own seat.
Then, together with Bhusuṇḍa and his troop of monkeys,
I sat down upon a seat in that grove of wish-fulfilling creepers.
Then, having offered water for the feet and other honors, the highly effulgent Bhusuṇḍa, with a delighted mind, spoke to me in words sweet with affection.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"Oh! After a long time, the Blessed One has shown us his grace, since we, along with the trees, have been sprinkled by the nectar-dew of your vision."
O Sage, most worthy of honor, impelled now by the long-accumulated store of my merit, from where have you come?
I hope that, while you have long dwelt in this great delusion,
your equanimity remains entirely unbroken within your pure mind.
Why have you troubled yourself with the hardship of coming here today?
You ought to grant us your command, for we are desirous of hearing your words.
O Sage, by the mere sight of your feet, everything has been understood by me;
we have been brought together by you through the merit of your arrival.
Through our discussions on long life, we have come to your memory;
therefore, you have now sanctified this tree with your feet.
O Sage, although the scripture is thus already known to you, I ask you this here because a longing for the taste of the nectar of your words is expanding within me.
Having spoken thus, that long-lived bird Bhusuṇḍa,
who perceives the stainless reality of the three periods of time, said this to me there.
Vasiṣṭha:
O great king of birds, what you say is true;
I have come today specifically to see you, the long-lived one.
With a heart cooled within, by good fortune you are well;
O pure-souled one, you have not fallen into the terrifying snare of worldly existence.
Therefore, O Blessed One, cut through this doubt of mine according to the truth:
in what family were you born, and how did you come to know all that is to be known?
O virtuous one, how long is your lifespan, what conduct do you remember, or by whom— some far-sighted being— was this dwelling place of yours pointed out?
Bhusuṇḍa said: O Sage, I shall tell you all that you ask;
this story of ours should be heard by a high-souled one without agitation.
When great beings of noble intellect like you— whose forms are worthy of worship by the lords of the three worlds— listen to what has been spoken,
that evil perishes through its proclamation, just as the heat of the sun is dispelled by the power of a cloud’s body.
The seventeenth canto, named "The Meeting with Bhusuṇḍa," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, O Rāma, that Bhusuṇḍa was neither overjoyed nor dejected;
he was dark-complexioned and beautiful in every limb, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
His speech was smooth and profound, and he always addressed others with a smile;
he weighed the three worlds like a merchant weighing goods on a scale held in his hand.
Having viewed all things as if they were blades of grass, having made the cycle of existence an object of his knowledge,
and having seen the state of worldly flux and agitation, he has realized both the higher and the lower.
Steadfast and of stable appearance, like Mount Mandara at rest;
full, even, and pure, like the unagitated, full ocean.
With his intellect resting upon the ultimate state, tranquil and reeling with supreme bliss,
he is the knower of the manifestation and disappearance of those born in saṃsāra.
Delightful in form with his impetuous speech, possessing words that are affectionate, sweet, appropriate, beautiful, and heart-pleasing,
he is like a new body assumed by himself— the supreme excellence who removes all fear.

With pure speech, with laughter-cleansed words, and with gentle steps free from agitation, he gradually began to relate his entire true nature, like a charming cloud expressing itself through sweet thunder.
The eighteenth canto, titled "The Description of Bhusuṇḍa," [spoken by] Bhusuṇḍa:
In this world, there exists the eldest of all the inhabitants of heaven,
the God of gods named Hara, who is worshipped by the God of gods.
She whose eyes were like rows of bees and whose breasts were like high clusters of blossoms was like a graceful creeper clinging to half the body of a mango tree.
The Gaṅgā, white as snow and nectar, entwined with clusters of waves and coiled upon his mass of matted hair, is his garland of flowers.
Born from the ocean of milk, with streams of nectar flowing forth,
the glorious moon— the reflected moon— is his crest-jewel.
He who was rendered immortal by the flow from the moon upon his head, for whom the *kālakūṭa* poison is an ornament on his neck like sapphire; (6.18.5)
For him, the white ash— produced from fire, pure,
a collection of atoms, and like a great whirlpool of dust— is the water for his ritual bath.
Even his bones are stainless jewels, surpassing the moon in brilliance; they have been polished and fashioned, and they possess a radiant luster within his very body.
Whose garment is the sky, which is as dark blue as a mass of clouds, possesses cool foliage in the form of the ten directions, and is variegated with the dots of stars.

The courtyard of his house was filled with wandering female jackals and crowded with cooked offerings of great meat and rice; yet the home of that man of abundant prosperity appeared as white as snow, like a cremation ground.
Adorned with garlands of skulls, drinking yellow and red juices and spirits,
and draped with wreaths of entrails— such are his kinsmen and mothers.
Whose bracelets were serpents with smooth bodies and the luster of shining gold, their crest-jewels flickering as they moved.
His conduct as Bhairava, which terrified even the gods in play, was intent on devouring the world, by the mere glance of whose eye the lord of mountains was consumed.
He who has restored the living beings of the world to health, whose mind remains fixed on its own natural function,
and for whom the mere movement of his hand by chance brought about the destruction of the cities of the Asuras.
Those who are single-minded in form, free from affection, passion, and hatred—
those kinsmen of his are like mountains, being both full of moisture and yet devoid of sap.
Whose attendants—the Pramathas—have heads, hooves, trunks, and tusks; arms, bellies, and faces like those of bears, camels, goats, and snakes, and who sportively play with him.
Of that Lord of the Immortals, whose face is resplendent with three eyes,
the other retinue consists of the Mothers, just like his hosts of attendants.
The Mothers dance before him, bowed down by hosts of spirits;
they are the sole consumers of the infinite multitudes of beings belonging to the fourteen classes.
With faces like those of donkeys, camels, and crows, drinking blood, fat, and marrow,
they wander about naked, wearing garlands made of the limbs of corpses.
They dwell upon mountain peaks, in the sky, and in other worlds;
they reside in forests, in cremation grounds, and within the bodies of embodied beings.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā— these,
who belong to the leftward current, are dependent upon Tumburu and Rudra.
Siddhā, Śuṣkā, Raktā, and Utpalā are the deities who,
resorting to the right stream, take refuge in Bhairava Rudra.
Of all these Mothers, these eight are indeed the leaders;
following them are other goddesses by the hundreds of thousands.
Raudrī, Vaiṣṇavī, Brāhmī, Vārāhī, as well as Vāyavī,
Kaumārī, Vāsavī, Saurī, and so forth— these [powers] exist by the thousands.
Following these, however, are other supreme goddesses who move through the sky,
originating from gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, humans, and asuras.
Following them, however, there stand tens of millions of other earth-dwelling beings known by the name Rūpikās, who subsist upon men on this earth.
Horses, elephants, donkeys, crows, camels, pythons, monkeys,
and other such mounts were used by these women as they roamed throughout the three worlds.
Some among them followed the ways of cattle, remaining fixed in trivial actions; others, having known what is to be known, stood in the state of liberation while living.
O Leader of Sages, O Giver of Honor, among those highly esteemed mothers, there exists one renowned as Mātā Alambuṣā.
And Vajrāśrituṇḍa, known as Caṇḍa, resembles a mountain of sapphire;
his vehicle is a crow, just as Garuḍa is that of Vaiṣṇavī.
Thus, those Mothers, endowed with the eight sovereign powers and characterized by fierce deeds,
once came together and held a gathering in the sky.
Having worshipped the two gods Tumburu and Bhairava, who are worthy of worship by the entire world,
they engaged in conversations of manifold meaning, gratified by the wine of blood.
Then, in the course of their conversation, this topic arose:
"Does the Lord Umāpati look upon us with indifference?"
We shall display our power to him so that he, having seen our great might, will not treat us with contempt.
Having thus resolved, those goddesses, with focused attention, brought Umā herself under their control and sprinkled her, whose face and limbs had turned pale.
The goddesses turned her— whose hair was disheveled, who had been snatched from her husband’s side by illusion, and who had met her destruction— into a ball of cooked rice.
On that day of Pārvatī’s consecration, a great festival took place there for all of them, enchanting with dance and song.
Others danced with unrestrained clamor, naked as the sky,
their hips and bellies revealed by the wide flinging of their long limbs.
Others laughed with unrestrained, loud shouts and deep roars,
their limbs quivering with agitation, while the forest resounded with the noise of ḍamaru drums.
Others, gratified by the drinking bout, sang with loud voices within the hollows of the sounding mountain caves,
as if in the interior of the world-tent where the drums were resonating.
Others drank their fill, chewing upon the moist heads and hooves of their prey,
while the hollows of the sky resounded with the playful *ghur-ghur* noise of their jaws.
They drank, they rose up on high, they crossed over, they arrived, they stayed, they laughed, they filled [the space], they offered oblations, they fell, they leaped aloft;
they danced incessantly and ate savory meat—the goddesses, dancing with wild abandon, brought the three worlds to a state of upheaval.
The nineteenth canto, titled "Description of the Discourse on the Mother," [spoken by] Bhusuṇḍa:
While this festival was thus proceeding, their excellent steeds likewise became intoxicated; they laughed, they danced, and they even drank blood.
There, in one place, the white swans of Brahmā’s chariot, intoxicated by the wine of their beloveds, danced in the sky; and the crow was the charioteer of Alambuṣā.
As the female swans danced and drank the wine,
their passion arose perfectly, like the tide upon the shores of the ocean.
Then all those female swans, having conceived passion and being intoxicated, took their pleasure one by one with that crow named Caṇḍa.
This crow was the beloved of seven young female swans; he took his pleasure with them one by one until each had attained their mutual desire.
Then those queens, having conceived, became exceedingly joyful; and the goddesses, having performed their dance, attained a state of perfect tranquility and freedom from intoxication.
The goddesses of great illusion offered Umā, who had become food and was dear to the Lord, as a meal for the wielder of the trident.
When the moon-crested Lord learned that she had said, "My dear [gave] food to me," he became enraged toward the group of Mothers.
Then, having brought her forth once more through the gift of their own limbs,
they gave Pārvatī again in marriage to the Moon-crested Lord.
Then the goddesses, Hara himself, and their respective retinues,
all with contented minds, departed each toward his or her own direction.
O Lord of Sages, those divine swans became pregnant; they then related to the divine Brāhmī the account of events exactly as it had occurred.
"O calves, my cows are now pregnant; you too are no longer capable of the work of drawing the chariot. Therefore, wander about freely for now."
Having thus dismissed the female swans, who were sluggish due to their pregnancy, the goddess Brāhmī, devoted to compassion, remained at her ease in unwavering meditative absorption.
Then, O Lord of Sages, those royal swans, languid from pregnancy, wandered within the lotus-pond of Brahmā that had arisen from his navel-lotus.
Thus, when their embryos had matured, those women gave birth upon the petals of the navel-lotuses to soft eggs, just as creepers produce sprouts.
When their time had arrived, those twenty-one eggs there split into two by the entry of the embryo, like cosmic eggs filled with essence.
"O Sage, it is from those very eggs that we were born—
these twenty-one crows, brothers born of Caṇḍa."
Born upon that lotus petal, they grew to maturity; having developed their wings, they became capable of soaring through the sky.
Then the Blessed Lady Brāhmī, together with her mothers who were like female swans,
having long propitiated [the Lord] correctly and being fully withdrawn in meditative concentration, remained there.
Then, at that time, the Blessed Lady herself, intent upon her grace,
favored our limbs in such a way that we remain liberated.
Having resolved, "We shall remain in a secluded place, our minds fully satisfied and tranquil, established in meditation," we went to the side of our father.
Then, embraced by our father, we were honored by Alambusā;
having been seen by her with favor, we remained there, self-restrained.
Caṇḍaka:
My sons, have you truly emerged from this net of saṃsāra, which is woven together by the threads of limitless latent dispositions?
If we do not [succeed], then let us entreat this Blessed One, who is so kind to her servants,
so that you may become those who have reached the further shore of knowledge.
The crows said:
"Father, by the grace of the Goddess Brāhmī, that which is to be known has been fully known;
however, we desire an excellent place for dwelling in solitude."
Caṇḍaka said:

Listen, my sons who desire a nest; I shall proclaim this supreme, most stable, and purifying place, free from defects. Dwell there for a long time, fully satisfied and without fear, where all activity has been stilled and delusion and fear have departed. MU 6,19.26.
The twentieth chapter, named "The Origin of Bhusuṇḍa," and the fierce [twenty-first] chapter.
There exists a mountain named Meru, the support for all collections of jewels and the refuge of all the gods, possessing immeasurable and great height.
The pillar of this pavilion of the universe, constructed of gold, supports the moving lamps of the sun and moon and has the multitude of living beings as its wife.
With its golden moon-stone for its jewel, its peaks for its fingers,
and its surrounding islands and oceans for its bracelets, it was like an arm raised up from the earth.
Surrounded by the neighboring mountain ranges, seated upon the throne of Jambudvīpa,
the king caused his eyes, like the sun and moon, to wander through the assembly of mountains.
He possesses a garland of jasmine flowers that is a flood of stars; he is the sole garment for the ten directions;
his self is supported by the pair of serpents; and he is the ornament of the lord of heaven.
He was fanned on all sides by beautiful women from every quarter, who served as ornaments to the city,
with thick yak-tail whisks that were cool and dripping with water droplets.
His feet, extending sixteen thousand yojanas below the earth, are worshipped by various asuras and great serpents.
His body, eighty thousand yojanas in extent, has the sun and moon for eyes;
he is worshipped by the inhabitants of heaven—the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
Just as relatives depend upon a householder, so do beings of fourteen kinds subsist upon him, who has not previously seen their mutual abode.
In the northeastern direction of this mountain, however, there exists a great peak made of ruby,
like another sun risen from the horizon.
Upon his back stands a great wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), surrounded by a multitude of beings,
appearing like a reflection in the mirror of the world’s summit.
On its right shoulder there is a branch with golden shoots,
densely covered with clusters of jewels, and bearing excellent fruit that has the luster of the moon's orb.
There, O sons, I had previously built a nest of shimmering jewels where, it is said, I used to take my delight while the Goddess sat absorbed in meditation.
It was covered with petals of jewel-flowers, endowed with fruits that were elixirs,
and its courtyards were fashioned with rods of wish-fulfilling gems.
It was completely filled with young crows whose behavior was guided by intelligence;
its interior was cool and pleasant, and it was strewn with heaps of flowers.
Therefore, go to your nest, which is difficult even for the inhabitants of heaven to reach;
staying there, you shall attain enjoyment and liberation without obstacle.
Having said this, our father there kissed us and embraced us,
and he gave that meat which had been brought for the Goddess to us as well.
Having eaten that and having paid homage at the feet of the goddess and our father,
we leaped from that place, the marsh of the Vindhya mountains, away from Ālambusa.
Gradually traversing the sky and emerging from the hollows of the clouds,
they ascended the mass of wind and paid homage to the celestial wanderers.
"O Lord of Sages, having left behind the Lord of Day (the Sun) and departed from the city of the other world, we have passed beyond heaven and reached the world of Brahmā."
Having first offered salutations, he immediately reported those words of his father exactly as they were to his mother, to the Blessed One, and to Brāhmī.
Having been embraced affectionately by those two and encouraged by their command, "Go," we offered our salutations and departed from the world of Brahmā.
Having leaped over the cities of the world-protectors, they move through the sky, radiant as the sun, fickle, and traveling upon the mass of wind.
"O Sage, having obtained this wish-fulfilling tree and entered our own nest, we remain established in silence, free from all affliction."

Just as we were born, and how we have come to this state, and how our minds have attained peace through the realization of awakening—this has been fully and flawlessly told by me to you. O Great-Souled One, instruct me with what remains.
The twenty-first canto, titled "The Attainment of the Ālaya," concerning Bhusuṇḍa.
In a former aeon, there once existed a world that has long been forgotten; it was by this very same arrangement that it exists today, though now it is exceedingly remote.
O Lord of Sages, this account has been described by me through practice while living in the present, for the sake of awakening, as one who formerly perceived the equality of the world.
Today my merits, accumulated over a long time, have borne fruit,
O Sage, since I behold you thus without any obstacle.
This nest, these branches, this tree, and I myself—
today all these have attained purification through the sight of you.
"O Sage, having accepted this water for honor and this water for the feet, offered according to my means, and having surely rendered them pure, instruct me with what remains."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, when that bird Bhusuṇḍa had spoken thus and had personally offered me water for my hands and feet once more, I spoke as follows."
O Lord of Birds, why are those brothers of yours—not possessing such courage and great intelligence—no longer seen here? For you alone are seen.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
O Sage, a great length of time has passed for us here;
O Sinless One, successions of ages have been exhausted like days.
In this much time, all my younger brothers,
having cast off their bodies like blades of grass, have been transformed into the supreme Śiva.
Even those who are long-lived, great, prosperous, and powerful— all are swallowed up by Time, whose nature is beyond reckoning.
Vasiṣṇṭha: My dear son, as the masses of wind, carrying the sun and moon upon their shoulders, blow incessantly with great speed, I hope you are not distressed?
O dear one, how is it that you are not distressed by the rays of the sun, which have long been in close proximity and have burnt the forest groves on the great mountains of sunrise and sunset?
Moreover, my dear, I hope you are not distressed by the cool rays of the moon, which have turned the water into stone as they draw closer?
O father, how is it that you are not distressed by these circles of clouds at the end of the aeon, which rest here incessantly and whose mists can be cut down even by axes?
Established in such a high state, how is it that this lofty wish-fulfilling tree does not tremble amidst the violent agitations of the world?
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"O Brahmin, this life of a bird among all living beings is without support or foundation, despised by the whole world, and utterly trivial."
That her dwelling was ordained by the Creator in such remote and solitary forests, or in the empty expanse of the sky-path—how strange! (MU 6.21.17)
O Lord, how can there be freedom from sorrow for one born in this world, living indeed with life, yet bound by the snares of hope— like a bird?
But we, O Blessed One, are always endowed with contentment in our own selves;
we are never deluded by the formless delusions of the world.
Content with our own nature alone, freed from hardships and from purposeful exertions,
O Brahman, we merely pass the time here in our own abode.
We do not obstruct the body’s life nor its death;
we remain just as it remains, with all our desires set at rest.
The state of the world has been observed, and various illustrative perspectives have been seen;
surely our flickering body has now been abandoned by the mind.
In the light of my own innate radiance, which is free from passion and eternally devoid of distress,
I always perceive the movement of the smallest units of time within the expanse of the eon.
O Brahman, in this house of the wish-fulfilling vine, richly illuminated by clusters of jewels,
I perceive unbroken time through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Even though day and night are unknown here upon this lofty mountain peak,
I discern through my own intellect the progression of time and the state of the world.
O Sage, through awakening, your mind has come to rest; having distinguished the essential from the non-essential, it has become tranquil and free from all agitation.
I do not fall into helplessness through the snares of hope arising from worldly affairs in saṃsāra— snares that are unreal— which are like the cries of a ground-crow.
Beholding the world’s illusion with an intellect that is cool with light and whose nature is supreme tranquility, we have attained steadfastness.
O one of great intelligence, even when terrible conditions arrive in their proper sequence, those whose minds are unshakable do not tremble, remaining like stones.
This worldly condition, though pleasant at its inception and yet flickering, is repeatedly scrutinized; herein, nothing whatsoever is real.
O Blessed One, all these nets of elemental beings surely depart and may or may not return; what cause for fear is there for us in this?
As the river of worldly existence, with its waves of the net of elemental beings, enters the ocean of time, we remain undisturbed, standing upon its bank.
We do not let go, nor do we grasp; we neither stand, nor are we stationary.
Though gentle, we are exceedingly cruel while remaining upon this tree.
We have been favored by you, the best of men, who are free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue; being satisfied with us, you have established us in a state free from all feverish distress.
O Blessed One, our mind is neither tossed here and there nor agitated in its functions; it has not failed to grasp the reality of the ultimate truth.
When our own self has become tranquil— changeless, free from agitation, and having attained peace—
we are full and waveless, like great oceans on a full-moon day.
O Brahmin, because of your arrival, our hearts are now filled with joy;
all our desires have borne fruit, and we have attained supreme fulfillment.
Whom indeed does the moonlight of association with the virtuous not delight? It consists of the essence of elixirs, it is cooling, and it bestows supreme bliss. (MU 6.21.38)
By what can this essence of bliss born from the company of the virtuous be compared?
It is that by which the Ocean of Milk, its waters churned by Mount Mandara, is surpassed.
I consider nothing to be more beneficial for myself than this:
that the virtuous follow one who has abandoned all desires.
What is obtained from enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight?
From the wish-fulfilling gem of association with the virtuous, every essence is obtained.
With speech that is smooth, deep, gentle, sweet, noble, and steady,
you alone act as a bee within this lotus-bud of the three worlds.

O Holy One, I believe that even for one who has realized the Supreme Self, this birth today has become fruitful through the sight of you, which has pacified my misdeeds; for the company of the virtuous removes all fear.
The twenty-second canto, titled "The Description of the True Nature of Bhusuṇḍa," begins with Bhusuṇḍa:
During the terrible upheavals of the ages and amidst violent, turbulent winds, this Kalpavṛkṣa remains perfectly steady; it never trembles.
This tree is inaccessible even to all beings who dwell in other worlds;
therefore, we abide happily in this lord of the forest.
When Hiraṇyākṣa swiftly seized the surface of the earth, encircled by the seven continents, even then the tree did not tremble.
When the divine mountain, its body swaying,
leaped from all sides, even then the tree did not tremble.
When Nārāyaṇa, who caused Mount Meru to bend by the pressure of his arms,
lifted up Mount Mandara, even then the tree did not tremble.
When the winds of portent blew, uprooting the rocks of the great mountains and shaking the very voice of Mount Meru,
even then that tree did not tremble.
When the world was violently agitated by the upheaval of the gods and asuras, causing the orbs of the moon and sun to tremble, even then the tree did not shake.
When the rows of clouds at the end of an aeon fell, shaken by the winds from the caves of the mountains tossing upon the milk ocean, even then the tree did not tremble.
When Mount Meru stood on all sides within the arms of Kālanemi, having been slightly uprooted, even then the tree did not tremble.
When the winds from the wings of the Lord of Birds blew during the struggle for the seizure of the nectar,
even as the Siddhas were falling, the tree did not tremble.
When Garuḍa went forth, dragging the remainder of its form because it had not yet completed its single coil, then the tree did not tremble.
When the flames of the fire at the end of the aeon, surging with mountains and oceans,
were cast aside by the hoods of Śeṣa, even then the tree did not tremble.
For those who dwell upon such a preeminent tree as this, O tiger among sages, whence could there be calamities? For it is indeed through instability that calamities arise for us.
Vasiṣṭha: O one of great intelligence, when at the ends of the kalpas the fire, water, and wind are surging forth,
and when the suns are thus scorching, how do you remain free from fever?
Bhusuṇḍa said:
When the activity of the end of the aeon approaches the stability of the world,
I then abandon my nest, like an ungrateful man leaving a true friend.
I abide in space alone, free from all conceptual construction,
with every limb motionless yet extended, like a mind devoid of latent impressions.
When the suns blaze forth, turning the mountains into liquid,
then, having fixed the Vāruṇī concentration, I remain with a steady mind.
When the winds of dissolution blow, shattering the great lords of mountains,
I remain motionless in the sky, having bound the mountain-like concentration (pārvatī-dhāraṇā).
When the world, including Mount Meru and all else, has dissolved and becomes a single ocean,
one should then bind the concentration on air and float in the sky with an unwavering mind.
Having reached the far shore of the cosmic egg at the end of the principles, in that stainless state,
I remain for as long as necessary in the state of deep sleep, with an immovable form.
Furthermore, as long as the Lotus-born remains engaged in the work of creation,
I shall enter the cosmic egg and remain there in the abode of birds.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Lord of Birds, why is it that other yogins do not remain as you do, unbroken by the powers of concentration even at the end of the kalpas?"
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"O Brahmin, this destiny of the Supreme Lord is indeed difficult to transcend; I must indeed be as I am, and others must be as they are."
It is impossible to weigh the inevitability of what must happen;
for whatever occurs in such a way, it is indeed the certain nature of intrinsic being (svabhāva).
By the power of my own resolve alone, in kalpa after kalpa, again and again,
this tree comes into being in this very manner upon the peak of this mountain.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O leader of birds, you shall indeed be exceedingly long-lived,
a hero endowed with knowledge and discernment, whose mental course is fit for yoga."
O auspicious lady, having witnessed the assembly of many various minor creations, what wonders do you remember in these three worlds?
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"I remember this earth below, which is as rough as a massive mountain rock, devoid of grass and creepers, and lacking the multitude of mountains, forests, and trees."
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
I remember this earth below, filled with a heavy burden of ashes.
I remember the earth below when the lords of the days had not yet arisen, when the orb of the moon was unborn, and when the light of day was undivided.
With its hollows half-revealed by the radiance from the slopes of its jewel-meru,
I recall the world as being like the primordial mountain Lokāloka.
I recall the gods fleeing in all directions, like men dying in the great battle against the asuras.
I remember this earth, which for fifty cycles of four ages was held by the intoxicated Kāśis, the Asuras, as their inner palace.
I meditate upon this hut of the world, whose interior is utterly secluded from the entire circle of asuras, and which remains as the sole remnant of the three unborn deities.
I remember this earth during the final half of the four ages, dense with thick trees and devoid of the creation of men, unseen by human eyes.
In this way, I remember this earth as being joined with dense, immovable [mountains] for more than four yugas, a time when the conduct of people had not yet begun.

I remember that hut of the world, where the six-faced one was yet unborn, where the gods were terrified by the intoxicated Tāraka, and which was overflowing with the victory of the faction of the Daityas.
I remember this earth, marked in its center by the pillar of Mount Meru, submerged up to its neck in a flood of water for three cycles of four yugas.
I remember the sky as being composed of darkness, where all the Vaimānika gods had vanished out of fear, and where the stars, the moon, and the sun were absent.
When the great Vindhya mountain was intoxicated and had reached the state of being a single mountain, swallowing the region of Agastya and making the world a mere hut, I remember that time.
I remember these and many other such events;
what is the use of speaking at length? Hear the essential point in brief.
O Brahmin, I remember hundreds of incalculable Manus who have passed away, as well as numerous creations and hundreds of cycles of the four ages.
I remember a creation consisting of a single deity, pure, devoid of humans and asuras, containing three worlds and a single heaven.
I remember a certain creation involving a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor while intoxicated, a Śūdra who has forbidden liquor, and a virtuous wife who has many husbands.
I remember a certain creation in which the world was so densely covered with trees that it seemed like solid ground, where there were no oceans, and where beings were born as men in heaven.
I remember a certain creation that was without mountains and without ground, where gods and humans stood in the sky, and which was not enriched by the light of the moon or the sun.
I remember a certain creation that was without Indra, without a great king, without middle or extremes, and without superior or inferior, in which all directions were equal.
At the division of time at the beginning of creation, within the three worlds,
there is the manifestation of gods and asuras, and the emergence of the circles of continents and oceans.
The configuration of the principal mountain ranges, their distinct locations within Jambudvīpa,
the perception of color and phenomena, and the division of creation according to the arrangement of the mandala.

The configuration of the circle of stars, the very construction of the Pole Star (Dhruva), the birth of the Moon, the Sun, and other celestial bodies, and the established positions of Indra and Upendra; [all these were created by him].
The seizing of Hiraṇyākṣa, the lifting of the earth by the Boar,
the establishment of kings, and likewise the bringing back of the Vedas.
The shaking of Mount Mandara and the churning of the ocean for the sake of the nectar; the birth of Garuḍa before his wings had grown, and the origin of the oceans.
O dear one, those memories which follow the sequence of very recent past events are remembered even by children; why then should there be such insistence on them?

I, whose life is unmeasured, have conceived Him who has Garuḍa as His vehicle and who has no vehicle other than Garuḍa; Him who has a white vehicle and who has a dark vehicle; Him who has a noble bull as His vehicle and who has no bull as His vehicle.
The twenty-third canto, titled "The Narration of the Life Story of Cirajīvin," by Bhusuṇḍa.
Then, O Blessed One, among those born in the world after you— namely Bharadvāja, Pulastya, Atri, Nārada, Indra, and Marīci— ...
Among Pulaha, Uddālaka, and others, as well as among Kratu, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras;
and among Sanatkumāra, Bhṛṅgīśa, Skanda, the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa), and so forth—
In Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Gāyatrī, and many others;
on Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, Dardura, and so forth.
Among Hayagrīva, Hiraṇyākṣa, Kālanemi, Bala, and others; among Hiraṇyakaśipu, Kratha, Baḍi, Prahlāda, and others.
In the playful dalliances of Nimi, Aṅga, Pṛthu, Protha, Vainya,
Nābhāga, Nala, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, and others;
Among Ātreya, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Vatsa, Vātsyāyana, and others;
among Upamanyu, Manīṣin, Maṅkin, Bhagīratha, Śuka, and others.
When [events] occurred only a short time ago, or when they were somewhat distant,
or even in the creations of today— what counting can there be for such things in memory?
O Sage, this is indeed the eighth birth of you, the Son of Brahmā;
I remember that in this eighth creation, you were united with me.
Sometimes you are born from the sky, sometimes you are born from water;
sometimes you are born from a mountain, and sometimes you are born from fire.
Whatever this creation is— whatever its conduct, whatever its configuration and its range of directions— I remember three other creations exactly like it.
I remember ten creations, consisting of gods and humans, whose conduct was entirely uniform in form, and who possessed stability throughout their entire duration for the same length of time.
The gods have vanished; they were raised up for five days, O Sage, like tortoises from the ocean during five creations.
I remember this twelfth [event]: the churning of the ocean of nectar, which threw the gods and asuras into utter confusion by the force of Mandara being pulled [as the churning-stick].
Hiraṇyākṣa dragged the earth down to the underworld three times, like a crocodile seizing an offering endowed with the essence of all medicinal herbs from the riverbank.
Having become the son of Reṇukā, Hari brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas for the sixth time, even across the interval of many creations.
O Leader of Sages, I remember that for a hundred Kali Yugas, the state of being a Buddha was attained by Hari solely through his birth as the Śākya King.
I remember thirty disturbances of the three cities, two destructions of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and ten instances of Śukra’s defeat, all performed by the Moon-crested Lord.
For the sake of the arrow, I remember the eight leaders of the fever-demons who agitated the hosts of the gods in the battle between Hari and Śarva.
O Sage, I remember the Vedas as being endowed with a variety of ritual components and recitations, due to the deficiency or excess of the intellects of men in every age.
O sinless one, my Purāṇas— focussed, complete, and rich in recitations— are being promulgated anew for each Yuga, with their meanings revealed.
Furthermore, I remember those very same ones, as well as others of the same kind, throughout age after age— these histories composed by divine sages and brahmins.
I remember another most wonderful history called the Rāmāyaṇa,
measuring one hundred thousand verses, which is a true scripture of knowledge.
"One should behave like Rāma, not like the dissolute Rāvaṇa"—
whereby such wisdom places knowledge in one's hand like a fruit.
This was composed by Vālmīki, and he will compose it again now;
today it remains unmanifest in the world, but in time people will come to know it.
By that very same soul named Vālmīki, or by another, this [work]—
which had been forgotten— is now being composed for the twelfth time, remaining unimpaired.
I remember a second work of his, equal in merit, named the Bhārata, composed by Vyāsa in a former age, which has now been forgotten in the world.
By the soul named Vyāsa, and likewise by another, this [work] was preserved unimpaired;
yet now, having been forgotten, it is being composed for the seventh time.
O Lord of Sages, I remember the narrative scriptures, revealed in each age with their various arrangements.
Furthermore, O virtuous one, I behold and remember those very same things, as well as others, in each successive age, amidst the multitude of objects.
For the destruction of the Rākṣasas, Viṣṇu will now undergo his eleventh incarnation, known by the name Rāma.
O Lord of Sages, for the sake of removing the burden of the earth, this will now be the sixteenth birth of Viṣṇu in the house of Vasudeva.
With his man-lion body, Hari struck Hiraṇyakaśipu three times, like a lion strikes an elephant.
This delusion of the three worlds is never non-existent,
yet it is never truly existent, persisting like a bubble upon water.
This undesirable delusion of the visible world, residing within the consciousness in the Self,
arises and dissolves instantly, as flickering as a wave in the water.
I remember the three worlds as having many uneven arrangements, some with uniform structures, and others appearing half-equal in form.
I remember those very same deeds and such other conducts of mine, as well as those other beings here who performed similar actions.

O Brahmin, at the end of every Manvantara, when the sequence of the world has been overturned, when its arrangement has become otherwise, and when the people have passed away as described; MU_6,23.37.
My other friends are indeed different, and your kinsmen are likewise different; my new servants are different, and my patrons are also different.

At times I dwelt in solitude at the foot of the Vindhya mountains, taking refuge among the creepers; at other times I took refuge among the creepers of the wish-fulfilling trees on the peaks of Mount Meru.
At times he has his abode on Mount Sahya, at times on Mount Dardura; at times he dwells in the Himalayas, and at times he takes refuge in the Malaya mountains.
Sometimes, reaching a mountain, a forest, a tree, or a branch with its former very same configuration, I build my nest.
O Leader of Sages, even as infinite ages have passed since then,
this tree has grown with its very same ancient configuration.
While my father was alive, this city possessed such splendor that,
having been established long ago by him, I have remained here with it.
In the past, this northern quarter did not exist, nor did this mountain;
previously, the northern direction was quite different, as was Mount Meru.
Having reached the arrival of the night of Brahman within the form of each individual body,
at the end of my meditation, while remaining in the sky, I perceive this creation and thus know it.
Because of the movement of the stars starting from the sun, and because of the fixed positions of Meru and so forth, the configuration of the directions would be otherwise;
for while that [system] remains as it is, the directions proceed in a different manner.
I consider the world to be neither existent nor non-existent; this is merely an illusion of the intellect.
This manifestation of the power of the self’s own vibration unfolds.
I remember how sons have become fathers, friends likewise have become enemies, and men have attained the state of women— and this has happened hundreds of times.

O Lord of Sages, I recall that in the Kali age one follows the practices of the Kṛta age, and in the Kṛta age one observes the conditions of the Kali age; this is likewise true for the Tretā and Dvāpara ages.
I remember certain creations here and there, in which those who had not seen the Vedas or their meanings dwelt according to their own conventions, and whose conduct was unrestrained.
