O Brahman, while I was absorbed in meditation upon Brahman, I remember two thousand cycles of four yugas during which the world, including its gods, asuras, and humans, was empty.

I remember, throughout the days of Brahmā, all those regions with their diverse specific configurations, whose storehouses of beings were busily engaged in various activities, and whose inhabitants possessed diverse arrangements, charms, and attire.
The twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Creation Long Past," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, O mighty-armed one, that best of crows was questioned by me once again for the sake of inquiry, while [I was] at the tip of the creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree.
O King of Birds, how is it that death does not afflict the body of those who move about within the treasury of the world, even while engaged in worldly affairs?
Bhusuṇḍa said:
O omniscient Brahman, although you already know [the answer], you ask me out of a desire to know; for masters always incite their servants to speak.
Nevertheless, I shall explain to you that which you ask me;
for they say that not violating the command [of the teacher] is the primary way of honoring the virtuous.
Death does not seek to slay him in whose heart the continuous thread of latent impressions (vāsanā) has not been strung together with the pearls of the defects (doṣa).
Death does not seek to slay him whom mental agonies do not pierce— agonies that are saws to the tree of trust and woodworms to the creeper of the body.
Death does not seek to slay him whose mind is not fickle, like a monkey that has leaped from one bush to another and is no longer agitated.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the floods of serpents that are bodies, nor the crests of the fire that is the mind, nor the quarters of space burn within.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the serpent of greed— whose abode is the cave of his own mind and whose flood consists of the poison of passion and hatred— does not devour.
Death does not seek to slay him whom anger— acting as a submarine fire in the ocean of the body— does not utterly consume, for it has drunk up all the water of discernment.
Death does not seek to slay that man whom the bodiless god of love cannot crush— that firm heap of sesame seeds, as if turbulent and fierce, which the god of love fails to press.
Death does not seek to destroy him by whom firm repose has been found in that single, stainless, and supremely purifying state.
O Brahmin, these great defects, which are the causes of the disease of saṃsāra,
do not disturb even in the slightest a mind that is singularly concentrated.
Sufferings arising from mental and physical ailments, accompanied by wrinkles and great delusions, do not overwhelm a mind that is singularly concentrated.
He neither gives nor takes, neither abandons nor begs;
his mind, concentrated on a single point, performs its duties as they arise.
The mind, when unified in one-pointed concentration, neither sets nor rises; it is neither forgetfulness nor mindfulness, neither asleep nor awake.
Thoughts born of the transformations of desire and anger do not afflict a mind that is one-pointedly concentrated, even though the space of their hearts has been blinded.

Those things that are ill-conceived, poorly undertaken, characterized by base qualities, wrongly expressed, or following an improper sequence— these do not cut through a mind that is focused on a single point.
All auspicious things— vast in purpose, great, and endowed with virtue— follow after the mind that is singularly concentrated.
One should direct the mind toward that supreme truth which is beneficial in its ultimate result, which is unfailing, free from delusion, and liberated from the state of evil intent.
O Sage, let that mind of mine be directed toward the Unseen, which is not defiled by the demon of desire that causes long-lasting alienation.
That which is beautiful, sweet, and wholesome, and which has been long and thoroughly exhorted in the beginning, middle, and end— that one should direct the mind toward as supreme.

One should direct the mind toward that which has been determined by the wise from the very beginning to be free from the state of misfortune, which is connected with virtue, and which is beneficial for the world.
One should cause the mind to be directed toward that which is skillful, sweet, pleasing to the heart, delicious, cooling, non-depleting, extremely sharp, and thoroughly refined.
One should direct the mind toward that which is beyond the intellect, which is to be perceived, which is primordial, which is the supreme nectar, and which possesses unsurpassed auspiciousness.
In heaven, together with the gods, the gandharvas, the vidyādharas, and the kinnaras, and along with the hosts of celestial women, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious.
O dear one, on this earth— including its kings, its mountains, cities, and villages, and even the oceans— nothing whatsoever is auspicious or stable.
In Pātāla, including the hosts of Nāgas and Asuras, as well as the women of the Asuras— and indeed throughout its entirety— not a single thing is beautiful or stable.
In this entire world— including the heavens, the celestial realms, the netherworlds, and the slopes of the mountains— there is nothing whatsoever that is beautiful or stable.
In this body— along with its face, hands, shoulders, feet, and the circle of the thighs, and including its blood and flesh— there is nothing at all that is beautiful or stable.
In activities that are restless with mental and physical afflictions, enveloped by floods of suffering, and eternally trivial, there is nothing whatsoever that is auspicious or stable.
In these thoughts that agitate the mind, crush the heart, and yet sustain life, not a single thing is stable or auspicious.
When the Mandara mountains of the surging milk-ocean of the heart are in constant motion,
there is nothing whatsoever that remains stable or auspicious amidst one's own conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations.
In these activities, which are incessantly subject to coming and going, intensely hot, and characterized by diverse modes of conduct, nothing whatsoever is stable or auspicious.

Neither is sovereignty over the entire earth a boon, nor is the various forms of the gods a boon, nor even the state of being a Naga beneath the surface of the earth; for that alone is a true boon where the minds of the virtuous find their abiding.

Neither is the investigation of confused treatises superior, nor is the critical analysis of excellent poetry superior, nor is the savoring of the sequence of sublime narratives superior— [none of these] compared to that wherein the minds of the virtuous find their firm abiding.
Neither is a long life consisting of mental distress preferable, nor is death preferable, nor is stubborn delusion;
neither is hell nor heaven preferable—that state wherein the minds of the virtuous do not abide.
Thus, all these various sequences of the world have become firmly rooted in a person through the dullness of a fickle mind;
how could the great ones allow them to endure for long regarding an object whose nature is most unstable?
In the *Bhusuṇḍopākhyāna*, the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Sole Refutation of the Resolve for Samādhi," Bhusuṇḍa said:
O best among all-knowers, there exists but one vision alone— unfailing, free from delusion, supreme among all, most excellent, and fully elevated.
Contemplation of the self brings an end to all sufferings;
it removes the long-accumulated fatigue of the tormented cycle of existence;
and it moves through the vast expanse of the stainless path of the mind.
By that [wisdom], an end is brought about within for all the sufferings of beings who revel in misfortune, just as darkness is dispelled by moonlight.
O Blessed One, that contemplation on one's own self is free from all conceptual constructions;
it is easily attained by those such as you, yet it is difficult to attain for those such as we.
How can those of ordinary intellect attain this state, which transcends all time and rests upon the supreme pinnacle?
O high-minded one, her friends, who delight in contemplating the Self,
exist here, cooled like the moon and having attained a certain degree of similarity with her.
O Lord of Munis, from among those various companions who are equal to me in their contemplation of the self, I have chosen one.
This reflection on the vital breath, when properly relied upon, brings about the destruction of all suffering, increases all good fortune, and is the very cause of life.
Vasiṣṭha:
Although I already knew this, I again questioned the bird Bhusuṇḍa, who had spoken thus, with an unperturbed mind and as if in play.
O you who cut through all doubts, O one of exceedingly long life! Tell me truly, O virtuous one: what is meant by "reflection on the vital breath"?
Bhusuṇḍa said:
"O Sage, you are a knower of all the Vedāntas and the destroyer of all doubts; yet you ask me about this crow merely for the sake of jest."
Or rather, I am merely repeating what has been learned from you yourselves;
what harm has come upon me?
Listen to this "concentration on the vital breath" (prāṇasamādhi) being described by me, which restores life to Bhusuṇḍa and grants Bhusuṇḍa his very self.
Behold, O Blessed One, this delightful house of the body,
with the three primary constituents as its great pillars and enclosed by nine doors.
It is protected on all sides by the householder ego, together with its wife, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and its kinsmen, the subtle elements (tanmātra).
It has the hollows within the ear-lobes as its attic rooms,
the hair as its roof-covering, and the large eyes as its windows.
The mouth was its principal gateway, the arms were its side-walls,
and the hollows of its doors were adorned with rows of teeth like garlands of *ketaka* flowers.
The door-keepers, whose tongues were incessantly rattling,
stood stationed at the thresholds of the foot-stalks, which were encircled by the light of their fingers.
It is entwined with networks of sinews smeared with blood, flesh, and marrow;
it has a firm structure of thick bones like sturdy timber, and it is well-scrubbed like a fine wall.
O Leader of Sages, within this body which is like a house— hollow, fragile in its center, and adorned with ribs as its walls— [what is there to cling to?]
The machine consists of a pair of lotuses, composed of bone and flesh, soft,
with stalks extending upward and downward, their calyxes meeting one another, and possessing shimmering petals.
By the wind, which moves through the entire sky in a state of constant vibration,
the soft petals of that machine were seized.
As those leaves wither, that wind increases,
as if blowing from all sides upon the mass of vine-leaves struck by the breeze.
Having increased and divided itself into many forms, that wind then spreads throughout this body— upward, downward, and in all other directions.
Then, that wind of the heart, characterized by diverse modes of conduct and activity, is designated by those who know it through technical terms such as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and so forth.
From the hollow of the mechanism of the heart-lotus, all the vital energies (prāṇa-śaktis) radiate upward and downward through the body, like rays from the orb of the moon.
They go forth and come back, they leap about, they seize and sport; they fly up and fall down swiftly—these are the powers of the vital breath (prāṇa-śaktis).
This very breath, situated within the heart-lotus, is called "prāṇa" by the wise;
O Sage, a certain power of this [breath] causes the eyes to blink.
One [of the fires] perceives touch; one carries [the breath] through the nose;
one digests food; and one utters words.
What need is there for much speaking here? The Blessed Vāyu performs everything within the body, just as a mechanic operates a machine.
In that regard, O Sage, the two winds that have spread upward and downward are designated by the pair of names *prāṇa* and *apāna*; these two are known as the manifest, excellent winds.
O Sage, I remain constantly following the course of those two,
who possess bodies of cold and heat and are ever travelers through the sky.
In the great machine of the body, when the two drivers— the sun and the moon in the sky of the heart— are free from fatigue, they possess the nature of fire and soma.
Of this mind, which is the guardian of the city of the body;
of this ego, which is the lord of the two chariot wheels; and of these two excellent and beloved horses.
As I followed those two vital breaths called prāṇa and apāna, which move through the body without obstruction until the dissolution of the body, I observed their course.
O Brahmin, for those who are always of the same nature throughout waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the days pass as if they were established in the state of deep sleep.
Even when their limbs are cut into a thousand pieces, subtler than even a fiber of a lotus stalk,
the movement of those two remains difficult to perceive, yet it exists.
Having understood the movement of the two winds that flow without ceasing, and having followed that movement impelled within the heart,
O Great-Souled One, the man whose mind is joyful and whose bonds are destroyed is not born here again.
In the *Bhusuṇḍopākhyāna*, the twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Inquiry into the Vital Breath," Bhusuṇḍa said:
O Sage, although you know everything, why do you ask me in jest? I shall speak according to what was asked; listen even to that, my words.
O Brahmin, this vital breath (prāṇa) is a power of vibration with constant motion;
it resides above within the body, both externally and internally.
O Brahmin, the downward-moving breath (apāna) is also a power of vibration with a constant flow;
within the body, both externally and internally, this apāna is situated below.
Listen now to that which, for the knower of reality, proceeds as the supreme prāṇāyāma both while awake and while sleeping, and which leads to the highest good.
The wise know that outward movement of the vital breaths from the hollow of the heart-lotus, occurring spontaneously without any effort, to be *recaka* (exhalation).
When the vital breaths, extending outward from the heart to a distance of twelve finger-breadths,
come into contact with the limbs, that is called *pūraka* (inhalation).
When, through the downward breath (apāna), [the air] enters from the outside into the interior without effort,
that sensation which fills the limbs is also known by the wise as pūraka.
As long as the prāṇa has not yet arisen in the heart after the apāna has set,
that is the state of kumbhaka experienced by yogins.
Inhalation, retention, and exhalation each exist in two ways;
they are situated outside, at the twelve-finger space known as the dvādaśānta, which is the place of the rising of the apāna.
O Great-minded One, listen to those who have been described by those of expansive intellect as abiding at all times by their very nature, gentle, and free from effort.
O Lord, from the exterior limit of twelve finger-breadths, the apāna breath has arisen; therein, by its very nature, reside the pūraka and the other [breath-control practices].
The wise know that state of the downward breath (apāna) which remains eternally within the space [of the heart], like an unformed pot situated inside a mass of clay, to be *kumbhaka*.
The outward orientation of the breath, which extends as far as the tip of the nose,
those who know yoga recognize as the first, the external inhalation (bāhyapūraka).
The wise know that movement of the breath which, having emerged even from the tip of the nose, extends as far as the *dvādaśānta*, to be the "external inhalation" (*bāhyapūraka*).
In this very state, as long as the prāṇa has not set and the apāna has not yet arisen,
they know that to be the full, external kumbhaka, a state of perfect equilibrium.
That inward-turned state which occurs without the rising of the apāna breath— one should know that as the external exhalation (bāhyarecaka), which, when contemplated, bestows liberation.
That which arises from the *dvādaśānta* and possesses a supreme density of form outside the *apāna*— the wise know that to be the other type of *recaka*.
Having continuously realized these internal and external breath-retentions (kumbhaka) and others,
which are of the nature of prāṇa and apāna, as one's own, one is not born again.
O one of great intelligence, these eight winds, when recollected day and night, have been described by me as bestowing liberation through their very nature.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, these do not come to a stop; for by its very nature, the wind is mobile.
Whatever a person does or eats while recollecting these [states] through the intellect,
that person is nothing at all as an agent within those [processes], such as the retention of breath (kumbhaka) and the rest.
Having completely abandoned external objects, the mind that is intensely focused on this practice attains the state of absolute liberation in just a few days.
For the person practicing this, the mind does not form an attachment to external sensory objects, just as a Brahmin does not take pleasure in a dog's sacrifice.
Those of perfected intellect who remain firm, grasping this view, have indeed attained everything that is to be attained; they alone are truly unwearied.
Whether standing, walking, waking, or likewise sleeping,
if this vision is constantly observed, then bondage is not incurred.
Through following the inhalation and exhalation, when the stainless awakening has been attained,
one will dwell here within oneself, healthy and with pride and delusion completely stilled.
Abandoning all undertakings, the wise person remains established in his own nature;
having attained the movements of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, he prospers happily in perfect well-being.
O Brahmin, the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) proceeds from the lotus-mechanism situated in the heart;
this breath sets outside at a distance of twelve finger-breadths.
O great sage, the rising of the apāna occurs from the external dvādaśānta,
while its setting takes place in the lotus-machine situated in the heart.
When the prāṇa comes to rest at the "end of the twelve" in the station of the sky,
immediately thereafter this apāna rises from that very place.
The prāṇa flows upward toward the external space like a flame of fire;
the apāna flows downward toward the space of the heart like water.
The apāna is the moon that nourishes the body from the outside;
the prāṇa is the sun or the fire that digests this physical form within.
For the vital breath, like the supreme sun, having first heated the space within the heart at every moment, subsequently heats the sky at the tip of the nose.
The moon of the downward breath (apāna), having first nourished the void at the tip of the mouth and the sky of the heart,
subsequently nourishes [the rest] immediately after a mere blink of an eye.
Having reached that state where the digits (kalās) residing within the moon of the apāna are swallowed by the sun of the prāṇa, one no longer grieves.
When the mind reaches that state where the digit of the sun of the prāṇa, situated at its end, is swallowed by the moon of the apāna, it no longer undergoes birth.
The vital breath (prāṇa) itself attains the state of the sun within the space both outside and inside;
subsequently, it assumes the state of the moon, which provides nourishment.
The vital breath itself, having abandoned its state as the moon which nourishes the body,
in an instant attains the state of the sun, which causes supreme desiccation.
As long as the vital breath has not completely abandoned its solar nature and attained its lunar state, one should investigate within; during that time, one does not grieve over place or time.
Having realized the constant setting and rising of the moon and the sun within the heart,
the mind is no longer born again, for it has found its own innate support in the Self.
He who beholds the divine Sun within his heart— along with its rising and setting, with the moon, with its rays, and with its conjunctions— he truly sees.
The darkness situated outside is neither diminished nor completely destroyed for the sake of perfection;
however, one should destroy the darkness within the heart, for upon its destruction, supreme perfection is attained.
When external darkness has been completely destroyed, the light of the world arises;
but when the darkness within the heart is destroyed, the supreme self-luminosity arises.

One should diligently observe the sun of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which destroys the darkness within the heart, bestows thorough knowledge, grants liberation, and possesses both its rising and setting.
When the moon of the apāna breath sets into the hollow of the heart-lotus,
from that very place the sun of the prāṇa rises within, facing outward.
When the apāna has set, the prāṇa rises from the heart-lotus,
just as heat quickly reappears in that very place when its shadow has vanished.
When the prāṇa has set, the apāna rises from the outside in an instant,
like a new shadow quickly appearing on the ground when the sunlight has vanished from all sides.
O noble-minded one, know that when the prāṇa has perished in the birthplace of apāna, and likewise,
understand that when the apāna has perished in the birthplace of prāṇa.
When the prāṇa has set and the apāna is tending toward its rise,
by resorting to external kumbhaka for a long time, one does not grieve again.
When the apāna has set and the prāṇa is slightly inclined toward rising,
by maintaining an internal kumbhaka for a long time, one no longer grieves.
Having practiced the natural *kumbhaka* (breath retention), which resides at the root of the exhalation (*prāṇa*) and reaches the limit of the inhalation (*apāna*), one does not suffer again.
Having perceived the kumbhaka established within itself— resting at the end of the exhalation of the apāna and the inhalation of the prāṇa— one does not suffer further.
When both the prāṇa and apāna have dissolved within,
by taking hold of that peaceful state, one does not suffer through the self.
Having discerned the external or internal location and time— wherein the apāna is oriented toward consuming the prāṇa and is partless— one does not grieve again.
When one observes the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— which is intent upon consuming the downward breath (*apāna*)— both within the heart and externally,
having fully considered place and time, the mind is no longer born again.

Behold those two— the breath and the downward breath— wherein the out-breath is swallowed by the in-breath and the in-breath by the out-breath, both externally and internally, as well as in space and time.
When for a moment the prāṇa has set and the rising of the apāna has ceased,
that effortless external kumbhaka established outside is known as the supreme state.
For a moment, with the downward breath subsided and devoid of the rising breath,
the internal *kumbhaka*— accomplished without effort— is the supreme state.
This is that very form of the Self; this is that supreme consciousness alone, pure.
This, appearing as both being and non-being, having attained which, one does not grieve.
Like fragrance within a flower, we worship the conscious Self (cidātman) abiding within the vital breath (prāṇa)— neither as the out-breath (prāṇa) nor as the in-breath (apāna).
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which stands at the end of the cessation of prāṇa, which reaches the limit of the cessation of apāna, and which resides in the middle between apāna and prāṇa.

We worship the conscious Self (cidātman), the foremost bearer who is the supreme vitalization of the vital breath (prāṇa), the highest life-force of the living being (jīva), and the sustainer of the body.
We worship that eternal Self of consciousness, in whom is all, from whom is all, who is all, who is everywhere, and who consists of all.

We worship the Self of Consciousness, which is the light that illuminates all, the merit that purifies all that is to be purified, and the contemplation of existence and non-existence, which is never diminished.
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), which abides in the heart at the mutual friction of the vital breaths, and likewise within and without in space.
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), free from parts and blemish, wherein the apāna has set and the prāṇa has not yet arisen for even a moment.
We worship that reality of consciousness, where the apāna has not arisen and the prāṇa has set, which is the whirlpool in the space at the tip of the nose.
We worship that reality of consciousness, the support for the state of the yogi, which exists as two [breaths] situated externally and internally at the place of origin of the prāṇa and apāna.

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is mounted upon the chariot of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, yet is itself beyond prāṇa and apāna, and which is the pervasive power-form of all powers.
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is the Lord as the kumbhaka of prāṇa within the heart, the kumbhaka of apāna outside, and that which is purified by the portions of pūraka.

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is to be attained through the contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇa), and which brings about the awakening to the nature of existence as the reflective awareness of the out-breath and in-breath.
We worship that essence of consciousness (cittattva), which is the vibration of the vital breath, which is the cause of the bliss of vibration, and which is the cause of all causes.

I take refuge in that supreme state, which is free from the stain of all worldly calculation, yet is eternally surrounded by a multitude of arts; it is the sovereign glory of experience, the highest station, and is bowed to by all the gods.
The twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of Prāṇasamādhi," in the Bhusuṇḍa Episode.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
For this rest within consciousness has been attained by me, through the meditative absorption of the vital breath (prāṇasamādhi), gradually, of its own accord, within my own stainless self.
"Grasping this view, O Great Sage, I stand firm;
I do not waver even for the duration of a moment, remaining as immovable as Mount Meru."
Whether walking or standing, whether waking or even sleeping,
this well-composed samādhi of mine does not waver, even in a dream.
Abiding amidst the ever-changing and unstable conditions of the world,
I remain inward-turned, established by myself within my own self through the Self.
Even the wind might be obstructed, or even water from its course;
yet I do not recall anything being so completely restrained as this well-composed concentration.
By following the inward and outward breaths and by beholding the Supreme Self,
I have attained the sorrowless, primordial state through great austerity.
O Brahmin, until the great dissolution, I continue to live with a steady mind, witnessing even today this rising and sinking of living beings.
I never think about what has been nor what will be;
I remain here relying upon the perception of my own present self.
Regarding duties as they arise, having abandoned all desire for their fruits,
I abide solely in a state of pure consciousness, like that of deep sleep.
Having abandoned thoughts consisting of existence and non-existence, and those accompanied by desire and aversion, I abide in the Self; I live for a long time, free from affliction.
Constantly recollecting the occasion of the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I find contentment within myself; by that means, I am long-lived.
"I have obtained this today; I shall obtain that beautiful thing tomorrow"—such thoughts I do not have; therefore, I live long and free from affliction.
O virtuous one, I neither praise nor blame anything anywhere at any time, whether it concerns myself or another; by this means, I live free from affliction.
I am not elated by attaining what is auspicious, nor do I feel distress over what is inauspicious; my mind is always equanimous, and therefore I live free from affliction.
Relying upon supreme renunciation, I have indeed always relinquished everything, including my very life; therefore, I live free from affliction.
O Sage, my mind is now stilled, its restlessness pacified, free from sorrow, and with all desires cast aside; by that peace I live, free from affliction.
I see wood, a graceful woman, a mountain, grass, fire, snow, and the sky as equal everywhere; therefore, I live free from affliction.
"What have I attained today, or what will happen again tomorrow?"—such a fever of anxiety does not exist for me; therefore, I live free from affliction.
I neither fear the sufferings of old age and death, nor do I rejoice in the pleasures of attaining a kingdom; therefore, I live free from affliction.
"This one is my kinsman, and this one is a stranger; this one is mine, and that one belongs to another"—O Brahmin, I do not recognize such distinctions, and by that I live free from affliction.
Whether eating, moving about, standing, rising, breathing, or sleeping, I do not perceive "I am the body"; by that I live free from affliction.
Regarding this cycle of existence as if it were deep sleep, I perceive it as if it were non-existent; by that means I live free from affliction.
"Gain and loss, occurring at their proper time through skillful means, are equal to me;
like two hands situated on the body, I live thereby free from affliction."
With a gaze that is steady, straight, clear-sighted, and tenderly innocent, I look upon everything with straightforwardness; by that means, I live free from affliction.
I have no sense of "mine" regarding this body from its feet to the top of its head;
having abandoned the mire of egoism, I therefore live free from affliction.
Whatever I do and whatever I eat, having renounced that—even though I possess it—my mind attains a state of actionlessness; by that means I live free from affliction.
O Sage, whenever I understand anything at all, then and there I bow down;
because of this lack of arrogance, I live free from affliction.
Even as a lord, I do not commit aggression; I am not tormented, nor am I distressed.
Even though I am poor, I have no longing; therefore, I live free from affliction.
While this body is perishing in form, the Self, which is the locus of consciousness, remains undestroyed;
from afar I laugh at the multitude of elements, and by that I live free from affliction.
Being composed, I do not allow the mental state, which is driven by the snares of hope, to come into contact with my inner self; therefore, I live free from affliction.
I perceive the non-existence of the world and the existence of the Self, like a bilva fruit in the palm of my hand;
having awakened from sleep, I see this, and therefore I live free from affliction.
I see everything—wasted, broken, slack, decayed, agitated, crushed, and gone to ruin—as if it were new; therefore, I live free from affliction.
I am happy when people are attached to happiness, and I am sorrowful when they are in sorrow;
as a beloved friend to everyone, I live free from affliction because of that.
In adversity I am steadfast-minded, and in prosperity I am a friend to the world; I am neither present nor absent in states of being and non-being, and therefore I live free from affliction.
"I do not exist, nor does anything else belong to me; I do not belong to anyone else"—such has been cultivated in my mind, and by that I live free from affliction.
I am the world, I am the ether, I am the succession of space and time; I am action—such is my understanding, and by that I live free from affliction.
The pot is consciousness, the cloth is consciousness, space is consciousness, the banyan tree and the cart are consciousness;
"everything is consciousness"—this is my state of being, and by it I live free from affliction.
Thus, O tiger among sages, I have been described as the long-lived crow named Bhusuṇḍa, the bee to the lotus of the three worlds.

Beholding and contemplating for a long time the three worlds as waves tossed about in the ocean of Brahman— appearing in diverse forms through the power of their arising and destruction, sometimes submerged, sometimes rising up, and with their visible appearances constantly fluctuating— I have remained here.
The twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Narration of the Causes of Longevity" within the *Bhusuṇḍopākhyāna*.
Bhusuṇḍa said:
This has been told to you, O Brahmin— both who I am and what I am here—
for the sake of accomplishing merely your command, through boldness, O you who have reached the further shore of knowledge.
Vasiṣṭha: Oh, how wonderful! O Blessed One, this account of your own self that you have narrated is an ornament to sacred learning and a cause of supreme amazement.
Blessed are those who inquire of you, the Great-Souled One who lives for so long, as if you were a second lotus-born Brahmā.
Today we are exceedingly fortunate that you have related in its entirety, exactly as it is, this purifying account of your own life, which is a complete awakening for the intellect.
Having wandered through all directions, I have seen the realms of the gods;
yet in this world, no one greater than you has been beheld.
Having wandered here, will any great person indeed find [you] by some means?
For a noble-souled one such as you is not easily found anywhere in the world.
Just as a pearl is produced within a certain section of a bamboo stalk,
so too is one such as you born within a certain fragment of the world.
Indeed, a very great and auspicious task has been accomplished by me today,
in that you, whose body is merit and whose soul is liberated, have been beheld by me.
May it be well with you; enter your auspicious inner cave.
This is my midday hour; I am departing for the abode of the gods.
Having heard this, Bhusuṇḍa rose from his tree and took with both hands, which he had previously consecrated, that excellent vessel adorned with golden leaves.
With the pollen from the flowers of the wish-fulfilling creepers and with the moonlight,
he of perfected intellect filled that vessel with a tribute of pearls.
With that vessel for the arghya and pādya offerings, my elder brother, out of devotion, worshipped me— though I am but three-eyed— from head to foot.
Saying, "Enough of the hardship of following me, O Lord of Birds," I rose from my seat and then leaped up like a bird.
Having followed me for a distance of one yojana through the sky,
that bird was forcibly restrained by grasping his claw with my own hand.
When I had traveled a long distance through the path of the sky and passed from sight, that lord of birds turned back; for the company of the virtuous is difficult to abandon.
When he and I had both vanished from sight into the sky like two waves in the ocean, I lost all memory of the sages.
Having reached the circle of the Seven Sages and being honored by my wife,
I then dwelt there, O Raghava, with a heart blossoming with wonder.
In that abode of the Kalpa-creeper, Bhusuṇḍa— possessing a noble beak,
equanimous, tranquil-minded, venerable, and established in his own meditative absorption— remained.
The wise one still lives even today upon that very leaf of the creeper;
he remains right there on that golden tree of Mount Meru, just as before.
Long ago, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, two hundred years after it had passed,
I met Bhusuṇḍa on Mount Meru beneath a tree on its peak.
O Rāma, now that the Kṛta age has waned, the Tretā age is turning;
you, O destroyer of enemies, were born in the midst of this Tretā Yuga.
Again, in his eighth year, that very Bhusuṇḍa, possessing an ageless form, met with him once more on the mountain above.
Thus has this wonderful and supreme account of Bhusuṇḍa been told;
having heard it and reflected upon it within yourself, perform that which is appropriate.

Thus, whoever of pure intellect shall here investigate this discourse of the sage Bhuṣuṇḍa will forcefully cross over the river of existence— the dense, miserable cycle of rebirth that is filled with the fear of worldly becoming.
The Bhusuṇḍa Episode is concluded.
The twenty-ninth canto. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, O sinless one, I have related to you the account of Bhusuṇḍa;
by means of this wisdom, Bhusuṇḍa crossed over the peril of delusion.
O mighty-armed one, by firmly grasping this view preceded by the practice of [controlling] your own vital breaths, become one who has crossed the ocean of existence, like Bhusuṇḍa.
Just as Bhusuṇḍa attained that state which is to be reached through knowledge and yoga born of continuous practice, so do you accomplish that same state.
Those whose intellects are unattached, being virtuous and observing the prāṇa and apāna breaths, attain a state of stability in the supreme reality, like Bhusuṇḍa.
These various philosophical views have been heard by you;
now, relying upon your own intelligence, do as you wish.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, by you, who shine as the earth with the rays of knowledge,
the entire darkness of unruly wickedness within the heart has been wiped away.
We are awakened; we are delighted; we have entered our own abode;
we stand with what is to be known already known—just like you, indeed.
"Oh, the life-story of Bhusuṇḍa is most wondrous!
O Blessed One, it has been narrated by you as that which bestows the realization of the supreme goal."

By whom indeed was that created, or from where did it arise?
How has it come to abide, or who dwells therein?
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāghava, for the sake of awakening to the supreme truth and for the removal of defects, listen to this which is being told by me according to its true nature.
O Rāma, this body-abode— with bones for its pillars, nine gates, and plastered with blood and flesh— was not created by anyone.
This is merely an appearance that manifests in this very way;
it has the form of the delusion of two moons, established as both existent and non-existent.
In the process of the illusion of two moons, the state of being two moons is indeed real;
yet in reality, there is only one moon, and the situation within the body is exactly like that.
For at the time when the body is perceived, this body exists as established;
yet in reality it is non-existent, and thus it is said to be of the nature of both being and non-being.
A dream is real during the state of dreaming, but at other times it is indeed in vain; a bubble is real during the state of being a bubble, but at other times it is indeed false.
The body is real within the limits of the body itself, yet unreal within the limits of anything else;
water is real during the perception of heat, but unreal at other times.
The body is remembered as existing during the limit of its appearance, and as non-existent at other times;
thus, this is now appearing as a mere manifestation.
"This am I by name"—thus it remains, with the internalizing function of thought (manana) contained within.
Abandon the delusion that the body is nothing other than a construction of flesh and bone; there are thousands of bodies constructed by mere conceptualization.
O Rāma, that body by which you wander the horizons in a dream while lying upon your bed— where does that body of yours reside?
While you wander through the celestial realms or Mount Meru within the kingdom of your mind during your waking state, where exactly does that body of yours reside?
And even in dreams, O Rāma, that body by which you wander through the slopes of the earth— where is it situated?
By means of which you wander here in this kingdom of the mind through lands of great splendor with bodies already gone— where does that body of yours now abide?
O mighty-armed one, in every mental kingdom you create those various activities of the world; where now do those bodies by which they were performed reside?
Where does that body reside by which you attain bliss through the union with your beloved created by imagination— a woman full of grace and passion?
O Rāma, just as these bodies are composed of the vibration of the mind,
so too this body is known as mental, having such a commencement.
This delusion that "this is wealth," "this is the body," or "this is the country"—
all of that is the manifestation of the mental energy of volition.
Know this saṃsāra, O descendant of Raghu, to be either a long dream, or a long delusion of the mind, or even a long reign of the imagination.
When you attain supreme awakening through your own self-will,
you will then clearly perceive this [universe] above and below as it truly is.
Just as the state of the world exists within the mental construction of a dream or a thought,
so indeed is this very mental construction merely a certain [mental] fabrication.
Just as I previously described the birth of the Lotus-born One,
which arose from within the mind itself through the formation of volitional constructs.
Endowed with various arrangements and possessing infinite hundreds of diversions,
this world appears as nothing more than the mere fabrication of conceptual construction.
Just as an appearance is imagined when the mind attains the state of being born from a lotus, so too is another body conceived as a body; for it remains exactly like that.
That body which was long practiced in the previous flow [of existence] is seen exactly as it was through the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā), by virtue of the emergence of its former form.
O Rāma, if this very resolve is cultivated otherwise through human effort, it becomes otherwise in this world.
O Rāma, when one contemplates, "This is that very self, and this is my saṃsāra," this reality shines forth, born from the firmness of such contemplation.
O Rāma, that very thing which has been cultivated with intense momentum is seen everywhere immediately, like a beloved wife who is exceedingly dear.
Just as the habitual activity of the day is seen even in a dream,
so too is cyclic existence perceived when it has been habituated through conceptual construction.
Just as the duration of a day appears quickly within the limit of a dream, so too this world, though existing for all time, is perceived as lasting for a long duration.
Just as a river is seen in the sky when it is heated by the sun's glare,
so too the earth, though non-existent, is seen through the power of conceptual construction.
Just as a tuft of hair is seen in the sky due to a visual disorder,
so too does this splendor of the world appear solely because of faulty cognition.
Just as even a coward does not fall into agitation regarding his own mental constructs,
so too the wise man does not experience fear regarding cyclic existence, even though it is his own mental construct.
For this very nature of one's own appears in this manner at present; through its abiding as the path of saṃsāra, who shines here, and what? MU 6.29.44.
When that very [mind] has been somewhat purified and, through purification, has attained stainlessness,
O Rāma, this flickering worldly delusion is no longer perceived within it.
By the mere sight of reality, one's own nature attains purity;
it no longer takes on impurity, just as gold does not again assume the state of copper.
"This triple world is merely an appearance; it is neither existent nor non-existent"—the wise know that such a complete relinquishing of other conceptualizations is right vision.
Death, life, heaven, knowledge, and even ignorance—none exist apart from the reflection of consciousness; this realization of oneness is right vision.
The wise know that the correct vision is this: that this entire cycle of transmigratory existence, beginning with "I" and "you," and these ten directions, are all nothing but one's own manifestation.
In this saṃsāra consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, through the vision of things as they truly are,
the mind— by means of perfect insight— neither sets nor rises.
Having determined that all phenomena are either non-existent or indeed existent,
the mind, through correct vision, attains peace free from desire.
It neither censures nor praises, it neither rejoices nor grieves;
through right perception, the mind attains the coolness of truth.
Since all kinsmen must inevitably die,
why do you grieve in vain over the separation from them?
Since it is certain that I must inevitably die,
why do you grieve in vain when my own death has arrived?
Since a person who has been born must inevitably obtain some degree of personal wealth and such, what occasion indeed is there for joy?
For every man engaged in worldly affairs within this cycle of existence, misfortune leads to ruin; for what opportunity is there for sorrow?
This web of living beings sinks, rises, and quivers like a mass of bubbles in the ocean; what lamentation can there be for this?
The existent is indeed always existent, and the non-existent is indeed always non-existent;
what cause for lamentation is there over this mere diversity of activity?
I do not exist, nor did I exist in the past, nor shall I exist now;
I am the body and this is a defect of the mind—what else is there to lament?
O friend, if I am indeed distinct from the body as the reflection of consciousness, then what are those states of existence and non-existence of mine, rooted in which one suffers so?
Thus, O Sage, because his mind possesses internal certainty through right knowledge,
it neither sets nor rises, nor does it suffer within.
Internally, he takes up that very state of transcendence established in the unsurpassed state,
just as a partridge seizes a soft, stainless tip of grass.
For this reason, not even the slightest reliance should be placed upon this unreality;
for by means of reliance, a living being is bound like an ox to a strong rope.
O sinless one, having determined through the intellect that this world is a firm, though unreal, dream, you should conduct yourself here with a vision free from attachment.
He for whom that which ought to be done no longer appears as a duty attains an inner coolness, just as the world does at the end of the day.
O sinless one, having abandoned the analysis of the multitude of categories of objects, behold this as a mere commonality of appearance.
O Rāma, that which is a mere appearance is stained by the touch of thought;
therefore, having abandoned even that, become the supreme one who is free from all appearances.
Consisting of the space of consciousness, eternal, all-pervading, and devoid of everything,
one becomes absolutely stainless upon the relinquishing of appearances.
When one has realized, "I do not exist, nor do my enjoyments truly exist," this display does not appear as something vain or leading to misfortune.
For when everything is indeed perceived as "I alone am consciousness," this display does not appear as something vain or leading to misfortune.
Both of these systems of philosophy are true and grant ultimate perfection; O Rāma, whichever one you find among them to be more beautiful, take refuge in that.
Therefore, O sinless one, dwelling here by means of these two very visions, bring about your own welfare through the complete destruction of passion and hatred.
Whatever is appropriate in this world, whatever is in the sky, or whatever is beyond—
that all is attained, O Rāma, through the complete destruction of passion and hatred.
O Rāma, whatever is performed by an intellect afflicted by passion,
that very thing quickly leads to the state of delusion for the ignorant.
In mental states obstructed by the fault of hatred, virtues find no footing,
just as deer do not set foot upon scorched ground.
For that wish-fulfilling tree in whose heart the two serpents of passion and hatred do not lurk—
my friend, what indeed cannot be obtained from it?
If those who are wise, well-restrained, clever, and learned in the scriptures are nonetheless filled with passion and hatred, then fie upon them— they are merely jackals!
"My wealth has been enjoyed by another; wealth has been enjoyed by me from another"—in worldly dealings such as this, what room is there for passion and hatred?
Wealth, kinsmen, and friends come again and go away; why should a wise man be attached to them, or why should he be repelled by them?
This supreme illusion of the Lord, which consists of the manifestation of existence and non-existence,
pervades the construction of saṃsāra and utterly consumes all attachment.
O Rāghava, in reality I possess neither wealth nor people, nor even truth; this which is perceived as "false" is seen to be merely a false manifestation of the false.
Everything is non-existent at the beginning and the end, and even in the middle it is unstable for one possessed by mental afflictions;
where, then, can a wise person find firm resolve in a tree created by another's imagination?
One man imagines a woman in the sky, while another, far away, enjoys her;
such, my dear, is the construction of this saṃsāra, and there is no other way.
In this world, the wise know this state of constant coming and going, agitated and pervasive, to be equal to the creation and destruction of a city of Gandharvas.
This world has arisen as something truly non-existent, like a city created by imagination in a dream;
yet, through the perception of long duration, it has come to be regarded as real by you today.
This cloth does not exist, nor does this object possessing the quality of being a wall-part exist;
this is merely a construction of conceptualization that has reached full development through habituation.
You are eternally established in the state of deep sleep within the expansive, eternal, supreme Self; indeed, there is nothing else whatsoever in which you abide.
Remaining right there, yet having fallen from the state of deep sleep, you perceive this entire long dream of saṃsāra with its vast delusion.
Having slightly deviated from your own true nature, which is profoundly dense with the sleep of ignorance,
you remain here, bewildered by the dream of saṃsāra.
Therefore, O Supreme Person, abandon this widespread sleep consisting of dense ignorance, just as one who has found a treasure abandons a female demon.
Awaken and behold the pure Self, ever-risen,
the manifestation of non-conceptual consciousness, just as a lotus beholds the sun at dawn.
Awake! Awake! Again and again you are being awakened by me, O mighty-armed one; behold the Sun of the Self, which is free from all ailment.
O Rāma, you have been awakened by me through this extremely cool rain of the water of knowledge, which resounds with beautiful words, like one awakened by a dense cloud.
Attain supreme awakening; O Rāghava, you are indeed awakened.
Behold the truth, having abandoned this false delusion of the world.
For you there is no birth, no suffering, no defect, and no delusion;
you are liberated from all conceptual constructions, established by your own self within the Self.
With the net of defects of conceptual construction completely dissolved, possessing a tranquil state like that of pure, essential deep sleep,
and beholding this vast and gentle form— abide, O Great-Souled One, in the Self of perfect peace.
The thirtieth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of the Ultimate Truth," by Vālmīki:
Thus, while Rāghava— whose mind was pure and equanimous— was listening,
he rested freely in his own self and attained supreme bliss.
And while all those present there remained characterized by tranquility,
their minds undisturbed, and established in their exalted selves;
When all vibration, sound, and worldly activity had been completely stilled, the earth stood as tranquil as the night, its surface like a peaceful assembly hall.
While the mute and bewildered bells were suspended in the vault of the sky,
and while the pure banners seemed to listen to the words of the Sage, [the gods departed].
While the birds had become motionless, their flight having ceased and their beaks stilled, and while those in the inner apartments were sleeping in their cages and dwellings;

While the members of the assembly—those who had attained expansion of intellect through the contemplation of the true meaning of reality and who were endowed with innate bliss—were investigating the essence of the truth; MU_6,30.6.
By means of that garland of excellent speech, which was radiant with supreme tranquility,
[he spoke] even to those play-monkeys who stood bowed in humility.
For the sake of establishing Rāghava’s rest within his own self, the sage ceased his flood of words, just as water ceases to flow once its momentum is spent upon reaching a dam.
Then, when half a muhūrta had passed and Rāghava had regained his composure,
Vasiṣṭha, the best among speakers, spoke again on that very same matter.
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāma, you are perfectly awakened; you have attained your own Self. Resting upon this very [realization], remain within yourself; do not indulge in pride regarding this.
O descendant of Raghu, this wheel of saṃsāra indeed revolves upon the hub that is mere conceptualization; when that movement is obstructed, it is brought to a halt.
Even when this wheel of saṃsāra is blocked with effort at the navel of the mind that has been awakened, it continues to flow with great force.
Relying on supreme human effort, and through the proper application of strength and wisdom,
one should bring to cessation the very mind that is the hub of the wheel of saṃsāra.
That which is not attained through manliness endowed with wisdom and goodness, and augmented by scriptural learning, cannot be obtained anywhere.
Having abandoned the sole reliance on destiny as conceived for the instruction of the ignorant,
one should first restrain the mind by relying upon one's own effort.
O sinless one, by means of this delusion consisting of ignorance which has proceeded from Viriñca, this world— which is indeed non-existent— is perceived as having the appearance of existence.
O sinless one, these bodies that wander here are all falsely manifested, arising from what is unreal, and consist of the expansion of ignorance and delusion.
O Rāma, a wise person should never allow the body— which is like a person created by imagination— to undergo the fluctuations of pleasure and pain.

The person within the body is considered even more hollow than a painted figure— one whose face is withered by suffering and moistened by tears, compared to one who is serene and free from such moisture.

In this body— which withers from mental and physical ailments, which is itself subject to decay, and which perishes— there is no stability at all, even as it is falsely imagined to be a variegated person.
For a body depicted in a painting perishes when that [supporting] body perishes, and not otherwise;
the body, being perishable by nature and subject to inevitable destruction, perishes of its own accord.
A person who is wonderfully composed assumes a very firm splendor;
however, the body, even when well-protected, perishes utterly and does not flourish.
Therefore, this excellent one has a variegated body; it is not a body born of mere conceptualization.
For those qualities that exist in a variegated body do not exist in a body born of conceptualization.
O sinless one, what reliance can you have upon this body composed of flesh, which is indeed more contemptible than even a dull, painted image?
O Great-minded One, what reliance can there be on this body born of long-standing volitions?
For it is indeed more hollow than even a body born of very slight volitions.
One whose volitions are very slight is not seized by long-lasting pleasures and pains;
yet this one, born of long-lasting volitions, is afflicted by long-lasting suffering.
For this body is composed of volition; it neither exists nor does it not exist.
Why then does this foolish person undergo suffering for its sake in vain?
Just as there is no injury to you when a man made of a painting is wounded or destroyed,
so there is no injury to you when a person created by imagination is wounded or destroyed.
Just as there is no injury to you when a wound consisting of a kingdom of the mind is destroyed,
so too there is no injury to you when the second moon is destroyed.
Just as when a wound incurred in a dream is healed, there is no injury to you;
and just as when water in thick clouds is exhausted, there is no injury to you.
Since this machine of the body is by its very nature perishable, being fashioned merely from mental constructs, there is no harm to you when it is wounded or worn away.
For in this body— which is like a long dream, fashioned by long-standing volitions, and whether adorned or defiled— there is indeed no injury whatsoever to consciousness.
O Rāghava, consciousness does not set, nor does the Self move;
Brahman does not undergo transformation—what loss is there for you when the body perishes?
For just as one standing upon a revolving wheel, even after the wheel has been abandoned, perceives the entire circle of directions as spinning due to extreme delusion; so it is with the mind.
By false knowledge that has suddenly arisen and is flourishing,
and by that which is likewise habitual, this wheel of the body is perceived in such a manner.
Under the influence of evil latent impressions, the body is whirled about and appears to whirl, it falls and appears to fall, and it is struck and appears to be struck.
Having abandoned the delusion born of ignorance and having beheld the true vision,
one should firmly rely upon steadfastness and cast off this dense delusion.
The body created by conceptualization through false knowledge is neither real nor unreal;
that which is produced by the unreal can never be real.
The body arises from what is non-existent, like a snake imagined in a rope;
and though it is itself unreal, it performs the activities of the world.
O Rāma, that which is done by the inert [body] is said not to have been done;
therefore, even while acting, the body is never indeed the agent.
For the body is indeed inert and devoid of effort; there is no desire belonging to the Self.
Since there is no agent whatsoever, the unborn Self is merely its witness.
Just as a lamp in a windless place remains fixed within itself,
so remain in the maintenance of the world, like a witness amidst all phenomena.
Just as the sun, remaining in its natural state, performs its daily tasks,
so too, O Rāma, perform these royal duties.
For when this empty house of a body, which is not composed of earth, has arisen and attained existence,
it is falsely [perceived], like a yakṣa imagined by a child.
Having come from somewhere unknown, devoid of substance and shunned by all virtuous people,
the wicked demon of egoism has entered that which bears the name "mind."
O Rama, do not become a servant to this evil-minded ego; for by serving it, one obtains hell as the fruit.
Within the house of the body, by the play of its own volitions,
the formless Vetāla of the intoxicated mind frolics with ease.
Having entered the empty house of the body, that was done by the yakṣa of the mind,
by which even great beings who remain absorbed in meditative concentration become terrified.
Having expelled the vampire of the mind from the single temple of your own body,
you shall never again fear the empty city of saṃsāra.
In this house of the body, which is overcome by the mind as its master, why do those who take delight in it remain unshaken even now, like stones, despite being struck by such wonders?
O Rāghava, that fortitude which exists in the house of the body when it is seized by the demon of the mind belongs to a demon; it does not belong to one who is free from demons.
O virtuous one, sport without attachment in this house of the great yakṣa of egoism, this body which is as good as burnt; for indeed, this is not yours and is not stable.
Having abandoned the habit of following egoism with an expansive intellect,
and having reached the death of egoism, let one quickly take refuge in one's own Self alone.
For those who, seized by the demon of egoism, seek only hell and are blinded by the disease of delusion, there are neither friends nor kinsmen.
Whatever action is performed with an intellect impaired by egoism, its fruit shall be like that of a poisonous creeper: death itself.
Know that the fool by whom his own great corpse of egoism is embraced— being devoid of discernment and fortitude— is swiftly destroyed.
Those wretched ones who have been brought under the sway of the demon of egoism,
O Rāghava, have become fuel for the fires of hell.
The tree of the body, in whose hollow the serpent of egoism writhes, is quickly felled by the wise.
O best among the great, whether this demon of egoism remains in this body or departs, do not regard it with your mind.
For once you have become an *avadhūta*, disregarded and even mentally despised,
the demon of egoism will no longer do anything to you here.
O Rāma, while this demon of the mind manifests within the abode of the body,
what of its own nature has come from this [mind] which possesses infinite diversions?
The extensive calamities that befall men who are overcome by the yakṣa of the mind cannot be fully enumerated even in hundreds of years.
"I am struck," "I am dead," "I am burned"—these are the wretched behaviors of the demon of egoism; they do not belong to anyone else, O sinless one.
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not connected to anything here,
so too the self, though all-pervading, is not joined with the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
O Rāma, whatever this moving machine of a body performs and whatever it grasps, that is the activity of egoism joined to the rope of the vital breath.
Just as the sky, though not an agent, is indeed the cause for the heightening of a tree,
so too the Self, abiding within itself, is the cause for the activities of the mind in this world.
By the mere presence of the Self, the mind— though pure like the form of a wall—
shines forth, assuming a body, just as by the mere presence of a lamp.
O Rāma, what connection can there ever be between the self and the mind, which are as utterly distinct from each other as heaven and earth, and as light and darkness?
O descendant of Raghu, through the delusion of ignorance, the mind— which is enveloped by its own powers of movement, vibration, and effort— is perceived as the Self.
The Self is indeed of the nature of light, eternal, all-pervading, and omnipresent;
know that the mind is deceitful egoism, while the Great One resides within the heart.
You are the Self, the very essence of the Raghu dynasty; you are not this dull stone of the mind.
Cast away the delusion of the mind; why have you become attached to this?
For this demon named "mind," dwelling in the empty house of the body, is a wicked soul that causes terror; O noble one, do not touch it.
Having dispelled the demon of the mind— which brings fear, is inauspicious, and robs one of the very essence of fortitude— be firm, for you are that very Self.
When a person is firmly seized by the yakṣa of the mind, neither treatises nor kinsmen,
nor even teachers, are able to protect that human being.
The kinsmen of the meaning of the teacher’s scriptures are able to rescue one whose mind-demon has been completely stilled,
just as [people rescue] a deer from a small amount of mud.
In this empty city of the world, everything has been utterly corrupted by the intoxicated yakṣa of the mind, which leaps about within the house of the body.
This forest of the world, in which every house and grove is haunted by the vampire of the mind— empty, for whom does it not cause fear?
In this city of the world, however, the body-house— wherein the demon of the mind has been stilled— is inhabited by only a few virtuous ones.
O descendant of Raghu, whatever direction one resorts to here is filled with the corpses of bodies— the vetalas of intoxicated delusion.
In this vast wilderness of the world, for even a moment, like an innocent child,
take hold of a portion of fortitude by yourself and rescue your own self.
O Rāma, in this forest of worldly decay where herds of living beings roam like deer, do not seek stability through the juices of grass like a young fawn.
O young deer among men, wandering in this forest of the earth's surface,
shatter the elephant of ignorance and adopt the conduct of a lion.
Other deluded human-beasts roam in their own jungles within Jambudvīpa; O Rāma, O sinless one, roam in that same manner.
One must not plunge for even a very short time into the mire-clinging waters of the cold season, lest one be submerged like a buffalo in a small puddle in the form of a young woman.
One should cast away the enjoyment and non-enjoyment of external objects and follow the path of the Noble One;
having investigated by means of the great Nobles, one should take refuge in one's own solitary self.
For the sake of this impure, worthless, unfortunate,
and misshapen body, one who is wise should not wallow in the grinding mills of anxiety.
The body is fashioned by one [agent], yet it is inhabited by another;
one experiences the suffering of another—strange indeed is this cycle of folly!
Just as a single stone possesses a uniform density within itself, so too does the Self;
for there exists no other possibility than this, since there is only the single universal of pure existence.
Just as the solidity of a stone is its very nature, so too is the mindness of the self;
for it is non-different from mere existence, since there is no consciousness other than itself.
Just as there is solidity in a stone, so too for this Supreme Self:
consciousness is of a single form, by virtue of its nature as the universal essence of existence.
O dear one, here in this world, neither insentience nor consciousness arises separately;
for these two are fashioned by false conceptualization, like a yakṣa imagined by a child.
Just as from a single measure of sugarcane juice, the illusion arises that "this is molasses" and "this is candied sugar," though it is composed of nothing other than that very [juice].
Since the one Supreme Self exists in the form of universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*),
this distinction between insentience and sentience has arisen in vain through delusion.
This [error] perishes as soon as it is perceived; it is destroyed by perception alone.
Like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is so.
The non-existent has no being; that which does not exist here cannot become existent.
Because it is established in its own nature alone, because of the impossibility of either duality or unity,
and because of the absence of any other consciousness, there is equality between the stone and the Self.
Just as the non-dual, infinite, single Self experiences its own existence, so too is the stone established in its own nature;
it is neither insentient nor sentient.
Because of the impossibility of anything else, due to the absence of the conjunction of permanence, duality, and unity,
and because of the impossibility of an object of cognition, the Self is neither insentient nor sentient.
The two perspectives—the inert and the non-inert—are like the son of a barren woman or a tree in the sky;
they have neither arrived nor not arrived, and they are neither perceived nor unperceived.
The referents of the words "insentient" and "sentient" do not exist, like a snake [projected] upon a rope;
how could those two be real without being based on mere non-investigation?
And that which was stated— that the self is conscious while the stone is insentient—
is for the purpose of making known such speech to those capable of understanding it.
By whatever reasoning one who is to be awakened is awakened to a more transcendent awakening, that instruction is not grasped by the fool; he does not suddenly seize that state.
The mind is distinct from these impaired faculties, yet no agent is perceived; this body is but a hollow house.
Some other being alone dances about, while this "I" is devoid of intrinsic nature—alas, what a great magical illusion!
In the restless cycles of worldly existence, amidst the successive births of beings and the play of the Supreme Person whose sole activity is consciousness,
the high-souled minister indeed delights after investigating the ultimate reality, just as one might sport with female serpents despite their virulent poison.
You are not the head, nor the eyes, nor the blood and flesh, nor the bones, nor indeed the mind, nor the aggregate of elements;
do not fall into delusion, for you are not the body—you are the serene consciousness, the refuge of all that is stainless and omnipresent.

Listen to that which was previously told by me in a cave of Kailāsa,

There exists the lord of mountains named Kailāsa, the abode of the lover of Gaurī, which shines with an abundance of moonbeams and extends beyond the heavens.
It was washed by the cascades of the Gaṅgā, its cave-dwellings resounded with the songs of the Gaṇas,

Clouds are hidden by tamāla trees, while clouds are likened to kadalī plants;
the forest is matted with swarms of bees and filled with the warbling of crying kalaka-piñjala birds.

The beauty of his hair was like a crystal cave; his garment was the surrounding forest;

There dwells the Blessed Lord Hara, the bearer of the crescent moon,
trident in hand, three-eyed, and surrounded by a multitude of his attendants.
He whose half-body was taken by Bhavānī, the sole cause of all the worlds, the crusher of Kama’s pride, the creator of the arts and the possessor of all arts.
His shadow is followed by six-faced ones; he has a rutting bull as his vehicle;

In former times, while worshipping that Mahādeva on that very mountain,

For the sake of austerity, he long maintained his station in the conduct of an ascetic;

Having performed his bath for the sake of dwelling there, having constructed a hut of blue leaves, having fixed his gaze upon young saplings, and having planted a fence of creeping vines; MU_6,31.17.

Surrounded by a multitude of disciples, having compiled the essential meaning of the scriptures,
having brought together a vast array of books, and having protected the noble seekers.
O Rāma, as I was thus engaged in ascetic practice within a grove of the Kailāsa forest, distinguished by such qualities, time passed me by.
Then once, on a certain occasion, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when half the night had passed and was coming to an end.
While the quarters of the sky had become perfectly still, as if established in the silence of wood,
and in the dense thickets where the darkness could be cut with a sword;
When the breeze was blowing with the laughter of falling dew-drops like pearls,

While they lick the nectar-fluid from the moonbeams upon the sprouts for their own nourishment—[the fluid] which flows like the rays of the moon, the possessor of nectar—*amṛtāṃśukara*. *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 6.31.24.
The night-blooming water-lilies, the female cakora birds,

In the third part of the sky, which was like a peacock’s plumage with its spreading clusters of stars— the Kṛttikās— resembling dark-blue cloud-sprouts resting upon the mountain.

On the mountain, where the crystal ground was doubled in its brilliance by the reflection of the multitude of stars, and where the clusters of blossoming flowers appeared as if multiplied; //MU_6,31.27//
While I lay upon a couch of tender leaves, with a mind freed from desire,
I contemplated the reality of the Self, which is of stainless luster and undecaying.
And in the second watch, when the constellation of the Seven Sages was in the sky,

The thirty-second canto, titled "Description of Vasiṣṭha’s Hermitage," Canto 32. Vasiṣṭha:
At that time, when the first watch of the night had passed,
I remained with my gaze fixed on the external world, having brought my concentration to a state of subtle refinement.
I beheld a brilliance suddenly arisen in the forest,
as radiant as the Ocean of Milk when it was agitated by the churning of Mount Mandara.
Resembling a hundred white clouds and like a multitude of dancing moons,
it was like a mountain of snow driven by the force of a fierce wind.
Like a mountain of fine crystal melted by the heat at the end of an eon,
like a cloud of butter, or like a mass of *ketaka* flowers that has risen up.
Like the whiteness of a conch shell flying up, like a mass of bright clouds gathered together,
like the surging foam of milk, or like the essence of pearls uplifted.
Like the mass of waves of the Gaṅgā entering a mountain cave, like a lump of fresh curd, he beheld the vast, pervasive laughter of Śarva.
Beholding that splendor which had revealed the directions, I looked upon it with a vision of the intellect shining with inner light, out of wonder.
Just as I beheld that mountain peak, the wearer of the crescent moon was wandering at his own pleasure and by chance upon his own delightful mountain, as if in mere play.
He was adorned by a multitude of attendants concealed behind the western thicket;
his hand was placed in the hand of Gaurī, while Nandin cleared the path ahead for him.
Behind him followed the bull, surrounded by all-night wanderers;
he was encircled by garlands of *kalhāra* lilies and wore a crest made of *mandāra* flowers.
Wearing matted locks crowned by the crescent moon, with earrings made of the lord of serpents,
resembling a moving mountain of snow, he is the bestower of all desired objects.
Then, having perceived the Blessed One with my mind alone, I bowed down and paid homage to him with a mandārava flower offered by my mind.
Thinking thus, I raised this body from its reclining posture in an instant, like a great corpse by a spirit.
Having awakened the disciples staying there and taken the water of honor (*argha*),
I, well-restrained, went before the Lord of the World, purified by his gaze.
There, having offered a handful of flowers from afar, the three-eyed god was saluted and worshipped by me after I had presented the water of honor (*argha*).
Then, with that gaze— moon-like, soft, upright, cool, removing all suffering, and leading to the eternal state— [he looked upon him].
Having observed me, the Lord, whose crown was formed by the half-moon and who was seated upon the flowery plateau, spoke to me with words white as a smile:
Īśvara said:
"O Brahmin, bring water for the guest-offering and water for washing the feet; welcome to you!
O sinless one, we have arrived today as guests at your hermitage."
O Brahmin, you shine with the splendor of asceticism, which is ever characterized by profound delight, constant tranquility, and joyful magnanimity.
Come and sit upon this natural lotus-seat,
soft, produced from the earth, and purifying through its accumulation of merit.
When he had spoken thus, I approached that wearer of the crescent moon and offered him water for honor, flowers, and water for his feet.
Before the feet, the hands, and the body of that Self-Existent One,
many garlands of Mandāra flowers were strewn.
Then the Blessed Goddess Gaurī, together with her companions and the circle of her attendants, was likewise worshipped with that same kind of service.
O Rāma, Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord, who are full of devotion and affection, graciously accepted that worship of mine with great respect.
At the conclusion of the worship, the bearer of the crescent moon spoke to me with a voice as cool as the rays of the full moon as I sat there.
Īśvara said:
O Brahman, do your consciousnesses, which are characterized by tranquility and have attained rest in the Supreme, remain established in that state which brings about all that is auspicious?
O Brahmin, are your disciples— those who follow you and are capable of gathering lotuses, water-lilies, and night-blooming lilies— free from illness?
O Blessed One, is all well with the innocent deer in your hermitage— those who partake of the sacrificial offerings and whose eyes are like those of my beloved?
I hope these lofty Mandāra trees are bestowing Mandāra flowers for the sake of honoring you and those like us.
I trust that the holy Mandākinī provides you with lotuses and water-lilies for your ablutions, even though she possesses but a single thicket of reeds.
O sinless one, O Lord of Munis, you are never distressed by my improper actions, nor even by the playful antics of my attendants.
O Sage, even the followers of the Lord of Wealth, who dwell in forests and wildernesses, do not disturb you as you remain here on this king of mountains.
O Brahmin, even as you dwell within the belly of this mountain, which is filled with a dense throng of ill-behaved yakṣas and restless night-stalkers, you remain unperturbed.
O descendant of Raghu, when the Lord of Gods, the sole cause of all the worlds, had spoken thus, I addressed him with words full of conciliation.
O Maheśvara, for those here who possess the auspiciousness of the recollection of the Three-Eyed One,
nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain, nor are there any fears.
For those whose minds are filled with the bliss of recollecting you,
there are none within the entire expanse of the world who do not bear devotion toward you.
Those lands, those provinces, those directions, and those mountains where men dwell with minds solely intent on recollecting you.
O Lord, the recollection of you is the fruit of past merit, the nourishment for present merit, and the seed for future merit, just like [the watering] of a tree.
O Lord, that which is called remembrance of you is indeed fruitful— pertaining to the past, the present, and the future— and auspicious throughout the three periods of time.
O Lord, recollection of you is the supreme friend of the mind, the remover of the spreading tide of all calamities, and the watering for the creeper of all prosperity.
O Lord, the remembrance of you is indeed the cause of great glories, of great deeds that are honored, and of all causes themselves.
O Lord, the remembrance of you is an ocean of the waters of discernment, a supreme mine of the jewels of merit, and a flood of suns for the darkness of ignorance.
O Lord, the remembrance of you is a jar for the flood of the nectar of knowledge, the moon for the moonlight of fortitude, and the gateway to the city of liberation.
O Lord, the remembrance of you is an axe for the creeper of craving, a mountain of clouds of fortitude, and a forest fire for the thicket of wretchedness.
Victorious is the unprecedented and supreme lamp of the recollection of you, O Lord, which illuminates the entire pavilion of the mind and the cycle of existence!
O Lord of Beings, by me, who possesses the noble wish-fulfilling gem of mindfulness of you,
the foot has been placed upon the summit of all calamities.
O Lord who removes the fear of all suffering, you have not been present before my mind here for even a moment;
O Giver of Boons, O Hero, O Maheśvara, I have forgotten you and thus I dwell in happiness like Bhava himself.

O Rāma, at this moment I reflected thus with my intellect:

Having reflected thus, O sinless one, that guru was questioned by me;

O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Cause of all causes!
By Your grace, this boldness has clearly come upon me.

O Maheśvara, tell me truly the procedure for the worship of the gods, which causes the destruction of all sins and the increase of all that is auspicious.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Brahmin, to this unsurpassed worship of the deity;
I shall speak it so that, by performing it even once, you shall indeed be liberated.
"Do you know, O twice-born one, who this god Mahādeva might be?
Neither the lotus-eyed one nor the three-eyed one is the god."
Neither is he the god born from the lotus, nor the god who is the lord of the thirty-three,
nor the god Wind, nor the Sun, nor Fire, nor the Maker of Night.
There is no Brahmin, no king, no "I," and no "you," O best of the twice-born;
there is no god in the form of a body, nor is there a god who assumes variegated forms.
