The deity is not of the nature of conceptual construction, nor is the intellect the deity;
that which is uncreated, without beginning or end, and pure awareness is called the deity.
How could that [consciousness] exist within an object delimited by forms and so forth?
The wise know consciousness to be the auspicious spirit (cic-chiva), uncreated and without beginning or end.
That very [reality] is expressed by the word "God"; one should worship that, since it alone exists as everything, assuming the nature of both being and non-being.
For those who do not know the true principle of Śiva, worship through forms and other such means is performed;
for one incapable of traveling the path of *yojana*s, a path of *krośa*s is devised.
The fruit obtained from Rudra and others is limited by such measures as "this much" and so forth;
however, the fruit of the Self is innate bliss, without beginning or end.
He who abandons the unartificial fruit and pursues an artificial one is like one who leaves a grove of mandāra trees to enter a forest of karañja bushes.
Awareness, equanimity, and tranquility are indeed the foremost flowers therein;
they know the Self to be auspicious, pure consciousness alone, partless, and stainless.
Know that when the divine Self is worshipped with the flowers of tranquility, awakening, and so forth, that alone is true worship of the deity; mere worship of an image is not worship.
But those people who, having abandoned the worship of the Divine which consists of self-realization,
are attached to artificial images, undergo long-lasting suffering.
For those virtuous ones who have known what is to be known do not regard [worldly matters] as a child's play;
O Brahmin, apart from meditation on the Self, they perform no worship of the gods.
The self alone is the divine Lord Śiva, the supreme cause;
he should always be worshipped incessantly with the offering of knowledge.
Know this space of consciousness to be the self, the imperishable living being, and one's own true nature; it is nothing other than the worship of the Self through the worship of the worshipful.
O Lord, just as this world has consciousness and space alone as its essence,
so too let it be explained how the state of being a living soul (jīva) and so forth belongs to consciousness itself.
Indeed, it is only the sky of consciousness that exists here, devoid of near or far; for that which remains at the end of aeons is the unthinkable, which cannot possibly exist anywhere else.
That which shines forth by itself—that very self-manifestation—is called "self-known" (svasaṃvidita); therefore, this is sufficient [to explain] what is meant by "this world."
Thus, the world, consisting of consciousness, appears like a city in a dream;
thus the world is purely of the nature of the space of consciousness, transparent and without foundation.

Because it is absolutely impossible [for anything else to exist], that which is seen as nothing but the sky of consciousness shines forth due to its nature as consciousness at the beginning of creation; that is what is traditionally known as the "world."

Therefore, as for this world that appears in the form of a city in a dream, what kind of otherness could there be therein, since its nature is nothing but the void of consciousness? From where could it arise?
The mountains are indeed pure consciousness alone; the world and the sky are pure consciousness alone.
The Self and the individual soul are pure consciousness alone; the succession of all elements is pure consciousness alone.

My dear friend, tell me: apart from the mere expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), what distinct thing could possibly exist at the beginning of creation, or within the perception of that creation, or even within a city of dreams?
"Space," "supreme space," "the space of Brahman," and "the consciousness of the world"— these are synonyms, just as the words *taru*, *pādapa*, and *vṛkṣa* are for a tree.
And this is experienced in dreams, mental constructs, illusions, and the like;
at that time, it is said that the space of consciousness alone shines forth as the world.
Just as this space of consciousness appears in the form of the world within a dream,
so too does that very same thing appear to us in what is called the waking state.
Just as in a dream-city, my dear, nothing whatsoever exists anywhere apart from the space of consciousness, so it is here in this world from the very beginning.

Since nothing else whatsoever is possible apart from this, therefore all this— whether it be the state of being consciousness or the object of consciousness— is established as the world, which is both conscious and yet devoid of an object of consciousness.
Just as in a dream, objects such as jars and cloths consist of nothing but the space of consciousness,
so too this creation at the very beginning of creation consists of nothing but the space of consciousness.
Just as nothing exists other than pure consciousness alone within a city of dreams,
so it is in these three worlds.

Whatever perceptions there may be, whatever existents and non-existents, and indeed whatever scriptures— along with their locations, times, and minds— all that is nothing but the space of consciousness.
This very God has been described, who is supreme from the perspective of ultimate reality;
he who is you, he who is I, or indeed the entire world in its totality.
For the body of every class of beings, of the world, of others, and of myself, is indeed the space of consciousness— the Supreme Self alone, and nothing else.
Just as in the city of a dream within a mental construction, there is no body whatsoever that exists apart from the space of consciousness,
so too, O Sage, in this creation, from the very first and unique beginning, there has been no other form.
The thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the World as Consisting of the Supreme Self," Lord Śiva said:
Thus, this entire universe is nothing but the Supreme Self alone;
it is Brahman itself, the supreme ether, known as the Transcendent God.
Therefore, this worship is most excellent; from it, everything is obtained.
He is the God, all-pervading, the All; everything is established in Him.
Therefore, that happiness which is uncreated, without beginning or end, non-dual, indivisible, and not to be accomplished by external means, is attained.
O best of sages, you are awakened; therefore, this is described to you.
You, a great soul, are not fit for worshiping the gods with offerings of flowers and incense.
For those children of unrefined intellect and feeble minds,
worship of the deity is said to consist of artificial images.
For they worship the God, whose nature is imagined within a form, with perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, lamps, flowers, and so forth— all of which are falsely imagined.
Having performed worship with rituals created by their own imagination,
the childish undergo distress through the worship of mere fragments of flowers and incense.
Having performed the worship of a deity in vain with objects created by their own imagination,
they offer the fruit of that act here to some false self from wherever it may be.
O Brahmin, the worship with flowers and incense is intended for those of childish intellect;
I shall now describe that form of worship which is unsuitable for one such as you.
But for those such as ourselves, O best among the wise, there is no deity whatsoever;
the deity who is the support of the three worlds is the Supreme Self alone, and none other.
Śiva transcends all states and surpasses all conceptual constructions;
though encompassed by all conceptualizations, he is neither the whole nor is he a part of it.
O Sage, he who is unconditioned by space, time, and the like; who is the performer of all types of undertakings; whose form is pure consciousness alone; and who is stainless—he is called God.
Consciousness transcends all parts, abides within all beings,
is the goddess who bestows existence upon all, and removes all suffering.
O Brahman, that which is the middle between being and non-being is called the Divine; known as both the Supreme Self and the Non-Supreme, that Being is proclaimed as "Om."
By its nature as the Great Being, it has attained equality everywhere;
it is called "Great Consciousness" (mahācit) and is known as the "Ultimate Reality" (paramārtha).
It abides everywhere in all seasons within the creepers, like sap;
it exists both in the form of the universal essence of being (sattāsāmānya) and as the nature of the Great Consciousness (mahācittva).

That which is the essence of mind in Arundhatī, that which is the essence of mind in you, O sinless one, that which is the essence of mind in Pārvatī, and that which is the essence of mind in the Gaṇas; //MU_6,34.17//
Those of supreme intelligence who know reality understand that the very essence of my mind and the essence of the mind in the three worlds are one and the same; they call that "the God."
O Brahmin, tell me: what essence can there possibly be in any other god who is conceived as possessing feet, hands, and so forth, if he is apart from pure consciousness?
O Brahmin, it does not stand at a distance, nor is it difficult for anyone to attain;
it is always established within the body, as well as everywhere in space.
He acts and he eats; he maintains and he departs;
he breathes and he is the knower; he knows each and every limb of yours.
Thus, by virtue of that [power], he becomes the lord of the city of the limbs within this city of manifold activities, which is manifest and bound to his own essential nature.
By his grace, he [the Self] dwells within this cave of the heart, which is like a deep cavern, while the body remains as a shifting mountain.
For that stainless Self, which transcends the existence of the activity of the six organs including the mind,
the designation "consciousness" (cit) has been conceptually fashioned for the sake of conventional discourse.
This very one, consisting of consciousness, subtle, all-pervading, and stainless,
produces this radiant manifestation and yet does not produce it.
That extremely pure consciousness colors this worldly activity for the sake of the world, just as a wise man colors a sweet vine with juice.
Those beautiful wonders which, as they exist within consciousness,
cause it to marvel— these are indeed certain things designated as "space."
Some are designated as "living beings" (jīva), some are designated as "mind" (citta),
some are designated as "time" (kāla), and some are designated as "space" (deśa).
Some denote actions, and some denote substances;
some denote states such as the modifications of being, as well as insentience and sentience.

Some are designated by names such as "light" and so forth, while others are designated by "darkness"; some are designated by "the sun," "the moon," and so on, and some are designated by the name "yakṣa."
Just as a sprout is produced by the spring season through its own nature of desirelessness,
even so is this splendor of the world produced by the conscious Self.
Indeed, within all these bodies taken together— which are like a web of lotuses situated in the ocean of the three worlds— consciousness alone is always one and the same.
The intoxicated sovereign consciousness tastes the honey of her own volition, which is gathered by the bee of the mind wandering within the lotus of the body.
The world, together with its gods, asuras, and gandharvas, and including its mountains and oceans,
moves upon consciousness like a blade of grass in a swirling eddy of water.
The wheel of saṃsāra, consisting of the restless mind and characterized by the constant movement of various conducts, revolves within the wheel of consciousness as a vessel of delusion.
In the form of a four-armed being, he struck down the host of asuras,
just as the sun destroys the heat with a mass of rain clouds accompanied by its rays.
O Brahmin, by virtue of his three eyes marked with the bull and the moon,
he has become like a bee hovering over the cluster of lotus-faces of Gaurī.
Having reached the state of being adorned by the lotus of Viṣṇu, consciousness— its mind dependent on meditation— assumes the status of Brahmā’s daughter, the lake for the lotus of the three Vedas.
O Brahmin, here in this world, diverse bodies arise in great abundance from the conscious principle,
just as leaves from a tree or as bracelets and other ornaments from gold.
She, whose feet are worshipped by the entire host of gods,
bears the status of the crest-jewel of the three worlds with the ease of Indra himself.

Having attained the state of gods and asuras within the grand display of the belly of the three worlds, consciousness rises, falls, and moves about by its own nature alone, like the waters of the ocean.
The moonlight of consciousness, spreading its radiance in all four directions,
causes the night-lotuses of the existence of all beings to blossom without exception.
The Great Lakṣmī, who is the mirror of consciousness, receives the triple world reflected within her by means of grace, just as a pregnant woman carries her own embryo within her womb.
The glory of water causes the vast mandalas of the fourteen elements to become manifest, just as the ocean brings about the state of being the sea.
With its flowers of diverse perceptions, its sprouts of dense volitions,
grown upon the field of the sky, it bears the fruit of the flood of sentient beings.
It is a mass of dust from the web of living beings, colored by the essence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), enveloped in the skin of perception, and crowded with the buds of mental activity.
She whose radiant form consists of the filaments of the three worlds throughout incalculable past ages,
and who smiles with the exuberant play of incessant vibration.
Harshened by the joints of all seasons, entwined with inert mountains and the like,
coiled with knots of birds, and devoid of both root and tip.
This mind is blossomed, its subtle body being both existent and non-existent;
it is a manifold flower of the visible world, variegated and unable to endure touch.
For here, by means of this [consciousness], even a mere shadow is produced everywhere;
the object is conceived, expanded, sung of, and even acted out.
By means of the great funeral pyre of consciousness, the sun and other luminaries shine eternally;
yet bodies appear to relish one another through the delusions of your and my consciousness and insentience.
This wind of consciousness dances along the path of its wide-spread whirlpools; it is the mass of dust in the net of the world, whose very existence manifests as the visible body.
Just as a lamp, the crest-flame that illuminates the three worlds, fully reveals the beauty of its colors, so does consciousness manifest this entire undertaking of the world.
Just as the moon, having attained union with the stainless lunar orb, becomes visible everywhere, so too does the splendor of all objects existing in the world become perceptible.
By the sprinkling of the elixir of consciousness, the series of multitudes of objects attains both form and fruit, just as a fine creeper does when watered by the rains.
By its own shadow alone, the insentience of everything is either quelled or arises,
just as the darkness of this corpse-like body is dispelled by the light of a lamp, as it were, within a house.
If these wonders of consciousness did not exist within the body,
then who would they be, and what forms would they assume, were the three worlds themselves the body?
In this house of the body, within the light of the illumination of consciousness, the flickering young bride of the multitude of actions, bearing the child of volition, shines forth.
Without the light of consciousness, how, when, or in what manner could a flavor become manifest, even while vibrating at the tip of the tongue? Or what indeed would that flavor be like?
Though possessing fine trunks, well-formed branches, and being surrounded by bees that are curls of hair,
how can the tree of the body shine at all without the blossom-cluster of consciousness?

Consciousness alone increases, desires, and consumes, acting as the creator of all that moves and is immobile; consciousness alone exists, nothing else exists—this entire world has arisen as mere consciousness.
Having spoken thus with a voice as clear as flowing nectar, O Rāma, the Three-eyed Lord was questioned by me once more, resplendent with humility and courtesy.
O Lord, if consciousness is all-pervading, unitary, and of the nature of that [Self],
then why is this one conscious of the manifold, while this other does not?
"How can this conceptualization— that 'this person was conscious in the past but has now become devoid of consciousness'— be based on direct experience in the world?"
Īśvara said: Listen to all this, O Brahmin; I shall speak to you according to what was asked.
This question you have posed is great, O best among the knowers of Brahman.
In this world, there exists Consciousness within the two bodies, whose nature consists of all beings;
however, that which is turned toward the object of thought is one, while the other is remembered as the supreme, free from conceptual construction.
Though her very self was bound by her own volition, she remained as if she were another;
like a woman who, having resolved upon a different husband, falls into immoral conduct.

For just as that very same person here, through anger, becomes as if another in an instant, so too does consciousness, marked by conceptual construction, attain a state of difference from its own true nature.
O Brahman, consciousness (cit), when fashioned by conceptual construction and fallen away from its own true nature,
gradually contemplates insentience and thus arrives at the state of objective manifestation.
Consciousness itself attains the state of being an object of cognition, first as the nature of the space-atom,
and subsequently as the nature of the sound-seed and the subtle element of air.
But through the successive divisions of space and time, enveloped by those subtle elements,
it first becomes the individual soul (jīva), then quickly becomes the intellect (buddhi), and subsequently the ego (ahaṃ) and the mind (manas).
When the mind arrives at the state of "mineness," it clings to saṃsāra;
just as a twice-born man becomes an outcaste through the thought, "I am an outcaste."

Due to the lack of awakening regarding its own conceptualizations, consciousness— though inherently self-awakened— assumes a variegated form through its inertia and proceeds incessantly with those conceptualizations.
Consisting of infinite volitions and thickened by the volition of inertia,
consciousness enters the body due to that inertia, just as water turns into the state of stone.
Thereafter, O Sage, that which is designated by the names *citta*, *manas*, and *māyā* is born within saṃsāra, having resorted to a subtle state of insentience.
Having reached a state of habitual delusion, she is oppressed by the shackles of craving;
possessed of desire, anger, and fear, she falls excessively into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Having abandoned her own infinite enjoyments, she is subject to the transformations of separation; scorched by the forest fire of suffering, her heart is withered by the thunderbolt of grief.
With the thought "I am this," she was rendered distraught by emptiness; grasping at mere distinctions, she has fallen into the utmost wretchedness.
Sunk in the great mire of delusion like an aged female elephant in the mud,
her body is tossed about on the swing of the creeper of existence and non-existence.
It deals with the transformations of this essence-less and inferior saṃsāra;
its heart is scorched by suffering, and it follows the disease of passion.
Like a doe strayed from her own herd, she has fallen into a state of helplessness;
her form appeared when it was manifest, and it has set when it has vanished.
A young girl flees even from unreal female vampires (vetālīs), who appear through her own imagination with terrified and agitated glances.
Like a camel longing for a drop of honey, one craves conditioned happiness;
falling away from the intermediate state due to faults, one descends from fault to fault.
She falls into utter helplessness, passing from distress to further distress;
fallen from sorrow into sorrow, she stands in calamity after calamity.
Possessed by a multitude of various misfortunes, her disposition rendered helpless by her own actions,
she has fallen from misery to even greater misery, consumed by the fire of remorse.
Having gradually attained a lack of skill in each successive new composition,
she became intent on creating various types of bonds and fell into the state of a worm.
Terrified on all sides by Śaṅkara and having reached the brink of death, she was like a fish in dwindling water, intent only on writhing about.
In childhood, all her faculties were powerless; in youth, she was carried away by anxiety;
in old age, she was tormented by the suffering of death; and having died, she was brought under the sway of karma.
She is born variegated with suffering; she dies while facing rebirth; she acts, helpless under the influence of obsession; and she swallows [existence] while bearing agony.
Exhausted and tormented by fatigue, she becomes as fragile as a water bubble;
with her heart overwhelmed, she weeps and, being scorched, she cries out aloud.
An Apsaras in the city of heaven, a Nāginī in the depths of Pātāla,
an Asurī in the caverns of the Daityas, and a human woman upon the surface of the earth.
A Rākṣasī on the support of a Rākṣasa, a Vānarī in a forest hollow,
a Siṃhī on the peak of a great mountain, and a Kinnarī on a Kulaparvata.
A Vidyādharī on Mount Devagiri, a serpent in a hole in the earth, a creeper on a tree, a bird in its nest, a vine on a mountain slope, and a doe in the forest.
Nārāyaṇa reclines in the ocean; the lotus-born Brahmā is absorbed in meditation in the city of Brahman; Hara is with his beloved on the mountain; and Hari, the best of gods, is in heaven.
The sun of sharp rays creates the day; the cloud pours down water;
the moon creates the night; and the great ocean holds the water.
The wheel of the seasons revolves together with the circle of the constellations and time; day and night arise, and in some places there is light and darkness.
In one place there is the vibrant sap of seeds; in another, the silence of stone;
in one place a river flows with its current; and in another, the profusion of flowers.

In some places there is the ripening of rows of fruits; in some places, decoctions produced by fire and other means; in some places, coolness from snow, the moon, and so forth; and in some places, the void where nothing exists at all.
In some places it has a blazing form, in some it is black, in some it is white; in some it is blue, then green, in some it is fire, and in some it is earth.
Because she is the self of all, because she is omnipresent, because she is kindled by universal power,
and because she is everything, that Supreme One is of a single form and is even clearer than the sky.
In whatever manner, by whatever means, wherever, and whenever one fashions oneself,
it immediately becomes exactly so, just as waves and the like arise from the flow of water.
The female swan, the female curlew, the female crane, the female crow, the female saras crane,
the female deer, the female cuckoo, the female heron, the female doe, the female monkey, the female elephant, and the female dog.
Caṭikā, Vañjulī, Śārī, Makṣikā, Ṣaṭpadī, and Śukī;
Dhī, Śrī, Hrī, Prīti, Ārti, Śavarī, Śarvarī, and Śaśī.
He wanders through these and other various wombs,
revolving in saṃsāra like a blade of grass in a whirlpool of water.
This [intellect] fears its own conceptual construction, just as a she-ass fears its own braying;
there is no other deluded, childish, weak, and fickle being like it.
O sage, this power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti) has been described to you by me;
it is wretched, subject to the sway of natural impulses, and characterized by the nature of a bound beast (paśu).
Having acquired the designation "the self of karma," this [individual soul] of the Supreme Self is to be pitied;
it has itself fallen into a state of agitation, thick with endless suffering.
Indeed, that which is overcome by this [ignorance] is non-existent, perishable, and an innate impurity;
it stands like the husk upon rice—non-different from it, yet appearing as if different.
Deprived of infinite splendor and tormented by misfortune,
it grieves upon attaining the state of a living being, like a heroine separated from her husband.

Behold the power of devotion to the insentient: without the remembrance of one's own state, it turns its back here and proceeds toward a downward fall, like the buckets on the wheel of a water-drawing machine at a well.
The thirty-fifth canto, titled "An Inquiry into the Nature of Consciousness Directed Toward the Object of Thought," [spoken by] the Lord:
In this way, through the contemplation "I am suffering," consciousness (cit) accumulates nothing but falsehood,
just as a wife who is drunk and asleep might falsely think, "I have fallen."
Just as a bride, her mind inverted, weeps thinking "I am dead" when she is actually alive, so too does the consciousness (cit) weep, thinking "I am lost" when it is not actually lost.
Just as this world, whose mind is inverted due to lack of cause, perceives even what is transitory as stable, so too does consciousness perceive the delusion of "I-ness."
For consciousness alone is the cause of that mind’s experience of saṃsāra;
and there is no other cause for it, because nothing else besides consciousness is possible.
Thus, because there is an absence of a cause and because that which is to be cognized is impossible,
it is not consciousness, nor is that its object, nor is that object cognized by it.
It does not possess the nature of the seen, the seeing, and the seer, like oil in a stone;
nor is it characterized by agent, action, and instrument, like darkness in the moon.

The measures of the mind are not perceived by the mind, just as a new sprout does not exist in the sky; nor are consciousness, the thinker, and the objects of thought present, like a khadira tree in the Nandana grove.
The notions of "I-ness," "you-ness," "that-ness," and so forth, do not exist in the Self as the nature of a mountain exists in the sky;
nor do "this-ness" and "other-place-ness" exist in it, as soot exists on conch shells.
There is neither multiplicity nor any interval between them, like Sumeru mountains within a single atom;
nor is there the splendor of the word for "meaning" and the word itself, like a great creeper upon a salt-waste.
"Not so, not so"— it is not like night in the solar orb,
nor is it like heat in snow, neither in reality nor in unreality.
Neither emptiness nor non-emptiness exist, like a tree within a stone casket;
even the emptiness of emptiness is not great, for it is as uncarved as space.
Only the state of being a Kevalin, which is sheer self-abidance, remains; no fault whatsoever belongs to anyone—this is attained through the nature of pure knowing.
By the mere non-contemplation of the meaning of "not," misfortune spreads from consciousness;
by the mere contemplation of the meaning of "not," misfortune is pacified.

"Except for the mere cultivation of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), no other auxiliary factor is required here—not even a blade of grass, nor even the three worlds; thus, in this matter, you possess complete independence."
For this goal, though dependent solely on oneself, remains difficult to accomplish due to a lack of cultivation;
indeed, how can that which is not accomplished by a person ever be obtained?
That consciousness which is non-conceptual and non-dual, which, while pervading all things, remains as the one supreme and transcendent reality, is the direct illuminator even of lights.
This very [consciousness] is the illuminator, all-pervading, eternally pure,
perpetually manifest, devoid of the mental organ, changeless, and stainless.
It is established in the pot, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, the monkey, the god, the asura, the ocean, the elemental being, the man, and the serpent.
Remaining like a witness, it does not vibrate anywhere;
like a lamp, it performs only the act of illuminating and no further action.
Though impure, she is pure; though rich in conceptual constructions, she is non-conceptual; though inert, her essence is non-inert; she is not everything, and yet she is indeed everything.
The supreme, subtle, and non-conceptual consciousness perceives its own self-awareness;
just as the wind causes the limbs, vital organs, and so forth, as well as mechanical devices, to move.
Consciousness, when conditioned by form, light, and mental attention, is non-aware;
yet through awareness, it becomes that very same [consciousness], for it is neither existent nor non-existent.
That supreme consciousness itself, being exceedingly pure, becomes the object of thought through the act of cognizing;
just as a virtuous person becomes the object of desire for the wicked through their perception of him as such.
Just as gold that has fallen into darkness attains a copper-like state through the removal of impurities,
yet returns again to its nature as gold— so too is the supreme consciousness.
Just as a mirror returns to its original state when the breath has subsided,
so too does consciousness, having entered into creation here, return to its own state through awakening.
From the non-realization of its intrinsic nature, this saṃsāra proceeds;
but from the realization of its intrinsic nature, it subsides, being indeed non-existent.
When, due to its nature as consciousness, it gathers within itself an unreal otherness,
then, as if having attained a state of "I-ness," it perishes as it were, though it is indestructible.
Just as a stone from the edge of a mountain peak falls downward with even the slightest movement,
so too does the Great Consciousness fall downward from its state of pure awareness.
But this existence of form and the rest is nothing other than consciousness itself, which is stainless consciousness;
when duality and unity, born of non-awakening, have dissolved through awakening.
The cognition of consciousness within the mind, senses, and so forth occurs by its mere existence,
just as worldly activity proceeds by the mere existence of light.
The trembling of the pupil arises from the vital wind (vāta); its radiance is called the "vision" (dṛṣṭi).
When that vision is cast outward, it perceives form; yet the supreme consciousness is the awareness of that form.
Skin and wind are inert and insubstantial; contact is said to be their conjunction.
The perception of contact is mental activity, but the supreme consciousness is the awareness of that [mental activity].
The connection between the subtle element of smell and the wind is the perception of smell; however, the experience of these [objects] when devoid of the mind is supreme consciousness itself.
Due to the attachment of the power of hearing the subtle element of sound to the mind, consciousness— when devoid of the mind—
is declared to be the supreme consciousness, resembling deep sleep.
The tendency toward action arises from volition; volition is the process of mental reflection;
and reflection is the turbidity of consciousness itself. Consciousness, however, remains inherently pure.
Consciousness, whose nature is luminosity, eternal, and established in its own self alone,
sustains this entire world within itself, just as a stone contains its internal structure.
Maintaining this non-dual state, free from modification and the like, it neither sets nor rises; it does not vibrate, nor does it increase.
Having entered the state of living beings through volition, she— by her own self which is devoid of volition—
remains established as consciousness itself, manifesting both insentient and sentient existence.
The vital breath (jīva) is known as the chariot of this [body];
the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is the chariot of the vital breath; the intellect (buddhi) is the chariot of the ego-sense; and likewise, the mind (manas) is the chariot of the intellect.

The chariot of the mind is the vital breath; the chariot of the vital breath is the collection of sense organs; the chariot of the multitude of sense organs is the body; and the chariot of the body is its vibration.
Vibration is action, which is saṃsāra, the cage of old age and death; thus has this wheel been set in motion, born from the manifestation of mental afflictions.
It appears within itself as something pervasive, like an unreal dream;
yet it possesses not even the slightest degree of reality, remaining like the water of a mirage.
O Lord of Sages, the vital breath (prāṇa) is traditionally held to be the chariot of this mental construction;
wherever the wind of the vital breath is, there the faculty of thought (manana) is firmly established.
Wherever this mental construction resides, it agitates that very place;
just as the wind that goes into a forest causes that very forest to tremble.
When the mind has dissolved into space, the vital breath no longer stirs;
when it has reached non-existence within the fire, it shines no more, like form [when the fire is extinguished].
When the vital breath has become tranquil, the mind does not perceive even the slightest internal object;
for when the wind has subsided, the dust indeed does not stir.
Wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) goes, there the mind remains;
wherever the chariot follows, there the charioteer is found.
Impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind travels to another place in an instant, like a stone released from a sling; it is not otherwise so swift.
Where there is a flower, there is fragrance; where there is fire, there is heat;
where there is breath, there is the mind; and where there is the moon, there is its luster.
Consciousness arises from the vibration of the vital breath through its contact with the channels by its own nature;
the expansion of that consciousness is the mind, which therefore resides within the cavity of the vital breath.
Consciousness exists everywhere—in both the insentient and the sentient—as clear as the sky;
yet it is experienced as if it were agitated by the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Abiding in insentient things as the very nature of pure existence,
it arises in the sentient as the essence of perception, awakened by the vital breath.
The vital breath (prāṇa), which previously leaped about through various expansive manifestations, no longer moves swiftly once thought has passed away.
O Sage, the Supreme Self shines forth within the city of eight constituents; it is reflected there just as a reflection is seen in a mirror, and not in stones or other such things.
Know the mind to be the city of eight constituents, the sole cause of all effects;
it is described by others through various divisions imagined according to their own inclinations.
Since that very thing from which the net of the manifold visible world arises as its fruit is experienced as being nothing other than the Reality, therefore know this:
the mind indeed revolves through the perception of the body, but all that is ultimately non-existent; understand that for yourself.
The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Unity of Mind and Vital Breath," [spoken by] the Lord.
O Sage, listen: how does consciousness—which performs actions, possesses vibration, and seems as if it were falling—attain for men that which is called death?
Through those past [deeds], as well as others here performed by one's own mental reflections and desires, which have become fully nourished by various winds of karma; //MU_6,36.2//
O Sage, that power of consciousness which has entered into the state of the mind, appearing as if utterly inert, vibrates, O Brahmin, by means of this self-consciousness acting as its witness.
O Sage, by her grace, that same Cit here, though possessed of a stain,
creates and yet does not create this world, which is like a city of Gandharvas.
Without its own existence, the living soul remains mute like a wall;
through its existence, it vibrates like a stone propelled by the sky.
Just as extremely inert iron vibrates in the proximity of a magnet,
so does this individual soul vibrate when the all-pervading Supreme is present.
This individual soul (*jīva*) manifests sufficiently by means of its own inherent power residing in all things;
it receives the reflection from the object itself, not even from that which is situated within.
Because its own true nature has been completely forgotten, this living being has fallen into a state of insentience;
due to delusion and the loss of its essential being, it is like a true twice-born man who has become a śūdra.
For consciousness, having forgotten its own true nature, has fallen into the state of being a mind;
due to its mind being afflicted by delusion, it experiences a state of great wretchedness.
The body is set in motion by an inert and involuntary power of movement, which is akin to the force of the wind,
just as a leaf is moved by a succession of ripples.
By this wretched living being, whose essence is karma, and by this mind,
the machines of bodies are set in motion, just as stones are moved by the wind.
For, O Brahmin, the Supreme Self has made the arising of the mind and the vital breath the two steadfast laborers for the drawing of the chariots of the body.
Having accepted this inert form as well as the state of being a living soul,
and having mounted the chariot of the mind, he drives the horses of the vital breaths.
In some places there is the state of having arisen objects; in some places, the state of having perished objects;
in some places, the state of having many objects; and in some places, the state of having various objects.
Like a river that has gone and yet remains as it was, not abandoning its own nature; like water appearing as waves, she is both that very same thing and yet not that, eternally manifest.
The supreme form of the Self shines forth within the mental modifications by depending upon them,
just as the beauty of form residing in material objects depends upon this light.
When the stainless supreme self, which is the essence of consciousness, is established,
the individual soul lives with its light, just as a house does when a lamp is present.
Mental anxieties and physical ailments indeed swell for her,
just as the state of waves arises from water and the state of foam arises from waves.
Overwhelmed by mental and physical ailments, the living being— like a bee in the lotus of the body— falls into a state of helplessness, just as water turns into waves.

Because the power of consciousness possesses all powers, yet through the contemplation "I am not consciousness," it falls into a state of helplessness by its own volition, just as the brilliance of the sun is obscured by clouds.
Possessing hope amidst helplessness, she does not find self-awareness due to her delusion,
just as one overcome by dense numbness does not feel the crushing of his own limbs.
The contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) perishes through delusion for this [individual],
just as the recollection of one's own duties perishes for a person possessed of dense delusion.
Then, due to delusion, one does not exercise coordination between the awareness of the limbs and the power of movement, just as a leper does not seek to move.
When the body vibrates without consciousness, the lotus-petal situated in the heart does not quiver;
untouched, it is like a wooden leaf outside.
When the lotus petal is motionless, these vital breaths within attain peace,
just as the powers of the wind outside subside when the palm-leaf fan ceases to move.
When the vital breath is stilled within through the absence of contact, the living being attains a state of subtle silence,
just as dust becomes invisible when the air in the sky is stilled.
Deprived of its chariot and lacking any support, it is seen as mere mind;
it remains within the Self like a seed of a tree that has not yet obtained soil, water, or other conditions.
Thus, when the entire multitude of instruments has come to a state of deficiency and the "city of eight" has met its destruction, the body falls motionless.
Due to delusion, the consciousness, though insentient by nature, undergoes vibration through latent impressions;
thus aroused, it remembers one thing and spontaneously forgets another.
Through the vibration of the heart-lotus mechanism, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) becomes manifest; when the flow within the heart-lotus mechanism is obstructed, the subtle body perishes.
As long as the city-of-eight exists within the body, so long does that [individual] live;
when the city-of-eight has ceased, O twice-born one, the body is said to be dead.
When, due to the obstruction of opposing impurities and by virtue of the states of cutting and piercing,
the mechanism of the heart-lotus does not vibrate within, [then the supreme state arises].
Then the city of eight constituents gradually attains peace in the void,
like a succession of winds when the mechanism of the wind has been obstructed.
Due to the power of his own lack of self-awareness, the individual soul falls into a state of helplessness;
lacking strength, it can no longer operate the lotus-machine situated within the body.
Those from whose hearts pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) do not depart,
who possess a stable and uniform life-force— they are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and long-lived.
When the lotus-machine is restrained and the vital breath has attained peace,
this body, losing its fortitude, falls upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of clay.
Just as the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) becomes merged in the wind of the sky,
even so, O Sage, the mind then attains dissolution right there.
The mind, accustomed to the latent impressions of states long practiced,
perceives wandering here and there through heaven, hell, and so forth.
Deprived of mind and breath, the body becomes a corpse,
just as a house falls into utter desolation when its inhabitants have gone far away.
The all-pervading consciousness, having become a living soul through its power of volition, abides as the mind;
having assumed the form of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), it becomes the possessor of a subtle, transportable body.
Having embraced the five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka) within itself, consciousness (cittva), abiding thus,
perceives a gross form as an object, like the delusion of a dream.
Through firm contemplation, she who is thereafter filled with aesthetic relish (rasa) there forgets her entire subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) in an instant.
Even while this body is unreal, the artificial imagination formed within it leads the unreal to the state of reality, and even reality to the state of unreality.
For consciousness, becoming the individual soul through its partial aspect, becomes the mind;
the mind then mounts the chariot of the city of eight constituents, and from that arises the world.
It thoroughly raises up the body consisting of the eightfold city and composed of wind;
for then the soul residing in the heart is said to be like a Vetāla.
When the eightfold city has been exhausted and the mind dissolves into the ether, then the body no longer throbs; it is said to be "dead."
By the power of its own nature, the living being encounters the incapacity of forgetfulness,
just as a leaf reaches a state of decay due to saplessness and the influence of time.
O Sage, when the lotus-mechanism is seized by the power of the individual soul and obstructed, and when the vital breath has reached a state of total arrest,
the human being dies.
Just as leaves, as they are born again and again, fall from a tree over time, so too do the bodies of men.
The bodies of embodied beings are born and die, just as the leaves of trees; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
These rows of body-bubbles flicker in the ocean of consciousness;
here one, there another—therefore, the wise man places no reliance upon them.
Although consciousness is all-pervading, it reflects within this mind;
for it does not take up an object within itself except through a mirror.

In the vast, pure sky of consciousness, which is not composed of those [phenomena], there flash forth rivers of delusion and torment arising from various bodies— rivers noisy with clamor, yet clearly beautiful in their manifestation.
The thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Reflection on the Fall of the Body," by Vasiṣṭha.
How has duality come to the great-souled *cittattva*, which bears the crescent moon as its crest-ornament, is infinite, and is of a single nature?
And how, O Mahādeva, does that which has taken root through the passage of time become a source of suffering and affliction when it is warded off by wisdom?
Īśvara: When the one, eternal, and real Brahman, which is consciousness and possesses all power, exists,
then this arising and subsiding of duality and unity is indeed rootless.
If duality exists, then indeed oneness would have to exist; if oneness exists, then there must be a dual nature.
Thus, these two parts alone constitute the form of consciousness, yet that too is unreal because it is of the nature of consciousness.
In this case, because one does not exist, both oneness and duality are absent;
for without the one, there is no second, and without the second, there is no oneness.
Because cause and effect possess a single essence, they have a single nature;
for even in the case of a seed and so forth ending in a fruit, [the notions of] transformation and the like are merely conceptual constructions.
The state of consciousness itself shines forth spontaneously as identical with that [object] through the non-conceptualization of subject and object;
therefore, it is that very [consciousness] appearing as modification and so forth, and because it is its essence, it does not differ from it.
This conceptualization of modifications and so forth, arising from that [consciousness] with respect to objects, attains significance through various notions of cause and effect and the like.
A wave is not different from the water; therefore, he for whom it exists is not [different] from us.
He for whom even that [water] is like a rabbit's horn is one for whom the sprout of the sky is real.
Now that the realization of the reality of things has been accomplished here, enough with your verbal fabrications!
For, O Brahmin, it is said that speech—being mere speech—is incapable of cutting through such difficult-to-sever matters as exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and the like.
The omnipotence of Brahman does not, in reality, differ from its own nature, just as the waves, foam, and other phenomena do not differ from the water of the ocean.
Just as flowers, sprouts, leaves, and so forth belong to the creeper and nothing else,
so too do duality, unity, the state of being the world, "thou-ness," and "I-ness" belong to consciousness alone.

Since whatever diversity there is—such as differences of place, time, and modification—is fashioned by consciousness (cit), it is said that it is consciousness itself; therefore, no question regarding this is appropriate for you.
The powers of space, time, action, existence, necessity, and so forth, are indeed of the nature of consciousness; they have descended from themselves because of the existence of consciousness.
And this consciousness, which is here to be contemplated as the object of thought, is known by such names as "Brahmā" and so forth;
it is like water that is rippled while remaining the very same water that bears the name "wave."
That which is like the state of being wavy for the great ocean of the play of consciousness— the wave of the sense of "I"— has not yet attained the status of an object of cognition.
This very supreme Brahman is celebrated by such names as Satya, Īśvara, Śiva, Śūnya, Eka, Paramātman, and so forth.
That form of the Supreme Self which is beyond such categories as "form" is not fit for naming; it is stainless and is not an object of words.
Whatever is seen here belongs to that great consciousness, the creeper;
for its fruits, shoots, flowers, and so forth, are not distinct from it, since they consist of that very essence.
Through the accumulation of the great "I" and the "object of thought," consciousness becomes a running entity;
it perceives itself as a living soul and that [world] as something external, seeing the non-dual as if it were dual.
Having contemplated by its very nature that "I am other than this," it attains,
as it were, a state of otherness, while its own selfhood consists of its own volition.
That form which possesses its own stain, having encountered a form that is stainless,
is perceived by consciousness alone as one fallen into saṃsāra.
This very body of consciousness itself attains the state of a living being from one side;
through the manifestation of the principle of consciousness, the living being lives, being composed of that.
The consciousness of living beings, having attained the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha),
becomes fivefold through mental cultivation and fully perceives, "I am this substance."
That substance, when consumed by a living being, quickly attains the state of *vīrya*;
from that, I am born as one possessed of life-force, knowing it through the nature of direct experience.
Through the sequence beginning with the sense of "I," by means of the rapid succession of experiencing the five [elements],
whatever one perceives— whether stationary or moving— that very thing one becomes completely.
Through a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," and through the wearing away of firm habitual practice,
it abandons its former form due to its connection with another latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Through its own cognition of duality, duality arises in that which is truly one,
just as a man appears radiant as a vampire through contact with a vampire.
From the realization of non-duality, duality ceases for the self,
just as the sense of agency in a person ceases through the resolve, "I do nothing."
In the ultimate sense, duality does not exist in the Self at all,
because it is eternally characterized by changelessness and so forth, and because it is omnipresent.
For that which is fashioned by one's own volition ceases when there is no further volition;
O Sage, it is like a kingdom of the mind or a city of the Gandharvas.
The fabrication of mental constructs is suffering, not their destruction;
effort directed toward mental construction is for the creation of a city of Gandharvas, not for its dissolution.
Since this suffering has arrived merely through the fulfillment of a desire, it can be destroyed merely by the absence of desire; what cause for distress is there in this?
By forming even the slightest conceptualization, a person sinks into suffering;
by not forming any conceptualization at all, one enjoys inexhaustible happiness.
If your consciousness remains free from the serpent of volitional thought,
then you shine brilliantly in the pleasure garden of the forest of bliss.
Having brought about the destruction of the clouds of conceptualization with the winds of your own discernment,
attain supreme purity like the expanse of the sky in autumn.
Drying up the intoxicated river of conceptualization with the machine of discernment,
you, whose mind is free from worldly existence, should console the self being carried away therein.
Shaken by the wind of volition and wandering like bits of leaves and straw,
behold yourself supported within the elemental space (bhūtākāśa).
Having warded off the impurity of your own mental constructs by means of yourself,
and having attained supreme clarity, become possessed of supreme bliss.
Because the Self possesses all powers, whatever it intensely contemplates in whatever manner,
it then perceives that very thing as such, manifested through its own volition.
This world has arisen falsely as mere volition;
O Brahman, it dissolves somewhere by mere non-volition.
The cluster of flames of birth, fanned by the wind of volitional thought,
is extinguished like a lamp upon contact with the wind of non-volition.
Make this thorny creeper of craving, which has reached such growth, withered away by uprooting its foundation, which is volitional construction.
The arising of appearances and the exhaustion of appearances—
just as a city of Gandharvas, so is the delusion of cyclic existence.
The king grieves for so long as he forgets "I am a common man," and as long as the realization "I am a king" has not arisen in his heart.
O Brahmin, innate memory is destroyed by the present [memory],
just as the dullness-altering rainy season is dispelled by the autumn that has arrived.
Whatever intense flow of mental desire there may be, that very thing increases; whatever high pitch there is of the string, that very thing ascends to the musical note.
Cultivate this single contemplation: "I am one; I am the Self.
Endowed with that contemplation, you will indeed become that very [Self] sufficiently.
For thus this Brahmanhood, which is impossible [to conceive as an object], luminous and undivided, is the supreme Lord, the highest state;
appearing in the forms of the worship, the portion of worship, the excellent worshiper, and the object of worship, He is like something and yet nothing, the single embodiment of the mind's delight.
The thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of the Deity," [spoken by] Īśvara:

Thus this universe stands, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, and having the nature of the Divine; it is free from the states of duality and unity, yet even that freedom from duality and unity has been transcended.
The form of consciousness, like a stain upon a mirror, has entered into the state of transmigratory existence;
yet that which is unstained and non-transmigratory is non-different from it, being of a dual nature.
The intellect, having acquired the stain of the notion "I am this," is bound;
by realizing that this very [intellectual] power is non-different from its own self, it is liberated.
Because it lacks the form of an object, consciousness abandons its dual nature and its status as an existent;
in an instant, when that [duality] is no longer real, it assumes the state of pleasure, pain, and so forth, yet is not truly existent.
Pure, partless, the one true existence— by such terms as these,
it is called "liberated" from all names, words, and meanings, even though it is the self-nature of all, like space.
All this is incomparable, peaceful, and flows through the three paths at the end of the mind;
this is Brahman, expanded by the Brahmic power which resembles the ether.
Vasiṣṭha:
When the mind has been severed within the mind, which is the source of all the senses—
at that second or third stage, what remains?
As long as there is the existence of a self, so long does it exist as a "Great Being" (Mahāsattva).
Once the cessation of all things has occurred, what kind of existence could there be, and from where?

Īśvara: When the mind has been severed within the mind—within that which consists of one's own senses and limbs—through investigation, through meditative absorption, through practice, or through mastery; //MU_6.38.9//

When the distinction between the conceptualization of duality and unity has dissolved, when the perceived self has been realized, and when the web of the world—swollen with the appearance of reality—has gone to its dissolution in the light of truth; MU_6,38.10.

What remains is the existence of the living being, named consciousness (cit), which consists of the dissolution of the mental constructions of saṃsāra that have been shattered; it is like a parched seed.
The state called *paśyantī* is undifferentiated, having abandoned the chewing upon objects of thought;
it is like the treasury of the autumnal sky, freed from the great clouds of the mind.
Pure consciousness, abiding as mere being, has fallen away due to the instability of the objectified mind;
yet it is not far removed from its Lord, who purifies by the mere falling at his feet.
The Self, conceived as the space of consciousness, has all conceptualization dissolved;
it possesses the universality of all things, yet has not descended into the ocean of worldly existence.
Having reached the further shore and come to rest in that vast state, she— plump with the scholarly mastery of the dreamless sleep of non-recognition— is finally at peace after long exhaustion.
This first step has been explained to you when the mind has become stilled;
now hear, O best of Brahmins, the second step of this most purifying power.
This very power of consciousness, liberated from mentation, is radiant with peace;
it is as beautiful as the vast sky, free from all light and darkness.
It is like a dense line of deep sleep within a stone,
like the moisture within salt, and like the power of vibration within the wind.
When, in the course of time, it reaches its ultimate transformation right there,
it then goes to the supreme ether, like the power of sound in space.
Surely they abandon their inclination toward the object of thought, just as water abandons its turbulence,
as a gust of wind abandons its movement, and as a garland of flowers abandons its fragrance.
Having abandoned temporality and spatiality, as well as all agitation, she is stainless;
neither inert nor non-inert, she sustains a vast, nameless existence.
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, attained through the state of Great Being (mahāsattā),
it is endowed with the fourth part of the fourth state (turyaturya), stainless and free from affliction.
He perceives her as having eyes like those of a large-eyed deer,
situated everywhere, at all times, and intent upon the enjoyment of every kind of pleasure.
This second state of the word has been explained to you, O observer of noble vows;
now listen, O best among those who know the words, as I shall speak of the third state.
This vision, through the dissolution of the perceived object, has reached the state of the nameless reality;
transcending the meanings of words such as "Brahman" and "Self," it arises as the absolute alone.
Through steadfastness over time, by virtue of its own purity, through its nature as the stainless state,
and even by being designated by names such as "beyond the fourth" (turyātīta), it attains the supreme state.
That is the highest beyond the high, the ultimate limit, the primary state by virtue of its nature as Śiva;
it is eternal, one, indivisible, the third, and purifying state.
O dear one, having long traversed the path of all hopes within this state,
she does not come within the range of my words either.
"O Sage, you have told me that it transcends the reckoning of the three paths;
remain forever in this state," said the eternal God.
O Sage, this entire universe consists of that; through the knowledge of being composed of that, and through the realization of truth, O Lord of Sages, it is neither "this" nor "not this."
Nothing here proceeds, and nothing here ceases;
it is peaceful, a uniform manifestation, and indeed non-material like the expanse of space.
Because of its non-dual unity, its lack of agitation, its state of being a dense mass,
and likewise because it possesses immutability and other such qualities, it remains eternally both permanent and impermanent.

Due to their nature as a mass of consciousness, there is not even the slightest difference between the worlds— which are like the interior of mountains— and the Self, whether they are real or as if unreal.
The All-encompassing, the Real, the Auspicious, the Quiescent, which transcends the play of speech— by means of its mere measure, "Om," and from the fourth part, it is the supreme "Om."
Vālmīki:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of pure vision, who is delightful through the cessation of all sound within this vast state,
remained silent for a moment there with that sage, his mental activities completely stilled.
The thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction of the Supreme Lord," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, in a moment, Hara, intent upon the blossoming of the lotus-lake that is Gaurī,
spontaneously underwent his own external unfolding.
He displayed three visions from his mouth, arising through the power of Time,
like a mass of sun-jewels rising from the casket of heaven and earth.
Withdrawing his splendor like twelve suns at an improper time,
yet not extinguishing the night, the Lord spoke somewhat to me as I stood before him with reverence.
O Sage, summoning your own power of reflection, let it immediately measure itself;
you must bring forth the object to be grasped, just as the wind brings about its own vibration.
Whatever is to be seen here has been seen; what is the use of these delusions regarding tranquility?
For I perceive nothing here, whether to be rejected or accepted, for one who knows that.
You have dissolved these conceptual constructions consisting of both the peaceful and the unpeaceful;
you have awakened to reality as it truly is—you alone are the vision of the self-nature of existence.
Either quickly resorting to this state of the visible for the sake of awakening the ignorant, or else listen to what I have said; for what is the use of remaining silent?
Having spoken thus and looking at me as I stood outside his awareness, the wielder of the trident struck me like the moon— the lord of the lake of moonlight— striking a white lotus.
[Īśvara:
Consciousness is the cause of the bodies' own movements through its state of indifference;
it is like the void sky to the trees, being the self of those things that are not the ultimate reality.
The body is perceived by consciousness, yet it is never moved anywhere;
the Lord is merely the seer, while the doer becomes the performer of action.
By means of the vital breath (prāṇa), this house of the body vibrates like a machine;
deprived of the vital breath, it remains motionless and mute.
The power that sifts and purifies is the power of consciousness; though embodied, it is clearer than even the ether. Here, its own existence alone is the cause.
The vital breath and the body perish, their very nature being that of separation;
but the conscious self, clearer even than the sky, does not perish—so why these delusions?
The principle of consciousness shines forth within the body composed of mind and vital breath,
just as a reflection appears in a mirror of stainless luster.
O Leader of Sages, even an object that is present and foremost does not perform the function of producing a reflection in a mirror covered with grime.
Likewise, even when the body has lost its vital breath, although it still exists,
the all-pervading consciousness is no less than before with respect to its vibration of awareness and so forth.
Through awakening, consciousness itself—entirely free from blemish—is known as the supreme Śiva, the God; likewise, the practice of that [consciousness] bestows the welfare of all beings.
He is Hari, He is Śiva, He is Aja, He is Brahmā, and He is the Lord of the gods;
He is the Supreme Lord whose body consists of wind, fire, moon, and sun.
He alone is known as the all-pervading Self, the Self, consciousness, awareness, and the sentient being;
he is the Lord of Gods, the sustainer of bodies, the Ordainer, the God of gods, and the Lord of Heaven.
Some indeed who arise as if from the great outburst of Consciousness—
namely these Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and others in the world—
are like sparks from heated iron or drops from the ocean.
When those seeds of delusion— which act as the weavers of the web of conceptual construction— have arisen from the supreme state as if they were slightly spinning, and remain present;
This thick ignorance arises with hundreds of thousands of branches,
entangled with the roots of the Vedas, the meanings of the Vedas, the gods, and the web of living beings.
Therefore, who would be capable of describing this infinite [compassion] which flows forth again and again, being perfectly suited to its place and time?
He who is considered the supreme father of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others,
is Mahādeva, the root-seed, like a tree to its sprouts.
He, whose names include Brahman and Tattva, is the sole cause of all consciousness, the bestower of existence to all, the radiant one; he is to be saluted and worshipped by those who know him.
Having as its object a directly perceived reality, it is ever-arisen in every respect; through its nature as pure awareness, it extends to the entire range of objects.
For him, no invocation-mantra or the like is of any use;
he who is eternally invoked, abiding everywhere, is attained from all sides by one's own consciousness.
O Sage, whatever state of an object you encounter, from that very state you attain auspiciousness, regaining your true nature through the vision of the mind’s eye.

Know him to be the primordial one, worthy of worship, to be saluted, to be praised, the recipient of the water offering (arghya), and the Lord of the Gods; he is the ultimate limit of all that is to be known, even among the great.
Having thus beheld the Self, which removes old age, sorrow, and fear,
a living being does not sprout again, like a parched seed.
O you of firm vows, having worshipped that primordial one who is known as the bestower of the state of being among all living creatures,
and who is the unborn, supreme state consisting of the Self— you, who have become that very Self— why do you sink into [worldly] views?
The fortieth canto, titled "The Determination of the Deities," Lord Śiva said:
The lords of Rudra know the Lord to be the one, pervasive form of consciousness alone, abiding within the existence of all beings, consisting of self-experience, and pure.
Know that the stainless element of consciousness (ciddhātu) is the seed of all seeds, the essence of the wandering in saṃsāra, and the supreme action among all actions.
The cause of the floods of causes, yet itself causeless and stainless;
the cultivation of the parts of cultivation, yet itself uncultivable and of a non-becoming nature.
It is consciousness among the floods of consciousness, perceived within the self of consciousness;
it is the non-objectified consciousness that is the object of consciousness, the supreme and manifold radiance.
The wise know it as stainless light-of-lights, unobservable, born of light, seedless, the flood of the seed of living beings, a mass of consciousness, and pure.
Know that which is unreal yet composed of reality, peaceful, and devoid of both truth and untruth;
know it to be pure consciousness alone—the continuum beginning with the Great Being—and nothing else.
One becomes passionate oneself, becoming a colorer and the coloring passion;
even though it is itself like space, one quickly becomes a decorated wall.
Within this vast radiance of consciousness, the mirages of the world have flickered,
will flicker, and do flicker by the millions.
This [world] is accomplished solely by its own existence within its own radiance;
nothing else whatsoever is accomplished therein, just as heat is not distinct from fire.
They know this atom to contain Mount Meru within it.
This blink of an eye is said to contain within it a great eon;
yet, even while occupied by such an eon, its nature as a blink of an eye is not abandoned.
Even with this [knowledge] which is subtler than the tip of a hair, the entire earth—including its seven oceanic enclosures—is pervaded; yet it does not reach the end of that [knowledge].
Without even acting, he has attained the state of being an agent of the construction of saṃsāra;
while performing great deeds, he does not do anything at all.
Though possessing substance, he is indeed without substance; for though without substance, he possesses substance.
Though bodiless, he has a great body; and though having a great body, he is without a body.
Even now this [world] is always "morning," yet it has reached the state of being "today";
and this is not "today" nor is it "morning," yet it is both "today" and "morning" at all times.
Huṇḍubhi, lli, ghale, matta, śulu, piṇṭhili, sālaghe,
vellighilli, salāvoli, lāsaguggulu, sussunī.
Such words are meaningless; likewise, he alone is the truth.
There is nothing that does not exist in him, and there is nothing that he does not exist in.
Salutation to that Self of all, to whom everything belongs, from whom everything arises, who is everything, who exists everywhere, and who is eternally composed of everything.
By the dense foliage of Pattrāntarāla, by the playful and rolling thunder of Vilāsavatī,
and by the darkness of Malla, the prosperity of the Mālava kings— who were like wrestlers— was as if coiled up, its growth entwined like a creeper.
The forty-first canto, titled "The Description of Maheśvara," Canto 41:
Īśvara said:
In this way, even the splendor of the meanings of words, which takes the form of truth,
resides within that Lord of All, who is the casket for the jewels of all existence.
What indeed are those stainless rays within that jewel of supreme consciousness,
which do not flash forth as they discern the manifold worlds?

This consciousness-existence (citsattā), residing within the seed and the grain, having realized its own form as consisting of clay, time, water, and so forth, brings about the impelling of the sprout.
Existing within the whirlpools and eddies of foam, taking the form of taste,
it produces the movement of the waters whenever there is contact with the sense organs.
This [fragrance], abiding within the clusters of flowers as scent and form, shines forth through the nostrils and brings about their full blossoming.

Abiding within the limbs of the rock, leading them to the state of being stone, she assumes the condition of being the support for creation through her effortless play of remaining upon the king of mountains, the very seat of truth.
And the skin-sense, whose nature consists of the sheath of the vibration of the wind,
brings about its own destruction, just as a father [brings about his own defeat] through the defeat of his son.

Having meditated upon even one's own self as the condensed essence of all things for the sake of attaining the sky-like state, one thoroughly effects the sky-like nature of that self, as if it were nothingness.
Within the interior of the sprout of space, which reflects the image of its own existence,
it bears a stainless body called Time, marked by the blink of a conceptual thought.
Until the transformation of the Great Fifth Lord occurs, Niyaṭi herself spontaneously determines: "This is thus; this is not so," for those who are free from disease.
When this witness, which is a vast and stable manifestation like a lamp,
exists, the successions of the world's variegated forms shine forth through its activity.
In the grounds of the dance pavilion of the city of supreme space,
she stands like a witness, observing the cycle of existence as the dance of her own power.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Lord of the World, how do those powers of this Śiva abide?
What is their witness-hood, and what indeed is their dance, and of what extent?
Īśvara says: O gentle one, [this applies] to Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is by nature immovable and tranquil,
whose form is pure consciousness alone, and who, though being everything, is yet formless.
The existence of desire, the existence of space, and likewise the existence of time; as well as the existence of destiny and the Great Existence, O observer of noble vows.
The power of knowledge, the power of action, agency, and even non-agency—
there is no end to such powers within the self of Śiva.
Vasiṣṭha:
From where do these powers arise, and how is there such multiplicity among them?
O Lord, how does their emergence occur, and of what nature is their difference and non-difference?
The Lord: That which is the pure consciousness-nature of Śiva, who possesses infinite forms, is indeed called "power" (śakti); it is not different from him even in the slightest degree.
Through the manifestation of knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, witnesshood, and so forth,
the powers assume various forms with manifold emergence.
Although one, Śiva appears as many by his own power through what is called the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti).

By means of the single Śiva, whose nature is all-powers, objects— which are essentially Śiva— appear as if they were separate selves, imagined through the desire for objects, while he remains like a witness.
These dance in the world within the theater of the cosmic egg,
having been gradually trained by Time as if by a dancer.
That which is the succession of these [factors] is called "niyati" (destiny);
it receives such designations as "action," "nature," "desire," "time," and so forth.

Because this world, from the great Rudra down to a blade of grass, exists in such a manner as it is, Niyati (the principle of necessity) is said to be that which governs the movements of Brahmā according to fixed rules.
Necessity (niyati), eternally free from agitation and supremely powerful,
constantly dances in the sky, performing the drama of the web of the world.

Rich with the playful display of various sentiments (*rasas*), accompanied by dramatic gestures and movements, it resounded with the roar of many Puṣkarāvarta clouds destroyed in an instant by the fire at the end of the aeon.
A dwelling with a mound of earth strewn with flowers of every season,
where a profuse spray of sweat-water falls again and again like a downpour of rain.
It creates the illusion of a dark blue garment fluttering like the leaves of a cloud,
and it is crowded with bracelets rich in jewels from the seven oceans, now full and now dried up.
The sky was streaked with side-glances that were like the day for the bees of her eyelashes;
the crests of the mountain ranges were busily engaged in sinking and emerging.
It possessed three strands of pearl necklaces formed by the Gaṅgā flowing through the revolving moonstones,
and it was marked by the rising and falling of the infinite hair-pores of the fourteen kinds of living beings.
With sprout-like hands flickering like clouds at the junction of day and night, both visible and invisible,
it was as delicate as the ornaments of the world constantly moving about.
He whose footsteps traverse the vast surface of the earth, the netherworld, and the expanse of the sky,
causing the dense masses of clouds and the clusters of stars to sink down and rise up like drops of sweat.
The face of the sky was made manifest by the smiles of the quivering orbs of the moon and sun,
while the door-panels and canopies of countless cosmic eggs trembled.
It possesses pearl-like sprouts that resound through the array of worlds as they tumble about,
and it contains the shifting flavors of the presence and absence of the defects of the states of pleasure and pain.

In this essence of the long drama called saṃsāra, which is a play of destiny transformed by modifications, this one Supreme Lord stands as the witness with his eternally risen form; he is neither distinct from that [saṃsāra] nor distinct from him [the individual soul].
The forty-second canto, named "The Dance of Niyati," Canto 42;
Lord Īśvara said:
This is the God, the supreme one, always to be worshipped by the virtuous;
he is pure consciousness, whose nature is self-experience, all-pervading, and the refuge of all.
Abiding in the pot, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, and the monkey,
he is Śiva, Hara, Hari, Brahmā, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
The Blessed One, who is the self of all, both external and internal, is always worshipped by those of excellent intelligence through this twofold sequence.
O Great Sage, first listen to how the external [worship] is performed in sequence, O Knower of Reality; thereafter you shall hear the internal sequence.
Among all the sequences of worship, there is no sacred thread (*pavitraka*) made of *darbha* grass here.
In this context, worship is indeed meditation, and meditation is indeed worship;
therefore, one should always worship that which is the support of the three worlds through meditation.
One should take refuge in one's own nature, which is of the form of consciousness, possessing the luster of a million suns, illuminating all manifestations,
containing within it the light of consciousness, and having the essence of "I-ness."
Whose neck has the expansive girth of the boundless, supreme ether,
and whose lotus feet are the source of the space that lies beneath the infinite.
Adorned by the circle of his arms which span the expanse of the infinite quarters of space,
he holds the supreme weapons of various kinds belonging to the great worlds.
Within the corner of the cavity of the heart rests a continuous succession of multitudes of universes;
its form is boundless, reaching the further shore of the supreme space of light.
One should contemplate this row of hair on his body as the splendor of all beings, headed by Brahmā, Indra, Hari, Rudra, and Īśa, and the foremost of the immortals.
All the powers, beginning with Will (icchā), which initiate various undertakings and serve as the ropes for the machine of the three worlds, should be contemplated as residing within the body.
Time is his gatekeeper— he who is the support of infinite single-footedness, whose singular form is pure existence alone, and by whom the web of the world is manifested as a transformation.
This entire sphere of the cosmic egg, with its vast expanse of mountains and worlds,
has become a mere limb within some corner of his body.
One should meditate upon Mahādeva, who has a thousand feet and eyes,
a thousand heads, who is peaceful, and adorned with a thousand arms.
Rich with the power of sight everywhere, possessing the power of smell in all directions,
consisting of touch everywhere, and endowed with the sense of taste on all sides.
Pervaded by hearing everywhere, accompanied by the mind everywhere,
yet transcending thought in every respect, it is the supreme auspiciousness (śiva) everywhere.
The eternal creator of all, the bestower of all desired objects,
dwelling within the interior of all beings, the All, the sole means for accomplishing everything.
Having reflected thus, one should then worship the Lord of Gods according to the rule.
O best among the knowers of Brahman, hear this procedure for worship.
One should not worship the God, who is one's own self-consciousness, with offerings, nor with lamps, nor with incense, nor by the presentation of an abundance of flowers.
Not by the giving of food and other gifts, nor by ointments of sandalwood, nor by saffron and camphor, nor by various enjoyments, nor by others.
He is honored by his own awakening alone— an ambrosia that is eternal, obtained without affliction, cooling, and indestructible.
This alone is the supreme meditation; this alone is remembered as the highest worship: the uninterrupted realization of pure consciousness alone abiding within.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing,
speaking, releasing, and grasping— one should remain composed of pure consciousness alone.
Having worshipped this very Self, who is the Lord, with the nectar of meditation—which is endowed with supreme savor—and with flowers that are free from worldly desires; //MU_6,42.24//
Indeed, his intended self-meditation is the very offering of meditation;
both the water for the guest-offering and the water for the feet consist of pure consciousness.
The wise know that the experience of meditative absorption is the supreme flower, incense, and lamp;
without that other [practice], this Self is simply not attained.
O Sage, through meditation, this self— having attained serenity— enjoys the glory of happiness throughout all worlds within the body, just as a king enjoys it within his palace.
