O excellent sage, by means of this meditation, even one who has completed only thirteen moments should worship the Lord; he shall indeed obtain the merit of gifting a cow.
Having worshipped the Lord for even a single hundred moments,
a person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
He who, by means of his own self and through the offering of the power of meditation,
worships himself for a single hour, shall obtain the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By performing the midday worship in this manner, one obtains the merit of a hundred thousand Rājasūya sacrifices;
having worshipped thus throughout the day, that person shall dwell in the supreme abode.
This is that supreme yoga; this is that supreme ritual act.
This is declared to be the external worship, which is the highest for the self.
That man who, even for a moment, practices this purifying rite which is the cause of the destruction of all sins without weariness—
him the hosts of gods and demons will honor, for he has attained a station in this world that is the very essence of the universe, like me.
The forty-third chapter, titled "The Outer Worship," Lord [Śiva] said:
I shall now describe that internal worship of the Self, which is the purifier of purifiers and the destruction of all darkness.
Whether walking or standing still, whether waking or even sleeping— this worship, consisting of constant meditation, belongs to one who maintains all proper conduct.
One should constantly meditate upon this supreme Śiva, who resides within the body,
as the creator of all cognitions— the Self by means of the self.
Whether lying down or risen, walking or standing, whether experiencing tactile sensations on all sides or abandoning them on all sides; MU 6.43.4.
Enjoying and renouncing enjoyments that are abundant and expansive,
he is the creator of the multitude of external objects and the bestower of the essential nature of all effects.

Having abandoned other external lingas and the like, one should worship the Linga of Awakening— which resides within the Lord of the Linga of the Body— through the realization of whatever objects are encountered as they arise.

But one whose mind has attained purity through the bath of enlightenment regarding matters that have entered the stream of consciousness should worship the symbol of awakening (bodhaliṅga) with the constant offering of awareness.
The sun that has cultivated the expanse of the solar nature,
and the moon that has cultivated the expanse of the lunar nature, are ever-risen.
He whose consciousness eternally perceives the flood of manifest objects through the bodily gates, and who carries [the breath] in the mouth in the form of *prāṇa*.
It has made the [inner] essence its own flavor; it has the vital breath and the mind as its noble steeds;
it is mounted upon the chariot of the prāṇa and apāna breaths; and it dwells hidden within the inner cave.
The knower of all objects of knowledge, the doer of all actions,
the enjoyer of all things to be enjoyed, and the rememberer of all cognitions.

One should contemplate Śiva, who is the flood of limbs fully and correctly perceived, who is cultivated through the meditation on existence, who is the abundant illumination of appearances, and who is all-pervading.
It is both partless and possessed of parts, situated within the body yet moving in the sky; it is both uncolored and colored, eternally through the consciousness of its own limbs.
Abiding in the power of mental reflection, it arises within the interval between the prāṇa and apāna;
situated in the heart, throat, and palate, it rests upon the seats of the eyebrows and the nostrils.
Abiding within thirty-six crores of locations, transcending the state that ends with *unmanā*,
it causes sound and the other objects to arise within, impelling the mind that moves like a bird.
It abides within the threefold path of speech— both conceptual and non-conceptual—
and is inwardly supported within all limbs, just as oil is within sesame seeds.
Free from the stain of parts, yet conceived through the multitude of mental constructions, it abides in one place within its own heart-lotus and throughout the entire body.
Pure consciousness alone, possessing a stainless luster, is the conceptualization of parts and their arrangement;
it is directly perceptible everywhere, consisting of the nature of one's own experience.
One's own inner consciousness, standing before one as the self,
quickly assumes the state of an object and, in an instant, becomes as if a duality.
One should contemplate: "I am this divine manifestation of consciousness, my own body complete with hands, feet, and limbs, along with hair, nails, and teeth."
Many diverse powers of various behaviors, perceived by the mind,
worship me as mental wives do a supreme husband.
This mind of mine is the gatekeeper who announces the three worlds;
this thought of mine is the female usher standing before me in her pure form.
My power resides in my limbs; my intellect and action reside in my other limbs;
and my various forms of knowledge are the ornaments adorning my body.
The organs of action are the doors, and the group of sensory organs are the courtesans;
I am that very Self, infinite in nature, consciousness devoid of all limitations.
"I abide as a single, filled self, full and filling all things"—
thus one should take refuge in the Goddess, the pure wonder of the Self.
Like a god, he remains within himself, perfectly complete and free from dejection;
he neither sets nor rises, and he neither rejoices nor suffers.
He experiences neither satiety nor hunger; he desires nothing and abandons nothing.
He is equanimous, his conduct is perfectly equal, his appearance is equal, and his form is equal.
Having attained gentleness, he is beautiful in disposition on all sides; as long as the body lasts, he remains truly one, his great intelligence uninterrupted.
Thus he performs the worship of the deity day and night for a very long time;
his body, permeated by the reality of consciousness (cittattva), is proclaimed to be the deity.
With every object as it is obtained, he honors that Supreme Being who is beyond the body, using a mind that is pure through its commitment to the vow, consisting of pure consciousness alone.
One should worship with all things arising in their natural sequence as they are obtained;
one should not exert even the slightest effort toward anything that is not already present.
O sinless one, one should daily worship the all-pervading Consciousness in the morning with the horse of Dharma, then with purposeful action, and finally with the experience of desire.
One should honor the funeral pyre with various kinds of food, drink, and delicacies of diverse abundance, as well as with beds, seats, and vehicles as they are obtained.
One should worship the Self by means of awakening through every form of happiness, such as the passionate delight in the enjoyment of beloved food, drink, and sensual pleasures.
One who is overcome by mental and physical ailments, possessed by delusion and agitation,
and beset by all manner of calamities and suffering, should worship the Self.
One should worship oneself with the boundaries of prosperity, the activities of the world’s existence, and the living beings who have attained both death and life.
Whether through poverty or through sovereignty, which come to one by the force of natural flow,
and which have their flowers in various activities— one should worship the Self after realizing it.
One should worship the gentle Self with the playful display of passion and hatred, which is characterized by the splendor of the surging waves of various quarrels.
One should worship the Self residing within the heart with a friendliness that captivates the hearts of the virtuous, which is as cool as the moon and possesses the quality of sweetness.
One should worship one's own awakened self by either renouncing or, alternatively, through attachment to enjoyments that are neither prohibited nor forbidden at all times.
One should worship the Self with whatever has been obtained— whether it be desirable or undesirable, appropriate or inappropriate, pleasant or painful— having abandoned all attachment to it.
One should remain indifferent toward what is lost and gather what is obtained;
for this state of changelessness is indeed the supreme worship of the Self.
Always maintaining supreme equanimity toward all perceptions, whether they be desirable or undesirable, one should practice the vow of constant worship of the Self.

A man who is devoted to the constant worship of the Self should perceive everything as exceedingly beautiful, and he should perceive everything as unlovely; he should make all things consist of the Self.

Having understood that everything which is delightful at first sight and everything which is unbearable at first sight are all exactly the same, one should practice the vow of worshiping the eternal Self.
One should abandon the distinction between "this is I" and "this is not I," and having resolved that "all is Brahman," one should practice the vow of constant self-worship.
At all times, in every form, with every kind of transformation,
and in every possible manner— whether as the whole or as the part— one should worship the Self once it has been attained.
Neither desiring nor rejecting, the wise man has attained the planes of enjoyment by their very nature; they are to be experienced like rivers by the ocean.
One should not be agitated by views, whether trivial or profound,
just as the sky is not disturbed by objects of various forms that fall and rise within it.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious arises through the conjunction of place, time, and action—
one should worship the Self with that very thing, having grasped it as changeless.
In this ritual for the worship of the Self, whatever riches of material substances have been prescribed are permeated by the single flavor of tranquility.
They are neither sour, nor pungent, nor bitter, nor astringent; though smeared with various flavors, those perceptions are perceived as only sweet.
O Lord of Sages, that which is perceived when permeated by that power of aesthetic flavor— which is delightful, beautiful, and sweet with equanimity— becomes nectar in an instant.
Whatever is contemplated through the flood of the nectar of equanimity attains a supreme sweetness, like the nectar flowing from the moon.
When one has become equanimous like space, that posture which is free from mental impressions,
changeless, and effortless is called the worship of the Divine.
One should become like the full moon— full with the radiance of tranquility and equanimity,
transparent, consisting solely of the density of consciousness, and wise even while appearing in the form of a stone.
Clear as the inner space within, yet performing external natural functions;
free from the mist of passion, the wise devotee is complete.
When the clouds of ignorance have vanished, the autumnal sky of the Knower shines forth, its inner landscape invisible even in dreams and its mist of "I-ness" and other such notions stilled.
With the commonality of subject, object, and means of knowledge having set, like the pervasive sensation of a newborn infant,
with the intellect, consciousness, mind, and vital breath perfectly stilled— remaining as a living knower established in the supreme state, abide.
With a mind whose every longing has been stilled, remain with your body eternally honored by the Guide, amidst all the delusions of pleasure and pain arising from the sequence of time and space.
The forty-fourth chapter, titled "Reflection on the Worship of Deities," spoken by Īśvara:
Whether you do not act according to your desire or your undertaking, or whatever you do,
that which occurs within the auspicious Śiva who is pure consciousness is itself the worship of the Self.
By that very means, the Lord himself attains joy and likewise manifests in his own form as it truly exists.
The referents of words such as "attachment" and "aversion" do not exist as distinct entities within the auspicious Self, just as particles of frost cannot exist within fire.
Whatever experience there may be— whether of kingship or servitude, pleasure or pain, and so forth—
whether belonging to oneself or to another, each and every one of those is an act of worship toward the Self.
Know that consciousness itself is the object of worship; for the Self knows only the Self, O Brahmin, either as the nature of objects such as jars or simply as its own self-nature.
Auspicious, peaceful, without appearance, one, radiant, and all-pervading— this entire world, though appearing as a mental construct, exists as the very form of the Self.
Oh, how wondrous! It is the Self alone that exists as other things such as jars;
yet the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, though established within itself, have surely forgotten this, as it were.
Within Śiva himself— the infinite Self who is the essence of all—
this delusion consisting of the worshipped, the worshipper, and the act of worship has arisen in vain.
Nor is a state of fixed form and tranquility possible in Īśvara, since,
O Brahman, the sequence consisting of the worshiper and the object of worship is conceived by him.
A deity who is separated from the act of worshiping the worshipful is impermanent; he is not a fit vessel for lordship over the infinite, pure-souled, and omnipotent one.
O Brahman, for the Self, whose nature is the purest consciousness pervading the three worlds, no designation whatsoever is appropriate except that of "Lordship."
Those for whom the Supreme Lord is limited by space and time are our teachers; they are not truly wise, though they may call themselves wise.
Having abandoned that view and likewise having adopted this one,
he becomes equanimous, with a healthy mind, peaceful, free from passion, and free from affliction.
Worshiping yourself with the offerings of your duties as they arise from all sides, remain with an undaunted mind amidst pleasure and pain, and the auspicious and inauspicious.
O virtuous one, when you have thus attained [realization], surely no suffering of birth and so forth will quickly touch your agitated life-force;
for it does not cling to you who are completely pure, just as a blemish does not appear within a flawless crystal palace.
The forty-fifth canto, titled "An Inquiry into Divinity," by Vasiṣṭha:
O Lord, what is Śiva called? What is the supreme Brahman called?
And what is the Self (ātman) called? Or what is the supreme Self (paramātman) called?
O Blessed One, Lord of the Three Worlds, why is there this distinction— such as "that is existent," "it is nothing at all," "emptiness," and "consciousness alone"— spoken of?
Īśvara:
There exists here a certain Reality that is without beginning or end and without manifestation;
because it does not manifest through the senses, it remains as if it were nothing at all.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Lord, since the senses have attained invisibility even when joined with the intellect and other faculties, tell me, by what means is that [Self] perceived?
Īśvara:
He who desires liberation is merely a portion of ignorance that is purely *sāttvika*;
he is [bound] by those very *sāttvika* portions of ignorance known as the scriptures and so forth.
Washing away ignorance, both superior and inferior, he remains here like a skilled washerman who removes dirt with dirt.
When the destruction of ignorance arrives later, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit, the Self perceives itself by means of itself; this is the certainty regarding its own nature.
Just as a child, by somehow rubbing away soot and washing it off, attains purity of hand through the removal of the blackness of the charcoal; so too [does one attain purity].
Just as one who is rich in scriptural knowledge analyzes a portion by means of various parts,
so too, through the destruction of the tamasic by means of the sattvic, there arises the exaltation of the Self for both.
The Self alone perceives itself and investigates by means of itself;
the Self alone exists here, and there is no ignorance—those who know this understand the destruction of ignorance.
To whatever extent this entity is not understood as non-different from the Self,
to that extent the sequence of instructions from the guru and so forth is not a cause for the knowledge of the Self.
The Guru is indeed the self of the aggregate of the senses; Brahman is attained through the cessation of all the senses.
Whatever object is to be reached by the cessation of something, that object is not attained while that thing still exists.

O twice-born one, even those things which are not causes have attained the status of being causes in due order— beginning with the instruction of the guru— for the sake of accomplishing self-knowledge.
When the sequence of the guru’s instructions proceeds through the awakening of the disciple,
the Self, though indescribable and invisible, becomes manifest of its own accord.
O sinless one, the Self is not understood through the meanings of the scriptures, nor by the words of a teacher;
it is understood by itself alone, through the power of its own awakening from within.
Without the meaning of the scriptures and the instructions of the guru, the Self is not realized;
it is only through the existence of this conjunction that the knowledge of one's own Self is illumined.
Through the long-standing association of the teacher, the meaning of the scriptures, and the disciples, self-knowledge proceeds just as the conduct of people proceeds through the passage of days.

The cessation of karma, the sense organs, and the like, as well as pleasure, pain, and so forth, is called the Self (ātman), which is Śiva; it is designated by such names as "That" (tat) and "Being" (sat).
That wherein this entire world does not exist, yet exists in its very form—
that which is more transparent than space, infinite, and real— indeed exists here.
Because they do not rest therein, those seekers of liberation who possess limited ignorance have their souls stained by the blemish of various pure mental constructions.

Standing not far from the state of being liberated while living, they [composed] this work for the purpose of explaining the means to liberation and for the formulation of the meaning of the scriptures.
By the world-protectors headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, together with the learned,
who had cultivated their selves for the sake of establishing the doctrines of the Purāṇas and the Vedas.
Cid, Brahmā, Śiva, Ātman, Īśa, Paramātman, Īśvara, and so forth—
these are names conceptually constructed for the one Lord who is beyond all naming, though he appears as distinct.
Such is the reality of this world; it is one's own reality, named Śiva.
Worshipping it in every way, at all times, and with everything, O friend, remain in happiness.

In such terms as "Śiva," "the Self," and "the Supreme Brahman," there is a distinction created by those possessed of latent impressions; for the knower, however, there is no difference in the Reality itself.
O leader of sages, the wise one who thus constantly performs the worship of the gods goes to that supreme state where we and others like us are servants.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"This [world] is indeed non-existent, yet it stands as if it were existent.
O Blessed One, you should explain to me how that is, in brief."
Īśvara said:
Know that which is the referent of words such as "Brahmā" and so forth to be nothing but pure consciousness;
even the clear sky is gross compared to it, like Mount Meru is to an atom.
Perceiving the object of knowledge, she attains the fitness for the state called *citi*;
indeed, even when devoid of an object of knowledge, she remains established in the state at the end of *unmanā*.
In an instant, because its state of being experienced has been brought forth, it follows after the "I-ness," just as a man, by virtue of his humanity, assumes the form of a new elephant in a dream.
When this [consciousness] has attained non-duality, space, time,
and the void itself become its very friends, being of the nature of emptiness.
Then, that existence conjoined with those [powers] and designated as the "living being" (jīva) becomes the knower of vibration, like a streak of wind.
The power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), being of such a nature and delighting solely in its own resolve,
follows the state of the intellect (buddhi) and comes to abide in the station of the ignorant.
She is followed by the power of sound, the power of action, and the power of knowledge;
she vibrates within each [of these] individually, her form unmanifested.
Having quickly joined together and conforming to the sacred revelation,
this group becomes the mind— the seed of the tree of volition, which is empty of self-nature.
The wise know that to be the vehicle of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha),
which, through the power of Brahman residing within it, perceives the Self by itself as the form of the Knower.
For these powers, while this very mind is coming into being, arise as if simultaneously with it, even though they have not yet manifested, as if they were already there afterwards.
The existence of wind, the existence of vibration, and likewise the existence of touch;
the existence of the skin, the existence of fire, and likewise the existence that is illuminating.
The existence of vision, the existence of water, and likewise the existence of taste;
in the same way, the existence of flavor and likewise the existence of smell.
Existence as earth, existence as body, existence as a physical mass, and that which is plump; existence as space and existence as time—all these are devoid of form.
In this way, having embraced the multitude of beings within its own nature,
that which has attained the state of life vibrates like a seed from which leaves and other parts have emerged.
Know this to be the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), and this body is the subtle transport-body (ativāhika). Due to the lack of higher awakening, it manifests as if divided into parts.
That which is endowed with limbs, when fully analyzed, is nothing at all;
it is not born, nor does it possess the nature of existence, nor is it consciousness and so forth, nor anything else.
The other shines forth from the other, being solely the nature of the Absolute (kevalātman),
like the play of liquid water within the belly of a mass of water.

This world, whose sole essence is consciousness and its perception, appears as something separate when it is not reflected upon; yet when fully understood, it becomes like a city of one's own imagination.
Through the thorough knowledge of consciousness, one attains the state of Śiva;
but how can that which is unborn possibly attain the status of a real entity?

Then, when it attains its own interiority through volition, it becomes minute by its very nature; these [elements], existing as mere subtle essences (*tanmātra*), perceive the body of that minute being.
One quickly perceives that very [self] as having attained both atomicity and grossness;
one perceives its apertures consisting of the subtle elements according to their respective locations.

Then, through the singular contemplation of the form of the Puruṣa, having seen [the deity] possessing the shape of a person— just like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit— one becomes fully satisfied and nourished.
Then the living being, remaining in this state, perceives the body as something non-existent, like a city of Gandharvas or a city in a dream.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The world has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and is like a city seen in a dream; since it leads only to suffering, what logic is there for its destruction?
Īśvara said:
Suffering arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), and those impressions exist only while the world exists;
yet the world is non-existent, like the shimmering water of a mirage.
Therefore, what is being perfumed, by what, whose is the perfuming, or from where?
How, my dear, can the water of a mirage be drunk by a man in a dream?
But when the creator, as well as desire, mind, and ego,
no longer exist within the world, that which is real remains.
Where there is neither latent impression (*vāsanā*), nor that which perfumes (*vāsaka*), nor that which is to be perfumed (*vāsya*),
there is only the state of absolute oneness (*kevalībhāva*), in which all delusion has been completely stilled.
For one for whom even a yakṣa—whether real or unreal—is indeed empty, that [yakṣa] has dissolved through absolute oneness; what else remains?
For this mental impression called "the world" has arisen in this way as something utterly empty, like a ghost; when it is stilled, peace remains unimpaired.
He who is equally composed toward egoity, the world, and the water of a mirage— that mass of pure consciousness— he cannot be described by saying "this is he."
Those who know reality teach that the discerning soul alone exists here, while the ignorant, deluded, and unreal body is abandoned by the noble.
He who instructs the ignorant indeed gives his daughter—who is as bright as gold—to a man seen in a dream.
The forty-sixth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Falsity of the World," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then that living being, O Blessed One, having witnessed the agitation of the body at the time of the primal creation while stationed in the ether, indeed attained what state?
The Lord: In the supreme ether beyond the other, the individual soul perceives a body formed according to the previously described sequence,
just like a man in an unreal dream.
For since the mass of consciousness is all-pervading, just as a man in a dream quickly performs an action, so too does the living being perceive its body.
Because he designates himself as "I am the eternal, unmanifest Person," he is therefore called the first Person (puruṣa).
Thus, in a certain creation, that first principle is called Sadāśiva; in another, he is called Viṣṇu, and not the Grandfather (Brahmā) born from the navel.
That grandfather was one thing, and the other was something else entirely;
he was a personification of volition, existing as volition itself embodied in form.
Nourished by his initial resolve and established in that mental form,
whatever he conceives in whatever manner, he experiences that exactly and immediately in abundance.
All that, being of the nature of non-existence, is like a ghost in an empty place;
yet, through the vision of delusion, it appears as having the nature of existence—such is the course of the ego and the world.
Indeed, he who is the primordial Person, the Creator, thus becomes manifest by himself;
he arises and then dissolves within the ether at every moment.
In a mere blink of an eye, one fully experiences the succession of aeons, intermediate aeons, and great aeons,
through nothing more than the error of mental appearance.
Indeed, in every atom, in every void, and in every moment,
there arise the existence and non-existence of creations, kalpas, and great kalpas.
Some are seen by one another due to hundreds of similar latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
some are not seen by others; and some see no one else at all.
Some creations are not seen by others, even though they are perceived as having a non-existent nature;
such creations do not arise anywhere in the auspicious state.
In the supreme ether, they themselves become of the nature of ether;
and being themselves of the nature of both the existent and the non-existent, they dissolve like mountains in a dream.
Neither space, nor time, nor agency is pervaded by creations;
nor are these of the nature of reality, neither for an eon nor for even a moment.
Nothing whatsoever is born here, nor does anything whatsoever perish;
consciousness manifests as wonder within consciousness by means of its own wondrous nature.
Like the construction and the falling and rising within a city in a dream,
the world does not even allow the mind to traverse space and time.
Just as the infinite expanse of space and time is not actually overcome by a mountain created through mere imagination,
so too the unreal world does not truly overcome [the Self].
Just as that primordial Person, the creator of the world, comes into being, so too does a worm here come into being in an instant by this very same sequence.
In this very same way, the four classes of beings that remain stationary—
beginning with the Rudras and ending with trees— come into being anew at every moment.
There are some that are supreme, others that are inferior, and likewise some that are like atoms;
this is their sequence, whether a creation exists or does not exist.
Through the cultivation of the true nature of this illusion of saṃsāra,
when its distinctions are stilled through practice, there arises auspicious peace.
If the supreme consciousness, which lasts for no more than half of a hundredth part of a blink of an eye,
were to roll about within its own nature, then this state arises.
If that [consciousness], whose nature is knowledge, remains within itself like a stone casket,
then it is designated by the term "Brahman," which is essentially beginningless manifestation.
When this creation has reached maturity, the Great Consciousness (mahācit) attains a new awareness by coming into contact with the directions, space, time, and the constituent atoms.
For living beings, [the body] arises through the sequence of the fluctuations of the elements and subtle essences;
it becomes a god, an asura, a plant, a tree, a deer, a beast, a creeper, an insect, and so forth.
In that eternal, extended, and firm thread, the entire universe— composed of both the existent and the non-existent— rests like a garland upon Viśvakarman, whose limbs are the universe.
It is neither far nor near, neither above nor below; it is not yours, nor mine;
it was not in the past, nor today, nor in the morning; it is neither being, nor non-being, nor something situated in between.
Apart from the occurrence of direct experience, there can be no knower even when all forms of conceptual construction are present;
the series of means of valid cognition, though possessing the vast power of results, does not attain stability, just as fire does not exist in water.
O Sage, you have answered what was asked; may prosperity be yours.
We shall now depart for our desired destination; arise, O Pārvatī!
Having spoken thus, that blue-throated one, while I was still holding the handful of flowers,
crossed into the expanse of the sky together with his retinue.

When that Lord of Umā, the sovereign of the three worlds, had departed, I stood for a moment and then, as if out of a renewed sense of purity, accepted that seat of darbha grass which I had previously resolved upon, just as one who is weary accepts the great learning he has acquired.
The forty-seventh canto, titled "An Inquiry into the Designation of the Supreme Self," consisting of the dialogue between Īśvara and Vasiṣṭha, is completed.
Vasiṣṭha: This has been declared by the Supreme Lord himself, and I too know it;
O Rāma, you also know how this world is established.
In this illusory cycle of existence (*saṃsāramāyā*), where the unreal is perceived by means of the unreal— what therein is real, and what is composed of the unreal?
Just as that which is conceptualized by whichever conceptualization and by whatever conceptualization, so too it is not experienced even while existing, because it lacks that very nature of selfhood.
Just as liquidity exists in water, as movement exists in the wind,
and as emptiness exists in space, so does the state of manifestation exist within the Self.
From that time onwards, I have remained here, free from distraction, performing my own worship according to that very same sequence until this day.
O Rāma, by means of this method of worship, these latent tendencies are passed through by me without distress, even while remaining engaged in worldly affairs.
The worship of myself with the flowers of ritual conduct as they were obtained was never interrupted by me, even for a single day or night, though it had been severed.
When all embodied beings possess a commonality regarding the relationship between the grasped and the grasper,
that state of attentiveness which the yogi maintains therein is the worship of the Self.
O Lord of the Raghus, by means of this vision and with a mind liberated from attachment,
you wander in this vast wilderness of saṃsāra without being distressed.
When great suffering has arisen, born from the loss of wealth and kin, hold fast to this view and engage in reflection, O observer of noble vows.
One should not experience pleasure or pain due to the rise or fall of wealth and kinsmen;
indeed, all such perceptions of cyclic existence are constantly of this nature.
You surely know the various courses of the sense-objects, which are so turbulent—
how they proceed, how they return, and how they overcome us.
In this very way do affections and riches arise;
in this very way they perish through unexamined causes.
They are not yours, nor are you theirs; you are stainless, while the activities of the world belong to them.
This world is merely such as it is—what is the point of grieving in vain?
You alone are the form of the universe, pure consciousness with an expansive manifestation;
when one is enveloped by one's own limbs [of existence], what room is there for the sequence of joy and sorrow?
Having attained a state of one-pointed consciousness resembling that of deep sleep,
from this day forward, O Rāma, you shall abide in the nature of the fourth state (turya).
Equal, appearing as equal, with a radiant body and noble intellect,
remain always according to your own nature, like the perfectly full ocean.
You have heard all this; you stand here with a perfected intellect. O delight of the Raghus, if you wish to ask anything else, then ask it.
"Regarding that which you asked in the first aeon— 'How can there be impurity for Brahmā, who possesses infinite forms?'— bring that forward again today."
Rāma:
O Brahmin, now my doubt has especially ceased;
everything that was to be known has been known, and an unartificial satisfaction has arisen.
There is no duality, nor unity, nor even conceptualization regarding the Self;
at that time I was ignorant, but now that [ignorance] has been stilled.
That delusion which I previously held, under the influence of ignorance, that there was a stain upon my self, has now ceased through your grace.
The Self is neither born nor does it die, nor is it ever defiled;
indeed, I have declared that everything is composed of Brahman. MU 6.47.23
From questions, from doubts, and from all desires,
my mind has emerged purified, like a carpenter’s tool released from the whirling of its lathe.
When most of the essential instructions have been proclaimed by the virtuous,
I remain within myself free from longing, like Mount Sumeru amidst gold.
There is nothing wherein there is no hope; there is nothing that is not desired;
there is nothing that is not to be taken up by me, nor to be abandoned, nor even that which is neutral.
"This is to be abandoned, this is to be accepted; this is existent, and this too is non-existent"—O Sage, such delusion of thought has been stilled by you, the most skillful and supreme one.
I do not long for heaven, nor do I hate the Raurava hell;
for I abide in the Self alone, like Mount Mandara free from clouds.

The Mandara mountain that is Rāma, having long been agitated, has now come to rest; he is free from delusion, and the succession of the milk-ocean of the three worlds is scattered grain by grain within him.
In the heart of one who possesses the impurity of conceptualizing "this is non-existent" and "this is existent," the web of evil doubts blazes all the more intensely.
O Lord of Sages, that world which is known by one as "this world is thus," when he encounters misfortune regarding that very world, it is no longer found.
O Blessed One, by your grace we have crossed the ocean of existence, which is filled with various turbulent waves and revolved by the movements of the dull-witted.
The limit of prosperity has been known, and the boundary of calamities has been seen;
we are undaunted amidst all essential things, we are fulfilled, we are supreme lords.
In the battle of saṃsāra, his mind has attained a perfect fortitude that is supreme, indivisible by others, and which crushes the elephant of desire.

Victorious in the three worlds is my unsurpassed mind, which has attained the state of being free from conceptual construction, which has shed all longing, whose essential strength is undaunted, and which is exultant within with its well-known form.
The forty-eighth canto, titled "Attaining Rest," by Vasiṣṭha:
Whatever you do with the mind alone, together with the senses directed toward present objects, that which is performed without attachment is as if not done at all.
Just as an object at the very moment it is attained brings initial satisfaction, who has not experienced that it does not do so after even a single moment of attainment? MU 6.48.2
Just as an object brings satisfaction at the time it is desired, but not otherwise,
therefore only a fool, and no one else, binds his satisfaction to momentary pleasure.
At the moment of desire, it is the desire itself that is the cause of satisfaction;
yet satisfaction ends in dissatisfaction. Therefore, abandon desire.
If you should ever attain that state through the passage of time,
you must never again plunge into the form of egoistic contemplation.
O Rāma, you have found rest upon the peak of the mountain of self-knowledge;
you ought not to fall again into the great abyss of egoism.
For one who possesses the infinite, true vision that has spread forth and stands upon the summit of the Meru of knowledge,
how could there again be a fall into the abyss within the darkness of the womb?
This nature of yours is seen to consist of the truth of equanimity;
I believe you have exhausted all conceptual constructions, you are born [in the ultimate sense], and you are free from time.
"O gentle Rāma, this stability of yours makes it seem as if it were announcing to me that this is your true nature; your equanimity is stainless and resembles the full ocean."
May hope turn into hopelessness, and may the tendency toward mental construction turn into non-existence; may the mind turn into no-mind for you who live in non-attachment.
Whatever perception of an object you may have, in each and every one of them, there resides the dense mass of consciousness expanded as Brahman, in the form of the universal nature of existence.
One who does not know the Self is bound; one who knows the Self is not bound. Therefore, O Rāma, by your own effort, you must awaken the Self through the Self.
Know that state to be the absence of latent impressions (avāsanatva), as gentle as the sky, wherein an object does not taste sweet to oneself, yet tastes sweet as it comes.
Performing actions with internal organs free from latent impressions,
you do not undergo modification even through hundreds of disturbances, remaining like the sky.

O fortunate one, experiencing the peaceful Self in which the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge— this triad— are unified within the Self, you shall no longer be subject to further existence.
The emergence and dissolution of saṃsāra occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of the mind;
by restraining the latent impressions and the vital breath, make the mind free from such opening.
The emergence and dissolution of transmigratory existence occur through the opening and closing of the vital breath;
by means of practice and application, render that [breath] devoid of its opening.
The dissolution and emergence of karmas occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of ignorance;
therefore, forcibly dissolve that [ignorance] by means of union with the meaning of the scriptures and the Guru.
Just as the perception of pillars and clouds arises from the movement caused by the contact of wind and dust,
so too does this world appear through the vibration of consciousness as the object of thought.
This movement of the world, which is to be conquered through the vibration of the relationship between the seen and the seeing,
manifests like the cognition of color arising from the contact of light with a wall or other objects.

In the absence of the vibration of the relationship between the seen and the seeing, no sensation arises that appears as existence, just as [no image arises] in the minds of men depicted in a painting.
Illusion arises from the vibration of the mind; in its absence, it dissolves. A wave arises from the vibration of water; in its absence, it subsides.
Whether through the relinquishing of the portion of latent impressions, through awakening, or through the restraint of the vital breath,
when the mind has attained a state of vibrationlessness, how could there be the possibility of vibration?
By the mere cessation of the vibration of non-awareness, the mind reaches the state of no-mind;
or else, by the suppression of the vital breaths, that very same supreme state is attained.
In the relationship between the seen and the seer, that supreme bliss which exists is attained through the final, exclusive realization; by means of the vision of Brahman, the mind is extinguished.
Wherever the mind has not arisen, there that happiness is unconditioned;
it does not exist even in heaven and the like, just as a house of ice does not exist in a desert.
The bliss born from the tranquility of the mind is expansive, inexpressible by words,
free from decrease or excess, and neither arises nor ceases.
Through awakening, the end of the mind occurs; through non-awakening, the mind arises.
Therefore, like a child’s ghost, the splendor of delusion has attained solidity.
For even though this mind exists, it dissolves through awakening;
though real, it appears as if unreal, just like copper when it has been turned into gold.
The mind of the Knower is not called "mind"; the mind of the Knower is said to be *sattva*.
Through awakening, the mind undergoes a change in both name and substance, just as copper becomes gold.
The nature of mind is not possible; therefore, it dissolves.
Delusion is stilled by awakening; there is no non-existence of that which exists.
This mind and so forth, being of the nature of conceptual construction, is a non-entity like the horn of a hare;
because the Self is all-pervasive, it dissolves through the awakening to that [Self].
The mind, having attained the state of being a sentient being for some time during the existence of the world,
dwells in the fourth state (turya) and thereafter becomes that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
Brahman alone, through the flood of delusions consisting of the manifold wanderings of the world, exists thus as the one in its multiplicity;
it becomes the self of all, and nothing else whatsoever, my dear—just as various forms exist within a golden heart, so too do mental states and the like exist within it.
The forty-ninth canto, titled "The Indication of the Non-existence of the Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this regard, O Rāma, listen to this unprecedented and beautiful story in brief, which causes the hair to stand on end with wonder for the sake of awakening.
There exists a great bilva fruit, thousands of yojanas in extent, vast, stainless, and manifest, which remains undecaying even through the ages.
It possesses the essence of indestructible flavor, like the sweet core of nectar;
though ancient, it is as beautiful and soft as the crescent of the young moon.
It was not shaken even by the force of the great winds at the end of a kalpa, which could move a mass of grass consisting of the vast and insurmountable mountains of Mahāmeru and Mandara.
Even by hundreds of lakhs of millions of ten-thousand yojanas,
the extent of the first fruit of the world’s existence is immeasurable.
The universes, though vast, are near to this bilva fruit;
on the mountain below, they bear the likeness of a mere row of mustard seeds.
O Rāghava, there is no one who surpasses him in the marvelous sweetness of his flavor, which is filled with a flowing essence and possesses all six tastes.
That which never meets its end through cooking, and which, though always cooked, my dear friend, is not afflicted by old age; [that is the body].
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and others like them are merely some who have grown old; they do not know his origin, nor his root, nor even the tree itself.
But for one who has not seen the sprout or the tree, and has not seen the emergence of the flower,
the fruit alone is observed— [a fruit] whose stem, root, and branches are invisible.
Of that which possesses a grossness pervaded by the form of a single, solid mass,
no transformation such as birth or alteration is perceived.
Within this great fruit, which is the essence of all fruits,
there exists an extensive, changeless inner pith consisting of a distinct flavor.
Like a solid rock that is yet permeated by the flowing orb of the moon,
he flows with the nectar of truth, tasting within himself the essence that is his own self-awareness.
The initiation is the source of all happiness, the creator of cooling light;
it is like a mountain, like a mass of nectar, and the essence for abiding in the fruit of the self.
Therefore, that supreme marrow which is a sweet wonder,
eternally undisturbed within and non-different from the limb of the Śrīphala fruit— [that is the true essence].
By that slender girl, though she was stout and very young, her own arrangement of limbs— which resulted in a state of non-difference from him— was not abandoned.
From the conceptualization "I am this," there arises the impurity of the distinction between the non-existent and the existent;
having produced this [distinction] by itself, it is then cultivated, since [in reality] distinctions and the like are impossible.
Immediately following the arising of the ego-sense,
she [the world] was formed by the atoms of the three worlds, whose limbs were the sounds of the revolving sky.
Thus, proceeding in this sequence, that power of consciousness (saṃvit) attains the state of being marrow,
without ever abandoning its own prior internal structure.
By that power of consciousness, which there assumes a fluctuating form, the vision is thus expanded within its own supreme nature.
This is the great infinity of space; this is the great portion of time;
this is destiny engaged in action; this is activity characterized by vibration.
This is the expansion of conceptual construction; this is the delusion of the burden of hope;
this is the state of attachment and aversion; and this is the intellect that discriminates between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
This is you, this is I, this is yours, and this is the established order;
this is the flood of cosmic eggs situated above, this is in front, and this is also below.
"This is in front, this is at the side, this is behind, this is near, and this is far; this is a real thing, this is present, and this is also future. MU 6.49.24.
This is the abode of the lotuses of manifold mental constructions situated within,
the circular pavilion for the play of the cosmic egg.
This pericarp of the heart-lotus of Hari, which has fully blossomed with the reality of infinite time, is the rosary of lotus-seeds that constitutes the worlds.
This long path, strewn with the sprouts of the seeds of great Rudras in its hollows, possesses a luster that strives to dispel the darkness.
This Mount Meru is the pericarp of the world-lotus whose petals are the cardinal directions;
it is frequented by the bees that are the gods, who are greedy for the nectar of the shimmering moon.
This cluster of blossoms from the flower-creepers of celestial splendor, possessing unrestrained fragrance,
belongs to the world— a withered tree whose roots are in the dust of hell.
And this blue lotus of the sky, with the stars as its filaments, stands upon the rim of the cosmic egg; it is boundless, extending to the very limits of the infinite.
This river of action has rows of rafts in the form of wind-driven waves; it is the place where the succession of numerous beings revolves within the whirlpools of creation.
This is the lotus-plant of Time, whose bees are darkness, whose sprouts are moments and eons,
whose lion is radiance, and whose lotus is the sky.
These views on the meaning of the scriptures are rich in the transformations of existence, filled with old age, death, and cholera, and abounding in the fluctuations of knowledge and ignorance.
Thus, that very wonder of the wood-pulp of the bilva tree has established itself in this manner within the internal structure of its own conceptual arrangement.
Peaceful, established in its own nature, free from affliction, and abandoned by all that is other than the gentle;
having rendered both agency and non-agency as if they were performed, it remains exactly as it is.
Though appearing as manifold and diverse when perceived individually, it is indeed neither of a single nature nor manifold;

rather, it is that very same [reality]—the power that is consciousness itself, which is established in truth, whose uniform form is the peace of all things, which is the self of all, and which is exceedingly great.
The fiftieth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Conceptualization of the Existence of Consciousness," [ends here].
Rāma:
O Blessed One, Knower of all Dharmas, it is my understanding that you have described this entity, which has the form of a bilva fruit, as the "mass of great consciousness" (mahācidghanasattā).
This entire expanse, beginning with the ego-sense, is of the nature of pure consciousness;
there is not even the slightest difference consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as the arrangement of Mount Meru and other features is the marrow within the gourd of the cosmic egg,
so too this arrangement of the world, beginning with the cosmic egg, is the marrow within the wood-apple of consciousness.
The creation known as the world is the wondrous manifestation of the marrow of the consciousness-wood-apple;
it remains within the tranquil interior of deep sleep, like a structure carved within a stone.
In this regard, O moon-faced one, listen to another delightful and wonderful narrative being recounted by me, which is truly astonishing.
There exists somewhere a great rock— glossy, clear, soft to the touch, possessing vast dimensions, dense, and eternally without fissures.

Within it, there are also very many lotuses in full bloom; some have their roots arising from the pericarp, while others have the pericarp within their roots; some have roots above, some have roots below, and others are rootless.
And near them are conchs by the hundreds of thousands,
and great masses of discs arranged like lotuses.
Rāma:
This is true; I have seen that great stone of such a kind.
It exists, surrounded by its retinue, in Sāligrāma, the abode of Hari.
Vasiṣṭha said: "It is so; you understand this. You have seen those stones;
whatever stone is there, each one is entirely of such a nature."
But this unprecedented stone of yours is described by me as one within whose vast interior everything both exists and does not exist.

This consciousness has been described by me to you as a "fragment" (cicchilā), within which the worlds exist in space; because of its nature as a single mass of density, this consciousness is like a stone.
Even within one whose body is exceedingly dense and whose form is without interstices,
the Supreme Brahman exists within, just as the vast wind exists within the sky.
The sky, the earth, the wind, space, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions exist within it;
yet that stone is not even slightly porous.
Within this [reality], which is a single solid mass of being, the lotus of the world unfolds;
there is nothing other than this substance, nor anything else that possesses a dual nature.
The past, the present, and the future are like a carved figure on a block of stone;
thus, everything exists there exactly as the configuration of the object.

Just as a collection of stones, though consisting of many distinct entities, assumes the state of a single mass, so too this consciousness, though manifold, appears as a single, solid, and compact whole.
Just as a lotus, though not distinct from the stone matrix,
consists of its own form, so too the creation, though not distinct from the form of consciousness, consists of its own form.
Just as the lines of lotuses on a wheel remain within a stone during deep sleep, so too does this series of worlds exist within consciousness.
Just as a row of lotus designs within a stone or a flash of brilliance within black pepper neither arises nor sets, so too is creation within consciousness.
Just as the interior of a wood-apple fruit is filled with pulp so that there is no space between it and the rind,
so too the sphere of the universe is contained within consciousness, which is richly endowed with all possible transformations.
The statement that "the modification and so forth are that very [reality]" is purposeless;
for it quickly attains that state of reality, like a drop of water in water.
Because consciousness is infinite, this [universe] and its modifications are said to "belong to consciousness";
through speech it is manifested, and by merging into that, it is dissolved.
This world, consisting of modifications and so forth, is indeed Brahman alone, devoid of the reality of modifications and the like;
for, due to its infinite nature, Brahman alone exists whether there is the exclusion or non-exclusion of objects.

The state of Brahmā, the transformations, and so forth—know that all these were produced from Brahman alone in succession; understand that those who perceive them as something else are like one who seeks water in a mirage.
The seed situated within the flower and fruit does not consist of anything other than the end of the seed;
such is the nature of that seed-existence which will likewise exist subsequently.
That which is the density of consciousness within the mass of consciousness is itself the sequence of the three worlds;
their oneness and duality exist together, for in the absence of one, both are lost.
The world never arises from anything other than itself; it was never otherwise. Consciousness and the unconscious are never non-existent, nor are these two ever separate from one another.

Just as within a great, indivisible stone there exist many lines, so too within the dense mass of consciousness (cidghana) exists the movement of the three worlds, which is neither different from nor non-different from it— like marrow and other internal constituents.

Just as lines and the like carved within a stone are not distinct from the stone itself because they consist of its very essence, so too the world— including the states of being a thinker or an agent— is not distinct from Consciousness.
Just as the arising and ceasing, the movement and stillness of lotuses within a rock do not become objects [of perception],
so too the creators of the world do not become objects [of perception].
This is never created, nor does it ever perish;
like a mountain, its nature consists of the experience of the play of subsidence and manifestation.
Just as, wherever, and in whatever form [something appears], so indeed is that very thing;
for Brahman, which is the self of all and everything, remains established in the state of deep sleep.
Know that this great delusion of the world, which is rich with the manifold transformations of existence,
is indeed like deep sleep, comparable to a lotus and the like within a stone.

O dear one, because it consists of the tranquil, uniform, dense consciousness that is the self of space, the world’s play is eternally nothing but the state of deep sleep; thus, from the perspective of one's own essence, the various stages of creation do not differ in any way from a lotus carved out of stone.
The fifty-first canto, titled "The Instruction on the Casket of Stones," by Vasiṣṭha.
Just as the fruit of the *cittattva* is variegated and beautiful, so too,
its internal arrangement of its own existence that occurs in succession is established as "creation" (*sarga*).
Because space, time, action, and so forth are of such an extremely subtle nature,
it is not possible here to say, "this is one thing" and "that is another."
For those who know that all conceptual constructions of words and their meanings are but latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
how could this world be described as "other" than that, since it is of one single nature?
Just as the internal arrangement of a fruit appears in various sequences— appearing as if non-various yet varied, as if agitated yet unagitated—
so too is the existence within the fruit, and the mass of consciousness within consciousness.
The city of the world is reflected in the mirror as if in a funeral pyre; it seems to shimmer and yet does not shimmer, like a structure within a stone.
Within the supreme jewel of consciousness, even hundreds of millions of worlds exist,
just as infinite desired fruits are fully present within a wish-fulfilling gem.
This entire world appears like a pearl inlaid upon that vast casket of consciousness; it shines forth as composed of its rays, appearing as something other than itself.
Creating days and nights, this radiant sun of consciousness stands manifesting the substances of the world, alternating between sensations of pleasure and pain.
Like the playful movement of water in the whirlpools and hollows of the ocean,
the three worlds exist within consciousness, neither manifest nor unmanifest.
Possessing a body whose essence is the single, pure consciousness within the rock, the self-possessed one remains gentle even while engaged in worldly activity, like a gem within its casing.
Consciousness is an indivisible, dense vibration;
it is non-dual yet appears as manifold, like the internal arrangement within a stone.
That which exists in the stone body of the statue is the statue; that which does not exist in the stone body of the statue is the statue.
That which is the truth amidst both existence and non-existence is the very brilliance of consciousness;
for the splendor of all objects has consciousness as its core essence, and it is indeed composed of that alone.

Just as a lotus, having abandoned various sounds and meanings, remains within the interior of a stone, so too is this manifold; though it appears manifold, it is not composed of that multiplicity, for it is non-dual.
Just as a solid mass of clouds or a stone interior is neither manifold nor one, being an indivisible whole, so too is this internal expanse of consciousness.

Just as a stainless vessel of water appears to exist or not to exist depending on whether the reflection of the sun rests upon its bottom, so too does the density of consciousness appear as both being and non-being.
Just as the hollow interior of a water-filled cloud is about to form, being both quivering due to its fluidity and yet motionless, so too is this interior of the mass of consciousness.

Know that the world— consisting of the flood of consciousness, stone, conch, and lotus, both composed of that and not composed of that— is the meaning of words such as "lotus" and so forth, which exists within consciousness and stone.
This mass of consciousness, though like a great solid rock, has a hollow interior;
it is without internal cavities, non-dual, and transparent, like the arrangement of things beneath the surface of water.
This world falls away from Brahman, like water flowing from a gentle stream.
This world exists as Brahman alone, appearing like deep sleep, non-different [from it] like a lotus carved from stone;
the world is Brahman itself, just as the kernel within a bilva fruit is nothing but the wood itself.
Just as emptiness resides in space, fluidity in water,
and motion in the wind, so does this world reside in Brahman.
Just as the state of Brahman exists within Brahman, so too does this world exist;
no difference exists between these two, just as there is none between a tree and a plant.
These worlds that exist here are the entrails of the form of Consciousness;
for them, there is never any existence or non-existence, just as there is none for that [Consciousness] itself.
The world-appearance is Brahman alone, just as water [is] vapor;
through the perception of Brahman, it becomes pure, just as water [becomes clear] from heat.
The form of Mount Meru, of grass and shrubs, of the mind and so forth, and even of the entire world, when analyzed down to its atoms— that they know to be the ultimate.
That collection is indeed the lofty mountain of the mind, consisting of grass and the like;
for even in its subtlety it is substantial in essence, and in its grossness it is even more substantial.
Just as the power whose essence is taste exists within the objects of the world in the form of atoms, so too does the state of Brahman exist within them as the nature of milk.
Just as the power of taste arises from water in the form of grass and shrubs,
so too does that very Brahmanhood arise here in manifold forms through its own manifestation.
That which constitutes the ultimate atom of light within these playful manifestations of form—
possessing the nature of both the qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), as well as the objects and the self— is that supreme Selfhood.
In the principle of consciousness (cititattva), which is the essence of its manifestation, there exists the mountain and so forth,
just as there is the density of the mass of feathers in the fluid of a peacock's egg.
There is diversity within the principle of consciousness, which consists of its own manifestation,
just as there is a mass of variegated tail-feathers within the fluid of a peacock's egg.
For just as the various things within an egg, though devoid of essence,
are seen through the vision of discernment, so too are the existence of Brahman and the world perceived.
Just as the peacock exists both as one with and as distinct from the fluid within the egg,
so too the delusion of the world and Brahman consists of the essence of both non-duality and duality.

Know that supreme state to be one's own true being, from which comes the existence and substantiality of both the existent and the non-existent, from which comes stability, and from which comes the form of both that and not-that.

Surely you have not perceived the manifold diversity of things, which is indeed impossible; behold rather the blazing of consciousness within the world, like a peacock feather emerging from the essence of the egg.
Just as the reality of mind is in the world and the world is in the reality of mind,
so too it is both manifold and non-manifold, and yet one, like the fluid within a peacock's egg.
The conscious self (cidātman) is the essence of the egg of the world-peacock, filled with the plumage of the delusion of various objects;
know that while it has the form of a peacock, it is not a peacock here, for it is the state of pure existence—wherein could there be any differentiation?
The fifty-second canto, titled "The Instruction on Truth," from the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa].
In that [reality], where this entire extended universe exists as its own unmanifest nature,
non-duality (ahantva) has been declared to be like a peacock within its seed.
In that, nothing has arisen, yet everything exists therein;
it is inexpressible by words, and even the essence of the bliss of heaven does not exist [as such] there.
And likewise, the sages, gods, hosts, perfected beings, and great seers,
constantly relishing their own true nature, abide forever in the fourth state (turyapada).
Those whose gaze is fixed with unblinking eyes are established in the relinquishment of the vibration of attachment to the seen and the seeing.
Those for whom meditation does not abide, even though they are engaged in activities,
and who remain established in the relinquishing of the vibration of the relationship between consciousness and its object— [they are liberated].
Their vital breath does not stir, like figures depicted in a painting;
having abandoned attachment to the mind and mental factors, they abide in their own true state.
Just as armies achieve their purpose through the movement of their commander,
so too do the mind and mental factors bring about cyclic existence through their movement.
Just as a clear ray of moonlight refreshes a sprout,
so does the Self refresh the inner self upon the union of the seen and the seer.
The form of the moon's radiance that has traveled far from its orb and has not yet fallen upon the wall—
that is the form of pure consciousness.
It is not visible, nor is it fit for instruction; it is neither near nor far.
That pure form of the self is attainable through direct experience alone.
It is neither the body, nor the collection of senses, nor the mind, nor latent impressions;
it is neither the individual soul, nor even vibration, nor consciousness, nor indeed space.
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor situated between; it is neither empty nor non-empty.
It does not consist of space, time, substance, and so forth; that alone exists, and nothing else.
That which is liberated from all these, even when it has entered the sheath within the heart,
where this invisible one vibrates— that indeed shall be the state of the Self.
And that [Self], neither today nor at the end of an aeon, is altered by weapons, fire, wind, or other such things; it never becomes otherwise from its true nature, neither here nor in the hereafter.
Thousands of bodily jars are born and die;
yet there is no destruction of this space of the Self, which exists both within and without.
And all that, beginning with the body, O best of those who know the Self, is indeed the Self alone;
it appears only slightly separate due to the absence of pure awakening.

Having realized through your own perfected intellect that the pure Self pervades all things, remain free from the sense of "mine" and be extinguished even while engaged in activities, like a fire that has been quenched.
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving— all that is Brahman, devoid of attributes, devoid of qualities, and characterized by a self free from the sense of "mine."
It is eternally devoid of parts, one, absolutely pure, changeless,
without beginning or end, eternal, peaceful, and of a uniform nature.
For you who have seen that everything— death, its performance, its cause, its agent, its effect, birth, maintenance, dissolution, transmigration, and so forth—
is Brahman, why, my dear friend, do you still wander with attachment as if through the vision of a personal self?
The fifty-third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman," [from] the Rāmāyaṇa: Canto 53. Rāma:
If there is no modification or the like within the expanded Brahman,
then how does this world, consisting of existence and non-existence, appear?
Vasiṣṭha: That which is the non-returning to the previous state and the reversal of one's own nature— that is what is called "modification" (vikāra) and so forth, as found in milk and the like.
Having become curd, it returns again to the state of milk, yet curd is not milk;
so too, the Buddha is Brahman alone—stainless and pure—in the beginning, middle, and end.
Therefore, Brahman possesses no quality of being subject to transformation, like milk and other such substances;
for that which is without beginning or end and devoid of modification cannot possibly undergo the process of becoming a composite whole.
Know that this transformation of consciousness which is observed for a moment at the beginning and end of a problem is an illusion; there is no modification in that which is unchanging.
When there is an object of cognition, there is consciousness; that does not exist in Brahman.
That which is called by the word "Brahman" is the conscious self (cidātman) devoid of any object of cognition.
Whatever the nature of a thing is at its beginning and end, that alone it is said to be;
any difference in it during the middle is merely the manifestation of ignorance.
The Self, however, is equal at the beginning, the end, and the middle; it is everywhere and at all times.
Even space undergoes change, but the reality of the Self never does.
Because he is of the nature of light, because of his unity, and because of his eternity,
this Lord never falls under the power of the modifications of existence.
Rāma:
While Brahman, which is eternally one and absolutely pure, exists,
what is the source of ignorance, whose very nature is the delusion of consciousness?
Vasiṣṭha:
This entire reality is the essence of Brahman; it has been, it is, and it will be.
It is changeless, without beginning or end, and it is certain that ignorance does not exist.

Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the signified and the signifier in the word "Brahman," even there, it was not done to establish a state of non-difference; rather, it was done for the purpose of instruction.
You, I, the world, the quarters, the earth, the sky, fire, wind, and so forth—all are nothing but Brahman, without beginning or end; there is not even the slightest trace of ignorance.
The wise know that this so-called "ignorance" is merely an error and is non-existent; for how can there be a name for that which does not exist?
Rāma:
O Lord, why was it said by you yesterday in the section on instruction: "This is ignorance; thus and so forth is it determined"? MU 6.53.15.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O scion of Raghu, you have remained unawakened for all this time;
indeed, you have been awakened by these well-reasoned arguments that were merely contrived.

This sequence of conceptual constructions, such as "this is ignorance" and "this is the individual soul," has been devised by the best among those skilled in speech for the purpose of awakening the unawakened.
As long as the mind remains unawakened,
it does not attain awakening even in hundreds of years, provided there is no delusion.
Having awakened him by means of reasoning alone, this living being is united with the Self;
for that effect which is accomplished through reasoning cannot be achieved even by hundreds of efforts.
The foolish person who, being unawakened, says "everything is Brahman," brings about the experience of suffering upon a post through the delusion that it is a friend.
The fool is awakened by means of reasoning; the wise man is awakened by means of the reality itself.
The fool attains wisdom not without being awakened by means of reasoning.
For so long you were unawakened; now, having been awakened through reasoning, you are fully enlightened and are being made aware of reality as it truly is.
I am Brahman; the three worlds are Brahman; you are Brahman; the ground of the visible world is Brahman.
There is no second conceptualization. Do as you wish.
The three worlds are merely the pinnacle of great consciousness that is beyond perception;
one who possesses such realization within is not defiled, even while acting.
"O Rāghava, remain—whether standing, walking, sleeping, or breathing—with the firm realization: 'I am the Supreme Self, whose nature is light, conscious, and all-pervading.'"
O Rāma, if you are wise, free from the sense of "mine," and free from egoism,
then become that peaceful realization of Brahman which abides in all beings.
Therefore, you are that very reality which is without beginning or end, the supreme state that shines forth;
you abide as the one omnipresent Self, whose nature consists of pure consciousness.
That which is Brahman, the pervasive Self, and that which is ignorance and primordial nature (prakṛti)—
all that is eternally one essence, just as clay is the single substance in hundreds of jars.
The nature of the Self is not distinct from the Self, just as the earthenness of a jar is not distinct from the jar;
or just as air is merely vibration, so too the Self alone is its own nature.
That which is the movement of the Self by itself, like the swirling of water, is indeed designated here by the word "prakṛti" (nature). For it is that very thing which is so described.
Just as the single vibration and the wind are distinct in name but not in reality,
so too the self and primordial nature are distinct in name but not in reality.
The distinction between these two, arising from non-awakening, dissolves through awakening alone;
non-awakening consists of unreality, like the delusion of a snake in a rope caused by error.
When this seed of mental construction falls, throbbing upon the ground of consciousness,
from it arises the sprout of the mind, which is the future grove of saṃsāra.
This very [seed], once burnt by the knowledge of the Self, is not capable of sprouting again, even if it is diligently watered with the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā).
If the seed of conceptualization does not fall into the field of consciousness,
then the sprouts of the mind— the trees that bear the fruits of pleasure and pain— will not arise.
Duality in this world is unreal, grasped through that which is born of ignorance; abandon it, for you have attained awakening, which is the destruction of ignorance.
Through the power of the singular nature of the Self, you are one whose being is fearless; "suffering does not exist at all"—this is our essence of the ultimate truth.
The fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Yoga of Contemplating Saṃsāra," [spoken by] Rāma.
All that is to be known has been known, and all that is to be seen has been seen without flaw;
O Brahmin, we have become fully satiated by your nectar of knowledge.
This fullness is of the nature of the Full; from the Full, the Full is filled forth.
Filled by the Full, it is the Full; the state of fullness remains as fullness alone.
O Brahmin, I ask this again as a mere play, for the sake of increasing my understanding; you ought not to be angry with me, as a father would not be with his child.
The ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and likewise the nose— though they exist, O Brahmin, and though they are clearly perceived— MU 6.54.4.
How is it that a living being does not perceive its own object when dead,
yet perceives its entire object while alive?

How is it that external objects such as jars, though perceived within the body by the sense organs— even though these organs are insentient— are not, moreover, perceived [by them] when they are inside?
In the case of the two— matter (ghaṭa) and the sense-faculty (indriya)—
which are like two iron rods, unjoined and devoid of moisture, how can existence be said to arise between them?
Although I already know this, I ask you again out of a desire for further detail; therefore, out of compassion, tell me everything without omission.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O dear one, neither the senses, nor the mind and so forth, nor even objects such as a jar,
can exist here separately apart from the stainless consciousness.
Even from the sky, that consciousness, by its own nature, has manifested its own form as the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) through the very activity of its own being, because it is consciousness.
This very world, having returned to its primordial nature, remains established;
its constituent parts consist of those things such as the sense organs and so forth, as well as jars and the like.
That very principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), which by its own nature has attained the state of the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*),
reflects objects such as jars within its own constituent parts.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, tell me what is the nature of my subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), which possesses the majesty of creating a thousand worlds and serves as a mirror for them?"
Vasiṣṭha:
That Brahman which exists is the seed of the world without beginning or end, free from affliction,
consisting of the nature of light, pure consciousness alone, and devoid of all parts or mental constructions.
When that [consciousness] becomes oriented toward temporal succession, it is known as the *jīva*.
Indeed, that *jīva* clearly accumulates karma and vibrates within this body.
From the state of "I-ness" it is called the ego (ahaṅkāra); from the act of thinking it is called the mind (manas);
from the determination of cognition it is the intellect (buddhi); and likewise, from the perception of Indra, it is the sense organ (indriya).
Through the contemplation of a body, it becomes a body; through the contemplation of a jar, a jar.
This self, whose nature is thus, is known as the *jīva* or the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
That consciousness which identifies with knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, witnesshood, and so forth, is called the *jīva*; for that is what they know as the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
From time to time, the individual soul itself becomes one thing and then another by its own nature,
due to the arising of infinitesimal particles of latent impressions (vāsanā) formed by past actions.
By means of the nature of the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), it assumes a form through time,
just as a seed reaches the state of a sprout due to the power of latent impressions (vāsanā) and through watering.
"I am the body and so forth, or the immovable world, or the gods"—
thus one sinks into false knowledge, [thinking] "I am not the primordial conscious Self."
Thus the living being, tossed about by latent impressions, wanders for a long time in this world,
like a piece of wood struck by waves in the ocean, moving up and down.
Someone, by virtue of being of a sattvic nature, immediately after being released from the bondage of worldly existence,
realizes his own Self and attains the state that is devoid of beginning and end.
After a long time, having passed through various successions of births,
someone attains the supreme state of the Self through the power of self-knowledge.
O wise one, listen to how that soul, having thus assumed the state of a body, perceives objects such as a jar through the eyes and other senses. MU 6.54.25.
Because of the mind's reckoning of that which has departed as being alive,
the collection of the six sense organs remains in the body as if it were still present.
When the body of the objective entity falls away along with its own body consisting of the senses,
then, through contact with the individual soul (jīva), it attains oneness with the living self (jīvātman).
In the perception of external objects, the constant connection of the sense organ with the mind is the cause;
never that of one who is liberated from the mind.
Whatever stands at the forefront within that most transparent [mirror] is reflected;
it becomes joined with the individual soul (jīva), and thus the soul lives externally.
When the pupils of the eyes possess the luster of freshly polished gems,
then external objects are reflected within them.
O Rāghava, because it is conjoined with the individual soul (jīva) by virtue of its reflection, an external object then becomes knowable by that soul.
For even a child perceives that which comes into contact;
why then should a living being—not even a beast or an immobile thing—not perceive it?
Furthermore, O virtuous one, the rays of the eye are enveloped by the living soul (jīva);
they fully embrace the visible object, and by that means, the soul perceives it.
This very same sequence applies to touch, wherein the arising of the cognition of relation occurs;
it is likewise described for taste and smell, arising from contact with the living soul.

But sound, because it resides in space, enters the space within the ear and from there instantly enters the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa); in this same way, the perceptions of the sense organs [enter].
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, tell me, what is the nature of this reflection which is seen in stainless mirrors, precious gems, water, and so forth?"
Vasiṣṭha:
