That which has long existed as something within the space of Brahman appears like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
that which remains for a moment and that which remains for a while—this alone is what constitutes these worlds of yours.
Meditating that objects are merely one's own existence, like [objects] in a dream,
one perceives the single, manifold-souled sky of consciousness as remaining stable, like a tree in a dream.
The cognition that external objects exist, as well as the notion that the world is the Self of Brahman— all this is real, because everything remains exactly as it is experienced.
First, when the nature of the atom is understood, then its subtlety, and then the ether;
those very [powers] by which the wise man today perceives the sky, the hand, the eye, and so forth.
From the very beginning of creation, the object is reflected in the stainless [intellect];
yet, because of the identity between the original object and its reflection, the state [of consciousness] remains undivided.
That which, at the beginning of creation, was perceived by the shining sky of consciousness as "this is the object," is that very configuration which has now come to abide.

By the power of the manifestation within the space of consciousness, there occurs a mutual attribution of qualities among non-existent entities, which is established as a reflection in that which is pure.
That mutual bestowing of existence which occurs by its very nature between two things that are utterly insentient, like two living beings, is called a reflection.
Or rather, between consciousness and the self, or between the insentient and that which consists of the Great Being (mahāsattā) and the insentient,
there is a mutual offering of the existence of the reflected image due to the necessity of their primordial nature.
O best among those who know the object of knowledge, understand that the reflection seen by the eyes is an illusion;
the world is merely that much. Therefore, let there be no further trust in this for you.
In the supreme ocean, the wave consisting of "I" and so forth, which possesses the whirlpools of creation and the rest,
does not exist at all as something produced by space, time, or action, due to its identity with that [ocean].
Always with an unattached mind and a joyful soul, experiencing the peace that transcends both pleasure and pain,
remain established in equanimity with a settled intellect, having eliminated all the delusions and diseases of worldly existence.
The fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Investigating the Perception of the Senses," by Vasiṣṭha.
Prior to his emergence from the lotus, the eyes and other faculties were already fully formed;
all this has been heard by you concerning the Lotus-born One.
Just as the consciousness of the senses was described at the beginning regarding the eightfold city of Brahmā,
so too does it always arise for every eightfold city.
Know that the "city of eight" is the individual soul (jīva); it is the emergence of the senses within the womb.
Whatever it conceives of in whatever manner, it immediately perceives that very thing in that same way.
Know that the senses and what is called the objects of the senses constitute one's own perception;
and how that is perfected, as it was explained to you regarding the initial state of the mind.
Pure consciousness is that which knows, the irreproachable act of cognizing;
therefore, from this internal awareness of "I," the individual soul as the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka) has emerged.
But the supreme state is not [defined] by oneness, nor by infinity, nor by being unknowable, nor by being free from affliction; it is not by non-duality, nor by multiplicity, nor by non-emptiness.

And so forth; it perceives nothing whatsoever, nor does it attain the state of the mind (manas), nor does it assume the state of a living being (jīva), nor is it of the nature of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka).
There is no play of ignorance and the like; that which always exists as if it were non-existent is called the Supreme Self, transcending the six senses including the mind.
Therefore, the living being (jīva), whose form is consciousness and whose nature is thinking, arises from that;
[the claim that it is] "merely an illusion" is sung [in the scriptures] for the sake of instruction.
When this disease consisting of ignorance has arisen from whatever cause,
it dissolves through inquiry by means of the instruction given to the disciple.
That knowledge remains, in which all activity has been completely stilled;
wherein even space appears as gross as a mountain amidst an atom.
In that state, even the world— which possesses emerging activity and exists as both real and unreal— stands as an object of knowledge for the wise, like something fashioned from mud.
The nature of ignorance consists solely of this:
that when it is truly perceived, it surely perishes and is no longer seen.
How indeed can that which is called "seen" be obtained as a non-entity?
Or by whom has the water of a mirage ever been attained, even with great effort?
That which is non-existent is always indeed non-existent; its appearance as real is due to ignorance.
Through knowledge, the object is seen as it truly is, and the delusion perishes.
For the sake of investigating ignorance, there is the conceptualization of the individual soul, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and so forth—
even though these are absolutely unreal— within the imagined self.

Therefore, this conceptualization of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth was fashioned by the scriptures for the purpose of instructing that [Reality] and awakening one to it; listen to it with a single-minded focus.
Having attained as it were the state of being a living soul, abiding in the condition of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), consciousness— free from parts and blemish— is oriented toward insentience.
Whatever one meditates upon in whatever manner, that very thing one experiences immediately and fully;
whether it be true or false, it is like a child [fearing] a yakṣa in the night.

In whatever place and in whatever manner she contemplates the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), there she perceives those very elements as having arisen in that same way within herself, with their respective openings.
The five elements existing externally, which have arisen from those very [faculties],
one perceives as non-different [from them] yet appearing as different, just as a sprout [perceives] its hundred branches.
Having then become certain that "this is internal" and "this is external," the living being firmly establishes whatever it grasps exactly as it is.
The manifestation of the self, like the web of rays from the moon,
is itself rendered into the form of external touch.
Just as there is sharpness in a mirage and emptiness in the sky, so too is the experience of the self; by means of that, it is itself perceived as if it were something else.
Having gained certainty in this very matter, the discipline was made very firm; "By this, it must be thus; by that, it must be thus," remained unbroken.

This [self], which is the regulator of its own volitions, exists at some place and at some time under the name of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) or by some other name; it exists only as intrinsic nature and not otherwise.
All this duality has arisen from the non-dual Self alone,
just as a eunuch [is transformed] by sweet wine, or as a great jar [is fashioned] from clay.
The arrangement, transformation, and so forth are possible here because they can occur in relation to space, time, and other factors;
however, this is not possible in the case of God (Īśa), because space, time, and the like are impossible for Him.
Just as the spring, arising within its own domain, takes away the duality from the non-dual essence by saying, "The flower is here, the leaf is here, and I am here," so too does the Self.

Thus, having arisen with the thought "the cloth is here, the wall is there, and I am here," Brahman— though non-dual and free from opposites— introduced duality into the Self, which is the essence of creation.
"Just as today I am a sprout, today I am the brilliance of the sun, and today I am a cloud— so does the Self, possessing both existent and non-existent forms, abide according to its circumstances."
Who in this world has the power to subvert the sequence proclaimed by the Lord of All, which dictates that "this must be brought about in such a manner"?
In a clear mirror, no form that is distinct from it is reflected; rather, because a separation is impossible, it simply shines forth as one with it.
But in Brahman, the Self alone, abiding as the Self, shines forth and reflects;
though bodiless, it appears as duality by its very nature, owing to its consisting of consciousness.
In whatever way the manifestation of the Self is perceived by the manifesting Self,
even though it is unreal, it never deviates from that [nature] here.

Just as the two states of being gold and a bracelet possess the natures of reality and unreality respectively within the cognition of a golden vessel, so too do consciousness and non-consciousness exist within the Self.

Because consciousness is all-pervading, its nature as consciousness is eternally present in the mind, just as the nature of gold is present in a bracelet; yet insentience remains [in it] at other times.
When the mind itself firmly cultivates its own nature as being either conscious or inert,
then it becomes exactly that state, in that very manner.
From time to time, the living being itself becomes variously manifest within,
assuming diverse forms through the arising of minute seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Just as a village seen in a dream momentarily attains the nature of reality,
so too does this living being (jīva) move from one body to another, which consists of mere appearance.
Just as in a dream a person may perceive a wall or a cloth,
so too, for us, that transition from one body to another occurs even though it is entirely unreal.
The unreal alone dies, and the unreal is born again;
the living being, through its own mental projection, appears like a dream or like another form within itself.
After such a period of time, he experiences for himself that this ordinary, firmly rooted conviction arises: "I must abandon this form."
An object, whether seen or unseen, is experienced in a dream;
know, O best among those who know what is to be known, that the world is the dream of the living soul.
That which is neither the waking seer nor the object seen does not differ from its own state—pure consciousness alone—when devoid of designation and the like; it is no different from the dream state.
Just as a man sees a great dream concerning things never seen before, so does this consciousness perceive its own self-awareness.
Formerly acquired latent impressions are quickly overcome by human effort alone;
indeed, through exertion today, yesterday's evil action turns into a virtuous deed.
Except through liberation, the eyes and other senses of living beings do not find peace;
they merely emerge and submerge according to place and time.
Because of the mental construction of that [body], the body stands as if it were real; though composed of five elements and cultivated from the unreal, it is like a great yakṣa conjured for a child.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, and likewise the five subtle elements—this is declared to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); this is the subtle, transportable body (ātivāhika-deha).
The mind-essence is indeed formless; its extreme bulkiness is its nature as space.
Its state as wind is its great ankles, and its state as body is Mount Sumeru.
This [self] possesses two states in succession, but when free from all states, it partakes in liberation;
its single state is like deep sleep, wherein the dawning of insentience is embraced.
This state, characterized by the perception of a body, is like a dream;
it wanders here until liberation, O moving and unmoving beings.
For sometimes abiding in deep sleep and sometimes established in dream,
this subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) persists for everyone.
When one abides in the state of deep sleep, about to be awakened by future suffering,
then one remains like a stone in the sky, with no form having arisen.
In states such as those of stationary objects and in the conditions of the wish-fulfilling tree,
this one remains in deep sleep, a mass of dense delusion as solid as a stone.
Its state of deep sleep is insentience; this transmigratory existence is its dream. That which is its awakening is liberation; that is its waking state, and it is the fourth state (turya).
For liberation is indeed the awakening of the living soul (jīva), and it is said here to be of two kinds:
the first is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and the second is liberation from the body (videhamukti).
For liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is the state of the Fourth (turya), and beyond that is the Supreme, which is beyond the Fourth (turyātīta).
Liberation is indeed the awakening of the living soul, and that occurs through the effort of the intellect.
For the living being, whose measure is knowledge, knows that which is within as being composed of that; therefore, let it know only consciousness itself, and it quickly becomes composed of that.
This living soul beholds this very long delusion of a dream,
falsely arisen within its own heart, which has become as solid as a crystal.
Within the individual soul (jīvāṇu), there exists nothing other than this fraction of consciousness (citkalā);
perceiving that very same [consciousness] as something else, one grieves in vain.
Within this individual soul there is nothing at all other than the Supreme;
that the world is perceived here and there—oh, how it is the unfolding of Māyā!
Just as the appearance of movement arises for grains of rice boiling within water in a pot,
so too does the illusory arising of transmigration occur for living beings within themselves.
Its bondage consists in possessing latent impressions (vāsanā), while liberation would be the destruction of those impressions. From these impressions, its states of deep sleep and dream manifest.
This dense latent impression (vāsanā) is delusion; it is known as the insentient nature of deep sleep.
It is accompanied by the dream that necessarily occurs within it.
The individual soul, drowsy from the sleep of the immersion in latent impressions, perceives delusion;
when this sleep of latent impressions wanes, it then awakens.

The attachment to the visible world and the state of being visible are said to be mere latent impressions (vāsanā); they do not exist at all within the Self of all, just as the nature of bracelets and such does not exist in gold.
If this [world] arose from non-awakening and dissolved through awakening,
then for you its emergence would indeed result from the exhaustion of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the impressionable mind (*vāsya*).

Having destroyed the dense delusion of one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one reaches the state of deep sleep; then, having attained the state of attenuated impressions, one perceives the dream of cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*).

This living being, possessing dense latent impressions and delusion, partakes in the state of stationary beings; one with middling latent impressions becomes an animal, while a person with attenuated latent impressions is a human.
When living beings such as jars and the like are grasped by the inner life-force, then,
due to the identity of the life-force in both, there is the existence of both the object of perception and the perceiver.
When the self is thoroughly embraced by the conscious self within and without, then the cognition of the grasped object and the act of grasping, along with its cause, vanishes like a mirage.
Nothing whatsoever is abandoned here, nor is anything whatsoever grasped here;
the one Self of Consciousness alone shines forth, devoid of external or internal forms and divisions.
The three worlds are but the wonder of consciousness; enough with conceptualizations of duality!
We have been perceived by consciousness within consciousness; we know nothing other than the external and so forth.

Just as the entire water of the ocean is stainless, free from all distinctions, sweet, clear, liquid, and purely one, so too this primordial, supreme state is understood to be entirely free from disease, having cast aside the entire collection of distinctions.
The fifty-sixth chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Perception of the Objects of the Senses," by Vasiṣṭha.
Know that this world-process (*saṃsāra*) is that very dream which has arisen for the individual soul (*jīva*), tender with various mental constructions; it is neither real nor composed of unreality.
A dream does not occur for the individual soul (jīva) anywhere as it does for a man;
therefore, these worldly states are the waking and the dream, for they are one here.

O best among those who know the objects of knowledge, understand that this long dream of the living soul appears both quickly and at length; though it is unreal, it is so because of its lack of substantiality.
Like those moving from one dream to another,
living beings perceive what is utterly unreal for a long time as if it were solid reality.
The non-inert has become inert, and within that inertia, non-inertia has arisen;
through the delusion of the individual soul's experience, unreality has become reality.
Perceiving the entire delusion of the three worlds even within the post of Śiva,
living beings wander here like those bewildered by a dream, their minds filled with the serpent of worldly existence.
Because one's own infinite consciousness is all-pervading,
whatever one contemplates and perceives, that very thing quickly attains the state of reality.
O mighty-armed one, that auspicious state free from attachment which was spoken by the lotus-eyed Lord, embracing which the great sage became liberated while living.
Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, will spend his life happily and free from suffering; therefore, spend your life in the same way.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, when will Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, appear?
And what kind of unimpeded power will Hari describe to him?"
Vasiṣṭha: There exists that which is pure being alone, designated by the name "Self," abiding within itself— beginningless and endless— like the great sky within the sky.
In that stainless [reality], this delusion of saṃsāra is seen,
just as bracelets and the like are seen in gold, or waves and the like in water.
Fourteen kinds of living beings flutter about sufficiently within this web of saṃsāra, like birds in a net.

There, Yama, Candra, Ārka, Śakra, and the others, who follow the sequence of transmigratory existence, have assumed the status of world-protectors (lokapāla) as the structural manifestations of the five elements.
"This merit is to be accepted, but this evil is to be abandoned"—
such is the established order fixed by the Veda, yet fashioned by their own conceptual constructions.
The powerful world-protector named Yama, the son of Vivasvat,
is established in the restraint of living beings whose existence is marked by death.
O sinless one, until this very day, his mind has remained steady and as immovable as a mountain in its own duty, which has come down to him like a continuous stream.
That Lord Yama performs a certain vow at the beginning of every cycle of four ages; nevertheless, he does so out of apprehension regarding the sin arising from the destruction of living beings.
Sometimes for eight years, or even ten or twelve;
sometimes for five or seven, and sometimes even for sixteen.
While he remains seated like one indifferent, established in his discipline,
death does not harm any beings within the web of the world.
By that, the surface of the earth becomes a dense mass of beings with no passage for movement,
like a sweat-dripping bower filled with mosquitoes during the rainy season.
Then, O Rāma, those various beings, by means of many stratagems, brought about the destruction of the gods for the sake of relieving the burden of the earth.
In this way, thousands of Yamas and hundreds of legal disputes,
as well as infinite beings and worlds, have passed away.
"O virtuous one, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, who is indeed the leader of the ancestors, has today,
now that some [of his followers] have been exhausted, been overcome by this."
In each age, for the sake of destroying sin, one whose cruel deeds have been cast far away must perform the practice of vows here in his twelvefold form.
Therefore, this earth will become densely packed with mortal beings who are immortal,
and it will become a burdened mass, like a thicket of thickets.
The Earth, her limbs overwhelmed by the burden, will seek refuge with Hari,
like a beloved wife, distressed and oppressed by bandits, seeks her dear husband.
Then Hari shall descend to earth with two bodies,
together with all the portions of the gods who have assumed the state of leaders of men.
But the son of Vasudeva alone shall be known as Vāsudeva;
he will be one body of Hari, while the second shall be the Pāṇḍava Arjuna.
He shall be known as Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma;
that knower of righteousness will be the son of Pāṇḍu and the sovereign of the earth girdled by the oceans.
He will have a brother born of his paternal uncle known as Duryodhana,
with whom Bhīma will engage in a firm duel, like that of a mongoose with a snake.
As those two strive to seize the earth from one another,
eighteen terrifying akṣauhiṇīs, eager for battle, will indeed clash here.
Upon their destruction, Viṣṇu will bring about the division of the earth through the bodies of Rāghava and Arjuna, the wielder of the great Gāṇḍīva bow.
This one named Arjuna, having assumed a natural state belonging to Viṣṇu,
will possess a body subject to human laws, filled with joy and indignation.
Seeing his own kinsmen belonging to both armies on the verge of death,
he will fall into despair and will not exert himself for battle.
O Rāghava, Hari will awaken that body named Arjuna by means of his own intellect-body for the sole purpose of accomplishing the task at hand.
The Blessed One said:

"O lion among kings, your inner self has been struck down by the human [condition]; through being overwhelmed by dejection and delusion, you have lost consciousness. Having perished, you have abandoned your own supreme light—that very essence of the Self—and are indeed [lost]."

O self of consciousness, behold the Self—endless, unmanifest, without beginning or middle; you are the expansive body of consciousness, untouched by defects; you are unborn, eternal, and free from all affliction.
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be again.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
The fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Incarnation of Nārāyaṇa," [spoken by] the Blessed One:
He who perceives this as a slayer, and he who thinks of it as slain—both of them do not understand; this does not kill, nor is it killed.
Of the infinite, uniform, existent, and subtle Self, who is even subtler than space, the Supreme Lord— what can destroy him, how, and by what means?
You are not Arjuna, nor are you the slayer; abandon this pride sufficiently.
You are yourself the eternal Self, liberated from old age and death.
He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not tainted—
even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
Whatever consciousness arises within, that alone is experienced;
therefore, abandon the notions of "this is he," "I am this," and "this is mine" regarding that consciousness.
And by this very [chain], O Bhārata, you are dragged helplessly from all sides by pleasure and pain, thinking "I am joined" and "I am destroyed."
Actions performed by the qualities through their own constituent parts are [misconstrued] by one whose self is deluded by egoism as "I am the doer."
Let the eye see, let the ear hear, and let this skin touch;
let the tongue go to its taste—what single "I" remains here?
Even when the mind is intent upon the activity of conceptualization, O Mahāmati, there is no one here who possesses the affliction of "I"; who indeed could you possibly be?
O Bhārata, that which is accomplished by many through their collective effort is seized by a single person for mere mockery, due to the suffering caused by his pride.
Having abandoned attachment, yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, for the sake of self-realization.
Those whose bodies have not been permeated by the powder of the poison of "I-ness"— whether they are giving or taking— these very people are free from the cholera of craving.
Nowhere does this body shine, being defiled by the impurity of the sense of "mine," just as a man, though wise and even very learned, is like one of immoral conduct.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, equal in suffering and happiness, and patient— he who acts, whether performing what ought to be done or what ought not to be done, is not defiled.
And this, O son of Pāṇḍu, is your own duty as a Kṣatriya,
which, though exceedingly cruel, is superior for the sake of well-being and prosperity.
Even a deed that is contemptible, base, unrighteous, or insignificant may lead to one's own welfare; yet the nectar of immortality does not do so here in this world in such a manner.
Even for a fool, one's own action alone leads to the highest good; how much more so for one of noble mind?
A mind from which egoism has fallen away is not defiled, even when it has fallen [into worldly circumstances].
Established in yoga, perform actions while abandoning attachment, O Dhanañjaya; if you are free from attachment and act as circumstances arise, you will not be bound.
Having become one whose body is the peaceful Brahman, perform action consisting of Brahman;
with your conduct dedicated to Brahman, you will become Brahman itself in an instant.
With all your purposes surrendered to the Lord, with the Lord as your very self, free from affliction, you shall become the Lord—
the Self of all beings— adorning the surface of the earth.

Having renounced all volitional constructions, equanimous, with a tranquil mind, a sage whose self is joined to the yoga of renunciation— performing [your duties], remain one whose intellect is liberated.
Arjuna said: O Blessed One, [please explain] the renunciation of attachment, as well as the offering unto Brahman,
which consists of the offering unto the Lord, and renunciation itself, O All-pervading One.
Likewise, O Lord, what is the distinction between knowledge and yoga?
Tell me this in due order, for it brings about the cessation of great delusion.
The Blessed One said:

When all conceptual constructions have completely subsided, that state of singular, intense awareness which takes the form of meditating on "nothing whatsoever"— that they know as the supreme Brahman.
Those of perfected intellect know that exertion to be knowledge and yoga;
they understand the offering to Brahman to be the realization: "Brahman is the universe, and I am it."
Empty within and empty without, resembling a heart of stone;
it is tranquil, as clear as the expanse of space, yet neither void nor merely a stone.
Then, that slight emergence which arises as a slight otherness—
this manifestation of the world is emptiness, like space.

"This is a portion of me"—thus has this [individual] arisen in each instance from consciousness, divided into parts of millions upon millions of parts; what kind of attachment can there be toward such a one?
When the various manifestations of conceptual construction flash forth within the self whose essence is pure consciousness—
even though it is not diverse in its manifoldness— why do you still cling to the notion of "one" even in that single [reality]?
Though not distinct, this [Self] remains as if it were distinct;
though the ocean is boundless and separate, it does not perceive itself as "I am."
Just as "I" am here, so too is "you" here; there is a jar and so forth here, and a monkey is here;
space is likewise here, as are water and the like—why then is there this grasping at "I-ness"?
Thus, that destruction of duality through the knowledge of non-differentiation,
which is the relinquishing of the web of volitions, is called non-attachment.
The contemplation of the oneness of the Lord within the entire web of conceptual constructions,
wherein the appearance of duality has dissolved— this alone is the offering to the Lord.
Due to the power of non-difference, their distinction exists only in name within the conscious self;
the entire world, as the referent of all words, is the one conscious self—of this there is no doubt.
I am hope, I am the world, I am the sky, and I am action as well;
I am time, I am non-duality, I am duality, and I am the universe.
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
thus regarding Me as your very Self and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone.
Arjuna said:
O Lord of Gods, you have two forms—the supreme and the non-supreme.
Of what kind is that [supreme] form, and at what time shall I abide by resorting to it for the sake of perfection?
The Blessed One said:
"O sinless one, know that my forms are twofold: the common and the supreme.
The common form is endowed with hands and other limbs, and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace."
The supreme form of mine, which is without beginning or end, unique, and free from all affliction,
is expressed by such terms as Brahman, Ātman, and Paramātman.
As long as you remain unawakened, dwelling in the ignorance of selflessness,
so long remain devoted to the worship of the four-armed deity.
Through that sequence, you will become fully awakened; from that, you will come to know my supreme form, which is without beginning or end, by means of which you shall not be born again.
Or if you have been recognized by me, O crusher of enemies,
then quickly take refuge in that Self of mine, which is the very Self of yourself.
When I declare, "This am I" and "That am I," this very thing is the reality of the Self; I shall explain it clearly and repeatedly.
I believe, O virtuous one, that you have awakened; you have found rest in the supreme state.
You are now liberated from all mental constructs; become one whose sole essence is truth.
Behold the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self; with your mind disciplined by yoga, see the same everywhere.
He who, established in unity, worships the Self residing in all beings—
no matter how he may conduct himself— is not born again.
Oneness is the meaning of all words; oneness is the meaning of the word "Self" (ātman).
That Self is neither existent nor non-existent; he who quickly attains that is truly existent.
That internal light within the minds of the three worlds which arises from illumination and has ascended to the level of direct experience— this is the certainty that "this is the Self."
O Bhārata, that experience of flavor which exists within the waters of the three worlds— both those produced from cows and those born of the ocean— that very self am I.
That subtle experience which exists within all bodies, and which is itself free from anything to be experienced— that is this all-pervading Self, and I am that.
Just as clarified butter exists within a collection of milk,
so does the Supreme abide within all objects and bodies.
Just as light exists within and without all the jewels of the oceans, so do I abide within bodies, though appearing as if not established therein.
Just as space exists within and without thousands of jars,
so do I abide as the Self within the bodies of the three worlds.
Just as a thread has its body strung through a multitude of hundreds of pearls, so do I exist as the Self, unperceived, within hundreds of thousands of bodies.
In this multitude of objects, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
that which is the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) is known as the unborn Self.
That Brahman, its form slightly vibrating, remains as Brahman alone;
yet, through a delusive process, it sequentially manifests as the ego-sense (*ahantā*) and the world-phenomenon (*jagattā*).
This entire world is indeed the Self; what is it here that is slain or that slays?
O Arjuna, how can this [Self] be tainted by the auspicious or inauspicious sufferings of the world?
He who sees that which remains undestroyed when things are destroyed, standing like a witness equally present in all reflections as in a mirror— he truly sees.
"This am I" and "this am I"—this is what is spoken by me.
Thus you are the Self, the Self of all; know me thus, O Pāṇḍava.
All these transformations of creation and dissolution proceed from the conscious one, who is self-dependent and resides within, like the movement of waves in the ocean.
Just as there is stoneness in mountains, woodness in trees,
and waterness in waves, so too is there the nature of the Self in all things.
He who sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self,
and likewise sees the Self as the non-agent— he truly sees.

Just as water remains the same amidst waves of various forms and transformations, or as gold remains the same in bracelets and other ornaments, so too, O Arjuna, does the Self remain amidst the elements.
Just as various groups of waves are restless in water,
or as bracelets and other ornaments exist in gold, so do the elements exist within the Self.

O Bhārata, know that the entire collection of categories, beginning with the elements and including the Great Brahman, is truly one alone; it does not exist as something separate in the slightest degree.
Is there anything within the three worlds that is subject to the modifications of existence?
Where are they, or where is this world? Why do you delude yourself in vain?
Having heard this, understood it within, and cultivated it with complete certainty,
the virtuous, liberated while living, wander here with minds of equanimity.
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, possessing knowledge of the inner self and with desires turned away,
they— liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain— go, undeluded, to that imperishable state.
The fifty-eighth canto, titled "The Instruction to Arjuna," the Blessed One said:
Once more, O mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word,
which I shall speak to you, who are pleased with me, out of a desire for your welfare.
But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata.
But they are not distinct from the one Self; where then is suffering, or where is happiness?
In that which is without beginning or end and without parts, how can there be filling or diminishing?
In this infinite Supreme Self, which has no beginning such as a specific arrangement, there exists a subtle part called "mere touch," just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold.
For he whom these delusive contacts of the senses do not disturb,
being steadfast and equal toward pleasure and pain— he is fit for immortality.
Since the Self is all-pervasive, these appearances exist as if established;
yet they are unreal in nature—how can that which is unreal not be tolerated?
Pleasure and pain do not exist even slightly in that which is not all-pervading;
since the reality of the Self is all-pervasive, how could there be any existence of these two?
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being;
pleasure, pain, and the like do not exist at all; there exists only the omnipresent Supreme Self.
Having abandoned the notions of existence and non-existence regarding these two— the world and the self—
and having abandoned even the "nothingness" that lies between them, remain firmly established in what remains.
The self does not rejoice in pleasure, nor does it languish in sufferings, O Arjuna;
for the conscious self, though situated within the body, remains like a stone.
The insentient mind and so forth, having attained the state of a body, are the vessel of suffering;
yet, when this [body] is injured or destroyed, not the slightest injury occurs to the Self.
That this inert body and so forth are established as the "experiencer" of suffering and the like—
know that, my dear, to be nothing but the delusion of māyā, arisen through the power of ignorance.
Nothing whatsoever—neither the body and so forth, nor suffering and so forth—exists as something separate from the self; therefore, what could be experienced by whom?
O Bhārata, that which I am speaking of here— by means of this, this delusion of yours, which arises from difficult-to-comprehend ignorance, shall perish through right awakening.
Just as the fear of a snake in a rope perishes through knowledge because it was born of ignorance,
so too do the body and the like, as well as suffering and the like, perish through knowledge because they were born of ignorance.
"The unborn Brahman, all-pervading and universal, neither perishes nor is born;
know this to be the supreme truth—this indeed is the highest awakening. (MU 6.58.16)
You are a wave of the ocean of Brahman; having become something slight, you dissolve.
Today you flash forth in the whirlpool of Brahman; you are indeed Brahman itself, free from all affliction.
The world, time, action, space, you, I, and the soldiers—all such movement exists only within Brahman; herein, the sequences of being and non-being do not exist.
Abandon pride, intoxication, grief, fear, envy, and pleasure and pain;
this duality is unreal in nature—be one who possesses the nature of Reality.
Through the destruction of millions of human akṣauhiṇīs, which is of the nature of experience,
make this battle— which has been expanded by Brahmā— into Brahman, consisting of Brahman.
Unaware of pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat,
attain the state of oneness with Brahman in battle, O Bhārata, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Becoming equal toward gain and loss, and truly possessing nothing at all, move about like a dull-witted man or the wind, performing whatever task presents itself.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, and whatever you shall do, O son of Kuntī—regard all that as the Self; remain steadfast in this conviction.
Whatever one’s inner nature is, that one undoubtedly attains;
therefore, in order to attain the truth of Brahman, become one whose very nature is the truth of Brahman.
Having become Brahman and contemplating "I am Brahman," the knower of Brahman performs action exactly as it comes, solely out of habit, without regard for its fruit.
He who perceives inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is called a doer of all actions.
Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let there be attachment to inaction;
established in yoga, perform actions having abandoned attachment, O Dhanañjaya.
Without relying on attachment to action, nor likewise relying on delusion,
and even without relying on inaction, remain poised in equanimity as you are.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent,
even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all.
They say that attachment constitutes agency; even for one who is not the agent, that [agency] arises when the mind remains in a state of ignorance. Therefore, one should abandon ignorance.
But by relying on that supreme state of knowing, for the great-souled one who is free from attachment,
the sense of agency never arises, even though he may be engaged in all kinds of actions.

Due to the absence of agency, there is the absence of being an enjoyer; due to the absence of being an enjoyer, there is equanimity and oneness; from equanimity and oneness comes infinity, and from that, the pervasive nature of Brahman.
Having completely abandoned the sense of diversity and attained oneness with the Supreme Self,
you are not truly an agent, O Arjuna, whether performing what is to be done or what is not to be done.
The wise call him a sage whose every undertaking is free from desire and purposeful intent, and whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
He who remains even-minded, gentle, steadfast, self-abiding, tranquil, and free from longing for all objects— even when intensely busy, he has attained a state of complete composure.
Free from dualities, ever established in purity, devoid of the pursuit of acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self,
follow whatever comes to you and adorn the surface of the earth.
He who restrains his organs of action but sits dwelling upon the objects of the senses with his mind is a deluded soul; he is called a hypocrite.
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action without attachment— he is preeminent.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, even so all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
The Fifty-Ninth Chapter: The Instruction on Self-Knowledge in the Arjunopākhyāna.
The Blessed One said:
One should not renounce enjoyments, nor should one cultivate an attachment to enjoyments;
one should remain perfectly equanimous, following whatever circumstances arise.

Do not conceive of a self in the body, which is non-self; do not conceive of a self in worldly existence, which is not the Self. Rather, conceive of the nature of the Self alone—the True, which is of the nature of non-existence.
O mighty-armed one, upon the destruction of the body, nothing at all is destroyed;
for if the self were destroyed, there would be destruction, yet the self is never destroyed anywhere.
The wise know the Self to be indestructible, without beginning or end, and ageless;
let there be no such misconception in you—that the Self perishes—for it is difficult to understand and brings excessive suffering.
Those supreme ones who have realized the Self never perish;
for those who do not know the Self, perishing occurs, as they imagine the self to reside in what is not the Self.
Arjuna said:
"If this is so, O Lord of the Universe, bestower of honor even upon the foolish,
I consider that nothing at all is lost when the destruction of the body occurs."
The Blessed One said:
"Just so, O mighty-armed one, nothing whatsoever perishes anywhere.
Only the self exists, which is by nature indestructible; what of it could perish, and where?"
Apart from delusion and error, I do not perceive anything else such as "this is lost" or "this is joined," just as one does not perceive the son of a barren woman.
The unreal has no being; the real never ceases to be.
The truth of both these ends has been perceived by those who see reality.
But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable.
These bodies are said to have an end, but they belong to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable embodied Self; therefore, fight, O Bhārata!
The Self alone exists; there is no duality. How could that which is non-existent come into being?
It is indestructible and infinite; for that which is existent, destruction does not occur.
When duality and unity are both abandoned, that which remains as the residue—
the peaceful middle between being and non-being— that is the supreme state here.
Arjuna said:
"O Blessed One, since I am as good as dead, what is the basis for the continued existence of men? Or how, O Lord, do heaven and hell exist for people while they remain in this world?"
The Blessed One said:
Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, and intellect— this self, whose nature consists of these subtle elements, exists as the individual soul (jīva) within bodies.
He is dragged along by latent impressions as if a young animal were pulled by a rope;
he remains within the body like a bird in a cage.
By the power of time, as the body has become worn out,
it departs due to the force of latent impressions, just as sap flows from the leaves of a tree.
Having taken up the ear, the eye, touch, taste, and the nose,
it departs just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
This body of his consists solely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is not produced by any other cause;
it perishes when the latent impressions are abandoned, and when that [body] has perished, one attains that state.
Having previously been nourished by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the individual soul (*jīva*) wanders through various wombs,
taking on the form of a mass of delusions, like a person created by *māyā*.

Under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the individual soul (*jīva*) departs from the body, taking with it all the sense-faculties along with their inherent natures, just as the wind carries away fragrances from a flower.
O son of Kuntī, when the life-force has departed, the body becomes motionless;
with its limbs and expanse devoid of movement, it is like a tree from which the wind has ceased.
Devoid of activity and subject to defects such as cutting and breaking, the body, having lost its life-force, becomes invisible; it is called "dead" in the world.
Wherever that living soul, whose form is breath, abides in the ether,
there it perceives an expansive form through the habitual force of its own latent impressions.
For this body is perceived by the living being as truly non-existent;
upon its destruction, it likewise quickly perceives another [body] just like a dream.
Just as he perceives their forms, so too does he perceive their destruction;
for it is said that at the beginning of creation, he was thus fully manifested through meditative cultivation.
At the very moment of its sudden arising, whatever appears before it,
until the final nirvāṇa, that alone is the inseparable consciousness of this [mind].
The web of past latent impressions is quickly overcome by human effort through present exertion, just as one overcomes the exertion of yesterday.
That very portion of a preceding or succeeding moment which is perceived by a powerful human agent in an instant clearly triumphs.
Even if the cosmic egg were to burst asunder or the wind of universal dissolution were to blow,
a wise person must certainly not abandon human effort in accordance with the scriptures.

Under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the living being (*jīva*)— whose intellect is clouded by long-standing delusion— perceives everywhere the creation of hells, heavens, and so forth, as it has been practiced for a long time.
Arjuna said:
O Lord of the World, tell me what is the cause of this living being’s birth and existence amidst the tumultuous cycles of creation such as hell and heaven?
The Blessed One said:
Know this living being, the body, to be of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Its very existence, consisting of its own latent impressions, is the cause of cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*).
Samsara persists only as long as latent impressions (vāsanā) manifest;
since it is like a dream, therefore here the destruction of latent impressions leads to the highest good.
Arjuna said:
O Lord of the gods, from what does this mature latent impression (*vāsanā*) that causes the delusion of worldly existence arise due to long-term habituation, and how is it destroyed?
The Blessed One said:
O virtuous one, from the height of the delusion of ignorance, through the cultivation of the notion of a self in that which is not-self,
and due to the lack of knowledge regarding the self, latent impressions come into being.
O son of Kuntī, you have cultivated the self and have realized the truth;
abandon the latent impressions that "this is he," "I am this," and "these people are mine."
Upon the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā), the individual soul (jīva) dissolves of its own accord;
for whatever has swollen through the existence of something else, it dissolves upon the destruction of that thing.
When the body has dissolved due to the alteration of place and time,
who is it that becomes the vessel for birth and death?
O Mahāmati, know that very same turbid form of the self, which consists of its own imagined conceptualizations, to be the individual soul (jīva) characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā).
O Bhārata, know that liberation to be the immutable nature of the Self, which is independent, free from volition, and released from latent impressions through awakening.
O mighty-armed one, even while living, having perceived reality as it truly exists and being released from the snare of latent impressions, one is designated as "liberated."
He who is not free from latent tendencies is certainly not one who is devoted to all dharmas;
even if he were omniscient, he would be bound on all sides like a bird confined in a cage.

He within whom no latent impression (vāsanā) flickers, even though it be subtle, like a peacock feather in the sky of the difficult-to-perceive [mind], is indeed liberated here; for latent impression alone is the bondage of the sinless one, and its destruction is surely liberation.
In the *Arjunopākhyāna*, the sixtieth canto, titled "The Determination of Life," the Blessed One said:
Thus, through the state of being free from latent impressions and liberated while living, having attained inner coolness within yourself, completely abandon the sorrow for your kinsmen.

O sinless one, you are free from fear regarding old age and death; your disposition is as clear as space; having abandoned all thoughts of the desirable and the undesirable, you are devoid of passion.
Perform whatever task has come to you as it falls into the stream of events;
act without meanness, and nothing here will be lost.
For that action which is performed as it spontaneously falls into the stream of events is indeed the very nature of one liberated while living; otherwise, there is no liberation while living.
"I shall abandon this action" and "I shall resort to this"—such is the nature of the mind of the deluded person, which is not stainless; but the mind of the wise person remains in equanimity.
Performing actions that have fallen into the natural flow of life with peaceful minds,
those liberated while living remain as if in deep sleep, yet they manifest like those who are half-awake.
The senses of the wise man naturally withdraw from their objects into the heart, becoming steady in their withdrawal on all sides, like the limbs of a tortoise.

The entire universe, woven together from the existent and the non-existent, is established like a garland upon the firm, expansive thread of pure consciousness— the architect of the universe whose very limbs are the universe itself.
When it is extended, it expands; when it is contracted, it vanishes;
a web of diverse arrangements exists within the single canopy of consciousness.
Though non-different from it, this world appears as if different, like the form of one's own limbs appearing as if they were a separate body; it stands as a wondrous canopy within consciousness.
Just as a painting, once completed by the efforts of a painter,
remains fixed, so too does the entire universe— both that which is born and that which is unborn— subsist within the Self.
Just as a painter manifests various forms upon a canvas,
so does the Universal Self manifest the entire universe, consisting of the emergence of the three periods of time.

The painter of the mind creates the painting of the three worlds without a wall, even though it consists of space itself, yet it appears clearly in the sky through the application of its various modes of activity.
First, a manifold painting was spread out by the painter that is the mind;
afterwards, the wall was made to have the nature of space—oh, what a delusion!
Truly, this is an unprecedented and great illusion, wherein there is not even the slightest difference between empty space and a wall, despite their being clearly perceived.
O lotus-eyed one, know that these walls which appear to be produced by the painting of the mind are actually the emptiness of space.
Just as the destruction and arising of the world appear in the mind in an instant,
so too is this entire universe— both internal and external— the void, whose nature is space.
In this which is merely a long-standing mental construction, how could there be truth even when it is perceived? There is no truth at all in an illusion.
When perceived through delusion, reality dissolves upon the arrival of light;
though it appears, it becomes as thin as a cloud in the sky during autumn.
The various paintings created by the mind reside within the mind like painted figures;
because there is no wall, the external world, including the three realms, is without support.
These do not exist, nor do you exist; what is obstructed by what?
Abandoning the delusion of the obstructed and the obstructor, become as pure as space.
What activity can there be for space? Indeed, activity itself has the nature of space.
Therefore, time, action, walls, parts, and so forth, are all the pure sky.
Just as a painting resides within the mind and, though appearing as a real form, is essentially of the nature of space,
know this entire world to be likewise the most void of the sky.
The painting created by the artist of consciousness upon the wall of the mind does not differ in the slightest from the sky of emptiness.
Just as the manifestation and dissolution of the world appear within the mind,
know, O friend, that these two likewise exist externally in an instant.
In the kingdom of the mind during the first moment— named for various worlds—
which exists only for a moment, the state of being an eon (*kalpa*) has been imagined through delusion.
Just as the mind is capable of creating a kingdom of the imagination that is entirely non-existent,
so too is the powerful mind capable of transforming a single moment into an eon.
It turns a moment into an eon, and likewise makes the small appear great;
it quickly renders the non-existent existent—thus has this delusion arisen.
For a moment, a mental projection appears by its own nature;
that which consists of manifold forms is established as this web of the world.
Since this creation culminates in nirvāṇa, it has arisen in a mere moment; its adamantine essence is here imagined as being merely a matter of appearance.
The world-picture, painted by the mind and residing within consciousness, shines forth; though without a wall and devoid of colors, it appears as if vast before one's eyes.
"Aha! How wondrous is this brilliant painting that has arisen without a wall;
it stands as a delightful ornament for the world, a mere deception of the eye."
It is inscribed with the soot of manifold darkness, colored by the rays of manifold light,
composed of parts that are manifold stains, and tinted by manifold passions.
Rich with the play of various views, possessing eyes of diverse experiences,
with the fierce formations of various clouds, and having various forms as its foremost and final features.
The sky is a blue lake with the blossoming lotuses of the stars, moon, and sun,
and the rows of clouds are its clusters of leaves, busily engaged in diverse arrangements.
In its own inner chamber, it depicts the daughters of gods, asuras, and men;
it has the supreme light for its illumination and the sky-wall white as an *akkola* flower for its surface.
This charming little daughter, who enchants the three worlds, is fashioned from space alone—a single stage for her own manifestation;
she colors all the worlds with the face of pure consciousness, brought into playful activity by the painter of the flickering mind.
Her vine-like limbs are of gold, her mass of hair is thick, and she gazes upon the world by moving her eyes like the sun and moon;
she is clothed in the scriptures that restrain the triad of dharma, artha, and kāma, and her hips are as high as the earth while her feet reach down to the netherworld.
Her four arms are as formidable as those of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and Hari; her body is the staff of the quarters, with breasts raised by truth and falsehood;
and the great interior of the world, including the mountains, serves as the petals for the lotus-seat of the earth's surface encircled by the ocean.
With a face trembling in the darkness of night, laughing loudly with stars as its terrifying bristling hair, and rows of planets for its teeth;
with the rising fourteen kinds of fierce spirits for its bristling body-hair, it possesses a mass of conch-shells in the form of the roaring clouds of the cosmic dissolution.

The three worlds, endowed with living beings, created within the very sky by the mind— which is itself of the nature of space— as a marvelous and long-unprecedented painter, like a choice doll fashioned from various playful movements by one skilled in the art of painting.
The sixty-first canto, titled "The Description of the Variegated Colors of the World," spoken by the Blessed One.
Know this, O Arjuna, to be a great marvel here:
that indeed, the variegated form first comes into being, and only afterwards does the wall arise.
When a painting is produced without a wall, the extended wall is seen;
oh, how wondrous is this illusion! The stone has sunk, yet the gourd has floated.
In the three worlds, which are like a painting situated within the mind and whose nature is space,
how can this "I-ness" (ahantā) arise from you, whose nature is space?
The space of creation is made by space; in space, space dissolves;
space is experienced within space, and space is spread throughout space.
O Arjuna, that long-lasting bond of worldly existence which is entwined by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā) is unraveled here precisely by the unraveling of those latent impressions.
Just as a reflection appears in a mirror, so does this [universe] appear within Brahman itself;
it is inaccessible to cutting, piercing, and the like, because it is non-different from its substratum.
In Brahman there is no cutting, splitting, or the like; and Brahman is space.
What is cut, how, whose, by what, or where is this cut, or where is it split?
Brahmanhood shines within the fullness of Brahman like water in water;
it abides as perfectly even as the sky, stainless and peaceful within the Self.
Therefore, the relationship between the impressioner and the impressed does not differ even slightly;
thus, for you, the state of being free from impressions is already fully accomplished through awakening.
He who is not free from latent tendencies is surely not one who is devoted to all dharmas;
even if he were omniscient, his self would remain bound, and even if he were an ascetic, he would still possess passion.
For one who possesses even a very small seed of latent impressions (vāsanā) residing in the ground of consciousness,
the vast forest of saṃsāra arises once again.
The seed of latent impressions, once completely consumed by the fire of the awakening to truth that has taken root in the heart through practice, does not sprout again.
But when the seed of latent impressions has been burnt, one does not sink into objects such as pleasure and pain; one remains pure like a gourd leaf upon water.
You are one whose self is peaceful, free from the disease of worldly existence, born into Nirvāṇa, and who has shattered the great delusion of the mind;
having understood that purifying sacred learning through right knowledge, remain as the activity of the Self alone, in the form of absolute peace.
The sixty-second canto, titled "Arjuna’s Rest," begins with Arjuna:
Delusion is destroyed and memory has been regained by me through Your grace, O Acyuta;
I stand firm with my doubts dispelled, and I shall do as You have commanded.
The Blessed One said:
"If the mental fluctuations have clearly subsided within the heart through awakening,
know that this mind has quickly become peaceful and has attained the state of pure being."

In this context, that which remains is the reality called direct consciousness (*pratyak-cetana*), which is devoid of "that" and "this," liberated from everything, and which is itself entirely free from all else.
No afflictions of the world can obstruct that state,
just as the elements cannot hinder a bird that has flown up from the earth into the sky.
Know this Self here to be inwardly conscious, appearing as pure and devoid of volition— an unattainable [object] for those of impaired vision.

For one who stands in the state beyond all, purified by consciousness, latent impressions are unable to perceive that state, just as the vision of ordinary people cannot perceive a snake [in its true nature].
When that is attained, all these things such as jars and cloths are utterly exhausted;
what then can wretched latent impression (*vāsanā*) do there in the supreme state?
Just as even a trace of snow dissolves upon reaching the Fire Mountain,
so too does ignorance dissolve upon attaining the pure reality of the mind.
Where is this wretched, trivial, and binding desire for enjoyments, which is mere dust?
And where is the vast wind of the reality of consciousness (cittattva), which fills the entire web of the world?
This ignorance, which undergoes various transformations into manifold forms,
continues to flicker as long as this pure Self has not been thoroughly realized by the self.
All perceptions of the visible have ceased; pure reality alone has arisen and expanded within that state, which is one's own self, filling everything like the sky.
That supreme reality, which possesses all forms yet is devoid of all forms,
and which transcends speech— by what indeed can it be compared?

Therefore, having skillfully struck down the cholera-like poison of sensory objects and abandoned the latent tendencies for worldly existence through the method of striving to avoid what is undesirable, become free from disease— the very embodiment of the sole Lord of the world.
Vasiṣṭha:
When the Lord of the Three Worlds had spoken thus and remained silent for a moment before him,
then the son of Pāṇḍu was about to address him there, like a bee approaching a cluster of blue lotuses.

Arjuna said: O Blessed One, through your word, this mind of mine has attained the highest exaltation, with all states of sorrow completely dissolved, like a lotus-pond awakened by the sun, the lord of the world.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, Arjuna, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow whose charioteer is Hari, having risen and being free from doubt, will perform the sport of battle.
He will turn the earth into a land where great rivers of blood flow swiftly from wounded elephants, horses, and charioteers;
and he will shroud the sky—the eye of which is the sun—with circles of clouds formed by the spreading flight of his arrows.
The chapter titled "Arjuna’s Rest," the sixty-third chapter,
the *Arjunopākhyāna*, is completed.
Vasiṣṭha:
Holding fast to this vision, which destroys the sins of the descendants of Raghu,
remain established in that state consisting of selfless renunciation and the offering of all to Brahman.
Know that Supreme Self in whom all is contained, from whom all proceeds, who is all, who is everywhere, and who is eternally composed of all.
Though situated at a distance, you are not distant; you are all-pervading and indeed your very self.
Abiding within that [universe], you attain its nature; of this there is no doubt.
Know that to be the supreme state which is stainless consciousness, free from the object of cognition, and the manifestation of consciousness liberated from all that is thinkable.
She is the highest beyond the high, the ultimate goal; she is the unsurpassed vision among all visions.
She is the greatness of all greatnesses, and she is the teacher of teachers, the supreme Guru.
That is the Self, and that is consciousness; that is the void, that is Brahman, that is the supreme.
That is the highest good, that is the auspicious, the peaceful; that is knowledge, the ultimate state.
This inner conscious self, whose nature consists of all experience,
in which all substances take their relish through the existence of its own self.
He is the essence of the sesame oil within the world; he is the lamp for the house of the world;
he is the sap of the tree of the world; he is the protector of the cattle of the world.
He is the thread upon which the pearls of all beings are strung, the vast sky of the heart;
he is the pervasive, supreme pungency of the mass of black pepper that is all beings.
He is the substantiality of a substance, and he is the insubstantiality of what is non-existent;
he is the existence of an existing thing, and he is the non-existence of what is non-existent.
He is the illuminator of the world, its house, its activities, and its utensils;
by the light of the moon, the sun, and the stars, this universe is made manifest.
Everything has emanated from this conscious Supreme Self;
by means of inquiry into one's own self-awareness, this very Self is attained by oneself.
All worldly phenomena are charming only so long as they are not investigated;
their true existence is non-existent, for they fall apart under investigation.
In the beginning, having become what, within this web of the world whose nature is a mass of false delusions, do I cling to where, and how can I maintain an unreal resolve?
I am the beginningless and endless space of Brahman, beyond the mental constructions of beginning, middle, and end; what limit can there be to my own self?
Thus, he who possesses internal certainty, while maintaining outward conventional conduct,
remains forever infinite, liberated from both rising and setting.
He who neither sets nor rises, in whom equanimity remains constant and even,
whose emptiness is like that of space— he is the Great-Souled One here, possessed of the true form.

One who has ascended to the state of non-duality of existence with an intellect as profound as deep sleep does not experience agitation of the heart even while engaged in worldly activity, just like a person reflected in a mirror.
Even though he engages in worldly activity like a man looking into a mirror,
he whose heart is not touched by even the slightest impression is a partaker of liberation.
In the jewel of the Knower, which is indeed non-differentiation, all worldly activity is reflected as it occurs, due to the supreme purity of consciousness.
This very wonder of consciousness manifests as the world;
herein there is neither unity nor duality, for even the teaching is composed of that.
Through its own self-manifestations known as the signified, the signifier, the disciple, the seeker, and the teacher, consciousness— which is inherently tranquil— wonders within consciousness itself.
For transmigratory existence is the vibration of consciousness, while the supreme state is its non-vibration;
by the stilling of the vibration of consciousness, this cycle of birth and death comes to rest.

That which is the cessation of non-contemplation— the manifestation of a portion of the meaning of the negative particle within the Great Consciousness— is described as a vibration of consciousness, though it is by its very nature as if non-existent.
That emptiness which is non-inert is said to be the supreme body of consciousness;
the absence of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) therein is what is experienced as cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*).
That [state] consists merely in the dissolution of all mental cultivation and is devoid of any substantial form;
only the pure state of oneness remains as one's own true being.

The wise know that the very vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) is the turning of the wheel of saṃsāra, just as bracelets and other ornaments are nothing but gold. The knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, are likewise [nothing but consciousness].

There is no vibration of consciousness that exists separately from it which could constitute transmigratory existence; rather, the very nature of consciousness is its vibration, for it is the non-awakening to that [nature] which is indeed transmigratory existence.
The mere absence of awakening is a vibration of consciousness that has arisen like the state of being a bracelet;
when this dissolves into mere awakening, pure conscious gold remains.
By the mere realization of truth, the tendency toward enjoyment perishes;
indeed, the absence of such a tendency here is the supreme characteristic of one who possesses knowledge.
All these enjoyments are by their very nature undesirable to the wise man; for who, indeed, being fully satiated, would ever long for bad food?
Know this alone to be the supreme characteristic of true knowledge:
that which is indeed the absence of longing for enjoyments by their very nature.
The certainty that "consciousness alone, whose nature is the self of all,
exists" is what is remembered by the term "knowledge" when it has taken root within through one's own practice.
The unintelligent person who does not enjoy even the objects of enjoyment being offered to him,
merely for the sake of conforming to worldly custom, is striking at the sky with sticks.
Without artificial reasoning, success is not attained anywhere—
whether regarding the self or the world— even by means of cutting off one's own limbs.
As long as this unawakened self, whose nature is vibration, quivers in the form of movement, so long does it perceive the delusion situated at the limit of the "this" and the "not-this."
But upon the arising of perfect awakening, the successive stages of its movement and stillness,
along with their designations, seem to vanish somewhere, like a lamp that has been extinguished.
For the intellect, which by its very nature is a lamp whose form is light,
there is not even the slightest possibility here of any discourse regarding vibration or non-vibration.
That very form of the motionless one— which neither was, nor is not, nor is intermediate— becomes the vibration of consciousness when it is characterized by tranquility.
The vibration of this consciousness is non-different from it, possessing the essence of pure consciousness;
it exists solely within the Self, leading neither to bondage nor to liberation.
If one does not perceive even the slightest cognition of the meaning of "not," as if in nirvāṇa,
then even the name of the categories of bondage and liberation does not exist.
The thought "let there be liberation" is itself bondage; the desire for the exhaustion of fullness is also bondage.
Even the thought "let there not be [liberation]" is bondage; for you, supreme non-perception is the highest good.
Know that which is non-manifest and non-inert to be the supreme state— the abiding in the true nature of consciousness, characterized by the absence of orientation toward any object of cognition.
That vibration of the Great Consciousness which consists of the forms of conceptualization and words—
the very thing subject to bondage and liberation— is stilled when it is scrutinized.
When the ego-sense has been completely stilled through mere observation and is left without a basis,
we do not know by whom, what, or for whom one is bound or liberated.
If the intellect (citi) were indeed nothing but volition (saṅkalpa) and devoid of differentiation,
then everything that has arisen would be unobstructed— free from volition and free from movement.

Because it is always identical with consciousness, the world of manifestation is swallowed by consciousness through its very non-manifestation; thus, when one abides in the motionless mass of consciousness, saṃsāra is utterly exhausted.
In the awakened one, the vibration of consciousness (citspanda) is nothing other than the energy of consciousness itself; no vibration of consciousness remains that is distinct from it.
In this long dream consisting of the visible world, one who moves from one dream to another does not incur delusion, because of the all-pervasive nature of one's own consciousness.

Realize through meditation that inner Self within you, wherein the existence of all consciousnesses rises forth forcefully and incessantly, upon which all the chisels of manifold mental constructions strike, and wherein all perceptions arise, beautiful in their own experience.
The sixty-fourth canto, titled "The Realization of the Inner Self," by Vasiṣṭha.
They say of him: "Know him as the supreme reality; know him as the highest state.
I know him as the one alone; he alone exists, and nothing else.
This very inner self, which is the single mirror for all beings,
from this the world has arisen, just as a tree arises from a seed.
Having abandoned the intellect, ego, mind, and so forth, which are insentient by nature— that within which the experiencer comes to an end— know that to be the supreme state.
That which is pure experience alone, devoid of mind, intellect, and the like, called the Great Consciousness and meritorious— that is this supreme state.
Abiding in that [Supreme Reality], these great forms— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—
shine forth intensely with their manifold powers, like subjects before a gratified king.
He sports for a long time with pastimes such as traveling through the sky,
together with the very people residing there, just like a dweller of heaven in the celestial realm.
Having attained that, my dear, one does not die; having attained that, my dear, one does not grieve;
having attained that, my dear, one does not decay; having attained that, my dear, one is not bound.
If even the slightest form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) of the Supreme Self— which has the nature of the infinite, supreme ether— is clearly contemplated, [then all is attained].
In that very moment, the living being becomes a sage whose mind is liberated;
performing the actions of worldly existence, he is no longer tormented by them.
Rāma:
That wherein the mind, intellect, and ego have come to an end—what is that manifestation called, and of what nature is it said to be? It is the universal existence (sattāsāmānya).
Vasiṣṭha said:
That Brahman which, residing within all bodies, eats, drinks, moves about,
takes up, destroys, and consumes, is devoid of both consciousness and the objects of consciousness.
That which is all-pervading, devoid of beginning and end, established, and powerful— this entire universal essence of existence is here called the reality of things.
It exists as space within the ether, it exists as sound within sound;
it exists as touch within touch, and it exists as skin within the skin.
It is perceived as taste through its nature as taste and is absorbed in the tongue through its nature as that;
it is seen as form through its nature as form and is absorbed in the eye through its nature as sight.
The nose is seen as nasality; fragrance is declared to be fragrance;
the body is nourished as the body; and even the earth is perceived as earthiness.
It exists as liquidity in water, as the nature of air in air,
as the nature of fire in fire, and as the nature of intellect in the intellect.
Through its nature as the mind, it has taken root within the mind by means of the ego-function (*ahaṅkṛti*);
through consciousness, it has arisen in consciousness as the intellect (*citi*) by means of the faculty of thought (*cittva*).
It is attached to the tree as the tree-ness, it abides in the cloth as the cloth-ness;
it is established in the jar as the jar-ness, and it abides in the banyan tree as the banyan-tree-ness.
In the immobile as immobility, in the mobile as mobility,
in the stone as stoneness, and in the sentient as sentience.
Among the immortals by way of immortality, among men by way of humanity, among animals by way of animality, and among worms by way of being a worm; MU 6.64.20.

In the sequence of time, the all-pervasive Lord exists as time; in the seasons, He exists as the seasons; and in moments such as the *tuṭi*, the *kṣaṇa*, and the *nimeṣa*, He exists as those very things.
It is born as whiteness in the white, it abides as blackness in the black;
it exists as vibration in actions and as restriction in destiny.
The Supreme Lord abides as stability in that which is stable, as destruction in destruction, and as arising in that which arises.
In childhood, he rests through childhood; in youth, through youth;
in the state of old age, through old age; and in death, through death.
Thus, the Supreme Lord is non-different from all things, just as the mass of water in the ocean is non-different from its waves, spray, and ripples.
This diversity is indeed unreal; for by means of this very reality, it is imagined through the nature of consciousness, just as a ghost is imagined by a child.

"O Great-Souled One, remain at ease with a mind entirely tranquil, realizing: 'This entire universe is pervaded by Me, who am omnipresent, free from all affliction, and possessed of manifold manifestations; for it is by My own conscious nature that the world is both fashioned and un-fashioned.'"
Vālmīki:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
The assembly, having offered their salutations, departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
The sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Manifest Power," [spoken by] Rāma:
O Sage, just as for us the circle of dream-cities and towns is [unreal],
so too is the assumption of a body for Padmajā and the others.
If all this has arisen in that very way and consists entirely of non-existence,
then how has such a firm conviction arisen in us?
Vasiṣṭha said:
The Prajāpati of the previous creation appears like my own creation;
he exists as the nature of the manifestation of his own individual soul, but not as something real.
Because consciousness is all-pervading, the individual soul (jīva) is everything, and thus transmigration occurs everywhere;
yet that [transmigration] is unreal, arising from false perception, and it destroys right vision.
This appearance of his, which has arisen of its own accord like a dream, is essentially of the nature of the notion of "I"; it remains exceedingly firm.
Just as the momentary destruction [of objects] in a dream is not perceived by a person,
so too this [destruction] is not observed even by Brahmā in the dream of creation.
Whatever dream or mental appearance may arise for this Supreme Person,
it would be exactly like that creation consisting of Rāma, myself, and others.
That which is born from a dream-person is of the nature of that dream-person;
for it is experienced as such, just as a fruit is of the nature of its seed.
Know that to be truly unreal which is accomplished by means of the unreal;
even when an object is capable, attachment to its existence is not appropriate.
Since the cultivation of existence is possible even for an object that lacks functional capacity,
one must therefore abandon the cultivation of the cultivation of what is non-existent.
Whatever arises from a person in a dream who is firmly believed in,
that [arising] within oneself as the creation and so forth is likewise held with firm conviction.
This dream-creation exists as a mere twinkling of an eye;
within that very twinkling, our state of being a kalpa has been imagined.
Just as this vast thicket of long sleep arises for Prajāpati,
so too do the beginnings of creation arise individually for all living beings.
Through the very existence of the reality of consciousness alone, successions of creations and dreams flash forth,
just as whirlpools and eddies manifest through the fluidity of water.
Since this splendor of creation is merely of the nature of a dream and not real,
the question of whether "this is possible" or "this is not" has come to an end.
