Whatever is seen in whatever manner and of whatever kind exists exactly so;
for the principles governing dreams and delusions are not subject to critical inquiry.
There is nothing in this world that cannot occur within delusion;
for diverse perceptions of reality are seen throughout the three realms.
Fire burns within the water, like the submarine fire in the ocean;
cities exist in the sky, as the abodes of those who dwell in celestial chariots.
Lotuses grow upon stones as trees do on the Golden Mountain; all flowers exist in a single place, just as they do on the wish-fulfilling tree.
The rocks bear fruit like clusters of jewels;
within the rocks there exist living beings, just as frogs exist within a rock.
Water flows from stones just as it does from a moonstone;
in the blink of an eye, a jar turns into a cloth, like one under a curse.
They perceive even their own non-existence, just as one perceives one's own death in a dream;
or like water flowing downwards appearing to fly through the sky when it is within a cloud.
Water stands in the sky like a canopy, just as the celestial river [flows];
massive rocks fly upward like winged mountains.
Indeed, everything is obtained from the stone, just as from a wish-fulfilling gem;
for thoughts bear fruit swiftly, like those in the inner gardens of the gods.
O Raghava, those very [actions] do not bear fruit quickly, like liberation and other such goals;
even one who is insentient performs action, like a mechanical man.
Such and other various bewildering undertakings,
impossible even for the playful illusions of Śambara or the Gandharvas, have been seen.
Arising from place, time, action, substances, jewels, spells, and curses;
produced by illusion and by Gandharvas; infinite and born of truth.
Even here, the impossibility of possibilities is accepted;
the establishment of the aspects of possibility and impossibility are like the delusions of a dream.
There is nothing that is not real, and there is nothing that is not false;
everything, by everything, everywhere, within this dream designated as "creation."
Just as a living being whose intellect is immersed in a dream perceives stability,
so too does one whose intellect is immersed in the dream of creation perceive stability.
Moving from one delusion to another, passing from one dream to another,
the living being here becomes utterly bewildered, caught in a state of extremely firm conviction.

Just as a bewildered deer, falling into the fault of plunging into a chasm, enters another abyss, so too does the living being, deluded by the fall into cyclic existence, enter a state of confusion whose sole nature is that of a downfall.
The sixty-sixth canto, titled "The Narration of the Dream of the World," by Vasiṣṭha.
In this regard, O Rāghava, I shall relate this ancient history; listen to it, concerning what occurred to a certain meditative mendicant at some place.
There was a certain great monk who was devoted to the practice of meditative concentration,
constantly spending the entire day in his own spiritual discipline.
That mind of his, purified by the practice of meditative concentration, instantly contemplates whatever it thinks of and quickly attains that state, just as water becomes waves.
Once, having ceased from that meditative absorption and remaining one-pointed in mind,
he sat upon his seat and reflected for a moment on the sequence of his duties.
As he was reflecting thus, this realization then arose spontaneously within him:
"I shall quickly manifest the conduct of an ordinary person for the sake of sport."
Having reflected thus, his mind remained fixed upon some other person,
like water in a whirlpool that ceases its movement and shape through mere abandonment [of its previous state].
Then that man of the mind, by his own desire, suddenly gave himself a name; "I am Jīvaṭa"—thus it was established, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
Then Jīvaṭa, that man created by a dream, wandered for a long time through the streets of a certain city within that city fashioned by a dream.
There he drank the drink, intoxicated like a bee drinking the nectar of a lotus;
ground down as if by a stone, he fell into a deep sleep.
In a dream, he saw his own state as a Brahmin, satisfied with recitation and ritual performance,
endowed with mere intuition, just like reaching another region of the mind.
Once, that best of the twice-born, through his devotion to the performance of his daily rites,
fell into a deep sleep, just as a tree sinks into its state of seed.
Then, in a dream, he himself beheld his own status as a sovereign,
adorned by a garland of clouds consisting of an army of banners, chariots, elephants, and horses.
Having finished his meal, that vassal king once fell into a deep sleep,
with all internal activity ceased, like a tree whose seeds have entered a state of dormancy.
In a dream, he saw her in royal splendor, garlanded with the circle of the quarters, cherished by a multitude of enjoyments like the season of spring graced by a profusion of flowers.
Once, that king, being at ease and having ceased all exertion, fell asleep as if his own future conduct were already present within the cause of his current action.
In a dream, he beheld within himself the irreproachable state of a celestial woman,
like a blossoming kesara tree manifesting as a cluster of flowers.
She took delight among the celestial armies and in the grounds of the divine gardens,
like the beloved of Hari, restless upon the waves of the milk ocean.
Once, that young woman slept in a bower of garden creepers,
her mental fluctuations completely stilled, like a fragrance resting upon a lotus.
Then, in a dream, he beheld within himself the state of being a female deer, arisen through the power of association, just as the nature of water freely manifests as the whirling of a whirlpool.
Once that doe with tremulous eyes, overcome by sleep,
saw in a dream her own state as a creeper, grown within herself through the force of her habitual practice.
Even animals perceive dreams due to the nature of the mind;
in this regard, the examples of the parrot, the horse, and the elephant’s recollection of their names remain unimpaired.
She became a creeper, resplendent with flowers, fruits, and tender shoots,
sporting like a forest goddess within a bower of creepers in a woodland garden.
By means of an internal consciousness that had ascended to the form of a sprout situated within the seed,
she clearly perceived her own being cut down.
After experiencing a state of dense insentience for some time through a portion of deep sleep,
he then beheld himself existing as a bee.
Then that six-footed one roamed in the forest among the forest creepers and in the blooming lotus ponds, like a lover among young women.
Parting his bimba-like lips and tasting the honey of flowers,
he would sleep upon beds of blossoms after enjoying the playful vine-like women.
He became as distressed in the lotus pond as one is by a lotus stalk;
for even the mind of a dull-witted person finds delight only in some particular thing.
An elephant came to that lotus pond to stir it up;
for the minds of the foolish expand only for the destruction of beautiful things.
Along with that very churning of the Nalinī lake, the bee likewise attained a state of powdering, just as the establishment of excellence within another leads to its own destruction.
A bee, through its perception of an elephant and by cultivating that perception of an elephant, saw itself arisen as a swaying, intoxicated elephant.
The elephant fell into a pit as deep as a dried-up ocean,
like a living being in this empty world, dense with the thick mass of darkness.
He became the king’s great favorite, a destroyer of enemy forces,
who was always intoxicated by the power of his own pride, like a night-stalker reeling as if drunk.
Once, severed by the sword of his enemy, he went to his end,
like the life-force within the self when its form has been lopped off by the blade of discernment.
Seeing the bees emerging from the jewels on the frontal globes of the herd of elephants,
that soul, as it departed from the elephant, instantly became a bee once again.
While enjoying the forest creepers, he returned once more to the lotus pond;
for the long-standing habituation of latent tendencies is difficult to overcome due to a lack of awakening.
There, by being trampled by the elephant's hoof, it was reduced once more to powder;
yet, through the perception of a swan standing nearby, it became a *kalahaṃsaka* (a type of fine cloth).
That swan, wandering for a long time among lakes of blooming lotuses,
shone resplendent once upon a time, accompanied by many other swans.

Consciousness, whose essence is the Brahman-goose, was for the most part devoid of words and their meanings; yet within it, that consciousness blossomed forth like the first peacock emerging from the fluid of the primordial egg.

As he was contemplating her from afar, he was struck violently by the son of Daśaratha; through the continuous recollection of that perception, he was born as a swan in the lake of the Lotus-born One.
There, awakened by the playful expressions of words concerning uninterrupted solitude, and having attained the vision of the purifying reality, he remains liberated;
indeed, at the time of the end of the age, he must necessarily become one who is liberated while still in the body (videha-mukta).
The sixty-seventh canto, titled "The Example of the Monk's Saṃsāra," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, on one occasion, that bird beheld Rudra in Rudrapura,
who was engaged in the playful sport of trumpeting like an elephant upon the stalks of Brahmā’s lotus-pond.
Then the thought arose in him with the certainty, "I am Rudra";
for a reflection instantly appears in a fine mirror as the very image itself.
There, his body having become that of Rudra, he cast off that physical form,
just as fragrance, upon becoming wind, leaves behind a cluster of flowers.
Then Rudra sported at will in the abode of Rudra, according to the various customs of Śiva’s city and through his preeminence in the assemblies of the Gaṇas.
But Rudra, through that singular manifestation of his unsurpassed knowledge, perceived with his intellect his entire former history.
That Blessed Lord Hara, whose form is unobstructed consciousness,
spoke of his own accord in private, amazed by the hundreds of his own dreams.
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion, which deludes the entire world! Though it is unreal, it appears as real, firmly rooted like water in a mirage.

For the first time, having transcended the object of thought, I have attained the state of pure consciousness, through the contemplation of the sky and other elements that existed from the beginning of creation.
While living as one who exists by chance, colored by the elements and subtle essences,
I became a monk, entirely unperturbed, during a certain creation.
When, through that which is bound to the non-abode, one perceives that delight consists in wandering at will in the external world with a form agitated by playful charm; //MU_6,67.10//
At that time, through the force of that practice and by the dissolution of all phenomenal existence,
that monk experienced only that [reality], having abandoned any other arising of mental construction.
Whatever wonder has taken root in the mind, that alone unfolds;
the summer creeper sheds its blossoms even when it has drunk the water of spring.
Having become that monk Jīvaṭa, a living being whose latent impressions had grown old,
he wandered through those regions like an ant through crevices.
Then, because of his devotion to the twice-born within himself, he perceived his own state as that of a twice-born;
for when there is a reversal of one's disposition, that very disposition grows exceedingly strong.
That Brahmin attained the state of being constantly contemplated;
for a sap, when drunk continuously, reaches fruition in a tree.
Because he was the performer of the duties of sovereignty, wealth, and dharma, he became a king;
yet, due to his lustfulness, that king attained the state of a celestial woman.
Out of greed for her flickering eyes, that deer became full of passion; alas, the delusion of latent tendencies leads only to suffering for living beings!
The doe remained with her mind constantly fixed on the vine in the forest;
she experienced the inevitable cutting down of that creeper.

Then, through the constant cultivation of that state, she— whose mind was always permeated by that very disposition— beheld within herself the condition of being a bee, long practiced through internal perception.
Having experienced the crushing under the hooves of elephants,
he then wandered again and again through the delusions of the great cycle of existence.
At the end of hundreds of cycles of transmigration, I stand here as this very Rudra,
within this frantic bustle of saṃsāra which is produced solely by one's own mind.
Thus have I wandered extensively through the many forest lands of saṃsāra, which, though appearing utterly tranquil, were as if never empty of beings.
In one creation I was named Jīvaṭa;
in another, I was an eminent Brāhmaṇa; and in another, a lord of the earth.
Having been a swan in a lotus grove and an elephant on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains,
and a deer on the Hehaya mountain, I have now reached this present state.
Here, infinite thousands of years and hundreds of four-age cycles have passed, composed of days and seasons.
From the supreme state that first flashed forth for me, there arose,
through the nature of being a sentient being, that sequence of knowledge established in my state as a monk.
Even though he had repeatedly transcended [worldly existence] and attained the state of a Brahman-swan,
that very former habit bore fruit through the arising of association.
Whatever firm habit arises for this living being without obstruction,
even after a hundred other births, that very same one it pursues.
Sometimes, by a chance occurrence like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" maxim, through association with the virtuous,
the impure habitual tendencies of the individual soul are brought to an end.
This [consciousness], for its own arising, depends solely upon a slight cause consisting merely of the prior habitual practice of latent impressions (vāsanā) such as association and the like.
Whatever is practiced continuously, even in another body,
is experienced as real— even if it is unreal— during both waking and dreaming states.

That very thing which performs purposeful action for the sake of both suffering and happiness arises from cultivation; therefore, victory consists in the cultivation and non-cultivation of that [cultivation].
Meditation itself perceives its own self as "this body," which is merely the expansion of its own existence,
just as a sprout perceives its own bushiness.
When this cultivation is scrutinized, not even the slightest thing remains;
since it does not exist at all, let us have enough of that delusion.
This delusion, which consists of non-existence, having arisen like the color of the sky,
must in reality be cleansed away solely through its own non-perception.
It is better that this very existence, though of an unreal nature and harsh in form, be cherished;
let it proceed for our diversion—for what will the unreal do for us?
Therefore, having arisen, I shall look upon all those various worlds of my own;
by bestowing light upon some, I shall unify them with myself.
Having reflected thus, that Rudra went to that creation where the mendicant, staying in the monastery, lay asleep like a corpse.
Then, having awakened that monk through his own mind and intention, he joined him [to the truth]; the monk also remembered his own delusion.
Beholding Rudra as his own self, yet likewise consisting of Jīvaṭa and others, he—
though not subject to astonishment due to his awakening— was filled with wonder for the sake of maintaining the world.
Then Rudra and the mendicant both rose up and departed together for some unknown place—
the world of Jīvaṭa, situated in a single corner of the space of consciousness.
Having gone there to that dwelling, to that island, to that region,
to that district, to that city, and to that tavern;
They beheld Jīvaṭaka sleeping, his consciousness lost, like a corpse who,
having cast off the burden of his body, was wandering through the realms of existence.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him through both his mind and his conscious self,
those [beings]— Rudra, Jīva, and the mendicant— became either uniform or threefold in form.
Though they were enlightened, they appeared as if unenlightened; though filled with wonder, they remained without wonder.
For a moment, they stood silent, like figures depicted in a painting.
Then they all went to a certain part of the conscious void where the cycle of existence of the Brahmins was situated, resounding with the humming of beings engaged in their various undertakings.
Having gone there to that palace, that island, and that region, they reached that district, that village, and the abode of the brahmins.
They saw the Brahmin asleep in his house, surrounded by his wife,
with his arm held around the neck of the brahmin woman, appearing as if he were still alive.
Having awakened him and quickly engaged him with both their minds and their conscious wills,
those many who were there stood as one, filled with wonder yet free from pride.
Then they went to the assembly of neighboring kings, which was reflected in the sky of their consciousness and perceived by them, and which was beautiful with the weight of its undertakings.
There they reached that palace, that island, and that circle;
they saw the sovereign lying asleep on a lotus-throne, intoxicated with pride.
Like a female bee resting upon the interior of a lotus bud, she placed that gold-bright [child]— who resembled a honey-bee sleeping within a lotus calyx— into the hollow of her golden-limbed breasts.
He was surrounded by beloved women like a tree with its clusters of blossoms,
standing amidst a network of lamps like a mass of gold set with jewels.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him with their mind and consciousness, those many beings stood there thus, filled with wonder yet free from pride.
Then, having awakened him there, they entered the royal cycle of existence;
thereafter, together with him, they wandered through other realms of transmigration.
Having attained that state of Rudra— the desire for the Brahma-swans— all of them came together and shone as the hundred supreme Rudras.
The Supreme Lord is a single consciousness whose body is divided, both active in manifold movements and yet motionless; He is of a single nature and yet possesses many forms.
Know that the hundred Rudras are, moreover, composed of unobscured consciousness;
they pervade the entire cycle of existence and abide as the sustenance of the whole world.
"O Rāma, there are ten great hundreds of Rudras here;
know this to be the eleventh, established in relation to saṃsāra."
For whatever cycle of worldly existence arises for whichever individual soul,
therein the multitudes of unawakened souls do not perceive one another.
For Buddhas meet with one another like waves and water in the ocean;
those who are unawakened, being established solely in their own individuality, remain like clods of earth.
Just as waves of water mingle thoroughly with one another due to their liquidity,
so too do the multitudes of awakened living beings mingle thoroughly with one another because of their consciousness.
These multitudes of living beings have arisen individually within saṃsāra;
yet, because the element of consciousness is all-pervading, they exist as if real though they are unreal.
Just as whatever is dug out of the earth is called by that very name,
O dear one, so too in this case, whatever is piled up in the universal funeral pyre is designated as such.
Just as you perceive the five elements everywhere here in this world,
so too is the nature of consciousness— the self of all beings— found everywhere here.
Just as when one looks at a limb upon a stone pillar in a group of carved figures, that very part is nothing but stone; so too the world is composed of consciousness within consciousness.
That which the worlds perceive as sensation within the supreme, pure state of non-sensation is indeed without cause,
just like the emptiness of the sky.
In the density of consciousness, the perception of the visible world is bondage, while non-perception is liberation;
whatever may be pleasing to you, that very thing you should quickly make firm.
Creation and non-creation, bondage and liberation, consisting of sensation and the absence of sensation—these two are non-different from the perspective of awakening; therefore, act as you wish.
Since that which does not exist simply because it is not perceived cannot be destroyed, what cause for distress is there?
Know that whatever is to be attained through silence has already been swiftly attained.
That which consists of mere sensation perishes when sensation ceases;
therefore, practice that which is desired regarding both sensation and the absence of sensation.
Just as a ripple is a movement in water, so the variegated world is a movement in consciousness;
O descendant of Raghu, the difference here is merely this much.

While place, time, and intrinsic nature exist in the case of waves and the like within water, at the beginning of the world, however, place and the other factors do not exist; they are merely constructed by consciousness.
The three worlds appear as radiant, for luminous consciousness is the accumulation that is the very nature of the single awareness.
This [consciousness] remains in speech with its distinctions brought forth and becomes afflicted; yet, when its speech is stilled, it is the auspicious Supreme Self.
In this context, the two words "consciousness" (saṃvedana) and "creation" (sarga) are never distinct in their meaning;
it is not appropriate for one who knows to say that "the wave and the water are two," yet such a statement is indeed fitting for one who lacks knowledge.
In the narrative of the Hundred Rudras in the Dream, the sixty-eighth canto, titled "The Search for Hundreds of Saṃsāras," Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, what has transpired beyond this for Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others ending with the Haṃsa, whose bodies were merely the dream-forms of the mendicant?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having come together with Rudra, they have all awakened;
having mutually perceived the cycle of existence, these portions of Rudra remain established in happiness.
Having observed that Māyā thus addressed by Rudra,
his own partial manifestations were sent back once more to that very state of worldly existence.
Rudra said:
"Go quickly to your own abode; having enjoyed pleasures there with your wives for some time, you shall come back into my presence."
"You shall become my portions, my hosts, and the ornaments of my city;
then, after the great dissolution, we shall go together to that state."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished from their sight and went into the midst of the other Rudras established throughout the cycle of existence.
Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others also returned to their own abodes; then, having spent their lives together with their wives, they eventually passed away.
Having reached the world of Rudra, they will become the foremost of the Gaṇas;
sometimes they are seen in the sky, bearing the form of stars.
Rāma:
Those [beings] such as Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and others, were merely the forms of the mendicant’s mental constructs;
how did they attain reality? For there is unreality in the objects of a mental construct.
Vasiṣṭha said:
In the Lord, the reality of intention exists; in the Unborn, the unreality of intention exists.
Wherever something does not exist, that is not there; for that state is the Self of all.
Whatever is seen in a dream and whatever is perceived through mental constructs exists in that very way there, being of that nature at all times.
It is established by that very state which consists of that place and time,
just as [a traveler] reaches another location by means of a movement consisting of that place and time.
Just as one cannot go from one place to another without effort, movement, and so forth,
so too a dream cannot be attained without its reality.
Everything exists within the treasury of consciousness; in whatever manner it perceives, consciousness attains that very thing exactly so, for it is unimpaired by virtue of being the self of all.
O dear one, that state by which objects of thought and dream are attained cannot be reached here without the practice of supreme meditation and yoga.
But those for whom the insights born of the knowledge of yoga have borne fruit and are firmly established— they, such as Śaṅkara and others, see everything everywhere.
He who desires this foremost object, which has been conceptualized in such a way, incurs the ruin of both, because he relies upon both.
For every desired task is accomplished by one who is single-minded;
what person, while traveling toward the southern quarter, can reach the northern direction?
The object of intention is understood only by those intent upon the object of intention;
the object situated at the tip is understood by those intent upon the object situated at the tip.
When this [object] is established by the cognition situated in front, he who desires to attain that which is imagined—
because of his lack of steadfastness in either one— he would then destroy both.
Therefore, because it is fixed upon a single object, the life-force of the monk, having attained the state of Rudra as the self of all, obtains everything from that state through its remaining thus.
To those whose lives are sustained by the resolve [to be] monks, that world appears as distinct for each of them;
and they do not perceive one another, except through the knowledge of Rudra.
Unawakened living beings are born from the Awakened Living Being,
by His will, just as fools are produced from the wise, like sons from a father.
"May I be a Vidyādhara here; may I be a ewe here"—this is the illustration of the fruitfulness of single-minded meditation within this state of ritual action.
Oneness and hundredfoldness, folly and wisdom,
divinity and humanity— all these arise through the sequences of place, time, and action.

Through the effort of concentration and meditation, it is indeed possible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to adorn [the body] simultaneously, because it possesses the nature of being capable of all powers and is undecaying.
Its nature, by its very essence, is both infinite and yet possessed of limits;
it is subject to expansion and contraction, like that of the *haṃsa*, the conscious self.
Whatever one desires exists; indeed, it is accomplished of its own accord through these self-conceived sequences of place, time, and action.
Yoginīs and yogins stay here and go elsewhere;
they desire both this world and the next—this has been seen many times over.
Just as Kārtavīrya, while remaining in his home, became a rain-cloud and showered down,
so too Viṣṇu, while remaining in the ocean of milk, becomes a person on earth.
While the yoginīs remain within the assembly of yoginīs, they go for the sake of the sacrificial animal;
and Śakra, while remaining on his celestial throne in heaven, goes to the earth for the sake of the sacrifice.
In this same way, within this Self of the universe, one thousand [beings] exist;
hundreds of devoted men attain union with Him while still in their bodies.
Just as one becomes a thousand, so too does this Janārdana;
alone, he enjoys thousands of beloved women at the same time.
Thus those [beings], such as the monks, the Saṅkalpajas, the Jīvakas, the Brāhmaṇas, and others,
have gone to their own cities of mental construction through the power of Rudra’s consciousness.
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time and thereafter attained the city of Rudra,
they shall obtain the status of Gaṇas and remain there together with their retinues.

Then, in various worlds and in cities and towns, those wearing stainless crowns take their pleasure with Rudra in dwellings of ever-blooming new kalpa-latas and amidst clusters of vast jewels, as well as among the vidyādharīs.
The sixty-ninth canto, titled "The Resting of the Bhikṣu," by Vasiṣṭha.
Just as this delusion of volition was seen by this monk,
so too does one perceive each element as real, yet sees them separately after death.
For every living being, a state consisting of birth and death certainly occurs;
even for that which is of the nature of the space of consciousness, it assumes a formal manifestation.
The forest of saṃsāra proceeds individually and separately for each self,
just as a grove of flowers proceeds individually for a caravan of merchants seeking fragrance.
Every living being, once dead, perceives its own individual manifestation; likewise, the embodied soul, though possessing its true nature, remains agitated until liberation.
O Bhikṣu Rāma, by this discourse I have explained to you this living soul (jīva) as being the self moved by the Supreme; it is not, however, the absolute (kevala) one.
The living being whose life is worn out goes from delusion to further delusion,
just like a stone fallen from a mountain peak that sinks lower and lower.
Fallen from the state of the Supreme Self, the individual soul perceives this dream as solid;
from this dream, it passes once again into another dream.
Falling even from one dream into another dream, this body within— which is as solid as stone— is perceived as a mere falsehood, worn out by illusion.
Sometimes, by some means, or perhaps at some time,
this [being] is released from the sleep of delusion by means of the body itself and becomes fully awakened.
Rāma:
Oh, how terrible is this delusion that arises for this living being!
Even by falling a mere step from its state, it produces manifold forms of transformation.
Alas! How truly terrible is this disparity resulting from the fall from one's own state, brought about by Māyā—that fierce night of false knowledge—acting with such skill!
O Blessed One, you have stated that everything is always and in every way possible within the existence of the world; and that very thing is experienced by me.
O great-souled one, look within and tell me quickly: does there exist anywhere a mendicant whose self is distinguished by such qualities?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Remaining in meditative absorption during this night, I shall observe whether or not this monk exists within this small hut of the three worlds, and speak of it in the morning."
Vālmīki:
While the sage was speaking thus, the midday drum resounded outside, as deep and resonant as the thundering of clouds agitated at the time of universal dissolution.
The kings and the citizens showered successive handfuls of flowers at his feet, like trees dropping their blossoms when stirred by the wind.
Having honored the best of sages, that protector of the earth rose from his seat together with the sage, like the sun rising from the mountain of sunrise.
Thereupon the assembly rose, exchanging mutual salutations;
then the sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers departed in due order, just as they had come the previous day.
In their own abodes, all of them respectfully carried out their daily activities according to the scriptures, as was appropriate for the sequence of their respective duties.
Reflecting upon the knowledge proclaimed by the Sage, those who move upon the earth and those who move through the sky passed their nights as if they were a moment, yet also like an eon.
In the morning, when the people had again become intent on their succession of duties, the assembly of sky-dwellers, earth-dwellers,
and perfected beings remained just as before, arranging themselves in their respective seats, honoring those worthy of worship through mutual salutations.
The seventieth canto, titled "Description of the Inner Wonder of Awakening," by Vālmīki.
It was joined by the sage Vasiṣṭha and attended by Viśvāmitra and others;
it was filled with throngs of Siddhas dwelling in the sky, and the leaders of kings had found rest there.
Then that very same assembly hall shone forth, together with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
it was as serene as a lotus pond when the wind has subsided, possessing a gentle and perfectly even expanse.
Then the Lord of Sages spoke, even without waiting for a question;
for the virtuous, being compassionate, instruct others by their very power.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, delight of the Raghus, moon in the sky of the Raghu dynasty!
Yesterday, that mendicant was gazed upon by me for a long time with the eye of meditation."
For a long time I wandered through meditation, desiring to see such a monk as you,
across the seven vast continents and likewise the mountain ranges that support the world.
Until such a monk is found anywhere at all,
how indeed can a kingdom of one's desires be perceived even in the external world?
Then, when one-third of the night remained, I again set out toward the northern region with my mind, like a coastal wind moving across the ocean.
Now, there is a great and glorious province there named Cīna;
upon an anthill there stands a monastery dedicated to the Jina.
In that monastery, within his own small cell, there lived a monk named Dīrghaśaya with tawny hair, whose future destiny was as follows.
And for twenty-one nights, while he remained in such a state,
they did not enter his house— which was secured with firm bolts— fearing the interruption of his meditation.
"His servants generally remain in that state, and he himself remains as one who has plenty; today it has turned out this way for him—such is the nature of destiny."
Twenty-one nights passed for him as he remained fixed in meditation;
yet in his mind, he experienced [the passage of] thousands of years.
In a certain previous eon, there was once a monk such as this;
today, however, there is a second here, but a third is not to be found.
Furthermore, with my fourfold mind, like a bee within the lotus of the world, I have searched for another such third monk.
But from this creation, we have not found a third one with such an intention;
thereafter, other creations were observed by me as mere play.
As long as there exists even a single creation resting within some corner of space,
there will be a third monk and a brahmin of such a character.
In this very manner, with that very same arrangement, entities have come to be, are being, and will repeatedly come to be throughout the succession of creations.
In this assembly as well, those sages, brahmins, and kings—
and indeed many others— must likewise be possessed of such conduct.
O sinless one, this Nārada must become someone else again;
likewise, Atri must now become someone else again.
Thus, by means of wife and karma,
and through such births and so forth, Vyāsa and Śuka were repeatedly endowed with these very conditions.
Furthermore, Janaka was to be attended by Kratu,
Pulaha, Agastya, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, and also Aṅgiras.
These very things, as well as others, will thus become the locus of such actions after a long, long time, because this illusion is so widespread.
Those very beings and many others, born with similar conduct,
revolve again and again through successive creations like waves in the waters.
Some are absolutely similar; some follow the sequence of being half-equal;
some are slightly equal; and some are never like that again.
Thus, this vast illusion that deludes the mind has neither a moment nor an aeon here; for it is the manifestation of one's own realization that unfolds.
Where are the endless twenty-one days and nights, and where are the miserable births?
Where is their perception? Alas, how truly terrifying is the course of the mind!
This [world] is merely a flash of intuition that has thus blossomed white;
it is as restless with waves of various strife as a lotus at dawn.
This entire web of saṃsāra, though impure, has arisen from pure consciousness alone, just as a mass of fire arises from a spark of fire.
Thus has each cluster of appearances been described; and within those, there are likewise various other clusters.
Indeed, they are all not false, for they manifest within this very self of all, the ultimate cause of causes.
The seventy-first canto:
Daśaratha said,
"O leader of sages, let these men go and awaken that mendicant."
Men dispatched by me have swiftly gone to the Chinese Buddha-hut.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O King, that body of that great mendicant, deprived of life, has become moist and discolored; it is no longer a vessel for life."
And having become the life-force of that monk, this lotus-born crane remained liberated while living; he was no longer a vessel for the cycle of worldly existence.
At the end of that month, having been forcibly expelled from his house,
they will look for the monk of unimpaired mind within [the city].
The monk remains liberated even with that very body;
how can he be awakened when his little physical frame has perished in the monastery?
This illusion, composed of the qualities, is difficult to overcome for one who lacks understanding; it is easily transcended by the constant realization of truth.
Just as the state of being a bracelet made of gold is produced by something unreal,
its arising has as its sole cause the error of appearance.
This illusion is measured as belonging to the Supreme Self alone;
like a wave in water, it perishes upon mere observation.
Even though the knower proceeds from one long dream consisting of the visible world to another dream,
he does not undergo any change of identity, for the seer of the all-pervading Self remains distinct through discernment.
Whatever appearance may arise for this [consciousness], that is itself the Self from the perspective of awakening;
it is that very same [Self] which arises as the vision of the thicket of *karañja* trees in the forest of saṃsāra.
Each individual being has arisen as a separate sphere of cyclic existence,
like a dream within the state of a monk, or like a wave from the water.
From the very beginning, this dream of the world has issued forth from the Lotus-born [Brahmā] himself;
likewise, it has now ascended upon the form of one's own mind toward every person.
The creation, extending back to the great-grandfather, shines forth like the play of a dream;
by that [process], millions of cosmic eggs arise here one by one.
Vibrating within the supreme, each individual soul perceives delusion in the heart as something capable of producing its objects, long and internal, like a dream.
Merely through the lapse of the perception of the universal that is the mere existence of consciousness,
someone has become a vessel for the sufferings of old age and death.

Whether it be the netherworld or the realm of Brahmā, she who is characterized by wondrous power remains ever established, having repeatedly created them through the mere vibration of a fraction of the mind.
The consciousness, whose nature is vibration, having entered into itself by means of that which is called "life," rolls about elsewhere as something other than itself, becoming laden with agitation.
O Supreme Self, why do you fear the Supreme Self alone—
this one who bears the name of "living being," "body," and so forth, like a child fearing its own reflection?
In Brahman alone does the supreme Brahman exist as the world-appearance; it is real only through the perception of the world, like pure space within space, or like stainless water within water.
This world belongs to Brahmā alone as he exists in the form of the universe;
it fears what is perceived as other, just as a child fears its own reflection.
When the mind, through awakening, is rendered motionless, its ideation ceases;
that [ideation], too, by means of complete transformation, dissolves like ghee in fire.
It is consciousness itself that unfolds within the vibration of consciousness as the self of all;
thus, vibration and non-vibration, unfolding and so forth, are merely conceptualized and have no reality here.
Here there is neither vibration nor non-vibration, neither unity nor duality;
there exists only pure consciousness alone, and everything exists exactly as it is.
Through the ultimate transformation, when both the world and the sense of "I" have subsided,
even pure consciousness does not exist, nor does the notion that "it does not exist" remain.
Through the contemplation of difference, difference arises as the characteristic of primordial nature;
when everything has dissolved through the realization of non-difference, the Supreme alone remains.
There is no diversity due to lack of awakening; that lack of awakening exists because of a failure to investigate.
Furthermore, there is no observer at all; therefore, there is supreme fearlessness.
Therefore, there is neither dream nor waking splendor, neither deep sleep nor the fourth state;
there is neither bondage nor liberation, nor anything else consisting of conceptualization.
Peace alone is named the World; this [world] is established within peace.
Therefore, since ignorance is truly non-existent, where can there be the seen, the seer, and the act of seeing?
Even the vibration of this consciousness is indeed non-vibration due to its freedom from conceptual construction;
for consciousness, devoid of conceptual construction, is neither distinct in vibration nor in non-vibration.
The mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), which consists of the forms of duality, unity, and so forth, is the cultivation of the mind;
that [construction] dissolves through mere non-cultivation, and Brahman remains.
That which appears like a dark spot on the disc of consciousness is not a blemish at all; know it rather to be the dense body of the mass of pure consciousness itself.
"The mass of consciousness is neither existent nor non-existent; abide in that expansive state.
Thus has been made this compendium of the essence of the entirety of great awakening.

By you, through your state of being whose nature is the destruction of both existence and non-existence, the stain of conceptual construction has been wiped away from the lunar orb of consciousness, which is the very embodiment of nectar.
Having brought the conceptualization of existence, non-existence, and so forth to the state of pure consciousness by means of the intellect,
remain at ease in equanimity at the conclusion of the play of tranquility and radiance.

Vibration and non-vibration, as well as the parts consisting of conceptualization and non-conceptualization, are not other than consciousness because it is consciousness; yet consciousness is nameless, partless, omniform, unobstructed, the existence of peace, and remains like a single ocean filled with sentient beings.
The seventy-second canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman," by Vasiṣṭha.

Having become possessed of the silence of deep sleep, and having shaken off the mental construction consisting of duality and unity, O beloved one, remain established in that state, assuming the form of consciousness.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, I know the silence of speech, the silence of the senses, and the silence of wood;
tell me, what is called the silence of deep sleep, the Lord of Silences?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, the sage is described here by the best of sages as being of two kinds:
one is the ascetic of wood, and the other is the one liberated while living.
One whose self is uncultivated, who is firmly resolved upon dry ritual action,
and who forcibly subdues the collection of his senses, may be a sage, yet he is merely a wooden ascetic.
Having understood this as it truly is, one whose self is cultivated remains established in the Self; though appearing like the world, he is inwardly satisfied—he is remembered as a liberated sage.
Whatever state belongs to these two Lords of Sages who have attained peace— a nature consisting of the certainty of the mind— that is remembered by the term "mauna" (silence).
Those who know silence say that it is of four kinds:
silence of speech, silence of the senses, wooden silence, and the silence of deep sleep.

Vocal silence is the restraint of speech; sensory silence is the forcible control of the senses; and the silence of the limbs is the abandonment of all physical movements, characterized by being like a piece of wood.
The fifth is mental silence, which exists in the deceased wooden ascetic;
while that which is called deep-sleep silence exists in the living liberated one while he is still alive.
Among the three specific types of silence, the wooden ascetic (*kāṣṭhatāpasa*) is the object;
and the one whose intellect is liberated is the object of the fourth state, that of deep-sleep silence.

Silence of speech alone is established as true silence; yet that which is defiled by a fraction of the mind leads to the bondage of the living soul—those who abide in such [silence] are merely "wooden ascetics."

Whether by force or through the application of yoga, the restraint of one's own senses is called "silence of the senses" (akṣamauna); those ascetics who remain in that state are known as "wooden ascetics" (kāṣṭhatāpasa).
Neither remembering nor recollecting, not touching the two-fold speech regarding the visible world,
and indeed not seeing while seeing, he remains in wooden silence.
This triad of silences, which consists of the flickering of the mind's activity, is traditionally taught for ignorant sages; it does not occur spontaneously among those who possess true knowledge.

In this matter, there is no need for the acquisition of knowledge regarding these three forms of silence; indeed, those who know them may practice them or not, either with ease or even with indifference.

This, however, is the silence of deep sleep, established in the mind of one liberated while living; listen to this ornament for the ears, which leads a living being to the state of no further rebirth.
In this state, speech is neither restrained nor abandoned in its threefold form; nor are the perceptions of all the sense organs made to exult or overcome one another.
For this perception of multiplicity neither leaps forth nor subsides;
it is neither mind, nor non-mind, nor non-mind; it is neither being, nor non-being, nor space, nor the earth.
O dear one, that state which is undivided, effortless, and without beginning or end,
whether one is meditating or even running— that is the silence of deep sleep.
Having understood, as it truly is, this delusion of the world's diversity, that which remains as an unattached state free from longing— that, my dear, is the silence of deep sleep.
O dear one, that which is infinite and remains as the state of deep sleep— the single, pervasive Self whose nature consists of manifold consciousness— that indeed is the silence of the supreme state.
Space is not space at all; I am everything, yet I am not.
That which remains thus—equal and tranquil—is the silence like deep sleep.
All is empty, without support, peaceful, and mere representation;
neither existent nor non-existent—this is the natural state, the supreme silence.
That which is the non-reflection within consciousness upon the various manifestations of the states of existence and non-existence arising from the unreal— that the wise know as the supreme silence.

That which is the non-returning of the movement of consciousness— by means of the mind, whose nature is its own activity, whether directed toward the unreal or as if toward the real— that is the imperishable silence (mauna).
"I am not, nor does another exist; there is no mind, nor anything mental"—this non-perception of consciousness is uninterrupted supreme silence.
"I exist" and "the world exists"—these are merely the referents of the word "exists";
since they are nothing other than the universal of being (*sattāsāmānya*), this is called the silence of deep sleep.
Since consciousness alone exists, how could there be other constructions such as dreams?
The state of deep sleep is indeed infinite; therefore, all is pervaded by that silence.
Know this very state of deep-sleep silence to be like awakening due to its infinity;
it is the stainless fourth (turya), or even that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
Whether it be the samādhi of deep sleep alone, or the samādhi of the fourth state (turya),
or even the samādhi beyond the fourth (turyātīta), these may indeed occur even while one is awake.

Abiding in the fourth state (*turya*), with all mental fluctuations stilled and purified, even while engaged in worldly activity during the waking state as if dreaming skillfully—whether still embodied or indeed disembodied—be forever the Brahman-sky; for that alone, O virtuous one, you truly are.
"Om! Remain as the One, with the latent impressions of worldly existence cast aside; for here there is nothing true such as 'you' or 'I.
Yet everything exists here like the interior of a stone; therefore, O Knower, remain established solely in the single digit of the treasury of the sky of consciousness."
The seventy-third canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Great Silence," [spoken by] Rāma.
O leader of sages, from whence has the number one hundred come for the Rudras?
And as for those who are the Gaṇas, are they Rudras or not? Tell me this.
Vasiṣṭha said: "The monk has seen a hundred dreams, each consisting of a hundred bodies;
all were known by way of summary, therefore they were not described by me."
Whatever forms appear as a hundred in a dream, that is remembered as a hundred of the Gaṇas;
that very same thing is a hundred of Rudras, for even the Rudras are designated as Gaṇas.
Rāma:
O Blessed One, how is it that from a single mind a hundred minds are produced,
like a hundred lamps lit from a single lamp by means of the Śatarudra-mantra performed in a dream?
Vasiṣṭha:
Whatever those whose true being is unconditioned conceive of, that very thing immediately comes to be exactly so; this is not the case for those whose consciousness is conditioned.

Because the Self is all-pervading and omnipresent, whatever is meditated upon in whatever manner and wherever, that very thing is experienced there in that same way by the knower of reality, without the aid of the intellect.
Rāma: O Brahmin, Maheśvara is adorned with a garland of skulls, smeared with ashes, naked, dwelling in cremation grounds, and yet he is a lover.
Vasiṣṭha:
For the great lords, the perfected ones, who possess bodies while already liberated in life, there is no restrictive rule of action here; for such a rule is devised only for the ignorant.
But the ignorant, because their minds are unsubdued, and lacking restraint over their actions,
indeed go to supreme suffering through greed, according to the "law of the fish."
But those who know that do not sink into attachment toward desirable or undesirable objects,
because they have conquered their senses, attained awakening, and are free from these latent tendencies.
They always perform actions that have become customary like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence;
or some do not perform them at all, for they have no attachment to anything whatsoever.
Like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit, Viṣṇu alone has been impelled by the Supreme to perform such actions;
the Three-eyed One performs such actions, and the Lotus-born One performs such actions.

For the one who possesses knowledge, there is never anything in the sphere of action that is blameworthy or blameless, nothing to be accepted or rejected, and nothing that belongs to oneself or another.
Just as heat and other qualities became established in fire and the rest at the beginning of creation,
so too did the activities of Hara and others, as well as the castes of the twice-born, become established.
When the creation has reached full development, conceptual constructions (kalpanā) are then fashioned for their own sake through the power of convention, based on previously experienced results.
O scion of Raghu, I have described to you the fourth silence concerning the one liberated while living; I have not yet spoken of the fifth silence concerning the disembodied one.
The space of the Self, which consists of consciousness, is even more transparent than the sky;
the attainment of that is the supreme good—listen now to how it is attained.
Those who have awakened through the realization of perfect knowledge by means of constant, single-pointed concentration,
having understood through enumeration itself— they are remembered as the Sāṅkhya yogins.
Those who have attained the state through the complete pacification of the vital breaths and other winds,
reaching that which is free from affliction and without beginning or end— they are remembered as the yogis of yoga.
But that peaceful, unconditioned state is to be accepted by all;
it is attained by some through calculation and by others through yoga from the body.
He truly sees who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one;
for the supreme state that is attained by the followers of Sāṅkhya is indeed the very same as that attained by the followers of Yoga.
Know that to be the supreme state where the activity of the mind, though it has reached there, is no longer perceived at all, being transcended by the snare of latent impressions.
They say that the mind itself is the latent impression (vāsanā), for it is the cause of saṃsāra;
when it dissolves within the karmas of existence, it ceases to be a cause.
The mind indeed perceives the body as a child perceives a ghost;
having brought the self to dissolution, one no longer perceives it.
The mind has arisen in vain and is indeed non-existent due to a lack of discernment;
like one observing the form of one's own death in a dream, it is not found to exist.
In the absence of the mind, there is no cyclic existence; where is joy without a flower?
Where, then, can there be the teacher and the taught, or bondage and liberation?
The intense practice of a single principle, the subsequent dissolution of the vital breaths,
and the restraint of the mind— these are the causes for the meaning of the word "liberation."
Rāma:
O Sage, if indeed the dissolution of the vital breaths were the cause of liberation, then surely all living beings would be liberated simply by dying; that is what I think.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Among these three practices, the pacification of the mind is the best;
know that it alone is what must be accomplished quickly, so that it may become auspicious.
When the vital breaths, free from latent impressions, abandon this little body,
they no longer enter into union with the subtle elements in the ether.
Know that the subtle elements (tanmātras) consist precisely of the portion of latent impressions (vāsanā).
The vital breaths (prāṇas) adhere to those [subtle elements] which possess a mental nature, and not to others.
But if these vital breaths, along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), abandon the body,
they enter into union with the space and wind for the sake of suffering, like a scent.
Like a rain cloud with its moisture, the mind does not become tranquil as long as it possesses latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
indeed, life-breaths devoid of the mind do not exist, just as suns without light do not exist.
The mind never abandons the vital breaths without knowledge,
just as a partridge does not leave the tip of a blade of grass without the rest of the grass.
Through knowledge, the mind indeed attains its own destruction by becoming free from latent impressions; it no longer sustains the vibration of the vital breath, and thereafter, peace alone remains.
From the knowledge that all things are non-existent, [the realization] fully arises;
then, my dear, through the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), there occurs the dissociation of the vital breath and the mind.
Then the mind, being utterly tranquil, no longer perceives the state of a body;
having attained the state through its own dissolution, the wise know that the mind is nothing but latent impression (*vāsanā*).
For the mind consists merely of latent impressions; its absence is the supreme state.
And that is accomplished through knowledge; they call knowledge discernment.
Thus, O Rāma, the end of this cycle of existence proceeds by means of discernment alone,
like the cessation of the delusion of a snake in a rope.
The practice of a single object, the restraint of the vital breath, and the dissolution of the mind—
when even one of these is fully perfected, they all become perfected through mutual influence.
Just as the wind is stilled when the movement of the palm-leaf fan ceases,
so too the mind is stilled when the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) ceases.
Upon the dissolution of the body, the vital breaths attain the state of space and wind;
and there, they perceive this very mind according to how it has been conditioned.
Just as the Videhas perceive their bodies in the ether, so too do they,
together with their minds, experience all conduct and everything else.
Just as fragrance subsides when the movement of the wind has ceased,
so too do the vital breaths subside when the movement of the mind has ceased.
The vital breath and the mind are always inseparable in living beings;
they exist mixed together like the fragrance and the flower, or like sesame oil and the seeds.
The vibration of the mind is the vital breath; the vibration of the vital breath is the mind.
These two always move together like a chariot and its driver.
Like the container and the contained, these two perish when one of them is absent;
and through their own destruction, they bring about the supreme effect known as liberation.
Through the intense practice of a single reality, the mind becomes thoroughly stilled;
because its very nature is absorption in that, the vital breath is also stilled by it.
Having reflected upon that reality of the infinite Self, one should lead the mind to identification with it; then, through absorption in that, the mind becomes steady as that very reality.
Whatever is the supreme good regarding both non-perception and perception—
since both are non-existent— remain steadfast therein, or likewise in what remains.
One should contemplate the state of being within a single, firmly established reality until,
through the full extent of one's own practice, that state of being arrives at the nature of non-being.
Through the power of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the mind dissolves along with the vital breaths, as if through the exhaustion of its objects of enjoyment; only the Supreme remains.
When the mind becomes one-pointed, it instantly becomes that in which the entire flood of diverse [mental states] has been stilled, by virtue of its nature resulting from long-term cultivation.
Having understood through reasoned intellect that this ignorance does not exist, the supreme attainment comes from knowledge alone; therefore, its cultivation is best.
When the mind is stilled, this mirage of saṃsāra subsides,
just as a great mist vanishes when the clouds have reached their dissolution.
Regard ignorance as mind-only; by that very means, bring about its destruction.
For that which consists of form and name is the experience of the nature of mind, the supreme state.
If the mind attains nirvāṇa for even a moment in the supreme state, know that it has been transformed by that; therein, the true taste has been found.
If the mind has found rest in the state [of liberation] through Sāṅkhya or Yoga, having attained the nature of pure being for even a moment, it is not born again.
The mind from which ignorance has dissolved is described by the term "sentient being" (sattva);
once the seed of saṃsāra is burnt, it will not produce a sprout again.
The knower, whose ignorance has dissolved away, established in purity and with tranquilized latent impressions,
beholds the peaceful light that is equal and like unto the void, and thus attains peace.
O fortunate one, the mind that has dissolved its state of ignorance and is stainless is here called "sattva";
it does not return again to the state defiled by the parts [of passion], just as copper that has attained the state of gold does not revert to its former condition.
The seventy-fourth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into the Union of Vital Breath and Mind," by Vasiṣṭha.
Through discernment, the living soul quickly becomes non-living, and the mind attains the state of no-mind;
thus, the end of ignorance is designated as liberation.
Like the water of a mirage, this creation—consisting of the sense of "I" and so forth—is perceived; though it is utterly non-existent, it dissolves upon investigation even as it appears.
Upon the cessation of this dream of saṃsāra, listen to these auspicious questions posed by the Vetāla, which have come to my memory through the course of our conversation.
In the great Vindhya forest there was a Vetāla of massive form;
out of greed for some sacrificial circle, he arrived there driven by hunger.
Formerly, that Vetāla dwelt in a certain abode of the virtuous,
happy because he was constantly satisfied by the offering of many sacrifices.
Being signless and blameless, he does not kill a man standing before him even when hungry; for attachment is the instructor of injustice.
In time, that forest-dweller went to another city,
driven by hunger, to consume people through fraudulent means.
There he encountered the king, who had gone out on his nocturnal round;
that fierce night-stalker addressed him with a deep and terrible voice.
The Vetāla said:
"O King, you have now been caught by me, the Bhīma Vetāla!
Where will you go? You are ruined; you shall be my food today!"
The King:
O night-stalker, if you devour me here by force against all justice, then your head shall split into a thousand pieces; of this there is no doubt.
The Vetāla said:
"I do not devour you; rather, this justice is being proclaimed by me:
you are a king, and the hopes of all supplicants must be fulfilled by you."
O King, fulfill this request of mine for the sake of its realization;
you ought to explain correctly these questions posed by me.
To what sun are the universes like tiny, minute atoms?
In what wind do the great particles of the vast sky flutter?
Moving from one dream to another by the hundreds and thousands,
though abandoning them, who could abandon their own clear and radiant essential nature?
Just as the trunk of a plantain tree consists of nothing but layers upon layers, so too,
when one goes deeper and deeper within, that very same atom is found to be likewise.
For whom, without abandoning their atomicity, could the Brahma-egg, space, the flood of elements, the solar orb, and Mount Meru be mere atoms?
Within the solid, single interior of a mountain as vast as an atom— which is itself partless— the marrow of the three worlds exists.
If you speak thus to me, O evil-souled one, then I shall swallow you here, O self-destroyer,
and having approached you by force, I shall devour your entire circle like a fruit, just as the God of Death devours the world.
The seventy-fifth canto, titled "The Question of the Vetāla," by Vasiṣṭha.
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, the king, his face brightened by the luster of his teeth, smiled and spoke these words to answer the questions.
The King said:
"This universe is a peppercorn fruit whose essence is consciousness,
enveloped by successive layers of elemental skins that have come into being."
Indeed, there exists a lofty, vast branch with trembling foliage, upon which there are thousands of such fruits.
Furthermore, there exists such a great tree, vast in form and difficult to perceive, in which there are thousands of such branches.
Where there exist thousands of such trees,
there is a lofty forest with infinite trees and shrubs.
Furthermore, where there are thousands of such forests,
there stands a great peak, exceedingly high and of massive form.
Furthermore, there exists a great mountain such that it possesses thousands of peaks like those, filling the entire expanse of the quarters.
Furthermore, where there are thousands of such mountains,
there exists a vast region with extensive caverns.
Furthermore, there exists a vast continent surrounded by great lakes and rivers, wherein there are thousands of such regions.
Furthermore, where there exist thousands of such islands,
there is likewise a surface of the earth endowed with various wonderful arrangements.
Furthermore, where there exist thousands of such worlds,
there exists such a vast universe, a great cage of worlds.
Furthermore, there exists a great cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) like a seat of fierce splendor, wherein there are thousands of such worlds.
There exists a vast ocean with such waves of thousands of cosmic eggs, possessing such incessant motion.
There exists a great ocean, pure and whose essence is its own play, wherein even a wave is as delicate as the mere appearance of such an ocean.
Suppose there were some man of such exceedingly tall stature that the waters of thousands of oceans filled his belly.
There is another man who is the foremost among all beings, upon whose chest a garland made of hundreds of thousands of such men rests.
Thousands of such great-souled persons flash forth within his mandala like the network of hairs on his own body.
Such is that Great Sun who shines within these perceptions;
all these mental constructs are but its own radiance.
To this sun, the entire universe is like a mote of dust in its rays;
he is called the Sun of Consciousness, and he illumines all this.
This supreme sun, whose nature is consciousness, is the illuminator of all that is to be; these expansive worlds are but its motes of light.
By the radiance of the supreme sun that is consciousness, these splendors of day for the world come into being and shine forth, just as the splendors of day belong to the sun.

Since the multitude of living beings consists of a self that is nothing but consciousness, and since the assembly of the three worlds is a pavilion in full bloom, there are here no traces whatsoever of the agitation caused by sinking or emerging; therefore, remain peaceful.
The seventy-sixth canto, titled "The Description of Paramamahāmārtāṇḍa," Canto LXVII.
The King:
The existence of time, the existence of space, the existence of motion,
and the existence of pure consciousness— all these and so forth are purifying.
In the great wind of the supreme Self, the quality of passion (rajas) flickers restlessly; like fragrance within a flower, it is by its very nature both identical with and distinct from that [Self].
In this great dream called the world, one passes from one dream to another;
yet Brahman, which is augmented by its own tranquility, does not abandon its peaceful form.
This [consciousness], which is infinite radiance by its very nature, is nourished by its own volitions;
in whatever manner it is nourished by those acts of nourishing, it expands accordingly.
And volition does not differ even slightly from that Supreme; because it consists of consciousness, there is therefore neither anything to be expanded nor anything that expands.
Just as a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers within layers,
so too this entire universe, when transformed, is indeed Brahman.
That which is denoted by these words such as "Brahman," "Self," and so forth, is the void that is indefinable; it is neither nothingness nor something.
Whatever existence is conceptualized is constructed by experience;
therefore, like the trunk of a plantain tree, that which is spread forth is pure consciousness alone.
Because of its subtlety and because it is unattainable, the Supreme Self is the supreme atom;
yet, because of its infinity, that very same Self is said to possess the dust of Mount Meru and all other things.

Even before this [Self], which is subtler than the subtle and infinitely greater than the great, even the beginning of the world appears like an atom, because it is an object of cognition and thus lacks true form.
This person is an atom because he cannot be grasped; he is a great mountain because he fills [all space]; though consisting of all limbs, the person is devoid of limbs.
The three worlds are merely the marrow of this representation-only;
O virtuous one, know that the three worlds are indeed the very center of consciousness-only.
The worlds are mere consciousness, ungrasped by parts, peaceful, naturally delicate, and of infinite form;
that state is like a child’s play with a ghost—indeed, it is not to be transgressed. Thus, O one free from pride, experience this and remain in peace.
The seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Resolution of the Vetāla’s Questions," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having heard this from the mouth of the king, the Vetāla attained peace through his purified nature and through the wisdom arising from reflection upon that matter.
Having become serene in body and having gone to a solitary place,
the blameless one became absorbed in unwavering meditation, forgetting his agonizing hunger.
This web of questions from the Vetāla has been told to you by me, O Rāma;
in this manner, this entire world is situated within the atom of consciousness alone.
The entire universe, which resides within the sheath of the atom of consciousness, dissolves through inquiry;
that which remains is the Supreme, like the anger of a Vetāla [dissolving] upon its master.
Withdrawing the mind from all directions with a tranquil inner self,
making it fall into a continuous flow, remain free of desire with a peaceful intellect.
Having made the mind itself as clear as space, the sage should remain with a single, tranquil, and peaceful self, his disposition as pure as the sky.
For a king of steady intellect, free from delusion, who follows what has been attained, even that which is difficult to accomplish is achieved— just like King Bhagīratha.
For one whose mind is completely tranquil, whose conduct is fully satisfied, and who always abides within the Self— which is perfectly equanimous— the desired goals,
even those most difficult to attain, are accomplished, just as the ocean was for the great-grandson of Sagara at the descent of the Gaṅgā.
The chapter titled "The Narrative of the Vetāla. The narrative of the Vetāla is concluded.
This is the seventy-eighth chapter.
Rāma:
O Lord, tell me how King Bhagīratha’s descent of the Gaṅgā was accomplished through the wonder of his mind.
Vasiṣṭha said:
There was a king named Bhagīratha, supremely righteous,
who was like an exquisite tilaka ornament upon the earth consisting of its oceans and islands.
Immediately after their resolve, those seekers obtained whatever they desired from him,
whose face was as serene as the moon, as if from a wish-fulfilling gem.
He who constantly gave away wealth for the sake of establishing the righteous takes back only as much as a blade of grass, like a "grass-gem" (tṛṇamaṇi).
Just as an iron gem pierces an iron machine even when not glowing, so did he shatter even that which was strung with the essence of diamond— such is the conduct of the wicked.
For he was smokeless yet burning, cool yet capable of removing the hardness of men's hearts;
he dispelled the darkness of people like a jewel dispels the night-darkness within houses.
Scattering a shower of sparks born from his own prowess in all directions,
he blazes against his enemies like the fire produced by a sun-gem at midday.
With a soft, cool, and pleasant touch that gladdens the earth,
he flows with affection toward his own kin, like a moonstone melting at the sight of the moon.
By him, the third strand of the Ganges’ current— serving as the sacred thread for the world and flowing through both heaven and the netherworld— was replenished upon the earth.
The ocean, which had been dried up by Agastya, was filled again by the flood of the Gaṅgā—
just as a great caravan of supplicants, though difficult to satisfy, is replenished.
By him, the friend of the world, those who dwell in the netherworld were joined with the realm of Brahmā by means of a flight of stairs made from the Ganges.
Worshipping Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu through ascetic penance,
he experienced weariness again and again, yet never like one whose resolve has been shattered.
Then, while that lord of the earth was still in his youth,
he reflected upon this worldly course of life which is so full of turmoil.
By chance, even in his youth, there arose within his mind a tiny spark of reflection on the wonder of self-detachment, like a creeper in a desert.
Then that lord of the earth reflected in solitude upon this course of the world, which is perpetually crowded with contradictions.
Again there is day, again night; again the taking and giving of food, yet that very same food is tasteless and sour—how shameful it is for one performing such actions!
I consider that to be well-done by which, once attained in this world, nothing remains unattained; everything else is merely a cholera-like affliction of karma.
One of deluded intellect performs an action again and again even when it has become stale and does not feel shame; but who indeed, being undeluded, would act like a child?
Then once, his mind agitated and fearing the cycle of worldly existence, Bhagīratha questioned his teacher Tryuttala in private.
Bhagīratha: O Lord,
having wandered for a very long time within the worldly conditions that are empty at their core—
like wandering through vast wildernesses— we are utterly exhausted.
O Blessed One, how does the end come about for all sufferings— those which take the form of old age, death, delusion, and so forth, and which produce existence?
O King, [the soul] is three-foldly lightened by the full awakening of what is to be known— a state that is pure through long-standing equanimity, delighting in the indivisible, and filling the self.
All sufferings perish, all knots are completely severed,
all doubts come to rest, and all actions are dissolved, O sinless one.
The wise know the Knowable to be the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness;
it is omnipresent and eternal, neither setting nor rising.
Bhagīratha said:
"O Lord of Sages, I know that there exists only pure consciousness—omnipresent, peaceful, stainless, and immutable; that nothing other than this, such as the body and so forth, exists."
But in this matter, my comprehension does not become clearer;
O Blessed One, how might I possess even this much realization?
The Tryuttula:
Through knowledge, the mind within the heart attains absorption in the object of knowledge;
then, having become the universal body, the living being is no longer born again.
Non-attachment and absence of possessiveness toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
The constant cultivation of the true being through non-dual yoga with the Self,
dwelling in solitary places, and a distaste for the assembly of people.
Devotion to the knowledge of the inner self and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge; that which is otherwise is ignorance.
O King, through the aspect of the destruction of passion and hatred, which is the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra,
knowledge is attained when the sense of "I" has been stilled.
Bhagīratha said:
"The great-scaled egoism, which has long been rooted in this body like a tall tree upon a mountain— tell me, how is it to be abandoned?"
The *tryuttula*:
Having abandoned the cultivation of the flood of enjoyments through manly effort,
and having gone and searched with the intellect for the reality, the ego-sense dissolves.
As long as the cage of the [mental] instruments— including shame and all the rest— is not shattered,
so long does egoism remain manifest, with nothingness as its only residue.
If you remain motionless, having abandoned all mental constructs,
then you yourself, with the dissolution of the ego, are the supreme state.

With all distinctions stilled, free from fear, and having abandoned all desires, you have surely attained a state of nothingness; having given up your entire fortune to your enemies, with pride extinguished and the perception of a body vanished, you wander for alms among those very same people and have even forsaken me—if you are truly exalted, then you are indeed most highly exalted.
The seventy-ninth canto, titled "The Instruction of Bhagīratha," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, having heard this from the mouth of his guru, Bhagīratha,
having resolved upon what must be done in his mind, became intent on his own task.
Then, after only a few days had passed,
he performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for the sole purpose of attaining perfection through total renunciation.
Discerning between the virtuous and the non-virtuous, he gave away his entire wealth— cows, land, horses, gold, and so forth— to the twice-born, the gods, the afflicted, and his kinsmen.
Abandoning everything in this manner within merely three days,
King Bhagīratha was left with nothing remaining but his own clothes.
Then, having become devoid of all resources and seeing his subjects and citizens exhausted, he gave away his own kingdom to a neighboring enemy like a blade of grass.
When his kingdom, city, palace, and realm were seized by his enemy,
he departed from his own domain with nothing remaining but his lower garment.
In those villages or forests where he was not known by name, nor recognized by his face, there the steadfast one dwelt in distant places.
Thus, in a very short time, having stilled all desires,
he attained rest within himself through supreme tranquility.
While wandering through the islands upon the surface of the earth, he once, by the turn of time,
reached that very city which had been seized by his enemy king.
There, remaining composed, he begged for alms from those very enemies, as well as from the citizens and the ministers, following the sequence as it presented itself like a flowing stream.
Then his enemies, the citizens, and the ministers, perceiving [his intent], honored Bhagīratha with reverence, though they were filled with despondency.

Although entreated by his enemy with the words, "O Lord, accept the kingdom," the sage did not accept it, being indifferent to everything except for food, which he regarded as no more than a blade of grass.
Having spent a few days there, he departed for another place;
Bhagīratha was lamented by the people, crying, "Alas, what misery!"
Then, his self pacified elsewhere, his intellect fully rested, and happy,
delighting in the Self, he once encountered the teacher Tryuttula.
Having offered his own hospitality to him, Bhagīratha dwelt with him for some time on the mountain, in the forest, in the village, in the city, and among the people.
Having attained equanimity, those two—the teacher and the disciple—stood as equals; established in themselves, they regarded the maintenance of the body as a mere diversion.
Why is this body maintained? What is gained for us by abandoning it?
Let it remain as it is, according to its natural state, following its proper sequence and conduct.
Having thus resolved, as they remained traveling from forest to forest,
those two felt neither joy nor sorrow, neither pleasure nor anything intermediate.
Wealth, women, riches, and the eightfold sovereignty—
even when offered by the Siddhas out of satisfaction— they considered it as worthless as withered grass.
Thinking, "This body must be maintained by one's own karma alone until its end,
even against one's will," they then remained there by means of their own karma.

The two supreme sages, who were by nature equanimous, equal toward all, like the sky, and self-restrained, welcomed his arrival; for they were indifferent to both pleasure and pain, being free from desire for what is sought.
The eightieth canto, named "The Liberation of Bhagīratha," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then once, in a certain district within a preeminent city,
death carried off a childless king like his own prey.
