There, the subjects, exhausted and having lost their sense of order, sought out a king endowed with vast excellence and glory.
Having approached Bhagīratha, who was staying in the city subsisting on alms,
they recognized him, brought him back, and made him their sovereign with their army.
In an instant, Bhagīratha was suddenly mounted upon an elephant by his heavy army, which covered him with dust like a lake filled with water during the rainy season.
The great caves of the lords of mountains became completely filled with the dense roar of "Victory to Bhagīratha, the Lord of the World! as it resounded.

While that king was protecting the kingdom there, the original subjects, having become respectful toward him, approached him whose former lords had died and spoke thus: *Note: The term *mṛtādhipāḥ* (literally "those whose lords have died") implies that the previous rulers had passed away, leaving a power vacuum which the new king filled.*
The subjects said: "O King, he who was formerly made our sovereign by you has been swallowed up by death, like soft meat by a fish."
Therefore, you ought to show favor by protecting this kingdom;
for it is not proper to abandon wealth that has come to one unasked.
Vasiṣṭha: Thus entreated, the king accepted those words and became the lord of the earth, which bears the marks of all the oceans.
Equanimous, with a tranquil mind, silent, free from passion and envy,
devoted solely to performing what ought to be done, he was filled with wonder.
He heard that the water of the Gaṅgā is capable of delivering his ancestors, who had perished in the depths of Pātāla and had once been like the ocean itself.
At that time, it is said, the celestial river did not flow upon the earth;
therefore, the offering of a handful of Gaṅgā water became difficult for the ancestors to obtain.
Then, in order to bring the Gaṅgā down from heaven to the earth, King Bhagīratha undertook a vow of ascetic discipline; from that time forward, he remained steadfast.
Then, having renounced the kingdom, the peaceful king, whose desire for action had ceased, went to the deep forest for the sake of asceticism along with his ministers.
There, having propitiated Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu again and again for thousands of years, he brought the Gaṅgā down to the earth.

From that time forth, the three-pathed river, possessing waves of exceeding purity and clinging to the moon-bright body of the Lord of the World, falls from the vault of heaven to the earth like the continuous stream of great merit belonging to noble souls.
With its shimmering waves, laughing with its masses of foam, and possessing clusters of blossoms of serene merit, that river— like the flow of dharma in motion—
became known on the surface of the earth as the *Trimārgagā* (the Three-pathed) from that time onwards, serving as the thoroughfare for the spread of King Bhagīratha’s fame.
The eighty-first canto, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," by Vasiṣṭha.
Adopting this view, which was chosen by Bhagīratha, remain equanimous and composed; with a tranquil mind, accomplish whatever task arises as it may.
Having first abandoned this [world] and then having embraced it yourself,
remain as one who is peaceful within the self, immovable like Śikhidhvaja.
Rāma said:
Who was this one named Śikhidhvaja, and how did he attain that state?
O Brahmin, tell me this further for the sake of increasing my awakening.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"In the Dvāpara age you two were previously such, and now you shall be so again; by that very same disposition, you shall be a husband and wife, affectionate and noble."
Rāma said: "O Blessed One, that which existed previously is indeed exactly as it will be now;
for what purpose is this? Tell me, O best among speakers."
Vasiṣṭha: Such is the eternal and unavoidable state of this self-awareness of Brahmā, born of its own nature, which constitutes the law of the creation of the world.
That which, having become manifold, becomes abundant once again;
that which, having not existed at all, comes into being, and then no longer exists sufficiently—this is another [state].
One [cognition] manifests clearly through similarity with a prior configuration;
another flashes forth through partial similarity with a prior configuration.
Just as waves in a lake are both similar and dissimilar,
so too are the various states of existence seen in saṃsāra— both the same and yet different.
Therefore, O Raghava, that lord of men, possessed of great splendor, shall yet again be spoken of; hear this account of his.
In the past, during the seventh Manu who has passed away,
in this fourth cycle of four ages (caturyuga) within this creation crowded with elephants, it occurred in the Dvāpara age.
In Jambudvīpa, not far from the Vindhya mountains,
there was a glorious lord named Śikhidhvaja in the city of the Mālavas.
Endowed with fortitude, magnanimity, and compassion, possessed of patience, tranquility, and self-control,
he was a hero of auspicious conduct, honorable, and a mine of manifold virtues.
He is the performer of all sacrifices, the conqueror of all archers,
the accomplisher of all tasks, and the sustainer of the earth with his unprecedented form.
He was gentle, affectionate and sweet, clever, pleasing to refined people, handsome, blessed with virtuous character, majestic, and devoted to the Dharma.
He is the knower who understands all meanings, the giver of all prosperity,
the enjoyer free from attachment, and the excellent listener of all that is heard.
Disregarding floods of enjoyments and casting aside women like blades of grass, he—
while still a child— ascended to heaven through his supreme splendor when his father had passed away.
Having reached the age of sixteen and having conquered the quarters,
that self-controlled one surely united the circle of the earth with the perfection of righteous sovereignty.
Free from apprehension, the wise king remained protecting his subjects according to dharma, while together with his ministers he whitened the quarters of the sky with his glory.
Then, as the years passed, when spring was in full bloom,
while the flowers were unfolding and the moonbeams were shimmering, [he went forth].
In the inner apartments of the branches, upon swings formed by clusters of flower-buds,
where the pollen was white as camphor and the moving petals served as door-panels.
In that fragrant place, where canopies of shimmering flower clusters hung above,
pairs of bees sang loudly together in the dense thickets.
When the sweet breeze, cool as the rays of the moon, arrives, gliding over the groves of plantain and *kandalī* trees and the tender foliage of the marshy banks;
His heart became newly eager for his beloved,
as if intoxicated by the sweet liquors fragrant with the abundance of flowers.
Nourished by the intoxication of spring, he indulged in this kingdom of his imagination within the garden groves,
upon the swings, and amidst the playful lotus ponds.
When shall I place upon my lap, on the couch, my beloved and charming young woman, whose breasts are like the buds of a lotus and who is adorned with flowers?
When shall I, like a bee among lotus creepers, lead this young girl— who clings to my vine-like arms— to freedom from her trembling, as a bee leads its mate upon the swings?
When will Indusundarī, tormented by love on my account, desire a bed made of lotus stalks, jasmine garlands, and clusters of moons?
Thus becoming absorbed in thought and intent upon gathering flowers,
he wandered through the forest edges and among the flowery groves.
Upon the swings in the groves and gardens, amidst the playful lotus ponds,
within the bowers of creeping vines, and throughout the various grounds of the pleasure-groves.
And his mind was entirely absorbed in stories filled with the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), which were interspersed with descriptions of the arrangement of forests and groves.
He worshipped young maidens whose creeper-like tresses were tossed by breath shimmering with enchanting smiles, and whose breasts resembled golden jars.
Thus do wise ministers understand his new resolve;
for the ability to discern intentions from outward appearance is the supreme qualification for the office of a minister.
Then, for his marriage, the deliberative circle of ministers requested the daughter of the lord of Surāṣṭra, who was endowed with youth.
He married her, who was endowed with beauty and youth, as his most excellent wife according to the prescribed rites— a woman who was like a very image of himself.
Known on earth by the name Cūḍālā, that beautiful queen shone like a blossoming lotus upon finding him as her husband.
Out of affection, Śikhidhvaja caused Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like blue lotuses, to bloom with beauty, just as the sun causes a lotus pond to blossom.
The affection between those two, whose hearts were offered to one another, grew like a young creeper nourished by the sprinklings of gestures, expressions, and amorous charms.
Having entrusted all affairs to his ministers, he was exceedingly happy, with his subjects well-established;
like a royal swan upon a lotus pond, he took delight with that beloved wife.
In the inner apartments, upon swings, in avenues of sandalwood and aloe-wood, on swings draped with garlands of *mandāra* flowers, and amidst plantain and *kandalī* trees;
In the outskirts of cities, at the edges of forests, at the ends of the quarters, and by the lakes;
in the jungles, at the close of day, and among the *jambu*, *jambīra*, and *śāli* trees.
Every mutual gesture of theirs was a source of delight,
like the union of heaven and earth through the rain of the clouds and the performance of sacrifices.
Because they were constantly inseparable and because of their mutual fondness for artistic performance, those two became experts in the entire range of the arts.
These two, having attained a state of union, assumed a single essential nature;
it was as if their respective forms had been transferred to one another, remaining intact because each dwelt within the heart of the other.

Like children taking toys from a chest, she received from the mouth of her lord proficiency in all the sciences and other arts, as well as painting and the like; thus she became learned in every subject.
From the mouth of Cūḍālā, he learned dancing, instrumental music, singing, and so forth;
thereafter, he became exceedingly proficient in all the arts.
In the Kali age, like the moon and the sun at the new moon,
those two, dwelling within each other's hearts, shone together as if they had attained oneness.
The two of them remained together, of one essence and devoted to no other;
they were inseparable like a flower and its fragrance, like two Śivas dwelling upon the earth.
Possessing intellects beautiful with wit and proficient in the meaning of all scriptures,
they were like Kamalā and Kamalādhava who had descended to earth as if in play.
Out of affection, they remained gracious and gentle, possessing equal knowledge and wisdom; devoted to following one another's lead, they were both conversant with the ways of the world.
Endowed with the full complement of artistic skills, possessing the essence of shimmering elixirs,
their limbs were cool, smooth, and charming, like two risen moons.

He abandoned that couple of unsurpassed splendor, who were as lovely as the enjoyments and pleasures of a king, moving slowly with the intoxication of passion within the inner apartments like a pair of royal swans in the hollows of a lotus thicket in Brahma’s world.
The eighty-second canto, titled "The Play of Śikhidhvaja," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, for many years, the couple, filled with intense longing,
took delight day after day in the endless sports of youth.
Then, after many years had passed in their recurrence,
youth gradually ebbed away like water from a broken jar.
Like an autumn leaf, the heart of this couple, through the passage of time, touched a state of complete detachment with a slight fading of passion.
Overcome by the latent impression of dispassion and standing in solitude, he reflected upon that couple and this impermanent course of the world in such a manner.
What indeed is truly captivating here in this wandering through the cavern of saṃsāra, where worldly affairs are as fragile as a multitude of ripples?
Death is as unavoidable as the falling of a ripe fruit; old age stands ready to strike down like a frost-bolt upon a lotus.
Life flows away incessantly like water from the palm of the hand;
while life is like a gourd-vine in the rainy season, craving alone has grown long.
Youth passes away like the current of a mountain river;
life is as unreal as a magician’s illusion, its duration lasting but a moment.
Pleasures flee away like arrows shot from a bowstring;
miseries fall upon the mind boldly, like vultures pouncing on raw meat.
The body is as fragile as a bubble in the water during the rainy season;
worldly activity is as pithless as the core of a plantain tree, bringing about detachment.
Youth has quickly departed like a beloved who desires what is unloved;
discontent has come by force, like saplessness to a tree.
In this wretched cycle of existence, what indeed could there be that is truly auspicious,
by attaining which the mind is no longer tormented amidst the various conditions of life?
Having thus resolved upon that pair as the medicine for the disease of worldly existence,
he reflected for a long time upon the spiritual scripture esteemed by the wise.
Having resolved that the cholera of what is called worldly existence is pacified solely by the mantra of self-knowledge, let those two remain devoted to that alone.

Their minds were fixed on him, their lives were centered on him, their talk was of him, and they took refuge in those who knew him; devoted solely to his worship, they became intent upon his activities.
In that very place, intensely practicing together and awakening one another,
they remained for a long time, filled with mutual affection and engaged in those same undertakings.

Then that young woman, having heard from the mouths of those who know the inner self the words of the scriptures— words of beautiful phrasing and capable of delivering one across [the ocean of existence]— was never satiated.
Thus she reflected upon herself day and night,
whether inactive or active, with a mind that was pure in its inner disposition.
Let me first examine myself: "What might this be?
Of whom is this delusion of the world, how has it arisen, and where?
The body is indeed inert and mute; the certainty that "I am not this" is well-established even among children, and it is experienced at the time of death as well.
Furthermore, its group of organs of action is not distinct from it as a composite whole;
because there is no difference between the part and the whole, it is indeed insentient.
In this same way, the group of sense organs is seen to be entirely insentient,
since it is impelled by the mind, just as a clod of earth on the ground is driven by a staff.
I consider the mind itself to be inert, possessing the power of volition; it is impelled by the determinations of the intellect, just as a stone is propelled by slingshots.
Thus, the certainty that the intellect is of the nature of determination alone, and that it is insentient and non-existent,
is carried along at its own will by the ego-sense, like a river by a channel.
The ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is likewise devoid of substance and purely inert; it is like a corpse, yet it is produced by the living soul, just as a delusive phantom is created by a child.
And the individual soul (jīva), whose form is conceptualization and whose nature is wind, resides in the heart;
it lives within by means of some other essence of semen (śukrasāra).
Ah, now it is understood by this [intellect] stained by the conceptualization of "this" and "that":
the living being lives through the *jīva*, which is of the nature of consciousness and has the form of the Self.
The individual soul, though possessing the delusion of being an object of thought, lives by its very nature as consciousness,
just as fragrance exists in the wind or the current of a river in the sky.
By taking recourse in unreal, insentient, and objective aspects, the body of consciousness becomes insentient;
for even fire, when entering a great mass of wood, abandons its own form.
Whether it be real or unreal, whatever appears, consciousness itself consumes it;
casting off its own form, it becomes that very thing in an instant.

In this way, although its nature is consciousness, this very [consciousness], by being oriented toward an object of thought, itself becomes insentient, void, and devoid of volition; it perceives only when awakened by another.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā thought, "By what means does this consciousness perceive? After reflecting for a long time, she understood it in this way.
Ah! After a long time, that which is to be known has been known as the state free from affliction—that which, once realized through the mind, causes no further suffering whatsoever.
For these—the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth—though ultimately nothing but the play of consciousness, appear as if they were real; alas, they abide like a second moon.
In this world, there exists only one Great Consciousness, which is called the "Great Being";
it is stainless, equal, pure, and characterized by the absence of ego.
It exists as the form of pure consciousness, auspicious, pure awareness alone, undecaying,
once-manifested, stainless, and eternally risen.
That which is designated by names such as "Being," "Brahman," and "Supreme Self"—the objects of cognition, the insentient, and the mind—is not different from Her; nor is She separate from them.
By her this Śrī-consciousness is perceived; she is the primordial consciousness, known as "Cid.
This state of consciousness, which is itself unperceivable, is her undiminished form.
In this way, it manifests within itself through the forms of the mind, intellect, senses, and their objects, just as water does through the movements of ripples, droplets, and waves.
The existence of all beings and objects in the world manifests within it;
that which is this [world] is indeed the supreme form of that Great Consciousness.
This very Great Lioness of pure consciousness has arisen in perfect equilibrium; she abides through the unfolding of the world, which is both non-different and yet as if different from her.
For here, existence cannot possibly exist as something other than that [Being],
just as various golden ornaments are not indeed anything other than gold.
Just as it arises, it perceives itself in that form by its own nature,
through its own consciousness and fluidity, like the state of waves and so forth in water.
Because the great consciousness is the thinking of the world, it arises as if it were arising, though it is without arising;
it is of that very nature, just as a whirlpool with form arises from the fluidity of the ocean.
Thus, I am indeed pure consciousness alone, expanded and devoid of the sense of "I";
for such a one, there is neither birth nor death, nor do the states of existence and non-existence exist.
The destruction of this sky of pure consciousness is never possible;
this conscious self is indivisible, unburnable, and eternally stainless.
Ah! After such a long time, I have become peaceful and fully extinguished;
with my mind exiled from worldly thoughts, I sit liberated like the ocean when Mount Mandara has been removed.
Resting upon the space of the Self— which appears as non-existent, utterly transparent, infinite, unborn, and immutable— I rejoice for a long time, free from effort.
This space is infinite, as are the multitude of beings beginning with the mountains;
this entire universe, including the gods and demons, is composed of that and is uncreated.
Just as an entire army made of books is nothing but clay,
so too the existence of the seer, the seen, and the seeing consists solely of pure consciousness.
"This is unity, this is duality, 'I,' and 'not-I'—what delusion and confusion is this? How, whose, from where, or where could it be?"
Therefore, I am infinite and effortless, established in the tranquil void;
having attained final nirvana, I am extinguished and abide in truth, free from all fever.
Whether it be insentient or sentient, whatever one conceives of by name, its form consists of mere existence; it is established within the Great Consciousness as its own self.
Therefore, here there is neither I nor another, nor the occurrence of existence or non-existence;
everything is peaceful, without support, and established as the absolute alone.
Thus, intent on inquiry, she realized this reality of the Supreme Self as it truly exists through supreme awakening;
with the playful movements of passion, fear, and delusion stilled in her mind, she became tranquil like a streak of cloud in an autumn sky.
The eighty-third canto, titled "The Awakening of Cūḍālā," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, day after day, by virtue of that delight in her own self and her constant inward orientation,
she became established in her natural state.
Free from passion, free from disease, free from attachment, free from dualities, and free from desire,
she neither abandons nor grasps, moving according to her natural conduct.
Having crossed over the ocean of existence, with the web of doubts stilled,
their inner being is completely filled with the supreme attainment of the Great Self.
Having rested for a very long time, weary from its long journey, it found its footing within the Self;
and because it transcends all comparison, it entered into a state beyond description.
Thus, in a very short time, that queen Cūḍālā, of excellent complexion, attained the state of one who has known all that is to be known.
She shone forth as one who had understood how this world has come into being as some kind of delusive vibration of consciousness, and how everything dissolves again.
Having attained rest in that state where all delusion is no longer seen,
she shone, free from agitation, like a streak of autumn cloud that has become clear.
With an unconfused gaze, she remained within herself, breathing deeply,
like an old bull standing upon a mountain peak covered with grass.
By the power of her intense practice of self-discrimination and through the awakening of the Self,
that beautiful woman shone like a splendid flowering creeper newly emerged.
Then, on one occasion, having beheld that woman of faultless limbs and unprecedented beauty, Śikhidhvaja spoke with a smile:
O slender one, you shine all the more like one endowed with renewed youth, adorned again and again,
as if you were the sovereign lady of the world.
O beloved, you shine most intensely, as if filled with the essence of nectar, as if having attained a state that is difficult to reach,
and as if overflowing with a flood of bliss.
Bearing a beautiful body that was both tranquil and lovely, you approach, O passionate one,
surpassing the moon with an indescribable splendor.
O beloved, I behold your mind as free from worldly attachment yet compassionate, tranquil yet powerful, attained to equanimity, profound, and serene.
O beloved, I behold your mind as something that treats the three worlds as mere straw, which has swallowed up the entirety of the triple universe, infinitely radiant, and serene.
O highly fortunate one, no object of worldly prosperity or pleasure can equal your mind, which is as beautiful as Mount Meru or the Ocean of Milk.
With those very limbs, as tender as the sprouts of a young plantain tree or a lotus stalk, you appear to have attained growth even while remaining stationary.
Thus, though remaining in that very same position and configuration,
you have undergone a transformation like a creeper at the change of seasons.
Have you drunk the nectar of immortality, or have you attained universal sovereignty? Or have you achieved the practice for the sake of deathlessness through the methods of yoga?
O lady with eyes like blue lotuses, what unattainable thing have you obtained that is superior to sovereignty, or even the wish-fulfilling gem, or the three worlds?
Cūḍālā said:
"Having abandoned this form of 'nothing-at-all,' I have come;
because [I have realized] the form of 'nothing-at-all,' I remain as the Illustrious One."
Whatever exists and whatever does not exist, I know that as it truly is—how it arises and how it perishes; by this, I abide in glory.
I am content with enjoyments that remain unenjoyed, as if they were already consumed and far away; I neither rejoice nor am I provoked to anger, and by that means I abide in prosperity.
I delight in the one, solitary heart that resembles space;
I do not delight in royal pastimes, and for that reason I remain possessed of glory.
For I abide in the Self alone, not in forests, gardens, or palaces;
nor do I dwell amidst the floods of enjoyments or upon couches; therefore, I remain established in glory.
"I am indeed the sovereign of the worlds, yet I exist in the form of nothing at all;
thus I abide in the Self alone, and for that reason I am established as Śrīmatī."
I am indeed other than this, yet I am not other than this; or rather, I am both this and that.
I am everything, or I am nothing at all; therefore, I abide as the Illustrious One.
"That which I see, I do not see; that which I see is something else entirely"—thus I perceive correctly, and by that I abide in glory.
I do not long for pleasure, nor wealth, nor misfortune, nor any other state;
I am content with whatever comes to me, and by that I abide in prosperity.
Accompanied by those female companions who possess slender aversion and passion and who understand the perspectives of the scriptures, I take delight; therefore, I remain possessed of splendor.
O Lord, whatever I see here with the rays of my eyes, or with the sense-faculties, or with the mind, that is indeed nothing at all;
but when devoid of those, I see that which appears as nothingness, and thus I see correctly—this has been long dawning upon me.
The eighty-fourth canto, titled "The Attainment of Cūḍālā's Self," by Vasiṣṭha.
To that fair-faced woman who was speaking thus, resting her mind within the Self, he said slowly, "You are a child; you are one whose talk is incoherent."
Suspecting his beloved to be deluded by a mind greedy for enjoyments,
and failing to understand the meaning of her words, the king laughed and said:
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O fair-complexioned one, you are a girl who utters incoherent prattle;
you delight in the play of words, so delight in them, O daughter of a king!"
How indeed can he shine, who, having abandoned something, has gone to a state of "nothingness" that is directly present,
and who has thus renounced the truly existent nature of direct perception?

How indeed can he appear dignified who renounces enjoyments while saying, "I am satisfied even with enjoyments not yet consumed," as if he were rejecting food, drink, and other necessities out of anger?
How indeed can he who, having abandoned everything— vehicles, food, beds, and so forth— remains alone by himself, appear beautiful, O man of steady intellect?
How indeed can that person of evil intellect shine, who possesses the conviction: "I myself am nothing at all, yet I am the Lord of the World"?
How indeed can he who remains alone with himself in solitude, having abandoned all social associations,
appear beautiful, like one dwelling in a pit?
"I am not the body; I am something else; I am nothing at all; indeed, I am everything"—how indeed can he who utters such rambling talk appear beautiful?
How indeed can he who says, "That which I see I do not see; I see something quite different," shine, when such talk is merely empty chatter?
Therefore, you are bewildered, you are a child, and you are fickle, O playful one;
you sport with various conversations and charms—sport on, O beautiful lady!
Laughing aloud with a boisterous laugh at his beloved, saying "Śikhidhvaja," he rose to bathe at midday and departed from the women's quarters.
"Alas! He did not find rest within himself and did not understand my words;
he is but a king," Cūḍālā thought, distressed by the failure of her own efforts.
Then, my dear friend, as those two shared such dispositions,
that day passed for them amidst those royal pastimes.
Gradually, O Rāma, many months, seasons,
and years passed there for that affectionate couple.
Once, although she was eternally satisfied and free from desire, Cūḍālā herself felt a longing for the playful act of traveling through the air.
Then, for the sake of attaining the power of moving through the sky, that princess disregarded all enjoyments and went to a secluded place.
Delighting in solitude alone, with her limbs settled in her own posture,
she practiced for a long time the upward movement of the vital breath.
Rāma:
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, is experienced as the fruit of vibration, which is known by the name "action."
Tell me, O Brahmin, what playful movement and what intense practice of mine— characterized by singular effort— is this fruit, namely, the traveling through the sky and so forth?
O Lord, tell me truly how one— whether knowing the Self or not knowing the Self— accomplishes this for the sake of perfection, as if in play.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O dear Rāghava, in this world, every object to be accomplished arises in three ways: as something to be accepted, as something to be rejected, and likewise as something to be disregarded."
That which is beneficial to oneself should indeed be diligently adopted;
that which is to be abandoned is discarded once known; and that which is neutral between these two is disregarded.

Whatever is pleasing and acceptable to one of right-mindedness is considered unacceptable and to be disregarded by one of wrong-mindedness; that which is neutral between these two is known as the middle path.
When everything for the wise, learned sage consists of the Self,
then only three sides are possible, none other.
Perhaps all this is merely a play, or perhaps not;
he either looks upon it with indifference as if casting a glance from his eye, or perhaps he does not.
O Rāma, that which is characterized by equanimity is to be disregarded by the wise, yet it becomes something to be accepted by the fool;
for one of expansive dispassion, it is to be abandoned. Now hear how the sequence of attainment proceeds.
All accomplishments— whether achieved through place, time, ritual action, or material substances—
delight the living being here, just as spring delights the earth.

Among these four, the practice of the first stage is for the purpose of accomplishing success (*siddhi*) and so forth; for those stages are, in sequence, identical with that [goal] for the practitioner.
The description of the sequence of rituals involving pills, collyrium, the sword, and so forth—
let that remain for now, as such elaboration here would detract from the subject at hand.
The detailed description of gems, medicinal herbs, austerities, mantras, and ritual procedures—
let that be set aside for now, as such elaboration here would detract from the subject at hand.

The claim that "perfection" arises from residing on Śrīśaila, in a land of the Siddhas, or on Mount Meru and the like, is merely an elaboration; being born of ritual action, it destroys the intended meaning.
Therefore, listen to this practice of training in the vital breaths and other winds, which yields the fruit of supernatural powers, as it arises in the context of the story of Śikhidhvaja.
Having completely abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanā) other than those concerning the goal to be accomplished, along with their very roots,
[the practitioner proceeds] by means of the sequence of actions such as the postures (sthānaka), through the contraction of the apertures beginning with the anus.

Through purity of food and seat, through contemplation on the meaning of the scriptures of the virtuous, through one's own proper conduct, through association with good people, through total renunciation, and through a comfortable posture.

O Rāma, O observer of noble vows, through the intense practice of breath control over some period of time, and by the abandonment of anger, greed, and the like, as well as the renunciation of worldly enjoyments, [the mind becomes purified].
In the acts of relinquishing, grasping, and restraining,
all the vital breaths come completely under the control of that man who knows his own sovereignty, just like servants.
O Rāghava, all prosperities, from sovereignty up to liberation, are achieved by everyone through subjugating the body and the vital breaths.
Circular in shape and situated at the location of the bulb (kanda),
the channel named Antraveṣṭanikā is supported by hundreds of channels.
It resembles the whorl at the tip of a lute, similar to a whirlpool in water;
it is established in the form of the syllable *Oṃ* of the scripts and so forth, and exists like a curl of hair.
It is declared to exist among gods, asuras, and humans; among deer, crocodiles, birds, and the like;
and among all living beings, from insects up to those born from lotuses.
Her body is coiled in a circle like the coils of the lord of serpents asleep from the cold;
her white [garment] and her bound earrings resemble the moon melting away before the fire at the end of an aeon.
Flickering within the clear waters of the channel below the aperture between the eyebrows of the mind, it remains as if constantly floating upon the streams of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Within this [body], which is as delicate as the core of a plantain tree,
there vibrates a power of wind with a radiant movement, like that within a flute.
She is called by the name Kuṇḍalinī because she flows in a coiled form;
she is the supreme power of living beings, bestowing the vitality of all powers.
Constantly sighing like an angry female serpent,
she remained with her face upturned, becoming the very cause of all throbbings.
When the vital breath enters the seat of Kuṇḍalinī in the heart,
then consciousness arises within, which is the source of the seeds of the elements and their subtle constituents.
When Kuṇḍalinī vibrates within the body like a bee upon a lotus, then consciousness arises within through the awakening brought about by the power of subtle touch.
Just as consciousness arises intensely through the touch of a soft reed upon the penis, the lingam, or the parasol, so too does Kuṇḍalinī arise with speed.
In that [space], all the interconnected channels leading to the cavity of the heart arise and dissolve like rivers into the great ocean.
Because it is eternally of the nature of wind and is ever intent on vibration,
it is declared to be the one primordial seed of all cognitions.
Rāma:
Consciousness (*cit-saṃvit*), indeed, exists as all-pervading and unconditioned by space, time, and so forth.
For what reason does its manifestation clearly arise from the sheath of Kuṇḍalinī?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, consciousness and awareness exist always and everywhere as truth;
however, its manifestation occurs in certain instances due to the influence of the elements and their subtle constituents.
Consciousness, though present everywhere, appears flickering within bodies;
though all-pervading like sunlight, it shines forth intensely within the finest jewels.
In one place a thing is destroyed, in another it is asleep, and in another it has become swollen;
whatever is thus observed as one thing within another is the manifestation of its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
O sinless one, listen further as I shall explain to you in due order how this sequence, consisting of pure consciousness, arises intensely within the very bodies.
The entire collection of elements, both conscious and unconscious, as well as the whole of space—
all this is nothing but pure consciousness, nothing but pure existence, and nothing but emptiness, just like the sky.
For that [reality] is pure consciousness and pure existence, changeless and free from affliction;
though situated in some [substratum], it has by its own consciousness alone fashioned the five subtle elements.
That pentad has attained duality, beginning with the nit (likṣā) and ending with itself, through its own consciousness;
it contains within it modifications and so forth, just as a hundred lamps arise from a single lamp.
By their mere existence, which consists of a fragment of volition,
certain groups of five here attain the state of deities.
Some [atoms] possess the state of being animals and so forth, some the state of being gold and so forth;
some possess the state of being stones and so forth, and some the state of being substances and so forth.
Thus it is established that the world is merely the vibration of the five elements; O descendant of Raghu, the consciousness of pure awareness (citsaṃvit) is present here everywhere.
It is solely by virtue of the five elements that there is the designation "consciousness" in the body and so forth,
or the designation "insentient vibration" in water, and the designation "insentient" in stationary objects and so forth.
Just as in the oceans, water exists here as a wave and there as the bottom,
so too within the five aggregates, consciousness exists here in a flickering form and there as inert matter.
Just as one who is restless might wonder, "Is this ocean here or there?",
so too is this group of five— both the insentient and the sentient— subject to such conceptualization.

O sinless one, by the power of their own nature, the fivefold group beginning with the body vibrates while living, whereas mountains and the like are inert; and stationary objects such as trees vibrate due to the wind.
Nor should the natures of things be questioned, O descendant of Raghu; for who would be ridiculed for asking why snow and fire possess coldness and heat?
For the continuities of the five [aggregates], which have grasped portions of latent impressions and undergo transformations of intensified states, are indeed fit for critical inquiry.
A wise man who skillfully investigates them can easily lead those impressions, which are distorted by their own partiality, here and there.
Whether it be regarding the impure or the pure, he is questioned by that [consciousness];
for there is nothing other than the fivefold [aggregate] with awakened latent impressions, nor one with dormant latent impressions.
One should apply that [inquiry] where the fruit of inquiry is experienced; one should not strike at the sky with one's fists.
From the tip of a blade of grass up to Mount Meru and so forth are the aggregates of the five elements;
from Viriñca down to insects and so forth are these moving and stationary beings.
Some have dormant latent impressions, such as the species of stationary beings;
some have awakened latent impressions, such as humans, gods, and so forth.
Some have the filth of their own latent impressions, such as animals and the like;
others have their latent impressions exhausted, such as these who partake in liberation.
Just as within their respective cognitions, names are constructed by means of the mind, intellect, and so forth, together with hands, feet, and the like, through the five aggregates.
Other designations have been devised by others, such as animals and the like; and perceptions have been established otherwise by others, such as stationary beings and the like.
Thus, O virtuous one, these various pentads of dispositions manifest through forms that are moving or unmoving, and sentient or insentient, in their beginning, middle, and end.

For among these, O Mahāmati, even a single atom of volitional construction (*saṅkalpa*) is the seed of the trees of space— the various creations— and within those [creations], these [phenomena] arise.
The sense faculties, my dear, are indeed the flowers that possess the fragrance of their objects; the desires are the bees, and the flickering activities are the shimmering flower-clusters.
The various worlds are its clusters, the Malaya and Meru mountains its thickets; here, the clouds are its sprouts, and the ten directions display the grace of its creepers.
O descendant of Raghu, the worlds that exist now and those that will come to be are as innumerable as the fruits [of these actions].
O Rāma, these five trees indeed have such seeds;
they arise by themselves from their own nature and perish by themselves in the course of time.
They themselves undergo diversity and, due to long-standing dullness, they manifest;
yet, when thoroughly distinguished, they come to rest like waves in the ocean.
From whence they rise to swell and from whence they subside of their own accord—
these states arise through dullness and discernment, like waves from the ocean.

O Rāma, those heaps of the play of the five [senses] who have attained dissolution through the power of discernment do not return here to worldly existence; others wander repeatedly throughout the world.
The eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Discerning the Five," by Vasiṣṭha.
This is the seed-syllable of the pentad which resides within the interior of Kuṇḍalinī;
it vibrates within her at all times in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Within her is Kuṇḍalinī, the stainless digit of consciousness consisting of vibration and touch; she is called "Kalā" because of her quickening, and "Cit" because of her awareness.
Through living it becomes the life-force (jīvana) of those who live; through thinking it abides as the mind (manas);
through volition it is itself volition (saṅkalpa); and through awareness it is known as the intellect (buddhi).
Having entered into a portion of the ego (ahaṅkāra), this very one, known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka),
abides in the body as the unsurpassed power of the individual soul (jīvaśakti) called Kuṇḍalinī.
Having reached the lower part, it flows constantly downward;
that which is situated in the middle is named Samāna, and that which is located above is called Udāna.
In a healthy man, [the breath] always remains below in the form of apāna, in the middle as soma,
and from the back as udāna.
If it goes downward despite every effort and is not held back by exertion,
then the person meets death because of that [breath] having forcefully departed.
If the entire [vital force] rises upward and is not restrained by means of yoga,
then the person meets death because it has forcefully departed.
If it should remain entirely within the self, having abandoned its upward and downward movement,
that becomes a disease for the living being due to the obstruction of the waste and the vital air.
From the impairment of the general channels, general diseases arise;
from the impairment of the principal channels, principal diseases arise.
Rāma:
O Lord of Sages, what are the causes of destruction and what are the causes of production for the mental afflictions and physical diseases in this body? Tell me quickly and exactly as they are.
Vasiṣṭha:
Mental anxieties and physical ailments—these two are the causes of suffering.
One should know that the cessation of these is happiness; their destruction is called liberation.
Sometimes mental anguish and physical disease arise in the body one after another, sometimes simultaneously, and sometimes in alternation.

They know bodily suffering to be disease, and that which is called mental anguish to consist of latent impressions; for they should understand both to have their root in ignorance, which is destroyed by the knowledge of reality.

Due to the power of ignorance regarding reality, while they incessantly diminish passion and hatred within their hearts without first bringing their own senses under control, [the mind] abandons its attenuation.
"This has been obtained, this has not"— such anxieties, which produce the dense delusion of the blindness of dullness,
arise like mist during the rainy season.
When desires throb violently because the mind has not been conquered through folly,
and by the consumption of bad food and the traversing of evil lands;
Through the conduct of a bad time, through the manifestation of evil deeds,
through the fault of association with wicked people, and through the arising of evil intentions;
Or, due to the depletion or the overfilling of the channels during the movement of the breath,
when the vital energy (prāṇa) falls into a state of distress, it is like a traveler on a new path who has entered upon a wrong road.
Due to a defect, a disease arises in the body as the cause of its instability,
just as the alteration of the river's form occurs due to the rainy season and the summer heat.
Whether it be from a previous life or this one, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whichever cognition is predominant, that very one directs him accordingly in that sequence.
In this way, mental anxieties and physical ailments arise within the five elements;
hear now, O upholder of the Raghu lineage, how they are destroyed.
For there are two kinds of pledge here: the common and the essential.
The common pledge pertains to legal transactions, while the essential is said to consist of the very nature of birth.
Worldly sufferings perish through the attainment of what is desired;
mental afflictions are destroyed by the exhaustion of their objects, and even physical diseases are thoroughly subdued.
Without the knowledge of the Self, O Raghava, the essence of the world-spirit does not perish;
indeed, it is only through the realization of the rope that the rope-snake is destroyed.
O Rāma, the destruction of the essence of all mental and physical afflictions is the eradicator of their very root, just as a river in the rainy season uproots the shrubs on its banks.
But diseases not born of mental afflictions are destroyed by means of substances, mantras, and auspicious rites—
as taught in the medical treatises and other sciences— just as heat is dispelled by clouds.
The medical treatises, along with their bathing rites, mantras, medicinal herbs, and therapeutic methods, have been mastered by you; what else remains to be taught?
Rāma said:
How does disease arise from the primary cause (ādhi), and how is it destroyed—
either by means other than [physical] substances, or through methods preceded by mantras, merit, and the like?
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the mind is disturbed, this body does not experience things correctly;
for just as a person who is enraged does not see what is right before him.
Disregarding what has been attained, he pursues the wrong path,
abandoning the natural course like a deer afflicted by an arrow.
Due to agitation, the vital breaths abandon their equilibrium and flow through the body like waters on a riverbank disturbed by a herd of elephants.
When the vital breath flows unevenly, the channels fall into disorder,
just as the order of the castes and stages of life collapses when the king is improperly situated.
Some channels reach a state of fullness while others become empty,
depending on where the vital breath (prāṇa) is displaced, just as rivers behave during all seasons.
Food that is undigested, incompletely digested, or even over-digested leads only to harm through the improper movement of the vital breaths.
Just as the current of a river carries logs to the place it has reached,
so the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) carries the food inward to its own seat.
Those very foods that remain in conflict within the body turn into diseases by the very nature of their transformation.
In this way, illness arises from poverty, and it perishes through the absence of poverty;
just as diseases are destroyed by mantras, hear now that method.
Just as myrobalan fruits cause purgation by their very nature,
so too do the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and others perform their function through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
O virtuous one, through pure and meritorious action and service to the holy,
the mind attains purity, just as gold does by means of a touchstone.
O Rāghava, when the mind is pure, bliss increases within the body,
just as clarity appears in the world when the full moon has risen in a cloudless sky.
When the sattva is purified, these vital breaths flow in due order;
likewise, they digest the foods, and by that means, disease is destroyed.
The sequences of the destruction and arising of mental and physical afflictions have been explained to you;
now, through the discourse on Kuṇḍalinī, hear that which is relevant to the present topic.
Know that Kuṇḍalinī, residing within, is the primary support for the individual soul (jīva), which is otherwise called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), just as a flower-cluster is for fragrance.
When, by means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*), one remains for a long time having filled [the body] with that [breath],
then the stability of Meru is attained, as well as the swelling of the body.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is not released within the interior filled by inhalation,
it is led upward by consciousness alone, having endured the fatigue and exhaustion caused by the heat.
Like a serpent provoked to fury, it moves upward with great force;
having assumed the likeness of a staff, it takes hold of all the channels in the body and becomes bound like a creeper.
Then it completely floods this entire body, just as a leather bag,
when tightly filled with air and submerged in water, causes a man [inside] to float.
Thus, through yoga— the playful exercise of repeated practice—
yogins attain the lofty state of moving through the sky, just as the wretched attain a state of great fortune.
When the Kuṇḍalinī power, by means of the flow through the Brahma-nāḍī, flows outward and upward to the top of the head at a distance of twelve finger-breadths; MU 6.85.50.
By means of the practice of exhalation (recaka) which restrains the other channels, one attains stability for a moment; then, the vision of the sky-dweller arises.
Rāma:
O Brahmin, what kind of perception could there be without the multitude of rays from the eyes?
And how could such be the true nature of the other sense organs as well?
Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, no beings who move through the sky can be seen by those who move upon the earth with their human faculties, which are non-divine and devoid of knowledge.
O Rāghava, by means of the eye of the intellect situated not far from consciousness,
the perfected ones moving through the sky are seen like dreams, even though they grant their own desired objects.
The vision of the perfected ones (*siddha*) is just like the observation of a dream;
the only difference is that upon attaining the state of a perfected one, there is stability of the object.
By means of the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), once the vital breath has been brought to remain for a long time outside the mouth at the *dvādaśānta*, they enter the supreme city.
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, tell me how the state of one's own nature does not waver;
for compassionate speakers do not feel weary even when asked a difficult question."
Vasiṣṭha: It is certain that the power known as the inherent nature of things manifests itself through creation and so forth, and in that very same way, it attains its state of persistence.
Because ignorance is not a real entity, its power over objects may sometimes be differentiated;
for indeed, my dear, autumnal fruit is seen [to appear] in the spring.
All this is indeed Brahman of such a nature; through this manifold diversity, it is perceived for the sake of conventional usage, while its stability is merely conceptualized.
Rāma:
How is it that this body is made either minute or gross, for the purpose of passing through subtle apertures and the like, or for the purpose of filling space?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a cut occurs from the joining of wood and a saw,
so too fire arises from their friction by its own inherent nature.
The flesh-and-lotus machine situated in the abdomen has its openings joined to one another;
its bases meet above and below, like the surfaces of heaven and earth.
His Kuṇḍalinī Lakṣmī was hidden within her own abode,
like a string of pearls within the casket of a ruby.
Like a garland of foam from a whirlpool, it is constantly hissing; like a female serpent struck by a staff, it repeatedly coils itself up in deep contractions.
Stationed between heaven and earth like action itself in the form of vibration,
consciousness is a bee within the hollow of the heart-lotus, arisen from the awakening of the honey of [pure] awareness.
All that— the powers, the lotuses, and so forth— is constantly shaken about within the heart by internal and external winds, like a mass of clouds on all sides.
Whatever manifests in the sky by its own nature, my dear, the winds thoroughly cause that which is thin and soft to tremble.
Struck by the winds, that lotus and the rest tremble,
just as the sprouts and other parts on a tree quiver against one another through mutual friction.
The cause of bodily heat, intent upon digesting all tastes and so forth,
generates fire through mutual friction, like a dense bundle of bamboo.
His body, being by nature cool and cold in essence,
attained intense heat throughout all its limbs, just as the world is heated by the risen sun.
That splendor, radiating rays in all directions and having the form of a star,
should be meditated upon by yogis as having entered the golden bee within the heart-lotus.
That knowledge, consisting of light, when contemplated,
bestows the power by which an object situated even a hundred thousand yojanas away is seen even at night.
For that fire, like the submarine fire (vāḍava), water is its fuel;
it dwells within the treasury of the heart-lake, which is rich with clusters of lotuses made of flesh.
That which is the coolness of the lotus is called the Moon, whose nature is the downward breath (apāna);
that fire has arisen from the Moon, for the body consists of both Agni and Soma.
They know that whatever is of a hot nature is designated as *tejas*, the sun, and fire; and that which is of a cold nature is called *soma*. The entire world is composed of these two alone.
The entire world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, is produced by this duality of knowledge and ignorance; it is that very same [reality] which is thus divided.
The wise know that true light, consisting of knowledge and the like, to be the sun and fire;
the learned call the unreal, inert darkness, consisting of ignorance and the like, the moon.
Rāma said:
"O Sage, best among speakers, I have heard that fire arises from the moon, which is of the nature of water;
now tell me of the origin of the moon."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Agni and Soma, being mutually both effect and cause within their own established state,
are equal in turn and are produced from one another.
Their existence is like that of the seed and the sprout of a tree, or like day and night; it would be as distinct as shade and sunlight.
For the coexistence of shadow and sunlight is perceived simultaneously;
their existence would otherwise be perceived one at a time, like day and night.
And the causal relationship between these two is said to be twofold:
that which arises from the transformation of an existing form, and that which arises from the transformation of destruction.
When a second arises from one, as in the case of a seed and a sprout,
that is the relation of cause and effect, born from the transformation of an existent form.
When one perishes, the existence of the second occurs like day and night;
this is the relationship of cause and effect, born from destruction and transformation.
Since the transformation into the form of an existent— such as the sequence of clay and jar—
is perceived by the senses, no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is required.
Even the non-existence of the sequence of day and night, which consists of destruction and transformation,
has attained the status of a primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it arises from a single entity.
Those who argue on the basis of logic that there is no agency in one's own destruction and so forth should be treated with contempt and cast out; they deny their own direct experience.
O descendant of Raghu, even non-existence is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), just like direct perception;
for the absence of fire is a proof of cold for all living beings.
That portion of fire which, by becoming smoke,
attains the state of a cloud through a transformation of its true nature— that fire becomes the cause of the moon.
Since fire attains the state of water due to its coldness by means of the transformation of destruction,
that fire has Soma as its cause.
Having drunk the waters of the seven oceans, the submarine fire (vāḍava) produces that very same water in abundance through its emission of smoke, which has assumed the form of clouds.
Having drunk the lord of the night again and again on the new moon day, the sun regurgitates it during the bright fortnight,
just as a crane spits out a lotus stalk.
Having drunk the cool nectar-like Soma that has reached the tip of the mouth, it becomes the downward-moving breath (apāna) and fills the body with water.
That portion of water which, by virtue of its subtlety,
enters into the state of the sun’s rays through a transformation of its own nature— that water is the cause of fire.
Since water attains the state of fire due to heat by way of its nature as destruction,
that water, through the transformation of its destruction, becomes the cause of fire.
Upon the destruction of fire, the moon is its transformation in the form of existence;
upon the destruction of the moon, fire is its transformation arising from friction.
Just as fire, having reached its end, becomes the moon,
and just as the day, having reached its end, becomes the night.
Between darkness and light, between shadow and sun, and between day and night, a form that is distinct from both is not perceived even by the wise.
Even that which is turbid as a conjunction is the very nature of these two;
for just as existence and non-existence are intertwined in a single thing, so too are these two.
Indeed, all beings manifest through the two principles of consciousness and inertia,
just as day and night appear on the surface of the earth through darkness and light.
This existence of the world has been initiated by the two forms of consciousness and insentience,
like the body of the moon formed from the mixture of water and nectar.
Know, O Rāghava, that the luminous fire and the sun are of the nature of consciousness;
know that which is of the nature of inertia and darkness is the body of the moon.
When the stainless sun of consciousness is seen, the darkness of the disease of worldly existence is destroyed,
just as the darkness of a black night vanishes when the sun in the sky is seen outside.
When the body, which is insentient, is perceived, the light of consciousness would appear as if non-existent,
just as the mass of solar radiance appears [faint] when the moon shines at midnight.
Fire reveals the moon, its body shining with long-lasting radiance;
and the moon illuminates the fire, bestowing its own form upon its body.
But the intellect, being inactive and without manifestation, is not perceived in its isolation;
it is understood only through the body, just as light is understood by means of a lamp.
The mind’s gain consists in its orientation toward objects of thought, and that itself is saṃsāra;
but for that which is free from objects of thought, there is no gain, for that indeed is nirvāṇa.
Know that these two, Agni and Soma, joined together like a wall and its light, possess their very existence only through mutual dependence, even as the body and the embodied soul.
O dear one, when there is an excess of nirvāṇa and an excess of dullness,
the state of fire and moon remains alone.
Prāṇa is fire, whose nature is heat; apāna is the moon, which is cool.
These two are situated like shadow and sunlight, moving along the paths of the mouth.
When the apāna becomes cool, the warm fire of prāṇa enters it,
just as a reflection appears in a mirror, and it likewise appears in that [fire].
The fire of consciousness, by its radiance, produces from the moon situated within the lotus-machine that which consists of water,
through experience here, just as light outside produces the appearance of a wall.
For whatever consciousness there was at the beginning of transmigration, characterized by cold and heat, attained the designation of Agni and Soma; that very thing is the creation of men here.
Where the sixteenth digit of the moon is swallowed by the sun for a moment,
stand with your feet firmly planted at a distance of one span (vitasti) in front of its mouth.
Surely Soma has reached the station of the Sun within the sky of the heart;
surely, remain there with steadfast composure, having established your footing.
Fire is said to be heat and the sun is heat; the moon is said to be coldness.
Wherever these two exist as reflected images, there establish your firm footing.
O sinless one, you are a knower of the transits of the bodily moon, sun, and fire;
for here, even at night, you perceive an object situated a hundred thousand yojanas away.
Indeed, in this context, the external times of transit are considered as insignificant as blades of grass.

O dear one, if you perceive the transits, the northern solstice, the correct time, and likewise the equinoxes— just as if they were situated within or outside the bodily winds— exactly as they are experienced, then you will not grieve here again once you have attained the Supreme.
The eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Investigation of Agni and Soma," by Vasiṣṭha.
O Rāma, listen now as I correctly explain how the body of yogis attains both minuteness and grossness. MU_6,86.1
Within the heart, a spark of fire arises from the interior of the lotus-petal sheath;
it throbs like a golden bee at twilight, or like a flash of lightning within a cloud.
Through the consciousness of growth, it increases rapidly like a whirlwind;
through its nature as pure consciousness, it surely rises like the sun.
Resembling the first rays of the sun amidst twilight clouds, having attained growth in an instant,
it melts away the entire body along with its limbs, just as fire melts gold.
By means of reasoning, one who is unable to endure the touch of water can even drain away stones and the like;
this is true of the external movement of fire, but it is especially so of the internal.
That fluidity of the body is subsequently shaken off and carried away somewhere by the vital breath agitated by consciousness, just as mist is dispersed by a whirlwind.
Devoid of the foundational channels, the Kuṇḍalinī power remains situated in the void alone,
having emerged like a streak of smoke from fire.
Having embraced the ego-sense consisting of mind, intellect, the individual soul, and so forth, she possesses an inner,
shimmering wonder, like a column of smoke rising from the *tāgara* tree.
Whether in a wound, a wall, a stone, the sky, or the ground—
just as she is applied wherever it is necessary, by that means she emerges perfectly in that very way.
If that very consciousness, my dear, through the successive taking up of the flavors,
becomes filled with flavor, it then becomes like a mist saturated with water.
O Rāma, whatever form one contemplates while filled with aesthetic relish (rasa), that very thing quickly assumes its likeness,
just as lines in the mind of a painter take on a particular shape.
Then, by the power of firm disposition, it enters within [the womb] among the bones;
it is like one seated in the mother's womb, or like the state of a sprout that has been well-watered.
O Rāghava, the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti) attains whatever form it desires and whatever measure it chooses, whether it be as Mount Sumeru or as a blade of grass.
You have heard of the attainment of powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) which is accomplished through yoga;
now listen to that which is accomplished through knowledge, which is an ornament for the ears.
There exists here only one pure, gentle, and unperceivable Consciousness alone;
it is subtler than the subtlest, peaceful, and neither the world nor the activities of the world.
When that [consciousness], having turned toward volitional ideation (saṅkalpa), accumulates itself by means of itself and has thus become turbid,
it is then called the "living being" (jīva).
Through the delusion of mental construction, the ignorant soul perceives this unreal body as if it were real, just as a child sees a towering phantom.
But when perfect illumination has arrived by means of the lamp of knowledge,
the delusion of conceptualization in the living being perishes like an autumn cloud.
When all mental constructions have ceased, O Rāghava, this body attains peace, just as a lamp is extinguished entirely when its oil is exhausted.
Just as a living being does not see a dream once sleep has passed away,
so too the individual soul, when the Truth has been cultivated, no longer perceives the body.
The living being, shrouded by the body, dwells perceiving the unreal as real;
yet, through the singular contemplation of reality, he becomes bodiless, illustrious, and happy.
That which is the conceit of a self in what is not-self, such as the body and so forth—
O dear one, that is the terrible darkness of the heart, difficult to pierce even by the light of the sun and other luminaries.
Through the sun of knowledge, one perceives: "I am the stainless, pure consciousness alone, pervading all by way of my very self within the Self."
In every Manvantara, O Rāma, Hari, whose nature is immeasurable, assumes the state of a Buddha by relying on some cause during the Kali age.
O Rāghava, those who possess devotion for that Lord of Sages, who is designated as Buddha, and who are wise and desirous of the path to liberation—
Whether it be emptiness, mere consciousness, or some middle position between these two,
they designate Brahman as "it exists" by means of the presentation of logical reasons.
For among them, those who know consciousness, once duality has been brought to an end,
perceive the world as nothing other than a mere conceptualization of delusion.
The Mādhyamikas, who understand the doctrine of momentary destruction, declare the middle way;
they remain established in the view that this is neither emptiness nor consciousness, but rather "this is nothing whatsoever."
But those other proponents of emptiness, who possess a firm cultivation of emptiness,
abandon all attachment to the world as being even more empty than space.
O Rāma, those whose intentions are as clear as space perceive only the one, lofty space; they do not perceive themselves or the world and its origins as separate.
They emerge from stone walls as if unimpeded by the sky;
they are not pierced by weapons or winds, remaining as immovable as portions of the firmament.
Even those things as vast in form as Mount Sumeru abide like atoms within the rays of the sun, within the fibers of a lotus stalk, and within the clouds.
Having attained a state as if they were emptiness itself, with their meditation fixed upon emptiness,
they remain in the void, free from fever, like portions of the sky that are empty.
And those who have realized the self within emptiness cultivate whatever it may be; through their own firm cultivation, they see that very thing exactly as it is, swiftly.
O Rāghava, by maintaining a firm conviction, even those who are deluded transform poison into nectar and nectar into poison as well.
"In this way, however one cultivates a firm cultivation here, it becomes exactly so quickly; this has been observed again."
When this body is viewed with the sense of reality, it truly becomes a body;
however, when viewed without the sense of reality, this physical frame attains the state of space.
O Rāma, you have now heard from me the method of knowledge for attaining the states of aṇimā and the rest; listen now to this other method.
Through the practice of exhaling (recaka), the individual soul is drawn out from the abode of Kuṇḍalinī and joined with the vital air, just as fragrance is extracted from a flower.

This body, devoid of movement, is abandoned like a piece of wood or a clod of earth; when the life-force has departed from the body, what regard can there be for it, any more than for a lifeless bamboo stalk?
Whether in an immobile or a mobile being, according to its own desire and intention,
the individual soul is properly placed within it in order to enjoy its prosperity.
Having thus enjoyed the glory of accomplishment, if that body remains, one may re-enter it,
or another body, whichever one prefers here.
Or else, having emerged from the body and pervaded the ether and wind in every direction,
one remains completely filling the entire world with consciousness.

O Rāma, having known the Lord who is ever-risen and free from defects, whatever the light of consciousness desires in whatever manner, it attains that very thing without delay; they know the state of perfection to be nothing other than this state of being unobstructed.
The seventy-seventh chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Aṇimā and Other Powers," by Vasiṣṭha.
Endowed with the sovereign powers of the *aṇimā* and other qualities, that noble lady Cūḍālā became thus, being possessed of intense meditative practice.
She traveled by way of the sky, entered the hollow of the ocean,
and moved across the surface of the earth like the Ganges— pure and cool.
Not having departed from her husband’s chest for even a moment, she likewise dwelt within his heart,
as Lakṣmī resides in all kingdoms and throughout the worlds.
Moving through the air, dark-complexioned, and adorned with ornaments as flickering as lightning,
she wandered over the surface of the earth like a streak of cloud upon a range of mountains.
He entered wood, grass, stone, earth, space, wind, fire,
and water without obstruction, just as a thread passes through a pearl.
Above Mount Meru, he wandered at his pleasure among the peaks, the cities of the world-protectors, and the hollows and openings of the quarters and the sky.
She engaged in worldly affairs with animals, piśācas, and other beings, as well as with nāgas, gods, asuras, vidyādharas, apsarases, and siddhas.
And with great effort, she repeatedly instructed her husband regarding the nectar of self-knowledge, just as a mother instructs her young son.
And her husband, the king, found no rest within himself,
like a pearl that has fallen unattached into the depths of the underworld.
Even after such a length of time, that king, being foolish, did not recognize Cūḍālā, who was endowed with such virtues, any more than one might fail to recognize a magical spell.
"She is skilled in the arts, yet innocent; she is my young wife"—it was only by thinking thus that the king recognized her as Cūḍālā.
Since she had not yet attained repose within her own self, she did not reveal that glory of her spiritual perfection to the king, just as one would not show the performance of a sacrifice to a Śūdra.
Rāma:
Even Śikhidhvaja did not attain awakening despite the efforts of that great Siddhayoginī; O Lord, how could anyone else awaken?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, what is called the 'method of instruction' is merely the maintenance of formal discipline; the true cause for the arising of knowledge is the pure intelligence of the disciple alone."
The object of knowledge of the self is not known through sacred learning nor through merit;
the self alone knows the self, just as a snake [knows] its own tracks.
Rāma:
This being so, O excellent sage, how is it that this has been heard in popular report,
and that the instruction of a guru is the cause for the knowledge of one's own self?
Vasiṣṭha said:
"There is a certain merchant who, though extremely wretched, possesses wealth and grain;
he lives with his family on the edge of the Vindhya forest like a worm in a wound."
Once, O Rāma, as he was walking through the Vindhya jungle covered with a thicket of grass and chaff, a single cowrie shell fell from him.
Out of stinginess, he diligently shook everything— grass, chaff, and so forth—
for three days all around, for the sake of a single cowrie shell.
From one cowrie shell, two, then four, eight,
and from that time on, by means of the mind, [one perceives] a hundred, a thousand, and another thousand.
Gathering [the husks] in the jungle, miserable yet untiring day and night,
he endured the laughter of the people for three days while winnowing the chaff.
Then, at the end of three days, he obtained from that thicket of trees a great wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) resembling the orb of the full moon.
Having attained that, with a contented heart, he returned home happy;
having obtained the prosperity of the entire world, he remained with all fears pacified.
Thus, just as that jewel, worth the entire world, was obtained by the Kirāta through his search for cowrie shells, without being distressed day or night.
Thus, through the instruction of the scriptures, knowledge of one's own self is attained; indeed, by following the lineage of gurus, one thing is sought and another is obtained.
Brahman transcends all the senses; therefore, O sinless one, the reality of the Self is not attained through the cognition of the senses of hearing and the rest, nor by means of instruction.
And without the instruction of a guru, there can be no attainment of the reality of the Self;
by whom has the wish-fulfilling gem ever been obtained without searching for cowrie shells?
The teacher’s exposition of this highly precious reality has reached its conclusion;
it is like a cowrie shell being treated as the cause [of value] for a gem, though it is not actually the cause.
Behold, O Rāghava, this illusion which deludes even the great:
one thing is sought with effort, yet another fruit is obtained.
A person performs one action, yet he obtains a quite different result; moreover, the fixed order of things is observed.
Therefore, for the sake of the world-process whose power is infinite, the better course is to pass through it with detachment and indeed with indifference.
The Eighty-Eighth Sarga, titled "The Narrative of the Kirāta": Vasiṣṭha said:
Then King Śikhidhvaja, lacking the state of knowledge of reality,
fell into a supreme delusion, like the surface of the earth falling into the blindness of night.
With his mind set ablaze by the fire of suffering, he took no pleasure even in those splendors brought before him, as if they were tongues of flame.
In solitary places, at the ends of the earth, by waterfalls, and in caves—
places free from living beings— he found delight, like one addicted to vice.
O Raghava, like you, every king is made to perform his daily duties by his servants when entreated with conciliation, persuasion, and exhortations.
Always possessing unrestrained dispassion and a tranquil intellect like a wandering mendicant,
he remained amidst riches without enjoying them, even while censuring great pleasures.
The bestower of honor gave away abundant gifts— cows, land, gold,
and so forth— to the gods, the brahmins, and his own kinsmen.
And he practiced austerities, performing the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other penances;
he wandered through sacred fords, forests, and shrines.
Nevertheless, he did not obtain even the slightest freedom from sorrow,
just as one seeking a treasure who digs the earth finds no treasure when there is none to be found.
Wasting day and night with an endless fire of grief,
he reflected again and again upon the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.
Overcome by anxiety and dejected, he viewed his kingdom as if it were poison;
with a distressed mind, he no longer perceived even the great splendor before him.
Then, on one occasion, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words in a sweet voice to Cūḍālā, who had come into his lap while they were in a secluded place.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I have enjoyed the kingdom for a long time and have experienced the heights of prosperity;
now, joined with dispassion, I am going to the forest."
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither calamities nor successes,
embrace the sage dwelling in the forest.
There is no delusion caused by the ruin of one's country, nor the loss of life in battle; I consider the happiness of those dwelling in the forest to be even greater than that of kingship.
Bearing clusters as breasts, with red shoots for hands,
they laugh with their masses of blossoms while their white clouds flutter like shifting silken garments.
They captivated the limbs of both themselves and others, were adorned with artificial floral ornaments,
and shone with the slopes of their hips like well-serviced golden rocks.
Enveloped by pearl necklaces in the form of rivers threaded with pearls that are the waves,
they are embraced by their companions in the form of creepers— the most charming young fawns.
Possessing a natural fragrance that is unrestrained, they offer food in the form of fruit;
their eyes are like rows of bees, and their bodies are bent under the weight of blossoms.
O fair-faced one, these forest paths, having become a source of consolation for me with their cool and pure-limbed trees, delight me just as you do.
As the mind becomes secluded, solitary, and tranquil,
it does not find such peace in the orbs of the moon, nor even in the abodes of Brahmā and Indra.
O slender one, you ought not to place an obstacle in this request of mine;
for noble women do not thwart the desire of their husband even in a dream.
Cūḍālā said:
"O Lord, an action performed at the appropriate time shines, and nothing else;
a flower shines in spring, and fruit shines in autumn."
It is appropriate for those whose bodies are worn out by old age to take refuge in the forest;
but it is not fitting for young men such as yourself, and therefore this does not please me.
O Great King, as long as we have not been abandoned by youth,
we shine within our home like trees laden with a profusion of flowers.
When the forest, white with flowers, becomes old along with us,
we shall go together from our home like swans from a tree to a lake.
For a king who neglects the protection of his subjects at the improper time,
a great sin does not perish, just as the affliction of consumption does not leave the moon.
The subjects indeed restrain a king who acts prematurely;
for masters and servants restrain one another from improper actions.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Enough, O lady with eyes like blue lotuses, with this obstacle to my desired goal;
know that I am departing from here for a distant, solitary forest.
"You are but a child with faultless limbs; you must not come to the forest.
For even for men, O soft-limbed one, dwelling in the forest is difficult to endure."
Even women who are hardened are not capable of dwelling in the forest;
for what kind of flower-clusters are able to endure the heat of the sun?
You must remain here in this supreme state, protecting the kingdom;
for when the husband has departed, the duty of a woman is to bear the burden of the household.
Having spoken thus to his beloved, whose face was like the moon, the self-controlled king rose up to bathe and performed all his daily duties.
Then, having abandoned all activity for his subjects, Ravi went to the western mountain,
just as Śikhidhvaja had gone to the forest, which was inaccessible to all people.
Withdrawing her diffused form, the radiance followed that very Lord who had departed from his palace, like a devoted female crest-jewel.
The dark night arrived, making the world grey with ash, as if the sister of Yama had come out of envy toward Śiva, who bears the celestial river upon him.
While the quarters of the sky stood with twilight clouds for hands, marked by the curls of darkness as their forelocks, it was adorned by the rising smile of moonlight.
As the husband and wife proceeded toward the further shore, they reached the Mairava forest,
