which was like a celestial garden for the couple to enjoy, as it were for the splendor of the day and the lord of the day.
And for the two lords of night and day as they arrive at this shore, there is a heart-pleasing [abode] free from harsh rays; furthermore, for the couple, there is that which belongs to Mount Meru.
The host of stars was also seen shattered upon the pavement of the sky,
like a handful of auspicious parched grain released by the maidens of the quarters.
The night— moon-faced, dark as the gloom, cool, and smiling with white water-lilies—
attained her youth, her breasts being the buds of lotuses.
Having performed his evening rituals together with Cūḍālā,
the king lay down upon his bed like Mount Maināka in the ocean.
Then, at the hour of midnight, when the region had become silent and all people were nestled within the stone-wombs of deep sleep;
While she was fast asleep on that bed of soft silk, utterly overcome by slumber like a female bee upon a lotus, he—
King Śikhidhvaja gradually abandoned his sleeping beloved from his embrace,
just as Rāhu gradually releases the splendor of the sun and moon from his mouth.
He rose from his white silken bed, where his young bride lay nestled,
like Hari rising from the milk-ocean with its shimmering waves and its goddess Lakṣmī.
He emerged from the house into the courtyard where the servants were sleeping in a state of intoxication,
like a lion emerging from a cave into a forest where herds of deer are asleep.
Accompanied only by his sword and covered by two cloths,
he reached the gateway where the gatekeeper was half-asleep.
Thinking, "I am going for the sake of the Hero's Gait," that one of perfected intellect departed from the city, having secured the series of gates right there.
Having said, "Salutations to you, O Fortune of Kingship," he departed from the circle [of kings] and entered the formidable forest alone, like a river entering the ocean.
And that night in the vast forest, thick with dense darkness and harsh with swarms of petty spirits,
was passed by him together with her.
Having traversed the vast expanse of the empty forest at dawn throughout the long day,
he rested together with the sun upon a certain woodland floor.
When the sun had gone out of sight, she performed her bath and other preliminary rites there, ate some fruit and such, and led him into the darkness of night.
Again at dawn, O Rāma, he forcibly leaped over cities, high mountain ranges, and rivers for twelve nights.
Then he reached a forest situated on the slope of Mount Mandara, inaccessible to people, where the cities of men lay at an extreme distance.
The trees were encircled by ponds whose water flowed through gurgling conduits;
the ancient hermitage of the twice-born was recognizable by its ruined altars and other remains.
It was free from small creatures, a bower of creepers frequented by the Siddhas,
filled with trees and vines, and provided with fruits that sustain life.
There, in a certain place that was pure, level, garlanded with water, cool, dark-green with grass, and lush with fruit-bearing trees; //MU_6,88.57//
With creepers adorned with clusters of blossoms, he constructed a leaf-hut,
like a cage made of dark clouds accompanied by lightning during the rainy season.
A smooth bamboo staff, a vessel for eating fruit,
a water-offering bowl, a flower-basket, a rosary, and a water-pot.
Having brought a patched cloak to ward off the cold, as well as a cushion and a deer-skin, the king prepared them within that small hermitage cell.
Whatever other object was suitable for the practice of asceticism,
he established that there, just as the Creator establishes the order of things upon the earth.
Then, during the first watch of the morning, he performed his recitation preceded by the twilight prayers;
thereafter, he gathered flowers, bathed, and worshipped the deity.
Afterwards, having eaten some forest fruit, wild tubers, lotus stalks, and the like, that self-controlled man spent the night alone, devoted to his recitation.
Thus the Lord of Mālava spent the day without weariness within a hut constructed on the shore near Mount Mandara;
nor did he remember that royal splendor—for what indeed can the glories of sovereignty carry away when discernment flashes in the heart?
The eighty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of Śikhidhvaja’s Renunciation," by Vasiṣṭha.
Thus Śikhidhvaja remained in the forest in a leaf-hut;
now hear what Cūḍālā did at home.
There, at the time of midnight, when Śikhidhvaja had gone far away,
Cūḍālā woke up in fear like a doe sleeping in a village.
She beheld her bed, bereft of its lord and fallen into emptiness,
like the sky when the sun has vanished and the moon is not full, its beauty stilled.
She rose up with her face somewhat withered and full of weariness,
like a great creeper poorly watered, its sprouts— the limbs of her body— devoid of vigor.
Neither clear nor stainless, having fallen into agitation,
she remained like the beauty of day turned grey by mist.
Seated upon her couch for a moment, she reflected with deep anxiety:
"Alas! Having abandoned his kingdom and his sovereign power, he has gone from his home to the forest."
Therefore, what should I do now? I shall go into his presence;
for destiny has ordained that the husband alone is the refuge of women.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā rose up to follow her husband; emerging through a wind-cleft, she ascended into the sky.
The yoginī wandered through the path of the sky by means of the wind-current, creating the illusion of another moon with her face before the caravan of the *siddhas*.
Then, traveling along the path at night, she saw her husband wandering alone in a secluded spot with a sword in his hand, appearing like a risen lord of vetālas.
Beholding such a husband, she remained confined within the hollow of the sky and reflected upon everything concerning her future that would remain unimpeded for her lord.
O Rāghava, you must proceed in such a manner, at such a time, in such a place, for as long as necessary, according to how the task arises, and so that your extensive liberation may be attained.

it has arisen solely from ignorance as something unreal, like a mirage-ocean in a desert.
For that wise one in whom delusion has been destroyed through the contemplation that "all is Brahman," no latent impression arises, just as a mirage does not arise from the ocean in a desert.
By abandoning even the mere traces of latent impressions, the living being within attains that state which is free from old age and death,
and is devoid of further rebirth.
The mind accompanied by latent impressions is ignorance; the mind free from latent impressions is the object of knowledge.
Having attained the state of being known through knowledge, the living soul is not born again.
Cūḍālā said:
"O royal sage, even the great ones, beginning with Brahmā, have declared that knowledge alone is the supreme good; why then do you remain in ignorance?"
"The water-pot is here, the wooden staff is there, and the grass mat is over there;
O Lord of the Earth, why do you take delight in this display of useless things?"
"Who am I? How was this born? And how is it extinguished? O King, why do you not consider these things; why do you remain as if ignorant?"
Citing such questions as "What is bondage? What is liberation?", why, my dear, do you not serve the feet of those who know both the higher and the lower?
Why do you remain like a stone-insect in the hollow of a mountain cave, wasting your life with this activity of barely perceptible consciousness?
That method, by which one is liberated, is obtained through inquiry, service, and association with the virtuous who possess equal vision.
Do not remain in a forest hollow eating your fill like the lowest of men, with your wicked deeds exposed, like a worm in a hole in the earth.
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus enlightened by that beloved woman of divine form,
Śikhidhvaja, his face filled with tears, spoke these words.
Śikhidhvaja:
Oh, son of a god, today at long last I have been awakened by you!
Out of folly, having abandoned the company of noble beings, I lived in the forest.
"Aha! Indeed, the darkness of my delusion has vanished entirely, since you yourself have come here and awakened me."
"You are my guru, you are my father, you are my friend, O fair-faced one;
as your disciple, I bow before your feet—please show me your compassion."
Teach me quickly that Brahman which you know to be most sublime, by knowing which one does not grieve, and through which I may become liberated.
There are manifold manifestations of knowledge, such as the cognition of a jar and so forth;
among these various forms of knowledge, which one would be the supreme knowledge that acts as a savior?
Cūḍālā said:
"O royal sage, if my words are worthy of being accepted, then I shall speak them to you;
I will say this little according to my knowledge, and not like a crow perched on a pillar."

When questioned in jest by one whose words are not to be accepted, the speech of such a speaker bears no fruit— or rather, it bears fruitlessness— just as the perception of the eyes fails in the darkness.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Whatever you say must be carried out by me, just as the injunction of the Veda is by the ritualist;
this truth shall be my vow, remaining forever unchanging."
Cūḍālā said:
Just as a child accepts his father’s word even when it is devoid of reasons and supporting arguments,
so too should you accept these words of mine.
Immediately upon hearing it, contemplate it as something auspicious with your intellect;
listen to my words like a song, setting aside the desire for logical reasons.

O Udayantī, listen as I relate in due order this pleasing account of the great poets, which accords with your own conduct, brings about the awakening of the intellect after a long time, and shatters the fear of worldly existence.
The Ninety-second canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," concerning Cūḍālā.
Is there some illustrious man who is the abode of two qualities that are eternally opposed, in their entirety, just as the ocean is the abode of both the submarine fire and water?
Possessing the arts, skilled in the scriptures, and discerning in worldly affairs,
he does not know the unborn state that lies beyond the limit of all conceptual constructions.
He has set out to accomplish the attainment of the wish-fulfilling gem, which can only be achieved through infinite effort,
like the submarine fire attempting to dry up the ocean.
Through great effort and resolute perseverance over time, he attained the wish-fulfilling gem; for what indeed cannot be accomplished by those of lofty spirit?
If one applies oneself with perseverance, effort, and wisdom without weariness,
then even though possessing nothing, one attains the state of Śakra without hindrance.
Standing on the peak of Mount Meru, he beheld the jewel that had come before him, within reach of his hand, like the risen moon seen by a sage.
Although he was among the sovereign lords of jewels, he remained devoid of certainty;
when the kingdom was suddenly attained, he became like a wretched commoner.
He reflected upon this with a mind full of wonder,
having attained equanimity toward the agitation caused by long-standing suffering.
"This is a gem; this is not a gem—if it were so, it would not be that [gem].
I touch it, yet I do not touch it; at some point, through contact, it would pass away."
It is said that the supreme jewel is not accomplished by this much time alone;
according to the sequence of the scriptures, it is accomplished through effort until the end of one's life.
With my eye narrowed by the act [of squinting], I perceive the light of the jewels as resembling the surface of a flickering firebrand, like the appearance of two moons due to delusion.
Whence has such vast and abundant good fortune come to me,
that even now I obtain this sovereign jewel which grants all accomplishments?
Indeed, only those few are truly great and highly fortunate for whom prosperity comes face-to-face in a short period of time.
"I am but a poor human being, a mere ascetic of little merit;
how can the supernatural powers come to me, who am the sole vessel for misfortune?"
Thus, for a long time, the ignorant man, reflecting with conceptual constructions and mental fabrications,
was deluded by his own folly and made no effort to grasp the jewel.
When something is not to be obtained by someone at a certain time, he does not obtain it then;
even though the wish-fulfilling gem has been acquired, it is cast aside with indifference by one of dull intellect.
Thus, while he remained in that state, the jewel flew up and the supernatural powers departed; for those who treat them with contempt abandon them, just as discharged arrows leave the bowstring.

Having first taken away a person's wealth, that [Yakṣa] indeed departs; once he has gone, the supernatural powers (siddhis) that had arrived bestow everything, but when they have departed, they take it all away completely.
The man again made an effort toward the means of obtaining the supreme jewel;
for resolute people do not falter in their undertakings.
Then the fool saw a piece of glass with a glittering appearance,
which had been cast down before him by laughing, deceptive siddhas who remained unobserved.
Thinking "this is a wish-fulfilling gem," the fool perceives reality in that [clod of earth];
for the ignorant person, deluded, regards clay as gold.
Eighty-eight things— the enemy, the friend, the rope, the serpent, land, water, two moons, and the notions of nectar and poison— create delusion in the mind of a child.
Taking that burnt gem, he abandoned his former prosperity, thinking:
"Everything is obtained from this *cintāmaṇi*; what is the use of other riches?"
This land is unpleasant and harsh, filled with sinful people;
what is that home which is almost destroyed, and who indeed are my kinsmen?
"Having gone far away, I shall dwell happily according to my desire through this prosperity"—
thinking thus, the fool took the jewel and went to the empty forest.
There, by means of that glass shard, he met with that calamity which is equal,
my dear, to the night of Mount Kāñjilādri or to the very state of ignorance.
Those sufferings which arise through the power of folly do not come from calamity, nor from old age or death;
for folly alone stands at the head of all misfortunes, like the mass of black hair upon the bodies of people.
The ninety-third canto, titled "The Narrative of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem," Canto 93: Cūḍālā.
Now, O King, listen to this other delightful account,
which is a supreme awakening of the intellect and worthy of yourself, O virtuous one.
In the Vindhya forest there was an elephant, the leader of a great herd,
who had grown by his own nature as much as the Vindhya mountain itself, which increased when its growth was halted by Agastya.
His two fangs are sharp, long, and as crooked as a thunderbolt; they are equal to the crest of the fire at the end of an eon and capable of uprooting Mount Sumeru.
Bound by the elephant-trainer with a net of iron, he was deceived like Mount Vindhya by the Lord of Sages, or like Bali by Upendra.
Bound by the noose of restraint and placed within a cage of weapons, that heroic elephant experienced such agony as cannot be described in words.
While his enemy, the elephant-driver, watched him from afar in concealment,
the elephant spent three days within that iron cage.
Out of weariness, he made an effort to break his fetters with a *jhaṇajjhaṇa* sound,
like the tinkling of small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*) produced by the jolting of a chariot.
With those two teeth, he exerted himself for two muhūrtas and broke the network of chains, just as an asura breaks the bolt of heaven.
From afar, his enemy saw that severing of his fetters,
just as Hari [Vishnu] saw the rending of the wings of Mount Meru from its slope.
As he was thus bound by the noose, his enemy, Hari, fell upon his head like a palm tree, as if leaping from Mount Meru to heaven.
Falling through delusion and failing to reach the heads of the elephants,
he fell like a ripe fruit shaken down by the wind, tossed about in the air.
Seeing him fallen before him, the great elephant felt compassion; for virtuous beings, whose noble qualities are ever-vibrant and expansive, exist even among those of the animal realm.
"What manliness is there in my merely thinking, 'I shall crush him who has fallen'?
Even though he was an elephant, he did not kill that enemy, considering [him as such]."
Having swiftly burst through the array of fetters,
he departed like a vast torrent of water sweeping away a wide-spreading dam.
Disregarding him, Mātaṅga broke through the net and sped away with speed,
like the sun in the sky parting a mass of clouds.
When the elephant had departed, the elephant-keeper stood up, his body and mind restored to health;
along with the elephant itself, his distress had gone far away.
Even though he fell from the tall palm tree in that manner, he did not suffer any injury; I think the bodies of the wicked are difficult to break.
The strength of the wicked increases in their evil deeds like a cloud in the rainy season;
at that time, he was exceedingly eager to attack the elephant.
That lion among elephants, having lost his elephant, fell into misery;
he vanished once it had gone, like a pauper losing a hidden treasure.
He diligently searched for the elephant hidden within the thickets of the forest,
just as Rāhu seeks the moon in the sky when it is shrouded by clouds in order to devour it.
After a long time, he obtained the lord of elephants dwelling in a certain forest,
resting at the foot of a tree as if he had just emerged from battle.
Then, at the place where the elephant was stationed, [the king] employed a supreme array of royal forces, appearing eager to seize the elephant, capable of binding it.
In the forest, that elephant trainer constructed a new circular pit extending in all directions, just as the Creator fashioned the oceanic ring upon the earth.
That rogue covered it from above with a mass of withered creepers,
just as the autumn season covers the empty sky with a thin web of clouds.
Within just a few days, while roaming in that forest,
the elephant fell into a pit like a mountain falling into a dried-up ocean.
While walking, he fell into a well that had the form of a serpent, terrifying as the depths of Pātāla,
resembling a dry ocean trench, and serving as a casket for the jewel of an elephant.
Thus, having been bound even more firmly by that elephant-keeper,
he remains even today in pain within the subterranean dwelling, like a fish on dry land.
If he had struck down the enemy who had come before him earlier,
then that elephant would not have suffered the pain of being bound by his own digging.
Due to folly, a man who fails to purify his future time through the sequence of present actions goes to suffering, just like the elephant of the Vindhya mountains.
"Even though the elephant was satisfied, thinking, 'I am freed from weapons and shackles,' he was bound again even while at a distance; where indeed does folly not cause affliction?"
O Great-souled One, know that ignorance is the supreme cause of bondage; there is no other bond here for one whose mind is free from it.
When the Self has risen, the entire three worlds consist of the Self; indeed, for one seated upon a horse, the whole earth is its own companion.
The Ninety-fourth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Elephant," [spoken by] Śikhidhvaja:
O son of an immortal, please reveal once more to me that web of excellent stories which you have indicated by means of the acquisition of jewels, the taming of wild elephants, and other such tales.
Cūḍālā said:
Through the perfection of the vision of the meaning of words, within the house of the heart upon the walls of the mind, listen; I shall unfold for you the wondrous painting of the sacred narrative.
O Lord of the Earth, you alone are that person who is skilled in the meaning of the scriptures yet unlearned in the knowledge of reality, as described in the context of acquiring jewels.
You are a knower of the scriptures, like the sun upon the slopes of Mount Meru;
yet you have not found rest in the knowledge of reality, remaining instead like a stone in the sky.
Know, O virtuous one, that unartificial renunciation of everything is the wish-fulfilling gem;
with a pure intellect, you shall thereby accomplish the end of all sufferings.
O sinless one, through pure renunciation of everything, everything is attained;
for the renunciation of all is indeed sovereignty—what need is there for the wish-fulfilling gem?
O virtuous one, you have accomplished that total renunciation which diminishes the worldly prosperity of the entire universe,
just as the rising of the Vindhya mountain eclipses the splendor of the world.
You have renounced the kingdom, along with your wife, wealth, and kinsmen,
just as Brahmā abandons the activity of creating the world at the onset of his own night.
You have come from a place extremely distant from your own country to this hermitage on the border,
like Garuda with the tortoise, who came to the edge of the earth for rest.
In the total renunciation of everything, only the notion of "I" has been left behind by you,
who have wiped away every stain, just as the wind leaves only its own presence in the sky.
As long as you have not abandoned the mind alone within the heart and it has not reached fullness,
so long will conceptualization obscure you, just as a cloud obscures the sky.
"This is not that supreme bliss, this great success consisting of total renunciation;
it is something else entirely, lofty, difficult to achieve, and vast."
When thought gradually increased through the grasping of volition,
your renunciation flew away like the trembling of a tree in a whirlwind.
How could there be renunciation for one who even conceals his own thoughts?
How could a tree that is joined with the movement of the wind possess stillness?
They say that thought itself is the mind, which has other names such as "volition" (saṅkalpa);
while that very [thought] is vibrating, how could the mind be abandoned?
O holy one, when the mind— which is the seed-grain of the net of the three worlds— is grasped, how can the stainless renunciation of everything be accomplished in an instant?
By grasping at mental constructs, O dear one, your renunciation has flown away from within you,
just as a village bird flies away upon hearing a sound.
Having taken all the wealth of freedom from anxiety through renunciation, he has departed;
indeed, he who departs after taking leave and being honored causes suffering for others.
O lotus-eyed one, since all things are thus like jewels of total renunciation, you have perceived the jewel of asceticism with the eye of your resolve.
By you, in that very asceticism which arose from the delusion of vision,
a single-pointed cultivation was fixed upon what is to be grasped, just as a child fixes its attention on the moon reflected in water.

The practice of austerity that is performed without a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is blissful, whereas that which is undertaken with a latent impression is fraught with discordance in its beginning, middle, and end, leading only to suffering.

He who abandons that which is easily accomplished and brings immeasurable bliss, and instead exerts himself toward a limited object that is difficult to achieve, is considered a rogue who destroys his own self.
Beginning with the renunciation of everything, you have not brought it to completion,
being bound in the forest hermitage by your singular devotion to the suffering of asceticism.
O virtuous one, having emerged from the bonds of kingship like an elephant into what is called forest-dwelling— a place filled with suffering— you are now bound by firm fetters.
Those anxieties regarding cold, wind, heat, and so forth are indeed doubled;
I consider dwelling in the forest to be more than a mere bondage for one who is unaccustomed to it.
"You thought, 'I have obtained a wish-fulfilling gem'—enough of that!
O virtuous one, you have not even obtained a fragment of crystal."

Thus, O lotus-eyed one, I have fully revealed this to you, which is like the story of the jewel and the effort; having awakened pure understanding by your own intellect, bring what I speak to its full realization within the treasury of your mind.
The ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Account of the One Who Procured the Cintāmaṇi Jewel," [spoken by] Cūḍālā.
Now, O tiger among kings, for the sake of understanding the matter,
hear the account of the Vindhya-elephant, which will cause you wonder.
That elephant which was in the Vindhya forest is you here upon this earth;
that detachment and discernment of yours are its two sharp tusks.
And that elephant-driver who stood intent on mounting the elephant—
that is ignorance, intent on mounting you, which brings you suffering.
O King, though you are exceedingly powerful, you are led by your own folly from sorrow to sorrow and from fear to fear by your incapacity, just as an elephant is led by a mahout.
Just as an elephant is bound by a rope made of iron,
so have you fallen into calamity because of the snare of the net of desire.
For hope is more treacherous, more extensive, and more firm than iron ropes;
iron may decay with time, but craving only increases.
Just as an enemy, remaining unobserved nearby, watches an elephant that has been bound,
so too does ignorance watch you alone, bound for its own sport.
Just as an elephant breaks free from the bonds of its net of chains and weapons,
so have you abandoned this kingdom, a land of enjoyment free from all thorns.
O virtuous one, at times it may be easy to break through the net of weapons and chains, but it is not so easy to ward off the desire for enjoyments from this mind.
Just as the elephant-driver, when he splits those two [tusks], falls from his high perch,
so too did ignorance fall and perish when it abandoned that kingdom to you.
When a dispassionate person desires to abandon the hope for enjoyment,
then ignorance trembles like a tree-demon that is about to be cut down.
When the discerning person remains having renounced enjoyments,
then ignorance flees like a demon from a felled tree.
When the flood of enjoyments has surely been released, ignorance falls away without support,
just as a nest situated in a tree falls when the tree is cut by a saw.
When you departed for the forest, that ignorance was wounded by you;
yet, having fallen, it was not destroyed by the great sword of the renunciation of the mind.
Rising up once more and remembering [the past], he committed an insult;
you were cast into this thicket, a pit dug by the elaborate display of his asceticism.
If you had caused it to be destroyed at that very moment when ignorance fell upon you,
then it would not have killed you as it reached its end during the act of renouncing the kingdom.
That the enemy caused the elephant to be encircled by a trench was an incomparable suffering of penance inflicted upon you through ignorance.
That collection of royal resources which the king brought forth against the enemy of elephants has now spread forth as the mental manifestation of your king who is ignorant of you.
O Lord of Elephants, although you had gone to the vast forest dug up by your asceticism,
you were swiftly cast into this fire-pit by that enemy, ignorance.
That trench which was once concealed by young creepers is now covered by the slight hardships of asceticism, resembling the conduct of the virtuous.
Thus, even now, O King, you remain in this most terrible pit of suffering created by your own asceticism, bound at the bottom of the underworld like a fish on a hook.
The elephant is you; the shackles are the directions; the enemy is delusion; the stake is fierce bondage;
the surface of the earth is the Vindhya mountains—such is your description. Now, do what you must do.
The ninety-sixth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Elephant":
That which was spoken by her, who is endowed with political wisdom and has known all that is to be known—
Why, then, was that knowledge not accepted by Cūḍālā?
For she is the foremost among those who know reality; whatever she says and whatever she does, my dear, all that is indeed true and should be practiced with reverence.
But if her words were not carried out by you, O King,
then why was that total renunciation not perfected?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"The kingdom has been abandoned, the home abandoned, and likewise the country; even the wife has been abandoned. Yet, my dear friend, why has total renunciation not been performed?"
Cūḍālā said:
"Wealth, wife, home, kingdom, land, parasol, and kinsmen—all these are yours, O King; what renunciation is there for you here?"
There remains for you a supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished;
by renouncing that entirely, you shall attain the highest state of sorrowlessness.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"If my entire kingdom were not mine, then even this entire forest would be mine—rich with *sāla* trees and thickets; yet even that, I shall renounce."
Vasiṣṭha:
O Rāma, even as he was speaking thus, urged by the words of Kumbha,
the self-controlled hero Śikhidhvaja, in a mere twinkling of an eye—
With a very firm resolve, he thoroughly wiped away that desire for the forest from his heart,
just as the monsoon wind sweeps away a streak of dust from its own bank.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Indeed, I have completely abandoned all latent impressions (vāsanā), even from the forest with its trees, caves, and ravines; thus, the renunciation of everything stands established within me."
Kumbha said:
"The forest on the mountain slope, the chasm, the water, the trees, the dry land—none of these belong to you; how then can you claim total renunciation?"
There remains for you a supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished;
by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain the highest state of sorrowlessness.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Sage, if all this does not belong to me, then let all that—including the pond, the ground, and the hut—be my own hermitage; I shall abandon it immediately."
Vasiṣṭha: O Rāma, even as he was speaking thus, the self-controlled hero Śikhidhvaja, impelled by the words of Kumbha, [attained his goal] in a mere moment of meditation.
Wipe away that state of weariness from within your heart by means of pure consciousness,
just as the wind sweeps away a streak of dust with its very movement.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Indeed, even from my own hermitage—with its trees, huts, and creepers—my latent impressions have been abandoned by me; thus, the renunciation of everything is established within me."
A water-jar,
a tree, a pond, dry land, a shrub, a hut, or a fence of creepers—
none of these belong to you; how then can you have renounced everything?
There remains for you one supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished;
by renouncing that entirely, you shall attain the highest state of sorrowlessness.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If all this of mine is not [what I seek], then I shall renounce all that— my vessels and so forth,
my leather tent, my rosary, and the rest."
Vasiṣṭha,
having spoken thus, rose up from his seat with an unagitated and tranquil mind,
his soul pure like an autumnal cloud rising from a mountain peak.
But Kumbha remained for a year watching that performance with steady gaze,
seated upon his throne like the sun upon his chariot amidst its worldly duties.
"Let him do whatever he does; this is his supreme purification.
Having said this, Kumbha remained silent and gazed at Śikhidhvaja.
Śikhidhvaja, however, brought all that household utensils and equipment from the hermitage to one single spot, just as the ocean-born [Vasiṣṭha] gathered the waters of the earth.
Having established that [fire], he kindled the flame with dry fuel,
like the sun, moving its rays, igniting the surface of a sun-crystal.
He entered [the fire] to cast away that collection of vessels and utensils,
as the sun ascends the peak of Mount Meru to burn up the world upon its seat.
O you who are dear to those who observe vows, let my debt to you be paid off by the very fact that for all this time I have chosen you, without any differentiation in my understanding.
Now that delusion has been dispelled, you no longer serve me;
by the grace of the son of a god, O wooden staff, homage be to you!
Having said this, Śikhidhvaja cast his bamboo staff into the fire,
just as the ocean casts its long-flowing stream of the Gaṅgā into the submarine fire.
O friend, like countless births enumerated by you and me, these words of counsel have been counted today; depart, for you no longer benefit me.
I have wandered for a long time in the forest of mantras and moved along the paths of ritual duties;
I have seen the stations of the Dharma, my friend, and now I rest.
Having spoken thus, Śikhidhvaja cast the rosary into the fire,
just as the wind casts the pure streaks of stars into the sky during the conflagration at the end of an aeon.

By me, who am but a human deer, you have for a long time been held fast through lack of understanding— like a forest deer caught by a forest deer— with a livelihood that was like compassion, as if by a deer-skin.
Go now, O you who possess true luster; may your paths be auspicious. Go to the state of fire, and let the starry sky be equal to your own space.
Having released it from his body and grasped it with both hands,
the king cast off the hide, just as the wind casts a cloud from a mountain into a forest fire.
"By you being held by me, water has been held by you for me;
O virtuous water-pot, a proper return has been made for what was done."
You alone are the supreme abode of all that is lovely friendship, steadfast benevolence, and every form of goodness.
O friend, go by that very same fire by which you came to me after purifying your body; may your paths be auspicious.
Having spoken thus, he then gave that water-pot to the wife of the Vedic scholar, saying:
"Whatever is good should be given even to a great fire."
Like the mind of a fool, you always dwell in concealment beneath [the surface]; what kind of destiny is fitting for you? O grass-mat, turn to ashes!
Having said this, he took up a seat that increases the fuel of the fire,
and for the sake of purification and as a seat, he cast it into the blazing fire.
That which is to be abandoned must indeed be abandoned by the virtuous without delay;
however, when that which is to be accepted is considered desirable, the virtuous employ the appropriate means.
I shall quickly cast this entire collection of vessels into the fire;
for fire, by burning its fuel all at once, finds satisfaction.
O virtuous one, you who possess the instruments of action yet are yourself devoid of action, I abandon you.
You should not feel any distress here; for who would maintain that which is of no further use?

Having spoken thus, the king instantly offered into the fire his entire collection of vessels and utensils suitable for the pleasures of forest life; that mass of implements was cast into the flames all at once, as if the world were burning in the fire at the end of an aeon.
The ninety-seventh canto, titled "The Renunciation of Everything," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, rising up, he burned that dry leaf-hut,
which had been vainly imagined and constructed by his own ignorant mind.
Whatever remained there, Śikhidhvaja,
with an unagitated mind and observing silence, gradually [perceived] through his composed intellect.
In his rage, he burned, cast far away, abandoned, and broke the collection of vessels, as well as his own clothes, food, and so forth.
That hermitage of his became one whose own stability was burnt away and destroyed,
resembling the hermitage of Dakṣa’s sacrifice when it was devastated by the power of Vīrabhadra.
The deer and birds fled from that hermitage, abandoning their rumination,
like terrified people fleeing from a great city consumed by fire.
The king, who was satisfied with his mere outward appearance and devoid of affection, said: "That collection of goods is being consumed in the fire along with the dry fuel. (MU 6.97.6)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Oh! After a long time, O Son of the Gods, I have been awakened;
I have become perfected, solitary, pure, happy, and enlightened."
What indeed could this thing be that follows the sequence of mental construction,
which serves as the support for vessels, utensils, places, dwellings, and so forth?
To the extent that the obstacles, which are the causes of bondage, are abandoned,
to that same extent the mind attains supreme peace.
I am at peace, I am fully extinguished, I am happy, and I am victorious;
my obstructions have been destroyed, and I have accomplished the relinquishment of everything.
"Naked, with the directions as my garment and the directions as my friend, I stand here;
O son of a god, through such great renunciation, what else remains?"
Kumbha said:
"O King Śikhidhvaja, you have not abandoned anything at all;
do not vainly pretend to experience the supreme bliss of universal renunciation."
There remains for you a supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished;
by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain the highest state of sorrowlessness.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed Rāma, lotus-eyed one, having heard this, that king reflected for a moment and spoke as follows.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O son of a deity, when all has been completely renounced, only this body remains for me— a mass of venomous serpents that are the senses, and a form composed of blood and flesh."
Therefore, having risen and brought about my own destruction through a leap from the cliff before the city— free from all obstacles— I shall become one who has renounced everything.
Vasiṣṭha,
having said this, was just as he was making a swift effort to rise in order to cast his body into the chasm standing before him, when Kumbha addressed him.
Kumbha said:
"O King, why do you cast away this innocent body in the great forest? For even a bull, when enraged, kills a calf though it be ignorant."
This wretched body is indeed inert, mute in nature, and miserable;
it is nothing at all belonging to you—do not, therefore, direct your anger toward it in vain.
This deluded soul remains as if absorbed in meditation within itself alone,
yet it is moved by another, just as a piece of wood is driven by a wave.
Another person, who deserves to be restrained, repeatedly and forcibly agitates him,
just as a drunken thief disturbs an ascetic dwelling in solitude.
For the body is not at fault for the experience of pleasure and pain;
nor is the tree at fault for the falling of its fruit because of its own movements, just as it is not the fault of the self.
The quivering wind brings about the falling of fruits, flower-tops, and blossoms;
what offense has the young tree committed against itself by being virtuous?
O lotus-eyed one, it is said that even though you have abandoned your body,
your renunciation of everything has not reached completion, for that is indeed difficult to achieve.
You are pointlessly casting away this innocent body of Bhrigu; by abandoning the body, you do not become a true renunciant.
If you abandon that evil by which this body is agitated, like a tree by a rutting elephant, then you are one who possesses great renunciation.
O King, when that [ego] is abandoned, everything including the body and so forth is abandoned;
for if it is not, then even though this [body] has been utterly consumed by fire, it sprouts again and again.
Śikhidhvaja said:
By what is this body moved? What is the seed of births and karmas? O handsome one, when what is abandoned does everything become relinquished?
Kumbha said:
"O virtuous one, for human beings, the renunciation of everything does not occur through the abandonment of the body, nor by the relinquishing of a kingdom, nor by the burning of huts and such."
When everything from every side, and whatever exists within that single cause of all,
has been completely relinquished, then the renunciation of all has been accomplished.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Everything is all-pervading and belongs to all; it must be abandoned and relinquished in every way.
Tell me, O best among those who know the reality of all things, what is meant by 'everything'?"
Kumbha said: "O virtuous one, that which is the support of all arts (kalās), known by such names as the individual soul (jīva) and vital breath (prāṇa),
which is neither inert nor non-inert, and which is deluded— that is traditionally remembered as the 'all' (the mind)."

O Lord of the Earth, the mind is the seed of everything— of sovereignty and the like, of the body and the like, and of the stages of life and the like— just as the seed of a tree is the source of the tree itself.
When the seed of everything has been abandoned, everything is fully abandoned;
through the repeated realization of both the possible and the impossible, there comes to be the relinquishment of all.
Everything— whether dharma or adharma, kingship or the forest—
is supreme suffering for one with a mind, but supreme happiness for one without a mind.
All this revolves as nothing but the mind appearing in the form of the world,
like a seed appearing in the form of a tree through the web of forms such as the body.
Just as a tree is moved by the wind, a mountain by an earthquake,
or a bellows by the one who blows it, so too is this body moved by the mind.
Know that the mind is the very firm casket for those great jewels— birth, old age, death, and all things experienced by living beings.
O Sage, by means of designations and functions corresponding to its activities— such as "mind," "living soul," "intellect," "illusion," and "vital breath"— the mind is so called.
They say that the mind is everything; when it is relinquished, O Lord of the Earth, one has made the renunciation of all, reaching the end of all mental anguish and physical disease.
O best among those who know renunciation, the wise understand that the renunciation of the mind is the renunciation of everything;
when that is accomplished, O mighty-armed one, truth is realized by someone.
When the mind is relinquished, duality and even unity dissolve everywhere;
something remains that is peaceful, pure, singular, and free from ailment.
The wise know that the mind is the field for this continuous harvest of cyclic existence;
once the field has become non-field, how could rice possibly arise?
Mind alone, sporting with existence and non-existence, evolves here in manifold forms as objects, just as water manifests in the form of waves.
O King, by means of total renunciation— which takes the form of uplifting the mind—
one properly attains everything at all times, just as through universal sovereignty.
O King, just as there is another object for your universal renunciation, so too do you become an object for another if you, O renouncer, accept anything from him.
By him who has renounced everything, the entire web of the world spanning the three times is encompassed within, just as a string of pearls is contained within a single pearl.
By whom everything has been relinquished, even in that void he remains established,
like a thread within a pearl, sustaining the entire world throughout the three periods of time.
By him everything has been illuminated as by a lamp filled with oil;
yet he stands having abandoned everything, peaceful like a lamp devoid of oil.
He by whom everything has been obscured, as if by a lamp lacking oil,
shines forth as the luminous self, equal to a lamp filled with oil.
Just as when all things have been removed, only space remains,
so too when the relinquishing of everything has been accomplished, only consciousness remains.
For just as space, O King, is indifferent toward all things and nothing else,
so too, my dear, the relinquishment of everything is called nirvāṇa.
For total renunciation, though itself empty of self-nature, is the support of all prosperities—
of infinite and noble things, just as space is for the inhabitants of heaven.
Through drinking the elixir of the essence of total renunciation, no fears of old age and death afflict one at all,
just as streaks of dirt do not stain the sky.
The renunciation of everything is the cause of greatness for that which possesses stainless luster;
because it relinquishes all, space is pure, stable, and vast.
The renunciation of everything is supreme bliss; anything else is most terrible suffering.
Having accepted this with the word "Om," do whatever you wish.
For one who renounces everything, everything indeed stands at his service;
just as water enters the fire, so too does it flow back into the ocean.
Within the very midst of total renunciation lies the knowledge that brings clarity to the self;
for indeed, it is within the emptiness of a vessel that jewels and such are contained.
Precisely because of his total renunciation, even at the time of his passing during the Kali age,
the Śākya Sage remained as steadfast as Mount Meru, free from all fear.
O Great King, the renunciation of everything is the foundation of all prosperity;
for to him who does not grasp at anything, everything is given.
Having renounced everything, peaceful, pure, and equal to the sky, you have become gentle;
O King, be of that very nature which is yours.

Having renounced everything, O Great-Souled One, you have abandoned that which is sufficient for its sake; having relinquished even that renunciation along with its acceptance, become one whose nature is liberated, O Protector of the Earth!
The Ninety-Eighth Chapter, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," by Vasiṣṭha.
While Kumbha was thus repeatedly speaking of the renunciation of the mind,
the gentle King, reflecting within himself, spoke these words.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"The bird of the sky of the heart, the monkey of the tree of the heart—
though repeatedly driven away, the mind indeed returns to me again and again."
I know how to seize this fish, yet I am as agitated as a child; I do not know how to let it go, as bewildered as a blind man regarding that which is supreme.
O Blessed One, tell me truly first the essential nature of the mind;
thereafter, O Blessed One, tell me truly how to relinquish the mind.
Kumbha said:
"O Great King, know that latent impressions alone are the very nature of the mind;
indeed, the word 'citta' is cited as a synonym for 'vāsanā'."
But this renunciation is exceedingly easy to perform and simple to accomplish;
it brings greater bliss than even worldly pleasure and is more beautiful than even a flower.
But for a fool, the renunciation of the mind has indeed become difficult to accomplish—
like a universal empire for a Pukkasa, or like Mount Sumeru becoming a blade of grass.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I know the true nature of the mind to be agitated and composed of latent impressions (vāsanā). I consider its abandonment to be more difficult to accomplish than even the shattering of a diamond."
Of the flower of the fragrance of saṃsāra, and of the sesame seed of the oil of suffering;
of the lotus fiber of the world's youth, and of the void of the wind of delusion.
Tell me how the effortless relinquishing of the mind occurs— that which drives the machine of the body and acts as the bee within the heart-lotus.
Kumbha said:
O virtuous one, that which is the destruction of this mind— the cessation of saṃsāra—
is itself called the renunciation of the mind by those of far-reaching vision.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I believe that for the sake of one's own perfection, the destruction of the mind follows from the relinquishing of the mind;
how then can this non-existence of the mind be experienced?"
Kumbha said:
Uproot the tree of the mind, which has "I" as its seed and possesses branches, fruits, and shoots— uproot it along with its very root, becoming as pure as the sky.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, what is the root of the mind? What is its sprout, and what is its origin? What are its branches, and what are its trunks? And how is it uprooted?
Kumbha said:
Know that this which arises as the sense of "I," the conscious self whose nature is sentience, is the seed of this tree of the mind that pervades the entire world.
The nature of consciousness, which consists of the sense of "I," is declared to be the seed of the mind;
it is the field for the state of the Supreme Self and the eye of that which is composed of illusion.
That sprout which arises first from this [seed], having the form of experience,
consisting of certainty and being formless, is called "cognition" (buddhi).
The swelling of this sprout called "intellect," which consists of volitional constructs, is termed "mind" (citta) and is designated as "manas."
The living being consists of false perception; though its nature is empty, it is like a mirage. This body of his is a mere pillar, composed of sinews, bones, and flesh.
Those branches of this tree of the mind which extend from one country to another distant land for one who knows space and time are long, reaching far, and widely spread.
Furthermore, the sense faculties and enjoyments— consisting of waves of existence and non-existence—
are its great trunks, crowded with the fruits of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Cutting away the branches of this tree-like mind at every moment, apply yourself primarily to the excavation of its root.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, while I am merely pruning the branches and such of the tree of the mind, how can I effect the complete eradication of its very root?
Kumbha said:
The various latent impressions (vāsanā) are like branches endowed with fruits, trunks, and so forth;
when they are not cultivated, they are severed within by the power of pure consciousness (saṃvid).
One whose mind is unattached, who observes silence, and whose speech and deliberations are stilled,
who acts only when the time is right— he is one whose inner creeper of the mind has been cut down.
He who stands firm while cutting through the web of the tree and creepers of the mind by means of human effort would be fit for the testing of its very root.
The pruning of the branches of the tree of the mind is secondary; the cutting of the roots is primary. Therefore, be intent upon scraping away the very roots of that tree.
O one of great intelligence, thoroughly perform the burning of the root by means of the primary [method];
in this way, the thicket of the mind's thorns becomes indeed stateless (acittatā).
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, what fire would be capable of burning and thus serving its purpose for that seed of the tree of the mind which consists of the sense of "I"?
Kumbha said:
O King, this inquiry into one's own self, taking the form of "Who might I be?",
is known as the fire for burning the seed of the wicked tree of the mind.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, I have reflected upon this many times with my great intelligence, until I realized that I am neither the world, nor the earth, nor even the circle of the mandala.
Neither the bank of a river, nor the forest, nor the leaf-hut and such;
neither the body and so forth due to its insentience, nor the flesh, bones, blood, and so on.
Neither are the organs of action, nor are the organs of perception;
neither is the mind, nor even the intellect, nor the sense of "I," because of its insentience.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, so does the state of being the "I" exist in the conscious self;
whereas the insentient [body] is unreal by its very nature, therefore, O Sage, I am not that.

In the supreme state, which consists of a particular arrangement [of consciousness], there exist no objects such as the self or words, because of its absolute infinity, just as a great tree does not exist in space.
"O Blessed One, although I know that the purification of the 'I'-notion is sufficient,
when I do not know it within myself, I suffer for that reason, O Great Sage."
Kumbha said:
O Lord of the Earth, if you had not been so dull-witted, you would have known that this was merely a small group; therefore, O one of great intelligence, tell me who you truly are.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O best of the wise, I am pure consciousness alone, the clear self-awareness,
wherein these entities take their flavor and by which they are created.
For one such as I, this clinging is surely groundless;
yet, because I am [bound] by that which has a cause, I do not know how to abandon it.
O Sage, since I am unable to wipe away this non-existent, non-self-defining impurity from my soul, I suffer most grievously because of it.
Kumbha said: "Tell me, O mighty-armed one, what is that great impurity clinging to you,
by which you remain a transmigrating being, whether through the existent or the non-existent?"
Śikhidhvaja said:
"The sense of 'I' (ahaṃbhāva) is the seed of the tree of the mind; that is my impurity.
Yet I do not know how to abandon it; though abandoned again and again, it returns to me."
Kumbha:
An effect arises from a cause; that which [arises] must exist everywhere.
But anything else, being non-existent like the appearance of a double moon, is not found even when perceived.
The effect arises from a cause, consisting of the nature of ego;
therefore, having investigated that cause, tell me quickly with your own self.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Sage, I understand that the perception of 'I' is the cause of this fault;
tell me, O Lord of Sages, how that may come to rest."
Because the mind is oriented toward objects of thought, it remains as the "I" for the sake of suffering;
O Sage, tell me how to bring about the cessation of those objects so that it may be pacified.
Kumbha said:
"O knower of causes, tell me quickly the cause of sensation;
then I shall instruct you in the sequence of causes and non-causes."
Tell me, how did that which consists of the object of knowledge and the knower, and of the thinkable and the thinker, come to become a cause when it is itself without a cause?

Śikhidhvaja said: O Sage, this existence of objects, consisting of the body and so forth, which takes the form of the perception of the knowable— whether in the nature of the conscious or the unconscious— is the cause here.
Sensation arises through the existence of objects as having a body and so forth;
it is like the movement caused by the appearance of a non-existent streak in the wind.
I do not perceive the non-existence of the reality of things by means of which the perception of "I-ness"—
the seed of the mind— might be completely stilled.
Kumbha said:
If the existence of entities such as the body and so forth were real, then that [consciousness] would belong to you;
but since there is no existence of the body and so forth, upon what is your cognition based?
Śikhidhvaja said:
How could that which possesses some perceivable nature consisting of conceptualization be of an unreal form? How could light be darkness?

O Sage, how can it be that the body—which is endowed with hands, feet, and so forth; which possesses the manifestation of the fruits of action; and which is constantly being experienced—does not exist?
Kumbha said:
O protector of the earth, that effect for which no cause exists is not found here; the perception of such an effect is merely an illusion.
An effect never exists without a cause;
where indeed could that substance be produced which has no seed?
But know that which is causeless yet appears as if it were a real effect at the outset to be the delusion of the observer, comparable to the water of a mirage.
Know that this which has arisen from false delusion is indeed non-existent;
even by one who exerts great effort, the water of a mirage cannot be obtained.
The observation of a cause is not logical for that which is non-existent, such as a double moon-image;
for whom does the decoration of all the limbs of the son of a barren woman shine?
O King, know that this effect— the body and so forth, this skeleton of bones— does not exist at all, because it is impossible for an effect to exist without a cause.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Lord of Sages, why is the father not considered the cause of this body, which is endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs, and is constantly perceived?
Kumbha said: O King, because of the absence of a cause, that which is called "father" does not exist.
That which has arisen from what is non-existent is itself said to be non-existent.
The seed is said to be the cause of all things and effects;
indeed, my dear, no sprout can arise in this world without a seed.
Therefore, for that effect whose cause is not found here, it does not exist when the seed is absent; yet the cognition of it is an illusion.
That which is necessarily non-existent and without a seed is a delusion of the mind;
it is equal to the vision of two moons, water in a desert, or the son of a barren woman.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Among the grandfathers, sons, and fathers within the three worlds,
why is the primordial Grandfather not considered the cause, since he was born first?"
Kumbha said: O King, even that primordial grandfather does not exist at all;
for since there is an absence of a cause, no effect can ever belong to anyone.
O Grandfather, because its own seed— the cause— is eternally non-existent,
that which is perceived as the "first" being does not exist as anything other than an error.
Like the water of a mirage, the Grandfather (Brahmā) appears as a mere form of delusion; moreover, his capacity for causal efficacy is itself of the nature of an error.
"Because of this false notion regarding my grandfather and the others, their density has indeed ceased; now I shall wipe away the rest."
Therefore, that which is the sky of consciousness within the Self, shining eternally and beautifully by its own nature as the essence of consciousness—that is this very God.
By that very [consciousness], the Self has declared itself to be "the Lotus-born" (Brahmā) and "the one whose form is space"; thus, all this is peaceful.
The ninety-ninth canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja. Śikhidhvaja:
If this delusion, extending from the Brahma-world down to a blade of grass,
appears and is capable of causal efficiency, then it remains established as the cause of suffering.
Kumbha:
Thus, the thinning of this delusion of the world has now occurred,
like the solidification of water by cold is brought about by heat.
The wise know that ignorance has indeed perished once it has become slackened;
for there is no disappearance of its former state without its destruction.
Indeed, that very attenuation of the awareness of creation is the cause for the attainment of the cessation of creation and for the realization of the supreme state.
When attenuation is observed in him, then, through the gradual disappearance of his former constitution, his own pacification also becomes possible.
O King, by this very sequence, you should understand this Primordial Person as the arising of the form of delusion, like water produced from a mirage.
Even in the absence of a grandfather, this continuity of beings is non-existent;
for that which is established by what is itself unestablished is never established.
For this perception of a real entity has arisen like the water of a mirage;
through investigation, it dissolves just as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does.
As for the claim that an effect comes into being from the absence of a cause after having not existed,
its nature cannot be established except through false cognition.
False view has never been observed even once;
by whom could jars ever be filled with the water of a mirage?
Śikhidhvaja said: Why is the Supreme Brahman— the infinite, unborn, unmanifest, Lord, peaceful, and immutable— not the cause of the First Creator?
Kumbha says:
Because it lacks the state of being a cause, and because it lacks the state of being an effect, Brahman is therefore the non-dual, unitary, and changeless Self— neither an effect nor a cause.
How could Brahman— which is without agent, object, or instrument, without cause, without seed, inconceivable, and unknowable— be an agent?
When that [reality] becomes devoid of the nature of an effect due to its lack of causality,
then there is the perception of that non-dual unity which is without beginning or end.
How, for whom, by what means, and at what time could that which is inconceivable, unknowable, auspicious, peaceful, and immutable become an agent, an enjoyer, or anything at all?
Therefore, nothing here has been created, nor does the world and so forth exist;
there is no agent and no enjoyer; everything is peaceful, unborn, and auspicious.
Due to the absence of a cause, this world is not the effect of anything; and because it is not an effect, it does not exist—thus, creation is not found.
When the world is not the effect of any cause, then the non-existence of all things is established; and when that is established, whose is the cognition?
Thus, in the absence of sensation, there is no cause for the sense of "I";
therefore, you are pure and you are liberated—what use are mere words regarding bondage and liberation?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Ah, I am awakened, O Blessed One! What you have spoken is most excellent and appropriate.
Because of the absence of a cause, I now understand that there is no creator here in this world, nor is there Brahman as such."
Due to the absence of an agent, the world does not exist; therefore, there is no perception of objects.
Consequently, there is no mind or the like, nor is there any seed for it, nor is there anything such as the sense of "I."
This being so, I am pure, I am awakened, and yet I am not; I bow to myself and bow to the Supreme, for from the perspective of awakening, there is nothing at all.
The perception of objects is merely false; it appears as something that does not exist at all.
Enough with this "I" and so forth; I abide in peace like the hollow of space.

The vision that distinguishes the objects of the world—including space, direction, time, divisions, and the flood of activities—has, alas, after a long time been stilled; or rather, it has surely become established as Brahman alone.
I am stilled; I am extinguished; I abide in the Supreme; I do not go, nor do I rise, nor do I set.
I remain as the unending Self as it truly is; I am the auspicious, the pure, the holy, and the silent.
The hundredth canto, titled "The Resting of Śikhidhvaja," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having thus attained rest in Brahman, Śikhidhvaja remained for a moment with his mind completely stilled, like an extinguished lamp.
Having reached the state of cessation through the transformation of non-conceptual meditative absorption, he was suddenly awakened by Kumbha with the words, "It is my own sport! (svalīlayā).
Kumbha said:
O King, you have awakened from the sleep of ignorance and stand as Śiva; therefore, there is no further task for you, whether by setting or by not setting.
O dear one, you have now become liberated while living— your self shining forth all at once, abiding as the nature of the state beyond desire, and entirely free from the perception of parts.
Vasiṣṭha:
Thus awakened by Kumbha, he became fully enlightened;
having emerged from the casket of great delusion, he shone forth intensely.

With his intellect resting in an instant upon perceiving the non-existence of all visible objects, the liberated soul spoke thus with ease: The liberated soul, having attained rest in a mere moment by seeing the non-existence of the perceptible world, spoke thus with effortless ease.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Although this is already largely understood by me, let that which I ask be told once more for the sake of my refined awakening, O giver of honor, O destroyer of delusion!
In that which is auspicious, peaceful, without appearance, supreme, and the untransgressible Self—
whence could there arise the cognition called the seer, the seeing, and the seen, which constitutes the essence of the universe?
Kumbha said:
Well asked, O Great King; you shine with the light of awakening.
For this alone remains for you of all that is to be known; therefore, listen to this.
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving,
all of it— abounding in every variety— is destroyed at the end of the aeon.
Then, neither light nor darkness spreads forth;
that which is real and essential remains at the end of the play of the great aeon.
Pure consciousness alone— stainless, beautiful, and shining like the stainless sky— is liberated from all mental constructs and endowed with supreme splendor.
That which is uniquely arisen, utterly transparent, peaceful, pervasive, and radiant—
the splendor whose nature is the Supreme Self, motionless and consisting of pure consciousness alone.
Brahman is inconceivable, unknowable, equal, auspicious, and immovable; it is the fullness of liberation, as if overflowing with prosperity.
It is subtler than the subtlest, and more massive than the most massive;
it is weightier than the heaviest, and even the most excellent among the excellent.
Such is that supreme, subtle reality, compared to which this sky appears as gross as Mount Meru would appear next to an atom.
Such is that supreme grossness, before which this world appears like an atom; it shines forth only in some places, or does not shine at all.
Such is that most precious sovereignty over the world which remains unimpaired;
yet once one has realized this stainless peace, it becomes like a mere scrap of withered straw.
Such is that supreme good which exists in the Lord:
that the splendor of the multitude of objects in the world arises from the awareness of its own existence.
O King, that single essence alone exists here, pervasive;
it is grasped by the intellect as one through its absolute oneness, yet even as one, it is not manifold due to its state of non-duality.
Therefore, no second conceptualization whatsoever exists;
the reality of the Self alone shines forth, complete and unimpaired.
Everything is always established as if arisen in every form;
because it is inexpressible and unattainable, it is neither effect nor cause.
Because it is inaccessible to perception and other means of knowledge, that one supreme reality is something indescribable;
it is everything, the essence of all, subtle, and consists solely of pure experience.
How can that ineffable form, which has emerged as something like a perceiver—
and whether it exists or does not exist— possess the status of a cause?
Indeed, from that whose nature transcends all means of valid cognition, nothing whatsoever is born, because it is not the seed of anything and, due to being ineffable, is not a cause.
It is devoid of agent, object, and instrument; it is reality, a mass of consciousness, and unimpaired.
It is the nature of the Self, without appearance, characterized by self-awareness.
Therefore, O Sage, nothing whatsoever is born from the supreme Brahman;
tell me, how indeed could there be a sequence of produced and producer in the unmanifest?
In the tranquil state, nothing whatsoever is born, nor does anything whatsoever perish;
Brahman abides by its own existence, being neither seed nor cause.
That is pure experience alone; therefore, nothing else exists apart from it.
Whatever there is in the world, such as the sense of "I" and so forth, that indeed is the infinite itself.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Śiva, O Sage, I know that in the world there is no such thing as a creator or a destroyer; yet this perception of creation appears—tell me quickly how this is so.
Kumbha said:
That essence of consciousness, which is without beginning or end, abides within its own self-awareness;
the wise know that world to be that very state of being, utterly transparent, and consisting of nothing but thatness.

Know that which is called the manifestation of one's own conscious self— wherein the vision of an object of consciousness is impossible— to be the awareness of "I," the Virāṭ Self in which the world is established.
Just as no distinction exists between the wind and the movement of the wind,
so too there is no distinction between pure consciousness and the sense of "I," which are comparable to emptiness and space.
Just as waves and the like exist in water due to place and time and possess a cause,
so too the world exists in the Supreme— which is devoid of place and time— and is thus without a cause.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"In this world, that which consists of waves and the like within water and so forth may indeed have a cause;
however, I do not perceive the 'I'-sense and the world in the Supreme to be without a cause."
Kumbha said: "Now, O Lord of the Earth, you have understood this truth:
this world, consisting of 'I'-ness and so forth, does not exist here at all."
The world exists as Śiva in essence, devoid of the meaning of the word "world";
it is fashioned within space itself, peaceful, or even more subtle than space.
Just as emptiness exists in the sky, so does this [Brahman] abide in Brahman;
it exists neither in the form of an existent nor a non-existent thing, nor in any form whatsoever.
This world, being of such a nature, becomes auspicious through right knowledge;
by the power of right knowledge, even poison becomes nectar.
All incorrect knowledge brings supreme suffering to the entire world;
even nectar, when consumed with the perception that it is poison, acts like the essence of poison.
Because he is the Lord, whatever this conscious Lord perceives,
that very thing immediately comes to be as such, auspiciously manifesting in that form.
Just as a flame or a circle of light persists in its very same nature despite the delusions of various forms, so indeed does the reality of Brahman persist.
That which exists within the Self as the supreme essence of consciousness, yet remains latent,
is perceived by that [Self] as this very world of "I-ness" and so forth.
Only the supreme Śiva shines here in this way as the ultimate; whence could there be a world, an "I," and so forth? Thus, a question regarding these is simply not appropriate here.
A question is appropriate regarding a thing that actually exists;
but what is the use of an examination or a question concerning that which does not exist at all?
Just as existence is not found in gold without its particular configuration, so the Lord has no established existence without the world and the sense of "I."
Because it lacks any other cause, this [world] does not exist; rather, Brahman alone unfolds in this manner.
Even while not unfolding, it remains here established as the "I" and as the world.
Impelled by that very same [power] within me, these states of being mutually stir one another's hearts, like a multitude of couples at the onset of the five-arrowed god of love.
Pure consciousness alone is accumulated by pure consciousness through pure consciousness itself;
even the Self, though non-different from itself, appears as if it were non-self, as if it were different, through its own self.
From the Full they draw forth the Full; from the Full they have made full things.
From the Full come full things, yet the Full itself remains.
It is pure consciousness alone that shines within itself by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness;
yet, when that very same [consciousness] does not shine [in that way], it is called the perception of creation.
I am indeed consciousness, and this [other] becomes as if consciousness itself by its own nature;
yet, though it appears so, it does not truly become [consciousness], for it does not abandon its own stainless form.
The conscious form is without beginning or end, an infinite form of the mind;
it appears as the sovereign body of the Self-existent One.
Then one perceives this [world] as either entirely non-existent because of its lack of intrinsic nature, or indeed as existent;
through intense contemplation, the object of perception attains density and gradually comes into being.
This world, in its nature as a pervasive expansion, is described by the term "intrinsic being" (svabhāva) as being tranquil; it is ineffable and one.
Established as a reality, it is the essence of the true nature of experience, free from the state of "worldliness," consisting in the vision of its own inherent wonder.
The One Hundred and First Chapter, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," by Kumbha.
There is no object consisting of consciousness, nor is there an external one, nor even emptiness;
because its essence is nothing but feeling, it is called an "object" according to how it is perceived.
Just as fluidity belongs to water, know that consciousness is without cause;
it is the space-like self, eternal and infinite, abiding exactly as it is.
Because there is no exclusion of the counter-correlate for either non-existence or existence,
others do not establish the status of existence or non-existence through that [negation].
If the supreme reality were something tranquil that could become fit for the state of being a cause,
how could it be immovable, without appearance, and beyond conceptualization?
Therefore, Brahman is never the cause nor even the seed of any effect whatsoever; consequently, no creation exists.
For no other origin for this creation is possible;
therefore, apart from pure consciousness alone, a creation consisting of insentient matter does not exist.
Whatever is seen here is but a mass of consciousness, undifferentiated,
devoid of the possibility of existence, and colored by the taste of the word and its meaning "world."
An entity consisting of duality, unity, and so forth, does not arise as an object because of the absence of a cause; it is like a flower in the sky, [known] only through one's own experience.
Because it culminates solely in the destruction of the entity, that which is unborn is not logically possible;
for when there is perception, destruction is certain, and the birth of what has been destroyed is also certain.
Or else, if you perceive this entire mass of objects as always existing, eternal, and yet also destroyed— then since this reality is of a single nature here, why this distress?
But this perception which occurs is the wonder of the nature of consciousness;
there exists only the reality of the nature of consciousness, and duality and unity do not exist at all.
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, since the existence of objective entities is absent,
and since there is no possibility of cultivation [of them], the cultivation of "I-ness" does not exist for you.
Since the existence of the sense of "I" is impossible, what else can be called the mind?
Thus, the mind does not have the form of "I"; therefore, O Lord, be free from delusion.
Free from latent impressions, with a tranquil mind, silent, and composed of the supreme ether— whether possessing a body or bodiless, whether stationary or moving— be thus.

Because of the purity of the vision of all-ness, because of the establishment of the non-existence of objective entities, and because of the absence of mental cultivation within the mind, the "I" does not exist at all; therefore, there is auspiciousness (śiva).

Through the cultivation of the meaning of the Vedas— that "all is Brahman"— and through direct experience, because the perceived object alone is realized as true, that which is called "mind" does not exist.
Therefore, you are that stainless, causeless, eternally liberated Brahman—eternal, entire, manifold yet one;
empty, devoid of transformation, non-existent yet existent, without beginning or middle; everything, yet not anything at all—abide as you truly are.
The one hundred and second canto, titled "The First Awakening of Śikhidhvaja. Śikhidhvaja:
Tell me that other [reasoning] by which my understanding that "the mind does not exist" becomes clear through logic; I have not understood the Buddha’s teaching skillfully.
Kumbha said:
O royal sage, the mind does not exist at all, anywhere, or at any time;
that which appears as if it were a mind is the imperishable one called Brahman.
Where the world itself, consisting of the knower and the known, does not exist,
how can there be the mental constructions of "I," "you," "that," and so forth?
This world that has been described as something existing does not exist at all;
it is Brahman alone that shines within itself—listen to this, for how can it be understood?
This world was impelled at the very beginning of creation after the great dissolution;
however, this explanation was given by me elsewhere for the sake of your understanding.
Because causes such as the nature of grasping (*upādāna*) do not exist,
and because it is impossible for all entities to be without a cause.
Since the world does not exist apart from the Self realized in this way,
therefore that which appears here is nothing but the manifestation of Brahman.
"It is false to say that the God, who is ineffable and formless, creates this;
such speech is not consistent with reason, nor is it experienced as truth."
The statement that "the Lord— who is inexpressible, non-obstructive, of the nature of space, and formless—
creates the worlds" is merely for the amusement of those lacking wisdom.
By this very reasoning, O King, the mind does not exist; O virtuous one, the world itself is not real—how then could that which is derived from it, such as consciousness and so forth, exist?

For the mind is merely a latent impression (vāsanā), and an impression exists only when there is something to be impressed; that which is to be impressed is the world, and since that very world is non-existent, how can the existence of the mind be established?
That which shines as Brahman itself, by itself, through itself, within itself—
that very thing has been given such names as "mind" (citta) and so forth.
This visible world is its clothing; it has not arisen at all.
Since there was no cause prior [to it], how could there be the state of mind?

Therefore, this world does not exist here as something other than this expansive awareness itself, which is of the nature of pure consciousness-space and is called the supreme ether; it merely shines forth.
Whatever supreme space shines forth slightly due to the inherent clarity of the mirror of consciousness— that is the mind, and that has created the world.
This cognition that "I," "you," and "the world" exist is not real;
appearing falsely like a dream, it surely does not fulfill any purpose.

Since there is no world for one who is free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and because such impressions do not exist at all, what kind of mind could there be, where, from what cause, and how could it exist, given that it is composed of those very impressions?
This world, which is perceived as an object by the unawakened, is merely mental;
it is non-existent, formless, and has never arisen at all from the beginning.
Because of the absence of a cause, [the world] has never arisen at all, even at the beginning of creation; for such a thing is never seen in the world, in the scriptures, or through experience.
Neither beginninglessness, nor birthlessness, nor even stability can be established for this world,
which possesses form and consists of gross, resistant shapes.
Because all causes are absent according to worldly experience, scriptural authority, and direct perception,
the occurrences of the great dissolution cannot be denied.
Furthermore, whoever says that these things— established by scripture, experience, and the meaning of the Vedas,
such as dissolution and so forth— do not exist, is indeed a madman.
He for whom the worlds, the scriptures, and the Vedas are no authority when he speaks untruth—that utterly deluded one is a beast; one should not take refuge in him.
And it is not possible for that which is resistant and visible to have as its cause something non-resistant anywhere; nor can that which possesses form have as its cause that which is formless.
If this world were not perceived in such a manner, it would not appear at all;
nor would it be capable of causal efficiency, for this universe is indeed perceived in this way.
