Therefore, this [universe] belongs to that partless space of consciousness, which is unobstructed in form,
formless, infinite, and existing as prior even than the prior.
Of Brahman, who possesses all forms, that which is peaceful and of the peaceful is the equanimity;
it is the self-manifestation by its own nature, assuming the forms of creation and dissolution.
By that very [knowledge], his own body and this entire world were known for a moment;
yet in the next moment, he remained as the awakened, eternal Brahman within his own self.
All this is indeed Brahman; so where is this notion of the world and so forth?
Where is the mind and its like, where the body and its like, and where the conceptual constructions of duality, unity, and the rest?
All is without support, unborn, and profoundly peaceful; it is the beginningless and middleless inner self, existing exactly as it is.
This is neither manifold nor even non-manifold; remain as you are, established in the silence of perfect stillness.
The one hundred and third canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja. Śikhidhvaja:
Delusion has perished and mindfulness has been regained by me through your grace, O Sage;
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled, my mind at rest, and established in the Self.
Having known that which is to be known, I am the great silent sage who has crossed the vast ocean of illusion; peaceful, devoid of the sense of "I," and wise, I abide free from all affliction.
Alas! For how very long a time have I wandered in the interim;
now, at last, I have reached this imperishable and unshakable state.
This being the case, O Sage, the three worlds beginning with Sāhaṃtā do not exist;
I know that this which appears as the intellect of the ignorant is Brahman.
Kumbha said:

Where even the world itself does not exist, how could there be the manifestation of "I-ness"? Where, from where, of what kind, and in what manner could the entire mass of the sky-like cycle of existence (saṃsāra) be?
O friend, remain as a silent sage with a tranquil mind, conducting yourself according to the way things truly are, like the movement of a whirlpool within the belly of a gentle ocean.
This exists as it is, peaceful in its nature as Brahman;
"I" and "this world" are but the pure sky, consisting of the essence of words and their meanings.
This sky, which is devoid of beginning and end and is designated by the names "creation" and "dissolution," shines forth as the very essence of the wonder of consciousness.
Just as gold exists within the perception of various ornaments when those perceptions have ceased,
so too does this Brahman exist when the world and its primary objects have subsided.
Just as the intention of the self-arisen ones is its own destruction,
so indeed are these two— bondage and liberation— established as dependent upon one's own cognition.
The thought "I am" is indeed a conception that leads to bondage and utter destruction;
the thought "I am not" is the conception for liberation, O one of pure self.

That which is the knowledge of the true nature of the concepts and words regarding bondage and liberation— whether they be existent or non-existent— is called "Being" (Sat) and "Isolation" (Kaivalya).
The realization of "I am not" is success; the realization of "I am" leads to calamity.
He who possesses the pure awakening that "I am indeed that which is not-I" is one whose self is established in Being.
Through the mere absence of conceptualization, which consists in the arising of right knowledge,
conceptualization— which is by nature unreal— perishes of its own accord for the sake of accomplishment.
For in Śiva, whose essential nature is beyond conceptualization, there is no causality;
due to the absence of a cause, neither an effect nor any category of entity exists.
When the non-existence of objective entities is established, cognition is not tenable;
due to the absence of a cause, the ego-sense never arises.
In the absence of the arising of the sense of "I," whose is saṃsāra, and of what nature?
Since saṃsāra does not exist, only the Supreme remains as everything.
And that which shines here is the Real, abiding within the Supreme Self;
the Supreme, filled with the Supreme, unfolds as the Equal within the Supreme.
Know that by him all this world is rendered motionless, as if carved in stone; it stands as Brahman, appearing as if composed of rays of light.

Know that when the original architect is destroyed, the form of the city of imagination— which consists of both being and non-being— is like the world's appearance arising from the void, yet transparently clear.
The world throbs like a shadow-person; it is tranquil and devoid of mentation.
He who sees the world as being devoid of the referents of the word "world" truly sees.
The wise know that for one who possesses right knowledge, there is nirvāṇa when forms, light, and mental attention have become tasteless and their cultivation has ceased.
Just as there is wind that is motionless, and just as there is space that is not blue,
so too does Brahman exist as the world, like a configuration of gold.
These forms, light, and mental attentions— which are sapless, appearing as unreal, yet producing the cognition of the world— exist as the very form of Brahman.
Just as water, though possessed of many waves, is devoid of the word and the referent "wave," so too Brahman, though appearing as creation, is devoid of the word and the referent "creation."
Emanation itself is the supreme Brahman; the supreme Brahman is the vision of emanation.
This eternal meaning of the sentence is devoid of both the word "emanation" and its referent.

If the meaning of the word "Brahman" is established, how can there be a cognition of the meaning of the word "creation"? If the meaning of the word "creation" is established, how can there be a cognition of the meaning of the word "Brahman"?
When the manifestation and non-manifestation of all words and their meanings have arisen,
that certain pure space of consciousness is designated by the word "Brahman."
When both have been realized through right vision and there is no longer any perception of them,
speech turns back from that which remains— ageless and tranquil.

The entire flood of sensations belonging to all selves has been completely stilled; this world, as it exists, is of a single nature, having the form of space, the form of stone, and yet the supreme form of consciousness.
The one hundred and fourth canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja. Śikhidhvaja:
And thus, O Greatly Wise One, I understand that this very world is the effect corresponding exactly to its supreme cause.
Kumbha says:
Where there is causality, there the effect is appropriately produced;
but that which is not a cause from the very beginning—how could an effect arise from that?
Herein there is no cause whatsoever, nor is there ever any effect;
this entire world is Śiva, peaceful, unborn, and ever-existent.
An effect arises from a cause; therefore, it would possess the nature of a cause. But for that which does not arise at all here, how can there be any similarity?
Tell me, how can that which has no seed at all be born?
That which is inconceivable and inexpressible cannot possess the nature of a seed in this world.
Since all cognitions, by virtue of place and time,
possess causes, how can Brahman— which is without an agent— be the object of the two means of valid cognition?
In Śiva, who is devoid of agent, object, and instrument, there is no causality;
therefore, there is no perception of the world as a referent of words that is not caused by Him.

Brahman alone is its own true nature, which exists as that which is pervasive and sustains all; yet that very same [Brahman], when perceived by those of imperfect vision, appears as the accumulated world.
That which is pure consciousness alone—undecaying and tranquil—is proclaimed as the One.
By that very [consciousness], the unborn world is understood as the tranquil form of Brahman.
O Lord of the Earth, that very state which belongs to the mind itself is declared by the wise to be its destruction, and it is so experienced.
O King, know that the mind has the nature of destruction; it is essentially perishable.
It is the intention toward momentary destruction that is designated by the word "mind."
Merely by the absence of volitional construction (asaṅkalpana), even without the arising of perfect knowledge,
volitional construction— being inherently unreal in nature— is itself extinguished for the sake of accomplishment.
O lotus-eyed one, how could that which is called "ignorance" (avidyā)— whose non-existence is accepted by its very name— be something that actually exists as the mind?
How can he who, raising his hands, declares with a loud voice, "I am a Śūdra," become a Brahmin? Of what nature is his status as a Brahmin?
Know him to be truly dead, my dear, who cries out with a distorted throat, "I am dead," for his life is merely an illusion.
Whatever exists here that appears in the form of an illusion is seen like a whirling firebrand,
like a mirage, a double moon, and so forth, or like a child’s phantom and the like.
How indeed could that which consists of a mass of delusions be real?
Therefore, it is said that the mind is nothing but the error of ignorance.
Ignorance is said to be the mind, which, though non-existent, appears as if existent;
it is a false delusion, formless like a mass of hair seen in the sky.
Thus, it is ignorance itself that is expressed by the word "mind" (*citta*);
the destruction of that [ignorance] is the destruction of the mind, and that indeed is the relinquishing of the mind.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Lord, what is ignorance like, and how is it destroyed?
O Blessed One, best among speakers, tell me this in brief."
Kumbha said: O best of kings, that lack of awareness regarding a real object—
whether it be a jar or anything else, whether perceived or unperceived— is traditionally known as ignorance (ajñāna).
Non-cognition is ignorance, while cognition would be awareness;
because ignorance is not cognized, it ceases through the cognition that consists in awareness.
O virtuous one, the cognition of water in the mirages of a desert is a vain delusion;
it is dissolved by the realization that "this is not water."
This mature ignorance that firmly holds "this is the mind" in the heart is utterly destroyed, root and all, through the knowledge that "the mind does not exist."
Just as the appearance of a snake in a rope, which arises from the delusion of ignorance,
perishes once the knowledge that "this is not a snake" has taken root in the heart.
As long as the internal notions of "mind," "intellect," and "I" arise from ignorance, so long will the mind, the intellect, and illusion certainly persist; of this there is no doubt.
As long as the internal realization "there is no 'I' in the mind" has not arisen through knowledge, so long the mind and the mental faculty remain like an illusion; there is no doubt about this.
As long as there is the delusion of a false yakṣa, so long indeed is a yakṣa seen;
when the delusion of a false yakṣa has subsided, how could there be the existence of a yakṣa?
There is no mind, nor any mental factors associated with ego-grasping and the like;
in this world, there is only one stainless consciousness.
That deluded woman had previously formed intentions with her mind and so forth;
once she was awakened, she renounced everything that she had intended.
Whatever comes about through volition departs through volition,
O mighty-armed one, just as a mass of flames in fire is driven by the wind.
By that very being of Brahman, which is a single solid mass of the reality of the Self,
the entire world is pervaded, just as the ocean is pervaded by water.
I do not exist, nor does another; neither you, nor these, nor the mind;
neither the senses nor space—only the Self alone exists, stainless.
That very same [reality] is perceived in the form of objects such as jars;
what kind of false conceptualization is this, that "this is the mind" and "this is I"?
Nothing at all is born or dies in these three worlds;
it is only the Self that manifests through the nature of the conceptions of existence and non-existence.
Everything is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, eternally manifest and all-pervading; duality and unity do not exist—be free from delusion through truth.
O friend, you exist as the very form of the qualities of all the senses, like the sky;
O one of great intelligence, you are not burned, nor are you defiled anywhere.
O friend, it neither perishes nor does anything increase;
for it is of the nature of the stainless sky, singular and possessing infinite forms.
The two powers consisting of desire and non-desire belong to you alone;
for the moon is not perceived apart from its rays.

You are that primordial, unborn reality of the Self—ageless, unsurpassed, the supreme nature, eternally pure, constant, and of a single form; free from all mental constructions, yet manifesting as the play known as the creative arts, ever-arisen and uncreated.
The one hundred and fifth canto, titled "Śikhidhvaja’s Realization of the Ultimate Truth," by Vasiṣṭha.
Reflecting thus upon those sincere words of Kumbha, the king,
in that very moment, became transformed within his own true state of self.
With his mind and eyes closed, his speech stilled and free from fear,
he remained with the form of his limbs motionless, as if carved out of stone.
Then, after only a moment, Cūḍālā, who had assumed the form of Kumbha, spoke to him as he woke up with wide-open eyes, O mighty-armed one.
Kumbha said:
"Have you perhaps found rest in happiness upon this vast, pure, soft, and stainless couch, which belongs to those free from conceptual construction?"
Are you awakened within? Have you abandoned delusion? Has that which is to be known been fully understood, or has that which was to be seen been truly seen?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, I have beheld a great station, adorned with immense splendor, situated above all things."
Oh, how wonderful! The association of the great-souled ones—who have known that which is to be known—is composed of a unique, unprecedented nectar and bestows the fruit of the essence.
That great nectar which I did not obtain even through my birth has today been spontaneously attained in an instant through association with you.
O lotus-eyed one, why has this infinite, primordial, and immortal state of the Self not been attained by me? MU 6.105.9
Kumbha said:

When the mind has attained tranquility, when the desire for enjoyments has been abandoned, and when the ripening of the passions of the entire collection of sense faculties has come to an end; MU 6.105.10.
The stainless words of the Teacher find rest in the mind,
just as drops of saffron water settle upon a pure white cloth.
Today, the ripening of the infinite impurities accumulated within your little body— impurities whose very nature is your own latent impressions— has arisen for you.
O lotus-eyed one, O virtuous one, all impurities fall away from the body over time due to ripening,
just as fruits fall down from a tree when they have matured.
O friend, when the impurities consisting of latent impressions have gone to dissolution,
that which the Guru speaks within enters [the disciple] like an arrow into its quiver.
Now that the ripening of the astringent has been perfected, you have been awakened by me today;
therefore, O Mahāmati, the destruction of your ignorance has occurred this very day.
Today your impurities have been cooked away; today indeed your ignorance has been destroyed;
today you are worthy of instruction; today you have become awakened.
Today, the exhaustion of all actions, both auspicious and inauspicious,
has been brought to completion through your instruction on the company of the virtuous.
O Lord of the Earth, for as long as this was the former part of the day,
so long did your ignorance persist, thinking "I am the mind."
Now that, through understanding my words, [ignorance] has reached its end in your mind and has been completely cast out from your heart, O King, you are fully awakened.
As long as the existence of the mind persists within the heart, so long does ignorance remain established;
when the mind is relinquished by means of its very nature as mind, the emergence of knowledge occurs.
The mind that perceives duality and unity is called ignorance;
the dissolution of these two perceptions is knowledge, which is the supreme goal.
You are awakened, you are liberated; O King, the mind has been abandoned by you.
For that which is truly existent has been grasped by you, while the unreal state has been relinquished.
Free from sorrow, free from exertion, unattached, eternally self-possessed, of great exaltation, a sage, observing silence, established in your own true nature, remain stainless.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Indeed, O Blessed One, the land of the mind belongs only to the ignorant person;
for one who is awakened and knows that, there is, as it is said, no mind at all, O Lord."
Tell me, how do these very ones who are liberated while living move about?
For men such as you and others likewise have no mind that exists.
Tell me all this, and with other rays of speech such as these,
skillfully wipe away the darkness in my heart.
Kumbha said: O knower of dharma, it is exactly as you say and not otherwise;
for the mind of those liberated while living does not exist, just as there is no sprout from stones.
That latent impression (*vāsanā*) which is capable of producing rebirth is called "dense impression" (*ghanavāsanā*);
it is designated by the term "mind" (*citta*), and it does not exist for one who knows that [reality].
Know that latent impression by which those who know it engage in actions here to be what is called "sentient being," yet it is devoid of rebirth.
The great-souled ones who are liberated while living, established in purity and with senses restrained, move about free from attachment; their minds are never fixed on anything.
They say that the deluded mind is "citta," while the awakened is called "sattva.
For those who abide in the mind are unawakened, whereas those of great intelligence abide in the *sattva*.
The mind is born again and again, but the *sattva* is not born again;
there is bondage for the unawakened, O King, but none for the awakened.
You have been born endowed with courage and stand as one of great renunciation;
I know that today you have relinquished your mind entirely.
O King, you shine like a king, liberated from all latent impressions;
O sage, I believe your mind has attained equality with space.
You have attained supreme tranquility, pure and established in equanimity,
like the great ocean of milk when it is freed from the agitation of Mount Mandara’s churning.
You have completely renounced all attachment to the kingdom, as well as to asceticism,
to the forest, to the body, and even to the fruits of good and evil deeds.
Free from effort, devoid of attachment, with a mind renounced and free from latent tendencies— you have attained perfection, O mighty-armed one, having reached the state of the great relinquisher.
For this indeed is the great renunciation, wherein everything is abandoned:
heaven, liberation, the mind, and even the fruits of austerity and charity.
O virtuous one, when one awakens through the fire of the intellect and by means of supreme awakening,
what could mere austerity possibly be, other than a means for diminishing a limited amount of suffering?
That happiness which is free from decay and excess and consists of equanimity is real; it is that true entity, whereas heaven and the like are not so, for they are transitory.
For one who has ascended the scale of existence and non-existence and is pierced by mental and physical ailments, what joy is there in that which is called heaven? Even that remains subject to doubt.
As long as the accomplishment of one's own goal has not been attained, the section on action remains auspicious;
for would one who has not yet obtained gold ever abandon the ore?
Through association with Cūḍālā and others, you may easily attain the state of a knower;
so why are you immersed in this purposeless austerity?
O wise one, behold the beginning and end of this evil deed which is to be accomplished through the various stages of life and so forth; do not take delight in its middle alone.
Since these portions of conceptualization, which consist of austerity, from whence they arise and wherein they dissolve, have their footing bound there, remain established in that state.
All states of being have arisen from the sky of consciousness, which is clearer even than the physical ether;
they dissolve back into that very same place—dwell there and take delight therein.
"‘This must be done’ and ‘this must not be done’—these are but droplets of the Brahman.
O Śikhidhvaja, having abandoned these droplets, take refuge in the full cloud."
"Ask for what you desire"— why is it that a beloved husband is not asked for by a woman herself in the same way a female friend is asked?
Wise great-souled ones do not grasp these objects fashioned by conceptual construction, which are radiant only at first sight, just as they do not grasp reflections of the sun in water.
Whatever yields fruits such as heaven or liberation is all exactly the same; having abandoned that, become indeed that which appears as the equal of the equal.
Remaining free from desire, perceive this flood of objects as peaceful through their substantiality and perishing through their destruction; abide with a mind that is unmoving.

For one whose mind is free from agitation, the cycle of existence does not afflict him here, O virtuous one, just as misfortune arising from human agency does not affect a man who possesses sound judgment.
Whatever sufferings manifest here in the three worlds, O Lord of the Earth, they all arise solely from the restlessness of the mind.
He whose mind is steady, tranquil, motionless, and unwavering—
he is the all-pervading Lord, he possesses great bliss, and he is the vessel of universal sovereignty.
Therefore, O knower of reality, having brought both movement and stillness to a state of unity within the mind, remain as you wish, having attained eternal oneness.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Lord, how have these two—vibration and non-vibration—come to a state of unity?
O destroyer of all doubts, tell me this quickly.
Kumbha said:
The entire world is a single reality, consisting of pure consciousness alone, like water in the ocean.
That very reality either vibrates or does not, just as pure water [appears] with its waves.
That which is sung of by such names as Brahman, pure consciousness alone, stainless, and truth— this, O dear one, the deluded person perceives as the world.

Since all creation is indeed motionless, the cycle of worldly existence arises from that; for movement consists of waves and the like, whereas that which is without vibration is the equal, supreme reality.

If that very consciousness is cultivated as vibration (*spanda*) and likewise as non-vibration (*aspanda*), then by virtue of its single nature, it is indeed both that [vibration] and that [non-vibration], yet it remains immovable and auspicious (*śiva*).
When creation, whose nature is merely the vibration of consciousness, is seen correctly, it dissolves;
when its nature is not seen correctly, it arises, just like the delusion of a snake in a rope.
The consciousness that is in motion is designated as "consciousness" (cit), but this [consciousness] which is motionless and all-pervasive,
having ascended to the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), cannot be expressed by speech.
When the mind has attained purity over time through the continuous practice of contact with the scriptures and virtuous people— like the moon risen in the sky— then...
This has appeared solely as it is spread out by the word of one's own experience;
yet the nature of one's own experience is itself known by the self through itself.
You have attained your own true nature, which is without beginning or middle; remain right here, established in this desired state.
O virtuous one, you have indeed become the great conscious self, formless and undivided, truly free from sorrow.
The one hundred and sixth canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," [ends here].
Kumbha:
Thus, O King Śikhidhvaja, I have told you everything:
how all this has arisen and how it dissolves away.
O leader of sages, having heard this, understood it, and reflected upon it,
remain as you wish, with the clearly perceived state established in the ultimate ground.
"I am going to heaven; at this very time, the sage Nārada arrives there from the world of Brahmā for the assembly of the immortals."
If he does not see me there, he becomes angry;
for a worthy person should never cause distress to his teachers.
With all mental constructs abandoned and desiring nothing at all, you must dwell within the Self alone; this very vision is purifying.
Vasiṣṭha:
Just as Śikhidhvaja, with flowers in his hand, was about to offer a reply and perform a prostration, he vanished from sight.
Just as an object that has appeared before one is no longer seen right in front of one's eyes,
so King Śikhidhvaja did not see the jar before him.
When the jar had gone, the protector of the earth was filled with supreme wonder;
reflecting upon that very marvel, he became as if depicted in a painting.
Thus he reflected: "How wondrous is the play of Fate, that I have finally been awakened by this one under the pretext of being a water-jar!"
Where is Kumbha, the son of Nārada, and where am I, named Śikhidhvaja?
I have been awakened in this way solely by the power of time.
"Oh, how well-spoken by the son of the gods! It is indeed logical.
Oh, after a long time, I have truly awakened from the sleep of delusion!"
Where was I, submerged in the foul mud of the web of ritual actions,
practicing the false delusion of "this must be done" and "this must not be done"?
Oh, how cool, pure, and peaceful is this path of my own!
Having the appearance of a liquid elixir, it seems to cool my very being.
I am stilled, I am completely extinguished, and I abide in absolute bliss;
I do not even desire pure consciousness, for I remain established just as I am.
Reflecting thus, the king, with his mind intent on such renunciation,
remained in silence, as if carved out of stone.
Then, having attained a firm and unshakable foundation in that very state— silent, free from conceptual construction, and untainted— he remained like the peak of a mountain.
There, that great-souled one, his fear completely stilled, having attained rest after a long time and having regained his own stainless self after a long time,
then the conscious self slept in yoga.
The one hundred and seventh canto, titled "The Composure of Śikhidhvaja," by Vasiṣṭha.
Through non-conceptual meditative absorption, he remained like a piece of wood or a wall;
O Rāma, such was Śikhidhvaja—now hear about Cūḍālā.
Having awakened her husband Śikhidhvaja by means of that disguise as Kumbha, she vanished and swiftly crossed through the sky.
In the sky, he cast off his form as a son of the gods created by magic and assumed a beautiful feminine appearance, charming and innocent.
Having reached her own city through the sky, she entered the inner apartments in an instant;
she became visible to the world and performed the duties of a queen.
Having returned to the sky within three days,
she became a water-jar through her yogic power and went to the grove of Śikhidhvaja.
Likewise, while there on the forest ground, she saw that king established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, as if carved out from the very tree.
"Aha! Indeed, O Lord, by good fortune this one has here found rest in the Self;
he stands healthy, equanimous, and tranquil," he said before the Master.
Therefore, let me first awaken him from this supreme state;
why indeed does he abandon his body at this very moment?
After having flourished for some time here in either a kingdom or a forest,
we two shall go together to peace, having abandoned these bodies.
Therefore, as long as this [mind] does not undergo a fluctuating transformation,
I shall awaken it by means of this practice of yoga.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā let out a lion’s roar again and again before her lord, striking terror into the forest-dwellers.
When he did not move, like a rock upon a mountain, even though that sound was made again and again, then she caused him to move.
When the king was shaken and even cast down, yet did not wake up, Cūḍālā, who had assumed the form of Kumbha, reflected thus:
"Aha! This Blessed One has truly matured in his own state. Therefore, by what means shall I now awaken him?"
Or rather, why should I awaken this Great-Souled One?
Let him remain as he pleases, having attained awakening while being bodiless (videha).
I too, having abandoned this female body, shall go to the supreme state from which there is no rebirth; for what use have I here?
Having reflected thus, the great virtuous lady Cūḍālā, being prepared to renounce her own body, reflected once more.
I shall indeed examine this body of the lord of the earth to see if there remains within him any residue of vital essence, which is the seed of awakening in the heart.
In due time, this Blessed One will attain full awakening,
like a cluster of flowers nestled within the sap of their root-bud during the springtime.
Therefore, wandering here, he alone becomes one who is liberated while living; thinking, "Let him not be alone," I do not attain peace.
Having reflected thus, the fair-complexioned Cūḍālā, looking at her husband with apprehension through both touch and sight, spoke.
There still remains within his heart a residue of being that serves as the cause for awakening;
this body has not yet lost its form, so I shall not abandon this frame.
Rāma:

O Brahmin, how is one who possesses meditative concentration known to be one whose mind is utterly stilled, who remains like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, and in whom only the vital essence remains?
Vasiṣṭha: He in whose heart there exists a remnant of being (*sattva*), its subtle form difficult to perceive, which serves as the cause of awakening— just as flowers and fruit exist within a seed.
For him who is liberated from the vibration of the mind, whose true consciousness is free from vibration, who is devoid of duality and unity, and who abides equally and immovably; //MU_6,107.25//
The body maintains an even application; it neither flags nor exults, neither sets nor rises, but remains perfectly poised.
The body of one whose mind vibrates with notions such as duality and unity undergoes change; for one whose mind does not vibrate, it never does.
For the vibration of the mind, O Rāma, is the cause of the existence of the entire world and of all modifications of being, just as honey is the cause of flowers.
O descendant of Raghu, in whichever body the mind vibrates, that body repeatedly falls under the sway of joy, exhaustion, and delusion.
When the mind has attained tranquility, the physical body of that steadfast being no longer afflicts him,
for it is like a change of state in the sky.
Just as waves and the like do not arise from a continuous flow of water that is in equilibrium,
so too no defect is seen in the equilibrium of the mind established within a sentient being.
There is no perception of a sentient being other than its own cessation;
as long as the being exists, it remains the same, and merely subsides with time.
O Rāma, that body in which neither consciousness nor a living being exists dissolves into the five elements like snow under the heat.
This body of Śikhidhvaja is certainly devoid of mind, yet it is joined with a portion of *sattva*; therefore, it has not become a vessel for decay.
Beholding her husband’s body in such a state, that excellent woman did not abandon her own body, but reflected with haste.
Having entered the all-pervading, pure essence of consciousness, I awaken it;
for that lovely awakening which is yet to be, he is indeed established therein.
"If I do not awaken him, he will awaken by himself after a long time;
why then should I remain here alone?"—thinking thus, I am awakening him.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā abandoned her body, that cage of causes, and attained stability in the principle of consciousness (cittattva), which is devoid of beginning and end.
There, having made a conscious movement, she entered again her own body from the sky— like a bird entering its nest— from that powerful lord who possessed the essence of being.
Then, rising up in the form of a water-jar, she settled upon a bed of flowers and began to sing the Sāman, resonating with the humming of a swarm of bees.
Hearing that sound of the Sāman chant, the lotus-like [Queen] awakened within the body of the king, who was endowed with the quality of goodness, as if she were dwelling there.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, having attained the perfection of inner being, caused her vision to blossom, just as the sun causes the lotus to bloom.
He saw a jar standing before him, intent on chanting the Sāman hymns, endowed with a supreme form like another Sāmaveda.
"Oh, how blessed we are that the son of the Sage has come again!"—
saying this, the king gave a flower to Kumbha.
"By good fortune, O Blessed One, we abide within your purifying mind;
for indeed, O dear one, what great beings are not steadfast in their acts of grace?"
"Our purification is one cause for [your] arrival;
tell me, what might the second be that removes your sin?"
Kumbha said:
O subduer of enemies, from the very moment I departed from your presence,
from that time forth my mind has remained here together with you alone.
O sinless one, I find no delight in the celestial stages of heaven, nor in the divine gardens,
nor upon the peaks of Meru and Mandara, nor in the caverns of Kailāsa.
I desire only union with you, which is made beautiful by your auspicious conduct,
like a tree longing for the month of Madhu, which resembles a flow of nectar.
Therefore, I remain right here by your side for now;
for whatever is desired, O dear one, stands at the very forefront of all delightful things.
I believe there is no one like you in this world— a kinsman, a trusted confidant, a well-wisher, a friend, a companion, someone worthy of trust, and likewise a disciple.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Oh, how the trees of merit in our family-mountain have borne fruit,
since even you, though free from attachment, desire union with us!"
"This is the forest, these are the trees, and here I am, your attentive servant; if heaven does not please you, O Lord, then let it be stayed here."
O virtuous one, through the yoga-practice bestowed by you, I have found rest;
I consider that there is no such rest in heaven as this.
Relying upon that very pure and luminous state of your own being,
wander here as you desire, whether in heaven or upon the surface of the earth.
Kumbha:
Have you perhaps found rest in the supreme state of great bliss?
Have you perhaps completely abandoned this suffering consisting of duality?
O King, has your intense delight in those volitions that are pleasant at first sight been completely uprooted, like a creeper on a riverbank swept away by the current?
Has your mind become established— tranquil, abiding in perfect equanimity, beyond the states of what is to be rejected or accepted, and undisturbed by whatever has arisen as it may?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"By your grace, O Blessed One, the state that transcends all objects of sight has been seen;
the boundary of saṃsāra has been reached, and the certainty regarding what is to be attained has been gained."
After a very long time indeed, we have finally come to rest, free from ailment;
everything that was to be attained has been attained, and we remain satisfied for a long time, unhurt.
Nothing at all needs to be taught to us;
we are entirely satisfied in every respect, established in a state free from the fever of distress.
The known and the unknown, the unattained and the fully attained, the abandoned and the relied upon,
"you-ness" and "otherness," "I-ness" and "mine"— none of these exist in the void, just as nothing exists in empty space.

Free from worldly rebirth, delighting in the absence of delusion and fear, eternally awakened, with a perfectly equanimous disposition and universal gentleness; being the self of all, liberated from all mental constructions, as pure as the expanse of space, I abide in peace.
The one hundred and eighth canto, titled "The Yoga of Kumbha’s Return," by Vasiṣṭha:
Thus, those two, the knower and the known, sat together in the forest for three muhūrtas, conversing with one another on various topics concerning the inner self.
Then, having risen, they bathed in a certain lake abounding with cranes,
and they both sported in a forest resembling the Nandana grove.
By that conduct and through those conversations, the two forest-dwellers passed eight days in those woodland paths.
Then Kumbha said, "Let us go to another forest on the mountain. Thinking "So be it," the king agreed, and they both set out together.
Forests of many forms, jungles, riverbanks, lakes, thickets of shrubs, mountain peaks, and dense thickets.
Rivers, countries, as well as villages, towns, and cities;
deserts, formidable mountains, groves, sacred fords, and shrines.
Both stood there with equal affection, dressed alike, possessing equal strength and equal energy; they swam together and likewise remained standing together.
O Rāghava, they both worshipped the ancestors and the gods, partook of their meals together,
slept upon the same bed, and became equal in their understanding.
In the thickets of *tamāla* groves and amidst the dense *mandāra* trees,
that couple, with affectionate hearts like two friends, shone forth.
O Rāma, the mental construction of conceptualization— thinking "this is to be grasped" and "this is not"— did not carry away those two, just as a whirlwind cannot move a mountain of the gods.
He beheld those two friends in various states: in one place they were grey with dust, in another their limbs were smeared with sandalwood paste, and in another they were anointed with ashes.
In some places they wore divine garments, and in others they wore garments of bark;
in some places they were covered with sprouts, and in others they were adorned with flowers.
Within just a few days, because her mind was gone and due to the loftiness of her being,
the king shone like a jar.
Then, seeing Śikhidhvaja, who possessed the luster of a celestial being and had attained such splendor, the proud Cūḍālā reflected:
This husband is blameless in soul, as are these forest lands;
this state of being is effortless—he who is not desirous is the one who has been deceived.
For those whose intellects are liberated while living and who abide in enjoyment exactly as it comes to them,
that which is called "stupidity" would be merely a state of one-pointedness, though it is trivial.
A husband who is one's own, whose soul is blameless, freedom from debt, and fresh youth— she is not a woman who desires love who does not cherish these as her flower-filled home.
That wicked woman who does not take delight, free from sorrow, in her own beloved husband who has power over her within a bower of forest flowers and creepers, is truly ruined.
Fie upon that wicked woman who, having obtained a beloved husband as her wedded lord, does not take delight in him when they are in private.
If one who knows what is to be known were to abandon even that which has been attained—
which is blameless and of noble purpose— what could possibly have been accomplished by that knower?
Therefore, I shall quickly fashion some new artifice with my wit,
by which this lord of the earth, my husband and bestower of honor, may take delight in me.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, assuming the guise of Kumbha and standing within a forest thicket, spoke to her husband like a female cuckoo to a male cuckoo.
Kumbha said:
"O friend, today is the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra;
today, indeed, Hari’s great assembly in heaven takes place."
I must remain present there before my father;
for destiny, as it has been established, must never be abandoned.
"You must wait for me here today in this forest region,
sporting with the flowers of meditation and remaining free from agitation."
Today, at the end of the day, I have come from the sky, free from conceptual thought;
indeed, union with you brings me even greater joy than that of heaven.
Having spoken thus, Kumbha gave a cluster of flowers to Mitra,
as if giving his own beloved affection born from the trees of the Nandana grove for the sake of mutual joy.
"When the king spoke thus, 'You must come back very soon,' he leapt from the forest into the sky like a lovely autumn cloud."
As he moved through the sky, he shed the canopy of flowers produced from his floral garlands,
which was scattered by the forest wind like a snowy cloud in winter.
Śikhidhvaja beheld him as he was departing and vanished from sight, like a peacock waking from sleep at the sound of a cloud; for true affection is indeed difficult to relinquish.
At the end of Śikhidhvaja’s vision, she who had the form of a jar abandoned it in the sky;
like the beauty of water returning from a whirlpool on a mountain peak, the bewildered woman resumed her own form.
By way of the celestial path, he reached his own city, which was as delightful as heaven, adorned with fluttering banners, and resembled a wish-fulfilling tree in full bloom.
Without being seen, she entered the inner apartments filled with women,
like the great goddess Lakṣmī of the spring month entering a tree adorned with shimmering creepers.
Having swiftly completed all royal duties there,
he again leaped into the sky to go to the grove of Śikhidhvaja.
Having traversed the path of the sky, level with the rays of the sun,
she, remaining in the air, beheld the forest of Śikhidhvaja upon the mountain.
Seeing that form of Kumbha, he quickly seized it again,
and it fell before Śikhidhvaja like a flower in the sky.
There, with a face of faded luster, she made her mind unwearied, like the night making the moon appear as if covered in mist, or like the dawn making the lotus appear as if exhausted.
Seeing him in such a state, Śikhidhvaja rose up;
his heart became distressed, and with great respect, he spoke as follows:
"O son of the gods, homage be to you; you appear as if troubled in mind.
You are Kumbha; abandon your agitation and sit upon this seat."
Those who are virtuous and have known what is to be known do not resort to a state born of joy or dejection; established in themselves, they remain unaffected, like lotuses by the moisture of water.
When he was told, "Therefore, sit down," Kumbha sat upon the seat with a dejected voice that resembled the sound of a broken bamboo pole.
Those who, throughout the various states of the body, do not remain inactive due to their equanimity of mind toward the organs of action— they are not deceitful men lacking the wisdom of reality.
For those fools who do not know reality, O King, they flee from their own natural states because of their childishness, even though they have already grasped them.
As oil exists within every grain of sesame, so does the state of decay exist within every body;
he who does not fall into this bodily state cuts through the sky with a sword.
This indeed is the unsurpassed avoidance of the suffering inherent in the state of the body:
namely, equanimity of the mind through yoga, and not the mere steadiness of the organs of action.
O dear one, as long as the body lasts, one who understands should act according to the conduct of the ten states through the organs of action;
however, one should never abide in the organs of perception.
All beings, beginning with Parameṣṭhin, remain within the various states of the body with their intentions already awakened; such is the certainty of destiny.
For all this collection of visible things— whether ignorant, knowers of reality, or composed of the elements—
all of it indeed runs toward necessity (niyati), just as water flows toward the ocean.

Those who know this remain unimpaired as long as the body lasts, maintaining this destiny through the equality of intellect and other faculties, as well as by the movement of the hands and other limbs.
But the ignorant, O dear one, struck by states of pleasure and pain through the agitation of all things and shattered by hundreds of thousands of bodily marks, merely follow the course of destiny.

O friend, that which has been realized here by living beings—that one must remain thus in times of happiness as well as in states of suffering—is that very same manifestation of the mass of elements for both the wise and the ignorant; this fixed play of destiny is indeed difficult to overcome.

The one hundred and ninth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Conduct for One Liberated while Living," spoken by Śikhidvaja: Śikhidvaja said: "O venerable one, you have described the conduct of those liberated while living; now, please tell me about the yoga of their conduct. Vasiṣṭha said: "O King, listen with an attentive mind to the conduct of those liberated while living, which is free from all attachment and is the supreme state of liberation. For one who has attained the state of liberation while living, there is no distinction between day and night, nor between the internal and the external. Having transcended the world of duality, he remains established in his own nature. He does not perceive the body as 'I' nor the world as 'mine. He is neither a doer nor an enjoyer, yet he continues to act through the momentum of past impressions. He moves about like a cloud, unattached and free from desire. He experiences pleasure and pain without being affected, remaining as steady as a mountain. He may engage in worldly affairs or remain withdrawn, appearing to others as if he were still bound, though he is inwardly liberated. He may appear to be asleep, dreaming, or awake, yet he is always established in the state of pure consciousness. He may perform rituals, recite mantras, or practice meditation, yet he remains detached from the fruits of such actions. He may appear to be engaged in worldly activities, yet he is inwardly tranquil and free from all mental fluctuations. Such is the conduct of the liberated while living: it is beyond description, subtle, and difficult to comprehend. It is the very essence of wisdom and the ultimate goal of all seekers."
This being so, O illustrious one, how have you, though a god, come to experience such agitation even from heaven, that very abode of happiness?
Kumbha said: "Listen, O lord of the earth, to this wonderful matter of mine;
I shall relate to you in its entirety what has happened to me today in heaven."
Sorrow, when communicated to a friend, reaches a state of extreme attenuation,
just as a dense, dull, and dark cloud is diminished by a released shower of rain.
The mind of one who is questioned by a well-wishing friend attains clarity quickly, just as water does when approached by a devoted person using *kataka* nut.
I, for my part, having departed from here and given the *puṣpamañjarī* to you,
have crossed the sky and reached the third heaven.
There, having stood in due order in the assembly hall of Indra together with his father,
he rose when it was time to rise, being dismissed by his father.
Having abandoned heaven, I have come here to this sky;
together with the horses of the sun, I travel along the path of the wind.
Then, while the sun had gone in one direction, I returned by another path,
appearing as if fallen from the ocean of the sky.
Then, amidst the path of clouds filled with water ahead,
I saw the sage Durvāsas approaching with great speed.
With its mass of limbs washed by the downpour, covered by the clouds as if by a garment and adorned with circles of lightning, it resembled a woman going to meet her lover.
He stood upon the dark ground beneath the shade of a great cloud,
rushing forward with speed toward his beloved, as if toward the very goddess of ascetic splendor.
Having paid him homage, I spoke as I traveled:
"O Sage, you who are clothed in dark-blue clouds are like a woman going to meet her lover."
Having heard this, O giver of honor, he who destroys my honor became enraged toward me;
opening his blood-red eyes, he spoke with a deep resonance.
"Why are you so arrogant, saying, 'I am the grandson of the Lotus-born'?
For it is through their virtues that noble beings attain humility, just as trees do by means of their fruits."
"O you of wicked conduct, O fool, O celestial youth, you speak these inauspicious words to me, saying that you are like a woman going to meet her lover."
"O lovely woman with breasts and long hair, who displays such gestures and emotions, because of these harsh words you have spoken, you shall become a prostitute at night."
Having heard these inauspicious words uttered by the decrepit brahmin,
while I was reflecting for a moment, the sage vanished from sight.
"Thus, O virtuous one, with an agitated mind, I have arrived here from the surface of the sky;
I have told you all of this, for I have become the Night-Maiden."
"How can this womanhood of mine be passed through at the ends of days? What should I say to my father at night when I possess a vulva like a man?"
Alas, how treacherous indeed is the course of destiny within this cycle of existence!
Even I have, by fate, become like any other prey for young men.
Alas! Because of my abduction, a quarrel now arises here between the young gods in heaven, whose minds are agitated by desire.
Overcome by shame before my guru, the gods, and the twice-born, how could I, a woman of the night, stand properly in their presence?
Vasiṣṭha: Having spoken thus and remained silent for a moment, O scion of Raghu, Kumbha, the son of the sage, regained his composure and spoke again.
Why do I grieve like one who is ignorant? What injury has been done to my self?
This body, which is distinct from me, shall experience [the consequences] according to its own course.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Devaputra, what is the purpose of this lamentation for you?
Let that which comes come; the self of the body is not defiled."
Whatever sufferings or pleasures are ordained,
all of them belong to the body, and not at all to the embodied soul.
If even you, though unworthy of weariness regarding duties, feel such distress,
then what other means could there be for others, O ornament of the scriptures?
Furthermore, what did you say—that one should speak with weariness when it is appropriate for weariness? Now, having attained equanimity, remain as you are, free from fatigue.
Vasiṣṭha:
Having thus mutually consoled one another with such words,
those two affectionate friends remained together in the forest, both feeling weary at heart.
Then the sun, the lamp of the world, went to its setting as if producing womanhood in that jar, like a lamp going out due to the exhaustion of its oil.
Along with the burdens of worldly affairs, the lotuses underwent contraction;
and along with the travelers, the hearts of the wives of wayfarers did as well.
Like a fisherman gathering all birds together in one place,
the world— rich with a net of star-jewels— attained a state of darkness.
The lake of white water-lilies, rich with stars, attained a blossoming state as if laughing;
it resounded with the cries of ruddy geese and was filled with swarms of wandering bees.
Then those two friends rose up, performed their twilight devotions while the moon was rising,
and having likewise completed their silent recitations, they stood within a thicket.
Then Kumbha, gradually assuming a feminine form there,
spoke with faltering words to Śikhidhvaja who stood before him:
O King, I feel as if I am falling, trembling, and melting away with my slender limbs; I think that, out of shame, I am turning into a woman.
"Behold, O King, these hairs of mine are growing,
like a mass of shimmering stars in the darkness at the end of the day."
Behold these two breasts of mine growing upon my chest,
facing upward like the buds of a lotus plant in springtime, reaching toward the sky.
"O friend, behold how my garments, as they gradually slip from my body like those of a woman, have come to hang down only as far as my ankles."
Behold, my dear, these ornaments of vast jewels and various garlands that grow from their own limbs like flowers from trees.
Behold, my dear, how this frost, beautiful as the mass of rays from the rising moon,
has itself become a silken turban upon my head, like [a covering] on a mountain.
"O giver of honor, all the signs of a lover have appeared within me;
alas, what a misery! I am despondent—what shall I do? For I am but a woman."
Alas, what a tragedy! Oh, virtuous one, though I am situated as a woman, I experience within my own consciousness a buttock joined with a hip.
Having said, "Kumbha in the forest," he became silent and despondent;
and the king, beholding him, likewise remained dejected in spirit.
In just a moment, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words: "Alas! O lady of excellent complexion, this one has become a being of great essence."
O virtuous one, you have known all that is to be known and you understand the course of destiny;
do not let your heart be distressed over this matter which was inevitable.
O dear one, these calamities fall upon the mere bodies of the wise, but not upon those of the ignorant; for the latter, these afflictions seize both the mind and the body.
Kumbha said:
"So be it; I shall assume the female form of a night-walker.
I feel no distress, for by whom can destiny be transgressed?"
Having thus resolved and mutually diminished that grief,
they spent that long night in silence upon a single bed.
Then at dawn, having voluntarily cast off that youthful body,
Kumbha became possessed of a form with breasts as prominent as jars.
Thus that queen Cūḍālā, of excellent complexion,
having first assumed the state of a water-jar for her husband, subsequently returned to womanhood.
The virtuous maiden dwelt in the forest groves at night,
while by day she lived together with her husband and friend, assuming the form of a water-jar.

With unimpeded movement through yoga, that woman, adorned with garlands, necklaces, and large earrings, wandered at will with her beloved, her friend, and her lord across the peaks of Kailāsa, Mandara, Sumeru, Mahendra, and Sahya.
The Chapter on Attaining Womanhood;
the one hundred and tenth chapter; Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after only a few days had passed,
that virtuous woman, assuming the form of Kumbhī, spoke thus to her husband:
O King, lotus-petal-eyed one, listen to these words of mine:
every night, I remain right here as a woman.
Therefore, I wish to perfect such a womanly duty:
I shall give myself in marriage to some husband.
Therefore, you alone are pleasing to me as a husband throughout the three worlds;
accept me through marriage as your wife for all time, even at night.
O virtuous one, I wish to enjoy the pleasure of women together with my dear friend, which has come to me without effort; do not be an obstacle to me.
For one who performs their natural duty— which has proceeded sequentially since the beginning of creation, is easy to accomplish, and is delightful— what fault could possibly arise?
Because of the identity and equality of the views of desire and non-desire regarding all things, we have neither desire nor non-desire; therefore, we perform this which is desired.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O friend, O one of great intelligence, by performing this deed I perceive neither good nor evil; therefore, do as you wish."
With a mind that has attained equanimity, I see this triple world as being merely its own true nature; act as you wish.
Kumbha said:
"If that is so, O protector of the earth, then this very day is an auspicious moment for the wedding; for I have calculated all of this for you today on this full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa."
"O mighty-armed one, tonight when the moon has risen with its full and stainless digits, our wedding ceremony shall take place for both of us."
On this delightful peak of the summit of Mount Mahendra,
adorned with jeweled palaces illuminated by the light of jewel-lamps.
It was resplendent with tall trees bent low under the weight of their blossoms,
and enchanting with the dancing of forest creepers like women performing a dance.
At night, let the stars moving through the sky, together with their lord, the full moon,
gaze upon us with eyes reaching to the tips of their ears.
"Arise for the sake of our own marriage; O King, let us prepare from the depths of the forest an abundance of sandalwood, flowers, and other materials, combined with jewels."
Having spoken thus, Kumbha rose up together with that king and gathered flowers as well as a collection of jewels and other such things.
Then, in just a moment, upon a level and auspicious jeweled peak, they indeed fashioned heaps rich with unguents and flowers.
Those heaps of necklaces, garments, the finest jewels, and so forth, shone like the treasuries of good fortune accumulated over time by Kāma.
Likewise, having prepared the necessary provisions for their journey, those two great friends went to the golden cave to bathe in the Mandākinī river.
Then, with great reverence, Kumbha first performed the auspicious rites and bathed the great king, whose shoulders were like the frontal lobes of an elephant.
Having gone to Cūḍālā— who was in the form of a future wife and destined to become his future spouse— he bathed his beloved, who was bearing the form of a water-jar.
Having bathed there, the two of them worshipped the gods, the ancestors, and the sages;
they were just as indifferent toward the fruits of ritual action as they were toward the abandonment of such action.
Though eternally satiated by the essence of knowledge, those two auspicious ones, impelled by one another, established the practice of eating for the sake of maintaining order in the world.
Having put on white garments produced by the wish-fulfilling trees and having eaten fruits, the two of them gradually arrived at the place where their bridegroom was staying.
In this much time, as those two were longing for their place of birth, the sun suddenly entered the mountain of setting, as if to do them a kindness.
Then, when the twilight ritual had been performed and the recitation of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn completed,
the sky became filled with a multitude of stars as if to witness the wedding.
The night, the sole companion of the month of Mithuna, smiling with its abundance of white water-lilies,
arrived scattering a profusion of networks of frost.
On the mountain peak, the potter properly arranged many jewel-lamps,
like the Lotus-born [Brahmā] arranging the celestial lights joined with the sun and moon from the sky.
Assuming the form of a woman at the onset of night, she adorned the king with floods of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron.
With necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, as well as garments from the wish-fulfilling vine, with garlands, wreaths, and various ornaments and flower-bouquets;

Likewise, with clusters of wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*), *mandāra* and *pārijātaka* trees, with *santāna* trees abounding in many jewels, and with a crown having the form of the moon; ||| MU_6,110.31 |||
After this much time had passed, Kumbha attained the state of a young bride; with his broad chest pressed against her firm breasts, he quickly became full of amorous grace.
He reflected thus: "I am now a married man;
for the sake of desire, my very self must be given by me, for indeed, one's duty is that which is appropriate to the occasion."
"Here I am, your lovely bride; here stands my husband before you. Come, O Kāma, take me; this is your time, O dweller in the heart!"

Having reflected thus, she spoke to her husband, who stood before her adorned like the rising sun, as Rati speaks to Kāma: iti sañcintya bhartāram agrastham abhimaṇḍitam / udayantam ivādityaṃ ratiḥ kāmam ivāha sā // MU_6,110.35 //
"I am your wife, named Madanikā, O giver of honor; this salutation is performed by me with affection for you, my husband."
Having spoken thus, she of faultless limbs, her face bowed down with shame,
prostrated before her husband with her head and its dangling locks, out of a sense of propriety.
And she said this: "O Lord, adorn me with ornaments;
having gradually kindled the fire, perform my marriage ceremony."
O Lord, you shine exceedingly; you make me afflicted by love. Having surpassed Madana, you preside over the wedding of Rati.
O King, your garlands shine like the networks of rays from the moon;
the necklace upon your chest bears the luster of the flowing current of the Ganges on Mount Meru.
O King, you shine with your locks of hair entwined with mandāra flowers,
like a golden lotus with hovering bees grey with pollen.
O Lord, you stand surpassing Mount Meru with your nets of jewel-rays, flowers, splendor, steadfastness, majesty, and loftiness.
Speaking in this manner, those two future husband and wife,
who had previously been a hidden couple, became mutually delighted with one another.
King Śikhidhvaja himself adorned Queen Madanikā after seating her upon a golden, stainless couch.
With ear-ornaments, as well as garlands, with ornaments of gems and pearls, with garments, ointments, and flowers, each placed in its appropriate position; ||| MU_6,110.45 |||
Adorned, that slender woman, intoxicating and bestowing joy,
shone like Pārvatī longing for her wedding, or like a passionate woman beloved by Kāma.
The great king, having adorned the queen, said this to her:
"O fawn-eyed one, you shine like the goddess Lakṣmī newly arisen."
May that which Śacī has with Śakra, that which Lakṣmī has with Hari,
and that which Gaurī has together with Śambhu— may that be your auspiciousness.
With teeth like the sprouts of a lotus root and eyes like trembling blue lotuses,
you stand like a lotus pond, your form made fragrant and beautiful.
With hands of deeply red sprouts and bearing clusters as breasts,
I consider you alone to be the fruit-bearing creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree of love.
With limbs as white and cool as snow, with a smile that radiates like moonlight,
you delight us the moment you are seen, like the splendor of the full moon appearing in the sky.
Therefore arise yourself, O lady of beautiful limbs, and let us prepare the wedding altar in due order with nets of jewel-like flowers and creepers.
Having spoken thus, the lovely couple then prepared an altar for their own wedding in the jeweled cave of Mahendra.
With clusters of pearls accompanied by tinkling sounds, with flower-crests together with bees,
with jeweled garlands making a *ṭāṅkāra* noise, and with fluttering Vaijayantī banners;
With threads of *kalpa*-trees and creepers, with clusters of *kalpa*-blossoms,
with bands of *kalpa*-trees, and with heaps of *kalpa*-tree fruits;
With networks of deodar vines marked by their joint-jewels, and with heaps of pearls, flowers, and parched grain resembling stars;
And on the four sides, with four great coconut fruits fashioned as full water-pots filled with the overflowing waters of the Gaṅgā; ||| MU_6,110.57 |||
In its center, they kindled a fire with sandalwood logs,
its flames blazing, circumambulating it clockwise from the right.
Having first seated the lovely couple upon a seat of sprouts facing east in front of the fire, he himself sat down beside them.
Having offered sesame seeds, parched grain, and other oblations to the fire, Śikhidhvaja rose up,
raised his beloved with both hands, and took her by himself.
Shining with mutual splendor like two other newlywed Śivas,
that couple performed the circumambulation of the sacred fire.

Those two, worthy of honor, with the splendor of their smiling and radiant faces, mutually bestowed upon one another their own inheritance— the entirety of their knowledge, their hearts, and their unwavering love.
Having performed three circumambulations and offered parched grains into the fire,
they both saw my wife from the sky and gradually released their hands.
With smiling faces, the two lovely ones, like two newly risen moons,
entered their new bed of flowers prepared beforehand.
In the meantime, the moon slowly ascended one-quarter of the way toward the sky, as if to behold the splendor of these two.
On that plateau, O beautiful woman, the moon sent forth his trembling rays through the openings in the creepers on all sides, as if casting his glances to look about.
With various such conversations there, as the moon rose,
that lovely couple remained together for a short while.
Then, having risen, the two lovers entered the golden cave, which was previously prepared by them, secluded, and illuminated by blazing jewel-lamps.
There they beheld a new couch prepared with flowers,
surrounded on all sides by heaps of blossoming golden lotuses.
It was constructed with high, uniform flowers, such as mandāra and others, free from wilting,
and reaching the height of a man.
Resembling the long orb of the moon, cool as a bed of snow,
with the luster of a stream from the Ocean of Milk, and white like a mass of moonlight.
Like a reflection appearing on a wall of jewels, it is infinite,
fragrant, exalted, lovely, and free from perishability.
That couple fell upon that heap of pure white flowers,
which was as level and expansive as Mount Mandara in the ocean of milk.

Then, through various graceful expressions of speech consisting of humble prostrations, through endearments made auspicious by the duties of that moment, and through ever-new pleasures shared with their beloveds, those two long nights passed as if they were but a single moment.
The One Hundred and Eleventh Chapter, titled "The Playful Marriage," by Vasiṣṭha.
Then, while the interior of the world was colored by the rays of the sun,
Madanī, the wife of Śikhidhvaja, once again assumed the form of a water-jar.
Thus, on Mount Mahendra, both Kumbha and Śikhidhvaja were personally married by him; they became a beloved and accomplished newlywed couple.
Every day they sported in the various forest groves, which were laden with the weight of fully ripened fruits and abounded in flowers and tender shoots.
During the day they were more dear to each other as friends, and at night as beloved husband and wife;
like a lamp and its light, they remained joined and were never separated.
They remained in forest groves and mountain caves,
amidst thickets of *tamāla* and *sāla* trees, and in dense thickets of *mandāra* blossoms.
And on the Sahya, Dardura, Kailāsa, Mahendra, and Malaya mountains; and on the slopes of Gandhamādana, the Vindhya range, and the Lokāloka mountain.
When her beloved had gone to sleep after traveling for three days at a time,
Cūḍālā, having performed her royal duties, returned once more to her own place.
During the day they were friends, and at night they were husband and wife; clothed in various flowers, the two lords of Kumbha remained together in mutual joy.
For one month, they were honored by gods and kinnaras in a cave-dwelling on the peak of Mount Mahendra, which was filled with *sarala* trees and featured walls of jewels.
And when the risen moon was within reach of the hand and the Mandara grove was garlanded [with its scent],
thus, on the back of the Śuktimat mountain, month after month in a bower of creepers—
For two months, on the southern slope of Mount Ṛkṣavat,
in the Pārijāta grove within a pavilion of celestial flower clusters, [he dwelt].
At the foot of Mount Meru, beneath the Jambū grove on the bank of the Jambū river,
he dwelt for a month upon ground made of Jāmbūnada gold, amidst the juice of jambū fruits.
They spent ten days in the region of Uttarakuru and twenty-seven days in the areas situated to the north of Kailāsa.
In this manner, those two illustrious friends, a devoted couple, dwelt in various other lands belonging to different rulers.
Then, after some months had gradually passed,
Cūḍālā, who possessed the form of a son of the gods, reflected:
"I shall test Śikhidhvaja with a burden of celestial enjoyments,
so that his mind may never again find delight in worldly pleasures."
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, by means of her illusory power, caused her husband to see Hari arrived in the forest together with the gods and the Apsarases.
Seeing Indra arrived with his retinue,
Śikhidhvaja, dwelling in the forest, honored him according to tradition.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O King of the Gods, why have you subjected yourself to the hardship of coming from so far away? You ought to tell me the truth regarding this, by your grace.
Indra said:
"We have been brought here from afar by the excellence of your virtues,
like birds drawn by a string fastened to their hearts."
Arise and come to heaven; there all the hosts of celestial women stand, their faces turned toward you, filled with wonder at hearing of your virtues.
"Here are chariots, here is a vehicle, and here is the horse Uccaiḥśravas;
this is the elephant Airāvaṇa—take whatever shelter you desire."
Furthermore, having taken up sandals, pills, the sword, the elixir, and so forth,
attain the realm of heaven by means of the path of accomplishment.
Until the end of the kalpa, divine enjoyments are to be experienced by you, who are liberated while living, in the abode of the gods; for that reason, I have come to you.
Such truly virtuous people as you do not despise the prosperity that has arrived with insults, nor do they long for prosperity that has not yet been attained.
By your arrival today without hindrance and by your dwelling in happiness,
may heaven attain purity, just as the three worlds were purified by Hari.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O leader of the gods and others, I know heaven and its heavenly conduct;
however, for me, heaven is not restricted to any one place alone."
For I am satisfied everywhere, O Lord, and I rejoice everywhere;
because my mind is free from longing, I am full of bliss in all things.
"O Śakra, there is certainly nothing of this kind that leads to heaven which remains fixed in one place; I do not know how to go [there], nor do I perform what is unknown."
Indra said:
"O virtuous one, for the good whose wisdom is perfected and who have known what is to be known,
I consider the enjoyment of pleasures to be consistent with the conduct of the righteous."
When the Lord of the Gods had spoken thus and the king remained silent, Hari said, "Why do you not accept me in this way?"
Saying "So be it" very softly, Kāla spoke to Śikhidhvaja;
then, saying "May it be well with you, O Kumbha," he vanished from sight.

Then that entire host of gods, together with the Lord of the Thirty-three, vanished in an instant, dissolved there like a mass of waves in the ocean when the wind has subsided— a sea whose surging sounds of sea-monsters, foam, and lordly serpents have ceased.
The hundred-twelfth canto, titled "The Arrival of Śakra," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having brought that illusion to an end, Cūḍālā reflected:
"By good fortune, this lord of the earth is not being carried away by his desire for enjoyments."
In that assembly of Śakra, he remained tranquil and with perfectly equanimous engagement;
without agitation or disdain, he maintained his conduct.
I shall once again examine this matter with care through further elaboration,
by means of some captivating [argument] dominated by passion and hatred.
Having reflected thus, that virtuous Madanikā, adorned with ornaments, surely went at night into the forest when the moon had risen.
While the wind blew, rich with flowers and thick with the fragrance of wine,
Śikhidhvaja stood on the riverbank intent upon his evening prayers.
Intoxicated with passion, she entered the inner chamber of the forest goddesses— a bower of *santānaka* creepers densely covered with clusters of flowers.
There, upon the flower-bed she had imagined, garlanded with a wreath of flowers,
she stood holding her imagined lover, Śiḍga, by the neck.
Having arrived and searched through the groves, Śikhidhvaja beheld in a bower of creepers a charming paramour at Madanikā’s throat.
His shoulders were draped with locks of hair, his body was anointed with sandalwood paste,
and his crest-jewel was disarrayed by tossing and turning upon the bed.
Upon a golden-colored couch, twice as wide as it was long, with the arms of a young woman serving as pillows,
her single ear, the corner of her eye, the surface of her cheek, and her locks of hair were submerged.
Then he beheld that couple, their faces smiling at one another,
with their mouths joined together, concealed by the garments of the Kalpa-creeper.
With their garlands and beds swaying, and agitated by the pangs of love,
they bestowed upon one another their own passion under the guise of applying cosmetics.
Intent on passion, filled with intense bliss, and possessed of unrestrained and intoxicated love,
they struck one another with flowers while pressing their breasts together against each other's chests.
Beholding that with an unchanging mind,
Śikhidhvaja was pleased and said, "Oh, what happiness these two youths find in their station!"
"Stay, dear ones, as you please and happily, just as you are; do not create obstacles to our pleasure. Having spoken thus, he departed.
Then, in just a moment, having disregarded her own elaborate display, she emerged, revealing her body agitated by the battle of passion.
She saw the king seated upon a golden stone slab in a secluded spot,
established in meditative absorption, with his eyes slightly opened.
Having arrived at that place, the woman Madanikā, her face bowed down with shame, sat in silence for a moment, distressed and withered.
