O slender one, why have you returned so soon, having had your joy thwarted?
Whatever beings there may be, they all strive only for bliss.
Go once more and satisfy that beloved with acts of affection;
for mutual love desired by both is indeed rare throughout the three worlds.
For this reason, O proud lady, I do not feel agitation;
for that which is most cherished in the world should be given away by one who understands.
"O slender-limbed one, Kumbha and I remain here free from passion; you, young woman, are born from the curse of Durvāsas—do as you wish."
Madanikā: Thus it is, O noble one; for the nature of womanhood is fickle.
Women possess eightfold passion; you ought not to be angry.
"I am a weak woman who has been carried off by him into the dense forest; while you are intent on your evening prayers, what can I, a wretched creature, do?"
A woman effects the imprisonment of a man by her mere word alone,
until a blade has been driven into his own body.
When a beautiful woman has gone to the embrace of another man's body, what will her anger, her refusal, or her lamentation avail regarding her chastity?
I am a weak woman, as well as young and foolish; I have committed an offense.
O Lord, you ought to forgive me, for the virtuous are indeed forgiving.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"My anger toward you, O young girl, does not exist within me, like a tree in the sky;
it is only because you are censured by the virtuous that I do not desire you as my daughter-in-law."
O lady, as before, let us always delight together in the forest retreats with equanimity, as friends, through the practice of austerity alone, being free from passion.
[Vasiṣṭha:
While Śikhidhvaja remained there in such equanimity, Cūḍālā, her intentions awakened by the truth of that state, reflected:
Oh, how great is this supreme equanimity! This Blessed One has arrived;
free from passion, fear, and anger, he abides as one liberated while living.
Neither desires for enjoyments, nor even great supernatural powers, nor pleasures, nor pains, nor calamities, nor successes can carry him away.
All blameless women of great supernatural power, as soon as they are thought of, come to him, just like another Nārāyaṇa.
I shall remind him of my entire life story;
having abandoned this form of a jar, I shall become Cūḍālā once again.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, having abandoned the form of Madanikā, quickly revealed her own unimpaired form as Cūḍālā right there.
Therefore, as if she had emerged from the body of Madanikā,
Cūḍālā appeared like a spotless pearl released from its casket.
He beheld before him that lady of faultless limbs,
Cūḍālā, his beloved wife, standing there as charming as Madanikā through her affectionate demeanor.

The king beheld his own beloved wife, appearing like a cluster of spring lotuses in full bloom, like the goddess Śrī herself descended from the surface of the earth, or as if manifested from an open casket of jewels.
The one hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Elaboration of the Lover," by Vasiṣṭha:

Then, seeing his beloved, Śikhidhvaja’s eyes blossomed with wonder, and he spoke these words in a voice agitated by amazement: Śikhidhvaja said: "O you who possess the splendor of a goddess, O you who are like a celestial nymph, O you who are adorned with all ornaments, O you who are as beautiful as the moon! O you whose face is like the full moon, O you whose eyes are like lotuses, O you who are radiant with the beauty of your limbs, O you who are the very essence of loveliness! O you who are the source of joy to the world, O you who are the delight of the gods, O you who are the supreme ornament of the three worlds, O you who are the embodiment of the highest bliss! O you who are the mother of the universe, O you who are the consort of the Lord of the World, O you who are the refuge of the virtuous, O you who are the supreme power of the Creator! O you who are the manifestation of the Supreme Spirit, O you who are the primordial nature, O you who are the sovereign of all beings, O you who are the eternal and imperishable one! O you who are the source of all prosperity, O you who are the dispeller of all misfortune, O you who are the giver of all boons, O you who are the supreme reality!"
Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? From where have you come, O beautiful lady? What is your purpose, for how long [have you been here], and for what reason do you stay here?
By your gestures, your conduct, your smile, and your conciliatory manner, you are perceived as my wife through your playful charm, like Cūḍālā herself.
Cūḍālā said: "It is even so, O Lord; know that I am Cūḍālā, there is no doubt.
Today I have been obtained by you in person with my unartificial body."
This elaborate display of mine, consisting of the construction of bodies such as the pot and so forth, has reached a hundredfold branching here within the forest of this world in order to awaken you.
When you abandoned the kingdom and went to the forest for asceticism out of delusion,
from that very moment I have been striving for your awakening.
By means of this pot-body, you have been awakened by me in this way;
yet, O Lord of the Earth, nothing such as a pot or anything else is real through illusion.
O Buddha, you who have realized what is to be known, through meditation this remains unimpaired; O knower of reality, you see everything—behold it swiftly through meditation!
Then, when Cūḍālā said, "So be it," the king girded his loins and beheld the entirety of his own life's story through meditation.
From the moment of his renunciation of sovereignty until the point of seeing Cūḍālā,
he beheld his entire life-story in a single moment of meditation.
Having observed the entire succession of present moments up until the total renunciation of his kingdom, the king ceased from his meditative absorption.
Abandoning his meditative concentration, his lotus-eyes blossoming with joy,
he quickly extended his arms, which became radiant with horripilation.
With his limbs trembling, his affection shining forth, tears rising, and longing surging,
he embraced his beloved for a long time, as a male mongoose embraces a female.
The state of being that arose during their embrace cannot indeed be described even in years by the tongues of Vāsuki.
Like figures fixed in a painting, or like two bodies cast from molten metal,
or as if carved out of a mountain, the two lovers remained embraced for a long time.
In a moment, their two beloved arms— dripping with networks of sweat and thick with horripilation— gradually became slightly slackened.
With his heart filled with nectar yet resembling a void heart,
let him remain with arms outstretched and eyes fixed on the imperceptible.
Having remained silent for a moment in intense bliss, the king, his hand resting on the chin of his beloved, spoke words tender with affection.
Ah! How sweet, tender, and lovely is this meritorious outflow of the conduct of noble women—more delicious even than nectar!
O slender-limbed one, how great was the terrible suffering experienced for a long time by you, who are as charming as the young moon, for the sake of your husband?
By what indeed can that intellect be compared, by which I have been rescued from this cave of saṃsāra so difficult to cross?
Arundhatī, Śacī, Gaurī, Gāyatrī, Śrī, and Sarasvatī—
all these appear delicate in comparison to the slender lady’s splendor of virtuous character.
O beautiful one, among those lovely qualities such as wisdom, grace, beauty, patience, friendliness, and compassion—
qualities that are themselves beautiful in form— you appear to be the very first.
I have been awakened by you through your supreme resolve;
by what recompense could my virtues ever equal it?
Out of delusion, noble women, even when falling into a beginningless, profound, and infinitely treacherous abyss, rescue their husbands by remaining devoted to them.
Neither the meaning of the scriptures, nor the guru, nor the mantras, and so forth,
are capable of delivering one in such a manner as these noble women of the family, who are full of affection for their husbands.
A wife of noble family is everything to her husband: she is his friend, brother, well-wisher, servant, teacher, counselor, wealth, happiness, scripture, sanctuary, and slave.
Women of noble family should always be honored with every effort;
all happiness in both worlds is properly established upon them.
For you who have departed without desire to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra,
how shall I ever perform a return service for such a kindness?
I believe that now, in this world, the entire community of noble women will become the subject of reference in all discussions concerning female virtue.
I believe that Arundhatī and the other women must surely have been provoked to anger by the Creator when he fashioned you, who surpasses them all with your web of virtues.
O casket of the jewels of virtues such as chastity, beauty, and goodness!
Come, grant once more an embrace to me, who am so devoted to your qualities.
Having spoken thus to Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like those of a young fawn, Śikhidhvaja embraced her firmly once more, as a mongoose embraces its mate.
Cūḍālā said:
"O Lord, while you were intent upon a web of dry rituals and your own mind was agitated,
I indeed became thus exceedingly distressed on your account."
Thus, you have established your own purpose, which consists in awakening me;
therefore, O Lord, why do you offer words of praise to me in this matter?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, just as you have accomplished your own auspicious purpose,
so now may all virtuous women of noble family accomplish theirs."
Cūḍālā said:
O Lord, you in whom the entire web of the world has come to rest solely within a portion of the intellect—
do you still perceive that former delusion today?
"I am doing this, but I do not attain that; rather, I obtain this from here"—do you perhaps inwardly laugh at such a mind whose hope is as fragile as a blade of grass?
O Lord, those trivial stirrings of thirst and those wicked imaginings of conceptual thought are no longer seen in you today, just as mountains are not seen in the sky.
Who are you, endowed with such a body today? What is your ultimate aim, and what do you seek?
O Lord, how do you perceive the future sequence of the body's states?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O you who perceive the essence of the garland of blue lotuses filled with flowers—whatever that is, you alone know it; I have arrived for that very purpose."
I am effortless, I am partless, I am as pure as the sky, and I am free from desire;
I am peace, I am the very form of the ultimate reality, and I have long remained as the Self.
I have reached such a state, O Caṇpakavarṇinī,
that even great beings like Hari, Jina, and others appear pitiable to me.
I am established in my own state, resting in the pure consciousness that is nothing at all;
I have had enough of delusion, O lovely-eyed one, for I am now liberated from saṃsāra.
I am neither pleased nor distressed; I am not this, nor am I the other;
I am neither gross nor subtle, O beautiful one, yet I am everything.
I am indeed equal to a light that has departed from a luminous orb, that has not fallen upon a wall, and that is free from both decay and excess.
I am peaceful; I am equanimity itself; I am pure and free from ailment;
I am indeed in final nirvāṇa; I exist in the most excellent vow.
I am able to say only that which truly exists, and nothing else:
"O you whose side-glances are tremulous like waves, you are my guru; salutations be to you!"
Through the grace of the large-eyed lady, I have crossed over the ocean of existence;
I shall not take up defilement again, like gold that has been smelted a hundred times.
Established in my own nature, peaceful, gentle, self-controlled, free from passion, and possessing an undivided intellect;
transcending all and omnipresent, I abide like the sky.
This being the case, O Great Being, Lord of Life, beloved of the heart:
tell me now, O Master, what pleases you, O High-minded One?
Śikhidhvaja said: "I do not know your refusal, nor do I know your longing;
whatever you do, O slender one, I may or may not know it at any time."
O beloved, the mind, like the pure vow of the sky, does not know how to perceive any portion of destruction, nor any portion of persistence.
Whatever you know, O beautiful one, do that very thing;
I shall hold it just as a gem reflects an image.
With a mind free from desire, O blameless one, I neither praise nor blame you regarding what you have obtained; do as you wish.
Cūḍālā said:
"If it is so, then O illustrious one, listen to my thought;
having heard it, O you whose self is liberated while living, you ought to carry it out."
Now, through the realization of universal oneness— which arises from the destruction of ignorance—
we remain free from desire, as clear as the sky.
Just as this seeking is for us, so too is this non-seeking;
for when there is the shining forth of pure consciousness alone, what distinction can there be between seeking and non-seeking?
Therefore, O Supreme Person, those among us who have abandoned ignorance at the beginning, middle, and end are the very ones established here.
"Now, O Lord, having spent this time according to our current purpose, we shall gradually attain the state of being bodiless through some means of time."
Śikhidhvaja said:
O fickle one, tell me, what kind of people are we at the beginning, middle, and end?
Or rather, how can we remain, having abandoned this singular delusion?
Cūḍālā said:
"O best of kings, we have been your subjects from beginning to middle to end;
having now abandoned our sole delusion, we remain once again yours."
"Be you the king in your own city, established upon your own throne;
I shall become your queen, the most excellent among lovely women."
The city, with its intoxicated inhabitants and their king, was filled with dancing young women; it was adorned with banners, resounded with the music of trumpets, and strewn with showers of flowers.
O Lord, may it be long for us as if it were a row of spring forest groves, filled with flowering creepers, accompanied by humming bees, and equal to a cluster of blossoms.
When Cūḍālā had spoken thus, Śikhidhvaja smiled and spoke these sweet words, unperturbed and without haste.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"If that is so, O large-eyed one, then those lands of the Siddhas' enjoyments in the triple heaven are under our own control; why then, my dear, do we not dwell in them?"
Cūḍālā said:
"O King, I have no desire for enjoyments nor for riches; O Monarch, I rejoice simply by the power of my own nature in whatever comes to me."
Neither heaven, nor sovereignty, nor even liberation brings me happiness;
rather, I remain established as I am, unshaken, with my conduct centered in well-being.
When the mental conceits of "this is pleasure" and "this is not" have come to an end,
I abide here at ease in this peaceful state of absolute equanimity.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O large-eyed one, you have spoken rightly with this balanced intellect.
For what purpose indeed could there be in either the grasping or the abandoning of a kingdom?"
Having abandoned concern for states of pleasure and pain and being free from envy,
let us both remain exactly as we are, having attained composure.
Thus, through their conversation there,
the day drew to a close for those two beloveds who had been husband and wife for so long.

Then, having risen, those two blameless ones, though full of longing, performed their daily duties as they occurred without any sense of yearning; skilled in their task, they remained with their minds complete, disregarding the attainment of heaven.
On that very same bed, through various acts of affection,
the night passed for those two who were liberated while still alive.

That long night passed like a mere moment for those two lovers, who were longing for the supreme bliss of worldly enjoyment and liberation; it brought to its fullness their yearning, which was filled with the playful charm of their affectionate words.
The one hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "The Manifestation of Cūḍālā," by Vasiṣṭha:
Then, when the sun had risen and stood in a sky free from darkness,
this jewel of the world emerged as if from a casket.
The lotus-pond blossomed at the edge of the dawn like two eyes,
as the rays of the sun spread forth through the worlds as if through established customs.
Having risen and performed their twilight rituals, the two beloved spouses sat upon soft and smooth leaf-seats in a golden cave.
Then Cūḍālā rose up there and, with a jeweled pitcher held in her hand, she,
as a wife, consecrated her husband in private within her own kingdom.
When he was seated upon a magnificent throne, consecrated on a lion-seat brought forth by his own volition,
that slender Cūḍālā, possessing a divine form, addressed him.
O Lord, setting aside your mere silence, you ought to withdraw this peaceful splendor in order to take back the energies of the eight world-protectors.
Thus addressed as "Cūḍāla" in the forest, King Śikhidhvaja said,
"I shall do so," and attained the status of a great king.
Then he said to the proud woman standing in the position of a doorkeeper:
"O Queen, I shall consecrate you to the rank of Great Queen."
Having spoken thus and established her upon the throne in the position of the Great Queen, King Meghavāg, after performing her consecration, said to his beloved:
"O dear one, lotus-petal-eyed lady, you ought to summon in an instant an army of vast power and unrestrained might, born of mere thought."
Having heard these words of her beloved, the fair-complexioned Cūḍālā conjured up an army as formidable as a mass of monsoon clouds.
The two of them beheld that army, crowded with horses and elephants,
its banners filling the sky and making the forest appear dense.
The mountain caves resounded with the blare of trumpets, the deep interior of the forest was filled with intoxicated vassals, and the wild elephants were fleeing in terror.
It was fierce in its tearing apart, like a great roaring lion rising up; it was a victorious elephant trumpeting with the scent of flowing temple-ichor in the forest.
It was thick with the creaking of wheels from the collision of multitudes of celestial chariots,
and it shattered the veil of dust and darkness by the dense radiance of the jewels in their crowns.
There, upon that excellent fragrant elephant, within a royal pavilion protected by haughty vassal lords, the king and queen ascended.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, together with his beloved queen,
leading a mighty army crowded with foot soldiers and chariots, marched forth.
The army, impetuous and causing even mountains to tremble,
moved with great force, swiftly splitting the rocks as a whirlwind splits the clouds.
Therefore, that lord of the earth set out from Mahendra, the king of mountains,
beholding on his way the mountains, regions, rivers, and villages together with their jungles.
And showing that collection of his own adventures to his beloved,
he reached his own city, which was as beautiful as heaven, in a very short time.
There, his vassals, honoring his arrival, understood his coming by the sound of "Victory! and went forth with their intentions stirred.
Accompanied by those two armies, which had joined as one and resounded with the blare of trumpets, the king entered the city.
Showered with handfuls of parched grain and flowers by the city women as he proceeded along the merchant's road, he beheld the city most magnificently adorned.
Crowded with banners and flags, beautiful with nets of pearls,
and filled with women devoted to dance and song, it was like heaven fallen to earth.
Then, having entered the palace accompanied by various royal auspicious rites,
he duly honored the multitude of subjects who bowed before him.
Having celebrated a magnificent festival for seven excellent days,
the king, having honored the women of his inner apartments, attended to his royal duties.
Having ruled over the earth for ten thousand years,
the king, together with Cūḍālā, desisted from maintaining the body.
Having cast off the body, O Rāma, that one of great intelligence attained nirvāṇa like a lamp without oil, so as not to be born again.
Having ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years with that impartial vision, he attained the state of Nirvana.
Free from fear and dejection, liberated from pride and envy, performing his natural and innate duties with a mind unattached and free from passion—
thus, that noble one, possessing a perfectly balanced vision, conquered death and ruled over ten thousand winters as a sole sovereign.
Having enjoyed infinite pleasures on earth and having remained for a long time as the crest-jewel of all sovereign rulers, he indeed attained that supreme state of immortality;

just as he did, so you, following the course of events that has come upon you through Rāma, remain free from sorrow while attending to your duties, and arise! By your own effort, forcefully experience the foremost glory of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The story of Śikhidhvaja is concluded;
this is the one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "Vasiṣṭha."
All this story of Śikhidhvaja has been told to you;
go by this path, and you shall never again experience weariness.
Grasping this view which destroys the sins of Rāghava,
remain with a mind eternally free from passion, firmly established in that state.
Just as Śikhidhvaja ruled his kingdom, so too, O Rāma, conducting yourself in the realm in such a manner, become one who possesses both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Rāghava, understand it in this way: just as Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, attained awakening through the very method of Śikhidhvaja.
Rāma said:
"This venerable Kaca is the son of the blessed Bṛhaspati;
O Blessed One, tell me how he became awakened, in brief."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, how that glorious Kaca, born of the preceptor of the gods, attained supreme awakening just like Śikhidhvaja.
Having transcended childhood and being intent on crossing over saṃsāra,
Kaca, who understood both words and their meanings, spoke to Bṛhaspati.
Kaca said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, tell me how a living being, bound by the thread of life, may emerge from this cage of saṃsāra."
Bṛhaspati said:
"O son, one crosses this ocean of saṃsāra— which is a house made of the fires of misfortune— without agitation by means of renouncing everything."
Vasiṣṭha:
Having heard these most purifying words of his father,
Kaca abandoned everything and went to a solitary forest.
That departure of Bṛhaspati did not cause him any distress;
for the great remain equanimous in both union and separation.
Then, O sinless one, when eight years had passed,
Kaca once again encountered his father in a certain great forest.

Having fully honored and saluted him, and having embraced his son, Kaca again questioned the Lord of Speech with a weary voice: *paripūjyābhivandyainaṃ samāliṅgitaputrakam / apṛcchad vākpatiṃ bhūyas sa kacaḥ klāntayā girā //* MU_6,115.13*
Kacha said:
"Today marks the eighth year since I made this total renunciation;
yet even so, O father, I do not attain blameless rest."
Vasiṣṭha:
While Kaca was speaking thus with a distressed mind in the forest,
the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), having said "Abandon everything," ascended to heaven.
Once he had departed from the body, Kaca cast off even his bark garments and all else without exception, just as the sky sheds rain-clouds and the like at the onset of autumn.
He dwelt alone at the ends of the quarters, peaceful, with a body as empty as space, breathing like the autumnal sky from which the moon, clouds, sun, and stars have departed.
Then, after another three years, with a grieving mind, he reached that very same father and preceptor in a certain part of the forest.
Having performed the sequence of worship with devotion and having embraced his son,
he questioned him once more with a voice faltering from grief.
Kaca said:
"Father, everything has been renounced—even my patched garment, my bamboo staff, and my girdle of munja grass—yet there is still no rest in my own true state; what shall I do?"
Bṛhaspati said:
"They say that the mind is everything; having abandoned that, O son, you shall shine.
Those people who know renunciation understand that the abandonment of the mind is the abandonment of everything."
Vasiṣṭha, having spoken thus, the Lord of Speech, flew swiftly into the sky after his son;
Kaca, however, with an undaunted mind, sought to abandon his life.
When he could not perceive his own mind even while reflecting upon it in the forest, he then pondered this with an undaunted intellect:
*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 6.115.23* (as cited) When he could not perceive his own mind even while reflecting upon it in the forest, he then pondered this with an undaunted intellect.
[Kaca said:
"The entire collection of objects, such as the body and so forth, is not said to be 'all' in this context. Why, and wherefore, should I abandon this which is useless and innocent?"
I shall go into the presence of my father to recognize the great enemy that is the mind;
and having recognized it, I shall quickly abandon it, and thereafter I shall remain free from fever.
Vasiṣṭha:
Having reflected thus, Kaca ascended to heaven;
having reached the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), he affectionately paid homage and prostrated before him.
And in private he asked him: "O Blessed One, what is the nature of my mind?
Tell me the true form of the mind, so that I may renounce it."
Bṛhaspati said:
Those who know the mind understand the innate ego to be the mind;
that internal sense of "I-ness" which exists in a living being is called the mind.
Kaca said: "I think that his renunciation is difficult and does not lead to perfection;
how indeed, O best of yogins, is it possible for him to renounce?"
Bṛhaspati said:
Even from the plucking of flowers or even from the closing of the eyes, the abandonment of egoism is easy; there is not the slightest difficulty in this.
Kaca said:
O Great-minded One, tell me quickly how this [happened] regarding the host of gods, whose teacher you are and who number thirty-three times ten million.
Bṛhaspati said:
Listen, my son, as I tell you this very thing:
an object established solely through ignorance perishes through knowledge.
In reality, O son, there is no such thing as egoism; it is indeed a false delusion. Though non-existent, it appears as if existent—deceitful like a child’s phantom.
Just as the state of being a serpent appears in a rope, and just as the notion of water appears in a desert,
so too does the false ego manifest through a false appearance.
Just as duality, though non-existent, is perceived in the moon due to delusion,
so too does the ego-sense flash forth, appearing as if real though it is not real.
There exists the one, devoid of beginning and end, pure consciousness alone, stainless and all-pervading; clearer even than the sky, it is the knower of all.
In all places, at all times, and in every manner, that very same one shines within all living beings, like the water in shifting waves.
In this regard, what is this sense of "I," from where does it arise, and how has it emerged?
Where could a mass of dust be born from the ocean, and where could water rise from fire?
Abandon, my son, this vain notion of "I am this," which is hollow,
limited in form, and rendered subservient by space and time.
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, transparent, eternally manifest, all-pervading,
consisting of all objects yet having a single object, you are the stainless pure consciousness alone.
Like the sap of fruits, flowers, and leaves situated in every direction, you are ever-present within all worlds;
as the most stainless conscious self, eternally and infinitely vast, O embodiment of being, how indeed could there be any notion of "I" in you?
The one hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Awakening of Bṛhaspati’s Hair," by Vasiṣṭha.
Having thus attained this supreme yoga, the unsurpassed instruction,
that son of the preceptor of the gods became liberated while living.
Free from objective existence, free from egoism, with the knots of the heart severed and the intellect profoundly tranquil—
O Rāma, remain as Kaca remained, free from all modification.
Know that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is non-existent; do not rely upon it, but abandon it.
For how indeed can there be the acts of abandoning or grasping in relation to a non-existent thing, such as the horn of a hare?
When egoism is impossible, where are your birth and death? By whom can a fruit be gathered that has been sown in the expanse of space?
You are partless, with all conceptual constructions stilled, the self-nature of all beings, all-pervading,
subtler than even the most subtle atom, pure consciousness alone, and free from all affliction.
Just as waves and the like arise from water, or as bracelets and the like from gold,
so too the conception of "I" appears from consciousness as if it were something other than that very [consciousness].
Through lack of awakening, O sinless one, the entire world remains as if composed of illusion; through awakening, everything becomes the very form of Brahman.
Abandoning the notions of duality and unity, remain happy as one who abides in the remainder;
do not be miserable in vain like a deluded person.
This illusory nature of saṃsāra, which is exceedingly difficult to cross and has attained the status of substantiality,
quickly comes to attenuation through awakening, like autumnal mist.
Rāma:
I have attained the highest inner satisfaction through the nectar of your knowledge, just as a cātaka bird, overcome by the fear of drought, finds relief in a refreshing downpour of rain.
As if sprinkled with nectar, I experience an inner coolness;
I stand, as it were, above all incomparable attainments.
I do not attain satiety while you speak these words, just as the cakora bird, parched with thirst, finds no satisfaction in the rays of the moon.
O Lord, though already satisfied, I ask you this further question:
who indeed, even when satiated, would not drink the nectar-liquor standing before him?
O best of sages, what is said regarding that which is named the "false person"? Please tell me quickly how the multitude of worldly entities is rendered unreal.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, listen to this beautiful narrative uttered by me, which produces laughter and serves to awaken you from the delusion of being a person.
O mighty-armed one, there is a certain person consisting of illusion and machinery,
whose intellect is as tender as a child's, who is deluded and hidden solely by his own ignorance.
Having arisen somewhere in solitude, he remains right there in that void,
like a mass of hair in the sky or like a mirage in the desert.
Therefore, there is nothing else there; that which exists is that very thing itself.
And as for that which is other, it is a mere appearance of existence—the one of dull intellect does not perceive this.
As he grew up there, a fixed resolve arose within him:
"I am space, I am space, space is mine, and I protect space. MU 6.116.19.
"Having established myself in the sky, I shall protect my beloved object with diligent care.
Thinking thus, he built a house for the purpose of guarding the sky.
He fixed his mind on that treasury, thinking, "The space within me has been protected by me";
thus, O descendant of Raghu, he remained content with the space inside his house.
Then, in the course of time, that house of his went to ruin,
just as one season passes away by another, or as a wave is driven away by the wind.
"Alas, O house-space, you are lost! Alas, where have you gone in an instant?
Alas, alas, you pure one, you are shattered! Thus did he lament.
Having thus lamented for a long time, the evil-minded one once again dug a well right there for the sake of his donkey; he became intent on the empty space within the well.
Then, in the course of time, even his well met its destruction; consequently, he became overwhelmed by a great sorrow as vast as the space of that well.
At the conclusion of his discourse on the space within the well, he placed the water-jar right there;
having become one with the space within the jar, he himself attained final liberation.
O descendant of Raghu, even Kumbha was brought to destruction by him in due time;
whichever direction he takes up, that too perishes, being as if ill-fated.
At the conclusion of his prattle regarding the space within the jar, he dug a pit right there for the sake of a donkey;
because of that, he became obsessed with the space within the pit.
In time, even his sacrificial pit met its destruction in the forest;
because of that, like darkness by light, he grieved for the state of the pit.
At the end of his grief over the pit and the sky, he built a great four-winged mansion for the sake of his wife; then he became intent upon the sky.
Time, which devours all creatures, swiftly snatched that away from him as well, just as the wind carries off a withered leaf; he became utterly consumed by grief for it.
At the edge of the four-pillared palace, he constructed a granary for the sake of protection against wild beasts;
it was shaped like a water-jar, and he remained within it, situated beyond the reach of space.
Time quickly snatched that away from him, like the wind from a cloud;
because of that grief over the space within the granary, he was consumed by torment.
In this way, with the house, the four-sided hall, the water-jar, the bowl, and the granary, this time of his, which is without end, passes away.

Thus situated, that one of deceitful intellect, grasping at the sky within a cave as if it were his own home, yet not truly possessing a home through the sky due to his deluded self-conception, O friend, this fool goes and comes from state to state, entering a denser suffering than even the net of thick misery.
In the narrative of the False Man, the one hundred seventeenth canto, titled "The Protection of the Sky," Rāma said:
O Lord, why have you spoken of this illusory person (māyāpuruṣa) in connection with the pursuit of a false man? And why is the protection of the sky being mentioned?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, Rāma, as it truly is; I shall reveal this to you. Now, let me tell the narrative of the story of the illusory man.
O descendant of Raghu, know that this person who is said to consist of the machinery of illusion is indeed the ego (ahaṅkāra), arisen from the empty sky.
O holy one, that corner of space within which this world resides is itself infinite,
non-existent, and void at the beginning of creation.
Then, from that cavity of sound— the space of Brahman situated within and extremely difficult to perceive—
egoism arises, like the first vibration from the wind.
Having increased in the sky, that rogue imagines it to be his own self;
through the conceit of "I" regarding what is not the self, he then exerts himself.
For the sake of protecting the Self alone— which is non-self— this world repeatedly creates these various bodies, having observed that they have perished again and again.
That very person is a person of illusion; he is indeed a false person.
Though non-existent, he has arisen in vain, and even the ego-sense is produced by illusion.
Having fashioned the body as a house, a sacrificial pit, a quadrangle, a jar, and so forth, and thinking "the self has been protected," he directs his contemplation toward that space [of the heart].
O Rāghava, hear these names of that very egoism, by which delusions at the beginning of the world it falls into infatuation.

It is also well known as the living soul (jīva), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), consciousness (citta), illusion (māyā), primordial nature (prakṛti), volition (saṅkalpa), conceptualization (kalanā), time (kāla), and a digit of time (kalā).
Through these and other such names that have multiplied, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), possessing a thousand forms, expands by means of imagined objects.
Within the vast and empty space of the elements, the person has long remained in a state of utter falsehood, experiencing pleasures and pains through the fabrications of the world.
Just as this false person, fearing for his own self,
guards the space within jars and so forth [as if it were his own], do not become afflicted in such a manner.
The Self, which is more vast than even space, pure, subtle, auspicious, and beautiful— how and by whom can it be protected or likewise grasped?
While the Self resides within the space of the heart just as the space within a jar [resides within a jar],
living beings vainly mourn at the time of dissolution, thinking, "The Self is destroyed."
Just as space remains undivided when jars and other objects have perished,
so too the embodied self is eternally indestructible when bodies have perished.
This Self is pure consciousness alone, subtler than even space;
for it does not perish, O Rāma, being like the sky, consisting solely of the portion of one's own self-experience.
Nothing whatsoever is ever born, nor does anything ever die anywhere;
it is only Brahman that expands in the form of the world's manifestation.
All this is one, peaceful, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and liberated from existence and non-existence; having realized this, be happy.

Having abandoned through awakening the entire locus of egoity— which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking self-mastery, prone to downfall, devoid of discernment, essence-less, and ignorant— you remain in the perfectly established state and attain the highest excellence.
The One Hundred and Eighteenth Chapter, titled "The Narrative of the False Man," by Vasiṣṭha:
Before the Supreme Brahman, the mind first arose;
consisting of thought and expansive in its reach, it attained its state of existence while remaining established in Him alone.
O Raghava, the mind is in Brahman like fragrance in a flower-bud, like a great wave in the ocean, and like a network of rays in the sun.
O Rāma, the state of that invisible reality of the self has come about solely through forgetfulness; it did not come through any other means, just like the appearance of a snake in a rope.
O Raghava, for one who contemplates this web of rays as being distinct from the sun, it appears as something other than that luminous body.
For one by whom the armlet is conceived as being distinct from gold, that for him is merely an armlet;
it is not gold for him.
For one who perceives a wave as distinct from water,
only the notion of a wave remains for them, not the ocean.
He by whom the wave is perceived as non-different from the water,
and who possesses the awakened cognition of the commonality of water, is called "free from conceptual construction" (nirvikalpa).
He by whom the armlet is perceived as not distinct from the gold,
possessing the great wisdom that gold alone exists, is called one who is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
For one who conceives of a series of flames as distinct from the fire itself,
the cognition of "fire" vanishes and only the cognition of "flames" remains.
That state is likewise colored by the flickering mass of flames;
the agitated mind, being absorbed in that, adopts that very same condition.
He by whom a series of flames is perceived as non-different from fire possesses only the cognition of fire; he is said to be free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
He who is free from conceptual construction is great; he is a sage whose mind has been utterly stilled.
That which is to be attained has been attained by him, and he does not sink into worldly objects.
Having abandoned all diversity within the hollow of pure consciousness alone, O sinless one, become a portion of pure awareness, free from all objective perception.
When the Self itself quickly brings forth by its own power the creative faculty called *saṅkalpa*,
it becomes manifest, just as the wind produces the power of motion.
Then the mind, consisting of the fabrication of conceptualization, appears as if separate; it becomes the self of the universe and itself fashions its own form.
That mind, whose nature is volition, whatever it conceives of as this entire world,
that very thing becomes so for the volitional being in an instant.

The mind— designated by such names as ego, intellect, and consciousness— has likewise attained the state of an insect, the state of being born from a lotus, the state of Mount Meru, and the state of an atom.
Having attained the state of Viriñci through its own volition, the mind extends the maintenance of the world;
subsequently, within that very maintenance, it itself undergoes manifoldness.
This expansive world is seen as consisting solely of mental construction;
it is neither real nor yet unreal, having arisen like a web of dreams.
Just as a person’s kingdom of the mind shines forth with various undertakings,
so does this vast kingdom of Brahmā expand.
Just as a dream is neither unreal because it appears nor is it real, so too, O Sage, the world and the divine realm of the mind are neither non-existent nor existent.
For this which has attained density is merely a false appearance;
because it is cultivated through the reality of things as they truly are, it dissolves away.
If it is seen from the perspective of ultimate truth, this is nothing at all;
but when seen from the perspective of what is not ultimate, it branches out into a hundred directions.
Just as the ocean, by its very nature, manifests a body that is fit for the calculation of waves, ripples, and surges, so too does the all-pervading Lord manifest his form.
Even while performing thousands of actions, the agent does nothing new apart from the vibration of consciousness; therefore, abandon all notions of duality.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, speaking, acting, and sleeping—realize with certainty that one does not perform anything unprecedented. MU 6.118.26.
Whatever you do, that is in truth the stainless, pervasive Pure Consciousness;
it is Brahman whose form is expanded, and nothing other than that exists.
Since the entire multitude of objects exists with consciousness as its essence, this whole world is nothing but consciousness; there is no other conception.
In this mere radiance of consciousness called the web of the world,
how can there be the false grasping that "this is one thing" and "that is another"?
Since everything arises from a single consciousness alone in all its forms, even the object of cognition does not exist; therefore, whence can there be bondage or liberation?
Having forcibly cast aside all thoughts such as "this is liberation" or "this is bondage," and having abandoned every conceit of partiality,
remain as one who is silent, self-controlled, free from pride and intoxication, a great soul performing his own duty, truly devoid of egoism.
The one hundred and nineteenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of the Ultimate Truth," by Vasiṣṭha.
O sinless one, you are a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer;
having abandoned all doubts, take hold of eternal fortitude.
Rāma said:
What is meant by "the great doer"? What is meant by "the great renouncer"? What is meant by "the great enjoyer"? O Lord, tell me correctly.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, in former times this triad of vows was declared as supreme by the one who bears the crescent moon on his crest to Bhṛṅgīśa, by which he became free from all affliction.
Formerly, on the northern peak of Mount Sumeru, which resembled fire, Śaśikalādhara dwelt together with his entire retinue.
O Rāma, the highly resplendent Bhṛṅgīśa, having bowed down with joined palms, questioned the Lord of Umā out of his own desire to know through wisdom.
Bhṛṅgīśa said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, omniscient Supreme Lord,
please tell me quickly that which I am asking out of compassion.
O Lord, beholding this construction of saṃsāra, as flickering as a wave, I am bewildered, being deprived of rest in reality.
Having firmly embraced which beloved internal certainty do I remain in this dilapidated house of the world, free from the fever of distress?
Īśvara said:
O sinless one, having abandoned all doubts and resorted to eternal fortitude, become a great renouncer, a great doer, and a great enjoyer.
Bhṛṅgīśa said: Why is he called the great renouncer? Why is he called the great enjoyer?
Why is he called the great agent? O Lord, tell me correctly.
The Lord:
He whose disposition is free from apprehension regarding the arising or passing away of merit and demerit,
and who acts according to what has come to him, is called a great doer.
He who acts without any regard for passion and hatred, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, or fruit and lack of fruit— he is called a Great Agent.
He who acts with silence, free from egoism, devoid of pride, and liberated from envy,
performing his duties without agitation, is called a great doer.
He whose mind is not stained by doubt regarding dharma and adharma in matters both auspicious and inauspicious is called a great doer.
He who is free from attachment everywhere and remains like a witness,
acting in his duty without desire— he is called a great doer.
Free from both agitation and bliss, acting according to his own pure will,
he who neither grieves nor arises is called the Great Agent.
The wise sage who, at the time of action, remains unattached in mind and abides in conduct appropriate to the task, is called a great doer.
He whose intellect, by its very nature, never abandons equanimity toward the end [of all things],
even while performing both auspicious and inauspicious deeds— he is called a great doer.
He whose mind remains perfectly equanimous during birth, existence, and destruction, as well as during rising and setting, is called a great doer.
He who hates nothing and praises nothing himself,
and who enjoys everything as it arises, is called a great enjoyer.
He who does not take even while taking, who does not act even while acting,
and who does not enjoy even while enjoying— he is called a great enjoyer.
He who, with an unwearied mind, observes the entire course of worldly affairs like a witness and has no desire for their cessation— he is called a great enjoyer.

He whose mind does not deviate because of pleasures or pains, through ritual actions or their absence, nor by those things that cause delusion through existence and non-existence— he is called a great enjoyer.
He who perceives old age and death, misfortune and even kingship as well as poverty as truly delightful— he is called a great enjoyer.
He who receives great joys and sorrows with equanimity, like the ocean receiving its waters, is called a great enjoyer.
Non-violence, equanimity, and contentment never depart from him, just as rays do not leave the orb of the moon; therefore, he is called a great enjoyer.
He who eats the bitter, the sour, the salty, the pungent, the unpalatable,
and the palatable with equanimity— he is called a great eater.
He who views with equanimity both the flavorful and the flavorless, as well as sexual union and its cessation— he is called a gentle one, a great enjoyer.
He for whom equanimity is well-established toward alkaline substances, various kinds of sugar, and likewise toward the auspicious or the inauspicious— he is called a great enjoyer.
Having abandoned the conceptual distinction that "this is edible" and "this is inedible," he who eats with all longing gone is called a great eater.
He who experiences adversity and prosperity, delusion and bliss, the inferior and the superior,
with an even-minded intellect, is called a great enjoyer.
He by whom merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, anxiety, death,
and birth have been abandoned through wisdom is called a great renunciant.
He by whom all desires, all doubts, all fancies, and all certainties have been abandoned through wisdom— he is called a great renouncer.
He by whom the existence of the body, the mind, the intellect, the senses, and the world is truly abandoned— he is called a great renouncer.
"I have neither body nor birth, nor am I affected by action, whether appropriate or inappropriate"—
he who possesses such certainty within is called a great renunciant.
He by whom dharma and non-dharma, as well as the mental conceits and desires,
have all been completely renounced within, is called a great renouncer.

Having abandoned the mind, meditation, austerity, splendor, selfhood, and the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as the auspicious and the inauspicious— he who remains established in his own nature is called a great renouncer.
He who honors his own mind yet neither desires nor rejects it,
being free from latent tendencies toward all this, is called a great renunciant.
Whoever has completely renounced this entire range of perceivable objects that is observed here is called a great renouncer.
He who desires nothing, who is free from the pairs of opposites, whose mind is unshaken amidst pleasure and pain,
who is steadfast, self-abiding, gentle, self-controlled, and a great renouncer— he is called such.
He who, even while performing his duties, does not abandon the state of being as if in deep sleep— he, being full, is called a great renunciant.
Thus was it spoken by the God of gods to Bhṛṅgīśa in the past, O sinless one:
"O Rāma, maintain this vision and remain as you are."

"O Rāmabhadra, on Mount Meru— which possesses a single peak of the finest radiant sapphire-stone and takes the form of a blazing fire— Hara spoke thus, his matted hair adorned with a crescent moon bound amidst a garland of fragments of glorious skulls."
Adopting this perspective, perform your graceful and beautiful duties at the proper time with a disciplined intellect;
you are eternally risen, stainless, and free from affliction—abandon all doubt, be happy, and remain as you truly are.
In the Bhṛṅgīśa-episode, the chapter titled "The Yoga of Instruction Concerning the Great Creator and Others."
